sections.heading: Multi-bike: the main reason to be here
sections.html:
Riders who own more than one machine — a commuter and a weekend bike, a project in the garage, a classic — usually pay considerably more insuring them separately than together.

Admiral's multi-bike arrangement puts several machines on one policy with a combined discount and a single renewal date. If you own two or more bikes, this is the first quote to get.

It also works alongside MultiCar, so a bike can sit on the same household policy as cars — useful for a rider whose partner drives, or a household with a van and a bike.

Two things to confirm rather than assume: that the machines are kept at the same address, and how a claim on one affects the no-claims bonus on the others. Policies vary on the second point and it matters more than the discount.

sections.heading: Storage and security: declare it accurately
sections.html:
Motorcycle theft is concentrated and opportunistic, and insurers price it hard. Where the bike is kept overnight — locked garage, driveway, on the street — moves the premium substantially, and so do declared security measures like a ground anchor, chain, disc lock, tracker or alarm.

Declaring a garage you do not use, or security you have not fitted, is the fastest way to have a theft claim declined. Insurers investigate theft claims closely because the fraud rate is high, and the security question is the first thing they check.

Conversely, if you have fitted a Thatcham-approved immobiliser or tracker and not told them, you are paying more than you need to. Re-declare after any security upgrade.

sections.heading: Your gear is not covered by default
sections.html:
Add it up honestly. A decent helmet is £300 to £600. A textile or leather jacket, £200 to £500. Boots, gloves, trousers — another £300. Most riders are wearing £1,000 to £1,500 of equipment before the bike is considered.

Standard comprehensive cover insures the motorcycle. Riding gear is normally a separate add-on, and when you buy it there are two things to check:

  • The limit. Some policies cap gear cover at £500, which does not replace a helmet and a jacket together.
  • Whether the helmet is covered after any impact. A helmet that has been dropped or crashed in must be replaced whether or not it looks damaged — the protective structure is single-use. A policy that only pays for visible damage misses the point.

This add-on is usually cheap relative to what it covers, and it is the one most worth taking.

sections.heading: European riding and the tour trap
sections.html:
If you ride abroad, check the European allowance rather than assuming comprehensive cover follows you.

Many policies include a limited number of days of European use, and drop to third-party-only beyond it. A rider on a two-week Alpine tour can find that days eleven to fourteen are uninsured for damage to their own bike — the point at which the roads get most interesting.

Where the allowance is short, extending it for the trip is usually inexpensive. The mistake is discovering the limit after the trip rather than before.

Breakdown cover deserves the same treatment. Recovery of a motorcycle from mainland Europe is expensive and specialist, and standard UK breakdown cover generally does not extend to it.

pros: Multi-bike discount for riders with more than one machine on a single policy
Works alongside MultiCar, so a bike can sit with household cars
Full range from third party through to comprehensive
Covers scooters through to sports bikes rather than a narrow band
Helmet, leathers, breakdown and legal cover all available as add-ons
Single renewal date across multiple machines
cons: Riding gear is an add-on, not standard — and default limits may not replace a helmet and jacket
European cover is day-limited; exceeding it can drop you to third party abroad
£60–£160 cancellation fee, which bites if you sell the bike mid-season
Multi-bike generally requires machines at the same address
Declared security and storage must be accurate or a theft claim can be refused
UK breakdown cover does not usually extend to European recovery
verdict: The strongest case for Admiral is multi-bike — if you own two or more machines, or a bike alongside household cars, the combined price is hard to beat by shopping separately. Whichever insurer you end up with, take the helmet and leathers add-on and check its limit against what you actually wear, because £1,200 of gear is not covered by a standard comprehensive policy. If you tour, confirm the European day allowance before booking rather than after, and be scrupulously accurate about where the bike is kept overnight.

faqs.q: Is my helmet and riding gear covered?
faqs.a: Not as standard. Helmet and leathers cover is normally an optional add-on. Check the limit — some cap at £500, which will not replace a helmet and jacket together — and confirm the helmet is replaced after any impact rather than only when visibly damaged.

faqs.q: Can I insure more than one bike?
faqs.a: Yes. Admiral's multi-bike arrangement covers several machines on one policy with a combined discount and one renewal date. Bikes generally need to be at the same address. Ask how a claim on one affects the no-claims bonus on the others.

faqs.q: Am I covered riding in Europe?
faqs.a: European cover is available but usually limited to a set number of days. Beyond the allowance you may drop to third-party-only. Check the limit before a long tour and extend it if needed.

faqs.q: How does where I keep the bike affect the price?
faqs.a: Substantially. A locked garage prices very differently to street parking, and declared security like a ground anchor, chain, tracker or alarm reduces the premium. Declare it accurately — theft claims are investigated closely and this is the first thing checked.

faqs.q: What does it cost to cancel?
faqs.a: Between £60 and £160 depending on circumstances, plus around £15 for amendments. Worth factoring in if you might sell the bike at the end of the season.

title: Admiral Van Insurance Review
meta_title: Admiral Van Insurance Review 2026: Cover, Tools and MultiCar
meta_description: Admiral van insurance and where it fits. Social versus commercial use, tools cover, MultiCar with your car, and the fees to know about.
intro:
Van insurance turns on one question that car insurance never asks: what is the van actually for?

Social-only, carriage of own goods, and hire-and-reward are three different products at three very different prices, and declaring the wrong one is the most common reason a van claim gets refused. A tradesman who insures for social use because it was cheaper has effectively bought nothing.

Admiral's van proposition is built on the same foundations as its car cover — MultiCar, MultiCover, tiered comprehensive policies — but the use-class question sits in front of all of it, and it deserves more attention than the premium does.

key_facts.value: Social only · Carriage of own goods · Hire and reward — each priced differently

sections.heading: Get the use class right or nothing else matters
sections.html:
Three classes, and the gap between them is the whole ballgame:

  • Social, domestic and pleasure — the van is personal transport. Cheapest, and useless to anyone working from it.
  • Carriage of own goods — you carry your own tools, stock or equipment for your own business. This is what most tradespeople need.
  • Hire and reward — you carry goods belonging to other people for payment. Couriers, deliveries, man-and-van work.

Insurers check use class when a claim is made, not when the premium is taken. A plumber insured social-only who crashes on the way to a job can find the claim declined and the policy voided — which then has to be declared on every future application.

The saving from under-declaring is typically modest. The consequence is total. If you use the van for work in any capacity, buy the class that reflects it.

sections.heading: Where MultiCar changes the calculation
sections.html:
Admiral's MultiCar scheme lets a van sit on the same policy as household cars, each keeping its own no-claims bonus.

This is genuinely useful for a sole trader with a work van and a family car, or a small operation running two vans and a car. The combined price is usually below the sum of separate policies, and there is one renewal date instead of three.

MultiCover adds home insurance to the bundle for a further discount — relevant if you are self-employed and working from home anyway.

The same caveat applies as with cars: vehicles generally need to be at the same address. A van kept at a yard or lock-up rather than your home may not qualify, and that is worth confirming before building a renewal strategy around it.

sections.heading: Tools are usually not covered, and that surprises people
sections.html:
Van insurance covers the van. It does not automatically cover what is inside it.

Tools cover is generally an add-on, and when you buy it there are three things to check rather than assume:

  • The limit. A working tradesman's van can hold £5,000 to £15,000 of equipment. Add-on limits are often far lower.
  • Overnight conditions. Many policies exclude theft from a van left on the street overnight, or require tools to be removed entirely between certain hours. This is the clause that defeats most tools claims.
  • Whether individual high-value items need listing. A £900 laser level may need naming specifically to be covered.

If tools are your livelihood, read this section of the policy wording before comparing premiums. A cheaper policy with a £1,000 tools limit and an overnight exclusion is not cheaper in any meaningful sense.

sections.heading: Two things to confirm before buying
sections.html:
Does the courtesy vehicle come as a van? A courtesy car is worthless to someone whose van is their working vehicle. Some policies provide a like-for-like van, some provide a small car, and some provide nothing on van policies at all. If your income depends on the vehicle, this is the most important line in the policy.

What are the cancellation terms? Admiral's fees run to £60–£160 to cancel and around £15 to amend. Vans change hands more often than cars — upgrading as a business grows, or downsizing when work is thin — so mid-term cancellation is a realistic scenario rather than a hypothetical one.

pros: MultiCar allows a van and household cars on one policy, each keeping its own no-claims bonus
MultiCover extends the discount to home insurance, useful for home-based sole traders
One renewal date instead of several across vehicles
Wide voluntary excess range for tuning the premium
Established insurer with 24/7 claims support
cons: Tools cover is generally an add-on rather than standard, with limits and overnight exclusions to check
Courtesy vehicle may not be a like-for-like van — confirm before buying
Cancellation fees of £60 to £160 matter more for vans, which change hands often
MultiCar generally requires vehicles at the same address, which rules out yard-kept vans
Use class must be declared accurately or a claim can be refused and the policy voided
verdict: Worth a quote if you have other vehicles to bundle — MultiCar is the strongest part of Admiral's proposition and a van sits in it naturally alongside a family car. Before comparing premiums, settle two things: declare the correct use class, because under-declaring voids the policy at the worst possible moment, and check whether tools cover and a like-for-like courtesy van are included or extra. For a working van those two clauses matter more than the price difference between insurers.

faqs.q: What use class do I need?
faqs.a: Social only if the van is purely personal transport. Carriage of own goods if you carry your own tools or stock for your business — this covers most tradespeople. Hire and reward if you carry other people's goods for payment. Declaring the wrong class can void the policy.

faqs.q: Are my tools covered?
faqs.a: Not usually as standard. Tools cover is generally an add-on. Check the limit, whether high-value items must be listed individually, and any overnight conditions — many policies exclude theft from a van left on the street overnight.

faqs.q: Will I get a courtesy van?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Some policies provide a like-for-like van, some a small car, some nothing at all on van cover. Confirm this specifically if the van is how you earn.

faqs.q: Can I put my van on a MultiCar policy?
faqs.a: Yes. Vans can sit alongside cars on one Admiral policy, each keeping its own no-claims bonus. Vehicles generally need to be at the same address, so a van kept at a separate yard may not qualify.

faqs.q: What does it cost to cancel?
faqs.a: Between £60 and £160 depending on circumstances, plus around £15 for amendments. Worth factoring in if you change vans regularly.

headline.label: Cheapest SIM-free handset

intro:
Affordable Mobiles listed 13 SIM-free handsets on 24 September 2026, running from a Samsung Galaxy A57 5G at £479 to an iPhone 18 Pro Max at £1,299. Every one is sold outright and unlocked — no credit check, no minimum term, no airtime attached — and the prices above were read that morning from the shop's own SIM-free page.

The shop is part of AO. AO World plc turned over £1,266.6m in the year to 31 March 2026, up 11.4%, with adjusted profit before tax of £50.5m and 13.3 million customers on its books, and it took on 720,000 new ones during the year. That matters on a purchase you make outright, because the money goes to a listed British retailer with published accounts rather than to a name with nothing behind it.

Read the footer and the terms together and you get the useful detail early: the website belongs to Affordable Mobiles Limited, company 15476278, but the order itself is fulfilled by AO Retail Ltd, company 03914998, trading as Mobile Phones Direct, and clause 1.2 of the terms makes AO Retail the party to your contract. So the company you ring about a late parcel or a dead handset is AO Retail, and its registered office in Bolton is where a formal letter goes.

sections.heading: A brand that outlived the company that built it
sections.html:
Affordable Mobiles has been a familiar name in phone retail for a long time, and the business that built it no longer exists. A1 Comms Limited, company 04455131, ran the site from Derbyshire and had traded since 1997. On 2 February 2024 the High Court appointed David Kemp (IP number 24510) and Richard Hunt (IP number 21772) of SFP Restructuring Limited as joint administrators, under case CR-2024-000622. AO bought the intellectual property and the websites — affordablemobiles.co.uk, buymobiles.net and mobileshop.com — out of that administration for £2.2m in cash, saving 73 jobs; A1's gross assets of £41.6m, mostly contract assets and stock, stayed behind. The administration ran until 29 October 2025, when the old company passed into creditors' voluntary liquidation with Rachael Wilkinson and Peter David Dickens appointed the same day.

The company now behind the website was incorporated a week after the administrators walked in. Affordable Mobiles Limited (15476278) was registered on 9 February 2024 under SIC codes 47421 and 47910 — retail sale of mobile telephones, and retail by mail order or internet — with its first accounts made up to 31 March 2025 and the next due by 31 December 2026.

None of that is a warning. A brand rescued by a larger buyer is a better outcome for customers than a brand that disappears, and the buyer here is substantial. It is simply worth knowing that a guarantee, a cashback promise or a dispute from before February 2024 belongs to a company in liquidation, and that everything since belongs to AO.

sections.heading: Three companies, one Bolton postcode
sections.html:
Put the three registrations side by side and the structure is plain. Affordable Mobiles Limited (15476278), AO Retail Limited (03914998) and musicMagpie Limited (12977343) all give their registered office as 5a The Parklands, Lostock, Bolton, BL6 4SD.

AO Retail is the oldest of the three and has worn two other names: it was incorporated on 28 January 2000 as Appliances Online Limited, became DRL Limited on 2 May 2000, and took its present name on 30 April 2014. musicMagpie arrived by takeover — AO acquired it through a scheme of arrangement under Part 26 of the Companies Act, and the register records the company dropping its plc status on 20 January 2025, which dates the completion better than any press release.

That last point has a practical edge. The trade-in valuation offered on the Affordable Mobiles site is musicMagpie's, so the firm quoting you for your old phone and the firm selling you the new one are in the same group. The terms are good ones — a free instant valuation, a pre-paid label, payment by bank transfer on the day the phone is delivered, and a price promise that you either get the first figure offered or the handset comes back free — and musicMagpie will not take a phone snapped in half, bent, crushed, or missing components. But a valuation from a connected company is still worth checking against one that is not, and it takes five minutes.

sections.heading: What you give up, and what you get back, by paying once
sections.html:
The whole argument for a SIM-free phone is that the two purchases come apart. You buy the handset, then you buy airtime, and neither decision traps the other. Three consequences are worth spelling out because the bundled alternative hides all of them.

There is no credit agreement. A bundled phone contract is a rolling commitment with a network, and the site runs credit checks and security ID checks on those orders; a SIM-free order is a single purchase of goods, so nothing is searched and nothing is recorded. There is no minimum term and therefore no early termination charge to calculate. And the phone is unlocked from the start — the shop's own SIM-free page says that its phones "are unlocked, which means they can be used with any compatible SIM card without restrictions" and that "you can change networks at any time", which since Ofcom's ban on selling locked handsets took effect on 17 December 2021 is what every new phone sold in the UK should offer anyway.

Against that, paying once means paying it all at once. £479 is a single debit rather than £20 a month, and nobody is spreading it for you unless you arrange that separately. It also means the airtime is your problem: the page shows logos for more than a dozen networks that its SIM-free phones work with, and choosing between them is a job the bundle does for you.

The airtime the shop itself sells is worth counting, because the menu is longer than the choice. Six brands appear: O2, Three, Vodafone, Talkmobile, SMARTY and VOXI. SMARTY's own terms describe it as "a trading name of Hutchison 3G UK Limited" (03885486). VOXI's help pages say "Vodafone Limited, trading as VOXI". Talkmobile Limited (04154716) records Vodafone Limited as holding 75% or more of its shares and votes, notified on 6 April 2016. Since Vodafone and Three combined into VodafoneThree, five of those six brands sit inside one merged operator and only O2 is outside it — so six tiles represent two networks, which is a fair thing to know before you treat the list as a comparison.

sections.heading: Modified stock, and why a phone here can cost less than the maker charges
sections.html:
This is the most useful thing on the site and it is tucked into a help page rather than printed beside the prices. Some handsets sold here are modified stock, described in the shop's own words as "mobile phone stock that's sourced globally" and "inspected and officially modified by authorised partners to ensure it includes UK-compatible software and settings". The reason given for the price is equally plain: the shop sources "from a wider range of official suppliers to find the best possible price in the market", which makes modified stock "cheaper than UK stock".

Four consequences follow, and the page states three of them itself. Boxes "may arrive resealed as part of our routine quality testing process", so a factory seal is not guaranteed. Some models have no eSIM, which on a phone bought to move freely between networks is the one specification that decides whether you can switch in five minutes or must wait for a plastic SIM in the post. Modified devices are ineligible for AppleCare+ Theft & Loss in the UK. And the cover is capped: "your device comes with a 12-month warranty, provided through a combination of the manufacturer's warranty and our own cover".

That last figure is where the arithmetic bites, and the shop's own faults page supplies the comparison. It sets out UK manufacturer warranties as Apple 12 months on handset and battery, Samsung 24 months on the handset and 6 months on the battery, and Google 24 months on both. A modified Samsung or Google handset therefore carries twelve months where the same model bought as UK stock carries twenty-four. On an Apple handset nothing is lost on duration; on the other two, a year is.

The honest summary is that this is a legitimate grey-import practice, disclosed in writing, that trades warranty length and eSIM certainty for price. Plenty of buyers will take that trade knowingly and be pleased with it. The criticism is not the practice — it is that the disclosure lives on a help page while the decision is made on a product page.

sections.heading: Who fixes it, and when the fixing stops being theirs
sections.html:
The fault route is short and it changes hands at day 30. Inside the first 30 days on a new phone, Affordable Mobiles says it "will exchange it free of charge if we can identify a manufacturer's fault". After that the customer is sent to the maker: Apple on 0800 107 6285, Samsung on 0330 726 7864, Google by online support only. Refurbished devices work the other way round — the manufacturer's warranty does not apply to them and the shop handles the exchange itself.

Two rights sit above all of that and neither can be signed away. Under section 22 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 a buyer has a 30-day short-term right to reject goods that are not of satisfactory quality, and the Act says in terms that an agreement under which that right would be lost earlier "is not binding on the consumer" — so the shop may extend the window and may not shorten it. Separately, the 14-day cancellation right on a distance sale is for changing your mind and has nothing to do with faults; the shop's returns page quotes exactly that, "you have 14 days to return it". Readers conflate the two constantly, and a shop that prints only the 14 days on its returns page does nothing to stop them.

After the retailer, there is nowhere obvious to go. Handset retail has no ombudsman and no compensation scheme. Ofcom's approved complaints schemes exist, but they adjudicate the network contract, not the phone — which on a SIM-free purchase you do not have. A dispute that the shop will not settle ends in the county court.

sections.heading: The prices against what the makers charge for the same phone
sections.html:
A shop called Affordable Mobiles invites the test, so here it is, all read on 24 September 2026.

The iPhone 16 at 128GB is £799 here. Apple's own UK store shows the identical phone at £799.00. Not a pound of difference, and Apple will spread it at 0% APR over 24 months at £33.29 a month, which this listing does not offer.

The Galaxy A57 5G at 256GB — the cheapest phone on the page, and the one that sets the entry price for the whole range — is £479. Samsung's own UK product page for the same 256GB model showed "Buy from £404.00 with code A5754" the same morning. That is £75 between a shop whose name is a price claim and the manufacturer's own website, in the manufacturer's favour.

The range itself is the second finding, and it is easily counted. Thirteen tiles appeared on the SIM-free page; twelve carried a price and the Pixel 9a tile showed none on either read. Of the twelve priced, five are iPhones, six are Pixels and one is a Samsung. The filter offers four manufacturers — Apple, Samsung, Google and Motorola — and no Motorola handset appeared. For comparison, the Carphone Warehouse page on this site recorded 165 SIM-free devices on 4 September 2026. Thirteen tiles with a floor of £479 is a narrow shelf for a shop selling outright phones, and it is the single biggest limitation here: if the phone you want is not one of those twelve, there is no version of this page that helps you.

sections.heading: Two charges that arrive after the sale
sections.html:
Neither of these belongs to the SIM-free purchase, and both are waiting on the same website, so a buyer should know them.

The first is cashback, which on this site is a network-deal mechanism rather than a discount. The help page says the shop will "automatically pay it to your bank account by BACS, 90 days from the day your order was shipped", with no claim to submit — which is materially better than a cheque you have to bank. The condition is in clause 18.1 of the terms: the money is "paid directly into your bank account within 90 days" and "your network contract must be active for 90 days" or it "will become void". A cashback offer that requires you to keep a contract running for three months is the exact opposite of what the no-contract shelf is for, and the two sit side by side in the same shop.

The second is Complete Savings, a paid subscription promoted around the checkout and described by the shop as "a subscription-based savings programme, offering members exclusive cashback rewards" — a minimum of 10% back at over 1,000 UK online retailers and up to 20% off gift cards, for a monthly membership fee. It is not run by Affordable Mobiles: the programme's own site names Webloyalty Sàrl, a Swiss company with registered number CHE-344.043.246. Two details are worth carrying to the checkout. The charge appears on a bank statement as WLY*Completesave.co.uk, which is not a name anyone would connect to a phone order. And cancellation is by an online service, by email to cancel@completesavings.co.uk, by phone on 0800 389 6960 (Monday to Friday 8am to 8pm, Saturday 9am to 4pm), or by post to Complete Savings, PO Box 5305, Lancing, BN11 9WD. Anything that turns a one-off purchase into a monthly debit deserves to be read before it is agreed to, not after.

sections.heading: Where a returned phone can cost you money
sections.html:
The change-of-mind return is generous in length and exacting in condition. Clause 13.5 gives 14 days after you or a nominated person receives the goods. Clauses 14.6.1 to 14.6.5 then require the phone to be "in a resalable condition", the "original box and packaging which must remain undamaged", the "original charger, and all other in box accessories", and "pin locks or passcodes removed". The returns page repeats it in plainer words — "the phone is in a pristine condition" — and adds the sentence that costs money: "if any accessories are used, damaged, or missing, you may be charged."

Timings are published, which many retailers avoid. A refund is quoted at 14 days from the day the cancellation is confirmed, and where a network has already billed you, up to 28 days for those charges to come back. The shop pays return postage on a faulty item and the customer pays it on a change of mind, which is the ordinary position in law and worth no complaint.

Two things about that list are worth weighing rather than resenting. A screen protector peeled off and thrown away, or a charger cable used for one night, sits inside "used, damaged, or missing" as written, and the amount of any charge is nowhere published. And "pristine condition" is a higher bar than the statutory one, which allows you to handle goods as you would in a shop. If you intend to try a phone properly before committing, keep the box intact and every cable in its bag.

sections.heading: What could not be established
sections.html:
Four things resisted checking and are set down rather than guessed at.

The monthly fee for Complete Savings is not published on the shop's help page or on the programme's own homepage or terms, which say only that "the period and amount of this fee will be notified during the enrolment process". Anyone signing up should read the figure off the enrolment screen before agreeing, and the trial length is unpublished on the same pages for the same reason.

The proportion of stock that is modified could not be worked out. The help page explains the practice but nothing on the SIM-free listings read on 24 September said which of the twelve priced handsets were modified and which were ordinary UK stock — and since that decides whether a Samsung carries 12 months of cover or 24, it is the question a buyer most needs answered before paying.

No independent rating of this retailer exists. There is no Defaqto equivalent for a phone shop, Ofcom rates networks rather than the shops that sell them, and Which? does not score handset retailers. That is an absence across the whole trade rather than a mark against this shop.

Finally, the Motorola filter returned no priced handset on either read, and nothing on the page explains whether that is a temporary stock gap or a filter left in place after the range changed. Prices and counts here are a snapshot from one morning; treat them as a benchmark to check against rather than a quote.

pros: Every SIM-free phone is sold outright and unlocked, with no credit check, no minimum term and no early termination charge to calculate
Backed by AO World plc, which turned over £1,266.6m in the year to 31 March 2026 with £50.5m of adjusted profit before tax and 13.3 million customers
The terms name the seller plainly in clause 1.2 — AO Retail Ltd, company 03914998, trading as Mobile Phones Direct — so there is no doubt who the contract is with
Modified stock is disclosed in writing, with the resealed boxes, the missing eSIM on some models and the 12-month warranty all stated rather than discovered
Cashback is paid automatically by BACS 90 days after shipping, with no claim form to submit and no cheque to bank
Warranty lengths for each maker are published in a table — Apple 12 months, Samsung 24 months and 6 on the battery, Google 24 months — with the repair numbers beside them
A free exchange inside the first 30 days where a manufacturer's fault is identified, which sits alongside rather than instead of the Consumer Rights Act
Trade-in through musicMagpie pays by bank transfer on the day the phone arrives, with the quoted price guaranteed or the handset returned free
Refund timings are published — 14 days for the shop's own refund, up to 28 days for network charges — which most phone retailers leave vague
cons: Only 13 SIM-free tiles appeared on 24 September 2026 and 12 of them carried a price, against 165 SIM-free devices recorded at Carphone Warehouse on 4 September
Of the 12 priced handsets, exactly one was a Samsung and none was a Motorola, despite Motorola appearing in the page's own manufacturer filter
The iPhone 16 128GB at £799 matches Apple's own UK price to the pound, and Apple spreads it at 0% APR over 24 months while this listing does not
The cheapest phone on the page, the Galaxy A57 5G 256GB at £479, was £75 more than the £404.00 shown on Samsung's own UK product page with code A5754 the same morning
Modified stock carries a 12-month warranty, so a Samsung or Google handset bought that way has half the 24 months the shop's own faults table gives for UK stock
Nothing on the SIM-free listings said which handsets are modified stock, which is the fact that decides how long the cover lasts
Modified devices cannot be covered by AppleCare+ Theft & Loss in the UK, and some models have no eSIM at all
Cashback requires a network contract to stay active for 90 days or it becomes void, which is the opposite of what a no-contract buyer is looking for
Complete Savings is promoted around the checkout with no monthly fee published on the shop's page or the programme's own site, and it debits as WLY*Completesave.co.uk
A change-of-mind return demands pristine condition and undamaged packaging, and the charge for a used or missing accessory is not published anywhere
Six network brands are offered but five of them sit inside VodafoneThree, so the menu represents two networks rather than six
The trade-in valuation comes from musicMagpie, a company in the same group at the same Bolton address, which the trade-in page does not mention
verdict: As a place to buy a phone outright, Affordable Mobiles is straightforward and better documented than most: the terms say who the seller is, the faults page prints each maker's warranty length, the refund timings are published, and the modified-stock practice that explains the pricing is described in the shop's own words rather than left to be discovered. AO World's accounts sit behind it, which is more than the brand had on 2 February 2024 when its previous owner went into administration. The two things to settle before paying are the range and the stock. Thirteen tiles with a £479 floor is a narrow shelf, and on the two handsets that could be checked against the makers themselves the shop matched Apple exactly and came in £75 above Samsung — so check the manufacturer's own store before assuming the name is a price promise. Then ask, in writing, whether the handset you are buying is modified stock, because that single answer decides whether you get 12 months of warranty or 24, and whether the phone has an eSIM to switch networks with.

faqs.q: Who actually sells the phone when I order from Affordable Mobiles?
faqs.a: AO Retail Ltd, company 03914998, trading as Mobile Phones Direct. The website belongs to Affordable Mobiles Limited (15476278), but clause 1.2 of the terms makes AO Retail the party to your contract, and the site's own footer says orders "will be fulfilled by AO Retail Ltd". Both companies are registered at 5a The Parklands, Lostock, Bolton, BL6 4SD.

faqs.q: What is modified stock and should I avoid it?
faqs.a: Modified stock is handset stock sourced globally and altered by authorised partners so it carries UK software and settings, which is why it is cheaper than UK stock. The trade-offs are stated by the shop: boxes may arrive resealed, some models have no eSIM, the device cannot be covered by AppleCare+ Theft & Loss in the UK, and the warranty is 12 months made up of the manufacturer's cover plus the shop's own. On a Samsung or Google phone that is half the 24 months the shop's own table gives for UK stock, so ask which you are buying before you pay.

faqs.q: How cheap is the cheapest phone?
faqs.a: £479, for a Samsung Galaxy A57 5G with 256GB, read on 24 September 2026. That was the lowest of 13 SIM-free tiles, of which 12 carried a price, running up to £1,299 for an iPhone 18 Pro Max. Samsung's own UK page for the same 256GB model showed "Buy from £404.00 with code A5754" the same morning, so the manufacturer was cheaper on that handset.

faqs.q: Can I send a SIM-free phone back if I change my mind?
faqs.a: Yes, within 14 days of delivery, but the conditions are strict. The phone must be in resalable, pristine condition, the original box and packaging undamaged, the charger and every in-box accessory returned, and all locks and passcodes removed. The returns page warns that "if any accessories are used, damaged, or missing, you may be charged", and the amount of that charge is not published. A refund is quoted at 14 days from confirmation of the cancellation.

faqs.q: What happens if the phone develops a fault?
faqs.a: Inside 30 days the shop exchanges a new phone free of charge where it can identify a manufacturer's fault. After that you deal with the maker — Apple on 0800 107 6285, Samsung on 0330 726 7864, Google through online support. Refurbished devices are the exception and go back to the shop. Your section 22 right under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 to reject faulty goods within 30 days runs alongside all of that and cannot be shortened by any term of sale.

faqs.q: Is there an ombudsman if the shop will not help?
faqs.a: Not for the handset. Ofcom approves complaints schemes for telecoms providers, and they deal with the network contract rather than a phone bought outright, which on a SIM-free order you do not have. Handset retail has no ombudsman, no regulator and no compensation scheme, so an unresolved dispute ends in the county court under the Consumer Rights Act 2015.

faqs.q: What is the Complete Savings charge on my statement?
faqs.a: Complete Savings is a paid subscription cashback programme promoted around the checkout, run by Webloyalty Sàrl, a Swiss company registered as CHE-344.043.246. It appears on bank statements as WLY*Completesave.co.uk. The monthly fee is not published on the shop's help page or on the programme's own terms, which say only that the amount is notified during enrolment. You can cancel online, by email to cancel@completesavings.co.uk, by phone on 0800 389 6960, or by post to Complete Savings, PO Box 5305, Lancing, BN11 9WD.

title: Agoda Hotels
meta_title: Agoda Review: What Moves a Hotel to the Top of Its List
meta_description: Agoda lists over 6 million properties and publishes what a hotel pays for a top-three slot: 10%, 12% or 15% extra. Prices and small print, 24 September 2026.

headline.label: Cheapest advertised London room, per night
headline.value: £49 a night — Travelodge's own published London lead-in rate, the class of room Agoda resells; Agoda itself publishes no city lead-in price, checked 24 September 2026

intro:
Agoda's press office puts the catalogue at "over 6 million hotels and holiday properties, plus flights, activities, and more", sold in more than 200 markets, in 39 languages, with customer support in 16 of them. Those are the company's own figures, read on 24 September 2026. Behind them sits Booking Holdings (Nasdaq: BKNG), which turned over $26.9 billion in 2025 and employed about 24,300 people at the end of it.

The useful part for a British traveller is the pricing model rather than the size. Agoda grew up selling Asia to Asia — Booking Holdings' own annual report still describes it as "a leading online accommodation reservation service catering primarily to consumers in the Asia-Pacific region, with headquarters in Singapore" — and it carries habits from that market: heavy discounting, a large share of rooms you pay for at the desk rather than in advance, and a search page that is openly, published-price-list openly, influenced by what hotels pay to sit near the top of it.

That last point is the reason this page is worth reading before you book. Agoda prints the rate card for its own search results on its partner site, and the Competition and Markets Authority made it promise, in writing, to tell you when money has moved a hotel up the page.

key_facts.label: Who you are booking with
key_facts.value: Agoda Company Pte. Ltd., the Singapore company named in its 2019 undertakings to the CMA at 30 Cecil Street, Prudential Tower, Singapore; its partner-facing terms give the address as 36 Robinson Road, #20-01 City House

key_facts.label: UK presence
key_facts.value: Agoda International Pte. Ltd., overseas company FC030522 (Singapore registration 200914710H), UK establishment BR015519 registered on 25 October 2011 at 2nd Floor, The Monument Building, 11 Monument Street, London

key_facts.label: Parent
key_facts.value: Booking Holdings Inc. (Nasdaq: BKNG) — revenue $26.9bn in 2025, about 24,300 staff; sister brand Booking.com lists roughly 4.4 million properties

key_facts.label: Catalogue
key_facts.value: "over 6 million hotels and holiday properties", 200-plus markets, 39 languages on the platform, 16 languages of support, about 7,500 staff

key_facts.label: What a top-three slot costs a hotel
key_facts.value: Sponsored Listing buys spots 1–3 or 11–13 on a cost-per-booking basis; the Agoda Growth Program charges 10%, 12% or 15% extra commission per booking for a ranking boost and a Preferred Partner badge

key_facts.label: How you pay
key_facts.value: Prepaid to Agoda, or Property Collect — "Agoda's solution for guests to pay for their booking upon arrival at the property", with Agoda's cut offset against the hotel's other payouts

key_facts.label: Binding promises to the regulator
key_facts.value: Undertakings signed under Part 8 of the Enterprise Act 2002, in force from 24:00 on 1 September 2019, covering ranking disclosure, labelled paid slots, total prices and countdown timers

key_facts.label: Rules that apply
key_facts.value: No financial regulator; a hotel-only booking is outside ATOL, which covers "a package trip that includes a flight"; no independent ratings body assesses booking platforms

sections.heading: What a London room costs, and where the number actually comes from
sections.html:
Agoda does not publish a lead-in price for a city. LateRooms tells you London starts at £34 before you type anything; HotelPlanner prints a London average of $111.36 for a three-star group rate. On Agoda the price exists only inside the search tool, which means the cheapest advertised London room is whatever the platform decides to show you on the day, and it cannot be quoted in advance.

The floor is still knowable, because the cheapest large supplier in London publishes it. Travelodge, which runs over 80 hotels across Central and Greater London and more than 625 in total, advertises rooms "from £49 in London" and thousands under £35 elsewhere in the country, bookable up to 355 days ahead. It also says, flatly: "You will always find our lowest prices on our website." On a budget chain room, then, an Agoda price beating £49 is a genuine find and a price above it is worth a thirty-second check on the hotel's own site before you commit.

Where Agoda tends to earn its place is the opposite end of the catalogue — independents, Asian city hotels and apartments that never appear on a British chain's booking engine at all, and where there is no direct rate to compare against.

sections.heading: The ranking has a price list, and Agoda prints it
sections.html:
Most platforms keep the mechanics of their search results vague. Agoda does the opposite on its partner site, and the numbers are specific enough to be useful to a traveller reading them from the other side.

The first product is Sponsored Listing, described as "the only marketing solution that guarantees prominent placement in the search results on Agoda's platforms" — a guaranteed slot in positions 1 to 3, or 11 to 13, bought on a cost-per-booking basis rather than by auction, because a flat rate is "not available…due to variances in market demand". Agoda's pitch to hotels reports campaigns running 30 days or more since January 2024 averaging 124% more impressions, 32% more clicks, 23% more bookings and a 13x return. The sentence that matters most to a shopper sits in the same pitch: "90% of bookings are made with properties listed in the top 5 search ranks."

The second is the Agoda Growth Program, a longer commitment with three tiers of extra commission on every booking — 10% on basic, 12% on standard, 15% on premium — in exchange for a search ranking boost, a Preferred Partner badge on the listing and the property page, up to 90% more spending on metasearch engines such as Google Hotels and Kayak, up to 80% more on pay-per-click advertising and exposure across what Agoda counts as 10,000-plus affiliate networks. There is a 90-day minimum commitment and one free two-week trial per property. Agoda's 2024 figures for the standard tier: 1.5 times the impressions, 37% more revenue, 42% more net room nights.

Read those two products together and a hotel paying 15% above its contracted commission is buying a documented advantage over the identical hotel next door that did not. That is not a scandal — every marketplace sells visibility — but it is the reason the first result is not the best result, and it is why the regulator took an interest.

sections.heading: The promises Agoda made to the CMA, and what they oblige it to show you
sections.html:
On 6 February 2019 the Competition and Markets Authority announced enforcement action against six booking sites — Expedia, Booking.com, Agoda, Hotels.com, ebookers and trivago — over search ranking, pressure selling, discount claims and hidden charges. Agoda Company Pte. Ltd. signed undertakings under Part 8 of the Enterprise Act 2002, in relation to the Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008, and paragraphs 1 to 23 took effect at "24:00 hours on 1 September 2019".

The document is worth knowing in outline because it is still the clearest statement of what Agoda has to do. "Money Earned" is defined as a payment received by Agoda "which may affect the Position of a Hotel", and Agoda must state clearly and prominently that money earned may affect the ranking of results. A "Guaranteed Slot Listing" — a hotel guaranteed a pre-determined position solely because it paid — must be labelled as such and set apart from the rest. The total price, including compulsory charges, must appear next to its constituent parts, and a sort by price must sort by the total. A price cannot be presented as time-limited if it survives the deadline, and a countdown timer may not imply a deadline that does not exist.

The CMA's own summary of the commitments is blunter: the sites agreed not to give "a false impression of the availability or popularity of a hotel" and to display "all compulsory charges such as taxes, booking or resort fees in the headline price". Agoda had to report on implementation by 1 March 2020 and on effectiveness by 1 March 2021, and must produce a further report within one month whenever the CMA asks in writing.

sections.heading: Two ways to pay, and they protect you differently
sections.html:
Some Agoda rates are prepaid; many are Property Collect, which Agoda describes to hotels as "Agoda's solution for guests to pay for their booking upon arrival at the property". On those bookings the hotel takes the whole selling price at the desk and Agoda recovers its share by deducting it from the property's other payouts — "Agoda will deduct the compensation of Property Collect bookings from your other prepaid bookings to avoid manual invoicing". There is also a variant that holds the room without a card at all.

For the traveller, the difference decides what happens when something goes wrong. Pay the hotel on arrival and Agoda has never touched your money, so there is nothing for it to refund. Prepay by credit card and section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 makes the card issuer jointly liable with the seller on purchases above £100 and up to £30,000, which is the strongest protection available on a hotel booking; a deposit paid on the card is enough to bring the whole price into scope. Pay by debit card and you are left with a card scheme chargeback, which is an industry arrangement rather than a statutory right.

One more boundary is worth stating plainly. A room on its own is not a package holiday, so ATOL does not apply: the scheme covers "a package trip that includes a flight", and it explicitly does not cover accommodation-only bookings. Agoda does sell flights, and whether it holds a UK ATOL for flight-plus-hotel sales could not be confirmed for this review — the CAA's ATOL holder search is the place to check before booking the two together.

sections.heading: Who you are contracting with, and where the argument would be heard
sections.html:
Agoda is a Singapore business with a long-standing British footprint. Agoda International Pte. Ltd. is registered at Companies House as overseas company FC030522, Singapore registration 200914710H, and its UK establishment BR015519 has been open since 25 October 2011, currently at 2nd Floor, The Monument Building, 11 Monument Street, London, with accounts filed to 31 December 2025. The consumer-facing company named in the CMA undertakings is a different one, Agoda Company Pte. Ltd., given there as 30 Cecil Street, Prudential Tower; its partner terms of use put it at 36 Robinson Road, #20-01 City House, and make that agreement subject to Singapore law and the "exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore".

The group above it is regulated harder in Brussels than in London. The European Commission designated Booking a gatekeeper under the Digital Markets Act on 13 May 2024 for the intermediation service Booking.com (case DMA.100019), and Booking Holdings' 2025 annual report records that the designation, together with Booking.com's status as a Very Large Online Platform under the Digital Services Act, brought "new requirements and scrutiny". Neither designation names Agoda. In the UK the relevant instrument is the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, whose consumer provisions came into force on 7 April 2025: they prohibit drip pricing, ban fake reviews, and let the CMA decide for itself that consumer law has been broken and fine up to 10% of global turnover.

The terms themselves move often — version 8.0 of the property agreement took effect on 8 June 2026, version 7.0 on 21 February 2025 and version 6.0 on 8 December 2023 — and a UK and EEA exhibit covering the Platform-to-Business Regulation 2019/1150, which requires marketplaces to disclose the main parameters behind their rankings, has been attached since January 2021.

sections.heading: What the listing does not tell you about the property
sections.html:
A large share of Agoda's six million properties are apartments and holiday homes rather than hotels, and the British rules for those have been changing under everybody's feet. In England, a letting is subject to fire safety, gas, carbon monoxide and electrical obligations enforced by the Health and Safety Executive and the fire service rather than by any travel body, and the promised mandatory national registration scheme for short-term lets is still "not yet in force", expected to begin during 2026. Until it starts there is no register a guest can search, and a listing's own description is the only account of what the place is.

Star ratings on the results page are not an inspection either. In Britain the assessing bodies are the AA and VisitEngland, whose inspectors stay anonymously and grade the property; a star count typed into a listing by its owner is a claim, not an assessment. The same distinction applies to the guest score beside a price: it is an average of past customers, useful in bulk, and not an award from anybody.

On the product side Agoda is moving quickly. It opened a limited public beta of an AI assistant that turns "travel ideas into bookable trips" on 15 September 2026, and has been publishing a steady run of partnership and technology announcements through the year — with Singapore Tourism Board in August 2026 among them.

pros: Publishes the actual rate card for its own search results — 10%, 12% or 15% extra commission for a ranking boost, and guaranteed slots at positions 1–3 or 11–13 — which almost no rival platform puts in writing
Bound by dated, specific undertakings to the CMA covering ranking disclosure, labelled paid placements, total prices and countdown timers, in force since 1 September 2019
Over 6 million properties in more than 200 markets, with depth in Asian cities and independents that British chains and direct booking engines never list
Property Collect rates let you hold a room and pay the hotel on arrival, with a variant that does not need a card at all
Backed by Booking Holdings, a $26.9bn-revenue parent with about 24,300 staff, rather than a thinly capitalised intermediary
Support offered around the clock in 16 languages, with the platform itself running in 39
cons: No lead-in price is published for any city, so you cannot see what a destination starts at without running a search — LateRooms and HotelPlanner both publish theirs openly

The order of the results is for sale: a hotel paying 15% above its contracted commission buys a ranking boost over an identical hotel that did not, and the shopper sees only a Preferred Partner badge with no published explanation of how far a payment moves a listing

Agoda's own pitch to hotels states that 90% of bookings go to properties in the top five ranks, which is precisely why paid placement is worth buying and why the first screen should not be read as the best value
On a Property Collect booking Agoda never holds your money, so it has nothing to refund if the room is not as described, and a card payment made only at the hotel desk is outside section 75

The consumer contracts with a Singapore company, and the partner-facing terms are governed by Singapore law with exclusive jurisdiction in Singapore courts; the UK establishment is a branch of an overseas company, not a British contracting party

The consumer terms of use, the best price guarantee wording and the cancellation rules could not be read for this review — those pages return no text to anything other than a live browser session, so the liability cap and the guarantee conditions remain unverified
Reports Agoda made to the CMA on implementation (due 1 March 2020) and effectiveness (due 1 March 2021) are not published, so there is no public record of how well the 2019 promises were kept
verdict: Agoda is the most candid of the big booking platforms about how its search results are built, and that candour is the reason to use it carefully rather than a reason to avoid it: when a marketplace tells hotels that 90% of bookings land in the top five ranks and then sells those ranks at 10%, 12% and 15%, the sensible traveller scrolls. It earns its keep on independents and Asian city hotels, where there is often no direct rate to check against, and it is least useful on a British chain room, where Travelodge's own £49 London lead-in and its promise that its website always has its lowest price are one click away. Prepay by credit card if the booking matters, because section 75 is worth more than any platform guarantee, and read what the price excludes before you agree to pay the hotel on arrival.

faqs.q: Is a hotel booked through Agoda financially protected?
faqs.a: Not by a travel scheme. ATOL covers "a package trip that includes a flight" and does not cover accommodation-only bookings, and no financial regulator oversees hotel booking. The protection that does apply is your card: a prepaid booking over £100 and up to £30,000 on a credit card brings section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 into play, making the issuer jointly liable with the seller. A room paid for at the hotel desk has neither.

faqs.q: Does paying Agoda more move a hotel up the search results?
faqs.a: Agoda says so itself, to hotels. Sponsored Listing guarantees positions 1 to 3 or 11 to 13 on a cost-per-booking basis, and the Agoda Growth Program charges 10%, 12% or 15% extra commission per booking for a ranking boost, a Preferred Partner badge and heavier metasearch and pay-per-click spending. Under its 2019 undertakings to the CMA, Agoda must tell you clearly that money earned may affect the ranking and must label guaranteed slots.

faqs.q: Why can I pay some Agoda rooms at the hotel and others in advance?
faqs.a: They are two commercial models. Prepaid rates are collected by Agoda; Property Collect rates are collected by the hotel on arrival, with Agoda's share deducted from the property's other payouts rather than invoiced. Paying at the desk keeps your money in your account for longer, and it also means the platform is holding nothing on your behalf if the stay goes wrong.

faqs.q: Who is Agoda owned by, and who would I sue?
faqs.a: Agoda is part of Booking Holdings Inc. (Nasdaq: BKNG), which reported $26.9bn of revenue for 2025. The trading company named in Agoda's undertakings to the CMA is Agoda Company Pte. Ltd. of Singapore; a separate group company, Agoda International Pte. Ltd., has had a registered UK establishment (BR015519) in the City of London since 25 October 2011. Agoda's partner-facing terms are governed by Singapore law with exclusive jurisdiction in Singapore.

faqs.q: Are the star ratings and guest scores on Agoda independent?
faqs.a: No. In Britain the assessing bodies are the AA and VisitEngland, whose inspectors stay anonymously and grade the hotel; a star count on a listing is supplied by the property or a third party. Guest scores are averages of past customers' ratings, which are useful in volume and are not an award, an inspection or a ratings-agency assessment.

title: Airport Lounges Airport Lounge
meta_title: Airport Lounges: What a UK Lounge Pass Really Costs
meta_description: Pre-booked UK airport lounge entry runs £29.99 to £64 an adult. What Airport Lounges sells, who runs the rooms, and the booking rules that decide refunds.

headline.label: Cost of one lounge visit
headline.value: £29.99–£64 per adult, pre-booked — UK lounge operators' own published prices, checked 21 September 2026

intro:
Airport Lounges sells lounge entry one visit at a time, and a pre-booked UK visit costs between £29.99 and £64 an adult at the prices the companies running those rooms were publishing on 21 September 2026. There is no membership, no annual fee and no card to hold: you pick an airport, pick a date, pay once and walk in.

That suits the traveller who flies twice a year. A lounge pass bought outright is the only route into these rooms for anyone without a premium bank account or a business-class boarding pass, and it is priced the same whether you fly once or fifty times. UK airports handled 302 million passengers in 2025, a record the Civil Aviation Authority confirmed on 24 February 2026, and a paid seat away from the gate is one of the few things at an airport you can still fix in advance for a known price.

What you are buying, though, belongs to somebody else. Airport Lounges is a reseller: the rooms are run by Swissport, by Manchester Airports Group's CAVU business and by Plaza Premium, and it is their rules on how long you may stay, how late you may arrive and whether you get your money back that apply to your booking. Check the operator's own price before you pay, because that is the number the reseller is marking up or matching.

key_facts.label: What it sells
key_facts.value: Single-visit airport lounge entry, pre-booked for a named date and flight

key_facts.label: Who runs the lounges
key_facts.value: Third parties — Swissport (Aspire, No1, Club Aspire, My Lounge, Clubrooms), CAVU Experiences (EMEA) Limited (Escape) and Plaza Premium

key_facts.label: Typical UK price
key_facts.value: £31 at Humberside and Inverness, £38 at Gatwick North, £50 at Heathrow Terminal 3, £64 for Suite by Aspire at Newcastle

key_facts.label: Standard stay
key_facts.value: Three hours before your scheduled departure; extra hours sold separately

key_facts.label: Cancellation
key_facts.value: Typically 24 hours' notice; inside that window the operators keep the money

key_facts.label: Regulated?
key_facts.value: No. A lounge pass is not a package holiday, carries no ATOL protection and has no financial regulator behind it

key_facts.label: Corporate identity
key_facts.value: No company registered at Companies House under the name Airport Lounges — checked 21 September 2026

sections.heading: What a UK lounge visit costs in September 2026
sections.html:
Swissport publishes a price for every Aspire-family lounge it runs in the UK, and the spread is wider than most people expect. The cheapest are £31 at Humberside and Inverness and £32 at Aberdeen's Northern Lights and Glasgow's Upperdeck. In the south, Club Aspire at Gatwick South is £34, the No1 Lounge at Gatwick North is £38, Club Aspire at Heathrow Terminal 5 is £40, My Lounge at Heathrow Terminal 3 is £44 and the No1 Lounge in the same terminal is £50. Manchester Terminal 3 is £37; the C Gates lounge in Terminal 2 is £46. At the top, Luxe by Aspire at Liverpool and Newcastle is £57 and Suite by Aspire at Newcastle is £64.

CAVU's Escape Lounges, which you will find at Manchester, Stansted, East Midlands and Edinburgh among others, start at £29.99 per person pre-booked. Children under three go in free, and a single booking may carry no more than three children or infants.

Two levers move the number. Booking ahead rather than paying at the door is worth up to 20% by No1 Lounges' own reckoning, and a pre-booked visit there carries delay cover, so a late flight does not cost you a second entry. Arriving early costs extra: the three hours before departure are included and additional hours are sold as an add-on. Against that, Which? researchers paid an average of £42 across the lounges they visited, with individual entries ranging from £16.99 to £68 — so a reseller quoting much above the operator's own published figure is not saving anyone anything.

sections.heading: The rooms belong to somebody else
sections.html:
Edinburgh Airport is the clearest illustration. Three lounges sit airside — an Aspire Lounge, the Turkish Airlines Lounge run by Plaza Premium Group, and an Escape Lounge — and all three are operated by third-party companies rather than by the airport. Book any of them through any seller and the contract behind your ticket is with that operator.

Swissport GB Ltd is the name in the footer of the Aspire estate, which now runs to more than 100 lounges worldwide across the UK, Europe, Australia, the Middle East, Africa, North America and Asia. The No1, Clubrooms, My Lounge and Club Aspire brands all sit inside it, which is why one price list covers all four. The Escape Lounges are run in the UK by CAVU Experiences (EMEA) Limited, 6th Floor Olympic House, Manchester Airport, M90 1QX — the commercial arm of Manchester Airports Group — with sister companies in Chicago and Carlton South, Victoria handling the American and Australian rooms.

This matters for one practical reason. If the room is full, the coffee machine is broken or staff turn you away at the desk, the seller who took your card is not the party that can fix it, and the operator's terms are the ones a complaint is judged against. Keep the operator's name and the booking reference together, and raise a problem with whichever of the two the terms name — on a resold booking that is usually the seller first, the operator second.

sections.heading: Three hours, one hour late, and no refund
sections.html:
The booking rules are tighter than a restaurant reservation and looser than a flight, and almost nobody reads them before paying. Outside the United States, Escape Lounge bookings must be made at least 12 hours before your arrival time, so there is no walking up to the website from the departures hall. Cancellation needs at least 24 hours' notice; inside that window the wording is blunt — bookings cancelled within 24 hours of the arrival date “will not be refunded”. Once the booking has started, no amendment can be made at all.

Arrive late and the seat may be gone. Escape reserves the right to free a seat if you have not turned up within one hour of the booked time. Edinburgh's lounge terms say a booking that goes unused simply expires and is not refundable, and that bookings are not transferable to another person or another lounge — you cannot hand a pass you cannot use to the friend you are travelling with. Amendments there can be made online up to 24 hours before departure.

Stay lengths vary by brand rather than by seller: three hours at a standard Escape Lounge, two at a 1903 Lounge, two and a half to three at the Executive and Essence rooms. Only an adult of 18 or over may make a booking. There is a smart-casual dress code, footwear at all times, clothing with offensive slogans refused, and an expectation that guests “drink sensibly” — the free bar is not unlimited in practice, and staff can refuse entry or ask you to leave.

sections.heading: Which? sent researchers into 28 lounges
sections.html:
There is no Defaqto or Fairer Finance for airport lounges, so the nearest thing to an independent rating is the survey Which? published on 22 November 2025. Its researchers visited 28 UK lounges, mostly between July and September 2025, scoring each on food, comfort, space and views.

Only about a third managed three stars or better. The best of them were Clubrooms at Gatwick South at 3.5 stars for £44 to £50 and Clubrooms at Birmingham, also 3.5, at £48. The worst was Club Aspire at Heathrow Terminal 5, which scored one star at £42, while Suite by Aspire at Newcastle — the most expensive room in the survey at £68 — managed 2.5 and the Escape Lounge at Manchester Terminal 1 scored two. Prices have run well ahead of inflation: the average of £42 compares with £25 in 2017, a rise of 68%.

Which? travel editor Rory Boland put the value case plainly: “Instead of paying over £40 for a lukewarm buffet breakfast on a dirty plate, you can get a lot more for your money by visiting a bar or restaurant.” That is worth weighing before booking, and it cuts both ways — the cheaper regional rooms at £31 and £32 have to beat a sit-down breakfast and a drink by a much smaller margin than a £64 suite does.

sections.heading: Where the money protection stops
sections.html:
A lounge pass sits in an awkward gap in consumer law, and a reseller sits in the middle of it.

Start with the card. Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 makes a credit card company equally liable with the trader for misrepresentation or breach of contract — but section 75(3)(b) excludes any single item with a cash price of £100 or less, or more than £30,000. At £29.99 to £64, one lounge pass falls under the floor, and so does a pair of them. Paying by credit card buys you a chargeback claim against the card scheme and nothing stronger; debit card holders have chargeback alone.

Then the cooling-off period, which does not exist here. Regulation 28(1)(h) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 removes the usual 14-day right to cancel an online purchase where the contract is for “catering or services related to leisure activities” on a specific date. A lounge booked for a named flight is exactly that, so the operator's own 24-hour rule is the only cancellation right you have.

Nor is any of this a package. Buy a lounge pass on its own and there is no ATOL cover, no Package Travel Regulations protection and no financial regulator standing behind the seller, because selling entry to a room is not a regulated activity. If the seller fails between your payment and your flight, recovering the money is a chargeback question rather than a claim against a protection scheme. That is a reason to book close to travel rather than months out.

sections.heading: The checks we could not complete
sections.html:
Two things about Airport Lounges itself could not be verified, and both should be resolved before a reader hands over card details.

The first is corporate identity. A Companies House search on 21 September 2026 for a company registered under the name Airport Lounges returns no results at all. That does not mean the business is not real — plenty of sites trade under a name that differs from the registered one — but it does mean the trading name alone will not tell you which company takes your money, where it is registered or what its accounts look like. The site's own terms should name the legal entity and a company number; look for both before booking, and treat their absence as a reason to pay by credit card.

The second is the site itself. Both www.airportlounges.com and www.airport-lounges.co.uk block automated retrieval, so the prices, the lounge list, the cancellation terms and the complaints route on those pages could not be read or quoted here. Every figure on this page therefore comes from the companies that run the lounges, from the Civil Aviation Authority, from Which? or from the legislation itself. Compare the seller's quote against the operator's published price for the same room on the same date — Swissport and CAVU both publish theirs — and check the cancellation deadline in writing before you pay, because a resold booking can carry the seller's terms on top of the operator's.

pros: One purchase, no membership and no annual fee — the only route into these rooms for an occasional flyer without a premium card
Regional lounges are genuinely cheap: £31 at Humberside and Inverness, £32 at Aberdeen and Glasgow
Pre-booking beats the walk-up price by up to 20% and, at No1 Lounges, includes delay cover if your flight slips
Children under three go free at Escape Lounges, which takes the sting out of a family booking
A known price fixed in advance, at airports where almost nothing else is
cons: The prices, terms and complaints route on airportlounges.com and airport-lounges.co.uk cannot be read by automated checks, so none of the seller's own claims could be verified here
No company is registered at Companies House under the name Airport Lounges, so the trading name does not identify who takes your money
You are buying a third party's room under that third party's rules — the seller controls the stay length, the capacity and the refund, and none of them are its own
At £29.99 to £64 a pass, every booking falls below the £100 Section 75 floor, so a credit card gives you chargeback and nothing more
There is no 14-day cooling-off right on a dated leisure booking, and inside 24 hours the operators keep the money whether you turn up or not
Which? found only about a third of 28 UK lounges worth three stars or better, at an average price of £42 — the room may not be worth the pass
verdict: Airport Lounges is a booking front for rooms run by Swissport, CAVU and Plaza Premium, and it is competing on price and convenience rather than on anything it owns. That is a perfectly reasonable thing to buy — a single visit at £31 in Aberdeen or £34 at Gatwick South is decent value against airport food prices, and there is no membership to carry. Do two things first. Check the same lounge on the operator's own site for the same date, because the operator publishes its price and the reseller's margin sits on top of it. And read the cancellation deadline: outside 24 hours you are usually fine, inside it you have bought a non-refundable ticket to a room you may not like, with no Section 75 claim to fall back on.

faqs.q: How much does a UK airport lounge cost to book?
faqs.a: Between £29.99 and £64 an adult on the operators' own September 2026 price lists. Escape Lounges start at £29.99, Aspire charges £31 at Humberside and Inverness, £38 at Gatwick North and £50 for the No1 Lounge at Heathrow Terminal 3, and Suite by Aspire at Newcastle is £64. Which? found an average of £42 across 28 lounges in its November 2025 survey.

faqs.q: Can I cancel a lounge booking and get my money back?
faqs.a: Usually only with at least 24 hours' notice. Escape Lounges will not refund a booking cancelled within 24 hours of the arrival time, and no amendment is possible once the booking has started. Edinburgh's lounge terms say an unused booking expires unrefunded and cannot be transferred to another person or lounge. The 14-day online cancellation right does not apply, because regulation 28(1)(h) of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 excludes leisure services booked for a specific date.

faqs.q: How long can I stay in the lounge?
faqs.a: Three hours before your scheduled departure at a standard Escape Lounge and across the Aspire and No1 estate, with extra hours sold as an add-on if you want to arrive earlier. A 1903 Lounge allows two hours and the Executive and Essence rooms two and a half to three. Turn up more than an hour after your booked time and the seat can be released.

faqs.q: Is a lounge pass protected if the seller goes bust?
faqs.a: Not by ATOL, and not by Section 75 either. A lounge pass bought on its own is not a package holiday, so the Package Travel Regulations and ATOL do not apply, and at under £100 a pass it falls below the Section 75 threshold in the Consumer Credit Act 1974. The practical remedy is a card chargeback, which is why booking close to the travel date rather than months ahead is the safer habit.

faqs.q: Can I take children into an airport lounge?
faqs.a: Yes at most, with limits. Escape Lounges admit children aged three to 15 at a charge, let infants under three in free, and cap a single booking at three children or infants. The booking itself must be made by someone aged 18 or over. The 1903 Lounges are adults-only unless a child is accompanying an adult whose access came with an airline ticket.

title: Airport Parking Shop Review
meta_title: Airport Parking Shop: Prices, Partners and Cancellation
meta_description: Manchester parking at £4.82 a day and Gatwick at £7.20 on 24 September 2026. The eight brokers behind the results, the cancellation fees and who you pay.

headline.label: Cheapest park and ride
headline.value: £5.16 a day at Manchester · £8.09 at Gatwick · £9.78 at Heathrow — lowest week recorded in the seven days to 24 September 2026

intro:
The cheapest tile on Airport Parking Shop's Manchester page on 24 September 2026 was Avian Parking All Inclusive at £4.82 a day, with a ten to twenty minute transfer. Gatwick opened at £7.20 and Heathrow at £7.60. All three came off the site's own airport pages that afternoon, and each is a daily equivalent of a week's parking rather than a rate you pay by the day.

The site has been doing this since 2003, which makes it one of the older price engines in British travel, and it is unusually large for its age: "An amazing 660 car parks across 32 airports", from Heathrow and Gatwick through Inverness, Norwich and Teesside to Belfast City, Dublin, Shannon and the Dover ferry terminal. It is run by Fubra Limited, an internet publisher in Aldershot incorporated on 7 April 2000 and still on the register as company 03967214, and the search itself is Fubra's own code rather than a widget bought in.

What makes it different from the rest of this trade is what it is comparing. Most parking sites rank car parks. This one ranks the eight booking companies that sell car parks — APH, BCP, Essential Travel, FHR, Holiday Extras, Park and Go, Purple Parking and SkyParkSecure — and shows their prices for the same car park side by side. It takes no money itself. Your card goes to whichever of the eight you clicked through to, your confirmation email comes from them, and if the barrier will not lift at six in the morning they are the number on the voucher. Knowing that before you book decides who you ring.

key_facts.value: Fubra Limited, registered in England and Wales, 03967214, incorporated 7 April 2000; VAT 733667024

key_facts.label: What it is
key_facts.value: A comparison of eight parking brokers. Its own terms: "we are a comparison website and do not provide the Car Park Service itself"

key_facts.value: 2003; the site claims "millions of bookings" since launch

key_facts.value: 660 car parks at 32 airports, plus Dover ferry port and two Irish airports

key_facts.value: Eight on the homepage and in the FAQ; the terms and conditions name only seven
