key_facts.value: 41%, from Ofcom's Technology Tracker 2024 as reported in its audio study of 21 May 2025

intro:
Amazon guarantees software security updates on an Echo for at least four years from the day you buy it new from Amazon as the seller on Amazon.co.uk, and Ring makes the same four-year promise on its doorbells and cameras. Both then publish a hard end date for every model, and those dates run as far out as 31 December 2031 on the newest Ring cameras. Every figure here comes from Amazon's and Ring's own support pages and was checked on 27 September 2026.

Publishing the dates at all puts Amazon in the better half of this market. When Which? surveyed 128 connected-product brands in June 2024, weeks after the law requiring that disclosure took effect, 29 of them - 23% - had published nothing usable or did not reply, and a further 23 offered a policy with no end date in it. Amazon's tables name the model and give the day. The estate they cover is large: the company says 56 million smart home devices are connected to Alexa across the UK, and Ofcom's Technology Tracker found a smart speaker in 41% of British households.

One thing to hold on to before reading a single listing. That four years is Amazon's promise about hardware Amazon itself makes - Echo, Fire TV, Ring and Blink. Most of the smart-home catalogue is other companies' products sold by other companies, and each of those carries whatever update period its own manufacturer chose to publish. In law Amazon is a distributor there rather than a manufacturer, and a distributor's duty is a different and much thinner one.

sections.heading: Four years from the till, and the day it stops
sections.html:
The commitment is written the same way across the three ranges. Amazon's Echo page promises "software security updates until at least four years from when you bought it new, from Amazon as the seller, on Amazon.co.uk", or until a later date published against the model - whichever comes last. Fire TV carries the identical wording. Ring's is "at least four years from when you bought it new", again with a published date as the floor.

The tables behind those sentences are short and blunt. Every Echo falls on one of two dates. 31 December 2029 covers the Echo Dot 3rd, 4th and 5th generation, the Dot Kids, the Dot with Clock, the Echo Show 10 3rd generation, the Show 8 1st and 2nd generation, the Show 5 2nd generation, the Show 15 1st generation, the Show Kids 3rd generation, the Echo Link, the Link Amp, the older Echo Studio and the Echo Sub. 31 December 2030 covers the Echo Pop, the Echo 4th generation, the Show 5 3rd generation, the 2025 Show 8, the Show 11, the Show 15 2nd generation, the Show 21, the Echo Hub, the 2024 Echo Spot, the 2025 Echo Studio and the Echo Dot Max. Fire TV is simpler still: almost the whole range ends on 31 December 2030, with the first-generation Fire TV Stick 4K alone on 2029.

Set the dates against the prices Amazon announced on 30 September 2025 and the guarantee acquires a unit cost. An Echo Dot Max is £99.99 and an Echo Studio £219.99, both supported to 31 December 2030 - five years and three months from launch, which on the Studio is about £42 a year of guaranteed patching. The Echo Show 11 is £219.99 and the Show 8 £179.99 on the same date. The adjustable stand, if you want one, is £34.99 and has no software in it at all.

The "whichever is later" mechanic is worth following through, because it decides which number applies to you. Buy an Echo Dot Max in September 2026 and four years from purchase lands in September 2030, three months short of the published date, so the published date governs and you get four years and three months. Buy the same device in 2029 and the published date has almost gone, so the four years governs instead and support runs into 2033. The promise is generous late in a product's life and barely binding early in it.

Ring is candid about what sits on the far side of the date, in wording most manufacturers would have left out: "After that time, we may continue to provide software security updates for as long as we can (subject to technical and other limitations)", followed by the line that matters most - "the update period is not a guarantee as to how long your device will last". That is an honest sentence about a four-year floor under a device screwed to a door frame.

sections.heading: The law that made them print a date
sections.html:
None of this was voluntary. The Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022 took Royal Assent in December 2022, and the regulations that put it to work - the Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure (Security Requirements for Relevant Connectable Products) Regulations 2023, SI 2023 No. 1007 - were signed on 14 September 2023 and came into force on 29 April 2024. A further amendment on 25 February 2025 added vehicle exemptions.

Three duties fall on the manufacturer, and they are narrow enough to check. Passwords must be unique to the product or set by the user, and a product-unique password may not be built from an incremental counter, from publicly available information, or from a product identifier unless it is encrypted. There must be a published point of contact "to allow a person to report to the manufacturer security issues", with stated timelines for acknowledging a report and for status updates on it. And the defined support period must be published: the minimum length of time, expressed as a period with an end date, for which security updates will be provided, in language a buyer can understand without technical knowledge, and available without giving personal data or asking first.

That last clause is why a page like Amazon's exists and why you should be able to find one for any connected product on sale here. It is also where the regime draws an odd line. Schedule 3 excepts a short list of products: those covered by relevant EU legislation for the Northern Ireland market, electric vehicle smart charge points, medical devices, smart meter products assured under National Cyber Security Centre schemes, and desktop and laptop computers along with tablets that have no cellular connection. So the laptop you use to set the whole smart home up is outside the rules that govern the smart plug it is talking to.

Enforcement belongs to the Office for Product Safety and Standards. Its powers under the Act run from a compliance notice under section 28, through a stop notice under section 29 - which may be issued without prior notice where there is an urgent need - to a recall notice under section 30 requiring arrangements for the return of the products. The money at the end of that ladder is serious: the maximum penalty is the greater of £10 million or 4% of the person's qualifying worldwide revenue for their most recent complete accounting period, with daily penalties of up to £20,000 while a breach continues.

sections.heading: Ask for the statement of compliance - Ring's is online, signed and dated
sections.html:
There is a second document the regime creates, and it is the one a shopper has a direct claim on. Section 22 stops a distributor making a relevant product available in the UK unless it is accompanied by a statement of compliance. The Government's own guidance concedes that the Act "does not define the terms 'document' or 'accompany'", so it can be paper in the box or something digital, and each business works out how to satisfy it. The contents are prescribed: the product, the manufacturer, a declaration of conformity, the defined support period, the signatory and where and when it was issued.

Ring publishes its. The UK statement is version 2.3, filed by Ring LLC of 12515 Cerise Ave, Hawthorne, CA 90250, USA, first issued on 29 April 2024 - the day the regime began - and signed on 27 March 2026 by Jason Mitura, VP. It covers 31 products across indoor, outdoor, spotlight, floodlight and peephole cameras, wired and battery doorbells, chimes, alarm components, an intercom and access control units, and it declares that they "are in conformity with the relevant statutory requirements for sale in the United Kingdom, including: the security requirements; and the compliance requirements, of the Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022".

Read it beside the support page and the two do not say the same thing. The statement promises "guaranteed software security updates until at least four years after the device is last available for purchase". The support page promises four years from when you bought it new. Those are different clocks, and the statement's is the kinder one for anyone buying early in a product's life, because a device is typically on sale for years after your purchase. Which? recorded Ring in June 2024 as giving four years after discontinuation, which is the statement's version rather than the shop's. Both are Ring's own words and both are current; printing them together is fairer than picking one.

The dates inside the statement are mostly 31 December 2030 or later, with three exceptions worth knowing before buying old stock: the Stick Up Cam Elite and the Video Doorbell Elite run to 2029 and the second-generation Video Doorbell to 2028. Devices whose support has already lapsed are simply absent, because the document covers what is still sold - which is correct, and is also why a statement of compliance tells you nothing about the doorbell already on your wall.

No equivalent public UK statement of compliance could be found for Echo, Fire TV or Blink, only the security-update help pages. That may well exist somewhere in the packaging or the app; it could not be established from outside and needs confirming with Amazon.

sections.heading: 67 entries on the recall register, and none of them found by searching for wi-fi
sections.html:
Britain's public register of unsafe products is at gov.uk, and it is worth running before any purchase in this category. Searched on 27 September 2026 it returned 67 reports for the word smart, 13 for camera, one for doorbell, and nothing at all for wifi.

The freshest entry with a household name on it is the Silentnight Smart Wi-Fi Plug, model A6, EAN 5012701485418, recalled on 27 March 2026 after being sold from 2017 to 2022 - individually, in packs of four, six and eight, and bundled with Silentnight electric blankets. The register records a serious risk of electric shock because the mains plug did not meet the dimensional requirements of BS 1363, breaching the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016 and the Plugs and Sockets etc. (Safety) Regulations 1994. It was made in China, recalled by Comfy Quilts on 0330 107 1052, and notified by local authority Trading Standards. Nine years is a long time for a plug to be on bedside tables.

A second entry shows the other way these devices fail. A Cloud Storage Intelligent Camera, published on 19 January 2026 and notified by OPSS itself, carried a serious electric shock and fire risk: no fuse in the plug, live parts reachable without tools, and transformer windings touching each other. That import was rejected at the border and destroyed, so it never reached a customer.

Now notice what the register does not hold. Every one of those 67 entries is about electricity, flammability or a physical hazard. Not one is about a software vulnerability, an unpatched device or a default password - the things the 2024 regime was written for. Product safety has a public register with a search box; product security has a statute, a regulator and no register at all. OPSS's own enforcement page for the connectable products regulations, updated on 8 August 2025, sets out the compliance notices, stop notices, recall notices, monetary penalties, forfeiture orders and court orders available to it, and names not one case. Whether the £10 million ceiling has ever been approached is not something a shopper can find out.

sections.heading: A doorbell camera makes you a data controller at your own gate
sections.html:
The part of a smart doorbell nobody mentions on a product page is that pointing one at the street brings you inside data protection law. The Biometrics and Surveillance Camera Commissioner's guidance on domestic CCTV, first published on 20 October 2016 and last updated on 21 May 2026, puts it plainly: "If your CCTV system captures images of people outside the boundary of your private domestic property - for example, from neighbours' homes or gardens, shared spaces, or from public areas - then the GDPR and the DPA will apply to you."

What follows from that is short and practical. You should be transparent about the recording, which the guidance describes as "putting up a notice informing people that recording is taking place". You should not keep footage indefinitely - "you should not store any information or images for longer than is necessary to protect your property which means you should delete the information once it is no longer required". And you have to honour the rights of the people you have filmed, because if you do not "you may be subject to appropriate regulatory action by the ICO, as well as potential legal action by affected individuals".

The deadline attached to that last duty is a real one. The Information Commissioner's Office gives an organisation - or a householder who has stepped into this position - no later than one calendar month from the day the request is received, extendable to a maximum of three calendar months where the request is complex or where more than one has been made. The month runs to the same date in the following month, rolls to the next working day if it falls on a Saturday, Sunday or bank holiday, and becomes the last day of the month where no matching date exists.

Put that beside the retention the subscription sells. Every Ring plan, from £4.99 a month upwards, offers "Up to 180 Days of Video Playback". Six months of recordings of a pavement is not obviously "no longer than is necessary to protect your property", and it is the householder rather than Ring who has to reconcile the two. None of the hardware prices announced on 30 September 2025 - the Ring Wired Video Doorbell Pro at £219.99, the Wired Video Doorbell Plus at £159.99, the Outdoor Camera Pro at £179.99, the Floodlight Cam Pro at £249.99, the Indoor Cam Plus at £49.99, the Blink Mini 2K+ at £39.99, or the Blink Outdoor Floodlight Camera and Blink Arc at £89.99 each - includes an answer to it.

sections.heading: What the microphone is doing between wake words
sections.html:
Amazon's own privacy page for Alexa and Echo devices is more specific than most people expect, and it answers the question the marketing never raises. By default, "No audio is stored or sent to the cloud unless the device detects the wake word (or Alexa is activated by pressing a button)". When it does, "a recording of what you ask Alexa is sent to Amazon's cloud, where we process your request".

Three of the controls are hardware or near enough. A light ring turns blue, or a blue bar appears on an Echo Show, whenever the device is streaming to the cloud. An Echo can be set to play a short audible tone every time audio is sent. And the microphone button does something better than a software switch: press it and "the power to the microphones is disconnected and a dedicated red light is illuminated".

On retention, Amazon offers automatic deletion of voice recordings, text transcripts and typed requests "after a specified period of time (3 or 18 months)", or the option "to not save any voice recordings" at all, with manual review and deletion under More then Alexa Privacy in the app. Eighteen months is the default-shaped option and three months is the one worth choosing.

The distinction to hold on to is that not saving is not the same as not sending. The setting governs the copy Amazon keeps, not the journey the audio makes; the same page says the recording goes to the cloud to be processed. Anyone who wants speech recognition to happen inside the room is asking for something this product does not offer.

On the security of the hardware itself, the only independent testing found is old and should be read that way. Which? commissioned ethical hackers to attack eight connected devices in a mocked-up home and published the result on 1 June 2022: 37 vulnerabilities across the eight, of which 12 were rated high risk and one critical, with a first-generation Echo among them and remote microphone access among the findings. That is four years ago and first-generation hardware, and no comparable test of the current range has been published since.

sections.heading: The subscription can cost more than the camera
sections.html:
The hardware is the cheap half. Ring's UK plans run Solo at £4.99 a month or £49.99 a year for one device at one address; Multi at £7.99 or £79.99 for every device at that address, adding multi-camera live view and a daily event summary; Pro at £15.99 or £159.99, adding video descriptions, single event alerts, video search and familiar faces; and Guard Response at £29.99 or £299.99. All four carry up to 180 days of video playback.

Guard Response is the newest and the most interesting, announced on 15 July 2026. It sends a licensed guard from RSPNDR, usually within 30 minutes, around the clock, with no charge per dispatch - automatically if a registered Ring Alarm goes off, or on demand from a doorbell or camera. The guard walks the outside of the property checking doors, windows, gates and passages, can call the emergency services, and sends a report afterwards with images. The limits are published and sensible: guards cannot go inside without explicit consent, cannot detain anybody, and have no access to your Ring footage. It is a limited release in Birmingham, Bristol, Manchester and Cardiff, so for most of the country it is not yet a product at all.

Two sums are worth doing before subscribing to anything. Paid monthly, Guard Response is £359.88 a year against £299.99 paid annually, so the monthly option costs £59.89 more for the same service - and £359.88 in year one is more than the £249.99 Floodlight Cam Pro it is watching over. The same gap scales down: Solo is £59.88 a year monthly against £49.99 annually. Guard Response includes Ring Pro, which is £15.99 a month bought alone, so the guard service itself is the other £14 a month.

The assistant has a price now too. Alexa+ reached the UK in Early Access on 19 March 2026 at £19.99 a month once that period ends, free for every UK Prime member, and running on the Echo Show 8, Echo Show 11, Echo Dot Max, Echo Studio, Fire TV and a browser at alexa.com. £19.99 a month is £239.88 a year, which is a good deal more than Prime's £95 for twelve months - so the cheapest route to Alexa+ is a Prime membership rather than the product itself, which is presumably the point. Amazon puts the scale of what it is upgrading at 114 billion customer interactions with Alexa in the UK over the past three years.

sections.heading: Whose four years is it, when the seller is not the maker?
sections.html:
Almost everything else in this part of the shop belongs to somebody else, and Amazon's own seller price list shows how the category is sorted. A smart-home device can land on either side of a wide line: Consumer Electronics takes 7%, Electronic Accessories 15% up to £100 and 8% above, Home Products 8% at or below £20 and 15% above, Tools and Home Improvement 13%, and anything unclassified 15%, all with a 25p minimum. A £39.99 wireless camera therefore costs its seller £2.80 in one category and £6.00 in another, on identical hardware. Selling plans are £25 a month or 75p an item on top.

What the law asks of Amazon on those listings is not to publish the support period - that duty sits with the manufacturer - but not to make the product available without the statement of compliance that carries it. The Smart Technology (Product Safety) Stakeholder Group's guidance, updated on 29 April 2024, states the duty in the same terms and adds that it bites on everything made available in the UK "regardless of source or method of sales". Whether a given marketplace listing actually surfaces that number to a shopper could not be verified here, because amazon.co.uk refuses automated access; it needs checking in a browser, and it is the single most useful thing a buyer could ask for.

The reason it matters is what the rest of the market does with the same obligation. Which?'s June 2024 survey of 128 brands found 76 - 59% - publishing a clear period, and the spread among them was enormous. One year on AEG tumble dryers, Beko washing machines and dishwashers and Grundig ovens. Two years on Hisense dishwashers, Hive radiator valves and Hubble and Owlet baby monitors. At the other end, ten years from Bosch, Miele and tado°, eight from Fairphone, and seven from Google and Samsung phones, Epson printers and Ezviz doorbells. TP-Link gave three years from discontinuation on smart plugs; Samsung and LG gave five years from launch on televisions; Apple gave a five-year minimum on an iPhone. Amazon's four years from purchase sits in the middle of that, and is measured from a better starting point than most.

Set the periods against how long the things actually live and the problem is obvious. An earlier Which? survey, of 119 brands across 20 smart categories in November 2022, found only 49% giving a clear minimum support period, and estimated average lifespans of 13 years for a dishwasher, 13 for an inkjet printer, 11 for a washing machine and 6.8 for a television. A one-year update policy on an appliance with a thirteen-year life is not a policy. Of 1,051 Which? members asked in October 2022, about nine in ten said security updates mattered when buying a smart product.

And the worst case is not a lapsed update but an abandoned platform. On 25 July 2022 Hive told customers it was discontinuing the Hive View and View Outdoor cameras, the Homeshield burglar alarm with its sirens, keypads and sensors, and its leak sensors, with support ending on 1 September 2023 for the sensors and 1 August 2025 for the cameras and alarms, and subscriptions honoured for a minimum of two years. That is a different company and not a criticism of Amazon; it is the thing a published, dated, four-year floor is insurance against, and it is why the floor is worth reading before you buy rather than after.

pros: Publishes a security-update end date for every Echo, Fire TV and Ring model rather than a vague promise - 23% of the 128 brands Which? surveyed in June 2024 published nothing usable at all
Measures the four years from the day of purchase rather than from launch, which is a better starting point than the five-years-from-launch most television makers offer
Ring's UK statement of compliance is public, versioned, dated and signed, and covers 31 products by name
The newest Ring cameras and doorbells are covered to 31 December 2031, and almost the whole current Echo and Fire TV range to 31 December 2030
The Echo microphone button disconnects power to the microphones rather than switching them off in software, with a dedicated red light to show it
Voice recordings, transcripts and typed requests can be set to delete automatically after 3 months, or not to be saved at all
Alexa+ costs nothing on top of a Prime membership, against £19.99 a month standalone
Ring's entry plan is £4.99 a month for up to 180 days of video playback on one device
cons: Four years is short against how long this hardware lives. Which? put the average life of a dishwasher at 13 years and a television at 6.8, and a £219.99 Echo Studio's guaranteed patching stops on 31 December 2030 whether or not the speaker still works

Ring publishes two different clocks for the same promise: its statement of compliance says four years after the device is last available for purchase, its UK support page says four years from when you bought it new

That support page describes the qualifying purchase as one made "on amazon.com where Amazon is the seller or on ring.com" - the US domain rather than amazon.co.uk. Checked 27 September 2026, and which UK purchases the four years covers needs confirming with Ring
Security updates for the first Ring Video Doorbell and the first Ring Chime ended on 31 December 2024, so devices still screwed to door frames have been unsupported for close to two years

No public UK statement of compliance for Echo, Fire TV or Blink could be found - only the help pages - so the one document the regime asks a distributor to pass on is easier to read for Ring than for Amazon's own devices
Choosing not to save voice recordings is not the same as keeping them off the cloud. Amazon's own page says the recording is sent for processing either way, and there is no on-device option
Whether a third-party smart-home listing shows its manufacturer's support period could not be checked, because amazon.co.uk refuses automated access - and that number is the one a buyer most needs

OPSS publishes enforcement guidance for the connectable products regulations, last updated 8 August 2025, but no record of any action taken, so nobody outside can tell whether the £10 million maximum penalty has ever been used
Ring Guard Response costs £29.99 a month and is a limited release in four cities - Birmingham, Bristol, Manchester and Cardiff
verdict: On the one question this category ought to be compared on, Amazon answers clearly: at least four years of security updates from the day you buy, with a published end date for every model, and nothing in the Echo range finishing before 31 December 2029. That is better than most of the market manages and it is easy to check. The honest caveats are that four years is short measured against a decade of hardware life, that Ring's two published versions of the same promise do not match, and that the four years covers Amazon's own devices rather than the marketplace catalogue around them. Read the support page for the model you want before you buy, and price the subscription alongside the hardware - on a Ring camera the plan can cost more in its first year than the camera did.

faqs.q: How long does Amazon guarantee security updates on an Echo?
faqs.a: At least four years from the day you bought it new from Amazon as the seller on Amazon.co.uk, or until the end date Amazon publishes against that model, whichever is later. Every Echo falls on 31 December 2029 or 31 December 2030; almost all of Fire TV is on 31 December 2030, with the first-generation Fire TV Stick 4K on 2029. Ring devices run to 31 December 2031 at the newest end.

faqs.q: What is a defined support period, and where should I find one?
faqs.a: It is the minimum length of time, with an end date, for which a manufacturer will provide security updates. Since 29 April 2024 every connectable product sold in the UK has had to publish one under SI 2023/1007, in plain language, without you having to ask or hand over personal data. If a product you are looking at has no published period, that is itself the answer.

faqs.q: Does the four years cover a smart plug I buy from a marketplace seller on Amazon?
faqs.a: No. The four years is Amazon's own commitment on Echo, Fire TV, Ring and Blink. A third-party product carries whatever period its manufacturer published, and those range from one year to ten across the brands Which? surveyed in June 2024. Amazon's duty on those listings is a distributor's: not to make the product available unless it is accompanied by a statement of compliance.

faqs.q: Do I have to tell my neighbours about a Ring doorbell?
faqs.a: If the camera captures anyone beyond your property boundary, data protection law applies to you, and the official guidance on domestic CCTV - updated on 21 May 2026 - says you should put up a notice saying recording is taking place, keep footage no longer than necessary, and honour requests from people you have filmed. The ICO allows one calendar month to answer such a request, or up to three where it is complex.

faqs.q: Can I stop Alexa keeping recordings of what I say?
faqs.a: Yes, in the Alexa app under More then Alexa Privacy. You can delete recordings manually, set them to delete automatically after 3 or 18 months, or choose not to save any at all. What you cannot switch off is the trip to the cloud: Amazon's own page says a recording of the request is sent to be processed there. Pressing the microphone button cuts power to the microphones entirely.

faqs.q: What does a Ring subscription cost, and do I need one?
faqs.a: Solo is £4.99 a month or £49.99 a year for one device, Multi £7.99 or £79.99 for a whole home, Pro £15.99 or £159.99, and Guard Response £29.99 or £299.99. All include up to 180 days of video playback. Without a plan the cameras still work live; recorded history is the thing you are buying. Paying annually saves £59.89 a year on Guard Response and £9.89 on Solo.

title: Amazon Televisions Review 2026: Fire TV Prices, Power and Parts
meta_title: Amazon Fire TV Review 2026: Prices, Power and Parts
meta_description: Amazon's own Fire TV sets start at £249.99 with a one-year guarantee. We read the compliance sheets for the watts, the parts period and the update date.

headline.label: Free guarantee included in the price
headline.value: 1 year on every Amazon-built Fire TV, 90 days on the remote — and nothing from Amazon on another brand's set (checked 28 September 2026)

intro:
Amazon's own-brand televisions start at £249.99 for a 32-inch Fire TV 2-Series and run to £849.00 for the 55-inch Omni Mini-LED, and every one of them carries a one-year limited warranty from Amazon EU S.à r.l. in Luxembourg. Those prices come from Amazon's UK newsroom buying guide, published 30 September 2025 and last modified 27 December 2025; the warranty term is from Amazon's own device warranty page, both checked on 28 September 2026.

Amazon is unusual among the shops on this list because it is also a manufacturer. It builds the 2-Series, the 4-Series, the Omni QLED and the Omni Mini-LED under its own name, licenses the Fire TV software to Hisense, Panasonic, TCL and Xiaomi, and sells every other brand alongside them. Amazon says customers have bought 300 million devices with Fire TV built in.

What makes the range worth a serious look is not the price. It is that Amazon publishes a safety and compliance sheet for each set, and those sheets carry numbers most retailers never put in front of a shopper: the watts the panel draws, the energy class, the standby draw, and how long the company will keep making spare parts. We have read them, and the figures below are all Amazon's own.

key_facts.label: Published on-mode power, Omni QLED (2025)
key_facts.value: 140.0 W at 50 inches, 180.0 W at 55, 200.0 W at 65 and 250.0 W at 75 — Amazon's own compliance sheet

key_facts.label: Guarantee
key_facts.value: One-Year Limited Warranty on devices, 90-Day Limited Warranty on separately bought remotes and accessories

key_facts.label: Guarantor
key_facts.value: Amazon EU S.à r.l., 38 avenue John F. Kennedy, L-1855 Luxembourg

key_facts.label: Declared for compliance by
key_facts.value: Amazon.com Services LLC — a United States company, on every Fire TV sheet we read

key_facts.label: Energy class
key_facts.value: G in both SDR and HDR on the Fire TV Omni 65 (QL65F601U); the 2025 sheets publish no class at all

key_facts.label: Spare parts
key_facts.value: 7 years after the last unit is placed on the market, and 15 working days to deliver one

key_facts.label: Security updates
key_facts.value: At least 4 years from purchase, or 31 December 2030 for the whole current television range

key_facts.label: Range sold
key_facts.value: £249.99 (32in 2-Series) to £849.00 (55in Omni Mini-LED), plus every other brand on the marketplace

sections.heading: The price, the guarantee and what Amazon is promising when it gives you one
sections.html:
Four Fire TV lines are sold in the UK under Amazon's own name. The 2-Series is HD at 32 and 40 inches from £249.99; the 4-Series is 4K at 43, 50 and 55 inches from £429.99; the Omni QLED runs 43 to 65 inches from £549.00; and the Omni Mini-LED covers 55, 65 and 75 inches from £849.00. The Fire TV Stick 4K Select, which turns any set into a Fire TV, is £49.99.

Every one of those televisions comes with what Amazon calls a One-Year Limited Warranty. It runs "one year from the date of original retail purchase", covers "defects in materials and workmanship under ordinary consumer use", and is given by Amazon EU S.à r.l., 38 avenue John F. Kennedy, L-1855 Luxembourg. Remotes, game controllers, IR extenders and the Fire TV Blaster bought separately get a 90-Day Limited Warranty instead.

A guarantee of that kind is not a favour. Section 30 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 says a guarantee "takes effect, at the time the goods are delivered, as a contractual obligation owed by the guarantor" — so the year is enforceable in its own right, on top of the statutory rights that run for six years in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and five in Scotland. The same section requires the guarantee to be written in English where the goods are offered in the UK, to set out the claims procedure in plain language, to state that statutory rights are unaffected, and to give the guarantor's name and address, the duration and the territorial scope. Amazon's wording does all of that, and says so explicitly: "If you are a consumer, this One-Year Limited Warranty is provided in addition to, and without prejudice to, your consumer rights."

One year is what Amazon adds. On a television made by somebody else and sold through the marketplace, Amazon adds nothing to the guarantee at all — the cover is whatever the manufacturer or the seller offers, and it varies set by set.

sections.heading: The watts Amazon prints, and the bill they turn into
sections.html:
The single most useful document on an Amazon television is the safety and compliance sheet, and it is not on the product page. For the 65-inch Fire TV Omni, model QL65F601U, the sheet gives on-mode power demand of 104 W in Standard Dynamic Range and 164 W in High Dynamic Range, standby at 0.44 W and networked standby at 0.53 W, at a resolution of 3,840 by 2,160.

Those figures do something a star rating cannot: they price the set for the years after you buy it. Four hours of viewing a day is 1,460 hours a year. At 104 W that is 151.8 kWh, and at the Ofgem price cap direct debit electricity rate of 26.11p per kWh for 1 July to 30 September 2026 it comes to £39.65 a year. From 1 October the capped rate rises to 26.32p, which takes the same viewing to £39.96. Watch in HDR instead and the same four hours a day draws 239.4 kWh, or £62.52 — £22.87 a year for the brighter picture. Leaving it in networked standby all year, which is what it does when you are not watching, costs about £1.21.

Across the seven years Amazon commits to supplying spare parts, that SDR figure is £277.55 of electricity behind a television that cost a few hundred pounds. It is the sort of sum a shopper can only do if the retailer publishes the wattage, and Amazon does.

The 2025 sheets extend the ladder. The Fire TV 4-Series is given as 100.0 W at 43 inches (4K43N402U), 135.0 W at 50 and 150.0 W at 55, all at 220–240 V, 50 Hz. The Omni QLED is 140.0 W at 50 inches, 180.0 W at 55, 200.0 W at 65 and 250.0 W at 75. Those newer numbers are not split between SDR and HDR, so they are not directly comparable with the 104 W on the older Omni sheet, and we have not treated them as if they were.

sections.heading: Class G is normal, and the label explains why
sections.html:
The Omni 65 sheet rates the set G for energy efficiency in both SDR and HDR. That reads alarmingly and it should not. The GB energy label for electronic displays was rescaled to a plain A to G range that applied from 1 March 2021, with the printed-label duty biting from 1 November 2020, and the scale was deliberately set so that almost nothing qualified for the top letters at the start. Under the retained regulation on the energy labelling of electronic displays, class A needs an Energy Efficiency Index below 0.3 and class G covers anything at 0.9 or above. Large 4K panels sit at the bottom of that scale almost by construction.

The label itself is a mandated disclosure with a fixed content list, which is what makes it useful. A GB label must carry the model number, the supplier's name or trademark, the consumption data, the class, the UK flag, English text and, where applicable, a QR code. The duties are split: the supplier has to provide the label free and promptly, include the product information sheet and keep the technical documentation for 15 years for inspection; the dealer has to display the label clearly and, for distance selling, put the label and the information sheet in front of the buyer before they buy. For internet sales the electronic label must appear "in proximity to the price of the product", with a nested display permitted so long as it opens on the first click.

There is one quiet divergence worth knowing. In Great Britain the QR code on the label points to "the required model information on a publicly accessible website" — the supplier's own. In Northern Ireland it still points to EPREL, the EU's central database. So a Northern Irish buyer can look a television up in one place and cross-check the maker's claims against a public register; a buyer in England, Scotland or Wales is sent to whatever page the supplier decided to put up.

sections.heading: Seven years of parts, fifteen working days to get one
sections.html:
Energy labelling is only half of the rulebook. The ecodesign regulation for electronic displays sets minimum efficiency and, more usefully for a buyer, minimum repairability. From 1 March 2021 the maximum Energy Efficiency Index was 0.9 for HD and 1.1 for UHD-4K; from 1 March 2023 it tightened to 0.75 and 0.9. Standby is capped at 0.5 W, off mode at 0.3 W and networked standby at 2.0 W.

Set the Omni 65's own figures against those caps and the result is mixed in an interesting way. Networked standby at 0.53 W is comfortably under the 2.0 W ceiling. Standby at 0.44 W is inside the 0.5 W limit with very little room left.

The repair provisions are the part almost nobody reads. Manufacturers must make the internal power supply, connectors, capacitors, batteries, and the DVD/Blu-ray and HD/SSD modules where fitted available to professional repairers for seven years after the last unit of the model is placed on the market, and the external power supply and remote control to end users for the same period. Orders must be delivered within "15 working days after having received the order". Repairers must be given an exploded view, a list of the test equipment needed, wiring diagrams and fault codes within one working day of asking. Plastic parts over 50 g must be marked with the polymer type, joins must not prevent removal of the components listed in the WEEE rules using ordinary tools, and "the use of halogenated flame retardants is not allowed in the enclosure and stand of electronic displays."

Amazon's own compliance sheet for the Omni 65 states spare parts availability of 7 Years and product support of 7 Years, which matches the regulation rather than beating it.

sections.heading: Three documents, three different answers on how long the set is supported
sections.html:
The same compliance sheet says software and firmware updates are guaranteed for 8 Years. Amazon's customer-facing security update page says something different: "We'll support your device with software security updates until at least four years from when you bought it new", or the published date if later. The published date for every current Fire TV television — Omni QLED at 43, 50, 55 and 65 inches, 4-Series at 43, 50 and 55, 2-Series at 32 and 40 — is 31 December 2030, as it is for every current Fire TV Stick. Only the first-generation Fire TV Stick 4K sits earlier, on 31 December 2029.

Both statements are Amazon's and they do not say the same thing. Buy an Omni QLED on the day we checked, 28 September 2026, and 31 December 2030 is four years and three months away, so the four-year floor and the published date land in almost the same place. Buy one in 2029 and the date, not the four years, is what you get — unless Amazon extends it. The eight-year figure on the compliance sheet is the most generous of the three and the one no customer-facing page repeats. We have printed all three rather than choosing between them.

The update page also carries its own caveat, and it is a fair one: "Please note the update period is not a guarantee as to how long your device will last." For context, Samsung and LG have both told Which? they support their televisions for five years from launch, which is measured from a different starting point again.

sections.heading: Who actually answers for the set, and which regulator is watching
sections.html:
Three Amazon entities appear across the documents for one television. The compliance declaration is made by Amazon.com Services LLC, a United States company, and the sheets we read give no address for it. The guarantee is given by Amazon EU S.à r.l. in Luxembourg. The shop is Amazon's UK store. None of the three is a UK address a buyer could write to, and the compliance sheets point readers to a support page rather than naming a responsible person in Great Britain.

Enforcement is split in a way that matters on a marketplace. The Office for Product Safety and Standards is the market surveillance authority for suppliers under the energy information rules; local authorities enforce the same rules against dealers. When Amazon sells a television it has built, it is the supplier and OPSS is the body concerned. When a third-party seller on the same site lists a Hisense or a Toshiba, that seller is the dealer, and the duty to show the energy label beside the price falls on them, policed by their local trading standards service rather than by Amazon or by OPSS.

The Fire TV compliance sheets state the devices "are in compliance with Directive 2014/53/EU and relevant UK statutory requirements" and meet the public exposure thresholds for electromagnetic fields in Council Recommendation 1999/519/EC. On recycling they say only that you should "dispose of, or recycle, your device in accordance with your local laws and regulations".

sections.heading: The badge on the bezel is not always the company that built it
sections.html:
A television is one of the few purchases where the brand on the front tells you very little about who made the thing. The public product safety register makes the point better than any argument. Searching it for television on 28 September 2026 returns two reports, both dated 15 June 2026, and both about the same component in different boxes.

Report 2606-0078 covers Vestel UK plugs fitted to televisions sold between November 2024 and February 2026 under Toshiba, JVC, Mitchell & Brown, Polaroid, Finlux, Techwood and Panasonic badges — models running from the Toshiba 32WF2F53DB to the Panasonic TV-65W80AEY. The fault is that "the plug's fuse does not meet the dimensional requirements of BS 1362", giving a risk of fire; the origin is Turkey, the breach is of the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016 or the Plugs & Sockets etc (Safety) Regulations 1994, it was notified by local authority Trading Standards, and the remedy is a free replacement power cable or fuse. Report 2606-0164 is the same defect in Bush TiVo televisions sold by Argos.

Seven brand names, one manufacturer, one fuse. Amazon sells several of those brands, and so does everybody else. It is the strongest argument there is for reading the compliance sheet rather than the badge — and Amazon, for its own sets, is one of the few sellers that publishes one you can find.

sections.heading: How Amazon's sets rate for reliability against the rest
sections.html:
The independent measure worth having on a television is not a picture-quality score but a fault rate, because a set that dies in year three costs more than one that was £100 dearer. Which? surveyed more than 15,000 members and members of the public in May 2026 about more than 43,000 televisions, with 5,911 sets behind the brand rankings and 14 brands covered, Amazon among them alongside LG, Sony, Samsung, Hisense, TCL, Sky, Toshiba, Sharp, Bush, Panasonic, JVC, Philips and Hitachi.

The headline finding that is readable without a subscription is blunt: of those fourteen brands, "just four of them manage five stars for reliability". The three most common faults reported were picture problems such as dead pixels and fuzzy images, sound faults including crackling and speaker failure, and hardware failure that stops the set powering on at all. The per-brand fault percentages and the average time to first fault sit behind the Which? paywall, so we cannot tell you where Amazon lands — and we are not going to guess at it. Anyone deciding between two sets on reliability should pay for one month of access and read the table, because it is the only UK figure of its kind.

sections.heading: The set is also a screen Amazon sells advertising on
sections.html:
Amazon's television business is not really a hardware business. The company says customers have bought 300 million devices with Fire TV built in, and it sells advertising against that audience in more than 20 countries including the UK. Its own case for Fire TV advertising cites 93% incremental reach when added to a Prime Video campaign and 88% exclusive reach, measured in the United States between 1 July and 31 December 2025.

Amazon also publishes the number that explains its interface design: customers spend an average of 12 minutes looking for something to watch, up from 10.5 minutes in 2023. The redesigned interface launched on 5 January 2026 and updated on 22 June 2026 claims 20% to 30% speed gains on existing hardware, and the newest set, the Ember Artline at 55 and 65 inches, is a picture-frame television with more than 2,000 works of art built in. A buyer should go in knowing that the home screen is inventory. That is the trade behind a 4K set at £429.99, and it is a defensible one — but it is a trade, not a discount.

pros: Publishes a safety and compliance sheet per model giving on-mode watts, standby draw and, on the older Omni, the energy class — detail most television retailers never put in front of a shopper
One-year manufacturer guarantee on every Amazon-built set, given by a named company at a stated address, with statutory rights expressly preserved
Seven years of spare parts and product support stated on Amazon's own sheet, matching what the ecodesign rules require
Networked standby of 0.53 W on the Omni 65 is well inside the 2.0 W legal ceiling, which keeps the always-on cost near £1.21 a year
Four own-brand lines from £249.99 to £849.00 plus almost every rival brand on the same site, so the range genuinely spans the market
Fire TV software is licensed to Hisense, Panasonic, TCL and Xiaomi, so the interface a buyer learns is not locked to Amazon's own hardware
cons: The 2025 compliance sheets for the 4-Series and Omni QLED publish on-mode wattage but no energy efficiency class at all, while the older Omni 65 sheet gives one — a step backwards in disclosure on the figure the label regime exists to communicate

Three Amazon documents give three different support periods for the same television: 8 years of software updates on the compliance sheet, at least 4 years from purchase or 31 December 2030 on the customer support page, and 7 years of spare parts
No UK address appears anywhere in the chain. Conformity is declared by Amazon.com Services LLC in the United States and the guarantee is given by Amazon EU S.à r.l. in Luxembourg

One year of manufacturer cover is short against a television's working life, and on any set Amazon did not build it adds nothing at all — the cover is the maker's or the seller's, and it is not consistent across the marketplace
Standby draw of 0.44 W on the Omni 65 is inside the 0.5 W legal cap by six hundredths of a watt, which leaves no headroom at all
The newer wattage figures are published without the SDR and HDR split the older sheet used, so they cannot be compared with it or with a rival's label figure without guesswork

In Great Britain the label's QR code points at the supplier's own website rather than a public database, so there is no independent register to check a claim against — a Northern Irish buyer can still use EPREL
verdict: Amazon is worth buying a television from for a reason that has nothing to do with the price: it publishes more hard numbers about its own sets than almost any shop publishes about anybody's. The 65-inch Omni's 104 W in SDR, 164 W in HDR and 0.53 W in networked standby are the difference between guessing at a running cost and working one out — about £39.65 a year at four hours a day on the capped rate in force when we checked. The guarantee is one year, which is short, and the support dates disagree with each other across three Amazon documents. Read the compliance sheet for the model you want before you buy, and if the set is not one of Amazon's own, find out from the listing who is actually giving you a guarantee.

faqs.q: How long is the guarantee on an Amazon Fire TV?
faqs.a: One year from the date of original retail purchase, given by Amazon EU S.à r.l. in Luxembourg, covering defects in materials and workmanship in ordinary consumer use. Remotes and other accessories bought separately get 90 days. It sits on top of your statutory rights, which run for six years in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and five in Scotland.

faqs.q: What does a Fire TV cost to run?
faqs.a: The 65-inch Fire TV Omni draws 104 W watching standard content. Four hours a day for a year is 151.8 kWh, or £39.65 at the 26.11p capped direct debit rate for July to September 2026, rising to £39.96 at the 26.32p rate from 1 October. HDR content draws 164 W, which takes the same viewing to £62.52.

faqs.q: Why is the energy rating G?
faqs.a: Because the A to G scale for televisions was rescaled from 1 March 2021 and set deliberately hard. Class A needs an Energy Efficiency Index under 0.3 and class G covers 0.9 and above, so most large 4K sets from every brand sit at the bottom. A G rating is not a sign that one television is worse than its rivals — compare the kWh per 1,000 hours instead.

faqs.q: Can a Fire TV be repaired?
faqs.a: The ecodesign rules oblige the maker to supply professional repairers with the internal power supply, connectors, capacitors and other listed parts for seven years after the last unit of that model is sold, delivered within 15 working days, and to hand over wiring diagrams and fault codes within one working day of a request. Amazon's own sheet states seven years of spare parts and seven of product support.

faqs.q: How long will Amazon send security updates to a Fire TV?
faqs.a: Amazon's support page promises at least four years from the day you buy it new, or a published date if that is later. Every current Fire TV television and stick carries 31 December 2030; the first-generation Fire TV Stick 4K carries 31 December 2029. The compliance sheet for the Omni 65 says eight years, which no customer-facing page repeats.

faqs.q: Does Amazon guarantee televisions made by other brands?
faqs.a: No. Amazon's one-year warranty applies to devices Amazon makes. On any other brand the guarantee is the manufacturer's or the seller's and it varies by listing, so check who is named on the set's own guarantee before ordering.

title: Amazon Women's Fashion: Pre-Owned Designer, Marketplace Rules and the Chemistry Small Print
meta_title: Amazon Women's Fashion: Pre-Owned Designer and the Rules
meta_description: Amazon has sold pre-owned designer womenswear since February 2024. What the resale shelf holds, the metal and dye limits it must meet, and the gaps.
intro:
Amazon has sold pre-owned designer womenswear in the UK since 6 February 2024, when Hardly Ever Worn It — a London resale business trading since 2012 and shipping to more than 40 countries — became the first second-hand seller inside Luxury Stores at Amazon, launching in the UK, Germany, Spain and Italy on the same day. Figures here were checked on 28 September 2026 against Amazon's own newsroom, its UK selling fee schedule, Companies House and the government's product safety register.

Everything else is the marketplace: third-party sellers listing new clothing, shoes, bags and jewellery beside Amazon's own retail stock, with free returns on fashion items for 30 days and no minimum spend. On 5 January 2026 Amazon cut the referral fee it charges those sellers on clothing to 5% on anything priced at or under £15, rising to 10% up to £20 and 15% above it — the lowest entry rate in any category it publishes, and the reason a great deal of cheap clothing has arrived on the site.

The rest of this page is the part a product listing does not show: which rules a dress, a pair of earrings or a leather jacket has to satisfy before it can legally be sold at all, what the recall register has stopped at the border this year, and what Amazon does and does not publish about the clothes it marks as sustainable.

key_facts.value: Hardly Ever Worn It, founded 2012, women's ready-to-wear, shoes, accessories, jewellery and watches

key_facts.value: Hardly Ever Worn It UK Ltd, company number 16812843, incorporated 27 October 2025

key_facts.value: Like New, Very Good, Good, Acceptable — up to 50% off recommended retail prices

key_facts.value: 20% of the first £225, then 5% — the highest rate of any fashion category

key_facts.value: 0.5 micrograms per square centimetre per week; 0.2 for piercing posts

sections.heading: Where the second-hand womenswear actually sits
sections.html:
Two routes, and they are not the same thing. The first is Luxury Stores at Amazon, where Hardly Ever Worn It has sold pre-owned designer pieces since 6 February 2024 — women's ready-to-wear, shoes, accessories, jewellery and watches, screened by the partner rather than by Amazon, and launched across four markets at once. Ruth Diaz, then vice-president of Amazon Fashion Europe, announced it alongside the resale company's chief executive, Tatiana Wolter Ferguson. The business itself dates from 2012 and ships to over 40 countries, so the inventory is not new even if the shop window is.

The second is Amazon Resale, which is customer returns sold on at a discount. Amazon grades them Like New, Very Good, Good and Acceptable, prices them at up to 50% off recommended retail, and covers them under the ordinary returns policy rather than a separate clearance rule. Its Second Chance pages, updated 27 August 2025, name apparel explicitly in the list of what can turn up there, alongside electronics, kitchen appliances, office supplies, books and toys.

What does not exist is a route in the other direction. Amazon's own guidance for people selling clothing states plainly that only new clothes may be listed and that used or refurbished clothes cannot be sold, and that apparel must be authentic with permission obtained from the retailer, wholesaler, manufacturer or designer. So the pre-owned shelf is Amazon's own supply chain and one invited partner; nobody else gets to put a worn dress on the site.

sections.heading: Who takes the money for a pre-owned dress
sections.html:
Hardly Ever Worn It UK Ltd sits at Companies House under number 16812843, incorporated on 27 October 2025 with a registered office at 167-169 Great Portland Street, London W1W 5PF and a single trading classification, 47910 — retail sale via mail order houses or via the internet. It is an active company with nothing filed: first accounts are due by 27 July 2027 for a period ending 31 October 2026, and the first confirmation statement by 9 November 2026.

That gap between a brand trading since 2012 and a UK company eleven months old is worth understanding rather than worrying about — group structures get rearranged, and a new entity for a new market is ordinary. But it does mean the usual check a careful buyer makes before a large purchase is unavailable. There are no accounts, no turnover, no balance sheet and no filing history to read, and on a pre-owned designer handbag that can be a three-figure or four-figure decision.

One thing could not be established. Amazon's own shopping pages refuse automated reading, so whether the storefront is still live on the UK site in 2026 could not be checked from a primary source. The announcement is dated and real, the UK company is active on the register, and the rest needs a look at the site or a question to Amazon's customer service.

sections.heading: The chemistry rules behind a £6 pair of earrings
sections.html:
Costume jewellery is where womenswear meets its strictest rulebook. Anything in prolonged contact with skin — necklaces, bracelets, chains, anklets, finger rings, wristwatches and their components — must release less than 0.5 micrograms of nickel per square centimetre per week, and anything inserted into a pierced ear or body part must stay under 0.2. The reference method is BS EN 1811. Lead is prohibited in jewellery at 0.05% or more by weight, and cadmium is capped at 0.01%, which is 100 mg/kg. The official trading standards guidance carrying those figures was last reviewed in April 2024, and local authority Trading Standards enforce them.

Fabric has its own set. Azo colourants that can release listed aromatic amines are limited to 30 mg/kg in dyed textiles and leathers that touch skin, tested to EN ISO 14362-1:2017 for textiles and EN ISO 17234-1:2024 for leather. Chromium VI in finished leather must be under 3 mg/kg, tested to EN ISO 17075-2, which matters on a dyed leather jacket because the dye masks the result under the older method.

Then there is the restriction that swept up everything else. Since 1 November 2020 a single entry has capped 33 substances classed as carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic for reproduction across clothing, footwear, textile accessories and household textiles: formaldehyde at 75 mg/kg, quinoline and three disperse dyes at 50 mg/kg, benzene at 5 mg/kg, eight polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons at 1 mg/kg, the solvents NMP, DMFa and DMAC at 3,000 mg/kg, five phthalates at 1,000 mg/kg, and extractable cadmium, chromium VI, arsenic and lead at 1 mg/kg each. Garments made entirely of natural leather, fur or hide sit outside it, as do medical devices and personal protective equipment. None of this appears anywhere on a listing, which is the point worth taking away: compliance here is a promise made by the seller, not a published figure the shopper can read.

sections.heading: What the register stopped at the border this year
sections.html:
The government's product safety alerts, reports and recalls database is the check a shopper can actually run, and it is free. Searched on 28 September 2026, the keyword nickel returns 33 reports, and the three most recent are all jewellery and all rated serious.

A Bees Jewellery hand chain, bangle and earring set, reference 2601-0411, was published on 3 February 2026: the earrings exceeded the permitted limits for both lead and nickel and the hand chain and bangle exceeded the nickel limit, a breach recorded against the REACH Enforcement Regulations 2008, country of origin India, notified by local authority Trading Standards. The import was rejected at the border and destroyed. A Lost Souls 'S' initial necklace, 2512-0348, was published on 9 January 2026 and also destroyed. A Shop TJC diamond silver bracelet, 2512-0330, was published on 7 January 2026 and rejected at the border.

None of the three names Amazon as the seller, and that is worth saying rather than leaving implied. The register is evidence that the system catches cheap jewellery with too much nickel in it wherever it is sold, and the sensible use of it is as a habit: search the brand name on the register before buying unfamiliar costume jewellery, from any shop.

sections.heading: The green tick on a listing, and who stands behind it
sections.html:
Amazon's sustainability label is Climate Pledge Friendly, which covers over 1.4 million products and leans on more than 50 external certifications rather than any judgement of Amazon's own. For clothing the one that matters is STANDARD 100 by OEKO-TEX, which tests every component of a textile product — thread, buttons and trims included — against harmful chemicals; for leather goods it is the Leather Working Group. Amazon co-founded The Climate Pledge in 2019 and last updated its explainer on 21 April 2025.

The regulator's line on this sits just outside Amazon's door. The Competition and Markets Authority opened an investigation into environmental claims by ASOS, Boohoo and George at Asda on 29 July 2022 and closed it on 27 March 2024 on formal undertakings: published criteria for any named green range, the actual percentage behind an organic or recycled claim, filters that match what the garment is made of, and no natural imagery overstating a benefit. Its sector guidance of 18 September 2024 sets almost no thresholds and offers at least 50% recycled content only as an example of a filter label that works. Amazon was not one of the three firms investigated, and leaning on a third party's certification rather than an in-house claim is the approach the guidance points towards.

What is missing is an outside score. Fashion Revolution's What Fuels Fashion reviewed 250 brands and retailers with turnover above 400 million US dollars against over 70 data points on climate disclosure, producing an average score of 18%, a top score of 75% and 32 brands on zero. Amazon does not appear in it, and no UK consumer body publishes a rated survey of clothing shops, so there is no independent figure to set beside the company's own.

sections.heading: Fees, fakes and the numbers Amazon does publish
sections.html:
The selling costs explain the shape of the range better than any description of it. Clothing pays 5% at or under £15, 10% between £15 and £20 and 15% above, with a 25p minimum, after the cut dated 5 January 2026. Footwear, handbags, rucksacks and luggage pay a flat 15%. Watches pay 15% of the first £225 and 5% above it. Jewellery pays 20% of the first £225 and 5% above — the steepest rate anywhere in fashion, and a reason a small jeweller may price higher here than on its own site. Sellers using Amazon's warehouses also pay monthly storage of £0.62 to £0.76 per cubic foot from January to September, rising to £0.82 to £1.51 from October to December.

On counterfeits, Amazon's Trustworthy Shopping Experience report of 22 April 2026 gives the year to 31 December 2025: 15 million counterfeit products identified, seized and disposed of worldwide; more than 32,000 bad actors pursued through litigation and criminal referrals across 14 countries since the Counterfeit Crimes Unit opened in 2020; over 100 websites shut down; more than 70 raids alongside Chinese law enforcement; and 12 million products analysed through its Omniscan system. Those are real, dated, auditable numbers of a kind most clothing retailers never publish.

They are also group-wide. Not one of them is broken out for apparel, footwear or jewellery, which are the categories a shopper buying a designer-lookalike bag would want them for. The figures say the enforcement machine is large; they do not say how well it works on the shelf this page is about.

sections.heading: The gaps a shopper cannot close from the listing
sections.html:
Three things sit unresolved after a day of reading Amazon's own documents. The seller's compliance with the nickel, azo and 33-substance limits is asserted nowhere the shopper can see, so on marketplace jewellery the practical protection is the returns policy and the recall register rather than anything on the page. There is no independent rating of Amazon as a clothing retailer from any consumer body or transparency index, which is unusual for a company this size and leaves its own reporting unchecked. And the pre-owned shelf, which is the best thing on this page, rests on a single partner whose UK company is eleven months old with no accounts filed.

None of that makes the site a bad place to buy a coat. It does mean the confidence a shopper can take from a listing runs out sooner here than at a retailer that owns its whole supply chain, and that the £6 end of the jewellery range deserves more care than the £600 end.

pros: The only large UK general retailer with a pre-owned designer womenswear shelf built in, rather than a separate app or a marketplace of private sellers.
Returns on clothing, shoes, handbags, jewellery and watches are free for 30 days with no minimum spend, and the prepaid label is paid for by Amazon on anything it sold or dispatched.
The referral fee cut of 5 January 2026 took the rate on sub-£15 clothing down to 5%, which is the cheapest selling rate Amazon publishes and shows up in the price of basics.
Amazon Resale sells graded customer returns at up to 50% off recommended retail prices under the ordinary returns policy, so a reduced item is not a final sale.

Amazon publishes an annual account of its counterfeit enforcement with dated figures — 15 million products removed in 2025 and more than 32,000 sellers pursued since 2020 — which most clothing retailers do not publish at all.
cons: No test evidence is published against a listing. Nothing on a product page shows whether a pair of earrings was tested against the 0.5 microgram nickel release limit or a dress against the 30 mg/kg azo dye limit, and on a marketplace the duty sits with whichever seller shipped it.

There is no independent transparency or customer score for Amazon as a clothing retailer. Fashion Revolution's 250-brand review of climate disclosure does not include it, and no consumer body publishes a rated survey of clothing shops, so there is nothing external to weigh the company's own numbers against.

Second-hand runs one way only. Amazon's own seller guidance states that used or refurbished clothes cannot be sold on the site, so a customer has no route to resell a garment bought here, and the pre-owned shelf depends entirely on one curated partner.

Hardly Ever Worn It UK Ltd was incorporated on 27 October 2025 and its first accounts are not due until 27 July 2027, so a buyer spending several hundred pounds on a pre-owned handbag has no filed financial information to look at.

Whether the Hardly Ever Worn It storefront is still trading on Amazon UK in 2026 could not be confirmed from any Amazon page that can be read automatically; the announcement stands, the UK company is active, but the current position needs confirming directly with Amazon.

The counterfeit figures are group-wide and cover every category. Amazon publishes no apparel, footwear or jewellery breakdown, which are the categories fakes are most often reported in, so the numbers cannot be read as a statement about fashion specifically.
verdict: As a place to buy women's clothes, Amazon is two businesses wearing one logo. One is a curated, authenticated pre-owned designer shelf with a named partner behind it and free 30-day returns; the other is an open marketplace where a 5% referral fee on sub-£15 clothing has drawn in a very large number of very cheap sellers, and where the metal and dye limits that make a garment legal are enforced after the fact by Trading Standards rather than before the fact by the shop. Buy the pre-owned items and the branded stock with confidence; on the £6 jewellery, check the seller's name and keep the receipt, because the 33 results the recall register held for nickel on 28 September 2026 are what enforcement looks like when it works.

faqs.q: Can you buy second-hand clothes on Amazon UK?
faqs.a: Yes, by two routes. Pre-owned designer womenswear is sold inside Luxury Stores at Amazon by Hardly Ever Worn It, live in the UK since 6 February 2024, covering ready-to-wear, shoes, accessories, jewellery and watches. Separately, Amazon Resale sells graded customer returns at up to 50% off recommended retail across categories including apparel. What you cannot do is sell used clothing yourself: Amazon's seller guidance allows only new clothes on the site.

faqs.q: Are returns on Amazon clothing really free?
faqs.a: On fashion items, yes for 30 days with no minimum purchase, covering clothing, shoes, handbags, jewellery and watches. The prepaid label is paid for by Amazon on anything it sold or dispatched itself. Items must go back new and unworn with original packaging, tags and any certificate of authenticity, and resized or altered items are refused.

faqs.q: How do I check whether cheap jewellery is safe?
faqs.a: Search the brand or product name on the government's product safety alerts, reports and recalls register, which is free to use. On 28 September 2026 it held 33 reports under the keyword nickel, including a Bees Jewellery set published 3 February 2026 that exceeded both the lead and nickel limits and was destroyed at the border. The legal limits are 0.5 micrograms of nickel per square centimetre per week for anything worn against skin and 0.2 for piercing posts.

faqs.q: What does Climate Pledge Friendly actually certify?
faqs.a: Nothing on its own. It is a badge Amazon applies to over 1.4 million products that hold one of more than 50 external certifications. For clothing the relevant one is usually STANDARD 100 by OEKO-TEX, which tests every thread, button and trim for harmful chemicals; leather goods may carry Leather Working Group certification instead. The certification is the substance, so it is worth reading which one a garment holds rather than the badge.

title: American Express UK Credit Cards: One 29.1% Rate and Nine Price Tags
meta_title: Amex UK Credit Cards: One 29.1% Rate, Nine Price Tags
meta_description: Nine American Express UK cards share a single 29.1% purchase rate. The fees, the £10,000 cashback crossover and the £700 limit, checked 11 Oct 2026.

headline.label: Representative APR
headline.value: 29.1% to 685.3% variable across nine personal cards, every one quoted on an assumed £1,200 credit limit

intro:
Every one of the nine personal credit cards American Express issues in Britain charges the same 29.1% a year variable on purchases — the no-fee Rewards card, the £195 Preferred Rewards Gold and the £650 Platinum are identical on that one number. Figures re-checked on 11 October 2026 against Amex's own product pages and pre-contract summary boxes. What separates the nine is the fee, and the fee is the whole reason one representative APR reads 29.1% and another reads 685.3%.

American Express Services Europe Limited issues all of them, authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference number 661836, registered in England and Wales as company 1833139 and based at Belgrave House, 76 Buckingham Palace Road in London. Amex is unusual among UK card issuers in running the payment scheme as well as issuing the plastic, so there is no bank behind the brand and no network in front of it — the same company signs up the shop and lends the cardholder the money.

The range is also better documented than most. Each card's summary box prints the simple monthly rate beside the annual one, names the minimum credit limit, states the assumed limit the representative example is built on, and — rarest of all — splits the rate into the margin Amex sets and the Bank Rate it tracks. Where the marketing stays quiet, the paperwork says it anyway: the £3,000 a year of spending the free cashback card needs before it pays anything is in the terms, not the advertising.
