sections.heading: One purchase rate, nine price tags
sections.html:
Read the nine personal cards side by side and the pricing stops looking complicated. Purchases cost 29.1% a year variable on all of them, printed in the summary boxes as a 2.15% simple monthly rate and a 25.81% simple annual rate. Cash costs 36.3%, again on all of them, shown as 2.62% a month. The published representative APRs, every one worked on an assumed £1,200 credit limit, run: 29.1% on the Rewards card, the Cashback Everyday card and the British Airways card, all free; 34.6% on the £25 Cashback card; 42.2% to 44.7% on the Vitality card; 52.5% on the £95 Marriott Bonvoy card; 85.8% on Preferred Rewards Gold at £195 a year; 135.7% on the £300 British Airways Premium Plus; and 685.3% on the £650 Platinum.

Nothing in that ladder is a lending decision. A representative APR folds any compulsory fee into the cost of credit, and on a £1,200 assumed balance a £650 fee is more than half the assumed borrowing, so the percentage detonates. Amex has not hidden this — it prints the assumed limit beside the number on every product page — and the practical reading is the opposite of what the figure suggests: the fee-paying cards are built for someone who clears the balance monthly and wants the benefits, and 685.3% is what a benefits package looks like when the law makes you express it as an interest rate.

The Vitality card is the proof, because it has no cardmembership fee and still cannot reach 29.1%. It is sold only to Vitality policyholders, who pay Vitality between £0 and £6.50 a month for the partner benefits that make the card work, and that payment is compulsory enough to belong in the APR even though Amex never receives it. The summary box, reference 303 87U (T1) of February 2026, assumes the top £6.50 tier and prints 44.7%; the product page assumes £5.50 and prints 42.2%; the pre-contract document says the figure runs from 43.4% down to 29.1% for the cheaper tiers. Three different numbers for one card, none of them wrong, and the card grid does not carry it at all.

The one figure worth arguing with is the £1,200 itself. The Gold, British Airways, Premium Plus, Marriott and Vitality summary boxes all set the minimum credit limit at £700. An applicant approved at the floor carries the same fee against a little over half the assumed balance, so their real cost of credit is higher than the advertised representative figure, not lower.

sections.heading: The 29.1% is Bank Rate plus a margin, and both halves are published
sections.html:
A rate quoted to one decimal place on nine cards looks fixed, and it is not. The pre-contract documents break the 25.81% simple rate into two parts: a Personal Rate, "which may change but is currently 22.06%", and the Bank of England Base Rate, assumed at 3.75% — the level the Bank held it at on 17 September 2026. Add them and you get 25.81%, which compounds to the 29.1% on the advertising. Almost no card issuer shows the reader that join, and it means a Bank Rate decision moves this rate without Amex deciding anything.

The protections round it are published too. The Base Rate portion "will never be less than 0%", a change to it appears on the monthly statement before it takes effect, and a rise in the Personal Rate needs at least 60 days' notice. If the Base Rate stops being published, Amex says it will substitute the closest equivalent it reasonably judges.

The archive on Amex's own servers shows what that structure has done. The pre-contract document for the £25 Cashback card, reference 422 83D of May 2021, prices the same product at 22.2% compound — a 20.19% simple rate made of a 20.09% Personal Rate and an assumed Base Rate of 0.10%. Set that against today's document and the quoted rate has risen 6.9 percentage points in five years. Of the 5.62 points of movement in the simple rate, 3.65 came from Bank Rate and 1.97 came from Amex widening its own margin. A cardholder told only that the rate is variable cannot see that split; the two documents make it arithmetic.

Where a payment does not cover the balance, the order is set out in the same boxes: arrears first, then the monthly instalment amount and instalment fee, then "the remaining amounts you owe at the highest interest rates before amounts charged at lower interest rates", and statemented balances before ones that have not appeared yet. That order works in the cardholder's favour and it is worth knowing before assuming a payment has cleared a cash advance.

sections.heading: What £650 buys, and the date it stops buying it
sections.html:
The Platinum Card is the range's outlier and the one where the arithmetic deserves time. The fee is £650 a year, the minimum income is £35,000, the first supplementary card is free and each one after that costs £285. Against the fee Amex sets the Global Dining Statement Credit, lounge access to "over 1,550 airport lounges across more than 140 countries worldwide" with one guest admitted free, eight lounge pre-booking entitlements a calendar year from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2027, Hertz Gold Plus Rewards at up to 15% off standard rates and up to 25% off the Prestige Collection, status in five hotel programmes from Hilton Honors Gold to ALL Accor Gold, and the Fine Hotels + Resorts and Hotel Collection booking benefits.

The dining credit is the part most often quoted at £400 and it does not arrive that way. It is up to £200 a year for participating UK restaurants and a further £200 abroad, but each £200 is split into £100 for January to June and £100 for July to December, enrolment is required, supplementary cardmembers are excluded, and only the charge for the meal counts — booking fees and deposits do not. Amex also publishes an end date: the benefit "will start on the date you save the benefit to your Card and end on 31 December 2026". A card bought today on the strength of £400 of dining credit has one £100 tranche per territory left to use and a published expiry less than twelve weeks away.

The travel insurance is generous and narrower than it looks. The January 2025 documentation, underwritten by Chubb European Group SE (Financial Services Register number 820988) with Europ Assistance S.A. UK Branch on assistance, carries up to £2,000,000 of medical, surgical and hospital costs, on trips that "must not exceed 90 consecutive days with a maximum 240 days during each 12 month period". The limit the marketing does not lead on is the age one, and it is wider than a reader might assume: Medical Assistance and Expenses benefits are excluded "if aged 70 years or over at any time during the trip" — the whole section, not only claims arising from a pre-existing condition. Those are separately excluded unless they appear on Amex's accepted conditions list.

Gold sits a long way below it and is the more conventional proposition — £195 a year with the first year free, 1 Membership Rewards point per £1 spent, 2 points per £1 with airlines or in a foreign currency, 3 points per £1 booking through Amex Travel, 5,000 bonus points at £10,000 of annual spend up to a 10,000-point ceiling, four Priority Pass visits a year at up to 1,300 lounges, Travel Accident Insurance up to £250,000 and £5 back on Deliveroo twice a month. The first supplementary card comes with the fee; further ones cost £45 a year, or £4 a month on the monthly-fee version of the product. The two British Airways cards hang on one threshold — £15,000 of spending in a membership year releases a Companion Voucher, economy cabins only on the free card and any cabin on the £300 one, with the free card earning 1 Avios per £1 and Premium Plus 1.25. Marriott Bonvoy pays 6 points per £1 at Marriott properties and 2 elsewhere, and its Free Night Award arrives at £25,000 of spending capped at a redemption level of 25,000 points.

sections.heading: The cashback crossover sits at exactly £10,000
sections.html:
Amex sells two cashback cards and the choice between them turns on one number the company never prints. The Cashback Everyday card is free and pays 0.5% on annual spending up to £10,000 and 1% above it. The Cashback card costs £25 a year and pays 0.75% up to £10,000 and 1.25% above. Both drop to 0.5% at warehouse retailers in the United Kingdom, and both measure the tiers over the preceding twelve months rather than the tax year.

Set them against each other and the crossover lands on exactly £10,000 of annual spending: 0.75% of £10,000 is £75, less the £25 fee, leaving £50 — and 0.5% of £10,000 is £50. Spend less and the free card wins; spend more and the paid one pulls ahead, because 1.25% beats 1% with no further fee to recover. At £20,000 of spending the paid card returns £200 and keeps £175 of it after the fee, against £150 on the free card — a £25 difference, which is the fee back and no more.

The introductory offers have changed since this page was last checked, and they have swapped places. The free card now opens at 2% for the first twelve months capped at £200, where it was 5% for five months capped at £125; the £25 card still opens at 5% for three months capped at £125. Both caps bind well before the period ends — £200 at 2% is reached at £10,000 of spending and £125 at 5% at £2,500 — so the free card's offer is now both longer and £75 larger than the card you pay for. Referrals pay at least £30 each on the £25 card and at least £20 on the free one, capped at £150 a calendar year, with £5 for adding the first supplementary card.

Two conditions sit underneath the whole calculation. The free card pays nothing unless annual spending reaches £3,000 — "You must have made purchases on your Card Account of at least £3,000 within the Cardmembership year" — so a light spender earns zero rather than a small amount, and Amex does not say on either page whether that floor also applies to the introductory 2%, which is worth asking before applying. And cashback on both cards is "paid by crediting your Account during each Credit Card anniversary month", once a year, so it is earned up to twelve months before it is usable.

sections.heading: A scheme with no interchange cap behind it
sections.html:
The reason a British shop is likelier to refuse an Amex than a Visa has a regulatory explanation rather than a snobbish one. Visa and Mastercard are four-party schemes: an issuing bank, an acquiring bank, the cardholder and the merchant, with an interchange fee passing between the banks that UK law caps. Amex is a three-party scheme — issuer and acquirer at once — so there is no interchange fee to cap, and the merchant service charge it negotiates sits outside that ceiling.

The Payment Systems Regulator has put a boundary on the exemption and published where it falls. In a statement dated 27 March 2018 the regulator set out that a three-party scheme keeps its exemption only while "the value of an exemptible three party card scheme's annual UK card-based payment transactions must not exceed 3% of the annual value of all card-based payment transactions made in the UK". Amex crossed that line: the regulator found the value of its UK transactions in 2017 exceeded 3% of the market, and the scheme was brought inside the caps from 1 April 2018 until 9 December 2018, except where it operated as a genuine three party scheme under Article 2(18) of the Interchange Fee Regulation. That time-limited arrangement expired on 9 December 2018.

Amex spent the years after that buying its way out of the acceptance problem. Its own acceptance page records more than 150,000 new UK locations added during 2018 alone — 89,000 retail, 37,900 restaurant, 5,400 lodging and 1,000 supermarket sites, "based on American Express merchant locations setup between January 2018 and December 2018". That is a serious piece of work and it is also still the most recent figure the company publishes: there is no current total for UK acceptance anywhere on the site, which leaves a shopper choosing between this card and a Visa without the one statistic that would settle it.

sections.heading: Fifty-six days, £12 and a 3% transfer fee
sections.html:
The charge schedule is short and published in full, which is more than several larger issuers manage. Purchases carry "maximum 56 days on purchases if you pay the full amount you owe on each statement date on time each month". Miss that and interest runs from the transaction date at 29.1%. A late payment costs £12 and a returned payment costs £12. Every transaction in a currency other than sterling carries 2.99% "of the amount after we've converted a transaction into sterling", and no card in the personal range waives it — awkward on a portfolio sold hard on travel, and worth setting against the Gold card's promise of double points on foreign-currency spending.

Cash is the expensive corner: 3% of the amount with a £3 minimum, then 36.3% a year from the day the money is taken, with no interest-free period at all. Transfers are the other one, and they cost twice. Every summary box in the range sets a "balance/money transfer fee 3% of the amount of the transfer" and then charges the transferred balance at the purchase rate of 29.1% from the day it lands, with no promotional window anywhere. Moving £3,000 across costs £90 before a penny of interest, and the interest starts immediately — so the range holds no answer at all for the commonest reason a British consumer applies for a new credit card.

The minimum repayment is the higher of £25 and a sum made up of interest, default fees and any repayment protection insurance on the current statement, one twelfth of any annual cardmembership fee or the full monthly fee where the product has one, any instalment amounts and fees, and 2% of what is left outside those instalment balances. The references to a monthly fee are not boilerplate: several of these cards now exist in a monthly-billed version, which is also why the Gold supplementary card is priced at £45 a year or £4 a month depending on which one you hold.

sections.heading: 439 million transactions, and 47.6% of balances paying interest
sections.html:
Context matters on a card sold to people who intend to clear it. UK Finance counted 439 million credit card transactions in June 2026, 8% more than in June 2025, worth £24.4 billion and 9.2% up on the year, with outstanding balances growing 9.3% over the twelve months. The figure that decides whether an Amex makes sense is the last one in that release, published on 16 September 2026: 47.6% of outstanding balances incurred interest, against 47.8% in June 2025. A little over half of British card balances are cleared in full, and this range is priced for that half and punishing for the other.

On complaints, the FCA's own aggregate data for the second half of 2025 — first published on 28 April 2026 and revised on 15 May — recorded 218,456 credit card complaints across the industry, up 3.1% from 211,903 in the first half, within 857,757 for banking and credit cards as a whole and 1.74 million across financial services. Banking and credit card complaints actually fell 4.7% over the same period, from 899,910, so cards moved against their own sector.

Amex publishes its own timetable for handling one. It aims to resolve a complaint inside three business days, acknowledges within five business days where it cannot, provides an update after fifteen, and says a case can go to the Financial Ombudsman Service where resolution takes more than 35 business days — or up to eight weeks on general insurance and pure protection matters. The referral is free, and the firm's FCA authorisation under reference 661836 is what brings it into the scheme.

sections.heading: Where the published detail stops
sections.html:
Four gaps are worth naming, and one of them is smaller than this page previously reported. Amex does publish a complaints return of its own: the tables sit on its UK complaints page under "How we resolve our complaints", with columns for complaints opened and closed, complaints per 1,000 accounts and the proportion upheld, broken out for credit cards and for general insurance. The problem is the label. The data is described as "relating to the first half of 2018", and the cells themselves returned no readable figures on 11 October 2026. An eight-year-old return with blank tables is a stranger result than no return at all, and every large UK issuer manages a current one.

The second gap is acceptance. The 2018 expansion figures are the newest numbers Amex publishes about where its cards work in Britain, and a current percentage or merchant count would be easy for the company to produce and genuinely useful to a reader weighing a 29.1% card against a cheaper Visa.

The third is independent rating. Defaqto rates insurance rather than credit, so there is no star rating to point at on any UK credit card, and Fairer Finance's American Express brand page returned "Failed to load this content" in place of both its customer experience and its product rating panels on 11 October 2026. Neither absence is Amex's fault, but it leaves a reader with the company's own documents and the regulators' data and very little in between.

The fourth is housekeeping on the documents themselves, and it matters because these are the papers a court would read. The £25 Cashback card's pre-contract information is still served as reference 422 83D of May 2021, quoting 22.2% on purchases and 27.1% on cash against an assumed Bank Rate of 0.10%, while its sister card's equivalent document carries reference 421 883 (T1) of February 2026 and the current 29.1% and 36.3%. The live product page is right. The regulated disclosure beside it is five years out of date, and that is the one document a customer is handed before they sign.

pros: A single 29.1% purchase rate across the whole personal range, so the borrowing cost does not change with the card you pick
Up to 56 days interest-free on purchases where the statement balance is cleared on time
The summary boxes split the rate into a 22.06% Personal Rate and the Bank Rate, so a cardholder can see which half moved and why
Four cards in the range carry no annual cardmembership fee at all, and the £195 Gold card waives its fee for the first year
The free Cashback Everyday card now opens at 2% for twelve months, capped at £200 — a longer and larger introductory offer than the £25 card's £125
Platinum sets up to £200 of UK dining credits and a further £200 abroad against its £650 fee, plus over 1,550 lounges in more than 140 countries and £2,000,000 of medical cover
Both British Airways cards release a Companion Voucher at £15,000 of spending in a membership year, and the Premium Plus voucher is valid in any cabin
Gold pays 2 Membership Rewards points per £1 with airlines or in foreign currency and 3 per £1 through Amex Travel, with four Priority Pass visits a year
Payments are allocated to arrears, then instalments, then to the highest-rate balance first, so a cash advance clears before cheaper purchase debt
The first supplementary card is free on both Gold and Platinum
cons: No 0% balance transfer offer exists anywhere in the range — a transfer costs 3% of the amount up front and then 29.1% from the day it lands, with no interest-free window
The Cashback Everyday card pays nothing at all until annual spending passes £3,000, so a light spender earns zero rather than a small amount
Every representative APR assumes a £1,200 credit limit while the summary boxes set the minimum at £700, so an applicant approved at the floor pays more than the advertised rate
A 2.99% non-sterling transaction fee applies on every card in the range, including the ones sold on foreign travel and foreign-currency points
Cash advances cost 3% with a £3 minimum and then 36.3% a year, running from the day the money is taken
Platinum's Medical Assistance and Expenses cover is excluded outright for anyone aged 70 or over at any point in the trip, not merely for a pre-existing condition
The £400 of Platinum dining credit arrives as four £100 half-year tranches that cannot be carried over, and the benefit is published as ending on 31 December 2026
Cashback is credited once a year in the account's anniversary month rather than monthly, so it is earned long before it can be spent
Welcome bonuses are closed to anyone who has held any personal American Express card in the previous 24 months
One live pre-contract document, Platinum Cashback 422 83D of May 2021, still prices the £25 card at 22.2% on an assumed Bank Rate of 0.10% while the product page says 29.1%
The firm's own complaints return is published for the first half of 2018 and its tables carry no readable figures
The newest UK acceptance figures Amex publishes are its 2018 merchant additions; no current total appears on the site
verdict: American Express prices its UK range on fees rather than on rate, and the 29.1% running through all nine cards is the proof: the distance between a 29.1% representative APR and a 685.3% one is the fee, not the lending. That makes the range a good fit for someone who clears the balance every month and wants dining credits, lounges, Avios or cashback out of spending they were going to do anyway — and a poor one for anyone carrying debt, because there is no 0% transfer offer, no cheap cash and no rate to negotiate down. Work out which half of the market you are in first. If you clear in full, the crossover between the two cashback cards at £10,000 of annual spending is the most useful sum on this page; if you do not, the cheapest card here is still 29.1%, and 3.75 points of that is Bank Rate rather than anything Amex chose.

faqs.q: Why is the Platinum Card's representative APR 685.3% when the interest rate is 29.1%?
faqs.a: A representative APR has to include any compulsory annual fee as part of the cost of credit, and the calculation assumes a £1,200 credit limit. A £650 fee set against £1,200 of assumed borrowing dominates the arithmetic. The rate you actually pay on a balance is 29.1% a year variable, the same as on the free cards.

faqs.q: Does American Express offer a 0% balance transfer card in the UK?
faqs.a: No. The summary boxes across the range charge a transfer fee of 3% of the amount moved and then interest at the purchase rate of 29.1% a year variable from the day the transfer lands, with no promotional period. Anyone moving existing card debt needs a different issuer.

faqs.q: Which Amex cashback card is better value?
faqs.a: It turns on £10,000 of annual spending. Below that the free Cashback Everyday card wins; above it the £25 Cashback card does. At exactly £10,000 they pay the same £50, because 0.75% of £10,000 less the £25 fee equals 0.5% of £10,000. At £20,000 the paid card nets £175 against £150. Remember the free card pays nothing until spending reaches £3,000 a year.

faqs.q: Is the Amex purchase rate fixed at 29.1%?
faqs.a: No. The pre-contract documents show it as a Personal Rate of 22.06% plus the Bank of England Base Rate, assumed at 3.75%, giving a 25.81% simple rate and a 29.1% compound equivalent. Amex has to tell you about a Base Rate change on your statement before it takes effect, and must give at least 60 days' notice before raising the Personal Rate.

faqs.q: Why do fewer UK shops accept American Express?
faqs.a: Amex is a three-party scheme — it issues the card and signs up the merchant itself — so the interchange fee caps that apply to Visa and Mastercard transactions do not bite on it in the same way, and the charge a retailer pays is negotiated rather than capped. The Payment Systems Regulator set the boundary at 3% of the annual value of UK card transactions in its statement of 27 March 2018.

faqs.q: What does Amex charge for spending abroad?
faqs.a: 2.99% of the transaction value after conversion, on every personal card in the range. A cash withdrawal abroad adds the cash advance fee of 3% with a £3 minimum, and interest at 36.3% a year from the day the cash is taken.

faqs.q: What income do I need for an Amex card?
faqs.a: £15,000 a year for the Rewards, Cashback Everyday and British Airways cards, £20,000 for Preferred Rewards Gold, the Cashback card, Marriott Bonvoy and Vitality, and £35,000 for the Platinum Card and the British Airways Premium Plus card. Approval also depends on Amex's credit assessment, and the minimum credit limit it will set is £700.

faqs.q: How do I complain about an American Express card?
faqs.a: Complain to American Express Services Europe Limited first. Its own published timetable is a resolution inside three business days where possible, an acknowledgement within five business days otherwise and an update after fifteen. If the complaint takes more than 35 business days, or eight weeks on an insurance matter, it can be referred free of charge to the Financial Ombudsman Service. The firm is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority under reference number 661836.

title: Anglo Welsh Canal Boat Holidays: Nine Wharves, 2 to 12 Berths and the Small Print
meta_title: Anglo Welsh Canal Boats: Prices, Bases and Small Print
meta_description: Anglo Welsh hires narrowboats for 2 to 12 from nine wharves. Week and short-break prices, the £110 fuel deposit, the £50 waiver and what it leaves out.

headline.label: Typical price for a week's hire
headline.value: From £995 a week for a boat for two (short breaks from £735) — before the £110 fuel deposit and £50 damage waiver

intro:
A self-drive narrowboat holiday with Anglo Welsh starts at £735 for a short break on a two-berth boat and £995 for a full week, and no licence or previous boating is needed because a member of staff walks every crew through the boat before it leaves the wharf. Figures checked on 29 September 2026 against Anglo Welsh's own boat pages and booking terms. For its 2026 season the company cut summer prices by 11%, which it puts at £40 off a boat for two and up to £300 off a boat for ten.

The firm has been hiring canal boats for close to sixty years and now runs nine bases: Bath, Bradford on Avon and Monkton Combe on the Kennet & Avon, Bunbury on the Shropshire Union, Great Haywood on the Trent & Mersey, Silsden on the Leeds & Liverpool, Trevor and Whixall on the Llangollen, and Wootton Wawen on the Stratford Canal. A tenth, at Tardebigge on the Worcester & Birmingham, is due to open for 2027 and takes telephone bookings only. Boats run from compact 48ft two-berths up to Ocean Class boats that sleep ten, and a wide beam at Silsden sleeps eight.

The hire price includes more than some rivals bother to list: parking at the base, bed linen, towels, gas, water, pump-outs, a smokeless log or two for the stove and unlimited Wi-Fi on board, though the company admits the signal rides a mobile network and can be patchy. The first dog travels free. Diesel is the main thing you pay for on top, through a refundable fuel deposit.

sections.heading: Who runs the boats, and from where
sections.html:
Behind the brand is Anglo Welsh Limited, company number 04062985, incorporated on 31 August 2000 as Aquatravel Limited and renamed on 26 October 2007. It is registered in Bath and classed at Companies House under SIC 55209, other holiday and collective accommodation. The hire business itself is much older than the company number — the 2021 brochure already spoke of more than 55 years of experience.

Ownership has sat inside the same Bath office for several years. Chatleigh Limited became the controlling shareholder in March 2020, Anglo Welsh (Holdings) Limited took over in December 2021, and since 3 February 2026 the person with significant control is SG Aerospace (UK) Limited, a company incorporated in 1972 and registered at the same Oldfield Road address. Nothing about that reshuffle changes who a customer books with or rings.

The network has grown rather than shrunk. In April 2024 Anglo Welsh took over Sally Narrowboats at Bradford on Avon Marina and put three new Ocean Class boats built at Silsden onto that stretch of the Kennet & Avon. Two more Ocean boats join the Trevor and Wootton Wawen fleets for 2026, and the selected-boats list now names five: Aurora, Mirabella, Phoenix, Selene and Vanora. Day boats run from six bases, and Trevor also operates the 48-seat trip boat Seren Fach across the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct, with 2026 tickets held at £10 for adults and £6 for children.

sections.heading: What £735 and £995 buy, and the three charges added on top
sections.html:
Anglo Welsh prints a single starting price on each boat page and leaves the date-by-date figure to its online availability search. Chertsey 2, a 48ft two-berth at Bunbury, shows from £735. The Admiral 2 boats at Trevor and Wootton Wawen and the four-berth Village class both show from £835, the eight-berth Firefly at Great Haywood and Butterfly at Bunbury from £1,080, and the ten-berth Ocean class from £1,450. The boat pages do not say how many nights those figures buy; the Trevor base's listing on North Wales Tourism's site gives £735 as the short-break price for two and £995 as the weekly one, and the weekly figure for 2026 should be confirmed on the booking screen before you rely on it.

Three things are added to the hire price. A fuel deposit of £110 for a week or longer, or £70 for a short break, is payable up front — the terms say eight weeks before departure, the pricing page says at booking; the boat leaves with a full tank, is refilled on return and the difference is charged or refunded. A damage waiver of £50 is compulsory and never returned. And pets beyond the first cost £25 each on a short break or £35 each on a week, up to three animals.

Money moves in two stages. A 25% deposit secures the boat and the balance is due eight weeks before the start date, or at once if you book inside that window. Pay late and the terms allow interest at 4% a year over Bank of England base rate. Holidays run for three, four, seven, ten, eleven or fourteen nights, and each length can only start on set weekdays — most seven-night routes leave on a Monday, Tuesday, Friday or Saturday.

sections.heading: Stacking the discounts: loyalty, second weeks and early 2027 bookings
sections.html:
The regular offers are generous for returning crews. The loyalty bonus climbs from 2% (capped at £40) after one holiday to 10% (capped at £190) after five years, and it sits on top of most other offers. Rebook within 14 days of getting home and the next holiday is 20% off, though that one cannot be combined with anything. A second consecutive week is half price on bookings of two weeks or more, except for the week of 22 to 29 May 2026, and 10- or 11-night holidays between 13 March and 1 November 2026 carry 20% off the brochure price.

Groups taking two or more boats from the same base on the same day get 10% off every boat after the first. Members of the British Armed Forces get 15% and Blue Light Card holders 10%, neither combinable with other offers. For 2027, week-long holidays booked by 31 January 2027 earn £25 off for every crew member under 12 or over 60, up to 10% of the basic price. Anglo Welsh also runs a price promise: find the same size and standard of boat for the same dates cheaper elsewhere and it says it will match it.

sections.heading: Routes measured in locks and hours, not miles
sections.html:
Canal holidays are planned by cruising time, and Anglo Welsh publishes it for each route. From Bradford on Avon, the run to Bath and back is 18 miles through 2 locks in about 7 hours — an easy first short break. From Great Haywood, Fradley Junction and back is roughly 12 hours through 10 locks. At the other end of the scale, Wootton Wawen to Warwick and back covers 28 miles and 76 locks in about 23 hours, and Monkton Combe to Pewsey Wharf takes around 44 hours through 74 locks, which is a full week of hard work at the paddles.

Those times assume the canal speed limit, which the Canal & River Trust sets at 4mph on narrow canals, and daylight only: Anglo Welsh's terms forbid moving the boat between sunset and sunrise and bar it from sea and tidal water altogether. The hirer has to be at least 18 when booking, and at least two adults of 18 or over must be aboard whenever the boat is under way, so a parent with young children cannot take a boat out alone.

sections.heading: The Llangollen breach and the two bases beside it
sections.html:
In December 2025 the Llangollen Canal breached near Whitchurch in Shropshire. The Canal & River Trust has closed the canal and towpath between Bridge 31A at the Whitchurch bypass and Lock 6 at Grindley Brook, and its six-month update on 22 June 2026 said it aimed to reopen by the end of the year, and its breach page puts the repair at several million pounds. About 40 million litres a day are being pumped around the site to keep water flowing downstream.

For Anglo Welsh's Trevor and Whixall bases that means about 30 miles of the canal remain open, including the whole 11-mile World Heritage stretch and the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct, plus 8 navigable miles of the Montgomery Canal from Frankton Junction to Crickheath. What is lost is anything that needs to pass Whitchurch, including the week-long Trevor-to-Whitchurch route, so check that a Llangollen itinerary does not depend on the closed length before paying the balance.

sections.heading: The clause about lock cills, and the other limits in the hire agreement
sections.html:
The £50 damage waiver is narrower than its name suggests. The terms exclude "damage arising from speeding, contact with a lock cill causing damage to the rudder, skeg, stern gear or boat, negligence, malicious or intentional damage", and leave the hirer responsible for any loss caused by breach of the agreement or by negligence. The cill is the stone step at the top end of a lock chamber, and the Canal & River Trust's Boater's Handbook warns that it can stick out by up to 5ft (1.5m) and only becomes visible as the lock empties. A stern caught on it is exactly the kind of damage these terms leave as the crew's bill rather than the waiver's.

Two other clauses are worth reading before booking. Anglo Welsh may ask for a pre-authorised deposit of £1,000 per boat, and its own boat pages say this is aimed at larger celebration parties. And if a boat cannot be provided and no substitute is available, the company may end the agreement, refund what has been paid and "have no further liability"; its total liability in any case is capped at the price you paid. The company's insurance does not cover personal accident or your belongings, so travel or home insurance needs to pick those up.

sections.heading: Cancelling, complaining and what stands behind the payment
sections.html:
Cancellation charges are a percentage of the hire price and climb steeply: 25% if you cancel 56 or more days out, 50% between 43 and 56 days, 70% between 29 and 42 days, 80% between 8 and 28 days and 90% inside a week. The deposit and any insurance bought are not refundable in any band, so a 25% deposit is effectively lost the moment it is paid. Cancellation insurance, bought separately, is what covers a cancellation forced by illness or a family emergency.

Complaints must reach Anglo Welsh by post or email within 30 days of the end date of the holiday, and the agreement is under English law with English courts. The terms carry no ABTA, ATOL or package-travel protection statement, so paying by credit card is the simplest safeguard if the firm cannot deliver. No Which?, Defaqto or Fairer Finance assessment of Anglo Welsh or of canal boat hire generally was found, and the North Wales Tourism listing shows no Visit Wales grading.

sections.heading: Where Anglo Welsh's own pages disagree with each other
sections.html:
The company's website is less consistent than its boats. The home page and contact page list nine bases, and the home page and a fleet page count 150 narrowboats; the 2026 brochure announcement says ten bases and 140 boats, the tenth being Tardebigge, which does not open until 2027. The home page claims nearly 60 years of experience while another fleet page says over 55. The 2026 announcement describes the new Ocean Class boats as 60ft; the Ocean Class page calls them 69ft.

The pricing page still carries the 2024 price charts and a promise of 10% off for Blue Badge holders, while the current offers page gives the 10% to Blue Light Card holders instead. A 2025 article offered 2026 holidays for a £150 deposit, against the 25% stated on every boat page. None of these is serious on its own, but together they mean the booking screen and the written confirmation, not the marketing pages, are what to rely on.

pros: No licence or experience needed, with a full handover demonstration and buoyancy aids at the base
Parking, linen, towels, gas, water, pump-outs and Wi-Fi are all in the price
Nine bases on six different canals, from Bath to the Llangollen and the Leeds & Liverpool
Boats for two to twelve, including new Ocean Class boats for up to ten
11% off 2026 summer prices, half-price second weeks and a loyalty bonus worth up to £190
First pet free, with dog-friendly boats in the fleet
Route guides give locks, miles and cruising hours for each itinerary
cons: The £50 damage waiver excludes lock-cill damage, speeding and negligence, so the costliest mishaps in a lock stay with the hirer
Cancellation costs at least 25% of the hire price however early you cancel, and 90% inside seven days
The company's total liability is capped at the price paid, and a boat that cannot be supplied ends the contract with a refund only
Date-specific 2026 prices sit behind the booking engine, and the pricing page still shows 2024 charts
The terms carry no ABTA, ATOL or package-travel protection statement
Complaints must be lodged within 30 days of the holiday ending
The Llangollen Canal is closed at Whitchurch after the December 2025 breach, cutting routes from Trevor and Whixall
verdict: Anglo Welsh is one of the easiest ways onto the English and Welsh canals: nine bases, boats from two to twelve berths, a short break from £735 and a week from £995 for two, with parking, linen and Wi-Fi included and an 11% cut to 2026 summer prices. Budget £110 for fuel and £50 for the waiver, read the lock-cill exclusion before your first flight of locks, and treat the booking confirmation rather than the website as the final word on price and boat. For a first canal holiday, a short run from Bradford on Avon or Great Haywood is a gentle place to start.

faqs.q: How much does an Anglo Welsh canal boat holiday cost?
faqs.a: Starting prices are £735 for a short break and £995 for a week on a boat for two. Larger boats start higher: £835 for four-berth Village class boats, £1,080 for eight-berth boats and £1,450 for the ten-berth Ocean class. Add a £110 fuel deposit for a week (£70 for a short break) and the £50 damage waiver.

faqs.q: Do I need a licence or boating experience?
faqs.a: No. A member of the base team demonstrates the boat before you leave. You must be 18 or over to book, and two adults aged 18 or over must be aboard whenever the boat is moving.

faqs.q: What does the £50 damage waiver cover?
faqs.a: Accidental damage, but not damage caused by speeding, by the boat catching a lock cill, by negligence or by deliberate acts. The waiver is compulsory and non-refundable.

faqs.q: Can I take my dog?
faqs.a: Yes, on pet-friendly boats. Up to three pets are allowed; the first is free and the second and third cost £25 each for a short break or £35 each for a week.

faqs.q: What happens if I cancel?
faqs.a: You pay a share of the hire price: 25% at 56 days or more, then 50%, 70%, 80% and finally 90% inside seven days. The booking deposit is not refundable.

faqs.q: Is the Llangollen Canal open for Anglo Welsh holidays from Trevor and Whixall?
faqs.a: Mostly. Since the December 2025 breach the canal is closed between the Whitchurch bypass bridge and Grindley Brook Lock 6, but about 30 miles stay open, including the 11-mile World Heritage section over Pontcysyllte Aqueduct. The Canal & River Trust aimed in June 2026 to reopen by the end of the year.

title: APH Airport Parking Review
meta_title: APH Parking Review: Prices, Which? Score, Free Cancellation
meta_description: APH has parked cars since 1980 and scored 80% with Which? in March 2026. Gatwick park and ride from £7.49 a day, plus the cancellation tiers to read first.

headline.label: Cheapest park and ride
headline.value: £7.49 a day at Gatwick · £6.17 at Heathrow (APH's own advertised floors)

intro:
APH advertises Gatwick park and ride from £7.49 a day and Heathrow parking from £6.17, and its own Gatwick results page returned a cheapest park and ride of £93.89 for seven nights — £13.41 a day — when searched on 15 September 2026. Both figures come from APH's own airport pages on that date.

APH stands for Airport Parking and Hotels, and it has been doing exactly that since 1980. It owns and staffs its own car parks rather than only reselling other people's: around 7,000 spaces in total, roughly 300,000 cars a year, and a comparison table of more than 150 car parks, hotels and lounges for the airports where it does not. It is still a family firm, registered in Copthorne, West Sussex, and it has taken the British Travel Award for airport parking in each of the last 15 years.

The award that matters more is the independent one. In research published after fieldwork in March 2026, Which? made APH a Recommended Provider for park and ride with a customer score of 80%, ahead of every Gatwick and Manchester operator it tested bar one. There is no booking fee and no card charge on top of the quoted price.

key_facts.label: Company
key_facts.value: Airport Parking and Hotels Limited, registered in England and Wales, 01539777

key_facts.label: Trading since
key_facts.value: Incorporated 19 January 1981 as Airport Parking (Gatwick) Limited; renamed 26 April 1996

key_facts.label: Owner
key_facts.value: Crawley Down Holdings Limited (07123465) holds 75% or more, notified 1 July 2016

key_facts.label: Own car parks
key_facts.value: Gatwick, Manchester and Cardiff; around 7,000 spaces

key_facts.label: Independent rating
key_facts.value: Which? Recommended Provider, park and ride, customer score 80% (March 2026)

key_facts.label: Security award
key_facts.value: Park Mark Plus at Gatwick (June 2023) and at Manchester; renamed Safer Parking Plus from 1 April 2026

key_facts.label: Trade body
key_facts.value: Independent Airport Parking Association, one of 14 members

key_facts.label: Booking fee
key_facts.value: None advertised; APH states “no hidden fees or booking charges”

key_facts.label: Complaints
key_facts.value: Acknowledged within 5 working days, written decision aimed at within 30 days; no ombudsman covers parking

sections.heading: A family firm that still answers to a family
sections.html:
Airport Parking and Hotels Limited was incorporated on 19 January 1981 under the name Airport Parking (Gatwick) Limited, and took its present name on 26 April 1996. The marketing says 1980, which is a year earlier than the register; the gap is the kind of thing that usually separates the start of trading from the date the paperwork was filed, and it is worth nothing more than a footnote.

Ownership runs through Crawley Down Holdings Limited (07123465), which has held 75% or more of the shares and voting rights, plus the right to appoint and remove directors, since 1 July 2016. Both companies sit at APH House, Snow Hill, Copthorne, Crawley RH10 3EQ — the same address the car park operates from.

The register also records a handover. Frederick James Caunter and Harry Nicholas Caunter were appointed directors on 25 June 2025, and Bertram George Voller and John William Voller ceased to be directors on 27 August 2025, with Frederick Caunter also taking over as company secretary. Nick Caunter, the managing director quoted when the Gatwick site won its security award in June 2023, remains in place. Accounts to 31 December 2024 were filed on 28 August 2025 and the next set is due by 30 September 2026; the filed accounts themselves could not be opened during this check, so no turnover or profit figure is quoted here.

Why any of this matters: almost every other name on APH's own results pages belongs to a group, a platform or a private-equity roll-up. An operator whose owner, directors and car park share one postcode is a genuinely different proposition, and it is checkable in about four minutes on the public register.

sections.heading: The 80% score, and who it beat
sections.html:
Which? surveyed 5,030 people about 8,121 separate parking experiences at Birmingham, Gatwick, Heathrow, Luton, Manchester, Stansted and other large UK airports, with fieldwork in March 2026. Four park and ride operators came out as Recommended Providers: Sentinel at Leeds Bradford on 86%, APH on 80%, Secure Airparks on 76%, and Cophall and Maple at Gatwick on 75%.

Two things follow that APH does not say out loud. The first is that its 80% is second of four, not first — a small regional operator at Leeds Bradford scored six points higher. The second is more useful to a reader choosing between the pages on this site: in the meet and greet half of the same research, Maple took 76% and Purple Parking 75%, and APH's own valet product does not appear among the recommended names at all. The park and ride is the rated product. The forecourt service is not.

The lowest scores in the study went to airport-operated car parks rather than independents, with Belfast International's long stay at 61%. That is the finding APH's marketing leans on hardest, and on this evidence it is fair: the airport's own car park is not automatically the safe choice.

sections.heading: What £7.49 a day becomes once you put dates in
sections.html:
APH's Gatwick page carries the line “Park from just £7.49 per day”; the Heathrow page says £6.17. Those are floors reached by booking many months out, and the distance between them and a real search is the single most useful number on this page.

Searched on 15 September 2026 for seven nights, APH's Gatwick results ran: Cophall Parking £93.89, APH's own Park and Ride £103.92, Airparks Park & Ride £103.92, Bubble Park & Deliver £105.50, Bubble meet and greet £126.00, Ace £128.00, I Love £130.00 and APH's own Meet & Greet Forecourt £135.75. The cheapest park and ride was therefore £13.41 a day, not £7.49, and it was not APH's.

Manchester tells the same story more sharply. APH's own Park and Ride there was £134.95 for the week and its Self Park £199.95, while Maple Park & Ride on the same page was £70.49 — a little over half the price, for a 20 to 25 minute transfer against APH's 10. At Heathrow, where APH owns nothing, its meet and greet was £137.90 against Edward Lloyd at £110.00 and Maple Express park and ride at £119.95.

An operator that lists a rival above its own product, on its own booking page, at its own airport, has given away the easiest sale it has. That is the strongest argument for using the site, and it costs nothing to verify: put your dates in and see which name is at the top.

Gatwick's own APH site is a 10 to 12 minute bus ride from either terminal, with buses every 10 to 15 minutes round the clock, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, more than 120 camera positions, barrier entry and floodlighting. It was the first airport park and ride in the UK to be given the Park Mark Plus security award, in June 2023, and Manchester has the same award; the scheme was renamed Safer Parking Plus on 1 April 2026 when the police-backed body took it over.

sections.heading: One banner, four sets of cancellation rules
sections.html:
The Gatwick landing page is titled “Free Cancellation” and says “free cancellation up to 24 hours before departure”. The booking conditions describe four different products, and only one of them behaves like that.

Non-Flexible bookings cannot be cancelled or amended at all and no money comes back. Semi-Flexible must be cancelled a stated number of days ahead. Flexible must be cancelled “24 hours before 00:01 on the booked arrival date”. Super-Flexible can be cancelled at any time up to the booked arrival time, which is what the APH Gatwick car park page describes.

The Flexible wording is the one to read twice. Because the clock runs from one minute past midnight on the day you arrive rather than from your arrival, a car booked in for 22:00 on a Friday has to be cancelled by 00:01 on the Thursday — 46 hours before the barrier, not 24. Read as “24 hours before departure”, as the banner puts it, a traveller would miss that deadline by most of two days and pay the full booking.

Three further terms sit alongside. Chargeable services begin 30 minutes before the booked arrival time, so a refund inside the window is of everything except those. Coming home early earns nothing back: there is no partial refund for collecting the car sooner than booked. And an amendment that changes the price is processed as a fresh booking with the original refunded, so the new price is whatever the site is charging that day.

The genuine good news is that none of this carries a fee. APH publishes no amendment charge and no booking charge, and no card surcharge appeared in the conditions. In a trade where a non-refundable card fee is close to standard, an operator that does not levy one deserves to be told so plainly.

sections.heading: What the company will not pay for once it has your keys
sections.html:
At the three car parks APH runs itself, it accepts responsibility for death or personal injury caused by its negligence, and for damage to paint and bodywork caused by its negligence where that damage is not already recorded on the inspection report. Everything else is carved out: minor scratches, dents and chips to paintwork; glass and windscreens unless negligence is proved; theft, vandalism, mechanical failure, terrorism and natural disaster; personal property left in the car or on the transfer bus; and indirect losses such as lost earnings.

Two conditions sit on the driver rather than the company, and both can be missed. The car must hold a current MOT certificate valid for the whole parking period, and vehicle excise duty must be paid for the whole period too — so a trip that straddles an MOT expiry date is a breach of the contract you have just signed. Keys are left with the car park unless Self Park is booked, steering wheel locks and other manual security devices are not allowed, and house keys must come off the ring.

Damage has to be reported before you drive off the site, and APH must be allowed to inspect before any repair. That is a normal enough condition, but it is paired with one that is not: a Vehicle Inspection Report recording the marks already on the car, which is the document the exclusion above turns on, costs £5. Charging for the evidence that decides a later claim sits awkwardly beside “no hidden fees”, even at that price.

Height limits differ by product and are easy to trip over. The Gatwick park and ride takes vehicles up to 2.4 metres and no trailers; the Gatwick meet and greet takes 2 metres, or six feet six inches. A roof box or a tall van can be fine for one product and refused at the other, at the same airport, on the same booking.

sections.heading: Principal at three airports, booking agent at everywhere else
sections.html:
The conditions split cleanly in two, and the split decides who a complaint goes to. At the car parks APH owns and operates — named in the terms as Gatwick, Manchester and Cardiff — APH is the principal: its staff take the keys, its contract governs, and its liability wording applies. Everywhere else, including every Heathrow product and the hotels and lounges, “APH acts as a booking agent for the relevant service provider and does not operate”, its own liability runs only to negligence in processing the booking, and claims must go “directly to the relevant service provider”, whose contact details APH supplies on request while stating it cannot guarantee the outcome.

Vehicles at those third-party sites are parked at the owner's risk, and the operator accepts no responsibility for theft, loss or damage unless negligence is proved. In practice a customer who books a Heathrow meet and greet through APH and finds a dent has bought from APH and must claim from a company they have never dealt with.

One detail could not be settled and should be checked before booking in Wales. The terms list Cardiff among APH's own car parks, while APH's Cardiff page describes the site as operated through its partner network. Those two statements are both APH's and they point at different contracts. Ask which applies before you hand over keys there.

sections.heading: The trade body registered at APH's own address
sections.html:
Airport parking has no financial regulator, no ombudsman and no statutory compensation scheme. What stands in their place is the Independent Airport Parking Association, which has 14 member companies and a ten-point code of conduct. Members must use land authorised for airport parking, run courtesy transport with qualified drivers, have transport “normally available within 20 minutes” of arrival and customs clearance, keep insurance and fire precautions, and hold a clear procedure for complaints, cancellations and refunds, with the limits of their liability given to the customer in writing at or shortly after booking.

That twenty-minute figure is the only hard number in the code, and APH clears it comfortably: 10 to 12 minutes at Gatwick, 10 at Manchester, 5 to 7 at Cardiff. The rest of the code asks members to have procedures rather than to meet standards, and there is no external audit, no assessor and no published sanction behind it.

There is also an awkwardness worth stating. The association's contact address is given as care of APH, Snow Hill, Copthorne, West Sussex RH10 3EQ — the member's own building. A trade body run from one member's offices is common enough in small industries, and it is not evidence of anything improper, but it does mean the code should be read as an industry undertaking rather than as independent oversight.

APH's own complaints procedure is published and dated, which is more than several of its rivals manage: receipt acknowledged within five working days, a written decision aimed at within 30 days, and a phone line on 01342 645062. After that the route is the county court, under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 duty to carry out a service with reasonable care and skill and the old law of bailment that applies from the moment a member of staff takes the keys. No ombudsman will look at it and no scheme will pay if the operator fails.

pros: Owns and staffs its own car parks at Gatwick, Manchester and Cardiff rather than only reselling, with around 7,000 spaces and roughly 300,000 cars a year
Which? Recommended Provider for park and ride with a customer score of 80%, from research covering 8,121 parking experiences with fieldwork in March 2026
No booking fee, no card charge and no amendment fee anywhere in the published conditions
Gatwick was the first airport park and ride in the UK to be awarded Park Mark Plus, in June 2023, and Manchester holds the same award
Transfers of 10 to 12 minutes at Gatwick with buses every 10 to 15 minutes, 24 hours a day, against the trade code's 20-minute standard
Lists competitors above its own car parks on its own results pages, including Cophall at £93.89 against APH's £103.92 at Gatwick
Independent and family-owned since 1980, with ownership and directors visible on the public register
A Super-Flexible fare exists that can be cancelled at any time up to the booked arrival
cons: The “free cancellation up to 24 hours before departure” banner covers four different fare types, one of which cannot be cancelled or refunded at all
Flexible bookings run their 24 hours from 00:01 on the arrival date, so a 22:00 arrival must be cancelled 46 hours ahead, not 24
The advertised £7.49 a day at Gatwick was more than 40% below the cheapest park and ride actually returned by its own search on 15 September 2026
APH's own car park was not the cheapest at Gatwick and cost nearly twice Maple's price at Manchester
The Vehicle Inspection Report that records pre-existing damage, and on which the paintwork exclusion turns, costs £5
Minor scratches, dents, chips, glass, theft, vandalism and anything left inside the car are all excluded, and damage must be reported before leaving the site
Drivers must hold a valid MOT and paid vehicle excise duty for the whole parking period, which is easy to miss on a long trip
At every airport other than Gatwick, Manchester and Cardiff, APH is a booking agent and claims must be taken up with an operator the customer never dealt with
The terms list Cardiff as an APH-operated car park while APH's Cardiff page calls it a partner site
No ombudsman, no compensation scheme and no external audit behind the trade code, whose association is registered at APH's own address
The Which? recommendation covers park and ride only; APH's meet and greet is not among the recommended names
verdict: APH is the most straightforward proposition in UK airport parking: a family-owned operator that has been doing this since 1980, owns the car parks it sells at Gatwick, Manchester and Cardiff, charges no booking or amendment fee, and holds the only independent rating in the trade that is worth anything — a Which? Recommended Provider score of 80% for park and ride, from March 2026 fieldwork across 8,121 journeys. It also ranks rivals above its own car parks on its own booking pages, which is the single best reason to trust the results it shows you. The care needed is on two things. Check which of the four fare types you are buying, because the “free cancellation” banner covers one that cannot be cancelled at all and another whose deadline runs from midnight on the arrival date rather than from your arrival. And treat the £7.49 a day headline as a booking-far-ahead price: on real dates the cheapest park and ride at Gatwick was £13.41 a day, and it belonged to Cophall.

faqs.q: Does APH own the car parks it sells?
faqs.a: Some of them. APH owns and staffs its own car parks at Gatwick, Manchester and Cardiff, and at those three its booking conditions apply directly. At every other airport, including Heathrow, it is acting as a booking agent for another operator, whose own terms govern the parking and to whom any claim must be made.

faqs.q: Is APH parking really free to cancel?
faqs.a: It depends which fare you bought. Super-Flexible can be cancelled up to the booked arrival time and Flexible up to 24 hours before 00:01 on the arrival date, but Semi-Flexible has a fixed number of days' notice and Non-Flexible cannot be cancelled or amended at all. There is no cancellation fee as such; the charge for missing the deadline is the whole booking. Coming home early is never refunded.

faqs.q: How much does APH cost at Gatwick?
faqs.a: APH advertises Gatwick parking from £7.49 a day, which needs booking months ahead. A seven-night search made on 15 September 2026 returned £93.89 for Cophall, £103.92 for APH's own Park and Ride and £135.75 for APH Meet & Greet Forecourt, so the cheapest park and ride worked out at £13.41 a day.

faqs.q: Is APH secure?
faqs.a: The Gatwick car park was the first airport park and ride in the UK to be awarded Park Mark Plus, in June 2023, and Manchester holds it as well; the scheme was renamed Safer Parking Plus on 1 April 2026. Gatwick has more than 120 camera positions, barrier-controlled entry, floodlighting and staff on site. APH still excludes theft, vandalism, minor scratches, dents, chips, glass and anything left inside the car from its own liability, so your motor insurance remains the cover that matters.

faqs.q: What happens if my car is damaged?
faqs.a: At an APH-run car park you must report it before you drive off the site and let APH inspect before any repair. APH accepts liability for paint and bodywork damage caused by its negligence where the mark is not already on the inspection report, which is a document that costs £5. Complaints are acknowledged within five working days with a written decision aimed at within 30 days. There is no ombudsman for airport parking, so an unresolved claim ends in the county court.

faqs.q: Who owns APH?
faqs.a: Airport Parking and Hotels Limited, company number 01539777, is controlled by Crawley Down Holdings Limited (07123465), which has held 75% or more of the shares and votes since 1 July 2016. Both are at APH House, Snow Hill, Copthorne, Crawley RH10 3EQ. Two Caunter family directors were appointed on 25 June 2025 and the two Voller directors stepped down on 27 August 2025.

title: Apple Watch: What £219 to £900 Buys, and Which Health Features Apple Stands Behind
meta_title: Apple Watch from £219: Prices, Cover and Health Claims
meta_description: Apple Watch runs £219 to £900 in the UK: the one-year guarantee, AppleCare+ at a £49 excess and which sensors a regulator has seen. Checked 29 Sept 2026.
intro:
Apple Watch starts at £219 for the SE 3 and runs to £369 for the Series 12, £650 for the Ultra 4 and £900 for the Hermès Ultra 4. Those are Apple's own UK store prices, read on 29 September 2026, and they are the same whichever shop you buy from, because Apple sets them.

What the money buys is unusually well documented. Apple publishes tech specs down to the glass — Ceramic Shield 2 on the Series 12, which Apple says is 60 per cent tougher than the Ion-X it replaced, a 2,000-nit display, 64GB of storage, 50-metre water resistance to ISO 22810:2010 and an IP6X dust rating. It publishes battery behaviour: up to 24 hours of everyday use on the Series 12, up to 50 hours on the Ultra 4 and up to 84 hours with that watch in Low Power Mode, and a battery designed to hold 80 per cent of its original capacity after 1,000 complete charge cycles. And for the health features that a regulator has actually looked at, it publishes the trial that got them there — which almost nothing else on a wrist does.

One rule decides whether any of it is relevant to you. An Apple Watch cannot be set up without an iPhone: Apple's own specifications for the Series 12, the Ultra 4 and the SE 3 all require an iPhone 11 or later, or an iPhone SE from the second generation onwards, running iOS 27. There is no Android app and no standalone mode. A £369 watch paired to a Pixel is a paperweight.

headline.label: Guarantee behind the device
headline.value: 1 year of hardware cover from Apple — extendable to 24 months with AppleCare+ for Apple Watch, which charges a £49 excess per accidental-damage repair and replaces the battery once it falls below 80% of its original capacity (checked 29 September 2026)

key_facts.label: Price ladder
key_facts.value: SE 3 £219, Series 12 £369, Ultra 4 £650, Hermès Series 12 £850, Hermès Ultra 4 £900

key_facts.label: Standard hardware guarantee
key_facts.value: 1 year, on top of your Consumer Rights Act 2015 rights against the retailer

key_facts.label: AppleCare+ term and excess
key_facts.value: 24 months (36 for Hermès and Edition); £49 per accidental-damage repair, £55 on Hermès and Edition

key_facts.label: Theft and loss cover
key_facts.value: £89 excess, up to 2 claims in any 12 months, underwritten by AIG

key_facts.label: Who carries the insurance risk
key_facts.value: American International Group UK Limited, FCA firm reference 781109 — not Apple

key_facts.label: Sleep apnoea notification accuracy
key_facts.value: 66.3% sensitivity and 98.5% specificity in a 1,499-person study (Apple's UK instructions for use)

key_facts.label: Blood Oxygen and wrist temperature
key_facts.value: Apple labels both “not for medical use” in its own tech specs footnotes

key_facts.value: 80% of original capacity at 1,000 complete charge cycles

key_facts.label: Return window
key_facts.value: 14 calendar days from delivery, from Apple Retail UK Limited (company number 04996702)
