sections.heading: Three watches, £431 apart
sections.html:
The range splits cleanly. The SE 3 at £219 is the cheap way in: a 1,000-nit display, up to 18 hours of normal use and 32 hours in Low Power Mode, seven hours of outdoor workout, 64GB of storage and 50-metre water resistance. Apple's own comparison table marks two things as not applicable on it — the ECG app and the Blood Oxygen app — while listing heart rate tracking, heart rate variability, high and low heart rate notifications, irregular rhythm notifications, sleep score and sleep apnoea notifications as present.

The Series 12 at £369 adds the electrical heart sensor, a third-generation one, plus a blood oxygen sensor, a depth gauge good to six metres and a water temperature sensor. Apple puts it in 42mm and 46mm cases, on an S11 chip, with a peak brightness of 2,000 nits and 24 hours of everyday battery. Fifteen minutes on the charger now returns up to 12 hours of use, which Apple says is 50 per cent more than the model before it, and outdoor workout life is up 25 per cent to ten hours.

The Ultra 4 at £650 is a different proposition again: 50 hours of normal use, 84 hours in Low Power Mode, 45 hours in Max Extended Workout mode, a 3,000-nit display, 100-metre water resistance and certification to EN13319 for recreational scuba to 40 metres. It weighs 63.0 grams in natural titanium and Apple rates it for operation between 0°C and 35°C off the wrist, widening to −20°C to 55°C on it. The Hermès versions — £850 on the Series 12 case, £900 on the Ultra 4 — are the same watches with different straps and a dial.

sections.heading: The sensors a regulator has seen, and the ones Apple disclaims
sections.html:
This is the useful distinction on any wrist device, and Apple is one of the few makers where you can settle it from the manufacturer's own paperwork rather than guessing.

Some features go through a medical device route. Sleep apnoea notifications have a formal instructions-for-use document, published in British English on Apple's regulatory portal, which describes the feature as analysing sensor data “to identify patterns of breathing disturbances suggestive of moderate-to-severe sleep apnoea”. It names Apple Inc. at One Apple Park Way, Cupertino as the manufacturer and gives a dedicated address, medicalcompliance@group.apple.com, for regulatory correspondence. The ECG app and irregular rhythm notifications sit on the same side of the line, and both carry a 22-year age floor in Apple's tech specs.

Other features do not, and Apple says so in its own footnotes rather than burying it. The Blood Oxygen app is described as being “for wellness purposes only and not for medical use”. Wrist temperature sensing is “not intended for medical use”. Both readings appear in the Health app beside numbers that have been through a regulator, with nothing on the watch face to tell them apart.

That asymmetry is worth more than any accuracy claim, because it is the only reliable signal a buyer gets. A feature that has been assessed publishes a number and a list of things it cannot do. A feature that has not publishes neither.

sections.heading: A third of cases missed, and Apple prints the figure
sections.html:
The sleep apnoea instructions give the trial. The validation study ran on 1,499 participants aged 18 and over and produced a sensitivity of 66.3 per cent against a specificity of 98.5 per cent.

Read those two numbers together. High specificity means a notification is unlikely to be a false alarm — if the watch tells you something, it is probably worth acting on. Sensitivity of 66.3 per cent means roughly a third of people who do have moderate-to-severe sleep apnoea will never get the notification at all. Silence from the watch is not a clean bill of health, and the document does not pretend otherwise.

The mechanics matter too. The feature works in sequential 30-day windows and needs at least ten days of breathing disturbance data inside one before it can say anything, so a watch worn only at weekends will never produce a result. It is indicated for adults 18 and over who have not already been diagnosed.

Hypertension notifications follow the same shape on a different schedule — 30-day evaluation periods, a prompt to confirm any finding with a proper blood pressure cuff over seven days, and a set of exclusions that rules out anyone under 22, anyone pregnant and anyone already diagnosed with hypertension.

sections.heading: Upgrading can take a health feature away from you
sections.html:
Apple's own support documentation carries a sentence that ought to be on the buying page: “Hypertension Notifications might not be available on Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 in your region.” The feature is otherwise supported on a Series 9 or later and an Ultra 2 or later.

The reason is regulatory rather than technical. Each new sensor array is a new device in the eyes of a national regulator, and clearance for the 2026 hardware has not landed everywhere the 2025 hardware is already cleared. The practical result is that somebody trading in a Series 11 for a Series 12 can find a feature they had has gone, and there is no way to get it back other than waiting.

Check the feature availability page for your own country before ordering, and check it again rather than relying on this paragraph — it is the sort of fact that changes without announcement. If hypertension notifications are the reason you are buying, that check is the whole purchase decision.

sections.heading: One year from Apple, twenty-four months from AIG
sections.html:
The standard position is one year of hardware cover from Apple, sitting on top of whatever the Consumer Rights Act 2015 gives you against the shop that sold it. AppleCare+ for Apple Watch extends that to 24 months, or 36 on Hermès and Edition models, and adds accidental damage at a £49 excess per repair — £55 on Hermès and Edition. It also replaces the battery once capacity drops below 80 per cent of the original specification, which is the same threshold Apple uses to define the end of the battery's design life.

The part most buyers never read is who is actually on the hook. AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss is underwritten exclusively by American International Group UK Limited, of The AIG Building, 58 Fenchurch Street, London EC3M 4AB, FCA firm reference number 781109. Apple sells and administers it as an insurance intermediary on AIG's behalf: Apple Retail UK Limited holds firm reference number 598851, and Apple Distribution International acts as its appointed representative. Theft and loss claims carry an £89 excess and are capped at two in any 12 months.

Apple's terms of business are candid about the money. The document states plainly that Apple receives commission from AIG as a percentage of the premium, and that AIG pays Apple a flat fee per policy to handle claims on its behalf. It also states that neither Apple nor AIG gives advice or a personal recommendation. That is a sale, not guidance, and the paperwork says so.

Because it is a regulated insurance contract, the consumer protections are the familiar ones: complaints escalate to the Financial Ombudsman Service at South Quay Plaza, 183 Marsh Wall, London E14 9SR, and the Financial Services Compensation Scheme would cover 90 per cent of a claim with no upper limit if the insurer failed. Cancel within 30 days of buying the plan outright and the refund is in full; after that it is pro rata, less the value of anything already claimed.

sections.heading: AppleCare One changed the arithmetic on 4 August
sections.html:
Apple brought AppleCare One to the UK on 4 August 2026. It costs £16.99 a month and covers up to three products, with further devices at £4.99 a month each. Apple's own example is a household protecting an iPhone, an iPad and an Apple Watch together, which it says saves up to £11.48 a month against buying three separate plans.

Two conditions do the work. Products can be added if they are up to four years old and in good condition, which is a genuine opening — a watch bought in 2023 can be brought under cover, where AppleCare+ has to be bought close to purchase. Headphones are the exception at under one year. Devices may need a diagnostic check first, and only hardware signed in to the same Apple Account qualifies.

Run the sums before signing up. £16.99 a month is £203.88 a year, which is most of an SE 3 and more than half a Series 12. Against three devices with a history of cracked screens it is straightforward value; against one watch it is not.

sections.heading: Batteries, repairs and the number Apple will not print
sections.html:
Apple states the battery is designed to keep up to 80 per cent of its original capacity at 1,000 complete charge cycles. On a watch charged daily that is roughly three years before a noticeable decline, and the figure is a design target rather than a promise.

What Apple does not publish is what fixing it costs. The Apple Watch service page offers a pricing tool and a caveat — an inspection is needed before a personalised estimate, and estimated fees are for out-of-warranty service and subject to VAT — but no printed price per model. For a category where the repair bill decides whether the watch is worth keeping, that is a real gap, and it is the one number a shopper cannot get before they walk in.

The selling entity for the UK online store is Apple Retail UK Limited, 13th Floor, One Angel Court, London EC2R 7HJ, company number 04996702. Its published policy gives 14 calendar days from delivery to return standard hardware with the receipt, packaging and accessories, for any reason.

sections.heading: What the public registers show
sections.html:
Two independent records are worth checking on any wearable, and both are free.

The first is the Office for Product Safety and Standards register of alerts, reports and recalls. A keyword search on “apple watch” returned 23 entries on 29 September 2026 — the search matches any of the words, so most concern unrelated watches and toys. No Apple Watch appears on it. The two Apple-adjacent entries are a recall of the Belkin BoostCharge Pro Fast Wireless Charger for Apple Watch and Power Bank 10K, references 2410-0061 and 2411-0129 dated 6 November 2024, and a counterfeit “Apple” branded USB-C power adapter, reference 2507-0047 dated 28 July 2025. Neither is Apple's own hardware, and the second is a warning about the accessory market rather than about Apple.

The second is the Advertising Standards Authority's rulings index. Checked on 29 September 2026 it showed no formal ruling upheld against Apple and five cases resolved informally — an outcome where the advertiser amends or withdraws the ad without a published adjudication. The largest of those attracted 41 complaints and was closed on 11 January 2023. Informal resolution is not the same as vindication, but for a company advertising at this volume it is a clean-ish record, and the ASA index is searchable if you want to check it for yourself before the next campaign.

On measured accuracy the picture is also good. Which? tested 58 devices against medical-grade chest straps in a report published on 3 February 2026 and put Apple at the top on wrist heart-rate error, at 1.1 per cent. The full model-by-model table is behind a membership.

pros: The regulated health features come with published evidence: a 1,499-person validation study, 66.3% sensitivity and 98.5% specificity, in a document written for the UK market
Apple labels its unassessed features honestly in its own tech specs — Blood Oxygen is “for wellness purposes only and not for medical use” and wrist temperature is “not intended for medical use”
A real entry price at £219 for the SE 3 that still carries irregular rhythm notifications, sleep apnoea notifications, sleep score and 50-metre water resistance
AppleCare+ is a properly regulated insurance contract, not a shop guarantee: AIG carries the risk under FCA firm reference 781109, with the Ombudsman and FSCS behind it
AppleCare One accepts hardware up to four years old, so an older watch can be brought under cover rather than being stuck outside it
Battery design life is stated rather than implied — 80% of original capacity at 1,000 complete charge cycles — and AppleCare+ replaces the battery at that threshold
The Ultra 4 is genuinely specified for the job at £650: 50 hours of normal use, 100-metre water resistance and EN13319 certification for scuba to 40 metres
cons: Buying the newest watch can cost you a health feature: Apple's own support pages say hypertension notifications “might not be available on Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 in your region”, while a Series 9 or Ultra 2 has them
Sensitivity of 66.3% means roughly a third of moderate-to-severe sleep apnoea cases produce no notification at all, and nothing on the watch tells a user that silence is not reassurance

Blood Oxygen and wrist temperature readings sit in the Health app next to regulated measurements with no visible distinction, and the disclaimer is a footnote on a specifications page most buyers never open
None of it works without an iPhone 11 or later on iOS 27 — there is no Android app and no standalone mode, so a £369 watch is unusable to anyone outside Apple's phone range

Apple publishes no out-of-warranty repair or battery price for Apple Watch: the service page requires an inspection for a personalised estimate, so the cost of the most likely repair is unknowable before you commit
AppleCare One at £16.99 a month is £203.88 a year, more than half the price of a Series 12, and it only makes sense across three or more devices

The health exclusions rule out several groups most likely to want the features: hypertension notifications are closed to under-22s, to anyone pregnant and to anyone already diagnosed, and the ECG app and irregular rhythm notifications both carry a 22-year floor

AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss is sold without advice or a personal recommendation, and Apple is paid commission by AIG as a percentage of the premium plus a flat fee for handling claims — disclosed in the terms of business, not at the point of sale
verdict: Apple Watch is the best-documented wearable you can buy in the UK, and that is the reason to buy one rather than any single specification. Prices are fixed and clear — £219, £369, £650 — the battery design life is stated, the guarantee is one year with a regulated 24-month extension behind it, and the health features that have been through a regulator publish the trial that got them there, including the unflattering half. A sensitivity of 66.3% on sleep apnoea is a number most makers would never print. Against that, three things deserve care before ordering: the Series 12 and Ultra 4 may not carry hypertension notifications in your region when the cheaper, older model does; Blood Oxygen and temperature are wellness readings dressed in the same typeface as clinical ones; and no Apple Watch does anything at all without a recent iPhone. Check the feature availability list for your country, decide whether £49 an incident is worth £203.88 a year across your household rather than on this watch alone, and buy on the model that has what you actually want cleared.

faqs.q: How long is the guarantee on an Apple Watch in the UK?
faqs.a: One year of hardware cover from Apple as standard. AppleCare+ for Apple Watch extends it to 24 months, or 36 months on Hermès and Edition models, and adds accidental damage at a £49 excess per repair (£55 on Hermès and Edition). Separately, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 gives you rights against the retailer that are not limited to a year.

faqs.q: Does Apple Watch work with an Android phone?
faqs.a: No. Apple's specifications for the Series 12, Ultra 4 and SE 3 all require an iPhone 11 or later, or an iPhone SE from the second generation onwards, running iOS 27. There is no Android app and no standalone setup.

faqs.q: Which Apple Watch health features are actually regulated?
faqs.a: Sleep apnoea notifications, the ECG app, irregular rhythm notifications and hypertension notifications go through a medical device route and publish evidence and limits — the sleep apnoea instructions for use, for instance, give a 1,499-person study at 66.3% sensitivity and 98.5% specificity. Blood Oxygen and wrist temperature do not: Apple's own footnotes call them wellness features not intended for medical use.

faqs.q: Will the Series 12 have hypertension notifications?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Apple's support documentation states that hypertension notifications “might not be available on Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 in your region”, while listing the feature as supported on a Series 9 or later and an Ultra 2 or later. Clearance is granted country by country, so check Apple's feature availability page for the UK before upgrading if the feature matters to you.

faqs.q: Who insures AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss?
faqs.a: American International Group UK Limited, FCA firm reference number 781109, at The AIG Building, 58 Fenchurch Street, London EC3M 4AB. Apple sells and administers it as an intermediary — Apple Retail UK Limited holds firm reference 598851 — and receives commission from AIG plus a flat fee per policy for handling claims. Complaints go to the Financial Ombudsman Service, and the FSCS would cover 90% of a claim with no upper limit.

faqs.q: What does an out-of-warranty Apple Watch battery replacement cost?
faqs.a: Apple does not publish a figure. Its Apple Watch service page offers a pricing tool but states that the product must be inspected for a personalised estimate, and that estimated fees are for out-of-warranty service and subject to VAT. Under AppleCare+ the battery is replaced at no extra fee once capacity falls below 80% of the original specification.

faqs.q: How long do I have to return an Apple Watch bought online?
faqs.a: Fourteen calendar days from delivery, for any reason, with the receipt, original packaging and accessories. The seller is Apple Retail UK Limited, 13th Floor, One Angel Court, London EC2R 7HJ, company number 04996702.

title: Argos Gaming and Accessories: What It Costs to Buy, and to Send Back
meta_title: Argos Gaming: Delivery, Returns and Argos Pay Explained
meta_description: Argos sells gaming from 1,133 collection points: £4.95 small-item delivery, free over £100, 30-day returns and Argos Pay at 34.9% APR. Checked 29 Sept 2026.
intro:
Argos took £4.1bn of sales in the year to 28 February 2026, up 0.7%, and it did it through 667 Argos store locations and 466 separate collection points — 1,133 places to pick up a console, a controller or a boxed game. Those figures are Sainsbury's own, from the preliminary results published on 23 April 2026, and were checked again on 29 September 2026. Volumes rose 3.7% while the average selling price fell 3.0%, so the business is shifting more items at lower prices, which is exactly the shape of a gaming aisle.

Two things about buying gaming kit here are worth knowing before you click. Collection costs nothing at any of those 1,133 points; home delivery of a small item is £4.95 and free once the order passes £100. And the credit behind the counter has changed hands: the Argos Card became Argos Pay and the lender is now NewDay Ltd, not Sainsbury's. If you are ringing about an Argos balance, you are no longer ringing Sainsbury's.

On returns Argos is more generous than the law requires. You get 30 days from the day you collect or take delivery, against the 14 days the Consumer Contracts Regulations give, and anything bought between 23 September and 25 December can go back until 31 January. Beyond 30 days and inside 12 months, a fault gets a repair or a replacement at no cost, and a refund if neither works.

sections.heading: What it costs to get a controller to your door
sections.html:
Argos charges by the size of the parcel rather than the value of the order. Its own delivery page gives “Small Item Delivery £4.95, free over £100”, and it prices other ranges separately — standard delivery on Tu clothing is £3.95 per order. Delivery slots, the same page says, are “subject to stock, postcode and availability”, so a same-day slot is not a promise you can bank on before you reach the basket.

For anyone buying gaming kit more than a few times a year the pass is the cheaper route. Argos Plus costs £40 and, in Argos's words, “gives you access to same day, next day and standard delivery services at no additional cost for 12 months”, on orders totalling £20 or more and with an Argos account. Nine small-item deliveries at £4.95 come to £44.55, so the pass pays for itself on the ninth order and every delivery after that is free.

The cheapest route of all is not to be delivered at all. Collection is free, and the number of places to do it is the real argument for buying a game here rather than online: 667 Argos store locations and 466 collection points, 1,133 in total. Sainsbury's results table lists 203 Argos stores separately from that 667, and it does not explain the gap in the table itself — the likeliest reading is that 203 are standalone shops and the balance are Argos counters inside Sainsbury's supermarkets, but Sainsbury's does not say so there and that split needs confirming.

sections.heading: Thirty days to change your mind, and the things that never come back
sections.html:
The statutory floor is set out on Argos's own page about the Consumer Contracts Regulations: “you may cancel your order provided you exercise your right to do so within 14 days”, and “the 14 days starts the day after the date of delivery”, with the goods to be returned within 14 days of cancelling. Argos doubles the first half of that: “You have 30 days from the date of collection or from the date of delivery to request to return your item(s).” Anything bought between 23 September and 25 December can go back until 31 January, which as of today already covers this week's purchases.

The mechanics are published and worth reading before you post anything. Refunds go back to the card used at purchase “within 5-7 days of our receipt”. “Returns are at your cost except where we state otherwise”, and Argos refunds the standard outbound delivery charge only “provided all goods are returned” — send back one item of three and the £4.95 stays spent. Argos also reserves the right to “deduct from any refund an amount to reflect the loss in value of the goods as a result of any unnecessary handling by you”.

Four exclusions matter more in this category than in any other. “Sealed video games, DVDs, CDs or any computer software that has been opened, downloaded or redeemed” cannot be returned. Neither can “digital content (including apps, digital software, eBooks, MP3, etc.) which is not supplied on a tangible medium”. Neither can “Pokémon card packets or other sealed mystery collectables, once the packet is opened”. And earphones sit on the hygiene list, alongside razors and toothbrushes, so a gaming headset whose seal you have broken is outside the 30 days too. Between them, those four cover the two most common things a gamer buys: the game and the headset.

sections.heading: The credit behind the counter belongs to NewDay now
sections.html:
On 31 October 2024 Sainsbury's announced the sale of the Argos Financial Services card portfolio to NewDay Group for “around £720 million, broadly in line with the expected net value of loan balances and associated provisions”. The book it sold serves roughly two million customers and supports about 20% of Argos transactions. Beneficial title was expected to pass at the end of the first quarter of 2025, with legal title following around twelve months later after a migration period.

Two Argos documents date the consumer end of that differently, and both are worth having. Sainsbury's preliminary results describe Argos Pay as launched in partnership with NewDay in February 2026; the Argos help centre says “As of 26 April 2026, certain Argos Store Card accounts updated to Argos Pay”. Read together they are a product launch and a migration date rather than a contradiction. The help centre also names the parties plainly: “NewDay Ltd is the lender, Argos Limited is the credit broker.” NewDay Ltd is company 7297722, FCA firm reference 690292; Argos Limited's own firm reference as a broker is 713206.

The published terms are specific. Argos Pay carries 34.9% APR representative (variable). The interest-free tiers are laid out as 0% Buy Now Pay Later for “3 months when you spend £149+”, “6 months when you spend £199+”, “12 months on products £499+” and “12 months on furniture products £199+”. Instalment plans run over “12, 24, 36 or 48 fixed monthly payments” with a minimum spend of £150, and Argos says there are “no early repayment fees”. Third-party options sit alongside: Klarna's pay-in-30-days and pay-in-3, and PayPal Pay in 3, which splits purchases between £20 and £3,000 into “3 interest-free payments over 2 months”. The Argos Pay helpline is 0333 240 8002, open 9am to 7pm Monday to Friday and 9am to 5pm Saturday.

For a gaming basket the tier that matters is the first one. A console and a spare controller will clear £149 and open the three-month interest-free window; almost nothing in this category reaches the £499 that opens twelve months. Read the £499 line as a white-goods threshold that gaming rarely touches.

sections.heading: Boxed games are the one part of this market going backwards
sections.html:
Ukie's UK Games Market Valuation for 2025, published in April 2026, puts the consumer games market at £8.76 billion, up 7.4%. Underneath that, the lines move in opposite directions. Console hardware grew 12% to £811 million and gaming PCs grew 11% to £790 million. Console game accessories fell 9% to £420 million. And boxed software fell 1.0% to £319 million, the smallest and the only shrinking software line.

That last figure is the one to hold against a shop with shelves. The hardware Argos sells is in a market growing at 12%; the discs it sells alongside are in a market of £319 million and falling, against £6.03 billion of software sales overall once downloads are counted. A physical retailer's gaming business is therefore mostly a hardware business now, and the accessories that used to ride along with it are shrinking on a growing installed base — which is the condition in which cheap unbranded kit multiplies, and the reason the safety register below reads the way it does.

sections.heading: The batteries in your controller are Argos's problem too
sections.html:
Wireless controllers, headsets and light guns run on portable batteries, and there is a free, enforceable duty attached to selling them. The Waste Batteries and Accumulators Regulations 2009 (SI 2009/890, in force 26 April 2009) say at regulation 31 that a distributor of portable batteries must, at any place it supplies them to end users, “take back waste portable batteries at no charge” and “inform end-users about the possibility of such take back at the distributor's sales points”. It may not charge for doing so and may not “oblige end-users to buy a new battery”, and it must not dispose of what it takes back. Regulation 34 separately forbids showing the cost of collection, treatment and recycling to the customer.

The only escape is size. Regulation 31(5) defines a small distributor as one supplying “less than 32 kg of portable batteries to end-users in a year”, and a retailer turning over £4.1bn is not within a country mile of that exemption. So the duty to take your dead AAs back, free, at the counter, applies to every one of those 1,133 points.

A search of Argos's own help centre for “recycling” on 29 September 2026 returned no article about batteries and no article about electrical take-back. The single recycling entry on the page was “Furniture Recycling”, pointing at a third-party collection service. That is a gap in what is published rather than evidence about what happens at the counter — the obligation is on the shop, not the shopper — but regulation 31(1)(b) is specifically about informing you, so it is fair to say the information is not where you would look for it. Ask at the desk before you throw a set of controller batteries in the bin.

sections.heading: What the safety register actually shows about gaming kit
sections.html:
The Office for Product Safety and Standards publishes every alert, report and recall it handles. A search of that register for Argos returns 17 notices, and not one of them is a console, a controller or a headset. They are sofas and footstools (2212-0201, 2302-0155, 2303-0001 and 2303-0003, all in early 2023), a car seat and a pushchair, an air fryer, a tumble dryer, a ride-on toy, jewellery and two Tu clothing lines — the most recent dated 28 September 2026. For a retailer selling gaming hardware at this scale, an empty gaming column on the register is a meaningful result rather than an absence of data.

The nearest thing to a gaming hazard on the register is instructive about where the risk actually sits, and it is not an Argos product. The Ultrapods Pro True Wireless Headset, model AP092, brand Jinhua Jiebo Electronics Co. Ltd, made in China, was recalled on 7 January 2026 under reference 2510-0030 because “the product presents a serious risk of burns as the supplied USB cable cannot handle outputs from standard USB power sources”. It breached the Radio Equipment Regulations 2017, was recalled from end users by A Plush Limited and was notified by local authority Trading Standards. The headset was not the hazard; the cable in the box was.

That is the pattern across this category: the danger is rarely the branded device and almost always the cheap mains or USB part travelling with it. It is a good reason to buy the charger from the same place as the console, and a good reason to read the brand name on a marketplace listing rather than the shop name above it.

sections.heading: The one thing you cannot read on Argos's own website is an Argos price
sections.html:
This page carries no Argos price, and that is not an oversight. On 29 September 2026 three Argos URLs were opened and read directly: the video games and consoles category (c:29993), the Maxx Tech MX40 LED gaming headset page (product 7796087) and the Nintendo Switch 2 console page (product 7624867). All three returned a complete page of navigation, breadcrumbs and category menus, and no price at all. The price is fetched by the browser after the page arrives, so it exists only for a human with a browser open. The Switch 2 page's own description says nothing more than “Thousands of products for same day delivery, or fast store collection”.

For a business that built its name on a printed price list this is a strange place to end up, and it has a practical cost. Anything that reads pages rather than renders them — an answer engine, a price tracker, a shopping comparison — sees the catalogue and not the prices. So the delivered cost of the cheapest gaming item at Argos cannot be quoted here or compared against another shop from Argos's own pages; only the £4.95 on top of it can. Argos's help centre lists an article titled “Do we price match with other brands?”, which could not be opened on 29 September 2026, so whether any price promise exists needs confirming with Argos directly.

One more distinction is worth drawing before you buy. Some listings are Argos's and some belong to its Trusted Sellers, and the returns route is not the same. A Trusted Seller purchase still gives “30 days from the date of collection or from the date of delivery to request to return your item(s)”, but “refunds will be processed once the Trusted Seller has received and inspected the item” and “will be issued within 14 days after the day on which the Trusted Seller receives the goods back”. Against 5–7 days on an Argos-owned item, that is a fortnight of difference, and the Trusted Seller page says nothing about what Argos itself will do if the seller does not play ball.

pros: 1,133 places to collect, and collection costs nothing — 667 Argos store locations plus 466 collection points
30 days to change your mind, against the 14 the Consumer Contracts Regulations require, and until 31 January on anything bought from 23 September
Repair or replacement at no cost on a fault beyond 30 days and inside 12 months, with a refund if neither settles it
Argos Plus at £40 for 12 months pays for itself on the ninth £4.95 small-item delivery
0% credit at three published thresholds — 3 months on £149+, 6 months on £199+, 12 months over £499 — with no early repayment fees
Sales volumes up 3.7% in the year to 28 February 2026 while the average selling price fell 3.0%, so the pricing pressure is running the buyer's way
Not one of the 17 OPSS safety notices naming Argos concerns a console, controller or headset
cons: Argos publishes no readable price. The video games category and two product pages checked on 29 September 2026 returned full pages with no price in them, so nothing on this site or any other can quote or compare an Argos gaming price from Argos's own pages.

Argos's help centre carries no article on waste battery or electrical take-back, checked 29 September 2026, even though regulation 31(1)(b) of the Waste Batteries and Accumulators Regulations 2009 requires a distributor to inform end users about it at its sales points. Only furniture recycling appears, via a third party.

An opened game is gone. “Sealed video games, DVDs, CDs or any computer software that has been opened, downloaded or redeemed” cannot be returned at all, digital content not on a tangible medium cannot be returned, and earphones fall on the hygiene list — which takes most gaming headsets out of the 30 days as soon as the seal breaks.
34.9% APR representative (variable) on Argos Pay outside the promotional tiers, and the 12-month interest-free tier needs £499 of spend that a gaming basket rarely reaches.
Return postage is the customer's cost unless Argos says otherwise, and the outbound delivery charge is only refunded if the entire order goes back — so a partial return leaves the £4.95 spent.

A Trusted Seller refund arrives up to 14 days after the seller receives and inspects the goods, against 5–7 days on an Argos item, and the Trusted Seller policy does not set out Argos's own liability if the seller does not perform.
Same-day and next-day slots are “subject to stock, postcode and availability”, so the delivery speed that justifies the £40 pass is not guaranteed at the point you buy it.
verdict: Argos is the most convenient way to buy gaming hardware in Britain and the least transparent way to price it. The convenience is real and measurable: 1,133 places to collect for nothing, £4.95 to have a small parcel delivered and nothing over £100, 30 days to change your mind rather than the statutory 14, and 12 months of free repair or replacement on a fault. The £40 Argos Plus pass is good value for anyone ordering more than eight times a year. The credit is now NewDay's rather than Sainsbury's, at 34.9% APR representative outside the 0% tiers, and the £149 three-month tier is the one most gaming baskets will reach. What you cannot do is compare it: Argos's own pages carry no price that anything but a browser can read, so the cheapest delivered route into its gaming range has to be worked out in the basket. Go in knowing that an opened game and an unsealed headset are both non-returnable, that a partial return forfeits the delivery charge, and that a Trusted Seller listing is a different contract with a slower refund.

faqs.q: How much does Argos charge to deliver a game or a controller?
faqs.a: Small-item home delivery is £4.95 and free once the order passes £100. Collection is free at any of Argos's 1,133 points of presence — 667 Argos store locations and 466 collection points. If you order often, the Argos Plus pass costs £40 for 12 months of same-day, next-day and standard delivery on orders of £20 or more, which is cheaper than nine £4.95 deliveries.

faqs.q: Can I return a video game to Argos if I have opened it?
faqs.a: No. Argos's returns policy excludes “sealed video games, DVDs, CDs or any computer software that has been opened, downloaded or redeemed”, and that exclusion reflects regulation 28 of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, which removes the 14-day cancellation right for sealed audio, video or software once unsealed. The same applies to digital content not supplied on a tangible medium, and to opened Pokémon packets and sealed mystery collectables. An unopened game goes back within 30 days like anything else.

faqs.q: Who lends the money on Argos Pay?
faqs.a: NewDay Ltd, company 7297722, FCA firm reference 690292. Argos Limited acts only as the credit broker, firm reference 713206. Sainsbury's sold the Argos Financial Services card portfolio to NewDay for around £720 million in an announcement dated 31 October 2024, covering roughly two million customers and about 20% of Argos transactions, and Argos says certain store card accounts updated to Argos Pay on 26 April 2026. The representative rate is 34.9% APR variable.

faqs.q: Will Argos take my old controller batteries back?
faqs.a: It is required to. Regulation 31 of the Waste Batteries and Accumulators Regulations 2009 obliges any distributor supplying more than 32 kg of portable batteries a year to take waste portable batteries back at no charge wherever it supplies them, without obliging you to buy a replacement. Argos is far above that threshold. Its own help centre carried no article explaining this on 29 September 2026, so ask at the counter rather than relying on finding it online.

faqs.q: How long is an Argos guarantee on gaming hardware?
faqs.a: Beyond the 30-day change-of-mind window and within 12 months, Argos offers a repair or replacement at no cost on a faulty item, and a refund if neither resolves it. Inside the first 30 days a faulty item qualifies for a refund outright. Those are Argos's own terms and sit on top of, not instead of, your statutory rights.

faqs.q: Is the gaming market still growing?
faqs.a: The UK consumer games market reached £8.76 billion in 2025, up 7.4%, on Ukie's figures published in April 2026. Console hardware grew 12% to £811 million and gaming PCs 11% to £790 million, but console game accessories fell 9% to £420 million and boxed software fell 1.0% to £319 million — the only shrinking software line, and the one a shop with shelves depends on.

title: Argos Televisions Review 2026: The 12-Month Guarantee, the Bush Recall and the Missing Energy Label
meta_title: Argos TVs 2026: 12-Month Guarantee, Bush Recall Checked
meta_description: Argos gives 12 months repair or replace on every TV, sells Freely-ready Bush sets, and has 16 Bush TiVo models under a plug recall. Checked 30 September 2026.

headline.label: Free guarantee included in the price
headline.value: 12 months — repair or replace on any television, with nothing free beyond that; longer cover is sold separately as Argos Care (checked 30 September 2026)

intro:
Argos promises to repair or replace a faulty television free of charge for 12 months, and its own Bush brand was the second in Britain to ship Freely, in May 2024, a month behind Hisense and a year ahead of four bigger names. Both figures come from Argos's own help centre and Everyone TV's press releases, read on 30 September 2026.

Collection is the part Argos still does better than anyone: nothing to pay at over 1,100 collection points, against a lorry delivery for anything the shop classes as large. The Bush sets built for it carry Freely, the broadcaster-owned platform that now lists more than 70 live channels over Wi-Fi, so a £150-class 32-inch set from Argos reaches the same live channels as a set costing four times as much.

One piece of corporate news belongs here rather than three sections down: on 31 July 2026 Sainsbury's agreed to sell Argos, and completion is expected in February 2027. Nothing about buying a television changes today, and the detail is set out further down the page.

key_facts.label: Own-brand television maker
key_facts.value: Bush sets are built by Vestel UK Limited (company 04771550, Vestel House, Langley, Berkshire), and Bush is sold only by Argos

key_facts.label: Free guarantee
key_facts.value: Refund inside 30 days; repair or replace at no cost after 30 days and inside 12 months

key_facts.label: Extra cover
key_facts.value: Argos Care, provided by Domestic & General Insurance PLC, can be added in store up to 45 days after purchase

key_facts.label: Open safety notice
key_facts.value: OPSS report 2606-0164, published 15 June 2026: 16 Bush TiVo catalogue numbers sold December 2024 to March 2026

key_facts.label: Freely requirement
key_facts.value: Broadband of at least 10Mbps; an aerial is optional and adds further live channels

key_facts.label: Collection points
key_facts.value: Over 1,100 Argos and Sainsbury's collection points, free to collect

key_facts.label: Ownership
key_facts.value: Sale to Swift Partners agreed 31 July 2026 for at least £120 million, completion expected February 2027

sections.heading: What the 12-month guarantee promises, and what it leaves out
sections.html:
Argos states the position in one short passage on its returns and repairs page: a fault inside 30 days of receipt means you are “entitled to a refund”, and “if something goes wrong after the first 30 days but within 12 months, we'll offer to repair or replace the item at no cost to you”. If repair or replacement fails, takes too long or “causes significant inconvenience”, Argos says it will refund. Damaged or faulty goods do not need the original packaging.

That is clear, and it is also the whole of it. There is no free two-year or five-year television guarantee at Argos, and a search of its help centre for the word “guarantee” on 30 September 2026 returned no article by that name at all — the promise lives inside the returns article rather than in a guarantee document with terms you can read before buying.

Longer cover is a separate purchase. Argos Care “policies are provided by Domestic & General Insurance PLC, who are an insurer not an intermediary”, and Argos says it covers “many of the items not covered by your standard manufacturer's guarantee, including both parts and labour (although some exclusions apply)”. Where a set already carries an extended parts guarantee, Argos Care pays for labour only. You have 45 days from purchase to add it in store with your receipt, which is a genuinely useful window. What the help centre never publishes is the price, the term, or which exclusions apply — the phrase is simply “some exclusions apply”, and the policy documents sit behind the product page, which is discussed below.

sections.heading: Bush is Argos's own brand, and the law notices
sections.html:
Most of the sets on the site are other companies' brands, where Argos is the shop and nothing more. Bush is different: it is Argos's own label, sold nowhere else, and the hardware is built in Turkey by Vestel. The safety notice discussed in the next section names Vestel UK Limited — Companies House 04771550, incorporated 20 May 2003, registered at Vestel House, 1 Waterside Drive, Langley, Berkshire SL3 6EZ — as the manufacturer of the part that failed.

Two separate rulebooks treat an own-brand retailer differently from a shop. Under the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016, a “manufacturer” is “any person who manufactures electrical equipment, or has electrical equipment designed or manufactured; and markets that electrical equipment under that person's name or trade mark”, while a “distributor” is “any person in the supply chain, other than the manufacturer or the importer, who makes electrical equipment available on the market”. Regulation 31(1) then closes the gap: a distributor who “places electrical equipment on the market under A's own name or trademark” takes on the manufacturer's duties in regulations 4 to 13 — design, conformity with the safety objectives, technical documentation and marking.

The energy rules draw the same line in different words. Government guidance defines the supplier as “the manufacturer, authorised representative or importer” that places a product on the market, and the dealer as the retailer that displays the label. Enforcement splits accordingly: the Office for Product Safety and Standards polices suppliers, and local authorities police dealers.

So on a Samsung or an LG, Argos is a dealer with a display duty. On a Bush, the brand is Argos's own and the manufacturer's duties are in play. Exactly how they are allocated between Argos and Vestel is set by contracts nobody outside the two companies can read, and the OPSS notice records Vestel UK as the manufacturer, so this page does not claim to settle it — it needs confirming from Argos directly. What is not in doubt is that a Bush television is not a third party's product that Argos happens to stock.

sections.heading: Sixteen catalogue numbers, one fuse
sections.html:
Product safety report 2606-0164, published by OPSS on 15 June 2026, is headed “Vestel UK Plugs in Bush TiVo Televisions sold by Argos”. The fault is small and serious: “the plug's fuse does not meet the dimensional requirements of BS 1362”, and if a fault develops “the plug may overheat and catch fire”. The risk is recorded as fire, the country of origin as Turkey, the notifier as local authority Trading Standards, and the measure as a modification programme rather than a full recall.

Sixteen Argos catalogue numbers are listed: 7623916, 7615436, 7623930, 5024232, 7623057, 7140585, 6799418, 7049662, 5816505, 4743868, 5420001, 5024373, 6826271, 4723668, 7041251 and 7086388. They were sold by Argos between December 2024 and March 2026 — a 16-month window, which is wide. The remedy is a free replacement power cable or fuse, and the owner has to go and get it: register on the Argos Product Check site, then dispose of the old cable through WEEE recycling facilities.

Two legal instruments are cited as breached, and neither has appeared on this site before: the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016 and the Plugs and Sockets etc. (Safety) Regulations 1994. The 1994 rules are the reason a British plug is the shape it is. Regulation 8 requires a standard plug to be “of a type approved by a notified body” satisfied that it conforms to BS 1363, that the maker can reliably produce conforming plugs, and — where a sample fails — that “such plugs shall be treated for the purposes of this regulation as not conforming to the standard”, with no retest. An approval lasts “seven years or such shorter period as may be specified”. A fuse a fraction of a millimetre out of tolerance is exactly the sort of thing that regime exists to catch, and in this case it was caught by a council officer rather than by the supply chain.

For scale: a keyword search of the OPSS register for “Bush” on 30 September 2026 returns exactly one notice, this one. That is a good record for a brand Argos has sold since 2008, and it is the honest way to read an empty column on a public register.

The disposal instruction is worth one more line. Argos tells affected owners to take the old cable to WEEE recycling facilities, and a search of its own help centre for “recycling” on 30 September 2026 returned no electrical or television take-back article of any kind — only a furniture clearance service run by a third party. Ask at the counter; do not assume the shop will take it.

sections.heading: The energy label that never arrives
sections.html:
Since 1 March 2021 televisions sold in Great Britain have carried the rescaled A-to-G energy label, and for distance selling the rules require the class and the range of classes to be shown to the buyer before they commit. Argos does not manage it in the page it serves. Three URLs were opened and read directly on 30 September 2026: the television category at /browse/technology/televisions-and-accessories/televisions/c:30106/ and the product page for catalogue number 7623916, the Bush 32-inch 32FT25CB Smart FHD HDR LED Freely TV. The category page returned navigation, breadcrumbs and subcategory links and no product, no price and no energy class. The product page returned the set's name, its model number and its 32-inch screen size — and no price, no energy efficiency class, no link to a label and no guarantee wording.

None of that means Argos is hiding anything. The prices and the label arrive by script once a browser has the page, which is a design choice thousands of retailers make. It has two consequences a reader should know about. The first is practical: an Argos television price cannot be quoted by anything that reads the page rather than running it, this page included, so every figure here is a published document rather than a shelf price, and the price you see is the one on your own screen. The second is regulatory: the duty to put the class beside the product in distance selling is enforced by local authorities against dealers, and a document that arrives without it is an odd way to meet it.

The supplier half has a gap too. A GB energy label's QR code “must link to the required model information on a publicly accessible website” — the supplier's own, since Great Britain does not use the European product database. Argos runs a manuals and support portal at argos-support.co.uk, searchable by product name, catalogue number or model number, and it carries “instruction manuals, user guides, videos and telephone helplines” for televisions among other categories. It does not publish energy labels or model information sheets. Suppliers must keep the technical documentation behind those figures for 15 years after manufacturing stops; for a Bush set, that paperwork is not on the public side of the wall.

sections.heading: Seven years of spare parts, and a spares site run from Yeovil
sections.html:
The ecodesign regulation for electronic displays is the half of the rulebook nobody markets. Annex II, point D.5(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2021 requires a manufacturer to keep spare parts available to professional repairers for at least seven years after the last unit of a model goes on sale: “internal power supply, connectors to connect external equipment (cable, antenna, USB, DVD and Blue-Ray), capacitors, batteries and accumulators, DVD/Blue-Ray module if applicable and HD/SSD module if applicable”. Two parts — “external power supply and remote control” — must be available to ordinary owners as well, which is the reason the recall remedy above is a cable rather than a workshop visit. Orders must be delivered “within 15 working days after having received the order”, and from two years after a model launches, repairers must be given the disassembly map, the test equipment list, wiring diagrams and the fault codes.

The same annex sets the rest of the physics: an Energy Efficiency Index no higher than 0.75 for HD sets and 0.9 for 4K since 1 March 2023, off mode capped at 0.3W, standby at 0.5W and networked standby at 2.0W, polymer marking on plastic parts, and a flat prohibition — “the use of halogenated flame retardants is not allowed in the enclosure and stand of electronic displays”.

Against a seven-year parts duty, a 12-month guarantee looks short, and Argos's own signposting to parts is thin. Its help centre says only that “we can provide spare parts for some items, just head over to our Argos Spares site to find out more”, with no list of which items, no statement of how long parts stay available, and no price. The site it sends you to is more interesting than the sentence suggests: argosspares.co.uk is operated by Screwfix Spares Limited — Companies House 03593012, incorporated 6 July 1998, registered at Trade House, Mead Avenue, Houndstone Business Park, Yeovil BA22 8RT — “in association with 4ourhouse”. Screwfix belongs to Kingfisher, not to Sainsbury's, and the catalogue leans heavily towards white goods and floorcare, with televisions represented mainly by remote controls. A reader after a Bush panel or power board should not expect to find one there.

sections.heading: Freely needs 10Mbps before it needs an aerial
sections.html:
The reason to look at a Bush set rather than an unbranded one is Freely, and Argos got there early. Freely is run by Everyone TV Limited, company 05422613, the joint venture owned by the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5. It launched on Hisense sets in April 2024 and on Bush sets in May 2024; Everyone TV's release of 24 June 2024 confirmed Toshiba, Sharp, Panasonic and Metz as the next four partners, with their models “due to launch later this year”. Bush was therefore the second brand in the country to carry it, which for a catalogue own-label is a real achievement.

The platform has grown since. Everyone TV's release of 14 October 2025 puts Freely at “over 70 live channels over Wi-Fi”, records more than 500,000 weekly users reached earlier that year, and names 10 further streaming channels arriving in 2026 from Hearst Networks, Bloomberg TV+ and AMC Networks International UK, including BLAZE, Bloomberg TV+, Talking Pictures TV, TRUE CRIME UK and Local TV. Freely's own site claims “97% of the UK's most watched shows” and lists Hisense, Bush, Toshiba, Panasonic, Sharp, TCL, Amazon Fire TV and METZ as supported.

The catch is the connection. Freely delivers live channels over the internet, and the service asks for a minimum broadband speed of 10Mbps; an aerial is optional and unlocks more live channels rather than fewer. A buyer replacing an old set in a room with a good aerial socket and slow or no Wi-Fi has the arrangement backwards, and on a cheap Bush set the streaming platform is much of what they are paying for. Check the speed in the room the set is going in, not the speed on the router.

sections.heading: New owners from February 2027
sections.html:
Argos is changing hands. Sainsbury's announced on 31 July 2026 that it had agreed to sell the business to Swift Partners — Swift Whistle Midco Limited, backed by Richard Pennycook, Trevor Strain, Matt Truman and True Capital — for at least £120 million in cash: a minimum £70 million at completion and £50 million deferred over the three years afterwards, including proceeds from the sale of the Daventry distribution centre. Completion is expected in February 2027, with full separation by February 2029. Simon Roberts, Sainsbury's chief executive, said the agreement “allows us to focus all our resources and investment on the significant opportunities ahead”; Richard Pennycook said Argos has “an excellent platform for growth”.

The sale takes in the standalone shops, the Argos counters inside Sainsbury's stores, the sales channels, the logistics network and the sourcing offices in Shanghai and Hong Kong — and, relevant to anyone buying cover with a television, Argos Care and Argos Pet Insurance. Sainsbury's keeps the Argos defined benefit pension scheme, and the in-store counters continue under a long-term commercial agreement with rent paid to Sainsbury's.

This is the second attempt. On 13 September 2025 Sainsbury's confirmed discussions over a sale of Argos Retail Group Limited to JD.com — a company it described as 44th on the Fortune Global 500, with 2024 revenue of $158.8 billion and around 600 million annual active customers — and added that “no agreement has been reached and there is no certainty at this stage that any transaction will proceed”. It did not proceed. That release is also the source of the scale figures worth having: Argos is the UK's second largest general merchandise retailer, with “over 1,100 collection points” and the third most visited retail website in the country.

For a television buyer the practical reading is narrow. A 12-month repair-or-replace promise is a promise by Argos Limited, which continues to exist and continues to trade; an Argos Care policy is an insurance contract with Domestic & General, which is unaffected by who owns the shop. But a five-year service plan bought this autumn will spend most of its life under an owner who has not yet taken possession, and that is worth knowing before ticking the box.

sections.heading: Where the 12 months sits against the other shops
sections.html:
Argos's answer to the question this category is compared on — how much guarantee comes free with the set — is 12 months of repair or replace. John Lewis includes five years on every television it lists. Amazon gives one year on the Fire TV sets it builds itself and nothing at all on another brand's panel. Argos sits between the two, and closer to Amazon.

An independent customer score for Argos could not be verified from a free primary source this run, and it is not asserted here. For context on the benchmark rather than the shop: the UK Customer Satisfaction Index published on 7 July 2026 put the all-sector average at 78.3 out of 100, up 1.0 point year on year across the 13 sectors it tracks, with Nationwide top on 87.3, John Lewis second on 87.1 and first direct third on 86.0. Argos is not named in the public summary.

What Argos genuinely wins on is the last mile. Collection is free at over 1,100 points, most of them inside a supermarket that is open late, and a 32-inch set is a one-person carry. Home delivery is the opposite: anything the shop classes as a large item “come[s] on a lorry and need[s] 2 people to handle”, and Argos's own tell is the order number — “if it starts with a 1, it's a small item. If it starts with a 2, it's a large item”. For a big screen going up a narrow staircase, that distinction matters more than the guarantee does.

pros: Repair or replace at no cost for 12 months is stated plainly, in Argos's own words, with a refund if repair fails or drags on
Free collection at over 1,100 Argos and Sainsbury's points, with supermarket opening hours behind them
Bush was the second brand in Britain to ship Freely, in May 2024, ahead of Toshiba, Sharp, Panasonic and Metz
Argos Care can be added in store up to 45 days after purchase, and is provided by Domestic & General Insurance PLC as insurer rather than intermediary
A keyword search of the OPSS safety register for Bush returns exactly one notice
Manuals, user guides and helplines are searchable by catalogue or model number at argos-support.co.uk
cons: Nothing free beyond 12 months: no multi-year television guarantee, and a help-centre search for the word guarantee returns no article by that name
Argos Care's price, term and exclusions are not published anywhere readable before purchase — the help centre says only that some exclusions apply

The served product page carries no price and no energy efficiency class: on catalogue number 7623916 (Bush 32FT25CB) the class, the label link and the price all arrive by script, which is an odd way to meet a distance-selling display duty enforced by local authorities

16 Bush TiVo catalogue numbers sold between December 2024 and March 2026 have a plug fuse that fails the dimensional requirements of BS 1362, with a fire risk, and the owner has to register on a separate site to get the free cable
Argos tells owners of those sets to dispose of the old cable through WEEE facilities, yet its help centre publishes no electrical or television take-back article at all

No statement of spare-part availability for televisions, against a seven-year ecodesign duty, and the Argos Spares site is operated by Screwfix Spares Limited, a Kingfisher company, whose television parts are mostly remote controls
The business is being sold, with completion expected February 2027 and Argos Care included in the sale
verdict: Argos is the right shop for a cheap television you want to pick up today and a poor one for paperwork. The 12 months of free repair or replace is a fifth of what John Lewis includes, the extra cover is sold without a published price or exclusion list, and the served page gives you neither a price nor the energy class the distance-selling rules expect beside it. Against that, the Bush own-brand sets were second in the country onto Freely and now reach more than 70 live channels over broadband, collection is free at over 1,100 points, and the one open safety notice — 16 catalogue numbers with a BS 1362 fuse fault, remedied with a free cable — is the register working rather than a pattern. Buy on the screen and the collection slot, check your broadband is above 10Mbps before you rely on Freely, and if you want cover past the first year, ask for the Argos Care price and exclusions in writing before you pay.

faqs.q: How long is the guarantee on an Argos television?
faqs.a: Twelve months. A fault inside 30 days of receipt entitles you to a refund; after 30 days and inside 12 months Argos says it will “repair or replace the item at no cost to you”, and refund instead if that fails, takes too long or causes significant inconvenience. There is no free multi-year television guarantee, and no separate guarantee document published in the help centre.

faqs.q: Is my Bush television part of the 2026 plug recall?
faqs.a: Check the catalogue number against OPSS report 2606-0164, published 15 June 2026. Sixteen Bush TiVo numbers are listed — 7623916, 7615436, 7623930, 5024232, 7623057, 7140585, 6799418, 7049662, 5816505, 4743868, 5420001, 5024373, 6826271, 4723668, 7041251 and 7086388 — sold by Argos between December 2024 and March 2026. The plug's fuse does not meet the dimensional requirements of BS 1362 and may overheat. Register on the Argos Product Check site for a free replacement cable or fuse, then dispose of the old cable at a WEEE recycling point.

faqs.q: Do Argos televisions need an aerial or broadband?
faqs.a: The Freely sets, which include Bush, need broadband of at least 10Mbps, because live channels come over Wi-Fi. An aerial is optional and adds further live channels rather than being the main route. Freely lists over 70 live channels and is run by Everyone TV Limited, the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5 joint venture.

faqs.q: Is Argos Care worth buying with a television?
faqs.a: It depends on numbers Argos does not publish. The policy is provided by Domestic & General Insurance PLC as insurer, covers parts and labour on faults outside the manufacturer's guarantee, pays for labour only where an extended parts guarantee already exists, and can be added in store within 45 days of purchase. The price, the term and the exclusions are not published in the help centre, which says only that some exclusions apply, so ask for both before paying — and note that Argos Care transfers with the business when the sale to Swift Partners completes, expected February 2027.

faqs.q: Can I get spare parts for an Argos television?
faqs.a: Only up to a point. The ecodesign rules require seven years of spare parts to professional repairers after the last unit of a model is sold, including the internal power supply, connectors and capacitors, with the external power supply and remote control available to owners too, delivered within 15 working days of an order. Argos itself says only that it can supply parts “for some items” and points at argosspares.co.uk, which is operated by Screwfix Spares Limited and stocks mainly remote controls on the television side.

title: Asda Groceries: The £40 Threshold, the Delivery Pass and the Date You Cannot See
meta_title: Asda Groceries: £40 Minimum, £4 Charge, Cheapest Brands
meta_description: Asda was cheapest of eight supermarkets on a 220-item branded basket in August 2026 at £771.27. Delivery needs £40 or a £4 charge. Checked 30 September 2026.

headline.label: Delivery: what it costs and the basket that makes it free
headline.value: £40 minimum spend, or a £4 minimum basket charge below it — and slots included on a Delivery Pass from £3.95 a month (Asda's own figures, checked 30 September 2026)

intro:
Asda came out cheapest of eight supermarkets on a basket of 220 branded groceries in August 2026, at £771.27 against £782.39 at Tesco with a Clubcard and £869.16 at Sainsbury's without a Nectar card. Those are Which?'s figures, from daily price tracking across the month, checked on 30 September 2026. Asda's own accounts put the gap at 4–7% against the other traditional supermarkets.

The delivery side is built around one number. An Asda delivery order needs £40 of shopping, a Click & Collect order needs £25, and an order below the line attracts a £4 minimum basket charge rather than being refused. You can keep adding to a booked order until 11pm the night before, an Express slot brings a full-range shop within four hours and sometimes inside one, and there are more than 450 Click & Collect points across the UK. A Delivery Pass from £3.95 a month covers the slot fee on up to one delivery a day.

One term is unusually generous and worth knowing before you order. If Asda substitutes something it cannot pick, its own policy is that “if it costs less, we charge you less. If it costs more, we won't charge you the extra” — so a swap can only move the bill downwards. Weights on loose fruit, vegetables and meat are settled when the item is actually weighed, so those lines can move either way by a few pence.

key_facts.label: Who you are buying from
key_facts.value: Asda Stores Limited, company 00464777, incorporated 19 February 1949, Asda House, South Bank, Great Wilson Street, Leeds LS11 5AD — with Asda Delivery Limited (03873501) a separate active company at the same address

key_facts.label: Minimum spend
key_facts.value: £40 for delivery, £25 for Click & Collect, with a £4 minimum basket charge applied below either line

key_facts.label: Express delivery
key_facts.value: £8.50 to £8.99, no minimum spend at all, delivered within 4 hours of ordering and in as little as 1 hour

key_facts.label: Express Click & Collect
key_facts.value: £3.50 for a full-range shop collected within 4 hours; order by 12 noon for collection after 4pm

key_facts.label: Delivery Pass
