sections.heading: Three products share the name, and they do not cost the same
sections.html:
Search for an Aviva pension and you can land on any of three products. Sorting out which one you are looking at is the first useful thing you can do, because the charge is the main thing that differs and each of the three answers the question differently.

The Aviva Pension, badged as a SIPP. This is the one you can open yourself in an afternoon. It sits on Aviva's consumer platform alongside its stocks and shares ISA and investment account, and the Aviva Charge is 0.35% a year on the first £500,000 of investments held across all three, with nothing charged above that. Cash is outside the calculation altogether: the charge "is based on the total value of your investments apart from any cash you have in your account", in Aviva's own words. Its worked example takes £40,000 in a SIPP and £60,000 in an ISA and charges 0.35% of £100,000, which is £350 a year.

The workplace pension. Aviva's group personal pension carries more than 4.8 million members, offers up to 200 funds from more than 30 fund managers, and now advertises its annual management charge as "usually 0.3% to 0.75% of the member's pension a year". That range is new enough to be worth saying plainly: until recently there was no published figure at all. It is still a range rather than a price, because the charge is negotiated scheme by scheme on member numbers and contribution levels, so the only number that applies to you is on your own annual statement. The default investment sits in Aviva's My Future range, whose returns the governance committee publishes and which are set out further down this page. Automatic enrolment minimums are unchanged: 3% from the employer, 5% from the member, 8% in total.

Pension Portfolio. The adviser-sold version, on Aviva's advised platform, with its own charge scale and — as the last section shows — a less generous split of the interest on your cash. If a financial adviser set your pension up, this is almost certainly the one you hold.

The simplest test is who you pay. A charge appearing on a statement you receive at home, with no employer and no adviser in the picture, is the 0.35%. Anything else and the number you need is on your scheme documentation rather than on Aviva's website.

sections.heading: What 0.35% buys, and the four things that sit on top
sections.html:
The Aviva Charge is worked out daily on the value of your investments and taken monthly out of the cash account, from each product separately. If there is not enough cash sitting there, the terms (RD01003 06/2025, section 18) say Aviva disinvests from your funds, adding "an additional 10% of the disinvestment" to cover market movement between the sale date and the charge date, subject to a £10 minimum. That is tidier than it sounds: a pension held fully invested with no cash float will be nibbled at twelve times a year by small forced sales. Aviva gives 30 days' notice of any change to the Aviva Charge or the trading charge.

Four things are charged separately from the 0.35%, and all four are easy to miss.

The first is the fund's own cost, shown as an ongoing charges figure. Aviva's examples are blunt enough to be useful: £1,000 in one of its ready-made funds with an OCF of 0.35% costs £3.50 a year, and £10,000 in a fund with an OCF of 1% costs £100. Aviva does not take that money — "it's taken from your investments by the fund itself" — but on a portfolio of active funds it is routinely larger than the platform charge, which makes the 0.35% a floor rather than a total.

The second is dealing. Funds are free to buy and sell, and so is the ready-made range including the Universal Retirement Fund. Anything traded on an exchange — a UK share, an ETF, an investment trust — costs £4.99 a go, so a four-holding rebalance is £19.96. The third is tax and levies: 0.5% stamp duty reserve tax on most UK share purchases, plus the £1.50 Takeover Panel levy on trades over £10,000.

The fourth is money Aviva keeps rather than money it charges, and it is now large enough that Aviva counts it in its own worked example. The investor in that example pays £350 of Aviva Charge, £19.96 across four trades and £9.82 of interest retained on the cash in the account: £379.78 for the year. The last section explains where the £9.82 comes from, and it is the only one of the three a customer can do anything about.

sections.heading: Getting money in: £25 a month, 30 days to change your mind, and the transfers Aviva will not take
sections.html:
The entry points are low. £25 a month opens the pension; so does a single £5,000 payment, or £1,000 if you also set up £25 a month. You can open one from 18 and keep paying in until 75, after which Aviva "are unable to accept new payments". There is no upper age limit on transferring a pot in. Tax relief works the usual way at source — £80 of your money becomes £100 in the pension — with higher and additional rate taxpayers claiming the rest back, up to 45%, or 48% in Scotland.

The allowances are set by HMRC rather than Aviva, and the 2026/27 figures on GOV.UK are a £60,000 annual allowance, a money purchase annual allowance of £10,000 once you have flexibly accessed a pension, a lump sum allowance of £268,275 and a lump sum and death benefit allowance of £1,073,100. The taper is a separate mechanism from the £10,000 above and both tests have to be failed before it bites: threshold income above £200,000 and adjusted income above £260,000, grinding the £60,000 down to a floor of £10,000.

Transfers in are free from Aviva's side — "we don't charge you a penny" — take three to six weeks in its own estimate, and currently carry cashback for new Aviva Pension customers. The ladder runs from £100 on a transfer of £20,000 to £49,999 up to £2,500 at £1,000,000 or more, one payment per customer, applied for by 23 November 2026 with the money kept in the SIPP until 22 May 2027. Transfers of existing Aviva pensions are excluded.

There are hard limits on what can come across. Aviva will not take a defined benefit or final salary pension, a pension you have already started drawing, or one carrying a guaranteed annuity rate or other safeguarded benefit. Its own transfer page also lists what you might be giving up elsewhere: a tax-free lump sum above 25%, loyalty bonuses, enhanced life cover or death benefits, a protected pension age, or the right to take the money before 55. Transferring safeguarded benefits worth more than £30,000 requires regulated advice first.

The cooling-off period is 30 days from Aviva receiving your first payment, or from its confirmation that a transfer has been invested. Regular payments made in that window come back in full; a single payment is refunded "less any amount by which your investments might have fallen in value", and on a cancelled transfer Aviva pays back the lower of what it received and the value on the day you cancel. Charges tied to buying or selling investments are not refunded, so the money back is not guaranteed to be pound for pound.

sections.heading: Two Aviva companies, two reference numbers, and one that was worth re-checking
sections.html:
The Aviva Pension is assembled from two regulated entities, and both the product page and the key features document now give the same pairing. Aviva Wrap UK Limited, registered in England and Wales as company 4470008 with firm reference 231530, runs the platform. Aviva Pension Trustees UK Limited, company 2407799 with firm reference 465132, provides the pension itself and acts as trustee of the scheme the money sits in. Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited appears as the insurer behind any insured funds, and the small print attributes the MyAviva service to Aviva Insurance Limited without giving a number for it. All of them are Aviva, so there is no third-party administrator between you and the brand on the statement — which is not true of every pension sold under a household name.

An earlier version of this page flagged a possible documentation error in those reference numbers. Re-reading both sources on 11 October 2026, they agree: 231530 belongs to the platform operator and 465132 to the pension provider, and anyone checking the chain on the Financial Conduct Authority register will find the two numbers where the documents say they are.

Compensation cover is where a pension platform differs from an insured pension fund, and the distinction is worth more than it looks. The key features document sets Financial Services Compensation Scheme protection on collective and exchange-traded investments at "100% of the first £85,000 held per person per fund management firm", on shares at £85,000 per person per stockbroking firm, and on the account provider itself at £85,000 per person shared across any other Aviva Pension Trustees plans you hold. Insured funds are different again: there the FSCS "currently provides cover at 100% of the policy value without limit". Cash in the pension's cash account is protected to £120,000 for each bank Aviva places it with, the higher limit the Prudential Regulation Authority confirmed on 18 November 2025 and which took effect on 1 December 2025. So the same pension can carry three different levels of protection depending on what you buy with it, and the unlimited one is the insured fund most self-directed investors never touch.

For a workplace pension there is a second layer the direct product does not have. Default funds in automatic enrolment schemes are capped by law at 0.75% a year under regulation 7 of the Occupational Pension Schemes (Charges and Governance) Regulations 2015, and Aviva's workplace book is overseen by an Independent Governance Committee that reports publicly every year. Mark Thompson is listed as its independent chair; the 2026 report was signed by Sam Burden, who took the role on an interim basis in June 2026, and Simon Ellis joined as a firm-appointed member the following month.

sections.heading: What Aviva's own governance committee found
sections.html:
That committee's 2026 report, covering 1 January to 31 December 2025, is the most useful document on Aviva's pensions anywhere, and it is unusual in being written by people whose job is to criticise the firm paying them. Its conclusion is favourable: Aviva "continues to provide good value for money for members of its workplace pension schemes". The detail is more mixed.

On price, 65% of Aviva policyholders pay 0.5% a year or less. The full distribution is 22.3% under 0.3%, 23.4% between 0.3% and 0.4%, 19.1% between 0.4% and 0.5%, 10.1% between 0.5% and 0.6%, 24.8% between 0.6% and 0.75%, and 0.3% above 0.75%. Set that against the 0.3% to 0.75% range Aviva now advertises for the workplace product and two things fall out of it. Roughly a fifth of members are paying less than the bottom of the advertised range, which is the good news. But a quarter are paying between 0.6% and 0.75% — up to twice what the direct Aviva Pension charges — and a small group sit above the statutory cap, which is possible because the cap binds default arrangements rather than every fund a member can choose.

Performance to 31 December 2025 was strong in the growth funds: My Future Growth returned 14.3% over the year, My Future Focus Long Term Growth 14.2% and My Future Focus Growth 13.1%, against consumer price inflation of 3.3%. The committee was blunter about the Stewardship range, recording that it "challenged Aviva that the Stewardship Fund has not performed well against its benchmark over recent time periods" and that the fund "has performed less well over the last one, three and five years". It also thinks the name itself "risks misleading members about how it invests", and has gone on pressing for a change. It criticised the pace of Aviva's own fund migration too: a "significant cohort of members have not yet benefited from the new My Future Strategy", and it has asked Aviva to accelerate the transition. On investment pathways — used by about 27,000 policyholders holding roughly £1.5bn at the end of 2025 — it looked at proposed asset allocation changes to pathway 4 due in late 2026 or early 2027 and said it was "not yet persuaded the changes go far enough".

Two service figures from the same report are worth having. Aviva proactively traced about 41,000 lost members during 2025 and re-established contact with 44% of them, leaving its "gone away" population at 7% — in line with the industry average, which is another way of saying roughly one member in fourteen cannot be contacted. And 71,218 members attended one of 1,348 seminars during the year, against 70,869 at 1,195 seminars in 2024.

sections.heading: 20,143 complaints in six months, and what they were about
sections.html:
Aviva publishes its own complaints returns, which most providers bury. The numbers for 1 January to 30 June 2026 are the strongest argument against the product on this page.

In the decumulation and pensions grouping Aviva opened 20,143 complaints and closed 20,070 in those six months, a rate of 2.4 per 1,000 policies in force. It upheld 72.4% of them, and the single largest cause is recorded as "delays / timescales". The investments grouping on the same return opened 4,088 and closed 4,005, at 4.8 complaints per 1,000 client accounts and an uphold rate of 83.8%, with the same leading cause.

Read the two speed columns carefully, because they are separate groups rather than a running total. They are headed "Percentage closed within 3 days" and "Percentage closed after 3 days but within 8 weeks", and on pensions they read 25.5% and 63.2%. Added together, 88.7% of pensions complaints were resolved inside eight weeks and 11.3% took longer than the regulatory window; on investments the pair is 19.3% and 65%, so 84.3% inside eight weeks and 15.7% beyond it. Taking the second column on its own would make Aviva look far worse than its own return says it is.

An uphold rate above 70% is not evidence of a firm being hard on customers — upholding a complaint means agreeing with it. It is evidence of a firm generating a very large number of complaints it then agrees were justified, overwhelmingly about taking too long. For a product whose worst-case failure is a transfer or a drawdown payment arriving late, that is the risk worth pricing in, and it is the one thing a glossy charges page will never tell you.

For context from outside Aviva, the Financial Ombudsman Service published its 2025/26 annual data on 21 May 2026: 214,600 new complaints across all financial products and an average uphold rate of 30%. Personal pensions accounted for 3,777 cases with a 49% uphold rate. Aviva's own first-stage figure is well above both, though the two are not directly comparable — the Ombudsman sees only cases a firm has already refused.

sections.heading: Cash sits outside the 0.35%, and that is not a kindness
sections.html:
Aviva does not apply the Aviva Charge to cash. It makes money on cash a different way, and it publishes exactly how in document RD06102, dated April 2026.

Interest earned on the pension's cash account is split in bands. The customer gets 60% of the first 1.5 percentage points, 75% of the next 1.5, and 90% of anything above 3%. The factsheet's current figures run at an underlying rate of 3.05%, where the customer receives 2.08% and Aviva retains 0.97%; the illustration now on the consumer charges page uses 3.00%, where the customer gets 2.03% and Aviva still keeps 0.97%. If the rate from the bank is zero or negative, Aviva keeps no margin. Bank Rate has stood at 3.75% since the Monetary Policy Committee held it there on 17 September 2026, and neither Aviva page states the rate actually being credited this week — the April factsheet is the most recent dated figure there is, which is a long time for a number that moves with the base rate.

The terms are candid about the mechanism in a way the marketing is not. Section 7 of RD01003 06/2025 says "the interest rate applied is not the rate We receive from the banks", that Aviva "will deduct an amount (margin) from the banks' rates and pass the remaining amount (if any) on to You", and that where it receives more than it credits, "We will keep the excess and it will not be paid to Your Cash Account and will not be Your money".

Measured as a charge, 0.97% on cash is almost three times the 0.35% Aviva charges on invested money. On £5,000 of cash that is £48.50 a year that does not reach you, and it is the £9.82 that turns Aviva's own £369.96 of visible charges into £379.78. The practical lesson is that the cash account should hold roughly what the monthly charge needs and little more, because money parked there is the most expensive money in the pension — and unlike the other charges, this one you can avoid by staying invested.

The split is also not the same across Aviva's platforms. Its separate note on charge changes for the advised platform — Pension Portfolio, ISA Portfolio, Investment Portfolio and the Junior ISA, with the change applying no earlier than 17 August 2026 — sets the first band at 50% to the customer rather than 60%. Aviva's own example there is £1,000 of cash earning 3.05%: £30.50 of interest, of which the customer receives £19.30 and Aviva keeps £11.20. The same £1,000 on the consumer platform passes on £20.80, so an advised customer is £1.50 a year worse off per £1,000 of cash held. Two Aviva documents, two first-band splits — check which applies to your own plan rather than assuming the better of the two.

pros: Nothing is charged by Aviva above £500,000, which is rare — most platforms tier downwards but keep charging
Cash is excluded from the 0.35% calculation altogether
Buying and selling funds costs nothing, including the ready-made range, and exchange trades are £4.99
£25 a month, or £1,000 with a monthly payment, is a genuinely low entry point
Over 5,000 self-select funds plus UK shares, ETFs and investment trusts, with ready-made options and an Experts' Shortlist for people who do not want to choose
Defaqto put Aviva top of the SIPP market for adviser recommendations in the first half of 2026
No charge to transfer in, three to six weeks typical, and £100 to £2,500 cashback on £20,000-plus transfers applied for by 23 November 2026
Aviva now publishes a 0.3% to 0.75% range for the workplace charge, where it used to publish nothing
The workplace book is independently reviewed every year and the report is published in full, criticisms included
30 days to cancel, 30 days' notice of any charge change, and every company involved is Aviva rather than an outsourced administrator
cons: Aviva opened 20,143 decumulation and pensions complaints in the six months to 30 June 2026 and upheld 72.4% of them, with "delays / timescales" the main cause
11.3% of those complaints took longer than eight weeks to close, and on the investments side 15.7% did
On cash, Aviva retains 0.97 percentage points of a 3.00% to 3.05% rate — nearly three times what it charges on invested money, and £48.50 a year on £5,000
The most recent cash rate Aviva publishes is in a factsheet dated April 2026; the live rate credited to a cash account is not on its consumer pages
The first-band cash split differs between Aviva's own documents, 60% on the consumer platform and 50% on the advised one, which costs an advised customer £1.50 a year per £1,000 of cash
The 0.35% is effectively flat for almost everybody, since the only break is at £500,000, and cheaper platforms exist below that
Badged a SIPP, but the published asset list is funds, UK shares, ETFs and investment trusts — not the commercial property and unlisted holdings a full SIPP allows
FSCS cover on collective investments is £85,000 per person per fund management firm, not the unlimited protection that applies to an insured pension fund
The workplace charge is published only as a 0.3% to 0.75% range; 24.8% of policyholders pay between 0.6% and 0.75% and 0.3% pay more than the statutory cap

Aviva's own governance committee says the Stewardship fund has underperformed its benchmark over one, three and five years, that its name risks misleading members, and that a significant cohort are still waiting for the My Future transition
The committee is also "not yet persuaded" that the pathway 4 asset allocation changes due in late 2026 or early 2027 go far enough
No defined benefit pension, no pension already in payment and nothing with a guaranteed annuity rate can be transferred in
Monthly charge collection disinvests from your funds with a 10% buffer and a £10 minimum if the cash account is short, so a fully invested pot gets twelve small forced sales a year
verdict: As a place to hold a pension you manage yourself, the Aviva Pension is priced in the middle of the market and built better than its price suggests: 0.35% to £500,000 with nothing above and nothing on cash, free fund dealing, £4.99 exchange trades, more than 5,000 funds and a £25 monthly minimum. The free transfer in and the cashback running to 23 November 2026 make consolidating old pots into it cheap to do, provided none of them carries a guarantee worth keeping. Two things should temper the decision. The first is service: Aviva's own published return shows 20,143 pensions complaints in six months with 72.4% upheld and delay the leading cause, and 11.3% of them took longer than eight weeks to close. The second is cash, where Aviva keeps 0.97 of about 3 percentage points — fine if you hold a float for charges, expensive if you drift into cash and leave it there, and the figure it publishes for that is now six months old. If you already have an Aviva workplace pension, none of the 0.35% applies to you; find your own annual management charge on your scheme statement, because Aviva publishes only a 0.3% to 0.75% range and a quarter of its workplace members are paying between 0.6% and 0.75%.

faqs.q: What does the Aviva Pension actually cost a year?
faqs.a: The Aviva Charge is 0.35% a year on the first £500,000 of investments you hold across your Aviva pension, ISA and investment account combined, nothing above £500,000, and nothing on cash. On £100,000 that is £350, which is Aviva's own worked example. On top sit each fund's ongoing charges figure, £4.99 per trade on shares, ETFs and investment trusts, 0.5% stamp duty on most UK share purchases and a £1.50 levy on trades over £10,000. Aviva's own example totals £379.78 for the year once £9.82 of retained interest on cash is counted. The charge is calculated daily and taken monthly from the cash account.

faqs.q: How do I find out what my Aviva workplace pension charges?
faqs.a: Your annual statement, or your scheme documentation from your employer. Aviva advertises the annual management charge on its group personal pension as "usually 0.3% to 0.75% of the member's pension a year" and negotiates the actual figure scheme by scheme on member numbers and contribution levels. For scale, its governance committee reported that 65% of policyholders pay 0.5% a year or less, 22.3% pay under 0.3%, 24.8% pay between 0.6% and 0.75%, and 0.3% pay more than 0.75%. The 0.75% statutory cap applies to default arrangements, not to every fund you can pick.

faqs.q: Can I move an old pension into the Aviva Pension?
faqs.a: In most cases yes, and Aviva does not charge for it — three to six weeks is its own estimate, and there is no upper age limit on transferring in. It will not accept a defined benefit or final salary pension, one you have already begun taking money from, or one with a guaranteed annuity rate or other safeguarded benefit. Check what you would lose before moving anything: a tax-free lump sum above 25%, a loyalty bonus, enhanced death benefits, a protected pension age or an early access right can all be worth more than a charge saving. Transferring safeguarded benefits over £30,000 requires regulated advice. Cashback of £100 to £2,500 is available on transfers of £20,000 or more applied for by 23 November 2026, excluding existing Aviva pensions.

faqs.q: When can I take the money out?
faqs.a: From 55 at present, rising to 57 on 6 April 2028 unless you hold a protected pension age. Normally 25% comes out tax free, up to the lump sum allowance of £268,275 for 2026/27, and the rest is taxed as income. On the consumer platform the income route is drawdown; buying a guaranteed income for life means moving the money to an annuity provider, which can be Aviva or anyone else. Anyone aged 50 or over can get a free appointment with Pension Wise through MoneyHelper before deciding.

faqs.q: Is my money safe if Aviva fails?
faqs.a: The pension's assets are held separately from Aviva's own, and the scheme's trustee is Aviva Pension Trustees UK Limited, company 2407799, firm reference 465132. The key features document puts Financial Services Compensation Scheme cover on collective and exchange-traded investments at 100% of the first £85,000 per person per fund management firm, on shares at £85,000 per person per stockbroking firm, and on the account provider itself at £85,000 per person — not the unlimited protection that applies to an insured pension fund, which is a real difference between a platform pension and an older-style insured one. Cash in the pension's cash account is covered to £120,000 per bank, the limit that took effect on 1 December 2025.

title: Avonline Broadband Satellite Internet
meta_title: Avonline Broadband: What Happened and Where It Went
meta_description: Avonline sold satellite broadband from 2002 and hit 30Mbps in 2016. The brand was renamed Bigblu in 2018. Here is the record and where the service is now.

headline.label: Cheapest advertised monthly price
headline.value: No longer sold — the last package advertised under the Avonline name was 30Mbps down and 2Mbps up, and the satellite business was renamed Bigblu on 31 August 2018

intro:
Avonline began installing television and telecommunications equipment in 1981, started putting satellite broadband into British homes in 2002, built fibre networks past more than 2 million UK premises and installed digital services in over 4 million homes and businesses. By 31 October 2016 it was advertising a 30Mbps satellite connection to anyone in England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland, two years before the government's own universal service floor of 10Mbps came into force.

The brand is no longer sold. Avonline Satellite Services Limited (company 10201939) became Bigblu Services Limited on 31 August 2018; Avonline Network Services Limited (company 10201726) became M Group Telecom Limited on 1 April 2025; and Avonline Limited, registered as Avonline plc until 2019, was dissolved on 16 March 2026. Nothing can be bought under the name today. Every figure on this page was checked on 4 October 2026 against Companies House, Ofcom, the London Gazette and the companies' own websites.

The service itself did not disappear with the name. It is sold today as Bigblu, run out of the same Oxfordshire town on a phone number one digit group away from the old one, at £24.99 a month for an average of 21Mb/s with no data cap. The complication is that avonlinebroadband.com is still live, still advertises the 2016 product in the present tense, and has had cryptocurrency link-spam injected into its home page. That is the gap this page is here to close.

sections.heading: Thirty-five years of rural installs, and the numbers behind them
sections.html:
Avonline was not a reseller that appeared when satellite broadband became fashionable. The company dated itself to 1981 and had been selling satellite broadband since 2002, which made it one of the first in Britain to do so. By its own account in October 2016 it had built fibre networks past more than 2 million UK premises and installed digital services in over 4 million UK homes and businesses — a contractor's record rather than a retailer's, and the reason councils took its calls.

The product that made its name arrived on 14 April 2014. Running on Avanti Communications Group's HYLAS 2 satellite, roughly 22,000 miles up, it was sold from £19.95 a month with a minimum £50 upfront payment and hardware rented at £5 a month on a two-year term. The service guaranteed a 9Mbps minimum average download with up to 20Mbps available, and installation inside a week.

What stood out was the granularity. Allowances ran from 5GB to 150GB a month, unlimited overnight downloads were thrown in free on every package above 50GB, speed was measured on a 30-day rolling basis, and customers had a three-month window to move up or down tiers without charge. Mark Wynn, then managing director, claimed at the time that "no-one else in the UK can give such a specific service commitment and so many different payment options". On the published tier structure that was a fair claim; a decade on, most satellite packages are a single flat tariff.

By 31 October 2016 the ceiling had risen to 30Mbps. Avonline's own framing of why that mattered holds up: it put the figures at 8% of UK homes, some 2.4 million, unable to receive 10Mbps or more, rising to 48% — about 1.5 million — in rural areas, against a government superfast definition of 24Mbps and fibre-to-the-cabinet plans covering 97% or 98% of premises by 2020. A 30Mbps dish beat the superfast threshold in places the cabinet programme was never going to reach, and it saved roughly £200 a year in line rental for anyone who dropped their landline.

sections.heading: The name came off the register in three dated steps
sections.html:
Satellite Solutions Worldwide bought Avonline's satellite arm on 7 July 2016, and rebranded itself Bigblu Broadband Group in May 2018. The paperwork behind that is public, free and exact, and it is the only reliable way to tell what happened to which half of the business.

The satellite retail business. Avonline Satellite Services Limited, incorporated 26 May 2016, became Bigblu Services Limited on 31 August 2018, company number 10201939, SIC code 61300 for satellite telecommunications. Its parent, Avonline Satellite Services Holdings Limited, incorporated 12 May 2016, became Bigblu Services Holding Ltd on the same day, company number 10177312. Both are registered at 60 Gracechurch Street in London. That is the entity a former Avonline customer's contract now sits under.

The network and installation business. Avonline Network Services Limited, company 10201726, kept the name far longer and became M Group Telecom Limited only on 1 April 2025. It is registered in Stevenage, is up to date on its filings — accounts to 31 March 2025 filed, next due 31 December 2026 — and carries all three telecoms SIC codes. It is a contractor that builds networks for other people, not a service a householder can buy.

The holding companies. Avonline Holdings Limited (10177556) was dissolved on 8 June 2021. Avonline Network Services Holdings Limited (10177313) was dissolved on 4 April 2023. Avonline Limited (03756315), incorporated on 21 April 1999 and registered as Avonline plc until 24 April 2019, filed its last accounts to 30 June 2019, its last confirmation statement on 21 April 2020, and was dissolved on 16 March 2026. Its registered office by then was care of an accountancy firm in Bristol.

Read in order, those dates say something useful: the trading business was sold and renamed in 2016 to 2018, the contracting business carried the name until 2025, and the original company was wound up in March 2026. There is no insolvency in that sequence and no customer was left without a service. The brand was retired commercially, in stages, over a decade.

sections.heading: The website nobody switched off
sections.html:
Eight years after the rename, avonlinebroadband.com is still resolving and still selling. Its home page carries the headline "Superfast 30Mbps broadband now available in England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland", quotes 30Mbps download and 2Mbps upload, and gives a phone number, 01869 222 895. Nothing on it says the company has been renamed.

The regional pages are worse, because they are more specific. The Northumberland page offers "up to 22Mbps speeds and unlimited data" with uploads to 6Mbps, promises "now get connected FREE this month", describes Avonline as "the UK's largest satellite broadband provider", and states that it "has been hand picked by Northumberland County Council as their satellite broadband partner" under the iNorthumberland programme. It names a regional coordinator and offers a mobile demonstration vehicle for community groups.

Northumberland County Council's own broadband pages, last updated 20 June 2025, name no satellite provider at all. What they describe is Project Gigabit — the government's £5 billion fibre programme — with £7.3 million going into more than 3,750 rural premises in north Northumberland, a national voucher pot of up to £210 million and individual vouchers raised to £4,500 a premises, plus council top-ups for properties below 30Mbps. A reader who rings the number on that regional page expecting a council-endorsed satellite install is working from a prospectus about a decade out of date.

There is a further problem, and it is the one that should decide whether anybody follows a link to this domain at all. The home page now carries a paragraph of injected search-engine spam promoting cryptocurrency presales: "Satellite broadband enhances crypto transactions by providing high-speed, global connectivity... For investors exploring best crypto presales 2025, satellite technology ensures uninterrupted access to platforms". That is not marketing copy anyone at a telecoms company wrote. It is the signature of an unmaintained site that has been compromised or sold for links, and it is dated to 2025 by its own text. Several pages that would let a visitor check anything — the FAQs and the contact page among them — return a 403 error and cannot be read.

sections.heading: Where the satellite service actually went
sections.html:
Bigblu still sells satellite broadband to British households from a consumer site, and the continuity with Avonline is not a guess: the contact number is 01869 722 425, in the same Bicester dialling code as Avonline's 01869 222 895. The advertised offer on 4 October 2026 was £24.99 per month for "average speeds of 21 Mb/s" with an "uncapped, unlimited data allowance", and a 14-day risk-free cancellation period. Hardware and installation charges were not stated on the page, and the contract term was not either.

Priced against history, that is a reasonable deal and a sobering one. A household paying £19.95 in 2014 for a guaranteed 9Mbps minimum average now pays £24.99 for an advertised 21Mb/s average with no cap — roughly 25% more money for more than double the speed and no allowance to watch. Over twelve years that is barely a real-terms rise. But the ceiling has gone nowhere: 21Mb/s in 2026 is below the 24Mbps superfast line that Avonline's own 2016 release used as its benchmark, and well below the 30Mbps the brand was advertising when it was sold.

The corporate picture behind that offer needs stating plainly. On 4 October 2026 Companies House showed both Bigblu Services Limited and Bigblu Services Holding Ltd as "Active proposal to strike off". Neither has filed accounts since those for the period ending 30 November 2022, filed on 30 November 2023; accounts have been due since 30 November 2024. Bigblu Services Limited's last confirmation statement was dated 17 May 2024 with the next due 31 May 2025; the holding company's was dated 23 May 2024 with the next due 6 June 2025. A first Gazette notice for compulsory strike-off was published for Bigblu Services Limited on 28 January 2025 and that action was suspended on 14 March 2025, which is what a company does when it objects or starts filing again. The London Gazette holds 31 notices against the name across eighteen years.

A proposal to strike off is not insolvency and is not a closure. It usually means paperwork, and it was suspended once already. It is still the single most important thing to know before paying a deposit, and the clock is readable: anyone considering a two-year commitment can check the same status word on Companies House before they sign, for nothing, in a minute.

sections.heading: What satellite is for now, and what Ofcom will accept instead of a cable
sections.html:
The case for a dish has narrowed to a sharp point, and the regulator has drawn it. Ofcom's guidance on the right to request a decent broadband connection, published 8 August 2023 and last updated 19 June 2026, sets the floor at 10 Mbit/s download and 1 Mbit/s upload. If the only decent service available to a property costs more than £59.60 a month, the householder can request a connection instead. Where the cost of building or upgrading their share of the network is £3,400 or less, BT pays for the work — or KCOM in the Hull area. Above that figure, the customer covers the difference, and those bills have historically run into tens of thousands of pounds.

In July 2026 Ofcom confirmed that an available Starlink service can count as a decent alternative, which means a request can be refused on the strength of it. Trade reporting of Ofcom's January 2026 data put roughly 39,000 UK premises beyond the reach of decent fixed-line or fixed-wireless broadband — about 23,000 in England, 9,000 in Scotland, 6,000 in Wales and 1,500 in Northern Ireland. Those figures come from the trade press rather than from an Ofcom page this page could read directly, and are worth confirming with Ofcom before anyone relies on them.

Two things follow for a reader who arrived here looking for Avonline. First, a geostationary service of the kind Avonline sold — signal travelling 22,000 miles each way, with the latency that implies — is now the third choice rather than the first, behind fibre where it exists and behind low-orbit satellite where it does not. Second, the universal service route is free to try and is worth trying before buying any dish, because the same regulator that will accept satellite as an answer also obliges BT to spend up to £3,400 trying to avoid needing one.

sections.heading: The consumer protections a retired brand cannot give you
sections.html:
This is where the gap between satellite and the rest of the broadband market is widest, and it has nothing to do with Avonline's conduct. Ofcom's automatic compensation scheme pays £10.34 for every calendar day a fault goes unrepaired beyond two working days, £32.31 for a missed engineer appointment and £6.46 for each day a new service starts late, with the amounts rising annually with inflation. The scheme is voluntary, and exactly ten providers have signed it: BT, EE, Hyperoptic, Plusnet, Sky including NOW Broadband, TalkTalk, Utility Warehouse, Virgin Media, Vodafone and Zen Internet. No satellite provider is among them, and none ever has been. A rural customer therefore gets no automatic payment for the outage that the dish was bought to prevent.

The same pattern repeats in Ofcom's quarterly complaints tables, which name only providers above a market-share threshold. No satellite ISP is large enough to appear, so there is no published complaints rate for any of them — not a good one and not a bad one. That is an absence rather than an accusation, but it leaves a buyer with nothing comparable to check.

Telecoms providers must belong to an alternative dispute resolution scheme, which in this sector is CISAS, run by CEDR, or the Communications Ombudsman, reachable after eight weeks or on a deadlock letter. Which scheme covers the successor could not be established for this page: the terms and complaints pages on the Bigblu consumer site are blocked to automated reading, and nothing on the surviving Avonline pages names a scheme. It should be confirmed on the phone before signing anything. The practical backstops remain Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 for anything bought on credit above £100, and card chargeback below it.

pros: A genuine rural pioneer rather than a reseller — trading from 1981 and selling satellite broadband from 2002, six years before the first UK superfast targets
A contractor's track record behind the brand: fibre networks past more than 2 million UK premises and digital services installed in over 4 million homes and businesses
The 2014 tier structure was unusually flexible for satellite — allowances from 5GB to 150GB, free unlimited overnight downloads above 50GB, and a three-month window to change tier without charge
A 30Mbps service from October 2016 beat the government's 24Mbps superfast definition in places the fibre-to-the-cabinet programme was not going to reach
The service was not abandoned: it continues under Bigblu from the same Bicester base at £24.99 a month for an uncapped 21Mb/s average
Twelve years on, the successor's price is only about 25% above Avonline's 2014 entry tariff for more than double the speed and no data cap
cons: Nothing can be bought under the Avonline name. The satellite business was renamed Bigblu on 31 August 2018, the network business became M Group Telecom on 1 April 2025, and Avonline Limited was dissolved on 16 March 2026.
avonlinebroadband.com is still live and still advertises the 2016 product in the present tense, with a 30Mbps headline and a working phone number, and says nothing anywhere about the rename.

The home page carries injected search-engine spam promoting cryptocurrency presales, dated 2025 by its own text — the clearest possible sign that nobody is maintaining the site. Pages a visitor would use to check anything, including the FAQs and the contact page, return 403 errors.

The regional pages make two claims that nothing published today supports: that Avonline is "the UK's largest satellite broadband provider", and that it was "hand picked by Northumberland County Council as their satellite broadband partner". The council's own pages, updated 20 June 2025, name no satellite provider and describe a fibre programme instead.

Both successor companies, Bigblu Services Limited and Bigblu Services Holding Ltd, were shown as "Active proposal to strike off" on 4 October 2026, with accounts overdue since 30 November 2024 and confirmation statements overdue since mid-2025.

No current price, data allowance, contract term, installation charge or early termination fee is published anywhere under the Avonline name. The £19.95 and £50 figures are from April 2014 and are history, not quotes.

Satellite customers get nothing from Ofcom's automatic compensation scheme — no satellite provider is among its ten signatories — and no satellite ISP is large enough to appear in Ofcom's published complaints tables.

Which alternative dispute resolution scheme covers the successor could not be confirmed, because its terms and complaints pages are closed to automated reading and the surviving Avonline pages name none.
verdict: Avonline earned its reputation honestly. A company trading since 1981 that put satellite broadband into British homes from 2002, built fibre past more than 2 million premises and sold a 30Mbps rural connection in October 2016 was doing something the national programme could not, and the 2014 package range was more thoughtfully built than most satellite tariffs sold today. None of that is available to buy. The satellite arm became Bigblu Services Limited on 31 August 2018, the network arm became M Group Telecom Limited on 1 April 2025, and Avonline Limited was dissolved on 16 March 2026. The service continues under Bigblu at £24.99 a month for an uncapped 21Mb/s average, from the same Oxfordshire base — though both Bigblu companies stood at "Active proposal to strike off" with accounts overdue when this page was checked, which is worth looking up again before paying a deposit. Anyone who followed a search for Avonline to its old website should know that the site is unmaintained to the point of carrying cryptocurrency link-spam, and that its council endorsement and "UK's largest" claim are not supported by anything either party publishes now. The better first move is free: ask BT for a universal service connection, which obliges it to spend up to £3,400 on your behalf before a dish becomes the answer at all.

faqs.q: Is Avonline Broadband still trading?
faqs.a: No. Avonline Satellite Services Limited became Bigblu Services Limited on 31 August 2018, Avonline Network Services Limited became M Group Telecom Limited on 1 April 2025, and Avonline Limited — registered as Avonline plc until 2019 — was dissolved on 16 March 2026. The website avonlinebroadband.com is still online and still advertises a 30Mbps service, but no company sells under the name.

faqs.q: What happened to my Avonline satellite broadband contract?
faqs.a: It sits with Bigblu Services Limited, company number 10201939, which is the same legal entity renamed on 31 August 2018. The company is registered at 60 Gracechurch Street, London EC3V 0HR. The consumer sales line is 01869 722 425, in the same Bicester dialling code as the old Avonline number.

faqs.q: What did Avonline satellite broadband cost?
faqs.a: From 14 April 2014 it started at £19.95 a month with a minimum £50 upfront payment and hardware rented at £5 a month on a two-year term, with allowances from 5GB to 150GB and free unlimited overnight downloads above 50GB. It guaranteed a 9Mbps minimum average with up to 20Mbps available, and by 31 October 2016 the top speed was 30Mbps. Those are historic figures and not available today.

faqs.q: Why does the Avonline website still show prices and a phone number?
faqs.a: Because nobody has taken it down. The domain still serves pages written around 2014 to 2016, including regional pages offering a free connection "this month" and naming a county council partnership. The home page has also had cryptocurrency link-spam inserted into it, and the FAQ and contact pages return 403 errors. Treat the whole site as an archive rather than a shop.

faqs.q: Can I still get satellite broadband where Avonline used to install it?
faqs.a: Yes. Bigblu advertised £24.99 a month for an average of 21Mb/s with unlimited data and a 14-day cancellation period on 4 October 2026. Low-orbit services are the other route, and Ofcom confirmed in July 2026 that an available Starlink connection can count as decent broadband for universal service purposes.

faqs.q: Should I ask BT for a universal service connection first?
faqs.a: It costs nothing to ask and it can save a great deal. Ofcom's rules, last updated 19 June 2026, set decent broadband at 10 Mbit/s down and 1 Mbit/s up, and let you request a connection if the only decent service available to you costs more than £59.60 a month. If building your share of the network costs £3,400 or less, BT pays for it — KCOM in the Hull area. You only pay anything above that.

faqs.q: Do satellite broadband customers get Ofcom automatic compensation?
faqs.a: No. The scheme pays £10.34 a day for an unrepaired fault, £32.31 for a missed engineer appointment and £6.46 a day for a late start, but it is voluntary and only ten providers have joined: BT, EE, Hyperoptic, Plusnet, Sky including NOW Broadband, TalkTalk, Utility Warehouse, Virgin Media, Vodafone and Zen Internet. No satellite provider is among them.

title: AXA Home Insurance Review
meta_title: AXA Home Insurance 2026: What £196 a Year Actually Buys
meta_description: AXA paid 80.9% of home claims in 2025 and quotes from £196. The tier limits, the broker-only wordings and the excesses, taken from AXA's own documents.
intro:
AXA is one of the few home insurers in Britain that sells the same risk two ways: direct to you at axa.co.uk, and through brokers under its AXA Connect arm. Both routes lead to the same underwriter, AXA Insurance UK plc, firm reference 202312, which sits inside a group that wrote €116bn of premium in 2025. Buy direct and you choose between three named levels — AXA Home Insurance, AXA Plus and AXA Premier — with a quoted starting price of £196 a year, a figure 10% of AXA Plus customers paid or beat between 1 May and 31 July 2026.

The number worth carrying into a quote is 80.9%. That is the share of home insurance claims AXA says it paid across the 2025 calendar year. Set it against the FCA's own market data, published on 21 July 2026, which put claims acceptance across the home market at 62–71%, and AXA is claiming to settle a good deal more often than the sector average.

Every tier carries the same spine: guaranteed repairs for three years on work done by AXA's approved contractors, trace and access to find a leak before it can be fixed, architects' fees and debris removal, emergency access to the building and to the garden, and £2,000,000 of property owner's liability. Premier removes the rebuild ceiling altogether and folds in the extras that the other two charge for.

key_facts.label: Underwriter
key_facts.value: AXA Insurance UK plc, firm reference 202312

key_facts.label: Cover levels
key_facts.value: AXA Home, AXA Plus, AXA Premier

key_facts.label: Quoted from
key_facts.value: £196 a year (10% of AXA Plus customers, 1 May – 31 July 2026)

key_facts.label: Claims paid
key_facts.value: 80.9% of home claims, January–December 2025 (AXA's figure)

key_facts.label: Property owner's liability
key_facts.value: £2,000,000 on every tier

key_facts.label: Complaints
key_facts.value: 5.17 per 1,000 policies in the six months to 30 June 2026

sections.heading: Three price points, and the limits that separate them
sections.html:
The tiers are not a discount ladder with the same policy underneath. The ceilings move at every step. Buildings are capped at £500,000 on AXA Home, £1,000,000 on Plus and left unlimited on Premier. Contents run £50,000, £75,000 and £100,000. The valuables sub-limit inside that contents figure — jewellery, watches, collections — moves £10,000, £20,000, £30,000, and anything worth more than £1,500 on its own has to be listed by name on the schedule whichever level you buy.

Alternative accommodation is where the gap opens widest. If the house is uninhabitable, the buildings section pays up to £30,000 on Home, £50,000 on Plus and £100,000 on Premier, with a further £15,000, £20,000 or £25,000 sitting under the contents section. On a long subsidence or fire claim that difference is the whole argument.

Smaller limits repeat across all three: £500 for money in the house, £1,000 to replace keys and locks, bicycles covered to £350 each and £1,500 in total unless named separately. Garden contents and anything in an outbuilding are capped at £1,500, £3,000 or £4,500 by tier — low enough that a shed full of tools is worth checking before you assume it is covered.

Two extras are optional on Home and Plus but built into Premier: legal expenses, £50,000 as an add-on against £100,000 included, and home emergency, £1,000 per claim as an add-on against £1,500 included. Personal possessions cover away from the house is an add-on at any level, running from £1,000 to £15,000 of total cover with a £1,500 ceiling on any single item, and students away at university can be covered for £5,000 of belongings.

sections.heading: Who carries the risk, and who you argue with
sections.html:
AXA Insurance UK plc holds the permissions, and its firm reference of 202312 is printed on the product documents rather than left to be inferred; it is dual-regulated, prudentially by the Bank of England's Prudential Regulation Authority and for conduct by the Financial Conduct Authority, and the entry is checkable on the FCA Register. The parent group reported €116bn of gross written premium and €8.4bn of underlying earnings for 2025 when it published on 26 February 2026, with personal lines growing 7%.

Complaints follow the standard British route with one detail worth noting: the claims department handles claims complaints itself first, on 0330 024 6841 for the broker-sold wordings, and you have six months from AXA's final response letter to take the matter to the Financial Ombudsman Service. The Ombudsman is free to use and its decision binds the insurer if you accept it.

On flooding, AXA signed up to Flood Re's Build Back Better scheme on 26 January 2023, which makes up to £10,000 available on an eligible flood claim for resilience work — raised sockets, solid floors, flood doors — over and above simply putting the house back as it was. Flood Re itself has taken about half a million homes since 2016, and by AXA's account 98% of homes at flood risk can now get quotes from more than five brands, with four in five previously flooded homes seeing prices fall by more than half.

sections.heading: 80.9% paid, in a market the regulator measures at 62–71%
sections.html:
The FCA's general insurance value measures release of 21 July 2026 covers the whole of calendar 2025 and is the only place the home market gets marked publicly. Home insurance accepted 62–71% of claims. Motor accepted 99%. Travel sat at 83–86%. Home also carried the worst complaints record of any product line measured, with claims complaints running at 7–13% of claims registered while most other products stayed inside 0–6%.

Two more findings from that release change how a premium should be read. Claims costs held at 48% of premium across combined buildings and contents, up from 46% in 2024 — so a little under half of what a household pays comes back out as claims. And the average payout on buildings and contents rose 17% in a single year, which is the clearest reason quotes have moved regardless of provider.

AXA's 80.9% is self-published rather than taken from that dataset, and the FCA is explicit that firms have reported home claims acceptance inconsistently, so the two figures are not strictly like for like. Treated as a claim about AXA's own book rather than a league table position, it still points the right way. AXA also states that accidental damage makes up over one in three of the home claims it handles — a figure that matters more than it first appears, for reasons two sections down.

sections.heading: The broker version is not the same policy
sections.html:
Ask a broker for AXA home cover and you may be sold AXA Extra, AXA Exclusive or AXA Advanced instead. Same underwriter, same firm reference, materially different policy book — and on high-value contents the broker wordings are the stronger buy by a distance.

The January 2025 AXA Extra wording allows £15,000 for any one valuable and £30,000 for valuables in a single claim, against the £1,500 threshold that forces an item onto the schedule direct. Money is covered to £750 rather than £500. AXA Advanced goes further again: buildings unlimited, contents chosen anywhere between £75,000 and £300,000, a single valuable or personal effect covered to £15,000 and up to £25,000 if specified, total valuables capped at 40% of the contents sum insured rather than a flat figure, personal and property owner's liability at £5,000,000 apiece rather than £2,000,000, and alternative accommodation running for up to three years instead of against a cash ceiling.

The trade is that these come with a broker's fee and a broker's advice, and the excess structure is spelled out rather than hidden — AXA Advanced carries a £100 compulsory excess with a £1,000 minimum on subsidence, heave and landslip and £350 on escape of water. If your contents are ordinary, the direct route is simpler and probably cheaper. If you own one thing worth more than about £5,000, the broker wordings deserve a look before you fill in a comparison form.

sections.heading: A third of the claims, and two tiers charge extra for it
sections.html:
AXA's own material says accidental damage accounts for more than one in three of the home claims it deals with. It is also an optional add-on on AXA Home and AXA Plus, and included as standard only on Premier. The single most likely thing to go wrong — a foot through a ceiling, a drill through a pipe, a television off its stand — is the cover the cheaper two tiers leave off the base price.

That is legitimate product design and every insurer does some version of it, but it makes the headline £196 harder to read as a like-for-like number. A Plus policy without accidental damage is not the same product as a Premier policy, and a quote comparison that treats them as equivalent is comparing different things. Price the add-on in before deciding which tier is cheaper, and be aware the £196 figure describes the tenth percentile of Plus customers over a three-month window, not a typical price.

sections.heading: Thirty days empty, £500 for a leak, and the numbers that only surface on the quote
sections.html:
Leave the house unoccupied and the cover thins. AXA Home restricts after 30 consecutive days without anyone staying overnight; Plus and Premier allow 60. The broker-sold AXA Extra wording also stops at 30 consecutive days, after which escape of water and several other perils fall away. A long winter abroad, a probate property or a slow renovation can cross that line without anyone noticing until a claim is refused.

Excesses are the weaker part of the public disclosure. The direct site publishes tier limits in detail but no excess figures at all — the sample documents are offered for download and the real wording appears only once you have a quote. What can be verified comes from the broker side, and it is not trivial: AXA announced on 29 September 2023 that the escape of water excess on AXA Extra would rise from £350 to £500 for new business and renewals from 1 November 2023, with AXA Buy to Let following from 1 January 2024, saying plainly that "the performance of these products is not where intended". Escape of water is among the most common household claims there is, so a £500 excess on it is a real cost. Whether the direct tiers carry the same figure is not published, and needs confirming at quote stage.

The complaints numbers deserve the same flat treatment. In AXA's own FCA return for the six months to 30 June 2026, AXA Insurance UK plc recorded 5.17 complaints per 1,000 policies in force, closed 30.7% within three days and 61.7% within eight weeks, and upheld 59.2%. A high uphold rate cuts both ways: AXA agreeing with almost six in ten complainants means a complaint is worth making, and also that a lot of them had merit in the first place. The figure to watch is the other one — close to four in ten complaints were still open after eight weeks, which is the point at which you can take the case to the Ombudsman without waiting for AXA.

pros: 80.9% of home insurance claims paid across 2025 on AXA's own published figure, against an FCA-measured market range of 62–71%
Premier removes the rebuild ceiling entirely and includes accidental damage, £100,000 legal expenses and £1,500 home emergency as standard
Guaranteed repairs for three years, trace and access, and £2,000,000 property owner's liability on every tier including the cheapest
Up to £10,000 for flood resilient repairs under Flood Re's Build Back Better scheme, which AXA joined in January 2023
The broker wordings cover a single valuable to £15,000 and liability to £5,000,000, so high-value contents have a route that does not need a dozen specified items
cons: Accidental damage is an optional extra on AXA Home and AXA Plus despite AXA saying it accounts for over one in three of its home claims
No excess figures are published anywhere on the direct site before you get a quote; the broker wordings that do publish show £1,000 on subsidence and £500 on escape of water since 1 November 2023
The cheapest tier restricts cover after just 30 consecutive days unoccupied, half the 60 days allowed on Plus and Premier
Only 61.7% of complaints were closed inside eight weeks in the six months to 30 June 2026, leaving close to four in ten running longer
Entry-tier ceilings are tight for a family home — £50,000 contents, £10,000 of valuables within it, and £1,500 for everything in the garden and outbuildings combined
verdict: AXA Premier is a genuinely strong home policy — unlimited rebuild, accidental damage included, £100,000 of alternative accommodation — and the 80.9% claims-paid figure is a better number than the home market usually manages. The entry tier is a different proposition: £50,000 of contents, 30 days of permitted absence and accidental damage priced separately. Anyone with valuables should get a broker quote on AXA Extra or Advanced before buying direct, because the same insurer will cover a single item to £15,000 through that door and £1,500 through this one. Whichever level you look at, ask for the excesses in writing before you commit, since the public pages do not carry them.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites AXA home insurance?
faqs.a: AXA Insurance UK plc, firm reference 202312, whether you buy direct or through a broker. It is regulated for conduct by the Financial Conduct Authority and prudentially by the Prudential Regulation Authority, and the registration is checkable on the FCA Register.

faqs.q: Is the £196 price realistic?
faqs.a: It describes the cheapest tenth of AXA Plus customers between 1 May and 31 July 2026, not an average. It also excludes accidental damage, which is an optional add-on at that level, so a comparable Premier quote will look higher for reasons other than the insurer taking more margin.

faqs.q: What happens if I go away for a few months?
faqs.a: AXA Home restricts cover after 30 consecutive days with nobody staying overnight, and Plus and Premier after 60. The broker-sold AXA Extra wording uses 30 days as well. Tell AXA before you go rather than after — unoccupied property terms are one of the more common reasons a household claim is turned down.

faqs.q: How much of my jewellery is covered without listing it?
faqs.a: Direct, anything worth more than £1,500 has to be specified by name. The valuables total inside your contents sum is £10,000 on Home, £20,000 on Plus and £30,000 on Premier. The broker wordings are far more generous — AXA Extra allows £15,000 for any one valuable and £30,000 in a single claim.

faqs.q: If AXA turns down my claim, what can I do?
faqs.a: Complain to AXA first and wait for its final response, then take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service within six months of that letter. If AXA has not resolved the complaint within eight weeks you can go to the Ombudsman without waiting, which in the six months to 30 June 2026 applied to nearly four in ten of its complaints.

title: AXA Landlord Insurance Review
meta_title: AXA Landlord Insurance: 10 Properties, One Policy, From £15
meta_description: AXA covers up to 10 rental properties on one policy from £15 a month, with liability to £10m and 36 months of lost rent. Limits, excesses and gaps explained.
intro:
AXA sells landlord cover through AXA Business Insurance rather than alongside its household policies, and the product is shaped for people who own more than one address. Up to 10 rental properties sit on a single policy with one renewal date, the online quote starts at £15 a month for a single property — a figure 10% of customers paid or beat between April and June 2026 — and monthly instalments carry 0% interest rather than the credit charge most insurers add.

The standard cover is fuller than the price suggests. Subsidence, ground heave and landslip are built into the residential cover rather than sold as an extra — the commercial landlord product lists them as an option — and so are trace and access, cables and underground pipes, and the cost of rehousing tenants if the property becomes uninhabitable after a claim. Property owners' liability runs up to £10,000,000, and on the direct residential product the range on offer starts at £1,000,000. Houses, bungalows, individual flats, converted flats, whole blocks and land-only risks all quote online, and student lets are accepted — a tenant type several insurers refuse outright.

Behind all of it is AXA Insurance UK plc, company number 00078950, registered in England and dual-regulated by the Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority. Its firm reference, 202312, is printed on the product documents themselves and can be checked on the FCA Register. If loss of rent is added, the shortfall is covered for as long as 36 months, which is longer than a good many landlord policies will run.

key_facts.label: Sold by

sections.heading: Three AXA landlord policies, and they are not the same policy
sections.html:
Ask for AXA landlord cover and you can end up with one of three products, all underwritten by the same company and carrying materially different numbers.

Buy on axa.co.uk and you get the residential landlord wording: up to 10 properties, liability from £1,000,000 to £10,000,000, subsidence included, students welcome. Ask a broker and you may be sold the AXA Buy to Let personal-lines wording instead, where landlord's contents are chosen between £5,000 and £60,000, garden contents stop at £250, anything in a garage or outbuilding stops at £1,000, public liability is fixed at £2,000,000 and the legal expenses section is not AXA's at all — it is underwritten by AmTrust Europe Limited, firm reference 202189.

Ask the same broker for the commercial SME landlords product and the scale changes again: buildings to £10,000,000 per location, landlord's contents to £75,000, loss of rent to £2,500,000, employers' liability to £10,000,000, legal expenses at £100,000 any one claim and £1,000,000 any one period, and up to 20 locations on one schedule. That wording adds a 25% day-one uplift to the buildings figure as standard, pays up to £5,000 to make good a property used for drug cultivation and up to £2,500 for theft from outbuildings. It also declines students, which the direct product accepts. Establish which of the three you are being quoted before comparing the price to anything else.

sections.heading: Rent cover pays after damage, not after a tenant stops paying
sections.html:
AXA's rental income protection is loss of rent, not rent guarantee. It answers when fire, flood or similar insured damage makes the property uninhabitable, and on that trigger it is generous: the shortfall is met for up to 36 months, and the leaseholder wording allows an indemnity period of 12, 24 or 36 months to be chosen at inception. If access is denied or a public supply fails, the payment is capped at the lower of £250,000 or 25% of annual rental income, for a maximum of 12 weeks. Tenant rehousing runs to 20% of the damaged building's sum insured for up to 24 months.

What none of that reaches is a tenant who simply stops paying. AXA states plainly on its own pages that rent guarantee is not covered, and that matters more in 2026 than it did two years ago. Section 21 was abolished on 1 May 2026 under the Renters' Rights Act 2025; existing tenancies converted to assured periodic tenancies on that date, possession now needs a Section 8 ground, and landlords had to serve the government information sheet or an equivalent written statement by 31 May 2026 or face a penalty of up to £7,000 for a first offence. Arrears cases take longer than they used to, and the AXA policy does not stand behind that gap. Rent guarantee has to be bought elsewhere.

One footnote from the Financial Ombudsman Service puts the size of that market in perspective: in the quarter to June 2026 it recorded fewer than 10 new rent protection complaints in the whole country, against 1,766 for buildings insurance. Very few landlords are buying the product at all.

sections.heading: Forty-five days is the number to write on the tenancy file
sections.html:
Every version of this cover tightens once a property is empty. The limit is 45 consecutive days. Past that point AXA's own summary says the property is no longer covered as normal, and the broker SME wording is more explicit again: 45 days of full cover mid-term, after which the risk is referred back to an underwriter. A wholly unoccupied property will not be taken on as new business at all, and no more than 20% of a portfolio can be empty when the policy starts.

Void periods between tenancies, a probate sale, a refurbishment between lets or a slow eviction can all cross 45 days without anyone thinking to telephone. That is the single most likely way a landlord holding this policy finds a claim refused, and it is worth a diary entry on the day a tenant hands the keys back.

Excesses vary by wording and are only partly published. The buy-to-let document shows a £100 compulsory excess with a minimum of £250 on escape of water; the SME wording runs variable property damage excesses of £100 to £500 that cannot be adjusted for flood, malicious damage, theft by tenant or subsidence; the leaseholder wording carries a £200 minimum on property damage and £1,000 on subsidence. The direct site publishes no excess figures before you reach a quote, so the number that will apply to you is one you have to ask for.

sections.heading: Complaints, and how AXA's own figures read
sections.html:
AXA publishes its regulatory complaints return, which is more than many insurers do voluntarily. For the six months to 30 June 2026, AXA Insurance UK plc opened 18,717 complaints and closed 18,093. It upheld 59.2% of them — above the 55.54% average across all financial services firms the FCA reported for the second half of 2025 — and the leading cause was general administration and customer service rather than claims decisions.

A high uphold rate can be read two ways. It means a large share of complaints were justified; it also means a customer who complains to AXA has a better than even chance of AXA agreeing without the matter going further. If it does go further, the Financial Ombudsman Service is free and its decision binds the insurer if you accept it. The Ombudsman took 6,399 new buildings insurance complaints across 2025/26 and upheld 38% of them, so a landlord dispute over a building claim is neither unusual nor a lost cause.

The regulator's own product data does not cover this market. The FCA's general insurance value measures release of 21 July 2026 reports claims acceptance for consumer lines only, and landlord and property owners' policies fall outside it — there is no published acceptance rate for this product from anyone, AXA included. Any comparison table claiming one is inferring it.

sections.heading: The starting price moves depending on which AXA page you land on
sections.html:
AXA quotes three different entry figures across its own landlord section, and each describes a different window. The main landlord page says £15 a month, based on the cheapest 10% of customers between April and June 2026. The multi-property page says £14 a month, drawn from January to March 2026. The landlord FAQ page quotes £173 a year. All three are honest tenth-percentile figures with the sample period disclosed, which is better practice than most, but they describe single properties on the cheapest risks — a terraced flat let to a working professional, not a four-bed HMO with students in it.

Price a landlord policy on the limits instead. The gap between £1,000,000 and £10,000,000 of property owners' liability costs very little and matters enormously if a tenant is injured by something structural. The £5,000 cap on malicious damage and theft by tenants is the figure most likely to disappoint after a bad let, and it is the same £5,000 on both the direct and the broker wordings. And landlord's contents at £5,000 to £60,000 on the buy-to-let wording is a decision about white goods and carpets, not furniture you would insure at home.

pros: Up to 10 rental properties on one policy with a single renewal date, and up to 20 locations on the broker wording
Subsidence, ground heave and landslip included as standard on the residential product rather than sold as an extra
Property owners' liability available up to £10,000,000, with £2,000,000 fixed on the buy-to-let wording
Loss of rent runs for up to 36 months once a property is uninhabitable after an insured event
Student tenants and HMOs are quoted online, where several insurers decline them
0% interest on monthly instalments, and AXA publishes its own complaints figures rather than leaving them to the regulator
cons: No rent guarantee at any price — a tenant who stops paying is not an insured event, and Section 21 possession ended on 1 May 2026
Cover changes materially after 45 consecutive days empty, and a wholly unoccupied property will not be accepted as new business
AXA Insurance UK plc upheld 59.2% of the 18,717 complaints it opened in the six months to 30 June 2026, above the 55.54% market average
No excess figures are published on the direct site before you get a quote; the broker documents show £250 on escape of water and £1,000 on subsidence
Malicious damage or theft by tenants is capped at £5,000, which will not re-fit a stripped property
Three separate AXA landlord wordings carry different limits and different rules on students, so a quote comparison needs the document reference as well as the price
verdict: A solid, well-documented landlord policy for someone with one to ten residential properties who wants the building, the liability and the rebuild covered without arguing about subsidence. The limits are competitive, the 36-month loss of rent is better than average, and the disclosure is more honest than most. Buy it for the bricks and mortar, watch the 45-day empty rule, and buy rent guarantee somewhere else.

faqs.q: How many properties can I put on one AXA landlord policy?
faqs.a: Up to 10 residential properties quote online on a single policy with one renewal date. The commercial landlord product also stops at 10 online. The broker-sold SME landlords wording stretches to 20 locations and can mix residential, commercial and mixed-use property in one portfolio.

faqs.q: Does AXA cover me if my tenant stops paying the rent?
faqs.a: No. AXA covers loss of rent after insured damage makes the property uninhabitable, for up to 36 months. It does not sell rent guarantee, which is the cover that responds to arrears. Since Section 21 was abolished on 1 May 2026 possession requires a Section 8 ground, so that is a gap worth filling with a separate policy.

faqs.q: What happens if my rental property is empty between tenants?
faqs.a: Cover holds for 45 consecutive days. Beyond that the property counts as unoccupied and the policy restricts — on the broker wording the risk is referred to an underwriter. Tell AXA before the 45 days run out rather than after a claim.

faqs.q: Are student tenants and HMOs accepted?
faqs.a: On the direct residential product, yes — AXA quotes student lets online and says an HMO may need additional cover, with property owners' liability available up to £10,000,000. The broker SME landlords wording declines students, so the answer depends on which AXA product you are being offered.

faqs.q: Who underwrites AXA landlord insurance and how do I complain?
faqs.a: AXA Insurance UK plc, company number 00078950, firm reference 202312, dual-regulated by the PRA and the FCA. Legal expenses on the buy-to-let wording are underwritten separately by AmTrust Europe Limited, firm reference 202189. Complain to AXA first; if you are not satisfied within eight weeks, or you get a final response you disagree with, the Financial Ombudsman Service will look at it free of charge.

title: AXA Tradesman Insurance Review
meta_title: AXA Tradesman Insurance: £10m Cover From £7 a Month
meta_description: AXA insures its own trades policies: £10m public and employers' liability with no excess on either, plus tools cover. What the £7 headline really buys.
intro:
AXA is one of the few names in trades insurance that carries the risk itself. There is no broker in the middle and no panel shopping your details around: the quote comes from AXA, the policy is underwritten by AXA Insurance UK plc (registered number 78950, firm reference 202312, Ipswich), and the claims line answers in the same building. The company says it protects over 867,000 businesses, and its trades list runs from electricians, plumbers and bricklayers through roofers, plasterers, tilers and kitchen fitters to locksmiths, glaziers, gardeners and window cleaners.

The headline covers are generous for a policy you can buy on a phone in ten minutes. Public liability runs to £10,000,000 and employers' liability to the same figure. Neither section carries a standard excess, so a third-party settlement is not reduced by a first slice you have to find yourself. Defending a health and safety prosecution is covered to £1,000,000, corporate manslaughter costs to another £1,000,000, and AXA pays £250 a day when you or a member of staff has to sit in court. Every business customer gets a legal and tax helpline whether or not they buy the legal expenses add-on. Prices, AXA says, start at £7 a month or £77 a year.

Around that core you bolt on what the trade needs: tools and own plant, hired-in plant, contract works, business equipment, professional indemnity, personal accident and legal expenses. It is a build-your-own policy rather than a packaged tradesman product, which suits a sole trader with a van and a drill as readily as a four-man firm on a site.
