intro:
Barclays advanced £17.7bn of new mortgages in the first half of 2026, up from £15.4bn a year earlier, and its UK mortgage balances stood at £176.7bn on 30 June 2026 against £166.8bn twelve months before. Those are the bank's own numbers, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and every figure on this page was re-checked on 16 October 2026.

Two things changed in the six weeks before that check, and both widen who Barclays will lend to. Its Fast-Track Remortgage service went live across the whole market on 7 September 2026 after an eight-month pilot with Mortgage Advice Bureau, offering an offer in 24 hours and completion in as little as five days. Then on 15 October 2026 Barclays began counting a limited company's profit after tax towards affordability for directors who own more than half the business, on residential and buy-to-let alike, with the restriction tied to property value removed.

The pricing has moved recently and in one direction. Barclays withdrew a market-leading 4.75% two-year fix and a 4.93% five-year fix on 29 September 2026, raising the two-year range by 30 basis points to 5.05% and the five-year to 5.03%, then repriced 62 further products upward on 2 October — its second increase inside a week. Across the ten biggest lenders, the average cheapest two-year remortgage fix moved from 4.68% at the start of September to 5.11% by the end of it, which on a £200,000 repayment mortgage over 25 years is almost £50 a month. No further Barclays repricing announcement could be found between 3 and 16 October 2026, so 5.03% is the most recent figure the bank has put its name to rather than today's shelf price.

What Barclays does better than most of the high street is lend against somebody else's money. Mortgage Boost puts a relative's income on the application without putting their name on the title deeds. Family Springboard was priced at 4.99% for 95% of a purchase price and 5.19% for the whole 100% in the June 2026 range. And since 8 April 2025 a council or housing association tenant exercising the Right to Buy can borrow the entire discounted price with no deposit of their own.

sections.heading: A year of repricing, rung by rung
sections.html:
Barclays reprices often, and the direction reversed in the autumn. Taking the bank's own announcements in order through 2026, the two-year fix at 60% loan to value with an £899 fee went from 3.57% to 3.65% on 5 February, to 4.25% on 19 March in a round that touched 62 residential products at once, then down to 4.39% on 29 May, 4.30% on 19 June and 4.25% on 10 July, before the September rises took the whole ladder past 5%. Read those two announcements together and a gap appears: the March round left that product at 4.25% and the May round cut it from 4.60%, so it had drifted back up by more than a third of a point in between without a consumer announcement either run of this page could find.

The 9 July round was the deepest cut of the year: reductions of up to 0.66%, which took the fee-free two-year fix at 90% loan to value from 5.45% to 4.79%, the Green Home version of the same product from 5.35% to 4.69%, and the fee-free two-year fix at 95% loan to value to 5.11%. The round Barclays announced on 6 August, and said was live that day, cut the ten-year fix at 60% loan to value with a £999 fee by a full 50 basis points from 5.62% to 5.12% and the 80% equivalent from 6.03% to 5.53%, took the five-year at 60% with an £899 fee from 4.67% to 4.58%, and introduced a Great Escape three-year remortgage fix at 4.88% fee-free with a £50,000 minimum and a £2m maximum loan.

Then it turned. On 7 September the two-year fix at 90% loan to value with an £899 fee rose from 4.96% to 5.14%, the fee-free equivalent from 5.11% to 5.29%, the two-year at 95% from 5.35% to 5.53%, the three-year at 90% from 5.04% to 5.22%, the five-year at 90% from 4.85% to 5.03% and the five-year at 95% from 5.30% to 5.48%. Three weeks later the 4.75% and 4.93% headline deals went, and the 2 October round followed. David Hollingworth of L&C Mortgages put it down to rising funding costs and warned of more to come; his firm's own tracking of the ten biggest lenders is where the 4.68% to 5.11% move comes from, and the £50 a month that costs a £200,000 borrower is about £600 a year.

Bank Rate itself has not moved. The Monetary Policy Committee held at 3.75% on 17 September 2026, against August CPI of 3.1%, and the Bank's own page gives 5 November 2026 as the next decision. Fixed rates are priced off swaps rather than Bank Rate, which is why Barclays could raise its range twice in a week with the base rate unchanged — and why a borrower watching the Bank rather than the swap market will keep being surprised.

sections.heading: £37,500 of income, £270,000 of mortgage: the Mortgage Boost sum
sections.html:
Mortgage Boost is a joint borrower sole proprietor arrangement, and Barclays publishes the arithmetic rather than describing it. A buyer earning £37,500 with a £30,000 deposit could borrow a maximum of £168,375, enough for a £198,375 home. Add a parent earning the same £37,500 to the application and the maximum becomes £270,000, enough for a £300,000 home. That is £101,625 of extra borrowing, a rise of 60%, from a person who will not own a square foot of the property.

Run the two sums against income and something useful falls out. On one income Barclays stretched to 4.49 times earnings. On two it lent 3.6 times the combined £75,000 — a lower multiple, not a higher one, because the deposit stayed at £30,000 and the purchase price rose, pushing the loan to 90% of value. The booster's income buys a bigger loan; it does not buy a better income multiple. Anyone modelling a boost on the assumption that two incomes attract the same 4.49 times would price themselves at £336,750 and be £66,750 out.

The obligations are real and worth reading before the call. Boosters are jointly and severally liable from completion, which means Barclays can pursue either party for the whole debt. Every booster is credit checked, the mortgage appears on their credit file, and each one has to take independent legal advice. Boosters are named on the mortgage and not on the deeds, so they carry the liability without the asset. Mortgage Boost also cannot be combined with Family Springboard, Right to Buy, the First Home Fund, Help to Buy Equity or the Mortgage Guarantee Scheme — it is one route or the other. Sian McIntyre, managing director of life moments at Barclays, framed the product around how much harder a first purchase has become; the mechanism is older than the framing, and the figures are the part to check.

sections.heading: The deposit somebody else puts up
sections.html:
Family Springboard is the other side of the same idea: instead of a relative's income, their savings. In the range Barclays announced on 19 June 2026 the five-year Springboard fix was 4.99% fee-free for 95% of the purchase price and 5.19% fee-free for the full 100%, cut from 5.32% and 5.54%. A 100% advance at 5.19% against a standard 95% five-year fix at 5.09% that same month is a 10 basis point premium for needing no deposit at all, which is a narrow gap by the standards of high loan-to-value lending.

The Right to Buy product, launched on 8 April 2025, is the most generous thing on the shelf and the least advertised. Barclays will lend up to 100% of the discounted price, provided that figure does not exceed 90% of the open market valuation, so the statutory discount does the work of a deposit. A tenant with a 40% discount is treated as having a 40% deposit and priced at 60% loan to value — the cheapest rung of the ladder rather than the dearest. Higher-value homes are capped more tightly, at 100% of the discounted price but no more than 80% of open market value, and the thresholds are published: houses valued at £640,000 or above and flats at £310,000 or above. Above those lines a deposit is still needed. Lee Chiswell, head of mortgages, described the point as removing the deposit barrier entirely, and on the published terms that is what it does for a tenant under the value caps.

Barclays is also lending at the top of the range far more than it was. Loans above 90% loan to value were 4.4% of new UK home lending in the first half of 2026, against 1.6% in the same period of 2025 — roughly £780m against £250m. Balances above 90% are now 2.1% of the portfolio, up from 1.7% at December 2025.

sections.heading: Retained profit started counting on 15 October 2026
sections.html:
The newest change is the one that will matter most to a reader who runs a company, and it arrived the day before this check. Barclays now includes profit after tax in its affordability assessment for limited company directors, counted in proportion to the applicants' combined shareholding — 60% ownership means up to 60% of the profit after tax can be considered. The applicant must own more than 50% of the business, individually or jointly, and qualifying gross annual income including the profit being counted must be at least £75,000 for a sole application or £100,000 for a joint one. The change covers residential and buy-to-let lending, and Barclays says eligibility is no longer dependent on property value, which is the restriction that used to confine this kind of assessment to larger purchases.

Two details decide whether it helps. Where profit after tax and dividends are both declared from the same business, only the profit after tax counts, so a director already drawing most of the profit as dividends gains nothing — the measure is aimed at owners who leave money in the company. And the declared figure has to be validated by the applicant's accountant by reference, which Barclays says is unchanged from its existing policy. Roland McCormack, head of intermediaries, put the reasoning plainly: "Many limited company directors retain profits to support future growth and investment." There are more than 5 million limited companies in the UK on Companies House's own count, which is the size of the pool this reaches into.

Alongside it Barclays published its own service times for intermediaries: live chat answered in under 30 seconds on average, a new case reviewed in an average of one day, a valuation completed in under three days, and residential purchase offers averaging eight days. Those are the bank's own measurements rather than an audited statistic, and they are the kind of claim worth repeating back to a broker who tells you a case is taking a fortnight.

sections.heading: What Premier status is worth, measured on one day
sections.html:
Barclays runs a Premier range alongside the core one, and the gap between them is measurable because both move in the same announcement. On 7 September 2026 the Premier five-year fix at 90% loan to value rose from 4.65% to 4.83% while the standard five-year at the same loan to value rose from 4.85% to 5.03%. That is a flat 20 basis point discount for Premier customers on identical terms. On a £250,000 loan over 25 years, 20 basis points is about £29 a month, or close to £8,700 across the full term if the gap held.

Premier pricing shows up elsewhere in the range too. The two-year tracker Barclays introduced on 19 June 2026 at 3.99% with a £999 fee up to 60% loan to value was a Premier product; in the 18 June round the Premier two-year fix at 75% loan to value was 4.47% against 4.50% for the standard product with an £899 fee; and in the 29 May round the Premier five-year at 90% went to 4.75% against 4.95% standard, the same 20 point gap four months earlier. Existing borrowers have a third range again, the Existing Mortgage Customer Reward: on 6 August its two-year fix at 60% loan to value was 4.66% with a £999 fee, and its ten-year fix at 75% was 5.12% with a £749 fee — the lowest product fee in any Barclays range this year.

Barclays does not publish the Premier qualifying test on any page this review could read, so the income or balance needed to reach that 20 basis points could not be confirmed and is worth asking about before an application is built around it.

sections.heading: £177.8bn falls due this half, and Barclays has built a product to chase it
sections.html:
Barclays publishes an analysis of the CACI Mortgage Market Database, and the June 2026 edition, using data to March 2026, found £177.8bn of UK mortgages maturing in the second half of 2026 — £154.5bn residential, up 5.1% on 2025, and £23.3bn buy-to-let. With the half now two-thirds gone, the heaviest part is still ahead: December alone carries £38bn of residential maturities against £16.2bn in November. By region the residential total splits £33.6bn in London, £31.1bn in the South East, £18.5bn in the East of England, £9bn in Scotland and £2bn in Northern Ireland. It is a whole-market figure, not Barclays' own book.

What happens to maturing loans is the single most revealing statistic in this market. UK Finance's half-year figures for 2026 show £143bn of internal product transfers against £41bn of external remortgaging — three and a half times as much money staying put as moving. Its December 2025 forecast put the full year at £261bn of product transfers against £77bn of remortgaging, and 2027 at £272bn against £80bn. Total gross lending was £145bn in the first half against a £300bn full-year forecast, of which £82bn was house purchase and £5bn buy-to-let. Barclays' own £17.7bn is about 12% of that half-year total.

Fast-Track Remortgage is Barclays attacking the easier half of that split from the outside. Victoria Thompson, head of strategic partnerships, described it as designed to prove a real alternative to product transfers, and the service is pointed squarely at customers approaching a product end date whose cases are straightforward: an offer in 24 hours, completion in as little as five days. A lender competing to take other lenders' maturing loans is the useful kind of competition, and the 24-hour offer is the first thing in this market to make an external remortgage sound as easy as clicking the switcher screen. Eligibility is subject to individual circumstances and criteria that Barclays has not published, which is the part to ask about.

A product transfer is also the one route where nobody has to look at the wider market. Under MCOB 4.8A.10R a lender can vary a rate on an execution-only basis provided there is no additional borrowing beyond fees and it shows the customer every product they are eligible for. MCOB 4.8A.14R then requires the firm to say plainly that it is not assessing suitability and that the customer loses the protections an advised sale carries. Those rules are a floor, not a recommendation: a borrower clicking through a switcher screen has been told, in terms, that nobody checked whether the deal suits them. Execution-only is barred outright for a statutory Right to Buy, for debt consolidation and for shared equity agreements under MCOB 4.8A.7R, and high net worth customers are exempted from parts of it under MCOB 4.8A.9R.

For scale, the Office for National Statistics and HM Land Registry put the average UK house price at £273,000 in July 2026, an annual rise of 1.4% and down from 2.0% in the year to June: £293,000 in England, up 1.1%, and £215,000 in Wales, up 2.6%. Annual growth has halved since May, when it stood at 3.0%. A 10% deposit on the English average is £29,300, which is within £700 of the £30,000 in Barclays' own Mortgage Boost illustration.

sections.heading: Who is actually lending, and what the complaints record shows
sections.html:
The lender is Barclays Bank UK PLC, firm reference 759676, company number 09740322, incorporated on 19 August 2015 and registered at 1 Churchill Place, London E14 5HP, with accounts to 31 December 2025 and SIC code 64191. That entity is the ring-fenced UK bank created out of the old Barclays Bank PLC, and it is the counterparty on a residential mortgage. The distinction matters when you go looking for figures: Barclays Bank PLC is a separate entity with its own regulatory returns, and the two are easy to mix up. The FCA's register is a JavaScript application that does not return firm data to an automated request, so the firm reference above was taken from a published FCA final notice rather than from the register; it is worth two minutes to check it yourself.

That final notice, dated 14 July 2025, fined Barclays Bank UK PLC £3,093,600 for breaches of Principle 3 and SYSC 6.1.1R over account opening checks for WealthTek. It concerns client money controls in another part of the bank, not mortgage lending, and it should not be read as evidence about either.

The complaints picture has improved since this page was first written, because the figure Barclays will not serve is published by its regulator instead. The FCA's firm-level complaints return for the second half of 2025 shows Barclays Bank UK PLC opening 85,996 complaints in the six months to 31 December 2025, of which 80,470 sat in banking and credit cards and 5,356 in home finance. Set that 5,356 against the 75,658 home finance complaints the FCA counted across the whole market in the same period and Barclays accounts for about 7% of them, while writing about 12% of the half-year's gross lending — a comparison in the bank's favour, and one nobody else draws. The same return gives 6.01 on the FCA's Context A measure for home finance; the regulator describes that only as complaints seen against the number of accounts or policies provided, without stating the denominator on the page that publishes it, so it is reported here as the FCA reports it. Note too that the firm-level set covers only firms reporting 500 or more complaints in six months.

On independent complaints outcomes, the numbers are thinner than they look. The Financial Ombudsman Service received 53,600 new complaints in the quarter to 30 June 2026, upholding 26% of them. First charge residential mortgages accounted for 1,291 of those with 26% upheld, buy-to-let 153 at 21% and lifetime mortgages 71 at 13%. That remains the Ombudsman's latest quarterly publication, dated 22 July 2026, when re-checked on 16 October. Mortgages are a quiet product at the Ombudsman compared with credit and motor finance, and that is worth saying plainly. The FCA's own aggregate data for the second half of 2025, first published on 28 April 2026 and revised on 15 May, recorded 1.74m complaints across financial services, with home finance falling 3.8% from 78,616 to 75,658; no newer aggregate had been published by 16 October 2026.

What is still missing is Barclays' own version. The bank publishes a six-monthly UK complaints return by product group, and the January to June 2026 page refuses automated access — a third attempt on 16 October 2026 was refused like the two before it. So the uphold rate, the three-day closure rate and the eight-week closure rate for its home finance line are not on this page. Those are the figures that would place Barclays against its peers on outcomes rather than volume, and they need confirming directly.

sections.heading: Three live documents, three different base rates
sections.html:
A review is only as good as the paperwork behind it, and here the paperwork is the story. Barclays' intermediary rate sheets and its criteria and packaging guide still return a 403 to an automated request, and so does every page on its corporate domain. The consumer pages now open, but the rate table on the fixed-rate mortgage page is a JavaScript component that serves "Loading mortgage data. Please wait..." to anything that is not a browser, so Barclays' current rates cannot be read from Barclays. Every rate quoted above therefore comes from the bank's own dated repricing announcements as reprinted by the mortgage trade press, not from a rate table and not from a comparison site, and the scale figures come from its SEC filing.

Two documents that do open are more revealing than the ones that do not. The Existing Mortgage Customer Reward customer rate sheet at Barclays' own mortgages document path is headed "Rates effective from 21 January 2022" and states the follow-on rate in terms: "3.74% variable BEBR (currently 0.25%) +3.49% for the term" on residential and "4.74% variable BEBR (currently 0.25%) +4.49% for the term" on buy-to-let. The two halves reconcile to the decimal, so the reading is sound: Barclays' reversion rate is base rate plus a stated margin for the whole remaining term, not an open-ended standard variable rate the bank can move at will. That is genuinely better than the alternative, and it is the single most useful thing on the page for anyone pricing the years after the fix. On the 3.75% base rate held since 17 September 2026 those margins would give 7.24% and 8.24% — this page's own arithmetic on a document nearly five years old, not a rate Barclays currently quotes. The same sheet shows the early repayment charge shape too: 2%, 3% and 5% of the balance repaid, falling away at dated milestones, with trackers at either no charge or 1% for two years.

The second is the Barclays Tariff of Mortgage Charges, which carries item reference 9914226_UK 09/2021 and print dates of 25 and 26 August 2021. It is more useful than its age suggests. The product fee is "Typically £999"; switching product between offer and completion costs £0; a funds transfer fee is £35 and a re-inspection £90, payable at each stage of a staged-release renovation mortgage; buy-to-let valuation fees run by value band from £175 to £1,945 with the top band "By negotiation"; and Barclays states that it does not charge for unpaid or returned Direct Debits or cheques, which several lenders do. The early repayment charge is the one thing it will not quantify: "The fee will typically be a percentage of the loan amount", with "Details available on request by calling 0800 022 4022". Note the mismatch in wording between the two documents — a percentage of the loan amount in the tariff, a percentage of the balance repaid on the rate sheet. On a part repayment those are very different sums, and it is a fair question to put in writing.

The third document is where the dates stop being an interesting footnote. Barclays' own page for mortgage customers, headed "Base rate change and mortgages", explains what a base rate move means for a fixed or tracker deal and then tells the reader: "It's the rate the Bank of England charges other banks and other lenders when they borrow money, and it's currently 5.25%." Bank Rate is 3.75%, held on 17 September 2026 and unchanged since. The page carries no last-updated date. So a Barclays mortgage customer looking up the one number that drives their tracker, or the follow-on rate waiting at the end of their fix, is handed a figure 1.5 percentage points too high on the bank's own website. The same page does carry one real term worth knowing: on a tracker, "The minimum interest rate that we'll charge is your current tracker rate", so if base rate fell below 0% the rate would floor rather than follow it down.

Collected up, three live Barclays mortgage documents quote three different base rates: 0.25% on the rate sheet, 5.25% on the explainer, and the 3.75% that is actually in force. None of that makes a figure on this page wrong, and none of it is evidence that Barclays is mispricing anything. It is evidence about how the paperwork is maintained, and a borrower who cannot get a reversion rate or an early repayment charge in writing should read the maintenance record as part of the product.

On independent ratings, the position has moved. Smart Money People scores the Barclays fixed rate mortgage 3.56 out of 5 from 95 reviews and the tracker 3.98 from 15, with the brand last reviewed within seven days of this check. Small samples, and a score to treat as a signal rather than a verdict — but it exists, and it is notably the fourth-lowest of the 22 Barclays products the site rates, against 4.31 for the current account and 4.51 for the personal loan. Defaqto does not rate mortgage ranges at all, and Fairer Finance's mortgages customer-experience table still returned "Sorry, there are no ratings to show here just yet" on 16 October 2026, the third such check since 22 September. Say which kind of absence each one is.

The credit signals in Barclays' own half-year numbers are mixed and belong here rather than higher up. Average loan to value on new lending held at 70%, but the whole portfolio rose from 54% to 57%, lending above 90% loan to value nearly tripled as a share of new business, and the credit impairment charge rose from £237m to £338m year on year. The bank also reported 14.1 million digitally active customers at 30 June 2026, against 13.7 million a year earlier, excluding Tesco Bank. None of that is alarming for a book of this size; all of it is the shape of a lender reaching further up the loan-to-value ladder, and a borrower at 95% should know they are part of that shift. Barclays' half-year results to 30 June 2026 remain its latest published figures as at 16 October 2026.

pros: Mortgage Boost adds a relative's income without putting them on the deeds, and Barclays publishes the worked figures: £168,375 becomes £270,000 on a second £37,500 income
Right to Buy tenants can borrow 100% of the discounted price with no deposit, and a 40% discount is priced as though it were a 40% deposit

Profit after tax has counted towards affordability for majority company directors since 15 October 2026, in proportion to shareholding, on residential and buy-to-let, with the old property-value restriction removed
Fast-Track Remortgage, live market-wide since 7 September 2026, offers an offer in 24 hours and completion in as little as five days on straightforward cases
The last published follow-on rate is base rate plus a stated margin for the term — 3.49% on residential — rather than a standard variable rate the lender can move at will
Family Springboard was 4.99% at 95% loan to value and 5.19% at 100%, both fee-free, in the June 2026 range
Premier customers got a flat 20 basis point discount on the five-year 90% loan to value product in both the 29 May and 7 September 2026 repricings
The tariff of charges is published and modest by high-street standards: £35 to transfer funds, £90 to re-inspect, £0 to switch product before completion and no charge for a failed Direct Debit
Existing borrowers have their own range with the cheapest product fee seen all year, £749 on the ten-year fix at 75% loan to value
Barclays took about 7% of the market's home finance complaints in the second half of 2025 while writing about 12% of the half-year's gross lending
A ten-year fix at 60% loan to value was cut 50 basis points to 5.12% in the 6 August 2026 round, which is a genuine long-term option few lenders price keenly
Green Home versions of the core products carried a visible discount, 4.69% against 4.79% on the two-year 90% loan to value fix in July 2026
cons: Barclays' own page for mortgage customers states the Bank of England base rate is "currently 5.25%" when it is 3.75%, held on 17 September 2026 — a figure 1.5 percentage points out, on the page explaining the number that drives a tracker and a follow-on rate, with no last-updated date anywhere on it

The most recent customer rate sheet that can be read is effective 21 January 2022 and quotes the base rate as "currently 0.25%", so the follow-on margin on it is nearly five years old and may have changed; the current sheets return a 403

The early repayment charge ladder is still not published: the tariff of charges says only that it is "typically a percentage of the loan amount" and tells you to ring 0800 022 4022, while the 2022 rate sheet describes it as a percentage of the balance repaid — two different sums on a part repayment

Barclays' current rates cannot be read from Barclays: the rate table on its own fixed-rate mortgage page serves "Loading mortgage data. Please wait..." to anything that is not a browser, and the intermediary rate sheets and criteria guide refuse access, so every rate here comes from the bank's dated announcements as reprinted by the trade press

Rates moved at least nine times in 2026 and twice in the week to 2 October, when 62 products were repriced upward; the 4.75% and 4.93% market-leading deals lasted weeks, not months, and no announcement at all could be found between 3 and 16 October
Mortgage Boost makes a booster jointly and severally liable for the whole debt, puts the mortgage on their credit file and gives them no share of the property
Two incomes did not attract a better income multiple in Barclays' own illustration: 4.49 times on one income fell to 3.6 times on the combined £75,000, a £66,750 difference against the naive sum
Mortgage Boost cannot be combined with Family Springboard, Right to Buy, the First Home Fund, Help to Buy Equity or the Mortgage Guarantee Scheme

Barclays' own half-yearly complaints return, which would show the home finance uphold rate and the eight-week closure rate, refused access for a third time on 16 October 2026, so only the FCA's complaint volumes are on this page and not Barclays' outcomes

The only independent score available is a small sample: Smart Money People's 3.56 out of 5 from 95 reviews on the fixed rate mortgage. Defaqto does not rate mortgage ranges and Fairer Finance's mortgage table was still empty on 16 October 2026
The Premier qualifying test is not published anywhere this review could read, so the income or balance needed to earn that 20 basis point discount cannot be confirmed before you apply

Eligibility for Fast-Track Remortgage is "subject to individual circumstances and criteria" that Barclays has not published, so there is no way to tell in advance whether a case qualifies for the 24-hour offer
verdict: Barclays is at its most useful when a borrower needs somebody else's income, somebody else's deposit or their own company's retained profit. The Mortgage Boost figures are published rather than hinted at, the Right to Buy product prices a statutory discount as a deposit, the profit after tax change of 15 October 2026 reaches owners who leave money in the business, and Fast-Track Remortgage is a serious attempt to beat the product transfer at its own speed. The last follow-on rate Barclays published was base rate plus a stated margin for the term, which is better than a standard variable rate, and its tariff of charges is cheap and specific. Against that, the paperwork is badly maintained: the readable rate sheet is from January 2022, the tariff from August 2021, and the bank's own explainer still tells mortgage customers the base rate is 5.25% when it is 3.75%. The rate position is unstable, with two increases in the week to 2 October 2026 and nothing published since. Go to Barclays for what it will lend and on whose income; get the current follow-on rate and the early repayment charge schedule in writing before you sign anything, because the published versions are years old.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest Barclays mortgage rate right now?
faqs.a: The most recent figure that can be verified from Barclays' own announcement is 5.03% on the five-year fix, effective 29 September 2026, replacing a 4.93% deal; the two-year equivalent went to 5.05%. Barclays then repriced 62 further products upward on 2 October 2026 without publishing the individual rates, and no later announcement could be found when this page was re-checked on 16 October 2026. Its own rate table is a browser-only component and its rate sheets refuse access, so treat 5.03% as a floor rather than today's number and ask for the current sheet.

faqs.q: What does a Barclays fixed rate revert to when it ends?
faqs.a: The last Barclays rate sheet that can be read, effective 21 January 2022, puts the residential follow-on at the Bank of England base rate plus 3.49% for the remaining term, and buy-to-let at base plus 4.49%. That is a tracking margin rather than a standard variable rate the lender can move at will, which is the better of the two structures. On the 3.75% base rate in force since 17 September 2026 those margins would work out at 7.24% and 8.24%, but the document is nearly five years old and the margin may have changed, so get the current figure in writing.

faqs.q: How much more can Mortgage Boost let me borrow?
faqs.a: On Barclays' own illustration, a buyer earning £37,500 with a £30,000 deposit could borrow £168,375. Adding one person earning another £37,500 took that to £270,000 — £101,625 more, a rise of 60%. Note that the multiple falls rather than rises: 4.49 times one income becomes 3.6 times the combined £75,000, so anyone assuming 4.49 times would price themselves £66,750 too high. The booster is named on the mortgage, not on the title deeds, is jointly and severally liable for the whole balance, is credit checked, has the mortgage recorded on their credit file and must take independent legal advice.

faqs.q: Can a limited company director use retained profit on a Barclays application?
faqs.a: Since 15 October 2026, yes. Barclays counts profit after tax in proportion to the applicants' combined shareholding, so 60% ownership allows up to 60% of the profit to be considered. You must own more than half the business, and qualifying gross annual income including that profit must be at least £75,000 on a sole application or £100,000 on a joint one. It applies to residential and buy-to-let lending, and eligibility is no longer tied to property value. If you already declare dividends from the same company, only the profit after tax is counted, so the change helps owners who leave money in the business rather than those who draw it out. Your accountant has to validate the figure.

faqs.q: Can I get a Barclays mortgage with no deposit?
faqs.a: In two situations. Family Springboard was priced at 5.19% fee-free for 100% of the purchase price in the June 2026 range, with a helper's savings standing behind it. And since 8 April 2025 a Right to Buy tenant can borrow 100% of the discounted price, capped at 90% of open market value, with the statutory discount doing the work of a deposit — though homes valued at £640,000 or more, or flats at £310,000 or more, are capped at 80% of open market value and still need a deposit.

faqs.q: Is it worth switching to a new Barclays deal or remortgaging elsewhere?
faqs.a: UK Finance recorded £143bn of internal product transfers against £41bn of external remortgaging in the first half of 2026, so most borrowers stay. An internal switch is quick and, under MCOB 4.8A.10R, can be done execution-only with no additional borrowing — but MCOB 4.8A.14R means the lender has told you it is not assessing whether the deal suits you. Barclays now sells against its own switcher screen with Fast-Track Remortgage, which promises an offer in 24 hours and completion in as little as five days. With £177.8bn of UK mortgages maturing in the second half of 2026 and £38bn of it in December alone, it is worth at least pricing the external market first.

faqs.q: Who regulates Barclays mortgages and where do I complain?
faqs.a: The lender is Barclays Bank UK PLC, firm reference 759676, authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority. Complain to Barclays first; if you are not satisfied, or eight weeks pass, you can take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which upheld 26% of the 1,291 first charge residential mortgage complaints it received in the quarter to 30 June 2026. For scale, the FCA's own firm-level return shows Barclays Bank UK PLC opening 5,356 home finance complaints in the six months to 31 December 2025.

title: Barclays Personal Loan: the Rate You Only See Once You Bank There

intro:
Barclays advertises its Greener Home Loan at 6.3% APR representative on £7,500 to £15,000 over two to five years, with up to £250 cashback, and it is the only personal loan rate the bank publishes as readable text anywhere on its site. Figures re-checked on 10 October 2026 against barclays.co.uk, where the same deal is advertised at 6.3% on the two greener-homes pages and at 6.5% on the main loans page.

Barclays lends between £1,000 and £50,000, repaid over two to five years. The quote is the selling point and the bank says so in its own words: “With some lenders, you won't know your actual rate until you've applied. And if you're not happy with the APR you're offered, your credit rating could still be affected even if you don't take out the loan. We're different – in many cases we can give you a personalised price quote up front, with no impact on your credit score.” Settle early and the charge is “a fee equal to 30 days' interest on the amount you're repaying”, which is a good deal less than the law lets a lender take; change your mind altogether inside 14 days and there is no settlement fee and, if you repay within a week of opening, no interest either. There is also a price guarantee: find a like-for-like unsecured loan at a lower APR within 30 days of signing and Barclays will “reduce the interest rate to produce an APR equal to the competing offer”.

The condition is that you already bank there. The provisional offer and the personal rate are for people who hold “a current account with us” — the loan pages also accept “a Barclays account – such as a Barclaycard” — together with Online Banking or Barclays Mobile Banking. Somebody arriving from a comparison page with neither cannot obtain a Barclays rate at all, and the representative example on the bank's open loan pages was still being served with its numbers missing on 10 October 2026, twenty-seven days after it was first found that way. That is worth knowing before you spend a click on it.

sections.heading: Two Barclays pages, two different rates for one loan
sections.html:
The Greener Home Loan rate is tied to a narrow slice of the product, and on 10 October 2026 Barclays was quoting it at two different levels. The dedicated product page at barclays.co.uk/sustainability/greener-homes/greener-home-loan and the greener-homes hub above it both head the offer “6.3% APR Representative on loans of £7,500 - £15,000 over 2-5 years, (your rate may differ*)”. The general loans page at barclays.co.uk/loans carries the identical sentence with “6.5%” in front of it. Both were read twice. Two of the bank's own pages therefore disagree by two tenths of a point on the one personal loan rate it publishes, and the figure used here — 6.3% — is the one on the page built for the product rather than the one on the listing page above it. On a £10,000 five-year advance the gap between the two is worth roughly £50 of interest: small, but it is the number a shopper is being asked to compare on.

Either way the rate reaches only part of the range. You get to it by selecting “Greener home” as the purpose in the application, and it is quoted for £7,500 to £15,000 over two to five years. Borrow £1,000, or borrow £40,000, and neither published figure tells you anything.

For the ordinary Barclayloan the picture is thinner still. On barclays.co.uk/loans, /loans/personal, /loans/calculator and /loans/home-improvement-loan, the representative APR was again served as “0 APR Representative on loans of 0 over 2-5 years” and the example beneath it as “APR Representative based on a loan of repayable over months at an interest rate of pa (fixed)”. The figures are plainly injected by the page's own scripts rather than absent from the product, and a shopper in an ordinary browser may well see them fill in — but they are not in the page as delivered, and no Barclays page that could be opened on 13 September or 10 October 2026 stated the standard representative APR or the maximum rate. Treat that as unestablished rather than as a gap in the product, and ask for the number before you apply. The maximum advance is at least published: “You can apply to borrow up to £50,000” on the home improvement page, and “between £1,000 and maximum of £50,000” on the greener loan page, which settles a minimum that could not be established in September.

One line on the loan calculator is worth keeping whichever rate you are shown: “The representative APRs shown are based on all loan applications made by Barclays customers.” A representative APR has to be available to at least 51% of the people who take the advertised product under CONC 3.5, so the other 49% can be charged more. Barclays repeats the point itself — the rate offered “will be based on your personal circumstances, the loan amount and the repayment term”.

sections.heading: The document the law promises you, and the moment it arrives
sections.html:
Every regulated loan in Britain comes with a standard disclosure form, and most borrowers have never heard of it. The Consumer Credit (Disclosure of Information) Regulations 2010 were made on 28 March 2010 and came into force on 30 April 2010. Regulation 3(2) says that “In good time before the agreement is made, the creditor must disclose to the debtor, in the manner set out in regulation 8, the pre-contract credit information”, and regulation 8(1) says that information “must be disclosed by means of the form contained in Schedule 1”. Schedule 1 is headed Pre-contract credit information (Standard European Consumer Credit Information), and it is the one place a borrower sees the rate, the total amount payable, the duration, the charges and the early settlement terms set out to a fixed pattern that can be laid alongside another lender's.

The timing matters as much as the content. “In good time before the agreement is made” is not the same as before you apply: it lands inside the application journey, once Barclays has decided what to charge you. So the comparison the form was designed to make possible happens at the point you are most committed, and on a product whose public pages carry one rate at two different values and no rate table at all for the standard loan, it is the first document with reliable numbers on it. Barclays publishes no specimen version of it for a personal loan that could be found on either 13 September or 10 October 2026, and the full terms of its price guarantee, linked from the loan page as “See our full price guarantee terms and conditions”, would not open on either date. Neither absence is proof that the documents are hard to get once you are in the application; both mean you cannot read them first.

sections.heading: A soft search now, a hard one later
sections.html:
The no-impact quote is real, and it is worth understanding what it does and does not settle. A quotation search leaves a footprint only you can see; the full application leaves one every other lender can. Between the two sits the assessment the FCA requires, and the rules are more demanding than most people expect.

CONC 5.2A.4R obliges a firm to carry out a creditworthiness assessment before entering into a regulated credit agreement or significantly increasing the credit provided. CONC 5.2A.10R makes the firm weigh two different things: “the risk that the customer will not make repayments under the agreement by their due dates (credit risk)” and the risk to the customer of not being able to make them at all. CONC 5.2A.12R(5) puts it in the borrower's terms — the question is whether repayments can be made “without the repayments having a significant adverse impact on the customer's financial situation”. CONC 5.2A.14R stops the lender counting any guarantee, indemnity or security when it judges that second risk. All four have carried the date 1 November 2018 since the affordability rules were rewritten.

The practical effect on this particular loan is that Barclays is assessing you partly from data it already holds. Your salary credits, your standing orders and your overdraft behaviour are all in the same bank, which is one honest explanation for why the personalised quote can be produced without a credit search, and why the product is closed to people who do not bank there. Barclays states the residual risk plainly: “All loans are subject to status” and borrowing is “Subject to application, financial circumstances and borrowing history”.

sections.heading: Fourteen days to change your mind, and the price of borrowing more
sections.html:
Two separate exits are worth keeping apart. The first is withdrawal, which is free: Barclays' own help page gives you “within 14 days of receiving your confirmation letter” to pull out, in writing, by phone on 0800 800 300 or in a branch, with no reason required and no early settlement fee. You then have “30 days to repay the loan amount, plus any interest” — and the useful part, which almost nobody mentions, is that “[i]f you repay us in full within 7 days of your loan being opened, we won't charge any interest”. A loan taken out and cleared inside a week costs nothing at all.

The second is settlement proper. “You have the right to repay your loan early, in part or full, at any time,” says the loan page, and that right comes from section 94 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 rather than from Barclays. What varies between lenders is the compensation they take for it. Barclays charges “a fee equal to 30 days' interest on the amount you're repaying, as well as any other interest that's due”. Under the Consumer Credit (Early Settlement) Regulations 2004, regulation 5 puts the settlement date 28 days after the borrower's notice and regulation 6 lets the creditor push it back by a further 30 on an agreement running more than a year, and most mainstream lenders take the whole 58. Barclays taking 30 is roughly half the industry maximum, and on a £10,000 balance at a mid-single-digit rate that is a difference of tens of pounds rather than hundreds — small, but in the borrower's favour and rarely mentioned.

The same fee is where a top-up quietly costs money. Borrow more from Barclays and it does not add a second agreement: “we set up a new loan for the remaining balance plus the extra amount you want to borrow” and pays off the first one, which means the 30 days' interest falls due on the loan being settled. The bank also warns that “the new loan may have a different interest rate from your initial loan”, so a top-up can reprice the original borrowing at whatever the bank is charging on the day, and you cannot do it immediately — “You'll need to have had your loan with us for at least three months.” The combined ceiling is £50,000. Barclays itself points at the alternative: “If you just want to take out a second loan instead of topping up, that could be an option too.” Anyone with a cheap existing loan and a small extra need should price that route first.

sections.heading: The cashback, and the twenty-year gap inside its own small print
sections.html:
The £250 attached to the headline is the top of a three-rung ladder, and the product page prints the whole thing: “£50 cashback on a loan up to £1,999”, “£100 cashback on a loan between £2,000-£4,999” and “£250 cashback on a loan of £5,000+”. The money is not automatic. “To claim the cashback reward, at least 90% of the loan proceeds must be spent on eligible home improvements”, the invoice has to come from a VAT-registered installer or tradesperson, solar and low-carbon heating installers “should be MCS certified”, and “[f]rom the day your loan application is accepted, you have 6 months to claim”. It is payable once per loan and once per property, only on your main home rather than a buy-to-let, second home or holiday home, and only if you are not in breach of the agreement; once the receipts are accepted the money arrives in your current account “in one go within 30 days”. Note the shape of that deal on the lowest rung: a £1,000 loan with £900 of qualifying work behind it returns £50, which is 5% of the advance back.

Seventeen measures qualify, and the list is specific: air source and ground source heat pumps, biomass pellet boilers, solar thermal, solar photovoltaic panels, solar battery storage, loft and pitched roof, flat roof, cavity wall, room-in-roof, underfloor, suspended wooden floor and solid wall insulation, A-rated double or triple glazing replacing single glazing, secondary glazing, new insulated external doors and an electric car charging point. “Spray foam insulation is excluded.”

One of those bullets does not say the same thing in both places, and a householder could spend money on the strength of the wrong one. The product page qualifies the door measure as “[n]ew insulated external doors (replacing single-glazed or solid doors installed before 2022)”. The offer's own terms and conditions, linked from it, qualify the identical measure as “replacing single-glazed or solid doors installed before 2002”. Both were read twice on 10 October 2026. Twenty years separates the two, and the terms are the document that governs a claim, so anyone replacing a door fitted in, say, 2010 is eligible on one Barclays page and ineligible on the other. Ask which applies before you order the doors, in writing.

sections.heading: Who the money actually comes from
sections.html:
The lender is Barclays Bank UK PLC, firm reference 759676 — the ring-fenced retail bank, a different authorised entity from Barclays Bank PLC (122702), which houses the investment bank. The distinction is not academic housekeeping: the help page telling you how to withdraw from a Barclayloan asks for the notice to be posted to “Barclays Bank plc, PO Box 362, M1 3BN”, which is not the entity named as lender on the product. Send it to the address the page gives, keep a copy, and telephone to confirm.

Barclays UK reported £220.8bn of loans and advances to customers at amortised cost and £245.6bn of customer deposits at 30 June 2026, with £1,767m of profit before tax for the half year, a net interest margin of 3.70%, a return on average allocated tangible equity of 20.1% and 14.1 million digitally active customers excluding Tesco Bank. Those are half-year figures and the next set is due at the end of October 2026, so they are the most recent audited picture rather than a current one.

The regulator has been in the file twice in recent years. On 16 July 2025 the FCA fined the group £42m over financial crime risk management, split as £3,093,600 against Barclays Bank UK PLC — reduced from £4,419,500 — and £39,314,700 against Barclays Bank PLC, reduced from £56,163,900; Barclays also agreed a voluntary payment of £6.3m to WealthTek clients facing a shortfall. The older penalty is the one that bears directly on a loan, and it is in the next section.

A borrower's protections are worth stating precisely, because one of them does not exist here. The Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers deposits, not borrowing; being a Barclays depositor changes nothing about a Barclays loan. What you do get is the Financial Ombudsman Service, free to use, whose decisions bind the bank if you accept them — and which has already been asked about this product.

sections.heading: If the payments stop
sections.html:
This is the part of a loan page most lenders would rather nobody read, and it is where Barclays has history. On 15 December 2020 the FCA fined Barclays Bank UK PLC, Barclays Bank PLC and Clydesdale Financial Services Limited £26,000,000 for failures in the treatment of customers in financial difficulty between April 2014 and December 2018, affecting at least 1,530,000 customer accounts. The penalty carried a 30% settlement discount from £37,223,500, breached Principles 3 and 6, and followed more than £273m of redress paid since 2017. Mark Steward, then the FCA's Executive Director of Enforcement and Market Oversight, said that “[c]onsumers should feel reassured that their lender will work with them to help resolve any financial difficulties”.

The rules he was enforcing are in CONC 7 and they are short enough to quote. CONC 7.3.4R: “A firm must treat customers in or approaching arrears or in default with forbearance and due consideration.” CONC 7.3.5BR requires a firm to “take all reasonable steps to ensure that any repayment arrangements agreed with customers are sustainable”. CONC 7.3.9R forbids a policy of refusing to negotiate with a customer developing a repayment plan; CONC 7.3.10R forbids pressing a customer to clear the debt in one or very few payments, within an unreasonably short time, or by selling property or borrowing more; CONC 7.3.11R requires the lender to suspend active pursuit of the debt for a reasonable period while a plan is being worked out. Those are entitlements, not favours, and they are worth naming on the phone.

Barclays' own support pages are a mixed picture, and twenty-seven days has not improved them. The dedicated page for a customer struggling with a Barclayloan or overdraft would not open on 13 September and would not open on 10 October 2026, which may be a fetching problem rather than a broken link. The general money-problems page did open on both dates, and it still names “The Money Advice Service” — a brand that stopped existing on 30 June 2021, when the Money and Pensions Service folded it together with The Pensions Advisory Service and Pension Wise into MoneyHelper — offering “free, impartial information and tools on how to manage your money”. The same page still carries the line “Check the government site for the latest advice and support on the coronavirus.” StepChange, the other organisation it names, is very much still there, still free, and described accurately.

sections.heading: The price guarantee, as an ombudsman read it
sections.html:
Matching a rival's APR is an unusual promise and it deserves testing rather than repeating. The Financial Ombudsman Service has published a decision on exactly this, reference DRN8017479, decided by ombudsman Rebecca Connelley against Barclays Bank Plc. A customer had applied for a loan elsewhere at a lower rate and expected Barclays to match it. The ombudsman found the bank had been entitled to insist on an actual loan agreement from the other lender rather than a completed application form, and declined to order the lower rate; the bank was told to pay £50 for distress and inconvenience because there was “enough evidence to conclude that the bank misrepresented the price match promotion”.

Read alongside the promise itself, that decision is the instruction manual. The claim window is 30 days from the date the Barclayloan agreement was signed, the comparison has to be like-for-like and unsecured, and the evidence has to be a real agreement rather than an indicative quote or a submitted application. Which means anyone intending to rely on the guarantee has to take out a second loan agreement, with a second lender, inside a month of taking the first — a sequence with real consequences for a credit file. The remedy if it works is a rate cut and recalculated monthly repayments, not a refund.

sections.heading: Where unsecured lending sits this quarter
sections.html:
The Bank of England's Credit Conditions Survey for 2026 Q3, published on 8 October 2026, found the opposite of the quarter before it on two of the four measures that matter to a borrower. Lenders reported that the availability of unsecured credit to households decreased in Q3, at a net balance of −11, and expected it to increase slightly in Q4; overall demand for unsecured lending was unchanged in Q3 and was expected to increase slightly in Q4; default rates on total unsecured lending increased in Q3 and were expected to increase again in Q4; and overall unsecured lending spreads were unchanged in Q3 and were expected to be unchanged in Q4. In Q2 the same survey had reported availability rising and spreads narrowing, so the direction of travel between July and September was tighter supply at a flat price with bad debts still climbing.

That is the commercial logic behind Barclays keeping this product inside its own banking app. When lenders are pulling back on availability and watching defaults rise, a bank that can see an applicant's salary credits and standing orders can price more finely than one buying applications from a comparison table — and it does not need to widen its spread to do it.

Independent scoring is thin on credit products. Defaqto rates insurance, not lending, so there is no star rating or ribbon to point at on any personal loan. Smart Money People, which does cover credit, lists the Barclays personal loan at 4.51 out of 5 from 108 individual reviews — against 4.32 from 4,963 for the current account, 3.56 from 95 for the fixed rate mortgage and 4.06 from 12 for car finance. The loan's score and review count are unchanged since 13 September; the mortgage score has moved from 3.44 to 3.56 on the same 95 reviews. No “last reviewed” date is shown against any individual product, only “Last reviewed within 7 days” for the bank as a whole, so treat the loan score as a modest sample of unknown vintage rather than a verdict.

pros: A personal rate before you apply, with no credit search and no mark on your file
Fourteen days to withdraw with no settlement fee, and no interest at all if the loan is cleared within 7 days of opening
Early settlement costs 30 days' interest, against a statutory maximum of 58
£1,000 to £50,000 over two to five years, with the minimum and maximum both published
A price guarantee that cuts your rate to match a cheaper like-for-like loan within 30 days of signing
6.3% APR representative on the Greener Home Loan at £7,500 to £15,000, with cashback of £50, £100 or £250 by loan size
A large, well-capitalised ring-fenced lender: £220.8bn of loans and £245.6bn of deposits at 30 June 2026
cons: Two Barclays pages quote the same Greener Home Loan at two different rates — 6.3% on the greener-homes product page and hub, 6.5% on barclays.co.uk/loans — both read twice on 10 October 2026
No rate for anyone who does not already hold a Barclays current account or Barclaycard, so most people arriving from a comparison page cannot be quoted at all

The representative example on four Barclays loan pages was still served with its figures missing on 10 October 2026, twenty-seven days after it was first found that way, and no standard representative APR could be established from any page that opened

The greener loan's door measure is qualified as “installed before 2022” on the product page and “installed before 2002” in the terms that govern the claim — a twenty-year gap on an eligibility condition

The Standard European Consumer Credit Information required by the 2010 Regulations arrives inside the application, so the one document built for comparing lenders reaches you after Barclays has priced you

The full price guarantee terms would not open on either 13 September or 10 October 2026, and a published ombudsman decision shows the bar is a signed agreement from another lender within 30 days, not a quote
A £26m FCA penalty in December 2020 for the treatment of customers in financial difficulty, covering at least 1,530,000 accounts between April 2014 and December 2018
A top-up settles the existing loan, triggering the 30 days' interest charge and repricing the original balance, and cannot be taken until the loan has run three months
The money-problems page still signposts the Money Advice Service, retired on 30 June 2021, and still carries coronavirus guidance — unchanged on re-checking four weeks later
The 10-year term for “selected existing customers” that Barclays' pages carried in September could not be re-found on 10 October 2026; treat five years as the published maximum and ask
verdict: For somebody who already banks with Barclays, this is one of the least stressful ways to borrow: a real rate on screen before any credit search, £1,000 to £50,000, fourteen days to walk away for nothing, a 30-day price guarantee and an early settlement charge at roughly half what the regulations permit. For everybody else it is close to unquotable, because the personal rate lives behind the app and the published pages carry a representative example with no numbers in it — and the one rate Barclays does publish statically is now showing as 6.3% on its greener-homes pages and 6.5% on its main loans page. Get the figure confirmed in writing, open the pre-contract credit information the moment it appears in the application, check the APR and the total amount payable against a rate you have been offered elsewhere, and remember that the guarantee needs a rival's signed agreement rather than a screenshot.

faqs.q: Can I get a Barclays loan without banking with Barclays?
faqs.a: Not on the same terms. The provisional offer and the personalised quote are described as being for people who hold “a current account with us” plus Online Banking or Barclays Mobile Banking, and the loan pages also accept “a Barclays account – such as a Barclaycard”. Barclays states that borrowing is “Subject to application, financial circumstances and borrowing history”. If you hold neither account, expect to open one first or to borrow elsewhere.

faqs.q: What is the Barclays personal loan rate?
faqs.a: The only rate Barclays publishes as readable text is for the Greener Home Loan, and on 10 October 2026 two of its own pages disagreed about it: 6.3% APR representative on the greener-homes product page and hub, 6.5% on barclays.co.uk/loans, both for £7,500 to £15,000 over two to five years. The standard Barclayloan's representative APR is served by the page's scripts and was blank on every page that could be opened, so ask for your figure in the application or in writing and do not rely on either published number.

faqs.q: What does it cost to pay a Barclays loan off early?
faqs.a: “A fee equal to 30 days' interest on the amount you're repaying”, on top of the interest already due. Section 94 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 gives you the right to settle at any time, in part or in full, and the Consumer Credit (Early Settlement) Regulations 2004 let a lender charge for up to 58 days. Barclays taking 30 is at the cheaper end of the market. Withdrawing inside the 14-day cooling-off period is different again: no settlement fee, 30 days to repay, and no interest at all if you clear it within 7 days of the loan opening.

faqs.q: How much can I borrow and for how long?
faqs.a: Between £1,000 and £50,000, including any existing Barclays loan you are topping up, repaid over two to five years. A 10-year term for “selected existing customers” appeared on Barclays' loan pages in September 2026 but could not be found on 10 October 2026, so treat five years as the published maximum and ask if you need longer. A top-up needs the existing loan to have run at least three months.

faqs.q: How does the £250 greener home cashback work?
faqs.a: It is £50 on a loan up to £1,999, £100 between £2,000 and £4,999 and £250 at £5,000 or more. At least 90% of the loan has to be spent on eligible improvements at your main home, the invoice must come from a VAT-registered installer, solar and low-carbon heating installers should be MCS certified, and the claim has to be made within 6 months of the application being accepted. It pays once per loan and once per property, and the money reaches your current account in one go within 30 days of the confirmation email.

faqs.q: Will checking my rate hurt my credit score?
faqs.a: Barclays says it can give “a personalised price quote up front, with no impact on your credit score” in many cases. The full application is different and will leave a search other lenders can see. The assessment behind both is governed by CONC 5.2A, which requires the bank to weigh the risk of you not repaying against the risk that repaying would have “a significant adverse impact on the customer's financial situation”.

faqs.q: What happens if I cannot keep up the repayments?
faqs.a: CONC 7.3.4R requires Barclays to treat you “with forbearance and due consideration”, CONC 7.3.5BR requires any arrangement agreed to be sustainable, and CONC 7.3.11R requires the bank to suspend active pursuit of the debt for a reasonable period while you put a plan together. Missed payments will still reach your credit file. Free help is available from StepChange and from MoneyHelper, the service that replaced the Money Advice Service on 30 June 2021.

title: Bigblu Broadband Satellite Internet
meta_title: Bigblu Satellite Broadband: £24.99 a Month, 21 Mb/s
meta_description: Bigblu advertises satellite broadband at £24.99 a month with 21 Mb/s average speeds and unlimited data. What the price covers, and what to ask first.

headline.label: Cheapest advertised monthly price
headline.value: £24.99 a month — average speeds of 21 Mb/s, uncapped unlimited data, cancel within 14 days of installation

intro:
Bigblu sells satellite broadband to British homes for £24.99 per month, quoting “average speeds of 21 Mb/s”, an “uncapped, unlimited data allowance” and the offer to “simply cancel within 14 days of installation” if the service disappoints. Orders go through one number, 01869 722 425, on the same Bicester dialling code the brand has used since it traded as Avonline. Figures checked on 12 October 2026 against the provider’s own site.

That is a genuinely low price for a dish, and for a property beyond the reach of a cable it may be the only offer on the table. The brand has real history behind it too: the business it grew out of had been selling satellite broadband since 2002, and at its height it served more than 49,000 European customers on revenue of about £34.6 million a year.

One thing belongs up here rather than further down, because it decides what a reader does next. The ordering page names no company. There is no trading name, no company number, no VAT number and no registered address anywhere on it, and the brand’s own terms, complaints and about pages cannot be read. Meanwhile the register shows every British company that has carried the Bigblu name either dissolved, in liquidation or filed for strike-off, the AIM-quoted parent gone private on 18 December 2025, and the operating company that used to run this service in a creditors’ voluntary liquidation that began on 7 March 2025. None of that proves the service is not being delivered — the site is live and taking enquiries. It does mean one question is worth asking on the phone before any money changes hands: which company am I contracting with, and what is its number?
