sections.heading: What £24.99 buys, and the four numbers the page leaves out
sections.html:
The offer is a single package rather than a ladder of tiers, which makes it unusually easy to read. £24.99 a month buys a service the provider describes as averaging 21 Mb/s with an uncapped, unlimited allowance, and a 14-day window after installation in which an unhappy customer can walk away. For a rural household that has been choosing between a copper line delivering 2 or 3 Mb/s and nothing at all, the headline rate is a fair price and the absence of a data cap matters more than the speed does.

Four numbers a buyer needs are missing. There is no contract length, so the commitment behind the £24.99 is unknown; there is no hardware charge and no installation charge, and a dish, a modem and a visit from an engineer are not free in any other part of this market; and there is no minimum or guaranteed speed. An average is not a floor. The brand’s own predecessor used to publish both halves of that pair, promising a 9 Mb/s guaranteed minimum average against an “up to” ceiling of 20 Mb/s, measured on a 30-day rolling basis, and renting the hardware at £5 a month on a two-year term with £50 upfront. The current page has the price and none of the structure.

Set the speed against the standard the regulator uses and the package clears it comfortably. Ofcom’s right-to-request guidance, published 8 August 2023 and last updated 19 June 2026, defines a decent connection as 10 Mbit/s down and 1 Mbit/s up, and lets a householder ask for one where the only decent service available costs more than £59.60 a month. At 21 Mb/s average and £24.99, this sits above the speed floor and well under half the price threshold — which is the strongest thing that can be said for it on paper, and worth saying before anything else.

sections.heading: Four company names, one brand, and a register that keeps score
sections.html:
Three separate corporate strands carry the Bigblu name at Companies House, and reading them in order explains why the ordering page is so thin. The first is the retail business a reader may remember: Avonline Satellite Services Limited, incorporated 26 May 2016, renamed Bigblu Services Limited on 31 August 2018 and carrying company number 10201939, with its parent Bigblu Services Holding Ltd (10177312, incorporated 12 May 2016) doing the same thing on the same day. Both are registered at 60 Gracechurch Street, London EC3V 0HR, both are listed under SIC 61300 — satellite telecommunications activities, and both show the status words “Active proposal to strike off”. Their last accounts were made up to 30 November 2022; the next set, to 30 November 2023, fell due on 30 November 2024 and the register flags them as overdue. Their confirmation statements are overdue too, one since 31 May 2025 and the other since 6 June 2025.

The second strand is the company that actually ran the service. Satellite Solutions Worldwide Limited was incorporated on 27 November 2008, became Bigblu Operations Limited on 31 August 2018, and was renamed again — to BRDY Broadband Ltd — on 18 July 2024, on a resolution dated two days earlier. Its company number is still 06759661 and its SIC code is still 61300. Its status is Liquidation.

The third is the listed parent, and its name has changed four times in eleven years. Cleeve Capital Limited was incorporated on 17 September 2014, became Cleeve Capital plc on 20 November 2014, Satellite Solutions Worldwide Group plc on 8 May 2015, Bigblu Broadband plc on 23 May 2018, and plain Bigblu Broadband Limited on 15 December 2025. That company, number 09223439, is the only one of the group still shown as straightforwardly active. It has moved to a law firm’s address — c/o Arch Law, Floor 2, 8 Bishopsgate, London EC2N 4BQ, changed on 11 June 2025 — its last accounts were made up to 30 November 2024 and filed on 9 June 2025 as a 106-page group filing, and no accounts for the year to 30 November 2025, due by 31 August 2026, appear in its filing history. Three directors left within six weeks of the delisting: Michael Tobin on 31 December 2025, and Philip David Moses and Paul Arthur Howard on 24 January 2026.

sections.heading: Sold to Eutelsat, sold on again, then wound up
sections.html:
The reason a 2002-vintage satellite business has three sets of names is that it was sold twice in three years, and both transactions are on the public record with figures attached.

On 31 July 2020 Bigblu Broadband plc announced the disposal of the entire issued share capital of Bigblu Operations Limited and its subsidiaries to Eutelsat S.A. The consideration was up to £39.3 million on a cash-free, debt-free basis: £36.8 million on completion, a further £1.0 million once the completion accounts were settled, and up to about £1.5 million more over the following twelve months, with Eutelsat also assuming around £13.9 million of net working capital creditors. The group’s European presence at the time covered eleven countries — France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and the UK — although the Norwegian business, BigBlu Norge AS, was excluded from the sale and stayed with the seller. On unaudited pro forma figures for the year to 30 November 2019 it turned over about £34.6 million with adjusted EBITDA of about £5.6 million and more than 49,000 customers, roughly 2,200 of them on fixed wireless in Italy. Shareholders backed it at a general meeting on 28 August 2020, with irrevocable undertakings and letters of intent over about 46.5% of the share capital, Harwood Capital alone accounting for 22.7%.

Eutelsat kept it for under three years. On 15 June 2023 the operator announced it was disposing of its European broadband retail activities, Bigblu Operations Ltd among them, across the same ten-market footprint, to what it described only as “an experienced private operator” — a buyer it did not name, then or since. The register dates the handover precisely: Eutelsat S.A. ceased to be a person with significant control on 21 July 2023. Eutelsat’s stated reason was its own shift to wholesale distribution rather than anything about the retail book.

What happened next is the part a prospective customer should know. The renamed BRDY Broadband Ltd passed an extraordinary resolution to wind up on 7 March 2025, and a creditors’ voluntary liquidation — the insolvent kind — commenced the same day. Two practitioners were appointed on 7 March 2025: Alan Brian Coleman of FTS Recovery Limited, 3rd Floor Tootal Building, 56 Oxford Street, Manchester M1 6EU, and Marco Piacquadio, of Ground Floor, Baird House, Seebeck Place, Knowlhill, Milton Keynes MK5 8FR. A statement of affairs was filed on 17 March 2025 and the liquidators’ statement of receipts and payments, covering the year to 6 March 2026, was filed on 13 May 2026 and runs to 19 pages. The registered office has moved three times during the liquidation, most recently on 21 August 2026 to Suite 4C, Manchester Club, 81 King Street, Manchester M2 4AH.

sections.heading: £25m for Australia, £6.1m back to shareholders, and the exit from AIM
sections.html:
While the European retail business was changing hands, the quoted parent was selling the rest of itself. The largest remaining asset was SkyMesh Pty Ltd, an Australian satellite retailer with more than 50,000 customers at 31 October 2024 and a 46% share of NBN Co’s Sky Muster service at 30 September 2024. Audited revenue for the year to 30 November 2023 was about £25.4 million with adjusted EBITDA of about £5.2 million, although net assets at 31 May 2024 were approximately negative £3.1 million.

On 2 December 2024, under a sale agreement dated 29 November 2024, the company announced the disposal of SkyMesh to SKM Telecommunication Services Pty Ltd, a bidco formed by Salter Brothers Asset Management, for up to AUD$50.20 million (about £25.67 million) — which the board called a return of up to 2.2 times the AUD$23.0 million the group had invested. The structure was 59.8% in cash on completion, capped at AUD$30.00 million, 26.5% in 13,320,581 shares in the buyer at A$1.00 each, and 13.7% — about AUD$6.88 million — deferred to the first anniversary, less an uncollected AUD$2.80 million of customer debt arising from a July 2023 system implementation. Because this was a fundamental change of business under AIM Rule 15, shareholders had to approve it; they did, on 20 December 2024, and completion followed on 23 December 2024.

By then the company had told its own shareholders what it had left: the New Zealand trading operations, a 2.8% stake in Quickline Communications plus loan notes carried at £3.9 million accruing roughly £15,000 of interest a month, around 33.7% of the Australian buyer (about 24.7% fully diluted), and a subsidiary distributing Starlink. The Quickline figure is worth pausing on: in 2020 the group had held 69.7% of it.

The last act came a year later. On 19 November 2025 the board proposed cancelling the AIM quotation, citing “the management time, the associated additional adviser costs and regulatory burden” and concluding that “the costs and constraints of remaining on AIM are no longer justified”. The figures in that notice are the clearest measure of what was left: a market capitalisation of about £8.1 million, interim revenue of £0.3 million, an adjusted EBITDA loss of £0.2 million, and remaining operations described as mainly in New Zealand. The Australian cash — AUD$30.0 million, about £14.9 million — had repaid the Santander facility and funded a tender offer returning £6.1 million to shareholders. Directors held 1,055,749 shares, about 2.42% of the company, which puts roughly 43.6 million shares in issue and the implied price near 18.6p — arithmetic from those two published figures rather than a quoted price.

Shareholders approved both resolutions on 8 December 2025: cancellation by 16,178,729 votes to 420,939 (97.46% in favour) and re-registration as a private company by 16,198,886 to 400,782, with 21,148 votes withheld on each. Re-registration was certified at Companies House on 15 December 2025, and admission to AIM was cancelled at 07:00 on 18 December 2025, the last day of dealings having been 17 December. A matched bargain facility with JP Jenkins was arranged so that shareholders could still trade, with the company reserving the right to review or withdraw it.

sections.heading: The Starlink company the group said it was keeping
sections.html:
The December 2024 circular named the subsidiary that was supposed to carry the group forward: Bigblu Broadband Group Services Ltd, described in terms as the company “which distributes Starlink”. Combined New Zealand and Starlink revenue was forecast at about £0.5 million for the year to 30 November 2024 and about £1 million for FY25. On a group that had just sold a £25 million-turnover business, that was the whole of the plan.

The register shows what became of it. Company 15960851 was incorporated on 17 September 2024 with a statement of capital of GBP 0.01. It never filed a set of accounts. It applied to strike itself off on 18 April 2026, a first Gazette notice for voluntary strike-off followed on 28 April 2026, and the final Gazette recording it as dissolved was filed on 14 July 2026. Nineteen months, one penny of capital, no accounts.

It did not go alone. Bigblu Broadband New Zealand Limited (15960667), incorporated the same day on the same GBP 0.01, followed exactly the same sequence to the same date, and so did Bigblu Broadband (EMEA) Limited (16298783). Three companies dissolved by voluntary strike-off on 14 July 2026, one of them the vehicle bearing the name of the country the board had described eight months earlier as where its remaining operations lay. These were UK-registered holding companies rather than the operating businesses themselves, so their removal is not proof that any trading operation has stopped — but it is the group’s own paperwork, and it points one way.

There is a smaller detail in the same filings worth noting, because it is the only sign of fresh money anywhere in the group. On 16 September 2025 the parent notified Christopher Harwood Bernard Mills as a person with significant control with effect from 4 September 2025; a new charge was registered on 23 December 2025, created the day after the delisting took effect, and runs to 29 pages. Three earlier charges were released on 15 December 2025 and formally satisfied in full on 26 March 2026. A capital reduction on 2 May 2025 cancelled shares and cleared the share premium account, moving stated capital to GBP 8,827,052.70.

sections.heading: Who answers when the dish stops working
sections.html:
This is the question the thin ordering page makes impossible to answer, and it is worth separating two things that are often run together. Ofcom’s automatic compensation scheme — £10.34 for each calendar day a fault goes unrepaired beyond two working days, £32.31 for a missed engineer appointment and £6.46 for each day a service starts late — is voluntary, and exactly ten providers have signed it. No satellite provider is among them and none ever has been, so a Bigblu customer has no claim to those amounts. That is a fact about the technology’s place in the market rather than about this seller.

Membership of a dispute scheme is different, because it is not voluntary. Ofcom states the obligation plainly: “All telecoms providers offering services to consumers and small businesses must be a member of one of these schemes”, the two approved schemes being the Communications Ombudsman and the Communications and Internet Services Adjudication Scheme (CISAS). Which of the two covers this service could not be established. The homepage names neither, and the site’s /complaints/, /terms-and-conditions/ and /about-us/ pages are all closed to automated reading, so the scheme, the early-termination charge and the contracting entity could not be checked from the documents. Treat that as unconfirmed rather than absent, and ask on the phone: the scheme name, and the company number behind it, are two sentences for a salesperson to supply.

The liquidation makes the question practical rather than academic. In a creditors’ voluntary liquidation an ordinary customer ranks as an unsecured creditor, behind the liquidators’ fees, behind secured lenders and behind preferential claims — which is the back of a queue that rarely reaches the end. A customer who had paid for hardware or a period of service in advance of BRDY Broadband’s wind-up on 7 March 2025 would have been in exactly that position. Anyone buying now should establish which company takes the payment before taking the dish, and should prefer a payment method with its own protection: a credit card purchase over £100 carries rights against the card issuer that a debit card or a direct transfer does not.

Independent measurement is no help here either, and the reason is structural. Ofcom’s quarterly complaints tables name only providers above a market-share threshold, which no satellite retailer reaches, and the annual consumer broadband surveys cover the large fixed-line names. No ratings body publishes a score for this service, so there is nothing to set against the corporate record above.

sections.heading: A brand with two addresses, one of which now sells something else entirely
sections.html:
The ordering site, broadband.bigblu.co.uk, was live and quoting £24.99 when it was checked on 12 October 2026. The domain a reader is far more likely to type is bigblu.co.uk, and that one no longer belongs to the business. On the same date it returned an HTTP 302 redirect to atomic-london.co.uk, a site whose content is a ranking of online casinos not covered by GamStop, carrying the notices “18+ Gambling can be addictive” and “We may receive a commission if you sign up via our links”, and whose own canonical tag points at a third unrelated domain. There is no mention of satellite broadband anywhere on it.

That is what an abandoned brand domain usually looks like once it has passed through the expired-domain market, and it is a hazard for anyone searching the brand by name rather than following a link. It is also the sharpest single illustration of the gap between the two halves of this review: one subdomain still selling a product, and the main address of the business pointed at a gambling affiliate.

It is worth remembering what this product was built for, because the policy backdrop has moved further than the dish has. In December 2015 the government rolled out a subsidy scheme for satellite connections aimed at an estimated 300,000 UK properties that could not get an affordable service of at least 2 Mbps, knocking around £350 off the cost of a dish and installation in return for a 12-month minimum subscription. The bar at the time was 2 Mbps. Ofcom’s current floor is 10 Mbit/s, and a household can require BT to spend up to £3,400 on building its share of a connection before satellite needs to be considered at all. A geostationary service averaging 21 Mb/s is a reasonable answer to the old question; the universal service request is free to make and is worth making first.

pros: £24.99 a month is a low headline price for a satellite connection, and it is a single package rather than a ladder of tiers a buyer has to decode

The data allowance is described as uncapped and unlimited, with no overnight-only window and no fair-use tier — the brand's predecessor sold allowances of 5GB to 150GB, so this is a real improvement on what the same business used to offer
An average of 21 Mb/s comfortably clears Ofcom's 10 Mbit/s definition of a decent connection, and at less than half the £59.60 monthly threshold that triggers a right to request one
Fourteen days to cancel after installation is counted from the engineer's visit rather than from the day the contract is signed, which is the point at which a customer can actually judge the service
A single UK sales line, 01869 722 425, on the same Oxfordshire dialling code the business has used since it traded as Avonline — a continuity worth something on a brand with this much corporate churn
The lineage is genuine: the business this grew out of had sold satellite broadband since 2002 and served more than 49,000 European customers on about £34.6 million of revenue before it was sold
cons: The ordering page names no company at all — no trading name, no company number, no VAT number and no registered address — so a buyer cannot tell who they would be contracting with before they ring

Contract length, hardware cost, installation cost and any minimum speed are all absent from the page. The brand's own predecessor published a 9 Mb/s guaranteed minimum, a £5 a month hardware rental and a £50 upfront charge; none of that structure is published now

The terms and conditions, complaints and about pages are all closed to automated reading, so the early-termination charge, the contracting entity and the compulsory dispute scheme could not be checked against any document
Ofcom requires every provider serving consumers to belong to the Communications Ombudsman or CISAS, and which scheme covers this service could not be established from anything the site publishes

BRDY Broadband Ltd (06759661), the company that previously operated this business under the name Bigblu Operations Limited, entered a creditors’ voluntary liquidation on 7 March 2025. Both Bigblu Services companies are filed for strike-off with accounts overdue since 30 November 2024, and three further group companies were dissolved on 14 July 2026

No automatic compensation. Ofcom's scheme pays £10.34 a day for an unrepaired fault, £32.31 for a missed appointment and £6.46 a day for a late start, and the ten signatories include no satellite provider — so the one failure a dish is bought to prevent carries no fixed redress
The main brand domain, bigblu.co.uk, redirected on 12 October 2026 to a site ranking online casinos outside GamStop, which is what a reader typing the brand name into a browser will find

No ratings body publishes a score for this service, and Ofcom's complaints tables name only providers above a market-share threshold, so there is no independent measurement to weigh against the corporate record
verdict: At £24.99 a month for an uncapped service averaging 21 Mb/s, this is priced where satellite broadband ought to be priced, and for a property that cannot get a usable fixed line it is a serious option. The obstacle is not the price and it is not the speed — it is that the page selling it names nobody. Every British company that has carried the Bigblu name is dissolved, in liquidation or filed for strike-off, the quoted parent left AIM on 18 December 2025 after selling its Australian business for up to AUD$50.20 million and returning £6.1 million to shareholders, and the subsidiary the board said would carry the group forward on Starlink distribution was dissolved on 14 July 2026 without ever filing accounts. Against that, a live site, a working sales number on the brand's original Oxfordshire code, and an offer that undercuts the £59.60 universal service price cap by more than half. Two things to do before paying, and both are free: ask the salesperson for the company name and number on the contract and for the name of its dispute scheme, and put in a universal service request first, because Ofcom can oblige BT to spend up to £3,400 on a fixed connection before a dish is the only answer. If the answers come back clearly, the price stands up.

faqs.q: How much does Bigblu satellite broadband cost?
faqs.a: The site advertises £24.99 per month for a service it describes as averaging 21 Mb/s with an uncapped, unlimited data allowance, checked on 12 October 2026. No contract length, hardware charge or installation charge is published alongside it, so the total cost of getting connected cannot be worked out from the page — ask for all three on the phone before ordering.

faqs.q: Which company would I be buying from?
faqs.a: The page does not say, and that is the single most important gap in it. Three corporate strands carry the name: Bigblu Services Limited (10201939) and Bigblu Services Holding Ltd (10177312), both filed for strike-off; BRDY Broadband Ltd (06759661), formerly Bigblu Operations Limited, in creditors’ voluntary liquidation since 7 March 2025; and Bigblu Broadband Limited (09223439), the former AIM-quoted parent, which remains active. Ask for the company name and number that will appear on the agreement.

faqs.q: Is Bigblu still in business?
faqs.a: The ordering site was live and quoting a price on 12 October 2026, so something is still selling under the name. What can be said from the register is narrower: the quoted parent cancelled its AIM admission at 07:00 on 18 December 2025 and re-registered as a private company on 15 December 2025; three group companies were dissolved by voluntary strike-off on 14 July 2026; and the former operating company is in liquidation. A live website is not evidence of a solvent counterparty either way, which is why the question above matters.

faqs.q: What happens if the service fails and I cannot get it fixed?
faqs.a: Ofcom’s automatic compensation scheme — £10.34 a day for an unrepaired fault, £32.31 for a missed appointment, £6.46 a day for a late start — is voluntary and has exactly ten signatories, none of them satellite providers, so it does not apply. A dispute scheme does: Ofcom requires every provider serving consumers to belong to the Communications Ombudsman or CISAS. The site names neither and its complaints page could not be read, so establish which one covers you before you buy.

faqs.q: Is satellite broadband still the right answer for a rural property?
faqs.a: It is now the third choice rather than the first. Ofcom’s right-to-request guidance, last updated 19 June 2026, sets a decent connection at 10 Mbit/s down and 1 Mbit/s up, and where building a property’s share of a fixed connection costs £3,400 or less, BT pays for the work. That request costs nothing to make. Satellite earns its place where a fixed line genuinely cannot be delivered, and a geostationary service averaging 21 Mb/s clears the speed bar when it is working.

faqs.q: Why does bigblu.co.uk take me to a gambling site?
faqs.a: On 12 October 2026 the bare bigblu.co.uk domain returned an HTTP 302 redirect to atomic-london.co.uk, which ranks online casinos outside GamStop and mentions satellite broadband nowhere. The ordering site is the separate subdomain broadband.bigblu.co.uk. Brand domains that lapse are routinely bought and repointed, so treat the short address as no longer connected to the business and go to the subdomain directly.

faqs.q: What happened to the rest of the Bigblu group?
faqs.a: It was sold piece by piece. The UK and European retail business went to Eutelsat S.A. under an announcement of 31 July 2020 for up to £39.3 million, covering eleven countries, more than 49,000 customers and about £34.6 million of revenue. Eutelsat announced its own exit from European retail broadband on 15 June 2023, selling to an unnamed private operator. The Australian business, SkyMesh, went to SKM Telecommunication Services Pty Ltd for up to AUD$50.20 million, completing on 23 December 2024, after which the parent returned £6.1 million to shareholders and left AIM.

title: Blackcircles.com Tyres Review: Fitted Prices, the Garage Network and the Small Print
meta_title: Blackcircles Tyres: £50.68 Fitted, Nothing on the Day
meta_description: Blackcircles sells tyres from £50.68 fully fitted, with VAT, fitting, balancing, valve and disposal in the price and 2,200 local garages doing the work.

headline.label: Cheapest 205/55 R16 tyre, fitted
headline.value: £50.68 — Wanli Sport Macro SA301 91V, fully fitted price including VAT, delivery, fitting, balancing, a new valve and disposal (checked 12 October 2026)

intro:
A 205/55 R16 tyre starts at £50.68 on Blackcircles.com, and that figure is the price on the car rather than the price in a box. The site states what sits inside it: “Fully fitted price includes VAT, delivery, fitting, balancing, new rubber valve & disposal of old tyres.” Four of them come to £202.72, with nothing to pay at the garage.

The company has been doing this since 2001 and it has been owned by Michelin since 2015, when the French tyre maker paid £50 million for it. Blackcircles says it has served more than two million customers and sold 36 million tyres. It owns no garages at all: you choose a fitting partner from a network the company puts at more than 2,200 across the UK, book a slot, pay online, and an independent business you have probably never dealt with does the half-hour of work. That arrangement is the reason the price can be a single number — the fitting is bought wholesale and bundled, not added at the counter — and the listings are honest about the product too, with the fuel, wet grip and noise grades printed against every tyre.

One thing to know before you book. Blackcircles puts the average gap between ordering and fitting at 48 hours, so this is not the route to a tyre this afternoon; a mobile appointment at home or work is usually included in the same fully fitted price, but it runs on the same lead time.

sections.heading: What £50.68 buys, and who turns the wheel nuts
sections.html:
Search by registration or by the three numbers on the sidewall and the 205/55 R16 page returns 21 distinct tyres. The bottom of the ladder on 12 October 2026 ran £50.68 for a Wanli Sport Macro SA301 in 91V, £55.21 for a Dynamo Street-H MH01 91V, £61.64 for a Triangle ReliaX Touring TE307 in 94W, and £66.66 for a Kumho Ecowing ES31 91H, with a Kumho 91V and a Yokohama BluEarth ES32 91V tied at £69.99. A separate brand table starts lower still, quoting Royal Black from £49.99, Westlake from £50.44 and Mazzini from £51.26, though it gives no model, load index or label grades to go with them.

Each listing carries the three graded figures a buyer is entitled to see. The Wanli is C for fuel and B for wet grip at 70 decibels; the Dynamo is D and C at 71; the Kumho is B and B at 69; the Yokohama is C and B at 68, which is the only A on the noise scale in the cheap half of the list. On a car tyre both letter scales now bottom out at E rather than G, and one step on the wet grip scale is worth several metres of stopping distance in the rain, so paying £16 more for the Kumho buys a measurable difference rather than a brand name.

The arithmetic that makes this kind of retailer worth a click is the fitting. Kwik Fit, which does own its centres, states that its tyre discounts “exclude charges for fitting, balancing, valve and disposal” and prices that work at £20.00 per tyre in one place on its own page and £20.50 in another, neither dated. Call it £82 on a set of four. Blackcircles has the same work inside the number on the screen, so £202.72 for four of the cheapest 205/55 R16 is the whole bill, and the only cash transaction at the garage is none. The company says so plainly: “nothing to pay on the day of your fitting.”

sections.heading: From Peebles to Clermont-Ferrand
sections.html:
The company was incorporated on 16 October 2001 as Online Tyre Store Limited, became Black Circles Limited four weeks later on 12 November, and took its present name on 26 September 2005. Mike Welch founded it in Peebles in the Scottish Borders, and it was among the first British businesses to sell a tyre online for fitting at a local garage. The registered office is now 1 Tanfield in Edinburgh and the registered activity is the retail trade of motor vehicle parts and accessories.

Michelin bought it in 2015 for £50 million. The person-with-significant-control register names Compagnie Générale des Établissements Michelin of 23 Place des Carmes-Déchaux, Clermont-Ferrand — a société en commandite par actions governed by French law — holding 75% or more of the voting rights since 6 April 2016. Blackcircles still sells every brand rather than only its parent's, which is worth saying because the only credit offer on the site is tied the other way: PayPal Credit at 0% for up to 12 months on spending of £500 or more, but on Michelin tyres specifically, against a representative 23.9% APR variable.

Unlike several of the online tyre shops it competes with, this one files full accounts. Thirty-two pages made up to 31 December 2025 went in on 23 September 2026, following the same for 2024 on 1 October 2025 and 2023 on 18 September 2024. A buyer who wants to know whether the company taking the money will still exist when a guarantee is claimed can read the answer rather than guess at it. For scale behind it, Michelin reported revenue of €12.7 billion for the six months to 30 June 2026, up 0.5% at constant exchange rates and down 2.6% as reported, with segment operating income of €1.45 billion at 11.4% of sales against 11.1% a year earlier, and free cash flow before acquisitions of €282 million against minus €102 million in the first half of 2025. The consumer tyre division alone turned over €6,926 million.

sections.heading: Four answers to one question: how many garages?
sections.html:
The network is the product here, and the company cannot settle on its size. On the fitting-network page itself the body text says “over 2,000 garages spread throughout the country” while the page's own meta description says “over 1,500 tyre fitting centres in the UK” and the site navigation above both says “Over 2,200 tyre fitters across the UK”. The about page says 2,200-plus and calls them fitting partners rather than centres. The mobile fitting page says over 2,000. None of the four figures is dated.

Whichever is right, the scale is real. For comparison, the National Tyre Distributors Association — the trade body for the whole British tyre trade, formed in 1930 — has more than 300 member companies between them representing over 2,000 tyre retail outlets. Blackcircles claims a booking network roughly the size of an entire national trade association's shopfront estate, and says 94% of the UK population lives within an eleven-minute drive of one of them, Northern Ireland included.

What the company publishes about quality is thinner than what it publishes about reach. A subset called Premier Garages, selected through a programme begun in 2010, is said to have “exceeded our rigorous criteria on capabilities, facilities and customer feedback” and to offer the highest standards of workmanship. For the other two thousand the site sets out no standard, no audit cycle and no minimum equipment at all, and there is no published way of telling from a search result whether the garage you have just booked has ever been inspected. A third strand, Blackcircles Pitstop, sits at what the company calls key Tesco stores and shopping centres, again without saying who owns or staffs it.

sections.heading: Two guarantees, one ladder, and a date in 2024
sections.html:
There are two products with similar names, and the free one is the problem. The Lifetime Guarantee was introduced in October 2021 and promises a replacement “where a tyre demonstrates a defect due to the manufacturing process or the materials used”, on car, van, 4x4 and SUV tyres from 22 named brands including Michelin, Continental, Goodyear, Pirelli, Bridgestone and Hankook. What you get depends on the tread left when the fault is assessed: 6mm or more brings a free replacement of the same model, 5mm to 5.99mm an 80% discount, 3mm to 4.99mm 60%, and 1.6mm to 2.99mm 40%, each against the price originally paid. Motorbike and truck tyres are out, and so is anything bought elsewhere.

Its own page then says: “Please note: Lifetime Guarantee is no longer active on orders placed after 12:00pm on 04/09/2024.” That is more than two years ago. The same page still carries the heading “Peace of mind, at no extra cost” and still says selected brands “now come with a Lifetime Guarantee, free of charge!”, and the about page still advertises the guarantee as a current reason to buy. A shopper reading either of those in October 2026 is reading about a benefit the company has withdrawn.

The paid Tyre Guarantee is live and it is the one worth understanding. It costs £6.99 a tyre where the pre-discount fitted price is under £49.99, then £7.99, £8.99, £10.99, £12.99, £14.99, £16.99, £20.99 and £21.99 as the tyre gets dearer, and it has to be bought for every tyre in the order. It covers accidental damage for 12 months from fitting and manufacturing defects for the tyre's legal life, which it defines as ending when the tread drops below 1.6mm. Inside the year it allows two puncture repairs with a £20 contribution from you on each, and one discounted replacement per tyre on exactly the same tread ladder as the free guarantee. Damage caused during fitting or removal is excluded, as are low pressures, overloading, snow chains, track use, malicious damage and fire.

Notice what is not stated. The page says Blackcircles provides the cover itself. It names no insurer, gives no Financial Conduct Authority firm reference and does not describe the product as insurance. The comparable product at Kwik Fit's counter names London General Insurance Company Limited, firm reference 202689, which brings the Financial Ombudsman Service and the Financial Services Compensation Scheme with it. Here, a disputed claim on a £21.99-a-tyre product is a contract dispute with the retailer and nothing more. Cancellation is 14 days from purchase, by emailing a form.

sections.heading: Clause 9.8 meets section 57 of the Consumer Rights Act
sections.html:
The terms of sale are clear that the fitting is subcontracted: the Fully Fitted Service means Blackcircles arranging fitting “using third party service providers”, and clause 7.1.2 refers to “the relevant tyre fitting agreement between Blackcircles.com and the relevant fitting centre”, which takes precedence where one exists. That agreement is not published, so the document actually governing the work on your car is one you cannot read.

Three clauses then narrow what the company answers for. Clause 9.4 requires a defect to be notified in writing within 48 hours of delivery or fitting, or within 24 hours of discovery where it was not apparent on reasonable inspection — a tight window for a fault that announces itself as a vibration at 60 miles an hour a week later. Clause 9.5 says the Blackcircles fitter must be given the chance to inspect and rectify any claimed fitting damage, and that work done by anyone else, at a garage the company has not designated or without written agreement, “will not be covered”; so a kerbed alloy cannot simply be repaired locally and invoiced. Clause 9.8 caps the company's entire liability at the price of the goods and excludes liability for loss arising from “the supply or fitting of the Goods”, apart from death or personal injury caused by negligence.

That last exclusion runs into statute. Section 49 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 treats every contract to supply a service as including a term that the trader must perform it with reasonable care and skill, and section 57(1) says a term is not binding on the consumer to the extent that it would exclude the trader's liability under section 49. Section 57(3) and 57(4) reach further, catching terms that restrict such liability, make a remedy conditional on something onerous, or stop the consumer recovering the price paid. Because Blackcircles sells the fitting as part of its own service rather than introducing you to a garage, section 49 bites on Blackcircles, and the remedies in sections 54 to 56 — repeat performance within a reasonable time and at the trader's cost, or a price reduction — are the consumer's whatever clause 9.8 says. The clause is in the contract; the statute says it is unenforceable to that extent. Anyone told otherwise on the phone should quote the section number.

sections.heading: Above the Head of Customer Care there is nobody
sections.html:
Clause 11.7 puts the contract under the law of Scotland and the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Scottish courts, wherever in the UK the customer lives and whichever garage does the work. The published escalation route stops inside the business: a customer care line on 01721 725 050, a WhatsApp number, and an invitation to write to Tracy Price, Head of Customer Care, who “will make sure your concerns are fully reviewed and put right as quickly as possible”. Naming a senior person is more than most retailers do.

Beyond that there is nothing. No ombudsman, alternative dispute resolution body, trade association or approved code scheme is named on the terms of sale, the help centre, the customer service pages or the contact page. The sector has a scheme and it is a good one: The Motor Ombudsman runs four codes of practice, all approved under the Chartered Trading Standards Institute's Approved Code Scheme, including a Service and Repair Code that covers exactly the work a fitting partner does. It can award up to £10,000 or the value of the vehicle, it gives a business up to eight weeks to issue a final response before it will look at a case, and it takes an average of 90 days to decide one; an adjudicator's view can be appealed by either side, and an ombudsman's final decision binds the business if the consumer accepts it.

Accreditation is applied for, paid for annually and spot-checked on site, and the scheme is blunt about the consequence of not joining: “We will not be able to take on a complaint about a business which is not accredited to a Code of Practice.” No accreditation for Blackcircles could be found, and it is not obvious how an online retailer that performs no work in its own premises would fit a garage code in any case. The practical effect is the same either way. If the company's final answer does not satisfy you, the next step is the small claims route in Scotland, not a free adjudication.

sections.heading: Mobile fitting, 48 hours and the £20 to send a tyre back
sections.html:
Mobile fitting is the quietly strong part of the proposition. The company says “the price of a mobile tyre appointment is included in the fully fitted price in most instances”, with an extra charge flagged on the fitter's listing before booking where one applies, typically in remote areas. A van comes to your home or to a workplace that allows access to the car, provided there is room to work safely, and the fitter installs the tyres, checks the balancing, fits a new rubber valve and takes the old tyres away for recycling. Evening and weekend slots exist. Allow about 30 minutes a tyre.

Cancellation is more generous than the law requires. The Consumer Contracts Regulations give 14 days on a distance sale; clause 8.1 allows 30 days from the day after delivery, or any time before the arranged fitting date, provided the tyres are unused and in the same condition. The cost of getting them back is yours, and a collection carries a “fixed return fee of £20” which the clause applies inside the fourteen-day cooling-off period as well as outside it. Return them yourself within 30 days of asking to cancel and that fee does not arise. Faulty, damaged or wrong goods are different: there the entitlement is a repair, replacement or refund under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 and no return fee applies. Anything beyond the statutory minimum, clause 8.2 says, is “entirely at the discretion of Blackcircles.com”.

Two smaller numbers from the same document. Delivery and fitting charges vary by location and by fitting centre, and some areas including the Isle of Man may carry a surcharge, so the headline price is not uniform across the country. And late payment on a trade or account order attracts interest at four per cent a year above the Bank of Scotland base rate.

pros: The advertised price is the fitted price: VAT, delivery, fitting, balancing, a new rubber valve and disposal of the old tyre are all inside it, and there is nothing to pay at the garage
£50.68 for a fitted 205/55 R16 is competitive once the £20.00 to £20.50 a tyre that a fitting charge costs elsewhere is taken into account
Mobile fitting at home or work is included in the same price in most cases, rather than being a paid extra or conditional on buying four tyres
94% of the population is said to be within an eleven-minute drive of a fitting partner, Northern Ireland included
Fuel efficiency, wet grip and noise grades are shown against every tyre in the listing, so the cheap options can be compared on something other than price
30 days to cancel an unused order, against the 14 the distance-selling rules require
Owned by Michelin since 2015 and files full 32-page accounts, most recently made up to 31 December 2025
The tread-depth credit ladder on a guarantee claim is published as exact percentages rather than left to discretion
cons: The free Lifetime Guarantee is still advertised as a current benefit on the about page while its own terms page says it stopped applying to orders placed after 12:00pm on 4 September 2024, more than two years ago
No ombudsman, alternative dispute resolution body or approved code scheme is named anywhere on the site, and the terms send a dispute to the Scottish courts wherever the customer lives

The paid Tyre Guarantee names no insurer and gives no FCA firm reference, so a disputed claim carries no Financial Ombudsman route and no compensation scheme behind it — unlike the equivalent product sold at a competitor's counter
The size of the fitting network is given four different ways across three of the company's own pages: over 1,500, over 2,000 and over 2,200, none of them dated

Nothing is published about how the roughly two thousand ordinary fitting partners are vetted, audited or equipped; only the Premier Garage subset has any stated criteria, and a search result does not say which is which
Clause 9.4 asks for a defect to be reported in writing within 48 hours of fitting, which is a short window for a fault that only shows itself at speed

Clause 9.8 purports to exclude liability for loss arising from the supply or fitting of the tyres, when section 57(1) of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 says a term excluding liability for failing to perform a service with reasonable care and skill is not binding on the consumer
The fitting agreement between Blackcircles and each garage takes precedence under clause 7.1.2 but is not published, so the document governing the work is one the customer cannot read
A 48-hour average lead time from order to fitment rules the site out for an urgent replacement
Returning an unwanted order costs £20 if the company collects it, and the clause applies that fee inside the statutory cooling-off period as well as outside it
verdict: As a way of buying tyres this works, and the reason it works is the single number. £50.68 fitted for a 205/55 R16, £202.72 for four, VAT and fitting and balancing and the valve and the disposal all inside it, and no card machine at the garage — that is a genuinely cleaner transaction than a tyre priced in a box with the labour to come, and the mobile option being included in most cases rather than sold as an upgrade is better than the market standard. Michelin's ownership since 2015 and 32 pages of filed accounts mean the company behind the guarantee can be checked. The caution is about what happens when something goes wrong, because that is where owning no garages shows. The work is done by one of two thousand independent businesses whose vetting is undescribed, under an agreement you cannot read, with a 48-hour notification window, a liability cap at the price of the tyres and no ombudsman above the company. Section 57 of the Consumer Rights Act makes the fitting exclusion unenforceable whatever the clause says, so the legal position is stronger than the contract reads — but enforcing it means the Scottish courts rather than a free adjudication. Buy on the fitted price, book a Premier Garage if one is near you, read the tread ladder before paying £6.99 a tyre for the guarantee, and do not count on the Lifetime Guarantee the site is still advertising.

faqs.q: Is the price on Blackcircles.com the final price?
faqs.a: For a fully fitted order, yes. The site states that the fully fitted price includes VAT, delivery, fitting, balancing, a new rubber valve and disposal of the old tyres, and that there is “nothing to pay on the day of your fitting”. The cheapest 205/55 R16 on 12 October 2026 was £50.68, so a set of four was £202.72 with no charge at the garage. Two caveats sit in clause 4.4 of the terms: delivery and fitting charges vary by location and by fitting centre, and some areas including the Isle of Man may carry a surcharge.

faqs.q: Does Blackcircles fit the tyres itself?
faqs.a: No. It owns no fitting centres. The terms describe the Fully Fitted Service as Blackcircles arranging fitting “using third party service providers”, and the company describes its network as the largest group of independently owned garages in the UK, put at over 1,500 on one page, over 2,000 on another and over 2,200 on a third. A selected subset called Premier Garages has published criteria; the rest have none stated. Because the fitting is sold as part of Blackcircles' own service, section 49 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 makes Blackcircles responsible for performing it with reasonable care and skill.

faqs.q: Is the Lifetime Guarantee still available?
faqs.a: Not on a new order. The Lifetime Guarantee page says the cover “is no longer active on orders placed after 12:00pm on 04/09/2024”, and tyres bought before it launched in October 2021 were never covered either. The same page and the about page both still present it as a free benefit, which is why it is worth checking rather than assuming. Claims on orders placed inside that window are still handled, on a tread ladder of a free replacement at 6mm or more, 80% off between 5mm and 5.99mm, 60% off between 3mm and 4.99mm and 40% off between 1.6mm and 2.99mm.

faqs.q: What does the paid Tyre Guarantee add?
faqs.a: Accidental damage cover for 12 months from fitting, which the free guarantee never included, plus manufacturing defect cover to the end of the tyre's legal life at 1.6mm of tread. It runs from £6.99 a tyre where the fitted price is under £49.99 up to £21.99 above £250, across nine bands, and must be bought for every tyre in the order. Inside the year it allows two puncture repairs with a £20 contribution each and one discounted replacement per tyre on the same tread ladder. Damage caused during fitting or removal is excluded. No insurer is named and no FCA firm reference is given, so a disputed claim is a contract matter with the retailer rather than one the Financial Ombudsman Service could look at.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if the fitting damages my wheel?
faqs.a: Blackcircles first, and clause 9.5 requires its own fitter to be given the chance to inspect and rectify the damage before anyone else touches it — repairs arranged independently will not be covered. Report it in writing quickly, because clause 9.4 asks for notification within 48 hours of fitting, or within 24 hours of discovery for a defect that was not apparent on inspection. If the answer does not satisfy you, there is no ombudsman: no alternative dispute resolution scheme is named anywhere on the site, The Motor Ombudsman cannot take a complaint about a business that is not accredited to one of its codes, and clause 11.7 points to the Scottish courts. Section 57(1) of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 still prevents clause 9.8 from excluding liability for poor workmanship.

faqs.q: How soon can the tyres be fitted?
faqs.a: Allow two days. The company puts the average lead time from ordering to fitment at 48 hours, and says a quicker supply can sometimes be organised. Fitting takes about 30 minutes a tyre, and evening and weekend appointments are available at both garages and mobile slots. For a tyre needed the same day, a retailer holding stock in its own centres is the better route.

title: boohoo Women's Fashion: Delivery, Returns and the Preloved Rail
meta_title: boohoo Review: Delivery, Returns and Preloved Prices
meta_description: boohoo delivery from GBP 2.99, Premier GBP 9.99 a year, 21 days to return and GBP 1.99 a parcel. Who you actually buy from, and what Preloved covers.
intro:
boohoo charges £3.99 for standard delivery, £2.99 to an InPost locker and £9.99 a year for unlimited Premier delivery, and it gives you 21 days to send something back — a week longer than the 14 days the law insists on. Returns cost £1.99 a parcel, deducted from the refund. Every figure here was read on 13 October 2026 from boohoo.com's own delivery, returns and terms pages.

The shop behind those prices is older than the brand suggests. Boohoo.com UK Limited was incorporated in Manchester on 27 February 2006 and traded as Wasabi Frog Limited until 14 April 2014; it still files from 49-51 Dale Street, M1 2HF. It is now one of five brands inside Debenhams Group, which describes itself as a platform carrying more than 25,000 partner brands, and which reported £795.6m of Youth Brands gross merchandise value before returns in its results for the year to 28 February 2025. That scale is why a £9.99 annual delivery pass and a seven-option delivery menu exist at this end of the market at all.

One thing is worth knowing before you fill a basket: not everything on boohoo.com is sold by boohoo. Third-party sellers, which the terms call Concessionaire Brands, contract with you directly, with DBZ Marketplace Online Limited (company number 13135555) acting as their "disclosed agent and not as principal". Those items are returned to the brand that supplied them rather than to boohoo, and the refund comes from the brand. Check the seller name on your order confirmation before you post anything back.

sections.heading: Seven ways to get a parcel, and the sum that decides whether Premier is worth it
sections.html:
boohoo publishes a seven-line delivery menu for the UK rather than the usual two, and the cheapest line is not the obvious one. A 24/7 InPost locker costs £2.99 and is quoted at about 3 working days. Standard delivery is £3.99 and quoted at about 4 working days, Monday to Saturday. An Evri ParcelShop drop is also £3.99 on a 4 working day estimate. Express is £4.99 and promises 3 working days, which makes the locker option both cheaper and, on boohoo's own stated timings, no slower. Next day is £5.99 with a cut-off of 12am, seven days a week. Northern Ireland standard is £4.99 on about 5 working days, and a bulky item is £4.99 on 5 to 7.

Premier is £9.99 for 12 months and covers standard, express, next day and Northern Ireland standard delivery. The arithmetic is ours rather than boohoo's, and it is simple: three standard orders at £3.99 come to £11.97, so the subscription has paid for itself on the third parcel. On next day it pays for itself on the second, because two orders at £5.99 come to £11.98. Anyone ordering monthly is better off with it by a wide margin; anyone ordering twice a year is not.

Two conditions sit underneath that. Subscriptions bought after 12am on 02.03.2023 carry a £20 minimum spend for free next day delivery, with free standard delivery still applying below £20. And the three cheapest or most specialised lines — the £2.99 InPost locker, the £3.99 Evri ParcelShop drop and the £4.99 bulky option — are not marked free with Premier, so the pass does not cover the single cheapest way to receive a boohoo order. To boohoo's credit the subscription does not roll over silently: the terms say it does not auto-charge for a second year, an email reminder goes out as the 12 months run down, and there is a 14-day cancellation window by email to customerservices@boohoo.com.

sections.heading: Twenty-one days, £1.99 a parcel, and the fourteen days you have regardless
sections.html:
boohoo gives 21 days from the day the order arrives to send something back, which is seven days more than the statutory minimum and more generous than several larger rivals. The charge is the trade-off: "a returns charge of £1.99 per parcel will be deducted from your refund amount", in the words of clause 10.5 of the terms. Send three parcels back from one order and that is £5.97 gone. Concession items work differently and better — a single £1.99 covers all of them regardless of how many parcels or partners are involved — while boohoo's own items are charged per parcel, so a mixed order can attract both.

Premier holders get one free return per order and pay for any further return against the same order. Once a parcel reaches the warehouse boohoo quotes up to 14 days to process the refund and up to 5 more days for a bank to show it, so the worst case from posting to money back is close to three weeks. A refund taken as a gift card is paid at 120% of the return value, which is a real 20% uplift for anyone who was going to spend it there anyway, though the card expires 90 days from receipt and the uplift is not offered to customers who paid with a gift card in the first place. Collection of a large electrical item costs a further £50.

The hygiene exclusions are longer than most: fashion face masks, cosmetics and beauty products, pierced jewellery, swimwear and lingerie where a hygiene or product seal has been broken, plus vitamins and supplements, medicines and toiletries. Clothing and footwear must come back unworn and unwashed with the original labels attached.

Set that against the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, which give a 14-day right to cancel an online order running from the day after the last item in it arrives, a refund due within 14 days of boohoo being told or of the goods coming back, and the basic outbound delivery charge refunded in full. The regulations forbid restocking and cancellation fees outright, but they do allow a retailer to make the customer bear the cost of return provided it said so up front, which is what the £1.99 is and why it is lawful. The exception matters more than the rule: on a faulty item, or one not as described, no return charge is properly payable at all, because the Consumer Rights Act 2015 remedy is not a change of mind. boohoo's own terms accept the principle, promising repair, replacement or refund on a faulty product, with a right to ask for evidence after 14 days.

sections.heading: A cancellation paragraph written for a customer in the EEA
sections.html:
The returns page explains the statutory right in these words: "If you are a customer in the European Economic Area (EEA) and you order an item online", you get "14 calendar days to cancel your order because you have changed your mind", and "This cancellation period starts from the day you have received all of the items in your order." It adds that "For the avoidance of doubt, your right to cancel does not apply to an in-store purchase."

The drafting has not kept up with the shop. boohoo.com's contracting company is registered in England and Wales, the United Kingdom is not a member of the European Economic Area, and the right a British shopper is exercising comes from the 2013 Regulations named above rather than from any EEA instrument — which the policy does not cite anywhere. The right is not in doubt and nothing here suggests boohoo refuses it; what is missing is any sentence telling a UK customer that the 14 days are theirs by law and sit underneath the 21-day goodwill policy. A shopper reading only that paragraph could reasonably conclude the cancellation right is for someone else.

It is worth knowing which of the two you are using, because they behave differently. Cancelling under the Regulations inside 14 days entitles you to the basic outbound delivery charge back as well as the price. Returning under boohoo's 21-day policy does not, and costs £1.99.

sections.heading: The company in the middle has had four names in five years
sections.html:
Where a boohoo order includes a third-party item, the terms name DBZ Marketplace Online Limited as the seller's agent. The register tells the rest of that story. Company 13135555 was incorporated on 14 January 2021 as Acraman 550 Limited, renamed Debenhams.com Online Limited eleven days later on 25 January 2021, renamed Debenhams Brands Limited on 30 March 2023, and renamed DBZ Marketplace Online Limited on 26 November 2024. It files from the same Manchester address as boohoo, 49-51 Dale Street, under the same mail-order SIC code 47910.

boohoo's documents have not converged on one of those names. The terms and conditions use "DBZ Marketplace Online Limited" at clause 2.2 and "Debenhams DBZ Limited" elsewhere in the same document; the returns policy heads its third-party section "Products bought from DBZ Brands:" and tells you to "return the item direct to the Concessionaire Brand that supplied the item"; and the help pages carry "Debenhams.com Online Limited", which the register shows was that company's name until March 2023. Two of the four names a shopper may meet are former names of one company, which is checkable in a minute on Companies House and not explained anywhere on boohoo.com.

None of this is hidden and none of it changes your rights, because the law makes the disclosed seller responsible either way. It changes the practical question of where a parcel goes and who owes the refund, so the useful habit is to read the seller name on the order confirmation rather than assuming boohoo sold you the dress. The same company number is the one named in Annex A of the green claims undertaking below, under the Debenhams Brands name it carried in March 2024.

sections.heading: What Boohoo Group actually promised the competition regulator
sections.html:
This is the most substantial document anyone has published about how boohoo describes its clothes, and almost nobody reads it. The Competition and Markets Authority began reviewing environmental claims in fashion retail on 10 January 2022, opened a case against three businesses on 29 July 2022, published it on 26 January 2023 and closed it on 27 March 2024 when all three signed formal undertakings. The CMA's own figures put Boohoo's 2022 global sales "in excess of £1.9 billion" with 20 million active customers worldwide, and the three businesses together on £4.4 billion of UK fashion sales a year.

The undertaking is given by Boohoo Group plc, Jersey registered number 114397, registered at 12 Castle Street, St Helier JE2 3RT with a UK principal place of business at 49/51 Dale Street, Manchester M1 2HF. It binds the five companies in Annex A — Boohoo.com UK Limited, Prettylittlething.com Ltd, KarenMillen.com Limited, Nasty Gal Limited and Debenhams Brands Limited — and it is expressly not an admission that anyone broke the law. The legal basis is Part 8, section 219 of the Enterprise Act 2002 in relation to the Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008.

What it commits boohoo to is unusually concrete for a voluntary document. Paragraph 1 bars new misleading environmental claims; paragraph 2 gave 2 months to remove or amend the ones already up. Paragraph 4 covers misleading icons, logos and imagery and paragraph 6 covers filter and navigation names, so a menu item called something green is itself a claim. Paragraph 7 requires the inclusion criteria for any environmental range to be published clearly and prominently, and paragraph 8 requires a summary of those criteria, including minimum thresholds, to travel with every purchasable item in the range. Paragraph 10 bans vague fabric language such as "eco-fabrics" in favour of objective characteristics, and paragraph 11 forbids labelling a product as part of a range it does not fully qualify for.

The two paragraphs a shopper can test on a product page are 18 and 19. Paragraph 18 bars a recycled or organic claim where the garment contains non-qualifying fibres in more than a negligible proportion, with fasteners, buttons, zips and threads left out of the calculation. Paragraph 19 requires the specific percentage of recycled or organic fibre, or at least the minimum percentage, evidenced by supplier due diligence or testing. Paragraphs 14 to 16 do the same job for target-based claims, paragraph 17 for claims covering only part of a product's life cycle, paragraphs 20 to 22 for third-party accreditations, and paragraphs 23 and 24 for overall-impact and comparative claims.

Then there are the enhanced consumer measures, which are the operational half. Paragraph 26(b)(ii) required spot checks on a representative sample of supplier certificates within 3 months and at least yearly after that; 26(b)(iii) required confirmations from existing suppliers inside the same 3 months; 26(c) says a claim must come down if a due diligence failure is not remedied or an error is not rectified within 10 working days. Paragraph 26(e) is the one with teeth: spot checks on at least 5% of new listings carrying an environmental claim, at least weekly, starting within 5 working days. Paragraph 26(h) gives 5 working days to pull or fix a misleading claim once boohoo knows about it. Internal documents were due within 6 months under paragraph 27, drafts to the CMA within 2 months under 28, and staff training by the same 6-month date and annually thereafter under paragraph 29.

sections.heading: Ready for the Future, and the clock that ran out in March 2026
sections.html:
The range all of that attaches to was called Ready for the Future, named as such in the CMA's own press notice of 27 March 2024. It is not on boohoo.com now. The site's /womens/looks/sustainability path, which is where an environmental edit would sit, returned no environmental range at all on 13 October 2026: no range name, no inclusion criteria, no stated recycled or organic percentage, and nothing in the navigation described as eco, sustainable, recycled or organic. Whether the range was withdrawn, renamed or simply moved could not be established from boohoo's own pages, and this page does not assert which.

The reporting machinery has a published end, and it has passed. Records had to be kept until the Reporting End Date, which the undertaking sets at 2 years after signature — 27 March 2026. The reporting periods ran 6 months, then a second 6 months to the one-year mark, then 12 months to the end; a declaration report was due within 20 working days of the first period under paragraph 34, further reports within 20 working days of each period under paragraphs 35 to 37, and spot check reports within 10 working days of each 3-month spot check period under paragraph 38. Annex B carries the whole timetable from "Immediately" to the two-year mark.

Two things follow, and the second is the one that matters to a shopper. The reporting obligations have run their course, and whether the CMA still treats any part of them as live is not something this page can settle. But the substantive conduct paragraphs, 1 to 24, carry no expiry date in the document at all. The ban on unquantified recycled claims, the requirement to publish range criteria, the prohibition on green filter names: none of that was time-limited, and all of it is still a commitment on the record. The sector guidance the CMA published afterwards, on 18 September 2024, deliberately sets very few numerical thresholds, so the undertaking remains the most specific thing boohoo has signed on the subject. If a recycled claim ever reappears on a boohoo listing without a percentage next to it, paragraph 19 is the sentence to quote.

sections.heading: The Preloved rail: eight subcategories and no explanation
sections.html:
boohoo does publish a second-hand department, which is more than the brand's reputation would lead you to expect. It runs to eight subcategories — Women's Preloved, Women's Preloved Shoes, Preloved Accessories, Preloved Fashion, Preloved Clothing, Preloved Jewellery, Preloved Bags and Men's Preloved — introduced on the site with the line "Introducing Preloved products here at boohoo!" The copy is aimed squarely at designer resale: the clothing page talks about "preloved Gucci outfits" and "pre-loved designer clothing", the bags page names Dior, Fendi and Gucci and promises "preloved designer bags and second-hand bags for timeless style at irresistible prices", adding that "Each piece has a story - and now it's ready for a new one with you."

What those pages do not carry is any explanation of the scheme. No partner, platform or consignment seller is named on any of the three pages read on 13 October 2026. Nothing states how items are sourced, who authenticates a designer bag, or how condition is graded — there is no equivalent of the four-step grading ladders used elsewhere in resale. The returns policy makes no mention of pre-owned goods anywhere, so a buyer is left to assume the standard 21 days and £1.99 apply to a second-hand Fendi bag on the same terms as a £8 top, and the hygiene exclusions list says nothing about used clothing either.

Two limits on what can be said about the size of it, stated plainly rather than guessed. No item count and no price could be read from any of the Preloved pages, and that is not evidence the rail is empty: boohoo.com serves no product grid at all to an automated read, which was confirmed by checking the ordinary women's dresses department, where no product or price appeared either. So the depth of the Preloved stock needs confirming by eye. And in the other direction the position is clear: there is no route on boohoo.com to buy a second-hand boohoo garment, no take-back or recycling scheme, and no sell-back — boohoo buys nothing from its customers. A boohoo dress reaching a second owner does so somewhere else entirely.

sections.heading: Paying in instalments stopped being unregulated on 15 July 2026
sections.html:
Fast fashion and deferred payment grew up together, and the rules changed this summer. From 15 July 2026 the Financial Conduct Authority regulates deferred payment credit, the formal name for interest-free buy now, pay later. Firms could register for the temporary permissions regime between 15 May 2026 and 1 July 2026 and then have 6 months from the start of the regime to apply for full authorisation. Agreements entered into before 15 July 2026 remain exempt, so the protections attach to new plans rather than old ones.

The FCA set out what that buys a shopper in its statement of 11 February 2026. Lenders must carry out proportionate checks that a customer can afford to repay before the option is offered. They must support customers in financial difficulty and, where appropriate, point them to free debt advice. Consumers get upfront information on payment dates, amounts and what happens if a payment is missed. The whole sector comes under the Consumer Duty, and a shopper who thinks something has gone wrong can complain to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which was not available on these agreements before. For scale, the FCA puts the market at £0.06bn in 2017 and over £13bn in 2024, with 20% of UK consumers — 10.9 million adults — having used it in the 12 months to May 2024.

boohoo's side of this is thinner than it should be. Its own documents refer only to a generic "buy now, pay later" service provider rather than naming one, and the returns wording passes the refund straight out of its hands: boohoo will "notify the relevant service provider that you have returned your Products to us", after which "the relevant service provider will process your full or partial refund as applicable, in accordance with its terms and conditions", with the note that "different refund processing times may apply" and an instruction to "review the applicable terms for your chosen service provider". Stack that on top of boohoo's own 14 days to process and up to 5 days for the bank, and a returned instalment order has two queues to clear. The payment page itself lists Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Maestro, Visa Electron and Apple Pay by icon, and names no instalment provider at all.

sections.heading: If it goes wrong, the escalation route runs out quickly
sections.html:
boohoo's terms do the ordinary things properly. Clause 1.1 names the operator, clause 4.1 warns that product images "are for illustrative purposes only" and that it "cannot guarantee" how a screen renders colour, clause 5.1(a) requires a customer to be at least 18 in England and Wales, and clause 8.5 reserves the position "where there is a pricing error that is obvious and unmistakable". Clause 16.1 accepts responsibility for "loss or damage you suffer that is a foreseeable result of our breach" while excluding unforeseeable loss, which is the standard formulation.

What is absent is the next step. No alternative dispute resolution body and no ombudsman is named in the terms or the returns policy, and boohoo is not on the published member list of RetailADR, the retail sector's certified ADR scheme and a trading name of Consumer Dispute Resolution Ltd, company number 09189773. Neither Boohoo.com UK Limited nor Debenhams appears on it, while ASOS, Footasylum, Boux Avenue, Damart, Hobbs, Miss Selfridge, Oliver Bonas, TK Maxx, Topshop and Topman all do (checked 13 October 2026). A customer who exhausts boohoo's own complaints handling is left with the county court or a card chargeback rather than a free independent decision.

Two registers are worth knowing about, and one of them reads in boohoo's favour. The Office for Product Safety and Standards publishes every product safety alert, report and recall in the UK, and a search on the keyword boohoo returned 0 reports on 13 October 2026. That is an absence rather than a clean bill of health, since reports name the product and not always the retailer, but it is a free check any shopper can run in thirty seconds. The other register is Companies House, where Boohoo.com UK Limited files audit exemption subsidiary accounts supported by a statement of guarantee from its parent: the parent guarantee and the notice of agreement to exemption from audit were filed on 4 March 2026 and the accounts for the year to 28 February 2025 followed on 21 March 2026; the next set, to 28 February 2026, is due by 30 November 2026. There is no auditor's opinion on the trading company's own numbers, which is lawful and common in a group structure, and worth knowing if you are wondering who stands behind a refund.

Seven separate UK delivery options, including a £2.99 InPost locker that is cheaper than standard delivery and quoted at a day faster
Premier at £9.99 for 12 months pays for itself on the third standard order or the second next-day order, and does not auto-charge for a second year
A 14-day cooling-off period on the Premier subscription itself, cancellable by email
A refund taken as a gift card is paid at 120% of the return value
A single £1.99 covers every concession item in a return however many separate partners and parcels are involved
