A Preloved department of eight subcategories exists at all, which is more than most fast-fashion sites offer
0 reports against the keyword boohoo on the Office for Product Safety and Standards register, checked 13 October 2026
cons: Returns cost £1.99 per parcel out of the refund, so a single order split across three parcels costs £5.97 to send back, and Premier covers only one free return per order

No alternative dispute resolution body or ombudsman is named anywhere in the terms or returns policy, and boohoo is absent from RetailADR's member list while ASOS, Hobbs, Oliver Bonas, TK Maxx, Topshop and Topman all appear on it

The Preloved pages name no supplier, platform or consignment partner, publish no condition grading and say nothing about how a second-hand return works, and the returns policy does not mention pre-owned goods at all
There is no route to buy a second-hand boohoo garment, no take-back or recycling scheme and no sell-back of any kind — boohoo buys nothing from its customers

The cancellation paragraph on the returns page is addressed to "a customer in the European Economic Area (EEA)", cites no UK regulation, and nowhere tells a British shopper that the 14-day right comes from the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013

Ready for the Future, the environmental range the CMA undertaking was built around, is not visible on boohoo.com: the sustainability path returned no range, no inclusion criteria and no recycled or organic percentage on 13 October 2026

boohoo's own documents give at least four names for the third-party seller arrangement — DBZ Marketplace Online Limited, Debenhams DBZ Limited, DBZ Brands and Debenhams.com Online Limited — two of which the register shows are former names of the same company
No instalment provider is named in the payment, returns or terms pages, which refer only to a generic "buy now, pay later" service provider whose own refund timings apply on top of boohoo's 14 days

No product price or item count can be read from boohoo.com by any automated means, including on the ordinary dresses department, so nothing on the site can be price-checked without browsing it by hand
The trading company you contract with files unaudited accounts under a parent guarantee, so no auditor has given an opinion on Boohoo.com UK Limited's own figures
verdict: On the things a shopper decides on before paying, boohoo is better than its reputation: a £2.99 locker delivery, a £9.99 annual pass that pays for itself on the third order, and 21 days to change your mind against a legal minimum of 14. The £1.99 per-parcel return charge is the price of that, it is lawful because it is disclosed, and it is worth remembering that it should never be charged on a faulty item. On the question this category is compared on — how many ways there are to buy the same clothes second-hand — the answer is one, and it is a designer resale rail with no partner named, no grading published and no returns wording of its own, while there is no route to a second-hand boohoo garment and nothing boohoo will buy back. The most interesting document in the whole picture is the undertaking Boohoo Group plc signed on 27 March 2024, which still commits it, with no expiry, to putting a percentage next to any recycled claim and publishing the criteria for any environmental range. The reporting clock behind it ran out on 27 March 2026 and the range it was written about is no longer on the site, which makes those paragraphs easier to forget and more useful to quote. Buy on the delivery terms, not on the green copy, read the seller name on your order confirmation, and if you pay in instalments remember that since 15 July 2026 the Financial Ombudsman Service is finally available on the credit even though it is not available on the shop.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to return something to boohoo?
faqs.a: £1.99 per parcel, deducted from the refund rather than paid up front, under clause 10.5 of boohoo's terms. Items from a third-party concession brand are charged a single £1.99 between them however many parcels or partners are involved, so a mixed order can attract both charges. Premier members get one free return per order and pay for any further return against that order. Collection of a large electrical item costs a further £50. No return charge should be applied to a faulty item or one that is not as described, because that is a Consumer Rights Act 2015 remedy rather than a change of mind.

faqs.q: How long do I have to send a boohoo order back?
faqs.a: 21 days from the day you receive the order, which is boohoo's own policy and seven days more than the law requires. Separately, the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 give you 14 days to cancel an online order, counted from the day after the last item arrives, and cancelling that way entitles you to the basic outbound delivery charge back as well as the price. Once a return reaches boohoo it quotes up to 14 days to process the refund and up to 5 further days for a bank to show it.

faqs.q: Is boohoo Premier worth £9.99?
faqs.a: It depends on how often you order, and the sum is short. Three standard deliveries at £3.99 cost £11.97, so Premier is ahead from the third parcel; two next-day deliveries at £5.99 cost £11.98, so it is ahead from the second. It covers standard, express, next day and Northern Ireland standard delivery for 12 months, but not the £2.99 InPost locker, the £3.99 Evri ParcelShop drop or bulky delivery. Subscriptions bought after 12am on 02.03.2023 need a £20 minimum spend for free next day. boohoo says it does not charge automatically for a second year.

faqs.q: Does boohoo sell second-hand clothes?
faqs.a: It publishes a Preloved department with eight subcategories, and the copy is about pre-owned designer pieces rather than used boohoo stock — Gucci, Dior and Fendi are the labels it names. No supplier, platform or authentication partner is identified on those pages, no condition grading is published, and the returns policy does not mention pre-owned goods. There is no route on boohoo.com to buy a second-hand boohoo garment, and no scheme of any kind for selling your old clothes back or recycling them through boohoo.

faqs.q: Who am I actually buying from on boohoo.com?
faqs.a: For boohoo's own stock, Boohoo.com UK Limited, company number 05723154, registered at 49-51 Dale Street, Manchester M1 2HF. For a third-party item the contract is with the seller, which the terms call a Concessionaire Brand, and DBZ Marketplace Online Limited (company number 13135555) acts as that seller's disclosed agent and not as principal. Those items go back to the brand that supplied them and the brand pays the refund, so it is worth reading the seller name on the order confirmation before posting anything.

faqs.q: What did boohoo promise the CMA about its green claims?
faqs.a: Boohoo Group plc signed a formal undertaking on 27 March 2024 under Part 8, section 219 of the Enterprise Act 2002, closing a case opened on 29 July 2022. Twenty-four conduct paragraphs cover misleading claims, imagery, filter names, fabric descriptions and accreditations. The two most testable are paragraph 18, which bars a recycled or organic claim where non-qualifying fibres are more than negligible, and paragraph 19, which requires the specific or minimum percentage to be stated. It was given without any admission of wrongdoing, and the reporting obligations ran to a date 2 years after signature.

faqs.q: Who can I complain to about boohoo if customer services cannot help?
faqs.a: There is no free independent scheme covering the shop. boohoo names no alternative dispute resolution body or ombudsman in its terms or returns policy and does not appear on RetailADR's published member list, where ASOS, Hobbs, Oliver Bonas, TK Maxx, Topshop and Topman do. That leaves a card chargeback or the county court for the purchase itself. Since 15 July 2026, though, an interest-free instalment plan used to pay for an order is regulated credit, so a complaint about the credit can go to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

title: Booking.com Hotels
meta_title: Booking.com: Why the Hotel's Own Site Can Now Be Cheaper
meta_description: Booking.com lists 4.4 million places to stay. Since July 2024 hotels have been free to price their own sites lower. How to use that before you book.
intro:
Booking.com carries roughly 4.4 million properties in over 220 countries and territories, of which about 500,000 are hotels, motels and resorts and about 3.9 million are homes, apartments and other places to stay. Travellers booked 1,235 million room nights through its parent in the year to 31 December 2025, worth $186.1 billion in gross bookings. Those figures come from Booking Holdings' own annual report on Form 10-K, not from an estimate.

That scale is the reason to start a search here. It is also worth knowing, before you start, how the site is put together. Booking.com's own terms say that "Our Platform only shows Accommodations that have a commercial relationship with us", and that when you book, "it's directly with the Service Provider" rather than with Booking.com. The company describes itself as providing the platform and says it is "not responsible for the Travel Experience itself". So the room is the hotel's, the contract is the hotel's, and the commission is Booking.com's. None of that is unusual for a booking site and none of it costs you anything at the point of sale, but it decides who you ring when a room turns out not to exist.

Signing in is worth doing before you search rather than after. Genius Level 1 is free on sign-in and gives 10% off the price of a stay before taxes and charges at participating properties; five stays in two years unlocks Level 2, worth "a 10% or 15% discount applied to the price before taxes and fees", plus free breakfast and a free room upgrade where the property offers them. Many rooms can also be held without payment and settled at the property.

sections.heading: Four and a half million places to stay, and 500,000 of them are hotels
sections.html:
The catalogue is the product. Booking Holdings' Form 10-K for the year ended 31 December 2025 puts it at approximately 4.4 million properties in over 220 countries and territories, split between approximately 500,000 hotels, motels and resorts and approximately 3.9 million homes, apartments, and other unique places to stay. The group's own factsheet gives a larger number still — 31 million or more reported listings on Booking.com — because a property with forty rooms types can be many listings. Both numbers are the company's own and they measure different things; the 4.4 million is the one to use.

Trade is growing and the growth is slowing. The year to 31 December 2025 produced 1,235 million room nights, up 8%, on $186.1 billion of gross bookings, up 12%, with revenues of $26,917 million and operating income of $8,825 million. Net income fell 8% to $5,404 million. The quarter to 30 June 2026, announced on 4 August 2026, gave 325 million room nights, up 5%, and $51.0 billion of gross bookings, up 9% — slower on both measures than the full year before it. The group employed approximately 24,300 people at the end of 2025.

One line in those accounts explains more about how a search result is built than anything on the consumer site. Marketing cost $8,186 million in 2025 against $26,917 million of revenue, and $4,439 million in the first half of 2026 against $12,884 million. By our own arithmetic that is about 30p in every pound of revenue in 2025 rising to about 34p in the first half of 2026. A platform spending a third of its income buying traffic is a platform under pressure to convert the traffic it buys, and that is the honest context for every scarcity message and every highlighted deal you will see on the page.

sections.heading: No London lead-in price appears anywhere on the destination pages
sections.html:
Most accommodation platforms publish a "from" price per city, which lets you see the floor of the catalogue before you commit to dates. Booking.com does not. Its Greater London page was read on 16 October 2026 and carried property names, guest scores — The Savoy at 9.2, Peckham Lodge at 6.6 — a count of 9,357 reviews and a line saying 38 guests from the United States had booked in the last minute, and not one price. The budget-hotels page for London was the same: ten named properties, no figures. There is no lead-in rate to quote because the company does not publish one.

So the honest comparison figure has to come from the operator whose rooms sit at the bottom of that catalogue. Travelodge states its own floor plainly: "Rooms under £35 are available throughout the UK and from £49 in London". A specific dated example from the same chain, read the same day: the nearby-hotels module on the Travelodge London City page at 20 Middlesex Street, London E1 7EX advertised £55.99 for one adult at London Central Aldgate East for the night of 18 October 2026 — two days out, which is exactly when a late booking is made.

Hold those two numbers next to each other and the shape of the London market appears without anybody's marketing: a published floor of £49, and £55.99 for an actual bed on an actual Sunday in mid-October. What Booking.com adds is not a lower floor. It is the ability to see that chain and four hundred others on one screen.

sections.heading: Sixteen years of argument about whether a hotel is allowed to undercut the booking site
sections.html:
This is the part worth knowing before you pay, and almost nobody writing about Booking.com covers it. For most of the site's life, contracts with hotels carried parity clauses — rules stopping a hotel from offering a better price elsewhere. A wide parity clause covered rival booking sites; a narrow one covered the hotel's own website. The second is the one that mattered to you, because it meant ringing the hotel direct could not legally get you a lower rate.

Britain's competition authorities went at this first and did not finish the job. The Office of Fair Trading opened an investigation in September 2010 into arrangements between InterContinental Hotels Group, Booking.com B.V. and Expedia over room-only bookings, issuing a Statement of Objections in July 2012 alleging the arrangements "restricted the OTA's ability to discount the headline rate". Commitments were offered in August 2013 and accepted in January 2014; the Competition Appeal Tribunal quashed that decision on 26 September 2014; and on 16 September 2015 the Competition and Markets Authority closed the case because it "no longer constitutes an administrative priority", stating plainly that this "does not amount to a decision or view as to whether a party acted illegally". Five years, no answer.

What filled the gap was voluntary. France, Italy and Sweden accepted commitments from Booking.com on 21 April 2015 and the amended parity terms took effect on 1 July 2015. The CMA's follow-on monitoring case records that those formal commitments on wide parity expired on 1 July 2020, and that on 20 August 2020 both Booking.com and Expedia said they would continue to act in line with them and that this would also apply in the UK. That CMA page has not been updated since. A separate CMA action on 6 February 2019 had already taken undertakings from six sites — Expedia, Booking.com, Agoda, Hotels.com, ebookers and trivago — on search ranking, pressure selling, discount claims and hidden charges, with changes required by 1 September that year, though the CMA made no finding that the law had been broken.

The answer arrived from elsewhere, twice, in the same summer. On 30 July 2024 Spain's competition authority fined Booking.com €413,240,000, in two penalties of €206,620,000, for conduct running "from at least 1 January 2019 to date", including a narrow parity clause which "prevents them from offering their rooms on their own websites below the price they offer on Booking.com". The regulator put Booking.com's share of Spanish hotel booking intermediation at between 70% and 90% across the period. Seven weeks later, on 19 September 2024, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in case C-264/23 that parity clauses "cannot, in principle, be classified as 'ancillary restraints'", finding that wide clauses "carry the risk of ousting small platforms and new entrants" and that even narrow ones "do not appear to be objectively necessary to ensure the economic viability of the hotel reservation platform".

What this means at the keyboard is simple. A hotel may now price its own website below Booking.com, and some say so outright — Travelodge's own guidance reads "You will always find our lowest prices on our website". Find the property on Booking.com, where the choice is, then spend thirty seconds checking the property's own site before you confirm. On a Genius rate Booking.com will often still win; on a plain rate it may not.

sections.heading: Being a designated gatekeeper means something specific, and it stops at the Channel
sections.html:
Booking.com is the only accommodation platform in the world carrying a formal gatekeeper designation. The European Commission received its notification on 1 March 2024 and designated it on 13 May 2024 in respect of "its online intermediation service Booking.com" under the Digital Markets Act. Obligations have bound it since 14 November 2024.

The Commission's own factsheet of 28 September 2026 sets out what that buys a traveller. Under Article 5(3), businesses active on Booking.com in the European Economic Area "can now freely set their prices and conditions on and off Booking.com", and the prohibition reaches "parity requirements of any kind (contractual or other measures having the same effect)". Removal of contractual parity requirements was completed in July 2024, and in September 2026 Booking.com stopped using prices found on other sites to decide eligibility for its Booking Sponsored Benefit. That last change is the interesting one: it closes the gap between dropping a clause from a contract and dropping the commercial consequence of breaking it.

Here is the part a British reader should hold on to. The Digital Markets Act is European law and the freedom it creates is a freedom for properties in the EEA. The United Kingdom's equivalent regime has so far given strategic market status only to Apple and Google in mobile platforms and to Google in general search. Booking.com has not been designated here. For a hotel in Manchester or Margate, the right to undercut rests on the statement Booking.com made on 20 August 2020 that it would keep acting in line with commitments that had expired seven weeks earlier — a company undertaking recorded on a regulator's page, not an enforceable duty. The practical advice does not change, but the strength of the backing behind it does, depending on which side of the Channel your hotel sits.

sections.heading: The Genius discount costs the property more than it costs you
sections.html:
Genius is a good deal and it is worth taking. It is also worth understanding who pays for it. Booking.com's own help article for property owners explains that commission is "a set percentage of the value of each reservation you receive through our platform", that the percentage "varies per country and can also vary depending on your property type or location", and that if the rate charged is higher than the contract rate, "you may be participating in a programme like Genius, Preferred Partner or Visibility Booster". The traveller's 10% or 15% comes out of the property's margin twice over — once as the discount, once as the higher commission that buys the placement.

Spain's regulator described the same machinery from the outside in its 30 July 2024 decision. It found that the Preferred, Preferred Plus and Genius programmes improve a property's position in search results in exchange for higher commissions or discounts, that entry to the Preferred tiers depends partly on how profitable the property is for Booking.com, and that the default ranking uses "the total number of bookings of a hotel through Booking.com" as one of its criteria. A property that sells well through other channels therefore ranks lower here than one of the same quality that does not.

The commission rate itself is never published — not on the consumer site and not in the partner help article that explains how it works. A few of its edges are. Commission falls due on a confirmed stay, on a non-refundable booking whether the guest turns up or not, and on a no-show or a cancellation where the property charges the guest. On an overbooking it is still charged, waived only "if your property has been live on our platform for fewer than 30 days" or "if you've had fewer than five overbookings in 12 months". The one entry on the consumer side pointing the other way is clause B7, which states that "Some of the price reductions you see are funded by us, not by the Service Provider" — Booking.com buying a sale out of its own margin, which is a real point in its favour and a rare thing for a platform to admit in writing.

sections.heading: Whose contract, whose courts, and what the liability cap is actually worth
sections.html:
The terms are numbered, in plain English, and clearer than most in this sector, which makes it easy to read what they say. Clause A3.1: Booking.com B.V. "provides and is responsible for the Platform, but not the Travel Experience itself". Clause B2.1: the booking is "directly with the Service Provider". Car hire and transport sit with a different company again, Booking.com Transport Limited.

Clause A18.3 sets the ceiling: "The cost of your Booking, shown in your confirmation email, is the most we, or any Service Provider, will be liable for." That is better than some rivals, whose caps are pegged to an unpublished booking fee, and it is still only the room. A cancelled room that costs you a missed flight and a replacement hotel is capped at the price of the room. Liability for death, personal injury, fraud, gross negligence and wilful misconduct is not limited, as it cannot be.

Clause A19 is the one to read twice. Disputes go to individual binding arbitration administered by the American Arbitration Association, with class and representative actions waived and jury trial given up; the agreement is governed by the US Federal Arbitration Act and New York law, and non-arbitrable disputes are to be resolved "exclusively in the federal or state courts of New York, New York". There is a fallback — where local law prevents a dispute being resolved in New York, local courts and local law apply — and a British consumer's own rights are not displaced by a contract. There is also an opt-out, and it is short: a written notice within 30 days, which Booking.com must receive within three days of that deadline. Before arbitrating you must file a written complaint and wait 60 days.

If that goes nowhere there is no ombudsman. The terms say Booking.com tries to resolve disputes internally and is not required to use independent alternative dispute resolution. Clause A15.3 offers European Economic Area residents the European Commission's Online Dispute Resolution platform instead — a platform that stopped operating on 20 July 2025 under Regulation (EU) 2024/3228, and which had not covered UK consumers since Brexit in any event. Clause A20 does set out EU and UK Package Travel Requirements and insolvency protection for linked travel arrangements, so a room booked alongside a flight is in a different and better position from a room booked on its own.

sections.heading: The British end of the business, which is older than the brand
sections.html:
Booking.com has a UK company and it predates the name by eight years. Booking.com Limited, company 03512889, was incorporated on 18 February 1998 as The Active Booking Company Ltd, became ActiveBooking.com Ltd on 17 May 2000, Active Hotels Limited on 14 July 2000, and took its present name on 27 November 2006. It is active, registered at 7th Floor The Monument Building, 11 Monument Street, London EC3R 8AF, under SIC code 82990, with accounts last made up to 31 December 2024 and the next due by 31 December 2026. Active Hotels was a Cambridge business, and the brand a British traveller uses today grew partly out of it.

Booking.com Transport Limited, company 05179829, the entity behind car hire and ground transport, files full accounts — 285 pages for the year to 31 December 2024, filed on 28 July 2025, against 211 pages for 2023. Full accounts from a subsidiary are worth noting because so much of this sector files under the small-company regime and publishes no profit and loss account at all.

Nobody rates a booking platform. Defaqto rates insurance, the tourist boards assess properties rather than the sites that sell them, and no ratings agency covers accommodation booking platforms at all. The guest scores next to a listing are crowd averages from people who stayed, not an assessment of Booking.com. The substitutes available to a reader are the ones used throughout this page: the company's audited filings, its own published terms, and the regulators' dated decisions.

pros: About 4.4 million properties across more than 220 countries and territories, including roughly 500,000 hotels, motels and resorts — a catalogue no competitor matches
Genius Level 1 gives 10% off before taxes and charges simply for signing in, and five stays in two years lifts that to 10% or 15% with free breakfast and room upgrades at participating properties
A great many rooms can be reserved with free cancellation and paid at the property, so nothing leaves your account before you arrive
The terms are numbered and written in plain English, and they state outright that your contract is with the property rather than with Booking.com
Clause B7 admits that some price reductions shown are funded by Booking.com rather than by the property — an unusually candid thing for a platform to put in writing
The liability cap is the full cost of the booking, which is better than rivals that peg the cap to an unpublished booking fee
Audited figures are published twice a year by a NASDAQ-listed parent, so the scale claims on this page are checkable rather than promotional
The EU gatekeeper designation gives EEA properties an enforceable right to undercut the platform, which works in a traveller's favour
Clause A20 sets out EU and UK Package Travel Requirements and insolvency protection where a room forms part of a linked travel arrangement
cons: No lead-in price is published anywhere. The Greater London and London budget-hotel pages were read on 16 October 2026 and carried guest scores, review counts and property names but not a single rate, so you cannot see the floor of the catalogue without running a dated search

For a UK property, the freedom to price its own website lower rests on a statement Booking.com made on 20 August 2020 after its formal commitments expired on 1 July 2020 — not on an enforceable duty. The Digital Markets Act obligation covers the European Economic Area, and the CMA has so far given strategic market status only to Apple and Google

There is no ombudsman and no alternative dispute resolution scheme. The terms say Booking.com is not required to use independent ADR, and clause A15.3 still directs EEA residents to the European Commission's Online Dispute Resolution platform, which ceased operating on 20 July 2025 under Regulation (EU) 2024/3228

Clause A19 puts disputes into individual arbitration under New York law before the American Arbitration Association, waiving class actions and jury trial, with only a 30-day written opt-out and a 60-day wait after a written complaint before relief can be sought

The commission charged to properties is never published — not to travellers and not in the partner help article that explains how the charge works, so the gap between the rate you pay and the money the property keeps cannot be calculated

Genius, Preferred Partner and Visibility Booster raise a property's commission above its contract rate and lift its position in results, and nothing on a listing tells a traveller which of those programmes it is in

Spain's competition authority found on 30 July 2024 that the default ranking uses a property's total bookings through Booking.com as a criterion, which pushes down a property that sells well elsewhere, and fined the company €413,240,000 for conduct running from at least 1 January 2019
Clause B2.3 states that the platform only shows accommodations that have a commercial relationship with Booking.com, so the "largest selection" is a selection of properties that pay to appear

Commission is charged to the property on no-shows and on cancellations where the property charges the guest, and on overbookings unless the property has been live under 30 days or has had fewer than five overbookings in twelve months
No independent assessment of the platform exists from any ratings body, so a traveller has nothing to weigh it against except the company's own filings and the regulators' decisions

Marketing absorbed $8,186 million of $26,917 million of revenue in 2025 and $4,439 million of $12,884 million in the first half of 2026 — by our own arithmetic about 30p and then 34p in every pound, which is the commercial pressure sitting behind every urgency message on a results page
verdict: Booking.com is the best place to find out what exists. About 4.4 million properties across more than 220 countries, 1,235 million room nights in 2025 and free cancellation on a large share of the catalogue is a combination nothing else offers, and Genius takes 10% to 15% off before taxes from the moment you sign in. Use it for that. What changed in July 2024, and what almost nobody tells travellers, is that the property at the other end is now free to price its own site lower — Travelodge says in terms that its lowest prices are on its own website. So the sequence that gets the best of both is to search here, sign in to pick up the Genius rate, then open the property's own site in a second tab before confirming. Go in knowing three things: the contract is with the property and not with Booking.com, the most either will ever owe you is the cost of the booking, and there is no ombudsman behind that if it goes wrong.

faqs.q: Is a hotel allowed to be cheaper on its own website than on Booking.com?
faqs.a: Yes. Contractual parity requirements were removed in July 2024, and the European Commission's factsheet of 28 September 2026 states that businesses active on Booking.com in the European Economic Area "can now freely set their prices and conditions on and off Booking.com" under Article 5(3) of the Digital Markets Act. The Court of Justice held on 19 September 2024, in case C-264/23, that parity clauses "cannot, in principle, be classified as 'ancillary restraints'". For a UK property the position rests on Booking.com's statement of 20 August 2020 that it would continue to act in line with commitments that had expired on 1 July 2020, which is a company undertaking rather than a legal duty. Either way, checking the property's own site before you confirm costs you thirty seconds.

faqs.q: Who am I actually buying the room from?
faqs.a: The property. Clause B2.1 of Booking.com's terms says that "When you make a Booking, it's directly with the Service Provider", and clause A3.1 says Booking.com B.V. "provides and is responsible for the Platform, but not the Travel Experience itself". Car hire and ground transport are sold by a separate company, Booking.com Transport Limited, company number 05179829. The practical effect is that a problem with the room is the property's to fix first, and a problem with the booking system is Booking.com's.

faqs.q: What is Genius worth and what does it cost the hotel?
faqs.a: Level 1 is free on signing in and gives 10% off the price of a stay before taxes and charges at participating properties. Five stays in two years unlocks Level 2, which Booking.com describes as "a 10% or 15% discount applied to the price before taxes and fees", with free breakfast and a free room upgrade where offered. The property pays for it twice: Booking.com's own partner help article says that where the commission charged exceeds the contract rate, "you may be participating in a programme like Genius, Preferred Partner or Visibility Booster". Spain's competition authority found in July 2024 that those programmes also improve a property's ranking.

faqs.q: If something goes wrong, who can I complain to?
faqs.a: Booking.com first, through its Customer Service and then the Dispute Resolution process, after which clause A19 requires a 60-day wait before relief can be sought and then sends most disputes to individual arbitration under New York law before the American Arbitration Association. There is no ombudsman: the terms say Booking.com is not required to use independent alternative dispute resolution. Clause A15.3 offers EEA residents the European Commission's Online Dispute Resolution platform, which closed on 20 July 2025 under Regulation (EU) 2024/3228 and never covered UK consumers after Brexit. Where a room is booked alongside a flight as a linked travel arrangement, clause A20 brings UK and EU package travel protections into play, which is a materially stronger position.

faqs.q: Why can I not see a "from" price for London before I search?
faqs.a: Because Booking.com does not publish one. Its Greater London page and its London budget-hotels page were both read on 16 October 2026 and gave property names, guest scores such as The Savoy at 9.2 and Peckham Lodge at 6.6, and a count of 9,357 reviews, but no rates at all. For a usable floor you have to go to an operator: Travelodge publishes "Rooms under £35 are available throughout the UK and from £49 in London", and its London City page advertised a nearby room at £55.99 for one adult on the night of 18 October 2026.

faqs.q: How big is Booking.com really?
faqs.a: Booking Holdings' Form 10-K for the year ended 31 December 2025 gives approximately 4.4 million properties in over 220 countries and territories, of which about 500,000 are hotels, motels and resorts and about 3.9 million are homes, apartments and other places to stay, with approximately 24,300 employees. The group took 1,235 million room nights and $186.1 billion of gross bookings in 2025 on revenues of $26,917 million. The most recent quarter, to 30 June 2026, gave 325 million room nights and $51.0 billion, growth of 5% and 9% — slower than the year before it.

title: Branded Beauty Review: Clearance Prices on High Street Makeup Brands
meta_title: Branded Beauty Review: 99p Lipsticks, Free Post Over £25
meta_description: Branded Beauty sells L'Oréal, Maybelline and MAC as clearance stock from 49p. Prices, delivery, the 14-day returns rule and what to check on the box.

headline.label: Deepest verified discount
headline.value: 90% off — L'Oréal Color Riche lipstick at £0.99 against a £9.99 comparison price, checked 17 September 2026

intro:
Branded Beauty was selling a L'Oréal Color Riche lipstick at £0.99 against a £9.99 comparison price when we read its sale pages on 17 September 2026, and a Maybelline Baby Lips crayon at 49p against £2.99. Delivery is £2.99 by Royal Mail 48, free once a basket passes £25.

The shop is run by Branded Beauty Limited, a company registered at Companies House on 30 April 2013 under number 08509792 and trading from Unit 8 Trafalgar Business Centre on River Road in Barking. It stocks makeup, skincare, haircare, fragrance, nails, sun care and bath and body from names most people already own something by — L'Oréal, Maybelline, MAC, NYX, Revolution, Benefit, Clarins and Essie among them.

The prices come from what the stock is. Branded Beauty's own terms tell buyers that products "may have superficial and cosmetic markings" and that they accept "slight visual defects and/or clearance stickering" when they order. That is a clearance operation, stated plainly by the shop rather than discovered by a reviewer, and it is the whole explanation for a 99p L'Oréal lipstick. A reader expecting the boxed, shrink-wrapped item from a department store counter should know that before they click; a reader who only wants the contents of the tube has just found the cheapest route to it.

key_facts.value: £2.99 Royal Mail 48, free over £25, 2–4 working days

sections.heading: What 99p actually buys
sections.html:
Four prices from the sale pages on 17 September 2026 give the range. A L'Oréal Color Riche lipstick at £0.99 against £9.99, marked 90% off. A L'Oréal Infallible Sculpt contouring palette at £0.99 against £7.99, marked 88% off. A Maybelline Baby Lips colour balm crayon at 49p against £2.99, marked 84% off. And, at the shallower end, a L'Oréal Matte Resistance lipstick in shade 665 First Move at £5.99 against £12.99, marked 54% off.

Postage is the number that decides whether those are bargains. Standard delivery is £2.99 on Royal Mail 48 with a 2–4 working day window, so a single 99p lipstick posted on its own costs £3.98 and the delivery is four times the item. Free delivery starts at £25, which at 99p a piece is a basket of twenty-six things. Express delivery is £5.99 on Royal Mail 24, quoted at 1–3 working days, restricted to England, Wales and Scotland and not running at weekends or on bank holidays. The shop says it aims to dispatch by the next working day but will not promise it.

The comparison prices are worth a moment of the reader's own checking. The Chartered Trading Standards Institute's guidance for traders on pricing practices, updated online on 14 August 2025 to take in the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, asks that a price comparison run for a period no longer than the higher price was actually charged, that a recommended retail price be labelled as an RRP rather than presented as a price the shop itself charged, and that an RRP "must not be false; it must not be created purely in order to present the appearance of a discount". It also says an "up to" claim should only be made where the top reduction applies to a significant proportion of the promotion. None of that is an accusation against this shop. It is the test any reader can apply in thirty seconds by opening the brand's own site in another tab, and on fast-moving cosmetics with a real recommended price behind them it is an easy test to run.

sections.heading: Clearance is not the same thing as counterfeit, and the difference is checkable
sections.html:
Deep discounts on branded cosmetics carry an obvious question, and there is now a good independent measure of it. Which? bought 34 cosmetic items from Amazon, eBay, TikTok Shop and Vinted in June 2025 and judged 23 of them — 67% — likely to be counterfeit: six out of six bought on Vinted, five of six on TikTok Shop, eight of eleven on eBay and four of eleven on Amazon. Rocio Concha, the group's director of policy and advocacy, called it "alarming that Which? was able to find such high volumes of what appeared to be potentially dangerous counterfeit cosmetics on popular online marketplaces".

That study was of third-party sellers on marketplaces, which is a different proposition from a named limited company selling from its own domain and its own warehouse. The legal position is different too. Under Article 6 of the cosmetics regulation as it applies in Great Britain, a distributor must check before putting a product on sale that the labelling required by Article 19 is present, that the information is in English, and that the date of minimum durability has not passed. If a distributor believes a product does not conform, it must not make it available until it does, and must withdraw or recall stock that has already gone out; where there is a safety risk it must tell the responsible person and the authorities. It must also keep storage and transport conditions such that the product still complies when it reaches the buyer.

Those duties sit on the shop, not the shopper. They are the reason a clearance retailer that has been filing accounts at the same Barking address since 2013 is a different animal from an anonymous listing, and they are also the reason the date on the box matters more here than it does on a full-price counter.

sections.heading: The date on the box is the number to check
sections.html:
Article 19 of the same regulation sets out what must appear on a cosmetic container in indelible, legible, visible lettering: the responsible person's name and address, the country of origin for imported goods, the nominal content by weight or volume except on packs under 5 grams or 5 millilitres, a batch number, the product's function, precautions for use and the full ingredients list in descending order of weight.

The durability rule is the one to apply to clearance stock, and it has a threshold. A product that keeps for more than 30 months carries no expiry date at all — instead it shows the open-jar symbol followed by the period after opening, in months or years, for which it stays safe. A product that keeps for 30 months or less must carry a date of minimum durability in month and year, or day, month and year. So a boxed foundation with no date anywhere on it is not necessarily a problem; it is a product with a shelf life over thirty months whose clock starts when the seal breaks. A mascara or a sunscreen bought at a deep discount is the case worth checking, because the shorter shelf life means a printed date and a distributor duty to have looked at it.

Behind all of it sits the Office for Product Safety and Standards. Its Submit Cosmetic Product Notification service launched in December 2020 after Great Britain left the EU system, and every product placed on the GB market has to be notified through a UK-based responsible person. OPSS published the numbers on 17 July 2026, in response to a parliamentary inquiry: as at 28 May 2026 there had been 861,686 notifications from 24,112 registered responsible persons. OPSS also said it had acted where notified products contained banned chemicals, requiring businesses to correct information or take the products off the market. A shopper can search those notifications themselves at the government's cosmetic product notification search service, which is more than most beauty retailers ever tell anybody.

sections.heading: Who is behind the shop
sections.html:
Branded Beauty Limited was incorporated on 30 April 2013 and is registered under SIC code 47750, retail sale of cosmetic and toilet articles in specialised stores. Its registered office, Unit 8 Trafalgar Business Centre, 77–89 River Road, Barking IG11 0JU, is the same address given on the shop's contact page, so the company an order is placed with and the building it ships from are one and the same — not a holding company in one county and a fulfilment house in another.

The public record is current rather than dusty. Accounts to 30 April 2025 were filed on 30 January 2026 as total exemption full accounts, which is the small-company route and means no turnover figure is published. The most recent confirmation statement was made on 3 April 2026. Michael Edward Wild was appointed a director on 11 March 2021, James Albert Phillips is also on the board, and Matthew John Phillips is recorded as a person with significant control, his details last updated in January 2025. There are no charges registered and no change of name.

One disclosure is missing from the shop itself. Regulation 25 of the Company, Limited Liability Partnership and Business (Names and Trading Disclosures) Regulations 2015 requires a company's website to carry the part of the United Kingdom in which it is registered, its registered number and the address of its registered office. The contact page gives the registered name and the address but we could not find the company number anywhere on the site; that is a small administrative gap rather than a warning sign, and it is worth confirming directly, because a shop can add a line to a footer between one visit and the next.

sections.heading: Returns: the policy and the statutory rights are not the same document
sections.html:
Branded Beauty gives buyers 14 days after receiving an item to request a return, by emailing returns@brandedbeauty.co.uk, and says that anything sent back without asking first will not be accepted. The item has to come back unopened, unused and in its original packaging with proof of purchase. The policy then lists what cannot be returned at all: perishable goods, custom items, hazardous materials, flammable liquids and gases, gift cards, personal care goods including beauty products, and sale items.

On a shop where the great majority of the catalogue is discounted, those last two exclusions cover most of what anybody buys, and they are drawn wider than the law draws them. The exception in the distance selling rules is narrower than "beauty products": regulation 28(1)(e) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 removes the cancellation right for "sealed goods which are not suitable for return due to health protection or hygiene reasons" only if they are unsealed after delivery. A lipstick still in its seal is not inside that exception. And there is no exception anywhere in regulation 28 for goods bought in a sale — a discounted price does not change the right.

A faulty item is a different matter again, and a different clock: the short-term right to reject faulty goods under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 runs for 30 days, and a trader can lengthen that window but cannot shorten it. Worth reading alongside the terms, which state that "superficial or cosmetics markings to products does not make your item eligible for a refund" — consistent with selling clearance stock, and fair enough as far as it goes, but it puts the line between a cosmetic mark and a defect entirely in the seller's hands.

None of this is exotic. It is the same wording used by a great many small online shops running on off-the-shelf store software, and it usually reflects a template rather than an intention. It still means a buyer who needs to send something back is relying on the shop being reasonable rather than on the policy as written.

sections.heading: If something goes wrong, there is no ombudsman to ring
sections.html:
A beauty retailer holds no FCA permission, sits under no ombudsman scheme and belongs to no compulsory alternative dispute resolution body. That is normal for retail and it is not a criticism of this shop, but it does change the route a complaint takes, and the arithmetic of a discount site makes one familiar protection unavailable.

Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 makes a credit card company jointly liable with the seller — but only where the cash price of the item is more than £100 and not more than £30,000. A basket assembled to clear a £25 delivery threshold out of 99p lipsticks does not come close, so section 75 simply does not apply to the typical order here. What remains is the card scheme's own chargeback process, which is a scheme rule rather than a statutory right and carries its own time limits, or a claim against the company itself.

Beyond that the route is Trading Standards, reached through the Citizens Advice consumer service on 0808 223 1133, open Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm and closed on bank holidays. Citizens Advice passes reports to Trading Standards, which a consumer cannot do directly. Product safety questions — an unlabelled item, a suspect batch, an ingredient that should not be there — go to OPSS.

The rules themselves may not stay still. The Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee is running an inquiry into the science and regulation of hair and beauty products and treatments, taking oral evidence in January and June 2026 from ministers and industry, and asking among other things how regulators assess safety evidence across different hair and skin types, how consumers can be made aware of potential harms, and what legal changes would protect them better. It is the reason OPSS published its notification figures in July 2026, and anyone buying cosmetics online has a stake in where it lands.

pros: Discounts are genuinely deep — 99p for a L'Oréal lipstick and 49p for a Maybelline crayon on the day we checked
The shop explains the price honestly in its own terms: clearance stock, with markings and stickering disclosed up front
A named UK limited company trading from one address since 2013, with accounts and officers on the public record
Free standard delivery over £25 and a flat £2.99 below it, with Royal Mail tracking from dispatch
Brand range is wide for a discounter — L'Oréal, Maybelline, MAC, NYX, Revolution, Benefit, Clarins and Essie across seven categories
Buying from a registered retailer's own site avoids the marketplace risk Which? measured at 67% in June 2025
cons: The returns policy excludes "sale items" and "personal care goods (beauty products)" outright, which covers most of the catalogue and is drawn wider than regulation 28(1)(e) allows
Only 14 days to request a return, and the item must be unopened and unused — shorter and stricter than most beauty retailers offer
No phone number anywhere on the site: contact is a single email address, which is slow when an order goes missing
The terms say superficial markings do not make an item eligible for a refund, leaving the seller to decide where a mark ends and a defect begins
The company registration number does not appear on the site, although regulation 25 of the 2015 trading disclosure rules requires it
Baskets are far too small for section 75 credit card protection, which needs a cash price above £100
No published policy on shelf life or expiry dating, which is the one thing clearance cosmetics buyers most want stated
verdict: Branded Beauty is a clearance retailer that says so, which is rarer than it sounds and is the strongest thing about it. At 99p for a L'Oréal lipstick and £2.99 for postage, the sums work as soon as a basket reaches the £25 free-delivery line, and the stock comes from a company that has been filing accounts at the same Barking address since 2013 rather than from an anonymous marketplace listing of the kind Which? found to be counterfeit two times in three. The weak point is what happens afterwards: a 14-day return window, exclusions for sale items and beauty products that go further than the distance selling rules permit, no phone number, and order values too small for section 75. Buy the things you already know you like, check the date of minimum durability or the open-jar symbol when the parcel arrives, and treat the price as the reason you are there.

faqs.q: Is Branded Beauty a genuine UK company?
faqs.a: Yes. Branded Beauty Limited has been registered at Companies House since 30 April 2013 under company number 08509792, at Unit 8 Trafalgar Business Centre, 77–89 River Road, Barking IG11 0JU — the same address the shop gives for contact. Its accounts to 30 April 2025 were filed on 30 January 2026 and its confirmation statement was made on 3 April 2026.

faqs.q: Why is it so much cheaper than the high street?
faqs.a: Because it sells clearance stock, and its terms say so: buyers are told products "may have superficial and cosmetic markings" and accept "slight visual defects and/or clearance stickering". The contents are the branded product; the box may have been round the houses. That is where a 90% cut on a L'Oréal lipstick comes from.

faqs.q: What does delivery cost?
faqs.a: Standard delivery is £2.99 on Royal Mail 48, quoted at 2–4 working days, and free on orders over £25. Express is £5.99 on Royal Mail 24, quoted at 1–3 working days, available in England, Wales and Scotland only and not running at weekends or on bank holidays. Orders are dispatched by the next working day where possible, though that is not guaranteed.

faqs.q: Can I send something back?
faqs.a: The shop gives 14 days from delivery to request a return by email, and requires the item unopened, unused and in its original packaging. Its policy also excludes sale items and beauty products entirely. Statutory cancellation rights are drawn more narrowly than that: regulation 28(1)(e) of the 2013 Consumer Contracts Regulations only removes the right for sealed goods unsuitable for return on hygiene grounds once they have been unsealed, and there is no exception for sale goods. Faulty items have their own 30-day right to reject.

faqs.q: How do I know a product is in date?
faqs.a: Look at the packaging. Cosmetics lasting 30 months or less must show a date of minimum durability; those lasting longer show an open-jar symbol with the number of months the product is safe once opened. A distributor is required to check the durability date has not passed before selling. Mascara, sunscreen and anything water-based are the products worth checking first.

faqs.q: What if something goes wrong with an order?
faqs.a: There is no ombudsman for a cosmetics retailer. Contact the shop at hello@brandedbeauty.co.uk first; if that fails, ask your card provider about chargeback, since section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act needs a cash price above £100 and beauty orders rarely reach it. Trading Standards is reached through the Citizens Advice consumer service on 0808 223 1133, Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm. Product safety concerns go to the Office for Product Safety and Standards.

title: breeze eSIM Review: Plans, Networks and the Small Print
meta_title: Breeze eSIM Review: What 190 Countries Really Costs
meta_description: Breeze sells data-only travel eSIMs across 190+ countries from $3.99. Who runs it, which networks you join, what 10GB costs and the clauses to read first.
intro:
Breeze is the consumer face of eSIM Go Limited, a Banbury telecoms company registered at Companies House as number 12465777, incorporated on 17 February 2020 and filed under SIC code 61200 for wireless telecommunications. It sells travel data eSIMs — a network profile your phone downloads instead of a plastic SIM — across 190+ countries, and says it reaches those countries through more than 1,200 networks. Fixed plans run from 1GB to 100GB, prices start at $3.99, the site promises a line that is live in under 60 seconds, and tethering is included on every plan rather than sold as an extra.

The name is less familiar than the business behind it. eSIM Go builds the platform that other travel brands put their own badge on, so the same engine sells the Wizz Air, SWISS, Lufthansa and Booking.com eSIMs, and the one Bristol Airport offers its passengers. Buying at breezesim.com is buying from the wholesaler rather than from a reseller with a licence to the same inventory. In May 2026 the company took an investment round led by TNS Global, a Eurasian wholesale telecoms group, to push further into travel data and UK mobile virtual network work.

Two things decide whether this product suits you before you spend anything. Breeze plans carry data only: no voice calls, no text messages and no phone number of their own, so your usual SIM has to stay switched on for anything that rings or texts, including bank verification codes. And the technology has an age limit — Breeze's own help centre states that "devices manufactured prior to 2018 will not be eSIM compatible", and the handset must be unlocked.
