sections.heading: The Banbury company behind the badge
sections.html:
Two registrations matter here. eSIM Go Limited is the older of the two, incorporated on 17 February 2020 and now filing accounts to 31 March each year, with its last set made up to 31 March 2025 and the next due by 31 December 2026. Breezesim Limited, company 16221665, was incorporated on 31 January 2025 with £4,000 of share capital and moved into the same First Floor office on 11 May 2026. Its filing history shows two charges registered, on 5 January 2026 and 7 April 2026, and a person with significant control — ESG Holdco Ltd — notified on 30 April 2026. The same director, Zacchary Couldrick, sits behind both the retail company and the platform that supplies it.

That structure explains the white labels. eSIM Go's business is selling connectivity to other brands, and its own May 2026 announcement names customers including Loopdl, SecondSIM, Faith Mobile and Symu, alongside a UK mobile virtual network arrangement with VodafoneThree. A traveller who has bought an airline-branded eSIM in the last two years may already have been a Breeze customer without knowing it: the terms document Wizz Air publishes for its own eSIM is headed "Breeze Terms and Conditions" and names eSIM Go Limited as the supplier.

sections.heading: How the plans are shaped, and when the clock starts
sections.html:
Breeze sells three shapes of plan. Fixed plans give a set number of gigabytes to use over a chosen number of days, from 1GB up to 100GB. Premium Unlimited plans are sold as 30GB over 5 days, 60GB over 10 days or 90GB over 15 days — unlimited in the sense that the line keeps working, because past the allowance the site says "your data speed will be reduced (but is still suitable for streaming 720p video)". Day plans give 1GB of full-speed data per 24 hours. Top-ups can be added mid-trip from your account, and the site states that it will "never let you go over your agreed data allowance", which removes the overage charge that made old-fashioned roaming frightening.

The timing detail is the one worth knowing before you fly. Breeze states plainly that "your plan validity starts on first use in [the destination] — not at purchase", so a 30-day plan bought a fortnight early still gives 30 days from the moment the phone first connects abroad. That is why the instruction to install before departure, while you still have reliable Wi-Fi, costs nothing: installing is not activating. Buying more than one plan attracts a stated 10% discount on two or more.

Prices seen on 6 September 2026: 10GB over 30 days in the United States at $13.99, reduced from a listed $19.00; the same size plan for Canada at $14.99; a Europe Lite 10GB plan at $12.99; and a North America regional plan at $13.99 against a struck-through $33.50.

sections.heading: Which networks your handset actually joins
sections.html:
Most travel eSIM sellers will not tell you whose masts you end up on. Breeze does, on each destination page, and that is unusually straightforward. In the United Kingdom the plan is carried by Telefonica UK Limited, Hutchison 3G UK Limited and Vodafone Ltd — the O2, Three and Vodafone networks, with the handset able to fall back between them rather than being stuck on one. In the United States the partners named are Verizon Wireless and AT&T Mobility, which between them are the two largest US carriers by subscriber base.

Technically the plans run on 3G, 4G LTE and 5G where the host network offers it, and the wording is careful: 5G is offered "where available" rather than promised. That caveat is doing real work, because a roaming profile is generally given whatever the local operator grants visiting customers, which is not always the same as what its own subscribers get. If a specific speed matters — uploading video, tethering a laptop for work — that is worth a question to support before you buy rather than an assumption afterwards.

The regional maths deserves a squint too. The Europe plan is described in one place as covering 34 countries and in another, on the same page, as "35 Countries and Networks", so check the specific country list for the trip you are actually taking rather than trusting the headline count.

sections.heading: Travel data sits outside the rules that protect you at home
sections.html:
Ofcom has spent several years tightening what a UK mobile provider must do when you cross a border, and it is worth knowing which of those protections travel with you and which do not. The statement Mobile roaming – Strengthening customer protections, published 22 March 2024 and in force from 1 October 2024, modified General Condition C3 so that providers must alert customers "without undue delay" on arrival, free of charge, explaining the charges and any fair use limits, and must point them to a free and easily accessible way of setting a bill limit. The same statement obliged providers to help customers avoid inadvertent roaming near borders, an issue Ofcom found affected 14% of customers nationally and 28% in Northern Ireland.

The research behind it is the useful part. Ofcom found 94% of people who had roamed were aware of the alerts, 84% said they read them and 72% changed their behaviour as a result, while 19% did not know whether charges applied in the EEA and 30% did not know for the rest of the world. Just 49% of pay-monthly customers had a bill limit set.

What no longer exists is the hard stop. The £45 plus VAT per day data cap that once halted a roaming session unless the customer agreed to carry on expired on 30 June 2022, as the House of Commons Library briefing on post-Brexit roaming records. Ofcom's own consumer guidance now suggests, in as many words, considering "a SIM card for the country you are visiting or an 'e-SIM'" as a way of controlling the cost — the regulator recommending the product category, which is a rare thing to be able to say on a comparison page. A prepaid data plan cannot generate a surprise bill because there is nothing to bill: you have already paid.

sections.heading: The clauses that decide whether you get your money back
sections.html:
The terms published under the Breeze name are more generous than the digital-goods norm in one place and stricter in others. You may cancel and be refunded "providing you do so within fourteen (14) days of purchase and have not Activated your Plan", and the sales pages put it more simply still: if no data has been used, the refund is available. Many sellers of digital content switch that right off the moment the file is delivered, so keeping it until first use is a real concession.

Against that sit three limits. An eSIM must be activated within twelve (12) months of purchase or it expires with no refund, and a profile left unused for twelve months may be cancelled outright, requiring a fresh one. The fair use policy restricts the service to "your own personal use during short-term travel" with a maximum of sixty (60) consecutive days in any one country, which rules out using a cheap foreign plan as a permanent home connection. And unused data does not roll anywhere: if the plan's days run out before the gigabytes do, the balance is forfeited.

Liability is capped at £1,000 for one incident or £3,000 for a number of incidents within any twelve (12) month period, with loss of income and profits excluded. English law governs the agreement. For a £12 data plan those caps are academic; for a business traveller whose week depends on the connection working, they are the ceiling on any argument.

sections.heading: One plan, three shops, three currencies
sections.html:
Because the same platform runs the airline and hotel storefronts, the identical plan can be bought in several places at prices that are not the same. On 6 September 2026 a 10GB, 30-day United States plan was listed at $13.99 on breezesim.com, at £12.00 (reduced from £16.00) on the Booking.com-branded Breeze store, and at €14.95 on the SWISS one. The Booking.com store also showed Turkey at £11.00, Italy at £12.00 against a struck-through £18.00, Spain at £10.00 from £12.00 and Greece at £10.00, with day rates quoted from £0.20 for the USA and £0.27 for Europe.

Nothing on any of those pages explains the gap, and a British buyer has a second question on top of it: the main Breeze site quotes in dollars, so the sterling amount that reaches your statement depends on the exchange rate on the day and on whether your card adds a non-sterling transaction fee. Check the currency shown at the checkout, not on the product tile. The partner stores are also geographically restricted — fetched from outside the UK, the Booking.com storefront returned "Sorry, [[store]] isn't available within the borders of [[country]] at this time", with the placeholders left unfilled, which is a small piece of housekeeping somebody should tidy.

The country counts wander in the same way. Breeze's own pages say 190+ countries and 1,000+ mobile network partnerships; eSIM Go's May 2026 announcement says more than 1,200 networks; and Bristol Airport, promoting the same product, tells passengers it covers 150+ countries. All three may be true of different things — countries with a plan, networks under contract, destinations the airport chose to list — but nothing published reconciles them.

sections.heading: Paperwork that has fallen behind the rules
sections.html:
Breeze's published complaints policy gives a phone number (+44 330 320 2064), an email address and a postal route, aims to resolve complaints within 10 working days, and offers escalation to a Complaint Escalations Team. It then tells the customer they may take the matter to an independent adjudicator once more than eight weeks have passed since first contact, or on receipt of a deadlock letter.

Eight weeks is no longer the rule. Ofcom announced on 8 July 2025 that the wait for alternative dispute resolution would fall from eight weeks to six, and the change took effect on 8 April 2026. The regulator's reasoning is worth quoting because it is exactly the situation a stranded traveller is in: between January 2022 and 2024, 79% of complaints were resolved within a week and 94% within six weeks, but roughly 700,000 consumers were still waiting at the six-week mark and only about 19% of them got a resolution or an ADR referral before the eight-week threshold. A customer who reads Breeze's page and waits the full eight weeks gives away two weeks of a right they already hold.

The two Breeze documents also point at different adjudicators. The complaints policy names Ombudsman Services – Communications at Daresbury Park in Warrington — a body that now trades as the Communications Ombudsman — while the terms and conditions document hosted by its airline partner points customers to the Communications and Internet Services Adjudication Scheme instead. Both are Ofcom-approved schemes, and being in one of them is more than many travel eSIM sellers offer, but a customer should not have to guess which one their complaint belongs to. That airline-hosted document is dated March 2023 and still carries an old registered address at 8 North Bar Street, OX16 0TB, three streets from the address the company uses now.

sections.heading: Nobody independent rates a travel eSIM
sections.html:
On an insurance page this is where a Defaqto star rating or a Fairer Finance ribbon would go. No such thing exists for travel data. Defaqto and Which? do not score eSIM sellers, the Financial Ombudsman Service has no jurisdiction because nothing here is a financial product, and Ofcom's quarterly telecoms complaints tables cover the large domestic providers rather than a specialist selling foreign data.

That is an absence rather than a black mark, and it is worth naming precisely, because the gap is filled on most eSIM comparison pages by review-collection sites where the merchant chooses when to ask. The verifiable things about Breeze are the ones in this page: a real UK company with filed accounts, a named registered office, named host networks, a published complaints route into an Ofcom-approved scheme, and terms you can read before paying. For a product bought once a year for a fortnight abroad, that list is a more useful test than a score.

pros: A genuine UK company with filed accounts, a named Banbury office and a published complaints route, rather than an app with an offshore support address
Names the host networks on each destination page — O2, Three and Vodafone in the UK, Verizon and AT&T in the USA
Plan validity starts on first use in the destination, so buying early costs you nothing
Tethering included on every plan, with top-ups available mid-trip and no charges beyond the allowance
Refund available within 14 days of purchase provided the plan has not been activated
The same platform that airlines, Booking.com and Bristol Airport put their own badge on, bought direct
cons: Data only: no calls, no texts and no number, so bank verification codes and 999 still depend on your usual SIM staying active
The complaints policy still tells customers to wait eight weeks for an adjudicator, when Ofcom cut that to six weeks on 8 April 2026
Two Breeze documents name two different Ofcom-approved adjudication schemes, and the older one still carries a previous registered address
The same 10GB, 30-day USA plan appeared at $13.99, £12.00 and €14.95 across three Breeze-run shops on the same day, with nothing published explaining the gap
Coverage claims do not agree: 190+ countries on Breeze's own pages, 150+ on Bristol Airport's, and a Europe plan described as both 34 and 35 countries
An eSIM not activated within twelve months expires with no refund, and unused data is forfeited when the days run out
Handsets made before 2018 will not work at all, and the phone must be network-unlocked
verdict: Breeze is the retail shopfront of eSIM Go, a Banbury wholesaler whose platform sits behind the Wizz Air, SWISS, Lufthansa, Booking.com and Bristol Airport eSIMs, so buying here is buying nearer the source than most travel data brands allow. It does the things that matter on this kind of product: it names the networks it puts you on, it starts the clock when you land rather than when you pay, it includes tethering, and it refunds an unused plan for fourteen days. The paperwork is where it lags — an eight-week complaints escalation that the regulator shortened to six in April 2026, two documents pointing at two different adjudicators, and the same plan priced in three currencies across its own storefronts. For a fortnight abroad on a phone made since 2018, with your normal SIM left switched on for calls, it is a straightforward way to avoid a roaming bill; read the country list and the checkout currency before you pay.

faqs.q: Can I make phone calls or send texts on a Breeze eSIM?
faqs.a: No. Breeze plans carry mobile data only and come with no phone number of their own. Calls and messages over apps such as WhatsApp or FaceTime work normally because they travel over data, but ordinary voice calls and SMS — including the one-time codes banks send — need your usual SIM left active in the phone. Keep that line switched on for calls and texts, and set the Breeze line as the one used for data.

faqs.q: When does my plan actually start?
faqs.a: On first use in the destination, not at the moment of purchase. Breeze states that validity begins when the eSIM first connects in the country the plan covers, so installing it at home the night before you fly does not eat into the allowance. There is an outer limit: an eSIM has to be activated within twelve months of purchase or it expires without a refund, and a profile left unused for twelve months may be cancelled.

faqs.q: What happens if I use all the data?
faqs.a: On a fixed plan the connection stops rather than running up a charge — the site says it will never let you exceed the agreed allowance — and you can buy a top-up from your account. On the Premium Unlimited plans the daily full-speed allowance is 1GB per 24 hours, after which the speed is reduced but the line keeps working, at a rate Breeze describes as still suitable for streaming 720p video.

faqs.q: Will my phone take an eSIM?
faqs.a: Breeze's help centre states that devices manufactured before 2018 will not be eSIM compatible, and the handset also has to be network-unlocked. Most iPhones from the XS onwards and most flagship Android phones of the last few years qualify, but the manufacturer lists on the help centre are the place to check a specific model before paying rather than after.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if something goes wrong?
faqs.a: Start with Breeze itself, by email to complaints@breezesim.com or on +44 330 320 2064; the company aims to answer within 10 working days and has an escalations team above that. If it is unresolved, you can take it to an Ofcom-approved adjudication scheme. Note that Breeze's own page still says eight weeks, but since 8 April 2026 the wait has been six weeks, or sooner if you are given a deadlock letter.

faqs.q: Is a travel eSIM cheaper than my network's roaming?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on your own tariff, which is why the comparison is worth doing before you go rather than at the airport. Some UK providers still include European roaming; others reintroduced daily charges after Brexit, and the £45-a-day data cap that used to stop a runaway session expired on 30 June 2022. Ofcom's own advice to travellers lists a local SIM or an eSIM as one way of keeping the cost down.

title: British Gas
meta_title: British Gas: 7.97p a Unit, and Who You Are Buying From
meta_description: British Gas gas sits at 7.97p/kWh and 29.68p a day, the Ofgem cap. The company behind it, the Ofgem record and the protections if you prepay.

headline.label: Gas unit rate
headline.value: 7.97p/kWh — Ofgem cap, Oct–Dec 2026, plus 29.68p/day standing charge

disclosure: we have no affiliate arrangement with British Gas and earn nothing if you switch to them. The link on this page goes to British Gas’s own site. We list it because it is one of the suppliers in this category, not because it pays us.
intro:
British Gas supplies gas at 7.97p per kWh with a 29.68p a day standing charge on its Standard Variable tariff, and publishes those figures itself as its October 2026 average. They are the Ofgem price cap for 1 October to 31 December 2026, to the penny. On the 11,500 kWh a year British Gas uses as a typical gas consumption, that is roughly £916 of gas and £108 of standing charge.

Being at the cap is not a criticism. It is simply the thing to know before you spend an afternoon comparing: the standard tariff from the UK’s largest gas supplier is the regulated maximum, so any saving has to come from a fixed deal, a payment method, or a different company.

What this page is actually for is the two questions a price comparison does not answer. Who is British Gas, legally and commercially? And what does its conduct record look like when you read the regulator rather than the advertising?

sections.heading: Who you are buying gas from
sections.html:
“British Gas” is a trading name, not a company. The entity that supplies your gas is:

  • British Gas Trading Limited, company number 03078711
  • Incorporated 6 July 1995, status active, a private limited company
  • Registered at Millstream, Maidenhead Road, Windsor, Berkshire SL4 5GD
  • Registered activity SIC 35220, distribution of gaseous fuels through mains, alongside 35130 for electricity
  • Owned by Centrica plc, company number 3033654

British Gas states it itself in its tariff terms: “British Gas is a trading name of British Gas Trading Limited (registered in England and Wales No. 03078711).” The brand and the flame logo are registered trade marks owned by Centrica, and the terms define “we” as covering British Gas Trading Limited, British Gas Services Limited “and all other Centrica plc group companies”.

How many customers? That depends which British Gas page you read. Centrica’s investor-facing page says 7.5 million residential energy customers. The main energy page says over 7 million. The price-cap page invites you to “join over 8 million customers”. A fourth page says “more than 8 million homes and businesses”. Only the 7.5m figure is attached to a defined unit, which is why it is the one we would use.

sections.heading: The 5% you cannot avoid, and the one you are not paying
sections.html:
Domestic gas carries 5% VAT, and it is inside the 7.97p unit rate and the 29.68p standing charge rather than added at the end. On a typical 11,500 kWh year that VAT is roughly £49 of the gas cost.

Electricity, unusually, is currently carrying none. A temporary measure removed VAT from electricity between 1 October 2026 and 31 March 2027. Ofgem warns that this makes its own cap figures impossible to compare directly with earlier periods, and the cap rose 4% to £1,723 for a typical direct debit dual-fuel household for this quarter.

For a gas decision the useful implication is narrow but real: nothing published says what happens to electricity VAT on 1 April 2027, so a fixed deal that bundles both fuels is fixing one fuel against a known tax position and the other against an unknown one.

sections.heading: The Ofgem record, in date order
sections.html:
Three entries, all from Ofgem’s own enforcement and compliance pages rather than press coverage.

January 2017 — closed. An investigation into breaches of standard licence condition 12.18 and 12.21, covering advanced meters for non-domestic customers. The financial penalty was £1. The redress was £4.5 million to the Carbon Trust. That structure — a nominal fine and a substantial payment elsewhere — is how Ofgem has handled several of these.

May 2026 — settled. Ofgem’s investigation into British Gas’s treatment of prepayment meter customers, covering conduct from 2018 to 2021, closed with a £20 million payment into Ofgem’s Voluntary Redress Fund and up to £70 million of energy debt written off for vulnerable customers, plus the remainder of a £22.4 million voluntary support package launched in 2023. Ofgem treated it as “alternative action”, so there was no financial penalty.

July 2024 — still open. A compliance engagement into smart meter obligations covering British Gas, EDF, E.ON, Octopus, OVO and Scottish Power, under electricity SLC 39A and 49 and gas SLC 33A and 43. Ofgem closed the installation-target half in June 2026 but British Gas remains, with three others, in reduced engagement on smart-mode obligations. Ofgem is careful to state that this “is not a finding of non-compliance”, and the case header still reads Open.

Ofgem has separately acted against British Gas Business over customer service failings and over switching and renewal errors. Those concern the business arm rather than domestic gas.

sections.heading: If you prepay for gas, these protections are the point
sections.html:
British Gas’s prepayment terms are more generous than its tariff pricing, and for a gas customer they are the part that matters most in February.

  • £10 of emergency credit on every Pay As You Go meter.
  • Friendly Credit — no disconnection on Sundays, English bank holidays, or between 6pm and 9am Monday to Saturday.
  • A free annual gas safety check through the Priority Services Register, subject to eligibility.
  • Free meter relocation and quarterly meter-reading visits with an optional password, also via the register.

The Priority Services Register itself covers the over-65s, anyone with a disability or long-term illness, anyone reliant on medical equipment at home, families with children aged five and under, and people recently bereaved, separated or out of work. It brings bills in Braille, large print or audio, and a free SignVideo BSL relay weekdays 9am to 5pm. Sign-up is 0800 072 8625 for credit customers and 0800 294 8604 for Pay As You Go.

On top of that the Warm Home Discount gives a one-off £150 for winter 2026/2027. It is applied to the electricity account rather than the gas one, or issued as a Post Office voucher if you prepay. DWP letters run from 20 October to 31 December 2026; if nothing arrives by 31 January 2027, contact DWP, and every payment lands by 31 March 2027.

sections.heading: Where it falls short
sections.html:
Escalated complaints have been climbing. The Energy Ombudsman’s accepted-disputes rate for British Gas, per 100,000 domestic accounts, reads 49.5 in Q3 2025, 53.0 in Q4, 58.1 in Q1 2026 and 54.9 in Q2 2026. The last figure is the second highest of the eight suppliers the Ombudsman charts. Sector-wide, accepted cases rose from 40,068 in the first half of 2025 to 46,532 in the first half of 2026, so British Gas is not alone — but it is near the top of a rising table.

On signposting it is last. Of those eight suppliers, British Gas had the lowest signposting score at 41% against a sector figure of 53%. Signposting means telling a customer the Ombudsman exists when a complaint stalls. Being bottom of that particular table is a choice about process, not an accident of scale.

You cannot see its absolute complaint numbers at all. The Ombudsman publishes per-supplier figures only as labels inside a quarterly chart. The last standalone British Gas data file is from Q4 2019, and the last Centrica Residential one from Q1 2023. Every recent British Gas figure is a rate per 100,000 accounts, which is the fair way to compare suppliers of different sizes but means nobody outside the company knows how many complaints there actually are.

And the cheaper tariffs will not show you a price. British Gas advertises Fix and Fall, Fixed Tracker and Fixed Fixed by name and publishes a rate for none of them. You need to complete a quote to see one.

£10 emergency credit on every prepayment meter
Friendly Credit blocks disconnection on Sundays, bank holidays and overnight
Free annual gas safety check through the Priority Services Register, subject to eligibility
Priority Services Register covers the over-65s, medical equipment users and families with under-fives, with Braille, large print, audio and a free BSL relay
£150 Warm Home Discount for winter 2026/2027, with published dates and a 31 March 2027 backstop
Legal entity, company number and parent all clearly stated in its own tariff terms
The British Gas Energy Trust helps households regardless of supplier and has reached over 2.2 million people
cons: The standard tariff is the price cap, so there is no saving in it by definition

verdict: British Gas sells gas at the Ofgem cap, which means the price is neither a bargain nor a risk — it is the regulated ceiling, and any saving has to come from fixing, from a payment method, or from somebody else. What the price comparison will not tell you is on this page instead. The company is British Gas Trading Limited, 03078711, owned by Centrica, and it has an Ofgem record you should read before deciding: a £20 million redress settlement in May 2026 over its treatment of prepayment customers between 2018 and 2021, with up to £70 million of debt written off, and a smart meter compliance engagement that has been open since July 2024. Escalated complaints have been rising and its signposting score is the lowest of the eight largest suppliers. Against that, the support for people who are struggling is genuinely among the best available: £10 emergency credit, Friendly Credit, a free annual gas safety check, and a £150 Warm Home Discount with dates you can hold them to. If that describes your household, the service record matters less than the safety net. If it does not, the cap price is available from companies that answer the phone faster.

faqs.q: What does British Gas charge for gas?
faqs.a: 7.97p per kWh with a 29.68p daily standing charge on Standard Variable, which is the Ofgem price cap for 1 October to 31 December 2026. On British Gas’s own typical consumption of 11,500 kWh that is roughly £916 of gas plus £108 of standing charge. The 5% VAT is already inside both figures.

faqs.q: Who actually owns British Gas?
faqs.a: Centrica plc, company number 3033654. The supplier itself is British Gas Trading Limited, company 03078711, incorporated on 6 July 1995 and registered at Millstream, Maidenhead Road, Windsor SL4 5GD. The British Gas name and flame logo are trade marks owned by Centrica.

faqs.q: Has Ofgem taken action against British Gas?
faqs.a: Yes, more than once. In May 2026 it settled an investigation into its treatment of prepayment meter customers from 2018 to 2021 with a £20m payment into Ofgem’s Voluntary Redress Fund and up to £70m of debt written off, taken as alternative action with no penalty. In January 2017 a closed case over advanced meters ended in a £1 penalty and £4.5m of redress to the Carbon Trust. A smart meter compliance engagement opened in July 2024 remains open.

faqs.q: What protections do I get on a prepayment gas meter?
faqs.a: £10 of emergency credit, and Friendly Credit, which stops disconnection on Sundays, English bank holidays and between 6pm and 9am Monday to Saturday. Through the Priority Services Register you may also get a free annual gas safety check and free meter relocation. Sign-up for Pay As You Go is 0800 294 8604.

faqs.q: How many customers does British Gas have?
faqs.a: Depends which of its pages you read: over 7 million, 7.5 million residential energy customers, or over 8 million. Only the 7.5 million figure, on Centrica’s investor page, is tied to a defined unit, so that is the one we would quote.

title: British Gas Business Dual Fuel
meta_title: British Gas Business Dual Fuel: the Most You Can Be Charged
meta_description: British Gas Business publishes a price ceiling, not a quote: 82.46p a unit for electricity, 14.71p for gas, and two standing charges. Checked October 2026.

headline.label: Maximum microbusiness price, both fuels
headline.value: 82.46p/kWh electricity and 14.71p/kWh gas — British Gas Business's published 1-year ceiling at 23 September 2026, before standing charges

intro:
British Gas Business publishes the most a microbusiness can be charged, and at 23 September 2026 that ceiling is 82.46p per kWh for single-rate electricity and 14.71p per kWh for gas on a one-year fixed plan. Both figures are maximum prices rather than quotes, and the distinction is worth holding on to: Ofgem obliges a supplier to publish the ceiling, and the deal a business is actually offered sits somewhere below it.

British Gas supplies energy to more than 350,000 businesses and dates the brand to 1815, which it describes as over 200 years of trading. The contracts are written by British Gas Trading Limited, company 03078711, incorporated on 6 July 1995 and registered at Millstream, Maidenhead Road, Windsor SL4 5GD. Every fixed-price and fixed-term British Gas Business electricity plan is sold as zero carbon, on a supply the company gives as 72% renewable and 28% nuclear.

One thing to settle before comparing anything. There is no British Gas Business dual fuel product and no dual-fuel discount: the price plans page sets out eight arrangements, none of them a both-fuels plan, and says nothing at all about taking gas and electricity together. A business buying two fuels signs two contracts and pays two standing charges. On the published ceiling those are 400.00p a day for electricity and 1,749.81p a day for gas — £7,846.81 a year between them, before a single unit is used.

sections.heading: The one price British Gas Business puts in public, and what it comes to
sections.html:
Business energy is quoted, not listed. What a supplier has to publish instead is the maximum it will charge a microbusiness, and British Gas Business prints that on a single page under the headers Fixed Rate Term, Standing Charge p/day, Unit Rate p/kWh and Estimated Contract £. The page says the figures "are the most microbusinesses will pay when entering a new contract or renewing with us", and that they are "current as of 23 September 2026 and can change at any time". New-customer and renewing-customer prices are identical, which is itself worth knowing.

On single-rate electricity the ceiling runs 82.46p, 96.66p, 104.37p and 111.78p per kWh across one, two, three and four year terms, with the standing charge pinned at 400.00p a day on all four. Gas runs the other way round: 14.71p, 12.92p, 11.89p and 11.72p per kWh, 20.3% cheaper per unit over four years than over one, while the gas standing charge climbs from 1,749.81p a day to 2,002.70p, up 14.5%. Longer electricity commitments cost 35.6% more per unit and nothing more per day; longer gas commitments cost less per unit and more per day. There are also two-rate and three-rate electricity ceilings — day and night at 84.22p and 75.16p on a one-year fix, evening and weekend against weekday day at 77.75p and 87.68p, and a three-rate set at 87.68p, 79.13p and 75.44p.

The page's own estimates make the units unambiguous, which matters because 1,749.81p a day is a startling number to read. British Gas assumes 21,000 kWh of electricity and 30,000 kWh of gas a year and prints £18,777 and £10,800. Work those back and the one-year electricity ceiling is £1,460.00 of standing charge plus £17,316.60 of electricity, which is £18,776.60; gas is £6,386.81 of standing charge plus £4,413.00 of gas, which is £10,799.81. Both land on the published estimate to the pound, so the standing charges really are per day. Taken together that is £29,576.41 a year before tax, of which £7,846.81 — 26.5% — is charged whether the premises uses any energy or not. That sum is ours, from British Gas's own rates and its own assumed usage.

sections.heading: Two standing charges, and on gas the fixed part is the bigger half
sections.html:
Electricity behaves the way most people expect. At British Gas's assumed 21,000 kWh, the £1,460.00 standing charge is 7.8% of the ceiling bill and the units are the other 92%. Use less and you pay a lot less.

Gas does not. At 30,000 kWh the gas itself costs £4,413.00 on the one-year ceiling and the standing charge is £6,386.81 — 1.45 times the cost of the commodity. A premises that burns a third as much gas, 10,000 kWh, still pays the same £6,386.81 and its gas bill falls only to £7,857.81. Two thirds less gas buys 27.2% off the bill. For a shop or a small office with a boiler that runs a few hours a day and little else, the fixed charge is most of what the gas supply costs, and no amount of efficiency touches it.

That is the part "business dual fuel" gets wrong as a phrase. The eight arrangements on the price plans page are a Fixed Price Energy Plan, Renewable Business Energy, British Gas Lite, deemed rates, the Lite Variable Price Plan, Standard Variable Rates, Flex Advantage for users above 500 MWh, and commercial landlord energy. Not one of them is a both-fuels plan and not one carries a discount for taking the pair. Two fuels means two contracts, two standing charges and two renewal dates, and the only thing they share is the envelope.

sections.heading: What the cap does for a house, and does not do for a shop
sections.html:
From 1 October to 31 December 2026 Ofgem's default tariff cap puts a direct debit household in England, Scotland and Wales at an average 26.32p per kWh of electricity with a 54.83p daily standing charge, and 7.97p per kWh of gas with a 29.68p daily standing charge. Set those beside the business ceiling and the electricity unit price is 3.13 times higher, gas units are 1.85 times higher, the electricity standing charge is 7.3 times higher and the gas standing charge is 59 times higher.

Those multiples are not what a business pays, and saying so matters more than the arithmetic. One number is a regulated cap on what a household is actually charged; the other is a published maximum on what a microbusiness can be charged, and the gap between that maximum and a real British Gas Business quote is not published anywhere. What the comparison does show is the distance between a priced market and an unpriced one.

Ofgem's retail market highlights of 27 January 2026 put some context round it. There are 65 active suppliers in the business market against 22 in domestic, so a business has more doors to knock on and less help choosing between them. Using DESNZ data for the second half of 2024, the report puts UK electricity prices for medium-sized businesses 92% above the European median, the highest in Europe, against 44% for households, and notes that very small firms pay the highest prices of all. On survey data for 2025 it found 70% of businesses keeping up with bills without difficulty, 19% keeping up but struggling from time to time and 6% constantly struggling. Smart or advanced meters cover 2 million non-household sites, 64% of the total.

sections.heading: Tax is where a business bill parts company with a household one
sections.html:
HMRC's guidance, updated 10 July 2026, is blunt: "Fuel for business use is usually standard-rated". So the £29,576.41 ceiling above carries 20% VAT, not the 5% a home pays. There are two ways out of it. A charity's non-business use qualifies for the domestic treatment, and so does low usage under the de minimis limits in VAT Notice 701/19: electricity at "not more than an average rate of 33 kilowatt hours per day, 1,000 kilowatt hours per month" and piped gas at "not more than an average rate of 5 therms or 145 kilowatt hours per day", 4,397 kWh a month.

Which produces an oddity on a dual fuel supply this winter. Great Britain has a temporary zero rate on qualifying electricity, and HMRC's brief of 8 September 2026 says it "applies from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027"; Northern Ireland stays at 5%. A small business under both de minimis limits is therefore paying 0% VAT on its electricity and 5% on its gas, from one supplier, for the same six months. On 1 April 2027 the electricity goes back to 5%. A business over either limit pays 20% throughout and the change passes it by entirely.

Then there is the levy a household never sees. Climate Change Levy is charged on business energy at £0.00801 per kWh from 1 April 2026 — the same rate on natural gas as on electricity, up from £0.00775 on both from 1 April 2024. On British Gas's assumed 51,000 kWh across the two fuels that is £408.51 a year. Holders of a climate change agreement pay 8% of the main rate on electricity and 11% on gas, which is the single largest discount available on a business energy bill and is not available to most of the firms reading this. Stack it up and the published ceiling becomes £29,576.41 of energy, £408.51 of levy and £5,996.98 of VAT: £35,981.90. That total is our arithmetic on British Gas's published rates, not a figure British Gas prints.

sections.heading: Which definition you fall inside decides what you are owed
sections.html:
British Gas Business sets out Ofgem's two definitions on its own help pages, and they are worth reading before a renewal rather than after one. A microbusiness uses no more than 100,000 kWh of electricity or 293,000 kWh of gas a year, or employs fewer than 10 people full-time equivalent with turnover or a balance sheet no greater than £2 million. A small business uses no more than 200,000 kWh of electricity or 500,000 kWh of gas, or employs fewer than 50 with turnover at most £6.5 million or a balance sheet of £5 million. British Gas adds the line that decides most arguments: "The consumption threshold applies to each fuel being supplied". On a dual fuel supply that can make one business a microbusiness for its gas and not for its electricity, with different protections on each bill.

The protections themselves arrived on dates worth quoting. Ofgem's microbusiness decision required principal terms to be put in front of a customer before a contract is agreed, and brokerage costs to be disclosed "as a total cost in pounds/pence covering the duration of the contract", from 1 October 2022; suppliers were barred from working with brokers outside a qualifying redress scheme from 1 December 2022. The Standards of Conduct were widened to businesses of any size on 1 July 2024, broker fees had to appear in the principal terms for every non-domestic customer from 1 October 2024, and from December 2024 complaints standards and Energy Ombudsman signposting were extended to small businesses. Ofgem's own framing of the problem it was solving: 5.3 million microbusinesses, 95% of all UK businesses, spending £4.2bn in 2021 across roughly 1.4 million electricity and 0.4 million gas meter points held by the largest suppliers.

Two limits are worth noting. The maximum price page states that the ceiling does not cover "businesses with a half hourly meter", and a half-hourly meter is compulsory once maximum demand reaches 100kW in any half-hour period, so a growing business can lose the published ceiling without changing anything about its ownership or headcount. And the Ombudsman route is real but lightly used: it opens at 8 weeks or on a deadlock letter, on 0330 440 1624, and in the year after its remit widened in December 2024 just over 400 small businesses used it against more than 13,000 microbusiness disputes. Across the whole energy sector it accepted 46,532 cases between January and June 2026 against 40,068 in the same half of 2025, 27,006 of them about billing, with supplier signposting improving from 48% to 53%.

sections.heading: Where the paperwork runs out
sections.html:
The default prices are the ones a business is most likely to end up on, and they are the ones hardest to read. The out-of-contract page describes the Variable Price Plan and the Standard Variable Rate, promises "at least 30 days' notice" of a change and says a standard variable rate is applied "only ... in exceptional circumstances" — and prints the rates themselves solely inside images. The equivalent PDFs on britishgas.co.uk refused a fetch on 16 October 2026. That is a different failure from a page being down, and it means the price a business is moved onto at the end of a fixed term is not published in text anywhere on the site.

The terms and conditions page, last updated October 2026, names fourteen documents — small business general terms, the fixed plan, the 30-day flexible plan, the Variable Price Plan, the multi-site plan, the deemed contract, metering and connections, enterprise and corporate terms, and two Lite versions split either side of 23 September 2026, the same date the maximum prices carry. It prints none of their contents. Security deposits, late payment charges and early termination charges are all in there somewhere, and none of them can be compared against another supplier without opening fourteen files.

Against that, credit where it is due on complaints. The page gives separate routes for British Gas Lite and British Gas business, acknowledges a complaint within 24 hours, aims to respond within 5 working days, publishes a customer service director mailbox, signposts Citizens Advice and the Energy Ombudsman for micro and small businesses, and tells a customer what to do about a broker as well as about British Gas. Ofgem has required microbusiness signposting since 1 July 2024 and it is there.

What no one publishes is how well any of it works. Ofgem's complaints guidance OFG1164, which applies from 4 November 2025, covers suppliers' domestic customers and records that microbusiness complaints data has moved into the non-domestic market monitoring return, which is not broken out by supplier. Smart Money People carries British Gas boiler repairs at 3.71 out of 5 from 42 reviews and home insurance at 4.00 from 34, and no business energy listing at all. Centrica's accounts give the commercial picture and nothing else: business energy supply made £58m of adjusted operating profit in the year to 31 December 2025 against £28m in 2024, on adjusted EBITDA of £60m against £31m, published on 19 February 2026. Neither the preliminary nor the interim results page gives a customer count, a meter-point count or a revenue figure for the business arm, so "largest business energy supplier" has 350,000 businesses behind it and nothing else.

pros: Publishes a maximum microbusiness price at all, covering 1, 2, 3 and 4 year terms on single-rate, two-rate and three-rate electricity and on gas, with an estimated contract cost printed beside each
Those estimates reconcile to the pound against the rates alongside them: 82.46p and 400.00p a day on 21,000 kWh really is the £18,777 the page prints
Every fixed-price and fixed-term British Gas Business electricity plan is sold as zero carbon, on a supply given as 72% renewable and 28% nuclear
Fixed terms of 1 to 3 years, with a renewal quote available up to 12 months before a contract ends
The complaints page signposts Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 and the Energy Ombudsman for micro and small businesses, and gives a separate route for a complaint about a broker
British Gas Lite comes with a free smart meter on joining and runs web chat 8am to 6pm, two hours longer than the main business line
A business that moves into premises on deemed rates is told it can switch to a cheaper plan through the business moves team
Scale and a traceable counterparty: more than 350,000 businesses supplied, on contracts written by a company that has existed since 1995
cons: The rates that apply by default — deemed rates, the Variable Price Plan and the Standard Variable Rate — are published on britishgas.co.uk only as images, and the PDF versions of the same documents refused a fetch on 16 October 2026. The price a business is moved onto when its fixed term ends cannot be read off the website at all.

The renewals page says a letter arrives 70 days before a fixed plan ends, and its own FAQ further down the same page says 60 days. The microbusiness help page says around 60. Two numbers, three statements, no date on any of them.

A blog post dated 27 August 2026, headed "Business Electricity VAT: Who Qualifies for 0% VAT?", tells businesses that VAT on electricity "will be reduced from 5% to 0% for eligible business customers" from 1 October and nowhere says the relief is temporary. HMRC's own brief of 8 September 2026 states that it "applies from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027".

"UK's largest business energy supplier" appears in the heading of the about page and "Britain's largest business energy supplier" in the paragraph beneath it, supported by a figure of 350,000 businesses and no meter-point count, market share or source. Ofgem publishes no business-market shares, so the claim cannot be checked either way.

Renewable Business Energy is sold only to businesses using more than 150,000 kWh of gas or electricity. Ofgem's microbusiness ceiling for electricity is 100,000 kWh, so no microbusiness reaches the green tariff on its electricity alone.

The published maximum prices exclude half-hourly meters, and half-hourly metering is required at a maximum demand of 100kW in any half-hour period. The protection therefore stops at a line drawn by the meter rather than by the size of the business.
The zero-carbon claim is an electricity claim. The gas arrives off the same network as everybody else's, and British Gas Business publishes no carbon or fuel-mix figure for it.

No independent assessment of British Gas Business exists. Smart Money People rates British Gas boiler repairs at 3.71 out of 5 from 42 reviews and home insurance at 4.00 from 34, and lists no business energy product; Ofgem's complaints guidance OFG1164, applying from 4 November 2025, collects domestic complaints and has moved microbusiness complaints into a non-domestic monitoring return that is not published per supplier.

The terms and conditions page names fourteen separate documents and prints the content of none of them, so every term that costs money — security, late payment, early termination — sits behind its own download.
verdict: British Gas Business is one of the few suppliers that puts a number in public at all, and the number is a ceiling: 82.46p a unit for electricity and 14.71p for gas on a one-year fix, plus £7,846.81 a year in standing charges, and a real quote should come in under it. Treat the published maximum as the worst case and the thing to negotiate down from, get the gas standing charge in writing before anything else, and remember that "dual fuel" here means two contracts with two renewal dates rather than one product with a discount attached. The reason to ask for a quote is that nothing on the website tells you what it will be.

faqs.q: Does British Gas Business give a dual fuel discount?
faqs.a: No. Nothing on the British Gas Business price plans page offers a discount for taking gas and electricity together, and none of its eight arrangements is a both-fuels plan. A business buying both signs two contracts and pays two standing charges — on the published microbusiness ceiling, 400.00p a day for electricity and 1,749.81p a day for gas, which is £7,846.81 a year between them.

faqs.q: What is the most British Gas Business can charge a microbusiness?
faqs.a: At 23 September 2026 the published ceiling for a one-year fix is 82.46p per kWh for single-rate electricity and 14.71p per kWh for gas, with standing charges of 400.00p and 1,749.81p a day. Four-year prices are 111.78p and 11.72p. All of it excludes VAT and Climate Change Levy, and the page says the prices "can change at any time". The ceiling does not apply to half-hourly meters or to a supply starting on a new connection.

faqs.q: Does the energy price cap apply to my business?
faqs.a: No. Ofgem's default tariff cap is a domestic cap: for 1 October to 31 December 2026 it sits at an average 26.32p per kWh and a 54.83p daily standing charge on electricity, and 7.97p per kWh with 29.68p a day on gas, for direct debit households in England, Scotland and Wales. A business has the published maximum microbusiness price instead, which is a ceiling on what it can be charged rather than a cap on what it will be.

faqs.q: Why does my business pay VAT and Climate Change Levy when my home does not?
faqs.a: HMRC treats fuel for business use as standard-rated, so most business supplies carry 20% VAT. Low usage takes the domestic treatment instead — not more than 33 kWh of electricity a day, or 145 kWh of gas — and so does a charity's non-business use. Climate Change Levy is a business-only tax at £0.00801 per kWh on both gas and electricity from 1 April 2026, up from £0.00775 from 1 April 2024, which is £408.51 a year on 51,000 kWh. Holders of a climate change agreement pay 8% of the main electricity rate and 11% on gas.

faqs.q: Can I take a British Gas Business complaint to the Energy Ombudsman?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are a microbusiness or a small business and the complaint is unresolved after 8 weeks or you have a deadlock letter. British Gas Business's own complaints page gives 0333 202 9766 and signposts the Energy Ombudsman on 0330 440 1624 and Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133. Access for small businesses — fewer than 50 employees, or up to 200,000 kWh of electricity or 500,000 kWh of gas — started in December 2024, and just over 400 of them used it in the first year.

faqs.q: What happens when a British Gas Business fixed plan ends?
faqs.a: You are moved to a Variable Price Plan unless a new deal is agreed. British Gas says a letter explaining the options arrives 70 days before the end on one part of its renewals page and 60 days in that page's own FAQ, and that a renewal quote can be given up to 12 months ahead. Online renewal may be unavailable if the plan ends within 4 days. The variable rates themselves are published only as images, so what you would be moved onto cannot be read in advance.

title: British Gas Dual Fuel
meta_title: British Gas Dual Fuel: There Is No Dual-Fuel Discount
meta_description: British Gas lists a dual-fuel discount as Not applicable on all 67 of its own tariffs. What you actually get for taking both fuels, and what it costs.

headline.label: Dual-fuel discount
headline.value: None — £0, on all 67 British Gas tariffs

disclosure: we have no affiliate arrangement with British Gas and earn nothing if you switch to them. The link on this page goes to British Gas’s own site. We list it because it is one of the six suppliers in this category, not because it pays us.
intro:
British Gas offers a £0 dual-fuel discount. Not a small one — none at all. Its own product catalogue carries a field called dual-gas-discount-description for every tariff it sells, and on all 67 of them the value is the same two words: “Not applicable”. The matching electricity field reads the same on 66 of the 67, with one left blank.

That matters because dual fuel is sold on the idea of a reward for consolidating. British Gas’s own guide hedges it carefully — you “may be able to access exclusive discounts and lower rates compared to managing them separately” — and then names no amount, no mechanism and no discount anywhere on the site. The same guide also tells you dual fuel “is not always the cheapest option”, which is the most useful sentence on it.

So what is dual fuel at British Gas? Convenience, stated plainly in their words: “one supplier, one contract, and one online account”. That is the whole of it.

sections.heading: Two fuels means two standing charges, and they add up before you use anything
sections.html:
This is the number dual-fuel marketing never leads with. You pay a daily standing charge on each fuel, and they are both charged whether you use a unit or not. On the figures British Gas publishes as its October 2026 averages, which match the Ofgem cap for October to December 2026:

FuelUnit rateStanding charge
Electricity26.32p/kWh54.83p/day
Gas7.97p/kWh29.68p/day
Both—84.51p/day

84.51p a day is £308.46 a year in fixed charges before a single kWh of either fuel. Against Ofgem’s typical dual-fuel figure of £1,723, the standing charges alone are 18% of the bill.

British Gas confirms the mechanism itself: standing charges “apply to both gas and electricity”. There is no combined or discounted daily charge for taking the pair, which is precisely the kind of saving a dual-fuel discount would have delivered if one existed.

sections.heading: The two fuels are not moving together this winter
sections.html:
A quirk of the current cap period makes dual fuel worth thinking about as two separate decisions rather than one. There is no VAT on electricity from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027. Gas still carries 5%.

So the gas half of your bill is being taxed and the electricity half is not, for six months. Ofgem is explicit that its cap numbers for this period “can’t be compared directly with earlier periods” because of it. The cap itself rose 4% to £1,723 for a typical direct debit dual-fuel household.

The practical consequence: if you are judging whether to fix, the gas and electricity sides of the same tariff are not facing the same risk. The VAT relief on electricity has a known end date of 31 March 2027, and nothing published says what happens on 1 April.

sections.heading: A stale figure on British Gas's own dual-fuel page
sections.html:
Worth knowing if you are reading British Gas’s own material to make this decision. Its dual-fuel benefits guide still cites “Ofgem’s estimate of about £1,862 a year” for a direct debit dual-fuel household.

The current Ofgem figure is £1,723. The page is out by £139, and in the direction that makes the bill look worse than it is. We checked both on 7 October 2026.

It is not the only number British Gas does not keep straight. Across four of its own and Centrica’s pages the customer count is given as “over 7 million”, “7.5m residential energy customers”, “over 8 million customers” and “more than 8 million homes and businesses”. Only the 7.5m figure, on Centrica’s investor-facing page, is tied to a defined unit. None of this changes your bill, but it is a reasonable reason to check a British Gas figure against Ofgem before relying on it.

sections.heading: What you do get for taking both
sections.html:
Set against the absent discount, there are real things on the table — they are just not price reductions on the energy.

  • One contract and one online account for both fuels, in British Gas’s own words.
  • Up to 15% off a Hive thermostat for British Gas energy customers — 10% on some models, 15% on others when bought with professional installation.
  • £106 a year claimed for paying by Direct Debit rather than on receipt of a bill.
  • Warm Home Discount of £150 for winter 2026/2027, applied to the electricity account.
  • The same time-of-use tariffs as the electricity-only range, including an EV tariff at 9.5p off-peak and a heat pump tariff with half-price electricity for 70 hours a week.

And one oddity that proves the point about the discount. The only place British Gas pays more for dual fuel than single fuel is its refer-a-friend scheme, where the voucher is £50 for a dual-fuel switch against £25 for a single fuel. That is a referral payment to whoever introduced you, not a reduction in your tariff, and British Gas’s own terms restrict the scheme to personal contacts the referrer already knows.

sections.heading: What is not published, and should be
sections.html:
Two basic dual-fuel questions have no answer anywhere on britishgas.co.uk, and we looked properly.

Is it one bill or two? British Gas says “one supplier, one contract, and one online account”. It does not say one bill. Its own guide notes that “most energy companies will send you a combined gas and electricity bill” — written generically, about the market, not as a statement about British Gas. We could find no page that answers it directly.

One direct debit or two? Also unstated.

The third gap is the exit fee. Fixed tariffs carry £75 on Winter Warmer 2026, £100 on The Longer Fix and £150 on Fixed Future, but whether that is charged per fuel or per account is not published — and on a dual-fuel contract that is the difference between £100 and £200 to walk away. The terms say only that any exit fees “will be sent by email or post and will be in your online account”. Ask before you fix.

sections.heading: How it compares in this category
sections.html:
Dual fuel at British Gas is a convenience product priced at the cap, so the comparison worth making is against suppliers who do something structurally different with the bundle.

Utility Warehouse discounts the services as you add more of them, which is the multi-service reward British Gas does not offer. Alfred, reviewed in this category, charges a £195-a-year membership and claims to sell the energy itself at cost with no margin — the opposite structure, and it has not launched yet. Octopus and E.ON Next both score far above British Gas on the Citizens Advice service table.

If your reason for consolidating is one company to call and one app to look at, British Gas delivers that. If your reason is that two fuels with one supplier ought to cost less than two fuels with two suppliers, British Gas is not the supplier that agrees with you.

pros: One contract and one online account for both fuels, which is what most people want from dual fuel
No exit fee and no end date on the Standard Variable tariff, so consolidating costs nothing to undo
Up to 15% off a Hive thermostat for energy customers
£106 a year claimed for paying by Direct Debit rather than on receipt
£150 Warm Home Discount applied to the electricity account for winter 2026/2027
The same time-of-use tariffs as the electricity range, including 9.5p off-peak on the EV tariff
No VAT on the electricity half of the bill until 31 March 2027
cons: There is no dual-fuel discount: “Not applicable” on all 67 tariffs in British Gas’s own catalogue
Two standing charges totalling 84.51p a day, or £308.46 a year before you use anything
British Gas’s own dual-fuel guide still quotes a £1,862 Ofgem estimate against the current £1,723
Whether dual fuel is one bill or two is not stated anywhere on their site, and nor is one direct debit or two
Whether a fixed-tariff exit fee is charged per fuel or per account is not published, which on dual fuel is the difference between £100 and £200
Standard Variable is priced at the Ofgem cap, so consolidating buys convenience and nothing else
Its own customer count appears as 7 million, 7.5 million and 8 million across four of its own pages
Utility Warehouse discounts services as you add them, which is the reward British Gas declines to offer
verdict: Take British Gas dual fuel if you want one company, one contract and one app for both fuels, and understand that this is the entire benefit. There is no dual-fuel discount — British Gas says so itself in the product catalogue behind its own website, on all 67 tariffs — and the Standard Variable tariff is priced at the Ofgem cap. You will pay two standing charges totalling 84.51p a day, which is £308.46 a year before either fuel flows, and 18% of a typical bill. The things genuinely worth having are the time-of-use tariffs if you have a smart meter and a load you can move, the £150 Warm Home Discount, and the Hive discount. If your reason for putting both fuels in one place is that it ought to be cheaper than splitting them, look at Utility Warehouse, which does discount for adding services, and read the Citizens Advice table before you decide service is a secondary concern.

faqs.q: Does British Gas give a dual-fuel discount?
faqs.a: No. The discount fields in British Gas’s own product catalogue read “Not applicable” on all 67 of its tariffs, and no amount or mechanism is published anywhere on its website. Its guide says you “may” access “exclusive discounts” without naming one, and also warns that dual fuel “is not always the cheapest option”.

faqs.q: What do two standing charges cost me?
faqs.a: On the October to December 2026 figures, 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p for gas — 84.51p combined, or £308.46 a year. You pay it whether you use anything or not, and it is about 18% of Ofgem’s £1,723 typical dual-fuel bill.

faqs.q: Is dual fuel one bill?
faqs.a: British Gas does not say. It states “one supplier, one contract, and one online account”, which is not the same claim, and its guide’s line about combined bills is written about the market generally rather than about British Gas. Whether you get one direct debit or two is also unpublished. If it matters to you, ask before switching.

faqs.q: Why is gas taxed and electricity not?
faqs.a: A temporary government measure removed VAT from electricity between 1 October 2026 and 31 March 2027. Gas keeps its 5%. It means the two halves of a dual-fuel bill are moving differently this winter, and Ofgem warns its own cap figures cannot be compared directly with earlier periods because of it.

faqs.q: If I fix and then leave, do I pay one exit fee or two?
faqs.a: Not published. The fees themselves are — £75 on Winter Warmer 2026, £100 on The Longer Fix, £150 on Fixed Future — but whether they apply per fuel or per account is not stated, and the terms defer to whatever is in your online account. On a dual-fuel contract that is the difference between £100 and £200, so get it in writing first.

title: British Gas Electricity
meta_title: British Gas Electricity: The Rate Depends Where You Live
meta_description: British Gas charges 26.998p/kWh in London and 28.447p in the North West on the same tariff, the same day. Regional rates, Economy 7 and the EV deals.

headline.label: Standard Variable unit rate
headline.value: 26.998p/kWh — London, Direct Debit, plus 47.109p/day standing charge

disclosure: we have no affiliate arrangement with British Gas and earn nothing if you switch to them. The link on this page goes to British Gas’s own site. We mention it because it is one of the six suppliers in this category, not because it pays us.
intro:
British Gas charges 26.998p per kWh for electricity on its Standard Variable tariff in London, with a 47.109p a day standing charge. Move to the North West and the same tariff, read from the same British Gas system on the same afternoon of 7 October 2026, costs 28.447p per kWh and 52.223p a day. Same supplier, same product, 1.449p and 5.114p apart.

That is the first thing to understand about any British Gas electricity quote you see written down, including the one on this page. There is no national British Gas electricity price. There are fourteen regional ones, and the gap between the cheapest and the most expensive is worth real money on an annual bill: British Gas’s own projection for 2,700 kWh is £900.86 in London and £958.66 in the North West.

The figure British Gas puts on its own price-cap page — 26.32p a unit and 54.83p a day — is not its price either. It is the Ofgem price cap average for October to December 2026, to the decimal place. Useful as a benchmark, misleading as a quote.

sections.heading: What it actually costs, and why the number moves with your postcode
sections.html:
British Gas publishes its Standard Variable rates through a postcode lookup. Two regions, both monthly Direct Debit, both read on 7 October 2026:

RegionUnit rateStanding chargeAnnual projection, 2,700 kWh
London26.998p/kWh47.109p/day£900.86
North West28.447p/kWh52.223p/day£958.66

Payment method moves it again, and in the direction you would not guess. In London, prepayment is the cheapest unit rate at 26.16p with a 47.1p standing charge, while paying on receipt of a bill is the dearest at 28.494p and 54.33p. Direct Debit sits between them. British Gas separately claims paying by Direct Debit saves £106 a year, which is a statement about its whole bill rather than about the electricity unit rate.

One change this quarter is worth knowing because it is temporary and it is not a British Gas decision. There is no VAT on electricity from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, while gas still carries 5%. Ofgem says plainly that its cap figures “can’t be compared directly with earlier periods” because of it. If your electricity looks cheaper than last winter, that is part of the reason, and it runs out at the end of March.

sections.heading: Standing charge first, unit rate second
sections.html:
At 47.109p a day in London, the standing charge costs £171.95 a year before a single unit is used, and £190.61 in the North West. On British Gas’s own 2,700 kWh projection that is 19% of the London bill and 20% of the North West one.

It matters because every low-usage household is paying a fixed entry fee. A flat using 1,500 kWh in London pays £171.95 standing charge against £404.97 of electricity — the fixed part is 30% of the bill. The arithmetic runs the other way for heavy users, which is why comparing suppliers on unit rate alone is a mistake if your consumption is low.

Economy 7 shifts the shape of the deal rather than the size. In London, British Gas Economy 7 pays 33.714p by day and 14.92p at night, on a 46.634p standing charge, with a projection of £867.34. The night rate is less than half the single rate, but the day rate is 6.716p above it. Economy 7 only pays if you can genuinely move load into the night; if you cannot, it is the more expensive tariff.

sections.heading: The time-of-use tariffs, and what each one asks of you
sections.html:
This is the part of the British Gas range that is genuinely competitive, and every one of them requires a smart meter and, in most cases, Direct Debit.

  • EV Power — off-peak electricity at 9.5p/kWh between 12am and 5am, or an equivalent 7.125p with Hive Power+. British Gas states it “does not work with Economy 7”.
  • Heat Power — half-price electricity 1pm to 4pm and 12am to 7am, every day. That is 70 hours a week. Credit customers only.
  • Charge Power — 50% off the unit rate from 12am to 5am, aimed at home batteries.
  • PeakSave — existing customers get 8 hours of half-price electricity every Sunday, 9am to 5pm.
  • Hive Solar Saver — up to 25% off electricity for Hive solar or battery installed after 22 May 2024.

Read the standing-charge clause on all of them. British Gas states for Heat Power that “you will still pay the full daily standing charge applicable to your tariff”, and the same applies to Charge Power. The discount is on units, never on the fixed charge.

One trap in the Electric Driver terms, which British Gas writes out itself: “when this tariff applies and you don’t have an electricity smart meter you will be charged the peak unit rate at all times.” Peak runs 5.01am to 11.59pm. Sign up without a working smart meter and you get the worst of both.

sections.heading: Fixed tariffs and the exit fees
sections.html:
British Gas’s own product catalogue lists the exit fee against each tariff, and they are not uniform:

  • Standard Variable — no exit fee, no end date
  • Winter Warmer 2026 — £75, ends 31 December 2026
  • The Longer Fix — £100, end dates from 31 October 2026 to 28 February 2027 depending on version
  • Fixed Future — £150, ends 31 October 2027

Across the full catalogue of 67 tariff records the exit fee ranges from £5 to £200, with £50 the most common value. Whether the fee is charged per fuel or per account is not published; the terms say only that any exit fees “will be sent by email or post and will be in your online account”. Ask before you fix if you think you might move.

British Gas also advertises three acquisition tariffs by name — Fix and Fall, Fixed Tracker and Fixed Fixed — and publishes a rate for none of them. Fixed Tracker is described as “guaranteed to pay up to £60 less” than the cap; Fix and Fall fixes for two years with a price review against the cap after twelve months. You cannot see either price without completing a quote, which is worth knowing before you spend twenty minutes on one.

sections.heading: Where British Gas is beaten, and by what
sections.html:
The service record is the weakest part of the case. Citizens Advice scores British Gas 2.61 out of 5 for customer service in its April to June 2026 table, ranking it 14th of the 16 suppliers it ranks. Octopus is on 3.67, E.ON Next 3.71, Outfox Energy 4.03. Only Utilita (2.53) and TruEnergy (1.38) score lower. Citizens Advice weights that score 35% on complaints, 30% on ease of contact, 25% on billing and metering.

Complaints that escalate are running high. The Energy Ombudsman accepted 54.90 disputes per 100,000 domestic accounts against British Gas in Q2 2026 — the second highest of the eight suppliers it charts, behind only ScottishPower on 65.10. The trend over four quarters reads 49.5, 53.0, 58.1, 54.9. On signposting — telling unhappy customers the Ombudsman exists — British Gas was lowest of the eight at 41% against a sector figure of 53%.

Ofgem has had cause to act. In May 2026 British Gas settled an Ofgem investigation into its treatment of prepayment meter customers between 2018 and 2021 with a £20 million payment into Ofgem’s Voluntary Redress Fund and up to £70 million of energy debt written off for vulnerable customers. Ofgem took it as “alternative action”, so there was no financial penalty. A separate compliance engagement on smart meter obligations, opened in July 2024, remains open; British Gas is one of four suppliers still in reduced engagement on smart-mode obligations, which Ofgem is careful to say “is not a finding of non-compliance”.

And the live prices are behind a quote. Of the named tariffs above, only Standard Variable, Economy 7 and the prepayment rates can be read without handing over a postcode and an email address.

sections.heading: What British Gas does well
sections.html:
Support for people struggling with bills is substantial and specific. The Warm Home Discount is a one-off £150 off the electricity bill for winter 2026/2027, applied as credit, or a Post Office voucher for prepayment customers. DWP letters go out between 20 October and 31 December 2026, and all payments land by 31 March 2027 at the latest.

The British Gas Energy Trust is an independent charity funded solely by British Gas since 2004, and it helps households regardless of supplier — it says it has supported over 2.2 million people. British Gas also cites a £140 million customer support package and says it helped over 300,000 of its own customers manage debt last year.

Prepayment customers get £10 of emergency credit and Friendly Credit, which blocks disconnection on Sundays, English bank holidays and between 6pm and 9am Monday to Saturday. The Priority Services Register covers the over-65s, anyone reliant on medical equipment, families with children under five and the recently bereaved, and brings bills in Braille, large print or audio, a free annual gas safety check subject to eligibility, and a free SignVideo BSL relay weekdays 9am to 5pm.

pros: Fourteen regional price areas are published through a postcode lookup, so you can get your actual rate before switching
Prepayment is cheaper per unit than Direct Debit in London — 26.16p against 26.998p
EV Power at 9.5p off-peak, or 7.125p with Hive Power+, is among the lower overnight rates on the market
Heat Power gives 70 hours a week of half-price electricity, which suits a heat pump on a timer
PeakSave gives existing customers eight hours of half-price electricity every Sunday
No exit fee and no end date on Standard Variable
£150 Warm Home Discount, £10 emergency credit and Friendly Credit protection on prepayment
The British Gas Energy Trust helps households regardless of who supplies them, and has reached over 2.2 million people
cons: Citizens Advice scores it 2.61 out of 5 and ranks it 14th of the 16 suppliers it ranks
Second-highest escalation rate of eight suppliers at the Energy Ombudsman — 54.90 disputes per 100,000 accounts
Lowest signposting score of those eight at 41%, against a sector figure of 53%
Settled an Ofgem prepayment-meter investigation in May 2026 with £20m of redress and up to £70m of debt written off
An Ofgem compliance engagement on smart meter obligations opened in July 2024 is still open
Fix and Fall, Fixed Tracker and Fixed Fixed are advertised by name with no published rate — you need a quote to see either price
The London standing charge of 47.109p a day costs £171.95 a year before you use anything, which is 30% of a 1,500 kWh bill
Economy 7 charges 33.714p by day, 6.716p above the single rate, so it punishes anyone who cannot shift load overnight
Whether a fixed-tariff exit fee is charged per fuel or per account is not published anywhere
verdict: British Gas is worth a quote if you have a smart meter and a load you can move: EV Power at 9.5p overnight, Heat Power’s 70 half-price hours a week and PeakSave’s Sunday window are real discounts, not marketing. It is also the supplier to look at if you need help paying, because the £150 Warm Home Discount, the £10 emergency credit, Friendly Credit and an independent charity that helps non-customers too add up to more than its rivals offer. What you are accepting in exchange is a service record that Citizens Advice puts 14th of 16, the second-highest escalation rate to the Energy Ombudsman of the eight largest suppliers, and a £20m Ofgem redress settlement from May 2026 over prepayment customers. On price alone the Standard Variable tariff is the price cap, nothing more, and three of the tariffs that might beat it will not show you a rate without a quote first.

faqs.q: Why is the British Gas electricity rate different from the one I was quoted?
faqs.a: Because there is no single British Gas rate. It prices fourteen regions separately, and on 7 October 2026 the Standard Variable unit rate was 26.998p/kWh in London and 28.447p/kWh in the North West — a 1.449p gap on the same tariff on the same day. Payment method moves it again. Always read your own postcode’s rate.

faqs.q: Is British Gas cheaper than the price cap?
faqs.a: Not on Standard Variable. The figure British Gas publishes as its October 2026 average, 26.32p a unit and 54.83p a day, is the Ofgem cap for October to December 2026 to the decimal place. Its Fixed Tracker tariff claims to beat the cap by “up to £60”, but no rate is published for it without a quote.

faqs.q: Do the half-price windows apply to the standing charge?
faqs.a: No. British Gas states for Heat Power that “you will still pay the full daily standing charge applicable to your tariff”, and the same holds for Charge Power. Every time-of-use discount applies to units only, so in London you are still paying 47.109p a day whatever happens.

faqs.q: What happens if I join a time-of-use tariff without a smart meter?
faqs.a: You pay the peak rate around the clock. The Electric Driver terms say it outright: “when this tariff applies and you don’t have an electricity smart meter you will be charged the peak unit rate at all times”, with peak running 5.01am to 11.59pm. Get the meter fitted before you switch tariff, not after.

faqs.q: Why does my electricity look cheaper this winter?
faqs.a: Partly because there is no VAT on electricity between 1 October 2026 and 31 March 2027. Gas still carries 5%. Ofgem says its own cap figures “can’t be compared directly with earlier periods” because of it, and the relief ends on 31 March.

faqs.q: What is the exit fee if I leave a fixed tariff early?
faqs.a: It depends which one. British Gas’s catalogue shows £75 on Winter Warmer 2026, £100 on The Longer Fix and £150 on Fixed Future, with no fee at all on Standard Variable. Across all 67 records in that catalogue the range is £5 to £200. Whether it is charged per fuel or per account is not published.

title: British Gas Plumbing and Drains Cover
meta_title: British Gas Plumbing & Drains Cover: £6.12 a Month
meta_description: British Gas plumbing and drains cover costs £6.12 a month with a £60 excess, unlimited call-outs and no claim cap. What the £1,000 access limit buys.
intro:
British Gas sells plumbing and drains cover at £6.12 a month — £73.44 across a year — with a £60 excess, unlimited call-outs and no cap on what the repairs themselves cost. On top of that sits £1,000 per repair, including VAT, to get at the pipe and put the floor, the wall or the driveway back afterwards. Every figure here was read on 16 October 2026 from British Gas's own product page, summary of cover and insurance documents.

Three separate companies stand behind that price and all three sit inside one group, which is unusual in this corner of the market. British Gas Services Limited (company 03141243, firm reference 490568) sells the policy and administers it. British Gas Insurance Limited (company 06608316, firm reference 490565) carries the risk and is authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority in its own right. And the engineer who arrives for a stubborn blockage works for Dyno-Rod Limited (company 01046906, incorporated 21 March 1972), which the Companies House register records as 75% or more owned and controlled by British Gas Services Limited — notified on 6 April 2016, with the same registered office in Windsor. Centrica's 2025 strategic report counts 7,000-plus field service engineers across the operation and 2,939,000 Home Services customers at the end of the year.

Three rules decide whether this policy is open to you before price enters the argument. You must own the home you are insuring, the cover is for domestic use on the mainland United Kingdom only, and claims in the first 14 days are not covered at all. British Gas prints that waiting period on the page where it takes your money, which is more than several of its rivals manage — but it still means a leak in the first fortnight is your bill.
