sections.heading: Eight prices, three terms, and what a year of commitment is actually worth
sections.html:
The 24-month Business Essential SIM table runs £5, £6, £7, £13, £15, £17, £19 and £25 against 0GB, 250MB, 500MB, 1GB, 10GB, 50GB, 100GB and unlimited data. The jump worth noticing is in the middle: £13 buys 1GB and £15 buys 10GB, so nine extra gigabytes cost £2. Below that the pricing stops making sense for anyone who uses a phone for data at all — 250MB for £6 is a month of email and little else.

The same plan is sold on three terms, and because EE prints all three the price of committing can be worked out exactly. On a rolling month the four data tiers are £21, £23, £25 and £31; on 12 months they are £17, £19, £21 and £27; on 24 months £15, £17, £19 and £25. The gaps are identical on every tier: a rolling month costs exactly £6 a month more than the two-year price, and a 12-month term exactly £2 more. So EE has put a number on lock-in rather than leaving the reader to guess at one. On 10GB, two years at £15 is £360 of payments against £504 on a rolling month over the same period — £144 for the right to walk away each month, and the same £144 on unlimited (£600 against £744). Twelve months is the awkward middle: £24 more than the two-year price across its own twelve months, and £48 less than a rolling month over the same twelve, for half the commitment either way.

Moving up the range costs a flat £5. Business All Rounder is £20, £22, £24 and £30 against Business Essential's £15, £17, £19 and £25, and what the £5 buys is one Inclusive Extra — EE's term for an add-on such as a streaming or productivity subscription. On the 10GB tier that is a third on top of the price of the airtime, which is worth checking against what the extra would cost bought directly. Business Full Works carries three Inclusive Extras, and the Apple One version swaps them for Apple TV+, Apple Music and 50GB of iCloud+; the SIM-only tables that could be read in the small business price guide cover Business Essential and Business All Rounder only, so no SIM-only price for either Full Works plan was found during this check.

sections.heading: Two brands in one group, two increase schedules, one day apart
sections.html:
Every mobile contract here carries an annual increase, and which kind you get depends on the date you signed rather than on anything you can choose today. A business that bought from BT Business on or before 1 December 2024 is still on the old inflation-linked formula: the December CPI rate “published by the Office for National Statistics on 21 January 2026 which was 3.4%”, plus a further 3.9%, giving 7.3% from 1 April 2026. BT Business states that where CPI is negative it will “take the CPI percentage (%) inflation rate to be 0%”, so the floor is 3.9% whatever happens to prices.

EE Business runs the identical 7.3% for 2026 and the identical 3.4% plus 3.9% derivation — but its cut-off is 1 September 2024, three months earlier than BT Business's, and its increase lands on 31 March rather than 1 April. Two brands inside one group, one regulatory change, two cut-off dates and two dates in the calendar a day apart. Nothing about that is improper and neither page mentions the other; it does mean a company with some lines bought through BT Business and some through EE Business can be on two schedules at once.

Contracts signed after those dates get a fixed amount instead of a percentage, and EE publishes the amounts: £3.00 a month for plans bought between 2 September and 18 November 2024, then from 19 November 2024 £3.00 on handset plans and £1.50 on SIM only, mobile broadband, connected device, router and watch plans, all excluding VAT. Selected add-ons and out-of-bundle charges rise by 5% instead.

Here is the part nobody states, and it is arithmetic rather than opinion. A fixed step is only cheaper than a percentage above a certain monthly price. At 7.3%, £1.50 is the same as the percentage on a plan of £20.55 a month: above that the fixed step is the better deal, and below it the fixed step costs more. On the £15 10GB plan, £1.50 is a 10% increase against the 7.3% an older contract pays — £16.50 rather than £16.10. On the £25 unlimited plan it is 6%, and the newer customer is better off. The pounds-and-pence regime made the rise legible, which was the point of it; on a cheap SIM it did not make it smaller.

And the amount is set per cohort, not once and for all. The SIM-only deal EE Business is advertising today prints its own steps on the tile: £19.00 a month now, £21.08 on 31 March 2027 and £23.16 on 31 March 2028 — a step of £2.08, which is 10.9% of the opening price and 39% larger than the £1.50 a late-2024 SIM-only customer pays. Taken over a 24-month term starting in November 2026, that is five months at £19.00, twelve at £21.08 and seven at £23.16: £510.08 ex VAT, or £612.10 with VAT, against the £456.00 you get by multiplying the headline by 24. The term ends with the customer paying 21.9% more than they agreed to. The month you sign moves that total, so treat it as a worked example rather than a quotation — but the method is the only honest way to read a price with two steps in it.

sections.heading: The line BT draws at ten employees is the same line Parliament drew
sections.html:
BT Business splits its mobile menu three ways: mobile plans for 1-10 employees, mobile plans for 11-249 employees, and Device Lifecycle Management for “businesses with 400+ devices”. That first boundary looks like ordinary sales segmentation. It is also the boundary of the law.

Ofcom's General Condition C1 carries the contract protections a mobile customer is likely to care about most — notice of “not shorter than one month” of any modification likely to cause material detriment, the right to exit within 30 days when one lands, and since 17 January 2025 the prohibition on writing inflation-linked or percentage-based rises into a new contract at all. Who gets them is set by section 52(6) of the Communications Act 2003, which defines a “Domestic and Small Business Customer” as a customer who is neither a communications provider nor “a person who is such a Customer in respect of an undertaking carried on by him for which more than ten individuals work”. Ofcom's own guidance puts it plainly: the prohibition “applies to small business customers with 10 or less employees”. Hire an eleventh person and the protection stops.

You can see that line in BT Business's own price-rise table. Digital Voice for Business “up to 10 employees” rises by a fixed £1.00 per user a month from 1 April 2026; Digital Voice for Business “11+ employees” rises by 6%. Same product, same company, same date, and the mechanism changes at exactly the headcount the Act changes at. Ofcom accepts that providers “do not routinely collect or hold information about the number of employees of their business customers” and will look instead at whether reasonable steps were taken to identify who qualifies, using proxies such as annual spend or the number of lines.

A third number is in play as well. EE's own General Condition C1.3 additional-information document, version 1.6 dated 18 January 2024, opens by stating it is “applicable to EE business customers with greater than 50 employees”, and sends anyone with fewer than 50 to the small business pay monthly terms instead. So one group operates a statutory threshold of ten, a product menu that breaks at ten and again at 249, and a documentation threshold of 50. A company of 30 people reading its way through this has to work out which of the three it is on.

sections.heading: What the regulated price list does not manage to say
sections.html:
The EE Price Guide for Small Business is a genuinely useful document — 24-month, 12-month and rolling prices for every tier in one place, which is more than most networks publish — and it is revised often: the copies dated 22 July, 26 August and 3 September 2026 were all read for this page. Not one Business Essential or Business All Rounder SIM-only price moved across the three. A confirmed figure is a result, and it says the range is stable rather than quietly creeping.

Two things in it cannot be read, though. The allowance row of the 24-month Business Essential table carries four entries for eight price columns — “Unlimited Texts and Minutes in the UK and ROI”, “250 Texts and 250 Minutes”, “500 Texts and 500 Minutes” and “Unlimited Texts and Minutes” — with nothing in the table saying which tier gets which. A buyer looking at the £6 250MB SIM cannot tell from the price guide whether the calls on it are unlimited or capped at 250 minutes. The data row and the price row line up cell for cell; the allowance row does not, and on three separate revisions of the document it has not been fixed.

The second is the exit charge, and it is the one a business signing for two years would most want. The guide's contents page lists Early Termination Charges on page 39, and that part of the document would not return readable text on any attempt here. BT's own help article for business mobile billing points customers at the BT Price List for “UK mobile and international mobile tariffs”, and that address is closed to automated readers by BT's robots file, so it was not read either. The charge itself is described in the terms rather than priced: clause 9.1.2 of the EE Pay Monthly terms for Small Business, version 11 dated 16 January 2026, makes it “calculated based on the sum of all outstanding Monthly Charges”, “factoring in any recurring monthly discount to which You are entitled”, “minus any costs we save from you leaving early”. No percentage is attached to the saving and no worked example is given anywhere a prospective customer can reach.

The same clause set holds one detail worth having: 30 days' notice or more is required to cancel, under clause 9.1, and that applies when the minimum term has already expired as well as during it. A business that simply stops paying at the end of 24 months has not ended the contract.

sections.heading: Running out of data slows the phone down rather than stopping it
sections.html:
Stay Connected is the best feature in the range and it is described in one line of the price guide: when the full-speed allowance is used, “speed drops to 0.5Mb per second until the next cycle or until a data pass is bought”. Half a megabit is enough for email, messaging and a maps lookup and not enough for a video call, which is the right trade for a working phone — and it means an engineer on site does not simply go dark on the 28th of the month.

Read the table carefully, because it is not on everything. The price guide marks Stay Connected “Not Included in price plan” on the cheaper tiers and “Included in price plan (except for Unlimited plans)” on the rest. Unlimited plans are excluded because they cannot run out, which is fair enough; the cheap tiers are excluded precisely where running out is most likely. On the 250MB SIM at £6 a month there is no soft landing at all.

Without it, the out-of-bundle rates take over, and they are the real reason to buy more data than you think you need. Data beyond the allowance in the UK and EU is 1.6p per MB, which works out at about £16.38 a gigabyte — more than the whole monthly cost of the £15 10GB plan, for one gigabyte. Calls to UK and EU mobiles outside an allowance are 69p a minute, so a ten-minute call is £6.90; texts are 45p each to UK and EU mobiles and 12p to UK and EU regional landlines, and a picture message is 69p. Calls to 0800, 0808 and 116 numbers are free. Calls to 084, 087, 118 and 09 numbers are 69p a minute plus the service charge set by whoever you are ringing.

Two more lines in the table are easy to miss. Network Boost, which prioritises traffic at busy times, is “Included in Unlimited price plan” only. 5G+ — the standalone network, which is where the low latency and the better indoor performance come from — is “Included in all new price plans from 13th May 2026”, so a business still inside a contract signed in 2024 or 2025 is not getting it on these terms.

sections.heading: Two documents, two answers on European roaming
sections.html:
Here the group's own pages do not agree, and both are worth printing. BT Business's plan page states that “Every plan is 5G-ready, with unlimited voice and roaming in our Europe Zone at no extra cost”. EE's price guide, pricing the same plans, says that without an Inclusive Extra, a roaming add-on or Business Connect, a day's use in the EU and EEA carries a charge of £2.26. Those two sentences cannot both be true for the same customer.

The likeliest reconciliation is in the tables rather than in either sentence. Inclusive Extras are marked “Not included in price plan” on Business Essential and “1 x Inclusive Extra” on Business All Rounder, so on the face of the two documents it is the cheaper plan that pays the daily charge and the dearer one that roams free — the opposite of what “every plan” implies. Neither document says that in terms, so confirm it for the tier you are buying before you travel rather than taking it from either page. If the £2.26 does apply to your plan, a fortnight away is £31.64, which is more than the £19 monthly price of the 100GB plan and over twice the £15 on 10GB.

Where the Europe Zone is included, fair use applies and the guide states it: plans above 50GB, 60GB and 100GB can use up to 25GB, 30GB and 60GB of roaming data in the zone before surcharges start. The passports are the expensive way to cover everything else, and they are quoted excluding VAT: the EE Business Passport is £9.32 a day for 1GB or £46.61 a month for 10GB with unlimited calls and texts, and the World Passport £11.64 a day or £69.93 a month on the same allowances. The monthly Business Passport is 2.45 times the cost of the airtime it is bolted onto. The cheapest route for a regular traveller is the Roam Abroad Passport at £11.90 a month ex VAT, which lets them use the minutes, texts and data they already pay for.

Full out-of-bundle roaming rates are not in this document at all — the guide refers them to a separate Non-Standard Price Guide, which is a second PDF a buyer has to find and open. On a price list that otherwise prints everything, that is the one gap that costs money.

sections.heading: Who measured the best-network claim, and what the complaints data can and cannot tell you
sections.html:
BT Business leads with “Together with EE, the UK's best mobile network for 13 years running”, and unusually for a superlative of that kind the working is published. The claim rests on RootMetrics' UK RootScore reports from H2 2013 to H1 2026; in the first half of 2026 RootMetrics “conducted approximately 609,000 coverage tests around the UK”, including in 16 major cities and driving 21,798 miles on UK roads, and EE serves the substantiation report itself. BT's own footnote then adds the line most advertisers leave out: “The Rootmetrics award is not an endorsement of EE.” Under CAP Code rule 3.34 a comparison with identifiable competitors has to be verifiable and the route to checking it has to be accessible rather than buried, and on this claim it is — the report is one click from the footnote.

The independent measure that is missing is complaints. Ofcom's quarterly telecoms data for Q1 2026, the quarter from January to March, puts pay-monthly mobile complaints at 1 per 100,000 customers for EE, level with Vodafone and giffgaff, against 2 for Three UK and Tesco Mobile, 3 for O2 and iD Mobile and an industry average of 2. Ofcom's own caveat belongs with the figures: where the measurable difference between providers is less than one complaint per 100,000, it considers the results comparable, so EE sitting a point below the average is a good result rather than a decisive one.

Two limits on using it here. The table carries no Q1 2026 figure for BT Mobile at all, so BT's own mobile base is not measured in it. And Ofcom compiles the data to understand dissatisfaction among residential customers — so even EE's figure describes consumer complaints, not business ones. There is no published complaints or satisfaction measure for UK business mobile from any regulator, which is worth saying plainly rather than borrowing the consumer number and hoping it transfers.

sections.heading: The gaps a business buyer should price in before signing
sections.html:
The plan prices in the price guide are not labelled for VAT. The roaming passports and the surcharges are explicitly marked “excl. VAT” and the sales pages label their monthly figures “ex VAT”, so the plan tables are ex-VAT figures too — but the document itself does not say so beside the numbers, and 20% on a £19 plan is £3.80 a month a non-reclaiming buyer would not have budgeted for.

The current offer carries a savings claim with no published basis. “Save up to £617 until 29 October” sits above a single product, the 100GB Business All Rounder SIM at £19.00, and nothing in the terms, footnotes or small print says what the £617 is measured against, whether it includes VAT, or how many connections it assumes. The price guide's own list price for that plan is £24, so the discount on the plan shown is £5 a month and £120 over the term. The ASA's position on “up to” savings claims is that a significant proportion of customers should be able to reach the advertised figure; no proportion is given here.

Version control on the price guide is loose in a way that matters for a document people cite. The copy served at a filename ending v21-2-03-09-2026 prints “V20.01 03.09.2026” in its own footer, and the copy at v21.1-26.08.2026 prints “V20.01 26.08.2026”. The dates are reliable and the filenames are not the same as the version strings inside. Quote the date, not the version number, and note that EE's terms page states “Any changes to the Price Guides take effect from the date of publication” — which means a price can change under a customer the day a new PDF goes up.

One last point about who you are dealing with. BT Business's mobile terms name BT Limited and set out the CPI-linked rise; the plans on sale today are EE Limited's, under EE's small business pay monthly terms, with EE's own price guide and EE's own increase dates. Both companies are inside BT Group and both sit at 1 Braham Street, so this is not a case of a brand badging somebody else's product. It does mean that when a bill or a price rise needs querying, the first question is which of the two companies the line was bought from, and the BT Business pages do not ask it for you.

pros: The full 24-month, 12-month and rolling price tables are published in one regulated document, which is more than most business networks disclose — eight data tiers from £5 to £25 a month ex VAT, with nothing to pay up front

Because all three terms are printed, the cost of commitment is exact rather than a guess: a rolling month is £6 a month dearer than the two-year price and 12 months is £2 dearer, identically on every tier
Unlimited UK and Republic of Ireland calls and texts on the headline tiers, and BT Business states that roaming in its Europe Zone is included at no extra cost on every plan
Stay Connected keeps email, messaging and maps working at 0.5Mb per second after the data allowance runs out, instead of cutting the line off, on every tier from 1GB upwards
5G+ standalone is included on every new price plan sold from 13 May 2026, and Network Boost traffic prioritisation comes with the unlimited plans

The best-network claim is substantiated rather than asserted: RootMetrics ran about 609,000 coverage tests in the first half of 2026 across 16 cities and 21,798 miles of road, and the report is linked from the claim
EE sits at 1 pay-monthly complaint per 100,000 customers in Ofcom's Q1 2026 data, level with the best in the table and below the industry average of 2
The price guide was revised on 22 July, 26 August and 3 September 2026 and not one Business Essential or Business All Rounder SIM-only price moved across the three revisions
BT Group's Business division is a substantial counterparty, with £1,293m of adjusted revenue and £302m of adjusted EBITDA in the three months to 30 June 2026
cons: BT Business publishes no price for any of its four mobile plans on its own site — the SIM-only page is a button reading “Go to EE for SIM-only plans”, so a buyer comparing BT against other networks has to leave BT's site to find out what BT charges

The allowance row of the 24-month price table gives four entries for eight price columns, so which tier carries unlimited minutes and which carries 250 or 500 cannot be read off the document — and three separate revisions of the guide have gone out that way

No pounds figure or worked example for the early termination charge is published anywhere reachable: the price guide's section on it would not return readable text, the BT Price List it points to is closed to automated readers, and the terms describe the charge only as the outstanding monthly charges less unspecified savings

The £1.50 fixed annual rise is worse than the 7.3% an older contract pays on any plan under £20.55 a month — on the £15 10GB SIM it is a 10% increase, so the cheapest customers gained the least from the move away from inflation-linked rises

The annual step is set per cohort and has been growing: the SIM-only plan on sale today steps £2.08 a year against the £1.50 a late-2024 customer pays, taking £19.00 to £23.16 and a 24-month term to £510.08 against the £456.00 implied by the headline

Two brands in one group run two schedules: BT Business's CPI-linked rise applies to purchases on or before 1 December 2024 and lands on 1 April, EE Business's cut-off is 1 September 2024 and its rise lands on 31 March, and neither page mentions the other

Neither BT Business price-change article lists mobile or SIM-only at all — the pounds-and-pence table covers broadband, Cloud Voice, Cloud Work and Digital Voice, so a BT Business mobile customer cannot find their own increase on BT Business's own pages

Stay Connected is excluded from the 0GB, 250MB and 500MB tiers, which is where a customer is most likely to run out, and out-of-allowance data then costs 1.6p per MB — about £16.38 a gigabyte, more than the entire monthly price of the 10GB plan

BT Business says every plan roams in its Europe Zone at no extra cost while EE's price guide charges £2.26 a day in the EU and EEA to anyone without an Inclusive Extra, which Business Essential does not include — so the two documents give different answers and neither resolves it, and a fortnight away on the charged reading is £31.64

The “Save up to £617 until 29 October” claim is published above a single £19 plan with nothing in the terms or small print saying what it is measured against, whether it includes VAT or how many connections it assumes

The plan tables are not labelled for VAT even though the roaming lines in the same document are, and the two most recent price guides both print “V20.01” in a footer that disagrees with their own filenames

A company of 11 or more people falls outside the General Condition C1 protections entirely, including the ban on percentage-based mid-contract rises — and BT's own Digital Voice price-rise table switches from a fixed £1.00 per user to 6% at exactly that headcount
verdict: This is a solid business mobile range sold behind a confusing shop front. The airtime itself stands up: £15 a month ex VAT for 10GB with unlimited calls and texts on a network Ofcom's own complaints table rates at 1 per 100,000 against an average of 2, Stay Connected keeping a phone useful after the allowance runs out, 5G+ on everything sold since 13 May 2026, and a published price guide that prints rolling, 12-month and 24-month prices side by side so the cost of commitment is £6 a month rather than a mystery. Very few business networks disclose that much. What costs the buyer time is the structure around it. BT Business prices none of its four plans on its own site, its own price-change pages do not list mobile, and the figures live in EE's price guide under a different company's name with a rise that lands a day earlier. Price the annual step before you sign, because it is the number that moves most: on the deal advertised today the term ends 21.9% above the opening price, and on anything under £20.55 a month the fixed rise is dearer than the inflation-linked one it replaced. If you are a business of 11 people or more, read the contract rather than relying on the regulator, because the protections stop at ten.

faqs.q: How much is a BT Business mobile SIM a month?
faqs.a: The 24-month Business Essential SIM runs from £5 a month excluding VAT for a 0GB voice SIM to £25 for unlimited data, with 10GB at £15, 50GB at £17 and 100GB at £19. Business All Rounder adds £5 a month on each tier for one Inclusive Extra. Add 20% for VAT if your business cannot reclaim it.

faqs.q: Why do BT Business's mobile pages send me to EE?
faqs.a: BT Business markets the plans and EE prices and contracts them. Its SIM-only page carries a button reading “Go to EE for SIM-only plans” and its plan page says the plans are “powered by EE”. The four plan names on BT's menu are the four priced in the EE Price Guide for Small Business. EE Limited (company 02382161) and BT Limited (02216369) are both BT Group companies registered at 1 Braham Street, London E1 8EE.

faqs.q: Will the price go up during my contract?
faqs.a: Yes, every year. A contract bought from BT Business on or before 1 December 2024 rises by CPI plus 3.9% each 1 April — 7.3% in 2026, from a CPI figure of 3.4% published on 21 January 2026. A newer contract rises by a fixed amount each 31 March instead: £3.00 a month on handset plans and £1.50 on SIM only for late-2024 purchases, and £2.08 on the SIM-only plan EE Business is selling today. Add-ons and out-of-bundle charges rise 5%.

faqs.q: Is the fixed pounds-and-pence rise cheaper than the old CPI one?
faqs.a: Only above about £20.55 a month. At the 7.3% applied in 2026, a £1.50 step is the same as the percentage on a plan of £20.55; above that the fixed step is smaller and below it the fixed step is bigger. On the £15 10GB plan £1.50 is a 10% increase, against 7.3% for an older contract. The fixed step is clearer, which was the point of the rule, but on a cheap SIM it is not smaller.

faqs.q: What happens when I use up my data?
faqs.a: On tiers from 1GB upwards, Stay Connected drops your speed to 0.5Mb per second until the next billing cycle or until you buy a data pass, so email and messaging keep working. It is not included on the 0GB, 250MB or 500MB plans, and it does not apply to unlimited plans. Without it, extra data costs 1.6p per MB in the UK and EU, which is roughly £16.38 a gigabyte.

faqs.q: Does my plan work abroad?
faqs.a: Check this one before you travel, because the group's two documents differ. BT Business says every plan includes roaming in its Europe Zone at no extra cost; EE's price guide says a £2.26 daily charge applies in the EU and EEA without an Inclusive Extra, a roaming add-on or Business Connect, and Business Essential carries no Inclusive Extra. Where the zone is included, fair use is 25GB, 30GB or 60GB on plans above 50GB, 60GB and 100GB. Beyond it, the Business Passport is £9.32 a day or £46.61 a month ex VAT, the World Passport £11.64 or £69.93, and the Roam Abroad Passport £11.90 a month lets you use your existing allowances.

faqs.q: What does it cost to leave early?
faqs.a: No figure is published. Clause 9.1.2 of the EE Pay Monthly terms for Small Business, version 11 dated 16 January 2026, makes the charge “the sum of all outstanding Monthly Charges”, allowing for any recurring discount and “minus any costs we save from you leaving early”, with no percentage attached to that saving. The Early Termination Charges section of the price guide and the BT Price List it refers to could not be read during this check, so ask for the figure in writing before you sign. Note also that 30 days' notice is required to cancel even after the minimum term has ended.

faqs.q: Does Ofcom's price rise ban protect my business?
faqs.a: Only if ten or fewer people work in it. Section 52(6) of the Communications Act 2003 defines a Domestic and Small Business Customer by excluding an undertaking “for which more than ten individuals work”, and Ofcom's guidance says the prohibition on inflation-linked and percentage rises in new contracts “applies to small business customers with 10 or less employees”. BT's own Digital Voice price-rise table switches from a fixed £1.00 per user to 6% at the same point.

faqs.q: Is EE really the UK's best mobile network?
faqs.a: It is the top-ranked network in the RootMetrics UK RootScore reports, which is what the claim rests on — from H2 2013 to H1 2026, with about 609,000 coverage tests in the first half of 2026 across 16 major cities and 21,798 miles of road. BT's own footnote adds that “The Rootmetrics award is not an endorsement of EE”. Ofcom's complaints data points the same way on the consumer side, at 1 per 100,000 against an average of 2, but it measures residential customers only and carries no figure for BT Mobile.

title: Burton Menswear Review: What a Return Costs, and How the Sizing Works
meta_title: Burton Review: Returns From £2.49 and the Suit Fit Rules
meta_description: Burton returns cost £2.49 to £2.99 a parcel out of your refund, and the policy quotes both 21 and 28 days. Delivery, Unlimited, Deliver+ and the fits.

headline.label: What a return costs when it does not fit
headline.value: £2.49 a parcel through InPost or ASDA and £2.99 through Evri or Royal Mail, taken out of the refund, with Burton's own returns page quoting both 21 days and 28 days to send it back (checked 16 October 2026)

intro:
Sending a Burton parcel back costs £2.49 through InPost or ASDA and £2.99 through Evri or Royal Mail, deducted from the refund, and Burton prints all four prices by carrier on its own returns page instead of leaving them to be discovered at checkout. Delivery is free over £60, a year of free delivery on every method costs £14.99, and the suit menu is split into eight ranges and four named fits with a Big & Tall department beside them. Figures checked 16 October 2026 against Burton's own pages.

There is no Burton shop to try the suit on in, and that is worth knowing before you click. boohoo group bought the brand on 8 February 2021 for “£25.2 million in cash”, and its own announcement to the market says the purchase covered “all of the e-commerce and digital assets and associated intellectual property rights, including customer data” plus the inventory, while “the Transaction does not include the HIIT brand and the Brands’ retail stores, concessions or franchises”. Burton has been an online-only name since. There is no branch, no fitting room and no alteration service anywhere in the proposition.

The company you contract with is DBZ Marketplace Online Limited, registered at 49-51 Dale Street, Manchester M1 2HF, and some listings on burton.co.uk are marked “Sold & Delivered by Debenhams” while others belong to concession brands you send returns to directly. The same navigation that sells tweed suits and Oxford shirts also sells duvets, rugs, curtains, garden furniture, home gyms, football boots and electric toothbrushes, because the shopfront runs on the group’s Debenhams platform.

key_facts.label: Who the contract is with
key_facts.value: DBZ Marketplace Online Limited, company 13135555, incorporated 14 January 2021, 49-51 Dale Street, Manchester M1 2HF, SIC 47910 (retail sale via mail order houses or via internet)

key_facts.label: Return charge
key_facts.value: £2.49 by InPost or ASDA, £2.99 by Evri or Royal Mail, deducted from the refund; a “one off return fee from £2.99” is quoted separately

key_facts.label: Return window
key_facts.value: The returns page states 21 days in one place and 28 days in another; the statutory route is 14 days to cancel plus 14 days to send the goods back

key_facts.label: Refund timing
key_facts.value: “Refunds can take up to 14 days from the date your return is posted”, then up to 5 more days to appear on the statement

key_facts.label: Store credit
key_facts.value: Valid for 90 days from the date you receive it

key_facts.label: Free delivery threshold
key_facts.value: Orders over £60

key_facts.label: Delivery subscription
key_facts.value: Unlimited Delivery, £14.99 for 12 months, one-off payment with no automatic renewal, 14 days to cancel

key_facts.label: Deliver+
key_facts.value: “powered by Seel and purchase will be direct with Seel” — Seel, Inc., terms under Delaware law, disputes in San Francisco County or the Northern District of California

key_facts.label: Concession items
key_facts.value: “Please return the item direct to the Concessionaire Brand that supplied the item”, under that brand’s own process

key_facts.label: Brand age
key_facts.value: Montague Burton opened the Cross-Tailoring Company in Chesterfield in 1903 on £100 borrowed from a relative, at 18

key_facts.label: Group reporting
key_facts.value: boohoo group plc, trading as Debenhams Group, reports Youth Brands, Debenhams and Karen Millen — Burton is not a named segment

key_facts.label: Product safety register
key_facts.value: 0 reports for the keyword “burton” on the government’s product safety alerts, reports and recalls service, 16 October 2026

sections.heading: Twenty-one days, twenty-eight days, and which of them is a right
sections.html:
Burton’s returns page answers the fit question twice and the two answers do not agree. One passage reads “From the day you receive your order, you must return your item to us within 21 days to secure your refund or store credit.” Another, on the same page, reads “You’ve got 28 days to send something back to us from the day you receive it.” Both were read verbatim on 16 October 2026. Nothing on the page says which route each sentence belongs to, so a man who opens the box, tries the jacket on a fortnight later and posts it on day 25 cannot tell from the policy whether he is in time.

The 28-day figure is not an act of generosity, and that is the useful half of the finding. Regulation 30(3) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 gives a 14-day cancellation period that “ends at the end of 14 days after the day on which the goods come into the physical possession of” the buyer. Regulation 35(4) then allows a further period to send them: the goods must go back “without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days after the day on which the consumer informs the trader”. Fourteen plus fourteen is twenty-eight, measured from delivery, and no retailer can shorten it. The 21 days looks like Burton’s own commercial window for a refund or store credit; the longer figure is the law.

The charge is lawful too, and for a reason worth stating plainly. Regulation 35(5) puts the direct cost of return on the customer unless the trader agreed to bear it or failed to say the customer would. Burton says it, four times over, with the carrier named against each price: InPost £2.49, ASDA £2.49, Evri £2.99, Royal Mail £2.99. On the refund side the page promises money back “up to 14 days from the date your return is posted”, which starts the clock earlier than regulation 34(5) requires — that provision runs 14 days from the day the trader gets the goods back, or from the day the customer supplies evidence of having sent them, whichever is sooner. Regulation 34(2) also obliges a trader to refund the delivery charge paid, capped at the cheapest common delivery option offered.

One limit sits above all of it. Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 a return fee cannot lawfully be charged on goods that are faulty, of poor quality or not as described, whatever a returns policy says about carriers and parcels. A shirt that arrives with a split seam is not a £2.99 problem for the buyer, and the £2.49 to £2.99 prices only bite on a change of mind or a size that is wrong.

sections.heading: A tape measure built this brand, and the fit guide has none in it
sections.html:
Burton’s own about page is unusually good on where the name came from. “In 1903, Montague Burton was only 18 years old when he borrowed £100 from a relative” “to open the Cross-Tailoring Company in Chesterfield”, selling made-to-measure suits on the slogan “A five guinea suit for 55 shillings”. “By 1929 Burton had four hundred shops, factories, and mills when the company went public.” He was knighted in 1931 “for his efforts in ‘furthering industrial relations and international peace’”, and when he died in 1952 the company was the largest multiple tailor in the world. The post-war demob suit, shirt and tie was the original Full Monty; the firm suited the England side in 1966 and became the F.A. official supplier in 1999.

What replaced the shop’s tape measure is a page called the online suit fit guide, and it contains no measurement at all. Skinny Fit “completely hugs the body”. Slim Fit garments “follow the natural contours of the body”, and “We’d recommend this one for slimmer to medium builds.” Tailored Fit “sits somewhere between a Regular Fit and a Slim Fit”. There is not an inch or a centimetre on it, no instruction on how to measure a chest or an inside leg, and no advice on whether to size up. The separate size guide page at /pages/informational/size-guide returned a client error on four attempts spread across this check, so the tables behind those four fit names could not be read either — that is a failed fetch rather than proof the page is empty, and it is worth saying which of the two it is.

Behind the label there is less law than a shopper would assume. Fibre composition has to be declared on a garment; size does not. The Trading Standards service’s own guide to textile labelling, last reviewed July 2026, deals only with fibre content and non-textile parts of animal origin, and says nothing whatever about sizes or measurements. The only instrument covering size is a voluntary British Standard, BS EN 13402-3:2017, “Size designation of clothes — Part 3: Size labelling based on body measurements and intervals”, published “under the authority of the Standards Policy and Strategy Committee on 31 October 2017” after CEN approved the European text on 26 June 2017, superseding the withdrawn 2013 edition. It “describes a flexible sizing system based on body dimensions” with pictogram examples and body measurement tables for men, women, boys, girls and infants, and it deliberately excludes garment dimensions. Part 1 covers terms, definitions and the body measurement procedure; Part 2 covers primary and secondary dimensions.

The British committee’s own note inside that standard is the part nobody quotes. It records that BSI was obliged to publish the European text but that the UK committee voted against its approval, objected that the title “Size Labelling” is misleading because the document covers designation rather than labelling requirements, and warned that making its content mandatory “would seriously harm the UK clothing industry”. The standard also states that “Compliance with a British Standard cannot confer immunity from legal obligations.” So a chest size printed on a Burton jacket is the retailer’s own arithmetic, not a regulated figure, there is no authority a buyer can appeal to if a 40 fits like a 38, and the £2.49 to £2.99 in the headline is the real cost of finding out.

sections.heading: Deliver+ is sold by a Delaware company and its clock runs for seven days
sections.html:
Alongside the ordinary return route Burton offers a paid add-on, and the returns page is candid about who sells it: “Burton Deliver+ is powered by Seel and purchase will be direct with Seel in accordance with their terms and conditions.” The same page carries Seel’s timings rather than Burton’s. “You must return the product within 7 days from initiating the return request”, and “Seel shall initiate the refund directly to you within 2 days from when Seel approved the return and refund of the product.” That is a third clock on one order, four days shorter than the shortest Burton window and three weeks shorter than the statutory one.

Seel’s own description of the product it sells to retailers explains the commercial logic. Its Return Assurance lets a shopper “Return to Seel for any reason”, Seel pays the refund once it has the parcel, and “merchants keep the full revenue from the original sale”. The price is not a flat fee: it is “Dynamic pricing based on each order’s probability of return”, estimated before the order is placed, so a shopper the model reads as likely to send things back is quoted more for the cover than one it reads as unlikely to. On a product where fit failure is the normal outcome rather than the exception, that is an unusual thing to be priced on.

Who the buyer is dealing with matters as much as the price. Seel’s terms of service name “Seel, Inc.”, are “governed and interpreted by and under the laws of the State of Delaware”, and send court disputes to “state courts located in San Francisco County, California” or “federal courts located in the Northern District of California”. A British customer who buys Deliver+ on a Manchester-registered company’s website has bought an American contract. Burton’s own Deliver+ page at /pages/deliver-plus could not be read on any attempt during this check, so the price range and the exact scope of the UK version are unconfirmed, and anyone considering it should read what Seel sends them before paying — particularly since the 2013 Regulations already give a free right to change their mind, and the Consumer Rights Act already covers a faulty garment at no cost.

sections.heading: Free over £60, or £14.99 for a year of it
sections.html:
The banner across burton.co.uk reads “Free Delivery On Orders Over £60”, which is a high threshold for shirts and a low one for a suit. Under it sits Unlimited Delivery, and that page does read cleanly: “For only £14.99 a year”, a one-off payment with no automatic charge at the end of the term, “you will have 12 months from the date of purchase” to use “free delivery across all of our delivery methods for a whole year”. The membership also carries next-day delivery, VIP member days, exclusive offers and savings that carry across the group’s other sites. There is a 14-day cancellation period, cancellation is by email, and an existing member cannot buy a second year until the current one runs out. Express Delivery “may take a little longer” to the Highlands and Islands and “is not available in the Channel Islands”.

The sum a reader actually wants — how many paid deliveries £14.99 replaces — cannot be done from Burton’s published figures, because the delivery page at /pages/informational/delivery returned a client error on four separate attempts across this check while the returns and Unlimited Delivery pages on the same host loaded normally. No individual delivery price is therefore quotable here. The Frequently Asked Questions page refused in the same way. What can be said is that the £60 free-delivery threshold and the £14.99 membership are the only two delivery figures Burton puts in front of a shopper who has not yet reached the basket.

Two smaller things sit on that page and are worth a sentence each. The family of brands the membership spans is given as Debenhams, Wallis, Oasis, Dorothy Perkins and Coast — a list that does not include Burton, the site selling the membership. And the address for cancelling it is customerservices@burton.com, while the returns page gives customerservices@burton.co.uk. Neither is likely to lose a customer their money, but a reader checking one page against the other will notice both.

sections.heading: A menswear name sitting on a department store's paperwork
sections.html:
Read the returns policy from the top and it becomes obvious it was not written for a menswear brand. Homeware such as “bedlinen, mattresses, pillows, and camping equipment” must come back “unused and in their original unopened packaging”. Vitamins, medicines and toiletries are excluded once a hygiene seal is broken, along with cosmetics, pierced jewellery, swimwear and lingerie. Installed large appliances and furniture not in saleable condition cannot be returned at all, and where Burton does collect “selected large appliances” a further £50 comes out of the refund. None of that is wrong — the site does sell duvets and home gyms — but a man buying a wedding suit is reading a document about mattresses.

One clause is stranger than the rest. The policy states that items bought in store “can only be returned direct to the store”. Burton has no stores: the 2021 announcement excluded “the Brands’ retail stores, concessions or franchises” by name, and nothing on the site offers a branch finder. The sentence is a department store’s, inherited whole.

The seller behind the badge takes a little work to pin down. Non-concession stock is labelled “Sold & Delivered by Debenhams” even on burton.co.uk, concession stock carries “Sold & Delivered By” a partner brand with the instruction to “return the item direct to the Concessionaire Brand that supplied the item” using that brand’s own process, and the contract itself is “under a contract with DBZ Marketplace Online Limited”. Companies House records that company as 13135555, active, incorporated 14 January 2021 at 49-51 Dale Street, Manchester M1 2HF, under SIC 47910, and shows it trading as Acraman 550 Limited for eleven days, then Debenhams.com Online Limited from 25 January 2021, then Debenhams Brands Limited from 30 March 2023, before taking its present name on 26 November 2024. Its accounts are filed under an audit exemption with a parent-company guarantee, last made up to 28 February 2025.

What could not be read is the paperwork a careful buyer would want next. The terms and conditions page, the concessionaire brand list and the size guide all returned client errors on repeated attempts from a host that was serving its returns page at the same moment, so the governing law, any named dispute-resolution body and the full concession roster are unverified here rather than absent. A reader who wants them should open those four links before ordering and ask customer services for the ones that do not load.

sections.heading: Where the growth sits inside the group, and why Burton is invisible in it
sections.html:
Burton’s owner is boohoo group plc, which trades as Debenhams Group and sits on the market under the ticker DEBS. Its half-year results for the six months to 31 August 2025, announced on 27 November 2025 and filed on the Financial Conduct Authority’s National Storage Mechanism, give the shape of the business the Burton site belongs to. “Revenue was £296.9m, down 23%”. “Gross margin remained broadly stable at 52.9%”, 60 basis points lower. “Adjusted EBITDA increased to £20.0m (H125: £19.0m)”. The loss before tax from continuing operations came in at £2.5m against £130.0m a year earlier, and “Net debt improved to £111.1m (H125: £143.1m)”.

The split inside those figures is the interesting part. The Debenhams brand grew gross merchandise value “20% to £318.8m” on segment revenue of £98.3m, with adjusted EBITDA up 50% at a margin of about 15%, while “Youth Brands GMV decreased 41% to £258.0m” on revenue of £172.4m. Marketplace stock accounted for 31.6% of gross merchandise value before returns. The reported segments are Youth Brands, Debenhams and Karen Millen, and Burton is in none of them by name — so there is no published revenue, order count or customer number for Burton itself, from the group or from anywhere else.

Set that against what the brand cost. The 8 February 2021 announcement priced Burton, Dorothy Perkins and Wallis together at £25.2m and recorded that in the year to 29 August 2020 the three brands had “unaudited revenues of approximately £427.8 million across all channels and an unaudited EBITDA loss of £14.3 million”, of which “The ongoing businesses for the Brands generated unaudited revenues of approximately £178.8 million”. Buying three national names and their customer data for less than a fifth of one year’s continuing revenue tells you what the high street was worth in February 2021, and it explains why the brand now lives on somebody else’s platform. The group’s annual results for the year to 28 February 2026 could not be read from a primary source during this check, because its investor site refuses automated access, so every figure above is the half-year to 31 August 2025 and should be read with that date attached.

sections.heading: The supply-chain statement a Burton shopper is sent to stops in 2022
sections.html:
The footer of every page on burton.co.uk carries a link marked Modern Slavery Statement, and it points off the site to a boohoo group PDF. That document “covers the FY22 reporting period from 1 March 2021 until 28 February 2022” and carries the date 31.08.2022 against a line headed Board Representative with no name or title beside it. Section 54 of the Modern Slavery Act 2015 expects a statement for each financial year, and four financial years have closed since this one. Burton is not mentioned anywhere in it.

Taken on its own terms the statement is numerate, which makes the age of it the only real complaint. It “covers our own operations and product supply chains for all of our group brands” across 13 brands, and reports 1,286 tier 1 factories as at 31 July 2022 across 29 sourcing countries — China 487, Turkey 228, India 157, the UK 80, Pakistan 78 and Bangladesh 71. The group accepts audits from 34 audit bodies provided they are within 12 months, says 95% of tier 1 factories are rated excellent, good or fair, and records 60% of audits graded critical as evidenced corrected. It gives 5,901 people employed directly at 31 January 2022 and 2,254 cotton farmers in a Pakistan programme. A menswear buyer gets none of it broken out: the only menswear-adjacent brand named is boohooMAN.

The public safety record is cleaner and shorter. A keyword search for “burton” on the government’s product safety alerts, reports and recalls service returned 0 reports on 16 October 2026, with the service reporting “There are no matching results.” That is an absence rather than an endorsement, and it is the only independent check available: there is no rated customer-satisfaction survey for clothing retailers from Which?, whose best-and-worst-shops guides cover baby shops, technology and appliances, and furniture, homeware and DIY, and nothing else.

pros: All four return prices are published by carrier on one page rather than appearing at checkout: £2.49 by InPost, £2.49 by ASDA, £2.99 by Evri and £2.99 by Royal Mail
Refunds are promised “up to 14 days from the date your return is posted”, which starts the clock earlier than regulation 34(5) of the 2013 Regulations requires
The 28-day figure on the returns page matches the 14 days to cancel plus 14 days to return that the law already gives, so the longer window is a right and not a concession
Free delivery over £60, and £14.99 buys 12 months of free delivery on every method as a one-off payment with no automatic renewal and 14 days to cancel
Four suit fits are each described in writing, across eight suit ranges, with a Big & Tall department beside them
Concession stock is labelled and the policy says plainly which seller a return goes back to
The brand’s own history page is detailed and dated, from the 1903 Chesterfield shop to four hundred shops by 1929 and the F.A. supply deal in 1999
A keyword search for burton on the government’s product safety recall service returned 0 reports on 16 October 2026
cons: The returns page gives two different windows for the same thing — “within 21 days to secure your refund or store credit” in one passage and “You’ve got 28 days to send something back to us” in another — so a shopper posting on day 25 cannot tell from the page whether a refund is still available

Two different return fees appear for Burton’s own stock: £2.49 and £2.99 by named carrier in one place, and “a one off return fee from £2.99” in another, with the word “from” never resolved into a ceiling
Three clocks run on one order — 21 or 28 days on the Burton route and 7 days on the Deliver+ route — and nothing on the page says which applies to an order carrying both

Deliver+ is bought from Seel, Inc., whose terms are “governed and interpreted by and under the laws of the State of Delaware” with disputes sent to California, so a UK shopper’s add-on sits outside UK jurisdiction and outside any UK redress scheme

Deliver+ is priced by “Dynamic pricing based on each order’s probability of return”, which means the shoppers most likely to need it are quoted most for it, and much of what it buys is already free under the 2013 Regulations and the Consumer Rights Act

The returns policy a menswear shopper reads is a department store’s: it governs mattresses, pillows, camping equipment, vitamins, medicines and installed large appliances, and deducts a further £50 from the refund for collecting one
The same policy says items bought in store “can only be returned direct to the store”, on a brand whose retail stores were explicitly excluded from the 2021 purchase and do not exist

The online suit fit guide carries no measurement in inches or centimetres and no instruction on how to measure — one fit “completely hugs the body” and another is “for slimmer to medium builds” — which is thin guidance on the one thing that decides whether the £2.99 return charge gets paid

The delivery page, the size guide, the terms and conditions, the Frequently Asked Questions and the concession brand list all returned client errors on repeated attempts, so the individual delivery prices, the size tables, the governing law and any dispute-resolution body could not be read at all
The Modern Slavery Statement linked from the footer covers 1 March 2021 to 28 February 2022, is dated 31 August 2022, names no signatory beyond “Board Representative”, and does not mention Burton

No product price could be read from burton.co.uk on any fetch, including the essential suits category page, so nothing on the site can be compared with another menswear retailer from published figures
The about page gives two founding dates: “We’ve been dressing men since 1904” in one sentence and Montague Burton opening his first shop “In 1903” in another
Burton is not a reported segment of its owner, which reports Youth Brands, Debenhams and Karen Millen, so no revenue, order count or customer number exists for Burton itself

The Unlimited Delivery page lists the brands the £14.99 membership spans as Debenhams, Wallis, Oasis, Dorothy Perkins and Coast — not Burton, the site selling it — and gives a customer service address ending .com where the returns page gives .co.uk

There is no independent customer-satisfaction score for any menswear retailer to set against any of this, because Which? publishes rated best-and-worst-shops surveys for baby shops, technology and furniture and none for clothing
verdict: Burton is a 123-year-old tailoring name sold as an online department store, and it is honest about the one number that matters most: £2.49 to £2.99 a parcel to send a suit back, printed by carrier before you buy. The 28 days on the same page is the law’s 14 plus 14, not a favour, and a faulty garment costs nothing to return whatever the policy says. Against that, the paperwork is a department store’s rather than a tailor’s — two return windows, a store-returns clause on a brand with no stores, a fit guide with no measurements and a Delaware add-on on a seven-day clock. Buy the suit on the strength of the range and the £60 free-delivery line, order two sizes if the fit matters, and send the wrong one back inside 21 days to stay clear of the argument.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to return something to Burton?
faqs.a: Burton deducts the return cost from your refund and publishes it by carrier: £2.49 through InPost, £2.49 through ASDA, £2.99 through Evri and £2.99 through Royal Mail. A separate passage on the same page describes “a one off return fee from £2.99”, and the word “from” is not resolved into a maximum anywhere. Start the return in the returns portal and print the label at home. Collection is only offered on selected large appliances, and that costs a further £50 out of the refund.

faqs.q: How long have I got to send a Burton order back — 21 days or 28?
faqs.a: Burton’s returns page states both, in different passages, and does not say which route each belongs to. The safe reading is that 21 days is Burton’s own window for a refund or store credit and 28 days reflects the statutory route, because regulation 30(3) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 gives you 14 days from taking physical possession to cancel, and regulation 35(4) then gives you a further 14 days to send the goods back. If you want to be certain of a refund without an argument, post it inside 21 days.

faqs.q: Can Burton charge me £2.99 for returning something faulty?
faqs.a: No. Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 a return fee cannot lawfully be charged on goods that are faulty, of poor quality or not as described, whatever a returns policy says about carriers and parcel prices. The £2.49 to £2.99 charge applies to a change of mind or a size that does not fit. If a seam has gone or the item is not what was advertised, say so when you start the return and ask for the postage back as well.

faqs.q: Is Burton Unlimited Delivery worth £14.99?
faqs.a: It is a one-off £14.99 for 12 months from the date of purchase, it does not renew automatically, it covers “free delivery across all of our delivery methods for a whole year” including next day, and it carries member days and offers that work across the group’s other sites. Whether it pays for itself cannot be worked out from Burton’s published figures, because the delivery page would not load on four attempts during this check and no individual delivery price is quotable. Delivery is free over £60 without it, so the membership is worth most to someone buying shirts one at a time.

faqs.q: What is Burton Deliver+, and do I need it?
faqs.a: It is a paid add-on at checkout, and Burton’s own page says it is “powered by Seel and purchase will be direct with Seel”. Seel describes the product as returns cover priced by “Dynamic pricing based on each order’s probability of return”, and the terms on Burton’s page give you 7 days to return after starting a request, with a refund within 2 days of approval. The contract is with Seel, Inc. under Delaware law, with disputes heard in California. Weigh it against the fact that the 2013 Regulations already give you 28 days to change your mind and the Consumer Rights Act already covers a faulty item at no cost.

faqs.q: Are there any Burton shops left?
faqs.a: No. boohoo group bought the brand on 8 February 2021 for £25.2 million in cash, and its announcement to the market says the deal covered the e-commerce and digital assets, the intellectual property and the inventory but “does not include the HIIT brand and the Brands’ retail stores, concessions or franchises”. There is no branch, no fitting room and no alteration service. The returns policy still carries a clause saying items bought in store can only be returned to the store, which is inherited from the Debenhams document it is built on.

faqs.q: Who am I actually buying from on burton.co.uk?
faqs.a: The returns page states that goods are supplied “under a contract with DBZ Marketplace Online Limited” — company 13135555, incorporated 14 January 2021 and registered at 49-51 Dale Street, Manchester M1 2HF. Non-concession stock is labelled “Sold & Delivered by Debenhams” even on the Burton site, and concession items are sold by a partner brand you return to directly under its own process. The terms and conditions page would not load during this check, so the governing law clause and any named dispute-resolution scheme could not be confirmed.

title: BusinessMobiles.com Review: Business Contracts Across EE, O2, Vodafone and Three
meta_title: BusinessMobiles.com Review: All Four Networks, One Dealer
meta_description: An independent West London dealer selling EE, O2, Vodafone and Three business contracts since 1999. Prices, price rises, contract terms and the catches.
intro:
BusinessMobiles.com is a West London dealer that has been selling mobile contracts to UK companies since 1999 and now says it manages more than 20,000 business mobile lines. What makes it worth a look is the range: it sells EE, O2, Vodafone and Three from one order desk, which very few independents do, and it will quote a sole trader on a single line as readily as a company with fifty. Headline prices at the time of writing start at £1 a month for a business SIM, £16 a month for a Samsung handset deal, £14 a month for mobile broadband and £22 a month for a business laptop, with free next-working-day delivery to most of the UK and a sales line on 0800 999 2999 open 8.30am to 5.30pm on weekdays.

One number needs reading carefully before you compare anything. Every price on the site excludes VAT, and the site says so plainly: "Our prices always exclude VAT." A £16 business tariff is £19.20 leaving the bank account, so setting it against a £19 consumer deal is not the like-for-like comparison it looks like. If the business is VAT registered it reclaims the difference and the ex-VAT figure is the real one; if it is not, the inclusive price is what it pays.

The company is an official partner of all four networks rather than a reseller of one, it won EE's 2025 Business Growth Award for Partners, and it offers an early upgrade from six months into a contract on selected networks — a good deal earlier than most dealers will touch a handset. Contracts run 12, 24 or 36 months.
