sections.heading: The name took three goes to arrive at
sections.html:
The trading story on the About page and the registry record agree on the year and differ on the detail, which is worth knowing if you are checking who you are dealing with. Companies House holds the firm as BUSINESSMOBILES.COM LTD, company number 03772025, incorporated on 17 May 1999 and active, at Suite 301, Boundary House, Boston Road, Hanwell, London W7 2QE, under SIC code 61200 — wireless telecommunications activities. Its last accounts were made up to 31 December 2024, the next are due by 30 September 2026, and the most recent confirmation statement was dated 16 May 2026.

The name changed three times before it settled. The company was incorporated as FAST FONES DIRECT LTD, became 31E CELLULAR OPERATIONS LIMITED on 24 May 2000, then 31E CELLULAR LIMITED on 13 July 2000, and finally took its present name on 17 January 2007. The About page tells the same story a year early — "In 2006, we became BusinessMobiles.com" — which is the sort of small drift that creeps into copy nobody has re-read for a while. The 1999 founding date, which is the part that matters, checks out exactly.

sections.heading: Buying as a business moves you outside the consumer rulebook
sections.html:
This is the fact that separates a business mobile purchase from the one a shopper makes, and almost nothing on any dealer's site explains it. The 14-day cancellation right people associate with buying online is a consumer right under the distance selling rules, and it does not follow a company that buys in its own name. Neither does the Consumer Rights Act 2015, whose 30-day short-term right to reject faulty goods is written for an individual acting for purposes wholly or mainly outside a trade or business. A limited company or a partnership buying handsets sits outside both.

Read that way, the return window in BusinessMobiles.com's own terms is a commercial concession rather than a legal minimum. The terms give "a 7-day right of return. The 7 days commencing on the date your order is activated or despatched, whichever is earlier". Seven days is half the consumer period and the clock can start at despatch rather than delivery, so a handset that spends two days in transit has five days left on arrival. That is still seven days more than the law obliges a business seller to give, and it is worth setting against dealers who give none.

Two charges sit alongside it. The customer pays the cost of return carriage, and an Incomplete Restocking Charge of £250 applies where a handset comes back without all of its parts. Keep the box, the cable and the paperwork.

sections.heading: Twelve, 24 or 36 months — and the longest one has a rule attached
sections.html:
The FAQ page puts contract length at "12, 24 or 36 months". The 12-month option is not a courtesy: Ofcom requires providers to offer at least one 12-month contract for each service, and that requirement covers business customers of any size. The 36-month option is the one that needs a question asked, because Ofcom's General Conditions cap the length of most small-business contracts at two years.

Condition C1.11 is explicit: "Regulated Providers shall not include a term in any contract, other than an Instalment Contract for a Physical Connection, with a Relevant Customer, that stipulates a Commitment Period of more than 24 months in duration." A Relevant Customer for that purpose covers consumers, microenterprise and small enterprise customers and not-for-profit organisations, unless the business has expressly agreed otherwise. So a 36-month term is available to larger companies, and to a small one only where it has knowingly signed away the cap. Nothing on the site says which of those applies to a given quote, and it is a fair thing to ask on the phone before you sign.

The same conditions give small business customers end-of-contract notifications and annual best-tariff information, so a company that stays put after its minimum term should be told, in writing, what it is paying and what it could pay instead.

sections.heading: The annual rise is pounds and pence on some tariffs and a percentage on others
sections.html:
Ofcom's statement of 19 July 2024 banned inflation-linked mid-contract increases, and from 17 January 2025 any rise written into a new contract has to be expressed in pounds and pence. The scope is wider than most coverage suggests. The statement applies the rules to services "purchased by residential customers, Microenterprise or Small Enterprise Customers and Not-For-Profit Customers" — small businesses are inside the protection, not outside it.

The catch is that a business tariff is not automatically a small-business tariff, and the networks this dealer sells are running several regimes at once. EE Business raises prices from 31 March each year: contracts taken between 2 September and 18 November 2024 go up by £3.00 a month across every plan type, while contracts from 19 November 2024 onwards go up by £3.00 on handset plans and £1.50 on SIM-only, tablet, laptop, watch and router plans. Anything signed before 2 September 2024 is still on the old CPI plus 3.9% formula.

Three Business steps its increase by tariff size each April — "Plans with an original Monthly Charge of £9.99 or less will increase by £0.50 per month. Plans from £10 to £20 will increase by £0.75 per month. Plans from £20.01 will increase by £1.50 per month" — but its Adapt and Dynamic plans are the exception and rise by 4.5% each April instead. Business broadband goes up £1.60 a month excluding VAT.

Vodafone Business is the clearest illustration that the pounds-and-pence rule has not reached every business bill. Contracts entered on or after 9 December 2020 are rising from 1 April 2026 by CPI of 3.4% plus 3.9%, a combined 7.3% — £1.61 a month on a £22 plan and £2.92 on a £40 one. Older contracts move with RPI at 4.2%, published on 21 January 2026. Vodafone's SOHO customers on contracts from 2 July 2024 get a fixed £1.50 excluding VAT instead, and contracts from 12 November 2025 rise by between £2.08 and £3.00. O2's business price page is built around RPI adjustments and offers a calculator rather than a published schedule; its figures load through JavaScript and could not be read directly, so the amount on an O2 business tariff needs confirming with the dealer.

The arithmetic is worth doing before you sign rather than after. Take the EE Business iPhone 17 deal the site lists at £33.00 a month excluding VAT on a 24-month term, bought in September. It runs seven months at £33.00, twelve at £36.00 and five at £39.00 — £858 across the term, against £792 if you simply multiply the headline by 24. That is £66 the advertised figure does not show, and £1,029.60 once VAT is added to what actually leaves the account.

sections.heading: One phone per employee, and the contract has to be in the company's name
sections.html:
The FAQ says a business contract "is also tax deductible", which is true and slightly undersells the mechanism. HMRC's guidance exempts a mobile phone provided to an employee from tax and from reporting entirely, but on conditions. The exemption applies where "you provide your employee with only one mobile phone or SIM card" and "the phone contract is between you and the supplier". A second handset for the same employee falls outside it, and so does a phone bought on the employee's own account and reimbursed. The exemption also does not apply where the phone comes through a salary sacrifice arrangement, which has to be reported.

That is the practical reason a company buys through a business channel rather than picking up a consumer deal in a shop. The contract has to be in the company's name for the exemption to work, and a dealer selling business tariffs puts it there as a matter of course. It is a genuine advantage of the route, and neither the FAQ nor any network page spells it out.

sections.heading: Who adjudicates a dispute depends on how many people you employ
sections.html:
Ofcom approves exactly two dispute schemes for telecoms: CISAS, the Communication and Internet Services Adjudication Scheme, and the Communications Ombudsman. Of the four networks on this site, O2, Vodafone and Three belong to CISAS while EE belongs to the Communications Ombudsman. Two companies buying the same kind of contract from the same dealer on the same day can end up in front of different adjudicators, depending only on which network they chose.

Eligibility is narrower than most buyers expect. Ofcom's own wording admits a residential customer, "a small business (up to 10 employees)" or a not-for-profit with up to ten working individuals, volunteers excluded. An eleven-person firm has no free adjudicator at all and is left with the courts. A complaint can be taken to the scheme once "it has been at least six weeks since you made the initial complaint", or straight away on a deadlock letter, which stays usable for 12 months.

None of that reaches the dealer itself. BusinessMobiles.com's terms route a dispute through negotiation, then mediation with LawBite, then arbitration if it is unresolved within 60 days. That is a private contractual ladder rather than an Ofcom-approved scheme, so a disagreement about what was promised at the point of sale — rather than about the network service — sits outside both CISAS and the Ombudsman. The terms also exclude liability for "loss of income, profit, business, data, contracts, goodwill or savings", while keeping responsibility for death or personal injury caused by negligence and for fraud.

sections.heading: Where the site's own numbers stop agreeing with each other
sections.html:
The savings claims are the weakest part of the site. The EE page leads on "Save 37% on Phone/SIM" and "over 30% off"; the Three page offers "Save over 20% on network prices". Neither page shows what the 37% or the 20% is measured against, over what term, or on which tariff. The CAP Code sets a clear standard for this: rule 3.34 requires that comparisons with identifiable competitors "objectively compare one or more material, relevant, verifiable and representative feature of those products", and CAP's guidance asks advertisers to signpost how a reader can check. The ASA has upheld against telecoms comparison claims on exactly that ground before, including Vodafone's "The UK's Best Network" in 2021, where the verification detail was there but out of reach. A dealer buying at trade prices very probably can beat a network's list price; publishing the comparison would make the claim worth more, not less.

Two of the company's own figures also disagree. The home page says 27 years of experience; the EE and Three pages both say 26 Years in Business. Counting from May 1999, 27 is right and the network pages are a year behind. The network awards quoted are also ageing: Three's Ookla "Fastest 5G Network" run is cited as five awards ending H1 2023, which is three years old, and predates the merger of Vodafone UK and Three UK.

There is no independent rating for a mobile dealer to fall back on. Ofcom's quarterly complaints data measures networks rather than the shops that sell them, there is no Defaqto equivalent for this trade, and the review score shown on the site is collected on the company's own behalf. The honest position is that the networks behind the contract are measured and the dealer in front of it is not.

pros: Sells all four UK networks — EE, O2, Vodafone and Three — from one order desk, which few independents do
No minimum number of lines: sole traders are quoted as readily as larger companies
Trading since 17 May 1999 under company 03772025, with a registry record that matches the founding date claimed
Early upgrade available from six months into a contract on selected networks, well ahead of the 10 to 40 day end-of-contract notification Ofcom requires
A 7-day right of return offered where the law gives a business buyer none
Prices start at £1 a month for a business SIM and £16 for a handset deal, with free next-working-day delivery to most of the UK
Named an EE Business Growth Award for Partners winner in 2025
cons: Savings claims of 37% on EE and over 20% on Three are published with nothing showing the comparison basis, which is the standard CAP Code rule 3.34 sets
The 7-day return window runs from activation or despatch rather than delivery, and a £250 Incomplete Restocking Charge applies if a handset comes back without all its parts
Disputes with the dealer go to LawBite mediation and then arbitration after 60 days, not to an Ofcom-approved scheme — and no free adjudicator exists at all for a business with more than 10 employees
A 36-month contract is offered without explaining that Ofcom's Condition C1.11 caps most small-business commitments at 24 months unless the customer expressly agrees otherwise
Annual price rises are not shown on the deal pages, and they vary sharply by network: £3.00 a month on an EE handset plan against 7.3% on many Vodafone business contracts from 1 April 2026
The company's own pages give its age as both 26 and 27 years, and the Three awards quoted were last won in H1 2023
verdict: A long-established West London dealer with a real advantage: it quotes all four networks, it takes single-line customers, and it puts the contract in the company's name, which is what HMRC's one-phone-per-employee exemption actually requires. The prices are ex-VAT and the advertised monthly figure is not the whole term — an EE Business plan at £33 a month costs £858 over 24 months once the 31 March increases land, not £792. Ring 0800 999 2999 and ask three things before signing: what the annual increase is in pounds for the tariff you are being quoted, whether the term offered is 12, 24 or 36 months and why, and which network's dispute scheme you would be using. The answers are all knowable and none of them are on the website.

faqs.q: Do the prices include VAT?
faqs.a: No. The site states that its prices always exclude VAT, so a £16 tariff is £19.20 including VAT at 20%. A VAT-registered business reclaims that; one below the registration threshold pays it. Comparing a business price against a consumer price without adding VAT first is not a like-for-like comparison.

faqs.q: Can a sole trader buy from BusinessMobiles.com?
faqs.a: Yes. Asked whether there is a minimum number of lines, the FAQ answers: "No. We are as passionate about serving our sole traders as we are about serving our corporates." Contracts run 12, 24 or 36 months.

faqs.q: What happens if the handset is faulty or I change my mind?
faqs.a: The terms give a 7-day right of return running from activation or despatch, whichever is earlier, with the customer paying return carriage and a £250 Incomplete Restocking Charge if parts are missing. The 14-day distance selling right and the Consumer Rights Act 2015 both apply to consumers rather than to a company buying in its own name, so this window is a commercial concession and not a statutory minimum.

faqs.q: Will my monthly price go up during the contract?
faqs.a: Almost certainly, and by an amount that depends on the network. EE Business raises prices each 31 March by £3.00 on handset plans and £1.50 on SIM-only and device plans taken from 19 November 2024. Three steps its April increase from £0.50 to £1.50 by tariff size, except Adapt and Dynamic plans which rise 4.5%. Many Vodafone business contracts rise by CPI plus 3.9% — 7.3% from 1 April 2026. Ask for the figure in pounds before signing.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if something goes wrong?
faqs.a: For a problem with the mobile service, the route runs through the network: EE is a member of the Communications Ombudsman, while O2, Vodafone and Three all belong to CISAS. You can escalate after six weeks, or immediately with a deadlock letter, if you are a business with up to 10 employees. For a dispute with the dealer itself, its terms use negotiation, then LawBite mediation, then arbitration after 60 days.

title: Buy Car Parts Vehicle Parts
meta_title: Buy Car Parts: a German Shop With a .co.uk Address
meta_description: Buycarparts.co.uk lists five million parts and charges £8.45 delivery. The seller is AUTODOC SE in Berlin, there is no UK company and no phone number.

headline.label: Who you actually buy from
headline.value: AUTODOC SE of Berlin, register HRB 247677 B — and no UK company at all

disclosure: we earn a commission if you buy through the link on this page. It costs you nothing. Everything below about the company structure, the postage costs and the core charge is reported as the site publishes it, including the parts that may put you off.
intro:
Buycarparts.co.uk is a big, properly built catalogue. It claims “over 5,000,000 car parts”, it finds them from your registration number or by make, model and engine, and prices are shown inclusive of 20% VAT with delivery at £8.45, free above £130. For common service items that is a competitive way to shop.

The thing to understand before you order is who is on the other end. The site owner is Partex Global GmbH of Gewerbering 38a, Röttenbach, Germany, registered at the District Court of Fürth under HRB 21524. The actual seller is a different German company again: AUTODOC SE of Josef-Orlopp-Straße 55, Berlin, named on the site as “the vendor of the products and exclusive contracting partner for sales contacts”.

No UK company is named anywhere — no Companies House number, no UK address, and no telephone number on the contact page. The .co.uk domain and the sterling prices are the only British things about it.

sections.heading: What delivery costs, and how long it takes
sections.html:
The postage table is short and clear, which is more than many rivals manage:

Destination or order valueCharge
UK orders under £130£8.45
UK orders over £130Free, excluding bulky items, tyres and core parts
Tyres£1.99, charged separately from the order total
Isle of Man, Jersey or Guernsey£15.00

Read the free-delivery line twice. It “excludes bulky items, tyres, or core parts”, so a £200 order containing an exchange part will still carry postage. Tyre delivery is quoted at £1.99 with the note “Tyre price not included in total order amount”, which means tyres do not count towards the £130 either.

In-stock items are “shipped within 1-2 days” of payment, with another one to two days if the part sits in a supplier’s warehouse rather than theirs. Weekend orders wait for Monday, because, as the site puts it, “delivery companies do not work on weekends”. The only carrier named is EVRI.

Three things we looked for and could not find: no order cut-off time, no next-day or Saturday option, and no mention of Northern Ireland or the Scottish Highlands at all — neither as a surcharge nor as an exclusion. If you are in either, ask before ordering rather than assuming the £8.45 applies.

So the realistic timeline for a UK buyer is two to four working days, with no way to pay for speed. For a brake job booked in for Saturday morning, that is a planning risk rather than a bargain.

sections.heading: Returns: a 14-day right, and you pay the postage
sections.html:
The headline is good: “You have the right to withdraw from this contract within 14 days without giving any reason.” No excuses required, no restocking fee published anywhere, and no clause banning the return of electrical parts — two exclusions that are common in this trade and absent here.

The cost side is less comfortable. “You will have to bear the direct cost of returning the goods”, and the notice goes to AUTODOC SE in Berlin. For a small filter that is a stamp. For a brake disc it is international parcel postage, paid by you, to decide you did not want it.

For anything that cannot go in the post, the site estimates the cost as “the shipping costs paid as part of the order plus 10 EUR”. That is a euro figure on a sterling website, which tells you how much of this policy is a straight translation of the German original.

Two conditions to note before you unwrap anything. You are “liable for any diminished value of the goods” if you handle them beyond checking how they work, and “if the original package will be damaged, you may have to recompense the value deduction”. Open the box carefully and keep it.

On fitted parts there is no outright ban, but there is a warning: the policy notes case law to the effect that installing vehicle parts counts as going beyond inspection. In plain terms, bolt it on and you may get back less than you paid. Test-fit without fluids and without torquing anything down if you can.

There is no right of withdrawal on goods “that are non-prefabricated” — made or configured to your order — and damaged hazardous items such as leaking batteries cannot be returned at all.

One gap we should flag because it matters: we could not find any warranty or guarantee length published on the returns, exchange or product pages we read. Plenty of parts carry a manufacturer’s warranty, but the shop states no period of its own.

sections.heading: The core charge, explained properly
sections.html:
If you buy a reconditioned part — a starter motor, alternator, steering rack, turbo — you will meet a core charge, and this is the part of the site worth reading before you spend. The example the site publishes is £25.39 including 20% VAT, added on top of the part price as a deposit on your old unit.

How it works, in their words and in order:

  • The charge “will be fully refunded after your old part has arrived at our warehouse” — in Berlin.
  • You have 12 months from purchase to send the old part back. Miss it and the deposit is kept.
  • Once your parcel arrives, they report the result of the examination within six to eight weeks.
  • If the old unit fails examination, the charge is not refunded. You then have two months to ask for it back, at their cost, after which it is scrapped.

Add that up and the worst case is this: you pay the deposit today, post a heavy part to Germany at your own expense, wait up to two months for a verdict, and lose the deposit anyway if your old unit is judged unusable. Core exchange is normal across the industry; the six-to-eight-week examination window and the self-funded international postage are the specific terms here, and they are why the free-delivery threshold excludes core parts.

Practical advice: photograph the old unit before you box it, send it tracked, and keep the receipt until the refund lands.

sections.heading: Finding the right part, and paying for it
sections.html:
The fitment tool is the strongest part of the site. You can search by registration number — “Find car parts by registration number” — or step through maker, model and engine. There is no VIN lookup, which is the one method that resolves mid-year specification changes, so for anything where the manufacturer changed supplier mid-production, check the dimensions on the listing against the part you are removing.

And do check them, because the site publishes no statement about who is responsible for choosing the right part. We looked. Some rivals say plainly that the customer carries that risk; this one says nothing either way, which is not the same as saying you are covered.

Two real listings, seen on 8 October 2026, to give you the pricing level:

  • MANN-FILTER CU 1719 pollen filter, 224 × 189 × 25 mm — £13.38
  • MANNOL Defender 10W-40, 5 litres — £30.48, or £6.10 a litre, though it was marked out of stock when we looked

Both are inclusive of 20% VAT and exclusive of delivery, which is how the whole site prices. Payment is by Visa, Mastercard, American Express, PayPal or bank transfer, and there is “no additional fee when paying via PayPal”. No Klarna, no Clearpay, and no trade or business account that we could find.

Customer service hours are published — Monday to Friday 7am to 8pm and Saturday 7am to 4pm — but there is no phone number to use them on, and the email address on the imprint is obfuscated so it cannot be read or copied.

sections.heading: What buying from a German seller means in practice
sections.html:
None of this makes Buycarparts a bad shop. AUTODOC is one of the larger parts retailers in Europe, the catalogue is deep and the prices are keen. But the structure changes three practical things, and you should price them in.

Returns go abroad at your expense. That is the single biggest cost difference against a UK seller with a free returns label. On a £13 filter it is irrelevant; on a £120 part you ordered in error it can swallow a tenth of the value.

There is nobody to ring. No phone number, no UK address, and a contact form as the way in. If a part arrives broken on the morning your car is on the ramp, that is a slow conversation.

Enforcement is harder. Your contract is with a company registered in Berlin, so a dispute you cannot settle by email is a cross-border problem rather than a county court one. The sensible protection costs nothing: pay by credit card or PayPal, and keep the order confirmation, the photographs and the postage receipts.

Our honest summary of when to use it: yes for planned maintenance you are ordering a week ahead — filters, oil, pads, discs, bulbs, wipers — where the saving is real and a delay costs you nothing. Be more careful for anything urgent, anything heavy, anything with a core charge, and anything where you are not completely certain of the part number.

£8.45 delivery and free over £130 on ordinary parts
Prices shown inclusive of 20% VAT, so the figure you see is the figure you pay before postage
A 14-day right to withdraw with no reason required and no restocking fee published
No electrical-parts exclusion on returns, unlike much of the trade

verdict: For planned maintenance a week ahead, Buycarparts does the job: a genuinely large catalogue, a registration-number lookup that works, VAT-inclusive prices, £8.45 postage and free delivery over £130. The 14-day no-reason return with no restocking fee is better than several UK rivals offer. What you are trading away is recourse. The seller is AUTODOC SE in Berlin, no UK entity is named, there is no phone number, you pay to send anything back, and the non-postable return estimate is quoted in euros. Add the core-charge mechanics — a £25.39 deposit, a part posted to Germany at your cost, and six to eight weeks for a verdict that can still go against you — and the picture is clear enough. Order ordinary service parts here and save money; for anything urgent, heavy, or where you are not sure of the part number, a UK seller with a phone number and a free returns label is worth the extra few pounds.

faqs.q: Is Buycarparts a UK company?
faqs.a: No. The site owner is Partex Global GmbH of Röttenbach, Germany, registered at the District Court of Fürth under HRB 21524, and the seller of the goods is AUTODOC SE of Berlin, described on the site as “the vendor of the products and exclusive contracting partner”. No UK company, Companies House number or UK address appears anywhere on the site.

faqs.q: How much is delivery and how long does it take?
faqs.a: £8.45 on UK orders under £130 and free above that, though the free threshold excludes bulky items, tyres and core parts. Tyres are £1.99 separately, and the Isle of Man, Jersey and Guernsey are £15.00. In-stock items ship within one to two days, with another one to two if the part is at a supplier’s warehouse, and the only carrier named is EVRI. There is no next-day option and no published cut-off time.

faqs.q: Can I send something back if I ordered the wrong part?
faqs.a: Yes, within 14 days and without giving a reason, but you pay the postage and the parcel goes to AUTODOC SE in Berlin. For anything that will not go in the post, the site estimates the cost as your original shipping charge plus 10 EUR. Keep the packaging intact: you can be charged for diminished value if the box is damaged, and fitting the part may also reduce what you get back.

faqs.q: What is the core charge on my order?
faqs.a: A deposit on your old part when you buy a reconditioned unit — the published example is £25.39 including VAT. It is refunded once your old part reaches their warehouse and passes examination, which they report within six to eight weeks. You have twelve months to send the old unit back, and if it fails examination the charge is kept, with two months to request the part back at their expense before it is scrapped.

faqs.q: Is there a phone number?
faqs.a: Not one we could find. The contact page publishes service hours of 7am to 8pm Monday to Friday and 7am to 4pm on Saturday, but no telephone number, and the email address on the company imprint is obfuscated so it cannot be read. Contact runs through the website’s own form.

faqs.q: How do I protect myself buying from abroad?
faqs.a: Pay by credit card or PayPal, so you have a route to a chargeback if something goes wrong. Check the dimensions and part number on the listing against the part you are removing, since there is no VIN lookup and the site makes no statement about who carries the risk of the wrong choice. Keep the order confirmation, photograph anything you return, and send it tracked.

title: BYD New Cars Review 2026: Prices, Warranty and the Missing Grant
meta_title: BYD New Cars 2026: UK Range Prices From £18,650
meta_description: What a new BYD costs in October 2026: £18,650 for a Dolphin Surf up to £58,990, six years of warranty, and why no BYD qualifies for the £3,750 grant.

headline.label: Cheapest new BYD, on the road
headline.value: £18,650 — Dolphin Surf Active, 30kWh, the entry point to a 15-line range (BYD UK media site, on-the-road price including VAT)

intro:
A new BYD starts at £18,650 on the road for a Dolphin Surf Active and runs to £58,990 for a Sealion 7 Excellence, and every one of them carries six years or 93,750 miles of vehicle warranty — twice the term most of the established marques offer. The battery is covered for eight years or 125,000 miles on top of that.

BYD has been selling cars in Britain since March 2023 and passed 100,000 UK registrations on 29 July 2026, from a network that had reached 143 sites by that date. Its own year-end release put 2025 at 51,422 registrations and a 2.55% market share, against 0.45% the year before.

The prices below come from BYD's own UK media site rather than from its consumer pages, which are closed to automated reading. Each one is an on-the-road figure including VAT, and each is a starting point for a trim rather than a quote for a particular car.

sections.heading: What £18,650 buys, and where the ladder ends
sections.html:
The Dolphin Surf Active opens the range at £18,650 with a 30kWh Blade Battery, a 65kW motor and 137 miles of WLTP combined range. Moving up to the 43.2kWh pack costs £3,300: the Boost is £21,950 and quotes 200 miles, and the Comfort at £23,950 trades range back down to 193 miles for a 115kW motor instead of a 65kW one. Three-phase 11kW AC charging is standard across all three, DC peaks at 65kW on the Active and 85kW on the other two, and BYD quotes 30 minutes from 10–80% on every trim.

Above that sits the Dolphin proper at £26,195 for a 44.9kWh Active, £27,195 for the 130kW Boost, and £30,195 or £31,695 for the 60.4kWh Comfort and Design, both rated at 265 miles. The Atto 2 arrived in August 2025 at £30,850 for a 51.1kWh Boost quoting 214 miles, and £34,950 for a 64.8kWh Comfort quoting 261 miles.

The top of the range is where the money is. The Seal saloon is £45,695 in rear-drive Design form, rated at 354 miles, and £48,695 for the 390kW Excellence AWD at 323 miles. The Sealion 7 SUV runs £46,990, £51,990 and £58,990 across Comfort RWD, Design AWD and Excellence AWD, the last of those on a 91.3kWh pack good for 312 miles.

One wrinkle worth knowing before you argue with a salesperson about battery size. BYD's own Seal page gives 82.5kWh in its technical data table and 80kWh in the prose above it, and labels neither as gross or usable. The gap is small and the explanation is probably mundane, but the document does not say which number is which.

sections.heading: The discount every rival gets, and BYD does not
sections.html:
The Electric Car Grant takes £3,750 off a Band 1 car and £1,500 off a Band 2 car at the point of sale. The government publishes the list of approved models itself, and on 15 October 2026 it held 20 entries in Band 1 — among them the Nissan Leaf, the Renault 5 and Megane, the Kia EV4, the Hyundai Kona Electric and both small BMWs — and roughly fifty in Band 2, covering most of Stellantis, Volkswagen, Skoda and Kia. No BYD model appears in either band.

Price is not the reason. The cap is £37,000 recommended retail, measured inclusive of VAT, mandatory extras, delivery and administration charges and the battery even where it is leased, with an interpolation family allowed up to £42,000 if one version in it comes under £37,000. A Dolphin Surf at £18,650 is barely half the cap, and six of the trims listed above sit comfortably beneath it.

What remains is the rest of the test, and it is worth reading because it explains the shape of the eligible list. An applicant must meet one of two sustainability criteria: a target verified by the Science Based Targets initiative, where a commitment alone is not accepted, or an assessment at Management Quality Level 4 or higher under the Transition Pathway Initiative with carbon performance at or below the sector 1.5°C benchmark for 2050. Separately, each vehicle is scored on where it is built, and the weighting is lopsided: battery production counts for 70% of the environmental score and final vehicle assembly for 30%, both measured against national electricity carbon intensity using the IEA's 2023 figures. A car built where the grid is dirtier scores worse.

BYD's absence is a fact; which limb of the test it turns on is not published, and this page is not going to guess. What a buyer can take from it is concrete enough. A Renault 5 at the 52kWh size comes down by £3,750 and a Dolphin Surf does not, so the gap between them is £3,750 narrower than the window stickers suggest. Ask the retailer what discount is on the table, because BYD has been funding its own offers rather than drawing on the scheme.

sections.heading: Six years and 93,750 miles, which outlasts most of the field
sections.html:
BYD's published warranty is six years or 150,000km — 93,750 miles — whichever comes first, with the drive unit covered for eight years or 150,000km and the traction battery for eight years or 200,000km, which BYD states as 125,000 miles. Set that against the three years and 60,000 miles that is still the standard offer from the German marques and the arithmetic favours a high-mileage driver heavily: a 20,000-mile year exhausts a 60,000-mile warranty inside year three, and leaves BYD's running until the end of year four.

The battery claim rests on cell chemistry rather than on a generous policy. BYD builds its own Blade packs on lithium iron phosphate, and the warranty page states a design life of over 5,000 charge and discharge cycles. On a 43.2kWh Dolphin Surf, 5,000 cycles is a number no private owner will approach.

Two things the page does not do. It attaches no figure to roadside assistance — the cover is described as including on-the-spot repair and towing, with no period or mileage attached to it — and it publishes no paint or anti-corrosion term at all, which most manufacturers state as a matter of course. The page also says the terms "may depend on model" without setting out the per-model table in any readable form, so the right move before signing is to ask for the warranty booklet for the specific car rather than relying on the headline figures.

One condition is stated plainly and is worth taking seriously: "If the vehicle isn't serviced to the manufacture recommendation it will invalidate your BYD Warranty." Six years of cover is worth having and it is conditional on six years of main-dealer-standard servicing, for which BYD publishes no price.

sections.heading: The tax line the Seal U DM-i misses by £95
sections.html:
Vehicle excise duty is where a list price quietly becomes a bigger number, and BYD's range sits across the line in an unusually instructive way. The expensive car supplement adds £440 a year for five years — £2,200 in total — to any car whose list price exceeds £40,000, or £50,000 where the car is electric. It is charged from the second time the vehicle is taxed, so it does not appear in the showroom conversation at all.

Run BYD's own ladder against those two thresholds and the results split by fuel. Of the fourteen electric derivatives priced above, exactly two cross the £50,000 line: the Sealion 7 Design AWD at £51,990 and the Excellence AWD at £58,990. The Seal Excellence AWD escapes by £1,305 and everything below it is clear by a wide margin.

The plug-in hybrids are judged against the lower threshold, because £50,000 applies only to zero-emission cars, and that produces the sharpest number on this page. The Seal U DM-i Design all-wheel drive is priced at £39,905. That is £95 below £40,000. A single factory-fitted option, or any dealer-supplied extra that lands in the list price, tips it over and costs the buyer £2,200 across the following five years — a return of roughly twenty-three pounds of tax for every pound of option. Anyone ordering that car should ask for the list price in writing before the order is placed.

The first-year rate runs the other way and favours BYD. A zero-emission car pays £10 in its first year against £115 for a plug-in hybrid emitting 1–50g/km, and both then join the £200 standard rate. The first-year saving on an electric BYD is real but small; the supplement is the figure that moves the total.

sections.heading: Half the range now burns petrol
sections.html:
BYD arrived in Britain as an electric-only brand and is not one now. Its franchised retailers list fifteen model lines, and seven of them are plug-in hybrids or range-extenders: the Dolphin G DM-i, Atto 2 DM-i, Seal U DM-i, Sealion 5 DM-i, Seal 6 DM-i, Seal 6 DM-i Touring and the Shark DMO pick-up, alongside a Ti 7 DM-p. BYD's own July 2026 release described a line-up that had gone "from one model to ten" in three years; the retail list has moved on again since.

The hybrids are the cheaper way into the larger cars. A Seal U DM-i Boost is £33,205 and quotes 49.7 miles of electric running and 671 miles on a full tank and a full battery, which is a usable commuting range on electricity with no range anxiety on a long trip. The all-wheel-drive Design is £39,905. Against the £46,990 entry price of the all-electric Sealion 7, the hybrid undercuts by £13,785.

There are two costs to that choice and neither is flagged at the point of sale. The plug-in hybrids face the £40,000 tax threshold rather than £50,000, as above. And they are outside the Electric Car Grant entirely by definition, which blunts the comparison between a BYD hybrid and a grant-eligible battery car of similar money. BYD's December 2025 figures record a 12.01% share of combined BEV and PHEV registrations, which is the honest way to describe a brand now selling both.

sections.heading: Nobody publishes who lends you the money
sections.html:
On most manufacturer pages the finance arm is easy to name: a captive lender with its own FCA firm reference, its own complaints ladder and its own regulatory history. BYD does not present one to a British buyer in any form this page could verify.

BYD's consumer site is closed to automated reading, so its finance terms could not be read. The franchised dealer group that does publish terms, Marshall Motor Group Limited, describes itself as "a credit-broker not a lender", operating under FCA firm reference 310503, and says an application goes to "our panel of lenders to see if they can offer you finance" without naming a single member of that panel or publishing a representative APR. The advertised offers run through the dealer: a Dolphin G DM-i Active at £275 a month with a £279 customer deposit at 2.9% APR representative, and an Atto 2 DM-i Boost at £329 a month with a £329 deposit at the same rate.

A Companies House search returns no BYD-named company in Britain carrying a finance or leasing activity. The only substantial BYD entity on the register is BYD (U.K.) CO., LTD., number 08458577, incorporated 22 March 2013, whose activities are listed as the sale and repair of motor vehicles and electrical installation, with accounts most recently made up to 31 December 2024. That is consistent with finance being arranged entirely through third-party lenders at dealer level, but it is not proof of it, and the arrangement should be treated as unverified until the paperwork is in front of you. Ask in writing who the lender is, what the APR is on the specific agreement, and what the total amount payable comes to.

sections.heading: Crash scores, and the scale behind a three-year-old brand
sections.html:
Euro NCAP has rated the range well. The Sealion 7 was assessed in 2025 and published on 9 April 2025 at five stars: 87% adult occupant, 93% child occupant, 76% vulnerable road users and 79% safety assist. The Dolphin Surf also took five stars, published 8 September 2025, which is a good result for the cheapest car in the range.

The Sealion 7's weaknesses are specific and worth knowing rather than being a reason to avoid it. Rear passenger chest protection in the full-width rigid barrier test was rated weak on dummy compression readings. Pedestrian and cyclist head protection was poor on the stiff windscreen pillars and at the base of the screen. Autonomous braking for pedestrians struck at the rear of the car was marginal, as was cyclist dooring prevention, which only warns the driver. Driver monitoring scored 0.9 of a possible 2 points.

On scale, BYD's own numbers are the only ones worth quoting, and they are substantial for a brand that sold its first UK car in March 2023. Full-year 2025 came in at 51,422 registrations and 2.55% of the market, up from 0.45% in 2024, with December alone at 7,683. The hundred-thousandth UK registration was announced on 29 July 2026, by which point the retail network stood at 143 sites. A car bought today is not an orphan, and the warranty behind it is written by a company selling at that rate.

pros: The cheapest new car in the range is £18,650 on the road for a Dolphin Surf Active with a 30kWh battery, which undercuts every grant-eligible small electric car even before the grant is taken off the rival.
Six years or 93,750 miles of vehicle warranty, against the three years and 60,000 miles still standard at most premium marques — a 20,000-mile-a-year driver gains well over a year of cover.
The traction battery is covered for eight years or 125,000 miles, and the drive unit for eight years or 93,750 miles, so the two most expensive components outlast the vehicle warranty.
Three-phase 11kW AC charging is standard across the whole Dolphin Surf range rather than reserved for higher trims, and BYD quotes 10–80% in 30 minutes on every version.
Euro NCAP gave the Sealion 7 five stars in April 2025 with 93% for child occupant protection, and gave the entry-level Dolphin Surf five stars in September 2025.
The Seal U DM-i Boost at £33,205 quotes 49.7 miles of electric range and 671 miles combined, undercutting the all-electric Sealion 7 by £13,785.
BYD publishes its UK prices openly on its media site with trim-by-trim specifications, which is more than several established manufacturers manage.
51,422 UK registrations in 2025 and 143 retail sites by July 2026 — enough network to make servicing and warranty work practical in most of the country.
cons: No BYD model appears on the government's Electric Car Grant list in either band, checked on 15 October 2026, so a rival at the same screen price can be £3,750 cheaper to buy. Price is not the obstacle — the Dolphin Surf is barely half the £37,000 cap — and BYD does not explain the absence anywhere a buyer will see it.

Nobody publishes who lends the money. BYD's consumer site cannot be read by automated tools, the franchised dealer describes itself as a credit broker with an unnamed panel, and no BYD-named finance company appears on the Companies House register. A buyer cannot find out who their creditor will be before walking in.

The Seal U DM-i Design is listed at £39,905, which is £95 under the £40,000 expensive car supplement threshold. One option tips it over and costs £2,200 in tax across five years, and nothing in the sales material warns about it.
The warranty page publishes no paint term and no anti-corrosion term at all, and attaches no period or mileage to roadside assistance, while most manufacturers state all three.
Six years of cover is conditional on servicing to BYD's schedule — the page says plainly that failing to do so "will invalidate your BYD Warranty" — and no service price is published anywhere.
The warranty page says terms "may depend on model" without publishing the per-model table in readable form, so the headline figures cannot be relied on for a specific car.

Euro NCAP rated rear passenger chest protection on the Sealion 7 as weak in the full-width barrier test, marked pedestrian head protection down on the stiff windscreen pillars, and gave driver monitoring only 0.9 of 2 points.
BYD's own Seal page gives 82.5kWh in its technical table and 80kWh in the prose above it, without saying which figure is gross and which is usable.
verdict: BYD has gone from nothing to 51,422 registrations a year and 143 UK sites in roughly three years, and the reason is visible in the price list: £18,650 buys a new electric car with a six-year, 93,750-mile warranty and eight years on the battery, which is more cover than almost anything else on sale. The range now runs to £58,990 and about half of its fifteen lines are plug-in hybrids rather than pure electric, so the brand is no longer the single-fuel proposition it arrived as. Two financial points deserve settling before signing. No BYD qualifies for the Electric Car Grant, so a Band 1 rival is £3,750 cheaper than its sticker suggests and the comparison needs redoing with that in mind; and if the car in question is a Seal U DM-i Design at £39,905, check the final list price in writing, because £95 of options turns into £2,200 of vehicle tax. Neither is a reason to walk away from the cars. Both are reasons to ask for the on-the-road price itemised, the first-year tax stated separately, the name of the lender, and the warranty booklet for the specific model rather than the summary on the website.

faqs.q: How much is the cheapest new BYD?
faqs.a: £18,650 on the road for a Dolphin Surf Active, which has a 30kWh Blade Battery, a 65kW motor and 137 miles of WLTP combined range. The 43.2kWh Boost is £21,950 for 200 miles and the Comfort is £23,950 for 193 miles and a 115kW motor. These come from BYD's own UK media site; the consumer site is closed to automated reading, so confirm the figure with a retailer before ordering.

faqs.q: Can I get the £3,750 Electric Car Grant on a BYD?
faqs.a: No. The government's list of approved models, checked on 15 October 2026, holds around 20 cars in the £3,750 band and roughly fifty in the £1,500 band, and no BYD appears in either. It is not a price problem — the cap is £37,000 and most of the BYD range sits below it. The scheme also tests the manufacturer against Science Based Targets initiative verification or a Transition Pathway Initiative Management Quality Level 4 assessment, and scores each car on where its battery and body are built, with battery production counting for 70% of the environmental score. Which of those BYD does not satisfy is not published.

faqs.q: What does the BYD warranty actually cover, and for how long?
faqs.a: Six years or 150,000km, which BYD states as 93,750 miles, whichever comes first, on the vehicle. The drive unit is covered for eight years or 150,000km and the traction battery for eight years or 200,000km, stated as 125,000 miles. BYD says cover will transfer to a new owner in most cases. It also says the warranty is invalidated if the car is not serviced to its recommended schedule, and it publishes no paint or anti-corrosion term and no roadside assistance period. Ask for the warranty booklet for your specific model, because BYD states the terms may vary by model and does not publish the per-model table.

faqs.q: Which BYD models pay the expensive car supplement?
faqs.a: On the prices published at the time of writing, two: the Sealion 7 Design AWD at £51,990 and the Sealion 7 Excellence AWD at £58,990, both above the £50,000 threshold that applies to electric cars. That adds £440 a year for five years, or £2,200. The plug-in hybrids are measured against the £40,000 threshold instead, and the Seal U DM-i Design at £39,905 clears it by only £95 — close enough that options could push it over.

faqs.q: Does BYD still only sell electric cars in the UK?
faqs.a: No. Franchised retailers now list fifteen BYD model lines, of which seven are plug-in hybrids or range-extenders, including the Seal U DM-i, Seal 6 DM-i, Sealion 5 DM-i, Atto 2 DM-i and the Shark DMO pick-up. BYD's December 2025 figures describe a 12.01% share of combined battery-electric and plug-in hybrid registrations. A Seal U DM-i Boost costs £33,205 and quotes 49.7 miles of electric range with 671 miles combined.

faqs.q: Who provides the finance on a new BYD?
faqs.a: This could not be established. BYD's UK consumer site is not readable by automated tools, no BYD-named finance or leasing company appears on the Companies House register, and the franchised dealer group publishing terms describes itself as a credit broker rather than a lender, operating under FCA firm reference 310503 and referring applications to an unnamed panel. Advertised offers quote 2.9% APR representative — £275 a month with a £279 deposit on a Dolphin G DM-i Active, for instance — but the lender behind them is not named. Ask for the credit agreement, the lender's name and the total amount payable in writing.

title: Campsites.co.uk Review: The Deposit the Park Sets, and the Price Promise Behind It
meta_title: Campsites.co.uk Review: 3,200 Sites, No Booking Fees
meta_description: Campsites.co.uk lists 3,200+ UK camping, glamping and touring sites with no booking fee. Who really sets the deposit, and what the price promise does.

headline.label: Deposit at booking
headline.value: From 15% of the stay, set by each park with a £5 minimum — and no booking fee on top

intro:
Campsites.co.uk lists more than 3,200 camping, glamping and touring sites across the UK, charges campers no booking fee of any kind, and takes a deposit starting at 15% of the stay with a £5 minimum. It has been running since 2003, added instant online booking in 2019, and says more than 475,000 campers now use it to find and hold a pitch. Figures checked on 17 October 2026 against the company’s own pages, booking terms and filings.

For a camper the economics are unusually plain. The booking terms state it outright: "We do not charge you any booking fees or add any fees to the prices quoted by the Park for your Booking." What you see on a listing is the park’s own price, with VAT included where it applies, because the money comes from the other side of the transaction — 10% plus VAT on each booking the site sends a park, with ordinary directory listings free and, in the company’s own words to owners, "No setup fees, contract, or exclusivity". There is nothing to join and nothing to cancel.

One structural point decides whose number you ring when a holiday goes wrong, so it belongs here rather than in the small print. The booking terms say "For all Bookings made or taken on your behalf through the Website, your contract is with the Park directly", and that the company "acts as an agent only in facilitating Bookings". Deposits, balance dates, cancellation windows and refunds are in practice each park’s own rules rather than one house policy applied to all 3,200 of them. That is a deliberate design choice, and understanding it is worth more than any other single fact on this page.

key_facts.value: No booking fee, no service charge, no membership

sections.heading: Where the 15% goes, and the £5 underneath it
sections.html:
The home page carries a heading marked Price promise and a single line beneath it: "Always get the best rate, with deposits from just 15% and no booking fees." The about page puts the same thing as "low deposits and no booking fees". Both are accurate, and both describe a floor rather than a rate. The binding version is in the booking terms, which say "Payments will be collected according to the terms set by Parks and comprise a deposit amount" and then add the only hard figure the company sets itself: "Deposit payments are subject to a £5 minimum and are non-refundable."

So two different people decide what you pay up front. The park decides the percentage, which can sit anywhere at or above 15%, and the platform imposes a £5 floor underneath it. On a £400 week that works out as £60 now and £340 later. On a single £30 night the floor is what bites, because 15% of £30 is £4.50 and the minimum takes £5. Neither the listing pages nor the terms publish a ceiling, which means the up-front cost of a specific booking is not knowable until the checkout page shows it.

The balance is handled the same way, by reference to somebody else’s rules. "If the Park’s terms for your Booking dictate that a Balance Payment should be collected automatically when it becomes due", the company says, "we will instruct the Payment Provider to process that charge using the same card as used to make the Deposit." If that payment fails, "the Park will contact you", and "[t]he Park may cancel your Booking if they have not received your Balance Payment by the due date". The deposit being non-refundable is not sharp practice, incidentally: regulation 28(1)(h) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 lifts the ordinary 14-day online cancellation right off accommodation booked for a named date, so every campsite, hotel and hostel in the country is in the same position.

sections.heading: The price promise, and who has to do the noticing
sections.html:
This is the clause worth reading twice, because it is the mechanism behind the headline claim and it is published in full. "Parks commit to matching their best rates in the prices quoted on our Website, but if you do notice any lower prices elsewhere please contact us using the details on our Contact Us page prior to your Booking and we will ask the Park to price match for you."

Read that slowly and three things fall out of it. The commitment is the park’s, not the platform’s. The trigger is the camper spotting a cheaper price somewhere else. And the remedy is that the company will ask — the sentence promises a request, not a reduction. The timing matters as well: the words are "prior to your Booking", so once the deposit has gone through there is no stated route back to a lower price at all.

What sits behind the clause is just as telling. The owner-facing pages promise "No setup fees, contract, or exclusivity" and say "[a]s a bookable listing, we won’t tie you into any sort of minimum allocation or minimum term". A park signs nothing, commits nothing and can walk away whenever it likes, which is a genuinely attractive offer to a small operator and also means there is no contractual parity obligation anywhere in the arrangement. Nothing can be suspended, because nothing has been agreed. The about page’s "you’ll never pay more than booking direct" therefore rests on the park’s own pricing discipline and on readers reporting exceptions.

There is a respectable argument that this is the better design. Wide retail parity obligations — the kind that forbid a hotel or a park from undercutting a platform anywhere else — are exactly what competition authorities across Europe have spent a decade objecting to. A platform that asks rather than compels avoids that problem entirely. It also, unavoidably, gives the reader a weaker promise.

sections.heading: 10% plus VAT, and the arithmetic behind the claim
sections.html:
The owner pages are blunter about money than the camper pages, and they are where the business model is legible. A bookable listing runs "at a commission rate of just 10% + VAT", a basic listing is "FREE", the model is "[p]ay as you go, on results", and parks are told they will "pay 20% less commission than the industry norm". The FAQ repeats it and names a competitor: "Our online bookings service is 20% cheaper than Pitchup."

That claim is worth checking rather than repeating, and it survives the check. Add VAT at 20% to a 10% commission and a park hands over 12% of the booking value. Pitchup’s own supplier pages state that for UK businesses "the commission (‘deposit’) we deduct from bookings includes 20% VAT", which puts its published 15% at 12.5% before tax. Twelve against fifteen is a fifth lower. Ten against twelve and a half is also exactly a fifth lower. The saving is 20% whether a park compares the two figures gross or net, which is unusually honest for a marketing percentage — on a £400 booking it is £48 including VAT against £60, a difference of £12.

The other side of the model is that the two percentages do not match each other. The camper’s deposit starts at 15% of the stay and the park’s commission is 12% of it including tax, and the booking terms say nothing about how the gap is reconciled or when a park receives its share of money the platform’s payment provider has already taken. That is normal for an agency arrangement and it is still unpublished. Parks are also told that becoming bookable will "typically get 75% more interest" and that even a free listing will "typically get thousands of pounds worth of booking enquiries from us each year", neither of which carries a date or a sample size.

sections.heading: If the park cannot honour the booking
sections.html:
The liability position is set out clearly, and it is narrow. "Subject to the limitations set out in these Terms and to the extent permitted by law", the company says, it "shall only be liable for direct damages actually suffered, paid or incurred by you due to an attributable shortcoming of our obligations in respect to our services, up to an aggregate amount of the aggregate cost of your Deposit and Balance Payment (where collection is initiated by us)". Indirect, consequential, special and incidental losses are excluded, and nothing in the terms limits liability "for death or personal injury resulting from its negligence; nor for the Company’s fraud or fraudulent misrepresentation".

Then comes the clause that matters most to anybody arriving at a full site. "We are not liable for any refunds in the event of changes to your booking (made by you or the Park), overbooking by the Park, Force Majeure (defined below) or any other cause beyond our control." A separate sentence disposes of the obvious follow-up question: "The Park are not liable for refunds or expenses you incur in the event they are prevented from fulfilling your Booking". Set those two beside "Deposits paid to confirm Bookings are non-refundable and cancellations are subject to the terms of each Park", and a park that overbooks, closes or simply cannot accommodate you leaves the deposit where it is, with no exception written anywhere for closure.

Nor is there an escalation route built in. The company "acts as an agent only in facilitating Bookings, but will provide support as a third party on a reasonable efforts basis", and it says in terms that "[a]lthough we are not obliged to mediate between you and the Park in the event of any complaint or dispute, we will make reasonable efforts to assist you and the Park in reaching a resolution wherever we can". A pitch booking sits outside financial regulation entirely, so no ombudsman stands behind it and no approved alternative dispute resolution body has jurisdiction. What is left is the park itself, a chargeback through your card issuer, section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 on a credit card purchase over £100, and the county court. The Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018 do not help either, because a pitch on its own is a single travel service and carries no insolvency protection — true of every accommodation platform rather than of this one in particular.

sections.heading: Reviews only exist where a booking went through
sections.html:
The review policy is one of the better things about the site and it is stated in one sentence on the home page: "Thousands of easy-to-search reviews, all from verified guests who booked through us." The about page calls them "honest and verified guest reviews". That is a stricter rule than most campsite directories apply, and it closes off the usual complaint about user-generated ratings, because nobody who has not paid for a stay through the platform can leave one. A long-established park such as Highlands End Holiday Park shows 207 reviews on its listing.

The consequence is less often spelled out. A park on the free basic tier takes no bookings through the platform, so it can never accumulate a single review there, however good it is. The score attached to a listing is therefore partly a measure of how long that park has been paying 10% plus VAT, not only of how well it runs its showers. And because the site does not publish how many of its 3,200-odd listings are actually bookable online, a reader looking at a listing with no reviews cannot tell whether they are seeing a park nobody rates or a directory entry nobody can book.

The booking terms contain no clause about reviews at all — nothing on moderation, nothing on how a park challenges a review it believes is unfair, and nothing on when a review is removed. For a site whose main editorial asset is its reviews, that is a gap worth closing.

sections.heading: The ratings the listings do not carry
sections.html:
The site runs its own annual recognition, the Outstanding Sites list, described as "[o]ur annual list of hand-picked camping, glamping and touring sites" that "offer campers a consistently excellent experience", alongside a 2025 awards programme. The word doing the work there is hand-picked. No scoring threshold, minimum review count, assessment visit or published methodology sits behind the list, so it reads as editorial selection rather than measurement — which is a perfectly legitimate thing for a magazine-style directory to do, and a different thing from an inspection.

An inspection regime does exist for this sector and no listing shows it. VisitEngland Assessment Services runs a Holiday Parks quality scheme whose standards document is public, and it is specific. The overall star bands are 60–74% for three stars, 75–86% for four and 87% and above for five, with the rule that "[n]o section to be more than one star rating band below the overall rating" and cleanliness never allowed to fall below the overall grade at all. Four stars requires electric hook-up on half of the non-seasonal touring pitches and five stars on 70% of them. Minimum facility ratios are set per 30 pitches — at four star, one urinal, one toilet, two washbasins and one bath or shower for gents, and two toilets, two washbasins and one bath or shower for ladies. Members receive a visit every year.

A park holding four stars under that scheme gets no visible credit on a Campsites.co.uk listing, and a camper who wants an independently assessed site cannot filter for one. Two details could not be established from the public document and are worth saying rather than guessing: the standards text does not state its own version date, and it does not say whether the annual visit is announced or made as a mystery guest.

sections.heading: What it costs to hold a pitch elsewhere
sections.html:
The sharpest way to see what a park-set deposit means is to put it beside an operator that owns its sites and can therefore impose one rule across all of them. The Caravan and Motorhome Club’s own booking terms, for stays booked from 4 July 2024, say the deposit "will usually be £5 per stay" and that "the £5 is a fixed amount regardless of the price of the stay". For bookings taken between 9 June 2023 and 3 July 2024 it was 10% of the stay with a £20 minimum, so the Club moved deliberately from a percentage to a flat fee. The balance is "due the evening before arrival (if you have selected automatic balance payments)".

The cancellation position is the part a platform cannot match. "Changes and cancellations are FREE when made more than 21 full days before your scheduled arrival date", and inside that window the charge is the proportion of the deposit attributable to what you cancelled, rising to "the entire deposit" if you drop the whole booking. Fail to turn up and fail to say so by 8pm on the arrival day and it is treated as a no-show, with no refund of "any element which has been paid, including the full deposit".

Hold the two side by side on a £400 week. Through the Club, £5 is at stake and nothing at all until 21 days out. Through Campsites.co.uk, at least £60 is non-refundable from the moment the card is charged, and whether any of it comes back is a question for that particular park’s terms. None of which is a failing of the platform so much as a description of what it is: a club with 3,200 of its own pitches could publish one cancellation policy, and a directory listing 3,200 independent businesses cannot. It is simply a cost the reader should price in before choosing which door to go through.

sections.heading: Addactive Limited, two addresses and no published turnover
sections.html:
The brand is not the company. The booking terms say Campsites.co.uk is "a trading name of Addactive Limited", "[r]egistered in England No. 5891444". Companies House carries it as ADDACTIVE LIMITED, number 05891444, an active private limited company incorporated on 31 July 2006, with SIC codes 62012 for business and domestic software development, 63120 for web portals and 79909 for other reservation service activities not elsewhere classified. The first two of those describe a software house, which is a fair account of what the business actually is.

There are two addresses and it is worth knowing which is which. The registered office is "Robert J Gogarty Chartered Accountants, Bank House Southwick Square, Southwick, Brighton, West Sussex, BN42 4FN" — an accountant’s office, which is ordinary for a company of this size and is not where anybody works. The operating address on the contact page is Oakfield House, 35 Perrymount Road, Haywards Heath RH16 3BW, with three separate numbers: 01444 676015 for general enquiries, 01444 676016 for existing site owners and 01444 676014 for parks thinking of joining.

Ownership has been stable and is fully disclosed. Martin Smith and Hannah Kate Smith each hold more than 25% but not more than 50% of the shares and of the voting rights, both notified on 31 July 2016 and both resident in England; Hannah Kate Smith is company secretary, her details last updated on 1 April 2026. Accounts to 31 December 2025 were filed on 24 September 2026 as total exemption full accounts, with the next set made up to 31 December 2026 and due by 30 September 2027. Micro-entity accounts were filed for the year to 31 December 2020. The practical effect is that no turnover, commission income or booking volume has ever been published, so every audience figure on the site — the 475,000 campers, the 3,200 listings, the survey of "4,000+ of our customers" in which 11% called themselves primarily glampers — is the company’s own count and none of it carries a date.

Three dates get quoted for the same business and none of them contradicts the others, which is worth saying plainly because it looks like an inconsistency and is not. The about page says "[f]ounded in 2003", the company was incorporated on 31 July 2006, and the footer reads © 2015-2026. A domain and a directory can easily predate the limited company set up to run them. The one figure that genuinely does not match itself is the site count: "more than 3,000" on the about page against "more than 3,200" on the home page, with neither dated.

pros: No booking fee or service charge of any kind for the camper, stated flatly in the booking terms rather than implied
The listed price is the park’s own price with VAT included where it applies, and parks "commit to matching their best rates" on the site
Commission of 10% plus VAT to parks with no setup fee, no contract, no exclusivity, no minimum allocation and no minimum term
Reviews are restricted to "verified guests who booked through us", so nobody who has not paid for a stay can post one
More than 3,200 listings with usable category counts, including 468 pod sites and 401 bell tent sites
A £5 deposit floor keeps the up-front cost of a single cheap night genuinely small
Agency status, the contracting party, the liability cap and the governing law are all stated in the booking terms without hedging
Trading since 2003 with online booking since 2019, under the same two shareholders since 31 July 2016
cons: "Deposits from just 15%" is a floor rather than a rate — the booking terms hand the amount to each park and publish no ceiling, so what a specific booking costs up front is not knowable before checkout
Deposits are non-refundable with no stated exception, not even for a park that closes, and the company is "not liable for any refunds" on overbooking either

The same terms also say "[t]he Park are not liable for refunds or expenses you incur in the event they are prevented from fulfilling your Booking", which leaves a failed stay with nobody holding the risk but the camper
The price promise is a request and not a guarantee: the camper must spot the lower price "prior to your Booking" and the company will only "ask the Park to price match"

Nothing in the owner terms obliges a park to keep its listed price in line, because there is no contract and no exclusivity, so "you’ll never pay more than booking direct" depends on each park’s own discipline

Liability is capped at the deposit plus any balance the platform collected, there is no obligation to mediate, and a pitch booking has no ombudsman behind it and no approved ADR body with jurisdiction
The site does not publish how many of its 3,200-plus listings can actually be booked online, so a listing with no reviews may be a free directory entry rather than an unpopular park
No scoring threshold, minimum review count or published methodology sits behind the hand-picked Outstanding Sites list, and VisitEngland holiday park star ratings are neither displayed nor filterable
Accounts are filed under total exemption, so no turnover, commission income or booking volume has ever been published and every audience figure is the company’s own
The about page says more than 3,000 sites and the home page more than 3,200, with neither figure dated
verdict: Campsites.co.uk does the thing a directory should do and charges the reader nothing to do it: more than 3,200 listings, the park’s own price with no fee bolted on, reviews only from people who actually booked, and a deposit floor of £5 that keeps a single night cheap to hold. Parks pay 10% plus VAT with nothing signed, and the claim that this is a fifth below the going rate stands up to the arithmetic in both directions. The weakness is the mirror image of the strength. Because the platform mirrors each park’s rules rather than imposing its own, the deposit percentage, the cancellation window and the refund position all belong to somebody the reader has not spoken to yet, the best-rate promise is a request rather than an obligation, and a park that cannot honour a booking leaves the deposit where it sits. Read the park’s own cancellation terms on the checkout page before the card goes in, pay by credit card if the stay is over £100, and treat the 15% as a starting point rather than a price.

faqs.q: How much deposit will I actually pay?
faqs.a: At least 15% of the stay, and possibly more. The home page quotes "deposits from just 15%", but the booking terms say payments "will be collected according to the terms set by Parks", so the percentage is the park’s decision and no maximum is published. A £5 minimum applies, which matters on a cheap single night: 15% of a £30 pitch is £4.50, so £5 is taken instead. On a £400 week expect £60 up front and £340 to follow. The exact figure appears at checkout.

faqs.q: Is the deposit refundable if I cancel?
faqs.a: No. The terms say "[d]eposit payments are subject to a £5 minimum and are non-refundable" and that "cancellations are subject to the terms of each Park", which may also carry a cancellation fee of the park’s own. There is no 14-day online cancellation right either, because regulation 28(1)(h) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 excludes accommodation booked for a specific date. That applies to every campsite booking in the UK, not just this one.

faqs.q: Does it really cost no more than booking the park direct?
faqs.a: That is the intention and there is a clause behind it, but it is softer than it sounds. Parks "commit to matching their best rates in the prices quoted on our Website", and if you find a lower price elsewhere you are asked to report it "prior to your Booking", after which the company "will ask the Park to price match for you". There is no contractual parity obligation on parks and no exclusivity, so no penalty exists for a park that prices differently. Checking the park’s own site before you book costs nothing.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if the pitch is not what was advertised?
faqs.a: The park, in the first instance, because "your contract is with the Park directly". The company says the listing information "has been provided to us by Parks and is subject to change" and that it cannot guarantee its accuracy, so a misdescription is the park’s. Campsites.co.uk is "not obliged to mediate" but says it will "make reasonable efforts to assist". Beyond that there is no ombudsman and no approved ADR scheme for a pitch booking, which leaves a card chargeback, section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 above £100, and the county court.

faqs.q: Can anyone leave a review of a campsite on the site?
faqs.a: No. Reviews are "all from verified guests who booked through us", so a stay has to have been paid for through the platform first. That makes the reviews harder to game than open ratings, and it also means parks on the free basic listing tier, which take no bookings through the site, cannot collect reviews at all. A listing showing no reviews is therefore not necessarily a badly rated park. The booking terms publish no policy on how reviews are moderated, challenged or removed.

faqs.q: Is a Campsites.co.uk booking financially protected if the park goes bust?
faqs.a: No, and this is true of accommodation platforms generally rather than of this one in particular. A pitch booked on its own is a single travel service, so the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018 do not apply and there is no insolvency protection or ATOL cover. The company’s liability is capped at "the aggregate cost of your Deposit and Balance Payment (where collection is initiated by us)". A credit card payment and a travel insurance policy that covers accommodation failure are the practical substitutes.

title: CarExamer Review: £142.99 Mobile Inspections and Who Actually Does Them
meta_title: CarExamer Review: £142.99 Inspections, Done By Whom?
meta_description: CarExamer sends a self-employed mechanic to the car: Basic from £142.99, 100+ checks in 70 minutes, report in five hours. Prices and terms checked.
intro:
CarExamer sends a mechanic to the car instead of asking you to drive the car to a garage. A Basic pre-purchase inspection is £142.99 including VAT and buys 100-plus checks, up to 70 minutes on site, a road test of up to 10 minutes and a photographic report five hours after the inspector starts work. Three larger packages follow at £189.99, £256.99 and £276.99, and booking two cars at one address takes 10% off, rising to 20% on five.

The independence behind that is real, and it is the whole point of paying for an inspection. CarExamer Ltd does not employ the mechanic and does not carry out the inspection itself. Its own customer terms say so in plain words: “CarExamer does not provide vehicle inspections – we help to connect customers and inspectors”, and “You buy a vehicle inspection from the inspector who accepts your booking – not from CarExamer.” Nobody in that chain is also trying to sell you the car. It does decide who you are dealing with if the report turns out to be wrong, and that sits further down this page.

Two things worth knowing before you book. The Basic package assumes you have already seen the car in person, is aimed at a newer, lower-mileage vehicle, and does not raise it off the ground at all. And the seller has to agree to the visit in advance — confirming they are the registered keeper, consenting to the inspection, providing “a safe and accessible location” and handing over the keys, the V5C and the MOT certificate. A private seller who will not do that ends the booking before it starts.

headline.label: Cheapest inspection
