sections.heading: Four packages, and the clock is the thing that changes
sections.html:
The price list is published in full, including VAT, which is more than one of the two national names manages. Basic, from £142.99, allows up to 70 minutes and runs 100-plus checks with a documentation check, a VIN check, a battery test, a diagnostic scan and a road test of up to 10 minutes — and only “when the vehicle is safe, road legal and available to drive”. The car stays on the ground. Standard, from £189.99, doubles the time to 120 minutes, raises the vehicle, runs 200-plus checks, adds a scratch report and a follow-up call with the inspector. Premium, from £256.99, takes three hours, runs 300-plus checks and adds paint thickness readings, accident-damage checks and video feedback. All three promise the report within five hours of the inspector arriving.

The fourth is different in kind. The Engineer's Report, from £276.99, is bought when something has already gone wrong: you supply a statement of the problem in the booking notes, the engineer examines that specific concern, and the report lands in 48 hours rather than five. The engineer will not dismantle anything, a revisit costs extra, and the escalation prices are published — £500 for court attendance, and where a full expert witness is needed, “from £1000 + £300 question round and £500 court attendance fee”. Very few firms in this trade print what a dispute costs before you are in one.

Read the ladder against the clock rather than against the check counts. Premium costs 1.8 times Basic and claims three times the checks, but it buys 2.6 times the inspector's time, and time on site is the part a reader can actually picture. The 300-plus figure is also the gap between the headline and the published checklist: CarExamer's own Premium list details 21 road-test items and 26 electrical-control items, with the rest of the count unitemised.

sections.heading: The contract is with the mechanic, and 35% of it never reaches him
sections.html:
This is the fact that separates CarExamer from an inspection bought from a motoring organisation, and it runs through every document on the site. The inspector terms say the inspector works “as principal on his own account” and that nothing in the agreement makes him an “employee, worker, agent or partner of CarExamer”. The customer terms say the inspection is bought from him, not from the platform. And the money follows that structure: Commission is defined as “35% of the Inspection Fee”, and on completion the payment gateway “shall transfer the Commission to CarExamer” and “transfer the balance of the Inspection Fee to the Inspector”.

That is a normal marketplace arrangement and there is nothing hidden about it — it is printed in the terms anyone can open. It is worth doing the sum, though, because CarExamer's recruitment page advertises that an inspector “could be earning up to £90 an hour!” On the published numbers, a Basic job at £142.99 leaves £50.05 with the platform and £92.94 with the inspector, which over 70 minutes is £79.66 an hour before any travel to the car, the diagnostic equipment he has to own or the insurance he has to carry. A Premium job at £256.99 leaves him £167.04 for three hours, or £55.68 an hour. Those three divisions are ours, not CarExamer's, but the inputs are all the company's own published figures. The advertising-standards guidance on a “from” or “up to” claim asks for a significant proportion of people to reach the advertised figure, and no proportion is published here.

The structure also decides who answers for a bad report. The inspector terms require him to indemnify CarExamer against “any negligent or reckless act, omission or default in the provision of the Vehicle Inspections”, and state that CarExamer is not liable for “any act, omission, negligence or other misconduct by the Inspector”. The customer terms put the same thing from the buyer's side: “Our sole liability relates to the provision of the CarExamer Platform to you.” The platform sells the booking. The mechanic sells the opinion.

sections.heading: Five years in the trade and a Level 2 certificate
sections.html:
CarExamer publishes its entry bar, which is unusual and useful. Its support pages say “All car inspectors are vetted to a high standard”, that it checks “the qualifications and experience of independent inspectors before they accept bookings”, and that an inspector must be a professional mechanic with at least five years' trade experience, must “Have a minimum level 2 or higher qualification or accreditation in Light Vehicle Maintenance or Repair” and must “Have liability and trade insurance”. The inspector terms define those policies precisely: commercial general liability, professional indemnity and public liability cover.

Set the qualification against the government's own scale and you can see what the floor is. GOV.UK lists a Level 2 qualification alongside “GCSE - grades 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4”, an “intermediate apprenticeship” and a “level 2 NVQ”. Level 3 is where A levels, advanced apprenticeships and Level 3 NVQs sit. So the minimum is the entry-level motor trade qualification, topped up by the five-year experience requirement, which is the part doing most of the work. The firm's own wording allows “qualification or accreditation”, and does not say which accreditations count.

One mismatch is worth flagging because it runs the other way. The recruitment page, which is where an applicant actually starts, lists the equipment an inspector needs and asks about experience, but does not mention insurance at all — while the inspector terms make three separate policies a condition of working. The requirement is real; the page that recruits against it leaves it out.

sections.heading: 97.4% of the cars it looked at had something adverse on them
sections.html:
CarExamer publishes a Car Market Health Index built from its own completed inspections, and it is the most interesting thing on the site. The series starts at 100.0 in 2019 and the latest reading, for a partial 2026, is 64.3 — described on the page as “the lowest recorded in the series”, 35.7 points below the baseline. It is drawn from 2,767 vehicles and 392,822 assessed checklist items, which works out at about 142 recorded checks per car.

The number a buyer should take from it is the one labelled “Vehicles with adverse items”: 97.4% for 2026. On CarExamer's own sample, very nearly every used car inspected had at least one thing recorded against it. The page is careful about what that means — “These findings describe the cars we inspected, rather than every used car in the UK” — and that caveat matters, because people commission an inspection when they are already uneasy. The page also shows an 8.5% adverse rate for the same year without defining how the two percentages relate, and no explanation appears anywhere on it. The second figure is presumably the share of individual checklist items failing rather than the share of cars, but CarExamer does not say so, and a published index should define its own measures.

For outside context, Citizens Advice said on 20 May 2024 that its consumer service had handled “almost 43,000 complaints relating to used cars in 2023 alone”, and that 3.5 million people (15%) were then looking to buy one. Its chief executive, Dame Clare Moriarty, put it as: “Year after year problems with used cars top the charts of consumer issues our expert advisers help with.” That is the market a £142.99 inspection is sold into.

sections.heading: A road test counted in minutes cannot be set beside one counted in miles
sections.html:
The two national providers both quote the road test as a distance — the AA stops at 10 miles at every tier on its own pages, and the RAC publishes 3, 10 and 20 miles by package. CarExamer quotes 10 minutes on Basic and 15 minutes on Standard and Premium. Ten minutes on a dual carriageway and ten minutes through a town are not the same test, and neither converts into the other provider's number, so the one specification this trade genuinely competes on cannot be compared across the three of them.

The same problem applies to the check counts, in every direction. CarExamer's 100-plus, 200-plus and 300-plus sit against the AA's 98, 214 and 221 and the RAC's 307, all of them published by the firms themselves, and none of them counted to a shared definition. A “check” is whatever each provider decides to list separately. The durations are the honest comparator CarExamer has given the market, and it would lose nothing by printing a mileage alongside them.

On price the picture is clearer. The AA's entry inspection is £110 and the RAC's starts at £132, both below CarExamer's £142.99 — but both of those are national organisations with age limits a 15-year-old car will not clear, and CarExamer sets no published age ceiling beyond a suitability note on the Basic package. For an older car, the comparison moves in CarExamer's favour before anyone mentions price.

sections.heading: What the report says about itself before you read a word of it
sections.html:
CarExamer publishes a guidance note that accompanies every report, and it is unusually blunt. The inspection is “visual and external”, “no dismantling, removal or inspection of any parts has been undertaken”, and “this report in no way constitutes any form of guarantee or warranty”, nor “a guarantee against defects arising in the future”. The customer terms add that “Reports are non-forensic and do not certify the vehicle's originality, authenticity or provenance” and that “all measurements in report's are approximate and based on the inspector's professional judgement”. The seller disclaimer confirms that the inspector “will not remove or tamper with any mechanical components of the Vehicle, including road wheels”.

None of that is a scandal. It is what a two- or three-hour non-invasive inspection can honestly promise, and saying it up front is better than burying it. Two scope questions are worth asking at booking, though. The guidance calls the inspection “visual and external” while the Standard and Premium packages raise the vehicle and include a diagnostic scan and paint thickness readings, which are neither purely visual nor purely external; the two descriptions can be reconciled, but only the inspector can tell you where the line falls on your car. And with the wheels staying on, nobody is looking directly at brake pads, discs or the inner faces of the tyres on any package at any price.

The free tools sitting alongside the paid ones are worth a sentence. CarExamer runs a free MOT history lookup, a free car data check and a vehicle recall check, and the MOT page describes its source only as “Official MOT records”, naming neither the DVSA nor the DVLA. The government publishes the same MOT history free on its own service, so the lookup is a convenience rather than a product. The paid history check is honest about its own limits: asked whether it guarantees a car is safe to buy, the page answers “No”, and says it “cannot confirm the car's current mechanical, electrical, structural or cosmetic condition”.

sections.heading: Four hours to cancel, £60 if you miss it, and three accounts of when you pay
sections.html:
The cancellation ladder is short and it is stricter than a distance-selling consumer would expect. You may cancel “without charge when giving a minimum of 4 hours' notice”; inside that, CarExamer “reserve[s] the right to make a late cancellation charge of £60 on behalf of the Inspector”; and in the final two hours there is no cancellation right at all, with “the full inspection fee” payable. A buyer who books the night before a Saturday viewing and has the car sold from under them at 8am is inside the £60 band before the working day starts.

A service bought at a distance normally carries a 14-day cancellation right under the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013. Where the customer asks for the service to begin inside that window, regulation 36 lets the trader charge a proportionate amount for what has actually been supplied up to the moment of cancellation — which is not obviously the same thing as a flat £60 on a £142.99 booking where no inspector has yet left home. CarExamer's terms make no reference to the 2013 Regulations anywhere. Ask for the statutory position in writing before you accept the charge.

Payment is described three different ways across three of the company's own pages, and they do not all say the same thing. The home page says “you only pay when the inspection is complete” and, a few lines later in its own FAQ, that “Payment is authorised when you book”. The support article says “we will reserve the booking amount on your card on the day of inspection” and “You will only be charged after the inspection is completed”. The customer terms say “you will not be charged until the Vehicle Inspection has been completed”. An authorisation is not a charge, so these can be squared — but they put the hold on your card at booking, on the morning of the inspection and nowhere at all, depending on which page you read, and the money is ring-fenced on your card either way.

sections.heading: No ombudsman, and the initials in the small print are not spelled out
sections.html:
If the report is wrong, the route is set out in the customer terms and it ends in the courts. You “contact the Inspector through our online resolution centre”, and if the matter is unresolved “within 30 days” the terms move to a further examination by “an appropriate body who will be a member of” “I.A.E.A”. The ceiling is set in the same clause: “Max inspectors liability in dispute is fee you have paid for inspection booking” — £142.99 on a Basic job. Where extra history data was bought, the claim limit is the price paid for that data. Clause 13.6 puts disputes under “the exclusive jurisdiction of the English courts”, and no ombudsman or alternative dispute resolution scheme is named anywhere on the site. A vehicle inspection is not a regulated financial service, so there is no Financial Ombudsman behind it either.

The initials are worth unpicking, because the terms never expand them. The automotive body of that name is The Institute of Automotive Engineer Assessors, a registered charity since 5 May 1977 with 13 trustees, gross income of £312.64k and expenditure of £181.70k in the year to 31 December 2024, whose objects run to “the science of their repair; and to further public education therein”. The same three letters belong to an unrelated international body in educational assessment, so a customer searching the abbreviation in the terms will land in the wrong place. One sentence giving the full name would fix it. Note also what the clause does and does not do: a re-examination by an independent engineer settles the technical question, it is not an adjudication, and it does not lift the cap on what the inspector can be made to pay.

The liability cap itself is not outrageous — the RAC's own terms cap at the inspection fee too, and section 57 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 stops a trader excluding liability for a service performed without reasonable care and skill, which puts the price paid on the floor rather than the ceiling of what a court could award. What differs here is who is behind it. At a motoring organisation the cap sits in front of a company with a balance sheet; here it sits in front of a self-employed mechanic and his professional indemnity policy, and CarExamer's own liability stops at the platform.

sections.heading: The law stops at the dealership gate, which is why this product exists
sections.html:
The strongest argument for paying £142.99 to look at a stranger's car has nothing to do with CarExamer. Buy from a trader and the Consumer Rights Act 2015 gives you goods of satisfactory quality and a short-term right to reject. Buy privately and almost none of that applies: section 14 of the Sale of Goods Act 1979 implies a term of satisfactory quality only “Where the seller sells goods in the course of a business”, and opens with the words “Except as provided by this section and section 15 below”. A private seller must describe the car accurately and must own it. They owe you nothing whatever about its condition.

That is the gap an inspection fills, and it is why the arithmetic works even at the top of the range. The Premium package at £256.99 is about 5% of what Citizens Advice puts as a typical used-car spend, and CarExamer's own index says 97.4% of the cars it looked at had something recorded against them. Against a private sale with no quality term behind it, the fee is cheap insurance against the wrong car; against a franchised dealer's used-car warranty it is a second opinion you are paying for twice.

Two structural points to finish on. CarExamer also sells inspections to the other side of the deal — “CarExamer Trusted” offers dealerships “independent inspection evidence” for their own stock — so a report produced for a seller is not the same thing as one you commissioned to your own specification. And it sells a £99 online inspection course (or £299 for a one-to-one session), which it says is part of onboarding for licence and franchise applicants while stating plainly that “Completing it does not by itself guarantee an inspector role, licence or franchise approval”. A firm that trains inspectors, recruits inspectors, franchises inspectors and takes 35% of what they are paid is a platform business first and an inspection business second, and reading its documents in that order makes all of them easier to understand.

pros: The full price list is published including VAT — £142.99, £189.99, £256.99 and £276.99 — with no telephone quote needed
The inspector comes to the car anywhere in the UK, and the report lands within five hours of the inspection starting
Genuinely independent of any dealer: the mechanic has no interest in whether you buy the car
No published upper age limit on the vehicle, where both national providers cap at 20 years
Premium at £256.99 raises the car and adds paint thickness readings, accident-damage checks and video feedback
Multi-car discounts of 10%, 15%, 17% and 20% for two to five inspections at one address — five Basic checks come to £571.96, or £114.39 each
An Engineer's Report for an existing dispute is available from £276.99, with court attendance priced at £500 up front
Inspectors must have five years' trade experience and carry professional indemnity, public liability and commercial general liability cover
The card is only held and charged around the inspection itself, not taken when you book
CarExamer publishes its own condition index with the sample size attached — 2,767 vehicles and 392,822 recorded checks
cons: The most you can recover from a bad inspection is the fee you paid — £142.99 on a Basic job — and there is no guarantee of any size behind the report, unlike the data-check products sold alongside it
No ombudsman or ADR scheme is named anywhere; the escalation route is an online resolution centre, 30 days, an engineer's re-examination and then the English courts
The dispute clause gives only the initials “I.A.E.A” and never expands them, and the same abbreviation belongs to an unrelated international body in education

Two of the company's own pages give different inspector counts on the same day — “30+ Inspectors nationwide” on the home page and “20+ inspectors available” on the coverage page, against 196 cities claimed
Payment timing is described three different ways across the home page, the support article and the customer terms
The entry qualification is Level 2, which GOV.UK lists alongside GCSE grades 4 to 9 and an intermediate apprenticeship; the five-year experience rule is doing most of the work
The recruitment page never mentions the three insurance policies the inspector terms make compulsory

A £60 late cancellation charge applies inside four hours and no cancellation right at all inside two, with no reference anywhere to the 14-day right the 2013 distance-selling regulations normally give
Support runs 10:00 to 18:00 Monday to Friday only, for a service most people use around a weekend viewing
The road test is quoted in minutes rather than miles, so it cannot be compared with either national provider's published figure
Seven straight years of micro-entity accounts mean no turnover is published anywhere, and the SIC code on file is the catch-all 96090 rather than a vehicle testing or repair code
No independent ratings body covers pre-purchase inspections at all, so the 4.9 score from 383 reviews shown on the site is collected and displayed by the seller
verdict: CarExamer is a marketplace with a mechanic at the end of it, and it is clearer about that than most marketplaces manage: the terms say outright that you buy the inspection from the inspector and not from the platform, and that the platform keeps 35% of the fee. At £142.99 for 100-plus checks in 70 minutes it undercuts nothing — the AA starts at £110 and the RAC at £132 — but it will look at a car neither of them will touch, it comes to the car, and the report is back the same day. The price of that structure is the redress: the ceiling is the fee you paid, the counterparty is a self-employed mechanic rather than a national company, and there is no ombudsman behind any of it. Worth booking for an older private-sale car where the alternative is no inspection at all, and worth asking two questions when you do — how many miles the road test will cover, and what the inspector will actually be able to see with the wheels still on.

faqs.q: How much does a CarExamer inspection cost?
faqs.a: Four packages, all quoted including VAT: Basic from £142.99 (100+ checks, up to 70 minutes), Standard from £189.99 (200+ checks, 120 minutes), Premium from £256.99 (300+ checks, 180 minutes) and an Engineer's Report from £276.99 for an existing dispute. Booking several cars at one address takes 10% off two, 15% off three, 17% off four and 20% off five. Every price is a “from” figure and the final number appears in the booking flow.

faqs.q: Who actually carries out the inspection?
faqs.a: A self-employed mechanic, not a CarExamer employee. The inspector terms say he acts “as principal on his own account” and is not an “employee, worker, agent or partner of CarExamer”, and the customer terms say you buy the inspection from him rather than from the platform. CarExamer vets him, takes the booking and keeps 35% of the fee. He must have five years' trade experience, at least a Level 2 qualification in Light Vehicle Maintenance or Repair, and liability and trade insurance.

faqs.q: What can I claim if the inspection misses something?
faqs.a: The fee you paid, and no more. The customer terms say “Max inspectors liability in dispute is fee you have paid for inspection booking”, which is £142.99 on a Basic inspection, and CarExamer's own liability “relates to the provision of the CarExamer Platform”. There is no £30,000-style guarantee attached to the inspection. You would raise it in the online resolution centre, and if it is unresolved after 30 days the terms point to a re-examination by an independent engineer, then the English courts.

faqs.q: Can I cancel a booking?
faqs.a: Free of charge with at least four hours' notice. Inside four hours CarExamer may charge £60 on the inspector's behalf, and in the final two hours there is no cancellation right and the full fee is payable. Nothing on the site mentions the 14-day cancellation right that the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 normally give on a service bought at a distance, so ask about the statutory position in writing if you are charged.

faqs.q: Will the inspector take the wheels off or get underneath the car?
faqs.a: No wheels come off at any price — the seller disclaimer says the inspector “will not remove or tamper with any mechanical components of the Vehicle, including road wheels”. The Basic package does not raise the car at all; Standard and Premium do. The guidance note that accompanies the report describes the whole exercise as “visual and external” with “no dismantling, removal or inspection of any parts”, and says the report “in no way constitutes any form of guarantee or warranty”.

faqs.q: Is CarExamer a big company?
faqs.a: CAREXAMER LTD was incorporated on 22 December 2017 as GLOBALCARCHECK LTD and renamed on 4 October 2018, and is registered at 124 City Road, London EC1V 2NX. It has filed micro-entity accounts every year since, most recently for the year to 31 December 2025, so no turnover figure is published anywhere. Its own pages claim 3,000-plus inspections completed, 196 cities covered and somewhere between 20 and 30 inspectors depending which page you read.

title: Carmoola Car Finance Review: Rates, Limits and What It Won't Fund
meta_title: Carmoola Car Finance: What 14.9% APR Really Buys You
meta_description: Carmoola lends direct with no dealer arranging the deal. Representative 14.9% APR, £2,000 to £40,000, used cars only. The rates, rules and gaps, checked.

headline.label: Representative APR
headline.value: 14.9% APR representative — hire purchase and PCP, with personalised rates from 9.9% to 29.9%

intro:
Carmoola lends its own money straight to the buyer at a representative 14.9% APR, and the dealership plays no part in arranging the loan. You get a budget on your phone before you go shopping, pay the dealer with a Carmoola card, and the garage never touches the credit application. Carmoola Limited is company 12992987, incorporated on 3 November 2020 at 1 Whittlebury Mews West, Primrose Hill, London NW1 8HS, and is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference number 958057.

Borrowing starts at £2,000, no deposit is required, and the only named charge is a £1 option-to-purchase fee at the end. On the lender's own worked example, £12,500 over 60 months at 14.9% fixed costs £290 a month, £4,901 in interest and £17,401 in total. An indicative budget takes 60 seconds, most applicants are fully approved within one to two working days, and the budget then stays open for 30 days while you look. Every figure on this page was re-read on 11 October 2026 from Carmoola's own pages, its published complaints reports and the public registers.

One rule decides whether any of this is relevant to you. Carmoola funds used cars only, bought from one of the dealerships on its network — "no vans, motorbikes or new cars" and "no private sellers, unfortunately", in its own words. Diesels must be registered from September 2015 onwards. If the car you have in mind is a van, a bike, a nearly-new registration or a private sale, this is not the lender for it.

sections.heading: What £12,500 costs on each of the two plans
sections.html:
Carmoola publishes a representative example for both products, and the difference between them is the whole argument about which to take. On hire purchase, £12,500 over 60 months at a representative 14.9% APR with a £0 deposit gives a monthly payment of £290, a total cost of credit of £4,901 and a total amount payable of £17,401, including the £1 option-to-purchase fee. Pay the last instalment and the car is yours, with — the lender's phrase — "no mileage limits" along the way. Both examples were unchanged when re-read on 11 October 2026.

On PCP, the same £12,500 over 48 months at the same 14.9% gives 47 payments of £267 followed by an optional final payment of £5,001. The total cost of credit is £5,050 and the total amount payable £17,550. The monthly figure is £23 lower and the total is £149 higher, and at the end you either find £5,001, hand the car back, or start a fresh agreement on a different car. That final payment is set from the predicted value of the car at the end of the term, which Carmoola calls the Guaranteed Minimum Future Value. Hand the car back and any mileage over the agreed allowance is charged — its own guidance says the rate "can reach 15p per mile, but it can vary" — along with anything beyond fair wear and tear.

The 14.9% is a representative rate, not a promise. Carmoola's eligibility checker states "personalised rates between 9.9% and 29.9% APR", and under the FCA's consumer credit rules in CONC 3.5 a representative APR only has to be available to at least 51% of the customers who take out the advertised product. Half of accepted applicants can be paying more than the number on the poster and the advert is still compliant. Worth knowing before you play with the calculator: its default illustration prices £12,500 at 9.9% APR for £221.00 a month, the very bottom of the published ladder, five percentage points below the rate the same site advertises as representative. On the £12,500 over 60 months in the formal example, the gap between 9.9% and 29.9% runs to thousands of pounds, so the figure that matters is the one in your own quote.

sections.heading: Who can borrow, and on what sort of car
sections.html:
The personal criteria are light: 18 or over, UK resident, proof of identity and address, and a credit and affordability check. Carmoola says it weighs current affordability rather than the credit score alone. The initial budget comes from a soft search that other lenders cannot see, and the hard credit check runs only after you have signed your agreements and are ready to buy — generous, unusual, and worth understanding before you sign rather than after.

The vehicle rules do far more filtering, and the lender sets them out as a plain list: "Petrol, diesel (from Sept 2015 only), hybrid or electric cars", "Cars sold at one of our approved dealerships (no private sellers, unfortunately)" and "Used cars (no vans, motorbikes or new cars)". On hire purchase the car must be less than 15 years old by the end of the agreement with less than 100,000 miles on the clock. On PCP the bar rises sharply: under 10 years old by the end of the agreement and under 70,000 miles, which rules out a large slice of the cheaper end of the forecourt. Annual mileage on a PCP is usually set between 6,000 and 12,000 miles.

The September 2015 diesel line is not arbitrary. It is the point at which Euro 6 became the standard for new registrations, and Euro 6 is exactly what Transport for London requires of a diesel car to avoid the Ultra Low Emission Zone daily charge — petrol cars only need Euro 4. A diesel that fails Carmoola's date test is generally the same diesel that would cost its owner a daily charge to drive into central London, so the rule protects the resale value of the security as much as anything else. On the other side of that trade, the market is moving the lender's way: diesel was the weakest fuel in the last used-car quarter SMMT has published, down 7.2% on 620,045 sales, while battery electric rose 67.0% to 110,761.

sections.heading: Where the money behind the loan comes from, and the accounts that followed
sections.html:
Carmoola was founded in March 2021 and its app launched in March 2022, which makes it young for a lender carrying its own credit risk. It has raised in stages: a £27 million seed round in April 2022 from investors including Jaguar Land Rover's venture arm; an £8.5 million Series A and a £95 million debt facility announced together on 22 February 2023; £15.5 million of further equity in January 2024; and a £300 million private asset-backed securities facility, which its own press centre says "brings the company's funding to over £540 million". That figure supersedes the roughly £146 million that stood as the total in January 2024. There are two dedicated funding vehicles on the register, Carmoola Funding 1 Limited (13325050, incorporated 9 April 2021) and Carmoola Funding 2 Limited (15641838, incorporated 13 April 2024), both active.

Scale is still harder to pin down, because a company that has raised over half a billion pounds continues to file small-company accounts. Carmoola Limited filed its accounts for the year to 31 December 2025 on 28 September 2026, two days inside the deadline, running to 17 pages; the previous set, for the year to 31 December 2024, was filed on 24 September 2025 and ran to 14 pages. Both are small-company filings, so no turnover, no loan book and no profit figure is published anywhere. The document itself could not be opened for this review, so only the filing is quoted here, not the numbers inside it. Note that the Companies House overview page was still serving the pre-filing position when checked on 11 October 2026 — "Next accounts made up to 31 December 2025 due by 30 September 2026" — while the filing history showed the accounts already in. The filing history is the record to trust.

What Carmoola does publish is counters, and they disagree with each other in a way that is worth a reader's scepticism rather than their alarm. Its refinance page reads "Trusted by 5900151 customers who applied" while its home page gives "20,000+" under "UK drivers sorted" — a ratio of nearly 300 applications to each completed loan, which is only coherent if the first number counts clicks on an eligibility check rather than people. The press centre separately says the app "has since processed around four million loan applications in the three years since the app first came to market". The dealership network is given three different ways on the same site: "9,000+" on the car finance page, "9780+" on the dealership page, and "over 10,000 dealerships across the UK" in the how-it-works questions. None of this is a scandal. It does mean no single audited number describes the business.

sections.heading: The £7.5bn redress scheme: three doors, and Carmoola has none of them
sections.html:
The defining story in UK car finance is money going backwards, and where a lender stands in relation to it is the most useful thing a review can establish. On 28 July 2020 the FCA announced a ban on discretionary commission models — arrangements that let a dealer or broker raise the interest rate a customer paid and be paid more for doing it — and the ban took effect on 28 January 2021, with the regulator estimating it would save customers £165 million a year.

The redress scheme followed in policy statement PS26/3 on 30 March 2026. It reaches finance taken out between 6 April 2007 and 1 November 2024, makes 12.1 million agreements eligible, and the FCA puts total redress at £7.5bn on an assumption that 75% of eligible consumers claim, at an average of around £830 an agreement. Read the scope closely and there are exactly three doors into it, and all three are held open by somebody standing between the lender and the buyer. The first is a discretionary commission arrangement, which the FCA describes as the case where "their dealer or broker set the interest rate to earn more commission". The second is commission of "at least 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan". The third is a tied arrangement, where "the dealer or broker was using one lender or gave one lender the right of first refusal". Commission of £120 or less before 1 April 2014, or £150 or less from that date, is excluded outright.

Carmoola's agreements sit inside the scheme's date range — it began lending in March 2022, comfortably between April 2007 and November 2024 — so it is not the dates that keep it out. What keeps it out is that every one of those three doors runs through a dealer or a broker, and in a Carmoola purchase neither arranges the credit: the customer applies in the app, the loan is approved before a car is chosen, and the garage is paid by Faster Payments like any other seller, usually the same day. No intermediary means no commission to mark up, to measure against the total cost of credit, or to tie to one lender.

The scheme itself, meanwhile, is not running. On 2 July 2026 the Upper Tribunal ordered a partial suspension on terms agreed with four challengers — Consumer Voice, represented by Courmacs Legal, together with Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services and Crédit Agricole Auto Finance. Until the Tribunal process concludes, lenders are "not required to calculate or pay redress, or send communications about compensation owed under the scheme". Everything else still binds: firms must keep identifying relevant complaints and agreements, gather commission and disclosure data, and answer complainants who are not owed compensation. The hearing is listed for 14 to 18 December 2026 or 16 to 26 February 2027, and the FCA expects payments to begin in 2027 if the scheme is upheld and not appealed. The dates that matter to a reader with a complaint in: an agreement from 1 April 2014 onwards, complained about by 30 June 2026, should get an answer by 18 November 2026; an older agreement complained about by 31 August 2026, by 18 January 2027; anything later, within five months. The separate complaint-handling pause under DISP App 5 expired on 31 May 2026.

sections.heading: Ending it early: what the 1974 Act gives you
sections.html:
Hire purchase and PCP are both regulated agreements under the Consumer Credit Act 1974, and that statute hands the borrower two exits that most finance advertising never mentions. Section 99(1) says that "at any time before the final payment by the debtor under a regulated hire-purchase or regulated conditional sale agreement falls due, the debtor shall be entitled to terminate the agreement by giving notice". Section 100(1) then caps what that costs: the borrower is liable "to pay to the creditor the amount (if any) by which one-half of the total price exceeds the aggregate of the sums paid and the sums due".

In practice that means once you have paid half the total amount payable, you can hand the car back and walk away owing nothing further. On the £17,401 hire purchase example, half is £8,700.50 — reached at around instalment 30 of 60. Two conditions bite. Section 100(4) allows the lender to add a sum where the borrower "has contravened an obligation to take reasonable care of the goods", so a damaged car still costs money. And section 100(3) lets a court order a smaller payment where the lender's actual loss was less, which cuts the other way.

Settling in full rather than terminating is the other route, and section 94 of the same Act gives the right to do it at any time with a rebate of interest. Carmoola confirms that "Early Settlement Quotes are valid for 28 days", and that "other fees may apply and you will still be charged interest" — without saying anywhere what those fees are. A 28-day quote on a figure that keeps accruing is a narrow window, and it is the one number in this part of the product the lender does publish.

sections.heading: The used market it is lending into
sections.html:
Carmoola only funds second-hand cars, so the health of that market is the health of its book — and the half of it that matters most to a lender has turned down. The Finance & Leasing Association's July 2026 release, published on 23 September 2026, reports its members financing 117,156 used cars in the month, down 7%, on advances of £1,819m, down 8%. Over the twelve months to July 2026 that is 1,382,326 used cars, down 2%, on £21,628m, flat at 0%. New car finance went the other way entirely: 740,677 cars and £21,143m over the same twelve months, both up 14%, and 54,313 cars on £1,549m in July alone, both up 10%. FLA members financed over 85% of private new car registrations in 2024. Geraldine Kilkelly, the association's Director of Research and Chief Economist, called it "a consumer car finance market that remains broadly resilient".

Do the division and the useful fact falls out. Used volumes fell 2% over the year while the total advanced held still, so the average amount financed per used car rose by roughly the same 2%, to about £15,650. That is the signature of rising prices on a shrinking number of transactions, and it is also the exact environment in which fixing the rate for the whole term — which both Carmoola products do — is worth more than it is in a falling one. Three months earlier, on the May 2026 release, used finance was down 5% on both volume and value and new finance up 12%, so both halves of the picture have moved since.

Unit sales, as opposed to finance, are the other half of the same paragraph, and here the most recent quarter SMMT has published on its own site is still Q2 2026, released on 11 August 2026: 2,009,318 used cars changed hands, up 0.7%, with 4,025,550 in the first half, up 0.2%. Battery electric reached 110,761, up 67.0%, for a 5.5% share; hybrids took 6.5% on 130,825 sales, up 31.2%, while plug-in hybrids slipped 6.8% to 22,856. Petrol at 1,121,243 and diesel at 620,045 still account for 86.7% between them. Superminis lead on 31.7% and lower-medium cars on 26.6%. SMMT had not published a Q3 figure on its own used-car pages when this page was checked, so nothing from that quarter is quoted here.

sections.heading: Sell My Car, and the first payment the site admits moving between it and a dealer
sections.html:
Carmoola now runs a second service alongside the lending, and it answers a question the finance side of the business has always left open. Its legal hub now carries Sell My Car customer terms, last updated 23 March 2026, and a separate set of dealership terms. The service "helps you find dealers in our network who may want to buy your car", and clause 1.4 states plainly that it is not a consumer credit product.

For the seller it is free, and the terms say so twice: clause 11.2 reads "Carmoola does not charge you any listing fee, success fee, commission or other customer fee for using the Service". For the dealer it is not. Clause 6.4 reads "Carmoola charges participating dealers a standard fee for completed sales", and clause 2.5 calls it a "fixed fee from the dealership purchasing your vehicle". The amount is nowhere in the document. That is the first place on the whole site where money is acknowledged to move between Carmoola and a dealership, and the shape of it is the right shape: a fixed fee per completed sale cannot be flexed by the size or the rate of anything, which is precisely the defect the FCA's 2021 ban was aimed at.

Two things a seller should know before using it. The contract is not with Carmoola on either count: clause 2.6 says "the contract for the purchase of your vehicle is between you and the purchasing dealer, not between you and Carmoola", and clause 17.5 says "these Terms are between you and Moola Asset Management Limited only" — a different legal entity from the lender. Moola Asset Management Limited is company 14712041, incorporated on 7 March 2023 at the same NW1 8HS address, with SIC code 70221 for financial management and Carmoola Group Limited recorded as its controlling party since 20 November 2024. It was dormant for the year to 31 December 2023, filed total exemption accounts for 2024 on 23 September 2025, and on 11 October 2026 Companies House showed it carrying the warning "Accounts overdue": its accounts for the year to 31 December 2025 were due by 30 September 2026 and nothing has been filed since a confirmation statement on 23 March 2026. The lender filed on time; the entity behind the free service has not.

sections.heading: What the site does not publish
sections.html:
For a lender that leans on transparency, the pre-sale paperwork is thin, and it was no thicker on 11 October 2026 than it was a month earlier. There is no specimen credit agreement, no pre-contract credit information document and no tariff of charges anywhere on the site. No late payment charge, default charge, arrears fee or missed payment fee is stated. The legal hub carries website terms, app terms, a complaints policy, a cookie policy, two privacy notices, an AI assistant policy, a mobile operating system support policy, the two Sell My Car documents and two promotional documents — and the app terms say in terms that they "do not apply to financial products or services offered by Carmoola", which closes off the obvious place a reader would look. The £1 option-to-purchase fee is still the only charge named anywhere on a finance product. A borrower cannot find out what missing a payment costs until they hold an agreement. The footer's own signpost to MoneyHelper, the government-backed free money guidance service, points at "#_" rather than at MoneyHelper.

The commission promise has been reworded since this page was written, and the new version is weaker. The sentence quoted here before — "We don't pay variable commissions based on interest rate or loan size. We don't reward upselling" — was a precise denial of the banned practice. The dealership page now says instead that "Carmoola doesn't receive commission from customer purchases" and "doesn't offer preferential rates for using Trusted Dealerships". Both are about money coming in rather than going out, and neither says what a dealership receives. Its August 2025 commentary adds "No hidden incentives. No markups. No middlemen trying to make more money by giving you a worse deal", which is a principle rather than a disclosure. The Sell My Car terms, as above, are the only document on the site that names a payment to a dealer at all.

Three smaller things. That August 2025 piece is the only commentary the site carries on the biggest story in its market, and it closes by noting that the FCA "has said it will announce its intentions to consult on such a scheme by Monday, 4th August, 2025" — fourteen months before this page was checked, and two regulatory stages behind where the scheme now stands. The refinance page advertises "Save up to £200 per month by switching to Carmoola", "Based on a sample of 1,378 customers who refinanced with Carmoola", and still does not say what proportion of them achieved it; the Advertising Standards Authority's published guidance on savings claims asks for a significant proportion of customers to reach the advertised figure and treats under 10% as unlikely to qualify. And two promotions remain published on the legal hub long after expiry: the free Warrantywise warranty, marked "no longer active", and the £75 Amazon voucher offer, which applied to vehicles bought on or before 22 June 2025.

sections.heading: The complaints numbers, now that they can be read
sections.html:
Complaints go to 020 3773 3901 between 8am and 8pm daily, to complaints@carmoola.co.uk, or by post to 1 Whittlebury Mews West, London NW1 8HS, and the lender promises a guaranteed update after four weeks and a written response within eight weeks. After that a customer has six months from the final response letter to take the case to the Financial Ombudsman Service on 0800 023 4567. To its credit Carmoola publishes its own half-yearly complaints returns, which most lenders of its size do not — and unlike the last time this page was written, both reports now open and can be read.

They are not comfortable reading. In the six months to 30 June 2026 Carmoola opened 2,294 complaints, a rate of 314 per 1,000 accounts or loans, closed 8.6% of them within three days and a further 80% after three days but within eight weeks — the two columns are separate, so 88.6% inside eight weeks — and upheld 44%. In the preceding half, to 31 December 2025, it opened 1,262 at 180 per 1,000, closed 3% within three days and 81% after three days but within eight weeks, and upheld 48%. So the volume has grown 82% in six months and the rate per 1,000 accounts by three quarters, while the uphold rate has eased four points and the speed of the quick wins has nearly trebled. Two things in Carmoola's favour are stated in its own notes: it records "all customer concerns as complaints, including issues relating to the quality of vehicles supplied under hire purchase agreements" even though vehicle quality is "not directly within Carmoola's control" — a wider net than the rules oblige — and the three-day and eight-week percentages exclude anything caught by a complaints-handling pause.

That pause is the figure a reader should sit with. Of the 2,294 complaints opened in the first half of 2026, 1,606 are recorded as paused, against 782 of 1,262 in the half before. The footnote explains why: "Complaints relating to motor commission arrangements are currently on hold while wider industry guidance is being finalised." Seven in ten of this lender's complaints in that half are commission complaints it cannot resolve. Being outside the redress scheme's three doors, as above, does not mean being outside the queue: the FCA's unsuspended rules still require Carmoola to identify those complaints, gather the commission and disclosure data behind them, and tell each complainant who is not owed compensation — by 18 November 2026 or 18 January 2027 depending on the agreement date — while the Upper Tribunal decides whether the scheme stands at all.

The sector context is not flattering to anybody. The Ombudsman's annual data, published on 21 May 2026 for 2025/26, records 37,673 new hire purchase (motor) complaints at a 24% uphold rate, plus 5,816 conditional sale (motor) cases at 24% and 346 point-of-sale motor loans at 22%, against 214,600 new complaints across all products and a 30% average. Independent ratings for credit are scarce — Defaqto rates insurance policies, not loans, so there is no star rating here and no ribbon to point at. The usable figure is Smart Money People, which scores Carmoola's car finance at 4.86 out of 5 from 1,118 individual reviews. Note the date: the most recent of those reviews is from 26 August 2026, so the sample has not moved in six weeks and the score is a customer-satisfaction reading collected after the fact rather than an assessment of the terms.

pros: Lends its own money direct, with no dealer or broker arranging the finance — which is what keeps it outside all three routes into the FCA's £7.5bn redress scheme
Fixed rate for the whole term on both hire purchase and PCP, with no deposit required and borrowing from £2,000
Soft credit search for the budget; the hard search only runs once you have signed
Budget stays valid for 30 days, so you can shop with a firm number in hand; 60 seconds for an indicative figure and one to two working days to full approval
The only named fee on a finance agreement is the £1 option-to-purchase charge at the end of a hire purchase deal
Unlimited free vehicle history checks while you shop, and the dealer is paid by Faster Payments, usually the same day
Publishes its own half-yearly complaints returns with volumes, uphold rates and response times, which most lenders its size do not — and counts vehicle-quality disputes it is not obliged to count
4.86 out of 5 from 1,118 reviews on Smart Money People, the one independent score that covers credit
Sell My Car is free to the seller: no listing fee, success fee or commission, with the dealer paying a fixed fee instead
cons: No specimen credit agreement, pre-contract credit information or tariff of charges is published anywhere on the site, so the cost of a missed payment, an arrears letter or a default is invisible until you hold an agreement
Personalised rates run to 29.9% APR, double the 14.9% headline, and under CONC 3.5 that headline only has to be available to 51% of accepted customers
The calculator's default illustration prices the loan at 9.9% APR, the very bottom of the published range and five points below the site's own representative rate
2,294 complaints opened in the six months to 30 June 2026, a rate of 314 per 1,000 accounts against 180 in the previous half, with 44% upheld
1,606 of those 2,294 complaints are paused as motor commission complaints the lender cannot resolve while the Upper Tribunal case runs — seven in ten of the half's total
Used cars only, from an approved dealership — "no vans, motorbikes or new cars", no private sellers, and no diesel registered before September 2015
PCP is limited to cars under 10 years old and under 70,000 miles, which rules out much of the cheaper end of the used market

The commission wording has been watered down: "Carmoola doesn't receive commission from customer purchases" replaces a specific denial of paying variable commission, and no finance page says what a dealership receives
The "save up to £200 per month" refinance claim, drawn from a sample of 1,378 customers, still does not say what proportion of them achieved it

Over £540 million raised and still only small-company accounts: the year to 31 December 2025 was filed on 28 September 2026 in 17 pages, with no turnover, loan book or profit figure published anywhere
Moola Asset Management Limited (14712041), the entity behind Sell My Car, was marked "Accounts overdue" at Companies House on 11 October 2026, its 2025 accounts having been due by 30 September
Dealership numbers are given three different ways on one site — 9,000+, 9780+ and over 10,000 — and the footer's MoneyHelper link points at "#_" rather than at MoneyHelper
Two promotions that have expired, the Warrantywise warranty and the £75 voucher that closed on 22 June 2025, are still published on the legal hub
verdict: Carmoola is the rare car finance company whose structure answers the thing that has gone wrong with car finance, and re-reading the scheme's own scope makes the case better rather than worse: all three routes into the FCA's £7.5bn redress scheme run through a dealer or a broker, and a Carmoola purchase has neither. The rate is fixed, the only named fee on the agreement is £1, the budget is good for 30 days, and the new Sell My Car service charges the dealer a fixed fee and the seller nothing. Against that, 14.9% is representative rather than typical, the ceiling is 29.9%, the calculator shows you 9.9%, and no fee schedule or specimen agreement is published for anyone to read before applying. Its own complaints return is the hard part: 2,294 complaints in six months at 314 per 1,000 accounts, 44% upheld, and 1,606 of them frozen as commission complaints until the Upper Tribunal rules in December 2026 or February 2027. Being outside the scheme is not the same as being outside the argument. If your car is a used petrol, hybrid, electric or post-2015 diesel from a dealer, this is a strong option and the quote costs a soft search. If it is a van, a bike, a new car or a private sale, look elsewhere.

faqs.q: Am I covered by the car finance compensation scheme?
faqs.a: Not through a Carmoola agreement, and the reason is the scheme's scope rather than its dates. PS26/3 of 30 March 2026 reaches 12.1 million agreements taken out between 6 April 2007 and 1 November 2024, and there are three ways in: a discretionary commission arrangement, commission of at least 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan, or a tied arrangement. All three need a dealer or broker arranging the credit, and in a Carmoola purchase neither does. The scheme is also partly suspended: on 2 July 2026 the Upper Tribunal froze the obligation to calculate or pay redress pending a hearing listed for 14 to 18 December 2026 or 16 to 26 February 2027, with payments expected in 2027 if it is upheld. If you have an older agreement arranged in a showroom, that one is worth raising with the lender who wrote it.

faqs.q: Does Carmoola pay dealerships commission?
faqs.a: On finance, no page on the site says either way. The dealership page states that "Carmoola doesn't receive commission from customer purchases" and "doesn't offer preferential rates for using Trusted Dealerships" — both about money coming in, not going out. The only document that names a payment to a dealer is the Sell My Car terms of 23 March 2026, where clause 6.4 says Carmoola "charges participating dealers a standard fee for completed sales" and clause 2.5 calls it a fixed fee. The amount is not published. In practice the dealer plays no part in the credit application: the loan is approved first and the garage is paid by Faster Payments like any other seller.

faqs.q: How many complaints does Carmoola get, and does it publish them?
faqs.a: It does, every six months, and both reports are readable. In the six months to 30 June 2026 it opened 2,294 complaints, a rate of 314 per 1,000 accounts or loans, closed 8.6% within three days and 80% after three days but within eight weeks, and upheld 44%. In the half to 31 December 2025 the figures were 1,262 complaints at 180 per 1,000, 3% and 81%, and 48% upheld. Of the 2,294, some 1,606 are paused as motor commission complaints awaiting the Upper Tribunal. Carmoola also records vehicle-quality disputes as complaints even though the cars are not its own, which inflates the count in its favour.

faqs.q: What credit score do I need?
faqs.a: Carmoola does not publish an acceptance threshold or a minimum score. Its eligibility checker says personalised rates run between 9.9% and 29.9% APR, and that it weighs current affordability and the overall financial profile rather than the score alone. You need to be 18 or over and a UK resident. The initial budget comes from a soft search that other lenders cannot see, so checking costs nothing; the hard credit check is run only after you have signed.

faqs.q: Can I hand the car back before the end?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 99 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 lets you terminate a regulated hire purchase or conditional sale agreement at any time before the final payment falls due, and section 100 caps the liability at one half of the total price less what you have already paid. On the £17,401 hire purchase example that is £8,700.50, reached at around the thirtieth of sixty payments. The lender can add a sum if the car has not been reasonably looked after. Settling in full instead is a section 94 right, and Carmoola's settlement quotes are valid for 28 days.

faqs.q: How much can I borrow, and over how long?
faqs.a: Hire purchase runs from £2,000 to £40,000 in £500 steps and PCP from £2,000 to £55,000, both over terms offered in nine lengths from 12 to 60 months. No deposit is required, though the calculator accepts up to £20,000. The representative example is £12,500 over 60 months at 14.9% APR fixed, giving payments of £290 and a total amount payable of £17,401 including the £1 option-to-purchase fee.

faqs.q: What happens at the end of a PCP agreement?
faqs.a: On the published example you make 47 payments of £267 and then choose one of three things: pay the optional final payment of £5,001 and keep the car, hand it back, or start a fresh agreement on a different car. That £5,001 is set from the car's predicted value at the end of the term, which Carmoola calls the Guaranteed Minimum Future Value. Handing it back triggers charges for mileage above the agreed allowance, usually set between 6,000 and 12,000 miles a year and charged at a rate Carmoola says "can reach 15p per mile, but it can vary", and for any damage beyond fair wear and tear.

faqs.q: Will Carmoola buy my car as well as finance one?
faqs.a: It will introduce you to a dealer who might. Sell My Car, whose customer terms were last updated on 23 March 2026, "helps you find dealers in our network who may want to buy your car". It is free to you — no listing fee, success fee or commission — and the dealer pays a fixed fee on a completed sale. Two things to note: the sale contract is between you and the buying dealer rather than Carmoola, and the terms themselves are with Moola Asset Management Limited, company 14712041, a separate entity at the same address. It is not a credit product and carries none of the protections of one.

title: Carphone Warehouse New Phone Contract Deals: The Real 24-Month Cost
meta_title: Carphone Warehouse Contract Deals: What 24 Months Costs
meta_description: Carphone Warehouse pay monthly deals from £11.99, the April rises that take them to £15.59, trade-in values, and what happens when the 24 months end.
intro:
Carphone Warehouse lists 131 pay monthly handset deals and does something most phone shops still avoid: it prints the price you will be paying at the end of the contract next to the price you start on. A Samsung Galaxy A16 4G shows as £11.99 a month, increasing to £15.59, with £5.00 up front. A Google Pixel 10a 128GB is £14.99 rising to £18.59. A Samsung Galaxy A57 5G is £19.99 rising to £23.59. Delivery is free and next-day seven days a week on mainland UK orders, an old handset can be traded in against the bill, and an existing customer can move to a new deal free of charge up to 75 days before the current one runs out.

Every deal on that page is a bundled contract: one monthly figure covering the phone and the airtime together, on a 24-month minimum term, with no separate finance agreement behind it. That single structural fact decides almost everything else on this page — what the deal really costs over two years, what happens on the day the term ends, and which regulator's rules you are relying on if something goes wrong. It is worth understanding before you pick a handset, because the arithmetic is not difficult and the retailer has already published every number you need to do it.

The choice is between two networks. iD Mobile carries 100 of the 131 handset deals and Vodafone the other 31, with Vodafone's own dedicated page listing 101 devices from £13.00 a month, increasing to £18.00, on up-front costs running from £9.00 to £199.00. A Samsung Galaxy S26 FE sits at £29.00 a month with £39.00 up front. Alongside the handset deals there are 72 SIM-only plans — Vodafone 46, iD Mobile 22 and VOXI 4 — starting at £6.00 a month for 10GB with unlimited minutes and texts on a one-month rolling term.
