sections.heading: The part of a car's life that stops at the Channel
sections.html:
A British vehicle check is built on British registers. The finance search, the stolen marker, the write-off category and the National Mileage Register readings all begin when a car is first registered here, and the Department for Transport's own definition of an import is exactly that: “vehicles imported into the UK at the point of first UK registration”. There were 682,375 first registrations in the April to June quarter of 2026, inside a licensed fleet of 42.9 million vehicles, on figures published on 23 September 2026.

For a car that spent five years in Germany or the Netherlands before someone shipped it over, that is the whole problem. HMRC gives an importer 14 days to notify the arrival through NOVA, the Notification of Vehicle Arrivals service, and the DVLA will not register the car until that is done — but neither step creates any record of what happened to the vehicle abroad. A UK check on that car can be entirely clean and entirely accurate at the same time.

carVertical is built the other way round. Its report sections include odometer readings, accident and damage history, theft records checked “against theft databases worldwide”, ownership history, a title check for US-registered vehicles, recalls, historical photographs, market value, whether the car was used as a taxi, rental or fleet vehicle, and a timeline of ownership changes, inspections and MOT records. The help centre is careful to say that “not all sections may appear in every carVertical report” and that data access varies by country.

The sharpest evidence that this gap is real comes from the incumbent rather than the challenger. HPI's own guarantee page promises up to £30,000 for inaccurate or incomplete information — and then excludes “the vehicle's descriptive information (including import status), mileage, value”. The British standard-setter will not stand behind import status. That is the ground carVertical is standing on.

sections.heading: The name on the website is not the name on the contract
sections.html:
Clause 1.2 of the UK terms is blunt about it: “carvertical.com is managed and administered by Sovian Epublishing Limited, company number 16582008, address 1 Princeton Mews, 167-169 London Road, Kingston Upon Thames, Surrey, England KT2 6PT (hereinafter – carVertical)”. Everything the terms go on to call “carVertical” is that company.

Companies House has it incorporated on 15 July 2025 — three months before this page was written — as a private limited company under SIC code 82990, “Other business support service activities not elsewhere classified”, with two officers and no resignations: a single director, Rokas Medonis, Lithuanian and resident in Lithuania, and a corporate secretary, M & N Secretaries Limited (03775091). Its first accounts are made up to 31 December 2026 and are not due until 15 April 2027, so there is no turnover figure, no balance sheet and no trading history published anywhere.

The data sits elsewhere. The vehicle data privacy notice, last updated on 18 February 2026, names three joint controllers: UAB “cV Group”, legal entity code 303134915, of Aukštaičių Str. 7, Vilnius; carVertical OÜ, legal entity code 14416655, of Narva mnt. 5, Tallinn; and Sovian Epublishing Limited. The Android app is published by CV GROUP, UAB at the same Vilnius address. Vehicle data “shall be retained for 30 years” from the date carVertical receives it.

Two of those facts are worth more to a buyer than the corporate trivia suggests. The contract is governed by English law, which is better than the alternative for anyone who has to enforce it. And the English company that signs it was formed in July 2025 and has filed nothing beyond a confirmation statement dated 14 July 2026.

sections.heading: Why you cannot find out what it costs before you start buying
sections.html:
On 17 October 2026 the pricing page at carvertical.com/gb/pricing returned a complete page with the pricing block showing the word “Loading” and three dashes where the plans should be. This is not a block: the page opens, the prices are fetched by the browser afterwards. The home page was read twice the same day and carried the claim “Save up to 40% to leave no car unchecked” without a single pound figure beside it, and the company's own articles on free checks, discount codes and outstanding finance all link to the pricing page rather than naming a price.

What the site does publish is the shape of the discount. The discount-code article states that “Comparing two cars cuts the report cost by 32%. Three is 45%”, that genuine codes “tend to sit in the 20 to 30% range”, that partner coupon sites offer “around 20%”, and that the built-in bundle discount “is bigger than most codes you'd find online”. The 45% on three reports and the home page's “up to 40%” do not agree, and neither carries a date.

The mechanics behind the missing number matter as much as the number. A purchase buys credits rather than one search: the help centre says “credits are valid 6 months after purchase”, a business subscription of 10 or 30 reports a month expires 30 days from the purchase date, and an account is created automatically once you have paid. So the cheapest route for a buyer looking at one car and the cheapest route for a buyer comparing three are different products, and the price of neither can be read without entering a checkout.

For context on what that price is being measured against: on the same day, the AA's own page offered “a single comprehensive vehicle history check for just £14.99” or five at “£6 per vehicle”, and HPI's own site offered its full check at £19.99, a Basic Check at £9.99 and a MultiCheck of three for £29.99. A reader who wants to know whether carVertical undercuts any of that has to begin a transaction to find out.

sections.heading: Nobody here is promising you £30,000
sections.html:
The British checks compete on a guarantee, and they print the number on the sales page. The AA's vehicle check page says “We guarantee you up to £30,000 to cover any inaccuracies in your report”, and notes that the checks “are provided by HPI Limited”; HPI's own site shows a “£30,000 guarantee” beside its £19.99 check. HPI's guarantee page sets the maximum at “up to £30,000 (£15,000 for written off vehicles)”, “valid for two years from the date of the check”, covering “reimbursement of financial loss you suffer arising from inaccurate or incomplete information”, with condition data capped at “up to £15,000 or 50% of the market value of the car, whichever is the lower” — and the page itself warns that it “may not be up-to-date with current terms”.

carVertical publishes no equivalent. The terms define a Report as “a digital publication (e-publication) that provides an analytical summary of a vehicle's history”, warn at clause 4.6.2 that “the information provided in the Report may not always accurately reflect all the facts of the vehicle” and at 4.6.5 that it “should not be the sole basis for making a decision to purchase or refuse to purchase a vehicle”, and then deal with the consequences of being wrong in a single line each: clause 10.1 says liability “is determined in accordance with applicable legal acts”, and clause 10.2 says that if the information “does not correspond to reality”, liability “is assessed in accordance with applicable law”. No sum, no cap, no claims process.

What is published instead is a return of the report. A check that comes back with no mileage records, no damage records and no timeline events is a “no-findings report”, and the system “will automatically add an unused report to your account”, live for six months. Anything else has to be asked for: email support with the VIN, the purchase date and an explanation, “within 30 days of generating the report”, after which “requests submitted after this period will not be accepted”. The remedy for a report that was wrong is another report.

Set against the British alternative, that is the trade. One side pays out money it has promised in advance on a narrow set of facts and excludes import status; the other searches wider, promises nothing in writing and hands back a credit.

sections.heading: The 14-day right dies the moment the report opens, and the law has a condition attached
sections.html:
Clause 7.1 of the UK terms gives the ordinary distance-selling right: a buyer may “without giving a reason, cancel such purchase within 14 days”, with money back “no later than within 14 days from the date of receipt” of the notice. Clause 7.2 then removes it for anything used — “the Right of Withdrawal does not apply to used Reports”, “as the service is considered to be fully provided at the time of vehicle history report generation” — while unused reports in a package keep the 14 days and part-cancelled packages are refunded proportionally.

That is a recognised position in UK law, with a condition on it that the terms do not spell out. Regulation 37 of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 is headed “Supply of digital content in cancellation period”, and it says a trader “must not begin supply of the digital content before the end of the cancellation period” unless the consumer has given express consent and acknowledged that the right to cancel will be lost. Regulation 37(4) then says the consumer bears no cost at all for content supplied where that consent was not given, or was given without the acknowledgement.

So the clause stands or falls on what the checkout asks you to tick, and the checkout is behind the payment page that also hides the price. Worth reading the box carefully before you confirm — the right exists until you knowingly give it up, and the words “you will lose your right to cancel” are the ones that do it.

sections.heading: Four counts of its own sources, and one rollback figure in two units
sections.html:
Read enough of carVertical's pages and the same quantity comes out differently each time. The UK home page says the search is “verified against 1000+ trusted sources across 45 countries” and that the company is “trusted by 6,000,000+ people across 37 countries”, with a second line on the same page putting it at “4.5+ million people”. The help centre says “over 900 trusted sources” on one article and “over 1000 trusted sources worldwide” searching “across 40+ countries” on another. The page explaining who owns the data says “hundreds of third-party sources”. The leasing page claims “1 000+” sources, “2 000 000+” unique users a year, and both “37 countries” and “38” markets in the same screen.

The mileage claim is the one that actually changes a figure a reader might use. The UK home page says a rolled-back odometer here is “off by around 35,000 miles on average”. The company's own transparency index for the United Kingdom gives the average rollback as “35,147 km”, which is about 21,840 miles. Both are carVertical's numbers, the digits are the same and the units are not, and nothing on either page is dated in a way that settles which is current. The same index page is served with a title reading “UK Used Car Market Transparency Index 2024” while its year selector shows 2026, and its methodology describes 12 months of report data running October to September without naming the sample size.

The index itself will not tell you which way its own number points. Its methodology says the “Market Transparency Index measures the level of potentially hidden or false information provided to a customer when buying a used car”, which makes the UK's 120.5 — the highest of the 23 countries listed — the worst result on the board; the page's own headline and description present first place as Britain being transparent. The page never reconciles the two, and it does not publish how the six weighted factors behind the score are combined, so the sub-rankings are the only part a reader can use directly: 7th of 23 on damaged cars, 13th on clocked odometers, 20th on average damage value and 1st on the size of the average rollback.

The damage figures sit in the same position: “around £2,100 per record” on the UK home page against an “average damage value” of €5,621 on the index. Those may well be measuring different things — a record against a vehicle — but neither page says so, and the counters further down the home page for cars checked, clocked vehicles found and damaged vehicles detected did not render at all on either read.

sections.heading: There is no regulator behind any of this, and the dispute route is unnamed
sections.html:
A vehicle history report is a data product, not a financial service. There is no FCA permission to look up, no Financial Ombudsman line, no claims-acceptance statistic and no ratings agency scoring the sector. That is true of every provider in this category, and it is the reason the paperwork each one publishes is the only thing a buyer can actually test.

carVertical's own escalation route is thin. Inaccuracies are reported “by filling out a special report form” at carvertical.com/gb/contacts, after which “carVertical will take reasonable steps to verify the information”. Clause 12.1 sends disputes to negotiation and then to “a competent court in accordance with the provisions of the applicable law”, and clause 12.3 says a UK-resident user may “contact an accredited Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) provider” — without naming one, which is a difficulty, because approved ADR schemes are sector-specific and no provider is signed up to hear complaints about vehicle data reports. The vehicle data privacy notice mentions “the right to lodge a complaint with the data protection supervisory authority” and does not name the Information Commissioner's Office either.

The security claim has the same shape. The information security policy states that the group holds “ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification” covering “all information technology products and related projects in the UAB ‘CV Group’ and carVertical OÜ”, and names no certification body, no certificate number and no expiry date. The claim is probably sound and it is entirely unverifiable from the page that makes it — which is a shame, because an external audit is a better argument than any of the marketing copy around it.

One practical consequence of the missing price: Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 only makes a card issuer jointly liable where the cash price is more than £100, so a cheap report almost certainly falls below it. A chargeback through the card scheme, or the county court for sums up to £10,000, is what is left.

pros: Covers the half of a used car's life that no British register holds: a report is searched against records in 40-plus countries, which is the whole point on an import
Sold under the law of England and Wales, with a UK company named on the contract and a UK address on it
A report with no mileage, damage or timeline records at all is handed back automatically as an unused credit, with no email and no argument
The free VIN decoder returns make, model, year and engine details without payment, and GOV.UK gives the MOT record away, so two of the easy checks cost nothing
Publishes its own dated market research rather than only marketing copy: the UK index gives 41.12% damaged, 3.98% clocked and an average damage value of €5,621

Says plainly that it does not own or create the data, that “not all events are recorded” and that the report “should not be the sole basis” for a purchase — which is more candour than the category usually offers
cons: No price is published anywhere a reader can see it before entering the checkout: the pricing page served “Loading” and three blank placeholders on 17 October 2026, and the home page carried no figure on two separate reads the same day

No data guarantee of any kind. Where HPI promises up to £30,000 for two years, carVertical's terms say only that liability “is assessed in accordance with applicable law”, and the published remedy for an empty report is a replacement credit rather than money

The company on the contract, Sovian Epublishing Limited, was incorporated on 15 July 2025 under the catch-all SIC code 82990 and has no accounts due until 15 April 2027, so nothing about its size or solvency is published

Its own pages give four different counts of its data sources (900, 1000, 1 000+ and “hundreds”), four different country counts (37, 38, 40+ and 45) and three different user figures (6,000,000+, 4.5 million and 2,000,000+ a year), none of them dated
The average UK odometer rollback is “around 35,000 miles” on the home page and “35,147 km” on the company's own transparency index — the same digits in two different units, which cannot both be right

The 14-day cancellation right is removed as soon as a report is generated, and the terms never set out the acknowledgement that regulation 37 of the 2013 Regulations requires before that removal bites

No named dispute route: the terms point a UK buyer at “an accredited Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) provider” without naming one, and the privacy notice refers to the “data protection supervisory authority” without naming the ICO
The ISO/IEC 27001:2022 claim comes with no certifying body, certificate number or date, and the transparency index page is served with a 2024 title while displaying 2026 data
verdict: Buy it for the car that has lived somewhere else. carVertical's reach across 40-plus countries is a real advantage over a British check whose records begin at first UK registration — and the strongest evidence for that is HPI's own guarantee, which excludes import status from the £30,000 it promises. For a car that has spent its whole life on British plates, the calculation is less kind: the free GOV.UK MOT history already gives you the mileage at every test since 2005, and the paid British checks put money behind their finance and write-off answers while carVertical puts a credit behind its. Add in a price you cannot see until you are in the checkout and a contract held by a company formed in July 2025, and this is a report worth buying for one specific job rather than as the default first check on any used car.

faqs.q: How much does a carVertical report cost in the UK?
faqs.a: carVertical does not publish it. The pricing page at carvertical.com/gb/pricing loaded with the word “Loading” and three blank placeholders on 17 October 2026, the UK home page carried no figure on two reads the same day, and the company's own help and blog articles link to the pricing page without naming a number. The only published prices are relative: 32% off per report when you check two cars and 45% off when you check three, against a home-page claim of “up to 40%”. For comparison, on the same day the AA offered an HPI-provided check at £14.99 for one vehicle or £6 each for five, and HPI's own site offered £19.99 full, £9.99 basic and three for £29.99.

faqs.q: Does a carVertical report show outstanding finance on a UK car?
faqs.a: Its report list includes a “Financial and legal status” section covering “financing limits, such as leases”, and the company's own UK article on outstanding finance says a report “can flag whether a car carries an active finance record”. What neither page does is name the British register the answer comes from, and the help centre says data access varies by country and that “not all sections may appear in every carVertical report”. If outstanding finance is the only thing you need answered, a check that names its finance source is the safer purchase.

faqs.q: What happens if the report turns out to be wrong?
faqs.a: There is no compensation scheme. Clause 10.2 of the UK terms says that where the information “does not correspond to reality”, liability “is assessed in accordance with applicable law”, and clause 4.6.4 says carVertical “will take reasonable steps to verify the information” once you report it. A report with no mileage, damage or timeline data at all is returned to your account automatically as an unused credit valid for six months. Anything else has to be raised by email with the VIN and the purchase date within 30 days, and requests after that window “will not be accepted”.

faqs.q: Who am I actually buying from?
faqs.a: Sovian Epublishing Limited, company number 16582008, of 1 Princeton Mews, 167-169 London Road, Kingston Upon Thames KT2 6PT, which clause 1.2 of the terms says manages and administers the site. It was incorporated on 15 July 2025 with one director resident in Lithuania. The data behind the report is controlled jointly by that company, UAB “cV Group” of Vilnius (303134915) and carVertical OÜ of Tallinn (14416655). The contract is under the law of England and Wales.

faqs.q: Is any of this free?
faqs.a: Partly. carVertical's VIN decoder returns the make, model, year and engine details without payment, and GOV.UK's MOT history service gives every test result since 2005, including the mileage recorded at each test, for nothing. Between them those two cover the specification and the recorded mileage. What they do not cover is damage abroad, theft markers, write-off categories, finance or historical photographs, which is what the paid report is for.

title: Carwow Sell My Car
meta_title: Carwow Sell My Car: Free to You, Dealers Pay From £199
meta_description: Selling through Carwow costs you nothing — free listing, free collection, payment on the day. The buying dealer pays from £199. Checked 17 October 2026.

headline.label: What selling costs you
headline.value: £0 — free listing, free collection and payment on collection day, with the buying dealer paying Carwow a fee from £199

intro:
Selling a car through Carwow costs the seller £0. There is no listing fee, no admin charge and nothing to pay for collection, and the car goes into one of Carwow's daily online auctions in front of what its own sell-my-car page calls “6,000+ trusted dealers”. Figures checked 17 October 2026 against Carwow's consumer pages, its dealer help centre, its terms of use and Companies House.

The money has to come from somewhere, and Carwow is more open than most about where. Its trade-facing auction page tells dealers that “Buyers fees start from as little as £199” with “no subscription”, and that its payment service, Carwow Wallet, is “Free when you use it, and free when you don't”. The dealers placing those bids have taken 345,000 vehicles off the platform since the auctions launched in 2021, and Carwow puts the current flow at 22,000-plus fresh cars a month, measured as the monthly average from August 2025 to July 2026. A seller who knows the winning dealer owes £199 or more on top of the hammer price reads that bid rather better than one who does not.

Two rules decide whether you can use the service at all, and both are published before you start. Carwow will not auction a car that has been a service vehicle — it names ambulances and taxis — or an insurance write-off. It will auction a car with finance still on it, and the buying dealer settles that finance “at no cost to you, the seller”, but where the winning bid falls short of the settlement figure “you will have to cover any shortfall yourself”. No age limit, mileage limit or condition threshold appears anywhere on the consumer pages.

sections.heading: The £199 nobody tells the seller about, and why it still matters
sections.html:
A free service for one side of a transaction is paid for by the other, and Carwow publishes its half of that arithmetic where most marketplaces do not: on carwow.co.uk/partners/auctions, written for the trade. Dealers are told buyer's fees “start from as little as £199” and are “on average 5% cheaper than our closest competitor”, that there is “no subscription”, and that Carwow Wallet settles “the seller, finance house and buyer's fees” in a single transfer at no charge. Bidding runs on an automatic proxy: “You only ever pay £1 over the next highest bid, and it never goes past your limit.”

None of that is hidden and none of it is improper. It does change how a bid should be read. A dealer working out the most it can pay for your car subtracts its own costs first, and the £199-plus fee is one of them, alongside transport, preparation and the margin it needs on resale. The seller sees a single number on a screen; the dealer sees that number plus its fee. On a £5,000 car a £199 fee is four pence in every pound of the bid.

The same trade pages price a risk the private seller cannot buy cover against at all. Carwow BuySafe costs “just £59 per vehicle”, covers “3,000 mechanical and electrical parts, including all internal engine and gearbox components” up to “£7,500”, and pays out “within 48 hours of invoice receipt”. Carwow's own survey of dealers, published 1 October 2024, found that “96% of dealers have bought cars that later required major repairs”, something it says “typically affects 20% of sourced stock”. For £59 the buyer can insure itself against your car. You get no equivalent, and no ombudsman, if the deal goes wrong in the other direction.

sections.heading: Your reserve price is Carwow's suggestion, built on a rival's data
sections.html:
The consumer pages describe the reserve as “the amount you'd be happy to sell your car for”. The dealer help centre, in an article dated 13 July 2026, is fuller and more interesting: Carwow “propose a Reserve Price that aligns with real-time market value”, based on the vehicle's appraisal and Auto Trader retail data, and defines it as “the minimum price both Carwow and the seller have agreed the vehicle can be listed for before auction”. Cars that do not meet Carwow's price guidelines never enter the auction.

Two things follow that no competitor page sets out. The first is that the floor under your car is calculated by Carwow from a competitor's retail index, and you agree to it rather than name it. The second is that the published mechanics are precise enough to work out what your reserve really buys you. A bid at or above the reserve with nothing else above the reserve “will win the listing at the Reserve Price” — not at the bidder's maximum. Where two bids clear it, the higher wins, and the proxy steps up in £1 increments. Where two identical maximum bids land on the reserve, “the first bid received will win”. Carwow also sets a Minimum Bid Amount per vehicle, below which no bid may be entered at all, and reserves the right “to refuse or remove bids and/or suspend, cancel or extend listings at our absolute discretion”.

Miss the reserve and the car is not sold, but it is not finished either. The best offer is “presented to you as the highest offer and you will have the opportunity to accept or relist into the next available auction”; the trade side calls that the holding pen, with the highest offering dealer, and lets a dealer add an Increase Offer or buy outright at the asking price. Carwow shows an unsold car “for two additional days”, after which it is “tagged as ‘unsold' and will be taken off the platform”. You can “end a listing at any time without prior notification to the bidders”, which is a genuine and unusual freedom — most auction terms bind the seller once bidding opens.

sections.heading: What the terms say happens when the dealer is standing on your drive
sections.html:
This is the part of a sell-side deal that decides whether the number you accepted is the number you bank, and Carwow publishes it. “The car buyer or their agent or our collection company will inspect your car prior to the transfer of payment.” The buyer “shall be entitled to withdraw its bid if upon inspection the information or photos disclosed by you in your listing was incomplete or inaccurate”, or if you have “engaged in fraudulent or misleading behaviour (and no price adjustment can be agreed)”, or where “there is outstanding finance which has not been fully disclosed”, or if the car “fails the test drive”. Four named grounds, published in advance, is a better disclosure than a general discretion to re-price.

And the sentence that matters most to a seller is in your favour: “You do not have to accept an amended purchase price.” Set that beside the obligation running the other way — sellers agree “to sell the car once the bid is successful in accordance with these terms of use” — and the balance is clearer than on most platforms. The collection itself is free to you because the car “must be collected from you directly at the buyer's sole cost”.

Three limits sit alongside it. Carwow “does not purchase any vehicles itself, nor does it acquire any risk or title to any vehicle”; “Carwow is not party to this contract of sale”, which the buyer may ask you to sign on its own paper; and the company “shall have no liability in the event that payment is made by the car buyer but the car is not delivered or is not as described”, adding that it is “not obliged to assist in any disputes between sellers and bidders or car buyers”. Payments made through Carwow Wallet are “processed by Airwallex” into the bank account you nominate. The terms also warn, sensibly, that outside the document collection service “no bank or other financial details should be shared via our site”.

sections.heading: Finance, the V5C, and the three clocks you are running against
sections.html:
Selling a financed car through Carwow turns on a settlement letter, and the requirements are specific: the name on it must match the car's V5C, and it must have “at least 7 days remaining” when the dealer collects. Carwow's own guidance adds the two figures a reader needs to plan around — a lender must provide a settlement figure “within 12 days” of being asked, and the letter is “typically valid for 10 days”. The buying dealer settles the agreement on collection, you keep “any surplus cash from the sale once the remaining finance amount has been settled”, and you fund any negative equity yourself. Carwow says it accepts cars with outstanding finance without naming which agreement types qualify, so a lease or a personal contract hire is worth a telephone call before you list.

The third clock is statutory and nothing to do with Carwow. Regulation 22 of the Road Vehicles (Registration and Licensing) Regulations 2002 requires a registered keeper selling to a private buyer to hand over the new keeper's slip and “forthwith deliver the remainder of the registration document to the Secretary of State”, completed with the buyer's name and address, the date of sale and signed declarations from both parties. Failing to comply with a regulation made under the Vehicle Excise and Registration Act 1994 is an offence under section 59(1) of that Act, punishable on summary conviction at “level 3 on the standard scale” where the Secretary of State has prescribed it as such and “level 2 on the standard scale” otherwise — £1,000 and £500 respectively. Which level attaches to regulation 22 depends on what has been prescribed, and that could not be established from the legislation pages; the widely repeated “£1,000 fine” is the level 3 maximum rather than a figure the regulations themselves state. Selling to a dealer through Carwow puts the car into trade hands, which is a different branch of the same regulations, so the practical advice stands either way: notify DVLA the day the car leaves, and keep the acknowledgement.

sections.heading: Who owns the auction, and who owns the reviews
sections.html:
Carwow Ltd is company 07103079, incorporated on 12 December 2009 under the name Digital Blurb Limited and renamed on 4 December 2015. Its registered office is 2nd Floor, Verde Building, 10 Bressenden Place, London SW1E 5DH, and its SIC codes are 58142, publishing of consumer and business journals and periodicals, and 62090, other information technology service activities. The publishing code is not an accident. In February 2024 Carwow bought Autovia, bringing Auto Express, Carbuyer, evo and DrivingElectric — and the Driver Power owner satisfaction survey — into the group, for an undisclosed sum, reaching “over 15 million car owners, buyers and enthusiasts every month”. Carwow's own release said the titles would be retained and named the opportunity: “embedding Carwow's e-commerce offering” across them.

It is also authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority “for credit broking and insurance distribution activities (firm reference number: 767155)”, and the group discloses that Carwow and Carwow Leasey Limited “may receive a commission from partners (including dealers) for introducing customers”. Publishing the firm reference is worth crediting: the comparable page on this site for a rival marketplace could establish no FCA permission at all.

The most recent corporate news is a retrenchment dressed, fairly, as focus. On 25 August 2026 Carwow Group and mobile.de announced “a definitive agreement for mobile.de to acquire Carwow Germany”, with terms undisclosed, subject to regulatory clearance, and with Carwow.de taking “a perpetual licence to use the Carwow brand rights in Germany” on completion. Chief executive John Veichmanis said the deal “allows us to sharpen our focus as we continue to innovate and accelerate our growth in the UK and Spain”. For a British seller that is good news: the UK is now one of two markets rather than one of three.

On the numbers, the newest figures Carwow itself has published are for 2024, in a release dated 29 September 2025: group revenue up 55% to £85.1m from £54.8m, an adjusted EBITDA loss narrowing to £6.7m, headcount from 338 to 509, and “over 75,000 cars sold, generating £1.1bn Gross Merchandise Value” through Sell My Car. Group accounts for the year to 31 December 2025 were filed at Companies House on 1 October 2026, running to 61 pages; the document would not open to this check and Carwow has issued no results release to go with it, so the 2024 figures above are the latest the company stands behind in public.

sections.heading: The market your car is being bid into
sections.html:
Two official datasets tell a seller more about timing than any valuation tool. The Department for Transport's vehicle licensing statistics for April to June 2026, published 23 September 2026, count 42.9 million licensed vehicles in the UK, up 1.5% on a year earlier, of which 34,888,140 were road-using cars at the end of the quarter. Zero emission vehicles reached 2,313,000, up 30.7%, taking 5.4% of all licensed vehicles, a gain of 1.2 percentage points; 2,017,093 of those are cars, which is 5.8% of the road-using car fleet. An electric car is still an unusual thing on a dealer's forecourt, and that is reflected in how confidently it gets bid for.

The second is the price direction. The ONS series for second-hand cars within CPIH, released 16 September 2026, shows an annual rate of -2.5% in August 2026, having run at +0.4% in March, -0.4% in April, -0.6% in May, -1.2% in June and -1.9% in July. Five consecutive months of deepening falls in what buyers actually pay is an argument for selling sooner rather than holding on for a better quarter, and it is the opposite of the picture the used market showed in 2024.

Against that, Carwow's own throughput looks healthy: 22,000-plus fresh vehicles a month in the daily auctions on the August 2025 to July 2026 average, auctions running Monday to Saturday, and 345,000 cars collected since 2021. Depth of bidding is the one thing a seller cannot create and cannot verify, and volume is the best available proxy for it.

sections.heading: Where Carwow's own pages stop agreeing with each other
sections.html:
The service is well documented. It is not consistently documented, and on a page about what your car is worth the inconsistencies are worth naming.

The dealer count has two values. The sell-my-car page and the about-us page both say “6,000+” trusted dealers. The sell-to-a-dealer page says “5,500+”, three times on one page, and the financed-car page says “5,500+” as well. Neither number is dated, and a 500-dealer gap is roughly the difference between the two figures being a year apart.

The volume figure is out by a factor of three, in Carwow's favour. The consumer pages say “Dealers like you have acquired over 100,000 vehicles with us already”. The trade auction page says 345,000 “based on volumes of actual vehicles collected since launch in 2021”. A brand understating its own scale by 245,000 cars on the pages a seller actually reads is a curious way to compete, and it is the clearest sign that the consumer copy is not being refreshed as often as the trade copy.

Same-day payment is a feature on one page and a tendency on another. The sell-my-car page lists “Free same-day payment” as a benefit and says the dealer “can pay you there and then”. The sell-to-a-dealer page is careful: “Most payments arrive on the same day as your car is collected”, adding that “some dealers have their own policies”. The terms of use, which are what govern a dispute, require only that the buyer “must pay for your car promptly following its collection”. Three documents, three strengths of promise, and the weakest one is the binding one.

Two headline claims come without their workings. “Most Carwow sellers surveyed got an average £1,000 more vs part exchange quotes” and “Nine out of 10 people who sold their car thought” they got the price they expected or more are both presented without a sample size, a survey date or the proportion of customers reaching the £1,000 figure — the last of which is what the advertising guidance on savings claims asks for. The about-us page carries the same undated quality: “Last year we grew over 50% with nearly £3 billion worth of cars bought on our site” has sat there across at least two financial years.

And there is no ombudsman at the end of any of it. Carwow's FCA permissions cover credit broking and insurance distribution; buying and selling a used car is not a regulated activity, so a dispute over the sale of your car falls outside the Financial Ombudsman Service, outside the motor industry's purchase-side codes, and back onto the contract you signed with the dealer. The published complaints route is the buyer first, then Carwow's support team on hello@carwow.co.uk or 0204 586 4000, and after that the county court.

pros: Genuinely free to the seller — no listing fee, no admin fee, no collection charge and nothing for Carwow Wallet
Carwow publishes what the buying dealer pays, “from as little as £199” with no subscription, which almost no marketplace does
The bid-withdrawal grounds are named in advance rather than left to a general discretion, and “you do not have to accept an amended purchase price”
A seller can “end a listing at any time without prior notification to the bidders”, which is unusually generous for an auction
Cars with outstanding finance are accepted and the buying dealer settles the agreement “at no cost to you, the seller”
Daily auctions Monday to Saturday, a sale possible in as little as 24 hours, and two extra days of exposure if the reserve is missed
The firm reference number (767155) and the corporate disclosures are published openly, and the dealer help centre explains the auction mechanics in more detail than the sales pages
345,000 cars collected since 2021 and 22,000-plus fresh vehicles a month gives a credible depth of bidding
cons: The reserve price is proposed by Carwow from the appraisal and Auto Trader retail data, not named by you, and cars outside Carwow's unpublished price guidelines never reach the auction
A bid that clears the reserve with nothing above it wins “at the Reserve Price” rather than at the bidder's maximum, so an agreed reserve can become a ceiling as easily as a floor
The £199-plus buyer's fee is a real cost of the transaction that is deducted before a dealer decides what to bid, and it is disclosed only on the trade pages
Same-day payment is sold as a feature but the terms require only payment “promptly following” collection, and the company accepts no liability if payment is made and the car is not as described
The dealer count is “6,000+” on two pages and “5,500+” on two others, and the cars-purchased figure is “over 100,000” on the consumer pages against 345,000 on the trade page
No published age, mileage or condition limit, so the first a seller hears of being outside the price guidelines is when the car does not enter an auction
The £1,000-better-than-part-exchange and nine-out-of-ten claims carry no sample size, date or proportion of customers achieving them
No ombudsman covers the sale of a car, Carwow is “not party to this contract of sale”, and it is “not obliged to assist in any disputes” — leaving the county court
Carwow has published no results release for the 2025 financial year even though group accounts were filed on 1 October 2026, so the newest figures it stands behind in public are 2024's
verdict: As a way of turning a car into money quickly, Carwow's auction is one of the better-documented options in the UK, and the documentation is what recommends it. The seller pays nothing, collection is free, finance is settled by the buyer, and the four grounds on which a dealer may walk away after inspection are published in advance alongside the plain statement that you do not have to accept a reduced price. Few platforms commit that much to writing, and fewer still tell you, as the trade pages do, that the winning dealer owes a fee from £199 on top of the hammer price. Read the bid in that light and the number makes more sense. The two things to go in with your eyes open about are the reserve and the recourse. Carwow proposes the reserve itself, from a competitor's retail data, and a lone qualifying bid wins at that reserve rather than at the bidder's maximum — so the figure you agree before the auction is doing more work than the word “minimum” suggests. And if the deal sours after the car has gone, there is no ombudsman: Carwow is not a party to the sale and says it is not obliged to help. Agree a reserve you would be content to be paid exactly, notify DVLA the day the car leaves, and keep the settlement letter and the acknowledgement. On those terms, a free sale in 24 hours to one of several thousand bidding dealers is a fair deal.

faqs.q: Does Carwow charge anything to sell a car?
faqs.a: No. Carwow says selling is “completely free” with “no hidden costs, no admin fees, nothing”, and that covers the listing, home collection and the Carwow Wallet payment service. The cost sits on the other side of the deal: Carwow's trade auction page tells dealers that buyer's fees “start from as little as £199” with no subscription, and the car “must be collected from you directly at the buyer's sole cost”.

faqs.q: Who decides the reserve price?
faqs.a: Carwow proposes it and you agree it. The dealer help centre, in an article dated 13 July 2026, says Carwow will “propose a Reserve Price that aligns with real-time market value” based on the car's appraisal and Auto Trader retail data, and describes the reserve as the minimum price “both Carwow and the seller have agreed”. Watch the mechanics: where one bid meets or exceeds the reserve and no other does, that bid “will win the listing at the Reserve Price” rather than at the bidder's maximum.

faqs.q: Can the dealer reduce the price after seeing the car?
faqs.a: It can withdraw its bid on four published grounds — incomplete or inaccurate listing information or photos, fraudulent or misleading behaviour where no price adjustment can be agreed, undisclosed outstanding finance, or the car failing the test drive — and it may offer you a lower figure instead. The terms are explicit that “you do not have to accept an amended purchase price”, so the choice at that point is yours.

faqs.q: Can I sell a car that still has finance on it?
faqs.a: Yes. You need a settlement letter in the same name as the V5C with “at least 7 days remaining” on collection day; a lender must supply the figure “within 12 days” of being asked and the letter is “typically valid for 10 days”. The buying dealer settles the agreement “at no cost to you, the seller” and you keep any surplus, but if the winning bid is below the settlement figure “you will have to cover any shortfall yourself”.

faqs.q: What happens if my car does not sell at auction?
faqs.a: The highest bid below your reserve is “presented to you as the highest offer” and you can accept it or relist into the next auction. Carwow shows an unsold car for “two additional days”, during which a dealer can increase its offer or buy at the asking price; after that it is “tagged as ‘unsold' and will be taken off the platform”. You can also end a listing yourself at any time.

faqs.q: Which cars will Carwow not auction?
faqs.a: Carwow says it can help “so long as your car hasn't been a service vehicle (think ambulances, taxis etc.) or an insurance write-off”. Beyond that, no age, mileage or condition limit is published on the consumer pages, though the dealer help centre notes that vehicles failing to meet Carwow's price guidelines do not enter the auction — so a very cheap or very tired car may be turned away without a published rule to point at.

faqs.q: If something goes wrong with the sale, who can I complain to?
faqs.a: Carwow's route is the buyer first, then its support team on hello@carwow.co.uk or 0204 586 4000. There is no ombudsman beyond that: Carwow's FCA permissions (firm reference 767155) cover credit broking and insurance distribution rather than vehicle sales, and the terms state that “Carwow is not party to this contract of sale” and that it is “not obliged to assist in any disputes between sellers and bidders or car buyers”. That leaves the contract with the dealer and, if necessary, the county court.

title: Catered Ski Chalets
meta_title: Catered Ski Chalets: No ATOL, No ABTA, a Dutch Bond
meta_description: Five chalets from 490 per person a week, and a financial protection position UK skiers should read twice. The bond it holds is not the one it appears to name.

headline.label: Cheapest catered week
headline.value: From 490 per person per week — Gerlos, Austria. Currency not published

intro:
CateredSkiChalets.com advertises a catered chalet week from 490 per person, and we cannot tell you in what currency. The price appears on its own pages as a bare number — the markup is literally 490 followed by “p.p.p.w.” with no symbol and no code. Every fee elsewhere on the site is in euros, so euros is the likely answer, but a UK skier comparing prices should not have to guess and we are not going to guess on their behalf.

The bigger thing to know before you book is the protection. This is a Dutch tour operator, Skichalets.nl, Chamber of Commerce number 78683297. It holds no ATOL and no ABTA bonding. Its cover is a Dutch scheme called SGR, membership number 3494.

And on every page, including the payment page, the footer says “Financial protection by The Trust Associaton”. There is no body of that name. The UK body it resembles is the Travel Trust Association — which this operator is not a member of, and names only as a comparison.

sections.heading: The protection position, carefully
sections.html:
This section matters more than the price, so here is exactly what the operator says and exactly what it means.

The operator’s own words: it holds “a fully-bonded membership in The Netherlands of the financial travel protection authority SGR, comparable with The Travel Trust Association, ATOL and ABTOT in the United Kingdom”. SGR is Stichting Garantiefonds Reisgelden, a real and long-established Dutch guarantee fund. The membership number given is 3494, and the operator notes the warranty certificate is available “only in Dutch”.

It claims the cover reaches UK customers: “not only our Dutch guests, but also all other international guests of ours are fully insured for a guaranteed refund of all your payments made to us, in the unlikely event of insolvency”, and “you won’t receive just a partial refund, but the full 100%”. There is a €10 mandatory consumer contribution per booking — per booking, the site is careful to say, not per person.

What it is not. It holds no ATOL licence; ATOL appears on the site only as a comparator. It is not an ABTA member — ABTA is not mentioned anywhere on the site at all. It is not ABTOT bonded and not a Travel Trust Association member. There is no client trust account; the protection is a bond, which is a different thing.

Why that may not matter much here, and where it does. No flights are sold. The word “flight” does not appear anywhere on the site; it sells chalet weeks plus optional transfers, lift passes, hire and lessons. ATOL covers flight-inclusive packages, so for an accommodation-only booking the ATOL question largely falls away. Where it bites is enforcement: if you book your own flights and the operator fails, your money sits behind a Dutch bond enforced in the Netherlands, with a certificate you cannot read, rather than behind a UK scheme. That is a workable position for some people and an unacceptable one for others, and it should be a conscious choice.

The naming is the real problem. “Financial protection by The Trust Associaton” in the footer of every page, with that spelling, is not a description of SGR. A UK reader seeing it on the payment screen could reasonably conclude they are covered by the Travel Trust Association. They are not.

sections.heading: What you actually get for the money
sections.html:
The catered package is well specified, which is to the operator’s credit. Per week it includes:

  • 7 nights’ accommodation
  • Daily breakfast — described as “a hearty continental breakfast” of fresh baguettes, eggs, cereals, fruit and hot drinks, prepared and cleared by staff
  • Afternoon tea on your return — “a sweet and salty afternoon tea” with homemade snacks, plus mulled wine, vin chaud or hot chocolate
  • A three-course dinner on six days, with free unlimited red and white wine served during the meal
  • Beer, soft drinks, juices, coffee and tea free and unlimited all day from the chalet fridge. Spirits are not included
  • Bed linen, towels, cleaning, and English-speaking Dutch chalet staff who cook, clean, shop and make beds. Towels changed midweek

Note the six days, not seven. The staff take one day off during your stay: “They still serve breakfast that day, but you make your own tea and coffee and usually eat out.” Budget for one restaurant dinner per person per week, and for drinks that evening, which are not covered.

Special dietary requirements “may carry a supplement”, with no figure published.

sections.heading: Five chalets, four resorts, and a country that is not there
sections.html:
The whole estate is five chalets, which the operator owns and runs rather than brokering — “the chalets are our exlusive properties so we can completely tailor the arrangement to your wishes”, in its own words and its own spelling. Trading since 1993.

ChaletResortFrom, per person per week
DenggGerlos, Zillertal Arena, Austria490
Selva PanoramaSelva Val Gardena, Dolomites, Italy590
AngelinaSt Anton, Ski Arlberg, Austria650
BlanchotLes Menuires, Three Valleys, France850
AlpkristallSt Anton, Ski Arlberg, Austria925

Three countries: Austria, France and Italy. The About page claims “our top resorts in the Austrian, French, Swiss and Italian Alps” — and no Swiss chalet is listed among the five.

The offers page is worth a look because it undermines the “from” prices. Blanchot appears as “Was 1550, Now 1150” per person per week, and Selva Panorama as “Was 1390, Now 1090”. Both discounted prices are higher than the “from” figures on the main listing — 1150 against 850, and 1090 against 590 — with no dates on any of the four numbers to explain the gap. The “from” price is presumably a quiet week in a shoulder season, but nothing on the site says which.

sections.heading: The booking terms, which are strict
sections.html:
To book: 25% of the total holiday cost, plus a €35 booking charge, plus the tourist tax, plus the €10 SGR contribution. Due seven days after the confirmation invoice is emailed. Book within six weeks of arrival and the full amount is due one day after the invoice.

Balance: at least six weeks before arrival.

Cancellation, calculated from the date written notice is received, and applied to the holiday cost plus the booking charge, the tourist tax and the SGR contribution:

When you cancelYou lose
More than 16 weeks before25% of the total
16 weeks to 3 weeks before90% of the total
Inside 3 weeks, including arrival day100%

That middle band is the one to notice. Cancel fifteen weeks before your holiday — nearly four months out — and you forfeit 90%. Most operators scale cancellation charges gradually; this goes from 25% to 90% at a single step, and the step is a long way from departure. If you book this, insure it the same day.

There is no snow guarantee. The booking conditions “exclude compensation for snowfall, avalanche danger, and weather conditions” and exclude liability for closed ski lifts. A poor season is entirely your risk.

sections.heading: The extras, and how they add up
sections.html:
The headline price is not the price. On top:

  • Tourist tax — “different per town between €1,50 and €5 p.p.p.n.”. For two people over seven nights that is between €21 and €70. Children under 12 are mostly free.
  • €35 booking charge and €10 SGR contribution per booking.
  • €25 per partial invoice if you split the payment on a whole-chalet booking.
  • Card fees of 4.5% on both Mastercard and Visa. On a €2,000 booking that is €90. iDEAL Wero costs €0.39, Bancontact €0.49 and Apple Pay is free. There is also a €2,500 cap per credit card transaction, so a larger booking has to be split — and splitting may trigger the €25 invoice fee.

In your favour: no caution deposit. Booking a whole chalet gets 30% off per adult above the chalet’s lower capacity figure, and €100 off per unoccupied bed. Children under 1 are free, 1 to 3 year olds pay €250, and 4 to 10 year olds get 30% off — which makes this materially better value for a family than the headline suggests.

One wrinkle on whole-chalet pricing: where a chalet shows two capacity figures, the lower is “ideal comfortable occupancy” and the higher is total beds, and the discount works off the lower one. The per-chalet figures themselves are not published, so you cannot do the arithmetic before you enquire.

sections.heading: Where it falls short
sections.html:
No currency on any price. Five chalet prices, two offer prices, and not one carries a symbol or a code.

No dates on any price either, which makes the “from” figures close to meaningless when the discounted offer prices are double them.

The protection is branded as something it is not. “The Trust Associaton” on every page, including at the point of payment.

90% cancellation from sixteen weeks out is among the harshest terms we have seen on an accommodation booking.

4.5% to pay by card, with a €2,500 transaction cap that forces larger bookings into instalments that may cost €25 each.

A Swiss claim with no Swiss chalet.

Two phone numbers and two email addresses for the same company, and booking conditions that refer to the entity as both “Skichalets.nl Ltd” and “Skichalets.nl B.V.” against a single registration number.

And no UK recourse at all. Not a UK company, no Companies House registration, no UK address, no UK licence. Your contract is with a Dutch company under Dutch arrangements.

sections.heading: Who it is right for
sections.html:
Strip away the presentation and there is a real product here. A fully catered chalet week with a cook, breakfast, afternoon tea, six dinners and unlimited wine, beer and soft drinks, in St Anton or the Three Valleys, from a company that has run its own properties since 1993. For a family it is better value than it looks, because under-ones go free, one-to-threes pay €250 and four-to-tens get 30% off. For a group taking a whole chalet, 30% off per adult plus €100 per empty bed is a serious discount.

It is right for someone who is comfortable contracting with a Dutch operator, who will insure the trip against the cancellation terms, and who understands that a bad snow year is their own loss. It is wrong for anyone who wants ATOL or ABTA behind their money, anyone who needs to know the price in pounds before committing, and anyone whose plans might change inside four months of departure.

Whole-chalet bookings get 30% off per adult plus €100 for every unoccupied bed
No caution deposit
Apple Pay carries no card fee, where Visa and Mastercard cost 4.5%
Chalets in St Anton, the Three Valleys, Zillertal and the Dolomites
cons: No ATOL and no ABTA — protection is a Dutch SGR bond, with the certificate published only in Dutch
Every page, including the payment page, claims “Financial protection by The Trust Associaton”, which is not a real body
Not one published price carries a currency symbol or code
No price carries a date or a season, and the discounted offer prices are higher than the “from” prices
Cancel between 16 and 3 weeks before departure and you lose 90% of the total cost
Cancel inside 3 weeks and you lose everything, including the booking charge and tourist tax
No snow guarantee — snowfall, avalanche danger, weather and closed lifts are all excluded
Dinner is served on six days of seven; you eat out on the staff day off at your own cost
4.5% to pay by Visa or Mastercard, with a €2,500 cap per transaction and €25 per extra invoice
The About page claims Swiss resorts and no Swiss chalet is listed
Not a UK company, so there is no Companies House record and no UK recourse
The booking conditions name the entity as both “Ltd” and “B.V.” against one registration number
verdict: The chalets look like a decent product and the catering is properly specified — breakfast, afternoon tea, six three-course dinners, unlimited wine and a cook who clears up, from an operator running its own properties since 1993. Families do well here: under-ones free, €250 for a toddler and 30% off for primary-school children is better than most. What a UK skier has to weigh is everything around the product. There is no ATOL and no ABTA; the cover is a Dutch SGR bond with a Dutch-language certificate, and the site describes it on every page as “The Trust Associaton”, which is not a body that exists and reads uncomfortably like the UK Travel Trust Association it is not a member of. The cancellation terms take 90% from sixteen weeks out, there is no snow guarantee, and not one published price tells you what currency it is in. Book it if you are happy contracting with a Dutch company, you insure the trip the day you pay the deposit, and you get the price confirmed in writing with a currency attached. If you want a UK licence standing behind your money, this is not the booking.

faqs.q: Is Catered Ski Chalets ATOL protected?
faqs.a: No. It holds no ATOL licence and no ABTA membership, and ABTA is not mentioned anywhere on its site. Its cover is a Dutch bond with SGR, membership number 3494, and the certificate is published only in Dutch. Since it sells no flights, ATOL would not normally apply to an accommodation-only booking — but if you book your own flights and the operator fails, your money sits behind a Dutch scheme rather than a UK one.

faqs.q: What is “The Trust Associaton” in the footer?
faqs.a: Nothing. No body of that name exists. The operator uses it on every page, including the payment page, to describe its Dutch SGR bond. The UK organisation it resembles is the Travel Trust Association, which this operator names only as a comparator and is not a member of. Read the footer as meaning SGR, not TTA.

faqs.q: How much is a week, and in what currency?
faqs.a: From 490 per person per week at Gerlos in Austria, rising to 925 at Alpkristall in St Anton. The currency is not published — the price appears as a bare number with no symbol or code, on both the listing and the detail pages. All the fees elsewhere on the site are in euros, so euros is the likely answer, but get it confirmed in writing before paying.

faqs.q: What does it cost to cancel?
faqs.a: 25% if you cancel more than sixteen weeks before, 90% between sixteen and three weeks, and 100% inside three weeks including the arrival day. Those percentages apply to the holiday cost plus the €35 booking charge, the tourist tax and the €10 SGR contribution. The jump from 25% to 90% happens nearly four months before departure, so insure the trip when you pay the deposit.

faqs.q: Is dinner included every night?
faqs.a: Six nights of seven. The chalet staff take one day off during your stay and the operator says plainly: “They still serve breakfast that day, but you make your own tea and coffee and usually eat out.” Wine is unlimited with the six dinners that are served, and beer, soft drinks, coffee and tea are free all day. Spirits are not included.

faqs.q: What happens if there is no snow?
faqs.a: You lose. The booking conditions exclude compensation for snowfall, avalanche danger and weather conditions, and exclude liability for closed ski lifts. There is no snow guarantee of any kind, so a poor season is entirely your risk and the only protection is your own travel insurance.

title: Cazoo Sell My Car
meta_title: Cazoo Sell My Car 2026: Fees, Payment and the Small Print
meta_description: Cazoo values your car free online and holds the offer for 7 days. What the £99 pickup covers, when you actually get paid, and which cars it turns away.

headline.label: What selling costs you
headline.value: £0 to drop off, £99 for home pickup — plus £49 if you cancel a pickup inside 24 hours

intro:
Cazoo's app was downloaded 412,527 times in the second quarter of 2026, more than any other car marketplace app in Britain and ahead of Auto Trader on 401,989, according to Sensor Tower figures reported that July. Downloads were up 80% year on year, and selling is now part of what the app does: Chief Product Officer Thomas Orthgiess lists a Sell My Car tool among the features added during 2026.

On the website the offer is a free valuation keyed off your registration, held open for seven days while you decide. Hand the car over at a drop-off point and there is nothing to pay; ask for it to be collected from your door and £99 comes off the price. Payment is promised on the day you hand the keys across.

One thing to establish before you start. The sell terms linked from that page are published in the name of Cazoo Ltd, company number 11624245, of 40 Churchway, London NW1 1LW. Companies House records that company as CL 1 REALISATIONS LTD, in administration since 29 May 2024 with Teneo Financial Advisory appointed, its administration extended again on 22 May 2026. The brand and the website are run by a different company, Motors.co.uk Limited (05975777). Ask which of the two is buying your car before you hand over the V5C. Figures on this page were checked on 15 September 2026.

sections.heading: Two companies have worn this name, and only one of them is trading
sections.html:
The business that built Cazoo into a household name bought cars outright and resold them. It was incorporated on 15 October 2018 as Cazoo Ltd, company number 11624245, and registered under SIC code 45112 — sale of used cars and light motor vehicles. Administrators were appointed on 29 May 2024, the registered office moved to Teneo's Birmingham office at 20 Colmore Circus Queensway, and on 8 July 2024 the company was renamed CL 1 REALISATIONS LTD so the trading name could be sold on. Its last filed accounts cover the year to 31 December 2023. Administrators' progress reports have been filed every six months since, the most recent on 30 June 2026.

The company behind the website you visit today is Motors.co.uk Limited, number 05975777, incorporated on 23 October 2006 and registered at 27 Old Gloucester Street, London WC1N 3AX. Its filed accounts run to 31 December 2025 and its SIC code is 62090 — information technology services, not car sales. That distinction is the whole business model: the relaunched site, which went live on 2 April 2025 with more than 200,000 listings from over 5,000 dealers, carries other people's stock rather than its own.

The dealer briefing issued for that relaunch puts it in one line: "the new Cazoo is not a retailer — it's a marketplace." Nothing in the relaunch announcement mentioned buying cars from the public. A seller reading the sell page in September 2026 is therefore looking at a journey written for the first company and hosted by the second.

sections.heading: Traces of the old operation are still on the live page
sections.html:
Three details date the sell journey rather precisely. The free hand-over option is described as dropping the car at "your nearest Customer Centre" — the staffed sites the pre-administration retailer ran, and which went with it. The page invites you to "browse our wide range of high-quality new and used Cazoo cars", stock the current business does not own. And the help articles that used to answer questions about handing a car over sat on support.cazoo.co.uk, a subdomain that no longer resolves at all: there is no DNS record for it, so every link pointing there is dead.

None of that proves the valuation form is broken. The app genuinely gained a Sell My Car feature during 2026, and a marketplace with thousands of dealers on it has an obvious way to turn a seller into a lead. What it does mean is that the written terms a seller is asked to accept, and the process described around them, have not been brought forward to the company now running the site. That is worth two minutes on the phone before you drive anywhere.

I could not verify, without submitting a real registration and a real address, which entity makes the offer today or completes the purchase. Treat that as unconfirmed rather than settled, and get the answer in writing.

sections.heading: What the published terms actually promise about money
sections.html:
The sell terms are more precise than the sales page, and in two places less generous.

The offer window. "Each Online Valuation is valid for 7 days after the date of issue and will expire at 23:59 on the 7th day." Seven clear days is longer than the four webuyanycar holds a valuation for, and it is the single best feature of the proposition.

When the money arrives. The sales page says payment is made on handover day. The terms say payment "will be made via bank transfer and will usually be processed within 2 hours, but we do not guarantee that payment will be processed on the same day as Pickup or Drop Off." Both statements can be true at once, but only one of them is a promise, and it is not the one printed in large type.

Whether the price holds. The sales page says there are no hidden fees and that the offer will not be chipped away. The terms reserve the opposite right in plain words: "We are not required to buy the Car from you, and any adjustment we make to the Online Valuation following inspection, is solely at our discretion." Every buyer of used cars inspects before paying and most adjust; the point is that the marketing and the contract describe different things, and the contract is the one that governs.

Two charges that only appear in the terms. There is a £49 fee "for any Pickup cancelled or rearranged by you with less than 24 hours' notice", and £20 for each fine the buyer has to process on your behalf after the handover. Neither figure is on the sales page.

sections.heading: The list of cars it will not take is long
sections.html:
The published criteria rule out a large slice of the cars people most want rid of. To qualify, the car must be under 15 years old, have covered fewer than 150,000 miles, hold at least two weeks of valid MOT at the point of booking, and you must have been the registered keeper for at least three months. You need the V5C, photo identification, evidence of service history and the keys, plus proof of address if you are dropping the car off.

Turned away outright: cars with outstanding finance, insurance write-offs, imports, vehicles with major accident damage or mechanical faults, modified cars, ex-rental cars, cars on illegal tyres, and anything that is a van, a motorbike or a truck.

Outstanding finance is the exclusion that matters most, because a large share of cars on British driveways carry it. Motorway accepts cars on hire purchase and PCP agreements and asks the seller for a settlement letter showing the payoff figure. webuyanycar publishes an even wider list — it buys cars with outstanding finance, with private plates, with damage, with under six months of MOT, on SORN, non-runners and imports, asking only that a car without a valid MOT is transported to the branch. Against either of those, Cazoo's criteria read like a retailer's stock-buying rules rather than a marketplace's, which is consistent with where they came from.

sections.heading: What the same handover costs at the two obvious alternatives
sections.html:
Selling a car to a trade buyer is rarely free, and the charges are structured differently enough to be worth a minute's arithmetic on your own car.

Motorway runs a daily auction across a network it describes as "8,000+ verified car dealers — that's two thirds of the UK market", and charges the seller on a sliding scale once a sale completes: nothing up to £1,000, £29.99 from £1,000 to £4,999, £49.99 from £5,000 to £9,999, £79.99 from £10,000 to £19,999 and £99.99 above £20,000. The winning dealer collects. Motorway says 83% of payments are made on the day of handover.

webuyanycar charges nothing if you are content to wait: payment lands by bank transfer within four working days of the sale. Next working day costs £24.75 and same day costs £29.75, with neither charged where the offer is below £500. Its valuation is secured for four days.

Cazoo's £99 pickup is therefore the most expensive collection charge of the three on a mid-priced car, and free only if you drive the car to the buyer yourself — which is the same deal webuyanycar offers at its branches. On a £17,000 car, the gap between a free Motorway sale and a £99 Cazoo pickup is real money for the same afternoon's work.

sections.heading: What your car is worth before anyone makes an offer
sections.html:
Two published datasets are worth knowing before you accept any instant figure, because they tell you whether an offer is close to the market or a long way under it.

The SMMT counted 7,807,872 used car transactions in the UK during 2025, up 2.2% on the year and a third consecutive year of growth. Petrol accounted for 56.7% of those sales and diesel 33.1%; battery electric cars reached a record 3.5% share on 274,815 units, up 45.7%. Black, grey and white made up 55.4% of everything sold, and superminis alone were 32.1% of transactions.

Auto Trader's retail price index for April 2026, published on 8 May, put the average used car retail price at £17,397, flat year on year but up 1.8% on the month — the strongest monthly rise since November 2021. The average car took 27 days to sell. Petrol cars averaged £14,988 and diesels £14,597, while electric cars averaged £23,555 and shifted in 28 days on demand up 59% year on year. Older cars did best of all: 10 to 15-year-old cars gained 8.4% year on year.

A trade buyer will not pay retail — it has to recondition, warrant and resell the car, and the margin comes out of your price. But the retail figure for your model is the number that tells you whether an instant offer is a fair trade discount or a poor one, and it is free to look up.

sections.heading: The paperwork is yours whoever buys the car
sections.html:
Selling to a trader does not move the registration duties off the seller. You must tell DVLA the vehicle has changed hands and give the buyer's full name and address; the buyer keeps the green new keeper slip from the log book. Once DVLA has the notification, the vehicle tax is cancelled and any full months remaining are refunded, with a direct debit stopped at the same time. If a car is being exported rather than resold here, the permanent export section goes to DVLA at Swansea SA99 1BD and the refund typically takes four to six weeks.

Do not leave it to the buyer to notify DVLA on your behalf. Until the change is recorded you remain the registered keeper for enforcement purposes, which is exactly the window in which parking charges and speeding notices arrive at your address. The £20-per-fine processing charge in Cazoo's terms is a reminder that the buyer expects that to happen often enough to price for it.

Keep a copy of everything you sign, note the date and time of the handover, and photograph the odometer and the car before it leaves you. On a sale where the contracting party is unclear, that record is the only thing you will have.

pros: The seven-day valuation window is longer than webuyanycar's four days, and gives you time to price the car against retail listings
Dropping the car off yourself costs nothing, so the £99 is avoidable
Terms specify payment by bank transfer usually processed within 2 hours of handover
The underlying marketplace is genuinely popular — 412,527 app downloads in Q2 2026, ahead of Auto Trader's 401,989
Valuation is free, needs only a registration number, and creates no obligation on you
cons: The sell terms are published in the name of Cazoo Ltd (11624245), a company in administration since 29 May 2024 and since renamed CL 1 REALISATIONS LTD — not the company running the site today
The sales page promises payment on handover day; the terms say same-day payment is expressly not guaranteed
The page says the offer will not be chipped away, while the terms reserve adjustment after inspection "solely at our discretion" and no obligation to buy at all
Cars with outstanding finance are refused outright, where Motorway and webuyanycar both accept them
A £49 charge for cancelling or rearranging a pickup inside 24 hours, and £20 per fine processed, appear only in the terms
The free drop-off option points at Customer Centres belonging to the failed retailer, and the old support subdomain no longer resolves
verdict: Get the valuation — it is free, it takes a registration number, it commits you to nothing and it is held for seven days, which is three days longer than webuyanycar will hold one. Use that week to check the retail price of your model against the £17,397 market average and to collect a Motorway figure, because a seven-day offer is only useful if you spend the week comparing it. Before you book a handover, ask in writing which company is buying the car and whose terms apply, because the sell terms currently published name a company that has been in administration since May 2024 while the site is run by another. If the answer is clear and the price is competitive, the drop-off route costs nothing and the money should arrive within two hours. If the answer is not clear, sell the car to a buyer whose contracting entity you can identify — and if your car carries finance, is over 15 years old, has done more than 150,000 miles or is a van, this route is closed to you anyway.
