faqs.q: Does Cazoo buy my car itself?
faqs.a: The sell journey reads as though it does, and the terms behind it are written as a purchase contract. The complication is whose contract. Those terms name Cazoo Ltd, company number 11624245 of 40 Churchway, London NW1 1LW — a company that has been in administration since 29 May 2024 and now trades under the name CL 1 REALISATIONS LTD. The website itself is operated by Motors.co.uk Limited, company 05975777, whose dealer briefing for the April 2025 relaunch says plainly that the business is a marketplace rather than a retailer. Ask which company is buying, and get the answer in writing before you hand over the V5C.

faqs.q: How long does the offer last?
faqs.a: Seven days. The published terms are specific: each online valuation "is valid for 7 days after the date of issue and will expire at 23:59 on the 7th day." That is longer than webuyanycar, which secures a valuation for four days, and it is genuinely useful — it gives you a week to check the retail price of your model and to collect a competing offer before the figure lapses.

faqs.q: Will I be paid the same day I hand the car over?
faqs.a: Not guaranteed. The sales page describes fast payment on handover day, but the terms say payment "will be made via bank transfer and will usually be processed within 2 hours, but we do not guarantee that payment will be processed on the same day as Pickup or Drop Off." Two hours is quick when it happens. If you are relying on the money landing that afternoon, the contract does not support that expectation, so plan around the slower case.

faqs.q: Can I sell a car that still has finance on it?
faqs.a: No. Cars with outstanding finance are on the published list of exclusions, alongside insurance write-offs, imports, modified cars, ex-rentals, cars with major damage or mechanical faults, and any van, motorbike or truck. If your car is on hire purchase or PCP, Motorway accepts it and asks for a settlement letter showing the payoff figure, and webuyanycar buys cars with finance outstanding as well. One of those is the route to take.

faqs.q: What does it cost to sell, and how does that compare?
faqs.a: Nothing if you drive the car to the buyer, or £99 deducted from the price for collection from your home, with £49 charged if you cancel or move that collection inside 24 hours. Motorway charges on a sliding scale after a completed sale — nothing up to £1,000, then £29.99, £49.99, £79.99 and £99.99 as the price rises through £5,000, £10,000 and £20,000 — and the dealer collects. webuyanycar charges nothing for payment within four working days, £24.75 for next working day and £29.75 for same day. On a typical car, collection is the most expensive part of the Cazoo route and the easiest to avoid.

faqs.q: Do I still have to tell DVLA?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is your job rather than the buyer's. Give the buyer the green new keeper slip from the log book and notify DVLA with the buyer's full name and address. Your vehicle tax is then cancelled, any full months remaining are refunded and a direct debit is stopped. Until that notification is recorded you remain the registered keeper, which is when parking charges and speeding notices still come to you — the £20-per-fine charge in the seller terms exists precisely because that happens.

title: ClickMechanic Pre-Purchase Inspection Review
meta_title: ClickMechanic Inspection: £79, Next Day, Mechanic To You
meta_description: ClickMechanic inspects a used car from £79 with 86 to 185 checks, a road test and same or next-day booking. Prices, limits and what it misses.

headline.label: Cheapest inspection
headline.value: From £79 — Basic, an 86-point mechanical and structural inspection with a road test of up to 5 miles

intro:
ClickMechanic will send a mechanic to look over a used car for £79, and the slot can be tomorrow morning. That buys an 86-point mechanical and structural inspection with a road test of up to 5 miles, carried out wherever the car is standing, with the report emailed as soon as the mechanic finishes. £95 takes it to 136 points and adds bodywork; £137 takes it to 185 points, adds a plug-in diagnostic check, photographs in the report and the car raised off the ground.

The company has been doing this since 2012 and says there are over 1600 mechanics and garages in the network, each one “vetted on their work history”, with an in-house team that “helped over 35,000 customers last year”. Booking is done entirely online: you give a registration and a postcode, the site returns what it calls an “instant fixed price” built from “industry-standard data”, and you pick a two-hour arrival window “of your choice starting from 8:00am”. It advertises same and next day bookings across the UK, and you do not have to be there — “You do not necessarily have to be present for the inspection.”

Two things are worth knowing before you book rather than after. The inspection “does not include any vehicle history checks on the vehicle”, so outstanding finance, a previous write-off and a mileage discrepancy are all outside it and have to be bought somewhere else. And three kinds of vehicle are refused outright: ClickMechanic says it is “unable to inspect vehicles written off by insurance, motor homes over 7.5t or imported vehicles”.

sections.heading: Three tiers, and what changes is how far the mechanic gets into the car
sections.html:
The three packages are priced from £79, £95 and £137, and the ladder is easy to read because the checklist grows in one direction. Basic is 86 points of mechanical and structural inspection with interior, electrical, engine-bay and tyre checks on top. Standard is 136 points and brings bodywork inside the inspection. Premium is 185 points, with a full interior, bodywork and paint inspection, a plug-in diagnostic check, photographs in the report, and what the site describes as the “Vehicle raised to conduct more thorough inspections”.

That last line is the one that matters most and the one the pricing page says least about. A car on its wheels on a driveway hides its underside, and raising it is the difference between looking at a suspension arm and looking under it. Nothing on the page explains how the car is lifted, where, or whether the Premium booking therefore has to happen somewhere other than the seller's kerb — and for a service sold on the promise that the mechanic comes to the car, that is the question a buyer would most like answered before paying the extra £42.

The road test is the same at every level. All three checklists carry a “Driving test (up to 5 miles)”, so the £137 package drives the car no further than the £79 one. Time on site is where the money shows instead: Basic and Standard “usually take between one and two hours” and Premium “typically takes between two and three hours, depending on the vehicle and its condition”. The report lands by email “as soon as the inspection is complete” and also sits in your ClickMechanic account, and only Premium carries photographs — a Basic report comes back as words.

sections.heading: The same website prices the bad news
sections.html:
This is what no other pre-purchase inspection in Britain can do. ClickMechanic's main business is booking repairs, so the company that tells you the clutch is slipping also publishes what replacing it costs, on the same site, before you have decided whether to buy the car at all. Its price-estimate tool is built from what it calls “millions of data points including official labour times, parts prices and regional labour rates”, and it will take a registration and a postcode and return a fixed figure.

The published averages give a used-car buyer a rough price list for the faults an inspection turns up. Brakes average £191.65, car electrics £218.58, suspension £232.73, ignition £235.75, the cooling system £270.96, the exhaust £267.63, engine work £397.36, the fuel system £406.28, and clutch and transmission £567.91. The company's own rule of thumb is “around £100-£250 for minor repairs and £250-£750 for major repairs”.

Take the clutch, because it is the classic thing a test drive catches and a forecourt does not mention. ClickMechanic gives the job at “on average £400, with prices ranging from £250 to £600”, taking “between 3 and 6 hours”, and then breaks it down by marque: £500 on a BMW, £576 on a Ford, £636 on a Volkswagen, £709 on a Vauxhall, £776 on a Land Rover, £791 on an Audi, £814 on a Renault and £816 on a Mercedes-Benz. By model it quotes £450 to £750 on a Fiesta, £550 to £900 on a Golf and £700 to £1100 on a 3 Series.

Set those against the inspection fee and the arithmetic is the argument for buying one. At the £400 average, a clutch costs about five times the £79 Basic inspection; at the £567.91 category average, about seven times; on a Mercedes at £816, more than ten. The quoted repair price includes the parts, the fitting, the fluids, disposal of the old parts, “VAT (if applicable)” and a 12-month parts and labour warranty, with the mechanic “Coming to you (under 1600cc)” — though a car over 1600cc that will not drive needs recovery, and ClickMechanic says to “budget around £100 for its collection”. None of this is a sales pitch the firm makes for its own inspection; the two halves of the site simply sit next to each other, and a buyer can do the sum.

sections.heading: Where the 50% saving comes from, and where it stops
sections.html:
The inspection page leads on a comparison: “Up to 50% cheaper than AA and RAC”, expanded underneath to “An average 50% saving when compared to the AA and RAC (AA: £142-£191, RAC: £116-£267)*”, with an asterisk that reads “*Prices as of February 2024”.

Dating the comparison is the right instinct and it is more than most advertisers manage — the Advertising Standards Authority's own guidance on verifiability says an ad should identify the specific products being compared and when the comparison was made, and CAP rule 3.34 requires a comparison with an identifiable competitor to “objectively compare one or more material, relevant, verifiable and representative feature of those products”. The trouble is that the date is now twenty months old and the two rivals have moved.

Read from their own pages on 17 October 2026, the AA charges £110 for Basic, from £199 for Comprehensive and from £279 for Advanced, with 10% off for members, up to 99, 214 and 221 points, and nothing older than 20 years inspected at any price. The RAC charges from £132, from £225 and from £290, with 307 points on the two upper tiers and road tests of up to 3, 10 and 20 miles. Neither range is the one in ClickMechanic's footnote: the real AA ceiling is £88 above the £191 printed, and the real AA floor is £32 below the £142.

The saving is real and it is worth having, but it is smaller at the bottom than the headline suggests and larger at the top. Against the AA's £110 Basic, the £79 Basic is 28% cheaper; against the RAC's £132 Basic, 40%. Against the AA's £279 Advanced, the £137 Premium is 51% cheaper, and against the RAC's £290, 53% — but that is the comparison between the least similar products, since 185 points and a five-mile drive is not 307 points and twenty miles. Even on ClickMechanic's own February 2024 figures the four comparisons available come out at 44%, 28%, 32% and 49%, and the page does not say which products were paired or how the average was struck. All of that is fixable with one afternoon's work and a new date.

sections.heading: A warranty that covers the repair and not the report
sections.html:
Every page on the site carries the same promise: “All repairs & services come with a 12-month warranty on both labour and parts.” The governing document behind it, ClickMechanic's Auto Service Warranty Requirements, puts it at 12 months or 12,000 miles, whichever is sooner, requires the work to be free from defects in materials and workmanship, and requires any part supplied by the mechanic to be “new and a match for the Customer's vehicle”. It is a minimum the platform imposes on its mechanics rather than a ceiling, and a mechanic may offer better.

It does not reach the product this page is about. The same document says a mechanic “need not provide this warranty in respect of inspections”, naming pre-purchase inspections, and adds that “Inspections and diagnosis are based on the condition of the vehicle at the time the auto services are provided.” The inspection page says it in four words of its own: “Inspections do not come with a warranty.”

That is not unreasonable in itself — an opinion about a car's condition on a Tuesday is a different thing from a gearbox that must keep working for a year — and it is stated plainly in two places rather than buried. What it means in practice is that the most expensive thing an inspection can do to you, which is miss something, is the one outcome with no contractual remedy attached. The terms narrow it further. Clause 1.1 says “The customer buys auto services from the mechanic who accepts their booking – not from ClickMechanic”, clause 9.2 says “Under no circumstances will we be liable in any way for any Auto Services”, and clause 19.3 says the company is “under no obligation to provide you with a refund or credit note” if you are unhappy with the work. Clause 19.2 sends you to the mechanic: “If you are unhappy with any Auto Services you should speak to the Mechanic to try and resolve the issue.” The terms were last updated on 3 December 2025, so this is current drafting rather than something left over.

A consumer is not left with nothing — a service bought in the United Kingdom has to be carried out with reasonable care and skill whatever a contract says — but the person who owes that duty is a self-employed mechanic you have never met, not the brand whose name is on the invoice, and there is no ombudsman behind either of them.

sections.heading: £50 and £79 buy two different documents
sections.html:
ClickMechanic sells a second thing that looks like the first. A Vehicle Health Check costs £50, “comes with a written report by a vetted mechanic”, runs to 28 points, and includes a road test. It covers seat belts, warning lights and the horn inside; the cambelt interval, fluid levels, cooling system, drive belts, oil and leaks under the bonnet; all four tyres, the spare and the wheel-nut torque; bodywork, lights, washers and wipers outside; and suspension, brakes, steering and the exhaust.

So £29 separates a 28-point health check from an 86-point pre-purchase inspection, and both end in a written report after a drive. On the arithmetic that is 58 extra checks for twenty-nine pounds, which makes the Basic inspection the better value of the two by a distance — and it is the kind of comparison a seller would normally keep off one page. Neither product page explains the difference, and the health check page does not mention the inspection at all.

Point counts across the trade are not comparable anyway, and nobody in it publishes a definition of a point. ClickMechanic's 86, 136 and 185 sit below the AA's 99, 214 and 221 and well below the RAC's 307, but a provider that counts each tyre separately has four points where a provider that writes “tyres” has one. The useful comparisons are the ones with units behind them: hours on site, miles driven, whether the car is raised, whether a diagnostic reader is plugged in, and whether there are photographs. On those, ClickMechanic's Premium is the only inspection of the three brands that both raises the car and reads fault codes for under £150.

sections.heading: What it costs to change your mind, and the labour rate hidden inside it
sections.html:
The charges are set out in a separate Auto Service Booking Policies document, and they are moderate. Cancelling or rescheduling is free with at least 24 hours' notice before the earliest scheduled arrival time. Inside that window a Late Cancellation or Late Rescheduling charge of up to £20 applies. Once the mechanic has started travelling it becomes an Extra-Late charge of up to £40. If work has already begun, an In-Progress Cancellation means paying for the labour incurred, any parts already fitted, and the labour to put the car back together if you ask for that.

Underneath all of it sits a Minimum Labour Charge of 0.9 hours, charged at the standard rate and stated as falling “between £34.44 and £75.30”. That is the most useful number on the document, because it is the only place the platform publishes what labour actually costs: 0.9 hours at £34.44 is an hourly rate of about £38, and 0.9 hours at £75.30 is about £84. That calculation is this page's own, not ClickMechanic's, but the two figures it rests on are the company's.

Three things in the same document are worth reading twice. Every one of the cancellation charges applies “at ClickMechanic's sole discretion”, which cuts both ways and is at least honest about who decides. A Forced Cancellation charge can land on the customer where the mechanic turns up and cannot do the work for reasons including “incorrect information affecting labour or parts” — a risk that falls on whoever filled in the booking form, which on a pre-purchase inspection is a buyer describing a car they have never owned. And the inspection page carries its own version: “It is not always possible for the mechanic to undertake all checks”, followed by “No refund will be made in these circumstances.” A partial inspection is still a paid inspection.

sections.heading: A software company, a mechanic, and a car on a stranger's drive
sections.html:
CLICKMECHANIC LTD is company 08297894, incorporated on 19 November 2012, active, a private limited company registered at 86-90 Paul Street, London EC2A 4NE. Its single SIC code is 62012, “Business and domestic software development” — which is a fair description of what the company does and a slightly startling one to find behind a service whose whole promise is a human being arriving with a toolbox. The business it is in is the booking engine; the spanner work is bought in.

The accounts say the same thing about scale that the marketing does not. ClickMechanic has filed “total exemption full accounts” every year, the most recent made up to 31 December 2024 and filed on 26 September 2025, running to 14 pages. Accounts for the year to 31 December 2025 were due by 30 September 2026 and had not appeared on the register when this page was written on 17 October 2026. A small company claiming audit exemption publishes no turnover, so there is no independently filed figure for the size of the business anywhere — only the company's own “over 1600 mechanics and garages”, “over 35,000 customers last year” and “212000+ Customer Reviews”.

Its own account of itself is that it was “founded in 2012” by two people it names only as Andrew and Felix, after one of them had run a car-parts aggregator, and that its institutional investors “include EF, Forward Partners, 500 Startups, and Imperial Innovations”, with the former chief executive of JustEat and chairman of Treatwell, Klaus Nyengaard, as an angel. No amounts are given for any of it. Companies House supplies the surname the about page leaves out: Andrew Jervis is recorded as a director and a person with significant control, with his details last updated in November 2023.

One more structural fact, and it flatters the firm. The same three packages at the same three prices appear on ClickMechanic pages built for other brands — the HPI partner page carries “From £79”, “From £95” and “From £137” and the same 86, 136 and 185 points, under the heading “HPI recommends pre-purchase inspections”. Other motoring names point their readers at this inspection rather than running one of their own, and the price does not change when they do.

sections.heading: What the inspection does not look at, and what the state looks at free
sections.html:
The clearest limit is one ClickMechanic states itself: the checklist “does not include any vehicle history checks on the vehicle”, and the page suggests those “can easily [be] purchase[d] elsewhere online”. An inspection answers what is wrong with the car today. It does not answer whether the car is still on finance, whether it has been written off and repaired, whether the mileage is what the dashboard says, or whether it is stolen. Those four questions have sunk more used-car purchases than a tired clutch ever has, and a buyer who books an £79 inspection believing it covers them has bought the wrong half of the job.

Part of the rest is free. GOV.UK's vehicle recall service, last updated on 9 September 2026, will “Find out if the manufacturer has recalled a vehicle, part or accessory because of a serious safety problem” from the registration alone, and also lists faults registered with the DVSA; where a recall applies, owners “will not usually have to pay for any repairs or parts”. Nothing in ClickMechanic's checklists mentions outstanding recalls, and nothing on its site points a buyer at the free check. The same is true of the MOT history service, which gives every recorded test, mileage reading and advisory since 2005 for nothing.

Two absences round it off. No ombudsman or alternative dispute resolution body is named anywhere on the site: the terms escalate to the mechanic, then to support@clickmechanic.com, then to the courts of England, with clause 19.4 setting English law and English jurisdiction. And no rating from an independent ratings body could be found for the brand — it does not appear on Smart Money People, and neither Defaqto nor Fairer Finance covers garage services at all, which leaves the company's own published review counts as the only measure of satisfaction available. Neither gap is unusual in this trade, and both are worth knowing before treating a brand name as a guarantee.

pros: £79 for an 86-point inspection is the cheapest pre-purchase inspection of the three national brands, £31 below the AA's Basic and £53 below the RAC's
Same and next-day slots across the UK, with a two-hour arrival window from 8:00am and no phone call needed to book
The mechanic travels to the car, and you do not have to be present for the inspection
Premium at £137 raises the car off the ground and plugs in a diagnostic reader, which no rival offers under £150
Photographs are included in the Premium report
The same site prices the repairs the inspection finds, with averages from £191.65 on brakes to £567.91 on clutch and transmission
Repair quotes include parts, fitting, fluids, disposal, VAT where applicable and a 12-month, 12,000-mile parts and labour warranty
Cancellation is free with 24 hours' notice, and the maximum late charge is £40
No vehicle age or mileage limit is published, where the RAC's Basic refuses anything over 10 years or 120,000 miles and the AA refuses anything over 20 years at any price
cons: Inspections carry no warranty at all, which the warranty document and the product page both state — the one service here with no remedy attached is the one that can miss a fault
The headline comparison is footnoted “Prices as of February 2024” and the AA and RAC ranges quoted in it no longer match either rival's own published prices
No vehicle history check of any kind is included, so finance, write-off, mileage and theft data all have to be bought separately
Clause 9.2 of the terms says “Under no circumstances will we be liable in any way for any Auto Services”, and clause 1.1 puts the contract with the individual mechanic rather than the brand
Where the mechanic cannot complete every check, the page says plainly that “No refund will be made in these circumstances”
The road test stops at 5 miles on all three packages, against up to 10 on the AA's two upper tiers and up to 20 on the RAC's Advanced
The Premium package raises the car but the site never explains how or where, on a service sold on the promise that the mechanic comes to you
No ombudsman or ADR scheme is named anywhere, and no rating from an independent ratings body could be found for the brand
Accounts for the year to 31 December 2025 were due by 30 September 2026 and had not been filed by 17 October 2026, and audit-exempt accounts publish no turnover in any case
Cancellation charges apply “at ClickMechanic's sole discretion”, including a Forced Cancellation charge that can follow from information a buyer gave about a car they do not own
verdict: For a mainstream used car with no history problem you already know about, £79 buys more than it looks like it should: a qualified mechanic at the seller's address inside a day, 86 checks, a short drive and a written report, for about a quarter of the cost of the cheapest clutch the inspection might save you from. The Premium at £137 is the better buy if the car is worth real money, because raising it and reading its fault codes are the two things a driveway inspection otherwise cannot do, and no rival sells both for less. What this is not is a complete pre-purchase check. Budget for a history check on top, read the sentence saying inspections carry no warranty before you rely on the report, and treat the “50% cheaper” line as twenty months out of date rather than as today's arithmetic.

faqs.q: How much does a ClickMechanic pre-purchase inspection cost?
faqs.a: Three packages are sold from £79 for an 86-point Basic, £95 for a 136-point Standard that adds bodywork, and £137 for a 185-point Premium with a plug-in diagnostic check, photographs in the report and the car raised. All three are “from” prices, so the quote for a particular car and postcode may be higher.

faqs.q: Does the inspection include a history or finance check?
faqs.a: No. ClickMechanic says the inspection “does not include any vehicle history checks on the vehicle”, and suggests buying one elsewhere. Outstanding finance, insurance write-off records, mileage discrepancies and theft markers are all outside every package. GOV.UK will tell you free whether a car has an outstanding safety recall and will show its full MOT history since 2005, but neither of those is a finance or write-off check either.

faqs.q: What happens if the inspection misses a fault?
faqs.a: There is no warranty to fall back on. ClickMechanic's warranty document requires mechanics to give 12 months or 12,000 miles on repairs but says a mechanic “need not provide this warranty in respect of inspections”, and the inspection page states that “Inspections do not come with a warranty.” Clause 1.1 of the terms puts your contract with the mechanic rather than with ClickMechanic, and clause 9.2 says the company will not be liable “in any way for any Auto Services”. A service still has to be performed with reasonable care and skill, but the person owing that duty is the mechanic, and no ombudsman scheme is named.

faqs.q: Can I cancel, and what does it cost?
faqs.a: Cancelling or rescheduling is free with at least 24 hours' notice before the earliest scheduled arrival time. Inside 24 hours a charge of up to £20 applies, and once the mechanic has set off it rises to up to £40. If work has started you pay for the labour already incurred and any parts already fitted, subject to a Minimum Labour Charge of 0.9 hours stated as falling between £34.44 and £75.30. All of these are applied at ClickMechanic's own discretion.

faqs.q: Which vehicles will ClickMechanic not inspect?
faqs.a: It says it is “unable to inspect vehicles written off by insurance, motor homes over 7.5t or imported vehicles”. No age or mileage limit is published, which is a real difference from the two motoring clubs: the RAC's Basic excludes cars over 10 years old or past 120,000 miles, and the AA inspects nothing over 20 years old on any package.

faqs.q: Is a £50 Vehicle Health Check the same thing?
faqs.a: No. The Vehicle Health Check is a 28-point visual check with a written report and a road test, sold at £50. The Basic pre-purchase inspection is 86 points at £79. For £29 more you get 58 more checks, so if the car is one you are thinking of buying, the inspection rather than the health check is the one to book.

title: Comfort Insurance Motorhome Breakdown Cover Review
meta_title: Comfort Motorhome Breakdown Review: Six Callouts, From £96
meta_description: Comfort Insurance sells motorhome breakdown cover from £96 a year. What the six callouts, the £300 UK limit and the 12-metre vehicle rule really mean.
intro:
Comfort Insurance has been arranging cover for motorhomes and campervans for more than thirty years, and it has stayed at it long enough to build a reputation the big direct insurers have never bothered to compete for. The business trades from Comfort House on Goresbrook Road in Dagenham, its flagship Horizon motorhome and campervan policy is underwritten by Aviva, and that policy took a Defaqto 5 Star rating in March 2025. The firm has been voted Insurance Provider of the Year by What Motorhome magazine on twelve occasions, and says it paid 98.3% of claims in 2025.

The breakdown cover reviewed here is the add-on that sits alongside that policy. It starts at £96 a year, it carries UK and European assistance in the same package rather than selling Europe separately, and it allows up to six separate breakdowns in a twelve-month period. Roadside repair, recovery, help at the house and a misfuelling service are all in the standard product, and there is a single UK number for callouts on 0330 303 1192, with +44 1206 812 868 for anything that happens abroad.

One thing to know before you get as far as a quote, because it decides whether this page is any use to you at all: Comfort will not sell this cover on its own. Its wording is blunt about it — breakdown is only available "if it is added to your Comfort Insurance motorhome or campervan policy at the time you purchase or renewal and cannot be bought as a stand-alone policy". If your motorhome is insured somewhere else, you cannot buy the assistance here, and if you skip it at renewal you are waiting until the next one.

key_facts.value: Victor Millwell Insurance Agency Ltd, trading as Comfort Insurance, FRN 300281

key_facts.label: Assistance provided by
key_facts.value: ARAG (formerly DAS) with Call Assist Ltd

key_facts.label: Callouts allowed
key_facts.value: Six breakdowns in any 12-month period

key_facts.value: £300 for any one breakdown

key_facts.label: European claim limit
key_facts.value: £5,000 for any one breakdown

key_facts.value: Up to one hour at the scene

key_facts.value: Up to 12 metres long and 2.55 metres wide; towed trailer up to 7.6 metres

key_facts.value: £35 new business or renewal, £35 mid-term change, £45 cancellation

key_facts.value: 14 days

key_facts.value: Not available — add-on only

sections.heading: Six callouts, one hour of labour and a £300 ceiling
sections.html:
The published wording splits the product into two halves. Sub-section A is the United Kingdom, the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands. Sub-section B is Europe. Both run off the same premium, which is unusual — most breakdown sellers price the Channel crossing as an extra.

In the UK half you get up to one hour's labour at the roadside, and if the vehicle cannot be fixed in that hour it is recovered to a single destination of your choosing. Where the breakdown leaves you stranded overnight, hotel costs are met at up to £50 per person per night. The overall ceiling on a UK breakdown is £300, and that £300 is the number to hold on to: it is not the cost of the tow truck, which the assistance company arranges directly, but everything else — beds, onward travel, the taxi to the hotel — comes out of it.

Europe is treated far more generously. The overall limit there is £5,000 for any one breakdown, hotel costs run to £500 rather than £300, and there is up to £750 towards hiring a replacement vehicle while yours is being repaired. Misfuelling carries its own £5,000 limit, and the agent removes the wrong fuel, moves the vehicle if needed and disposes of what came out. Comfort puts the scale of that problem at over 150,000 UK motorists a year, which is its own figure rather than an official one, but the service is genuinely useful in a vehicle with a 90-litre tank and a filler cap that sits at chest height.

Six breakdowns in twelve months sounds generous until you meet an older base vehicle with a temperamental starter. It is a real cap, and the seventh callout in a bad year is yours to pay for.

sections.heading: Dagenham, Bristol and Colchester: three firms behind one phone call
sections.html:
Three separate companies stand behind a single callout, and each does something different.

Comfort itself is Victor Millwell Insurance Agency Ltd, authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference number 300281 — a number you can check on the FCA Register. It is the broker: it arranges the cover, holds the premium and administers the policy from Comfort House, 8 Goresbrook Road, Dagenham RM9 6UR. Its terms of business confirm it advises on the sale rather than simply presenting options, and that premiums are held either in an insurance broking bank account or under risk transfer from the insurer.

The risk itself sat with DAS Legal Expenses Insurance Company Limited, registered in England as company number 103274 at DAS House, Quay Side, Temple Back, Bristol BS1 6NH. That name has since moved. ARAG Group completed its purchase of DAS UK from ERGO Versicherung AG on 16 January 2024, in a deal covering roughly £190 million of gross written premium and around 800 employees as at 2022, and the two businesses now trade under the ARAG name — ARAG plc holds FRN 452369 and ARAG Legal Expenses Insurance Company Limited holds FRN 202106. Comfort's own breakdown page has kept pace, and now refers to "our breakdown partners ARAG and Call Assist".

Call Assist Ltd is the operational half: company number 03668383, based at Axis Court, North Station Road, Colchester CO1 1UX, running what it describes as around 426 recovery operators across the UK and the Republic of Ireland with a separate network covering the rest of Europe. It is the firm that decides which local recovery operator gets sent to a layby on the A30, and it maintains dedicated networks for vehicles that a standard flatbed cannot handle.

For completeness: the insurance policy this cover attaches to is a different arrangement again. The Horizon motorhome and campervan policy is underwritten by Aviva, a relationship Comfort traces back to the mid-1990s when the insurer was still Norwich Union and Comfort was designing its first motorhome scheme.

sections.heading: Crossing the Channel on the same certificate
sections.html:
European assistance being standard rather than optional is the strongest single argument for buying this add-on at the same time as the policy. The territory listed in the wording runs well beyond the obvious: the European Union plus Albania, Andorra, Bosnia Herzegovina, Gibraltar, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Macedonia, Monaco, Montenegro, Norway, San Marino, Serbia, Switzerland and Turkey west of the Bosphorus.

That matters because the underlying Comfort motorhome policy carries a 365-day Green Card, so the insurance itself does not run out at ninety days the way a mainstream car policy's foreign-use clause does. A driver who takes six months in Portugal over the winter has insurance for the whole trip and assistance for the whole trip, from one broker, on one renewal date. Very little else in the motorhome market is arranged that way.

The limits abroad are the ones set out earlier — £5,000 overall, £500 of hotel, £750 of vehicle hire — and they are pitched at getting you home rather than at replacing the holiday. Ferry crossings are specifically excluded from the UK sub-section, so a breakdown on the boat itself is not what this covers.

Two smaller conditions are worth writing on the back of the certificate. Claims arising in the first 48 hours after the cover is taken out are excluded, unless it was bought at the same time as another insurance policy — which, given the add-on-only rule, will normally be the case here. And recovery is not available at all if the vehicle can be repaired at the scene within an hour; the assistance provider makes that call, not the driver.

sections.heading: The charges that sit outside the premium
sections.html:
Comfort publishes its fee schedule openly in its terms of business, which is more than a good many brokers manage, and the numbers are middling rather than punitive for a specialist.

New business or renewal carries a £35 charge. A mid-term change — a new address, a change of driver, adding a partner after a wedding — is another £35. Cancelling inside the 14-day cooling-off period costs £40; cancelling after it costs £45. A failed direct debit adds £20. Those sit on top of the insurer's premium and on top of any commission Comfort earns from the insurer, which the same document confirms it does.

The breakdown section itself carries the standard 14-day cooling-off right, with a full refund if nothing has been claimed, and can be cancelled later on 14 days' notice with a possible partial refund. The insurer holds the mirror-image right and can cancel on 14 days' notice too.

Should the firm fail, the Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers 90% of a claim with no upper limit for general insurance arranged this way, rising to 100% for compulsory motor insurance. That distinction catches people out: the motor third-party element of the policy is protected in full, the breakdown add-on is protected at 90%.

sections.heading: Twelve metres, 2.55 wide, and a sales page that says otherwise
sections.html:
Comfort's breakdown page states, in terms, that there are "no limits on the length or weight of your vehicle". The policy wording it links to says something different. The cover applies to a vehicle registered with the DVLA as a motorhome, motor caravan, campervan or van with side windows, and it excludes vehicles exceeding 12 metres in length or 2.55 metres in width. A towed caravan or trailer cannot exceed 7.6 metres, or 25 feet.

In practice, 12 metres clears almost everything on a British driveway — a large A-class is typically 8 to 9 metres, and 2.55 metres is the maximum width permitted for a vehicle on the road in any case. So the exclusion will rarely bite. But it is not nothing, and it is not what the page says. An American RV, a converted coach, or a long motorhome towing a car trailer over 25 feet is outside the wording while the sales page implies otherwise, and the wording is the document that will be read when a claim is being considered.

There is a second gap of the same kind. The breakdown page advertises "recovery limits up to £10,000". Neither the policy booklet nor the insurance product information document carries that figure; both put the ceiling at £300 for any one UK breakdown and £5,000 for any one European breakdown. It is possible that the current wording, revised in August 2023, raised it — but that document could not be read. The link Comfort publishes for it redirects from a secure address to an insecure one and then loops, so the current breakdown wording is effectively unreadable from the archive page, and the £10,000 figure needs confirming with Comfort directly before anyone relies on it. It is also worth noting that the breakdown documents in that archive stop at August 2023, while the motorhome and campervan insurance policies beside them have been refreshed in April 2024 and again in 2026.

One further piece of context, since the sales page mentions weight. Weight matters less to this policy than it does to your licence: a driver who passed the car test after 1 January 1997 is limited to 3,500kg, and anything heavier needs the C1 entitlement. Plenty of six-berth coachbuilts sit within a few hundred kilograms of that line once they are loaded.

sections.heading: What the national complaints figures say about this product
sections.html:
Roadside assistance is a quietly troublesome product line across the whole market, and the Financial Ombudsman Service's annual complaints data — published on 21 May 2026 for the 2025/26 year — is the place to see it. The Ombudsman took 214,600 new complaints across every financial product that year and upheld 30% of the ones it resolved. Roadside assistance insurance produced 950 new complaints, of which it upheld 44%.

That is a small line by volume and it says nothing about Comfort specifically, which is far too small to appear in it. But the gap is instructive: car and motorcycle insurance ran at 13,420 complaints and a 35% uphold rate over the same period, and commercial vehicle insurance at 1,429 and 44%. Complaints about assistance products are upheld appreciably more often than the average complaint about anything, which suggests the disputes tend to be about whether a promise made at the point of sale was kept.

Comfort handles complaints from Dagenham on 020 8984 0777. Anything about the breakdown policy itself goes to the insurer's customer relations department, historically on 0344 893 9013, and from there to the Financial Ombudsman Service at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR on 0800 023 4567 or 0300 123 9123. That escalation is free and the deadline is six months from the firm's final response.

An honest note on independent ratings: the Defaqto 5 Star that Comfort advertises, announced on 3 March 2025, was awarded to the Horizon motorhome and campervan insurance policy. It is not a rating of the breakdown add-on, and no independent star rating of this particular assistance product could be found.

pros: European assistance is built into the standard product rather than sold as a separate policy, and pairs with the 365-day Green Card on the underlying Comfort motorhome policy
Six callouts a year covering roadside repair, recovery, home breakdown and misfuelling, with up to one hour's labour at the scene
Generous European limits — £5,000 overall, £500 of hotel costs and £750 towards a hire vehicle
Fee schedule published openly in the terms of business rather than buried at the quote stage
Recovery run by Call Assist, with around 426 recovery operators in the UK and Ireland and specialist networks for awkward vehicles
Backed by an established legal expenses and assistance insurer now part of ARAG, following its completed purchase of DAS UK on 16 January 2024
A genuine motorhome specialist of more than thirty years, whose main policy holds a Defaqto 5 Star rating awarded in March 2025
cons: The sales page says there are "no limits on the length or weight of your vehicle", but the policy wording excludes anything over 12 metres long or 2.55 metres wide and any towed trailer over 7.6 metres
The advertised "recovery limits up to £10,000" appear in neither the policy booklet nor the product information document, both of which cap a UK breakdown at £300 and a European one at £5,000
It cannot be bought on its own — only bolted to a Comfort motorhome or campervan policy at purchase or renewal, so a miss costs you a year
Six breakdowns in twelve months is a hard cap, where several rivals sell unlimited callouts

The current breakdown wording, revised in August 2023, redirects from a secure to an insecure address and cannot be read from the document archive, while the insurance policies beside it have been updated twice since
The advertised price differs across Comfort's own pages — £96 on the motorhome breakdown page and £65 on an older campervan breakdown page that still discusses the UK leaving the EU as a future event
The Defaqto 5 Star rating belongs to the Horizon insurance policy, not to this breakdown cover, which carries no independent rating of its own
verdict: For anyone already insuring a motorhome or campervan with Comfort, this is an easy addition: £96 buys UK and European assistance on one certificate, six callouts, misfuelling cover and a recovery network used to vehicles that a standard patrol van cannot help. The European limits in particular — £5,000 overall with £750 of vehicle hire — are pitched at the kind of long continental trip motorhome owners actually take, and pair neatly with the 365-day Green Card on the main policy. Two things stop it being a straightforward recommendation. The £300 UK ceiling in the wording is modest, and it does not match the £10,000 the sales page advertises, so ask what the current limit is before you agree the renewal. And because the cover is add-on only, the decision is really a decision about the insurance policy: if the Comfort quote is competitive on the motorhome itself, take the breakdown with it, and if it is not, this add-on is not available to you at any price.

faqs.q: Can I buy Comfort breakdown cover without insuring my motorhome with Comfort?
faqs.a: No. The cover is only available as an addition to a Comfort motorhome or campervan insurance policy, and only at the point you take that policy out or renew it. There is no standalone version and no mid-term purchase.

faqs.q: How many breakdowns does it cover in a year?
faqs.a: Up to six in any twelve-month period. That is a genuine limit rather than a fair-usage clause, so a seventh callout in a bad year would be at your own cost.

faqs.q: How large a motorhome can go on the policy?
faqs.a: The wording covers vehicles registered with the DVLA as a motorhome, motor caravan, campervan or van with side windows, up to 12 metres long and 2.55 metres wide. A towed caravan or trailer must be no more than 7.6 metres, or 25 feet. Comfort's sales page says there are no length or weight limits, which the policy documents do not support — worth confirming in writing if you run something unusually large.

faqs.q: Is European cover included or an extra?
faqs.a: Included. The wording carries a European sub-section as standard covering the EU plus Albania, Andorra, Bosnia Herzegovina, Gibraltar, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Macedonia, Monaco, Montenegro, Norway, San Marino, Serbia, Switzerland and Turkey west of the Bosphorus, with an overall limit of £5,000 for any one breakdown.

faqs.q: What happens if I put the wrong fuel in?
faqs.a: A misfuelling service is part of the standard cover. An agent removes and disposes of the wrong fuel and moves the vehicle if that cannot be done where it stands, subject to a £5,000 limit for any one breakdown.

faqs.q: Am I covered straight away?
faqs.a: There is a 48-hour exclusion on claims after the cover starts, unless it was taken out at the same time as another insurance policy. Since this add-on can only be bought alongside a Comfort motorhome or campervan policy, that exception will normally apply.

faqs.q: What does it cost to cancel or change the policy?
faqs.a: Comfort's terms of business set out £40 to cancel within the 14-day cooling-off period and £45 afterwards, £35 for a mid-term change, £35 on new business or renewal, and £20 if a direct debit fails. The breakdown section itself can be cancelled on 14 days' notice.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if a callout goes wrong?
faqs.a: Start with Comfort in Dagenham on 020 8984 0777, or with the insurer's customer relations department for the breakdown policy itself. If you are not satisfied after eight weeks or a final response, you can take it free of charge to the Financial Ombudsman Service on 0800 023 4567. The Ombudsman upheld 44% of the 950 roadside assistance complaints it resolved in 2025/26.

title: Compare-Boat-Insurance.co.uk Boat Insurance
meta_title: Compare Boat Insurance Review: Four Insurers, £3m Cover
meta_description: CETA's four-insurer marine panel, £3m liability as standard, quotes held 30 days, and the fees that sit on top of the premium. What to check before you buy.
intro:
Compare-Boat-Insurance.co.uk is the marine arm of CETA Insurance Ltd, a Chipping Norton broker trading since 16 June 1993 — originally as Central Electronic Trading Agency Limited, renamed in July 2006. One proposal form goes to a panel of four marine underwriters: American International Group UK Limited, MS Amlin, Navigators & General and Towergate Mardon. You are quoted by insurers who write boat risk for a living, rather than by a general motor panel with a marine box bolted on the side.

The vessel list is wide for a site this size. Yachts, cruisers, motorboats, speedboats, narrowboats, RIBs, canoes, kayaks and fast-fishers all run through the same funnel, and third party liability starts at £3 million on the inland waterways product — comfortably clear of the £2,000,000 the Canal & River Trust demands before it will issue a licence. A completed quote is held for 30 days at the rate shown, and any premium above £100 can be spread by direct debit instead of being paid in one go.

CETA is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference 307824, with company number 02827690, both verifiable on the FCA Register. The site displays a customer score of 4.6 out of 5 drawn from 448 verified reviews collected by Feefo from CETA's own buyers. Boat cover is not compulsory under UK law — the pressure to hold it comes from marinas, harbour authorities and the bodies that licence the waterways — so the useful question is not whether to insure, but what the panel actually carries.

sections.heading: Four underwriters behind the badge
sections.html:
The brand is a shopfront; the risk sits elsewhere. CETA arranges cover and the four panel insurers carry it, and that distinction matters the day you claim, because the claims decision belongs to the underwriter rather than to the people who sold you the policy. MS Amlin business quoted through the site is backed by the financial strength of Amlin Syndicate 2001 at Lloyd's. Navigators & General has written small craft and inland waterways risk for decades. Towergate Mardon and AIG UK complete the panel.

CETA's terms of business, version 2.05 dated 15 July 2025, set out one arrangement that works quietly in the customer's favour: the firm does not hold client money and instead relies entirely on risk transfer, collecting premium as agent of the insurer. In practice, once your money reaches CETA it counts as having reached the insurer, even if it never travels the last step. That is a stronger position than a statutory trust account, and it is the sort of detail no boat owner thinks to ask about until a broker fails.

Payment is by credit or debit card at the point of submission, or by direct debit where the premium exceeds £100. Online quotes are verified internally before cover incepts, so a Friday afternoon purchase is not necessarily on risk by Friday evening — worth knowing if you are collecting a boat at the weekend.

sections.heading: What a standard inland waterways policy carries
sections.html:
Navigators & General publishes its inland waterways terms in full, and they are a fair guide to what the panel offers a narrowboat owner. Third party and passenger liability is £3 million as standard. The insured perils run to fire, lightning, explosion, theft, malicious damage and vandalism, weather events, freezing of machinery, accidental loss and damage, and damage in transit including the recovery costs that follow a loss.

Two extras are worth pricing into the comparison. Personal accident cover for the owner and non-paying guests aboard is included free up to £60,000 for any one event, and medical expenses after an accident on board are covered up to £500. There is no excess on a claim for loss while the boat is moored at an approved marina, which quietly removes the most common deduction from the most common type of claim. Up to 30 days of UK coastal use per policy period costs nothing extra, provided the vessel is suitable and you give notice first — enough for a summer trip out of the system without a mid-term endorsement.

Live-aboard and contents cover is available as an option, with legal liability extended to £3,000,000 on those policies. Occasional houseboat use is permitted only where an underwriter has agreed it in writing. One inconsistency to settle at the quote screen: the comparison site's own summary advertises emergency medical expenses of up to £1,000 per incident, while the underwriter's inland waterways page states £500. Those are likely different products, but they are not interchangeable, and the number that binds is the one on your schedule.

sections.heading: Your licence sets the liability floor
sections.html:
No UK statute obliges a boat owner to insure, but the bodies that licence the water do. The Canal & River Trust will not issue a licence without third-party cover of at least £2,000,000. The Broads Authority sets the same £2,000,000 bar, and the Environment Agency asks for £1,000,000. The panel's £3 million standard clears all three with room to spare, which removes the most common reason a licence application bounces.

The scale of that market is easy to underestimate. The Trust had 35,089 licences in issue across all types as at September 2025, generating £29.7m in private boat licence income and £3.5m from business licences in 2024-25. Its National Boat Count, carried out through March 2026, found overall numbers down 2.1% while boats without a home mooring rose 3.6% to 8,825 — close to a quarter of everything afloat on the network. The Trust also estimates around 10 per cent of boats are unlicensed, forgoing over £4 million a year.

The Trust's own insurance guidance carries a warning that belongs on any quote comparison: not all policies cover salvage following a sinking or a fire, and recovery costs frequently run to thousands of pounds. A hull that is a total loss still has to be lifted off the bottom, and whether that bill lands on you or the insurer is decided by wording most buyers never open. Ask the question before the premium, not after the sinking.

sections.heading: How CETA earns from your policy
sections.html:
The disclosure here is better than average. CETA is paid commission by insurers as a percentage of the annual premium and may also earn profit commission, and it receives commission from Premium Credit Limited where a policy is paid by instalments. Set against that, its sales staff are salaried rather than commission-paid, which removes the incentive that produces the hardest selling in this trade.

The fee schedule in the 15 July 2025 terms of business is published, and boat buyers should read it before assuming the quoted premium is the price. New business or renewal carries a fee of £40 to £100 depending on policy type. A mid-term change costs £20. Cancelling outside the cooling-off period costs £45 to £50. A rejected direct debit is charged at £27.50, and paying monthly adds a £7.50 administration fee. Because the headline range spans CETA's whole product set, confirm the exact figure attaching to a boat policy on the quote screen rather than working from the range.

The cooling-off period is 14 days from purchase, during which no cancellation fee applies. What comes back beyond that is the insurer's call, and CETA states plainly that some insurers offer no return of premium at all on a mid-term cancellation. On a seasonal product bought in spring and sold with the boat in September, that is a real cost rather than a technicality.

sections.heading: Where the comparison runs out
sections.html:
Four insurers is a panel, not a market. Craftinsure, GJW Direct, Noble Marine and Haven Knox-Johnston are all significant names in UK leisure marine cover and none of them appears on the panel named on the site. A quote from here is one broker's book, priced well, and it should be treated as a number to beat rather than as evidence that nothing cheaper exists.

The sale is also explicitly non-advised. The terms of business state: "You will not receive advice or a recommendation from us." Deciding the agreed value, the liability limit, the cruising range and whether you need salvage cover is left with you, and CETA acts as agent of the insurer rather than as your representative. That is a lawful and common arrangement, but it is the opposite of what most people assume a broker is doing for them.

The published exclusions are standard for marine and none the less sharp for it: wear and tear, corrosion and osmosis, machinery breakdown, damage from deliberate misconduct, racing or speed contests, commercial use, and any operation outside the agreed navigational limits. Osmosis alone writes off a good number of older GRP hulls and is never an insured peril. The site does not publish excess figures, survey requirements by hull age, or laid-up period terms anywhere a prospective buyer can read them — the FAQ page answers questions about SSL encryption and payment methods but not the ones that decide a claim. Getting those answers means entering the quote funnel or ringing 01608 647806.

sections.heading: Claims, complaints and the safety nets
sections.html:
Complaints go to the Complaints Manager, CETA Insurance Limited, CETA House, Cromwell Business Park, Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire OX7 5SR, or by telephone on 01608 647601. If the matter is unresolved after eight weeks, the Financial Ombudsman Service will take it, and where the risk sits with a Lloyd's syndicate there is a parallel route through Lloyd's own complaints process before the Ombudsman stage.

Compensation cover applies through the Financial Services Compensation Scheme. For insurance advising and arranging, protection is 100% of the first £2,000 and 90% of the remainder, rising to 100% of the claim for compulsory classes of insurance. Leisure boat cover is not a compulsory class, so the 90% tier is the one that applies.

One figure is missing and worth flagging rather than inventing. The Financial Ombudsman Service received 214,600 new complaints in 2025/26 and upheld 30% of those it resolved, with buildings insurance at 38%, pet at 41% and travel at 36%. Marine leisure insurance is not broken out as its own product line in that data, so there is no published uphold rate against which a boat insurer or broker can be measured. Anyone quoting one for this market is estimating.

pros: Four named marine underwriters, including business backed by Amlin Syndicate 2001 at Lloyd's, rather than a general panel with a boat option
£3 million third party and passenger liability as standard, above every UK waterway licensing minimum
Risk transfer means premium paid to CETA counts as paid to the insurer
Free personal accident cover up to £60,000 for any one event, and no excess on losses at an approved marina
30 days of UK coastal cruising included at no extra charge with prior notice
Quotes held for 30 days, which is long enough to arrange a survey or valuation
Sales staff are salaried, not paid commission on what they sell
Unusual craft — RIBs, canoes, kayaks, fast-fishers — quote through the same route as yachts
cons: "Compare" means four insurers. Craftinsure, GJW Direct, Noble Marine and Haven Knox-Johnston are absent from the named panel, so this is one broker's book rather than the market.
The sale is non-advised — "You will not receive advice or a recommendation from us" — so the agreed value, liability limit and cruising range are entirely your judgement.

Fees sit on top of the premium: £40 to £100 to set up or renew, £20 for any mid-term change, £45 to £50 to cancel after day 14, £27.50 for a failed direct debit and £7.50 a month to pay by instalments.
CETA acts as agent of the insurer, not of the customer, which is not the relationship most buyers assume they are getting from a broker.
Excesses, survey requirements by hull age and laid-up terms are not published anywhere on the site, so the details that decide a claim are only visible inside the quote funnel.
The site advertises emergency medical expenses of up to £1,000 per incident while the underwriter's own inland waterways page states £500 — the applicable figure needs confirming on your schedule.
verdict: A specialist broker's quote engine wearing a comparison site's clothes, and considerably better than that sounds. Four marine underwriters, £3 million of liability as standard, free personal accident cover to £60,000 and salaried staff who gain nothing from talking you into more than you need. The limits are equally clear: this is not a market sweep, nobody is advising you, and the £40 to £100 set-up fee is real money on a modest narrowboat premium. Use it as a strong quote to beat, pin down the excess and the laid-up terms in writing before you pay, and check whether salvage is covered — the Canal & River Trust flags that gap for good reason.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites a policy bought through this site?
faqs.a: CETA Insurance Ltd arranges the cover; the risk is carried by one of four insurers — American International Group UK Limited, MS Amlin, Navigators & General or Towergate Mardon. MS Amlin business is backed by Amlin Syndicate 2001 at Lloyd's. Your policy schedule names the insurer, and it is that company, not CETA, that decides a claim.

faqs.q: How much third party cover does a canal licence require?
faqs.a: The Canal & River Trust requires at least £2,000,000 of third-party cover before it will issue a licence. The Broads Authority sets the same £2,000,000 minimum and the Environment Agency asks for £1,000,000. The panel's £3 million standard limit clears all three. Boat insurance itself is not required by UK law — the obligation comes from the licensing body, the marina or the harbour authority.

faqs.q: What will it cost beyond the premium?
faqs.a: CETA's terms of business dated 15 July 2025 list a new business or renewal fee of £40 to £100 depending on policy type, £20 for a mid-term adjustment, £45 to £50 for cancellation outside the cooling-off period, £27.50 for a rejected direct debit and a £7.50 administration fee for paying monthly. Because that range covers CETA's whole product range, confirm the boat figure on the quote screen before paying.

faqs.q: Can I cancel if I change my mind?
faqs.a: Yes. There is a 14-day cooling-off period from purchase and no cancellation fee applies within it. After 14 days CETA charges £45 to £50, and what the insurer returns depends on its own terms — CETA states that some insurers offer no return of premium on a mid-term cancellation at all. If you expect to sell the boat mid-season, ask about the pro-rata position before you buy.

faqs.q: Is my money protected if something goes wrong?
faqs.a: CETA collects premium under risk transfer as agent of the insurer, so money paid to CETA is treated as received by the insurer. Beyond that, the Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers insurance arranging at 100% of the first £2,000 and 90% of the remainder; leisure boat cover is not a compulsory class, so the 90% tier applies. Complaints go to CETA first, then to the Financial Ombudsman Service after eight weeks.

faqs.q: Does the panel cover living aboard?
faqs.a: Live-aboard and contents cover is available as an option on the inland waterways product, with legal liability extended to £3,000,000. Occasional houseboat use is permitted only where an underwriter agrees it in writing beforehand. Continuous cruising without a home mooring is now close to a quarter of the network — 8,825 boats at the March 2026 count — so declare your actual arrangement rather than the one that quotes cheapest.

title: Compare Your Travel Insurance Review: 26 Insurers, One Gibraltar Licence
meta_title: Compare Your Travel Insurance: 26 Insurers, From £8.23
meta_description: Compare Your Travel Insurance puts 26 FCA-authorised insurers behind one form, with quotes from £8.23 and medical limits of £5m to £20m.

headline.label: Emergency medical cover
headline.value: £5m to £20m across the named panel — Post Office Economy up to Admiral Platinum

intro:
Compare Your Travel Insurance names 26 insurers on its panel, advertises over 200 prices from them, and its own medical page quotes single-trip cover from £8.23. Panel, prices and documents checked 17 September 2026 against the company's own pages. Its FAQ sets one rule most comparison sites leave unwritten: “Only travel insurance providers that are authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority are allowed on our panel.”

The names on it are recognisable — Admiral, Ageas, ERGO, Post Office Money, RAC, Rias, Sainsbury's Bank, Virgin Money, Coverwise, Esure — sitting alongside medical specialists such as Free Spirit, Good to Go and Travel Insurance 4 Medical. There is no upper age limit on who may ask for a quote, single trips run to 94 days, and gadget, winter sports and cruise cover are switches on the same form rather than separate journeys. You pay the site nothing; the insurer you choose pays it a percentage of your premium.

The firm behind all of it is Aequotech Limited, a Gibraltar company (number 111831) licensed by the Gibraltar Financial Services Commission under licence 20376 and appearing on the UK register under firm reference 677661. It trades under five names, and one of them — Medical Travel Compared — is a specialist version of this same panel. That matters more than it sounds, and both halves of it are set out further down.
