sections.heading: What the panel's medical limits actually run to
sections.html:
A comparison page is only as good as the numbers it puts side by side, so here are two panel members' published tables rather than a summary of them. Post Office sells three levels: Economy carries £5 million of emergency medical cover with a £125 excess, £1,000 of cancellation and £1,500 of baggage; Standard lifts medical to £10 million, drops the excess to £99 and raises cancellation to £3,000; Premier reaches £15 million on a £50 excess, with £5,000 of cancellation, £3,000 of baggage and £500 of money, rising to £750 if the currency came from a Post Office branch. Missed departure is absent from Economy, worth £750 on Standard and £1,500 on Premier.

Admiral, underwritten by EUI Limited (company 02686904, firm reference 309378), starts where Post Office finishes. Its base policy pays £10 million of emergency medical on a £100 excess, Gold pays £15 million on £75, and Platinum pays £20 million on £50, with cancellation climbing £1,500, £3,000, £5,000 and baggage £1,000, £2,000, £3,000 alongside it.

So the range this one form reaches across is roughly £5 million to £20 million of medical cover and £125 down to £50 of excess — a fourfold spread on the limit and a two-and-a-half-fold spread on what you pay before the insurer does. Two quotes eleven pence apart can sit either side of that. The form asks your destination early because it is the one answer that moves the medical limit you should be aiming for: a broken hip in Spain and the same break in Florida are not the same bill.

The Association of British Insurers puts a floor under how often this matters. UK travel insurers paid £472 million across more than 500,000 claims in 2024. Medical expenses were the single most common reason to claim at 34% of the total, worth £262 million between them, and one insurer alone settled a claim of over £1 million for emergency hospital treatment in the United States and a flight home.

sections.heading: A Gibraltar licence, a Surrey postbox and the question in between
sections.html:
The insurers on the panel must be FCA-authorised. The company running the panel is licensed somewhere else. Aequotech Limited holds permission from the Gibraltar Financial Services Commission under Gibraltar's own Financial Services Act 2019 for “taking up or pursuing insurance distribution – general”, and the firm's terms say it works into Britain “on a freedom of services basis” — selling from Gibraltar rather than from a UK office.

The FCA publishes a consumer page on exactly this arrangement, last updated 2 September 2026. It distinguishes a branch passport, meaning a physical UK presence, from a services passport, meaning none; and it says plainly that such firms “won't have been assessed or authorised by us or the Prudential Regulation Authority”. On complaints it is narrower still: where there is no UK branch, “you'll generally only be able to complain to the Financial Ombudsman if the firm has joined its voluntary jurisdiction.”

Compare Your Travel Insurance's own complaints page offers the Ombudsman without qualification — Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR, 0800 023 4567, available “if we do not provide a final response within 8 weeks” — and mentions no Gibraltar scheme at all. Complaints are posted to a UK address, PO Box 125, Hindhead, GU27 9HQ. Whether that adds up to a UK branch for Ombudsman purposes, or to voluntary-jurisdiction membership, is not something either the firm's pages or the FCA's answer for you, and it is a fair thing to ask by email before you buy. In practice it bites rarely: a complaint about the policy goes to the insurer, who is FCA-authorised and firmly inside the Ombudsman's compulsory jurisdiction. It is a complaint about the comparison itself — a price that changed between quote and checkout, a filter that hid a policy — where the answer matters.

There is a clock on the arrangement, too. Gibraltar firms reach the UK market through transitional provisions kept alive year by year while the permanent Gibraltar Authorisation Regime in the Financial Services Act 2021 is brought into operation. The most recent extension, the Financial Services (Gibraltar) (Amendment) (EU Exit) Regulations 2025, was made on 11 November 2025, came into force on 16 December 2025 and runs the current arrangements to 31 December 2026. Nothing about that threatens a policy you bought through the site — your contract is with the insurer — but it is why the regulatory wording on this site will probably be different a year from now.

sections.heading: One licence, five shopfronts, and the one you may actually want
sections.html:
The Gibraltar register lists five trading names against licence 20376: Compare Your Travel Insurance, Compare Your Cruise Insurance, Medical Travel Compared, Juxtify and Signposter Plus. It also records two former company names, CYTI (Gibraltar) Limited and Medical Travel Compared Limited, which is a useful clue about where the business started: the quote journey at quote.compareyourtravelinsurance.co.uk still identifies itself internally as CYTI.

The practical point is the sister site. Medical Travel Compared runs the same commission model from the same licence, and works with “over 30 specialist providers”, naming 33 of them — several of which, including Free Spirit, Good to Go and Travel Insurance 4 Medical, exist mainly to quote on conditions a mainstream insurer prices out of reach. If you are shopping with a heart condition, a cancer history or anything recently investigated, that is the panel to be on, and it belongs to the same company. Neither the medical-conditions page nor the FAQ on this site tells you it exists.

Two UK companies carrying the CYTI name also sat on the Companies House register until this year. CYTI Limited (number 07368288), incorporated on 7 September 2010 at 1 Dean Street, London, registered under the codes for non-life insurance and information technology services, and CYTI (Holdings) Limited (11080164, incorporated 23 November 2017, filing as dormant) were both dissolved on 24 March 2026. Public records do not state that either belonged to this group, and the site names no UK company anywhere, so treat the connection as unconfirmed — but it is the reason the only British address left in the chain is a postbox in Surrey.

sections.heading: The medical questions are the ones that decide a claim
sections.html:
The site is straight about declaration, and the wording deserves quoting because it is the sentence most travellers skim: “If you need to make a claim and your insurer discovers you did not disclose your medical history fully, they may deem your policy invalid.” Its FAQ adds two conditions people miss — cover applies only to conditions “you've declared and the insurer has accepted in writing”, and a condition that has not been diagnosed yet is not covered at all, however plainly it was brewing.

The Ombudsman's caseload says the same thing from the other end. Travel insurance complaints reached 4,466 in the year to 31 March 2024, up 19% on 3,745 the year before and well clear of the 2,510 recorded in 2019/20. Declined claims lead the list, and undisclosed or under-disclosed medical history leads the declines. The Ombudsman's own advice is blunter than any insurer's: you may have to declare a condition “even if you have fully recovered”.

Where this site falls short is the step the regulator built for precisely this reader. Since 26 April 2021, under policy statement PS20/3, firms selling retail travel insurance — intermediaries and comparison sites included — must point customers with serious pre-existing conditions towards a directory of specialist firms, of which two qualify: MoneyHelper's and BIBA's. The rules were tightened again from 1 January 2026: the premium level that triggers signposting rose from £100 to £200, it will be revised against the Consumer Prices Index every 5 years, and each firm may now hold only one entry per directory. The FCA's own review of the regime estimated it had produced about 21,000 additional policy sales.

Compare Your Travel Insurance's page on pre-existing medical conditions carries no link to either directory, and no directory link appears in its FAQ. The page instead describes medical screening as “a friendly chat about your health history”. That is a fair description of the questionnaire, and a thin substitute for a signpost — particularly from a firm that already owns a specialist panel it could send you to.

sections.heading: Where the website stops short of finishing itself
sections.html:
Small things, individually forgivable, and worth knowing before you judge the brand by its polish.

The Meet the Team page carries six profiles. One, Tommy Lloyd, has a photograph and a line of biography claiming 15 years in insurance. The other five have no photographs and placeholder Latin where the biography should be, under the names Daryl Dixon, Maggie Greene, Morgan Jones, Eugene Porter and Alicia Clark — a cast list borrowed from a television drama and never replaced.

Two different registered addresses are in circulation for the same company. The site's terms and privacy policy give PO Box 475, Suite 23 Portland House, Glacis Road, Gibraltar GX11 1AA; the Gibraltar regulator's register gives Unit 104, Royal Ocean Plaza, Ocean Village, at the same postcode. The about page dates the business to 2013 while the register dates the company to 18 July 2014. A /providers/ page returns a 404, so the panel list survives only on the about page. And the privacy policy names 18 firms that receive your data against the 26 shown as panel members, without explaining the gap.

None of that changes a quote. It does tell you how much of the site is maintained, which is worth a moment's thought before you hand over a date of birth and a medical history.

sections.heading: Money, timing and the two things to check at checkout
sections.html:
The service is free to use and paid by the insurer: “that provider gives us a small percentage of the policy cost. This is our commission.” The size of the percentage is not published, and the firm says it does not affect the order results appear in. Prices are described as live and set by the provider, so the same search an hour later can return a different number, and there are no site-only discounts to hunt for.

Every policy bought through the panel carries a 14-day right to cancel. Two checks are worth making inside those 14 days rather than at an airport. First, buy cancellation cover the day you book the trip, not the week you fly — cancellation is the one section that is working from the moment the policy starts, and a policy bought late covers nothing that has already gone wrong. Second, read the medical acceptance in writing: the quote screen shows a price, and the acceptance shows which of your declared conditions the insurer has actually agreed to carry.

Finally, the form is the fastest part and the documents are not. The journey asks for cover type, destination, dates, trip length, group size and dates of birth before it shows a price, which takes a couple of minutes; the policy wording behind the cheapest result takes rather longer, and it is where the excess, the limits in the table above and the activity exclusions live. The site itself gives no advice and makes no recommendation — its terms say so twice — which means every one of those judgements is yours.

pros: 26 named providers, all required to be FCA-authorised, including medical specialists alongside high-street brands
No upper age limit on who can request a quote, and single trips run to 94 days
Quotes advertised from £8.23, with gadget, winter sports and cruise cover as switches on the same form
Commission model disclosed in plain words on the about page rather than buried in terms
A 14-day right to cancel on every policy bought through the panel
A sister panel of 30-plus specialist medical providers sits behind the same licence
Complaints acknowledged within 5 working days, with a named UK complaints address
cons: The comparison company is licensed in Gibraltar, not assessed or authorised by the FCA, and its own complaints page offers the Financial Ombudsman without explaining the branch or voluntary-jurisdiction condition the FCA attaches to that
Its pre-existing medical conditions page links to neither the MoneyHelper nor the BIBA directory, which the signposting rules in force since 26 April 2021 exist to require
It never mentions Medical Travel Compared, the specialist panel of 30-plus providers run from the same Gibraltar licence and better suited to a serious condition
No advice or recommendation is given, so a £5m limit with a £125 excess and a £20m limit with a £50 excess are left to the reader to tell apart
The Meet the Team page shows five profiles with placeholder Latin text under names taken from a television series

Two different Gibraltar registered addresses are published for the same company, the about page dates the business to 2013 against an incorporation date of 18 July 2014, and the /providers/ page returns a 404
The commission percentage is not published, and the privacy policy names 18 data recipients against a panel of 26
verdict: A tidy, quick panel with real names on it and an honest line about how it gets paid, worth a couple of minutes if you want mainstream travel cover and a spread of medical limits from £5m to £20m in one list. Two caveats decide whether it suits you. If you have a pre-existing condition of any weight, the same company's Medical Travel Compared panel is the one you want and this site will not tell you so. And the comparison itself is run from Gibraltar rather than Britain, which is worth a question by email if a complaint about the comparison — rather than about the policy — is something you would want an Ombudsman to hear.

faqs.q: Does Compare Your Travel Insurance sell the insurance itself?
faqs.a: No. It is a comparison service run by Aequotech Limited and paid a commission by whichever insurer you choose. Your contract, your claim and your policy documents all come from that insurer, and its terms state twice that no advice or recommendation is given.

faqs.q: How much medical cover will I be shown?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on the policy. Across the named panel the published limits run from £5 million on Post Office's Economy level to £20 million on Admiral Platinum, with excesses between £125 and £50. Two results a few pence apart can sit at opposite ends of that range, so read the limit as well as the price.

faqs.q: Is the company regulated in the UK?
faqs.a: It is licensed by the Gibraltar Financial Services Commission under licence 20376 and appears on the UK register under firm reference 677661, working into Britain on a freedom of services basis. The FCA's own guidance notes that such firms have not been assessed or authorised by the FCA, and that access to the Financial Ombudsman generally depends on a UK branch or voluntary-jurisdiction membership. The insurers on the panel are separately FCA-authorised.

faqs.q: I have a pre-existing condition. Is this the right panel?
faqs.a: Possibly not. The same company runs Medical Travel Compared, which works with over 30 specialist providers including Free Spirit, Good to Go and Travel Insurance 4 Medical. For anything serious or recently investigated, start there, or with the MoneyHelper or BIBA directories. Declare everything either way: the site warns that an incomplete history can leave a policy invalid at claim stage.

faqs.q: What does it cost to use?
faqs.a: Nothing. The insurer pays the site a percentage of your premium after you buy, which the about page describes as commission and says does not influence how results are displayed. The percentage itself is not published, and prices are live, so the same search can return a different figure an hour later.

faqs.q: How long can a single trip be?
faqs.a: Up to 94 days on a single-trip policy, with the form offering duration bands of 35 days or under, 36 to 60 days, and 61 days or more. Longer stays are handled by a separate long-stay journey, and annual multi-trip cover has its own per-trip limit that is worth checking before you rely on it.

title: Coventry Building Society Mortgage Deals: Rates, Criteria and the Dates Its Fixes End
meta_title: Coventry Mortgage Rates: 5.10% Fixed, 6.5x Income
meta_description: Coventry Building Society's lowest fixed rate is 5.10% to 28 February 2029 at 65% LTV, and first-time buyers can borrow 6.5x income. Checked 22 Oct 2026.
intro:
Coventry Building Society's cheapest advertised mortgage for buying a home is 5.10% fixed to 28 February 2029, at 65% loan to value with a £999 product fee and a 6.4% APRC. The fee-free alternative at the same LTV is 5.21% fixed to 29 February 2032, and its 5.9% APRC is the only one under 6% anywhere in the range. Every figure on this page was read from Coventry's own pages and documents on 22 October 2026.

The Society was founded in 1884 by a Coventry businessman, Thomas Mason Daffern, and it is still owned by its members rather than by shareholders. Its group advanced £9.6 billion of mortgages in 2025 against £6.7 billion in 2024, taking the lending book to £72.9 billion and its share of the UK mortgage market to 4.2% from 3.1%. It paid members a £398 million premium over the year, it has been a certified B Corporation since 2023, and on 1 January 2025 it bought The Co-operative Bank outright. First-time buyers can borrow up to 6.5 times income at up to 95% loan to value, which is the most generous published multiple of any large lender.

Two things about the way Coventry sells its mortgages are worth knowing before you go any further, and neither is a criticism. First, it fixes rates to a date rather than for a term: every fixed product in both ranges ends on 28 February 2029, 28 February 2030 or 29 February 2032, so a deal that was a five-year fix in 2027 is a four-year fix by 2028 at the same price. Second, there is no online application. Coventry takes mortgage business by telephone on 0800 121 8899, where it warns that “it can take 45 minutes to 1.5 hours”, or through a mortgage broker; it does not have advisers in every branch, and its own advice is free but covers only its own mortgages.

sections.heading: Fixed to a date, not for a term
sections.html:
Most lenders sell a two-year or a five-year fix and the clock starts when your mortgage completes. Coventry does the opposite: it sets an end date and sells everything up to it. On 22 October 2026 every fixed product in both the purchase and the remortgage range carried one of three expiry dates — 28 February 2029, 28 February 2030 or 29 February 2032. Measured from that day those are 860, 1,225 and 1,956 days away, or roughly 28, 40 and 64 months.

So the familiar labels do not apply cleanly. The 5.10% deal to 28 February 2029 is not a two-year fix; it was a 28-month fix on the day it was read, and it will be a 24-month fix for somebody completing at the end of February 2027. The 29 February 2032 products were a 64-month fix in October 2026 and will be a five-year fix in March 2027. The rate does not change as the window shortens, which means two borrowers can pay exactly the same price for materially different lengths of protection depending only on when their purchase completes.

There is an argument in the Society's favour here, and it is worth making. A dated fix means the whole book reprices on the same three days, which is administratively simpler and lets Coventry tell a borrower precisely when their deal ends rather than approximately. It also means that if you are buying and your completion slips by two months, your fix does not quietly extend — you simply get less of it. The practical move is to work out the months remaining to the end date before comparing the rate with anybody else's, because a 5.10% fix with 28 months to run and a rival's 5.10% two-year fix are not the same product.

Coventry publishes no “information correct as at” line on either rate page, so there is no way to tell from the page itself how fresh the numbers are. Lenders that print one — Santander does on its card pages — hand the reader a free currency check. Here the only date on the page is inside the representative example, which assumes a mortgage “starting on 01.05.26” and is an illustration rather than a rate date.

sections.heading: What the two ranges actually pay
sections.html:
Coventry runs separate lists for buying and remortgaging, and the purchase list is cheaper at every loan to value. At 65% LTV with a £999 fee, a purchaser gets 5.10% to 28 February 2029 and a remortgagor gets 5.20%. At 75% the purchase rate is 5.20% and the remortgage rate 5.29%. The gap is a consistent nine or ten basis points, it is published on the Society's own pages rather than inferred, and it is the opposite of the loyalty argument a mutual usually makes.

The range itself is wide. On purchase it runs from 5.10% at 65% LTV up to 6.13%-equivalent pricing at the top of the ladder, with 95% LTV available at 5.69% with a £999 fee or 5.84% with no fee at all, both fixed to 28 February 2029. APRCs across the purchase products read between 5.9% and 6.6%. Every single product in both ranges reverts to the same 6.54% variable rate, and every one carries an early repayment charge.

Whether the £999 fee is worth paying depends entirely on the size of the loan, and Coventry gives you both halves of the sum. Take the two 65% LTV products ending on 28 February 2029: 5.10% with a £999 fee against 5.35% with none. Run both over 28 months on a 25-year repayment basis and the crossover sits at about £172,250. Below that the fee-free deal wins; above it the fee is cheaper, and at £250,000 it is about £451 cheaper over the fixed period. That calculation is this page's own arithmetic from Coventry's published rates and fee, not a figure the Society quotes.

At the top of the ladder the answer flips. The ONS put the average first-time buyer property at £230,097 in August 2026, in a release published on 21 October 2026. A 5% deposit on that is £11,504.85 and the loan is £218,592. On those numbers the 5.84% fee-free 95% product costs about £555 more in interest over the 28 months than the 5.69% product does — but the 5.69% product costs £999 up front, so the fee-free deal comes out roughly £444 ahead. A buyer at the national average is better off ignoring the headline rate and taking the one with no fee.

sections.heading: The rate after the fix, and what it is not tied to
sections.html:
This is the most consequential number on the page and it is the same on all 40-plus products: “Followed by 6.54% Variable for remainder of term”. Coventry names it the Standard Variable Rate, and it runs a second managed rate called the Privilege Rate at 6.29% for some older borrowers. Its own help page is unusually direct about what governs them: these rates “aren't linked to the Bank of England Base Rate or any other external rates”.

That sentence is doing a lot of work. Bank Rate was 3.75% on 22 October 2026, held at the 17 September 2026 meeting with the next decision due on 5 November 2026. Coventry's SVR therefore sits 2.79 percentage points above Bank Rate with no stated ceiling and no mechanical link to it, so a cut in Bank Rate obliges the Society to pass on nothing at all. Nationwide, by contrast, publishes two reversion rates on its own page, both effective 1 January 2026: a Base Mortgage Rate “guaranteed to be no more than 2% above the Bank of England base rate”, which on the same day stood at 5.75%, and a Standard Mortgage Rate of 6.49% that its page says has “no upper limit or cap”. Coventry's 6.54% is 0.79 points above Nationwide's capped rate and five basis points above its uncapped one, which is the fairer of the two comparisons and still does not flatter it.

The cost of drifting onto it is easy to state. On a £200,000 loan over 25 years, 5.10% is £1,180.86 a month and 6.54% is £1,355.42 — £174.56 a month, or £2,094.66 a year, for doing nothing at the end of a fix. Those two payment figures are calculated here from Coventry's own published rates, because the Society's rate listings show each monthly payment as a placeholder rather than a number. Ask for the reversion rate in writing, and ask whether it is capped against anything, because the published answer is that it is not.

sections.heading: Six and a half times income, and the sum that follows
sections.html:
Coventry's first-time buyer product guide advertises “Up to 6.5x LTI” alongside “Up to 95% LTV” and the line that eligible first-time buyers “can now purchase a home with a deposit of as little as 5%”. Gifted deposits are accepted from a wide family list including aunts, uncles and adopted children. The footnote attached to the 6.5x figure sets three conditions: “No applicant can be self-employed, min income £30k (sole), £50k combined (joint)”, and every application still has to pass the Society's lending checks including a minimum scorecard requirement.

Six and a half times income is the highest published multiple of any big lender; Nationwide's Helping Hand reaches six times and the market norm is 4.5. It is a genuinely useful product and it deserves to be said plainly. But the two published numbers only reach so far together, and the sum is worth doing before you ring. The minimum sole income of £30,000 multiplied by 6.5 is £195,000. At 95% loan to value that buys a property of £205,263. The average first-time buyer property in August 2026 cost £230,097, so a borrower on the minimum income taking the maximum multiple is about £24,800 short of the national average purchase — and to buy at that average on a £195,000 loan they would need a deposit of £35,097, which is 15.3% rather than 5%. To reach 95% of the average on the full 6.5 multiple you need an income of about £33,630. All of that division is this page's own arithmetic on Coventry's published minimum and the ONS average.

Note also where the multiple is not published. Coventry's residential criteria page sets out loan-to-value limits, age limits, acceptable income types and self-employed requirements in detail, and then says of the maximum loan only that “Our affordability calculator provides you with both the maximum loan amount and maximum monthly payments”. No income multiple appears on the criteria pages at all, and none appears on the affordability calculator page either. The 6.5x figure lives on one marketing page, with a footnote.

sections.heading: How far into retirement the Society will lend
sections.html:
Coventry publishes its age rules clearly, which is more than many lenders do. All applicants must be 18 or over and “they must be no more than 75 years old at the end of the mortgage term” on a residential mortgage; the ceiling rises to 85 on buy to let. The maximum repayment term is 40 years, so a 35-year-old is the oldest borrower who can take the full term.

The interesting part is what happens when the term reaches into retirement, because Coventry sets two separate thresholds. Where five years or more of the term falls after retirement, an underwriter assesses affordability in retirement. Where half the term or more falls after retirement, the maximum payment and the maximum loan are set by the lower of current or anticipated retirement income, both measured net of ongoing commitments. And where the applicant cannot evidence acceptable income past retirement at all, “the loan term will be restricted to the retirement age (maximum age 70)” — so the headline 75 collapses to 70 for anyone without pension paperwork.

Income treatment is set out line by line and it rewards reading. Basic salary counts at 100%; regular overtime, commission, shift allowance and bonuses at 50%; an annual bonus at 50% of the lower of the two-year average and the latest year. Non-pensionable allowances that form part of the package, London weighting among them, count at 100%. Child maintenance counts at 50% and only where the child is under 13. Daily-rate contractors need a “minimum income £50k (gross annual) using the calculation ‘day rate x5 x41’”. Self-employed applicants must have owned the business for at least two years, have been actively trading for at least three months, and produce two years of HMRC tax year calculations plus tax overviews.

Loan to value falls as the loan rises, on a ladder most lenders do not publish at all: 95% up to £600,000, 90% from there to £750,000, 85% to £1 million, 80% to £1.5 million and 75% to £3 million. On the ONS's England average of £294,000 in August 2026 a buyer sits comfortably inside the 95% band; on a £900,000 London purchase the maximum is 85%, which is a £135,000 deposit.

sections.heading: Interest-only, written out in full
sections.html:
Coventry still writes residential interest-only business and publishes the rules, which is rarer than it sounds. The maximum loan to value is 75% for all applications, with no additional borrowing permitted above it, and the minimum equity at completion is £200,000 outside London and the South East and £300,000 inside them. There is no minimum income, but the applicant “must have sufficient income to support an equivalent repayment mortgage” — so the affordability test is run as though the capital were being repaid.

The repayment plan is where the detail sits, and each acceptable vehicle takes a haircut. A stocks and shares ISA counts at 80% of its accrued value, an endowment at 100%, the tax-free lump sum from a defined contribution pension at 12.5% of the pot, a guaranteed defined benefit lump sum at 50%, sale of the mortgaged property at 75% of value, another unencumbered UK residential property at 60%, and FTSE-listed shares, unit trusts, OEICs and investment trusts at 80%. Two exclusions matter: “We do not accept new Interest-only applications on a part/part basis”, and debt consolidation “is not allowed when applying for an Interest-only loan on an Interest-only specific product”.

The 12.5% figure is the one to sit with. A borrower planning to clear a £150,000 interest-only mortgage from a pension lump sum needs Coventry to see a defined contribution pot of £1.2 million, because it will only count an eighth of it. That is a conservative rule rather than an unfair one — the tax-free element is 25% of the pot and Coventry is counting half of that — but it is the kind of number that ends a conversation, and it is better to know it before the 45-minute phone call than during it.

In August 2026 the Society changed the interest-only loan to value limits and the new build limits, on both residential and buy to let. Its own criteria updates page records all four changes as “Loan to Value (LTV) update” and effective August 2026, and names no figures for what moved, directing brokers instead to “read our revised lending policy prior to submitting any applications”. So the fact that the limits changed is published; what they changed from is not.

sections.heading: A mutual that bought a bank, and the court date that finishes the job
sections.html:
On 1 January 2025 Coventry Building Society bought The Co-operative Bank. The year-end results spell out the economics: the consideration was “over 40% below the fair value of the net assets acquired”, which produced a gain of £584 million, and the acquired balances included £20.4 billion of lending, £4.9 billion of personal current account balances, £3.4 billion of business and commercial deposits and £1.9 billion of Bank wholesale funding. Group total assets went from £64,031 million to £88,239 million in a single year.

That gain is why the 2025 statutory profit before tax of £801 million looks so different from the underlying figure of £374 million — the bargain purchase accounts for roughly 73% of the statutory number, on this page's own division. Underlying profit rose far more modestly, from £349 million to £374 million. In the same year the premium paid to members fell slightly, from £401 million to £398 million, and loans more than three months in arrears rose from 0.33% to 0.38%, or from 1,045 cases to 1,637. None of that is hidden; all of it is in the Society's own news release.

The merger is not finished. Coventry is proposing to transfer the Bank's business, including the smile brand, into the Society itself: “A Court hearing will take place on 2 December 2026 to decide whether to approve the proposed transfer”, and the Society expects it to happen on 1 January 2027, subject to that approval. For most members nothing changes — the Society says the transfer “will not impact your account with the Society” and “there's nothing you need to do to maintain your day-to-day banking”. For anyone holding savings with both organisations it does: once the two balance sheets are one, “your FSCS eligible deposit protection may be affected”, because two separate £85,000 limits become one. If you have a Coventry mortgage and Co-operative Bank savings, that is worth checking before the new year.

Behind all of this sits a statutory constraint on mutuals that almost nobody writes about. Section 7 of the Building Societies Act 1986 — the funding limit — requires that the excess of a society's total funding over the shares held by individual members “does not exceed 50 per cent” of that total, which in practice forces at least half the balance sheet to be funded by ordinary savers rather than by wholesale markets. The Building Societies Act 1986 (Amendment) Act 2024 carved out certain Bank of England liquidity facilities, some debt instruments and PRA-related sale and repurchase agreements from that calculation, which gave societies more headroom — and that headroom is part of what made buying a bank with £1.9 billion of wholesale funding possible at all.

The mutual sector it belongs to is larger than most readers assume. The Building Societies Association reported that in the six months to March 2026 building societies held £499 billion of mortgage balances, 29% of all outstanding UK mortgage loans, wrote almost a third — 32% — of all lending to new homebuyers, advanced 61,730 mortgages to first-time buyers, held 46% of all cash ISA balances worth £212 billion, and ran 35% of all high street branches. Two banks have been mutualised in that time: Virgin Money into Nationwide in October 2024 and The Co-operative Bank into Coventry in January 2025.

sections.heading: Reading the complaints return column by column
sections.html:
Coventry publishes its half-yearly complaints return openly, covering Coventry Building Society, Godiva Mortgages Limited and ITL Mortgages Limited together. For 1 January to 30 June 2026 the home finance line reads: 707 complaints opened, 706 closed, a Provision measure of 2.04, “Percentage closed within 3 days” 50%, “Percentage closed after 3 days but within 8 weeks” 50%, “Percentage upheld” 70%, main cause other general administration and customer service.

Those two closure columns are disjoint, which is easy to get wrong and worth stating carefully: 50% plus 50% means every single home finance complaint was closed inside eight weeks, which is a good result against the eight-week regulatory deadline, not a bad one. Half of them were resolved within three days. The Society's own summary adds that it received “fewer than 3 complaints for every 1,000 home finance accounts”.

The uphold rate is the figure that should give a borrower pause. Seven out of ten home finance complaints were decided in the customer's favour, against 55% on the banking and credit cards line in the same return — a 15-point gap inside one firm's own numbers, on the same methodology, in the same six months. A high uphold rate is not straightforwardly bad; it can mean a firm that concedes readily rather than one that errs often, and Coventry's three-day resolution rate points that way. But it does mean that if you think Coventry has got something wrong on your mortgage, the odds on its own published record are that it will agree with you, which is a reason to complain rather than to let it go. The credit-related line, on only six complaints, ran at 83% upheld; the banking and credit cards line opened 3,632 complaints at a Provision measure of 1.39.

sections.heading: The charges, and the gaps in the paperwork
sections.html:
The tariff of mortgage charges is a short document, reference 07591 11/25, carrying the line “Information correct at time of going to print (November 2025)” and the firm reference number 150892. What it quantifies is cheap: a funds transfer fee of £8, a change of parties administration fee of £80, and £40 for unpaid ground rent. For comparison, Nationwide's own intermediary fees page charges “a £20 fee if your client or conveyancer requests to send money by telegraphic transfer”, and Barclays' tariff of mortgage charges (item reference 9914226_UK 09/2021) sets £35 for “Electronically transferring the mortgage funds to you or your solicitor”. All three were read on 22 October 2026, and £8 is the lowest of them by a wide margin.

What the tariff does not quantify is more significant. Against “Early repayment charge” it says only “This will vary. Please refer to your mortgage illustration.” The same answer is given for the product fee, the legal fee, the additional lending valuation fee and the mortgage exit fee. So a prospective borrower comparing Coventry's deals cannot find out, from anything the Society publishes, what it would cost to repay a fix early — no percentage, no ladder by year, no ceiling. Nationwide publishes its whole early repayment ladder on its intermediary site, down to 6% for each of the first five years of a ten-year fix. Coventry's own page on charges for repaying early adds nothing numerical either, saying the details are in your mortgage offer and your annual statement.

Two further charges are published and worth knowing. Repaying in full or in part by cheque adds seven days' interest to cover clearance, which does not apply to cleared funds or to money moved from a Coventry savings account. And the mortgage exit fee is waived if less than a year remains on the mortgage and is refundable if you take your next Coventry mortgage within six months of redeeming — twelve months for borrowers on a former Stroud & Swindon Building Society scheme, a relic of the 2010 merger still sitting in the current terms. No annual overpayment allowance is published anywhere on the Society's site, which is the other standard figure a borrower would expect to find and cannot.

On the other side of the ledger, the remortgage transfer service is generous and clearly described. Coventry pays for the standard legal work of changing lender through a conveyancer from its own panel — Land Registry searches, preparing the mortgage deed, repaying the old lender — and arranges a valuation “up to £670 (£700 for a Buy to Let mortgage)”. The limit is stated too: Land Registry registration is covered only “up to a maximum of £30 … anything charged above this will be your responsibility to pay”, and a long list of extras is excluded, including resolving title problems, transfers of equity, first registration of unregistered property, landlord consent on leasehold and certifying identification documents.

Coventry's Consumer Duty paperwork is published for brokers and is partly unfinished. The residential repayment fair value statement concludes that “the products continue to deliver fair value for customers in the target market for the products”, and is dated February 2025 under reference CFI PDF 0076 02/25 — twenty months old on 22 October 2026, on a document the regulator expects to be kept current. The statements for the residential tracker and the residential Standard Variable Rate are listed on the same page with no working link at all, so the fair value assessment of the 6.54% rate every borrower eventually lands on cannot be read. A third card on that page carries the placeholder title “Header text” and the body text “Intro text for card catergory.”, misspelling included. The Society does deserve credit on one point here: buy to let lending sits outside the Consumer Duty, and Coventry states that it has “taken the voluntary decision to apply the same PRIN principles” to it anyway.

The unfinished paperwork is not confined to one page. The “First Time Buyer product range” section of Coventry's live first-time buyer product guide — the page carrying the 6.5x income claim — consists of two paragraphs of Latin placeholder text beginning “Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit.” It was read twice on 22 October 2026 to be sure, and the second read returned the same text. That is a cosmetic fault rather than a factual one, but it is on the page a broker is sent to for the product range.

Finally, the independent ratings. Coventry's own “why choose us” page displays three Fairer Finance “Gold ribbon for customer experience” awards for 2026, marked “(autumn 2026)”, two of them for mortgages. Fairer Finance's own mortgages customer-experience table returned “Sorry, there are no ratings to show here just yet” when checked on 22 October 2026, along with a loading failure, so the award cannot be confirmed from the rating agency's own published table and is reported here as the Society's claim rather than as a verified rating. Defaqto does not rate mortgage ranges at all. Smart Money People gives the Coventry brand 4.44 out of 5 from 165 product reviews, “Last reviewed within 14 days”, but its mortgages section is empty — there is no mortgage-specific independent score for this lender.

pros: 6.5 times income for first-time buyers at up to 95% loan to value is the highest published multiple of any large UK lender, against Nationwide's six times and a market norm of 4.5
The lowest purchase fix was 5.10% to 28 February 2029 at 65% LTV with a £999 fee, and the fee-free 5.21% to 29 February 2032 carries a 5.9% APRC — the only sub-6% APRC in the range
95% loan to value is available fee-free at 5.84%, so a buyer with a 5% deposit does not have to find a product fee as well
The remortgage transfer service pays for the standard legal work and a valuation up to £670, or £700 on buy to let
An £8 funds transfer fee undercuts Nationwide's £20 and Barclays' £35 on the same charge
Every home finance complaint in the six months to 30 June 2026 was closed inside eight weeks, and half of them within three days
Interest-only is still written on residential mortgages up to 75% LTV, with the acceptable repayment vehicles and their valuation haircuts published in full
Lending is considered to age 75 on residential and 85 on buy to let, over terms of up to 40 years, with the retirement-income tests set out openly
A certified B Corporation since 2023, owned by its members, and £398 million was paid back to them as a premium in 2025
Buy to let sits outside the Consumer Duty and Coventry says it has taken “the voluntary decision to apply the same PRIN principles” to it anyway
cons: The 6.54% Standard Variable Rate every fixed deal reverts to is uncapped, and Coventry's own help page says its variable rates “aren't linked to the Bank of England Base Rate or any other external rates” — it sat 2.79 points above Bank Rate on 22 October 2026, where Nationwide's Base Mortgage Rate is contractually capped at base plus 2% and stood at 5.75%, and above even Nationwide's uncapped Standard Mortgage Rate of 6.49%. On £200,000 over 25 years the drift from 5.10% to 6.54% costs £174.56 a month, or £2,094.66 a year

Nothing the Society publishes quantifies the early repayment charge. The tariff of mortgage charges (reference 07591 11/25, November 2025) answers “This will vary. Please refer to your mortgage illustration” for the ERC, the product fee, the legal fee and the mortgage exit fee alike, and no annual overpayment allowance appears anywhere on the site

Remortgage customers pay about ten basis points more than purchasers at the same loan to value and the same fee — 5.20% against 5.10% at 65%, 5.29% against 5.20% at 75% — on the Society's own published lists
Seven out of ten home finance complaints were upheld in the six months to 30 June 2026, against 55% on the banking and credit cards line in the same return
Neither rate page carries an “information correct as at” date, so there is no way to judge from the page how current the rates are

No income multiple is published on the residential criteria pages or the affordability calculator page; the 6.5x figure appears only on a marketing product guide, and the “First Time Buyer product range” section of that same live page is two paragraphs of Lorem ipsum placeholder text

The fair value statements for the residential tracker and the residential Standard Variable Rate are listed with no working link, so the Consumer Duty assessment of the 6.54% rate every borrower eventually reaches cannot be read; the residential repayment statement that can be read is dated February 2025

There is no online mortgage application. Applying direct means a telephone call the Society warns “can take 45 minutes to 1.5 hours”, advisers are not in every branch, and its own advice covers only its own mortgages

Members holding savings with both Coventry and The Co-operative Bank may lose part of their FSCS cover when the two balance sheets merge, which the Society expects on 1 January 2027 subject to a court hearing on 2 December 2026

No mortgage-specific independent rating could be verified: Defaqto does not rate mortgage ranges, Fairer Finance's mortgages table returned “Sorry, there are no ratings to show here just yet” on 22 October 2026, and Smart Money People's mortgages section for Coventry is empty
verdict: Coventry is a serious mortgage lender rather than a small society with a mortgage range: £9.6 billion advanced in 2025, a £72.9 billion book and 4.2% of the UK market, and it is pricing to compete — 5.10% at 65% loan to value, 95% LTV available with no product fee, and 6.5 times income for first-time buyers that no large lender beats. If you are buying near the national average with a small deposit, the fee-free products are where the value is, because at £218,592 the £999 fee costs more than the extra 0.15% saves. The two things to settle before you commit are both about what happens later rather than what you pay now: the 6.54% reversion rate is uncapped and explicitly not linked to Bank Rate, and the early repayment charge is not published anywhere, so get both in writing on your illustration. And check the months remaining to 28 February 2029, 28 February 2030 or 29 February 2032 before you compare the rate with anybody else's, because Coventry sells you a date rather than a term.

faqs.q: What is Coventry Building Society's lowest mortgage rate?
faqs.a: On 22 October 2026 the cheapest advertised fixed rate for a house purchase was 5.10%, fixed to 28 February 2029, at a maximum 65% loan to value with a £999 product fee and a 6.4% APRC. The cheapest fee-free product at the same loan to value was 5.21% fixed to 29 February 2032, carrying a 5.9% APRC — the only APRC under 6% in the range. Remortgage customers pay slightly more: 5.20% at 65% loan to value with the same £999 fee. All of these revert to a 6.54% variable rate at the end of the fixed period, and all carry an early repayment charge.

faqs.q: How long are Coventry's fixed rates fixed for?
faqs.a: Coventry fixes to a calendar date rather than for a number of years. Every fixed product in both ranges ended on 28 February 2029, 28 February 2030 or 29 February 2032 when the range was read on 22 October 2026, which was 860, 1,225 and 1,956 days away — about 28, 40 and 64 months. The length shortens every day while the rate stays the same, so two borrowers completing four months apart pay the same price for noticeably different lengths of protection. Work out the months remaining to the end date before comparing the rate with another lender's two-year or five-year fix.

faqs.q: Can I get a Coventry mortgage without going through a broker?
faqs.a: Yes. Coventry sells direct as well as through intermediaries, and it does not charge for its own advice — but it says plainly that “we only offer our own mortgages”. There is no online application. Applying direct means telephoning 0800 121 8899 and setting aside enough time, because the Society warns that “it can take 45 minutes to 1.5 hours”. It does not have advisers in all its branches, so a branch visit may still end in a phone call. Buy to let customers have to choose their product before they ring.

faqs.q: How much can a first-time buyer borrow from Coventry?
faqs.a: Its first-time buyer product guide advertises up to 6.5 times income at up to 95% loan to value, with a deposit “as little as 5%” and gifted deposits accepted from a wide family list. The footnote sets the conditions: no applicant can be self-employed, and the minimum income is £30,000 sole or £50,000 combined for a joint application. On the minimum sole income that caps the loan at £195,000, which at 95% loan to value buys a property of about £205,000 — around £24,800 below the £230,097 average first-time buyer price the ONS recorded for August 2026. No income multiple is published on the criteria pages themselves, so confirm the figure for your own circumstances before relying on it.

faqs.q: What rate does a Coventry mortgage go on to when the fix ends?
faqs.a: The Standard Variable Rate, which was 6.54% on 22 October 2026 and applies to every fixed product in both ranges. There is also a Privilege Rate of 6.29% for some existing borrowers. Coventry describes both as managed rates that “aren't linked to the Bank of England Base Rate or any other external rates”, and publishes no cap on either. With Bank Rate at 3.75% the Standard Variable Rate was 2.79 percentage points above it. On a £200,000 loan over 25 years the move from 5.10% to 6.54% adds £174.56 to the monthly payment, or £2,094.66 a year.

faqs.q: Does Coventry charge an early repayment charge, and how much is it?
faqs.a: Every fixed product in both ranges is marked “Early repayment charge: Yes”, but the amount is not published. The tariff of mortgage charges answers “This will vary. Please refer to your mortgage illustration”, and the Society's page on charges for repaying early says the details are in your mortgage offer and your annual statement. No percentage, no year-by-year ladder and no annual overpayment allowance appears anywhere on the site, so ask for all three in writing before you commit. Repaying by cheque also adds seven days' interest to cover clearance, which does not apply to money moved from a Coventry savings account.

faqs.q: What does the Co-operative Bank deal mean for a Coventry mortgage holder?
faqs.a: For the mortgage itself, nothing. Coventry bought The Co-operative Bank on 1 January 2025 and is now proposing to transfer the Bank's business, including the smile brand, into the Society. A court hearing is set for 2 December 2026 and the Society expects the transfer on 1 January 2027 if it is approved, saying it “will not impact your account with the Society”. The one thing to check is deposit protection: anyone holding savings with both organisations may find their FSCS eligible cover reduced once the two are a single institution, because two separate £85,000 limits become one.

title: Coverwise Travel Insurance Review: Five Levels, One Medical Limit
meta_title: Coverwise Travel Insurance: £20m Medical, Cover From £3.60
meta_description: Coverwise sells five levels of travel cover from £3.60, and every one carries £20,000,000 of emergency medical. What changes is the excess, not the limit.

headline.label: Emergency medical cover
headline.value: £20,000,000 on all five levels — Standard Plus to Platinum. Excess £100, £50 or nil

intro:
Coverwise advertises single-trip cover from £3.60 and annual cover from £10.95, and every one of its five cover levels carries £20,000,000 of emergency medical expenses — the same limit on the cheapest policy as on the dearest. Limits read off Coverwise's own policy wordings on 18 September 2026.

That is unusual, and it is the most useful thing about the range. Most travel insurers sell the medical limit as the reason to trade up, so the cheap tier gets £5 million and the expensive one gets £15 million. Coverwise does not ration it. Standard Plus, Bronze, Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum all stop at the same £20,000,000, and the money you spend moving up the ladder buys a smaller excess and a bigger cancellation limit instead. Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum each hold a Defaqto 5 Star rating, and there are optional gadget, winter sports and business extensions from £19.95.

The licence on the paperwork is a Gibraltar one — Coverwise Limited, company 103717, registered at 2 Irish Town and holding Financial Services Commission registration FSC1107B. The telephone is not. Sales and complaints both run through 01903 255 650 in West Sussex, and the complaints address in the firm's own terms is a fourth-floor office in Worthing. That gap between where a brand is licensed and where it is actually answered is worth understanding before you buy, and it is set out further down.

key_facts.label: Sold by
key_facts.value: Coverwise Limited, Gibraltar (company 103717, FSC registration FSC1107B, UK firm reference 533101)

key_facts.label: Underwritten by
key_facts.value: Inter Partner Assistance S.A. UK Branch (AXA Group, firm reference 202664) or AWP P&C S.A. (Allianz, firm reference 534384) depending on the scheme

key_facts.label: Cover levels
key_facts.value: Five — Standard Plus, Bronze, Silver Plus, Gold, Platinum

key_facts.label: Emergency medical
key_facts.value: £20,000,000 on every level; excess £100, £50 or nil

key_facts.label: Cancellation cover
key_facts.value: £1,000 on Standard Plus rising to £6,000 on Platinum

key_facts.label: Cheapest advertised price
key_facts.value: £3.60 single trip (age 20–40, Europe, 4 days); £10.95 annual (age 26–30)

key_facts.label: Age ceilings
key_facts.value: Annual multi-trip closes at 66; single trip closes at 76

key_facts.label: Trip length
key_facts.value: 24 days per trip on the two lower levels, 31 days on the three upper ones; winter sports capped at 17 days a year

key_facts.label: Right to cancel
key_facts.value: 14 days from receiving the documents, and no refund at all after that

key_facts.label: Advice
key_facts.value: None. The terms say the firm “does not seek to advise you on which particular product or service you should purchase”

sections.heading: The five levels, and the one number that never moves
sections.html:
Here is the ladder as the wordings print it, all five dated V.1.N 05/22 and all five underwritten by Inter Partner Assistance S.A. UK Branch.

Standard Plus pays £20,000,000 of emergency medical on a £100 excess, with £1,000 of cancellation, £1,000 of baggage, £200 of personal money, £50,000 of legal expenses and a £200 excess on the personal liability section. Bronze keeps the £100 excess and lifts cancellation to £1,500 and baggage to £1,750. Silver Plus halves the excess to £50 across almost every section, takes cancellation to £2,000, adds £1,000 of missed departure and drops the liability excess from £200 to £50. Gold holds the £50 excess and moves cancellation to £3,000 and baggage to £2,000. Platinum pays £6,000 of cancellation and £3,500 of baggage, lifts personal accident to £30,000 and delayed departure to £350, and charges no excess at all on most sections, including the medical one.

Read down that list and the medical column never changes. The gap between the cheapest policy and the dearest is £5,000 of extra cancellation cover, £2,500 of extra baggage and an excess falling from £100 to nothing. It is not more cover for a broken hip in Spain.

Which way that cuts depends on what you are protecting. If the trip cost £400 and your worry is a hospital bill, the £3.60 policy carries the identical limit to the expensive one and the upgrade buys you very little. If you have paid £4,000 up front for a fortnight and your real exposure is having to call it off, Standard Plus caps you at £1,000 and only Platinum's £6,000 covers the whole thing. Cancellation, not medical, is the section that should decide which row of this table you land on — which is the opposite of how the range is usually shopped.

One detail that is easy to miss on the cheaper levels: an excess normally applies per person and per section. Two travellers claiming on baggage and personal money on a Standard Plus policy meet £100 four times over, and on a £1,000 baggage limit that is a sizeable share of the claim.

sections.heading: Two insurers behind one brand, and the FAQ that is written twice
sections.html:
Coverwise is an intermediary, so it does not carry any of this risk itself, and the name on the certificate is not always the same one. The footer of the website says the insurance is underwritten by AWP P&C S.A. acting through its UK branch, authorised in France by L'Autorité de Contrôle Prudentiel et de Résolution and regulated here under firm reference 534384, and administered by AWP Assistance UK Ltd, trading as Allianz, under firm reference 311909. Every current policy wording served from the site's /Documents/UK/5/ path instead names Inter Partner Assistance S.A. UK Branch, part of the AXA Group, firm reference 202664, with claims run by AXA Travel Insurance. An older Gold wording sitting one directory across, at /Documents/UK/6/, is the AWP one.

The frequently asked questions settle the matter: every answer is given twice, once for AWP P&C S.A. and once for Inter Partner Assistance S.A. Both sets of schemes are live, in other words, and the honest reading is that this is a brand with two panels of paper behind it rather than a site that has forgotten to update itself.

The reassuring part is that the two sets of numbers match. The AWP Gold wording and the AXA Gold wording both pay £20,000,000 of emergency medical on a £50 excess, £3,000 of cancellation and £2,000 of baggage. Whichever insurer you are given, the cover summary is the same document with a different crest on it, and both firms are large European travel insurers rather than anybody obscure.

The answers do diverge in one place worth knowing about. Under an AWP policy, legal expenses pay up to the limit for you but “not more than twice this amount in total for all people insured under this policy”. Under an Inter Partner Assistance policy, legal expenses carry “a limit per policy (single trip) or a limit per trip (annual multi trip) irrespective of the number of individuals insured”. On a family annual policy making one legal claim between four people, those are different sums of money. Nothing on the quote screen tells you which rule you are buying.

sections.heading: What the free card does, and the part it never touches
sections.html:
A £20,000,000 limit sounds like a number invented by a marketing department, and it is worth saying plainly why it is not. The expensive half of a travel medical claim is rarely the treatment. It is the aeroplane: an air ambulance, a stretcher across three rows of a scheduled flight, a doctor and a nurse travelling with you, and a second seat home for whoever you were travelling with.

That is also exactly the part the state does not cover. The NHS Business Services Authority is unambiguous about the free UK Global Health Insurance Card: “Your UK EHIC or UK GHIC is not a substitute for travel insurance. It may not cover all health costs and never covers repatriation costs. Make sure you have travel insurance as well as a UK EHIC or UK GHIC.” The card is free to apply for and covers emergency treatment and A&E visits on the same terms as a local resident. It will not fly you home, and outside its list of countries it does nothing at all.

So the sensible way to read Coverwise's cheapest policy is as the repatriation cover the card cannot give you, bought for the price of a sandwich. At £3.60 for four days in Europe, that is 90p a day against a limit of £20 million, and even the £100 excess only bites on claims small enough that you would probably have paid them yourself. Carry the card as well — it costs nothing and it can settle the local bill before the insurer is involved — but the insurer is the one with the aeroplane.

Where the same arithmetic stops flattering the cheap tier is the ski page. Winter sports cover starts at £19.95 and is capped at 17 days in a policy year on an annual multi-trip, which is a fortnight and a long weekend. A second week on the snow is not covered by simply paying the premium again.

sections.heading: Gibraltar on the licence, Worthing on the telephone
sections.html:
Coverwise Limited is a Gibraltar company, number 103717, with its head office at 2 Irish Town, Gibraltar GX11 1AA, licensed by the Financial Services Commission there under registration FSC1107B and trading into the UK on a freedom of services basis under firm reference 533101. Read that on its own and you might expect an offshore shell.

The documents say otherwise. The complaints route in Coverwise's own terms is “The Operations Manager, 4th Floor, Southfield House, Liverpool Gardens, Worthing, BN11 1RY”, with a duty manager reachable on 01903 255 650. Its older policy wordings give a different West Sussex address, 77-79 High Street, Steyning, BN44 3RE. Both belong to Southdowns Insurance Services Limited, a UK broker at Companies House under number 07285096, incorporated on 15 June 2010 as Southdowns Contact Services Limited and renamed on 12 March 2013, which publishes its terms of business from the Worthing address, answers a duty manager on 01903 255659 and files its accounts to 31 March. Its documents sit behind the same directory structure as Coverwise's. Neither firm's public paperwork states the relationship, so treat the link as what the addresses and the file paths show rather than as a stated fact — but the practical point stands, which is that a Gibraltar licence here does not mean a call centre you cannot reach.

Two things about that paperwork are less impressive. The terms and conditions say Coverwise is licensed “under the Financial Services Act 1989”. Gibraltar replaced that regime on 15 January 2020, when the Financial Services Act 2019 came into force and consolidated roughly 90 separate pieces of legislation into one framework. The citation has been out of date for more than six years. And the About Us page carries no trading history, no customer numbers and no scale figures of any kind, under a copyright line reading 2010 — so how big this business is, and how long it has been doing this, is not something the site will tell you.

Nor will it tell you what it earns. The terms are clear that no advice or recommendation is given, which is fair and normal for an online travel policy, but the commission taken from your premium is not stated anywhere, and the Southdowns terms of business separately allow “an administration fee of up to £25.00 for any mid-term change to the policy”.

sections.heading: The ages, the dates and the declarations that decide a claim
sections.html:
Three eligibility rules do more to determine whether Coverwise suits you than any benefit limit, and none of them is on the front page.

The first is age. An annual multi-trip policy is “not available to anyone aged 66 or over”, and a single trip policy is not available to anyone aged 76 or over. Those are hard doors rather than loadings: a 66th birthday ends the annual product outright, and a 76th ends the relationship. For an older traveller this is the wrong provider, and the range gives no route round it.

The second is trip length. Standard Plus and Bronze cover “any trip not exceeding 24 days” on an annual policy; Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum stretch that to 31 days. A five-week visit to family, or a month plus a few days either side, falls outside the two cheaper levels entirely, and the difference costs less to fix at the quote stage than at the airport.

The third is your medical history. The Select wordings require disclosure of “any medical condition for which you have taken or been prescribed medication…within the last 2 years”, and an undeclared condition is treated as deliberate or reckless misrepresentation, which lets the insurer cancel the policy with no refund and decline the claim. Coverwise's own medical page puts it more directly: an omission “could affect the validity of your policy or result in claims being declined, even if the claim is not related to the undeclared condition”. To its credit, the firm says it does not sell policies that simply exclude undeclared conditions, and it points travellers it cannot quote for towards MoneyHelper's travel insurance directory on 0800 138 7777. Medical-screened cover starts at £15.00.

One last date. You have 14 days from receiving the documents to cancel for a full refund, provided you have not travelled and have not claimed. After that the terms give no refund at all, whatever is left of the policy year — so an annual policy cancelled in month two is paid for in full.

sections.heading: What a five-star rating is actually measuring
sections.html:
Coverwise puts Defaqto 5 Star against Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum, and the rating is real. Defaqto describes its method plainly: its experts “choose between 30 and 100 features and benefits, against which every policy/product in the market is scored”. A five-star travel policy is a policy with a long and generous feature list, independently scored.

What that sentence also tells you is the limit of the badge. It is a count of what is in the wording, so it says nothing about the price, nothing about how quickly a claim is settled, and nothing about the telephone. A 5 Star policy with a £100 excess and a 5 Star policy with no excess score on the same scale.

The rating on the Coverwise site also carries no year against it, which matters because Defaqto refreshes these and a wording dated 05/22 has had four years to be overtaken. If the star rating is part of why you are buying, it is worth asking which cover level and which year the award belongs to before you rely on it. The same goes for the two lower levels, Standard Plus and Bronze, which are not claimed to hold the rating at all — on a range where the medical limit is identical throughout, the honest summary is that the badge is marking the cancellation and excess columns, not the headline one.

pros: £20,000,000 of emergency medical cover on every level, including the £3.60 one
Prices advertised from £3.60 single trip, £10.95 annual, £15.00 with medical screening and £19.95 with winter sports
Platinum carries no excess at all on most sections, including emergency medical
£50,000 of legal expenses from the cheapest level upwards
Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum each hold a Defaqto 5 Star rating
Travellers the firm cannot quote for are pointed to MoneyHelper's directory, with the phone number given
No policies sold that simply exclude undeclared medical conditions
Sales and complaints answered on a UK number in West Sussex despite the Gibraltar licence
cons: The terms and conditions still cite Gibraltar's Financial Services Act 1989, replaced on 15 January 2020 by the Financial Services Act 2019 — a citation more than six years out of date
Annual multi-trip cover closes at 66 and single trip cover at 76, with no route round either, which rules the range out for many older travellers
You cannot tell before buying whether your policy will be underwritten by AWP P&C or by Inter Partner Assistance, and the two differ on how the legal expenses limit is shared between travellers
Cancellation cover on Standard Plus stops at £1,000, which is below the cost of the holidays most people insure
Excesses of £100 on the two lower levels, and £200 on their personal liability section, apply per person and per section rather than once per claim
No refund of any kind after the 14-day cancellation window, however much of an annual policy is unused
The commission taken from the premium is not published, and the About Us page gives no trading history, customer numbers or scale figures under a copyright line reading 2010
The Defaqto 5 Star claim carries no year and no cover-level detail beyond the three tiers named
verdict: A cheap, plain travel policy that is better value at the bottom of the range than at the top, because the £20,000,000 emergency medical limit — the number most people are actually buying — is identical on all five levels. Pay for Silver Plus or above if your exposure is cancelling a costly trip or if you want the excess down to £50 or nothing; the extra money buys nothing medical. The two rules that decide whether Coverwise suits you at all are the age doors at 66 and 76, and the 24-day trip limit on the two cheapest levels. Read which of the two insurers your certificate names before you need to ring anyone.

faqs.q: How much medical cover does the cheapest Coverwise policy have?
faqs.a: The same as the dearest. All five levels — Standard Plus, Bronze, Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum — carry £20,000,000 of emergency medical expenses. What rises with the price is the cancellation limit, from £1,000 to £6,000, and what falls is the excess, from £100 to £50 to nil on Platinum.

faqs.q: Who actually insures a Coverwise policy?
faqs.a: One of two firms. The current wordings name Inter Partner Assistance S.A. UK Branch, part of the AXA Group, firm reference 202664. The website footer names AWP P&C S.A., part of Allianz, firm reference 534384, administered by AWP Assistance UK Ltd, firm reference 311909. Coverwise Limited itself is the intermediary and carries none of the risk. The cover limits are the same either way; check your certificate for the name.

faqs.q: Is there an upper age limit?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is strict. Annual multi-trip cover is not available to anyone aged 66 or over, and single-trip cover is not available to anyone aged 76 or over. There is no loading or referral route past either point, so an older traveller needs a different provider.

faqs.q: Do I still need a GHIC if I buy this?
faqs.a: Carry both. The UK Global Health Insurance Card is free and covers emergency treatment abroad on local terms, but the NHS Business Services Authority states that it “never covers repatriation costs” and is “not a substitute for travel insurance”. Getting you home is the expensive part, and that is what the £20,000,000 limit is for.

faqs.q: How long can a single trip be?
faqs.a: On an annual multi-trip policy, 24 days per trip on Standard Plus and Bronze and 31 days on Silver Plus, Gold and Platinum, with winter sports limited to 17 days in total across the policy year. Single-trip durations are shown on the schedule you are quoted.

faqs.q: Can I get a refund if I change my mind?
faqs.a: Within 14 days of receiving the documents, yes, provided you have not travelled and have not made a claim. After those 14 days the terms give no refund at all, so an annual policy cancelled part-way through the year is paid for in full.

title: Cruise Critic Review: What Its Ratings and Prices Are Built On
meta_title: Cruise Critic Review: 700,000 Reviews, No Booking Fee
meta_description: Cruise Critic carries 700,000+ reviews of 1,100 ships and charges readers nothing. We checked its ratings, partner fares and small print on 23 October 2026.
intro:
Cruise Critic has been publishing cruise reviews since 1995 and now carries more than 700,000 of them, covering over 1,100 ships, 120-plus cruise lines and almost 500 ports. Its own at-a-glance figures give 2 million members, 55 million opinions, reviews and photos, and 5.6 million visitors a month. Reading all of it costs nothing, and the site says so in the plainest terms: “Cruise Critic is not a booking agent and does not charge any service fees to users of our site”.

That sentence is the most useful thing on the site, because it tells you what the next click does. Cruise Critic does not sell cruises and its terms of use say outright that it “is not a travel agency and does not provide or own transportation services or accommodations”. The fares on its deal cards belong to travel agencies that pay to be there and are named on the cards themselves: on the UK pages on 23 October 2026 those included Onyx Cruises, Panache Cruises and Cruise118, the last of them part of the World Travel Holdings group and both ABTA and ATOL protected. Whoever you click through to is the company that takes your money, holds your booking and answers the phone.

The UK site is a locale of the American one rather than a British business, and two lines of its own small print matter before you compare anything. On cruisecritic.com/en-gb the fares are quoted in sterling and the disclaimer reads “Rates are in GBP and valid for UK and Ireland residents” only, and “Taxes, fees and port expenses not included”. On the American version of the same page the same template says the opposite: “Taxes, fees and port expenses included”. A British reader comparing a sterling fare here against a dollar fare there is comparing a pre-tax price with a post-tax one.
