sections.heading: The £599 on the deal card, and what the small print takes off it
sections.html:
On 23 October 2026 the UK deals page carried 107 fares. The cheapest was £599 per person on MSC Euribia to the Canary Islands and the dearest £6,499 on Azamara Quest to South America, a spread of nearly eleven to one. Four of the five cheapest were MSC sailings: Euribia at £599, Fantasia at £649, Virtuosa at £679 and Euribia again at £679. Royal Caribbean’s cheapest was £899 on Rhapsody of the Seas, Celebrity’s £1,029 on Infinity and Cunard’s £1,590 on Queen Anne.

The disclaimer under those fares is fifteen sentences long and worth reading before you treat any of them as a price. The fares are “per person, double occupancy, and are based on specific cabin types and sailing dates” and “may not be available for all cabin types/sailings”. Taxes, fees and port expenses are excluded. A “fuel supplement may apply”. Average prices are “updated nightly”, the site “does not guarantee any specific rates or prices” and it “makes no guarantees for availability of prices advertised on our site”. Listed prices “may have blackout dates, qualifications or restrictions”. And the lowest figure of all is sourced to a company nobody names: “Lowest pricing is based on our 3rd party pricing supplier and valid as of 23 October 2026”.

Fifty-nine of the 107 fares show no number of nights at all, which means more than half of them cannot be set against each other even roughly. The page itself demonstrates the problem: Norwegian Encore to the Mexican Riviera appeared twice at the same £1,199, once as a seven-night cruise with three nights in Los Angeles and once as a fourteen-night sailing. Where nights are shown they run from a five-night Mediterranean cruise on MSC Virtuosa to twenty-nine nights on MSC Sinfonia across the Indian Ocean, so a bare per-person fare on this page can mean anything from about £100 a night to about £250.

One more labelling quirk, and it is on every card. The headline figure is printed as “£1,890 pp” and the detail box beneath it prints the identical number as “Price: £1,890 /night”. Three cards were checked on the UK site and three on the American one and all six did the same thing. A per-person cruise fare presented as a nightly rate is the kind of error that makes a cheap sailing look dear and a long one look like a bargain.

sections.heading: A 3.9 that reconciles to the decimal
sections.html:
The member score is the site’s main product and it is given as a single number out of five with a distribution beneath it. Royal Caribbean International carries 44,045 reviews and an overall “3.9”, built from 18,960 rated Excellent, 11,310 Very Good, 7,554 Average, 3,922 Poor and 2,296 Terrible. Those five bands account for 44,042 of the 44,045 the page counts. Expressed as shares, 43% of reviewers rated the line Excellent, 69% rated it Excellent or Very Good and 14% rated it Poor or Terrible.

Cruise Critic publishes no methodology, so we did the arithmetic. Scoring the bands five down to one and taking a plain average of the 44,042 gives 3.925, which rounds to the 3.9 on the page. That is this review’s own calculation rather than the site’s, and it establishes something the site never states: the score is an unweighted mean of every review ever left, with no recency weighting, no adjustment for sample size and no discounting of old sailings. A ship refurbished last year and a ship reviewed in 2014 contribute equally.

That matters more than it sounds, because the scores are then used to pick winners. The Best in Cruise Awards reached their seventeenth year in 2025 and run to nine categories, with the Cruisers’ Choice strand “based on the best-reviewed cruise lines of the past year from real cruisers” and the rest chosen by editors who “spend hundreds of nights at sea on dozens of cruise lines each year”. The page says “A minimum number of reviews is required to be considered” without saying what the minimum is, and it does not define “the past year” either.

sections.heading: What one review carries, and what it leaves out
sections.html:
An individual review is better documented than most platforms manage. It names the ship and the itinerary, gives a sail date, and identifies the reviewer by screen name, the number of cruises they have taken and an age bracket — one Allure of the Seas review from a September 2026 Western Caribbean sailing reads “5 Cruises” and “Age 20s”. Reviews can be tagged “With children” or “With accessible traveler”, carry member photographs, and can be marked helpful by other readers. Filters cover cruise line, ship and three-month sail-date windows. For working out whether a reviewer is anything like you, that is a genuinely useful set of fields.

What is missing is any statement about verification. Nothing on a review says it has been checked against a booking, and no page on the site sets out whether a reviewer must have sailed, how soon after a cruise a review may be left, or what happens to a review the cruise line disputes. The Competition and Markets Authority’s fake reviews guidance CMA208, in force since 7 April 2025, requires a publisher to take “reasonable and proportionate” steps to detect and deal with fake reviews and notes that it may, though it need not, restrict reviews to people it can verify. Cruise Critic does not say which side of that line it sits on.

The editor ratings are thinner still. The ship index prints an “Editor Rating” out of 5.0 — Noordam at 3.5, Viking Star at 5.0 — with no scale definition, no category breakdown and no explanation of how it relates to the member score. Four ships on the index carry “-- / 5.0” because they are too new to have been sailed, and review counts per ship run from five on Disney Destiny to 2,524 on Celebrity Summit, which is a thirty-fold difference in evidence presented identically.

sections.heading: The AI policy that bans AI from reviewing anything
sections.html:
Cruise Critic publishes an AI use policy, which almost no consumer travel site does, and it is unusually specific. “All opinions, reviews, rankings and editorial recommendations on Cruise Critic are created by humans”. “Cruise Critic does not permit freelance contributors to use AI tools to generate story content”. Quotes and expert commentary must “come directly from a real human expert”. On the member side, “AI-generated reviews are strictly prohibited”, AI-written forum posts are not allowed, member photographs must be original and not AI-generated or manipulated, and suspected AI content may be removed or rejected without notice.

Where AI is allowed, the uses are narrow and named: internal factual summarising for preview ship reviews and port guides from cruise line media materials, deck plans and itinerary maps; research by freelancers that the writer must verify and fact-check; and AI-generated stock-style images or artist renderings in limited cases. Everything so produced is reviewed by editorial staff before publication, “Materials created by AI will clearly be labeled as such”, and preview content is revised once staff have actually been aboard.

The weakness is the one that affects every policy on the site. The AI use policy carries no date and no version number, so there is no way to tell when it was written or whether it has been changed. A policy that forbids undated, unverifiable content would be stronger if it were dated itself.

sections.heading: Tripadvisor owns it and never mentions it
sections.html:
The corporate chain is longer than the site lets on. The privacy policy, effective 16 June 2026, states that “Tripadvisor LLC (d/b/a Cruise Critic) is the controller of personal information we collect” and that the services are owned and operated by that company through The Independent Traveler, Inc., whose name sits in the copyright line as “1995—2026, The Independent Traveler, Inc.”. The acquisition was announced on 23 May 2007, when TripAdvisor LLC — then described as “an operating company of Expedia, Inc.” — bought The Independent Traveler, Inc., publisher of Cruise Critic and IndependentTraveler.com, on undisclosed terms. The release said the business “operates profitably”, gave Cruise Critic “approximately five million visitors per year” and named founder and president Kathleen Tucker, who stayed on. IndependentTraveler.com had launched on America Online in 1990.

Set that five million a year against the 5.6 million a month the site claims now and the growth is roughly thirteen-fold. The UK end of it is thinner than the sterling pricing suggests. The privacy policy names Tripadvisor Limited of 10 Norton Folgate, London E1 6DB as the UK representative and Tripadvisor Ireland Limited, care of Matheson in Dublin, as the EU one. Companies House confirms Tripadvisor Limited as company 05612751, incorporated 4 November 2005 at that address, alongside Tripadvisor UK Holdco Limited (08279085, 2 November 2012) and two limited partnerships registered on 6 November 2012. A representative is not a contracting party, and no company called Cruise Critic or The Independent Traveler appears on the UK register at all.

The parent is listed and publishes audited numbers twice a year, which makes the silence about this business measurable. Tripadvisor’s second-quarter results of 6 August 2026, for the quarter ended 30 June 2026, give revenue of US$441.9 million, down 7% year on year, split between Experiences at US$278.6 million (up 3%) and Hotels and Other at US$163.3 million (down 21%), with net income of US$22.8 million and diluted earnings of US$0.19 a share against a US$10.0 million net loss for the half once discontinued operations are counted. The sale of TheFork to American Express “is expected to be completed by the end of 2026”. Neither the word Cruise Critic nor the word cruise appears anywhere in that announcement, so no revenue, profit or audience figure for this site exists in any audited document.

sections.heading: Massachusetts law, one hundred dollars, and no telephone number
sections.html:
The terms of use are short on comfort for a British reader. “[T]his Agreement is governed by the laws of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, USA”, and users “consent to the exclusive jurisdiction and venue of courts in Massachusetts, USA”. Liability is capped hard: “the Tripadvisor Media Group Companies’ liabilities will in no event exceed One-Hundred Dollars (US $100.00)”. The site warns in capitals that its content “MAY INCLUDE INACCURACIES OR ERRORS, INCLUDING RESERVATION AVAILABILITY AND PRICING ERRORS” and reserves the right to correct a pricing error even on a pending reservation. Where a booking is made with a third-party supplier, “Cruise Critic will have no liability” for that supplier’s acts or omissions.

Anything you post belongs to the site in perpetuity. Submitting content grants “a nonexclusive, royalty-free, perpetual, transferable, irrevocable and fully sub-licensable right” to use it, while the site “does not edit or control the User Messages” and may remove them at its discretion. Members writing thirty years of forum history on the Roll Calls boards, one section of which carries millions of posts, have signed that licence without any corresponding undertaking about the content’s accuracy.

The terms also appear not to have been looked at for a while. The page states that revision dates appear at the bottom, and no revision date is shown; the footer there reads “2022 The Independent Traveler, Inc.” while every other page on the site reads 1995 to 2026. There is no postal address and no telephone number anywhere on the site, including the contact page. The only channel is feedback@cruisecritic.com and a community help centre for forum problems, and no ombudsman or alternative dispute resolution scheme is named, because none covers a travel review website.

sections.heading: Where the money is protected, and it is not here
sections.html:
Because Cruise Critic takes no payment, nothing it does protects a penny of your holiday. Protection attaches to whoever sells you the cruise, and the two British schemes work differently. ATOL, introduced in 1973 and run by the Civil Aviation Authority, is “financial protection when you book a package trip that includes a flight” and the CAA states flatly that “It is not travel insurance”. You cannot claim from it “for cancellations, complaints, sickness, injury, or substandard hygiene during your holiday”, nor for a delayed flight. A claim must reach the CAA within twelve months of the ATOL holder’s failure; it aims to acknowledge within five working days and assess within twenty-eight working days of receiving everything it needs. Notably, the CAA’s own explanation of the scheme, last modified 30 April 2025, does not mention cruises once.

So a fly-cruise bought as a package should produce an ATOL certificate naming “the ATOL holder who is providing your protection”, and a cruise bought without a flight will not. For that, the protection comes from the seller’s own arrangements under the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018, which for a high-street cruise specialist usually means an ABTA bond. Cruise118, the sponsored seller against a Cunard sailing on the UK Norway listing, says it is “both ATOL and ABTA protected” and is part of the World Travel Holdings group. That is the right question to ask of any name you click through to, and the answer will not be on Cruise Critic’s pages.

Two further gaps are worth knowing about before you rely on a deal card. The UK home page was running a banner reading “Disney Wish is coming to the UK for the first time ever! Book your cabin now for just £1 pp deposit!* T&Cs apply” — and the asterisk leads to no footnote anywhere on the page. And the disclaimer’s own advice is the correct advice: “When you book with one of our partners, please be sure to check their site for a full disclosure of all applicable fees”.

sections.heading: Eighty-six out of a hundred, twice a year, unannounced
sections.html:
There is one scored, published, independent inspection of a cruise ship, and Cruise Critic does not show it. The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention runs the Vessel Sanitation Program, and the CDC’s own account of how it works — a Vessel Sanitation Program paper published in the Journal of Environmental Health in March 2008 — sets out the rules. Inspections are “twice-annual, unannounced”, they are “scored on the basis of a possible 100 points”, a passing score is “86 or higher”, a failure means a score below 86 and an unannounced re-inspection within 45 days. The scheme covers ships “sailing from foreign to U.S. ports and carrying 13 or more passengers”, which takes in most of the Caribbean and Alaska fleet a British holidaymaker would consider, and it is funded entirely by fees charged per inspection on a cost-recovery basis according to each vessel’s gross registered tonnage.

A number out of 100 from an unannounced government inspection twice a year is a harder measure than any average of member opinion, and it is free. Cruise Critic rates more than 1,100 ships on an undefined five-point scale and publishes none of it. The CDC’s current inspection-report index could not be opened during this check, so the individual ship scores are not quoted here and should be read from the CDC’s own site before being relied on; the scheme’s thresholds above come from the CDC’s 2008 description of it and should be confirmed against the programme’s current operations manual.

No ratings agency fills the gap either. Defaqto rates insurance, not travel websites; Smart Money People does not list cruise or travel platforms; and the national tourist board assessment schemes grade hotels and hostels rather than booking or review sites. On this page, an absence is the honest answer: there is no independent assessment of Cruise Critic’s ratings by anybody.

sections.heading: 2.54 million British cruises, and four different review counts
sections.html:
The market Cruise Critic is writing for is bigger than it has ever been. The Cruise Lines International Association’s UK and Ireland release of 22 April 2026 reports that British and Irish holidaymakers took 2.54 million ocean cruises in 2025, beating the previous high of 2.4 million in 2024. The Mediterranean took 34.5% of them, northern Europe 27.2% and the Caribbean 13.7%, the last growing 12% year on year. The average cruise ran 9.6 days against 9.7 in 2024, the average passenger was 54.6 years old, and the number of children under twelve rose 7%. “Cruise continues to appeal to a wide range of holidaymakers”, said Andy Harmer, managing director of CLIA UK and Ireland. On a market of that size and that age profile, a free library of 700,000 first-hand reviews is worth having.

Which brings us to the counting. The about page says “more than 700,000 cruise reviews” in its text and “more than 650,000 cruise reviews” in its own meta description. The ship index header says “650,000+ reviews”. The UK home page’s meta description — the line a British searcher reads before clicking — says “Over 150,000+ cruise reviews, ship ratings and the largest cruise forum”, which is less than a quarter of the figure two clicks away. Monthly audience is given twice on one page as “more than five million” and “5.6M+”.

None of those numbers is likely to be invented, and the review archive is plainly enormous whichever is right. The point is narrower and it is about maintenance: a site whose entire value rests on how many people have reported back cannot tell you, on four of its own pages, how many that is. The same pattern shows up in the undated AI policy, the 2022 copyright line on the terms, and an asterisk with no footnote.

pros: Free with no registration, no booking fee and no service fee of any kind, and the site says so in its own disclaimer
More than 700,000 member reviews across 1,100-plus ships, 120-plus cruise lines and almost 500 ports — an archive no cruise line or travel agent can match
An individual review names the ship, the itinerary and the sail date and shows the reviewer’s cruise count and age bracket, which is more context than most platforms publish
A published AI use policy that bans AI-written reviews, AI-written forum posts and AI-generated member photographs, and requires AI-assisted editorial content to be labelled
Editorial independence stated plainly: cruise lines are “forbidden from reviewing or approving any material before publication”, and press trips are disclosed rather than hidden
Thirty years of forum history, including per-ship Roll Call boards running to millions of posts, which is where a specific question about a specific sailing gets answered
Fares are shown with the seller named on the card, so the company you would actually be buying from is identifiable before you click
cons: No rating methodology is published anywhere. There is no scale definition, no category breakdown, no minimum review count and no stated relationship between the Editor Rating and the member score — and our own arithmetic on Royal Caribbean’s 44,042 banded reviews shows the headline 3.9 is a plain unweighted average of every review ever left, with no recency weighting at all

Nothing on the site says whether a reviewer has to have sailed. No review carries a verification marker and no page sets out how reviews are checked, which leaves the site silent on the standard the CMA’s fake reviews guidance has expected since 7 April 2025

Taxes, fees and port expenses are excluded from every fare on the UK pages and included on the American ones, so the two cannot be compared; and 59 of the 107 UK fares on 23 October 2026 showed no number of nights, which makes most of them incomparable with each other as well
Every deal card prints the same figure twice, once as a per-person fare and once as a nightly rate — “£1,890 pp” and “Price: £1,890 /night” — checked on three UK cards and three American ones
The cheapest fare on the page is attributed to an unnamed “3rd party pricing supplier”, so the one number a reader is most likely to act on has no identifiable source

Liability is capped at US$100 across the whole Tripadvisor group, the agreement is governed by Massachusetts law with exclusive jurisdiction in Massachusetts courts, and there is no postal address, no telephone number, no ombudsman and no ADR scheme anywhere on the site

Several of the site’s own documents are undated: the AI use policy carries no date or version, the terms of use say revision dates appear at the foot of the page and show none, and the footer there still reads “2022 The Independent Traveler, Inc.” while the rest of the site reads 1995 to 2026
The review total is given as 700,000, 650,000 and “Over 150,000+” on different pages of the same site, and monthly visitors as “more than five million” and “5.6M+” on one page
verdict:
Cruise Critic earns its place as the first stop rather than the last. Thirty years of forum history and 700,000-odd reviews of 1,100 ships cost nothing to read, the reviews carry the sail date and the reviewer’s cruise count, and the AI use policy and the ban on cruise lines approving copy before publication are commitments most travel sites do not make in writing. For narrowing 120 cruise lines down to three ships worth pricing, there is nothing else like it in Britain, and the 2.54 million ocean cruises CLIA counted in 2025 are a lot of people who could use it.

Treat the money side as a starting point and not a quote. The fares belong to agencies that pay to appear, the cheapest of them comes from a supplier the site does not name, taxes and port expenses are excluded on the UK pages and included on the American ones, and more than half the UK fares do not say how many nights they cover. Check the figure on the seller’s own site before believing it. And because Cruise Critic takes no payment, nothing here protects your holiday: that comes from the ATOL certificate on a fly-cruise or the seller’s ABTA arrangements on a cruise-only booking, so the name on the deal card is the one worth checking first.

faqs.q: Does Cruise Critic charge anything to use?
faqs.a: No. Its own pricing disclaimer states that “Cruise Critic is not a booking agent and does not charge any service fees to users of our site”, and there is no membership or registration charge for the reviews or the forums. The site is paid for by advertisers and by the travel agencies whose fares appear on its deal cards. Its parent, Tripadvisor, reported US$441.9 million of revenue in the quarter to 30 June 2026 but publishes no figure for Cruise Critic specifically.

faqs.q: Can you book a cruise through Cruise Critic?
faqs.a: Not with Cruise Critic itself. Its terms of use say it “is not a travel agency and does not provide or own transportation services or accommodations”, and clicking a fare hands you to a third party — on the UK pages on 23 October 2026 those included Onyx Cruises, Panache Cruises and Cruise118. That company takes the payment, holds the booking and handles any problem. The terms add that “Cruise Critic will have no liability” for a supplier’s acts or omissions.

faqs.q: Is a cruise booked this way financially protected?
faqs.a: That depends entirely on the seller, not on Cruise Critic. A package including a flight should come with an ATOL certificate naming the ATOL holder; the CAA describes ATOL as “financial protection when you book a package trip that includes a flight” and says plainly that “It is not travel insurance”. A cruise bought without a flight falls outside ATOL, and protection then comes from the seller’s own arrangements under the Package Travel Regulations 2018, usually an ABTA bond. Ask the company you are buying from and get the answer in writing.

faqs.q: How is a Cruise Critic rating worked out?
faqs.a: The site does not say, which is the central gap on it. A line or ship is given a single score out of five with a five-band distribution beneath it, and separately an “Editor Rating” out of 5.0 with no explanation of how the two relate. Royal Caribbean’s 3.9 can be reproduced by scoring its 44,042 banded reviews five down to one and taking a plain average, which comes out at 3.925 — our calculation, not the site’s. On that reading nothing is weighted for recency, so a 2014 review counts as much as last month’s.

faqs.q: Are the reviews checked to make sure the person actually sailed?
faqs.a: Nothing on the site says so. Reviews show a sail date and the reviewer’s cruise count but carry no verification marker, and no page sets out whether a reviewer must have sailed or how a disputed review is handled. The site does prohibit AI-written reviews outright — “AI-generated reviews are strictly prohibited” — and says suspected AI content may be removed without notice, which is a real control, but it is not the same thing as verifying a booking.

faqs.q: Why do Cruise Critic fares look cheaper than the cruise line’s own prices?
faqs.a: Usually because of what has been left out. On the UK pages the disclaimer reads “Taxes, fees and port expenses not included”, a “fuel supplement may apply”, the fare assumes two people sharing a specific cabin type on specific dates, and the lowest figure comes from an unnamed “3rd party pricing supplier” refreshed nightly. The same template on the American site says those charges are included. Price the sailing on the seller’s own site before comparing it with anything.

title: Cruise Nation Review: Smart Packages, Fares and Who Holds the ATOL
meta_title: Cruise Nation Review: Smart Packages From £395pp
meta_description: Cruise Nation sells 7-night cruises from £395pp and bundles flights, hotels and port taxes. Who you contract with, what the fees are and what is protected.

headline.label: Cheapest advertised fare
headline.value: £395 per person — 7-night no-fly cruise with a free balcony upgrade, two sharing the lowest cabin grade, on the cruisenation.com home page on 23 October 2026; gratuities excluded and a baggage charge may apply

intro:
Cruise Nation was advertising 7-night no-fly cruises from £395 per person on 23 October 2026, with a free balcony upgrade thrown in, and MSC Cruises out of Southampton from £419 per person for the same length of sailing. Nine-night holidays with flights and a hotel started at £549, and a 21-night Music Cities itinerary at £1,799. Every price is per person on two sharing the lowest cabin grade.

The company behind those prices is Really Great Cruises Limited, number 06908517 on the UK register, incorporated on 18 May 2009 and still run from Suite 4c, Conwy House, Castle Court on Swansea Enterprise Park. Philip Richard Evans and Stephen Roy Boardman, the two men who started it, were both appointed directors on 6 August 2009 and are still the only two in post. Companies House files the business under SIC 79110, travel agency activities, which is the clue to how the rest of this works.

When Cruise Nation packages a cruise with flights and a hotel, the contract is not with Swansea. Its own booking conditions say it plainly: “Your contract will be with Hays Tour Operating Limited” and “When we package your holiday for you we act as agents of Hays Tour Operating Limited (ATOL 10531).” Hays Tour Operating is company 03591401, incorporated on 2 July 1998 at Gilbridge House, Keel Square, Sunderland — the tour operating arm of Hays Travel, which has run from a first branch in Seaham since 1980, now has more than 530 high street shops and reported transaction value of £3 billion in 2025. For a reader handing over a deposit to a Welsh company of two directors, that is the most reassuring sentence on the site, and it is buried in clause one of the terms.

sections.heading: What £395 buys, and what the small print takes back out
sections.html:
The Smart Package is the product Cruise Nation built its name on, and the inclusion list is specific rather than vague. The company says each one carries “your cruise, return flights, hotel stay, and all port taxes and fees, clearly listed upfront”, a pre- or post-cruise hotel stay with a star rating attached, a choice of cabin grade, full board in selected ship restaurants, hot drinks, iced tea, lemonade, juice and water in selected buffet venues, use of the pools, hot tubs and gym, and the evening entertainment. Port fees, taxes and surcharges sit inside the headline figure, which is not true of every cruise seller and is worth knowing before comparing two prices.

Port taxes being inside the price matters more than it sounds. On a cruise booked elsewhere those can be presented as an extra at checkout, so a £395 fare with them included is not competing on level terms with a £379 fare that adds them later. Cruise Nation also says there is “No Booking fee is payable when you book online”, and lets you pick a departure airport from regional options, add hotel nights either side of the sailing, or upgrade to a four or five star property, with all of it priced before checkout rather than after.

Two things are outside every one of those prices and the site states both. “Gratuities are not included in any of these offers unless otherwise stated”, and “Baggage charge may apply.” On a seven-night sailing, ship gratuities commonly run to the better part of £100 for two people, so a £395 fare is not the sum a couple will actually pay, and the baggage line is the only mention of hold luggage anywhere in the package description. Transfers between airport, hotel and ship are not listed among the inclusions either, and seat selection is not mentioned at all.

The lead-in prices also move between banners on a single screen. On 23 October 2026 the no-fly banner carried “7-night cruises from £395pp” without naming a ship or a sailing date, while the Cruise Line of the Week panel on the same page read “Right now you can set sail with MSC Cruises from Southampton with 7-night sailings from just £419pp”. Both are seven nights, both sail from the UK, and the £24 between them is unexplained. The deal listings themselves are drawn by JavaScript and did not render on any fetch, so a lower fare may well sit behind the search; what is quotable is what the home page itself puts in front of a reader.

sections.heading: The contract is with a company in Sunderland, and that is good news
sections.html:
Clause one of the booking conditions does something most travel sites avoid, which is to name the principal. “Your contract will be with Hays Tour Operating Limited”, and Cruise Nation “act as agents of Hays Tour Operating Limited (ATOL 10531)”. The footer of every page repeats it: “Package holidays are sold by Cruise Nation as an agent for Hays Tour Operating Limited, ATOL 10531.”

Hays Tour Operating Limited is company 03591401 on the UK register, incorporated on 2 July 1998, registered at Gilbridge House, Keel Square, Sunderland SR1 3HA. It is the licensed tour operator inside Hays Travel, which calls itself “the UK’s largest independent travel agent” and has the trading history to argue it: a first shop opened in Seaham, County Durham in 1980, turnover through £500 million in 2012, past £1 billion in 2018 and £2 billion in 2024, transaction value of £3 billion in 2025, more than 530 branches, 2,500 former Thomas Cook staff re-employed in 2019 and 631 apprentices appointed in 2024.

ATOL 10531 is a licence of real size. The Civil Aviation Authority’s own ranked report of the largest ATOL holders, dated 29 November 2022, put Hays Tour Operating Ltd 36th with 59,692 licensed passengers. Set that against the 1,624 businesses the CAA said were licensed under ATOL in its release of 7 October 2026, and against the 20 million ATOL protected holidays it counted to the end of August 2026, and the shape is clear: the money behind a Cruise Nation Smart Package is sitting behind one of the larger licences in the country rather than a small one.

The Swansea company’s own filings are thinner, which is the other half of the picture. Really Great Cruises Limited files as a private limited company with last accounts made up to 31 December 2024 and the next set, to 31 December 2025, due by 30 September 2026. Crestvill Limited (05651282) was its registered person with significant control, holding more than 25% but not more than 50%, from 6 April 2016 until 31 December 2022; since a statement filed on 30 April 2023 the company has recorded no registrable person or legal entity at all, meaning no single holding now reaches the 25% threshold. The about page offers no headcount and no customer total either, only that the team has “more than 400 years combined experience in the travel industry”.

sections.heading: ATOL, ABTA and the cruise with no flight on it
sections.html:
This is where the site and its own paperwork part company, and it is the single most useful thing on this page. Under “Why Cruise Nation?” the home page states: “All holidays are fully ATOL protected. We are members of ABTA, so your booking is safe”. The booking conditions say the opposite twice. Clause 1.1: “ATOL protection does not apply to all holidays and travel services listed on this website.” Clause 17: “Not all holiday or travel services offered and sold by us will be protected by the ATOL Scheme.” Both are Cruise Nation’s own words, published on its own domain on the same day, and they cannot both be right.

The terms are the ones that match the law. ATOL covers flight-inclusive packages. The Civil Aviation Authority describes it as financial protection for a package trip that includes a flight, and the scheme does not reach a cruise with no flight attached. So the cheapest fare on the whole site — that £395 no-fly, seven-night sailing — is precisely the booking an ATOL certificate does not cover, while the banner three inches above it promises every holiday is fully ATOL protected. Clause 1.2 gives the reader the only reliable test there is: “When you buy an ATOL protected flight or flight inclusive holiday from us you will receive an ATOL Certificate”, and clause 1.1 adds that “If you do not receive an ATOL Certificate then the booking will not be ATOL protected.” Ask for the certificate, and if none arrives, the protection is not there.

The ABTA half of that sentence needs the same unpicking. A cruise with no flight falls under the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018, where a seller may protect the money by an ABTA bond, by financial failure insurance or by a trust account. ABTA’s own guidance is blunt about what membership alone does for a customer of an agent: where you book with an ABTA travel agent, “you cannot claim from the financial protection scheme administered by ABTA”, and “If the ABTA member did not financially protect your travel arrangements, you won’t be able to submit a claim to ABTA.” Cruise Nation is filed as a travel agency and describes itself as an agent. Its ABTA membership is a code of conduct and a route to arbitration; it is not, by ABTA’s own account, the thing that protects a deposit.

None of which makes a no-fly cruise unprotected. It makes the protection somebody else’s — the principal’s bond or trust arrangement — and Cruise Nation publishes no ABTA membership number anywhere on the site, so a reader cannot look it up. ABTA has been going for more than 75 years and says 89% of people are more likely to book with a member than not, which is exactly why the number is worth printing. Two safety nets exist regardless: a credit card payment between £100 and £30,000 brings section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act into play, and the 2018 regulations themselves cover the package, though ABTA notes that arrangements of under 24 hours or booked for business travel may fall outside them.

sections.heading: Deposits, balances and the price of running late
sections.html:
The money mechanics are set out in the terms rather than on the sales pages, and they reward reading. The deposit is described only as “A non-refundable deposit, to be advised per passenger”, with no figure attached anywhere in the conditions; the only numbers published are promotional, with the Summer 2027 banners quoting “low deposits from £103pp” and monthly payments “from £54pp per month”. Against that banner’s own lead-in fare of £689 per person, a £103 deposit is about 15% of the holiday, and eleven payments of £54 on top would come to £697 — eight pounds more than the advertised fare, which is this page’s arithmetic rather than Cruise Nation’s and the kind of sum worth doing on the confirmation invoice. The flexible payment option is available only on cruises departing in six months or more.

The balance falls due on the date printed on the confirmation invoice, which the terms say can be as much as 28 weeks before departure — roughly six and a half months of the money sitting with the operator. Miss it and the charges are fixed and published: £35 if payment lands 3 to 6 days late, £75 at 7 to 9 days late, and £20 per named person on a booking held under a Low Deposit Agreement. Changing your mind costs £25 per change per person, and transferring a booking to someone else is another £25 per person plus any increase in cost.

Cancelling is where the exposure sits. The terms say charges rise the nearer departure gets, but publish only one point on that curve: “a cancellation made within 50 days incurs a 100% cancellation fee.” Fifty days is early by the standards of most package holidays, and no graduated scale is given, so a customer cancelling at 60 or 70 days out cannot work out their liability from the website at all.

Clause 7 lets Cruise Nation pass on cost increases “up to an increase of 8% of the holiday price”, which on that £689 fare is £55. Clause 7.1 then sets out a rule that runs one way only: “Should the same holiday be advertised at a higher price, we will not contact you for more money”, and “should the same holiday be advertised at a lower price, no refund of the difference will be provided.” The first half protects the customer, the second half protects the seller, and the pairing is at least stated openly rather than left to be discovered.

When the company cancels or makes a significant change, compensation is tabulated per passenger across two scales. More than 56 days before departure it is nil on both. At 56 to 43 days it is £10 on Scale A and nil on Scale B; 42 to 29 days, £20 and £10; 28 to 15 days, £25 and £10; 14 days or fewer, £30 and £15. The ceiling of £30 is 7.6% of that £395 lead-in fare, so the compensation table is a gesture rather than a remedy — the refund rights under the 2018 regulations are what actually matter if a holiday is cancelled.

sections.heading: A 4.9 out of 5 that rests on 727 ratings, not 12,118
sections.html:
Cruise Nation uses Feefo, which independently collects feedback and says its “platform only reaches out to verified buyers” and that it verifies reviews “by matching them to a sale or transaction”. That makes the score meaningfully better evidence than an open review page anyone can post to, and the score itself is strong: a service rating of 4.9 out of 5, labelled EXCEPTIONAL.

The about page presents it as “a Feefo rating of 4.9/5 based on 12,118 verified reviews”. Feefo’s own page is more precise, and the difference is worth a paragraph. It displays all 12,118 reviews, but the star distribution sitting beside the 4.9 covers 727 ratings over the past year: 648 at five stars, 70 at four, 3 at three, 2 at two and 4 at one. Score those five down to one and take a plain average and the answer is 4.87, which rounds to the published 4.9 — so the headline figure is an unweighted mean of the last twelve months, not of the 12,118 reviews it is quoted against. Those 727 ratings are 6.0% of that total. This is arithmetic done on Feefo’s own published distribution, not a figure either company states.

What the distribution does show is a genuinely good recent record. Five-star ratings are 89.1% of the past year, and everything at three stars or below comes to nine ratings, or 1.2%. A seller shifting cruise packages at these prices with a one-in-eighty rate of mediocre-or-worse feedback is doing something right, and that is the honest reading of the number. The looser claim on the same pages is harder to stand behind: “Voted the UK’s number 1 cruise holiday company - over 720,000 can’t be wrong” and “Voted World’s No.1 cruise booking website” name no poll, no awarding body and no year, and 720,000 is not a figure that appears anywhere else on the site or in any filing.

sections.heading: Awards from four cruise lines, and not one of them named
sections.html:
The about page says the business grew “from being a small start up business to an award winning tour operator” and that “we have won awards from four different cruise lines, as well as awards for our innovation within the cruise market and our digital presence.” No cruise line is named, no award is named, and no year is given for any of them. The only specific award reference anywhere on the site is a blog headline, “Cruise Nation Nominated at British Travel Awards 2017”, which is a nomination nine years old rather than a win.

That is a shame, because the verifiable parts of the story are decent. The company dates itself to 2009, which Companies House confirms to the day, and it put its own booking platform live in 2017 so that Smart Packages could be bought online for the first time — a non-trivial thing for a two-director company in Swansea to build in a market where the large sellers buy their technology. The about page lists 20 cruise line brands it works with, including MSC Cruises, Norwegian Cruise Line, Princess, Cunard, P&O Cruises, Celebrity, Carnival, Oceania, Costa, Royal Caribbean and Virgin Voyages, and claims “over 200+ destinations worldwide”. Against its own observation that there are “more than 30 cruise lines out there”, 20 is a real proportion of the market and a checkable number, which is more than any of the award claims manage.

There is no independent rating of a UK cruise seller from anybody. Defaqto does not rate travel websites, Smart Money People has no listing, and the tourist board assessment schemes grade properties rather than agents. So the Feefo distribution above, the Companies House record and the ATOL report are the whole of the external evidence available on this company, and a page that pretends otherwise is guessing.

sections.heading: Where 2.54 million British cruises actually went last year
sections.html:
The market Cruise Nation sells into had its best year on record. Cruise Lines International Association’s UK and Ireland release of 22 April 2026 counted 2.54 million ocean cruises taken by British and Irish passengers in 2025, against a previous high of 2.4 million in 2024 — a rise of about 5.8%. The Mediterranean took 34.5% of those passengers, northern Europe 27.2% and the Caribbean 13.7%. The average cruise ran 9.6 days and the average passenger was 54.6 years old. Andy Harmer, managing director of CLIA UK and Ireland, put it as “Cruise continues to appeal to a wide range of holidaymakers”, with more children sailing than ever.

Two of those numbers bear directly on how Cruise Nation’s shop window is arranged. The 9.6-day average sits between its seven-night lead-ins and its nine-night packages, so the two cheapest tiers on the home page are aimed squarely at the middle of the market rather than at the long voyages that fill a brochure. And northern Europe at 27.2% explains the no-fly banner: more than a quarter of British cruise passengers sail from a UK port, which is the fare that comes in lowest and also, as the section above sets out, the one ATOL does not touch.

Scale is worth keeping in proportion. The 59,692 passengers Hays Tour Operating was licensed to carry in the November 2022 ATOL report represent 2.4% of the 2.54 million ocean cruises taken in 2025, and that licence covers the whole of Hays Travel’s tour operating, not Cruise Nation alone. This is a specialist seller inside a large agency group, not a volume operator, and the pricing reads accordingly.

sections.heading: Nobody shows you the ship’s inspection score
sections.html:
Every ship on Cruise Nation’s 20 cruise lines that calls at a United States port is inspected, scored and published by a public health authority, and no cruise seller in Britain displays it. The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention runs a Vessel Sanitation Program whose own published account of the rules sets out the method: inspections are twice yearly and unannounced, scored out of 100, with a pass at 86 or higher and a re-inspection within 45 days of a failure. It applies to ships sailing from foreign to US ports carrying 13 or more passengers, and it is paid for by fees levied on gross registered tonnage.

That is the only independent, scored, repeated assessment of the actual ships in this market, and it is free to look up. The programme’s current per-ship report index returned a client error on 23 October 2026, so no individual score is quoted here rather than quoting one that could not be read. A reader with a ship name and a sailing in mind can search that index directly before paying a deposit, which is a better use of ten minutes than any brochure.

Nothing about this is a criticism of Cruise Nation in particular. It sells cabins on other companies’ ships and has no more access to a sanitation score than a customer does. It is simply the most useful thing a cruise buyer is never told, and the gap sits across the whole category rather than on one seller.

pros: Smart Packages bundle the cruise, return flights, a hotel stay and all port taxes and fees into one advertised price, with no online booking fee
Lead-in fares are genuinely low for a UK seller: £395 per person for seven nights with no flight, £549 for nine nights including flights and a hotel
The booking conditions name the principal outright — the package contract is with Hays Tour Operating Limited, ATOL 10531, ranked 36th largest ATOL holder with 59,692 licensed passengers
Behind that licence sits Hays Travel, trading since 1980 with more than 530 branches and £3 billion of transaction value in 2025
A Feefo service score of 4.9 out of 5 from verified buyers only, with 89.1% of the past year's 727 ratings at five stars
Low deposits from £103 per person and monthly payments from £54 on cruises departing six months or more ahead
Fees are published rather than hidden: £25 to amend, £35 and £75 for late payment, and a compensation table with figures in it
Twenty cruise line brands including MSC, NCL, Cunard, P&O Cruises, Virgin Voyages and Royal Caribbean, and the same two founding directors in post since 2009
cons: The home page says “All holidays are fully ATOL protected” while clause 1.1 of its own terms says “ATOL protection does not apply to all holidays and travel services listed on this website”. The terms are right, and the £395 no-fly cruise is exactly the booking ATOL does not cover.

The claim that “We are members of ABTA, so your booking is safe” is not how ABTA works for an agent's customer. ABTA's own guidance says that where you book with an ABTA travel agent “you cannot claim from the financial protection scheme administered by ABTA”, and Cruise Nation publishes no ABTA membership number anywhere for a reader to check.
No deposit figure appears in the booking conditions at all — only “A non-refundable deposit, to be advised per passenger” — so the amount cannot be established before you call.
The cancellation scale is published at one point only: 100% of the price within 50 days of departure, which is early, with nothing at all for 60 or 70 days out.
Compensation when the company cancels tops out at £30 per person on Scale A, which is 7.6% of the cheapest advertised fare.
Clause 7.1 refunds nothing if the same holiday is later advertised cheaper, while the surcharge clause allows increases of up to 8% of the holiday price.
The 4.9 Feefo score is quoted against 12,118 reviews but is derived from 727 ratings over the past year, which is 6.0% of them.

“Voted the UK’s number 1 cruise holiday company - over 720,000 can’t be wrong” and awards “from four different cruise lines” name no poll, no body and no year; the only dated award reference on the site is a 2017 British Travel Awards nomination.
Gratuities are excluded from every advertised fare, a baggage charge may apply, and transfers and seat selection are not listed among the Smart Package inclusions.

The home page's own lead-in fares disagree: £395 per person for seven nights on one banner and £419 for seven nights with MSC from Southampton on another, with no ship or sailing date attached to either.
verdict: Cruise Nation does the hard part of a cruise holiday well. Putting the cruise, the flights, the hotel and the port taxes into one advertised number is the thing most sellers will not do, and at £395 per person for seven nights or £549 with flights and a hotel for nine, the prices are real rather than bait. A Feefo service score of 4.9 from verified buyers, with 648 of the past year's 727 ratings at five stars, says the delivery matches the promise more often than not — and the two founders who incorporated the company on 18 May 2009 are still the only directors, which in this market counts for something. Treat the protection wording as the one thing to settle before you pay. Your Smart Package contract is with Hays Tour Operating Limited in Sunderland under ATOL 10531, which is a licence for 59,692 passengers inside a group turning over billions, and that is a genuinely strong place for your money to sit. But the banner promising that every holiday is fully ATOL protected is contradicted by clause 1.1 of the company's own terms, and the cheapest fare on the site — the no-fly cruise — is the one ATOL does not reach. Ask for the ATOL certificate, ask which bond or trust account covers a cruise-only booking, ask what the deposit actually is, and pay by credit card. Get those four answers and the price is a good one.

faqs.q: Who am I actually buying from when I book a Cruise Nation package?
faqs.a: Cruise Nation is a trading name of Really Great Cruises Limited, company 06908517, run from Swansea and filed at Companies House as a travel agency. For a packaged holiday the contract is not with that company. Clause 1 of the booking conditions says “Your contract will be with Hays Tour Operating Limited” and that Cruise Nation acts “as agents of Hays Tour Operating Limited (ATOL 10531)” — company 03591401 of Keel Square, Sunderland, the tour operating arm of Hays Travel. Cruise Nation handles the sale and the customer service; Hays Tour Operating is the principal and the ATOL holder.

faqs.q: Is a no-fly cruise from Cruise Nation ATOL protected?
faqs.a: No. ATOL is financial protection for a package that includes a flight, and a cruise sailing from a UK port with no flight attached falls outside it. The company's own clause 1.1 says “ATOL protection does not apply to all holidays and travel services listed on this website” and clause 17 repeats it, even though the home page says every holiday is fully protected. The test clause 1.2 gives is the certificate: if no ATOL Certificate arrives, the booking is not ATOL protected. A cruise-only booking is instead covered under the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018, by whatever bond, failure insurance or trust account the principal holds — so ask which one, in writing, before paying.

faqs.q: How much is the deposit and when is the balance due?
faqs.a: The terms give no figure, only “A non-refundable deposit, to be advised per passenger”. The promotional banners quote low deposits from £103 per person and monthly payments from £54 per person, available on cruises departing in six months or more. The balance is due on the date printed on your confirmation invoice, which the conditions say may be up to 28 weeks before departure. Paying late costs £35 at 3 to 6 days, £75 at 7 to 9 days, and £20 per named person where the booking sits under a Low Deposit Agreement.

faqs.q: What does it cost to change or cancel?
faqs.a: An amendment is £25 per change per person, and transferring a booking to another person is £25 per person plus any increase in the cost. On cancellation the terms publish a single figure: a cancellation made within 50 days of departure incurs a 100% charge. No graduated scale is given for cancelling earlier than that, so get the figure for your own departure date confirmed in writing at the time of booking.

faqs.q: Can the price go up after I have booked?
faqs.a: Yes, within a limit. Clause 7 permits surcharges “up to an increase of 8% of the holiday price”, which on a £689 per person fare is about £55. Clause 7.1 then states that if the same holiday is later advertised at a higher price you will not be asked for more, and if it is advertised at a lower price “no refund of the difference will be provided” — so the published-price movement works in the company's favour, while a genuine cost increase can be passed on up to that 8% ceiling.

faqs.q: What is included in a Smart Package, and what is not?
faqs.a: Included: the cruise, return flights from a choice of UK airports, a hotel stay with a star rating, all port taxes, fees and surcharges, a choice of cabin grade, meals in selected ship restaurants, soft drinks and hot drinks in selected buffet venues, use of pools, hot tubs and leisure facilities, and the entertainment programme. Not included: gratuities, which the site excludes from every offer unless stated; hold baggage, where “Baggage charge may apply”; and transfers and seat selection, neither of which appears in the inclusion list. There is no booking fee if you book online.

faqs.q: How good is the Feefo score, really?
faqs.a: Good, and slightly narrower than it is presented. Feefo collects feedback only from buyers it can match to a transaction, so the 4.9 out of 5 service score is from verified customers. The about page quotes it “based on 12,118 verified reviews”, but the distribution published beside the 4.9 covers 727 ratings from the past year — 648 five-star, 70 four, 3 three, 2 two and 4 one. Averaging those gives 4.87, which rounds to the published figure, so the score reflects the last twelve months rather than all 12,118 reviews. On that year, 89.1% were five-star and 1.2% were three stars or below.

faqs.q: If something goes wrong, who do I complain to?
faqs.a: On holiday, the terms require you to tell the hotelier, local representative or local agent immediately. After you get home you have 28 days to put it in writing to Cruise Nation's Customer Relations Department in Swansea, by email to CustomerRelations@cruisenation.com or on 01792 705301. If that does not settle it, the company says that “As members of ABTA we are legally bound by the decision of the appointed Arbitrator”, under a scheme administered independently by the Chartered Institute of Arbitrators. That scheme is not available for claims above £5,000 per person or £25,000 per booking.

title: Cult Beauty Review: 287 Brands, Cult Status Points and the Four Brands Its Owner Makes
meta_title: Cult Beauty: 287 Brands, £5 Back per £100, 30-Day Returns
meta_description: Cult Beauty lists 287 brands, pays £5 of credit for every £100 spent and takes unopened items back for 30 days at £2.99. Checked 23 October 2026.

headline.label: Returning an opened beauty product
headline.value: Only if it is faulty — 30 days on an unopened item, hygiene seal intact, against a statutory 14, and £2.99 to post it back (checked 23 October 2026)

intro:
Cult Beauty’s own A to Z listed 287 brands on 23 October 2026, from 111SKIN and Augustinus Bader to Westman Atelier and Zelens. Spend £100 and the Cult Status scheme hands back £5 of credit; standard delivery is £3.95 and free over £30, next day is £5.95 and the shop will post an unopened item back for £2.99 inside 30 days.

It is a bigger business than the editorial tone suggests. Cult Beauty is one of three online beauty retailers owned by the listed group THG plc, which describes itself in its 2025 annual report as the “Owner and operator of three major online beauty retailers: Lookfantastic, Cult Beauty and Dermstore”. THG bought Cult Beauty on 4 August 2021 for £275m on a cash and debt-free basis, and its THG Beauty division turned over £1,107.9m in the year to 31 December 2025 and £500.2m in the first half of 2026. That means the audited accounts behind the shop are published twice a year, which is more than most beauty retailers can say.

One practical rule is worth knowing before you fill a basket. Nothing goes back once it has been opened: the returns policy wants items “Unopened, with all original product packaging and hygiene seals untouched”, and that is the industry norm rather than a quirk of this shop. The 30-day window on sealed items is longer than the 14 days the law requires, and the £2.99 return label is the one cost a Boots or a Space NK customer would not pay.
