sections.heading: What 287 brands adds up to, and the four the owner makes itself
sections.html:
The brand list is the product here. Cult Beauty’s A to Z carried 287 brands on 23 October 2026 — 289 entries if you count the two signposts sitting in the alphabet, “Recently Launched Brands On Cult Beauty!” and “LGBTQIA+ Owned Businesses”. The spread is the point: 111SKIN, 19/99 Beauty, Acqua Di Parma, Act+Acre, Aesop, Allies of Skin, Alpha-H, Amika, Anastasia Beverly Hills, Anua, Armani Beauty and Augustinus Bader are the first dozen, and the tail end runs VOTARY, VT Cosmetics, Vyrao, Weleda, WelleCo, Westman Atelier, WHO IS ELIJAH, Yu Ling Rollers, Youth To The People and Zelens. A good number of those are the kind of small, single-product, founder-run labels a department store will not touch.

Set that against the number THG published when it bought the business. The acquisition announcement of 4 August 2021 described Cult Beauty as stocking “c. 300” prestige third-party brands, with around two thirds of them not then listed on any existing THG Beauty site, serving “1.7m highly engaged customers” and “1.6m Instagram followers”. Five years and two months later the list is 287. That is a flat range, and on a shop whose whole promise is a curated edit it is defensible — an edit that doubles every year is not an edit. It is worth knowing all the same, because the group around it has grown: THG’s 2025 annual report calls THG Beauty a “Critical route to market for over 1,000 brands” and says it launched “over 80 new brands” during the year.

Four of the 287 belong to the company doing the editing. THG’s annual report names its “flagship skincare brands – Perricone MD, Biossance and ESPA”, and records that “Ameliorate completed a full rebrand in 2025”. All four — ESPA Skincare, Perricone MD, Biossance and Ameliorate — sit in Cult Beauty’s own A to Z alongside the third-party labels, and nothing on the brand pages says so. On the page’s own arithmetic that is about 1.4% of the list, which is a long way from a shop stuffed with house brands, and each of the four is a real brand with its own following rather than a white-label filler. The gap is one of disclosure rather than of substance: a reader taking the edit as independent expert selection has no way, from the site, of telling which four entries the editor profits from twice.

One name needs care in the other direction. Grow Gorgeous is on the Cult Beauty list too, and THG’s annual report mentions it only as a non-core brand exited during 2025 — so it is a third-party brand now, not a house one, and counting it would overstate the overlap.

sections.heading: A point a pound, and the 30-day fuse on what you earn
sections.html:
Cult Status is the loyalty scheme and the terms are unusually specific. You “earn 1 point for every £1 you spend on www.cultbeauty.co.uk (excluding shipping costs)”, and “For every 100 Points earned you will be eligible for £5 Credit”. That is 5% back on everything but the postage, paid in credit rather than cash, and it is a better headline rate than most high street cards manage. Enrolment happens once you have spent £100 or earned 100 points, whichever comes first, and writing a product review is worth 10 points, capped at ten reviews a month.

Three clocks run against it. Points “will expire 365 days following issuance if they are not converted into Credit”. Once converted, the credit “received from converting Points will expire after 30 days” and is “valid for a single transaction only”, so a £5 balance has to be spent in a single order inside a month or it is gone, and it cannot be put towards a Cult Beauty gift voucher. And conversion only works in multiples of £5, which means 99 points buy nothing at all.

Then there are the ceilings, which are the part nobody mentions. “The maximum Points available to earn per transaction is capped at 5,000” and “The maximum Points a Member can accumulate over a 12 month period is 10,000”. Those are the shop’s own figures; the sum is this page’s. At a point per pound, the annual cap means the scheme stops paying anything at all above £10,000 of spending in a year, and the most credit anyone can earn in twelve months is £500. For almost every customer that is academic. For the kind of heavy spender a prestige beauty retailer actually depends on, it is a real limit and it is not flagged anywhere a shopper would look.

The review route is the odd one. Ten points a review and ten reviews a month is 100 points a month, which converts to £5 — £60 a year of credit for 120 reviews, on the page’s own arithmetic, without buying anything extra at all. Reviews have to come through the review request email, so they are tied to real purchases, which is the right control to have.

There are tiers above the entry level — Silver and Gold, “previously Level Two” and “previously Level Three” — each lasting a 12-month “Membership Year”, with the level decided by points earned inside that year. Gold is worth having for one concrete reason: next day delivery becomes “FREE for Gold Cult Status Members on orders over £30” instead of over £100, and Silver pays £3.95 for it over £30. The terms point to a separate page for “the Points required for each Level” and that page returned no thresholds to a plain read on 23 October 2026, so how much a shopper has to spend to reach either tier could not be established.

sections.heading: Three company names and one checkout
sections.html:
A shopper who goes looking for the company behind the shop finds three. The footer reads “2026 The Hut.com Ltd t/a CultBeauty.co.uk”. The regulatory line a few pixels away reads “THG Beauty Limited (FRN: 1022963), trading as www.cultbeauty.co.uk”. And the company actually called Cult Beauty Limited is alive and filing: number 06195011, incorporated 30 March 2007, SIC code 47910 for retail sale via mail order houses or via the internet, status active, registered at Icon 1, 7-9 Sunbank Lane, Ringway, Altrincham WA15 0AF, which is THG’s own address.

THG Beauty Limited is company 13400467, incorporated 16 May 2021 — three months before the acquisition completed — and there is a THG Beauty I2 Limited, 16379955, incorporated 10 April 2025, at the same address. None of this is irregular; a group of this size reorganises its trading entities and the brand name survives the company that first carried it. It does mean that the entity a customer contracts with is not stated plainly on the pages a customer reads, and the firm reference number is the only regulatory identifier on offer. The FCA register page for FRN 1022963 would not load on 23 October 2026, so that number is the shop’s own disclosure rather than something confirmed against the register here.

Cult Beauty Limited’s last filed accounts were made up to 31 December 2024. The register shows the next set, to 31 December 2025, as due by 30 September 2026, and the company’s filing history page could not be read on three attempts, so whether they have since gone in could not be confirmed. The statutory accounts of that company are the one place a figure for Cult Beauty as a business would appear, which is what makes them worth asking after.

The terms of sale are the gap that matters more. The returns and delivery pages serve their text plainly and were read in full for this page. The terms and conditions page, the Klarna pages and the payment methods page all returned navigation and promotional banners and no terms at all on 23 October 2026, across both the ordinary and the alternate addresses. So the governing law, the jurisdiction, the point at which the contract is formed, the pricing-error clause and any cap on the shop’s liability could not be read, and none of them are quoted here. A reader who wants them should ask customer services for the document before ordering anything expensive.

sections.heading: The accounts behind the shop, and the one number they never print
sections.html:
Some context on the trade first, because it is a harder year than the marketing suggests. The British Beauty Council’s Value of Beauty 2026 report, compiled by Oxford Economics and announced on 1 July 2026, puts the industry’s contribution to the UK economy in 2025 at £28.3 billion — a “marginal 0.2% cash-terms decrease” on revised 2024 figures — supporting “more than 595,000 jobs”, with total employment down 2.8% and direct employment down 2.1%. Beauty services were the largest direct contributor at £5.7 billion. Millie Kendall OBE, the Council’s chief executive, said that “Successive budgets have made it increasingly difficult for beauty businesses to create and sustain jobs”.

Against that, THG’s preliminary results of 26 March 2026 for the year to 31 December 2025 read steadily enough. Group revenue was £1,717.0m, up 2.3% at constant currency and down 2.0% as reported, with adjusted EBITDA of £76.6m against £83.3m the year before, a 4.5% margin and an adjusted gross margin of 40.7%. Net debt before lease liabilities came down to £233.0m from £304.3m, with cash of £183.1m. THG Beauty, the division Cult Beauty sits in, took £1,107.9m of that — a 5.4% reported decline, growth of 0.2% at constant currency — on adjusted EBITDA of £65.8m, a 5.9% margin and a 39.3% gross margin.

The half-year numbers of 10 September 2026 are better. Group revenue of £828.7m, up 7.2% at constant currency and 5.8% as reported, adjusted EBITDA of £42.8m at a 5.2% margin and up 210 basis points, gross margin of 41.1%, and net debt before leases of £329.7m — £476.8m with lease liabilities in. THG Beauty grew 5.9% at constant currency to £500.2m. Group-wide, active customers were 7.5m in 2025 against 7.9m in 2024, and online revenue split 60% UK, 22% US, 16% Europe and 2% rest of world.

What none of those documents contains is a figure for Cult Beauty. It appears in the FY2025 preliminary results only in the notes to editors, and in the interim results only in the same boilerplate; the growth rates THG chooses to publish belong to Lookfantastic, which grew 16.2% in the UK and Ireland over 2025 and whose skincare was up 17.4% year to date at the half year, with UK TikTok Shop revenue up 26%. Lookfantastic rising 16.2% inside a division that fell 5.4% as reported means something else in the division fell further, and no published number says what. The 2021 acquisition announcement expected Cult Beauty to take “c. £140m” of sales in FY 2022 on adjusted EBITDA of “c. £10m”. Five years on, there is nothing to compare that against.

sections.heading: The number on a sunscreen is the one that gets tested
sections.html:
Most claims on a beauty label are hard to check. Sun protection factor is the exception: it is a laboratory measurement, and when it is wrong a regulator can prove it. The Office for Product Safety and Standards keeps a free, searchable register of alerts, reports and recalls, and a search for the keyword sunscreen returned 3 reports on 23 October 2026. Two of the three concern SPF50+ products sold widely in British beauty halls, which makes this the most useful ten seconds a sun cream buyer can spend.

The serious one is notification 2510-0095, a recall of Ultra Violette Lean Screen SPF50+ in the 50ml size, dated 15 October 2025 and last updated 9 April 2026. OPSS records the risk level as Serious, the country of origin as Australia, and the fault in plain words: the product “failed SPF testing with variable results, placing consumers at risk of sunburn”. Twenty-two batch numbers are listed, from A1399 through to A2550, the product was recalled from end users with refunds through the brand’s own form, and the notice was raised by Local Authority Trading Standards rather than by the brand.

Cult Beauty is named on that notice. So are Ultra Violette itself, Boots, Space NK, Liberty London, Harrods and Sephora — seven sellers of the same product, listed for the same reason, which is how a recall is supposed to work. Being on the list is evidence that the machinery reached the people who had bought the thing, and a shop that stocks hard-to-find imported brands will be on more of these notices than one that stocks six safe names. The second SPF50+ entry, 2512-0024 and 2602-0295 of 18 March 2026, is a recall of Bondi Sands Zinc Mineral Sunscreen SPF50+ body and face lotion.

The third entry shows the other risk in buying imported beauty, and it is about paperwork rather than chemistry. Notification 2607-0138 of 17 August 2026 concerns a Bubble Cosmetics Sunscreen Pack from the United States, graded High risk, where “Multiple mandatory cosmetic labelling requirements have not been met” — the missing items including the sunscreen use instructions and the traceability information — in breach of Regulation (EC) 1223/2009. The import was rejected at the border rather than recalled from shoppers, which is the system catching a problem a step earlier. For a shop whose appeal is American and Australian labels that British chemists do not carry, that is the category of risk to watch: not a dangerous formula, but a bottle that was never labelled for sale here.

Cult Beauty was running an “SPF 20% OFF” promotion on its home page on 23 October 2026. Nothing is wrong with that, and nothing in the register touches the products in it. It is simply the moment to run the two searches yourself: the register lives at gov.uk under product safety alerts, reports and recalls, it takes a keyword, and it prints a total so you can see whether you are looking at three results or three hundred.

sections.heading: Thirty days, an unbroken seal and £2.99
sections.html:
The returns policy is the thing a beauty shopper is most likely to need and it is written clearly. Cult Beauty is “happy to offer a refund/exchange for an unwanted item returned within 30 days of receipt”, and the condition is that items arrive “Unopened, with all original product packaging and hygiene seals untouched”. Anything else is refused outright: “We are unable to offer a refund, replacement or exchange on items that are not re-saleable”. A UK return costs £2.99 for the label; from outside the UK “you will need to cover the cost of return shipping”. If the order qualified for a free gift, the gift has to go back too before the refund is processed.

Measure that against the law and the shop comes out ahead on the window and level on the seal. The Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 give an online buyer 14 days to cancel, so 30 is more than double. The hygiene-seal rule is not an extra condition the shop invented — the same regulations lift the cancellation right for sealed goods unsuitable for return on health or hygiene grounds once they have been unsealed. Where the regulations bite harder is on what a trader may dock. Regulation 34(9) lets a trader recover any amount by which “the value of the goods is diminished by any amount as a result of handling of the goods by the consumer”, up to the contract price, and regulation 34(12) sets the test: handling goes too far if “it goes beyond the sort of handling that might reasonably be allowed in a shop”. A tester on a counter is allowed. Two weeks of using a serum is not.

The timings are where a reader should keep an eye on the calendar. Cult Beauty says processing “can take 3-5 working days from the date we receive the return”, after which a card or bank refund “can take up to 10 days to show on your statement from the time of issue”, and a Klarna refund arrives “within 5-10 working days”. Regulation 34(5) gives a trader 14 days from receiving the goods back, or from the day the customer supplies evidence of having sent them, whichever is earlier, and regulation 34(7) requires the same means of payment the customer used. Five working days of processing plus ten days on a statement can run past that 14-day mark, and the policy does not distinguish between the day the money is issued and the day it lands.

Two smaller wrinkles. The policy says 30 days “of receipt” in one sentence and asks for returns to arrive “within 30 days of delivery” in another, which are not the same start date on a parcel that sat in a collection point for a week. And the required condition is described as “saleable”, “re-saleable” and “pristine” in three different places, which are three different standards to be judged against if a refund is ever refused.

sections.heading: Four free-delivery thresholds, and two of them for the same service
sections.html:
The delivery page is one of the better ones in British online beauty, because it prints every option with a price beside it. Standard delivery is £3.95, “Allow 2-3 days for delivery”, and “FREE on orders over £30”. Next Day is £5.95 if you “Order before 1am” and “FREE on all orders over £100”, with the Cult Status variations noted above. Click & Collect is £3.95 over “over 8500 collection points”, and Click & Collect Next Day is £5.95 and “Free for orders over £90”. There is an Eco Delivery at £3.95 whose last mile “is completed on foot, by bike, or by electric vehicle” and which only appears at checkout for eligible postcodes.

A Same Day option sits at £5.95, described as “for a limited time only!” against a previous £9.95, with orders “placed before 1pm” and availability restricted to certain postcodes in the Birmingham, Walsall, Wolverhampton, Dudley and Tipton areas. Channel Islands customers pay £9.95 for a 5-7 working day standard service, free over £30, or £15 for a 1-2 business day priority service, free over £150. Orders going anywhere else should be placed through cultbeauty.com, and points earned on the international site do not count on the UK one.

Two of the shop’s own pages disagree about one of those figures, and both were read on 23 October 2026. The home page carries a banner reading “FREE NEXT DAY DELIVERY ON ORDERS OVER £150”. The delivery page, re-read a second time for the exact wording, says “FREE on all orders over £100”. Neither page is dated and neither mentions the other. The delivery page is the one carrying the cut-off times, the tier benefits and the carrier detail, so it is the likelier of the two to be current — but a shopper building a basket to a threshold cannot tell from the site which number applies, and £50 of unnecessary spending is the cost of guessing wrong. Check it in the basket before you add anything to reach a total.

Read as a ladder the thresholds are £30 for standard, £90 for next-day collection, £100 for next-day delivery and £150 on the banner. Collecting the parcel yourself qualifies £10 earlier than having it brought to the door, which is the right way round and not something every retailer gets correct.

sections.heading: Where a beauty complaint goes when nobody is obliged to hear it
sections.html:
There is no ombudsman for shopping. Banks, insurers and energy suppliers all answer to a statutory scheme; a beauty retailer answers to nobody unless it volunteers. The nearest thing is RetailADR, run by Consumer Dispute Resolution Limited, which says it “can be used to resolve disputes between consumers and Participating Member traders” and defines those as “Traders that have agreed to participate in the RetailADR scheme and be bound by our decisions”. Its member list was re-read on 23 October 2026 and carried no entry for Cult Beauty, THG, The Hut Group or Lookfantastic — and no beauty retailer at all, among fashion, homeware and general retail names such as ASOS, Topshop and Homesense.

So a disputed refund has three routes and none of them is an independent adjudicator. The first is the shop’s own service team. The second is a card chargeback through your bank, which is a scheme rule rather than a legal right; the Consumer Credit Act’s section 75 claim against a credit card issuer needs a cash price above £100, which a basket of two serums may or may not reach. The third is a small claim in the county court. Product safety is the one area with a proper destination: OPSS and local authority Trading Standards, which is who raised all three of the sunscreen notices above.

That is the normal state of affairs for online retail rather than a failing specific to this shop, and it is the reason the documents matter. A retailer that publishes its returns policy and its delivery prices in full, as this one does, has given a customer something to hold it to. A retailer whose terms of sale cannot be read has not.

pros: 287 brands on the A to Z on 23 October 2026, including small founder-run labels most department stores do not carry
Cult Status pays £5 of credit for every £100 spent, excluding shipping, which is 5% back
Thirty days to return an unopened item, against the 14 the Consumer Contracts Regulations require
Free standard delivery over £30, and six delivery options each priced on the page rather than only at checkout
Gold Cult Status turns free next day delivery from a £100 threshold into a £30 one
Owned by THG plc, so audited group accounts are published twice a year — THG Beauty revenue of £1,107.9m for 2025 and £500.2m for the first half of 2026
Product reviews earn 10 points each, up to ten a month, tied to a purchase through the review request email
Named openly on the OPSS recall notice for Ultra Violette Lean Screen SPF50+ alongside Boots, Space NK, Liberty London, Harrods and Sephora, so the recall reached its customers
Same day delivery at £5.95 in parts of Birmingham, Walsall, Wolverhampton, Dudley and Tipton
cons: The terms and conditions page, the Klarna pages and the payment methods page all returned navigation and banners rather than terms on 23 October 2026, so the contracting entity, the governing law and any cap on the shop’s liability could not be read at all
The home page advertises free next day delivery over £150 while the delivery page says £100; both were read the same day and neither is dated
Loyalty credit expires 30 days after conversion and is valid for one transaction only, so £5 earned has to be spent in a single order inside a month or it is lost

Points are capped at 5,000 per transaction and 10,000 in any 12 months, which on the scheme’s own earn rate caps credit at £500 a year and pays nothing above £10,000 of annual spending — and the caps are not mentioned where a shopper would see them
ESPA Skincare, Perricone MD, Biossance and Ameliorate are THG’s own brands and sit in the A to Z with no indication on the brand pages that the shop’s owner makes them

THG publishes no revenue, profit or customer figure for Cult Beauty in either its annual report or its interim results — the brand appears only in the notes to editors — against an expectation of “c. £140m” of FY 2022 sales at acquisition
The Silver and Gold points thresholds are not published in readable form, so the spend needed to reach the free-delivery benefit cannot be worked out before joining
Opened items cannot go back in any circumstances short of a fault, and a UK return costs £2.99 where some competitors pay the postage

Three to five working days of processing plus up to ten days to reach a statement can run past the 14 days regulation 34(5) allows a trader, and the policy does not separate the date a refund is issued from the date it lands
The returns policy gives the 30 days from “receipt” in one place and from “delivery” in another, and describes the required condition as “saleable”, “re-saleable” and “pristine” in three
No ombudsman and no ADR scheme: the RetailADR member list held no Cult Beauty, THG or Lookfantastic entry on 23 October 2026, so a disputed refund ends at a chargeback or the county court

Cult Beauty Limited’s accounts to 31 December 2025 were shown on the register as due by 30 September 2026, and the company’s filing history page could not be read on three attempts to confirm whether they have been filed
verdict: Cult Beauty is a genuine specialist rather than a general chemist with a beauty aisle, and the 287 brands on its A to Z are the reason to use it: a lot of them are small, imported or hard to find anywhere else in Britain. The money side is competitive without being remarkable — 5% back in credit, free standard delivery over £30, 30 days to send an unopened item back for £2.99 — and the tiered next-day benefit is worth having if you buy often. What a careful shopper should do before a big order is two things: confirm the free next-day threshold in the basket rather than off the home page banner, because the shop’s own pages give £100 and £150, and remember that loyalty credit dies 30 days after you convert it. The weakest part of the operation is documentary. A retailer owned by a listed company, publishing £1,107.9m of divisional revenue twice a year, should be able to serve its own terms of sale as readable text, and the four brands in the edit that THG makes itself should say so on their pages. Neither gap changes what arrives in the parcel. Both are the sort of thing worth knowing before you spend £150 to clear a delivery threshold that may not exist.

faqs.q: Can I return a beauty product to Cult Beauty once I have opened it?
faqs.a: No, unless it is faulty. The policy asks for items “Unopened, with all original product packaging and hygiene seals untouched” and says “We are unable to offer a refund, replacement or exchange on items that are not re-saleable”. On a sealed item you have 30 days from receipt, which is more than the 14 days the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 require, and a UK return label costs £2.99. If the order came with a free gift, that has to go back as well before the refund is processed.

faqs.q: How much is delivery, and when is it free?
faqs.a: Standard delivery is £3.95, takes 2-3 days and is free over £30. Next day is £5.95 if you order before 1am. The delivery page says next day is free over £100; the home page banner said over £150 on 23 October 2026, so check the figure in your basket before adding anything to reach it. Click & Collect is £3.95 across more than 8,500 points, or £5.95 for next day and free over £90. Gold Cult Status members get next day free over £30 and Silver members pay £3.95 over £30.

faqs.q: What is a Cult Status point actually worth?
faqs.a: Five pence. You earn one point per £1 spent excluding shipping, and 100 points convert to £5 of credit, so the scheme returns 5%. Conversion only works in multiples of £5. Points lapse 365 days after they are issued, and once converted the credit expires after 30 days and can only be used in a single transaction, not against a gift voucher. Earning is capped at 5,000 points per order and 10,000 points in any 12 months, which works out at a maximum of £500 of credit a year.

faqs.q: Who owns Cult Beauty?
faqs.a: THG plc, the listed Manchester group formerly known as The Hut Group, which bought the business on 4 August 2021 for £275m on a cash and debt-free basis. Its 2025 annual report describes THG Beauty as the “Owner and operator of three major online beauty retailers: Lookfantastic, Cult Beauty and Dermstore”. The site itself names THG Beauty Limited (company 13400467) in its regulatory line and The Hut.com Ltd in its copyright line, while the original company, Cult Beauty Limited (06195011, incorporated 30 March 2007), remains active at THG’s Altrincham address.

faqs.q: Is there an ombudsman if Cult Beauty will not put something right?
faqs.a: No. Retail has no statutory ombudsman, and the voluntary scheme RetailADR carried no entry for Cult Beauty, THG, The Hut Group or Lookfantastic when its member list was checked on 23 October 2026. That leaves the shop’s own service team, a chargeback through your card issuer, a section 75 claim if the cash price was over £100 and you paid by credit card, or a county court claim. Safety problems are different: those go to the Office for Product Safety and Standards or to local authority Trading Standards, which is who raised all three of the sunscreen notices on the public register.

title: Currys Gaming and Accessories: The Credit, the Cover and the Carve-Outs
meta_title: Currys Gaming: flexpay at 29.9% and the £99 Floor
meta_description: Currys gaming: interest-free credit over 12, 24 or 36 months but nothing under £99, breakdown cover priced above TVs, and free collection at 300+ stores.

headline.label: Cheapest way into the gaming range, delivered
headline.value: £0 — order online and collect free at any of 300+ Currys stores in the UK and Ireland; the item price cannot be quoted here, because currys.co.uk serves price placeholders rather than prices (checked 23 October 2026)

intro:
Currys will split a gaming order of £99 or more over 12, 24 or 36 months with no interest at all, or stretch it to 48 months at 9.9%, and it will hold the parcel at any of its 300-plus stores for nothing. Credit is no longer a sideline there: it ran through 23.7% of everything the company sold in the UK and Ireland last year, £1.2bn of sales, up 10% on the year before. Figures checked on 23 October 2026 against Currys' own service pages and its audited results for the year ended 2 May 2026.

The range behind that is wide. The gaming hub lists Console Gaming, PC Gaming, Gaming monitors, Gaming Accessories, Handheld Gaming, Gaming chairs, Components & Upgrades, Simulation gaming, Virtual Reality, Console games and Digital Downloads, with PS5, Xbox Series X, Nintendo Switch 2, Meta Quest and gaming laptops pinned at the top. Around 1,000 repair experts sit behind it, fixing more than a million products a year with a 12-month parts and labour guarantee on the repair itself, and any store will take old tech for recycling free of charge even if it was bought somewhere else. Recurring services revenue reached £873m last year, up 7%.

One thing is worth knowing before you click through. currys.co.uk does not send prices to anything except a browser. Fetched on 23 October 2026, the gaming landing page returned the full navigation, every category and every product name — and no price of any kind. In their place sat unrendered template tokens: $PRICE_10262507$ and $OFFER_10262507$. The delivery and collection page would not open at all across four attempts on the same day. So what follows is about the things Currys does publish in plain text — the credit, the cover, the repair promise and the returns — rather than about what a console costs on the morning you read this.

key_facts.label: Who you contract with
key_facts.value: Currys Group Limited, company 00504877, registered at Currys Newark Campus, Long Hollow Way, Newark NG24 2NH — incorporated 28 February 1952 as Dixon (Edgware) Finance Company Limited, and called DSG Retail Limited until 27 September 2021

key_facts.label: Credit
key_facts.value: Currys flexpay, 29.9% APR representative (variable) on an assumed £1,200 credit limit; Currys Group Limited is the credit broker and Creation Consumer Finance Ltd (FRN 311518) is the lender

key_facts.label: Minimum order for credit
key_facts.value: £99 — “paying with credit is available only on orders over £99”, which puts most controllers, headsets and games outside it

key_facts.label: Interest-free terms
key_facts.value: 12, 24 or 36 months interest free, or 48 months at a 9.9% purchase rate; buy now pay later promotions usually run 6, 9 or 12 months

key_facts.label: Online returns
key_facts.value: 30 days “even if you've opened it for inspection”; an in-store purchase has the same 30 days but must come back unopened

key_facts.label: Price match
key_facts.value: Against any other UK retailer, in store or online, claimable up to 7 days after purchase; exclusions and conditions are referred to but not set out on the page

key_facts.label: Breakdown cover on gaming
key_facts.value: Instant Replacement puts gaming in Group 2 and charges £13 to £40 for three years on items priced £20 to £150 — more than the £10 to £31 charged on a television in every band

key_facts.label: Recycling
key_facts.value: Free in store for any tech, bought there or not; WEEE registrations WEE/DE0065TW and WEE/FD0095VY, battery producer registrations BPRN00339 and BPRN00524

sections.heading: Spreading the cost stops dead at £99
sections.html:
Currys flexpay is a running credit account, not a point-of-sale loan, and the retailer is clear about its own role in it: “Currys Group Limited is a credit broker and offers the flexpay account under exclusive arrangement” with “the lender Creation Consumer Finance Ltd.” The standard rate is “29.9% Representative APR (variable)”, built on a 29.9% interest rate (variable) and an assumed credit limit of £1,200, with the usual rider that “Credit, offers and APR are subject to status and determined by the lender” and that applicants must be 18 or over.

Three promotional shapes sit on top of that. Interest free means “Pay in monthly instalments, interest free, over terms of 12, 24 or 36 months.” Pay monthly, low interest means “Spread the cost of your tech over 48 months, with a lower purchase interest rate of 9.9%” — twenty percentage points below the standard rate, which is a real saving rather than a presentational one. Buy now pay later runs for 6, 9 or 12 months and reverts: “Pay full balance by the end of the BNPL promotion period to avoid interest.” Miss a payment on any of them and “Late fees/charges may apply to missed payments and impact your credit file.”

The sentence that matters most on a gaming page is the quietest one. “Pay in monthly instalments for purchases £99 and over”, and separately, “paying with credit is available only on orders over £99.” A console, a gaming monitor, a gaming PC or a mid-range headset clears that bar. A controller, a keyboard, a mouse, a webcam, a boxed game or a capture dongle very often does not, and those are the purchases a gaming customer makes between consoles. There is a second restriction worth pairing with it: on the gift card terms, “Gift cards cannot be used towards Currys flexpay purchases when you purchase online”, so birthday money and a credit plan cannot be combined in the same online basket.

The scale of all this is in the audited numbers rather than the marketing. Flexpay sales reached £1.2bn in the year to 2 May 2026, “+10% YoY, with adoption rising +180bps to 23.7% of UK&I sales”, against UK and Ireland revenue of £5,438m. Twenty-three point seven per cent of £5,438m is £1,289m, so the two published figures sit together to within the rounding — that arithmetic is this page's, not the company's. Omnichannel sales reached 33% of UK and Ireland revenue, group adjusted profit before tax was £191m and the statutory figure £153m. A company incorporated in 1952 as a finance house, which then spent seventy years selling cameras and washing machines, now takes close to a quarter of its British sales on its own credit again.

sections.heading: The lender publishes its own complaints figures, and they repay reading
sections.html:
Creation Consumer Finance Limited puts its half-yearly complaints return on its own website, which most lenders do not, and the return covering 1 January to 30 June 2026 is specific. On fixed-term agreements it opened 8,629 complaints and closed 4,768 in the same six months — a gap of 3,861, which means the book of open cases grew over the period rather than shrank. The rate was 2.8492 complaints per 1,000 accounts. The headline cause is recorded as “Product Disclosure Information”.

The speed columns need reading in the regulator's own terms rather than at a glance. The return reports 7.38% closed within three days and 77.81% closed after three days but within eight weeks. Those two are separate buckets, not a running total, so the proportion resolved inside the eight-week deadline is 7.38 plus 77.81, or 85.19% — which also means a little under 15 in every 100 cases ran past it. Of the cases Creation closed, 49.52% were upheld in the customer's favour.

An uphold rate near half is not in itself an accusation; a complaint only reaches the figures because something had already gone wrong, and a firm that upholds readily is behaving better than one that does not. The pairing worth noticing is between that “Product Disclosure Information” heading and the thing a gaming customer is being asked to absorb at the checkout — a 29.9% running account, a 9.9% alternative, three promotional structures and a £99 floor, all decided in the few seconds before a console is paid for. Read the credit agreement on a screen bigger than a phone, and keep it.

sections.heading: Breakdown cover costs more on a controller than on a television
sections.html:
Instant Replacement is the cheap plan, sold in store only, for “most products between £20 and £150 which requires a one-off upfront payment”. It runs “for a total of 3 years, upon which your plan will expire”, covers breakdown “due to an electrical or mechanical fault”, excludes accidental and cosmetic damage, and can be bought on a product up to 12 months old. It can be paid in full or “over 10 instalments — ask in store for details”.

The price table is the interesting part, because Currys sorts products into three groups and gaming is not in the cheap one. Group 1 is televisions, monitors, printers and kitchen and household appliances. Group 2 is floorcare, gaming, headphones and electric transport. Group 3 is audio, home and outdoors, beauty, smart tech and gadgets. Across the six price bands, Group 2 is dearer than Group 1 every single time: £13 against £10 on a £20–£40 item, £17 against £13 at £41–£60, £24 against £17 at £61–£80, £30 against £22 at £81–£100, £35 against £27 at £101–£120 and £40 against £31 at £121–£150.

Set against the item it protects, the top of that ladder is steep. Forty pounds on a product at the bottom of the £121–£150 band is 33% of the purchase price; at the top of it, 26.7%. At the other end, £13 on a £20 accessory is 65% of what the accessory cost. Spread over the three years the plan runs, £40 is £13.33 a year to insure a controller against electrical failure. Currys does not publish the proportion of claims it pays or the average value of a replacement, and no regulator publishes an acceptance rate for retail breakdown plans of this kind, so there is no outside figure to measure that price against. The honest summary is that the premium is published, the payout record is not, and the gaming band is the dearest of the three.

sections.heading: Care & Repair, and the two words in its small print a gamer should find first
sections.html:
Care & Repair is the bigger plan, sold as a 2, 3 or 5-year upfront package or by monthly direct debit, priced on product category, price band and the length of the manufacturer's guarantee. Currys gives a worked example: a television priced £151–£175 with a one-year manufacturer guarantee costs £35 for three years upfront, £45 for five, or £1.50 a month. It covers parts, labour and call-outs, “if no fault is found you won't be charged”, and the stated target is to “repair products within 7 calendar days” — past which “you may request a replacement Product”. After two repairs, “if your tech has already had two repairs and it breaks down again, you can ask for a Currys gift card”. Televisions, computers and peripherals go to the company's repair centre in Newark. Upfront plans carry a 45-day cooling-off period with a full refund if unused; monthly plans carry 14 days.

Two sentences in it deserve attention before a gaming customer signs. The first is the status of the thing being sold: “Care & Repair is not an insurance policy and is an extended warranty plan only.” That wording is Currys' own, and it matters, because a service contract is not a general insurance contract and does not come with the complaints and compensation architecture a buyer might assume sits behind the word cover. The second is the pricing clause: “Care & Repair has fixed prices and we will therefore not price match.” The seven-day price promise described below applies to the console; it does not apply to the plan sold alongside it.

The third point is the one that sends a gamer back to the product page. The plan's extra benefits — the next-day replacement delivery, the 24/7 tech support, the built-in battery support and the annual valet — are not uniform, and the list of products shut out of them names “Monitors, eReaders, Networking, Printers, Scanners, Virtual Reality, Games Consoles”. Virtual Reality and Games Consoles. The two product lines a gaming buyer is most likely to be protecting are the two carved out of the extras, and the plan's own page says so without drawing attention to it. The core repair promise still applies; the add-ons that make the plan feel generous largely do not. Ask in store which benefits attach to the specific box before paying.

sections.heading: Seven days to claim the price match, and a test you can run on the sale price
sections.html:
The price promise is short and generous in outline. “We'll price match against any other UK retailer, in-store or online”, before or after purchase: “If you see the same item for less somewhere else, we'll refund you the difference”, and “We'll even price match 7 days after your purchase!” Currys Business runs a parallel “7 day price-match promise”. What the public page does not do is say which retailers count, which products are out, or how a claim is made; it says only “Exclusions and conditions apply. Claim within 7 days.” On a category where a marketplace seller and a high-street chain can both be the cheapest on a given Tuesday, the definition of an eligible competitor is the whole of the promise, and it is the part not published where the promise is advertised.

There is a free way for a reader to test the other half of the pricing — the struck-through comparison. The Chartered Trading Standards Institute's Guidance for Traders on Pricing Practices, reviewed and updated in October 2025 with a further amendment in November 2025, sets out what a defensible “was / now” claim looks like: the comparison should run for “a period that is the same or shorter than the period during which the higher price was offered”, and it asks “How recently was the higher price offered, compared to when the price comparison is being made?” Its worked examples treat a higher price charged “less than two months ago” as capable of giving a genuine indication of value, and prices “charged many months ago” as unlikely to. On recommended retail prices it is blunter still: “An RRP must not be false; it must not be created purely in order to present the appearance of a discount”, and “You should not recommend your own RRP.”

None of that is a finding about Currys, and it should not be read as one. It is a test a shopper can run without leaving the sofa: note the struck-through price on a gaming monitor today, check whether the same page shows the same comparison in a fortnight, and decide for yourself whether the higher figure was a price the shop actually charged for as long as the sale has run. The guidance exists precisely so that question has a published answer rather than an argument.

sections.heading: What the law calls a wireless controller, and where the hazard actually sits
sections.html:
Almost everything in the accessories half of this range is regulated radio equipment, and the definition is narrower and plainer than the phrase suggests. Regulation 2 of the Radio Equipment Regulations 2017 defines radio equipment as “an electrical or electronic product, which intentionally emits and/or receives radio waves” for “the purpose of radio communication and/or radiodetermination”, or one “which must be completed with an accessory, such as antenna, so as to intentionally emit and/or receive radio waves” for the same purpose. Radio waves are “electromagnetic waves of frequencies lower than 3,000 GHz, propagated in space without artificial guide”. A wireless controller, a Bluetooth headset, a wireless mouse and a VR headset all fall squarely inside that; anything mains-powered sits additionally under the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016.

Currys keeps its own product safety page, listing corrective action programmes and recalls with dates and model numbers, which is more than many retailers of its size publish at all. There were 28 entries on it on 23 October 2026, and the striking thing for anyone shopping the gaming range is what is absent: not one of them is a console, a controller, a headset or a gaming monitor. What is there instead is power. The Anker power banks A1681, A1689 and A1647 were recalled in July 2025 because “the lithium-ion batteries can overheat whilst in use”. Belkin's Power Bank 20K (BPB002) and Auto-Tracking Stand Pro (MMA008) followed in November 2025 over lithium-ion cells that “overheat”. The BenQ GV31 portable mini projector was recalled in June 2026 because its battery “may overheat and pose a fire risk”, and the Nutribullet Go blender in March 2025 over “isolated batteries that could overheat during charging”. In April 2026 Currys listed 44 separate Panasonic, JVC and Toshiba television models made between November 2024 and November 2025, every one of them over “the fuse in certain power cables not complying with the relevant safety standards”.

That pattern is the practical advice this section exists to give. A recall register with an empty gaming column is a good sign about the consoles, and it says nothing at all about the unbranded charger, the third-party dock or the cheap power bank bought to keep a handheld alive on a train. Buy the power supply from somebody who will be around to recall it, and keep the receipt — Currys' own guidance is to “always keep a hold of your sale receipt”, because that is how it reaches an owner if a programme is announced.

sections.heading: Consoles are growing, the headsets are not, and Currys is selling both
sections.html:
The trade body Ukie values the UK consumer games market at £8.76 billion for 2025, up 7.4% on £8.158 billion. Hardware was £2,172m of that, up 3%, and inside hardware the lines pull hard in opposite directions: consoles rose 12% to £811m and gaming PCs rose 11% to £790m, while virtual reality fell 26% to £151m from £201m. The fastest-growing line in the whole report is not a product at all — game culture, meaning merchandise, events, books and the rest, grew 42% to £566 million.

Set that beside what Currys puts in front of a shopper and the shape of the risk is clear. Virtual Reality is one of the eleven categories on the gaming hub and Meta Quest is pinned as a top category, in a segment that lost a quarter of its value in a year and now represents under 7% of all games hardware sold in Britain. There is nothing wrong with stocking a shrinking category — somebody has to — but it is the same category Currys has carved out of the Care & Repair extras, so the buyer is being sold the hardware in a declining line and offered a thinner support package on it than a dishwasher gets. A headset bought now will be supported by the manufacturer's guarantee and the statutory rights, and by rather less than the plan leaflet implies.

The console figures point the other way, and they are the better reason to shop here. A 12% rise in console sales on a market growing 7.4% overall is a line with momentum, and it is the line Currys is strongest in: PS5, Xbox Series X, Nintendo Switch 2 and handhelds including the ASUS ROG Ally X, MSI Claw 8 and Lenovo Legion Go all sit on the front of the gaming hub.

sections.heading: Sending it back, and getting rid of the old one
sections.html:
The returns position is better online than in store, which is the opposite of what most shoppers expect. An online purchase can be sent back “within 30 days — even if you've opened it for inspection”. An in-store purchase also has 30 days, but the item has to be unopened, so a game or a headset opened on the kitchen table after a Saturday trip to the retail park is in a weaker position than the identical item ordered from the sofa. Thirty days is more than twice the fourteen the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 require of a distance seller, so the extra sixteen days are a concession rather than a right. Some items “can't be returned if their seal is broken”, with hygiene given as the reason unless the goods are faulty, and the page points to each product's own Product Information for the exceptions. Faulty goods can be exchanged or refunded “within 30 days from when you bought it or had it delivered”, with damage, neglect, misuse and wear and tear excluded. The page does not say who pays return postage, and it gives no refund timescale.

On disposal Currys is strong and specific. “You can recycle all your tech for free at any of our stores — even if you didn't buy it from us”, items are checked and resold or donated to charity where they still work, and the company publishes its producer registrations in full: WEEE numbers WEE/DE0065TW for Currys Group Ltd and WEE/FD0095VY for Currys Retail Ltd, and battery producer registrations BPRN00339 and BPRN00524. Publishing those numbers is unusual and it is a genuine mark in the company's favour; a shopper who wants to check a retailer is inside the producer compliance regime can do it in one search. A million tonnes of tech have gone through it since 2010.

Two caveats. Free is the in-store position: collecting a large old appliance at the point of delivery is priced separately, at £25 for a washing machine, tumble dryer, dishwasher, cooker, oven, hob or fridge freezer and £30 for an American-style fridge freezer, with the recycling voucher scheme carrying a “Minimum £25 spend to redeem voucher” and a GB-only condition. And the gift card page, which is where a Care & Repair payout lands if a product cannot be fixed, is dense with expiry dates: a standard card runs 24 months, a Care & Repair eGift card 24 months, a No Fix Guarantee card just 3 months, and a loyalty card 3 months. That same page still carries a block of Home Electronics terms headed “Until December 31st 2018”, nearly eight years after that date passed — a small thing, but the kind of small thing that makes a reader wonder what else on the page has not been read recently.

pros: Collection is free at any of 300-plus stores in the UK and Ireland, so there is a £0 route into the range whatever home delivery turns out to cost.
Interest-free credit over 12, 24 or 36 months, and a 9.9% purchase rate over 48 months against a 29.9% standard rate — twenty percentage points of difference on a long plan.
Thirty days to return an online purchase “even if you've opened it for inspection”, against the fourteen a distance seller has to give.
Around 1,000 repair experts, more than a million products repaired a year, and a 12-month parts and labour guarantee on the repair itself.
Free in-store recycling of any tech whether or not it was bought there, with WEEE and battery producer registration numbers published openly.
Its own product safety register is public, dated and model-specific, with 28 corrective action programmes and recalls listed on 23 October 2026.
The credit page names the lender, the broker and the APR in plain words instead of burying them, and the lender publishes its own complaints return.
cons: No price on the site can be read without a browser. The gaming landing page returned unrendered tokens such as $PRICE_10262507$ and $OFFER_10262507$ where every price should be, so nothing here can be compared before clicking through.
The delivery and collection page would not load on four separate attempts on 23 October 2026, so Currys' own home delivery charge on a small gaming order could not be read or quoted at all.
Credit is closed off below £99. Controllers, keyboards, mice, headsets and boxed games mostly sit under that line, which is exactly where a gaming customer spends between consoles.

Instant Replacement charges more for gaming than for any other product group in every one of its six price bands — £40 against a television's £31 at the top — and Currys publishes no claims acceptance rate or average payout to set that against.

Care & Repair's extra benefits exclude “Virtual Reality, Games Consoles” outright, which is the heart of what a gaming buyer would take the plan for, and the plan is “not an insurance policy and is an extended warranty plan only”.

Creation Consumer Finance, the flexpay lender, upheld 49.52% of the complaints it closed in the first half of 2026 and resolved 85.19% inside eight weeks, leaving close to 15% running past the deadline; it opened 8,629 fixed-term complaints and closed 4,768 in the same period.

The price promise is advertised with “Exclusions and conditions apply” and the exclusions are not set out on the page — so the one thing a shopper needs in order to use it is the one thing not published beside it.
The gift card page still carries a section of Home Electronics terms headed “Until December 31st 2018”, and gift cards cannot be put towards a flexpay purchase online.
verdict: Currys is the most complete place in Britain to buy a console in person: 300-plus stores, free collection, a thousand repair engineers, a million repairs a year and free recycling of whatever the new machine replaces. It is also, increasingly, a credit business — £1.2bn of flexpay sales and 23.7% of everything it sold in the UK and Ireland last year — and the credit is genuinely good value if you clear the £99 floor and take the interest-free or 9.9% terms rather than letting a balance sit at 29.9%. Where the offer thins is on the attachments. Instant Replacement prices gaming above every other category it sells, Care & Repair strips games consoles and virtual reality out of its extras, and the price promise advertises exclusions it does not print. Buy the hardware here for the collection network and the repair operation, take the interest-free credit if the basket clears £99, and read the plan leaflet in the shop before adding cover to a console.

faqs.q: Can I spread the cost of a console at Currys?
faqs.a: Yes, on orders of £99 and over. Currys flexpay is a running credit account provided by Creation Consumer Finance Ltd, with Currys Group Limited acting as credit broker. The standard rate is 29.9% APR representative (variable) on an assumed £1,200 limit, but promotional terms run interest free over 12, 24 or 36 months, or at a 9.9% purchase rate over 48 months, with buy now pay later usually offered over 6, 9 or 12 months. Below £99 the credit option is not available at all.

faqs.q: Does Currys charge for delivery on a gaming order?
faqs.a: Its own delivery and collection page would not open on 23 October 2026 across four attempts, so the small-item charge could not be read first-hand and is not quoted here. What Currys does state elsewhere is that you “can order online and pick up your tech for FREE” at its stores, of which it counts more than 300 across the UK and Ireland. Large appliances are priced separately, from £20 for all-day standard delivery and from £30 next day, but those bands do not apply to a controller or a console. Check the charge in the basket before paying.

faqs.q: Is Care & Repair worth buying on a games console?
faqs.a: Read the exclusion list first. Care & Repair's headline extras — next-day replacement delivery, 24/7 tech support, built-in battery support and the annual valet — name “Monitors, eReaders, Networking, Printers, Scanners, Virtual Reality, Games Consoles” among the products they do not cover. The core repair promise still applies, with a target of seven calendar days and a gift card if the same product fails after two repairs, but it is an extended warranty rather than insurance and Currys says so in terms. For a cheaper item between £20 and £150 the alternative is Instant Replacement, which costs £13 to £40 for three years in the gaming band.

faqs.q: How long do I have to return something I bought online?
faqs.a: Thirty days, and Currys says you can send it back “even if you've opened it for inspection”. That is more than double the fourteen days the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 oblige a distance seller to offer, so sixteen of those days are a concession the retailer grants rather than a statutory right. A purchase made in a store also gets 30 days but has to come back unopened. Sealed items can be excluded on hygiene grounds, and the returns page gives no refund timescale and does not say who pays the postage.

faqs.q: Will Currys match a cheaper price I find elsewhere?
faqs.a: It says it will match any other UK retailer, in store or online, and that a claim can be made up to seven days after purchase, with the difference refunded. The page adds “Exclusions and conditions apply” without setting out what they are, so ask which sellers count before relying on it. One exclusion is stated plainly: “Care & Repair has fixed prices and we will therefore not price match”, so the promise covers the console and not the protection plan sold with it.

faqs.q: Can I recycle an old console at Currys?
faqs.a: Yes, free of charge, at any store and whether or not the item came from Currys — the company says it can “recycle almost any tech” and that working items may be resold or donated to charity. Its producer registrations are published: WEEE numbers WEE/DE0065TW and WEE/FD0095VY, and battery producer registrations BPRN00339 and BPRN00524. Collecting a large old appliance from your home at the point of delivery is charged separately, at £25 for most and £30 for an American-style fridge freezer.

intro:
Currys listed 360 SIM-free phones on 23 October 2026, running from a £24.00 Nokia 105 to a £1,899.00 Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, with a Motorola Moto G06 at £99.00 and a Samsung Galaxy A16 at £139.00 in between. Every price here was read that day from the shop's own mobile phone listing and its own product pages.

The useful thing about this particular shop is that the whole range is already what you came for. Currys sells phones outright and nothing else: there is no pay-monthly phone category anywhere in its own sitemap, no airtime attached to any tile, and the headings over the listing say “Choose your new SIM-free smartphone today” and “SIM-free mobile phones from top brands”. Contracts live on Carphone Warehouse, which sits in the Currys footer under “Our websites” and which the group's own recycling page identifies as a separate company, Currys Retail Ltd. So you do not have to filter the bundles out of this range. There are none in it.

Behind the till is a listed British retailer with audited numbers. Currys plc reported group revenue of £9,254m for the year ended 2 May 2026, up 6% with like-for-like growth of 4%, adjusted profit before tax of £191m (up 18%), statutory profit before tax of £153m, free cash flow of £157m and year-end net cash of £176m. It operates 691 stores in six countries and employs more than 24,000 people, it doubled its full-year dividend to 3.0p, and it started a £50m share buyback on the day it published. On a phone you are buying outright, with no ongoing relationship to fall back on, the solvency of the shop is the warranty behind the warranty.

sections.heading: What £24 buys, and the network that stops answering in 2029
sections.html:
The cheapest phone in this shop is a Nokia 105 (2023) at £24.00 in cyan or red and £24.99 in black. For that you get a 1.8-inch screen, 4 MB of storage and 4 MB of RAM, a 1,000 mAh battery rated at up to 12 hours of talk and up to 22 days of standby, a 3.5 mm headphone socket, a torch, an MP3 player and Snake. No camera, no WiFi, no Bluetooth, no NFC, no GPS. It weighs 78.7 g. As a second phone for a festival, a spare for a glovebox or a first phone for a child, that specification is honest about itself and the price is hard to argue with.

One line of it decides whether the phone works in five years, and it is not on the Currys page. HMD, which makes and sells Nokia-branded phones, publishes the specification for the same model — it calls it the Nokia 105 C (2023) — and gives its maximum network speed as 2G, with GSM bands 900/1800 and nothing else. No 3G bands. No LTE bands. The SIM slot takes a mini SIM, the full-size card most networks stopped posting years ago.

Now set that against Ofcom's own page on the switch-off, published 6 March 2024 and last updated 10 August 2026. Britain's 3G networks are already off. On 2G, EE has said it will begin switching off from May 2029, O2 from Summer 2029 and Vodafone during 2030, and every operator has confirmed to the Government that 2G will be gone by 2033 at the latest. Ofcom's instruction to anyone holding a 2G-only handset is four words long: such devices “will need to be upgraded to at least 4G”.

There is a sharper version of that, and it bites today rather than in 2029. Three has never run a 2G network at all. Ofcom's page says so in terms, and adds that Three customers with older devices must replace them to make calls, send texts and use mobile data now that 3G has gone. A 2G-only phone is therefore not a phone with a 2029 problem on Three or on SMARTY, the brand Three runs. It is not a working phone on those networks on the day you unwrap it.

The fix is £15.99. The Nokia 110 sits two tiles away at £39.99, and its Currys product page gives “4G network: 4G” and “Dual Nano SIM”, with 128 MB of storage, microSD support to 32 GB and a line about HD voice over 4G. HMD's own specification for the Nokia 110 4G (2023) confirms networks of 2G, 3G and 4G and a nano SIM. Same shape of phone, same two-year guarantee, a third more money, and roughly seven more years of network behind it. On a £24 purchase that is a 67% uplift; on the decision it is the whole thing.

sections.heading: The one specification row Currys leaves blank
sections.html:
Currys does better than most big retailers on its own product pages. Prices render. Full specification tables render. The delivery charges are printed on the page you are reading, rather than hidden behind a basket. On the Nokia 105's page you can read the processor (Unisoc), the operating system (Nokia Series 30+), the screen resolution (QQVGA), the dimensions (115 x 49.4 x 14.45 mm) and the manufacturer's guarantee (2 years). It even labels the product type, in its own words, as a “SIM-free mobile phone”.

Under Connectivity, that table lists a row called “4G network” and a row called “2G”, and shows a value against neither of them. Both are empty. A shopper reading the only page the shop gives them for this handset cannot tell from it which generations of mobile network the phone speaks — which, given everything above, is the single field that decides whether the £24 is well spent or wasted. The Nokia 110's page, for contrast, fills the same row in: “4G network: 4G”. One of the two phones that most needs the answer is the one that does not get it.

Credit where it is due: the 105's page does carry a warning, which is more than nothing and more than the 110's page bothers with. The sentence reads “2G and 3G mobile signals will begin to be phased out within the next year.” Read on 23 October 2026, it is wrong in both directions at once. 3G has not begun to be phased out within the next year; it has already finished, on Ofcom's own account. And 2G does not begin to be phased out within the next year either — the earliest operator start date any network has published is May 2029, a little over two and a half years away. The instinct to warn is right and the copy behind it has not been read since it was written.

The honest summary is that this is stale text rather than a misleading claim, and a shopper who takes it at face value errs on the side of caution, which is the safe direction. But it is a warning on the cheapest product in a 360-line range, and the correct version of it — that this handset will not work on Three now and will not work on anything by 2033 — is both shorter and more useful than the one printed.

sections.heading: Four in five of us are keeping a dead phone, and Currys counted them
sections.html:
Currys commissioned its own research into this and published it on 22 June 2026: a study of 2,000 UK adults through Opinium. Four in five of us are holding onto a defunct mobile. One in three still have their very first phone, and “a quarter of which are old Nokias”. Citing Material Focus, the release puts 880 million unused items in British homes, an average of 30 per household.

That finding and the shop's own entry price are the same object seen from two ends. The retailer whose research says a quarter of hoarded first phones are old Nokias is also the retailer whose cheapest new phone is an old-style Nokia with a published network expiry date. Neither fact is a criticism of the other. Together they are the best argument on this page for spending the extra £15.99: the thing people do with a cheap feature phone is keep it for a decade, and this one has rather less than a decade of network left.

The release is worth reading for the reasons people gave, because they are not the ones a retailer would choose. 33% simply had not got round to recycling, 27% keep devices “just in case”, 23% do not know how to recycle and another 23% worry about data security. Only a third had recycled any tech in the past year, while 81% knew batteries in household waste can start fires, 77% understood that recycling cuts the need to mine new material and 64% knew old tech can be worth money. The gap between knowing and doing is the whole story, and Currys published it about its own customers. 41% have bought refurbished, rising to 50% of 18 to 34-year-olds against 29% of the over-55s, and the group collected 5.5 million items of e-waste for reuse and recycling last year. Paula Coughlan, its Chief People, Communications and Sustainability Officer, is quoted as wanting “to give tech its longest life”.

What the shop does about it is genuinely good and comes with one piece of arithmetic attached. You can recycle any tech free at a Currys store, in the page's own words “even if you didn't buy it from us”, and the group publishes its producer registrations rather than referring vaguely to a scheme. In return you get £5 off a later purchase — and the same page states “Minimum £25 spend to redeem voucher”. The cheapest phone in the shop is £24.99 in black and £24.00 in cyan. Hand in your old Nokia, take the voucher, and the newest Nokia on the shelf is a penny short of being allowed to use it. The £39.99 Nokia 110 clears the bar comfortably, which is one more small reason the 4G phone is the better buy.

sections.heading: The monthly figure on the tile is the dear one, and the small print says so
sections.html:
Most tiles in this range carry a second price in bold underneath the first. The Google Pixel 10 at £499.00 shows “From £20.22 per month for 36 months*”. The Pixel 10 Pro XL at £849.00 shows £34.40. The Galaxy S26 Ultra at £1,129.00 shows £45.75.

Currys' credit page leads with a different offer. It advertises paying “in monthly instalments, interest free, over terms of 12, 24 or 36 months”, a 48-month option at a 9.9% purchase rate, and buy-now-pay-later over 6, 9 or 12 months with no interest if the balance clears inside the period. On that reading, 36 months on a £499 phone would be £13.86.

Follow the asterisk and the shop tells you plainly which figure you are looking at: “Monthly prices displayed are based on 29.9% Representative APR (variable).” So the instalment printed beside each price is the interest-bearing one, and the interest-free terms are a promotion the same footnote describes as “offered on selected products from time to time”, with no indication on the tile whether this handset is one of them.

Do the sum the footnote invites, and label it as ours rather than theirs. Thirty-six payments of £20.22 is £727.92 against a £499.00 cash price — £228.92 more, or about 46% on top. The Pixel 10 Pro XL comes to £1,238.40 against £849.00, £389.40 more. The Galaxy S26 Ultra comes to £1,647.00 against £1,129.00, £518.00 more. All three land on the same 45.9% uplift, and all three reconcile to the penny with a straight 29.9% APR amortised over 36 months — which is a point in the shop's favour, because the numbers it prints are arithmetically exactly what its footnote says they are.

Two smaller things sit alongside. Credit here requires a £99 minimum spend, so the four cheapest phones in the range — the £24.00 and £24.99 Nokia 105s, the £39.99 Nokia 110 and the £64.99 Nokia 2660 Flip — cannot be spread at any rate, interest-free or otherwise. And the terms are better than the headline rate suggests for anyone who can clear the balance early: no deposit is required, there are “no early payment fees”, and overpayments of some or all of the balance carry no charge. The lender is Creation Consumer Finance Ltd, with Currys Group Limited acting as credit broker under exclusive arrangements with it, on an assumed credit limit of £1,200.

sections.heading: Free to collect, £3.99 to deliver, and on this phone that is a sixth of the price
sections.html:
The page that is supposed to explain delivery would not open. Five separate attempts on /services/delivery-installation/delivery-collection.html returned a client error, and it is linked from the top navigation and twice from the footer. The charges are on the product pages instead, which is where a shopper is standing anyway, and they are complete.

Standard delivery is £3.99 on an order under £40 and free over it. Next day is £5.99. Weekend all day is £6.99. A four-hour time slot is £9.99, and a weekend morning slot before noon is £10.99. Store collection is free, and the listing advertises it as available “in as little as an hour”, subject to availability, across a store estate the annual results put at 691 in six countries.

That free-over-£40 threshold does something specific to the cheap end of this range. A £24.00 Nokia 105 delivered costs £27.99, so the carriage is 16.6% on top of the goods. A £24.99 handset delivered is £28.98, or 16.0% on top. The £39.99 Nokia 110 is a penny below the threshold, so it too attracts £3.99 and arrives at £43.98 — and adding a £4.00 phone case would make the delivery free and the whole order cheaper than the phone plus postage. The £64.99 Nokia 2660 Flip ships free.

None of that is a trick, and the collection route sidesteps it entirely: on every tile in the range the cheapest way to get the goods is £0, by walking in. It is simply worth doing the sum before you check out, because on a £24 phone the postage is the largest single percentage any charge on this page adds to anything.

sections.heading: Thirty days either way, with the statute left unmentioned
sections.html:
Currys is more generous on returns than the law obliges and quieter about the law than it should be. Buy online and you can return the phone within 30 days — the page says “even if you've opened it for inspection” — provided it comes back unused, in resaleable condition, in its original box with every accessory. Buy in a store and you also get 30 days, but the packaging must be “unopened and sealed”. A faulty item is covered for 30 days from purchase or delivery, and after that the page offers repair “if still under guarantee”, which it describes as “usually 12 months from when you bought it”.

That last figure understates what you actually have on the phones at the cheap end of this range. Both Nokia product pages give a manufacturer's guarantee of 2 years, in the spec table and again as a banner. A shopper who reads only the returns page would think their cover ran out twelve months early.

Three gaps are worth knowing before you buy rather than after. The returns page gives no refund timescale at all — not a number of days, not a working-day window. It does not say who pays return postage on a change-of-mind return, which on a phone is the difference between a free return and a tracked parcel at your own cost. And it does not mention the Consumer Rights Act 2015 or the distance-selling cancellation right anywhere, so the 30 days reads as a company policy that could be withdrawn rather than as a voluntary extension of rights a shop cannot take away. It is worth saying plainly that a phone bought outright here has no ombudsman behind it either: the Financial Conduct Authority reaches the credit agreement and Ofcom's approved complaints schemes reach an airtime contract, which on a SIM-free purchase you have not bought. A dispute the shop will not settle ends in the county court.

One exclusion catches people out and it is specific to this department. In-store returns do not cover “connected products with airtime, like a mobile phone, SIM contract or broadband connection”, and the same page notes that contracts with the iD network can be changed or cancelled within 14 days while Vodafone contracts cannot be changed or cancelled at all. None of that touches a SIM-free handset, which is exactly the point: the cash purchase is the simplest thing in the shop, and the complications all belong to the bundles Currys does not sell here.

sections.heading: Currys prints the dates behind its own was-and-now prices. Two of three survive the test
sections.html:
Plenty of this range is marked down, and Currys does something unusual with the markdowns: it prints the window during which the higher price actually applied. The Pixel 10 reads “£499.00 Save £200.00 Was £699.00 (from 22/07/26 to 01/09/26)”. The Pixel 10 Pro XL reads “£849.00 Save £250.00 Was £1,099.00 (from 23/09/26 to 13/10/26)”. The Galaxy S26 Ultra reads “£1,129.00 Save £150.00 Was £1,279.00 (from 08/09/26 to 06/10/26)”. Most retailers give you the two prices and leave the dates out, and the dates are the only thing that makes a saving checkable.

The yardstick is the Chartered Trading Standards Institute's guidance for traders on pricing practices, last reviewed and updated in November 2025. It asks two questions of a was-and-now claim: “How recently was the higher price offered, compared to when the price comparison is being made?” and “How long was the product on sale at the higher price, compared to the period for which the price comparison is made?” A comparison is more likely to comply where it runs “for a period that is the same or shorter than the period during which the higher price was offered”. Its worked example of a claim that is more likely to comply refers to a price “charged less than two months ago with no intervening prices”; one that is less likely to comply refers to prices “charged many months ago”.

Because Currys published the dates, a reader can run both tests, and the arithmetic below is ours. The Pixel 10 Pro XL held its £1,099 for 20 days and has been at £849 for 10: recent, and the discount period is shorter than the full-price period. Clear on both counts. The Galaxy S26 Ultra held £1,279 for 28 days and has been at £1,129 for 17. Clear again. The Pixel 10 is the one that does not sit comfortably: £699 applied for 41 days and the £499 has now been running for 52, so the comparison period has outlasted the period it compares against, which is the situation the guidance puts on the wrong side of the line. At 52 days it is also brushing up against that two-month example.

That is a narrow point and it is not an accusation — the guidance sets out factors rather than a deadline, the £200 is real money off a real price, and a £699 Pixel 10 genuinely was sold at £699 this summer. The reason it is worth printing is that nothing else on this page can be audited by a shopper and this can, because Currys chose to publish the dates. The price promise is the opposite case. It offers to “price match before or after you buy” and says “We'll even price match 7 days after your purchase!”, refunding the difference if you find the same item cheaper elsewhere — and that page names no retailers it will match against, publishes no exclusions and sets out no claim procedure. Seven days is a real promise; what it covers is not written down.

sections.heading: Pages that would not open, and the questions they leave
sections.html:
Six Currys pages could not be read on 23 October 2026, and the pattern is consistent: the product pages work and the service pages do not. /services/mobile-phone-insurance.html failed on three attempts, which matters because it is linked from the footer of every page and because phone insurance is the one financial product a SIM-free buyer is most likely to be sold. /services/instant-replacement.html and /services/care-services/care-repair.html also failed, so the price bands for Currys' two protection plans could not be checked against a handset. /terms-conditions.html failed, so the clauses on when the contract forms and what happens on a pricing error could not be read. /services/delivery-installation/delivery-collection.html failed five times, and /phones/mobile-phones/refurbished-phones failed as well, so the refurbished range could not be priced at all — the only figure available for it is the 12-month guarantee named in the June 2026 press release, against the two years on the new Nokias.

What did open is worth naming for anyone retracing this. Product pages under /products/ fetch reliably, which the site's own robots.txt confirms by explicitly allowing /products* while disallowing search, basket, checkout, wishlist and every filter and sort parameter. The practical consequence of those filter rules is that the 360-tile range cannot be sorted by price or filtered by budget from outside, so the cheapest handset here was found by reading the Nokia brand page, which returned “Showing 6 of 6” and all six prices.

Two further things could not be settled. Currys Group Limited's own FCA firm reference number is not printed on any page that invokes its authorisation — the credit pages say only “Authorised & regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority” — and the register itself would not load, so this page cites the wording rather than a number. And the listing's own product count moved while it was being read: the first two loads returned “Showing 20 of 360”, a load between them returned “Showing 40 of 377”, and a later load returned 360 again. That is a presentation quirk of a stock feed rather than a criticism, and it is the reason the 360 above is dated to the day. There is also no independent rating of handset retail from anybody — Defaqto and Fairer Finance do not reach it, and Ofcom's complaints tables measure networks rather than shops — so on the quality of this retailer, as opposed to the quality of its disclosures, there is nothing to cite.

pros: 360 SIM-free tiles read on one page on 23 October 2026, genuinely spanning a £24.00 Nokia 105 and a £1,899.00 Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra
Every phone in the range is sold outright, so there is no bundle to decline, no minimum term, no early termination charge and no credit search on a cash purchase
Free store collection on every tile, advertised as available in as little as an hour across 691 stores in six countries — a £0 route to the goods on any order
Prices and full specification tables render on both the listing and the product pages, including dimensions, battery capacity and guarantee length
Both Nokia feature phones carry a two-year manufacturer's guarantee, double the 12 months the retailer's own returns page describes as usual
Online returns run 30 days and expressly allow a box opened for inspection, more than twice the 14 days a distance sale must give
The exact dates each “was” price applied are printed beside the saving, which is what the trading standards pricing guidance asks for and most retailers do not supply
Delivery is free over £40 and the whole charge list is published on the product page itself, where the decision is actually made
No deposit, no early payment fees and free overpayments on flexpay, with interest-free terms of 12, 24 or 36 months available on selected products
Free in-store recycling of any tech even if it was not bought there, with WEEE and battery producer registrations published rather than gestured at
