A listed retailer behind the counter: £9,254m of revenue, £191m of adjusted profit before tax, £157m of free cash flow and £176m of net cash in the year to 2 May 2026
cons: The cheapest phone in the shop, the £24.00 Nokia 105 (2023), is 2G-only on its maker's own specification, which means it cannot work on Three or SMARTY today and will not work on any UK network by 2033

Currys' product page for that handset shows both the “4G network” and “2G” rows of its own specification table with no value against either — the one field that decides the purchase is the one left empty

The same page's only warning reads “2G and 3G mobile signals will begin to be phased out within the next year”, which on 23 October 2026 is wrong twice over: 3G is already off and the earliest published 2G start date is May 2029

The monthly instalment printed beside each price is the interest-bearing one — the footnote states monthly prices are based on 29.9% representative APR, so the £499 Pixel 10's advertised £20.22 over 36 months totals £727.92, about 46% on top
Credit carries a £99 minimum spend, so the four cheapest phones in the range cannot be spread at any rate, interest-free or otherwise
The £5 in-store recycling voucher carries a stated £25 minimum spend, which the £24.99 cheapest handset misses by a penny
The returns page gives no refund timescale, does not say who pays return postage on a change-of-mind return, and never mentions the Consumer Rights Act 2015 or the distance-selling cancellation right

Six service pages would not open, including the mobile phone insurance page linked in every footer, both protection-plan pages, the terms and conditions, the delivery page on five attempts and the refurbished phone listing
Sorting or filtering the 360-tile range by price from outside the site is blocked by robots.txt, so there is no way to confirm the cheapest handset except by reading brand pages one at a time
Currys Group Limited's own FCA firm reference number is not published on the pages that invoke its authorisation, and no independent rating of handset retail exists from any ratings body
The listing's own product count moved between 360 and 377 across three reads on one afternoon, so any range figure from this shop needs a date attached to it
verdict: As a place to buy a phone outright, Currys is better than its reputation for opacity suggests: 360 handsets from £24.00 to £1,899.00 with prices and full specifications on the page, free collection from any store, free delivery over £40, two-year guarantees on the cheap Nokias, 30-day returns that allow an opened box, and a listed parent with £176m of net cash standing behind the receipt. The whole range is already contract-free, so the thing you searched for is the default rather than a filter. Two sums are worth doing before you pay. The instalment figure under each price is the 29.9% one, not the interest-free one, and on the £499 Pixel 10 that is £228.92 of interest the tile does not mention — so ask at the till whether your handset qualifies for an interest-free term. And at the cheap end, spend the extra £15.99. The £24.00 Nokia 105 is a 2G-only phone in a country where Three has no 2G at all and the rest will have switched it off by 2033, and the £39.99 Nokia 110 beside it is the same phone with 4G, a nano SIM and the same two-year guarantee. Currys' own research says one in three of us still have our first-ever phone and a quarter of those are old Nokias. Buy the one that will still be ringing when you get sentimental about it.

faqs.q: Does Currys sell phones on contract?
faqs.a: Not on currys.co.uk. There is no pay-monthly phone category anywhere in its own sitemap, and every tile in the mobile phone range is sold outright. Airtime contracts sit on Carphone Warehouse, which appears in the Currys footer under “Our websites” and which the group's recycling page identifies as a separate company, Currys Retail Ltd. Currys does sell SIM cards separately, so you can buy the handset here and the airtime here too — just as two purchases rather than one.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest phone Currys sells?
faqs.a: £24.00, for a Nokia 105 (2023) with 4 MB of storage, in cyan or red; the black one is £24.99. That was the lowest of 360 SIM-free tiles read on 23 October 2026, and the lowest of six on the Nokia brand page, which showed “Showing 6 of 6”. Be careful with it: HMD's own specification gives the model's maximum network speed as 2G with GSM 900/1800 bands only. The cheapest handset that can use 4G is the Nokia 110 at £39.99.

faqs.q: Will a 2G phone still work in the UK?
faqs.a: For now, on three of the four networks. Ofcom's switch-off page, last updated 10 August 2026, says 3G is already off and 2G goes next: EE from May 2029, O2 from Summer 2029, Vodafone during 2030, and all operators have told the Government it will be gone by 2033 at the latest. Three is the exception that matters immediately — it has never had a 2G network, so a 2G-only handset cannot make calls, send texts or use data on Three or SMARTY at all. Ofcom's advice to anyone holding one is that it “will need to be upgraded to at least 4G”.

faqs.q: Is the monthly price shown next to a Currys phone interest free?
faqs.a: No. The footnote under the listing says “Monthly prices displayed are based on 29.9% Representative APR (variable)”. Interest-free terms of 12, 24 or 36 months do exist, but the same footnote describes promotional rates as offered on selected products from time to time, and the tile does not say whether a given handset is one of them. The arithmetic is worth seeing: the £499.00 Pixel 10's advertised £20.22 a month for 36 months comes to £727.92, which is £228.92 more than paying once. Credit also needs a £99 minimum spend, so the four cheapest phones cannot be spread at all. Ask whether your handset qualifies for an interest-free term before you sign.

faqs.q: What does delivery cost on a cheap phone?
faqs.a: £3.99 on any order under £40, free over it, with next day at £5.99, weekend all day at £6.99, a four-hour slot at £9.99 and a weekend morning slot at £10.99. Store collection is free and advertised as available in as little as an hour. On a £24.00 handset the £3.99 adds 16.6% to the bill, and the £39.99 Nokia 110 sits a penny under the free-delivery threshold — so collecting, or adding a cheap case to clear £40, is the sensible move at this end of the range.

faqs.q: Can I return a SIM-free phone to Currys if I change my mind?
faqs.a: Yes. Bought online you have 30 days, and the returns page expressly allows a box you have “opened it for inspection”, provided the phone comes back unused and resaleable with its original packaging and every accessory. Bought in store you also have 30 days, but the packaging must be unopened and sealed. Two things are not published: there is no refund timescale anywhere on the page, and it does not say who pays return postage. The page also never mentions the Consumer Rights Act 2015, under which a 30-day short-term right to reject faulty goods applies regardless of any shop policy.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to about a phone bought outright from Currys?
faqs.a: Currys first, and then there is nowhere obvious to go. Handset retail has no ombudsman and no compensation scheme. The Financial Conduct Authority reaches the flexpay credit agreement, where Creation Consumer Finance Ltd is the lender and Currys Group Limited the broker, and Ofcom's approved complaints schemes reach an airtime contract — which on a SIM-free purchase you have not bought. A dispute the shop will not settle ends in the county court. Currys Group Limited's own FCA firm reference number is not printed on the pages that cite its authorisation, and the register would not load to confirm it.

title: Currys Smart Tech: What You Buy, and How Long It Stays Safe to Use
meta_title: Currys Smart Tech 2026: Prices and Every Support Date
meta_description: Currys lists 274 smart cameras from £18.97 and 43 smart speakers from £44.99. We looked up every maker’s security-update end date so you don’t have to.

headline.label: Guaranteed security-update period
headline.value: 3 to 5 years, set by the maker and not by Currys — Philips Hue 5 years (3 on the Bridge), Google Nest at least 5, TP-Link 3 after end of life; Currys’ own listings carry no support date at all (checked 23 October 2026)

intro:
Currys lists 274 security cameras and CCTV products, priced from a £18.97 TP-Link Tapo C200 to a £419.95 Ring alarm bundle, alongside 45 video doorbells and 43 smart speakers and displays running from £44.99 to £550.00. Every one of those prices was readable on 23 October 2026, and each reduced item shows the window its old price applied in — the eufy C220 at £26.99 was £34.99 from 21/09/26 to 11/10/26, the Arlo AVD4001 at £69.99 was £139.00 from 20/06/26 to 09/08/26.

Behind the shop is a business that has had a good year. Currys plc reported audited results for the year ended 2 May 2026 on 2 July 2026: UK and Ireland revenue of £5,438m on like-for-like growth of 3%, Nordics revenue of £3,816m on 6%, statutory profit before tax of £153m, group free cash flow of £157m and year-end net cash of £176m after £74m of shareholder returns. The full-year dividend doubled to 3.0p and a £50m buyback began the same day. More than 24,000 people work there, and the smart tech aisles are staffed.

One thing is worth knowing before you start comparing. Almost nothing in the smart tech range is made by Currys: it is a distributor of other companies’ hardware, and under the 2023 connectable-product regulations the duty to publish how long a device will keep receiving security updates sits with the maker, on the maker’s own site. That number is the closest thing a smart plug or a doorbell has to a use-by date, and it is not printed next to the price here. This page collects it for the brands Currys actually stocks.

key_facts.label: What Currys is under the Act
key_facts.value: A distributor, not a manufacturer. Section 22 of the Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022 says it “may not make the product available in the United Kingdom unless it is accompanied by” a statement of compliance

key_facts.label: Range and prices read on 23 October 2026
key_facts.value: 274 security cameras and CCTV, 45 video doorbells, 43 voice-control devices, 6 smart plugs; £5.97 (WiZ smart plug) to £550.00 (Skylight Max 27-inch display)

key_facts.label: Security-update period shown on a Currys page
key_facts.value: None, on any of the four listings or either product page opened on 23 October 2026

key_facts.label: What is shown instead
key_facts.value: A guarantee — “2 year guarantee” on most tiles, and “Manufacturer’s guarantee: 2 years” in the Tapo D210 specification table

key_facts.label: Where the number does exist
key_facts.value: TP-Link, Signify, Google, Arlo and Ring each publish one, on five different websites, measured from five different starting events

key_facts.label: Minimum period the law sets
key_facts.value: None. The regulations require the period to be published, not to be any particular length

key_facts.label: Corporate identity
key_facts.value: Currys Group Limited, company number 00504877, incorporated 28 February 1952, registered at Currys Newark Campus, Long Hollow Way, Newark NG24 2NH

key_facts.label: Enforcement to date
key_facts.value: The OPSS enforcement page for these regulations was last updated 8 August 2025 and names no case; OPSS says it “publishes details of any Compliance Notice that we serve”

sections.heading: What £18.97 buys, and what 274 cameras look like once they are priced
sections.html:
The shelf is wide and the cheap end is genuinely cheap. On the security camera and CCTV listing, which showed “Showing 1 - 20 of 274”, the first twenty tiles ran from a £18.97 TP-Link Tapo C200 and a £26.99 eufy C220 up to a £219.99 Ring Wired Retinal 4K Video Doorbell Pro. The doorbell listing showed “Showing 1 - 20 of 45”, from a £34.99 Tapo TD20 to a £419.95 Ring Alarm, Indoor Camera and Battery Video Doorbell kit. Voice control showed 43 items, from a £44.99 Echo Pop to a £550.00 Skylight Max 27-inch display, with the Apple HomePod mini 2 at £149.00 and Apple HomeView at £299.00, both on pre-order.

Smart plugs are the thin category: six products in total, led by a £5.97 WiZ plug and two Currys own-brand Sandstrom plugs at £9.99 and £17.99. Two of the six were out of stock on the day. It is worth knowing that smart plugs sit inside the security camera path on Currys’ own navigation rather than in a category of their own, which is why they are easy to miss.

Reductions are dated, which is more than many retailers manage. The Tapo C510W at £34.99 shows “Was £37.99 (from 03/07/26 to 11/08/26)”; the Blink Whole Home Security Kit Plus at £69.99 shows “Was £119.00 (from 08/08/26 to 06/09/26)”; the Tapo C610 solar kit at £64.99 shows “Was £69.99 (from 19/08/26 to 24/09/26)”. Printing the window the higher price actually applied in is the hard part of a was-and-now claim, and Currys does it.

sections.heading: The number a maker has to publish, and the one it does not
sections.html:
Since 29 April 2024, anyone selling a connected consumer product in the UK has been inside the Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure regime. Schedule 1 of the 2023 regulations sets out what a manufacturer owes the buyer, and paragraph 3 is the one that matters at the till: “The defined support period must be published.” It has to be “accessible, clear and transparent”, available “without prior request for such information being made”, in English, free of charge, given without asking for the reader’s personal details, and written “in such a way that is understandable by a reader without prior technical knowledge”.

Two sub-paragraphs make it a promise rather than a slogan. Under paragraph 3(3), if a maker extends the period, the new one must be published “as soon as is practicable”. Under paragraph 3(6), the requirements are not met if the period is shortened after it has been published. A maker can be generous later; it cannot quietly claw the date back.

Here is the gap that explains this whole page. Paragraph 3(5) says that where a manufacturer publishes an invitation to purchase on its own website, the support information must sit alongside the price information, or be given equal prominence to it. That duty is written for the maker’s shop, not for somebody else’s. Currys is somebody else’s. Nothing in Schedule 1 obliges a retailer to put the support date next to the price, which is exactly why it is not there.

The second thing worth knowing is that the law sets no minimum. The Government’s own guidance describes the duty as “publishing information on minimum security update periods” — publishing, not providing. A manufacturer that states one year and sticks to it is compliant. The regime makes firms honest about the date; it does not make the date long.

sections.heading: Five brands on one shelf, and five different clocks
sections.html:
Put the makers Currys stocks side by side and the periods look comparable. They are not, because each one starts counting at a different moment.

Signify, for Philips Hue and WiZ. Its UK statement of compliance, issued 29-Apr-2024 and signed by Robert Sprott, Compliance Manager UK&I, declares a defined support period of “5 years, except 3 years for Hue bridge”, and names Signify Commercial UK Limited, Unit 3, Guildford Business Park, Guildford, Surrey, GU2 8XG as the UK authorised representative of Signify of 5600 VB Eindhoven. Its consumer end-of-support page measures that from purchase: “a minimum total of five (5) years from the date of your purchase from an authorised reseller” for lights and accessories, and “a minimum total of three (3) years from the date of your purchase” for the Bridge v2.

TP-Link, for Tapo. Its PSTI page is blunt: “The defined support period will end 3 years after the product’s end-of-life date.” Not from purchase — from the day the model is retired. The declaring entity is TP-LINK SYSTEMS INC., 5 Peters Canyon Road, Suite. 300, Irvine, CA 92606.

Google, for Nest. Its UK statement of compliance, signed April 8, 2024 by Louise Bohmann, Director & PA Compliance Lead for Google LLC, 1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View, CA 94043, puts Nest cameras, doorbells, thermostats, speakers, displays and Wifi in a group promised “at least five years from when the device first became available on the Google Store in the US”. Not from UK launch, and not from purchase. For contrast, the same document gives Pixel 8 seven years, Pixel Watch three, and Fitbit “at least two years after the device is last sold”.

Arlo. Its end-of-life policy sets the end-of-life date “no earlier than four (4) years from the date that volume manufacturing of such Arlo hardware devices last occurred”, and then promises “critical security updates for hardware to one year beyond the hardware’s EOL Effective Date”. Feature firmware stops at that date: the policy lists “No firmware upgrades” among the consequences.

Ring. Four years from purchase or the published end date, whichever falls later.

So: purchase, product retirement, first availability in another country, last factory run, and purchase-or-published-date. Five clocks. A shopper standing in front of a £79.99 Ring doorbell and a £74.99 Tapo D130 cannot compare “four years” with “three years”, because the two numbers are not measuring the same thing — and neither number is on either page.

sections.heading: Look the dates up and some of them have already gone
sections.html:
This is the part that repays ten minutes before you buy. Google publishes a full table of end dates for Nest hardware, written in US order, and on 23 October 2026 several products that are still familiar names had passed it: Nest Cam (battery) and Nest Cam with Floodlight both at 8/24/2026, Nest Cam (wired) at 10/5/2026, Nest Hub (2nd gen) at 3/30/2026, Nest Thermostat at 10/30/2025, Nest Audio at 10/5/2025, Nest Mini at 10/22/2024 and Nest Wifi at 10/28/2024. The older entries have been expired for years: Nest Hello ended 3/31/2023 and the original Nest Learning Thermostat 9/30/2020.

The same table carries the good news, and it is worth saying plainly. Nest Cam Outdoor (wired, 2nd gen) and Nest Doorbell (wired, 3rd gen) both run to 10/1/2030, the Nest Learning Thermostat (4th gen) to 8/20/2029, and the Google Home Speaker (2026) — which Currys sells at £99.99 — to 06/25/2031. Buy that one and you have a published commitment running almost five years out.

TP-Link publishes a model-by-model table too, and it shows something Currys’ pages cannot. The Tapo C200, the £18.97 camera at the top of the listing, is supported to 11/7/2027 in hardware versions V1, V2 and V3, to 20/2/2029 in V3.20, and to 16/1/2030 in V5. That is a spread of two and a half years across one model name. The Tapo C510W runs to 20/2/2029 in V1 and 31/12/2029 or later in V2. The Tapo P100 four-pack in hardware version V1 carries a defined support period of 8/10/2024, which expired two years ago.

Currys prints the model. It does not print the hardware version. On the £18.97 C200 the difference between the version you might receive and the one you might hope for is 11 July 2027 against 16 January 2030, and nothing on the product page, the specification table or the box description tells you which is in the carton.

sections.heading: A two-year guarantee and a support date are different promises
sections.html:
Most smart tech tiles on Currys carry the words “2 year guarantee”, and the Tapo D210 product page confirms it in the specification table as “Manufacturer’s guarantee: 2 years”. That is a good guarantee for a £44.99 doorbell and better than the statutory minimum the shopper would otherwise fall back on. It is also answering a different question.

A guarantee covers the device breaking. A defined support period covers the device staying safe to use while it still works perfectly. The two are not the same length and they do not expire together. On that same Tapo D210, the guarantee runs two years from purchase and TP-Link’s own table supports version V1 to 16/1/2030 — so the support outlasts the guarantee by years. On a Nest Cam (battery) bought shortly before its 8/24/2026 date, it runs the other way: a working camera, inside its guarantee, with no more security updates coming.

The National Cyber Security Centre puts it better than any retailer does. Its guidance on smart devices in the home, version 2.0, last reviewed 23 February 2024, describes the support date as “a ‘use by’ date for your device, so you’ll know how long it’s still safe to use”, advises buyers to “avoid buying devices that are no longer supported by the manufacturer, or whose support period will end soon”, and warns that out of support, “smart devices are easier to hack, or may stop working altogether”. Its instruction on where to find the date is one line: “Check the manufacturer’s website for details.” That is sound advice precisely because the shop will not have it.

sections.heading: What the Act puts on the shop, and what Currys shows of it
sections.html:
Retailers are not bystanders in this regime. The Act gives distributors five duties of their own, and they are worth knowing because they are the ones Currys is answerable for.

Section 21 requires a distributor to comply with the relevant security requirements where it intends the product for UK consumers or ought to know that is where it is going. Section 22 is the one with teeth at the point of sale: the distributor “may not make the product available in the United Kingdom unless it is accompanied by” a statement of compliance, or a summary of one. Section 23 forbids supplying a product where the distributor “knows or believes that there is a compliance failure in relation to the product”. Section 24 covers its own failures: it must “take all reasonable steps to remedy the compliance failure” as soon as practicable and notify the enforcement authority. Section 25 covers the maker’s failures: contact the manufacturer “as soon as possible”, and where a remedy is unlikely, “take all reasonable steps to prevent the product from being made available” to UK customers.

The statement of compliance is the document that carries the support period, and Government guidance is explicit that the duty is shared: “the manufacturer, importer and distributor must ultimately ensure that the SoC accompanies the product”. It also confirms that “the Act does not specify that the document must be physical; therefore it could be digital” — which means a link on a product page would satisfy it.

Currys’ own site does not take that option. Its footer carries Product recalls, which points at a safety page, along with privacy, terms, modern slavery and a sitemap. On 23 October 2026 there was no product-security page, no statement-of-compliance page and no support-period page anywhere in the navigation, and none of the four smart tech listings or the two product pages opened carried a word about security updates. Product safety at Currys has a public page with 28 dated recalls on it. Product security has none.

The regulator is quiet too. The Office for Product Safety and Standards publishes enforcement guidance for these regulations setting out compliance notices, stop notices, recall notices, monetary penalties and forfeiture orders. It was last updated 8 August 2025, it names no company and no case, and it states that “OPSS publishes details of any Compliance Notice that we serve, in line with our Enforcement Policy”. Read it for what it is — guidance on powers, not a register of their use — but two and a half years into the regime, there is nothing on it to read.

sections.heading: The own-brand question these pages do not answer
sections.html:
Two of the six smart plugs Currys sells are its own: the Sandstrom SSPMW26 at £9.99 and the Sandstrom SSPMW24 at £17.99, both advertised as working with Matter. Sandstrom also accounts for four of the smart digital calendars in voice control, at £99.00, £149.00, £199.00 and £399.00.

This matters more than its share of the range suggests. The distributor duties above are the light-touch end of the Act. A firm that puts its own brand on a connectable product is generally treated as the manufacturer, and the manufacturer is the party that has to publish the defined support period in the first place. If Currys is the manufacturer of a Sandstrom smart plug, the number is Currys’ own to produce.

It could not be established either way on 23 October 2026. The Sandstrom listings name no manufacturer, importer or responsible company, and the Sandstrom product page returned a client error on five separate attempts across the day, so its specification table could not be read. No Currys-published support period for a Sandstrom connectable product was found anywhere on the site. That is a gap in this page rather than a finding against the shop, and it deserves a second look by anyone buying one.

One further thing a camera buyer should know, because no retailer mentions it. A doorbell or camera that captures images beyond your own boundary makes you a data controller under UK data protection law, with a duty to tell people they are being recorded, to delete footage you no longer need, and to answer a request for a copy within one calendar month. Cloud plans that keep 180 days of playback are convenient and they do not alter that duty.

pros: Prices are printed plainly across the smart tech range, and reduced items carry the exact dates the old price applied — £44.99 down from £99.99 “from 15/04/26 to 07/08/26” on the Blink starter kit, which lets a shopper judge the saving rather than take it on trust

Real breadth at the cheap end: a WiZ smart plug at £5.97, a Tapo C200 camera at £18.97, a Swann EVO at £36.97 and a Tapo TD20 doorbell at £34.99, so a first connected device costs less than a takeaway
Most tiles carry a two-year manufacturer’s guarantee rather than the one year a shopper might expect, and it is stated on the tile as well as in the specification table

Where a maker does publish a long support period, the stock reflects it: the Google Home Smart Speaker (2026) sells at £99.99 and Google’s own table supports it to 25 June 2031, which is close to five years from the day it goes on a shelf

The specification tables are genuinely detailed — the Tapo D210 page lists power as a rechargeable battery with up to six months of life, the app, the box contents and the fact that a cloud plan needs a monthly subscription

Currys plc publishes audited numbers and is in good financial health: £153m statutory profit before tax, £176m year-end net cash and a doubled 3.0p dividend for the year ended 2 May 2026, which matters for a retailer you may need to go back to
cons: No security-update period appears anywhere on Currys’ smart tech pages. Four listings covering 274 cameras, 45 doorbells, 43 voice-control devices and 6 smart plugs, plus the product pages opened on 23 October 2026, carried nothing — so the one specification that decides how long a connected device stays safe to use has to be looked up on five separate manufacturers’ websites

Currys prints the model name but not the hardware version, and the version is what decides the date. The £18.97 Tapo C200 is supported to 11/7/2027 in V1, V2 and V3 and to 16/1/2030 in V5 — a two-and-a-half-year spread on one product page that shows neither number

There is no product-security, statement-of-compliance or support-period page anywhere in the Currys footer or navigation. The nearest is “Product recalls”, which is a safety page with 28 corrective action programmes on it and nothing at all about software

The “2 year guarantee” shown on most tiles is a repair promise, not a support promise, and the page offers nothing to tell the two apart. A shopper can reasonably read it as the length of time the device will keep working properly, which is not what it means

Currys’ own-brand Sandstrom smart plugs at £9.99 and £17.99 name no manufacturer, importer or responsible company on the listing, and the product page would not open across five attempts — so whether Currys publishes a defined support period for the connectable products it brands itself could not be established at all

Philips Hue’s own UK end-of-support page gives two different starting points for the same five years: sections 1, 2 and 4 measure “from the date of your purchase from an authorised reseller”, while a footnote to section 5 says “Durations are from the moment Signify stops selling this version of the product”. The page does not reconcile them

TP-Link’s statement of compliance carries no date and no signatory, and large parts of its table read “31/12/2029 or later*” with the asterisk left unexplained in the document — a floor rather than an answer, on the brand that supplies the cheapest cameras in the range
Smart plugs are filed inside the security camera and CCTV path rather than given a category of their own, and the whole category runs to six products, two of which were out of stock on the day
verdict: Currys is a good place to buy smart tech and a poor place to find out how long it will last. The prices are plain, the reductions are dated honestly, the two-year guarantee beats the minimum, and there are 274 cameras and 45 doorbells to choose between starting at £18.97. What is missing is one line per product, and the law does not require the shop to supply it — the duty to publish a defined support period falls on the maker, next to the maker’s own price. So the number exists for everything on these shelves; it is just somewhere else. Before you buy, spend ten minutes on the manufacturer’s support page, and on a TP-Link product check the hardware version in the box against its table, because that is where the years are won and lost. Buy the Google Home Smart Speaker (2026) at £99.99 and you have cover published to 25 June 2031. Buy a Tapo P100 four-pack in hardware version V1 and the published period ran out on 8 October 2024.

faqs.q: How long will a smart device bought from Currys keep getting security updates?
faqs.a: Between three and five years, depending entirely on who made it. Signify publishes 5 years for Philips Hue lights and accessories and 3 years for the Hue Bridge; Google promises Nest hardware at least 5 years; TP-Link gives 3 years after a product’s end-of-life date; Arlo sets end of life no earlier than 4 years after the last volume manufacturing run and then adds a year of critical security updates; Ring gives 4 years from purchase or its published date, whichever is later. Currys itself publishes no period for anything.

faqs.q: Why does Currys not show the support date next to the price?
faqs.a: Because the regulations do not ask it to. Paragraph 3(5) of Schedule 1 to the 2023 regulations requires the support information to sit alongside the price only where the manufacturer publishes the invitation to purchase on its own website. A retailer’s duty is different: under section 22 of the Act it may not make a connectable product available unless the product is accompanied by a statement of compliance. Government guidance confirms that document can be digital, so a link would do — but nothing compels one.

faqs.q: Is there a legal minimum support period?
faqs.a: No. The Government’s guidance describes the obligation as “publishing information on minimum security update periods”. The duty is to state the period, not to make it long. A manufacturer that publishes one year and honours it has complied. The one protection buyers do have is paragraph 3(6): once a defined support period has been published it cannot be shortened, and under paragraph 3(3) an extension must be published as soon as is practicable.

faqs.q: Does the two-year guarantee on Currys tiles cover security updates?
faqs.a: No. The “2 year guarantee”, shown as “Manufacturer’s guarantee: 2 years” in the Tapo D210 specification table, is a promise about the hardware failing. The defined support period is a separate promise about software. They are different lengths: on that same doorbell the guarantee runs two years from purchase while TP-Link supports hardware version V1 to 16/1/2030. On a Nest Cam (battery), whose published date was 8/24/2026, it works the other way round.

faqs.q: How do I find out which hardware version I am buying?
faqs.a: With difficulty, which is the awkward part. Currys lists the model name only. TP-Link’s own table separates the Tapo C200 into V1, V2 and V3 at 11/7/2027, V3.20 at 20/2/2029 and V5 at 16/1/2030. The version is normally printed on the label on the device or the box, so it can be checked on delivery and the item returned within the normal window if it is an older run than expected. Asking in store before paying is the simpler route.

faqs.q: What happens when a device goes out of support?
faqs.a: It usually keeps working and stops being patched. The National Cyber Security Centre warns that out of support, smart devices “are easier to hack, or may stop working altogether”, and calls the support date a “‘use by’ date for your device”. Arlo’s policy is explicit that end of life brings “No firmware upgrades”, while critical security fixes continue for one further year. Several Google Nest products — Nest Mini, Nest Wifi, Nest Audio, Nest Thermostat, Nest Hub 2nd gen and three Nest Cam models — were already past their published dates on 23 October 2026.

faqs.q: Has anyone been penalised under these rules?
faqs.a: Nothing has been published. The Office for Product Safety and Standards maintains an enforcement page for the connectable product security regulations setting out compliance notices, stop notices, recall notices and monetary penalties. It was last updated 8 August 2025, it names no company and no case, and it says OPSS “publishes details of any Compliance Notice that we serve”. That page is guidance on the powers rather than a register of their use, so read it as silence rather than as proof.

title: Currys Televisions: 395 Sets, a 12-Month Guarantee and the Fuse in the Cable
meta_title: Currys TVs: 395 Sets From £139.99, Guarantee Checked
meta_description: Currys lists 395 televisions from £139.99. What the 12-month guarantee covers, the 44 recalled models, the fuse behind them and how to check your own set.
intro:
Currys lists 395 televisions, running from a £139.99 32-inch JVC to a £3,699 77-inch LG OLED, and the guarantee the shop gives on any of them is, in its own words, “usually 12 months”. Every price, discount and date on this page was read from Currys' own television listing and service pages on 23 October 2026.

That listing is better documented than most. Each reduced set shows the price it used to carry and the exact window in which it carried it — the 55-inch Samsung R85H at £1,199.00 was £1,599.00 from 29/05/26 to 03/07/26, a £400.00 saving — and nearly every tile offers free collection from a store, which the page promises “in as little as an hour”. Currys trades from 691 stores in six countries with more than 24,000 colleagues, and in the 17 weeks to 29 August 2026 it reported like-for-like revenue up 6% in the UK and Ireland and 7% across the group.

It also does something few retailers of its size bother with. It keeps a public, dated, model-by-model record of the safety programmes affecting goods it has sold, and televisions are on it: 44 model numbers across three brands, all over a fuse of the wrong size. What that register says, what the regulator's version of it says, and what the longer guarantee badges on the listing are really worth are the three questions this page answers.

headline.label: Free guarantee included in the price
headline.value: 12 months — Currys puts its own cover at “usually 12 months”, and the longer badges on its listing belong to the makers: five years on 5 of the 20 television tiles read on 23 October 2026, two years on 3, and no guarantee wording at all on 12

key_facts.label: Who builds a Currys JVC television
key_facts.value: “Manufactured by Vestel Elektronik for Currys Group Ltd under license by JVCKENWOOD”, recorded in Office for Product Safety and Standards report 2606-0078, 15 June 2026

key_facts.label: Televisions listed
key_facts.value: 395 on 23 October 2026, 11 of them JVC

key_facts.label: Cheapest set on the listing
key_facts.value: £139.99 — JVC LT-32CR250 32-inch Roku TV, reduced from £169.99 (08/04/26 to 28/07/26)

key_facts.label: Dearest set on the first page
key_facts.value: £3,699.00 — LG G6 77-inch OLED, wall-mount version, reduced from £3,899.00

key_facts.label: Currys' own guarantee after the first 30 days
key_facts.value: Repair while the set is “still within its guarantee period”, which the returns page puts at “usually 12 months from when you bought it”

key_facts.label: Credit
key_facts.value: 29.9% APR representative (variable) from Creation Consumer Finance Ltd, with Currys Group Limited as credit broker; interest free over 12, 24 or 36 months; 48 months at a 9.9% purchase rate; orders over £99 only

key_facts.label: Televisions in the fuse programme
key_facts.value: 44 model numbers on Currys' safety page — 16 JVC, 14 Panasonic, 14 Toshiba — against 88 across seven brands in the regulator's report on the same defect

key_facts.label: How to tell whether a set is affected
key_facts.value: The serial number on the rear rating plate, or the marking YR-308 on the plug itself

key_facts.label: What the remedy costs
key_facts.value: Nothing — a replacement power cable or fuse, posted within “3-5 working days”, with no published closing date

key_facts.label: Where a television complaint ends up
key_facts.value: The “anything else” route on 0344 561 0000 — no arbitration scheme and no ombudsman, unlike the service-plan, insurance and credit routes

sections.heading: What £139.99 buys, and the guarantee badge that is not the shop's
sections.html:
The cheapest television in the range is the JVC LT-32CR250, a 32-inch HD-ready Roku set at £139.99, down from £169.99 between 08/04/26 and 28/07/26. Above it sit the JVC LT-32CT250 at £169.99, a 24-inch LG LB7000 at £179.00, and the 43-inch Hisense A6S at £259.00 against £329.00 earlier in the autumn. The first page of the listing tops out at £3,699.00 for the 77-inch LG G6 OLED in its wall-mount version. Between those two numbers are 395 sets, and the listing header counts them out as “Showing 1 - 20 of 395”.

The guarantee badges on those 20 tiles do not come from one place. Four printed “5 year guarantee” — the £1,199.00 Samsung R85H, the £1,399.00 and £1,899.00 LG C6 OLEDs and the £999.00 Hisense U7S. One, the £1,999.00 Sony BRAVIA 8 II, printed “Claim a 5 year guarantee”, which is a different promise with a step in front of it. Three Hisense A6S sets, at £259.00, £319.00 and £499.00, printed “2 year guarantee”. The remaining 12 tiles printed no guarantee wording whatsoever, including both JVC sets and six LG models between £179.00 and £3,699.00.

Currys' own position is on its returns page and it is short. A faulty item inside 30 days of purchase or delivery brings “an exchange or a refund”. After that the shop says it might be able to repair the set as long as it is still within its guarantee period, and gives that period as “usually 12 months from when you bought it”. Accidental damage, neglect, misuse and ordinary wear and tear are outside it. Longer cover is a separate purchase under the Care & Repair and Instant Replacement plans rather than part of the price.

So the twelve months is the shop's, and anything beyond it on this listing is the manufacturer's. Which maker stands behind each longer badge, whether it has to be registered for, and what it covers that the first year does not are not stated anywhere on the tile. Every television product page tried on this run returned a client error, which is where that detail would normally live.

sections.heading: Twenty-four months comes back to the cash price. Thirty-six does not.
sections.html:
Credit at Currys is lent by Creation Consumer Finance Ltd, with Currys Group Limited acting as “a credit broker and not a lender”. The published terms are 29.9% APR representative (variable) on an assumed £1,200 credit limit, instalments “interest free, over terms of 12, 24 or 36 months”, and a 48-month option “with a lower purchase interest rate of 9.9%”. Paying with credit is available only on orders over £99 — a floor that bites hard on controllers and cheap handsets and not at all here, because the least expensive television in the range clears it by £40.99.

The monthly figure printed on a tile is not always the interest-free one, and the term beside it is the tell. Five of the 20 tiles quote a 24-month figure, and every one of them multiplies back to the cash price: the £3,699.00 LG G6 at £154.12 a month comes to £3,698.88, twelve pence under; the £1,199.00 Samsung R85H at £49.95 comes to £1,198.80; the £1,899.00 LG C6 at £79.12 comes to £1,898.88. Those are the promotional rates the footnote mentions in passing, and they are a real saving against nothing.

The other 15 tiles quote a 36-month figure, each prefixed “From”, and those land roughly 45.9% above the price in cash. The £1,099.00 LG MRGB88 at £44.54 a month totals £1,603.44, which is £504.44 more. The £139.99 JVC at £5.67 totals £204.12, or £64.13 more. The £179.00 LG LB7000 at £7.25 totals £261.00, £82.00 more. None of that is hidden: the listing footnote reads “Monthly prices displayed are based on 29.9% Representative APR (variable)”, and the sums reconcile to the penny against that rate, which counts in the shop's favour.

The awkward part is narrower than it looks. Currys sells interest-free credit over 36 months on its own credit page, yet the 36-month number on the tile is priced at 29.9%. The cheaper version of the identical term exists; the listing simply does not quote it. Anyone spreading the cost of a mid-priced set should take the term they want to the checkout rather than the figure on the tile.

sections.heading: Forty-four model numbers on Currys' page, eighty-eight on the regulator's
sections.html:
Currys keeps a product safety page and in April 2026 it added three television notices to it. The wording is the same in each: “The issue relates to the fuse in certain power cables not complying with the relevant safety standards”, and “in the event of a failure in the electrical system, there is a rare possibility of a fire hazard.” Between them the three notices list 44 model numbers — 16 JVC, 14 Panasonic and 14 Toshiba — and tell owners that “For any affected product a replacement power cable or replacement fuse will be sent free of charge.” Nobody is told to stop using the television.

The same defect has a regulator's file. Report 2606-0078, published on 15 June 2026 and headed “Vestel UK Plugs in Various Televisions”, describes “Vestel UK-branded plugs fitted to various brands of television sold between November 2024 and February 2026”. Country of origin Turkey. Risk type fire, risk level low. Notified by Local Authority Trading Standards. The risk is put in one sentence: “The product presents a risk of fire as the plug's fuse does not meet the dimensional requirements of BS 1362.” The breaches cited are the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016 and the Plugs & Sockets etc (Safety) Regulations 1994.

The regulator's list is twice the length of the shop's. It runs to 88 model numbers under seven badges: 35 Toshiba, 17 Panasonic, 16 JVC, 15 Mitchell & Brown, two Finlux, two Techwood and a single Polaroid. The retailers named alongside Currys include Amazon, AO.com, Asda, Box, Buy It Direct, John Lewis, Marks Electrical, Richer Sounds, Virgin Media, The Very Group, Morrisons and Tesco stores. Seven brand names, one plug, one factory.

Currys lists the 44 it sold, which is a defensible place to draw the line, and the only model-level television page of its kind this run could find on any of those sellers. The gap still matters to a reader, because it is widest exactly where a Currys shopper is most likely to be caught: 14 Toshiba models on the shop's page against 35 on the regulator's. A set bought from Currys and listed only by the regulator is still a set with the wrong fuse in it.

sections.heading: Three documents, three date ranges, and the marking that settles it
sections.html:
Anyone trying to work out whether their own television is in the programme runs into a disagreement. Currys' page says “Models manufactured between November 2024 and November 2025”. The registration site the same page sends owners to says “certain TV models manufactured between November 2024 and February 2026”. Those two describe the same measure — when the set was built — and they are three months apart. The regulator's report measures something else again, sale rather than manufacture, and puts that at November 2024 to February 2026, with the per-brand detail showing Toshiba and JVC supplied from November 2024 to November 2025, Panasonic from December 2024 to September 2025, Mitchell & Brown from March to September 2025, Finlux from July to November 2025, Techwood from December 2024 and Polaroid from May 2025.

No manufacture date appears on this page, because the two documents that give one do not agree, and the difference is not academic: a set built in December 2025 falls outside Currys' window and inside the registration site's. The honest answer to the date question is that it is not the question to ask.

Two things do settle it. The serial number on the rating plate sticker on the back of the set, entered as the first eight digits where it starts with a 2 and the first seven where it starts with a 9. Or, for a television already on the wall where nobody can read the back of it, the plug: “If the wording YR-308 is present on the plug as shown above, the product is affected.” That second test is published by the regulator and repeated on the registration site, and it takes about four seconds. Anything bought before November 2024 is unaffected and needs no action.

The remedy itself is straightforward and free. Register online or by telephone on 03330 536 889, Monday to Friday 9am to 5pm, with a separate number for the Republic of Ireland, and a replacement cable or fuse follows “within 3-5 working days”, sent tracked and possibly needing a signature. No closing date is published, which is to the programme's credit. What is missing is a name: the site carries only the footer “© Pacifica Warranty 2026”, gives no company number and no registered address, and Currys' own page does not say who runs it either. For its own exclusive products Currys promises that “In the unlikely event of a safety recall, we'll contact you directly” — but only “as long as you gave us your name and address at the time of purchase”, which is why its standing advice is “Always keep a hold of your sale receipt.”

sections.heading: Three of the JVC sets on sale today share a model name with a recalled one
sections.html:
JVC is the badge where this gets closest to home. Currys lists 11 JVC televisions, describing the brand as one that “delivers affordable Smart TVs with HDR10/HLG, multiple HDMI ports”, and the brand page names LT-32CT150, LT-40CT450, LT-43CT450 and LT-32CR250 in its own text. The first three of those appear among the 16 JVC models in the fuse programme.

That is not evidence that a set on sale this week has the wrong fuse in it. The programme is defined by when a television was built and by its serial number, the fix is a cable, and a model name outlives the batch that caused the trouble. It is, though, the clearest demonstration of why the register works on serial numbers and a marking on the plug instead of on model names — and why a buyer who wants to check in two years' time will not be able to do it from the model number printed on the box.

The chain behind the badge is on the regulator's file rather than on the shop's. The JVC range is recorded there as “Manufactured by Vestel Elektronik for Currys Group Ltd under license by JVCKENWOOD”. JVC on a Currys television is a licensed name: the set is built in Turkey by Vestel and sold under a Japanese marque that no longer makes it. Vestel Elektronik says it ships to more than 160 countries from 11 offices, with almost 16,000 employees across 31 companies, 20 of them outside Turkey.

The plugs themselves are described throughout as Vestel UK-branded. Vestel UK Limited is company 04771550, incorporated on 20 May 2003, registered at Vestel House, 1 Waterside Drive, Langley, Berkshire SL3 6EZ, with accounts last made up to 31 December 2024 — and with SIC codes for financial management (70221), management consultancy (70229) and other business support (82990) rather than for manufacturing anything. Which company in that chain chose and fitted the fuse cannot be settled from public documents, and the regulator's report names no manufacturer or importer at all for most of the seven badges. Worth asking about rather than assuming.

sections.heading: The one part of a television the law describes on its own
sections.html:
A three-pin plug has a statutory instrument to itself. Regulation 6(2) of the Plugs and Sockets etc. (Safety) Regulations 1994 requires that a standard plug “shall contain or be accompanied by a fuse link which conforms to BS 1362”. The two standards are often run together and should not be: BS 1363 is the plug, BS 1362 is the fuse link inside it. The failure in this programme is dimensional — the fuse does not meet BS 1362's dimensional requirements — which is why the correction is a cable or a cartridge rather than a television.

What the law asks of the shop, rather than of the factory, is narrower than most readers would guess. Regulation 26 of the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016 sets out what a distributor must verify before it makes equipment available: that the UK marking is on it, that it is accompanied by “the documents that the manufacturer or importer is required to provide”, that instructions and safety information come with it in “clear, legible and easily understandable English”, and that the manufacturer and importer have met their own labelling and identification duties. Nothing on that list asks a retailer to measure a fuse.

Regulation 29 covers what happens afterwards. Where a distributor “considers, or has reason to believe” that equipment it has already made available does not conform, it has to ensure corrective measures are taken — bringing it into conformity, withdrawing it or recalling it — and, where the equipment presents a risk, immediately notify the market surveillance authority, stating the non-conformity and the measures taken. The published report records the notification as having come from Local Authority Trading Standards. The register does not show who told whom first, and this page does not guess.

Underneath both sits the general duty. Regulation 5 of the General Product Safety Regulations 2005 is as blunt as consumer law gets: “No producer shall place a product on the market unless the product is a safe product.” Regulation 8 then puts a distributor under a duty to act with “due care in order to help ensure compliance with the applicable safety requirements”, to help monitor the safety of products already sold, to keep records that trace a product's origin and produce them when asked, and to cooperate “in action taken by a producer or an enforcement authority to avoid the risks”. Read in that order, the model-by-model register Currys publishes looks less like an apology and more like regulation 8 being done in public.

sections.heading: A faulty television reaches no ombudsman at all
sections.html:
Currys splits complaints four ways, and the split is worth knowing before anything goes wrong. A dispute about Care & Repair, Instant Replacement or another extended warranty service starts on 0344 561 1234 or in writing to the Customer Focus Team at PO Box 194, Cramlington NE23 0DA, and escalates to Consumer Arbitration. An insurance complaint starts on 0800 049 0221, with Currys promising to “contact you with an update within 14 working days of receipt”, and escalates to the Financial Ombudsman Service at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR. A flexpay credit complaint starts on 0330 678 0511, writing to PO Box 1687 Sheffield S2 5YA, and also goes to the Ombudsman. Everything else goes to webchat or 0344 561 0000.

A television that stops working is in that fourth box. The arbitration scheme covers the service plan sold alongside the set; the Financial Ombudsman covers the insurance and the credit agreement; the television itself reaches neither. That is not peculiar to Currys — no ombudsman covers the sale of goods in Britain — but a shopper who has read the first three routes can easily assume the fourth works the same way, and it does not. The fallback is the Consumer Rights Act and, if it comes to it, the county court.

Where arbitration does apply, the terms are published and better than many. The route opens after a final resolution letter or once eight weeks have passed, and closes one year after that letter. The consumer pays £10 for a dispute up to £750 and £25 above it, and Currys refunds the fee if the customer wins. Consumer Arbitration is operated by Consumer Dispute Resolution Limited, company 09189773, incorporated on 28 August 2014. Currys gives its address as Unit 5 Homelands, Higher Union Road, Kingsbridge TQ7 1EQ; Companies House holds the registered office as Unit 12 Walker Avenue, Wolverton Mill, Milton Keynes MK12 5TW. The Chartered Trading Standards Institute's register of approved bodies lists the same two fees and records that “The outcome of the procedure is binding on both parties” — and carries the sentence “This service is free for consumers” on the same page, which cannot be true of both.

Two smaller things from the same page. The insurance behind Currys' cover is Aviva, named there as a member of the Financial Services Compensation Scheme, and on the Ombudsman the wording is unusually plain: “Whilst we are bound by the decision of the Financial Ombudsman Service, you are not.” And the line for customers who need reasonable adjustments, 0203 540 8063, is open on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday from 9:30am to 12:30pm — twelve hours a week, against a general enquiries line open 8am to 8pm on weekdays.

sections.heading: Two in three shoppers wish somebody would tell them what is worth buying
sections.html:
Currys asked. On 1 October 2026 it published a 3Gem survey of 2,000 UK adults, fielded between 4 and 8 September 2026, and the results read like a description of a television aisle. 69% said there is too much choice. 70% said technology is changing faster than they can keep up with. 64% said specifications make products sound more confusing than they are. 18% admitted to “winging it” when choosing something, 24% to pretending to understand a term they did not know, 28% to nodding along to an explanation they had not followed and 28% to looking a term up on their phone while standing in a shop. 21% had bought the dearer product on the assumption that dearer meant better, and 14% had bought something simply to end the decision.

61% had already used an AI assistant or an AI search tool to help choose a piece of tech; of those, 51% said it made the decision quicker or easier and 33% thought it produced a better choice. Asked who they would rather be helped by, 34% picked a human expert in store, 22% an AI assistant alone and 26% a combination. 79% would value independent expert guidance, 68% said an award judged by independent experts would make them more confident between similar models, and 66% simply wish somebody would tell them which products are actually worth buying. The release accompanied the second year of Currys' own Tech of the Year Awards across 13 categories, with Ed Connolly, Chief Commercial Officer, saying they are “about helping shoppers make decisions easier” and that the company is “using our unique position as the number one omni-channel tech retailer to help de-mystify the world of tech”.

Set that survey against this page and the two meet in an odd place. A Currys television comes with its price, its old price, the dates that old price applied, a monthly figure, a screen size, a brand and often a guarantee badge. The specification a worried owner actually needs — which fuse is in the cable, and whether YR-308 is stamped on the plug — is on neither the tile nor the box, and the one page that would tell them is a register most shoppers will never open.

The business asking those questions is trading well. The AGM update of 10 September 2026, covering the 17 weeks to 29 August 2026, reported like-for-like revenue up 6% in the UK and Ireland, 9% in the Nordics and 7% for the group, with gross margin stable in both regions, flexpay adoption up 30 basis points to 23.6%, iD Mobile past 2.7m subscribers and £23m of a £50m buyback completed. Company-compiled consensus puts group adjusted profit before tax at £199m for 2026/27, guidance was left unchanged, and interim results for the 26 weeks to 31 October 2026 are due on 17 December 2026. Fredrik Tønnesen, the group chief executive, said Currys “gained share in every category, in a market that was flat even with the help of the World Cup and Summer heatwaves”.

pros: 395 televisions listed on 23 October 2026, from £139.99 to £3,699.00 on the first page alone.
Every reduced set shows the price it used to carry and the exact dates it carried it, which is more than most listings publish.
Free store collection on nearly every television, promised “in as little as an hour”, and credit available across the whole range because the cheapest set clears the £99 floor by £40.99.
The five dearest sets on the first page are quoted over 24 months at figures that come back to within 20p of the cash price.
A public, dated, model-by-model safety register naming 44 television models and describing the defect in plain words — the only page of its kind this run found among the sellers involved.
The recall remedy is free, needs nothing but a serial number or a glance at the plug, arrives in three to five working days and has no published closing date.
On a service-plan dispute the arbitration fee is £10 or £25 and Currys refunds it if the customer wins.
Currys undertakes to contact owners of its own exclusive products directly if a recall is announced.
cons: Currys' own guarantee is “usually 12 months”. The five-year and two-year badges on the listing are the makers', 12 of the 20 tiles read carried no guarantee wording at all, and nothing on a tile says which party stands behind a longer promise or whether it has to be claimed.
Currys' safety page names 44 model numbers; the regulator's report on the same defect names 88 across seven brands, and the gap is widest on Toshiba — 14 models against 35.

Two documents in the same programme disagree about when the affected sets were built, Currys saying November 2024 to November 2025 and the registration site November 2024 to February 2026, so no manufacture date is quoted here.
The registration site that handles the remedy is badged only “© Pacifica Warranty 2026”, with no company number and no registered address, and Currys' page does not name the administrator either.
On the 15 sets quoted over 36 months the monthly figure is the 29.9% one, roughly 45.9% above the cash price, although Currys' own credit page sells interest-free credit over 36 months as well.

A faulty television itself reaches no ADR scheme and no ombudsman: arbitration covers the service plans, the Financial Ombudsman covers insurance and credit, and the set sits in the “anything else” route.

Currys' delivery and collection page would not open on any attempt, for the third page running, so the charge to deliver a television could not be read; nor would any television product page, so no energy class, weight or stated guarantee length could be taken from one.
Currys gives one address for its arbitration scheme and Companies House holds another.
The line for customers who need reasonable adjustments is open twelve hours a week.
verdict: A good place to buy a television and an unusually well documented one: 395 sets, prices and discount windows printed on the tile, free collection within the hour, credit on everything in the range, and a safety register that names 44 models and the defect behind them rather than hiding it. Three things are worth doing before and after buying. Check the term beside the monthly figure, because the 24-month quotes on the dearest sets are free and the 36-month quotes on everything else add about 45.9%. Treat the guarantee as twelve months unless the maker's badge says otherwise in writing. And whether the set is new or already on the wall, look at the plug: if YR-308 is stamped on it, a free cable is three to five working days away, and that is a four-second check on a fire risk the regulator has already graded.

faqs.q: What guarantee comes with a Currys television?
faqs.a: Currys' returns page gives the shop's own guarantee period as “usually 12 months from when you bought it”, with a faulty item inside the first 30 days bringing an exchange or a refund instead. Accidental damage, neglect, misuse and ordinary wear and tear are excluded. Some sets on the listing carry longer badges — five of the 20 tiles read on 23 October 2026 mentioned five years and three mentioned two — but those are the manufacturers' promises rather than Currys', and 12 of the 20 tiles carried no guarantee wording at all. Longer cover from Currys is a separate purchase under Care & Repair or Instant Replacement.

faqs.q: Is my television part of the fuse recall, and how do I check?
faqs.a: Two tests. The serial number on the rating plate sticker on the back of the set can be entered on the Television Safety Notice registration site — the first eight digits if it begins with a 2, the first seven if it begins with a 9. If the television is already wall-mounted, look at the plug instead: the regulator's report states that “If the wording YR-308 is present on the plug as shown above, the product is affected.” A set bought before November 2024 is unaffected. Registering brings a free replacement power cable or fuse within three to five working days, and the helpline is 03330 536 889, Monday to Friday 9am to 5pm.

faqs.q: What is actually wrong with the fuse?
faqs.a: It is the wrong size. Report 2606-0078, published by the Office for Product Safety and Standards on 15 June 2026, says “The product presents a risk of fire as the plug's fuse does not meet the dimensional requirements of BS 1362.” Regulation 6(2) of the Plugs and Sockets etc. (Safety) Regulations 1994 requires a standard plug to “contain or be accompanied by a fuse link which conforms to BS 1362”, so the defect is a compliance failure in a component rather than a fault in the television. The risk type is recorded as fire and the risk level as low, and the corrective measure is a replacement cable or fuse.

faqs.q: Which brands and how many models are affected?
faqs.a: Currys' own safety page lists 44 models across three brands it sold: 16 JVC, 14 Panasonic and 14 Toshiba. The regulator's report on the same Vestel UK-branded plug covers 88 models under seven badges — 35 Toshiba, 17 Panasonic, 16 JVC, 15 Mitchell & Brown, two Finlux, two Techwood and one Polaroid — sold through a long list of retailers that includes Amazon, AO.com, Asda, John Lewis, Richer Sounds, Virgin Media, The Very Group, Tesco and Morrisons as well as Currys. If a set is not on the shop's list it may still be on the regulator's.

faqs.q: Does the monthly price on a Currys television cost more than paying cash?
faqs.a: It depends on the term printed beside it. The five tiles quoting a 24-month figure all multiply back to the cash price — the £3,699.00 LG G6 at £154.12 a month works out at £3,698.88. The 15 tiles quoting a 36-month figure are priced at the headline 29.9% APR representative and come out roughly 45.9% higher: the £1,099.00 LG MRGB88 at £44.54 a month totals £1,603.44. Currys does sell interest-free credit over 36 months on its credit page, so the figure on the tile is not necessarily the cheapest version of that term.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if a Currys television develops a fault?
faqs.a: Currys itself, on 0344 561 0000 or by webchat. Unlike the other three complaint routes a television fault has no external body behind it: Consumer Arbitration handles disputes about the extended warranty plans and the Financial Ombudsman Service handles insurance and flexpay credit, but the sale of the set reaches neither. Beyond Currys, the remedy is the Consumer Rights Act and, if necessary, the county court. Where arbitration does apply, it opens after a final resolution letter or eight weeks, closes a year later, costs £10 up to £750 or £25 above, and the fee is refunded if you win.

faqs.q: Who makes the JVC televisions Currys sells?
faqs.a: Vestel. The regulator's report records the JVC range as “Manufactured by Vestel Elektronik for Currys Group Ltd under license by JVCKENWOOD”, so JVC on a Currys set is a licensed badge on a television built in Turkey to Currys' order. Currys listed 11 JVC televisions on 23 October 2026. Vestel Elektronik says it ships to more than 160 countries from 11 offices with almost 16,000 employees; the plugs in this programme are described as Vestel UK-branded, and Vestel UK Limited is company 04771550, incorporated on 20 May 2003 at Vestel House, 1 Waterside Drive, Langley, Berkshire SL3 6EZ.

title: DFDS Ferry Tickets: Fares, Fees and the Contract Behind Them
meta_title: DFDS Ferries: Dover Fares, Fees and Refund Rules
meta_description: DFDS ferry tickets from £114 for a car and five people Dover-Calais. The fares, the amendment fees, the cancellation rules and the cover you actually get.

headline.label: Cheapest car crossing
headline.value: £114 one way — car plus up to five passengers, Dover–Calais or Dover–Dunkirk, EU ETS charge included

intro:
DFDS sells a Dover–Calais crossing from £114 for a car and up to five passengers, one way, with the emissions charge already inside the price. The ship takes 1 hour 40 minutes and there are up to 30 of them a day. Dunkirk costs the same and runs up to 22 times a day over two hours. Figures checked 26 October 2026 against DFDS's own route pages and its January 2025 booking conditions.

The company behind that ticket is older than almost anything else you can buy a seat on. DFDS A/S has been running ships since 1866, is listed in Copenhagen, turned over DKK 30,947m in 2025 and ended the year with 68 ferries, around 30 routes and offices in more than 20 countries. It carried 5,247,000 passengers that year, and roughly three quarters of them — 3,862,000 — crossed the Channel.

One thing is worth knowing before you book rather than after. The cheapest Dover fare, the one called Economy, carries a 100% cancellation charge at any time, so the money is gone from the moment you pay it. The Flexi fare on the same route cancels free up to 48 hours before sailing. Which of the two you pick matters more than anything else on the booking page.
