sections.heading: Seventy-seven pence in every pound comes from lorries
sections.html:
The single most useful thing to understand about a DFDS ticket is that you are a minority customer on a freight business, and that this is mostly to your advantage. The audited 2025 accounts split the Ferry Division's DKK 16,999m of revenue into DKK 13,104m from freight and DKK 3,895m from passengers. That is 77.1% trailers and 22.9% people. On the Channel in 2025 the ships moved 16,910,000 lane metres of freight alongside those 3,862,000 passengers.

Frequency is the dividend. Lorries need sailings through the night and at awkward hours, and the economics of running a ship that often are carried by the freight deck rather than by your car. Up to 30 Calais departures and 22 Dunkirk departures a day is a timetable no passenger-only operator on that stretch of water could justify, and it is why a missed sailing at Dover is an inconvenience rather than a lost day.

The same accounts show why 2025 was a hard year. Group revenue rose 4.0% to DKK 30,947m, but EBIT fell from DKK 1,506m to DKK 520m and the group recorded a loss for the period of DKK 425m against a DKK 541m profit in 2024. The Logistics Division, which is now almost as large as the ferries at DKK 15,723m of revenue, lost DKK 30m. Passenger revenue across the group fell 17.5% from DKK 4,720m, and headline passenger numbers dropped 22.2% from 6,747,000. Almost none of that decline is on the Channel, where the count went up from 3,824,000; it sits on the Mediterranean and Strait of Gibraltar networks, where the half-year to June 2026 shows passengers down 24.8% again.

The half-year figures also carry a cost that no marketing page mentions and that shows how long shipping disputes run: a one-off charge of DKK 53m booked against the Channel in the second quarter of 2026, arising from a French court ruling about the chartering of two Channel ferries in 2015.

sections.heading: Three routes, six different opening prices
sections.html:
Every DFDS route page advertises a lead-in fare twice, once in the banner and once inside the frequently asked questions, and on 26 October 2026 the two did not agree on any of the three Channel routes.

Dover–Calais shows “From £114 per car + up to 5 people, one way* (INCLUDING ETS)” at the top of the page and repeats £114 in the route table. Its own FAQ, further down the same page, says: “Travel with DFDS by ferry from Dover to Calais from £99 for a car plus 5 passengers one way.” Dover–Dunkirk does exactly the same thing with exactly the same two numbers. Newhaven–Dieppe reverses it — the banner says “From £73 per car + 4 people one way*” while its FAQ says crossings “currently start from £117” on the same basis, and the Dover–Dunkirk page quotes Newhaven–Dieppe at £117 as well.

The likeliest explanation is innocent and it is still a problem. The banner prices carry the words “including ETS” and the FAQ prices do not, which suggests the FAQ copy was written before the emissions charge was folded in and has been maintained on a slower cycle. A shopper reading the FAQ expects to pay £99 and will be quoted £114. The gap is 15%.

The same page has a second disagreement with itself: the Newhaven route is described as running “up to 6 daily sailings” in one section and as departing “twice daily” in another. One ship, the Côte d'Albâtre, works that route in about four hours, or five on certain overnight crossings.

For completeness, the other published lead-in prices: short breaks to France from £79 per car and up to five people; Newcastle to Amsterdam from £74 per person based on four sharing a standard four-berth inside cabin with a car included, on a 16 hour 45 minute crossing leaving at 17:00 daily with check-in closing at 16:15. That route's FAQ says £69.

sections.heading: The cheapest Dover fare cannot be cancelled at all
sections.html:
DFDS publishes its cancellation scale in full in the January 2025 Passenger Booking Terms and Conditions, which is more than many operators manage, and the scale is unusually blunt. Section 14 sets a 100% cancellation charge on an Eastern Channel Economy fare at any time — not within 48 hours, not within a week, but from the moment the booking is made. The Western Channel Transportation fare is the same, and so are Long Sea transport-only tickets and the Mini and City Cruise breaks.

Flexi is the fare that behaves the way most people assume a ferry ticket behaves. On the Eastern Channel it cancels free if you give more than 48 hours notice and costs 100% inside that window. The Channel Islands fares sit between the two: Economy refunds half if you cancel more than 48 hours out and nothing inside it, while Flexi is free to the same 48-hour mark.

Only the Long Sea Holiday Collections and groups of 20 or more get a graduated ladder, and it starts early: 25% at 57 days or more, 50% from 56 to 36 days, 70% from 35 to 22 days, 90% from 21 to 11 days and 100% at ten days or fewer. Group bookings on the Western Channel and Long Sea take a 25% deposit with the balance due at least 56 days before departure.

Changing a booking is cheaper than losing it but it is not free. The amendment fee is £20 or €25 per change on the Eastern Channel and on Long Sea transport-only and cruise breaks, £10 on the Western Channel and £10 or €15 on the Channel Islands routes and for name changes. On top of that you pay the difference between your original fare and the fare on the day you make the change, which on a Dover crossing in August is where the real money goes. Booking by telephone or in person attracts a service fee as well; the terms say the amount is on the website rather than printing it.

Two surcharges in the same document are worth knowing about because they are large. Smoking outside a designated area carries a minimum penalty of €200 or DKK 1,500, and bringing your own alcohol to drink on board costs the bar price for it plus a cleaning surcharge if you drink it in a cabin. The vehicle rules are specific too: up to three gas cylinders with a combined weight of no more than 47 kg, up to 1,000 cartridges or shells per vehicle in original packaging, and no petrol or diesel cans at all.

sections.heading: What the ETS line in your fare is actually paying for
sections.html:
DFDS prints “including ETS” beside its Dover prices and explains the acronym nowhere a shopper will find it. It is the European Union Emissions Trading System, which has covered maritime transport since 1 January 2024 for cargo and passenger ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above.

Two details decide how big that component is, and both work in a Dover passenger's favour at the moment. The scheme counts only 50% of the emissions on a voyage between an EU port and a port outside the EU, which is what a Dover–Calais crossing now is; a sailing between two EU ports counts at 100%. And the obligation is still phasing in. Operators surrendered allowances against 40% of their reported 2024 emissions, 70% of 2025 emissions, and must cover 100% from 2027. Methane and nitrous oxide join carbon dioxide in the scheme from 2026.

So the charge inside today's £114 reflects seventy per cent of half a crossing's emissions, and the scheme's own timetable raises both halves of that. Absorbing it into the headline price rather than adding it at checkout is the better practice of the two available, and worth crediting, but it does mean the fare will carry an increase that has nothing to do with fuel or demand.

The United Kingdom's own emissions scheme does not reach this crossing. Its expansion to maritime covers vessels of 5,000 gross tonnage and above “operating on domestic routes within UK waters and/or generating in-port emissions”, with the draft legislation laid in January 2026, offshore vessels added from January 2027 and a review in 2028 that will consider “potential inclusion of international voyages”. An international sailing from Dover sits outside it until that review says otherwise.

sections.heading: A Special Drawing Right is worth about £1.01, and nobody tells you
sections.html:
Liability at sea is set by the 2002 Athens Convention and published in Special Drawing Rights, the International Monetary Fund's basket unit. DFDS prints the full set in section 16 of its conditions, which is more than most carriers do, and then leaves the reader holding a unit with no price on it. Here is the conversion, using the IMF's own valuation of 23 October 2026, when one SDR was worth US$1.355380 against a sterling rate of 1.33735 dollars to the pound — so one SDR is about £1.01.

Death or injury to a passenger is capped at 400,000 SDR, which is roughly £405,000. A vehicle and the luggage inside it is 12,700 SDR, about £12,871, with a deductible of 330 SDR or about £334 taken off any vehicle claim. Cabin luggage is 2,250 SDR, about £2,280. Other luggage is 3,375 SDR, about £3,421, with a 149 SDR deductible of about £151 per passenger. Money and valuables are excluded altogether, which is the clause that matters if you keep a laptop in the boot.

Set the vehicle limit against the thing it covers. The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders puts the average age of a car on British roads at close to a decade, so for most family cars £12,871 is ample; for anything newer or larger it is not, and the gap belongs to your own motor policy rather than to the ferry company. A claim under the Convention has to be notified within two years of the incident.

Delay is a separate régime and a weaker one. Assimilated Regulation (EU) No 1177/2010 gives a passenger the right to refreshments, and where necessary accommodation capped at €80 a night for a maximum of three nights, once a departure runs more than 90 minutes late, and compensation of 25% or 50% of the fare for arrival delays. DFDS reproduces the €80 cap in its own section 15. Article 20 of the same regulation switches the compensation off where the delay is caused by weather endangering safe operation, which in the Dover Strait in January is the usual reason a sailing goes wrong.

sections.heading: A Danish carrier, an English contract and a Lincolnshire registered office
sections.html:
The conditions name the carrier as DFDS A/S at DFDS House, Sundkrogsgade 11, DK-2100 Copenhagen Ø, operating “a subsidiary or branch of DFDS A/S” on any given route. The contract is nevertheless governed by the laws of England and Wales, and section 21 lets a passenger sue either where DFDS has its principal place of business or in their own country of residence where DFDS has a place of business there. For a British buyer that is a better arrangement than the carrier's nationality would suggest, and it is the same choice Brittany's French carrier makes.

Companies House shows the British arm as DFDS Seaways plc, company 01554521, a public limited company registered at Nordic House, Western Access Road, Immingham Dock, North East Lincolnshire DN40 2LZ and still active. It was incorporated on 2 April 1981 and has changed its name six times since: Scandinavian Seaways Limited, Longship Holidays Limited, Scandinavian Seaways again, DFDS plc from 2 January 1996, DFDS Tor Line plc from 8 December 2003 and the present name from 31 August 2010. Accounts were last made up to 31 December 2025 and the next confirmation statement is due by 12 February 2027.

Its registered activity codes are the detail that confirms the shape of the business. The plc files under 52101 for warehousing and storage for water transport, 52220 for service activities incidental to water transportation and 70100 for head office activities. There is no sea passenger transport code on the register at all. That is a filing choice rather than a statement about the service, but it does say where the company thinks its centre of gravity is.

Financial protection follows the same logic. DFDS holds membership 5448 of the Association of Bonded Travel Organisers Trust, which protects package bookings. Buy a crossing on its own and no bond attaches to it, because a single travel service is not a package; there is no ATOL cover either, since no flight is involved.

sections.heading: Jersey has bought twenty years of this company
sections.html:
The newest part of the network is also the clearest sign of how a government assesses a ferry operator when it has to. On 31 December 2024 the Government of Jersey confirmed DFDS as the island's ferry operator on a contract that “will run for 20 years”, with services beginning on 28 March 2025 across Jersey to Poole, Jersey to Portsmouth and Jersey to St Malo.

What DFDS committed to is on the record: “greater frequency of ferries to the UK and France in peak periods”, “faster ferries to the UK”, “investing in three new ferries by 2032” and “two dedicated high-speed ferries for the summer”. The company has since agreed to buy the ro-pax ferry Stena Vinga, currently working the Jersey–Portsmouth route, for delivery in November 2026, and its half-year report notes Jersey passenger volumes running above 2025.

For a traveller the practical point is that the Channel Islands routes run on their own fare rules, which are gentler than Dover's. Economy there refunds 50% if you cancel more than 48 hours ahead, against nothing at all on an Eastern Channel Economy ticket, and the amendment fee is £10 or €15 rather than £20. A twenty-year lifeline obligation and a commercial short-sea route are not the same product even when the funnel is.

sections.heading: Borders, and the one place Dover is easier than everywhere else
sections.html:
The European Union's Entry/Exit System began on 12 October 2025 and changes what happens at the far end of a crossing. Travellers create a digital record with fingerprints and a photograph at dedicated booths, and that record is “valid for 3 years”. The 90 days in every 180 limit on time in the Schengen area applies as before, and ETIAS is expected to start from autumn 2026.

Where the check happens is the part that favours a DFDS Dover booking. UK government guidance updated on 10 April 2026 says that at Dover, Eurotunnel Le Shuttle and Eurostar “any EES checks will be completed at the border, before you leave the UK”, while passengers using other ferry ports “will be registered at the border on arrival in their destination country”. Sail from Newhaven or Newcastle and you queue for biometrics after a night at sea; sail from Dover and you have done it before boarding. That is a genuine operational advantage of the short crossings and nothing on the booking page points it out.

sections.heading: Where the paperwork runs out
sections.html:
Four gaps are worth naming, and none of them is unique to this company.

The complaints window is short. Section 17 requires a written complaint within two months of the journey, sent to uk.customercare@dfds.com with the booking reference in the subject line; DFDS undertakes to say within one month whether the complaint is upheld, rejected or still under review, and to give a final answer on passenger-rights complaints within two months. Damage to a vehicle or luggage has to be reported before or at disembarkation if it is visible and within 15 days if it is not. Two months is less time than the law allows you to go to court, and a claim under the Merchant Shipping (Passengers' Rights) Regulations 2013 must be brought within six months of the infringement.

There is no ombudsman. The 2013 regulations name the Maritime and Coastguard Agency as the designated enforcement body, and enforcement means prosecution, which pays the court rather than the passenger. The conditions offer ABTA or the EU online dispute platform for unresolved matters, neither of which binds the carrier the way the Financial Ombudsman Service binds a bank.

Nobody rates ferry operators. Defaqto rates insurance, the national tourist boards assess accommodation and Ofcom measures telecoms. No agency publishes a star band, an acceptance rate or an uphold rate for any shipping line, so a comparison between carriers has to be built out of timetables, published fares and the documents themselves rather than out of a score.

And two figures a shopper would want are simply absent. The telephone and in-person booking service fee is referred to in the terms but not quantified there. Nor is there a published fee for carrying a dog, although the conditions reserve the right to apply freight tariffs to animals.

pros: Up to 30 Calais sailings and 22 Dunkirk sailings a day, with a Calais crossing of 1 hour 40 minutes
The emissions charge is folded into the advertised fare rather than added at checkout
EES biometric checks at Dover are completed in the UK before boarding, not on arrival in France
Flexi fares on the Eastern Channel and Channel Islands cancel free up to 48 hours before departure
The booking contract is governed by English law even though the carrier is Danish
Athens Convention limits for luggage, vehicles and deductibles are published in full, which many carriers omit
A 20-year Jersey lifeline contract with three new ferries promised by 2032 and the Stena Vinga arriving in November 2026
Group scale behind the ticket: 68 ferries, around 30 routes and DKK 30,947m of revenue in 2025
Channel passenger numbers rose to 3,862,000 in 2025 while the group total fell
cons: The cheapest Dover fare, Economy, carries a 100% cancellation charge at any time — the money is unrecoverable from the moment you book
Each of the three Channel route pages advertises two different lead-in fares, with Dover quoted at both £114 and £99 and Newhaven at both £73 and £117
Amending an Eastern Channel booking costs £20 or €25 per change on top of any increase in the fare itself
The Athens Convention limits are published only in Special Drawing Rights, with no sterling conversion anywhere on the site
Written complaints must be made within two months of the journey, against the six months the regulations give you to go to court
There is no ombudsman or binding adjudicator for ferry travel; the Maritime and Coastguard Agency enforces by prosecution, which pays the court rather than you
Statutory delay compensation of 25% or 50% falls away under Article 20 where weather endangering safe operation is the cause, which is the commonest reason a Dover sailing fails
The telephone booking service fee is referred to in the terms without an amount, and no pet carriage charge is published
Group passenger revenue fell 17.5% to DKK 3,895m in 2025 and the group recorded a DKK 425m loss for the year
The Newhaven–Dieppe page describes the service as both “up to 6 daily sailings” and “twice daily”
verdict: For a car heading to northern France, this is the operator with the timetable — up to 30 Calais crossings a day at 1 hour 40 minutes, from £114 for a car and five people with the emissions charge already counted, and biometric checks finished before you leave Kent. That frequency exists because lorries pay for 77.1% of the Ferry Division's revenue, and the passenger rides on a freight network with DKK 31bn of group turnover behind it. The thing to get right is the fare type, not the operator: an Economy ticket is unrefundable from the moment you buy it and Flexi cancels free until 48 hours before sailing, so unless your dates are certain the gap between the two prices is cheap insurance. Read the January 2025 booking conditions before you pay, because the cancellation scale in section 14 is blunter than the booking page suggests.

faqs.q: How much is a DFDS ferry from Dover to Calais?
faqs.a: DFDS advertises Dover–Calais from £114 one way for a standard car carrying up to five passengers, with the EU emissions charge included. Dover–Dunkirk is the same price over a two-hour crossing. Note that the FAQ on DFDS's own route page still quotes £99 for both, a figure that does not mention the emissions charge; the £114 banner price is the one repeated in the route table.

faqs.q: Can I cancel a DFDS ferry ticket and get a refund?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on the fare. An Eastern Channel Economy ticket carries a 100% cancellation charge at any time, so there is no refund however early you cancel. A Flexi ticket on the same route cancels free with more than 48 hours notice and 100% inside that window. Channel Islands Economy refunds 50% beyond 48 hours. Long Sea Holiday Collections use a ladder running from 25% at 57 or more days out to 100% inside ten days.

faqs.q: What does the ETS charge on a DFDS fare mean?
faqs.a: It is the EU Emissions Trading System, which has covered passenger and cargo ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above since 1 January 2024. Only 50% of emissions count on a voyage between an EU and a non-EU port, which is what a Dover crossing is, and the obligation is phasing in — 70% of 2025 emissions and 100% from 2027. DFDS includes the charge in the advertised fare rather than adding it at checkout.

faqs.q: What is DFDS liable for if my car is damaged on the ferry?
faqs.a: Under the Athens Convention limits in section 16 of its conditions, a vehicle and the luggage in it are covered to 12,700 SDR, about £12,871 at the IMF valuation of 23 October 2026, less a deductible of 330 SDR or roughly £334. Cabin luggage is capped at 2,250 SDR and other luggage at 3,375 SDR with a 149 SDR deductible. Money and valuables are excluded, and a claim must be notified within two years.

faqs.q: Is a DFDS ferry ticket financially protected if the company fails?
faqs.a: A package booking is: DFDS holds ABTOT membership 5448, which bonds package holidays. A crossing bought on its own is a single travel service rather than a package, so no bond, no insolvency protection and no repatriation promise attaches to it, and ATOL does not apply because no flight is involved.

faqs.q: Do I need to do EES biometrics before a DFDS crossing?
faqs.a: Yes, on a sailing into the Schengen area, but where it happens depends on the port. UK government guidance updated 10 April 2026 says Dover completes EES checks before you leave the UK, while other ferry ports register travellers on arrival in the destination country. The digital record lasts 3 years and the 90 days in every 180 limit still applies.

faqs.q: How long do I have to complain to DFDS?
faqs.a: Section 17 of the booking conditions requires a written complaint within two months of the journey, with DFDS replying inside one month and giving a final answer on passenger-rights matters within two months. Visible damage to a vehicle or luggage must be reported before or at disembarkation, and hidden damage within 15 days. Court proceedings under the Merchant Shipping (Passengers' Rights) Regulations 2013 must be started within six months.

title: Direct Ferries Tickets: Fees, Fares and Whose Contract You Get
meta_title: Direct Ferries Review: 314 Operators, Fees and Refunds
meta_description: Direct Ferries compares 314 ferry companies across 4,387 routes. What its service fee, the £10 amendment charge and a 14-day complaint window actually mean.

headline.label: Cheapest car crossing
headline.value: £160 — its own published average for a car on Dover–Calais; no lead-in car fare is advertised, and the £21 'from' price is not a car

intro:
Direct Ferries puts 314 ferry companies and Eurotunnel on one search screen, across 4,387 routes and around 930 ports, and its Dover–Calais page opens at £21. On that crossing alone it sells Irish Ferries, P&O Ferries and DFDS Seaways side by side, with sailings from 40 minutes. Figures checked 27 October 2026 against Direct Ferries' own pages, its booking conditions and Companies House.

The business has been doing this since 1999, which makes it older than most of the travel sites it competes with. Its own figures: more than 2.5 million customers, over 1.2 million crossings arranged a year, up to 1 million fares compared a day and 36 national sites. One practical thing it does better than most: nothing is charged to your card until the ferry company has confirmed the booking.

It owns no ships. Clause 2 of the booking conditions says Direct Ferries Limited “acts as an agent for the Operators” and that “you will be entering into a contract with the relevant ferry or train Operator”, and where the two sets of terms disagree the Operator Terms prevail. That decides who you ring when a sailing is cancelled, so it is worth knowing before you book rather than after.

sections.heading: Three carriers on one Dover results page
sections.html:
The product is breadth, and on the Channel the breadth is real. Dover–Calais is sold here across Irish Ferries, P&O Ferries and DFDS Seaways, which no single carrier's own website will do for you. The route page gives the usual crossing as 1 hour 35 minutes with the quickest sailing at 40 minutes, and prices starting at £21 against an average of £164.

Away from the Channel the gap between a reseller and a carrier widens considerably. Ferries to France are listed from 12 ferry companies; Greece is listed from 39, with up to 8,172 sailings a week and a cheapest crossing of £3 between Pserimos and Kalymnos. Nobody operating ships sells that range, and in the Aegean, where a dozen small operators run overlapping schedules, having them in one timetable is the whole point of using an agent at all.

The published averages per vehicle type are the other genuinely useful thing on these pages, because carriers rarely print them. On Dover–Calais: £67 for a foot passenger, £160 for one adult with a car, £76 with a motorcycle, £205 for a campervan, £210 for a cabin and £197 for a pet. Dover–Dunkirk is quoted from £22, Portsmouth–Caen from £18 and Newhaven–Dieppe from £30.

Note what the lead-in prices are not. The site says plainly that fares “are generally cheaper for foot passengers”, and neither the route page nor the France page gives a starting price for a car anywhere. The £160 car figure is an average, not a lead-in, so it is not the number to set against a carrier's own advertised from-price.

sections.heading: The fee that is never published, and the two that are
sections.html:
Direct Ferries is paid twice over: commission from the operator, and a charge to you. The charge is described on its own help pages as a service fee “calculated based on the total cost of your reservation”, varying “depending on your ticket type and the number of passengers”, and shown at the final checkout stage before you confirm. The booking conditions refer to a booking fee in two separate clauses. Neither the terms nor the help centre states a rate, a minimum or a maximum anywhere on the site.

That is the one number a shopper most needs in order to compare a reseller against the carrier, and it is the one number that only appears once the basket is full. A percentage fee also behaves differently from a flat one: it is modest on a £21 foot crossing and considerably less modest on a £210 cabin or a summer booking for a car and five people.

The administration charges, by contrast, are published in full and the gap between the channels is wide. An amendment made yourself through My Account costs £10 / €12 / $14 per booking. The same amendment asked for through the messenger or the contact form costs £20 on a booking under £100 and £35 on one above it. Cancelling costs from £10 / €12 / $14 online and from £20 / €25 / $27 offline. Changes made inside the first 24 hours escape the £10 online fee, which is a fair concession and worth using.

Three things then sit on top. The fare difference on the day you amend, which on a Dover crossing in August is where the real money goes. The ferry company's own cancellation terms, which the help pages confirm also affect the total. And card surcharges of 2% on corporate and commercial cards, and another 2% on consumer credit cards issued by banks outside the EEA. Roof boxes, bike racks and similar attachments carry an additional fee, and any deposit paid is not refundable.

The flexible products have to be bought at the moment of booking. Flexi fares and Cancellation Cover “can only be selected when you're making your booking and can't be added afterwards”, so a decision taken in thirty seconds at checkout cannot be revisited the following week when the plan starts to wobble.

sections.heading: Four of its own pages, four different route counts
sections.html:
Count the network from Direct Ferries' own copy and you get a different answer on every page. The home page says “from 4412 routes and 901 ports worldwide” at the top and “over 3000 ferry connections and more than 700 ports worldwide” further down. The about page says “4387 ferry routes across the globe”, “around 930 ferry ports” and “314 Ferry companies and the Eurotunnel”. The booking questions page says “almost 4,000 routes and over 270 ferry operators”. For reference, the senior lender on the company's 2023 refinancing described it in its own deal note as covering about 4,400 routes and more than 280 operators, which sits closest to the about page.

The route pages do the same thing at a smaller scale. The Dover–Calais page gives the average fare as £164 and the service as “24 daily sailings on average” in one place and “31 daily and 212 weekly sailings” in another. The France page gives the same route an average of £194.00 and 190 weekly sailings. That is an 18% difference in the price and twenty-two sailings a week between two pages of the same website.

Port counts drift too. The France page offers ferries “from 34 ports” and then states that “there are 21 ferry ports in France”. The Greece page says there are 100 ferry ports in Greece and that ferries from Greece go to 116. And the arithmetic on the same page does not hold: the cheapest crossing is given as £3 on the Pserimos–Kalymnos route while the average price for that identical route is given as £2.65, which is less than the cheapest.

The explanation is almost certainly dull. These are template figures pulled from live inventory on different cycles, and an average computed over a different window from the minimum beside it. It is still a problem, because the one claim the site makes about itself — that it is bigger than anyone else — is the claim its own pages cannot agree on, and a reader who checks two of them has no way to tell which is current.

sections.heading: Twice the fare is the whole of its liability
sections.html:
Clause 17 of the booking conditions limits Direct Ferries' liability “to a sum equivalent to twice the amount paid by you for a booking”. On the average Dover–Calais car fare of £160 that is £320. The cap does not touch liability for fraud, or for death or personal injury caused by negligence, which the law does not permit anyone to limit.

The clause beside it matters more. Direct Ferries is not liable for loss you suffer as a result of the operator's failure to perform the journey. Clause 15 adds that in events outside anyone's reasonable control you are “not entitled to a refund of the booking fee which you paid to us at the time of booking”. Put the three together and the position is consistent rather than sly: you have bought a search, a basket and a booking record, and the crossing itself is the carrier's promise.

That is also where your statutory rights sit. Assimilated Regulation (EU) No 1177/2010 gives a sea passenger care and compensation when a departure runs late, and those duties fall on the carrier, not on the website that sold the ticket. The Merchant Shipping (Passengers' Rights) Regulations 2013 name the Maritime and Coastguard Agency as the enforcement body, and enforcement there means prosecution rather than a payment to you. Nothing in that chain is Direct Ferries' doing, and none of it is explained on the booking page either.

Which conditions govern the voyage follows the same logic. The booking conditions state that in any conflict or inconsistency with the operator's terms, the operator's terms prevail. In practice you agree to a document you have read and a document you probably have not, and the second one wins.

sections.heading: Fourteen days to complain, and four separate refund clocks
sections.html:
Clause 18 requires a complaint “within 14 days of the completion of your booking”. That is tight. The carriers on this very route allow two months from the journey, and the 2013 regulations give a passenger six months to start court proceedings. Fourteen days from the completion of a booking can expire before a summer sailing has even taken place, and nothing on the page flags it.

Getting money back runs on four different timetables. A card refund is stated at 3 to 5 working days and a PayPal or iDEAL refund at up to 10 working days. A Cancel For Any Reason claim returns 80% of the ferry fare only, excluding the booking fee and the cost of the product itself, and must be requested at least 48 hours before sailing, with a limit of two uses per person per year. The last-minute version of that cover allows a cancellation up to 2 hours before the outbound departure and returns 80% of the ticket cost excluding its own fee, within 5 working days; a separate 48-hour version returns 70% including its own fee. A Best Price Promise claim is paid to the original card in approximately 10 to 14 business days, and the lower price you are matching against must include all mandatory taxes and charges while excluding optional extras.

Two operational details decide how painless any of that is. Cancellations cannot be requested by email — the help pages cite data protection — which leaves My Account or a contact form whose replies are “typically provided within 48 hours”. The telephone and messenger team works 08:00 to 20:00 daily with an automated assistant outside those hours. Anyone who cannot use the website is therefore pushed towards the channel that costs £20 to £35 rather than £10.

sections.heading: No bond, and the insurance the terms tell you to buy instead
sections.html:
Search the booking conditions for ABTA, ABTOT or ATOL and you find nothing at all. What you find instead is a recommendation: Direct Ferries “would recommend that you take out travel insurance which includes cover for End Supplier Failure”. That is an unusually candid sentence for a travel retailer, and it is the correct advice. A ferry crossing bought on its own is a single travel service rather than a package, so the bonding regime does not reach it, and ATOL only applies where a flight is involved.

It does mean the protection a reader might assume comes with booking through a large intermediary is not there. If a carrier stops sailing, the agent that took your money has told you in advance to insure against exactly that, and the £320 ceiling in clause 17 is what remains on an average car fare. The holiday-selling arm that might once have carried a bond is gone: Direct Ferries Holidays Ltd, company 06216807, incorporated 18 April 2007, filed its last accounts to 31 December 2015 as a non-trading company and was dissolved on 9 January 2018.

One structural protection does work in your favour and deserves saying. The booking conditions are governed by the laws of England and Wales with the English courts taking jurisdiction, and a customer resident in Scotland or Northern Ireland may choose their own courts instead. For a British buyer dealing with an Ipswich company that is a better position than the Irish contracting entity on the same terms might suggest.

sections.heading: Ipswich, Dublin, and a bidco called Elmo
sections.html:
Two companies can be on the other side of your booking and the terms name both. The British one is Direct Ferries Limited, company 03865405, incorporated on 26 October 1999 and registered at Units 2 & 3, Three Rivers Business Centre, Felixstowe Road, Foxhall, Ipswich IP10 0BF. The Irish one is Direct Ferries (RoI) Limited, registration 721008, at the Work Hub, 77 Camden Street, Dublin D02 XE80. Which of the two you contract with is set by the site you book on, and the liability and complaints clauses are written to cover either.

The register also shows a company that has recently changed hands. Until last year the controlling party was Direct Ferries (Holdings) Ltd, registered as such since 6 April 2016. On 25 September 2025 that entry ceased and Elmo Bidco Limited was recorded in its place, holding 75% or more of the shares and voting rights with the right to appoint and remove directors. The last full accounts were made up to 31 December 2024 and filed on 29 September 2025, and the latest confirmation statement is dated 26 October 2025. The register inspection address moved from Exeter to Bristol on 13 May 2026.

Behind that is a financing the company itself does not discuss. Investec's own deal record, dated 26 July 2023, describes providing senior debt in a club of three lenders to support a partnership investment by Intermediate Capital Group in what it calls “the leading ferry focused Online Travel Agency in Europe”, and the adviser on the other side records the seller as the private equity firm Livingbridge. The 2023 transaction and the 2025 change on the register are two separate filings and nothing published ties them together, so both are given here as they stand.

One small oddity in the filing is worth a line. The company's registered activity codes are 50200 for sea and coastal freight water transport and 79909 for other reservation service activities. The second describes the business exactly. The first describes carrying cargo by sea, which is not what this company does at all.

sections.heading: Three questions on its own help page have no answer
sections.html:
The making-changes page carries its questions as headings with the answers underneath, and three of them are published with the answer missing. One is “Do you charge for ferry booking cancellations?” Another is “FAQ - Do you charge for ferry booking amendments?”, where the answer field simply repeats the question. The third is the one that matters most: “Where can I find more information on my rights to refunds and compensation in the event of ferry cancellations and delays?”

Both fee questions are answered properly elsewhere on the site, so this is a maintenance fault rather than concealment. The passenger-rights question is different, because the answer does not exist anywhere else on the site either. A reader whose sailing has just been cancelled is sent to a heading with nothing under it, on the only page that promises to tell them what they are owed.

Two other absences are worth naming because they are not faults of this company so much as facts about the trade. There is no ratings body anywhere that scores a ferry retailer: the Financial Conduct Authority does not regulate ticket agency, Defaqto does not rate it, the tourist boards assess beds rather than bookings, and no regulator publishes an uphold rate for any of these sites. And because the company files small-company accounts, no revenue, booking value or margin figure exists in public for it at all — the only scale numbers available are the ones it prints about itself, which is why the four different route counts above are a problem rather than a curiosity.

Finally, a detail that is genuinely helpful and easy to miss. Timetables for most routes only appear three to six months before departure, and arrival at the port is required “between 30 minutes and 2 hours” before sailing depending on the operator, with the actual deadline given in the confirmation email rather than at the point of sale. Some bookings are confirmed provisionally and firmed up within 24 to 48 hours, and the card is not charged until the operator has confirmed.

pros: 314 ferry companies and Eurotunnel searchable in one place, across 4,387 routes and about 930 ports
Dover–Calais sold across Irish Ferries, P&O Ferries and DFDS Seaways on a single results page
Nothing is charged to your card until the ferry operator has confirmed the booking
Amendments made within the first 24 hours avoid the £10 online fee, though the fare difference still applies
Doing it yourself through My Account costs £10 against £20 to £35 through customer services
Average prices published per vehicle type — £67 foot, £160 car, £76 motorcycle, £205 campervan, £197 pet on Dover–Calais
Real depth outside the Channel: 39 ferry companies and up to 8,172 weekly sailings in Greece alone
English law and the English courts, with Scottish or Northern Irish courts open to residents there
The Best Price Promise is measured on the all-in price including mandatory taxes and charges
Trading since 1999, with over 1.2 million crossings arranged a year and 36 national sites
cons: The service fee is “calculated based on the total cost of your reservation” and no rate, minimum or maximum is published anywhere — it appears only at the final checkout step
Direct Ferries' liability is capped at twice what you paid for the booking, about £320 on the average Dover–Calais car fare, and it is not liable at all for the operator's failure to carry you
A complaint must be made within 14 days of the completion of your booking, against two months allowed by the carriers on the same route and six months to start court proceedings
Four of its own pages give four different route counts — 4,412, over 3,000, 4,387 and almost 4,000 — and three different operator counts
The Dover–Calais page and the France page disagree on the same route's average fare, £164 against £194, and on its weekly sailings, 212 against 190
Its fees sit on top of the ferry company's own: a cancellation starts at £10 before the operator's charge is applied, and an amendment adds the fare difference
Cancellation Cover and Flexi fares can only be bought at the moment of booking and cannot be added later
Cancel For Any Reason returns only 80% of the fare, keeps the booking fee and its own fee, and is limited to two uses per person a year
Cancellations cannot be requested by email, leaving My Account or a contact form answered in about 48 hours, and the staffed line closes at 20:00
A 2% surcharge applies to corporate and commercial cards and to consumer credit cards issued outside the EEA
Three questions on its own making-changes page are published with no answer, including the one about rights to refunds and compensation when a sailing is cancelled
No ABTA, ABTOT or ATOL protection on a crossing; the booking conditions recommend End Supplier Failure insurance instead
The Greece page gives the cheapest Pserimos–Kalymnos crossing as £3 and the average price for the same route as £2.65
verdict: If you know which ferry you want, book it from the company that owns the ship. If you do not — and on the Aegean, the Adriatic or the Irish Sea almost nobody does — this is the search that saves the afternoon, because 314 operators and 4,387 routes in one timetable is something no carrier will ever show you. The Channel is the weakest case for using it, since three operators run Dover–Calais and all three publish their own lead-in fares, and the strongest case is anywhere a journey needs two carriers who have never heard of each other. What to go in knowing: the service fee is a percentage of your basket and is not published until checkout, the amendment and cancellation charges sit on top of the ferry company's own, and the complaint window is 14 days from the booking. Buy the flexible fare at the moment you book if there is any doubt about the dates, because it cannot be added afterwards, and read the operator's conditions as well as these — in any conflict between the two, the operator's win.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to book with Direct Ferries or direct with the ferry company?
faqs.a: On a route with one operator it is hard to be cheaper than the carrier, because Direct Ferries adds a service fee “calculated based on the total cost of your reservation” that no carrier charges. On a route with several operators, or a journey that needs two of them, the comparison is the value — Dover–Calais alone is sold here across three carriers from £21. The fee is only shown at the final checkout step, so price the same crossing on the carrier's own site before you confirm.

faqs.q: What does Direct Ferries charge to change or cancel a booking?
faqs.a: Through My Account the fee is £10 / €12 / $14 per booking to amend and from £10 / €12 / $14 to cancel. Through the messenger or contact form an amendment is £20 on bookings under £100 and £35 above that, and a cancellation starts at £20 / €25 / $27. Changes made in the first 24 hours escape the £10 online fee. The ferry operator's own charges and any increase in the fare apply on top.

faqs.q: Who is responsible if my sailing is cancelled — Direct Ferries or the operator?
faqs.a: The operator. Clause 2 of the booking conditions says Direct Ferries acts “as an agent for the Operators” and that you contract with the carrier, and clause 17 states it is not liable for loss caused by the operator's failure to perform the journey. Care and compensation under assimilated Regulation (EU) No 1177/2010 are the carrier's duty, and the Maritime and Coastguard Agency is the body that enforces those rules.

faqs.q: Is a Direct Ferries booking financially protected?
faqs.a: Not by a bond. There is no ABTA, ABTOT or ATOL cover on a crossing, because a ferry ticket bought on its own is a single travel service rather than a package and ATOL only applies where a flight is involved. The booking conditions say Direct Ferries “would recommend that you take out travel insurance which includes cover for End Supplier Failure”. Its own liability is capped at twice the amount you paid.

faqs.q: How long do refunds take?
faqs.a: Credit and debit card refunds are stated at 3 to 5 working days and PayPal or iDEAL at up to 10 working days once the cancellation is confirmed. A Cancel For Any Reason refund of 80% of the fare is paid within 5 working days on the last-minute version. A Best Price Promise refund goes to the original card in approximately 10 to 14 business days. Cancellations cannot be started by email.

faqs.q: Can I add cancellation cover to a Direct Ferries booking afterwards?
faqs.a: No. The help centre states that flexible fares and cancellation cover “can only be selected when you're making your booking and can't be added afterwards”. Cancel For Any Reason has the same rule and must be bought at the time of booking, requested at least 48 hours before sailing, and is limited to two uses per person per year.

faqs.q: How many ferry operators and routes does Direct Ferries actually cover?
faqs.a: Its about page is the fullest answer: 314 ferry companies plus Eurotunnel, 4,387 routes, around 930 ports and over 276 countries and islands. Other pages on the same site say 4,412 routes and 901 ports, “over 3000 ferry connections” and “almost 4,000 routes and over 270 ferry operators”. The figures are template-driven and refreshed on different cycles, so treat any single one as approximate.

faqs.q: How far ahead can I book, and when do I need to arrive at the port?
faqs.a: Timetables for most routes appear three to six months before departure, varying by operator and season. Check-in requires arrival “between 30 minutes and 2 hours” before sailing depending on the carrier, and the exact deadline is given in the confirmation email rather than at the point of sale. Some bookings are confirmed provisionally and firmed up within 24 to 48 hours.

title: Direct Line Car Insurance
meta_title: Direct Line Car Insurance: What the Policy Actually Pays
meta_description: Direct Line's comprehensive limits, the five-year repair guarantee, and why the version sold on Compare the Market is a different policy. Checked August 2026.
intro:
Direct Line opened for business in Croydon in 1985 as the first UK insurer to sell car cover straight down a telephone line, cutting the broker out of the transaction, and it has been one of the largest names in British motor insurance ever since. At the last set of published accounts it carried 3.831 million motor policies and took £2,700m in motor premium and associated fees, part of a book of 8.827 million in-force policies across the group.

Buy the comprehensive policy direct and the standard inclusions are unusually complete for a mainstream brand. A hire car is guaranteed for the whole time an approved repairer holds your vehicle rather than for a fixed number of days; repairs done through that network carry a five-year guarantee on parts, materials and workmanship; the uninsured driver promise refunds your excess and protects your claim-free years when someone without cover hits you and you can give them the other registration; and Direct Line charges no fee at all for mid-term changes on a policy bought from it directly.

Ownership changed hands last summer. Aviva's takeover of Direct Line Insurance Group completed on 1 July 2025, with the shares delisted two days later, creating a combined business Aviva describes as serving 20 million UK customers. The underwriter behind every Direct Line motor policy is unchanged: U K Insurance Limited, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA and the PRA under firm reference 202810, which you can look up yourself on the Financial Services Register.

key_facts.value: 5 years on approved-repairer work, while you own the car

key_facts.label: Cooling-off period

sections.heading: The numbers inside the comprehensive booklet
sections.html:
The published motor policy booklet sets the limits out plainly, and they are worth knowing before a claim rather than during one. Personal belongings are covered to £250 on Comprehensive and £500 on Comprehensive Plus. Personal accident benefit runs to £5,000 and £10,000 respectively, with emergency medical expenses at £200 and £400. Lost, damaged or stolen car keys are covered to £1,000, and replacement child car seats after an impact carry no cash limit at all — a genuinely generous line, given a seat must be scrapped after any collision.

Glass is where the small print earns its keep. Use Direct Line's approved glass supplier and a repair or replacement is met in full. Go elsewhere and the payout is capped at £40 for a repair and £125 for a replacement. That cap has not kept pace with the vehicles it applies to: the trade body's own tracker puts the average windscreen repair at £283, up 7% in a single quarter, because a modern screen carries the cameras that drive lane assist and automatic braking and has to be recalibrated after fitting.

Two more worth carrying with you. A new car replacement applies if the vehicle is written off or stolen while under 1 year old on Comprehensive, or under 2 years old on Comprehensive Plus. And if a hire car cannot be supplied when it should have been, the policy pays £50 a day towards alternative travel up to £500 for the claim. Comprehensive Plus extends full cover in Europe for 90 days per period of insurance.

sections.heading: What the wider market is doing to your renewal
sections.html:
Judging a Direct Line quote needs a benchmark, and the most reliable one is the insurance trade body's premium tracker, which measures what drivers actually paid across more than 28 million policies a year rather than what was advertised. The average comprehensive premium paid was £566 in the second quarter of 2026, up £6 on the quarter before, and £560 in the first quarter, which was £20 below the same point in 2025. Adjusted for inflation the current figure sits £14 below where it was a year earlier.

Premiums are flat while claims are not. Insurers paid a record £3.2bn to motor customers in the second quarter of 2026, 7% more than a year earlier, with the average payout at £4,900 and the average accidental damage repair running at £3,699. The regulator's own value measures data, published on 21 July 2026, records motor premiums falling 7% across 2025 while claims costs rose to 59% of premium. Cover priced that tightly tends to be defended tightly at claim stage, which is an argument for reading limits rather than headline prices.

One rule works in your favour and is routinely forgotten. Since 1 January 2022 an insurer may not quote a renewing customer more than it would charge an equivalent new customer through the same channel. The regulator built that rule after finding that around 6 million loyal policyholders would have saved £1.2bn in a single year had they paid a price matched to their risk, and it estimated the change would return £4.2bn to consumers over 10 years. If a Direct Line renewal arrives above the price its own new-business quote returns for identical details, that is a question to put to them.

sections.heading: Buying it on a comparison site gets you a different policy
sections.html:
For most of its history Direct Line sold only direct, and the absence from comparison sites was the brand's defining trait. That ended on 20 December 2024, when three Direct Line motor products appeared on Compare the Market. The important detail is in Direct Line's own wording: these were designed for comparison-site buyers, and they are not the policies sold on the company's own site.

The comparison-site range runs Essentials Online, Standard Online and Premium Online. Windscreen cover is absent from the entry tier and only appears at Standard Online. Motor legal and roadside breakdown arrive at Premium Online. Features Direct Line lists as standard on its direct policies — misfuelling cover, the vandalism promise that protects your no-claim discount, and the guaranteed hire car — are not part of the online range, which is self-service by design and comes without call centre support.

There is also a fee. Change a comparison-site policy mid-term and Direct Line charges up to £19.04 including Insurance Premium Tax. On a policy bought direct, its published position is that no fee applies to policy changes. If you find a Direct Line price on a comparison site and like it, the sensible move is to run the same details through directline.com before buying and compare the two on cover rather than on price alone.

sections.heading: Where the complaints actually land
sections.html:
U K Insurance Limited publishes its regulatory complaints return, and the split inside it is more revealing than the headline. For the six months to 31 December 2025 the insurance side recorded 567 complaints opened, a rate of 0.34 per 1,000 policies, with 54% closed inside three days and 47% upheld by the firm.

The consumer credit line tells a different story: 37,282 complaints opened in the same six months, 4.54 per 1,000 active credit agreements, and 67% upheld. That category covers paying for insurance by monthly instalments, which is a regulated credit agreement rather than a payment plan. Two thirds of those complaints going the customer's way is a strong signal that if you intend to pay monthly, you should read the credit agreement and the APR as carefully as the policy wording, and keep the paperwork.

Beyond the firm's own complaints team, the Financial Ombudsman Service handled 13,420 new car and motorcycle insurance complaints in 2025/26 and upheld 35% of them. The service is free, and the route to it opens once your insurer has issued a final response or 8 weeks have passed without one.

sections.heading: A ten-million-pound fine, and what it was actually for
sections.html:
On 11 March 2026 the Prudential Regulation Authority fined U K Insurance Limited £10,625,000 — reduced by 50% from £21.25m under a scheme that rewards early cooperation, and the first case ever concluded that way. The firm had miscalculated its Solvency II balance sheet, overstating its capital position by roughly £99.9m at the end of 2023, with the error running from 1 June 2022 to 23 August 2024 before it was found.

It is worth being precise about what this was and was not. It was a failure of prudential reporting and internal control — wrong numbers filed with the regulator and published to the market — not a finding that customers were mistreated or claims wrongly declined. No policyholder lost money because of it. The PRA's deputy governor framed it as being about the reliability of the data supervisors depend on.

It still belongs in a buying decision, because it is evidence about the control environment behind the brand rather than about the marketing. A finance function that could not spot a nine-figure double count for fifteen months is a fair thing to weigh, particularly during the integration of two large insurers into one.

pros: Hire car guaranteed for the full length of the repair when an approved garage does the work, not capped at a set number of days
Five-year guarantee on approved-repairer parts, materials and workmanship for as long as you keep the car
No fee for mid-term policy changes when you buy direct
Uninsured driver promise refunds the excess and protects claim-free years if you can supply the other registration
Unlimited cover for replacing child car seats after an impact
Underwritten in-house by U K Insurance Limited rather than placed with a third party, so the insurer and the brand are the same company
cons: The version sold on comparison sites is a separate self-service product: no misfuelling cover, no vandalism promise, no guaranteed hire car, no call centre, and no windscreen cover at all on the entry tier
Mid-term changes on a comparison-site policy carry a fee of up to £19.04 including tax, where the direct policy has none
Glass work outside the approved supplier is capped at £40 to repair and £125 to replace, well short of the £283 average repair cost once camera recalibration is involved
Paying monthly is a credit agreement, and the consumer credit complaints line ran to 37,282 in six months with 67% upheld
The policy booklet published on the website is dated 07/06/2022, so the wording that applies to a new 2026 policy should be confirmed against the documents issued with your own schedule
The PRA fined the underwriter £10,625,000 in March 2026 over years of inaccurate solvency reporting
verdict: Direct Line is a strong pick if you buy it the way it was designed to be bought — direct, at Comprehensive or above, with the repair going through an approved garage. That combination gets you the guaranteed hire car, the five-year repair warranty, the fee-free amendments and limits that are competitive rather than merely present. Buy the same brand through a comparison site and you are buying a thinner, self-service product that charges for changes, so check which one you are being quoted. Price it against the £566 market average, and if you plan to pay monthly, read the credit agreement first.

faqs.q: Is Direct Line on comparison sites now?
faqs.a: Yes. Three Direct Line motor products launched on Compare the Market on 20 December 2024, ending a long run of direct-only selling. They are separate products built for that channel — Essentials Online, Standard Online and Premium Online — and they carry less as standard than the policies on Direct Line's own site.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites a Direct Line car policy?
faqs.a: U K Insurance Limited, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA and the PRA under firm reference 202810. It has been part of Aviva plc since the takeover completed on 1 July 2025. The reference number is on Direct Line's own disclosure and can be checked on the Financial Services Register.

faqs.q: What does Direct Line pay for a windscreen?
faqs.a: Through its approved glass supplier, the full cost of repair or replacement, subject to the glass excess shown on your schedule. Through anyone else, the booklet caps the payout at £40 for a repair and £125 for a replacement. Given the average windscreen repair now runs at £283, using the approved supplier is close to essential.

faqs.q: How long do I have to cancel?
faqs.a: 14 days from the start of the policy or from the day you receive your documents, whichever is later. Cancelling within that window means paying only for the days on cover, unless you have already claimed. Any cancellation charge is set out in your schedule, so confirm it against the documents you were sent.

faqs.q: Can I complain to the Ombudsman about a Direct Line claim?
faqs.a: Yes, once Direct Line has issued a final response or 8 weeks have gone by without one. The Financial Ombudsman Service is free to use and its decisions bind the insurer if you accept them. It received 13,420 car and motorcycle insurance complaints in 2025/26 and upheld 35%.

title: Direct Line Landlord Insurance
meta_title: Direct Line Landlord Insurance: Limits, Voids and Rent Cover
meta_description: What the Direct Line landlord policy pays: £1,500 emergency cover, £250,000 rent guarantee, £2m liability, and the empty-property rules. Checked August 2026.
intro:
Direct Line's landlord cover is not sold beside its car and household policies. It sits with Direct Line for Business, the arm of the group that writes commercial and property risks, and it has grown into one of the larger books in the private rented sector — the company says more than 350,000 properties are insured with it, and it has taken Best Landlord Insurance Provider at the what MORTGAGE Awards 13 years running.

The standard policy is fuller than most landlords expect before they read the wording. Buildings cover runs to the usual perils — fire, storm, flood, subsidence, escape of water, malicious damage, impact — and carries £2 million of property owners' liability, which can be raised to £10 million. Boiler and heating breakdown is built in rather than bolted on: parts, labour and call-out are met on failures such as a cracked heat exchanger, a failed expansion vessel or a dead circuit board, subject to a £200 excess, and a portable heater is supplied to the tenant while the repair is arranged. Permanent internal fixtures and fittings are insured to £50,000, replacement locks to £25,000, and if an insured event leaves the property unfit to live in the policy funds tenants' temporary accommodation to £100,000.

Where a landlord supplies white goods and furniture, contents are settled new for old with no deduction for age or wear, and floor coverings are included to £5,000 as standard with the option to increase that. Several addresses go on one schedule — Direct Line quotes up to 15 properties on a single policy — with discounts for adding between two and five further residential addresses. The underwriter throughout is U K Insurance Limited, firm reference 202810 on the Financial Services Register.

sections.heading: The numbers behind a landlord quote
sections.html:
Most of what separates one landlord policy from another sits in the optional layers, and Direct Line prices them individually rather than bundling them into tiers. Landlord Emergency pays up to £1,500 including VAT per claim to get a tradesperson out to a failed boiler, a burst pipe, a broken lock or a roof letting water in — useful on a let where the tenant rings at nine on a Sunday evening. One condition is easy to miss: on an address added to an existing policy part-way through the year, emergency claims in the first 7 days are not covered.

The personal accident benefit that comes with the policy pays up to £50,000 on death and £250 a week during temporary disablement, and applies between the ages of 16 and 75. Legal expenses can be added to fund repossession proceedings, the eviction of squatters and tax investigation protection. Loss of rent, accidental damage, employers' liability, terrorism, theft by a tenant or employee and malicious damage by a tenant are each separate additions rather than inclusions.

Glass and sanitary ware are replaced under the buildings section, and locks and keys are covered to £15,000 per claim on the buildings cover in addition to the contents limit. Leasehold flats are handled properly: fixtures inside the demise that the freeholder's block policy does not touch are insured under the landlord's own cover, which is where a lot of flat owners find a gap after a kitchen fire.

sections.heading: Rent guarantee after the end of Section 21
sections.html:
The ground moved under every landlord policy on 1 May 2026, the date section 21 no-fault eviction was abolished in England. Assured shorthold tenancies converted to periodic assured tenancies, and possession now runs through section 8 grounds — rent arrears, antisocial behaviour, the landlord selling, or the landlord moving in. Notices served before that date can still be used, but only if proceedings begin within six months of service or by 31 July 2026, whichever comes first.

That makes rent protection a different purchase than it was a year ago. Direct Line's Rent Guarantee pays up to £250,000 per claim and up to 12 months of arrears, with no excess and no cap on the number of claims in a policy year. If the property is damaged and cannot be let, it pays 50% of the rent previously received for up to 3 months or until the property is re-let. Against an average English private rent of £1,398 a month as at July 2025, twelve months of arrears is real money, and the private rented sector it protects covers roughly 19% of UK households, about 5.4 million homes.

The conditions are strict and worth meeting before a tenancy starts rather than after. Direct Line requires a written reference from the previous landlord or managing agent, a written reference from an employer or other source of income, and a credit check covering county court judgments. Rent must be at least one month overdue before a claim, claims are excluded if made more than 90 days after the missed payment, and on tenants already in place when a property is bought, claims are restricted for the first 90 days.

sections.heading: Judging the price with no comparison table
sections.html:
Direct Line for Business does not appear on any price comparison site, and says so on its own landlord page. For a product bought once a year that is a genuine inconvenience: the quote has to be obtained direct, and there is no screen on which to line it up against ten rivals. The quote holds for 30 days, which at least gives time to gather others by hand.

The nearest public benchmark is the trade body's quarterly figures for what householders actually paid, though they describe owner-occupier cover rather than let property. In the first quarter of 2026 the average combined buildings and contents premium paid was £375, down £5 on the year; buildings-only averaged £306, down 6%; contents-only £117, down 12%. Treat those as a floor rather than a target. A landlord policy carries property owners' liability, tenant damage exposure and loss of rent that a residential policy does not, so it should and does cost more.

What is not falling is the cost of a claim. Home insurers paid £846 million in that quarter, on an average claim of £6,340 — the highest recorded and up 20% year on year. Weather-related claims averaged £6,040, up 38%. Subsidence, the peril that most often leaves a rental uninhabitable for months, averaged £17,820, up 9% from £16,295. Those numbers are the argument for reading the alternative accommodation and loss of rent limits closely rather than the premium.

sections.heading: Empty weeks are where the wording tightens
sections.html:
The obligations on an unoccupied property are the part of this policy most likely to cost somebody a claim. A property must be reported to Direct Line within 30 days of becoming vacant. Cover continues in defined circumstances — newly purchased, between tenants, being redecorated — but restrictions bite after 60 days. While it is empty the landlord must inspect inside and out every 7 days, turn services off at the mains, and, between 31 October and 31 March, keep the heating running at a minimum of 10°C.

A weekly internal inspection is a demanding condition for anyone who does not live near the property. Letting agents commonly inspect quarterly, and a monthly visit — which most landlords would consider diligent — breaches it. The condition is not unusual in the market, but it is the sort of clause that is read for the first time after a burst pipe rather than before, and it applies to exactly the period when a house is most likely to suffer one.

The 60-day clock has also become harder to beat. With possession now running through the courts on section 8 grounds rather than a section 21 notice, the gap between one tenant leaving and the next arriving is less predictable than it was. That collides with a specific exclusion in the Rent Guarantee wording: arrears accruing during court delays caused by legislation or government guidance are not covered. Delays of precisely that kind are the most plausible consequence of the transition now under way, and it is the single clause a landlord buying rent protection this year should read twice.

sections.heading: Tenants and properties Direct Line will not take
sections.html:
Eligibility is narrower than the marketing suggests, and it is worth checking before spending time on a quote. At least one tenant must be employed, retired, in full-time education or in receipt of disability benefits. A property where every tenant is unemployed and claiming benefits is not covered at all. Houses in multiple occupation are handled case by case: student lets are commonly accepted, bedsits are declined.

The exclusions on the policy itself follow the usual shape but deserve stating plainly. Tenants' own belongings are not insured — that is their contents policy, not the landlord's. Wear and tear and routine maintenance are excluded, as they are everywhere. Pest infestation is excluded. Deliberate damage by a tenant is only covered if the optional malicious damage extension has been bought, which on a product sold specifically to landlords is a curious thing to leave off the standard schedule, given that tenant damage is one of the two risks that distinguishes letting from living in a house.

One inconsistency could not be resolved from the public pages and needs confirming with Direct Line directly: its multi-property page states that up to 15 properties can go on one policy, while the page metadata for the same product refers to 25. Anyone building a portfolio policy around that figure should get it in writing at quotation.

sections.heading: The company standing behind the cover
sections.html:
Two developments at the underwriter matter to anyone buying a multi-year relationship. On 11 March 2026 the Prudential Regulation Authority fined U K Insurance Limited £10,625,000 for miscalculating its Solvency II balance sheet across 2023 and 2024, overstating its solvency position to the regulator and to the market. The PRA found inadequate preventative and detective controls and staffing gaps in the finance and actuarial functions, and cited breaches of Fundamental Rule 6 alongside its notification and reporting rules. The firm settled early under the Early Account Scheme and received a 50% reduction; the penalty would otherwise have been £21.25 million. This was a reporting and controls failure rather than a claims-handling one, but it is a large fine and it is public.

The second is a change of legal insurer. Around 8.2 million in-force policies written by U K Insurance Limited — Direct Line, Churchill, Privilege, Green Flag, Darwin and By Miles — are proposed to transfer to Aviva Insurance Limited under Part VII of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, High Court case CR-2026-001308. The final English hearing is listed for 15 December 2026, the Jersey hearing for 18 December, with a proposed effective date of 31 December 2026. Terms, premiums, renewal dates and policy numbers are not expected to change. A policyholder who believes they would be adversely affected can object, ideally before 8 December 2026, on 0800 158 2502.

If a claim goes wrong, the route is a complaint to Direct Line first and then the Financial Ombudsman Service. The Ombudsman's own figures for April to June 2026 show 53,600 new complaints across all financial products with 26% upheld. Buildings insurance generated 1,766 of them at a 33% uphold rate, contents 472 at 24%, and home emergency 550 at 32%. Property claims are disputed successfully more often than the average across financial services, which is a reason to document the condition of a let property before a claim rather than during one.

pros: Boiler and heating breakdown included as standard, not sold as an add-on, with a £200 excess
£2 million property owners' liability as standard, extendable to £10 million
Tenants' temporary accommodation funded to £100,000 after an insured event
Rent Guarantee carries no excess, pays 12 months of arrears and up to £250,000, with no cap on claims per year
Contents settled new for old with no deduction for age or wear, floor coverings to £5,000
Several addresses on one schedule with discounts for adding two to five further properties
cons: Sold direct only and absent from every comparison site, so the premium cannot be benchmarked against rivals in one place
Rent Guarantee excludes arrears building up during court delays caused by legislation or government guidance — the most likely source of delay during the Renters' Rights Act transition
Unoccupied-property conditions are demanding: inspections inside and out every 7 days, mains services off, and restrictions after 60 days
Whole categories of tenant are refused — a property where every tenant is unemployed and claiming benefits is not covered, and bedsit HMOs are declined
Malicious damage and theft by tenants are optional extras rather than standard cover on a policy sold specifically to landlords
The underwriter was fined £10,625,000 by the PRA in March 2026 for overstating its solvency position across 2023 and 2024
Direct Line's own pages disagree on how many properties one policy will hold — 15 on the product page, 25 in its metadata
verdict: A well-stocked standard policy with unusually good bones — boiler breakdown included, £2 million of liability, £100,000 of tenant accommodation and new-for-old contents — wrapped in eligibility and empty-property conditions that are stricter than the sales pages let on. It suits a landlord with employed or student tenants, a property that is rarely empty for long, and the discipline to inspect weekly when it is. It suits far less anyone letting to benefit-dependent tenants, running bedsits, or holding property at a distance. Because it is sold direct only, the honest advice is to get the Direct Line quote and then price two or three brokered alternatives by hand before deciding.

faqs.q: Is Direct Line landlord insurance available on comparison sites?
faqs.a: No. Direct Line for Business sells this product direct only and states as much on its own landlord page. A quote must be requested from Direct Line, and it stays valid for 30 days, which gives time to gather competing quotes separately.

faqs.q: How long can the property be empty before cover is affected?
faqs.a: Direct Line must be told within 30 days of the property becoming vacant, and restrictions apply after 60 days of unoccupancy. While it is empty the property must be inspected inside and out every 7 days, services turned off at the mains, and heating kept to at least 10°C between 31 October and 31 March.

faqs.q: Does the policy cover damage caused deliberately by a tenant?
faqs.a: Only if the optional malicious damage by tenants extension is added. It is not part of the standard schedule. Theft by a tenant, employee or other lawful occupant is likewise a separate addition, and tenants' own possessions are never covered by the landlord's policy.

faqs.q: Who underwrites the policy and is it regulated?
faqs.a: The underwriter is U K Insurance Limited, firm reference 202810, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority and the PRA. That reference can be checked on the Financial Services Register. Around 8.2 million of its policies are proposed to transfer to Aviva Insurance Limited on 31 December 2026, subject to a High Court hearing on 15 December 2026.

faqs.q: What does Rent Guarantee actually pay, and what does it require?
faqs.a: Up to £250,000 per claim and up to 12 months of arrears, with no excess, plus 50% of previous rent for up to 3 months if damage makes the property unlettable. It requires a written reference from the previous landlord or agent, a written employment or income reference, and a credit check. Rent must be a month overdue before claiming, and a claim made more than 90 days after a missed payment is excluded.

title: Dragonpass Airport Lounge
meta_title: Dragonpass: £59 a Year, Two Passes, 1,400+ Lounges
meta_description: Dragonpass memberships start at £59 a year for two lounge passes. We price every pass, read the 1 October 2026 terms and work out a visit.
intro:
Dragonpass sells airport lounge entry by the pass, and the cheapest way in is £59 a year: a Solo Travel membership with two passes included, each one getting a person into any of more than 1,400 lounges across more than 130 countries. Prices read off Dragonpass's own membership page on 27 October 2026, and the contract from its terms and conditions dated 1 October 2026.

The company has been selling airport access since 2005. It says it now has over 40 million members, more than 400 corporate clients, offers at over 650 dining locations and premium retailers, and more than 200 Fast Track security lanes on the same membership. The UK business, Dragonpass International Ltd, has been filing at Companies House since 2013; its group accounts to 31 December 2025 went in on 25 September 2026.

Two things shape everything below, and neither is a criticism. A pass is not only a lounge visit — the same pass can be spent on £26 of airport dining credit or on a Fast Track lane that Dragonpass values at £11 to £19 — and the lounges belong to other companies, so the stay length, the capacity and the refund are theirs to set rather than Dragonpass's.
