sections.heading: What £59 a year buys, and what £329 buys
sections.html:
There are three plans and they are priced per pass, not per month. Solo Travel is £59 a year and carries two passes; the page is explicit that “Passes are for your personal use each trip”, so there is no guest entitlement on it at all. Better Travel is £229 a year for eight passes and lets one accompanying guest share them. Travel Together is £329 a year for twelve passes, shareable with up to five guests. Extra passes beyond the allowance cost £29, £28 and £27 respectively, so the larger the plan the cheaper the top-up.

Divide the fee by the passes and the included ones cost £29.50 on Solo Travel, £28.63 on Better Travel and £27.42 on Travel Together. That is the whole price list in three numbers, and it is unusually flat: the £329 plan buys a pass only £2.08 cheaper than the £59 plan does.

The guest rules are where the plans really differ, because Dragonpass is clear that sharing is not free capacity: “Each guest visit uses a separate pass from your annual allowance.” Twelve passes on Travel Together is therefore six trips for a couple, or two trips for a party of six, not twelve visits plus guests. A family of four taking a return flight spends eight of the twelve passes on one holiday.

Set against that, the £59 entry price is genuinely the cheapest published route onto a network this size, and it is cheaper than the plans Dragonpass itself was selling in the spring. It includes two passes rather than none, which is not true of every lounge programme.

sections.heading: A pass is the unit of account, and the three things it buys are not worth the same
sections.html:
The membership page offers three uses for one pass. A lounge visit. “One pass for $32£26€31 towards your bill at participating airport restaurants”, with anything above the credit paid separately. Or “one pass for airport Fast Track security at participating airports”, described on the same page as “a service that costs $15£11€13–$25£19€22 if booked separately”.

Those three uses have three different values, and Dragonpass publishes all the numbers needed to see it. A pass costs between £27.42 and £29.50. Spend it on the dining credit and you have paid £27.42 to £29.50 for £26, losing £1.42 to £3.50. Spend it on Fast Track and you have paid the same for something the seller itself values at £11 to £19, losing £8.42 to £18.50. Only the lounge visit returns more than the pass cost — which makes the flexibility a safety valve for an airport with nothing you can use, rather than three equal options.

The dining credit has its own rules and they are worth reading before relying on it. Clause 2.1.2 allows “only 1 (one) Dining Voucher per purchase”. Clause 7.3.6 says “No refund, cashback or credit will be offered in the event that the Dining Voucher is applied to a bill”, so a £20 lunch does not leave £6 behind. Clause 7.3.7 makes the vouchers “not exchangeable for cash, credit or other goods and services, and non-transferable”, and clause 7.3.8 subjects them to “certain local restrictions such as taxes, tips and alcohol”. Fast Track is “valid for 1 (one) use only” under clause 7.5.10, needs a separate booking for every guest, and is not refunded if cancelled “less than 72 (seventy-two) hours in advance”.

One oddity: the word the sales page is built on does not appear in the contract. The terms never define a Pass. They define a Dragonpass Membership at clause 2.1.5, Dining Vouchers at 2.1.2 and single-use Lounge passes at 7.15.5, each with its own expiry and its own rules. The single currency on the shop front is three separate products once you are inside.

sections.heading: The rooms belong to somebody else, and the booking fee is theirs too
sections.html:
Dragonpass says this twice and plainly. Clause 2.1.6: Participating Outlets “are not subcontractors, agents or representatives of Dragonpass”. Clause 7.7.17: the company is “in no way responsible for the management” of the lounges. Clause 7.7.19 follows from both — “access to a particular Lounge is not guaranteed and is subject to availability” — and clause 7.15.10 adds that a lounge may be unavailable when delays push traffic through it. The network itself moves: clauses 7.1.12 and 7.15.16 allow outlets to be “added or removed at any time without notice”, and clause 7.15.8 lets Dragonpass “amend the Lounge visit charges from time to time in its sole discretion”.

That third-party relationship is also where a cost appears that the price list does not carry. The comparison table on the membership page lists “Additional fee” against lounge pre-booking on all three plans and names no amount, and no figure for it appears anywhere else on the site. The operator publishes it instead: No1 Lounges, which runs the No1, Clubrooms and My Lounge rooms at Birmingham, Gatwick, Heathrow, Jersey and Luton, invites scheme cardholders to “Reserve your place at the lounge from just £6 using your Dragonpass”, and explains why in one sentence — “Without a pre-booking, we cannot guarantee you will gain access.”

Add that £6 to a £29.50 pass and a Solo Travel lounge visit costs about £35.50 in practice; on Travel Together it is about £33.42. Both are still below the £42 average entry price Which? measured in May 2026, but the gap is roughly £6 to £8 a visit rather than the half-price saving a membership implies.

The same operator page is useful for two other reasons. A pre-booking for the Clubrooms lounges at Gatwick “also includes complimentary access to the Fast track security lanes”, which is a pass saved; and Fast Track “is not available at Birmingham, Heathrow, and Luton Airports”, which is a pass that cannot be spent that way at three of the five airports it runs. It is also candid about the limits of a three-party arrangement: “No1 Lounges does not have access to any systems outside of its own”, so a membership question has to go back to Dragonpass or to the card issuer.

sections.heading: Two hours, one hour late, and forty-eight hours' notice
sections.html:
The timings are all in clause 7.15 and they are tighter than a lounge day out suggests. The stay is “usually 2 (two) hours”, and once it “has lapsed, you will be required to re-register your entry” — so a long connection is not one visit. A pre-booking or a cancellation “must be made at a minimum of 48 (forty-eight) hours in advance”, which rules out booking a lounge the night before an early flight. Arrive late and the lounge “will allow you entry to the Lounge for up to 1 (one) hour” past the booked time, after which the slot is gone.

Children are handled sensibly: under clause 7.15.18(g), “Children who are subject to free entry at the Lounge do not need to be included in the pre-booking”, so a free infant does not consume a pass. The free-entry age is the lounge's rule rather than Dragonpass's, which is another number to check on the room you are actually booking.

A bank reselling the same product spells out a rule Dragonpass does not. Revolut's own lounge pass terms, which name Dragonpass as the provider, say a pass is “valid for one visit per person”, that you “may not access more than one lounge within a two-hour period”, and that a valid boarding pass and ID or passport have to be shown at the door. On the Revolut route the pass also stays valid “as long as your Revolut account remains open”, where a Dragonpass single-use lounge pass bought direct is “valid for 1 (one) year from the date of purchase” under clause 7.15.5.

sections.heading: Where you buy it decides whether you can get your money back
sections.html:
Buy direct and the money is spent. Clause 7.1.2 makes memberships bought through Dragonpass channels non-refundable. Clause 4.8 lets you delete the membership in the app or on the website but gives “no refunds or compensation”. Clause 5.1 is the sharpest of the three: a membership “will need to be activated within 1 (one) year of the day on which you purchased” it, and if it is not, it is “terminated without any refund, extension of duration, or compensation of any kind”. Once activated it runs for one year under clause 5.2, and clause 5.3 ends the entitlement on expiry. Clause 4.3 allows suspension or termination without refund where the information given was “false, incorrect or incomplete”, and clause 12.1 lets Dragonpass end the services at any time by notice.

Buy the same lounge access through a reseller and the answer can be different. Revolut's terms say an unused pass “can be refunded if you request it within 14 days of purchase” through in-app chat. Same lounges, same provider named in the document, opposite refund position — and the only variable is where the purchase was made.

There is a question here we could not settle and it is worth asking before paying. Regulation 30(2) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 provides that for a service contract “the cancellation period ends at the end of 14 days after the day on which the contract is entered into”. The Dragonpass terms say nothing about any cancellation period, and clause 7.1.2 says the opposite. We are not able to reconcile the two from the published documents, so ask customer services to confirm the position in writing before you buy an annual plan you might not use.

sections.heading: Six directors, two countries, and the filings that are public
sections.html:
The company behind the brand is DRAGONPASS INTERNATIONAL LTD., number 08643888, registered in England and Wales. Its registered office moved to Floor 4, Charter House, 2 Woodlands Road, Altrincham WA14 1HF on 4 September 2025, and that is the address printed in the terms and on the about page.

The board has six serving directors and the dates tell you how the UK arm grew. Mark Ian Koch was appointed on 8 August 2013; Kehui Cai and Jiangnan Zhu followed on 23 October 2013, both recorded as resident in China; Andrew Harrison-Chinn joined on 20 October 2015; Peter John Hill on 7 February 2025; and Ming Sun on 31 December 2025, the same day Yik Long Ronald Tsang's appointment was terminated. Four of the ten officers ever listed have resigned.

The filing record is unbroken and current. Group accounts to 31 December 2025 were filed on 25 September 2026 and run to 32 pages; the previous year's ran to 30 and went in on 30 September 2025. A confirmation statement made on 22 December 2025 was filed with no updates. Group accounts are themselves informative: this is the parent of a group rather than a single trading company.

Scale has an outside witness too. Plaza Premium Group's own announcement of a network partnership names Mark Koch as chief executive of Dragonpass International, puts Dragonpass at 1,200 lounges against Plaza Premium's own 200-plus, and states a combined ambition of over 1,700 lounges for corporate clients. Read beside today's “1,400+”, that is a network that has grown by about 200 rooms since.

One check we could not finish: the persons-with-significant-control register at Companies House refused to load on three attempts, so the ultimate ownership of the UK company is not established on this page. The directors' recorded countries of residence point at a group with Chinese and British halves, and the company's own pages say nothing at all about who owns it.

sections.heading: What Which? measured, and the sum it stops short of
sections.html:
Which? published research on lounge memberships on 7 May 2026, written by senior researcher Amy Axworthy. Two of its figures matter more than the rest: the average UK lounge entry price is now £42 per adult, against £25 in 2017, and Dragonpass is accepted at roughly 65 UK lounges across 25 airports. It also worked out the mid-tier plan at about £21 a visit and made the same point about dining credit losing money, pricing a credit worth about £18 at £26 to redeem.

Be careful reading any write-up of this product from before the autumn, though, including that one. On 7 May 2026 Which? recorded Dragonpass selling a Classic plan at £68 with one visit included and a Preferential plan at £168 with eight. Neither name nor price is on sale now. The three plans above replaced them at some point between 7 May and 27 October 2026, and we could not date the change from Dragonpass's own pages.

The arithmetic nobody publishes is the break-even, and on today's prices it is unforgiving at the bottom of the range. Solo Travel costs £59 and the two passes still need reserving at about £6 each, so two lounge visits cost £71 against £84 at the £42 average — a £13 saving. Take only one visit in the year and you have paid £65 for £42 of lounge, which is £23 worse than paying at the door. The plan pays at two visits and not at one.

Higher up the range the sums are better and more demanding. Travel Together at £329 plus twelve £6 reservations is £401 for twelve visits, £33.42 each, worth about £103 against the average — but it needs twelve lounge visits inside one year from activation, with every guest visit eating a pass. Which?'s own worked example makes the opposite case for light users: three Manchester visits bought at £30.39 a person came to £91.17 against £132 on the Classic plan then on sale. The honest summary is that this product rewards people who already fly often and punishes optimism.

pros: £59 a year is the cheapest published route onto a 1,400-lounge network, and it includes two passes rather than none
More than 1,400 lounges in over 130 countries, plus 200-plus Fast Track lanes and offers at over 650 dining and retail locations on the same membership
One pass can be spent on a lounge, £26 of dining credit or a Fast Track lane, so a membership is not dead weight at an airport with no lounge you can use
Passes can be shared — one guest on Better Travel, up to five on Travel Together — which few lounge programmes allow at all
Top-up passes are priced below the included ones: £27 on Travel Together against the £27.42 an included pass works out at
The full terms are published and dated 1 October 2026, with clause-level detail on lounges, dining, Fast Track, delays and cancellations
Flight Delay registration gives lounge access by email when a tracked flight is delayed more than 60 minutes, provided the flight is registered at least 24 hours before departure
Dragonpass International Ltd has filed accounts every year since 2013, with group accounts to 31 December 2025 filed on 25 September 2026
The contract is governed by the laws of England and Wales, with the courts of England and Wales named for any dispute
cons: Two of the three things a pass buys are worth less than the pass costs: £26 of dining credit for a pass costing £27.42 to £29.50, and a Fast Track lane Dragonpass itself prices at £11 to £19. Only a lounge visit returns more than you paid

The lounge pre-booking fee is shown on all three plans as “Additional fee” with no amount published anywhere on the site. No1 Lounges prints it as “from just £6 per person”, and says that “Without a pre-booking, we cannot guarantee you will gain access”

Memberships bought direct are non-refundable under clause 7.1.2, deleting one in the app brings “no refunds or compensation”, and one not activated within a year is “terminated without any refund, extension of duration, or compensation of any kind” — while Revolut, reselling the same lounge pass, refunds an unused one within 14 days of purchase

Aggregate liability is capped at USD 100 by clause 10.3 on a membership costing up to £329 a year, and a complaint about anything within Dragonpass's control has to be in writing within 90 days of the event

The lounges are third parties that may be “added or removed at any time without notice”, entry to any particular one “is not guaranteed and is subject to availability”, and Dragonpass may “amend the Lounge visit charges from time to time in its sole discretion”
The stay is “usually 2 (two) hours” before you have to re-register, a booking or cancellation needs 48 hours' notice, and a late arrival has one hour before the slot is released
Used once in a year, a £59 Solo Travel membership plus a £6 reservation costs £65 for a visit Which? valued at £42 in May 2026 — £23 worse than walking up and paying
The plans on sale now are not the ones Which? recorded on 7 May 2026, and the change could not be dated from Dragonpass's own pages, so older reviews describe a price list that no longer exists
The persons-with-significant-control register would not load on three attempts and the company's own pages say nothing about ownership, so who ultimately owns the UK business is not established here
verdict: Dragonpass is a real network at a real price, and £59 a year for two passes is the cheapest published way onto 1,400-plus lounges that we can find. The catch is not hidden, it is just not added up: an included pass costs £27.42 to £29.50, the lounge adds its own reservation fee of about £6, and two of the three things a pass buys are worth less than the pass. At two or more lounge visits a year the Solo Travel plan beats the £42 average door price; at one it costs £23 more. Travel Together is the better deal per visit at about £33.42, but only if twelve passes genuinely get used inside twelve months by you and your guests. Read clause 5.1 before you buy ahead for a trip you have not booked, and ask in writing about cancellation rights if you are buying an annual plan on spec.

faqs.q: How much does one Dragonpass lounge visit cost?
faqs.a: An included pass works out at £29.50 on the £59 Solo Travel plan, £28.63 on the £229 Better Travel plan and £27.42 on the £329 Travel Together plan. Extra passes are £29, £28 and £27. On top of that the lounge charges its own reservation fee — No1 Lounges publishes it as “from just £6 per person” — so a real visit lands between about £33.42 and £35.50.

faqs.q: Can a pass be used for something other than a lounge?
faqs.a: Yes, and the membership page gives the values. One pass buys £26 of credit towards a bill at a participating airport restaurant, with anything above that paid separately, or one Fast Track security lane that Dragonpass says “costs $15£11€13–$25£19€22 if booked separately”. Both are worth less than a pass costs, so they are best treated as a fallback where no lounge is usable rather than as equivalent choices.

faqs.q: Can I bring someone with me?
faqs.a: Not on Solo Travel, where “Passes are for your personal use each trip”. Better Travel allows one accompanying guest and Travel Together up to five, but every guest visit “uses a separate pass from your annual allowance”, so twelve passes is six trips for two people. A child who gets free entry at the lounge itself does not need to be in the booking at all under clause 7.15.18(g).

faqs.q: How long can I stay, and how far ahead do I have to book?
faqs.a: Clause 7.15.9 puts the stay at “usually 2 (two) hours”, after which you have to re-register your entry. Pre-bookings and cancellations “must be made at a minimum of 48 (forty-eight) hours in advance” under clause 7.15.18(i), and if you turn up late the lounge will admit you for up to one hour past the booked time. Entry is never guaranteed: clause 7.7.19 makes it “subject to availability”.

faqs.q: Can I get a refund if I do not use the membership?
faqs.a: Not if you bought it from Dragonpass. Clause 7.1.2 makes direct memberships non-refundable, deleting one in the app brings “no refunds or compensation”, and a membership not activated within a year of purchase is terminated with nothing back. A pass bought through a reseller can be different — Revolut refunds an unused one within 14 days. Regulation 30(2) of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 gives 14 days to cancel a service contract, the terms do not mention it, and we could not reconcile the two, so get the position in writing before buying a plan on spec.

faqs.q: Who actually runs the lounges, and who do I complain to?
faqs.a: Third-party operators the terms call Participating Outlets, which clause 2.1.6 says are “not subcontractors, agents or representatives of Dragonpass”. Under clause 11.1 a dispute about what an outlet served or did goes to that outlet; anything within Dragonpass's own control has to be raised in writing within 90 days of the event. Total liability is capped at USD 100 by clause 10.3, and there is no financial regulator or ombudsman sitting behind a lounge membership.

title: Dunelm Furniture Review: Returns, Delivery and the Guarantee Ladder
meta_title: Dunelm Furniture: 28-Day Returns, 10-Year Frame Cover
meta_description: Dunelm allows 28 days to change your mind, collects anything over 15kg at home and guarantees sofa frames for 10 years. Prices and small print checked.

headline.label: Return window on a large item
headline.value: 28 days to change your mind — home collection for anything heavier than 15kg and over 120cm in any direction, and no large furniture item can be taken back to a store (checked 27 October 2026)

intro:
Dunelm gives you 28 days to change your mind about a piece of furniture, twice the 14 days the cancellation regulations require, and it will send a van to collect anything that weighs more than 15kg and measures over 120cm in any direction. Sales reached £1,825m in the 52 weeks to 27 June 2026, up 3.1%, across 204 stores in the UK and Ireland.

It is also one of the few homeware retailers on the high street that makes part of its own range rather than buying it in. Dunelm bought Bellbird Ltd in 2001 and turned it into its Made to Measure manufacturing centre, and the company you contract with — Dunelm (Soft Furnishings) Ltd, number 2129238 — still carries SIC code 32990, other manufacturing not elsewhere classified, alongside its two retail codes. The curtain hanging in the window was cut in Leicestershire.

That manufacturing is also the one part of the shop where the 28 days does not exist. Made to Measure and Made to Order products sit outside the change-of-mind policy entirely: Dunelm will take a Made to Measure item back only if it is faulty, damaged or has not been made to the specification, and its own help pages say a Made to Measure cancellation has to be raised with your consultant before the shop closes on the day you placed the order. Made to Order furniture gets a seven-day goodwill window instead. If you are shopping for blinds rather than a bookcase, that is the number that matters.

key_facts.label: Who you contract with
key_facts.value: Dunelm (Soft Furnishings) Ltd, company 02129238, incorporated 8 May 1987 as Dunelm Soft-Furnishings Limited and renamed on 5 January 2005; registered office Watermead Business Park, Syston, Leicestershire LE7 1AD; VAT GB 818 2840 21

key_facts.label: Listed parent
key_facts.value: Dunelm Group plc, company 04708277, incorporated 23 March 2003 as Tooley Limited, renamed Dunelm Group Limited on 2 April 2003 and Dunelm Group PLC on 3 October 2006, the year it floated

key_facts.label: Change-of-mind window
key_facts.value: 28 days from purchase, extended to 31 January 2027 for anything bought between 12 October and 24 December 2026

key_facts.label: Statutory cancellation
key_facts.value: 14 days from the day of delivery on an online or telephone order, with the customer paying the cost of sending the goods back

key_facts.label: Large item collection threshold
key_facts.value: Over 15kg and over 120cm in any direction; no collection charge is published for a change-of-mind return

key_facts.label: Delivery
key_facts.value: £3.95 standard and free over £60; £5.95 express; £12.95 on furniture and large items, with free two-person delivery over £600; Click and Collect free, same day, in as little as 2 hours

key_facts.label: Made to Order lead time
key_facts.value: 5 to 10 weeks, against as little as 7 days for a fitted Made to Measure order

key_facts.label: Sofa frame guarantee
key_facts.value: 10 years on the internal frame of both the Main Range Sofa Collection and Made to Order Upholstery; 25 years on the Edited Life and Natural History Museum ranges

key_facts.label: Made to Measure entry price
key_facts.value: From £62.10 on the made-to-measure curtains listing, which returned 414 results on 27 October 2026

key_facts.value: Video Check Measure free; in-home Check Measure £40, redeemable against fitting; fitting from £99 per order, paid at the time of ordering, with a 12-month guarantee on the fitting work

key_facts.value: 12 months interest free from Creation Consumer Finance Ltd on spends of £300 or more, with Dunelm acting as credit broker and not lender; no representative APR is published on the finance page

key_facts.value: 7 to 10 working days to the original payment method, or 3 to 5 working days on a card once the item is back with Dunelm

key_facts.label: Complaints
key_facts.value: 0345 165 6565, Monday to Saturday 8am to 5pm and Sunday 9am to 4pm; no ombudsman, arbitration or alternative dispute resolution scheme is named in the terms or on the contact page

sections.heading: Twenty-eight days, fourteen days, and the day the shop shuts
sections.html:
Three separate clocks run on a Dunelm order and they are not the same length. The longest is the voluntary one: the returns page offers returns and exchanges “within 28 days of purchase*”, with the asterisk pointing at an extended seasonal window. That window is currently open — anything bought between 12 October and 24 December 2026 can be returned until 31 January 2027, on proof of purchase. Dunelm did not have to offer any of this.

Underneath it sits the right nobody can take away. On an order placed online or by telephone the terms confirm that your rights “entitle you to cancel your order and obtain a full refund if you request one from the moment you place your order” and that the window runs “until 14 days from the day of delivery of the goods”. The same clause adds the part shoppers routinely miss: “you are responsible for the cost of returning the goods to us”. On a flat-packed wardrobe that is not a stamp.

The third clock is measured in hours. Because a Made to Measure blind is cut for one window, the returns policy says that “Each Made to Measure item or Custom Cut item are one of a kind and made just for you (and your window)” and that Dunelm “can only accept returns if they’re faulty, damaged, or they haven’t been made to the correct specification”. The help pages put the cancellation deadline at close of business on the day of the order, through the consultant who took it. Made to Order furniture is treated slightly more generously, with a seven-day goodwill change period before the piece goes into production, and the terms state plainly that “the Dunelm 28 day ‘change of mind’ returns policy will not apply to Made to Order items”.

Several categories are carved out of the 28 days whether they are bespoke or not: personalised items, cut-to-length fabric, perishable goods, ex-display and “less than perfect” products, live plants, gift cards, and paint and paint-your-own ranges. A second list turns on seals rather than customisation and covers mattresses, toppers, protectors, duvets and covers, pillows and pillowcases, bedsheets, throws and blankets, toilet seats and cosmetics — all of which have to come back unused, in the original packaging, with any hygiene or security seal intact. Once a mattress is out of its wrapper the policy is blunt: it “cannot be returned unless they are faulty”.

sections.heading: Getting a sofa back out of the house
sections.html:
The 28 days is only useful if there is a mechanism behind it, and on a large item that mechanism is a collection rather than a car boot. Dunelm states that “Large item furniture cannot be returned to any of our Dunelm Stores” and that “Home collections are available for items that weigh more than 15kg and measure over 120cm in any direction”. Those two numbers are the dividing line between a twenty-minute errand and a booked appointment, and they are published, which is more than several furniture retailers manage.

Booking one is less tidy. The policy says the fastest route to a refund is to arrange a collection, and the only two ways to do that are Live Chat or the Contact Us form — there is no self-service return portal, and no customer service email address is published anywhere on the contact page, which states that the addresses it does list are “for corporate and administrative enquiries only”. Live Chat runs Monday to Friday 8am to 8.30pm, Saturday 8am to 5pm and Sunday 9am to 4pm, with a virtual assistant outside those hours. The telephone line, 0345 165 6565, is open Monday to Saturday 8am to 5pm and Sunday 9am to 4pm.

The faulty route is the better one and it is worth knowing the difference. Within 30 days of receipt a faulty sofa, mattress or furniture item can be rejected outright for a full refund; after 30 days the remedy becomes a repair or replacement under the Consumer Rights Act. Where a faulty furniture item cannot be repaired, Dunelm says it “will arrange to collect the item free of charge” — language it does not use about a change-of-mind collection, where no charge is published either way. Repairs are assessed in the home by an independent expert, and on an order over £199 photographs are required before the visit is arranged.

Two smaller clauses are worth reading before you order. The delivery charge comes back “only if the whole order is damaged or faulty”, so one broken chair out of four leaves the £12.95 where it is. And purchases made in store, including Click and Collect orders, “can only be returned in-store” — which collides with the large-item rule, because a large item bought on Click and Collect cannot go back to the store that handed it over. Refunds take 7 to 10 working days to the original payment method, or 3 to 5 working days on a card once the goods arrive back.

sections.heading: What £3.95, £12.95 and £600 actually buy
sections.html:
Dunelm publishes its delivery ladder in full, which makes the thresholds easy to plan around. Standard UK delivery is £3.95 and free over £60, although furniture and large items are excluded from that threshold. Express is £5.95, again excluding furniture and large items, and is not offered to remote areas. Furniture and large items are a flat £12.95 with dates available Monday to Saturday, and Made to Order furniture is charged at the same £12.95 against a stated lead time of 5 to 10 weeks. Click and Collect is free, same day, and advertised “in as little as 2 hours”.

Spend £600 or more on qualifying large or furniture products and the two-person delivery service comes free. That is the line most sofa orders will clear, and it buys a service Dunelm runs itself rather than subcontracting: delivery “to your room of choice, up to the 2nd floor”, with a contact-free doorstep alternative if you prefer. The ceiling is literal — flats, apartments and townhouses are served to a maximum of the second floor “without the aid of a serviceable lift”.

The access rules are where a furniture order goes wrong, and Dunelm is clearer about them than most. An address judged unsafe may not get room-of-choice delivery, in which case the item is left on the doorstep or held until a safe location is agreed. If nobody is in, the item returns to the depot and has to be rebooked, and the page is explicit that items cannot be left in a safe place. There are no deliveries on public or bank holidays, and remote areas carry longer lead times.

Dunelm’s own satisfaction measurement says this is the part of the business it has been working on. The results for the year to 27 June 2026 report customer satisfaction up 2.4 percentage points overall, and then break it down by channel: stores up 3 points, Click and Collect up 6 points, and home delivery down 1 point. The commentary splits the difference the same way, recording that “satisfaction with our own two-person furniture delivery service improved” while “performance across third-party courier services declined during the year”. The service Dunelm staffs got better and the one it buys in got worse, and a furniture buyer over £600 is in the first group.

sections.heading: The measuring is the product, and Dunelm owns the factory
sections.html:
The made-to-measure curtains listing returned 414 results on 27 October 2026, starting at £62.10 and with other designs opening at £90, £99 and £118.80, from “hundreds of fabrics, colours and patterns”. Up to five fabric samples are free, the appointment is free, and the quote is described as “free, no-obligation”. Lead times run from “as little as 7 days”, which against the 5 to 10 weeks on Made to Order furniture is a different kind of operation.

It is a different operation because Dunelm built it. The 2001 purchase of Bellbird Ltd created the Made to Measure manufacturing centre, and the 2026 results record that “Made-to-Measure window treatments again grew strongly”, with “tech-supported growth drivers implemented in Made-to-Measure”. No figure is attached to either sentence, so the growth is a claim rather than a number, but the manufacturing is in the public registry: Dunelm (Soft Furnishings) Ltd holds SIC 32990 for manufacturing alongside 47510 for retail sale of textiles and 47910 for mail order and internet retail.

The commercially interesting part is what Dunelm charges to take the measuring risk off you. Measuring over video is free and “backed by our MeasureSafe guarantee”, which “covers any Made to Measure products measured through video assisted or in-home Check Measure” and promises that “If incorrectly measured, we’ll put it right, for free”. An in-home Check Measure by a fitter costs £40, redeemable against fitting. Fitting itself starts “from just £99 per order”, is paid when the order is placed rather than on completion, and comes with a 12-month guarantee on the workmanship; the fitter will also take the packaging away and remove the old window dressings on request.

Set that against the tolerance written into the returns policy, which allows 1cm of variance from the specification before an item counts as wrongly made. Measure the window yourself and anything inside a centimetre is your problem, on a product with no change-of-mind right. Let Dunelm measure it and MeasureSafe moves that risk across. The free video option makes that protection available at no cost, which is a genuinely good arrangement — and it is why the £40 and the £99 are better read as insurance against a non-returnable purchase than as service charges.

sections.heading: From a market stall in Leicester to 204 stores
sections.html:
Dunelm’s own history page dates the business to September 1979, when Bill Adderley and his wife Jean took on pitch D45 at Leicester market with their savings in discounted curtains, Marks and Spencer seconds and slippers, and reported a 600% profit inside a month. The first shop opened in Churchgate, Leicester in 1984; Will Adderley became managing director in 1996; the first Syston head office and warehouse followed in 1999; the website became fully shoppable in 2005; and the company listed on the London Stock Exchange in 2006. The registry dates the listing vehicle precisely — Dunelm Group plc, company 04708277, was incorporated on 23 March 2003 as Tooley Limited, renamed Dunelm Group Limited ten days later, and became a plc on 3 October 2006.

The current numbers come from the preliminary results of 8 September 2026, covering the 52 weeks to 27 June 2026. Sales of £1,825m were up 3.1% on the £1,771.0m of the year before. Gross margin rose 10 basis points to 52.5%. Profit before tax was £211m, described as in line with the prior year. Free cash flow improved to £155m from £127m. The estate stood at 204 stores across the UK and Ireland, with new openings in Wandsworth and Kingston-upon-Thames, and digital participation rose 2 points to 42% of sales.

Market share, measured on GlobalData UK data for the 12 months to June 2026, moved up 10 basis points to 7.9%. That is the figure worth holding on to, because it puts the company’s size in proportion: the largest specialist homeware retailer in the country still sells under eight pence in every pound spent in the category, which is why the terms a shopper actually gets are set by competition rather than by dominance. Shareholders took an ordinary dividend of 45.5p against 44.5p, plus a special dividend of 25.0p, for 70.5p declared in total against 79.5p the year before. Customer numbers “remained broadly stable across the year”, which is a flat line stated plainly rather than dressed up.

sections.heading: Spreading a furniture order over twelve months
sections.html:
Dunelm offers 12 months interest free on spends of £300 or more, with other finance options opening at £20, and the lender is named: the credit “is provided by the lender Creation Consumer Finance Ltd”, with Dunelm stating that it “is a credit broker, not a lender”. Klarna and PayPal sit alongside it. The eligibility conditions are published in full — applicants must be 18 or over, UK resident for three years or more, and on the 12-month offer “you’ll need an income of at least £10,000 a year”, all subject to status.

What the page does not carry is a representative APR. For a 12-month interest-free product that is less serious than it sounds, because at 0% there is nothing for an APR to measure, but the figure is the one number that lets a shopper compare the offer against a credit card if they fail the income test or want longer than a year, and it is absent. No firm reference number is given for the lender either, so a shopper who wants to check the credit provider on the Financial Conduct Authority register has to find it elsewhere.

The practical point for a furniture buyer is that the two thresholds do not line up. Free two-person delivery arrives at £600 and the interest-free credit opens at £300, so the sort of order that clears the delivery threshold comfortably clears the credit one; a single armchair or a cabinet may clear neither. Worth checking which side of £300 and £600 a basket falls on before adding a cushion to push it over.

sections.heading: Ten years, twenty-five years, and the five things both of them cover
sections.html:
Dunelm keeps a public guarantee library, which is rarer than it should be: a single index page lists the ranges that carry cover and states that “some of our own-brand buys come with a guarantee of between 2 and 25 years”, adding that the products “are tested way beyond what’s required”. The documents themselves are served as PDFs and can be read before buying. Most homeware retailers publish a badge and nothing behind it.

Read the two furniture documents side by side, though, and the numbers stop meaning what the badges suggest. The 10-year internal frame guarantee covers the Main Range Sofa Collection and Made to Order Upholstery for products bought from September 2018. The 25-year guarantee covers the Edited Life and Natural History Museum made-to-order ranges from September 2021. Both cover exactly five things, in the same order and the same words: “Loose joints”, “Timber breakage”, “Suspension spring and webbing breakage”, “Spring and webbing coming loose” and “Broken legs”. Both exclude exactly the same list, including the sentence that matters most — “It does not apply to fabric, fillings, cushions and mattresses including sofa beds” — plus “The metal mechanism for a recliner chairs or sofa beds is not included”, which the 25-year version extends with “This includes electric recliners”. Both are dated January 2023 and both carry the same typing error, promising nothing “If the timber is exposed to extreme moisture withing the home”.

So the difference between ten years and twenty-five years is the number on the cover, and neither number reaches a single component a customer touches. A sagging cushion, a flattened filling, a worn cover and a failed recliner motor are all outside both documents; a snapped leg is inside both. Dunelm is not alone in writing a frame guarantee this way, and a 25-year frame promise is still worth having — but a shopper choosing the Edited Life range over the main range on the strength of fifteen extra years is buying fifteen extra years of cover on the skeleton.

Four conditions apply across the furniture documents and all four narrow them further. Cover “only applies to the original purchaser of the item”, so it does not survive a house move with the sofa in it, and “any second-hand products that are still within their 25 Year Guarantee are excluded”. Domestic use only, within England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland and Jersey. Care instructions must have been followed, and proof of purchase is required — on a 25-year promise that means keeping a receipt until 2051. And the final remedy is not money: an independent service technician assesses the item at home, repairs it there if possible, offers a replacement or like-for-like if not, and where no replacement exists “you will be offered a credit for use with Dunelm” on a pre-loaded gift card, because “The Guarantee has no cash value and is non-transferable”. Ex-display and clearance items are outside all of it.

Two documents in the library are also not finished. The 2-year guarantee on Dunelm own-brand electrical heating and cooling products says in its “What do we offer?” section that a replacement “or credit will only be given strictly in accordance with the terms and conditions of the Lincoln Sliding Wardrobe Hardware Guarantee” — a different product’s paperwork, quoted in the operative clause of a live consumer document, checked twice on 27 October 2026 to be sure it was not a fetch artefact. And the Made to Measure guarantee page, which should cover the 414-product bespoke range, names exactly one thing: “Perfect Fit shutters - 5 Year guarantee”. There is no published guarantee length for a made-to-measure curtain, roller blind or Roman blind anywhere on it.

sections.heading: Who you are actually buying from, and who hears a complaint
sections.html:
Two companies share one brand. Dunelm Group plc (04708277) is the listed holding company and carries SIC 70100, activities of head offices. The contract is with Dunelm (Soft Furnishings) Ltd (02129238), incorporated on 8 May 1987 as Dunelm Soft-Furnishings Limited and renamed on 5 January 2005, registered at the Dunelm Store Support Centre on Watermead Business Park in Syston. Both filed their most recent accounts to 28 June 2025. Nothing about that is concealed — the terms, the contact page and the order paperwork all name the trading company and its number — but it is the entity to put on a letter, not the plc.

The terms themselves are short and mostly even-handed. Title passes on delivery “provided that we have processed and received payment in full” and risk “passes to you when the products are delivered”, which is the orthodox pairing. A pricing error is handled in the customer’s favour to the extent that the order is cancelled and refunded in full rather than repriced upwards. The limitation of liability clause is explicitly confined to non-consumer purchases and preserves liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence and for fraudulent misrepresentation. One drafting oddity: the main law clause says you “irrevocably submit to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of England”, while the gift card terms on the same site submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the English courts. Two clauses, one website, opposite words.

The gap that matters is what happens after a complaint fails. Neither the terms and conditions nor the contact page sets out a complaints procedure, and neither names an ombudsman, an arbitration service or any alternative dispute resolution scheme. The only dispute process written into the terms concerns alleged intellectual property infringement in user-generated content. The furniture trade does have a scheme: the Furniture and Home Improvement Ombudsman has operated since 1992, describes itself as “independent, not-for-profit, government-approved”, provides “impartial Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) services” and makes its outcomes binding on members — but membership is something a business chooses, and two attempts to open the consumer-facing member directory on 27 October 2026 returned errors, so whether Dunelm is a member could not be established here. What can be said is that Dunelm points no customer towards it. A furniture dispute that Dunelm will not resolve goes to the county court, which is the ordinary position in goods retailing and still worth knowing before a £600 order.

One last thing a reader should know before browsing rather than buying. Dunelm’s category listings are built client-side, and three furniture listings — sofas and armchairs, sofas, and made-to-order sofas — all returned “0 results are available” to a plain page request on 27 October 2026, while the made-to-measure curtains listing returned its full 414 products with prices. The delivery and returns pages load without trouble. It is a browsing quirk rather than a trading problem, and it is why the prices quoted above come from the Made to Measure range and the service pages rather than from a sofa.

pros: 28 days to change your mind, against the 14 the regulations require, and currently extended to 31 January 2027 on anything bought from 12 October 2026
Home collection is published with a threshold attached — over 15kg and over 120cm in any direction — rather than left to a phone call
A faulty furniture item that cannot be repaired is collected free of charge, and within 30 days of receipt it can be rejected outright for a full refund
Free two-person delivery to the room of your choice over £600, run by Dunelm itself; its own satisfaction measure says that service improved this year while bought-in couriers got worse
A public guarantee library of readable PDFs covering 2 to 25 years, which most homeware retailers do not publish at all
Measuring over video is free and carries the MeasureSafe promise, which moves the risk of a mismeasured non-returnable blind off the customer at no cost
Made to Measure is manufactured in-house, from the Bellbird business bought in 2001, with fitted orders turned round in as little as 7 days
cons: The 10-year and 25-year frame guarantees cover the same five faults and exclude the same list, and neither reaches fabric, fillings, cushions, mattresses or a recliner mechanism — so the extra fifteen years apply only to the frame

Both frame guarantees run to the original purchaser only, require proof of purchase, pay out in Dunelm credit rather than cash and are non-transferable, which on a 25-year promise means holding a receipt until 2051
The Made to Measure guarantee page covers one product — Perfect Fit shutters at 5 years — and publishes no guarantee length for a made-to-measure curtain or blind, which is most of the 414-item range

The 2-year guarantee on own-brand heating and cooling products binds its own remedy to the terms of the Lincoln Sliding Wardrobe Hardware Guarantee, a different product altogether, in a document dated January 2023

A change-of-mind collection on a large item has no published charge either way, and can only be booked through Live Chat or a web form; there is no self-service returns portal and no customer service email address
Neither the terms nor the contact page sets out a complaints procedure or names any ombudsman or ADR scheme, so an unresolved furniture dispute has nowhere to go but court
No representative APR is published alongside the 12-month interest-free credit, and the lender is named without a firm reference number
Both frame guarantee documents carry the same typing error, excluding timber exposed to extreme moisture “withing the home”, which suggests neither has been proofread since January 2023
verdict: Dunelm is the straightforward choice in this category on the two things a furniture buyer can check before paying: 28 days to change your mind rather than 14, and a published collection threshold of 15kg and 120cm instead of a conversation. At £1,825m of sales across 204 stores on a 7.9% market share it is big enough to run its own two-person delivery and honest enough to publish that the service improved while its bought-in couriers got worse. The Made to Measure side is better still, because the free video measure and the MeasureSafe promise take the risk off a product that cannot be returned, and the 2001 Bellbird purchase means the thing arriving at your window was made by the company selling it. Where it is weaker is on the promises that run longest. The 10-year and 25-year frame guarantees are the same document with a different number on it, neither covers a cushion, a cover or a recliner motor, and both pay in Dunelm credit to the original buyer only. Treat the frame cover as what it is, note that no guarantee length is published for a made-to-measure curtain at all, and remember that a dispute Dunelm will not settle has no ombudsman behind it. Buy the sofa on the 28 days and the £600 delivery threshold, not on the twenty-five years.

faqs.q: How long do I have to return Dunelm furniture?
faqs.a: 28 days from purchase under Dunelm’s own change-of-mind policy, with a seasonal extension to 31 January 2027 for anything bought between 12 October and 24 December 2026. Separately, an order placed online or by telephone can be cancelled under the regulations up to 14 days from the day of delivery, and on that route you pay the cost of sending the goods back. Made to Measure and Made to Order items sit outside the 28 days altogether.

faqs.q: Will Dunelm collect a sofa I have changed my mind about?
faqs.a: Yes. Home collections are offered for items weighing more than 15kg and measuring over 120cm in any direction, and large furniture cannot be taken back to a store instead. The collection has to be booked through Live Chat or the Contact Us form. Dunelm publishes no charge for a change-of-mind collection, so ask for the figure when you book; it does state that a faulty furniture item that cannot be repaired is collected free of charge. Refunds take 7 to 10 working days, or 3 to 5 working days on a card once the item is back.

faqs.q: What does the 10-year sofa guarantee actually cover?
faqs.a: Five things: loose joints, timber breakage, suspension spring and webbing breakage, spring and webbing coming loose, and broken legs. It applies to the internal frame of the Main Range Sofa Collection and Made to Order Upholstery bought from September 2018. It does not apply to fabric, fillings, cushions or mattresses including sofa beds, and it excludes the metal mechanism of a recliner or sofa bed. The 25-year guarantee on the Edited Life and Natural History Museum ranges covers and excludes exactly the same items. Cover runs to the original purchaser only, needs proof of purchase, and pays in Dunelm credit where no repair or replacement is possible.

faqs.q: How much is Dunelm delivery on a large item?
faqs.a: £12.95 for furniture and large items, on dates from Monday to Saturday, and the same £12.95 on Made to Order furniture against a lead time of 5 to 10 weeks. Spend £600 or more on qualifying large items and the two-person delivery service is free, delivered to your room of choice up to the second floor without a lift. Standard delivery on smaller items is £3.95 and free over £60, express is £5.95, and Click and Collect is free on the same day in as little as two hours.

faqs.q: Can I cancel a Made to Measure blind order?
faqs.a: Only immediately. Because each item is cut for one window, Dunelm accepts a Made to Measure return only if it is faulty, damaged or has not been made to the specification, and it allows 1cm of tolerance before an item counts as wrongly made. Its help pages put the cancellation deadline at close of business on the day you ordered, through the consultant who took the order. Made to Order furniture is more forgiving, with a seven-day goodwill change period before production starts.

faqs.q: Does Dunelm measure the windows for me?
faqs.a: Yes, and the video version costs nothing. A video-assisted Check Measure is free and an in-home Check Measure by a fitter is £40, redeemable against the fitting charge. Either route brings the MeasureSafe guarantee, which covers any Made to Measure product measured that way and promises that an incorrect measurement will be put right free of charge. Fitting itself starts from £99 per order, is paid when you place the order, and carries a 12-month guarantee on the workmanship. Dunelm does not publish the MeasureSafe terms or a duration for it.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if Dunelm will not help?
faqs.a: There is no escalation route published. Dunelm’s terms and its contact page set out no complaints procedure and name no ombudsman, arbitration service or alternative dispute resolution scheme. The customer service line is 0345 165 6565, open Monday to Saturday 8am to 5pm and Sunday 9am to 4pm. The furniture trade does have a voluntary scheme, the Furniture and Home Improvement Ombudsman, which has operated since 1992 and makes its decisions binding on members, but Dunelm does not point customers towards it and its membership could not be confirmed from the directory on 27 October 2026. Beyond Dunelm’s own process, the remaining route is the county court.

title: E.ON Next Dual Fuel
meta_title: E.ON Next Dual Fuel: £50 Off the Cap, £25 a Fuel
meta_description: E.ON Next's Next Pledge takes £25 a fuel off the price cap. What two standing charges really cost by region, and why Direct Debit is worth £139 a year.

headline.label: Dual-fuel discount
headline.value: £50 a year — £25 per fuel on the Next Pledge tracker, and £0 on the Next Flex variable tariff

intro:
E.ON Next's Next Pledge tariff is priced £50 a year below the Ofgem cap, and the supplier splits that saving evenly: £25 off each fuel, taken off the unit rates rather than the standing charge. That is the only quantified reward it publishes for taking gas and electricity together. Figures checked 27 October 2026 against E.ON Next's own Next Flex price sheet effective 1 October 2026, its charges list, its residential terms of 24 June 2025 and Companies House.

It is a big supplier with an unusually good service record for its size. Citizens Advice scored E.ON Next 3.71 out of 5 for April to June 2026, placing it third of the sixteen domestic suppliers it rates and ahead of every other large one — Octopus at 3.67, Ovo at 3.65, EDF at 2.96, ScottishPower at 2.76 and British Gas at 2.61. Its own quarterly report for the same three months counts 59,276 complaints opened at 760 per 100,000 customers, which puts roughly 7.8 million customer accounts behind the brand.

On Next Flex, the variable tariff a household lands on by default, there is no dual-fuel discount of any kind. The two fuels are priced from separate tables, the two standing charges simply add together, and nothing is taken off either for holding both. What does move a two-fuel bill at E.ON Next is the region the meters sit in and the way the bill is paid: the first is worth £89.87 a year in standing charges alone, and the second as much as £141.35.
