sections.heading: Where the meters sit is worth more than any discount in this market
sections.html:
E.ON Next publishes its variable prices as a single PDF covering all fourteen distribution regions, effective 1 October 2026. Reading the two standing charges together is the quickest way to understand what a dual-fuel account costs before a kettle is switched on.

A London household on Direct Debit pays 42.915p a day for electricity and 30.199p for gas: 73.114p combined, or £266.87 over a year. The same account on Manweb, which covers north Wales and Merseyside, pays 67.657p and 30.078p — 97.735p a day, or £356.73. The gap between the two is 24.621p a day, which is £89.87 a year, and every penny of it is decided by geography rather than by anything the household does.

Almost all of that gap is on the electricity side. Gas standing charges on Direct Debit move only from 29.157p in the Southern region to 30.199p in London, a span of 1.042p a day. Electricity runs from London's 42.915p to Manweb's 67.657p, a span of 24.742p. So the regional lottery on a dual-fuel account is really an electricity lottery with a gas bill attached, and a reader comparing suppliers on a single national figure will not see it at all.

Put the unit rates on top and the whole picture emerges. Using Ofgem's revised typical consumption of 2,500 kWh of electricity and 9,500 kWh of gas, in force since 1 July 2026, a Next Flex Direct Debit account costs about £1,672.22 a year in the East Midlands and £1,804.16 on Manweb — a £131.94 spread on identical usage. The headline cap of £1,723 for 1 October to 31 December 2026 is a Great Britain average across those same regions, so a regional figure sitting above it is arithmetic rather than a breach.

sections.heading: The price of not paying by Direct Debit is charged once per fuel
sections.html:
E.ON Next's price sheet carries three tables: Direct Debit, Other Payment Methods, and Prepayment and Smart Pay As You Go. The middle one is where a dual-fuel household quietly loses the most money, because every penny of the difference lands twice.

Take the Eastern region. On Direct Debit the standing charges are 51.835p and 29.339p; on other payment methods they are 60.621p and 37.498p. That is 16.945p more a day, or £61.85 a year, for nothing but the method of payment. The unit rates move as well — electricity from 26.613p to 28.109p and gas from 7.911p to 8.336p — and at typical consumption the full gap comes to £139.62 a year.

That pattern holds everywhere. Across the fourteen regions the standing-charge penalty alone runs from £54.32 in London to £62.58 on Sweb, and the total annual difference from £133.28 to £141.35. A single-fuel customer pays roughly half of it. The structure is entirely normal in this market and E.ON Next publishes it openly, which is more than some do — but it means the real dual-fuel decision at E.ON Next is not whether to consolidate, it is whether to set up a direct debit, and that is worth about three times what the Next Pledge discount is worth.

sections.heading: Prepayment carries the lowest unit rates on the sheet
sections.html:
The third table upends the usual expectation. On Prepayment and Smart Pay As You Go, E.ON Next's unit rates are the cheapest of the three — not the dearest. In the Eastern region prepayment electricity is 25.800p against Direct Debit's 26.613p, and prepayment gas is 7.679p against 7.911p. Across all fourteen regions prepayment electricity comes in between 0.775p and 0.852p below the Direct Debit rate, and gas between 0.228p and 0.298p below.

The standing charges are, to all intents, identical: the largest difference anywhere between the Direct Debit and prepayment figures is 0.009p a day, which is three pence a year. So the whole advantage sits in the unit rates, and on a dual-fuel account at typical consumption it is worth between £42.08 and £48.49 a year depending on region — £42.39 in the Eastern region, £48.23 on Manweb.

This is a consequence of the price cap's own structure rather than generosity, and it does not make prepayment a good idea for a household that could pay monthly instead: a meter that stops supplying energy when the credit runs out is a different product from one that does not. It is worth knowing because the folk assumption runs the other way, and because an E.ON Next customer already on a prepayment meter is not on the supplier's worst terms.

sections.heading: One gas standing charge for the whole country, unless you pay monthly
sections.html:
Here is a detail the price sheet gives away that nothing on E.ON Next's website explains. On Direct Debit the gas standing charge varies by region, from 29.157p to 30.199p a day. On Other Payment Methods it does not: the fourteen regional figures run from 37.483p to 37.501p, a total span of 0.018p a day across the whole of Great Britain. Four regions — Eastern, Manweb, Midlands and Scottish Hydro — are priced at exactly 37.498p.

In other words the regional gas differences that E.ON Next charges a Direct Debit household disappear entirely for a household that pays on receipt of a bill, which is instead charged a flat national figure about 7.3p to 8.3p a day higher than the Direct Debit rate for the same postcode. Nothing in the price sheet, the help pages or the residential terms sets out why, and no footnote marks it. It is not an error and it is not hidden — it is simply unexplained, and on a dual-fuel account the unexplained part is the larger of the two standing charges.

E.ON Next's help pages are candid about the one thing a standing-charge-averse reader will ask next: We don't currently offer a tariff with zero standing charge, so you'll need to pay it for any meters you have with us. Ofgem consulted on requiring every major supplier to offer at least one lower standing charge tariff, saying in a release of 24 September 2025 that if implemented, the tariffs will be offered by suppliers by the end of January 2026. Whether that requirement was made binding could not be established from Ofgem's own pages on 27 October 2026, so the honest statement is the narrow one: E.ON Next offers no zero-standing-charge tariff and names no lower-standing-charge one either.

sections.heading: Next Pledge: a £50 discount and a £50 door
sections.html:
Next Pledge is where the dual-fuel reward actually lives. It is described as a 12-month fixed term tracker tariff with variable rates that are always lower in comparison to the Ofgem price cap, and the discount is stated plainly in its footnote: £50 saving is applied as a reduction on unit rates split across both electricity and gas (£25 saving per fuel) based on Ofgem average dual fuel customer. Direct Debit is required and a smart meter is installed where possible.

Two things follow, and the first is in the customer's favour. Because the saving is applied to unit rates rather than the standing charge, a household that uses more than the Ofgem average gets more than £50, and the rates move down with the cap each quarter instead of being locked at today's level. Set against a cap of 26.32p for electricity and 7.97p for gas, a £25-a-fuel reduction at typical consumption works out at roughly 1.0p off each kWh of electricity and 0.26p off each kWh of gas.

The second is the arithmetic the page does not put side by side. Leaving Next Pledge for another supplier costs only a £25 exit fee per fuel — which on a dual-fuel account is £50. A full year's dual-fuel discount and the cost of walking away are the same number. Moving to a different E.ON Next tariff is free, so the fee is specifically a charge for leaving the company, and it is the mechanism that converts a tracker discount into a twelve-month commitment.

The fixed tariffs charge more to leave. Next Fixed 12m is £50 per fuel and Next Fixed 24m is £100 per fuel, so a dual-fuel household faces £100 and £200 respectively. Next Flex, Next Smart Saver, Next Optimise, Next Drive Smart and Next Pumped carry no exit fee at all. The EV tariffs are the outliers on price: Next Drive advertises lower-priced electricity 8.5p/KWh when you charge between 12am and 6am and Next Drive Smart a 6.5p/kWh off-peak rate for your whole home every night from midnight-6am, both against a national average standard variable rate E.ON Next gives as 26.322p from 1 October 2026.

sections.heading: The only charge with the words dual fuel beside it is £470
sections.html:
E.ON Next keeps a single page listing its additional charges, and it is worth reading before signing up for both fuels, because the one line that names dual fuel is a cost rather than a saving. Removing both smart meters is priced at £470; removing one, gas or electricity, is £235. The dual-fuel figure is exactly double, so there is no reduction for doing both in one visit.

The rest of the list is a tariff of its own. A residential late payment fee is £15, a debt collection fee £25, and a debt resolution visit — formerly pre-disconnection fee, in E.ON Next's own words — £55. A warrant costs £90 with a £60 application fee on top. Missing a booked meter appointment is £30. A standard load test is £103.93 and fitting an isolator £98.07. The open-ended one is the debt collection agency admin fee, given as up to 31% of the outstanding balance, which on a £600 dual-fuel winter arrear would be £186 before the £25 and £55 charges are added.

Credit should be given where the list is honest: these charges are published in one place, in plain figures, on a page a customer can find from the policies index. Several suppliers scatter the same information across separate downloads or do not publish it at all.

sections.heading: Two fuels, and the terms treat them as two accounts
sections.html:
E.ON Next's own guide to dual fuel states that you'll receive one combined bill showing your electricity and gas use. Its residential terms, last updated 24 June 2025, describe something closer to two ledgers under one roof. Where a customer is in credit, the terms say E.ON Next may use it to pay off a debt on any other account you have with us (for example for a different fuel or property) — a sentence that only makes sense if each fuel can carry its own account and its own balance.

The switching clause reads the same way: a customer paying in advance can move supplier provided they owe £500 or less for each fuel, which is a per-fuel threshold and therefore a £1,000 ceiling across a dual-fuel account. And where a customer has more than one account, the terms let E.ON Next decide which one a payment is applied to unless a payment plan says otherwise.

None of that is unfair and some of it helps — an electricity credit wiping out a gas debt is usually what a household would want. It is worth knowing because it is the opposite of how the marketing describes the product, and because it means the two fuels are not as consolidated as one bill implies.

The terms are thinner on the point a reader would most want pinned down. On a price rise they say only that we'll contact you before we put the prices up, with no number of days attached; the single 30-day notice period in the document applies to changes in how renewable electricity is sourced. The cooling-off period is 14 days from agreeing the contract, and an exit fee can be charged for switching more than six weeks before a tariff ends.

sections.heading: A good service record, and an electricity mix that is not
sections.html:
The Citizens Advice assessment for April to June 2026 is the strongest independent thing on this page and it breaks down into four parts. Fewer complaints received scored 3.0 out of 5 on a measurement of 27.1 complaints per 10,000 customers. Contact waiting time scored 3.6, on an average call-centre wait of 1 minute 57 seconds, 91.4% of emails answered inside two days and 100.0% of WhatsApp messages. Billing and metering scored 4.3, on bill accuracy of 98.51% for smart meters and 93.58% for traditional ones and 94.82% of smart meters working correctly. Customer commitments scored a full 5.

E.ON Next's own quarterly report fills in the volume behind that. For April to June 2026 it opened 59,276 complaints and resolved 59,138, settling 49.61% by the end of the next working day and 89.69% within eight weeks. The commonest causes were customer service at 32.28%, payments at 12.16%, general billing and meter reading at 11.19% and debt at 10.40%. Over the twelve months to 30 September 2025, 114,511 complaints were not resolved by the end of the next working day.

Half of a dual-fuel account is electricity, and that is where the company looks weakest. Its fuel mix disclosure for 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 gives 27.3% renewable, 53.2% natural gas, 9.3% coal, 5.8% nuclear and 4.4% other, at 322g of carbon dioxide per kWh. Coal at nearly a tenth of supply is unusual among large suppliers in 2026. The disclosure is an electricity figure only — E.ON Next publishes no carbon number for its gas, which arrives through the same network as everybody else's.

If a complaint stalls, the route out is the Energy Ombudsman, free to use, reachable on 0330 440 1624 or at PO Box 966, Warrington WA4 9DF, once eight weeks have passed or a final offer letter has arrived. E.ON Next's own complaints line is 0808 501 5200, open 9am to 5pm Monday to Thursday and 9am to 4pm on Friday, with email and WhatsApp staffed 8am to 10pm every day.

pros: Next Pledge is priced below the Ofgem cap by £50 a year, split £25 per fuel, and tracks the cap down each quarter rather than fixing at today's level
Third of sixteen suppliers in the Citizens Advice ratings for April to June 2026 at 3.71 out of 5, and the best-scoring of the large suppliers
A full regional price sheet is published as a dated PDF, so every unit rate and standing charge can be checked before signing up
Billing and metering scored 4.3 out of 5, on 98.51% smart bill accuracy and 94.82% of smart meters working correctly
Additional charges are listed in one place with plain figures, including the £15 late payment fee and the £55 debt resolution visit
No exit fee at all on Next Flex, Next Smart Saver, Next Optimise, Next Drive Smart or Next Pumped, and no fee for moving between E.ON Next tariffs
Prepayment and Smart Pay As You Go carry the cheapest unit rates on the sheet, between 0.775p and 0.852p below Direct Debit on electricity
An average call-centre wait of 1 minute 57 seconds, with 100.0% of WhatsApp messages answered within two days
cons: There is no dual-fuel discount on Next Flex, the default variable tariff — the two fuels are priced from separate tables and nothing is taken off either for holding both
A full year of the Next Pledge dual-fuel discount is £50, and leaving for another supplier costs £25 per fuel, which is also £50
Two standing charges on Direct Debit range from 73.114p a day in London to 97.735p on Manweb, an £89.87 annual gap decided by postcode alone
Paying by anything other than Direct Debit costs between £133.28 and £141.35 a year more at typical consumption, because every element of the difference is charged twice
The gas standing charge is flat nationally at about 37.49p a day on Other Payment Methods but regional on Direct Debit, and nothing E.ON Next publishes explains why
No zero-standing-charge tariff is offered and no lower-standing-charge tariff is named, which the help pages state outright
Its own dual-fuel guide still quotes an Ofgem average annual bill of £1,849 from February 2025, measured on consumption values Ofgem replaced on 1 July 2026, against a current cap of £1,723
The fixed-tariffs page claims the dual-fuel fixes are “certainly cheaper than taking out a single fixed one just for your electricity or gas” without naming a figure, a basis or a date
The electricity fuel mix for 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 is 9.3% coal and only 27.3% renewable, at 322g of CO2 per kWh, and no carbon figure is published for the gas at all
The residential terms promise only that “we'll contact you before we put the prices up”, with no notice period in days anywhere in the document
Removing both smart meters costs £470, exactly twice the £235 single-meter charge, so there is no saving for doing both in one visit
The debt collection agency admin fee is open-ended at up to 31% of the outstanding balance, on top of the £25 collection fee and the £55 debt resolution visit
verdict: Judged as a dual-fuel proposition, E.ON Next pays £50 a year for the business and charges £50 to end it, which is a modest offer honestly described. Judged as a supplier, it is a better one than that makes it sound: third of sixteen on the Citizens Advice ratings and ahead of every other large name, with a published regional price sheet, a published charges list and a published complaints report, none of which is universal in this market. Two things decide what a household actually pays, and neither is the dual-fuel question. Pay by Direct Debit, which is worth between £133.28 and £141.35 a year, and understand that the postcode moves the two standing charges by £89.87 whatever anyone does. Then take Next Pledge rather than Next Flex, because £25 a fuel off the cap for a £25-a-fuel exit fee is a fair trade for anyone not planning to move again inside the year. The gaps that remain are real — a coal share of 9.3% in the electricity, a price-rise clause with no notice period in it, and a national gas standing charge on one payment method that nobody has explained — but they are the sort of thing a reader can price in rather than be caught by.

faqs.q: Does E.ON Next give a dual fuel discount?
faqs.a: On Next Flex, the variable tariff, no — gas and electricity are priced from separate regional tables and nothing is deducted for taking both. On Next Pledge there is £50 a year, applied as £25 saving per fuel off the unit rates and based on Ofgem's average dual fuel customer. Direct Debit is required for it. E.ON Next's own guide to dual fuel says only that some suppliers give you a discount for choosing a dual fuel tariff and names no amount of its own.

faqs.q: What will two standing charges cost me a year?
faqs.a: Between £266.87 and £356.73 on Direct Debit, depending entirely on region. London is cheapest at 42.915p a day for electricity and 30.199p for gas; Manweb, covering north Wales and Merseyside, is dearest at 67.657p and 30.078p. Paying by any other method except prepayment adds a further £54.32 to £62.58 a year to those two figures. All of this is on the price sheet effective 1 October 2026.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to pay by Direct Debit?
faqs.a: Substantially, and twice over, because both the standing charge and the unit rate differ on each fuel. In the Eastern region a Direct Debit account pays 26.613p for electricity and 7.911p for gas against 28.109p and 8.336p on other payment methods, with 16.945p a day more in standing charges on top. At Ofgem's typical consumption of 2,500 kWh and 9,500 kWh that is £139.62 a year. Across all fourteen regions the gap runs from £133.28 to £141.35.

faqs.q: What does it cost to leave E.ON Next?
faqs.a: It depends which tariff, and on a dual-fuel account every figure doubles because the fee is charged per fuel. Next Pledge is £25 a fuel, so £50. Next Fixed 12m is £50 a fuel, so £100. Next Fixed 24m is £100 a fuel, so £200. Next Flex, Next Smart Saver, Next Optimise, Next Drive Smart and Next Pumped carry none. Moving between E.ON Next tariffs is free on all of them, and the residential terms allow a fee only where the switch happens more than six weeks before the tariff ends.

faqs.q: Is E.ON Next the same company as npower?
faqs.a: It uses npower's supply licence. E.ON Next Energy Limited is company 03782443, incorporated on 4 June 1999 as Hackremco (No.1496) Limited, renamed Nitrogen Two Limited that November, then npower Direct Limited on 18 September 2000, and finally E.ON Next Energy Limited on 3 June 2020. E.ON acquired npower in November 2019 as part of the Innogy purchase and began migrating customers to E.ON Next in July 2020. The registered office is Trinity House, 2 Burton Street, Nottingham NG1 4BX.

faqs.q: How good is E.ON Next's customer service?
faqs.a: Better than most large suppliers on the only independent measure that covers the whole market. Citizens Advice scored it 3.71 out of 5 for April to June 2026, third of the sixteen suppliers rated, behind Outfox Energy at 4.03 and 100Green at 3.90 and ahead of Octopus at 3.67, EDF at 2.96 and British Gas at 2.61. Its weakest component was complaints volume at 3.0 out of 5 on 27.1 complaints per 10,000 customers; its strongest was customer commitments at 5. Its own report for the same quarter shows 89.69% of complaints resolved within eight weeks.

faqs.q: Can I get a tariff with no standing charge?
faqs.a: Not from E.ON Next. Its help pages say plainly: We don't currently offer a tariff with zero standing charge, so you'll need to pay it for any meters you have with us. On a dual-fuel account that means paying two of them, every day, whether or not any energy is used. Ofgem said in a release of 24 September 2025 that it wanted to require all major suppliers to offer at least one tariff with a lower standing charge, adding that the change is unlikely to reduce bills, as tariffs with a lower standing charge will have a higher unit rate.

title: EBC Brakes Vehicle Parts
meta_title: EBC Brakes: Which Pads Are R90 Approved, and Which Not
meta_description: EBC makes brakes in Northampton and says plainly which products are ECE R90 approved for UK roads and which are not. Warranty: 12 months or 10,000 miles.

headline.label: Road legality
headline.value: R90 approved on the road pads — but RP-1 and SR race pads are not, by EBC’s own statement

disclosure: we earn a commission if you buy through the link on this page. It costs you nothing. The warranty limits, the five-day fault window and the restocking fees below are reported as published, including where they count against the sale.
intro:
EBC is a manufacturer rather than a shop, and a British one. Freeman Automotive (UK) Ltd, Companies House number 01690939, incorporated 13 January 1983, trades from the EBC Brakes World Headquarters on Upton Valley Way East in Northampton, where it says it makes its two-piece brake rotors and Apollo calipers.

What earns EBC real credit is something most brake brands avoid putting in writing: it states clearly which of its products are approved for road use and which are not. Its race pads — RP-1 and the SR sintered range — are described in its own words as “too grippy and therefore not tested or approved to R90 standards”.

That one paragraph is worth more than any amount of marketing, and it is the spine of this page. Below: what R90 actually is, which EBC lines carry it, the one range still in certification, the 12 months or 10,000 miles warranty, and a five-day fault window that is the harshest term here.

sections.heading: ECE R90, and why it decides what you can fit
sections.html:
ECE Regulation 90 is the European type approval for replacement brake pads and discs. A part that carries it has been tested to perform within a set band of the original equipment it replaces. EBC is blunt about its reach: “it only applies legally within Europe”, and “if you live outside Europe, it has no legal implications for the brakes you buy or use”. In the UK, it applies.

Where EBC says it holds approval:

  • OEM-style discs — plain, unslotted, undrilled — have “consistently passed testing for years”.
  • Road pads, with Yellowstuff listed as “fully ECE R90 approved, ensuring safe, legal, and reliable braking for road use” and an “R90 Approved” mark on the specification table.
  • Motorcycle organic and Double-H sintered pads, which EBC says are “now ECE R 90 brake safety test approved and fully TÜV tested”. It claims its DMX compound was “the first ever material to pass” the test.
  • Some two-piece floating discs, by named part number — among them SG2F022 and SG2F026 for the BMW M2 G87, M3 G80 and M4 G82, SG2F016 for the 991 Turbo and 718 Cayman GT4, and SG2FC7694 for the sixth-generation Mustang.

Where it says it does not:

  • RP-1 and SR sintered race pads. “These pads are simply too grippy and therefore not tested or approved to R90 standards.” EBC adds the obvious consequence: “brakes capable of racing cannot legally be used on highways in Europe”.
  • GD and USR slotted discs — still in certification. This is the sharpest detail on the page, and EBC volunteers it: the slotted rotors are “machined in the UK or USA using R90-approved plain rotors”, but “R90 requires that the actual slotted disc be tested separately”, and EBC said it was “currently undergoing these rigorous tests” as of June 2024.

Read that slotted-disc point carefully, because it is a distinction many buyers miss: a slotted disc machined from an approved blank is not itself an approved disc. EBC saying so, in public, is more candour than this trade usually offers.

One limitation to be fair about in both directions. EBC publishes no actual E-mark approval numbers for any product line. The codes above are EBC part numbers, not type-approval numbers. Some rivals do print the approval code — a Bosch disc we looked at elsewhere carries E4-90R-02C-0786/3289 on the listing — so if you want the number rather than the claim, ask before you buy or check the box when it arrives.

sections.heading: The warranty: twelve months, or ten thousand miles
sections.html:
Short and specific, and you should know the mileage limit before you fit anything.

ProductCover
Car disc brake pads12 months or 10,000 miles of highway use
Car brake rotors12 months or 10,000 miles of highway use
Motorcycle street pads12 months or 5,000 miles
Motorcycle street rotors12 months or 5,000 miles — and expires at 12 months regardless of mileage
Off-road, ATV and UTV rotorsManufacturing and fitment defects only; no period stated
Any product used for racingNo warranty at all

Three exclusions decide most claims. Cover is for “defects in materials or workmanship only”. It “does not cover brake noise or normal wear and tear” — so a squeal is not a warranty matter. And it is “invalid if product is used for taxi/hire car, racing, rally, drifting”.

On discs there is one more: “no warranty is offered for brake vibration suffered due to uneven rotor thickness wear”. Judder, in other words, is on you — which is a reason to bed new discs in properly and to replace pads and discs together.

EBC also states that “there is absolutely no warranty on any EBC product for race use” and that “riders must assess the performance and durability of EBC Brakes’ products themselves”. If you take your car on a track day, you are outside the warranty from that point, and the race-compound pads were never inside it.

sections.heading: Three different companies trade as EBC
sections.html:
This is worth getting straight, because it determines whose returns policy applies to your order.

WhoWhat they areNumber
Freeman Automotive (UK) LtdThe manufacturer and brand owner, Northampton01690939
EBC Brakes Direct LtdThe official direct-sales website, same Northampton HQ4835479
POTN Ltd, trading as EBC Brake ShopA separate retailer in Wellingborough04456778, per its own site

The third is a different business at a different address with materially different terms, so check which site you are actually buying from before relying on anything you read about returns. The policies below are EBC Brakes Direct’s, the official shop.

Even EBC’s own contact page muddles this, giving registration number 01690939 in the body and “Reg No. 4835479” plus VAT number 816150356 in the footer, without saying that they belong to two different companies.

Contact details, for the record: +44 (0) 1604 286028 for EBC Brakes Direct, +44 (0) 1604 583 344 for trade accounts and technical enquiries, and sales@ebcbrakesdirect.com. A technical line you can actually ring is a real advantage when you are choosing a brake compound.

sections.heading: Delivery, priced properly and with a carrier named
sections.html:
This is the best-documented delivery page of any parts seller we have looked at. All figures excluding VAT, and the carrier is named as UPS:

DestinationCharge
Great Britain, next working day£5.83
Great Britain, over £99 ex VATFree, including extended areas
Great Britain, extended postcode areas£15.00, next day
Saturday, on Friday orders only£16.67
Northern Ireland£10.00, 1–2 days
Republic of Ireland£14, 2–5 days
Europe, by band£19, £23 or £26

Two things stand out. Northern Ireland is priced rather than excluded, which several rivals cannot manage. And free delivery over £99 explicitly includes the extended areas, so remote postcodes are not quietly left out of the offer.

Cut-offs are published: 2pm Monday to Thursday, 11am on Friday. UK mainland delivery is stated as two to three working days once items are in stock, with delivery hours of 9am to 6pm weekdays. Standard insurance is £8.33 per kilo or £60, whichever is greater, with extra cover at £3.95. Jersey and Guernsey buyers can select their island as the delivery country and UK VAT comes off the order.

sections.heading: Returns: a five-day fault window, and 20% to change your mind
sections.html:
Here is the catch, and it is a real one. “We will accept no faulty goods claims, after 5 days of the goods being delivered.” The same five days applies to shipping damage, and to a short or wrong quantity.

Five days is tight for brake parts. They often sit in a cupboard until the car is booked in, and a casting flaw or a wrong-size pad may only become obvious when the wheel is off. Open the box the day it arrives, lay the pads against the old ones, check the disc diameter and thickness with a rule, and photograph anything wrong immediately.

On changing your mind, the charges are:

  • Wrong item ordered: 15% restocking fee on the Delivery and Returns page, reportable within 30 days of the invoice date — though the Terms say “minimum 20%” for the same thing.
  • Opened a sealed box: 20%.
  • Right to cancel with the packaging opened: 20%.
  • Wrong goods shipped by them: replaced free, claim within 30 days.

The cancellation window is stated three different ways across the site — a banner saying returns within 30 days, a distance-selling clause giving 14 working days, and the terms and the returns page giving 7 working days. Work to seven days and keep the box sealed and you are safe under any of them.

Two more conditions: brake kits must go back whole, with individual components refused, and goods “used in any way” cannot be returned under the right to cancel. There is no explicit no-returns-once-fitted clause, but that last line amounts to the same thing. Refunds go to the original payment method within 30 days of the goods arriving back.

Payment is by card through a Barclaycard Merchant Services page, with SagePay named as the gateway, and cheque or postal order by post. Note two firm refusals on the same page: EBC Brakes Direct “do not accept telephone orders” and “do not accept callers in person” — so the technical line will advise you, but you cannot order on it or collect from the factory. No Klarna, no Clearpay and no published finance.

sections.heading: Where it is made, and who picks the part
sections.html:
The British manufacturing is real but partial, and EBC itself tells you where the line falls. The two-piece rotors and Apollo calipers are made at the Northampton headquarters, with EBC claiming it makes “every component in house so we have total control over the entire process”. Ultimax2 pads are “crafted in the UK”, and the motorcycle organic pads are “manufactured in the UK”.

But the SR11 and SR21 race pads are “Made in the USA”, and the slotted rotors are “machined in the UK or USA”. So “British brakes” is true of much of the range and not all of it. If UK manufacture matters to you, check the individual product page.

On choosing the right part, EBC is unusually frank about the limits of its own catalogue: “We can only suggest what parts we think should be fitted to your vehicle”, and “EBC did not make your vehicle and therefore cannot guarantee what parts the manufacturer may have fitted.”

That is honest, and it is also a warning. Search is by part number or filter — there is no registration lookup and no VIN search — so measure the disc you are replacing and compare the pad shape before ordering. Garage labour for fitting the wrong part is not covered.

Product pages show both inclusive and exclusive VAT prices, which is the right way round for a brand selling to trade and public alike. Two live examples from 8 October 2026: Yellowstuff 4000 Series pads DP42424R at £249.52 inc VAT, or £207.93 ex, and DP41835R at £226.86 inc VAT, or £189.05 ex. The car ranges run Ultimax 2, Greenstuff, Redstuff, Yellowstuff, Bluestuff, then the RP and SR race compounds; discs come as standard, GD sport, USR slotted or BSD blade.

verdict: EBC is the brand in this category that tells you the truth about road legality, and that is worth paying for. It states which pads carry ECE R90 approval, says in plain words that its RP-1 and SR race compounds do not and cannot legally be used on the road, and volunteers that its slotted discs were still going through separate certification — a distinction most sellers would rather you did not know exists. Add genuine Northampton manufacturing, £5.83 next-day delivery free over £99, Northern Ireland priced rather than excluded, and a technical line you can ring, and the buying experience is a cut above the catalogue sites. Two things to handle carefully. The warranty is 12 months or 10,000 miles, excludes noise and judder, and ends the moment you take the car on track. And faulty-goods claims are refused after five days, so unbox the parts the day they arrive and check them against the old ones rather than leaving the box until the car is booked in. Buy the road compound for a road car, check whether the part is UK or US made if that matters, and keep the packaging sealed until you are certain.

faqs.q: Are EBC brake pads road legal in the UK?
faqs.a: The road ranges, yes. EBC lists its OEM-style discs and its road pads, Yellowstuff among them, as ECE R90 approved, and says its motorcycle organic and Double-H sintered pads are approved and TÜV tested. Its race pads are not: of RP-1 and the SR sintered range it says they are “too grippy and therefore not tested or approved to R90 standards”, and that “brakes capable of racing cannot legally be used on highways in Europe”. Buy the road compound for a road car.

faqs.q: Are the slotted discs R90 approved?
faqs.a: EBC says they were still in certification. Its own article explains that GD and USR slotted rotors are machined from R90-approved plain rotors, but that “R90 requires that the actual slotted disc be tested separately”, and that it was “currently undergoing these rigorous tests” as of June 2024. A slotted disc cut from an approved blank is not itself an approved disc, and EBC deserves credit for saying so. Ask for the current position before buying slotted if road legality matters to you.

faqs.q: How long is the warranty?
faqs.a: Twelve months or 10,000 miles of highway use on car pads and rotors, and twelve months or 5,000 miles on motorcycle street parts — with motorcycle street rotors expiring at twelve months whatever the mileage. Cover is for defects in materials or workmanship only. It excludes brake noise, normal wear and tear, disc vibration from uneven thickness wear, and any use for taxi or hire work, racing, rally or drifting. There is “absolutely no warranty on any EBC product for race use”.

faqs.q: What does delivery cost?
faqs.a: £5.83 excluding VAT for next working day in Great Britain by UPS, free on orders over £99 excluding VAT including the extended postcode areas, and £15.00 for extended areas below that threshold. Northern Ireland is £10.00 over one to two days, the Republic of Ireland £14, and Europe £19 to £26 by band. Saturday delivery is £16.67 on Friday orders only. Cut-offs are 2pm Monday to Thursday and 11am on Friday.

faqs.q: How long do I have to report a fault?
faqs.a: Five days from delivery, which is the tightest term on the site: “we will accept no faulty goods claims, after 5 days of the goods being delivered”. The same five days covers shipping damage and a wrong quantity. Unbox everything the day it arrives, compare the pads and discs against the parts you are replacing, and photograph any problem straight away rather than waiting until the car goes in.

faqs.q: Can I return pads I ordered by mistake?
faqs.a: Yes, but it costs. The returns page quotes 15% restocking for a wrongly ordered item while the terms say minimum 20% for the same thing, and opening a sealed box is 20% either way. Brake kits must go back whole, and anything “used in any way” is outside the right to cancel. The window is given variously as 30 days, 14 working days and 7 working days across the site, so work to seven days and keep the packaging sealed.

faqs.q: Is every EBC product made in Britain?
faqs.a: No, and EBC says so itself. The two-piece rotors and Apollo calipers are made at the Northampton headquarters, Ultimax2 pads are “crafted in the UK” and the motorcycle organic pads are UK made — but the SR11 and SR21 race pads are “Made in the USA” and the slotted rotors are “machined in the UK or USA”. Check the individual product page if country of manufacture matters to you.

title: Ebuyer Computers
meta_title: Ebuyer After Frasers: 28-Day Returns You Pay £4.99 For
meta_description: Ebuyer was bought out of administration by Frasers Group in August 2025. Same catalogue, new owner, and a returns policy written for a clothing shop.

headline.label: Who owns it now
headline.value: Frasers Group, which bought the business and assets for £2.07m on 11 August 2025

disclosure: we earn a commission if you buy through the link on this page. It costs you nothing. The administration, the new owner and the returns terms below are reported from Companies House and Ebuyer’s own pages, including the parts that may put you off.
intro:
Ebuyer still does the thing that made it useful: a deep computing catalogue with every price shown both inclusive and exclusive of VAT, which is exactly right for a shop selling to businesses and consumers at once. An Acer Predator Helios 18 with an RTX 4090 reads £2,999.98 inc VAT and £2,499.98 ex VAT on the same line, so you can budget properly either way.

Delivery is priced clearly too, from £4.99 standard to £11.99 for next day by DPD, with published cut-offs.

But this is not the same company you may have bought from before. Ebuyer went into administration in 2025, and Frasers Group bought the business and assets for £2.07 million on 11 August 2025. The entity selling to you today is EBYR (Investco) Limited, company number 16619700, incorporated on 31 July 2025 — eleven days before the sale — and registered at Frasers’ own Shirebrook headquarters.

sections.heading: What delivery costs
sections.html:
Four options, published with both the price and the cut-off, which is more than many rivals manage:

ServiceOrder beforeArrivesPrice

Next day by Evri21:00Next day£9.99
Next day by DPD21:00Next day£11.99

A 21:00 cut-off for next-day is genuinely late, and being able to choose DPD over Evri for £2 more is a sensible thing to offer rather than assigning you a carrier. Bank and public holidays are excluded, and options “can vary by product and region”.

Two gaps. There is no free delivery threshold published anywhere we looked — on a £2,999 laptop you still pay postage. And no Northern Ireland, Highlands or islands surcharge is published; the delivery page simply says to “refer to the checkout for the most up to date information”. If you are outside mainland Britain, get to the checkout before you commit to the price in your head.

One warning worth repeating because it is unusual: orders cannot be changed once submitted, including the delivery option. Choose carefully the first time.

sections.heading: The returns policy reads like a clothing shop's, because it now is one
sections.html:
The headline is reasonable: “You have 28 days to return your item.” That is longer than the 14 days the law requires for a change of mind, and longer than most of this trade gives.

Then the cost: “You pay from £4.99 per return.” For a change of mind you “will need to cover the return cost”, and the help centre says customer service cannot waive it. So sending back a mouse you did not want costs you £4.99 on top of the £4.99 you paid to receive it.

Now read the exclusions, which tell you more about the new ownership than any press release:

  • Items must be “unused, unworn, and unwashed”, in resalable condition with tags attached.
  • “Underwear, swimwear, and pierced jewellery” cannot be returned for hygiene reasons.
  • No returns on perishable items or magazines.
  • Computer games with broken seals cannot be returned — the one clause that is actually about computing.
  • Personalised items only if the text is wrong or the item is faulty.
  • Multiple orders must be returned separately.

Unwashed swimwear and pierced jewellery, on a computer retailer. That is a group-wide retail policy dropped onto a specialist business, and it is the clearest sign that the thing you are buying from is now part of a much larger general retailer. It also means the policy does not address what a computing buyer actually needs to know — opened software, bare processors, static-bagged components, bundled OEM licences. None of that is covered either way.

Online orders also cannot be returned to a store, including click-and-collect orders, despite the new owner having stores everywhere.

sections.heading: Faults, and the gap where a warranty should be
sections.html:
On a fault, the help centre tells you to “contact our Customer Service team and provide images of both the item and the fault” where the problem “has developed within a year of purchase”. All returned items “are inspected upon return”, and if no manufacturing fault is found the item is sent back to you.

That is workable, and the one-year window matches most manufacturers’ standard cover. But note what is not published: no warranty length of Ebuyer’s own, no statement of whether you deal with Ebuyer or the manufacturer after the first year, and no extended-warranty product with a price. For hardware that often carries two, three or five years from the maker — drives, power supplies, monitors — you are on your own working out who to approach in year two.

There is also a point of real substance for anyone with older kit. The help centre keeps a separate article for “orders prior to Monday 11th August 2025”, which is the exact date the business changed hands. If you bought before then, your contract was with a different legal entity — Ebuyer (UK) Limited, number 03941136, incorporated 7 March 2000 and registered at Ferry Road, Howdendyke, Goole. A new company that bought assets out of administration does not automatically inherit the old one’s obligations.

If you are relying on a pre-August-2025 Ebuyer purchase for a warranty claim, go to the manufacturer first, not the retailer. And if you paid by credit card, that route is worth remembering too.

sections.heading: What the administration actually involved
sections.html:
Worth setting out plainly, because it is a matter of record rather than rumour. FRP was engaged on 29 July 2025 to run a pre-pack sale. Frasers Group, through EBYR (Investco) Limited — a company owned by Sportsdirect.Com Retail Limited — bought the business and assets for £2.07 million on 11 August 2025.

48 employees transferred to the buyer under TUPE. The administrators’ report records that around 84 more were made redundant or were to be. Trade creditors were owed £33.3 million, with Westcoast owed about £5.2m, Exertis UK £2.5m, TD Synnex £2m, Spire £755,000, CMS £572,000 and Midwich £279,000. Four non-binding offers came in before the pre-pack route was taken.

Companies House confirms the buyer: EBYR (Investco) Limited, 16619700, incorporated 31 July 2025, active, registered at Unit A, Brook Park East, Shirebrook NG20 8RY, with Frasers Group Trading Limited (number 03406347) holding 75% or more of the shares and voting rights. Its SIC code is 47190, other retail sale in non-specialised stores — not the internet-retail code the old Ebuyer carried.

Why any of this matters to a buyer: a business bought for £2.07m with 48 staff is a far smaller operation than the one that owed £33m to its suppliers. Expect the catalogue and the website to keep working — they do — but set your expectations on depth of stock, specialist support and after-sales accordingly, and do not assume the pre-sale service levels came across with the brand name.

sections.heading: Prices, VAT and the credit offer
sections.html:
The pricing presentation is the best thing about the site. Every listing carries both figures. Eight laptops as we found them on 8 October 2026:

If you are buying through a limited company, that ex-VAT column saves you arithmetic on every page. There is a separate business arm at business.ebuyer.com, though no trade account terms, credit terms or bulk discount schedule are published on the main site.

On finance, read the wording carefully. The site states that “EBYR (Investco) Limited (FRN: 1042339), trading as ‘Ebuyer’, is an introducer appointed representative of Frasers Group Financial Services Limited (FRN: 311908)”, who “are authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority as a lender”.

So Ebuyer itself is an introducer, not the lender. The credit product is Frasers Plus, provided by Frasers Group Financial Services Limited. If you take credit at the checkout, your agreement is with that company and not with the shop — which is normal, and worth knowing before you click. No Klarna or Clearpay is published.

A deep computing catalogue, from a £679 MSI Prestige to a £2,999.98 RTX 4090 Predator
Four delivery options with published prices and cut-offs
A 21:00 cut-off for next-day delivery is genuinely late
You can choose DPD over Evri for £2 more rather than being assigned a carrier
28 days to return, which is longer than the 14 the law requires

verdict: Ebuyer remains a good place to price computer hardware, mainly because it shows inc and ex VAT on every line and prices four delivery options openly with a 21:00 next-day cut-off. What has changed is who stands behind it. The old company went into administration owing £33.3m to trade suppliers, and Frasers Group bought the business and assets for £2.07 million on 11 August 2025 through a company incorporated eleven days earlier. The new policies show it: 28 days to return, but you pay from £4.99 to do it, and the exclusions list covers swimwear and pierced jewellery while saying nothing about opened software or static-bagged components. Buy here for a well-priced, well-specified machine you have already decided on, pay by credit card, and keep the manufacturer's warranty details rather than relying on the retailer past the first year. If you bought before 11 August 2025, treat that purchase as being with a company that no longer trades and go to the manufacturer first.

faqs.q: Who owns Ebuyer now?
faqs.a: Frasers Group. It bought the business and assets out of administration for £2.07 million on 11 August 2025 through EBYR (Investco) Limited, company number 16619700, which was incorporated on 31 July 2025 and is registered at Frasers’ Shirebrook headquarters. Companies House records Frasers Group Trading Limited as holding 75% or more of the shares and voting rights.

faqs.q: I bought something before the takeover. Is my warranty still valid?
faqs.a: Treat it with care. Your contract was with Ebuyer (UK) Limited, number 03941136, a different company from the one trading today, and the help centre keeps a separate article for orders placed before Monday 11 August 2025 — the date the business changed hands. A buyer of assets out of administration does not automatically take on the seller’s obligations. Go to the manufacturer first for a hardware fault, and remember your card provider if you paid by credit card.

faqs.a: £4.99 standard over three to seven days with a 23:59 cut-off, £7.99 express within 48 hours, £9.99 next day by Evri or £11.99 next day by DPD, both with a 21:00 cut-off. Items must be unused and in resalable condition with the original packaging, computer games with broken seals cannot be returned, and online orders cannot be taken back to a store.

faqs.a: None is published. If a fault develops “within a year of purchase” you contact customer service with photographs and the item is inspected on return. Beyond a year, nothing on the site says whether you deal with Ebuyer or the manufacturer, and no extended warranty product is offered — so keep the manufacturer’s own warranty terms, which on drives, monitors and power supplies are often far longer than twelve months.

title: EDF Energy Business Dual Fuel
meta_title: EDF Business Dual Fuel: Gas 15.293p, Power 46.192p
meta_description: EDF prints its business energy prices every month. From 1 October 2026 a firm with no contract pays 46.192p a unit for power and 15.293p for gas.

headline.label: Maximum microbusiness price, both fuels
headline.value: 55.470p/kWh electricity and 19.526p/kWh gas — EDF publishes no price ceiling, so these are its dearest published rates: Extended Supply, effective 1 October 2026, before standing charges

intro:
EDF publishes what it charges a business that has no contract, re-dates the figures every month, and from 1 October 2026 those prices are 46.192p per kWh for electricity and 15.293p per kWh for gas. Both are deemed rates, the ones that apply when nobody has signed anything, and EDF puts them on its own website as dated rate cards alongside the standing charges that go with them. Very few suppliers publish this much, and none of it is behind a quote form.

The contracts are written by EDF Energy Customers Limited, company 02228297, incorporated on 8 March 1988 as LEB (Contractors) Limited and registered at Nova North, 11 Bressenden Place, London SW1E 5BY. Its business supply arm is the larger half of the company: 556,200 electricity meter points and 34.5 TWh sold to non-domestic customers in the year to 31 December 2024, on revenue of £8,674.9m, against 3,113,300 household electricity accounts and £3,037.1m. EDF describes itself on its small business pages as “Britain’s biggest generator of zero carbon electricity”, and its fixed business contracts run one, two, three or four years.

One thing to settle before any comparison. EDF sells very little gas to business: the same statement records 52,600 non-domestic gas meter points against those 556,200 electricity ones, which is roughly one gas account for every eleven. There is no both-fuels plan on the small business site, no dual-fuel discount mentioned anywhere on it, and the quote journey asks for a meter type rather than a pair of them. A firm buying gas and electricity here signs twice and carries a daily charge on each supply, and on the out-of-contract rates those two daily charges come to £10,389.21 a year in London before a single unit is burned.
