sections.heading: Three published prices, and which one you land on is about how you got there
sections.html:
Business energy is normally quoted rather than listed, so the striking thing about EDF is how much of it sits in the open. Its document library carries a dated rate card for every no-contract price it charges, replaced month by month, and on 27 October 2026 the current set all ran from 1 October.

There are three of them and they are not alternatives a buyer chooses between. Deemed prices apply when a business takes over premises and never signs anything: 46.192p per kWh of electricity and 15.293p of gas. Extended Supply prices apply when a fixed contract has ended and nothing has replaced it, which the small business terms define as “the price that you will pay for your Fixed Rate Supply if your Tariff comes to an end for any reason”, adding that they “may be higher than your existing prices”: 55.470p and 19.526p. And a third card, headed Former Tariff, prices electricity at 34.641p per kWh with a flat 491.21p a day for customers who have never changed supplier since 2001 and never signed a fixed deal.

Read in order that is an odd ladder. The cheapest published unit rate on EDF’s business electricity list, 34.641p, belongs to the group that has done nothing for twenty-five years; the dearest, 55.470p, belongs to the group whose contract lapsed. Between them sits the deemed rate at 46.192p, 33.4% above the legacy price. None of this is hidden and none of it is explained on the pages a buyer reads — the rate cards live in a document library on the large business side of the site, not on the small business pages where a shop or a café would look.

sections.heading: On electricity the lapsed-contract price is dearer by the unit and cheaper by the day
sections.html:
Put the two no-contract electricity cards side by side and they do not simply rank. Extended Supply charges 55.470p a kWh against the deemed 46.192p, which is 20.1% more. But its daily charge is lower everywhere: 341.34p against 404.10p in London on the lowest band, 995.30p against 1,178.32p on the Manweb network at the top band. The reduction is the same proportion in every one of the seventy cells on the two tables, 15.5%, which looks like a deliberate rebalancing rather than two prices set independently.

That has a consequence EDF does not spell out. For a small enough user the dearer-sounding price is the cheaper one. A London site on the No Residual band saves 62.76p a day by sitting on Extended Supply and pays an extra 9.278p on every unit, so the two cross at 2,469 kWh a year. Below that the lapsed-contract price costs less; above it the deemed price does. On Manweb at Band 4 the crossover is 7,200 kWh, because the daily saving there is nearly three times as large. Both of those sums are ours, from EDF’s own published cards.

Gas does not behave that way at all. The out-of-contract gas card is higher on both halves — 2,505.02p a day against 1,128.04p, which is 2.22 times, and 19.526p a unit against 15.293p, which is 27.7% more. So a two-fuel business whose contract lapses sees its electricity bill tilt and its gas bill simply rise. There is no crossover on gas and no usage at which the lapse is anything but expensive.

sections.heading: One gas price for the whole country, seventy for electricity
sections.html:
The gas card is four numbers wide. Meter type Standard, standing charge 1,128.04p a day, unit rate 15.293p, and a note that the charge is applied per meter. A corner shop in Truro and a unit in Inverness pay the same.

Electricity takes two pages. The unit rate is national, but the daily charge is set by a grid of fourteen distribution zones — Eastern, East Midlands, London, Manweb, Midlands, Northern, Norweb, Scottish Hydro, Scottish Power, Seeboard, Southern, Swalec, South Western and Yorkshire — crossed with five rows labelled No Residual and Bands 1 to 4. That is seventy published daily charges for one tariff, running from 404.10p in London on No Residual to 1,178.32p on Manweb at Band 4. The spread is 2.92 times, and nothing about it is within the customer’s gift: the bands come from the Targeted Charging Review, they are assigned from network data, and EDF’s own footnote says that “If a site’s banding can not be determined, an equivalent banding will be used”.

For a business taking both fuels that is the whole shape of the bill. At EDF’s deemed prices a London site pays £1,474.96 a year of electricity standing charge and £4,117.35 of gas standing charge: £5,592.31 before any energy. On the out-of-contract card the same pair is £1,245.89 and £9,143.32, or £10,389.21. Work out where the gas standing charge stops being the larger part of the gas bill and the answer is 26,923 kWh a year on the deemed card and 46,826 kWh on the out-of-contract one. A café with a small boiler will not reach either. Those three sums are ours, worked from EDF’s published rates over a 365-day year.

sections.heading: What nine months did to a price nobody is given notice of
sections.html:
Because the cards are dated and archived, the movement is provable rather than asserted, and it is the best reason to read them. The deemed gas card effective 1 January 2026 priced gas at 7.031p a kWh with an 893.86p daily charge. The card effective 1 October 2026 prices the same supply at 15.293p and 1,128.04p. The unit rate has more than doubled, up 117.5%, and the standing charge is up 26.2%, in nine months.

Electricity moved too, if less violently: the deemed unit rate went from 36.839p on 1 January to 46.192p on 1 October, up 25.4%, while the January daily charge for London on No Residual was 355.58p against today’s 404.10p. On the out-of-contract gas card the March 2026 figures were 2,092.10p a day and 13.007p a unit, so by October the unit rate had risen 50.1% and the daily charge 19.7% inside seven months.

What a business is told about any of this is the part worth knowing. The small business terms say a variable price “can increase (or decrease) at any time during the contract” and that “Any changes will apply from the date we publish them on our website or notify you”. Publication is enough. There is no stated number of days, and the practical effect is that the archive of rate cards is the notice: a firm that does not read a document library it has never been pointed at finds out when the bill arrives. Credit where it is due — the cards exist, they are dated, and the old ones are kept, which is more than most suppliers manage. The gap is in who is told they are there.

sections.heading: A tariff with no daily charge at all, described by two different numbers
sections.html:
EDF is one of the few business suppliers to publish a Zero Standing Charge tariff, and on a two-fuel supply, where the daily charge lands twice, it is the most interesting product on the site. The pitch is plain: “You only pay for energy when you’re active”, aimed at firms that trade seasonally or shut for part of the week. Given the arithmetic above — a gas standing charge that outweighs the gas itself below 26,923 kWh — a village hall or a holiday let is exactly the customer it should suit.

Two things stop the page doing its job. The first is that it contradicts itself on who qualifies: the body text reads “If your annual consumption is over 3,900 kWh for electricity and over 5,000Wh for gas, then you’ll be eligible for this tariff”, while the page’s own meta description — the line a searcher reads before clicking — gives 3,500 kWh for electricity. The gas figure, 5,000Wh, is five kilowatt hours written as five thousand watt hours, which no premises on earth would fail to exceed and is plainly meant to be 5,000 kWh. Three published figures, two of which cannot both be right.

The second is that no unit rate is published for it anywhere, so the trade-off that decides whether it is worth having cannot be examined without taking a quote. EDF’s own standing-charge explainer concedes the shape of it — “Small business customers are seeing some tariffs that offer zero standing charges but higher unit rates” — and that article carries the date “Posted June 26, 2024”. A business can work out its own break-even in a minute if it has the two numbers. It has one.

sections.heading: Leaving early costs twice as much if a broker signed you up
sections.html:
The early termination fee in the small business terms has two halves. The energy component is the difference between the original and the current market rate multiplied by unused volume, and the terms say that where that comes out negative or zero “there shall be no Energy Component” — so a customer leaving into a dearer market is not charged for the energy at all, which is fair and is not universal.

The fixed-cost component is the one to read. It multiplies unused volume and unused days by the contract’s rates and then by a contract percentage, and that percentage is “5% if you agreed your contract directly with EDF or 10% if you came indirectly via a Third Party Intermediary (TPI)”. The same customer, the same meter, the same remaining term: the exit fee doubles because a broker introduced the deal. EDF describes the total as “a genuine pre estimate of the losses”, and clause 6.4.4 adds that once the contract ends “you will be moved on to our Extended Supply Prices until you change supplier or agree a new contract with us” — the 55.470p and 19.526p rates above.

That clause sits in a market the regulator has only just begun to reach. Ofgem published a Third-Party Intermediaries Market Review call for input on 4 June 2026, with responses due by 16 July 2026, estimating that “there could be over 2,000 operating in the whole sector” and citing a departmental estimate that “approximately 50% of SMEs and 80% of industrial and commercial consumers use TPIs”. Half of small businesses, in other words, buy through the route that doubles this fee. Ofgem’s stated aim is powers to “set rules, monitor the market and take action where harm occurs, across both homes and businesses”. Until that lands, the 5% and the 10% are both lawful and both published, and the choice of door is the customer’s to make with the numbers in front of them.

sections.heading: The segmental statement says who this supplier is really built for
sections.html:
Standard Licence Condition 19A makes EDF publish a Consolidated Segmental Statement splitting its supply business four ways, and nobody quotes it. The 2024 edition, reconciled to EDF Energy Customers Limited’s accounts under FRS 101, is the clearest picture of the business available anywhere.

Non-domestic supply turned over £8,801.5m in the year to 31 December 2024 against £4,730.2m from households. Non-domestic electricity alone was £8,674.9m on 34.5 TWh across 556,200 meter points; non-domestic gas was £126.6m on 61.6 million therms across 52,600 meter points. Earnings before interest and tax came to £150.1m on business electricity and £6.4m on business gas, against £164.2m on household electricity and a loss of £92.0m on household gas. Divide revenue by meter points and the average business electricity account billed about £15,597 that year against roughly £976 for a household one, and the average business gas account about £2,407. Those three divisions are ours.

Two further numbers from the same statement put the margin in proportion. Business electricity revenue works out at about 25.1p per kWh across the year, direct fuel cost at 13.2p and total operating costs at 24.6p, leaving a little over 0.4p of EBIT on each unit — a 1.73% margin on the fuel that makes nearly two thirds of the company’s supply revenue. The statement also sets out how shared costs are split, “allocated using appropriate activity drivers, such as customer contact volumes and account volumes”, which is worth knowing before reading too much into either figure. What the document settles is simpler: this is a business-energy company with a household arm attached, and the gas side of the business book, at 52,600 meters, is the smallest thing in it.

sections.heading: The green claim, and the line underneath it in EDF’s own table
sections.html:
Business electricity is where EDF has something a competitor cannot copy, and it is worth stating plainly. Its disclosed fuel mix for April 2025 to March 2026 is 41.1% nuclear against a UK average of 13.7%, which is why its 173g of CO2 per kWh sits where it does even with 23.0% renewable against the national 48.0%. Its Fixed Renewable business tariff is matched unit for unit and backed by Renewable Energy Guarantees of Origin, with assurance from the Carbon Trust for the year ended 31 March 2025 under the Greenhouse Gas Protocol Scope 2 guidance.

The table also carries a product row headed Zero carbon, which is 100% nuclear, 0g of CO2 — and 0.0060g of radioactive waste per kWh, against 0.0025g for EDF’s supply as a whole and 0.0000g on the renewable product. That is not an accusation; it is a consequence of taking a zero-carbon product from a nuclear fleet, it is published by EDF itself, and a business choosing between the renewable tariff and the zero carbon one should see both columns rather than the carbon one alone.

One housekeeping failure sits on top of it. EDF’s central fuel mix page carries the April 2025 to March 2026 figures above. Its small business renewable tariff page still carries the previous year — 54.8% nuclear, 18.2% renewable, 135g of CO2 — and on that page EDF states that “Our fuel mix for the period April 2025 to March 2026 will be published on 1 October 2026”. It was. The business page has not caught up, and on 27 October 2026 a small business reading it was being shown a superseded mix with a nuclear share 13.7 points too high and a carbon figure 38g too low.

sections.heading: Where the paperwork gives out
sections.html:
EDF publishes a complaints performance page and the figures on it are specific: 46,534 complaints in April, May and June 2026, 965 per 100,000 accounts, 62% resolved by the end of the next working day and 86% inside eight weeks, with customer service the largest category at 33%. Every one of those figures is labelled domestic. There is no business or SME line anywhere on the page, so a firm comparing suppliers on service has household numbers or nothing, and no ratings agency fills the gap either: Defaqto and Fairer Finance do not reach business energy supply, and the Citizens Advice star rating covers domestic supply only.

The route out is better than it was. The Energy Ombudsman has handled microbusiness disputes for years and extended its remit to small businesses in December 2024; the maximum award for a non-domestic energy supply dispute rose from £10,000 to £20,000 on 19 December 2024, while the separate brokers scheme stayed at £10,000. In the first year of the wider remit the service reported “more than 13,000 microbusinesses” raising disputes and “just over 400 small businesses”, with Chief Ombudsman Ed Dodman saying it was “really encouraging to have seen over 400 small businesses use our service in its first year”. Four hundred, out of a population of millions, is the number that tells you how little known the route is.

Three smaller things did not stand up to a read. The document EDF’s own library lists as “Tariff Business NHH Electricity prices from 1 October 2026” is headed, inside, “Former Tariff Business Electricity Prices Effective from 1 April 2026” and says “The prices stated here apply from 1 April 2026” — six months between the label and the document. The small business terms promise a Statement of Renewal Terms “at least 60 days” before a fixed period ends while the small business FAQ says the renewal letter arrives “90 days” before the contract end date. And the business site gives three different sets of opening hours for the same customers across three pages, one of them twice on a single page: 9am to 5pm, 9am to 6pm and 8am to 6pm Monday to Thursday.

pros: Publishes a dated rate card for every no-contract price it charges, on both fuels, and keeps the superseded ones — so a business can prove what moved and when
Fixed prices for one, two, three or four years, with a quote promised in 60 seconds online and supply starting in about five working days
Offers a Zero Standing Charge tariff on both gas and electricity, which is rare and is worth real money to a seasonal or part-week business
41.1% of its electricity came from nuclear in the year to March 2026 against a UK average of 13.7%, and the Fixed Renewable tariff is REGO-backed with Carbon Trust assurance
Charges no energy component in the exit fee where the market has moved against the customer — the terms say there is none where the calculation is negative or zero
Sets out the microbusiness and small business thresholds in full on its own complaints page, including the 100,000 kWh and 293,000 kWh consumption limits
Signposts free independent advice by nation, with Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 and Advice Direct Scotland on 0808 196 8660
cons: No maximum microbusiness price is published anywhere on edfenergy.com that could be found on 27 October 2026, so the dearest figure a business can quote back is the 55.470p and 19.526p out-of-contract card
The rate cards live in a document library on the large business side of the site; nothing on the small business pages points a shop or a café at them

No notice period is attached to a variable price change: the terms say a change applies “from the date we publish them on our website or notify you”, and the deemed gas unit rate rose 117.5% between the January and October 2026 cards
The out-of-contract gas standing charge is 2,505.02p a day, which is £9,143.32 a year before any gas is used and 84 times the capped household figure of 29.68p
The early termination fee applies a contract percentage of 10% where a broker introduced the deal against 5% where the customer came direct, for an identical contract

The Zero Standing Charge page gives two different electricity eligibility figures, 3,900 kWh in the body and 3,500 kWh in its own meta description, writes the gas threshold as “5,000Wh”, and publishes no unit rate at all
The small business renewable tariff page was still showing the April 2024 to March 2025 fuel mix on 27 October 2026, almost four weeks after EDF’s own stated publication date for the newer figures

Complaints performance is published for households only — 46,534 in the second quarter of 2026 — with no business or SME split anywhere, and no independent rating of business energy supply exists from anybody
There is no dual-fuel plan and no dual-fuel discount: two fuels means two contracts, two renewal dates and two daily charges, £5,592.31 a year between them on the deemed cards in London
verdict: EDF is a better-documented business supplier than most and a worse-explained one. Almost everything a firm needs is published — three dated price cards a month, an exit-fee formula with its percentages written out, a segmental statement showing exactly how big the business book is — but it is scattered across a document library and a set of help pages that contradict each other on eligibility, renewal notice and even opening hours. For a business that will read the cards, that openness is worth something real: the deemed and out-of-contract prices are the two numbers a lapsed contract turns into, and knowing that gas out of contract costs £9,143.32 a year in standing charge alone is the argument for renewing on time. For a business that will not read them, the gap between the 34.641p legacy unit rate and the 55.470p lapsed one is the price of inattention. Get a quote before the renewal letter, ask what the Zero Standing Charge unit rate actually is, and ask whether you are being signed up direct or through a broker — on this supplier’s own terms that last answer doubles what leaving costs.

faqs.q: Does EDF give a dual-fuel discount to businesses?
faqs.a: No discount for taking both fuels is published anywhere on EDF’s small business pages, and there is no both-fuels plan to buy. Gas and electricity are separate contracts with separate renewal dates, and each one carries its own daily standing charge. On the deemed cards effective 1 October 2026 those two charges come to 404.10p and 1,128.04p a day for a London site, which is £5,592.31 a year before a unit of either fuel is used.

faqs.q: What will EDF charge my business if my contract runs out?
faqs.a: You move onto what EDF calls Extended Supply prices, which clause 6.4.4 of the small business terms states directly. From 1 October 2026 those are 55.470p per kWh for electricity, with a daily charge between 341.34p and 995.30p depending on your distribution zone and band, and 19.526p per kWh for gas with a daily charge of 2,505.02p. Against the deemed card the electricity unit rate is 20.1% higher and the gas unit rate 27.7% higher.

faqs.q: Why is the electricity standing charge different in different parts of the country?
faqs.a: Because it is banded. EDF’s cards print fourteen distribution zones crossed with five rows, No Residual and Bands 1 to 4, which is seventy daily charges for one tariff. On the deemed card they run from 404.10p a day in London on No Residual to 1,178.32p on Manweb at Band 4, a spread of 2.92 times. The bands come from the Targeted Charging Review rather than from EDF, and the footnote says that where a site’s banding cannot be determined an equivalent banding is used. The gas card has no regional split at all.

faqs.q: Is the Zero Standing Charge tariff worth taking?
faqs.a: It depends on a number EDF does not publish. The tariff removes the daily charge on both fuels and is pitched at seasonal businesses and those that do not open seven days a week, which matters most on gas, where the standing charge outweighs the gas itself below about 26,923 kWh a year on the deemed card. But no unit rate for the tariff appears anywhere, and EDF’s own explainer notes that zero standing charge tariffs come with higher unit rates. Ask for the rate and do the sum against your own usage before signing.

faqs.q: Can my business complain to the Energy Ombudsman about EDF?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are a microbusiness or a small business, once eight weeks have passed since you first raised the problem or you have been sent a deadlock letter. The maximum award for a non-domestic energy supply dispute rose to £20,000 on 19 December 2024, with the separate brokers scheme capped at £10,000. A microbusiness is one using under 100,000 kWh of electricity or 293,000 kWh of gas a year, employing fewer than ten people, or with turnover or a balance sheet no greater than 2 million Euros.

faqs.q: How much of EDF’s business is business energy?
faqs.a: Most of it, on the revenue line. EDF’s Consolidated Segmental Statement for the year to 31 December 2024 reports £8,801.5m of non-domestic supply revenue against £4,730.2m from households, across 556,200 business electricity meter points and 52,600 business gas ones. The average business electricity account billed roughly £15,597 that year against about £976 for a household account, which is our own division of those figures.

title: EDF Energy Dual Fuel
meta_title: EDF Dual Fuel: £100 Off, If You Go and Ask for It
meta_description: EDF's trackers cut 13.05p a day per fuel off the standing charge, worth £100 a year. Four EDF tariffs carry no dual-fuel discount at all — here is why.

headline.label: Dual-fuel discount
headline.value: £100 a year advertised — 13.05p a day per fuel off the standing charge on Simply Tracker Extra, worth £97.65 in cash while electricity VAT sits at 0%, and £0 on EDF's Standard (Variable) tariff

intro:
EDF takes 13.05p a day off the standing charge on each fuel for customers on its Simply Tracker Extra tariff, which its own tariff page puts at £50 a year per fuel — £100 across gas and electricity. That is one of the largest dual-fuel discounts any big British supplier publishes a number for. Figures checked 27 October 2026 against EDF's own rate card DM1903.08/26.AW16.V1 effective 1 October 2026, its tariff eligibility page, its deemed contract terms of 31 October 2024, its quarterly complaints return, Ofgem and Companies House.

The company behind it is the largest generator of zero-carbon electricity in Britain. EDF runs five nuclear power stations supplying about 12% of UK electricity demand, has put almost £9 billion into that fleet since 2009, owns more than 35 onshore and three offshore wind farms with over 2GW of renewable generation running and more than 10GW in construction or planning, and says it invests more than £100 million a week in British electricity infrastructure. Hinkley Point C and Sizewell C are expected between them to cover 14% of UK demand, enough for around 12 million homes. On the supply side it serves 5 million customers.

One thing decides whether the discount above is yours: whether you have ever chosen a tariff. EDF prints Standard (Variable), Deemed and Welcome prices on a single rate card at identical figures, adds its Safeguard Assist tariff on a second card at the same figures again, and none of those four carries any dual-fuel discount. The £100 sits only on the tracker range, and you have to go and take it.

key_facts.label: Company
key_facts.value: EDF Energy Customers Limited, company 02228297, incorporated 8 March 1988, Nova North, 11 Bressenden Place, London SW1E 5BY

key_facts.label: Previous names
key_facts.value: LEB (Contractors) Limited until 11 November 1994, then London Energy Company plc, London Electricity plc from 1 October 2001, London Energy plc from 30 June 2003 and EDF Energy Customers plc until 11 January 2018

key_facts.label: Dual-fuel discount, tracker range
key_facts.value: 13.05p a day per fuel excluding VAT on Simply Tracker Extra and New Home Tracker — EDF calls it 13.70p a day or £50 a year per fuel including VAT

key_facts.label: Dual-fuel discount, Standard (Variable)
key_facts.value: £0 — the same rate card prices Standard (Variable), Deemed and Welcome identically, with no reduction for taking both fuels

key_facts.label: Smaller tracker discount
key_facts.value: 6.53p a day per fuel excluding VAT on Simply Tracker and Ensure Tracker, which EDF puts at 6.8565p a day or £25.02 a year per fuel

key_facts.label: Window to claim it after moving in
key_facts.value: 28 days — New Home Tracker is only open to someone who moved into an EDF-supplied property within the last 28 days, and runs 12 months

key_facts.label: Smart meter condition
key_facts.value: Three months — miss the installation and EDF moves the account to a deemed contract, which it says most customers will be worse off on

key_facts.label: Ofgem cap, 1 October to 31 December 2026
key_facts.value: £1,723 a year, with electricity at 26.32p/kWh and 54.83p a day and gas at 7.97p/kWh and 29.68p a day on Direct Debit

key_facts.label: Independent rating
key_facts.value: 2.96 out of 5 from Citizens Advice for April to June 2026, tenth in its supplier table, with 2.0 of 5 on complaints and 5 of 5 on customer commitments

key_facts.label: Carbon intensity
key_facts.value: 173g CO2/kWh for April 2025 to March 2026 against a UK average of 147g, on 41.1% nuclear against a national 13.7%

sections.heading: Four doors onto a tariff you never picked
sections.html:
EDF publishes its default prices on a rate card headed “Standard (Variable), Deemed and Welcome - prices”, reference DM1903.08/26.AW16.V1, effective 1 October 2026. Three tariff names, one set of numbers: there are no separate rates for the Deemed or Welcome tariffs anywhere on it. A fourth name, Safeguard Assist, gets a card of its own — DM1905.08/26.AW15.V1 — and the figures on it match to the third decimal place. On Direct Debit in London, all four charge 42.915p a day and 26.595p a kWh for electricity and 30.199p a day and 8.146p a kWh for gas. In the East Midlands all four charge 51.452p and 25.355p for electricity and 29.414p and 7.823p for gas.

That uniformity is genuinely good news, and it is the opposite of how deemed supply used to work. A deemed contract is what governs your supply when there is no contract at all — EDF's residential terms put it plainly at clause 2.d: “Any supply made during any period where there is no contract between us will be governed by our deemed terms.” You arrive on one by moving into a house EDF already supplies, by having your account sold to EDF by another supplier, by failing a tariff's smart meter condition, or by your old supplier going out of business and Ofgem handing EDF the book. In each case EDF charges you its capped standard price rather than a penalty price.

What none of those four routes gives you is a dual-fuel discount. The entire reduction EDF publishes for taking gas and electricity together lives on the tracker tariffs, and a customer who has never opened a tariff page has never been offered it. EDF's own reading of the market is that around 19 million households — roughly 60% to 65% of British homes — are sitting on standard tariffs.

sections.heading: 13.05p a day, per fuel, and what the VAT holiday does to it
sections.html:
The mechanism is simple and unusually transparent. EDF's eligibility page states it for both Simply Tracker Extra and New Home Tracker in the same words: “We apply a discount of 13.05p/day (excluding VAT) to the standing charge for each fuel, this is equivalent to 13.70p/day or £50 a year, including VAT.” Simply Tracker and Ensure Tracker run the same machinery at half the rate — 6.53p a day per fuel before VAT, which EDF converts to 6.8565p a day or £25.02 a year. When EDF relaunched the Extra tariff on 27 June 2025 it described the effect as a guaranteed £100 dual fuel saving against the price cap, and quoted an average annual dual-fuel bill of £1,619 on the July 2025 cap against £1,681 on its twelve-month fixed deal.

Doubling EDF's own per-fuel figure gives the £100. The cash is slightly less than that this winter, and the reason is tax rather than anything EDF has done. Because the discount comes off the standing charge before VAT, the amount you keep depends on the VAT rate on that fuel. Gas carries VAT at 5%, so 13.05p becomes 13.7025p a day and £50.01 a year — EDF's figure exactly. Domestic electricity carries no VAT at all from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, so the electricity half is a flat 13.05p a day, or £47.63 a year. The pair comes to £97.65 rather than £100. That is this page's arithmetic on EDF's own numbers, and the gap closes again on 1 April 2027 when electricity VAT returns.

Worth knowing where the discount bites hardest, because a standing charge is a regional number and the discount is not. Against the East Midlands gas standing charge of 29.414p a day on Direct Debit, 13.7025p removes 47% of it. Against the London electricity standing charge of 42.915p, 13.05p removes 30%; against North Wales and Merseyside at 67.657p — the dearest of the fourteen distribution regions on the card — the same 13.05p removes only 19%. Identical discount, very different proportion of the bill, depending on the postcode.

sections.heading: Twenty-eight days after you move in, and then the door shuts
sections.html:
New Home Tracker is the most useful tariff EDF sells and the easiest to miss. Its eligibility condition is a single sentence — “Have moved into a property within the last 28 days that is supplied by EDF” — and it carries the full 13.05p a day per fuel discount, for a term that “will run for a period of 12 months starting from the day you agree the contract”.

Set that against what happens if you do nothing. Move into an EDF-supplied house and you are on a deemed contract from the moment supply starts: the Deemed Electricity Terms and Conditions, version 4.2, effective 31 October 2024, say at Schedule 1 clause 1.1 that the contract “will be regarded as coming into effect at the earliest of the following times”, which is when EDF began supplying the premises or when you began taking supply. The price is the capped standard price, which is fair, but the discount is not there. Twenty-eight days is a short window in the middle of a house move, and nothing about the deemed arrangement puts a clock in front of the customer.

Two details in the deemed terms are worth reading before you leave one. Ending it when you move out needs “not less than 2 working days notice” under clause 8.3, which is a short fuse for anybody who vacates on a Friday. And clause 4.1 allows EDF to “request a security deposit if we are concerned about your ability to pay our bills” — repaid with interest, and within 14 days under clause 4.2.1 if every bill in the previous full year was paid inside the payment period.

sections.heading: The smart meter condition that sends you backwards
sections.html:
Almost every EDF tariff now assumes a smart meter. On Standard (Variable) the consequence is mild and clearly stated: “If you don't already have a smart meter installed at your property, we will contact you to arrange an appointment for installation”, and “If you decide to decline the opportunity to have a Smart meter fitted, you may not be eligible for some of our discounts, services or Smart meter tariffs which may save you money.”

On the fixed and tracker tariffs it is sharper. The eligibility page states, for Ensure Tracker and Essentials Fixed among others, that “If you haven't had your smart meter installed within three months of your tariff start date we'll transfer you onto our deemed contract.” EDF then adds its own warning in the next breath: “A deemed contract may have different price to your current tariff and we recommend that most customers will be better off on their current tariff.” So a customer who signed a discounted tracker and then waited three months for an appointment can be moved to the undiscounted default, by a term they agreed to, on a timetable they do not control.

How much of that timetable is in the customer's hands is a fair question, and the regulator is asking it. Ofgem's consultation on smart meter guaranteed standards of performance, reference OFG1164, published 28 March 2025 with responses due by 9 May 2025, proposes that suppliers offer an installation appointment “within six weeks of the request being made” — defined in its own footnote as 42 calendar days or 30 working days — complete an initial assessment of a faulty meter within 5 working days, and restore a meter to smart mode within 90 calendar days, with a repeat payment every 365 days it stays broken. The existing compensation for a missed installation appointment was “recently raised from £30 to £40”. The rest of it remains a proposal: Ofgem says it would publish a statutory consultation and a draft statutory instrument before any of it binds anyone, and no commencement date is given. Six weeks is also longer than one third of three months.

sections.heading: A safeguard tariff that costs exactly what the standard one costs
sections.html:
Safeguard Assist is EDF's tariff for customers who qualify for the Warm Home Discount, and it has its own rate card, DM1905.08/26.AW15.V1, effective 1 October 2026. The prices on it are the Standard (Variable) prices. London on Direct Debit: 42.915p a day and 26.595p a kWh for electricity, 30.199p and 8.146p for gas. North Wales and Merseyside: 67.657p and 27.862p for electricity, 30.078p and 7.904p for gas. Both cards state that the prices are “only available for supplying electricity and gas to continuously occupied premises used only or mainly for domestic purposes”.

Nobody on it is paying more than a standard customer, there is no exit fee, and EDF describes the Deemed Safeguard Assist variant as providing “capped energy charges for eligible persons”. The name promises protection beyond the cap; the figures deliver the cap. Reading the two cards side by side is the only way to establish that, and it takes one minute.

The published eligibility rule has not kept up. To qualify, EDF says, you must “meet the criteria for the “core” or “broader” group as set out in the Warm Home Discount Regulations, or as otherwise directed by Ofgem from time to time; and be on years 6, 7 or 8 of the Warm Home Discount Scheme.” Ofgem's own social programmes pages say “Scheme Year 16 begins in 2026”, running 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027 in England and Wales and 1 May 2026 to 31 March 2027 in Scotland. Scheme years 6 to 8 ended in March 2019. The group names have moved on too: the Government's eligibility statement for England and Wales, published 7 August 2026 with a qualifying date of 23 August 2026, says that “From scheme year 16, core group 1 and core group 2 have been merged into one “core group””, and Ofgem's pages describe the broader group as operating in Scotland only, on individual application. The catch-all clause about Ofgem directing otherwise is presumably doing the real work, but an eligibility rule pointing at a window that closed seven years ago is not something a reader on a low income should have to decode.

sections.heading: Where 40,000 Utilita customers landed, and where Utility Point's did in 2021
sections.html:
The Welcome tariff on that rate card has a specific population behind it. On 13 October 2025 EDF announced that Utilita Energy had agreed to sell it “more than 40,000 of its credit customers”, with the transfer taking effect from 8 November 2025. The commitments were clear: “All accounts and credit balances will remain fully protected”, and “prices will remain unchanged during the current price cap period”. Philippe Commaret, managing director of EDF Customers, and Bill Bullen, Utilita's chief executive, both put their names to it. EDF's own customer page told the transferring households they would move to “an EDF tariff tailored to match your existing Utilita pricing”, that credit balances would follow their accounts, that EDF would start collecting Direct Debits “from December onwards” with no new instruction needed, that payment dates on the 29th or 30th would move to the 1st, and that Utilita's terms and conditions would continue to apply “until 1 Jan 2026”.

What “tailored to match your existing Utilita pricing” turned into is visible on the rate card: Welcome Utilita Smart and Welcome Utilita Premium are variable tariffs whose “standing charge and unit rates track those of the Ofgem cap”, priced identically to Standard (Variable). For customers moving from a cap-priced tariff that is a true statement and a fair outcome. It is also an open-ended variable tariff with no dual-fuel discount attached, reached without anybody choosing it.

EDF has done the harder version of this before. Ofgem appointed EDF Energy Customers Limited supplier of last resort for Utility Point Limited, announcing it on 17 September 2021 with the licence revocations and last resort supply directions taking effect the following day. Ofgem's decision letter of 23 June 2022 records that the bidders who volunteered offered deemed tariffs “set at or near the current price cap level”, that EDF was “willing to absorb the greatest share of costs claimable through the industry levy”, and that it would honour both existing credit balances and refunds owed to customers who had already switched away. On the two occasions a book of customers has landed on EDF without choosing it, they landed at the cap.

sections.heading: Electricity got cheaper to buy and dearer to make
sections.html:
The cap for 1 October to 31 December 2026 is £1,723 a year, up 4%. Ofgem's own figures for a Direct Debit customer are 26.32p/kWh and 54.83p a day for electricity and 7.97p/kWh and 29.68p a day for gas, and the critical footnote is that “There is no VAT on electricity from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027” while gas still carries 5%. EDF's own rate cards carry the same distinction in their own words: “All Electricity prices below reflect that VAT is charged at 0% on Electricity supplies” and “All Gas prices shown are inclusive of VAT charged at 5% and rounded.”

EDF's price cap explainer of 26 August 2026 then sets the old rates against the new: electricity 26.11p to 26.32p a kWh, described as up 0.8%, and 57.19p to 54.83p a day, described as down 4.1%. Gas goes 7.33p to 7.97p a kWh, up 8.7%, and 29.04p to 29.68p a day, up 2.2%. Those are accurate as cash: an EDF customer really does pay 4.1% less in electricity standing charge than in September.

They are not like-for-like, because the July figures include 5% VAT and the October ones include none. Strip the tax out of both and the picture inverts. The electricity unit rate goes from 24.867p to 26.32p, a rise of about 5.8%, and the standing charge from 54.467p to 54.83p, a rise of about 0.7%. The gas percentages are unaffected, since gas VAT did not move. So the whole of the electricity reduction on a bill this winter is the Treasury's doing and none of it is the supplier's, and it reverses on 1 April 2027. Neither Ofgem nor EDF has concealed any of this; both state the VAT position in terms. It simply means the one number a household will compare — last quarter's bill against this one — is comparing two tax regimes, and anybody budgeting past March should assume the electricity standing charge goes back up by about 2.74p a day before any cap decision at all.

sections.heading: Three times the nuclear, and more carbon than the national average
sections.html:
EDF publishes its fuel mix for April 2025 to March 2026: 41.1% nuclear, 28.5% gas, 23.0% renewable, 5.0% coal and 2.4% other, at 173g of CO2 per kWh and 0.0025g of radioactive waste per kWh. Beside it, credited to the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, sits the UK average: 13.7% nuclear, 31.4% gas, 48.0% renewable, 4.7% coal and 2.2% other, at 147g of CO2 per kWh.

EDF generates three times the national share of its electricity from nuclear and sells power that is about 18% more carbon-intensive than the British average. The explanation is in the same two columns: renewables are 23.0% of EDF's mix against 48.0% nationally, and its coal share is slightly above the average rather than below it. Nuclear displaces less of the gas than a reader would expect from the headline percentage. EDF does not spin this — it prints both columns next to each other and lists a separate per-tariff table for its zero carbon and renewable products, so a customer on one of those is not buying the whole-business mix.

On a dual-fuel account the figure covers one of the two fuels. A fuel mix disclosure is an electricity obligation, and no supplier publishes a carbon intensity for the gas it sells: EDF's gas comes off the same network as everybody else's, and on a typical dual-fuel home burning 9,500 kWh of gas against 2,500 kWh of electricity under Ofgem's revised consumption values, the unmeasured fuel is the larger one by a factor of nearly four.

sections.heading: The service record, and the paperwork that stops short
sections.html:
Citizens Advice scored EDF 2.96 out of 5 for April to June 2026, placing it tenth in its supplier table. The components are more useful than the total. Complaints scored 2.0 of 5 on a measured 47.7 complaints per 10,000 customers reaching the Citizens Advice consumer service, the Extra Help Unit, Advice Direct Scotland and the Energy Ombudsman. Contact scored 3.2 on an average call centre wait of 2 minutes 47 seconds, with 85.4% of emails answered inside two days, 91.0% of WhatsApp messages and 90.9% of texts. Billing and metering scored 3.2 on bill accuracy of 97.6% for smart meters and 90.75% for traditional ones, with 92.67% of smart meters working correctly. Customer commitments scored a full 5 of 5, EDF being a member of both the Switch Guarantee and the Vulnerability Commitment.

EDF also publishes its own quarterly complaints return, which most suppliers do not. For April to June 2026 it received 46,534 domestic complaints, 965 per 100,000 customer accounts, and resolved 42,360 — 62% by the end of the next working day and 86% within eight weeks, the second figure including complaints raised in earlier quarters. The causes are broken out: customer service 33%, billing and meter reading 17%, payment issues 12%, debt and debt-related disconnections 9%, and meter installation, exchange or failure 7%. Dividing the two headline figures gives a customer account count EDF does not publish anywhere — about 4.8 million — which sits sensibly below the 5 million customers its press material claims.

Where the documents stop is domestic charges. EDF's residential terms, last updated 1 September 2026, promise that “we'll give you advance written notice (a ‘variation notice’)” before a price change, and say that “Any changes will apply from the date we publish them on our website”, with no number of days attached. Clause 17.a refers to a debt “still not paid after 28 days”, and the fixed tariffs carry an exit fee if ended more than 49 days early. The deemed terms are thinner still: clause 3.7 says only that “The Deemed Contract Schedule of Charges set by us from time to time will remain in force until we change it”, with clause 3.6 entitling EDF to “vary, all or any of our charges by giving notice in writing to you” and clause 3.8.2 confirming that variations “shall not operate retrospectively” — and no notice period anywhere. The late payment, debt collection agency, premises visit, warrant, de-energisation and re-energisation steps are all described on EDF's own site with no amount against a single one of them, and that page is written for business customers. A household cannot find out what being late costs.

pros: The largest published dual-fuel discount of any big supplier: 13.05p a day per fuel off the standing charge before VAT on Simply Tracker Extra, which EDF puts at £50 a year per fuel
New Home Tracker gives anyone who moved into an EDF-supplied property in the last 28 days the full discount on a fixed 12-month term
Deemed and Welcome prices are identical to Standard (Variable) on the same rate card — arriving without choosing a tariff does not cost you a penalty price
Safeguard Assist matches the standard rate card to the third decimal place in every region, so no Warm Home Discount customer pays more than a standard one
No exit fee at all on Standard (Variable), Safeguard Assist, Warmwise Half Hourly, FreePhase Dynamic or the heat pump trackers
All fourteen distribution regions and three payment methods are published in one dated PDF rate card, reference DM1903.08/26.AW16.V1, effective 1 October 2026
A quarterly domestic complaints return is published in full, including 46,534 complaints for April to June 2026 and the five leading causes by share
Full marks from Citizens Advice on customer commitments as a member of the Switch Guarantee and the Vulnerability Commitment, with 97.6% bill accuracy on smart meters
Credit balances were honoured in both customer transfers — more than 40,000 Utilita accounts on 8 November 2025, and Utility Point's book in September 2021
41.1% of its electricity came from nuclear in the year to March 2026, three times the UK average of 13.7%, from five power stations supplying about 12% of national demand
cons: The published eligibility rule for Safeguard Assist still requires you to be “on years 6, 7 or 8 of the Warm Home Discount Scheme”, and Ofgem says scheme year 16 began in 2026 — scheme years 6 to 8 ended in March 2019
The same rule asks for the “core” or “broader” group, but core groups 1 and 2 were merged from scheme year 16 and the broader group now exists in Scotland only

The £50-a-year-per-fuel figure assumes 5% VAT on both fuels. With electricity VAT at 0% until 31 March 2027 the cash discount is £47.63 on electricity and £50.01 on gas — £97.65 for the pair, not £100
Four EDF tariffs — Standard (Variable), Deemed, Welcome and Safeguard Assist — carry no dual-fuel discount whatsoever, and all four are reached by doing nothing
Miss a smart meter installation by three months and EDF moves the account to a deemed contract, and its own eligibility page admits most customers will be better off staying where they were

The deemed contract terms set no notice period for a price change: clause 3.7 says the schedule of charges “will remain in force until we change it”, while the residential terms promise a variation notice
Only two working days' notice is accepted to end a deemed contract when you move out, under clause 8.3, and clause 4.1 allows EDF to demand a security deposit

EDF's October explainer calls the electricity standing charge “down 4.1%” and the unit rate “up 0.8%”, comparing July rates that include 5% VAT with October rates that include none; before tax the unit rate rose about 5.8%
At 173g of CO2 per kWh, EDF’s electricity is about 18% more carbon-intensive than the 147g UK average it prints beside it, on renewables of 23.0% against a national 48.0%
2.96 out of 5 and tenth from Citizens Advice for April to June 2026, with just 2.0 of 5 on complaints at 47.7 per 10,000 customers

No list of domestic charges with amounts anywhere on the site: the late payment, debt collection, premises visit, warrant and de-energisation steps are described without a single figure, on a page written for business customers
The 28-day window on New Home Tracker is never put in front of a customer who has just arrived on a deemed contract, and the deemed paperwork carries no clock
verdict: As a dual-fuel proposition EDF is the right way round and the wrong way round at once. The discount is real, it is bigger than most, and it is described in a single unambiguous sentence: 13.05p a day off the standing charge on each fuel, which EDF itself converts to £50 a year per fuel and £100 for the pair. The cash is £97.65 this winter because electricity VAT is zero until 31 March 2027, which is a quirk of tax rather than a failing of the supplier. But the discount sits only on the tracker range, and the four tariffs a household reaches without choosing anything — Standard (Variable), Deemed, Welcome and Safeguard Assist — pay nothing for taking both fuels. All four are priced at the Ofgem cap, which is a decent and unpenalising default, and all four leave £97.65 a year on the table. The sharpest version of that is the house move: 28 days to take New Home Tracker and the full discount, against a deemed contract that starts automatically and mentions no deadline. Judged as a supplier rather than a tariff, EDF is a mixed but improving picture: tenth of the Citizens Advice table at 2.96 out of 5 and weak on complaint volumes, strong on commitments and smart meter billing accuracy, honest enough to publish its own complaints return and both halves of its carbon comparison, and the owner of five nuclear stations and most of Britain's zero-carbon generation. The paperwork has two genuine gaps that are nothing to do with price: a Warm Home Discount eligibility rule pointing at scheme years that ended in 2019, and no published figure for what any late payment or debt action costs a household. Worth the click if you intend to pick a tariff rather than be put on one.

faqs.q: Does EDF give a dual fuel discount?
faqs.a: Yes, on its tracker tariffs only. Simply Tracker Extra and New Home Tracker take 13.05p a day off the standing charge for each fuel before VAT, which EDF describes as 13.70p a day or £50 a year per fuel — £100 across gas and electricity. Simply Tracker and Ensure Tracker run at half that, 6.53p a day per fuel or £25.02 a year. EDF's Standard (Variable), Deemed, Welcome and Safeguard Assist tariffs carry no dual-fuel discount at all.

faqs.q: Why is the discount £97.65 rather than £100?
faqs.a: Because it is applied to the standing charge before VAT, so the cash you keep depends on the VAT rate of that fuel. Gas carries 5% VAT, so 13.05p becomes 13.7025p a day and £50.01 a year. Domestic electricity carries 0% VAT from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, so the electricity half stays at 13.05p a day and £47.63 a year. The two add to £97.65. EDF's £50-per-fuel figure was calculated with 5% VAT on both, and it becomes right again on 1 April 2027.

faqs.q: What happens if I move into a house EDF already supplies?
faqs.a: You start on a deemed contract immediately — the terms, version 4.2 of 31 October 2024, say it takes effect when EDF began supplying the premises or when you began taking supply, whichever is earliest. The price is EDF's capped Standard (Variable) price, so you are not penalised, but there is no dual-fuel discount on it. You have 28 days from moving in to take New Home Tracker instead, which carries the full 13.05p a day per fuel for 12 months. Ending a deemed contract when you move out needs at least two working days' notice.

faqs.q: Is the Safeguard Assist tariff cheaper than EDF's standard tariff?
faqs.a: No. The two rate cards — DM1905 for Safeguard Assist and DM1903 for Standard (Variable) — carry the same figures in every region and on every payment method. On Direct Debit in London both charge 42.915p a day and 26.595p a kWh for electricity and 30.199p and 8.146p for gas. Safeguard Assist tracks the Ofgem cap and has no exit fee, so it protects you against paying above the cap and nothing more. Its published eligibility rule asks you to be on Warm Home Discount scheme years 6, 7 or 8, which ended in March 2019; Ofgem says scheme year 16 began in 2026, so ask EDF rather than relying on the wording.

faqs.q: Will EDF move me off my tariff if I do not get a smart meter?
faqs.a: On several tariffs, yes. The eligibility page states that “If you haven't had your smart meter installed within three months of your tariff start date we'll transfer you onto our deemed contract”, and warns in the same place that “most customers will be better off on their current tariff”. On Standard (Variable) the penalty is softer — EDF says only that declining a smart meter may make you ineligible for some discounts, services or smart meter tariffs. Ofgem is consulting on requiring suppliers to offer an installation appointment within six weeks, or 42 calendar days, but that proposal of 28 March 2025 has not yet been made binding.

faqs.q: What happened to Utilita customers moved to EDF?
faqs.a: More than 40,000 of Utilita's credit customers transferred on 8 November 2025 under an agreement announced on 13 October 2025. EDF said all accounts and credit balances would remain fully protected and that prices would be unchanged for the rest of that price cap period, and placed them on an EDF tariff “tailored to match your existing Utilita pricing”. In practice that is Welcome Utilita Smart or Welcome Utilita Premium, variable tariffs whose standing charge and unit rates track the Ofgem cap and which are priced identically to Standard (Variable). Utilita's own terms applied until 1 January 2026, and any balance outstanding with Utilita still had to be settled with Utilita.

faqs.q: Is EDF's electricity greener than average because of its nuclear fleet?
faqs.a: Lower in nuclear terms, higher in carbon terms. EDF's own disclosure for April 2025 to March 2026 gives 41.1% nuclear against a UK average of 13.7%, but 173g of CO2 per kWh against a UK average of 147g — because its renewable share is 23.0% where the national figure is 48.0% and its coal share, 5.0%, is slightly above the 4.7% average. EDF prints both columns side by side and lists a separate mix for its zero carbon and renewable tariffs. There is no carbon figure for the gas half of a dual-fuel account, because no supplier publishes one.

title: Eversure Breakdown Cover Review
meta_title: Eversure Breakdown Cover Review: Prices From £17.47
meta_description: Eversure breakdown cover reviewed: Silver, Gold and Platinum tiers, £17.47 starting price, the 15-year vehicle limit and who actually underwrites it.
intro:
Eversure sells UK and European breakdown cover starting at £17.47 a year, which is roughly what a month of patrol-branded membership costs. The Guildford firm has been arranging insurance since 2008 and says it has helped more than 250,000 people buy a policy, across a range that also takes in cycle, drone, camera, caravan and car hire excess cover. Breakdown is one line among ten rather than the whole business.

The breakdown product comes in three tiers — Silver, Gold and Platinum — and covers up to four people living at the same address rather than a single named driver. Eversure quotes an average response time of 46 minutes, says 85% of vehicles are fixed at the roadside and 76% of home callouts are fixed on the driveway. National recovery to your home address is included from the entry tier upward, which is not true of every budget policy.

Personal cover, which follows the person into any eligible vehicle they are travelling in, starts higher at £33.81. European cover is priced separately: £20.54 for a single trip, £50.28 for an annual policy covering trips of up to 90 days across 39 listed territories.

key_facts.value: Silver, Gold, Platinum

key_facts.value: £50.28 (trips up to 90 days)

key_facts.value: Up to 4 at the same address

sections.heading: What £17.47 gets you, and what the next tier adds
sections.html:
Silver is the base. It brings roadside assistance once you are at least a mile from home, local recovery to the nearest suitable garage within 25 miles, and national recovery to your home address if the garage cannot fix the car the same day. Onward travel is an alternative rather than an addition: rail or bus fares, a hotel capped at £150 for a lone driver or £600 for a group, or a hire car up to £300. You pick one of the three, not all of them.

Gold adds Home Start, which extends assistance to breakdowns at or within a mile of your home address. That is the single most common callout for most drivers, since a car that will not start usually will not start on the drive. Platinum adds misfuelling cover — draining the tank and, where needed, repairing engine parts damaged by the wrong fuel, up to £500.

The structure is worth reading carefully because the labels are doing real work. A great many cheap policies bury Home Start at the top tier and price the headline against the version without it. Eversure puts it at the middle tier, which is more generous than some and less generous than the patrol clubs that include it as standard.

Eligibility is tighter than the price suggests. The vehicle must be no more than 3,500kg including load, no longer than 7 metres, no taller than 3 metres and no wider than 2.25 metres. That comfortably covers cars and most vans, and quietly excludes larger motorhomes and anything towing at length.

sections.heading: The name on the certificate is not the name on the website
sections.html:
Eversure Limited arranges the policy; it does not carry the risk and it does not employ the mechanics. The breakdown wording is underwritten by Collinson Insurance, a trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both the PRA and the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference number 202846, company number 01708613, registered at 3 More London Riverside, London SE1 2RE.

That distinction matters for two reasons. The first is financial. Astrenska's most recent published solvency and financial condition report, for the year ended 30 April 2024, shows a solvency capital requirement of £15.5m against eligible own funds of £31.8m — a coverage ratio of 205% against an internal target of 150%. Gross written premium reached £221.4m in that financial year, up 30% from £170.8m the year before. Those are audited, public numbers, and they are a good deal more informative about whether a claim gets paid than any star rating.

The second is that Eversure uses different underwriters for different products. Its car hire excess policy, for instance, sits with American International Group UK Limited under firm reference 781109. Buying two Eversure policies does not mean buying from one insurer, and a complaint about one will not necessarily be handled by the same people as a complaint about the other.

Eversure Limited itself carries firm reference number 501311 and is registered in England and Wales as company 06751893, at Bury House, 1–3 Bury Street, Guildford, Surrey GU2 4AW. It was incorporated on 18 November 2008 under the name MYFINANCE.COM LIMITED and only became Eversure Limited on 14 September 2015 — worth knowing if you are searching Companies House and cannot find the earlier trading history. Cover is backed by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme.

sections.heading: Taking it across the Channel
sections.html:
European cover is bought separately and cannot be added to a UK policy after purchase, so the decision has to be made at the point of sale. The territory list runs to 39 entries and is broader than most drivers need: Andorra, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Channel Islands, Corsica, Croatia, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Gibraltar, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, the Isle of Man, Italy including Sardinia and Sicily, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal including Madeira, the Republic of Ireland, Romania, San Marino, the Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Spain including the Balearics and Canaries, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom.

Single-trip cover starts at £20.54 and works for a trip of one day or longer. The annual version at £50.28 allows repeated journeys of up to 90 days each. Benefits include recovery to a local garage, overnight accommodation, a replacement hire car, motorway fees and repatriation of the vehicle to the UK up to its market value.

That last phrase is the one to weigh. Repatriation capped at market value means an older car worth less than the cost of bringing it home will be abandoned rather than recovered, and you will be offered the value instead. For a fifteen-year-old estate stranded in southern Spain that is a real prospect rather than a theoretical one.

sections.heading: Where the cover thins out
sections.html:
Three limits do most of the work in Eversure's favour on price, and a buyer should see all three before clicking through.

The first is time. No breakdown assistance is available within 48 hours of buying the policy. This is standard practice across the budget end of the market and it exists to stop people buying cover from the hard shoulder, but it does mean a policy bought on a Friday afternoon is no use for a Saturday morning failure to start.

The second is age. The personal product carries a maximum vehicle age of 15 years. Eversure's own breakdown landing page states cover for vehicles under 20 years old, which does not match the 15-year figure on its personal cover page — a discrepancy in the company's own material that is worth resolving with them before you buy if your car is between those ages. Either way, the cap points the wrong way for the drivers most likely to need help. SMMT Motorparc data for 2025 puts 36,676,185 cars on UK roads out of a total parc of 42,549,649 vehicles, with the average car now 9.7 years old and ageing. Cars break down more as they get older, and this policy stops covering them at the point the risk starts climbing.

The third is money. Claims are capped at £15,000 across a policy period, local recovery on Silver reaches 25 miles, and the onward travel options are alternatives rather than a package. None of these is unreasonable at £17.47, but none of them is comparable with a patrol-network membership costing five times as much either.

sections.heading: How complaints are handled, and what the national data shows
sections.html:
Complaints go to complaints@eversure.com, through the contact form on the website, or by post to Eversure Limited at Bury House, 1–3 Bury Street, Guildford GU2 4AW. Eversure says it acknowledges promptly and issues a formal final response within 8 weeks. After that, or if 8 weeks pass without one, the case can go to the Financial Ombudsman Service at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR, on 0800 023 4567, free of charge.

The Ombudsman's annual complaints data for 2025/26, published on 21 May 2026, gives a useful backdrop. It received 214,600 new complaints across all financial products, close to 30% down on the previous year's 305,700, and upheld 30% of the cases it resolved. Roadside assistance insurance appears as its own product line with 950 new cases and a 44% uphold rate. For comparison, car and motorcycle insurance produced 13,420 cases at 35%, commercial vehicle insurance 1,429 at 44%, and motor warranties 511 at 41%.

A 44% uphold rate on roadside assistance is materially above the all-product average and above ordinary car insurance. That figure covers the whole product line rather than any one provider, so it says nothing about Eversure specifically — but it does say that when breakdown disputes reach the Ombudsman, the customer is more often found to have been in the right than in most other financial products.

One gap in the public record is worth flagging. The FCA's general insurance value measures data for 2025, published on 21 July 2026, is the standard place to check claims acceptance rates by product, and vehicle breakdown is partly exempt from it: under the reporting rules at SUP 16.27.7R to 16.27.9R and SUP 16 Annex 48R, breakdown and legal expenses firms do not have to report average claims pay-out, total claims pay-out cost, or the amount by which the top 2% of pay-outs exceed the rest. There is therefore no published acceptance rate to hold any breakdown insurer against, Eversure included.

pros: UK annual cover from £17.47, at the cheap end of a market where patrol memberships run into three figures
National recovery to your home address is included from the Silver tier upward, not held back as an upsell
One policy covers up to four people at the same address rather than a single named driver
Home Start arrives at Gold rather than being reserved for the top tier
Platinum adds misfuelling cover up to £500, including engine parts damaged by the wrong fuel
European annual cover at £50.28 spans 39 territories with trips of up to 90 days
Underwritten by Astrenska Insurance Limited, holding 205% of its solvency capital requirement at 30 April 2024, and backed by the FSCS
Claims line runs 24 hours from the UK, with a stated average response of 46 minutes
cons: No assistance at all within 48 hours of buying the policy, so it cannot rescue a problem you already have
The personal product stops at vehicles 15 years old, while the UK car parc averages 9.7 years and rising — the cars most likely to break down are the ones nearest the cut-off
Eversure's breakdown landing page advertises cover for vehicles under 20 years old while its personal cover page states 15, and the company has not reconciled the two
Home Start costs a tier upgrade, so the cheapest Silver price does not cover a car that will not start on your own drive
Claims are capped at £15,000 per policy period and Silver recovery reaches 25 miles, both well short of unlimited
Onward travel is one option out of three — hotel at £150 solo or £600 for a group, or a hire car at £300 — rather than a combination
European repatriation is limited to the vehicle's market value, which for an older car can mean it is written off abroad rather than brought home
Eversure arranges rather than underwrites, uses different insurers for different products, and does not publish the size of the recovery network its policies rely on
No Defaqto star rating for the breakdown product could be found on Eversure's own pages, so the cover has no published independent benchmark
verdict: Eversure is a broker selling a Collinson-underwritten breakdown policy at a genuinely low price, and the tier structure is more honest than most at this end of the market — national recovery from Silver, Home Start at Gold, misfuelling at Platinum. The catch is eligibility rather than benefits: a 15-year vehicle cap, a 48-hour wait and a £15,000 annual ceiling. For a newer car driven by a household of up to four, £17.47 is hard to argue with. For a fifteen-year-old runaround, check the age limit before you buy rather than after.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites Eversure breakdown cover?
faqs.a: Collinson Insurance, a trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited, under firm reference number 202846. Eversure Limited, firm reference 501311, arranges the policy and handles the sale. Astrenska is authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both the PRA and the FCA, and wrote £221.4m of gross premium in the year to 30 April 2024.

faqs.q: How old can my car be?
faqs.a: Eversure's personal breakdown page gives a maximum vehicle age of 15 years, while its main breakdown page refers to vehicles under 20 years old. The two figures do not agree and the discrepancy needs confirming with Eversure directly if your car sits between them. Size limits are firmer: 3,500kg including load, 7 metres long, 3 metres high and 2.25 metres wide.

faqs.q: Can I claim straight after buying?
faqs.a: No. The policy excludes any breakdown assistance within 48 hours of purchase. If the car is already off the road, this cover will not help with that particular failure.

faqs.q: Does the cheapest tier include help at home?
faqs.a: Not on Silver. Roadside assistance on the entry tier applies once you are at least a mile from your home address. Home Start, which covers a breakdown at or within a mile of home, begins at Gold.

faqs.q: What happens if the car cannot be repaired abroad?
faqs.a: European cover includes repatriation of the vehicle to the UK, but only up to its market value. Where recovery would cost more than the car is worth, expect a payment rather than a lorry.

faqs.q: Where do I go if a claim is refused?
faqs.a: Complain to Eversure first, by email to complaints@eversure.com or in writing to Bury House, 1–3 Bury Street, Guildford GU2 4AW. Eversure aims to issue a final response within 8 weeks. After that you can take the case free of charge to the Financial Ombudsman Service on 0800 023 4567. The Ombudsman upheld 44% of the 950 roadside assistance complaints it resolved in 2025/26, against 30% across all financial products.

title: first direct 1st Account: the £210 Switch, the 7% Saver and the HSBC Rule Behind Both
meta_title: first direct 1st Account: £210 Switch, 7% Saver
meta_description: first direct pays £210 to switch by 2 December 2026, then £175. What the conditions ask, what 7% on the Regular Saver pays, and who the HSBC rule shuts out.
intro:
first direct pays £210 for switching to its 1st Account if the account is opened by 2 December 2026 — £175 on the standing offer plus a £35 boost running since 14 September — charges no monthly fee, and lends the first £250 of an arranged overdraft at 0% EAR. Figures re-read on 9 October 2026 against first direct's own product, rates and charges pages. Account holders who also open the linked Regular Saver get 7.00% AER fixed for twelve months, the highest rate on first direct's own savings list.

It has been running since one minute past midnight on 1 October 1989, when it took more than a thousand calls in its first twenty-four hours as Britain's first telephone-only bank. Midland Bank built it; HSBC inherited it when it bought Midland in June 1992; and since the ringfencing reorganisation of July 2018 it has been a division of HSBC UK Bank plc, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both regulators under Financial Services Register reference 765112. Its home page claims two million customers and it still has no branches at all. In the independent service quality survey every large provider has to publish, dated August 2026, it came joint third of seventeen on 75% and third for online and mobile banking on 78%.

One rule decides whether the cash is available to you, and it is worth knowing before you click. first direct will not pay it to anyone who has held a first direct product before, and its own wording adds: "Sorry, we also can't offer this to people who have opened an HSBC current account on or after 1 January 2018." A great many people opened one in that period. The account itself is open to any UK resident over 18 who has not been bankrupt or in an IVA in the last six years; it is only the money that is restricted.
