sections.heading: Four things in forty-five days, and the £35 that stops in December
sections.html:
The money is not paid for opening an account. It is paid for completing a checklist, and first direct prints the whole checklist rather than burying it. Within 45 days of the account opening you have to switch to it using the Current Account Switch Service, bringing at least two Direct Debits or standing orders with you; pay in £1,000; make five or more debit card payments; and log on to digital banking at least once. Card payments count whether they are made in a shop or online, and whether they come from the plastic or a digital wallet.

Two of those are trivial and two are not. The £1,000 is a single deposit rather than a monthly commitment, which makes this a materially easier offer to complete than the ones that demand a pay-in every month for a year. The two Direct Debits are the real work, because they mean moving live commitments rather than opening an account alongside the one you already use. A switch that carries no Direct Debits does not qualify however much money passes through it.

The amount is the thing that has moved. The standing offer is £175; the £210 in the headline is that £175 with a £35 boost attached, and first direct's own wording limits the boost to accounts "opened between 14 September and 2 December 2026". An account opened on 3 December is worth £35 less on the same four conditions, so the deadline is a real one rather than a sales device. Note which clock it is: the boost depends on the date the account opens, and the 45 days for the checklist run from that date, so an account opened in the last week of the window still has until mid-January to finish.

Payment timing is stated plainly: "You'll get the money by the 20th of the following month in which all criteria has been met." Finish everything in late October and the cash arrives by 20 November. The offer is limited to one payment per customer or joint account, and first direct reserves the right to withdraw it at any time without notice, so a plan built around it a month from now is a plan built on something the bank can remove tomorrow.

sections.heading: Seven per cent, and what seven per cent comes to
sections.html:
The Regular Saver is the reason most people move here, and first direct publishes every number needed to work out what it is worth. The rate is 7.00% AER and gross, fixed for twelve months. You can pay in between £25 and £300 a month by standing order, one payment a month, to a maximum of £3,600 over the year. Interest is calculated daily and credited on the first anniversary. You must already hold the 1st Account to open one.

Now the sum the headline does not do. Pay in the full £300 every month and you finish the year with £3,736.50 — £136.50 of interest on £3,600 of your own money. That is a return of about 3.79% on the total deposited, because only the final month's balance ever earns 7% for any length of time; January's £300 is invested for twelve months, December's for a matter of days. The 7.00% is arithmetically correct and the £136.50 is what reaches your account.

The account is closed to withdrawals for the full term. There are no partial withdrawals: the only way to reach the money early is to close the account, and first direct's terms say that if you do, "you will receive interest up to the date of closure at our Savings Account variable rate" — 1.05% AER at the time of checking, so an early exit costs roughly five-sixths of the interest. At maturity the balance sweeps automatically into a sole Savings Account if you hold one, and if you do not, first direct opens one and moves it there. That takes up to five working days.

The missed-payment question has an answer now, and it is a generous one. first direct's product page says an underpaid month can be made up later — you add the difference to future payments, so long as the running total does not exceed the maximum, and an unused monthly allowance can be carried forward and caught up. Money paid in above the £300 ceiling does not earn the headline rate; it earns 1.05% AER, the same as the ordinary Savings Account. What the page still does not say is whether the 7.00% itself survives a month skipped entirely rather than underpaid, which is worth confirming on the phone before relying on it. The rate table that page sits above is stamped "Rates correct as at 1 December 2022".

sections.heading: The rest of the savings list, and the rung that was added
sections.html:
A current account is a gateway to whatever else the bank sells, and here the drop below the headline is steep. The Savings Account pays 1.05% AER and 1.04% gross on every balance from £1, effective 12 March 2026. The Cash ISA pays 2.75% AER and 2.72% tax-free on all balances, set on 10 November 2025 and variable since. The Bonus Savings Account pays 3.35% AER on balances up to £50,000 in any month you make no withdrawal and do not close the account, and 1.05% in any month you do.

Above all three sits a fixed-term option. The Fixed Rate Savings account's October issue pays 4.50% AER and 4.50% gross on £2,000 or more, with first direct's rate page giving the window as "Current rate available from 9 October 2026 to 18 November 2026" and the deposit maturing on 18 November 2027. The Fixed Rate Cash ISA matches it at 4.50% on £500 or more. Those are issue-dated products rather than standing ones, which is why they need checking on the day rather than taken from any page written a month ago — and the same table still carries a stray line reading "03 April 2025 to 08 May 2025" beside the fixed rate row, which is a superseded window nobody has taken down.

So the list runs 7.00%, 4.50%, 3.35%, 2.75% and 1.05%, and each rung costs something different to stand on. The 7.00% is capped at £300 a month. The 4.50% needs £2,000 locked away until November 2027. The 3.35% is forfeited for any month you touch the money. Only the 1.05% is unconditional, and it is the rate a large balance ends up on. A saver with £20,000 who moves here for the Regular Saver will earn the headline rate on at most £3,600 of it across a year, and has to choose between locking the rest up and accepting 1.05% or 3.35% on it. The 1st Account itself pays no credit interest on any balance, so money left sitting in the current account earns nothing at all.

The Bonus Savings Account is the one worth reading twice. The bonus is applied month by month rather than annually, so a single withdrawal costs you the bonus for that month only rather than for the year — better than the versions of this product that strip a year's bonus for one touch, and worth knowing before you treat it as untouchable.

sections.heading: One compensation limit, and two group pages that disagree about who shares it
sections.html:
Deposit protection rose from £85,000 to £120,000 on 1 December 2025, and to £240,000 on a joint account. Most comparison pages have not caught up. The part that matters more here is who the limit is shared with, because first direct is not a bank in its own right — it is a division of HSBC UK Bank plc, trading under one banking licence with several stablemates.

On this one point the group's own pages do not agree, so neither count is printed here as a fact. first direct's own page at firstdirect.com/fscs/ names the brands as "HSBC UK, HSBC Private Bank, first direct, and M&S Bank". HSBC's equivalent page at hsbc.co.uk/fscs/ gives the same four and adds M&S Savings and Investments. Four brands are on both lists and share one £120,000 between them; whether a fifth sits inside the same limit is answered one way on one page of the group and another way on the other. Anyone holding money with M&S Savings and Investments as well as first direct should get that confirmed in writing rather than assume a second limit exists.

What is not in doubt is the arithmetic on the four. A saver holding £80,000 at HSBC UK and £80,000 at first direct has £160,000 on deposit and £120,000 of protection, and first direct's wording is that anything above the limit across those brands is "unlikely to be covered". Nobody buying a savings account chooses a brand expecting it to share a ceiling with three others, and the structure is not mentioned on the product pages where the decision is made.

The flip side is real and worth saying. Being part of HSBC UK Bank plc means a ringfenced retail bank's balance sheet behind a brand with no branches, and the regulatory apparatus that comes with it: a route to the Financial Ombudsman Service at no cost, and a firm reference number a customer can check. The FCA has published a warning about a cloned site trading as thefirstdirect.com, with an overseas phone number and its own support email address, dated 12 November 2024. The genuine firm's reference is 765112 and its registered address is 1 Centenary Square, Birmingham B1 1HQ. Anyone dealing with the clone has neither ombudsman nor compensation scheme.

sections.heading: Borrowing works out at 23p a day, and the regulator has been here before
sections.html:
The first £250 of an arranged overdraft is free. Above it the rate is 39.9% EAR variable, which produces a representative rate of 30.5% APR variable on an assumed arranged overdraft of £1,200. first direct publishes worked costs rather than leaving the reader to compute them: borrowing £500 costs £1.63 over seven days, £7.00 over thirty days and £13.99 over sixty.

Those three figures are worth taking apart, because they show what the headline rate actually does. On a £500 overdraft only £250 bears interest, and £7.00 over thirty days is 23.3p a day on that £250 — the same 23.3p that produces £1.63 in seven days and £13.99 in sixty. Over a full year that is £85.16 on £250, or about 34.1% of it. The 39.9% is the EAR, which is what 34.1% of daily interest comes to once twelve monthly interest debits are themselves left on the balance. The practical consequence is that 39.9% must not be compounded a second time: an arranged overdraft of £1,200 run flat out for a year costs £379.05, because 39.9% applies to the £950 above the free slice, not £478.80 and not more. The £250 is also why a 39.9% EAR shows up as a 30.5% representative APR on £1,200: the free slice is a fifth of the assumed limit.

Two details sit outside the headline. From 19 May 2026 first direct stopped charging interest on unarranged overdrafts altogether, though it may still decline payments that would create one — a meaningful change, and one the bank admits has not reached its own paperwork: "We are in the process of updating our literature to reflect this change." And the interest-free £250 does not apply at all to customers with an Offset Mortgage linked to their 1st Account. That mortgage is closed to new customers, so the carve-out now affects only an existing cohort — but it is exactly the cohort most likely to assume it is getting the group's best terms. Interest is calculated daily and taken monthly, with at least fourteen days' notice, and money paid in before 11.45pm counts for that day.

The conduct record behind the lending is a matter of public record. On 23 May 2024 the FCA fined HSBC UK Bank plc, HSBC Bank plc and Marks and Spencer Financial Services plc £6,280,100 for failures in the treatment of customers in arrears or financial difficulty between June 2017 and October 2018. The regulator found the banks did not properly consider people's circumstances when payments were missed, did not always assess affordability before agreeing payment plans, and sometimes took disproportionate action. More than 1.5 million customers were put at risk of harm and £185 million of redress was paid. The penalty was reduced by 30% for settlement, from £8,971,600. HSBC identified the problem itself and spent £94 million putting it right, which the FCA took into account — but the period covered is recent enough, and the customer count large enough, that anyone planning to run an overdraft here should know it happened.

sections.heading: Two service records inside one legal entity
sections.html:
Because first direct is a division rather than a separate company, it reports its complaints inside HSBC UK Bank plc's return — but under its own name, which makes a direct comparison possible that is usually impossible. For the half year from 1 January to 30 June 2026, first direct opened 6,076 banking and credit card complaints at a rate of 1.47 per 1,000 accounts, closed 71.1% of them within three days, and upheld 48.4%. The same entity's combined figure was 73,367 complaints at 2.26 per 1,000, 60.1% closed in three days and 58.8% upheld.

Fewer complaints per account, settled faster, and fewer of them found justified: on its own regulatory return, the branchless division is running a better operation than the branch network it sits inside. General administration and customer service was the largest driver on both sides. That return is also the most recent one that exists — re-read on 9 October 2026 it still covered the first half of the year, because HSBC publishes on calendar half-years and the second-half figures are not due yet. Any page quoting a newer period for this bank is quoting something nobody has published.

The independent survey every large provider must publish, carried out by Ipsos for the Competition and Markets Authority between July 2025 and June 2026 across 17,055 people, put first direct joint third of seventeen on overall service quality at 75%, level with Nationwide and behind Monzo on 79% and Starling on 76%. It ranked third for online and mobile banking on 78%, behind Monzo on 85% and Starling on 83%. Its weakest showing was overdraft services, fifth on 70%. It is the one provider in the survey with no score at all for services in branches, for the obvious reason.

Not every product does as well. first direct's investments complaints over the same half year ran at 3.83 per 1,000 client accounts and were upheld 82.5% of the time — four in five decided against the bank, on a book small enough that the absolute number is only 83, and only 35.0% of them closed inside three days. Home finance complaints ran at 424 cases, 3.54 per 1,000 balances, and were upheld 60.4%. The current account is the strong part of this business, not the whole of it.

sections.heading: Charges that survive the no-fee headline, and a rate table dated 2020
sections.html:
"No monthly fee" is accurate and unusually complete here, because there is also no ongoing monthly pay-in to keep the account free — the £1,000 is a one-off condition of the switch cash, not a standing obligation. Travellers get more than that: first direct charges nothing of its own for debit card payments in a foreign currency, or for cash machine withdrawals outside the UK, though the machine's operator may still levy its own charge.

The tariff is not empty, and the remaining charges are the kind that arrive unannounced. An inward payment in a foreign currency worth more than £100 equivalent costs £8.00, which on a £120 payment from abroad is 6.7% of it. A status enquiry — the reference a bank gives a landlord or a lender about your account — costs £10.72 including VAT. An indemnity for a lost share certificate costs 0.5% of the value with a £50 minimum. Cancelling a cheque, copying a cheque, inward sterling payments and duplicate statements are all free.

What the paperwork does not do is keep pace with the product. The 1st Account's own rows on first direct's rates page carry the line "The rates are correct as at 14 March 2020", on the same page where the personal loan rows are stamped 6 August 2026 and the savings rows carry effective dates of 10 November 2025 and 12 March 2026. The numbers themselves are current — the 0% on £250, the 39.9% EAR and the 30.5% APR all match what the live product page advertises today, which is the reason they are printed here — but a six-year-old date stamp on a rate table is the sort of thing that makes a reader doubt the figure beside it. The same habit shows up in the customer count: the home page heading claims "2 million customers", while the description the same page publishes to search engines says "over 1.7 million UK customers", and neither carries a date. Both are first direct's own words, so no number is asserted here.

The structural cost is the one no tariff shows. There are no branches, and there never have been: everything is the app, the website or the telephone on 03 456 100 100. Paying in cash means using another bank's counter arrangements, and a customer who wants to sit opposite somebody to sort out a problem has bought the wrong account. That has been the deal since 1989 and the service scores suggest most customers are content with it, but it is a deal, not an oversight.

pros: £210 for switching on accounts opened by 2 December 2026, with a one-off £1,000 deposit rather than a monthly pay-in to keep it
No monthly account fee and no ongoing minimum funding requirement on the account itself
The linked Regular Saver pays 7.00% AER fixed for 12 months, and an underpaid month can be made up later
A fixed rate option at 4.50% AER sits above the instant-access rates, on £2,000 or more
First £250 of an arranged overdraft at 0% EAR, and no interest on unarranged overdrafts since 19 May 2026
No first direct charge on foreign-currency card spending or on cash withdrawals outside the UK
Joint third of seventeen providers on overall service quality at 75% in the August 2026 independent survey, and third on online and mobile banking at 78%
1.47 banking complaints per 1,000 accounts in the first half of 2026 against 2.26 across HSBC UK Bank plc as a whole, with 71.1% closed inside three days
Deposits protected to £120,000, or £240,000 jointly, behind a ringfenced bank authorised under firm reference 765112
cons: Anyone who opened an HSBC current account on or after 1 January 2018, or has ever held a first direct product, is barred from the cash — a rule that excludes a large share of the people most likely to look
The £35 boost stops on 2 December 2026, after which the same four conditions are worth £175
The 7.00% Regular Saver returns £136.50 on £3,600 paid in over a year, an effective 3.79% on the money deposited, because the cap is £300 a month
No withdrawals are possible from the Regular Saver during its 12-month term, and closing it early drops the whole balance to the standard variable savings rate of 1.05% AER
The 1st Account pays no credit interest on any balance, and the everyday Savings Account pays 1.05% AER from £1
Arranged borrowing above £250 costs 39.9% EAR variable — £379.05 a year on the assumed £1,200 limit
The interest-free £250 is withdrawn entirely from customers with an Offset Mortgage linked to the account

The group's two FSCS pages disagree about whether M&S Savings and Investments shares first direct's £120,000 limit, and the four brands that certainly do share it are not mentioned on any product page
The 1st Account's rate table is stamped "correct as at 14 March 2020" and the Regular Saver's "1 December 2022", on a site whose loan and savings rows carry 2026 dates
The home page claims two million customers while the description the same page gives search engines says over 1.7 million, and neither is dated
Investments complaints were upheld 82.5% of the time in the first half of 2026, against 48.4% on banking

HSBC UK Bank plc was fined £6,280,100 on 23 May 2024 over the treatment of customers in arrears between June 2017 and October 2018, with 1.5 million customers put at risk and £185 million of redress paid
No branches anywhere, and first direct still does not say whether the 7.00% survives a month skipped altogether rather than underpaid
verdict: Worth the switch for two numbers, one deadline and one exclusion. The £210 asks for a single £1,000 deposit rather than a year of monthly pay-ins, but £35 of it is a boost that stops on 2 December 2026, so the offer is better today than it will be in the new year. The Regular Saver's 7.00% is the best rate on first direct's own list, though it returns £136.50 on £3,600, not seven per cent of your savings. The exclusion is the thing to check first: open an HSBC current account any time since 1 January 2018 and the money is not available to you, whatever else you qualify for. Beyond the offer it is a well-run account with a better complaints record than its own parent, a genuinely free hand abroad, and a savings list that falls to 1.05% the moment you step off the top rung.

faqs.q: How much does first direct pay for switching, and what do I have to do?
faqs.a: £210 on an account opened between 14 September and 2 December 2026 — £175 plus a £35 boost. Within 45 days of opening you need to switch to first direct using the Current Account Switch Service bringing at least two Direct Debits or standing orders, pay in £1,000, make five or more debit card payments, and log on to digital banking. The money arrives by the 20th of the month after you finish the last of those, and it is limited to one payment per customer or joint account.

faqs.q: What happens if I open the account after 2 December 2026?
faqs.a: You would be on the standing offer of £175 rather than £210, on the same four conditions. The £35 boost is tied to the date the account is opened, not the date the switch completes, so opening inside the window still leaves the full 45 days to finish the checklist. first direct also reserves the right to withdraw the whole offer at any time.

faqs.q: Can I get the switch payment if I already bank with HSBC?
faqs.a: Not if you opened an HSBC current account on or after 1 January 2018, and not if you have ever held a first direct product. first direct's own terms exclude both groups. You can still open the account — the restriction is on the money, not on eligibility — provided you are over 18, resident in the UK and have not been bankrupt or in an IVA in the last six years.

faqs.q: How much will I actually earn on the 7% Regular Saver?
faqs.a: £136.50 if you pay in the maximum £300 every month for twelve months, on £3,600 of your own money — an effective return of about 3.79% on the total deposited. The 7.00% AER is correct, but the £300 monthly cap means most of your money is only invested for part of the year. No withdrawals are allowed during the term, and closing early drops the interest to the Savings Account variable rate, 1.05% AER at the time of checking. An underpaid month can be made up later; anything above the £300 ceiling earns 1.05% rather than 7.00%.

faqs.q: Is first direct a separate bank from HSBC?
faqs.a: No. It is a division of HSBC UK Bank plc, which is authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority and the PRA under firm reference number 765112. The practical consequence is deposit protection: the £120,000 limit is shared with HSBC UK, HSBC Private Bank and M&S Bank, so holding money at two of them does not give you two limits. The group's first direct and HSBC pages disagree about whether M&S Savings and Investments is inside the same limit, so check that one directly if it applies to you.

faqs.q: What does an overdraft cost at first direct?
faqs.a: The first £250 of an arranged overdraft is free, at 0% EAR. Above that the rate is 39.9% EAR variable, giving a representative 30.5% APR on an assumed £1,200 limit. first direct's own worked examples put £500 of borrowing at £1.63 for seven days, £7.00 for thirty and £13.99 for sixty — 23.3p a day on the £250 that bears interest. A £1,200 overdraft left outstanding for a year costs £379.05. Since 19 May 2026 first direct has charged no interest on unarranged overdrafts. Customers with a linked Offset Mortgage do not get the interest-free £250 at all.

faqs.q: What is the best savings rate first direct offers?
faqs.a: 7.00% AER on the Regular Saver, fixed for twelve months and capped at £300 a month. Next is the Fixed Rate Savings account's October issue at 4.50% AER on £2,000 or more, with the rate available from 9 October to 18 November 2026 and the deposit maturing on 18 November 2027; the Fixed Rate Cash ISA matches it at 4.50% on £500 or more. The Bonus Savings Account pays 3.35% AER up to £50,000 in a month with no withdrawal, the Cash ISA 2.75% AER, and the instant-access Savings Account 1.05% AER.

title: Game Over Bean Bags
meta_title: Game Over bean bags reviewed: prices, sizes and refills
meta_description: Game Over bean bags run £39.99 to £109.99 with free UK delivery and a 24-month guarantee. Prices, sizes, refill costs and returns, checked 18 September 2026.

headline.label: Cheapest gaming seat, delivered
headline.value: £39.99 delivered — Mini Gaming Bean Bag, 51 x 47 x 46cm, free mainland UK delivery, checked 18 September 2026

intro:
Game Over's Classic Gaming Bean Bag is £74.99, the Gaming Lounger £109.99 and the smallest seat in the range £39.99, each with free mainland UK delivery and, on the Classic, a 24-month guarantee. Those prices were taken from gameoverstore.co.uk on 18 September 2026. The shop belongs to Game Over Ltd of Handsworth, Birmingham, company number 12467164.

That company was incorporated on 17 February 2020 and files under SIC code 13921, manufacture of soft furnishings, which is consistent with the shop's claim that its bean bags are "designed and manufactured in the heart of the Midlands". Its registered office, Unit 15a Alexandra Trading Estate, Alexandra Road, is the same unit the site prints as its returns address. This is a maker selling its own output rather than a storefront forwarding orders to a warehouse abroad.

The range is narrower than a general retailer's and better documented than most small shops manage. Four seat shapes — a compact 8-Bit chair at £54.99, the Classic at £74.99, the Cloudrunner limited edition at £89.99 and the 120cm Lounger at £109.99 — sit alongside footstools, printed cushions at £22.99, a floor mat, a blanket and bags of replacement beads. Every item is quoted with its dimensions, dispatch is advertised at one working day and delivery at three to five.

key_facts.label: Who you are buying from
key_facts.value: Game Over Ltd, company number 12467164, incorporated 17 February 2020, SIC 13921 — manufacture of soft furnishings

key_facts.label: Price range
key_facts.value: £22.99 for a printed gaming cushion up to £109.99 for the Gaming Lounger; 28 products listed on 18 September 2026

key_facts.label: Classic chair
key_facts.value: £74.99 against a £84.97 comparison price, L83cm x W60cm x H83cm

key_facts.label: Filling
key_facts.value: Fire-retardant EPS polystyrene beads; a Classic chair takes 12 cubic feet, a Lounger 15

key_facts.label: Replacement beads
key_facts.value: £19.99 for 5 cubic feet, £29.99 for 10 cubic feet

key_facts.label: Delivery
key_facts.value: Free to mainland UK, dispatch quoted at 1 working day, arrival at 3 to 5 working days

key_facts.label: Returns and guarantee
key_facts.value: 30 days to return, 24-month guarantee advertised on the Classic chair

key_facts.label: Rules that apply
key_facts.value: No financial regulator; fire safety sits under the Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) Regulations 1988, amended 30 October 2025

sections.heading: What £39.99 to £109.99 gets you, measured
sections.html:
Game Over publishes a dimension for every seat it sells, which sounds unremarkable until you try to find the same figures on a marketplace listing. The Classic Gaming Bean Bag is L83cm x W60cm x H83cm and costs £74.99. The 8-Bit compact chair is L73cm x W49cm x H73cm at £54.99. The Lounger stretches to L120cm and stands 83cm high at £109.99, and the footstool is W60cm x H42cm x D40cm at £44.99. The printed cushions are L56cm x H27cm and £22.99 each.

The Mini Gaming Bean Bag is the outlier at 51 x 47 x 46cm and £39.99, sold as a saddle-shaped seat for children aged six to thirteen. It is the cheapest way into the range and the only product on the site aimed at a specific age band.

Construction is the same story across the range: a water-resistant polyester outer, double-stitched, filled with fire-retardant EPS polystyrene beads, with pockets, a velcro headphone hook and metal air vents. The fabric is water-resistant rather than waterproof — the shop says so itself — and the cleaning instruction is a damp cloth, not a washing machine. On a £74.99 chair that a teenager will eat crisps in, that is worth knowing before rather than after.

sections.heading: The beads are the part the law actually tests
sections.html:
A bean bag has no financial regulator, no ombudsman and no approved dispute scheme behind it. It does have one set of mandatory rules, and they are about fire. The Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) Regulations 1988 cover bean bags and floor cushions by name, and what they regulate is the filling: a non-foam filling material has to be tested to BS 5852: Part 2 using ignition source 2, and the finished item has to carry a durable permanent label securely attached to an outside surface.

Those regulations changed recently. The Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) (Amendment) Regulations 2025 were made on 28 April 2025 and came into force on 30 October 2025. They removed the separate display-label requirement at the point of sale, narrowed the definition of furniture so that products intended for babies and very young children fall outside it, and doubled the window for bringing a prosecution from six months to twelve. The permanent label on the item survived all of that; it is still the thing to look for when the parcel arrives.

The reason this is not a technicality is in the Office for Product Safety and Standards research report of April 2023. Upholstered items were the material first ignited in 12% of domestic fire incidents but accounted for 29% of the deaths, and were the main material driving fire development in 16% of fires but 43% of the deaths. The same report classifies bean bags as upholstered items, usually larger than 60cm x 60cm, filled with expanded polystyrene beads. Fire deaths across Great Britain fell from a peak of about 1,100 in 1980 to roughly 300 in 2019, and tighter furniture rules are part of why.

Game Over describes its beads as fire-retardant on every product page. It does not publish a test reference, a standard number or the wording of the permanent label anywhere on the site. Asking for it costs an email, and a seller who cannot produce it has a problem: an offence under section 12 of the Consumer Protection Act 1987 carries up to six months' imprisonment or a fine at level 5 on the standard scale, or both.

sections.heading: Refilling one, and what doing it properly costs
sections.html:
Every bean bag flattens. Game Over is straightforward about it — its own answers say the filling will compress with use and a top-up will be needed, and that a heavy-duty zip at the base is there for the purpose. The Classic chair also has an inner liner, so the beads are held in a bag inside the cover rather than loose against the zip.

The shop sells beads by volume and publishes a capacity guide: 12 cubic feet fills a bean bag, 15 fills a Lounger, 3.5 fills a footstool. A 5 cubic foot bag is £19.99, reduced from £21.99, and 10 cubic feet is £29.99, reduced from £32.99. There is a 2.5 cubic foot option listed at the same £19.99 as the 5 cubic foot bag, which is odd pricing; it was showing as sold out on 18 September 2026.

Run the arithmetic before you assume refills are cheap. Filling a Classic chair from empty needs 12 cubic feet, which means the 10 and the 5 together at £49.98 — two thirds of what the chair itself costs. A Lounger takes exactly 15 cubic feet, the same £49.98, against a £109.99 purchase price. A genuine top-up after a couple of years is a £19.99 job and that is the realistic case, but anyone planning to strip and refill a bag completely should price it first.

sections.heading: Game Over Ltd on paper
sections.html:
The register tells a short, consistent story. Game Over Ltd was incorporated on 17 February 2020 and filed dormant accounts for the years to 28 February 2023 and 29 February 2024. On 26 February 2025 it shortened its accounting period to 31 December 2024, and on 29 September 2025 it filed micro-entity accounts for that year. Micro-entity accounts do not include a turnover figure, so nobody outside the company knows what it sells in a year — that is the filing option a small company is entitled to use, not evidence of anything being hidden. Its latest confirmation statement was made on 10 January 2026 and the next set of accounts is due by 30 September 2026. A director was appointed on 3 January 2024 and another terminated six days later.

One loose thread is worth flagging rather than asserting. The shop's contact page lists social accounts under two different names, gameover_uk on some platforms and LOFT25Gaming on others. Loft 25 is a separate Birmingham bean bag and soft-furnishings brand; Loft 25 Ltd, company 06170952, was incorporated on 20 March 2007 as Changing Sofas Limited, renamed on 4 October 2019 and dissolved on 1 January 2026, while Loft 25 Group Ltd, company 12931054, remains active as a holding company at a different Birmingham address. No connection between the two businesses is published on either site, and the shared handle is suggestive rather than conclusive. It needs confirming with the company before anyone treats it as fact.

sections.heading: Where the price tags and the refund policy contradict each other
sections.html:
On 18 September 2026 every one of the 28 items in the shop's all-products collection carried a struck-through comparison price. Cushions were £22.99 from £25.29, the Classic £74.99 from £84.97, the Lounger £109.99 from £150.00, the blanket £29.99 from £32.99. The footstool was £44.99 from £45.99, which is a reduction of one pound presented as a sale.

The Chartered Trading Standards Institute's Guidance for Traders on Pricing Practices, free at businesscompanion.info and updated on 14 August 2025 to take in the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, sets out the test. A price comparison should run for a period no longer than the higher price was actually charged, and a recommended retail price must not be false and must not be created purely to present the appearance of a discount. That is a test a shopper can run without any help: note today's prices, come back in a fortnight, and see whether the sale ever ends.

The sharper problem is what the refund policy does with those price tags. It says, in terms, that only regular priced items may be refunded and that sale items cannot be. If every product in the shop is displayed as a sale item, that sentence refuses refunds on the entire catalogue.

It also claims more than the law allows. Under the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, a consumer buying at distance has 14 days from the day the goods arrive to cancel, and regulation 28 — the list of exceptions to that right — contains nothing at all about sale, clearance or discounted goods. Made-to-measure items are excepted, perishables are excepted, sealed goods unsealed after delivery are excepted. A discounted bean bag is not. To be fair to the shop, its 30-day window is more generous than the statutory 14 days; the carve-out inside it is the part that does not stand up.

Two smaller things sit in the same small print. Return postage is the buyer's responsibility and is deducted from the refund, which is lawful if you are told in advance but expensive on an item the size of a Lounger. And the terms of service say the agreement is "governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of 15a Alexandra Trading Estate, Alexandra Road, Birmingham, B210PG" — an address where a jurisdiction should be, which is store-platform boilerplate nobody finished filling in.

That same address is worth a second look. The site prints the returns postcode as B210PG. Companies House records the registered office as B21 0PD. One letter separates them, and it is the address a customer posts a £74.99 chair back to.

sections.heading: A bean bag for a six-year-old, and a warning Britain does not require
sections.html:
The Mini Gaming Bean Bag at £39.99 is sold for children aged six to thirteen, and the shop's own answers describe the range as suitable for all ages. That makes the safety question concrete rather than theoretical, because loose polystyrene beads are a choking and suffocation risk to small children and a bean bag is a container a child can climb into.

Australia has had a mandatory rule about this since 2014. Its Consumer Goods (Bean Bags) Safety Standard requires a child-resistant slide fastener on every opening through which filling can be added or removed — in practice a zip with the tag removed that locks shut — and a warning in fixed words on the bag, on any cover and on the packaging of refill beads: "WARNING: Children can suffocate if bean bag filling is swallowed or inhaled. Do not let children climb inside this bean bag. A bean bag is not a safe sleeping surface for an infant under 12 months of age."

Britain has no bean-bag-specific standard of that kind. What reaches a bean bag here is the 1988 fire regulations and the general duty on any consumer product to be safe. Game Over's design helps on the main risk — the inner liner keeps beads away from the outer zip — but its own answers describe a heavy-duty zip at the base for refilling, nothing on the product pages says whether that fastener is child-resistant, and no suffocation warning appears anywhere on the site. Neither point is an allegation, and both are worth an email before buying the Mini for a young child.

pros: Free mainland UK delivery on everything, with dispatch quoted at one working day and arrival at three to five
A 24-month guarantee advertised on the Classic chair, well beyond the 30-day returns window most small shops stop at
Dimensions published for every seat, so the space can be measured before anything is ordered
Replacement beads sold separately from £19.99, so a flattened bag is a £20 problem rather than a £74.99 one
Registered at Companies House under the code for manufacturing soft furnishings, which supports the made-in-the-Midlands claim
An inner liner on the Classic chair keeps the beads away from the outer zip
cons: The refund policy says only regular priced items can be refunded, and on 18 September 2026 all 28 products were displaying a struck-through comparison price
Regulation 28 of the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 lists no exception for sale or discounted goods, so that clause claims more than the law gives
No company number or registered office appears anywhere on the site, which Regulation 25 of the 2015 trading disclosures regulations requires of a company website
The returns address is printed as B21 0PG while Companies House records B21 0PD, on the address a customer posts a chair back to
The governing law clause names a Birmingham street address instead of a jurisdiction, which is unfinished store-platform boilerplate
Beads are described as fire-retardant but no test standard or permanent-label wording is published, on a product the 1988 fire regulations cover by name
Return postage falls on the buyer and is deducted from the refund, which is a real cost on an item the size of the 120cm Lounger
verdict: Game Over is a small Birmingham manufacturer that publishes more hard detail than most shops its size: prices, dimensions, filling volumes, dispatch times and a 24-month guarantee on its main chair. At £74.99 for the Classic and £39.99 for the children's Mini, with free mainland delivery and beads from £19.99 to keep them going, the product side of the proposition is honest and easy to check. The paperwork is where it slips. A refund policy that excludes sale items, in a shop where everything is a sale item, is both self-defeating and wider than the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 allow; the missing company number, the one-letter postcode difference and the unfinished governing-law clause all point the same way, at small-print nobody has read since the store was set up. None of that makes the bean bags worse, and all of it is fixable in an afternoon. Ask for the fire-safety label and the returns address in writing before you order, and buy on the product rather than the terms.

faqs.q: How much do Game Over bean bags cost?
faqs.a: On 18 September 2026 the Mini for children aged six to thirteen was £39.99, the compact 8-Bit chair £54.99, the Classic £74.99, the Cloudrunner limited edition £89.99 and the Gaming Lounger £109.99. Footstools were £44.99 and printed cushions £22.99. Delivery to mainland Britain is free on all of them.

faqs.q: What is inside them, and are they fire-safe?
faqs.a: They are filled with EPS polystyrene beads that Game Over describes as fire-retardant, inside a water-resistant, double-stitched polyester cover. Bean bags are named in the Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) Regulations 1988, which require the filling to pass BS 5852: Part 2 at ignition source 2 and the finished item to carry a permanent label. Game Over does not publish that test reference, so ask for it and check the label on the item when it arrives.

faqs.q: How much filling does one take, and what do refills cost?
faqs.a: Game Over's capacity guide gives 12 cubic feet for a bean bag, 15 for the Lounger and 3.5 for a footstool. Beads are £19.99 for 5 cubic feet and £29.99 for 10. A routine top-up is therefore about £20; filling a Classic chair from empty needs both bags at £49.98, which is two thirds of the price of the chair.

faqs.q: Can I send one back if I change my mind?
faqs.a: The shop advertises 30 days, which is longer than the law requires, but its policy also says sale items cannot be refunded — and every item in the shop was showing a sale price when this page was checked. Under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 you have 14 days from delivery to cancel a distance purchase, and regulation 28 lists no exception for discounted goods. Return postage is the buyer's and comes out of the refund.

faqs.q: Is a bean bag safe for a young child?
faqs.a: The risk is loose beads being swallowed or inhaled, and a child climbing inside. Australia has required a child-resistant zip and a fixed suffocation warning on bean bags since 2014; Britain has no equivalent standard, and no such warning appears on Game Over's pages. The Classic chair's inner liner reduces the exposure. If the Mini is for a six-year-old, ask the company directly whether the base fastener is child-resistant before ordering.

title: Gusto Camp Campsites and Resorts
meta_title: Gustocamp: No ATOL, and 100% Charged From 28 Days Out
meta_description: Gustocamp rents luxury mobile homes at Italian campsites for a 20% deposit. It sells no travel, holds no ATOL, and charges the full cost from 28 days out.

headline.label: Cancellation
headline.value: 100% of the total travel sum from 28 days before arrival

disclosure: we earn a commission if you book through the link on this page. It costs you nothing. The cancellation scale, the fees and the liability wording below are quoted from Gustocamp’s own booking conditions, including where they count against the sale.
intro:
Gustocamp does one thing and does it properly: it puts its own luxury mobile homes and safari tents on established Italian campsites and rents them to you fully equipped, with air conditioning and a shaded wooden terrace as standard. It has been at it “for over 25 years”, and the sites it uses — Union Lido, Marina di Venezia, Pra’ delle Torri, Park Albatros — are among the better-known camping villages in Europe.

The deposit is modest, at 20% of the rental, or 10% on an early booking, with the balance due six weeks before you arrive.

Two things to understand before you book, and we go into both below. Gustocamp sells you the accommodation, not the journey — there is no ATOL and no package protection, and it says in writing that it is not liable for flights, ferries, car hire or coach travel you arrange. And the cancellation scale is severe: 100% of the total travel sum from 28 days before arrival.

sections.heading: What you pay, and when
sections.html:
The payment structure is clear, which is to its credit. All amounts as published, in euros:

StageAmount
Deposit, regular booking20% of the rental, plus the reservation fee and any cancellation insurance, within two weeks of the invoice
Deposit, early booking10% of the total
Reservation fee€29.00
BalanceNo later than six weeks before the confirmed arrival date
Security deposit on arrival€100.00 for mobile homes and Premium safari tents, €50.00 for Gusto safari tents, reserved by SEPA form
Change of dates, accommodation or campsite€25.00 per reservation, plus any extra cost arising
Transfer of a reservation to someone else€25.00

A 10% early-booking deposit is genuinely low for this kind of holiday, and holding a pitch at a top Adriatic site for a tenth of the price nine months out is a reasonable deal. Note that the published discounts are percentages rather than prices — we saw up to 40% off selected September accommodation and up to 30% early-booking discount for 2027 — and no actual prices are published on the pages we read, so you have to run a search to find out what a week costs.

One practical point for a UK buyer on a .co.uk website: the fees are set in euros. The €29 reservation fee, the €25 amendment fee and the €100 security hold will each cost you whatever your card’s rate and non-sterling fee make them on the day. Use a card that does not charge for euro transactions.

sections.heading: The cancellation scale, which is the hardest thing here
sections.html:
Quoted exactly from the booking conditions, with the €29.00 reservation fee payable on top:

When you cancelYou pay
Up to 42 days before arrival20% of the total travel sum
From 42 days to 28 days before60% of the total travel sum
From 28 days to the day before100% of the total travel sum
On the day, or a no-show100% of the total travel sum

Read the middle row again, because it is the one that catches families. At six weeks out you already owe 60% — and six weeks out is also when the balance falls due, so the money is leaving your account at exactly the point the penalty jumps. At four weeks out you owe the lot.

For a July or August family holiday booked in January, that means your commitment becomes effectively total in June, before the school term has even ended and well before anyone knows whether a child will be ill or a job will change.

Gustocamp does sell cancellation insurance, and on this scale it is worth pricing rather than skipping. But read what it is: the conditions state that Gustocamp “offers only cancellation insurance, not travel insurance”. Those are different products, and you need the second one as well.

Note also that the conditions describe only one route for a change: €25 plus any price difference. Moving a date is cheaper than cancelling and rebooking, so if your plans wobble, ask about a change before you ask about a refund.

sections.heading: No ATOL, no package: what that means for your journey
sections.html:
This is the most important structural fact on the page, and it is not a criticism so much as a description of what you are buying.

Gustocamp rents you accommodation. It holds no ATOL and claims none, and it says plainly that it “cannot be held liable for any services booked by you (e.g. flight tickets, car rental, boat crossing, coach travel, etc.)”. Those are not part of its contract with you.

So the chain of risk runs like this. You book the mobile home with Gustocamp and the ferry or the flight with somebody else. If the crossing is cancelled, the airline fails or the strike is at the port, your accommodation booking stands and the cancellation scale above still applies. There is no package organiser to hold responsible for the whole trip, because there is no package.

That is normal for accommodation-only bookings and it is a legitimate way to sell holidays — it is also precisely why a flight-inclusive holiday with an ATOL number costs more. What it means in practice:

  • Buy travel insurance that covers travel disruption, not just medical cover, and buy it when you book rather than before you travel.
  • Book the crossing or the flight on a credit card, so you have a separate route if that supplier fails.
  • Do not book non-refundable travel for dates you could still lose to the 100% accommodation window, or you can end up paying twice.

Gustocamp is explicit that you need your own cover: “It is therefore very important that you have valid third-party liability insurance and travel insurance.” Take that at face value.

sections.heading: Who you are contracting with, and the gaps in the paperwork
sections.html:
The company is Dutch. The footer gives Gustocamp, Saturnusstraat 60, 2516 AH The Hague, the Netherlands, and the booking conditions state that “a contract between you and Gustocamp is formed” once you accept the travel conditions or complete a reservation.

Three things we looked for and did not find, each of which would normally be published:

  • No legal entity name. “Gustocamp” is a trading name; no limited company, BV or other registered entity is named on the pages we read.
  • No company registration number. There is no Dutch Chamber of Commerce (KvK) number and no UK company number anywhere we could see.
  • No governing law. The booking conditions do not say which country’s law applies to the contract — and with a Dutch seller, a UK customer and an Italian campsite, that is three candidates and no answer.

There is also no named dispute resolution scheme, no ABTA membership and no Dutch equivalent cited, and complaints have a hard deadline: they must be in writing “within one month after the end of the rental period”, and later complaints “will not be accepted”. If something goes wrong, write it up as soon as you are home, with photographs.

On liability the wording is broad: “Gustocamp is not liable for (including but not limited to) death, personal injury illness, loss, theft”, while you are liable for damage to the accommodation caused by you or your party — which is what the €100 SEPA hold is for.

The one thing that is better than we expected: there is a UK telephone number, +44 (0)1706 438006, and a uk email address. For a foreign operator selling into Britain, a real UK landline rather than a form is worth something.

sections.heading: Where you would actually be staying
sections.html:
The destinations are narrow and that is a strength, not a weakness — this is a specialist, not a catalogue.

Italy, Adriatic coast: Union Lido Mare, Marina di Venezia, Pra’ delle Torri, Garden Paradiso, Spiaggia e Mare, Tahiti, Sant’ Angelo and Eraclea Mare. Lake Garda: Bella Italia, Cisano San Vito and Villaggio Eden. Tuscany: Park Albatros, Norcenni Girasole and Montescudaio. Austria: Bella Austria in Styria.

Those are serious camping villages with pools, pitches on the sand and their own restaurants, and for a family who wants a resort without a hotel price they are a sound choice. The accommodation is Gustocamp’s own: three safari tent types and four mobile home types, including two- and three-bedroom homes and a “Gusto Baby”, with air conditioning and a terrace standard and free WiFi at some sites. Four arrival days a week are possible, which is more flexible than the Saturday-to-Saturday rule much of this market still runs on.

A small inconsistency to flag, since we counted: the UK site advertises 15 campsites while the pages name 12 in Italy and one in Austria. The partner listings we read give a slightly different set again. Check that the specific site you want is bookable rather than trusting the headline count.

And a word on what “we take care of your holiday from A to Z” means here: it covers the accommodation end to end — the unit, the equipment, the pitch, the campsite booking. It does not cover getting there. Read that claim in the light of the liability clause above rather than as a promise about your journey.

verdict: Gustocamp is a proper specialist: its own well-equipped mobile homes and safari tents, on a short list of genuinely good Italian camping villages, with a 10% early-booking deposit and four arrival days a week. If you are driving to the Adriatic or Lake Garda with children and you want a resort without a hotel bill, it does exactly what it says. Go in clear on two things. You are buying a pitch and a unit, not a holiday: there is no ATOL, no package, and the conditions state Gustocamp is not liable for the ferry, the flight or the hire car, so insure the journey yourself and avoid non-refundable travel. And the cancellation ladder is unforgiving — 60% at six weeks and 100% at four, with the balance falling due at the same moment the penalty jumps. Price its cancellation insurance properly rather than waving it away, buy separate travel insurance on top, pay with a card that does not charge for euros, and write any complaint up within a month of getting home, because after that it will not be accepted.

faqs.q: Is a Gustocamp holiday ATOL protected?
faqs.a: No, and none is claimed. Gustocamp rents accommodation rather than selling travel, so no ATOL applies and there is no package protection. Its own conditions say it “cannot be held liable for any services booked by you (e.g. flight tickets, car rental, boat crossing, coach travel, etc.)”. Book your travel separately, on a credit card, and take travel insurance that covers disruption.

faqs.q: What happens if I cancel?
faqs.a: It depends how close you are, and it gets expensive quickly. Up to 42 days before arrival you pay 20% of the total travel sum; from 42 to 28 days it is 60%; from 28 days to the day before, and on the day or for a no-show, it is 100%. The €29.00 reservation fee is payable on top. Gustocamp sells cancellation insurance, which on this scale is worth pricing.

faqs.q: How much do I pay up front?
faqs.a: 20% of the rental for a regular booking, or 10% on an early booking, plus the €29.00 reservation fee and any cancellation insurance, due within two weeks of the invoice. The balance must be paid no later than six weeks before arrival. On arrival a security deposit is reserved by SEPA form — €100.00 for mobile homes and Premium safari tents, €50.00 for Gusto safari tents.

faqs.q: Can I change my dates instead of cancelling?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is far cheaper. Changing the travel period, the accommodation type or the campsite costs €25.00 per reservation plus any additional cost arising from the change, and transferring the booking to someone else is also €25.00. If your plans look shaky, ask about a change before you ask about a refund.

faqs.q: Where does Gustocamp operate?
faqs.a: Italy and Austria only. On the Adriatic coast it uses Union Lido Mare, Marina di Venezia, Pra’ delle Torri, Garden Paradiso, Spiaggia e Mare, Tahiti, Sant’ Angelo and Eraclea Mare; on Lake Garda, Bella Italia, Cisano San Vito and Villaggio Eden; in Tuscany, Park Albatros, Norcenni Girasole and Montescudaio; and in Austria, Bella Austria in Styria. The site advertises 15 campsites while naming thirteen, so check your chosen site is bookable.

faqs.a: “Gustocamp”, at Saturnusstraat 60, 2516 AH The Hague in the Netherlands. No limited company or BV is named and no registration number is published on the pages we read, and the booking conditions do not state which country’s law governs the contract. There is a UK phone number on +44 (0)1706 438006. Complaints must be in writing within one month of the end of your stay or they “will not be accepted”.

title: Hastings Direct Car Insurance Review
meta_title: Hastings Direct Car Insurance Review 2026: £45 Excess
meta_description: Hastings Direct charges a £45 compulsory excess against a £160 market average. What that buys, who underwrites it, and where the money goes back on.
intro:
Hastings Direct has been selling car insurance from Bexhill-on-Sea since 1996, and it has grown into one of the larger names in UK motor. At 30 June 2026 the group carried 4.8 million live customer policies, up 13% on a year earlier, with gross written premiums and brokerage income of £1,300.9 million for the half year. Around 4,800 people work for it across Bexhill, Leicester and London.

The thing most worth knowing before you compare a quote is the excess. Which? put the Hastings compulsory excess at £45 on fire, theft and accidental damage claims in its January 2026 assessment, against a market average of £160. On a £700 windscreen-and-bumper job that difference is real money, and it is the single clearest reason a Hastings quote can look cheap and still pay out properly. Its Direct and Premier policies both carry a 5 Star Defaqto rating, and the company advertises cover from £295.

What follows is what the excess buys, who actually carries the risk on the policy, and the places where Hastings puts the money back on — because there are several, and they are not on the quote screen.

key_facts.label: Broker
key_facts.value: Hastings Insurance Services Limited, FCA firm reference 311492

key_facts.label: Underwriter
key_facts.value: Advantage Insurance Company Limited, registered in Gibraltar no. 85900

key_facts.label: Compulsory excess
key_facts.value: £45 on fire, theft and accidental damage (Which?, January 2026)

key_facts.label: Defaqto
key_facts.value: 5 Star on the Direct and Premier policies

key_facts.label: Live policies
key_facts.value: 4.8 million at 30 June 2026

key_facts.label: Cooling-off period
key_facts.value: 14 days

key_facts.label: Founded
key_facts.value: 1996, Bexhill-on-Sea

sections.heading: The £45 excess, and the parts of the policy it does not reach
sections.html:
A compulsory excess of £45 is unusually low. Most insurers set theirs somewhere between £100 and £250 before you add the voluntary excess you choose yourself, so the £160 average Which? recorded in January 2026 is roughly where the market sits. Hastings is well under it, and that applies to the three claim types people actually make: fire, theft and accidental damage.

Glass is where the arithmetic reverses. Hastings applies a £135 excess to a windscreen replacement, which is high enough to matter. The ABI put the average windscreen repair cost at £283 in the second quarter of 2026, up 7% in three months, so on a repair the excess can swallow half the bill and on some replacements it is the difference between claiming and paying yourself. Medical expenses are covered to £500, which is a mid-range figure rather than a generous one.

Two gaps are worth checking against your own habits. Which? recorded no cover for misfuelling and none for sunroof damage on the Hastings policies it examined. Misfuelling in particular is a common, expensive and entirely self-inflicted claim that a number of rivals now include as standard, and putting petrol in a diesel can run to four figures once the tank and lines are drained.

sections.heading: Hastings sells the policy; a Gibraltar company carries the risk
sections.html:
Hastings Insurance Services Limited is a broker, not an insurer. It is registered in England and Wales as company 03116518, incorporated on 20 October 1995, with its registered office at Conquest House, Collington Avenue, Bexhill-on-Sea, TN39 3LW, and it holds FCA firm reference 311492 — a number you can check yourself on the Financial Services Register. The company describes itself plainly as an intermediary acting on behalf of several insurers.

The risk on a Hastings Direct motor policy has long sat with Advantage Insurance Company Limited, registered in Gibraltar under number 85900. Advantage is part of the same group, so this is not a case of a broker shopping your risk around; it is the group underwriting its own book through a Gibraltar entity. That arrangement is ordinary in UK motor and it does not remove your protection: the Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers eligible UK policyholders of Gibraltar insurers, at 100% for compulsory third-party motor claims and 90% for everything else.

It is not a purely academic point either. When the Gibraltar-based Premier Insurance Company Limited went into administration on 14 October 2025, the FSCS stepped in for more than 16,000 UK motor policyholders, and those policies were disclaimed on 1 December 2025. Nobody is suggesting Advantage is in that position — Hastings reported an operating ratio of 89.6% for the first half of 2026 and a £95.3 million result, both healthy. It simply pays to know which company's name is on the certificate and what happens if that company stops writing.

sections.heading: Where a Hastings quote sits in a market that has stopped falling
sections.html:
Motor premiums came down hard through 2025 and then flattened. The ABI's tracker for the second quarter of 2026 put the average premium paid at £566, £6 higher than the previous quarter, though £14 lower than a year earlier once inflation is stripped out. Hastings' own commentary matches that: market prices for car insurance stabilised during the second quarter after falling for much of 2025.

The pressure is on the claims side. Insurers paid a record £3.2 billion to motor customers in the second quarter of 2026, 7% more than the same period a year earlier, with the average payout up 4% to £4,900. The FCA's general insurance value measures data, published on 21 July 2026 for calendar year 2025, shows the same squeeze from the other direction: motor premiums fell 7% across the year while claims costs rose from 54% to 59% of premium.

That matters to a shopper for one reason. When claims cost more and premiums are not rising to match, insurers recover the difference somewhere — usually in excesses, optional extras and administration charges rather than the headline price. A quote that wins on price today is worth reading to the end.

sections.heading: The telematics policies run to a hard number, and it is 30
sections.html:
Hastings sells black box cover as YouDrive and a mileage-based product as SmartMiles, both aimed at younger and newer drivers who cannot get an affordable price any other way. The app scores speeding, harsh braking, fast acceleration, hard cornering and handling a phone at the wheel.

The rule is explicit in the policy wording: your driving score needs to stay above 30 at all times, or your policy may be cancelled. A Financial Ombudsman Service decision published in 2025 shows how that works in practice. A driver's 16-minute journey on 8 March 2025 contained five speeding events and repeated phone use; Hastings sent a warning on 11 March and a cancellation letter on 20 March. The premium was £615.95 and £489.16 was refunded after deductions for time on cover. The ombudsman did not uphold the complaint, finding the cancellation fair and consistent with the terms.

Read that as the product working as designed rather than as a scandal — but a cancelled policy has to be declared to every future insurer, for years, and that is a heavy consequence to attach to an app-generated number. If a young driver in the household drives a work van hard or takes calls on a handset, this is the wrong product.

sections.heading: Charges that arrive after you have bought
sections.html:
Hastings makes a large part of its money as a broker, on fees and commission rather than the premium alone. A 2025 Hastings Direct policy pack sets out an arrangement fee of £20, a £12.50 charge for buying by phone rather than online, £20 to make a change to the policy, £45 to cancel after the first 14 days, and £12 for a missed Direct Debit. Fees already charged are not refunded when you cancel. These are the figures on one dated customer document rather than a published tariff, so confirm the schedule attached to your own quote before you buy.

The 14-day cooling-off period is the statutory one, and within it you can cancel for a pro-rata refund of premium. After that the £45 cancellation charge applies whatever the reason — including selling the car, which is the most common reason people cancel mid-term.

sections.heading: How it scores when somebody else does the marking
sections.html:
Hastings does not test well independently. In its January 2026 work, Which? gave Hastings Direct a customer score of 73%, twelfth of the twelve insurers surveyed, and a claims satisfaction score of 71%, joint twelfth of fourteen providers, from 97 customers who had made a claim. Its policy scores were 60% for the Premier, Standard and YouDrive policies and 45% for Essential, against an average of 62% — three of the four below average, and the cheapest one well below. Which? does not name it a Recommended Provider.

Complaint volumes across the sector give a sense of scale: the Financial Ombudsman Service logged 3,229 new car and motorcycle insurance complaints between July and September 2025, with 37% upheld in the consumer's favour, making it the most complained-about insurance product. Any Hastings complaint follows the usual route — the firm first, then the ombudsman free of charge within six months of its final response.

The company also has an enforcement record, albeit a distant one. The Financial Services Authority fined Hastings £735,000 on 24 July 2008 for breaching Principle 6, after it cancelled roughly 4,550 motor policies between June and September 2007 that its own quotation system had priced too low, rather than absorbing the shortfall. That is eighteen years old and the business has changed hands three times since, but it is on the public record and no comparison page mentions it.

pros: £45 compulsory excess on fire, theft and accidental damage claims, against a £160 market average
5 Star Defaqto rating on both the Direct and Premier policies
Replacement car included while yours is being repaired, with availability guaranteed
Scale and financial strength: 4.8 million live policies and an 89.6% operating ratio at the half year
Telematics and mileage-based options for drivers who cannot get an affordable standard price
Cover advertised from £295, and quotes are quick to complete online
cons: £135 windscreen replacement excess is high — roughly half the £283 average repair cost recorded by the ABI in Q2 2026
No cover for misfuelling and none for sunroof damage on the policies Which? examined, both of which several rivals include
Which? scored it 73% for customers, last of twelve insurers, and 71% on claims satisfaction, joint twelfth of fourteen — it is not a Which? Recommended Provider
The Essential policy scored 45% against a 62% average, so the cheapest tier is where the cover thins out most
Fees stack up after the sale: £20 to change the policy, £45 to cancel after 14 days, £12.50 to buy by phone
YouDrive policies can be cancelled if the app score falls below 30, and a cancellation must then be declared to insurers for years
Claiming for damage caused while the car is parked can still affect the no claims discount
verdict: Hastings Direct earns its place on a shortlist on one number: a £45 compulsory excess where most insurers want £160. If your realistic claim is a car park dent or a stolen vehicle, that is money straight back in your pocket, and the Direct and Premier policies are properly built — Defaqto rates both five stars. The reservations are specific rather than general. Glass is expensive to claim on, misfuelling is not covered, the Essential tier is thin enough that Which? scored it 45%, and the service scores are at the bottom of the table. Get a quote on Direct or Premier rather than Essential, check the windscreen excess against your own car, and read the fee schedule before you pay.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites a Hastings Direct car insurance policy?
faqs.a: Hastings Insurance Services Limited is the broker and holds FCA firm reference 311492. The policy itself has long been underwritten by Advantage Insurance Company Limited, registered in Gibraltar under number 85900 and part of the same group. Eligible UK policyholders keep Financial Services Compensation Scheme protection either way — 100% on compulsory third-party motor claims and 90% on the rest. Check the certificate on your own quote, as underwriting arrangements can change between products.

faqs.q: What excess will I pay on a Hastings Direct claim?
faqs.a: Which? recorded a £45 compulsory excess on fire, theft and accidental damage claims in January 2026, against a £160 average across the insurers it looked at. Windscreen replacement is the exception at £135. Any voluntary excess you choose at the quote stage is added on top of the compulsory figure, so a £250 voluntary excess would mean £295 out of your own pocket on an accidental damage claim.

faqs.q: Can Hastings cancel a YouDrive policy because of my driving score?
faqs.a: Yes. The policy wording states that your driving score needs to stay above 30 at all times or the policy may be cancelled, with speeding, harsh braking, fast acceleration, hard cornering and phone use the main things that pull it down. A 2025 Financial Ombudsman Service decision found such a cancellation fair where a single 16-minute journey included five speeding events. You would normally get a warning first, and a refund of the unused premium less deductions.

faqs.q: What does Hastings Direct charge to cancel or change a policy?
faqs.a: A 2025 Hastings Direct policy pack shows £20 to make a change, £45 to cancel after the 14-day cooling-off period, £20 as an arrangement fee, £12.50 for buying by phone and £12 for a missed Direct Debit. Fees paid before cancellation are not refunded. These figures come from one dated customer document rather than a published tariff, so confirm them on the schedule attached to your own quote.

faqs.q: Is Hastings Direct cheap for a reason?
faqs.a: Partly. The low compulsory excess is genuine value, and scale helps: 4.8 million live policies at 30 June 2026 and an 89.6% operating ratio mean it can price keenly. The market backdrop is tight, though — the FCA found motor claims costs rose from 54% to 59% of premium during 2025 while premiums fell 7% — and Hastings recovers some of that in glass excesses, excluded extras like misfuelling and post-sale fees. The Essential tier is where the cover is thinnest.

title: Haven Knox-Johnston Boat Insurance
meta_title: Haven Knox-Johnston Boat Insurance Review: £5m Liability
meta_description: Sir Robin's family name, Howden behind the desk and MS Amlin behind the risk. £5m liability as standard — and the 18-hour rule offshore sailors should read.
intro:
Haven Knox-Johnston has been putting British boats on cover since the 1970s, and the second half of the name is not marketing. Chris Knox-Johnston — brother of Sir Robin, who took the ketch Suhaili non-stop around the world in 1968 to win the Golden Globe — ran a marine brokerage that was bought by Murray Lawrence and Partners and folded into the Haven book. The firm that came out of it has spent five decades quoting yachts, narrowboats, RIBs, dinghies and motor cruisers, which is a longer run at the job than most of the names a search engine will put next to it.

Today it trades as Haven Knox-Johnston, a trading name of Howden UK Brokers Limited, authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference 307663. That parent is not a small one: Howden runs $51bn of premium under management for around 1.7 million clients, employs roughly 24,000 people across 100 countries, and is the fifth largest employee-owned business in the United Kingdom. The marine desk sits at Malling House in West Malling, Kent, on 01732 223650, with in-house underwriters and an in-house claims team rather than a call centre pointing at somebody else's.

The headline cover is generous by the standards of the market. Third party liability runs to £5 million as standard, no-claims discount starts at 5% and builds to 25% after five claim-free years, excesses can be cut by up to 50% on a clean record, and mid-term changes carry no administration charge. Feefo, which collects only from verified buyers, shows a service rating of 4.8 out of 5 from 11,625 reviews in the past year and a Platinum award. The risk itself is carried by MS Amlin Marine under a three-year underwriting agreement announced on 5 January 2024. What decides a claim, though, is none of those numbers — it is the cruising range printed on your certificate, and that is where this review spends most of its time.
