sections.heading: £3.38 to £12.23: the four plans and where each one stops
sections.html:
The plans are sold as a ladder rather than a single product. Plumbing & Drainage is advertised at £3.38 a month and covers burst pipes, blocked external drains, the water supply pipe and blocked toilets. Boiler & Heating is £4.90 a month and takes in gas, oil and LPG boilers, complete loss of heating and complete loss of hot water, the gas supply pipe and up to £50 towards an alternative heat source. Complete, at £9.78 a month, adds electrics — defined as the complete failure of at least one circuit — plus up to £250 towards a hotel if the house is left uninhabitable, and folds in an annual boiler service. Supercharged sits above all of it at £12.23 a month.

What separates the top plan is not the list of covered events but the ceiling on them. The September 2026 policy book sets Essentials cover at £1,000 for any one claim and £3,000 across the policy year, applied section by section: boiler, central heating, plumbing and drainage, electrics and security each answer to the same pair of numbers. Supercharged raises the per-claim figure to £5,000 and removes the annual cap altogether. Overnight accommodation stays at £250 a claim on both.

Two older products are still described in the same book and will be on some certificates. Essentials 500 pays £500 a claim and £1,500 a year — a third of the current Essentials limit — and Essentials 5K pays £5,000 a claim but stops at six claims in a year. If you bought before this September, check which of the four sets of numbers is actually yours before assuming the £1,000 applies.

The boiler replacement contribution is a separate pot again: up to £500 towards a new boiler if yours is written off as beyond economic repair, and nothing at all in the first six months of the policy. Excess is a choice of £0, £60 or £95, and the compulsory £60 sits on top of whichever you pick for any call-out in the first 90 days, or on any boiler more than ten years old.

sections.heading: Two £35 fees that no monthly price shows
sections.html:
The About Our Services document, version 3 of September 2026, sets out what the premium does not include. A £35 arrangement fee is charged when the policy is set up or renewed. It is refunded only if you cancel inside the 14-day cooling-off period with no claim made or pending. Cancel after that and the arrangement fee is kept and a further £35 administration fee is charged — £70 in fees on a policy you may have held for a fortnight.

On the cheapest plan the fee is the larger part of the bill. Plumbing & Drainage at £3.38 a month is £40.56 over a year; add the arrangement fee and the first-year cost is £75.56, with the fee amounting to 86% of the premium itself. On Complete the arithmetic is gentler but still material: £117.36 of premium becomes £152.36. Nothing on the plan pages carries those numbers, and the monthly figures quoted in advertising are premium only.

The same document confirms the sale is non-advised — "We won't recommend a specific policy, but we'll give you all the information you need to make the right choice for you" — and that the firm takes commission which is "included within the insurance premium". A non-advised sale means nobody is assessing whether this cover suits your house, your boiler or the cover you already hold, and there is no suitability report to fall back on if it turns out not to.

sections.heading: Four insurers behind one brand, depending on which document you read
sections.html:
The name on the website is not the name that pays the claim, and it has changed more than once. The current policy book, coded 0926 v3, states that cover is underwritten by Novus Underwriting Ltd — itself an appointed representative of Rokstone Group Ltd, FCA reference 1008277 — acting on behalf of Collinson Insurance, the trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited, FRN 202846. That arrangement is recent. Collinson announced on 1 August 2025 that Novus had granted it exclusive binding authority over a book of annually renewable warranty products running to more than 500,000 policies. Novus writes over £230 million of gross premium a year and has a five-year target of £550 million; its parent Rokstone underwrites around USD 1.1bn across specialty lines.

Documents still in circulation name two other insurers. The Essentials 5K product information document puts Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Ltd, FRN 202323, behind the £5,000 limit and its six-claim ceiling. The policy book issued in April 2025 names Financial & Legal Insurance Company Ltd, FRN 202915, with Legal Protection Group Ltd, FRN 749446, as administrator and a separate claims number on 0333 700 1040. Three insurers and two administrators across eighteen months of paperwork is a lot of movement for one product line, and it means the certificate you were sent is the only reliable guide to whose paper you are on.

Home Emergency Assist itself carries no FCA permission of its own. It is an appointed representative of Insure Group Limited, FRN 584710. The FCA's own description of that relationship is short and useful: "The principal agrees what activities the AR can do and is responsible for that business." So a complaint about the way the policy was sold is ultimately Insure Group's responsibility, even though the letterhead, the phone number and the brand all say something else.

sections.heading: The same cover is £1.83 a month cheaper through a staff-benefits portal
sections.html:
Home Emergency Assist runs partner pages for employee-benefit and affinity schemes, and the prices on them are not the prices on the main site. The Discounts for Carers page offers Complete at £7.95 a month against £9.78 on the public site, Boiler & Heating at £3.98 against £4.90, and Plumbing & Drainage at £2.75 against £3.38, using the code DFC35OFF for 35% off. On Complete that is £1.83 a month, or £21.96 a year — 18.7% less for the same plan name. The public site's own codes, SAVE20 on home emergency and SAVE10 on appliances, are worth less.

The partner terms are not identical either, which matters more than the money. That page offers excess options of £0 or £50 rather than £0, £60 or £95, and applies a £50 additional excess where the public site applies £60 — with the trigger stated as an appliance over six years old rather than a boiler over ten. It also carries the note "Prices correct as at 10.03.2025", so the figures on it are eighteen months older than the ones on the main site. Read whichever page you are buying from rather than assuming the plan names mean the same thing on both.

Neither the home page's claim of savings "up to £460 a year" nor the "up to 78%" figure beside it is supported by published workings. The terms and conditions page carries no basis for either, and no comparison methodology could be found on the site. Treat both as advertising until the company publishes the assumptions behind them.

sections.heading: Who actually turns up when the boiler goes out
sections.html:
Nobody employed by Home Emergency Assist will be at your door. The policy book says work is carried out by "one of our approved engineers", and the company's own FAQs describe "an extensive network of professionally qualified tradesmen" — a contracted network, arranged and paid by the claims operation. The network is not named, its size is not published, and the documents give no route to instruct your own plumber and claim the cost back afterwards. That could not be verified from any company source and is worth asking about on the phone.

Where gas is involved the law narrows the field regardless of who books the job. Under the Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 in Great Britain, and the equivalent 2004 regulations in Northern Ireland, anyone working on a gas appliance must be on the Gas Safe Register. That is a genuine floor under the quality of a boiler call-out, and it applies whether the engineer comes through this policy or you ring one yourself.

The performance figures the company does publish are specific enough to hold it to. It claims 75% of emergencies attended within four hours and 80% resolved on the first visit, 90% of calls answered within 20 seconds, and 70% of jobs booked while the caller is still on hold, with the average call under 15 minutes. None of it is audited or externally verified, but a firm that prints numbers in that shape is easier to argue with than one that says "rapid response".

One procedural rule catches people out. A claim must be reported within 48 hours of the problem starting; the claims page states that anything reported later "will not be accepted". A leak noticed on the Friday of a weekend away is a claim that needs making before you get home.

sections.heading: Ten years, fifteen years, and the service the sales pages call optional
sections.html:
The boiler is where this policy is most likely to disappoint, and the age rules are the first reason. Pass ten years and every claim carries an extra £60 compulsory excess on top of whatever voluntary excess you chose. Pass fifteen and the boiler is outside the policy altogether, as is anything above 238,000 Btu net input. Those are the ages at which a household most wants this cover, and they are the ages at which it costs more and then stops.

The servicing position is muddier than it should be. The current policy book describes a yearly boiler check as something "you can add as an optional extra to your policy, or you may choose to arrange it privately with your own contractor outside of your cover", and the FAQs say a service is not required, offering to add one for £90. Yet the same book's general exclusions rule out "general wear and tear, gradual deterioration, or lack of maintenance", and the April 2025 wording spelled the same clause out as "lack of maintenance or neglect by you, including where an annual boiler service has not been completed". The current book no longer names the annual service in that clause — that reading is ours, not a statement by the insurer — but a household that has skipped servicing for three years and is told its breakdown is wear and tear will find the argument lands in the same place. Keep the service receipts whether or not you buy the add-on.

The rest of the exclusion list is conventional and worth reading before you rely on the policy. Descaling and any work arising from hard-water scale is out. So is the replacement of water tanks, cylinders and radiators, and radiator valves other than as an emergency repair. Problems that existed before the policy started are excluded, as is anything caused by poor installation, faulty design or not following the manufacturer's instructions. Nothing at all is covered in the first 14 days, nothing under boiler replacement for six months, nothing while the home has stood empty for more than 60 consecutive days, and nothing in the first seven days after you move in or move back.

sections.heading: Three complaint desks, three addresses, and no independent rating
sections.html:
Where you complain depends on what went wrong, and the three routes do not share a phone number. Anything about the sale or the administration goes to Home Emergency Assist on 03330 034 999 or complaints@homeemergencyassist.com, addressed to the Complaints Department at the Arena Business Centre, Holyrood Close, Poole, Dorset BH17 7FJ, with an acknowledgement promised within three working days. Anything about how a home emergency claim was handled goes to a separate desk on 0330 094 8301, with five working days quoted on the online form; the policy book also routes some claims complaints to info@assuredresponse.co.uk, a name that appears nowhere on the sales pages. Appliance cover is different again — that one is handled by MB&G Insurance Services Ltd at the Cobalt Business Exchange in Newcastle upon Tyne, NE28 9NZ, on 0330 124 4531.

The backstop is standard. If the complaint is unresolved after eight weeks, or you disagree with the final response, the Financial Ombudsman Service will look at it free of charge on 0800 023 4567, and you have six months from the final response to refer it. The policy is covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme.

What is missing is any outside verdict on the product. No Defaqto or Fairer Finance rating for Home Emergency Assist could be found from a primary source, and Defaqto's public star-ratings pages do not list it. The company publishes no complaints volumes or uphold rates of its own, which larger sellers in this market now do, so there is no way to compare how often its claims decisions are challenged. On the evidence available, the documents are good and the track record is unreadable.

pros: A full policy book and five separate product information documents, each dated and version-numbered, all free to read before you buy
The underwriter and its FCA reference are named in the documents rather than left vague
A £0 excess option exists, which is rare at this price
£5,000 a claim with no annual cap on the £12.23 Supercharged plan
Complete at £9.78 a month includes an annual boiler service, and a one-off service is £90 as an add-on
Claims line staffed 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, with published answer and attendance figures
cons: A £35 arrangement fee and a £35 cancellation fee sit outside every advertised monthly price — on the £3.38 plan the arrangement fee alone is 86% of the annual premium
Boilers over 15 years old are not covered at all, and those over 10 carry an extra £60 compulsory excess on every claim
Three different insurers appear across the documents issued in the last eighteen months, so only your certificate tells you who actually carries the risk
The same plans are sold 35% cheaper through partner portals, on slightly different excess terms, with no explanation of the gap
The advertised savings of "up to £460 a year" and "up to 78%" have no published basis anywhere on the site
Claims must be reported within 48 hours or they will not be accepted, which is tighter than most home emergency wordings
Landlords, tenants, holiday homes and park homes are excluded outright, and there is no published route to use your own tradesman
verdict: Priced against what it pays out, this is a reasonable buy for an owner-occupier with a boiler under ten years old who wants a 24-hour number and can live with a £1,000 ceiling. The documents are better than the market average and the £0 excess option is genuinely useful. The catches are the £35 in and £35 out, which turn a £40.56 premium into £75.56 in year one, and the age rules that withdraw the cover exactly when an ageing boiler makes it worth having. Check your certificate for which insurer and which claim limit apply to you, because four combinations are in circulation, and get a quote through any staff-benefits portal you have access to before buying at the public price.

faqs.q: How much does Home Emergency Assist cost?
faqs.a: Plumbing & Drainage is advertised at £3.38 a month, Boiler & Heating at £4.90, Complete at £9.78 and Supercharged at £12.23, as at 19 September 2026. Add a £35 arrangement fee at purchase and at each renewal. A year of Complete is therefore £117.36 of premium plus £35, or £152.36 in total.

faqs.q: How much will it pay on a claim?
faqs.a: The current Essentials limits are £1,000 for any one claim and £3,000 in a policy year. Supercharged pays up to £5,000 a claim with no annual cap. Two older plans are still in force: Essentials 500 at £500 a claim and £1,500 a year, and Essentials 5K at £5,000 a claim but no more than six claims in a year. Overnight accommodation is capped at £250 on all of them.

faqs.q: Who underwrites the policy?
faqs.a: On the September 2026 policy book, Novus Underwriting Ltd — an appointed representative of Rokstone Group Ltd, reference 1008277 — acting for Collinson Insurance, the trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited, FRN 202846. Older documents name Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Ltd (202323) and Financial & Legal Insurance Company Ltd (202915). Home Emergency Assist itself is an appointed representative of Insure Group Limited, FRN 584710.

faqs.q: Is there a waiting period before I can claim?
faqs.a: Yes. No claim can be made for anything happening in the first 14 days of the policy, and the boiler replacement contribution of up to £500 is unavailable for the first six months. Cover is also suspended for the first seven days after you move into or back into the property, and while the home has been empty for more than 60 consecutive days.

faqs.q: Can a landlord or a tenant buy this cover?
faqs.a: No. The policy is sold to owner-occupiers for a UK property that is their permanent main residence. Let properties, holiday homes, park homes and social or housing association tenancies are all outside it, and detached garages, gardens, outbuildings and swimming pools are excluded from cover even at an eligible address.

faqs.q: Do I need an annual boiler service to claim?
faqs.a: The September 2026 policy book treats the yearly check as an optional extra you can add or arrange privately, and the FAQs offer one for £90. The general exclusions still rule out claims arising from wear and tear, gradual deterioration or lack of maintenance, and the April 2025 wording named a missed annual service as an example of that. Keeping service records is the safer course either way.

title: HomeServe Plumbing and Drainage Insurance
meta_title: HomeServe Plumbing Cover: 50p a Month, Then £16.45
meta_description: HomeServe plumbing and drainage cover is 50p a month in year one and £16.45 after it. What the £4,000 claim limit and £30 excess actually buy you.
intro:
HomeServe's Plumbing and Drainage Plus policy costs 50p a month for the first year — £6 for the whole twelve months — and pays up to £4,000 a claim, with no cap on the number of claims you make. The excess is £30 each time. Figures checked on 14 September 2026 against HomeServe's own product page and its Insurance Product Information Document.

The firm behind that price is one of the largest home emergency operators in Britain. HomeServe Limited reported 3,621,000 customers and revenue of £976.3m for the year to 31 March 2023, a retention rate of 82%, more than 6,000 staff with roughly half of them in the UK, and about 700 directly employed engineers rather than a list of subcontractors. Aviva Insurance Limited carries the risk. HomeServe Membership Limited sells, arranges and administers the policy, and publishes the full terms and the product information document on the buying page rather than after payment.

Two dates matter before you click. The 50p offer runs to 15 September 2026, after which the introductory price for new customers becomes £1 a month. And HomeServe prints the second-year figure on the same page as the first: £16.45 a month, or £197.40 for the year, for a customer who has not claimed. Sellers of this kind of cover rarely put the renewal price next to the offer price, and the arithmetic further down this page only works because this one does.

sections.heading: The cover itself: £4,000 a claim, £30 to open one
sections.html:
The policy is written around five named problems: leaking pipes inside the home, blocked drains, blockages to sinks and toilets, leaks or blockages to the water supply pipe, and dripping or seized taps. Each claim is met up to £4,000 in value, and the number of claims in a year is not capped. Where a part cannot be sourced within 28 days, or a repair would cost more than 85% of the price of a new appliance, the terms allow a replacement instead of a repair.

Set that £4,000 against the premium and the shape of the product becomes clear. At the second-year price of £197.40 a year, a single claim taken to the ceiling is worth just over twenty years of premiums. That is what a cheap indemnity policy is for, and it is a genuinely useful ceiling — the cover is not thin, it is narrow.

The £30 excess is charged per separate problem registered, by card, before an engineer is despatched. In the first year that single excess is five times the £6 the policy itself costs. A year with three unrelated jobs in it carries £90 of excess on top of whatever the premium was.

There is also a 28-day exclusion period running from the start date, and from the date of any change to the cover. A leak that appears in the fourth week of the policy is not a claim.

sections.heading: £6, then £197.40: the two-year sum
sections.html:
HomeServe publishes both numbers, so the sum is not a discovery. Year one is £6. Year two, for a customer who has made no claim, is an expected £197.40. Two years of continuous cover is therefore £203.40, an average of £8.48 a month across the twenty-four months, and the year-two monthly price is 32.9 times the year-one one.

Add claims and the gap widens. Two separate jobs in the second year put the year's outlay at £257.40. A customer who has claimed should also expect a different renewal figure again, because the terms state that claims history is taken into account when the renewal price is set.

None of that makes the offer a bad one. It makes the 50p a customer acquisition price rather than the price of the cover, and the honest way to judge it is to ask whether £197.40 a year is what you want to pay for a £4,000 drain and pipe indemnity with a £30 excess. The first year is close to free either way. The policy renews automatically, with a reminder before it does, so the decision arrives whether or not you go looking for it.

sections.heading: Who answers the phone, and who pays the bill
sections.html:
Two companies stand behind this policy and they do different jobs. Aviva Insurance Limited, registered in Scotland under company number 2116 and regulated by the Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority, is the insurer — it carries the risk and it funds the claims. HomeServe Membership Limited, registered in England and Wales under company number 02770612 and holding Financial Conduct Authority firm reference 312518, sells the policy, arranges it, administers it and sends the engineer.

The company was incorporated on 3 December 1992 and has traded under four names since; it became HomeServe Membership Limited in April 2008, and its registered office is Cable Drive, Walsall WS2 7BN. Its parent, HomeServe Limited, left the London Stock Exchange in January 2023 when Brookfield completed a take-private valuing the group at about £4.1bn.

Complaints go to HomeServe rather than to Aviva: 0330 0247 999, or customerrelations@homeserve.co.uk. The firm has up to eight weeks to reach a final answer, after which the Financial Ombudsman Service will look at the case. One caveat worth reading in the terms: the Ombudsman route is stated to cover the insurance, and not the features the documents describe as non-insured.

sections.heading: The renewal-price rule that protects your buildings policy stops short of this one
sections.html:
In January 2022 the Financial Conduct Authority stopped insurers charging existing customers more at renewal than an equivalent new customer would pay. Those rules sit in chapter 6B of the Insurance: Conduct of Business sourcebook, and the application rule is narrow. It says the chapter "applies where a firm carries out any of the following activities in relation to a home insurance or motor insurance policy or any related additional product sold to a consumer".

A standalone home emergency policy bought direct from HomeServe is not a home insurance policy, and it is not an additional product sold alongside one. On the plain reading of that rule the equivalent-new-business-price protection does not reach it, which is how a £6 first year and a £197.40 second year can sit on the same page without breaching anything. This is our reading of the application rule rather than a statement the regulator has made about this product, and it is worth confirming with HomeServe if the renewal is the part of the deal you care about.

The practical consequence is small but real: the discipline that stops your buildings insurer walking your price up year after year is not doing any work here, so the renewal figure is worth diarising rather than assuming.

sections.heading: A £30.6m fine in 2014, and the complaints book in 2026
sections.html:
On 13 February 2014 the Financial Conduct Authority fined HomeServe Membership Limited £30,647,400 — at the time one of the largest retail conduct penalties it had issued. The final notice covers January 2005 to October 2011 and describes mis-sold policies, unfair complaint handling between January 2010 and April 2011, and misleading telephone sales. Some 69,000 customers were mis-sold two insurance policies. The penalty would have been £43,782,058 without the 30% discount for early settlement, and about £12.9m of redress had been paid by the date of the notice against £16.8m expected. The regulator noted that a significant proportion of the customers affected were of retirement age.

Twelve years is a long time in a compliance department, and the more useful question is what the book looks like now. HomeServe publishes its own complaints return. For the six months from 1 January to 30 June 2026 it recorded 2,264 insurance complaints opened, a rate of 3.05 per 1,000 policies, with 53% closed inside three days, a further 46% closed within eight weeks, and 22% upheld.

That rate also gives a rough sense of the size of the UK book, which the group accounts do not break out: 2,264 complaints at 3.05 per 1,000 policies implies somewhere around 742,000 policies in force. That figure is arithmetic on the published rate, not a number HomeServe states, so treat it as an order of magnitude.

sections.heading: Where your water company fits in
sections.html:
Many people meet this policy through a utility bill rather than through HomeServe. The group's accounts for the year to 31 March 2023 record renewed relationships with three water partners covering 6.4 million households, and a three-year renewal with E.ON covering a further 5.0 million. Northumbrian Water and South West Water both carry the 50p offer on their own websites, described in Northumbrian's words as "50p a month in year one with £30 excess. New customers, homeowners only."

The arrangement is an introduction, not a sale by the water company. The contract is with HomeServe, the insurer is Aviva, and the water company's role ends at the link. Neither the Northumbrian Water nor the South West Water page states whether the utility is paid for making that introduction, and we could not establish it either way from a primary source — if that matters to you, it is a fair question to put to either company.

One eligibility point travels with the offer wherever it appears: it is for homeowners. Landlords are quoted on separate products, and the same is true of flats and of let or sub-let property, so read the restrictions on the product you are actually shown rather than the one you arrived from.

sections.heading: The jobs this policy will not send an engineer for
sections.html:
The exclusions are short, specific and worth reading before the first cold snap. The policy does not cover a boiler breakdown that leaves you without heating or hot water; that is a different and dearer HomeServe plan. It does not cover guttering. It does not cover soakaways. It does not cover shared drains, or drains and pipes you are not responsible for. And it does not cover mixer or digital showers, which between them account for most showers fitted in British homes in the last twenty years.

The terms add a second layer. Pre-existing faults are out. Removing sludge, scale or rust is out. A frozen pipe that has not actually leaked is out. And a system that has not been serviced in line with the relevant British Standards can be declined on that basis alone, which is a condition the reader controls and should keep paperwork for.

Nothing in that list is unusual for home emergency cover. The point is the shape of what remains: a policy for water escaping, water not draining and taps that have stopped working, sold at a price that assumes most people will not need it in any given year.

pros: Aviva Insurance Limited is named as the insurer on both the product page and the information document, rather than left for the buyer to work out
£4,000 per claim with no cap on the number of claims, which is a high ceiling for a plan at this price
The full terms and the Insurance Product Information Document are published before purchase, not after
HomeServe prints the expected second-year price of £16.45 a month alongside the 50p offer
Around 700 directly employed engineers rather than a subcontracted call-out list
The firm publishes its own complaints return: 53% of insurance complaints closed within three days in the first half of 2026
The first year costs £6, so the cost of finding out whether you value the cover is small
cons: The renewal is 32.9 times the offer — £6 in year one against £197.40 in year two — and that is the price quoted for a customer who has not claimed
A 28-day exclusion period runs from the start of the policy, so a leak in the first four weeks is not a claim
Mixer and digital showers are excluded, which rules out most modern shower installations
Boilers and central heating are not covered by this policy at all; that needs a separate, more expensive plan
The £30 excess applies to each separate problem, so three unrelated jobs in a year cost £90 on top of the premium
The renewal-price protections in chapter 6B of the Insurance: Conduct of Business sourcebook do not appear to reach a standalone home emergency policy
22% of the 2,264 complaints recorded in the first half of 2026 were upheld
No Defaqto or Fairer Finance rating for this product could be found from a primary source
Neither Northumbrian Water's nor South West Water's page says whether the water company is paid for introducing customers to it
verdict: A narrow policy with a high ceiling, sold at a first-year price that is close to free. The £4,000 claim limit and the absence of a cap on claim numbers are better than the 50p suggests, the insurer is named, and the wording is on the table before you pay — three things that are not true of every plan at this end of the market. The decision is not really about year one at £6; it is about whether £197.40 a year with a £30 excess is the right price for cover against escaping water, blocked drains and dead taps, given that boilers, guttering and mixer showers are all outside it. Diarise the renewal, because nothing in the pricing rules will hold it down for you.

faqs.q: What does HomeServe plumbing and drainage cover actually cost?
faqs.a: 50p a month for the first year, which is £6 in total, on the offer running to 15 September 2026. After that date the introductory price for new customers is £1 a month. HomeServe states an expected second-year price of £16.45 a month, or £197.40 for the year, for a customer who has not claimed. Each claim also carries a £30 excess.

faqs.q: Who underwrites the policy?
faqs.a: Aviva Insurance Limited, registered in Scotland under company number 2116 and regulated by the Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority. HomeServe Membership Limited, firm reference 312518, sells, arranges and administers it and is the company you claim against and complain to.

faqs.q: How much will it pay out on a single job?
faqs.a: Up to £4,000 in value per claim, with no limit on the number of claims in a policy year. Where a part cannot be obtained within 28 days, or a repair would cost more than 85% of the price of a new appliance, the terms allow a replacement instead.

faqs.q: Am I covered from the day I buy it?
faqs.a: No. There is a 28-day exclusion period from the start of the policy, and a further one whenever the cover is changed. A problem that arises inside that window is not covered, so this is not a policy to buy while a drain is already blocked.

faqs.q: Does it cover my boiler?
faqs.a: Not on this plan. A boiler breakdown that leaves you without heating or hot water is specifically excluded from Plumbing and Drainage Plus; HomeServe sells separate heating and boiler products for that. Guttering, soakaways, shared drains and mixer or digital showers are also outside this policy.

faqs.q: Can I buy it through my water company instead?
faqs.a: Several water companies and E.ON promote it — HomeServe's accounts for the year to 31 March 2023 record water partners covering 6.4 million households and an E.ON partnership covering 5.0 million more. The introduction comes from the utility, but the contract is with HomeServe and the insurer is Aviva either way.

title: Hostelling International Hostels: Membership, Booking Terms and What HI Actually Runs
meta_title: Hostelling International Hostels: Membership and Prices
meta_description: What HI membership costs in Britain, the 10% member discount, the 24-hour cancellation rule, and how far the HI quality audit really reaches.
intro:
Hostelling International is the federation that a great many British travellers have used without ever learning its name. Its member associations run more than 2,300 hostels, it counts “more than 2,63 million members from around the world”, and it traces the network back to a German schoolteacher, Richard Schirrmann, who opened the first youth hostel in his own school at Altena in Westphalia in 1914. The federation itself was founded in 1932 as the International Youth Hostel Federation, adopted the Hostelling International name in 2006, and still describes itself as working “for Good, Not For Profit”. In England and Wales its member association is YHA; in Scotland it is Hostelling Scotland. Both are registered charities, and a card bought from either one works across the whole federation.

What separates HI from an ordinary bed-booking site is that it publishes a standard and pays somebody outside the organisation to check it. Hostels in the HI Quality & Sustainability programme are, in HI's own words, “certified every 3 years by an external auditor”, and the management system behind that programme is recognised by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council. The GSTC's published register lists it as “HI-Q&S (Hostelling International Quality and Sustainability Management System)”, owner Hostelling International, United Kingdom, version 1 July 2018, with recognition dates of 14 January 2016 and 16 June 2019. Very few accommodation brands of any size submit to a fixed outside audit cycle at all.

One structural point is better known before you book than after. HI runs the search and takes the deposit, but it is not the party selling you the bed. Its own booking terms say so without hedging: “Booking made on hihostels.com are a contract with the hostel or Youth Hostel Association who runs the hostel, not HI.” Nor do you have to join to use it — “You do not need to be a member…in order to make your booking” — although membership is compulsory at the door in some countries, and elsewhere non-members “pay a small surcharge or can purchase a membership card at the hostel”.

sections.heading: A federation of charities, not a hotel chain
sections.html:
The organisation behind hihostels.com is a British one, which surprises most people who assume a global hostel network must sit somewhere warmer. The International Youth Hostel Federation is company 02250706, incorporated on 3 May 1988 as a private company limited by guarantee without share capital, using the exemption that lets it drop “Limited” from its name. Its registered office is 7 Bell Yard, London WC2A 2JR, its SIC code is 94990 — activities of other membership organisations — and its last accounts were made up to 31 December 2025. Its own website terms of use put the position in one line: “the International Youth Hostel Federation (IYHF) operating as Hostelling International (“HI”)”, Registered Charity No. 1117014. The company has carried three names in its life, trading as HOSTELLING INTERNATIONAL between 3 April 2006 and 15 April 2010 and as IYHF TRUST before that.

Underneath the federation sit the national associations, and the British ones are older than the federation's UK company by half a century. YHA (England and Wales) is company 00282555, incorporated on 12 December 1933 as the Youth Hostels Trust of England and Wales Limited, registered at Trevelyon House, Dimple Road, Matlock, and filed under SIC 55202, which is the code for youth hostels and almost nothing else uses. Its stated charitable object has not been modernised into blandness: “To help all, especially young people of limited means, to a greater knowledge, love and care of the countryside, and appreciation of the cultural values of towns and cities.” Hostelling Scotland is the Scottish Youth Hostels Association, a Scottish charity registered with OSCR.

This matters for a practical reason rather than a sentimental one. A charity that owns its buildings prices differently from a platform that owns none, it publishes accounts you can read, and it has a reason to keep a hostel open in a valley that no commercial operator would touch. It also means the money you spend has a visible destination, which is unusual in online travel.

sections.heading: Who you are actually contracting with
sections.html:
HI's booking terms are short and, on the points that matter, unambiguous. The contract for the stay is with the hostel or the national association, not with HI. HI “collect[s] a non-refundable deposit payment at the time of booking” and the balance is settled with the hostel. Cancellation is free provided “the cancellation must be made at least 24 hours prior to the arrival time”, and the terms fix that arrival time for you whether or not you told anyone when you were turning up: “The arrival time at your destination hostel is considered as 18:00 (6pm) local time to the hostel.” In practice that means a booking for a Saturday has to be cancelled by 18:00 on the Friday.

Miss that and the charge is set out plainly. “If a cancellation is not received and you do not arrive for a booking of 1 night you will be charged 1 night, plus applicable taxes. If a cancellation is not received and you do not arrive for a booking of 2 or more nights you will be charged 2 nights, plus applicable taxes.” Even where you cancel in time, “the booking deposit is always non-refundable, unless stated otherwise in the booking conditions”.

The limitation of liability follows from the same structure and is worth reading twice: “In the event of a problem arising, our liability, if any, is limited to the fees paid by you on this website.” Since what you pay on the website is the deposit, that is the ceiling on any claim against HI itself. Disputes about the room, the cleanliness or the money you paid on arrival belong with the hostel and its association. The terms are governed by “the laws of England and Wales” and “[t]he courts of England and Wales shall have exclusive jurisdiction”, which is a genuine convenience for a British reader booking a bed in Ljubljana and a point most international booking platforms do not offer.

sections.heading: What a card costs in Britain, and what it takes off the bill
sections.html:
HI's own site is coy about price. The membership pages say only that “[p]rices vary depending on your place of residence” and that a membership “is valid for 12 months” from the date of purchase; the actual figure appears nowhere on hihostels.com. For a British buyer the number comes from the national association, and it is small.

YHA charges £20 a year for adult membership paid by direct debit and £10 a year for ages 16 to 25, and the return is “10% off every booking including pre-booked breakfast”. Under-26s get “an additional 5% discount…stacked on top of your 10% discount”. Hostelling Scotland runs a longer ladder, with rates that “apply from 5 April” and are “non-refundable”: £15 per annum for adults aged 26 and over, £6 per annum for a young person aged 25 or under, £150 for life, £30 per annum for groups of ten or more, £25 per booking for a temporary group, and £3 per overnight if you would rather not join at all.

On a £25 dorm bed, 10% is £2.50, so a £20 YHA card pays for itself over eight nights, or over roughly five for a 21-year-old stacking the extra 5%. A Scottish £6 young person's card pays for itself faster still. Two conditions attach. “Individual adults (over 16) must have their own membership” unless a family or group card covers them, and membership becomes “non-refundable, non-transferable to another person after activation”, with cancellation permitted but carrying no refund. Buying the card through a third party is the one route HI warns against: “If you book through an online travel agent or 3rd party, we cannot guarantee your HI membership will be honoured.”

sections.heading: The standard behind the badge, and how far it reaches
sections.html:
HI-Q&S is the best thing on the site and it is undersold. It is described as “a long-term programme of continuous improvement that allows hostels and associations to advance their quality and sustainability practices”, hostels are “certified every 3 years by an external auditor”, and the management system is GSTC-recognised. The federation's About page goes further and tells the reader that “all our hostels meet the HI standards, which guarantee a range of good quality safe accommodation, in friendly surroundings at affordable prices”.

The programme's own page gives the scale, and it does not match that sentence. “HI-Q&S is used in 32 Associations and over 400 Hostels worldwide.” Against a network of more than 2,300 hostels and 57 or 58 associations, that is a little over one hostel in six and roughly half the associations. The audit is real, the coverage is partial, and only the first of those two facts is advertised.

There is a British yardstick to set beside it, and no hostel listing on hihostels.com carries it. VisitEngland runs a dedicated hostel assessment scheme in which “[o]ne of our professional assessors will visit as a mystery guest”, and it publishes the standards in full. Minimum entry requires self-catering facilities, wet clothing storage, daily cleaning, a first aid kit and emergency contact information; bedrooms need “a minimum floor space per bed (or bunk) of 4 square metres”, a two-metre ceiling, an external window and beds “at least 1.9m (6'3") x 0.76m (2'6")”; kitchens need “a minimum of 4 cooking rings”. Star bands run 60–74% for three stars, 75–86% for four and 87–100% for five, with sectional floors underneath — four stars requires “no area to score less than 67%” and a “cleanliness minimum score 76%”. The scheme also runs two lower tiers, Quality Assessed and Visitor Ready, and states that “[n]ot all types of hostel are given a star rating, but all of them must meet a set of minimum requirements”. If a hostel you are considering in England holds one of those ratings, it is worth more than any score collected by the seller, and HI does not show it.

sections.heading: Booking a bed is not a package holiday
sections.html:
Two pieces of British law shape what you get when you press the button, and neither is mentioned on the site. The first is the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018, which define a package as “a combination of at least two different types of travel services for the purpose of the same trip or holiday”, the types being “the carriage of passengers; the provision of accommodation; the rental of cars, other motor vehicles, or motorcycles; [or] any other tourist service”. A hostel bed on its own is one type, so a bed booked alone is not a package and carries none of the insolvency protection or organiser liability that a package carries. Nor is it an ATOL matter, because no flight is involved. Booking accommodation by itself is one of the least protected purchases in travel, and that is true of every hostel platform rather than of HI in particular.

That regime is about to move. The Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements (Amendment) Regulations 2026 come into force on 6 April 2027, remove the concept of linked travel arrangements altogether — the instrument directs simply “Omit regulation 26 (insolvency protection and information requirements for linked travel arrangements)” — widen the definition of a package to catch separate selections and separate payments made on “a single visit to, or contact with, the trader's point of sale”, and add a third-party refund obligation running to 14 days. A traveller who books a bed and a ferry in one sitting from one seller after that date may find themselves better protected than they are now.

The second piece of law explains the non-refundable deposit, and it is the answer to a complaint people often make unfairly. Regulation 28(1)(h) of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 excludes from the ordinary cancellation right “the supply of accommodation, transport of goods, vehicle rental services, catering or services related to leisure activities, if the contract provides for a specific date or period of performance”. The 14-day right to change your mind that applies to almost everything else bought online — “the cancellation period ends at the end of 14 days after the day on which the contract is entered into” for a service — simply does not attach to a room booked for a named night. HI's 24-hour rule is therefore a concession rather than a legal minimum, and a more generous one than a good deal of the hotel market offers.

sections.heading: The case for going straight to the hostel
sections.html:
Filter hihostels.com to England and you will find roughly seventy properties spread over seven pages, and all but a handful of them are YHA. That is not a criticism of the search — YHA is the English member association, so of course they are its hostels — but it does change the arithmetic for a domestic trip, because YHA sells the same beds itself and says openly what the intermediary layer costs it.

YHA's own book-direct page states that “[l]ast year, about £2 million of YHA's income was absorbed by third party booking agents”, money the charity would rather “invest…in improving young people's health, wellbeing and life skills”. It offers a price undertaking that no aggregator matches: “If you find a better rate elsewhere online, we will refund the difference”, applying where within 24 hours of booking on yha.org.uk you find an equivalent offer for the same property at a lower price. It says the direct site carries “our complete range of accommodation” and is “[t]he only way to redeem promotional codes and take advantage of special offers”. And critically, the 10% member discount and the extra 5% for under-26s are described throughout as applying to bookings “made online at yha.org.uk”.

The sensible conclusion is not that the HI site is worthless but that it earns its keep in different places. Abroad, where you have no account with the Slovenian or Portuguese association and no idea which properties are affiliated, one search across the whole federation with one membership number behind it is genuinely useful, and the same card that costs £20 in Matlock works at the door in Lisbon. At home, where the operator is a charity you can book with directly, is running a best-rate refund, and is quietly losing about £2 million a year to intermediaries, the case for the middle layer is much weaker.

sections.heading: Numbers on the site that do not agree with each other
sections.html:
Read HI's pages side by side and the network changes size. The About HI page describes “58 Member Associations operating over 2,300 hostels in hundreds of amazing destinations”. The network directory on the same site describes “57 Member Associations with over 2,300 hostels as well as affiliate hostels in 2 destinations”. One association is a trivial difference; publishing both figures on one website is the sort of thing that makes a careful reader check everything else.

The bigger gap is between the federation and its own members. HI says over 2,300 hostels. YHA tells its members that their card gives “[a]ccess over 4,000 hostels through automatic Hostelling International membership” and, on its dedicated page, “over 4.000 hostels in 90 countries”. Hostelling Scotland says membership “gives you access to over 4,000 hostels around the world with dual membership of Hostelling International”. Two national associations advertise a network almost twice the size the federation claims for itself, and nothing on any of the three sites reconciles the two counts. The likeliest explanation is that the larger number sweeps in affiliated and partner properties that HI does not count as its own, but no page says so, and a reader choosing on network size is being given two different answers by the same organisation.

A third gap is smaller and easier to fix. The membership pages promise “thousands of travel discounts at home and abroad”. The benefits page lists six partners: 15% off an Airalo eSIM, 15% off luggage storage with Bounce, 10% off European shipments with Eurosender, up to 10% on selected products through DiscoverCars, 25% off pickpocket-proof travel garments from Clever Travel Companion, and free or tip-based tours through Freetour.com. It adds that “[m]ore benefits and discounts might be available at your destination”, which is doubtless true and is not the same as thousands.

One page has simply been left behind. A Covid-19 measures page marked “Updated June 2022” is still published, still tells readers that “[m]any hostels in our network now require guests to present a proof of COVID-19 vaccination and/or a negative test result”, and still describes a refund concession “designed to ensure we survive during this turbulent time”. Four years on, that page is a liability rather than a service.

For scale, the market these beds sit in is growing slowly rather than quickly. VisitBritain's inbound forecast published on 27 August 2026 expects 44.2 million inbound visits to the UK in 2026 spending £33.9 billion, growth of 2% in both visits and nominal spending but a 1% decline in spending in real terms, putting volume at 103% and nominal value at 119% of 2019 while real spend is still only 90% of the 2019 level. European markets are forecast to grow 4% by volume and 7% by value while long-haul markets fall 3% and 2%. Short-haul European visitors are exactly the market a hostel bed is priced for, and they are the part of the market that is still expanding.

pros: One membership and one search across a federation of more than 2,300 hostels and 57 to 58 national associations
Participating hostels are “certified every 3 years by an external auditor” under HI-Q&S, whose management system is recognised by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council
The federation is a UK registered charity (1117014) and its British members, YHA and Hostelling Scotland, are charities too
You do not need to join to book, and membership runs 12 months from the date of purchase rather than to a calendar year end
British membership is cheap: £20 a year at YHA, £10 for 16 to 25s, £15 at Hostelling Scotland and £6 for those aged 25 and under
A 10% member discount on YHA bookings, with a further 5% stacked on top for under-26s
Free cancellation up to 24 hours before an assumed 18:00 arrival, which is more generous than the law requires for a dated booking
Terms governed by the laws of England and Wales, with exclusive jurisdiction in the English courts
cons: The booking deposit is non-refundable in almost all circumstances and the terms never state what percentage of the price it is, so you cannot tell what you are risking until you reach the payment screen
HI's liability is “limited to the fees paid by you on this website” — that is, the deposit — because the stay itself is contracted with the hostel or national association rather than with HI
HI-Q&S covers “32 Associations and over 400 Hostels” out of a network of more than 2,300, while the About page tells readers that “all our hostels meet the HI standards”
The price of membership appears nowhere on hihostels.com; you have to go to a separate site or ask at the hostel door to find out what a card costs
HI's own pages give 57 and 58 member associations, and its British members advertise “over 4,000 hostels” against the federation's “over 2,300”, with nothing anywhere reconciling the two
“Thousands of travel discounts at home and abroad” turns out to be six named partners on the benefits page
A Covid-19 measures page last updated in June 2022 is still live and still tells travellers that many hostels require proof of vaccination or a negative test
Hostel listing pages show no nightly price until you enter dates and no independent quality rating at all, even where an English hostel holds a VisitEngland star rating
For a stay in England or Wales you are almost always booking a YHA hostel, and YHA's 10% member discount, promotional codes and best-rate refund apply only to bookings made at yha.org.uk
verdict: Hostelling International is a well-run federation doing something unusual: publishing a quality standard, paying an outside auditor to check it every three years, and putting the whole thing behind a UK charity with accounts anybody can read. For a trip through several countries, one £20 card and one search across 2,300-odd hostels is a genuinely good deal, and the 24-hour cancellation rule is more generous than the law obliges anyone to be on a dated booking. The site's weaknesses are of presentation rather than substance — a membership price it never quotes, a quality programme that reaches a sixth of the network while the marketing implies all of it, three different network sizes across the federation and its own members, and a pandemic page four years past its usefulness. And for a hostel in England or Wales, the operator is YHA, which will refund the difference if you find the bed cheaper elsewhere and loses about £2 million a year to intermediaries. Use HI abroad, where the federation is the point; think twice before using it to book a bed forty miles from home.

faqs.q: Do I have to be a member to book an HI hostel?
faqs.a: No. HI states that “[y]ou do not need to be a member…in order to make your booking”. In some countries membership is compulsory to stay, and in others non-members “pay a small surcharge or can purchase a membership card at the hostel”. Where it is optional, a card bought in advance earns the member rate on the booking itself.

faqs.q: What does HI membership cost in the UK?
faqs.a: HI does not publish a price on its own site — it says only that prices “vary depending on your place of residence”. You buy through the national association. YHA charges £20 a year by direct debit for adults and £10 a year for ages 16 to 25. Hostelling Scotland charges £15 a year for those aged 26 and over, £6 for those 25 and under, £150 for life membership and £3 per overnight for non-members, with rates applying from 5 April.

faqs.q: When can I cancel without being charged?
faqs.a: The cancellation must be made “at least 24 hours prior to the arrival time”, and HI's terms treat your arrival time as “18:00 (6pm) local time to the hostel” regardless of when you actually intended to turn up. The deposit is non-refundable either way. Fail to cancel and not turn up and you are charged one night on a one-night booking or two nights on any longer booking, plus taxes.

faqs.q: Is my money protected if the hostel goes under?
faqs.a: Not by the package travel rules. A package requires “a combination of at least two different types of travel services for the purpose of the same trip or holiday”, and a bed booked on its own is one service, so the insolvency protection and organiser liability in the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018 do not apply. HI's own liability is capped at the fees you paid on its website. Paying by credit card, or holding travel insurance, is the practical answer.

faqs.q: Are HI hostels independently inspected?
faqs.a: Some are. Hostels in the HI Quality & Sustainability programme are “certified every 3 years by an external auditor” and the management system is recognised by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council, but the programme is “used in 32 Associations and over 400 Hostels worldwide” rather than across the whole network. In England there is a separate route: VisitEngland runs a hostel assessment scheme in which an assessor visits as a mystery guest, with star bands of 60–74%, 75–86% and 87–100%. HI does not display those ratings.

faqs.q: Should I book on hihostels.com or with the hostel directly?
faqs.a: Abroad, the HI search is genuinely useful and the membership discount travels with you. In England and Wales, the hostel is almost always YHA, which offers to “refund the difference” if you find a better rate online within 24 hours, applies its 10% member discount and 5% under-26 discount to bookings at yha.org.uk, and says direct booking is “the only way to redeem promotional codes and take advantage of special offers”. For a domestic stay, going direct is usually both cheaper and better for the charity.

title: Hostelworld Review: The Deposit, the Balance and What You Pay at the Door
meta_title: Hostelworld Review: What the Deposit Really Pays For
meta_description: Hostelworld lists around 17,000 hostels in 180+ countries. What the deposit covers, what you settle at the hostel, and how the guarantees work.
intro:
Hostelworld has been selling hostel beds since 1999, and it is one of the very few businesses in budget travel whose numbers you can actually check. Hostelworld Group plc floated on the London Stock Exchange's main market on 2 November 2015 at 185 pence a share, valuing the company at about £176.8 million, and it has published audited accounts ever since. The platform carries roughly 17,000 hostels across more than 180 countries and 13.7 million guest reviews, took 7.0 million net bookings in 2025 on net revenue of €93.8 million, and now sees 63% of its bednights booked through the app rather than the website.

The stay itself is not sold by Hostelworld, and its terms say so in plain words: "your contract for travel services (including accommodation) is with the travel services provider, not Hostelworld". You pay a deposit online — the company's own guide puts it at "about 12-15% of the total cost" — and you settle the balance in person at the hostel, usually alongside a local city tax the property is obliged by law to collect. That split decides who you deal with if anything goes wrong, so it is worth knowing before you book rather than after.

Free cancellation is offered on a large share of properties, and where a hostel sets a standard policy the deadline is, in Hostelworld's words, "normally at least 24 hours before your agreed check-in date". Cancel inside the window and the deposit comes back. There is also a Booking Guarantee for the rare occasion when a reception desk has no record of you, and a best price promise if you find the same bed cheaper elsewhere within a day of booking. Both have conditions attached, and both are set out further down this page.
