sections.heading: Seven cards, and a rate ladder that runs from 18.9% to 100.2%
sections.html:
HSBC publishes seven personal credit cards and prices them for seven different jobs rather than selling one card with options. The cheapest borrowing rate belongs to the Student Credit Card at 18.9% a year variable, open only to people who already hold an HSBC Student Bank Account, with a credit limit between £250 and £500 and a cash rate of 23.6% a year, which is the lowest cash rate in the range by a wide margin.

Above it sit the two promotional cards. Purchase Plus charges 24.9% variable once its offers run out and gives up to 24 months at 0% on purchases — HSBC's own comparison page adds “For new HSBC credit card customers only” to that offer, which is a condition the product page leaves out — plus up to 17 months at 0% on transfers made within 60 days, at a 3.49% fee with a £5 minimum. The Balance Transfer Credit Card charges 25.9% variable, runs the 0% transfer window out to 36 months at a lower fee, and gives only three months at 0% on purchases. Neither charges an annual fee and both ask for £6,800 of income.

The Rewards Credit Card is 26.9% variable and earns more than its headline suggests: HSBC advertises “up to 10 points for every £1 you spend” at selected retailers through Mastercard Pay with Rewards, which has to be registered for before the purchase is made, and 1 point for every £5 spent anywhere else. It pays 2,500 points as a welcome bonus on the first transaction, another 2,500 for £10,000 of spending in each of the first five years, six months at 0% on purchases and six months at 0% on transfers at a 2.99% fee. Classic is the plain card at 29.9% variable with no promotional period at all, a minimum credit limit of £250 and a maximum of £1,000.

The Premier Credit Card is the one the previous version of this page undersold. It matches Classic's 29.9% and is restricted to Premier customers, but it charges no annual fee and still earns 1.5 reward points per £1 of sterling spending and 2 points per £1 abroad, pays 30,000 points for £2,000 of spending in the first 90 days on an offer advertised as ending 1 December 2026, carries Priority Pass access to more than 1,700 lounges at £24 per person per visit, and advertises up to 5% cashback on selected Apple products.

At the top is the Premier World Elite Mastercard: a 29.9% purchase rate, a £290 annual fee, £60 a year for each additional cardholder, and a representative APR of 100.2% variable on an assumed £1,200 limit. It earns 3 points per £1 on sterling spending and 4 points per £1 on non-sterling spending against a 2.99% non-sterling fee, pays 70,000 points for the same £2,000 of spending in 90 days on the same 1 December 2026 deadline, and makes the same 1,700 lounges free rather than £24 a visit. Getting it means qualifying for Premier, which needs £100,000 of annual income paid into the account or £100,000 of savings and investments held with HSBC UK.

sections.heading: What three years of nothing actually costs
sections.html:
The arithmetic on the headline product is short enough to do in one line, and it has to be done twice because HSBC publishes two fees for it. At 3.09% a £3,000 transfer costs £92.70, which is £2.58 a month across 36 months, or an effective 1.03% a year for the use of the money. At the 3.19% HSBC quotes on its comparison and offer pages it is £95.70, £2.66 a month, 1.06% a year. The gap between the two is £3 on a three-year loan.

The number to set either against is not HSBC's own 25.9% go-to rate but the market rate a reader is probably already paying. The Bank of England's Money and Credit release for August 2026, published on 29 September 2026 and still the current one until the September figures appear on 29 October 2026, puts the effective rate on interest-charging credit cards at 21.55%, up from 21.45% the month before. A year of interest on £3,000 at that rate is about £646, so HSBC's one-off fee is worth roughly one-seventh of a single year's interest at the going rate, and the card then buys three years of silence. On that comparison the fee is cheap, and saying so is simply reading the two numbers next to each other.

The sum that matters more is what happens if the 36 months turns out to be 14, which is the shorter offer HSBC publishes on the same page. The fee does not shrink with the term. £92.70 spread over 14 months is £6.62 a month rather than £2.58 — two and a half times the cost per interest-free month for the same money. A reader comparing cards on the fee alone is comparing the wrong number; the figure that decides the value is the fee divided by the months actually granted.

The same Bank of England release explains why the product exists at all. Net credit card borrowing rose to £1.2 billion in August 2026 from £0.9 billion in July, within £2.5 billion of total net consumer credit, and credit card balances were growing at 13.3% a year against 12.6% a month earlier. Card borrowing is growing faster than consumer credit as a whole, which was running at 9.6%. A bank with 14.5 million retail customers competing for that flow has every reason to buy balances off its rivals with three years of free credit, and the fee is what pays for it.

sections.heading: Sixty days, two words, and one group exclusion
sections.html:
Three conditions sit between the advertised 36 months and the 36 months a particular applicant gets, and all three are on HSBC's own pages.

The first is the 60-day window. A transfer qualifies for the 0% rate only if it is made within 60 days of the account being opened, and the clock runs from opening rather than from approval or from the card arriving. The promotional period on the balance transfer card then runs from the date of each transfer, not from the date of the account, so a reader who waits eight weeks still gets the full term and a reader who waits nine weeks gets nothing. One version of the offer also sets a floor on the transfer itself, at “balances transferred of £100 or more”.

The second is the phrase “up to”, and HSBC is more candid about it than most issuers. Its balance transfer offer page names the alternatives outright: “0% for 36 months on balance transfers with 29.9% APR and 0% for 3 months on purchases” or “0% for 14 months on balance transfers with 29.9% APR and 0% for 3 months on purchases”, with the product page adding a third shape at “0% for 14 months on balance transfers with 29.9% APR”. Note what the alternatives are priced at: 29.9%, four percentage points above the 25.9% in the representative example, which is the rate that governs anything still owed when the 0% ends. Both the promotional length and the go-to rate are set on application.

The third is the group exclusion already stated above, and it has a second edge to it. Holding two HSBC cards is allowed — the maximum is two — but a balance cannot be shuffled between them, and no new card or credit limit increase is available for six months after one is opened, in either direction. The pairings are set as well: HSBC states that Purchase Plus and the Balance Transfer card are “Available for existing Rewards, Premier and Premier World Elite credit card holders only”, so the two promotional cards cannot be taken one after the other. A reader who takes Purchase Plus for its 24 months at 0% on spending has therefore used up six months, one of their two card slots, and their eligibility for the transfer card at the same time.

sections.heading: The bank behind the card, in the regulator's words
sections.html:
The lender is HSBC UK Bank plc, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both the Financial Conduct Authority and the PRA under Financial Services Register number 765112. Companies House records it as company 09928412, incorporated on 23 December 2015 and active, a public limited company registered under SIC code 64191 for banks, with its registered office at 1 Centenary Square, Birmingham B1 1HQ.

That 2015 incorporation date is worth a sentence, because the bank is younger than the brand on the card. HSBC UK Bank plc was created as the ring-fenced UK retail bank required by post-crisis banking reform, which is why the registered office is in Birmingham rather than at the group's Canary Wharf headquarters. HSBC's own description is that “HSBC UK is a ring-fenced bank and wholly owned subsidiary of HSBC Holdings plc”. For a cardholder the practical effect is that the entity carrying the lending is a separate legally ring-fenced company from the international business, and the Financial Services Compensation Scheme limit applies at that entity across HSBC UK, first direct and M&S Bank together rather than once per brand.

The scale is HSBC's own published figure, unchanged on this check: 14.5 million retail and wealth customers, 600,000 business clients, over 15 million active customers in total and more than 23,000 colleagues. Credit cards are a small line inside that, and HSBC does not publish how many cards it has in issue or what share of its card balances carry interest, which is a gap other large issuers also leave.

sections.heading: Two charges HSBC has quietly stopped making
sections.html:
The best news on this card range since it was last checked is a subtraction. HSBC's credit card fees page now states of the over-limit charge that “Previously, an over-limit fee of £12 was charged if you exceeded your agreed credit limit” and that “This fee has now been removed, and you will not incur any charges for going over your limit”; and of the returned payment charge that “Previously, a returned payment fee of £5 was applied if a payment from your Direct Debit or cheque was rejected” and “This fee has been removed, and you will not be charged for returned payments”. Both were live figures on this page a week ago. HSBC gives no date for either removal, so when they went is a question for the bank.

What survives is the £12 late payment fee, charged “If you're late paying your minimum monthly payment” and appearing on the next statement, plus reasonable costs if HSBC has to enforce repayment. Two charges gone and one left is a better charging structure than almost any rival publishes, and it is the kind of change a bank makes without a press release.

Cash is still the expensive corner of every card in the range and the rate depends on which card you hold. A cash advance costs 27.9% a year (2.075% a month) on the balance transfer card, 29.9% a year (2.207% a month) on Premier, 35.9% a year (2.592% a month) on Classic and 23.6% a year (1.784% a month) on the student card, in each case on a fee of 2.99% of the amount with a £3 minimum. Interest on a cash advance runs from the day it is taken, so the interest-free period on purchases does not reach it. Spending abroad costs 2.99% of the transaction converted into sterling. Every summary box in the range sets the interest-free period on purchases at a maximum of 56 days, and only where the transaction balance is paid in full and on time.

The minimum payment is the highest of three calculations: all interest added since the last statement plus any default charges plus 1% of the remaining balance; or 2.5% of the full amount owed; or £5. The first of those three is the one worth understanding, because a minimum payment built as interest plus 1% clears the principal at 1% a month and nothing faster. Payments are allocated to the most expensive balance first, which is the statutory order and works in the cardholder's favour.

sections.heading: Where HSBC's own documents stop agreeing with each other
sections.html:
This is the part of the range that needs reading with a pen. On 12 October 2026 HSBC was publishing three different prices for one card. Its product page and its single-card comparison page both give the Balance Transfer Credit Card a representative 25.9% APR with a 3.09% fee. Its four-card comparison page gives the same card 24.9% APR and a 3.19% fee. Its balance transfer offer page carries both fees in two adjacent sentences — “up to 36 months interest free for balance transfers (3.09% fee, min £5)” and “up to 36 months with no interest to pay on balances transferred of £100 or more (3.19% fee, min £5)”. The 36 months is the one term every page agrees on.

That resolves something the previous version of this page got wrong, and it is worth saying so plainly. It criticised HSBC for a worked example reading “would cost you £95.70” on a £3,000 transfer, on the grounds that 3.09% of £3,000 is £92.70. £95.70 is exactly 3.19% of £3,000, and 3.19% is a fee HSBC publishes on two of its own pages. It was never an arithmetic error; it was the other fee. The worked example itself could not be found on any HSBC page on this check, so it appears to have been taken down.

Behind the live pages sit the summary boxes, which are the documents a regulated lender points an applicant at before they borrow, and three of them have not been refreshed in years. The balance transfer box linked from HSBC's own comparison page carries the reference DCP140 and a copyright line reading ©HSBC Group 2021, and states a representative APR of 21.9%, a 0% transfer period of 29 months rather than 36, and a fee of 2.75%. The Premier box is DCP253, ©HSBC Group 2022, and gives a representative 23.9% APR against 29.9% on the product page. The Premier World Elite box is RFB1537 MCP55679, ©HSBC Group 2021, and is the widest gap of the three: “Representative 59.3% APR variable (including annual fee of £195)” with a purchase rate of 18.9% and a minimum credit limit of £5,000, against 100.2% APR, a £290 fee and a 29.9% purchase rate on the live page. The document understates the annual fee by £95 and the purchase rate by 11 percentage points on the most expensive card in the range.

All three boxes also still list the £12 over-limit fee and the £5 returned payment fee that the fees page says have been removed, which is the clearest sign that these are documents nobody has refreshed rather than two sets of terms. That is the fairer diagnosis and it is still a real problem: an applicant for the one product in the range with an offer worth having is reading a five-year-old price list, and every figure in it is wrong in the bank's favour on the rate and in the customer's favour on the fees. Which set of figures governs an agreement signed today needs confirming with HSBC before anybody relies on either.

There is a smaller mismatch of the same family on the student card, and it is the harmless kind. Its product page says “Based on an assumed credit limit of £250” while the card grid and its own comparison page both say £500. The summary box, DCP131 of 2021, settles what the two figures actually are: £250 is the minimum credit limit and £500 the maximum. The product page has put the minimum where the assumed limit belongs. Nothing material turns on it, because the card carries no fee and the representative APR is 18.9% either way, but it is the same lack of upkeep showing up in a second place.

sections.heading: Complaints, and the rule that caps how long a balance can sit
sections.html:
HSBC publishes its own complaints return, which is more than many issuers volunteer, and the figures for the six months from 1 January to 30 June 2026 are unchanged on this check. In the banking and credit cards category it opened 73,367 complaints at a rate of 2.26 per 1,000 accounts, closed 60.1% of them within three days and a further 39.3% after three days but within eight weeks, upheld 58.8%, and recorded general administration and customer service as the main cause. The two closure columns are separate groups rather than running totals, so the figure that matters is their sum: 99.4% of banking and credit card complaints were closed inside the eight-week regulatory window and 0.6% were not.

One correction to make here. The previous version of this page gave a total of 83,623 complaints opened across HSBC UK Bank plc. There is no total row on HSBC's table at all. Its six product categories — banking and credit cards 73,367, home finance 4,246, credit related 4,200, investments 1,207, insurance and pure protection 423 and decumulation and pensions 80 — add to 83,523, and that sum is this page's arithmetic rather than a figure HSBC prints. Credit cards sit in the best-performing of those categories: home finance closed only 29.3% of cases within three days and upheld 62.4%, and investments closed 13.5% within three days.

Two of the card figures point in opposite directions and both are fair. A rate of 2.26 per 1,000 accounts is low, and closing three in five cases inside three days is fast work. An uphold rate of 58.8% means nearly three in five complainants turned out to be right, which is the number a prospective cardholder should weigh rather than the headline volume.

Set against that is a protection the reader gets whichever card they take. Under the FCA's persistent debt rules, in force from 1 March 2018 with firms required to comply by 1 September 2018, a lender has to act when a customer pays more in interest and charges than they repay of the balance over an extended period. The FCA found around 4 million accounts in that position, paying roughly £2.50 in interest and charges for every £1 of balance repaid. At 18 months the firm must make contact and prompt a change in repayments, warning that the card may be suspended; at 36 months it must offer a way to clear the balance in a reasonable period and, where the customer cannot, show forbearance that may include reducing, waiving or cancelling interest, fees or charges. The FCA estimated the package would save consumers between £310 million and £1.3 billion a year, and that around 1.4 million accounts a year would stop receiving automatic credit limit increases. A 36-month 0% transfer and a 36-month persistent-debt intervention are the same length by coincidence, but a reader who reaches the end of one is close to the threshold for the other.

sections.heading: What a reward point is worth, on HSBC's own two numbers
sections.html:
HSBC publishes two valuations for its own points and they differ by a factor of three. The Rewards card's welcome bonus is advertised as “2,500 welcome points worth £25”, which makes a point a penny. The charity redemption on the same rewards pages is priced differently: “Every 1,500 points is worth £5 of support” for Shelter, which makes a point a third of a penny. For shopping vouchers, airline miles and hotel stays, the three redemptions most cardholders would use, HSBC publishes no rate at all and says only that “The cash equivalent of your points will be credited to your account”. Points have to be redeemed within three years from the end of the calendar month in which they were earned.

At the penny valuation the Rewards card returns 0.2% on general spending, because 1 point per £5 is a penny per £5. The anniversary bonus of 2,500 points for £10,000 of spending adds £25 on £10,000, which is another 0.25%, so a cardholder spending exactly £10,000 a year gets about 0.45% back. The 10 points per £1 at selected retailers is a 10% return at the same valuation, which is why HSBC caps it to a registered list rather than offering it on everything.

The interesting sum is the one between the two Premier cards, because HSBC prices the alternative itself. The Premier Credit Card is free and earns 1.5 points per £1; the World Elite costs £290 and earns 3. The fee therefore buys an extra 1.5 points per £1, which at a penny a point is 1.5% — so the fee is recovered at about £19,300 of annual sterling spending. On the charity valuation the same calculation needs about £58,000. Two things close the gap in the first year: the welcome bonuses differ by 40,000 points, worth £400 at a penny and £133 at the charity rate, and the World Elite makes lounge visits free where the Premier card charges £24 a person, so the fee is also about twelve lounge visits. A reader who will take twelve lounge visits or spend £19,300 is being offered a fair deal; a reader who will do neither is paying £290 for points.

That sum rests on a valuation HSBC has published for one card's welcome bonus and never confirmed for the Premier range, so treat the £19,300 as the best case rather than the answer, and ask HSBC what a World Elite point redeems at before paying the fee. On independent ratings there is a plain answer and it is a negative one: Defaqto rates insurance rather than consumer credit, and no ratings agency publishes a star rating or score for an HSBC credit card that could be quoted here. HSBC's own complaints return and its summary boxes are the only dated, primary numbers available on this product.

pros: Up to 36 months at 0% on balance transfers for a fee HSBC puts at 3.09% or 3.19% — £92.70 or £95.70 on £3,000, about 1.03% to 1.06% a year spread over the term
The £12 over-limit fee and the £5 returned payment fee have both been removed, leaving the £12 late payment fee as the only default charge HSBC still makes
Six of the seven cards carry no annual fee, and the minimum income on the four mainstream cards is £6,800
Purchase Plus covers the other need at up to 24 months at 0% on spending plus up to 17 months at 0% on transfers
HSBC names the alternatives to its own headline offer on the page itself — 0% for 36 months or 14 months, both at 29.9% APR — rather than leaving "up to" unexplained
The free Premier Credit Card earns 1.5 points per £1 with 30,000 points for £2,000 of spending in 90 days, so the rewards range does not start at the £290 card
99.4% of banking and credit card complaints were closed inside the eight-week window, and payments are allocated to the most expensive balance first
The lender is a ring-fenced UK bank, FCA and PRA regulated under reference 765112, with 14.5 million retail and wealth customers behind it
cons: A balance cannot be transferred from another card inside the group — HSBC's own page names First Direct and M&S Bank — so the 36-month offer is closed to the one debt HSBC's 15 million existing customers are most likely to be carrying

HSBC publishes three prices for one card: 25.9% APR with a 3.09% fee on the product page, 24.9% with 3.19% on its four-card comparison page, and both fees in adjacent sentences on its balance transfer offer page

The Premier World Elite summary box, reference RFB1537 MCP55679 and copyright 2021, states 59.3% APR including a £195 annual fee and an 18.9% purchase rate against the live page's 100.2%, £290 and 29.9% — a disclosure that understates the fee by £95

The balance transfer summary box (DCP140, 2021) gives 21.9% APR, 29 months and a 2.75% fee, and the Premier box (DCP253, 2022) gives 23.9% against 29.9%; all three boxes still list the two fees HSBC's own fees page says it has removed, and no date is given for either removal

Transfers must be made within 60 days of account opening and the fee does not shrink with a shorter offer: £92.70 over the 14-month alternative is £6.62 a month against £2.58 over 36, two and a half times the cost per interest-free month

The two promotional cards cannot be taken one after the other — HSBC offers Purchase Plus and the Balance Transfer card only to existing Rewards, Premier or World Elite holders, and locks out new cards and limit increases for six months

Representative examples assume £1,200, £1,000 and £500 while the minimum limits are £500 on the balance transfer card and £250 on both Classic and the student card, so an applicant approved at the floor pays more in percentage terms than the advertised APR implies

Cash is punitive and the pricing is easy to miss: 35.9% a year on Classic, 29.9% on Premier and 27.9% on the balance transfer card, plus a 2.99% fee with a £3 minimum, with interest running from the day of withdrawal

HSBC prices a point at 1p in one place and a third of a penny in another, and publishes no rate at all for vouchers, airline miles or hotel stays, so the break-even spend on the £290 annual fee cannot be settled from the issuer's own material
No ratings agency publishes a score for an HSBC credit card, and HSBC does not disclose how many cards it has in issue or what share of balances carry interest
verdict: Judged on the one thing a balance transfer card is bought for, HSBC's is at the front of the market: up to 36 months at 0% for a fee of 3.09% or 3.19% is £92.70 or £95.70 on £3,000, about a seventh of what a year's interest at the Bank of England's 21.55% effective rate would cost, and it buys three years rather than one. Purchase Plus covers the other half of the job at up to 24 months on spending, six of the seven cards charge nothing to hold, and HSBC has quietly dropped both its over-limit and returned payment fees since this page was last checked. The things to check before applying are all HSBC's own small print rather than anything hidden: the 60-day transfer window, the "up to" on both the term and the rate, the minimum credit limits of £500 and £250 behind the £1,200 and £1,000 assumed in the adverts, and the group rule that stops an HSBC, first direct or M&S Bank balance moving across at all. That last one disqualifies a large share of the people most likely to be reading, so it is the first thing to establish. What has not improved is the paperwork. Three cards are sold on live pages that disagree with their own summary boxes, and on the Premier World Elite the regulated disclosure understates the annual fee by £95. On price this is a competitive range; read your own agreement rather than the advert, and ask which figure governs it.

faqs.q: How long is HSBC's 0% balance transfer offer, and what does it cost?
faqs.a: Up to 36 months at 0% on the Balance Transfer Credit Card. HSBC quotes the fee as 3.09% of each transfer on its product page and 3.19% on its comparison and offer pages, with a £5 minimum either way. On a £3,000 balance that is £92.70 or £95.70, which is £2.58 or £2.66 a month across the 36 months. Transfers must be made within 60 days of the account being opened and the 0% period runs from the date of each transfer. The go-to rate afterwards is 25.9% a year variable, and the card gives only three months at 0% on purchases, so it is a card for clearing a balance rather than for spending on.

faqs.q: Can I move a first direct or M&S Bank balance to an HSBC card?
faqs.a: No. HSBC's second-card page states that you cannot transfer balances between two HSBC credit cards, including First Direct or M&S Bank, because all three brands sit inside HSBC UK Bank plc. The same applies to moving a balance between two HSBC-branded cards you hold yourself. If the debt you want to shift is already with one of those three, the 0% offer cannot take it, and this is the single most common reason an application of this kind is of no use to the applicant.

faqs.q: Does HSBC still charge an over-limit or returned payment fee?
faqs.a: No. HSBC's credit card fees page says the £12 over-limit fee “has now been removed, and you will not incur any charges for going over your limit”, and that the £5 returned payment fee “has been removed, and you will not be charged for returned payments”. The £12 late payment fee remains, as do reasonable costs if HSBC has to enforce repayment. HSBC gives no date for either removal, and every card summary box on its site still lists both charges, so ask which document governs your agreement.

faqs.q: Why is the Premier World Elite's representative APR 100.2% when the purchase rate is 29.9%?
faqs.a: Because a representative APR has to include compulsory charges, and the card's £290 annual fee is one. The calculation spreads that fee across the assumed £1,200 credit limit, which is a large proportion of a small balance, so the figure lands at 100.2% variable on a 29.9% purchase rate. Nobody pays 100.2% in interest. Note that the card's own summary box gives a different answer — 59.3% APR including a £195 annual fee, on an 18.9% purchase rate — and carries a 2021 copyright line, so the two documents are five years and £95 apart.

faqs.q: Is the £290 Premier World Elite worth more than the free Premier card?
faqs.a: It depends on how much you spend and how often you fly. The free Premier Credit Card earns 1.5 reward points per £1 of sterling spending; the World Elite earns 3, so the fee buys an extra 1.5 points per £1. At the penny a point HSBC puts on the Rewards card's welcome bonus, that recovers £290 at about £19,300 of annual spending. The welcome bonuses differ by 40,000 points, worth £400 at the same valuation, and lounge visits are free on the World Elite against £24 per person on the Premier card, so the fee is also about twelve lounge visits. HSBC does not publish what a Premier point redeems at, so treat those figures as the best case and ask before paying.

faqs.q: How many HSBC credit cards can I hold at once?
faqs.a: Two. The second has to be a different card from the first and the pairings are set: HSBC offers Purchase Plus and the Balance Transfer card only to existing Rewards, Premier or Premier World Elite holders, offers Rewards to holders of Balance Transfer, Purchase Plus, Classic, Premier or World Elite, and offers the two Premier cards to Balance Transfer, Purchase Plus and Rewards holders who also hold an HSBC Premier Account. Each card has its own credit limit, limits cannot be moved between them, and you cannot apply for a new card or a limit increase within six months of opening one.

title: Insurance2go Phone Insurance Review
meta_title: Insurance2go Phone Insurance: What £1.99 a Month Covers
meta_description: Insurance2go covers phones from £1.99 a month with unlimited claims and 94% accepted in 2024. The excess ladder, the insurers and the claim rules, checked.
intro:
Insurance2go has been selling mobile phone cover since 2007 and is the trading name of Loyal Insurance Services Ltd, a Portsmouth company registered on 2 February 2005 and authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference 430316. Since 28 March 2019 it has belonged to SPB, a European affinity insurance group, which runs the brand from 3000 Lakeside, Western Road alongside Better Buy Insurance. Cover starts at £1.99 a month for a phone, and the company says it accepted 94% of the mobile phone claims made in 2024.

The policy is more generous than most network and bank alternatives in one respect that matters: there is no cap on how many times you can claim while it is running. A single premium buys accidental damage, liquid damage, mechanical breakdown, malicious damage, loss and theft, worldwide cover, up to £1,000 of unauthorised calls, texts and downloads in the 24 hours after a theft, £100 against unauthorised e-wallet payments and up to £150 for accessories on any one claim. Claims are assessed within two working days, replacements go out in three to five, and repairs take around five to seven. Buying a year up front costs twelve months for the price of ten, and a second device takes 10% off.

One rule decides whether any of that is open to you. The phone must have been bought in the UK and must be no more than 36 months old on the day the policy starts. Once it is on cover it stays on cover as it ages, but a four-year-old handset cannot be added at all, and neither can one bought overseas or second-hand without a twelve-month warranty from a UK-registered supplier.

sections.heading: The two price tiers, and the gap the site never explains
sections.html:
Two levels are sold. Essential opens at £1.99 a month and Full at £3.49, both including insurance premium tax at 12%. On a named handset the difference is smaller than those headline numbers suggest: the iPhone 13 page quotes Essential from £2.49 and Full from £4.99, which is a gap of £2.50 a month, or £30 a year.

What that £30 buys is the part nobody at the company has written down. The comparison table on the mobile phone page, read on 1 September 2026, lists ten benefits — new or refurbished phones, accidental damage, mechanical breakdown, malicious damage, liquid damage, worldwide cover, loss, theft, e-wallet payments and unauthorised usage — and ticks every one of them for both Essential and Full. Read that table on its own and the cheaper tier looks identical to the dearer one.

The company's own Essential product information document says something different. Reference I2G-IPIDE-0920, published in 2020 and still the copy served from the site, lists accidental damage, breakdown, malicious damage, accessories and worldwide cover under what is insured, and puts theft and loss claims under what is not. Both documents belong to Insurance2go, they cannot both describe the same product, and the one that would settle it is six years old. Anyone buying Essential specifically for theft cover should get that confirmed in writing before paying.

There is a smaller version of the same problem on price. The home page advertises gadget cover from £2.99 a month; the gadget insurance page says from £4.49. Tablet cover is quoted at £4.49 and SIM-only phone cover at £2.99.

sections.heading: The excess is the number to check first
sections.html:
Insurance2go does not publish an excess table, and the figure only appears once you have run a quote. The iPhone pages are the exception, and they show a ladder that tracks the value of the handset rather than the type of claim. An iPhone 11 carries a £50 excess at £4.99 a month. An iPhone 12, 12 Mini, 13 or 14 carries £100 at £5.99. The Pro models sit at £125 and £7.49. An iPhone 13 Pro Max is £150 and £9.99 a month, or £99.90 for the year.

The company's own guide to low-excess cover puts the outer edges of the range at “around £150” for high-specification models and “as little as £25” for cheaper, older ones. Set the top of that ladder against the premium and the arithmetic of a first-year claim on a Pro Max is £99.90 in premium plus £150 in excess: £249.90, in exchange for a refurbished handset of the same age and condition as the one you lost.

A second charge sits on top of that in the first month. The Early Excess is described by the company as “an additional fee applied to claims made within the first 31 days of your policy's start date, or within 31 days of any changes to the covered device(s)”. During that window a claimant pays the standard excess, the early excess and, on monthly payment plans, the full first month's premium before the claim is processed. The amount is not published; like the standard excess, it appears on the certificate schedule. It is a reasonable enough guard against someone insuring a phone they have already broken, but it means the cheapest month of the policy is also the most expensive month in which to have an accident.

sections.heading: Three firms behind one phone number
sections.html:
Buying here puts three companies between you and your money, which is normal for this corner of the market but worth understanding before a claim. Loyal Insurance Services Ltd sells the policy. Citymain Administrators Ltd, company 03979666 and FRN 306535, takes the payments, handles the claims and answers the phone from the same Portsmouth address. An insurer carries the risk and is named only in the policy paperwork.

On the current gadget documents that insurer is Collinson Insurance, a trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited, FRN 202846. Astrenska is a real balance sheet rather than a brand: company 01708613, and its published solvency and financial condition report for the year to 30 April 2025 shows gross written premium of £297.2m, up from £221.4m the year before, and a profit of £4.289m against £3.198m. Its solvency capital requirement was £21.595m against eligible own funds of £38.026m, a coverage ratio of 176% — comfortably above the regulatory minimum, though down from 205% a year earlier. Mobile and gadget business sits inside the £35.3m the report books under fire and other damage to property, which makes it a modest part of a book dominated by travel and medical expense cover.

The business version of the product runs through two more entities, Square Pound Limited (company 07665065, FRN 564471) and Burnett & Associates Ltd (company 01472537, FRN 305511). All of these firm reference numbers can be checked on the Financial Services Register.

sections.heading: Four wordings, four insurers, and none of them current
sections.html:
The paperwork a shopper can read before buying is where this brand looks weakest, and it is worth setting out in order because the pattern is what matters.

The oldest document still served from the site is the full policy wording marked v7 and dated 14 May 2018. It names UK General Insurance Ltd, underwriting on behalf of Great Lakes Insurance SE. Next comes reference I2G/CW/0920, dated September 2020, which names UK General Insurance Limited on behalf of Watford Insurance Company Europe Limited. The mobile phone product information document, reference I2G_MPI_IPID_F_0521 and dated May 2021, names a third insurer again: Inter Partner Assistance S.A. UK Branch, FRN 202664. Only the gadget paperwork is recent — the product information document referenced I2G_FULL_GADGET_IPID_1024 from October 2024 and the terms and conditions referenced I2G-SINGLEGDGT-PD-1224 from December 2024, both naming Astrenska.

So the newest phone-specific document on the site is five years old, and the three phone documents between them name three different insurers. That does not mean the cover is unreliable; insurers change hands and schemes get re-papered, and the underlying benefits described in all four documents are broadly the same. It does mean that a customer buying a phone policy today cannot establish from the published documents who would actually be carrying their risk. That needs confirming on the phone before buying, and it is the single most useful question to ask.

One consequence is already visible. The excesses quoted in the 2018 wording run from £75 to £100 by model, which is not the £50 to £150 ladder the current iPhone pages show. Neither of the two current-era documents carries an excess table at all.

sections.heading: What a claim asks of you
sections.html:
The claims route is genuinely quick on paper. A claim goes in through the 24-hour portal, by phone, email or post; the company aims to respond within two working days; once authorised it emails instructions for paying the excess; a repair means posting the handset by registered mail in a padded envelope and takes around five to seven days, and a replacement arrives in three to five working days.

The evidence list is longer than most people expect. Every claim needs proof of purchase showing make, model and IMEI number. Theft and loss claims need a police or loss report reference, and the wording requires you to notify the local police as soon as possible after discovering the incident and to contact your network provider, also as soon as possible, to place a call bar. The company's claim documents page also asks, depending on circumstances, for a gifting letter, proof of exchange, proof of usage, an itemised phone bill, proof of blacklisting and proof of travel, and points customers to Immobilise and reportmyloss.com. A phone handed down from a family member without a gifting letter is a claim waiting to be argued about.

Two exclusions do more work than the rest. The wording states that you must not leave the phone unattended where it is accessible to the general public, and that no claim will be paid for property left unattended in publicly accessible places. And theft from a vehicle is excluded unless the windows and doors were closed and locked, the security systems were activated and the phone was out of view in an enclosed storage compartment, boot or luggage space. A phone taken from a table in a pub garden, or from a cupholder in a locked car, falls outside both.

The replacement itself is refurbished by design. The wording says the administrator “will endeavour to replace your mobile phone with an identical, fully refurbished (or new where a refurbished item is not available) mobile phone of the same age and condition”. That is standard across this market, but it is worth knowing before the parcel arrives — the Financial Ombudsman Service lists “replacement phone or gadget is refurbished and not a new one” among the recurring grounds of complaint it sees on these policies, alongside mis-selling, misleading policy wording, exclusions applied at claim time, automatic renewal and cover running on after the phone contract ended. All repairs and replacements are carried out in the United Kingdom, whatever the worldwide cover implies about where you can break the phone.

sections.heading: Gadget cover in the regulator's own numbers
sections.html:
The FCA publishes value measures data on retail general insurance, most recently on 21 July 2026 covering calendar year 2025, and gadget insurance is one of the lines it reports. Firms report where written retail premiums exceed £400,000 and more than 3,000 policies are in force, so the data covers the market rather than every seller in it.

Gadget cover paid out 36% of premiums in claims in 2025, down from 42% the year before. Policies in force fell 5% to 7.5 million, claims registered fell 8% and claims costs fell 12%, while premiums rose 3%. For comparison, motor insurance paid 59% of premium in claims over the same period. That gap is the honest context for any phone policy: as a class, these products keep a much larger share of the premium than motor or home cover does, which is the arithmetic behind the standard advice to weigh a year of premiums plus the excess against what the handset is actually worth.

What the FCA does not publish is a claims acceptance rate for gadget insurance. It gives them for home (62% to 71%), travel (83% to 86%) and motor (99%), and gadget is not among them. Insurance2go's 94% is therefore its own figure, defined by the company as authorised against rejected claims made in 2024, excluding pending and abandoned ones — a fair enough definition, but one with no published benchmark to sit against.

The Ombudsman's annual complaints data, published 21 May 2026, records 899 new mobile phone insurance complaints in 2025/26 at a 25% uphold rate, against 214,600 complaints across all products and a 30% average. That is a small line and a below-average uphold rate, and it says nothing about any individual firm. Ofcom's pricing report of 26 February 2026 explains why the standalone market exists at all: SIM-only plans accounted for half of pay-monthly subscriptions by June 2025 at around £18 a month, and taking the handset through the contract instead costs over £8 a month more, roughly £200 across 24 months. A phone bought outright is a phone with no insurance attached.

sections.heading: How much independent evidence there is
sections.html:
Less than the marketing implies. The company's own news page dates its Defaqto 5 Star rating to 1 February 2019 and attaches it to the full cover mobile phone policy. Defaqto reissues its ratings annually, so a badge from early 2019 tells you what the product looked like more than seven years ago, and no current rating for the brand could be read from Defaqto's own site.

Smart Money People carries a rating of 3.44 out of 5 for Insurance2go's gadget insurance, but from only five reviews, three of which are one star. Five reviews is far too small a sample to draw anything from, and it is quoted here only because it is the one independent score that exists.

There is a live award nomination: Insurance2go announced on 3 July 2026 that it had been shortlisted for Best Mobile/Gadget Insurance Service at the 2026 Mobile Industry Awards, with winners announced on 17 September 2026. A shortlisting is not a win, and this page was written before that date.

One last inconsistency, and a small one. The about page says the company has a 93% approval rate for claims, while the home page and the mobile phone page both say 94% of 2024 claims. The difference is a rounding argument rather than a scandal, but on a site where the claims acceptance rate is the headline selling point, two versions of it is one too many.

pros: No limit on the number of claims while the policy is in force
Cover starts at £1.99 a month for a phone, with loss and theft included rather than sold as a paid extra
Twelve months for the price of ten on annual payment, and 10% off a second device
Worldwide cover, plus £1,000 of unauthorised usage and £100 of e-wallet protection after a theft
Claims assessed within two working days, replacements dispatched in three to five
A phone stays covered once it passes three years old, even though it cannot be added after 36 months
The underwriter behind the current gadget wording, Astrenska, holds 176% solvency coverage on £297.2m of premium
cons: The excess is not published anywhere before you run a quote, and it is the number that decides whether the policy is worth having — £150 on an iPhone 13 Pro Max, which with the £99.90 annual premium makes one first-year claim cost £249.90
An unpublished Early Excess is charged on top of the standard excess for any claim in the first 31 days, along with the full first month's premium before the claim is processed

The newest phone-specific policy document on the site is dated September 2020, and the three phone documents name three different insurers — UK General with Great Lakes in 2018, UK General with Watford in 2020 and Inter Partner Assistance in 2021 — so who carries the risk on a phone policy sold today cannot be established from the published paperwork

The Essential and Full comparison table ticks all ten benefits identically for both tiers, while the published Essential product information document excludes theft and loss; the site never states what the extra £2.50 a month actually buys
Replacements are refurbished as a matter of policy, “of the same age and condition”, which the Ombudsman names as one of the recurring grounds of complaint on these products
The only independent rating the company publishes is a Defaqto 5 Star dated 1 February 2019; Smart Money People has just five reviews, three of them one star
The home page advertises gadget cover from £2.99 a month while the gadget page says £4.49, and the about page quotes 93% of claims approved where the rest of the site says 94%

The unattended exclusion is wide: nothing is paid for a phone left where the general public can reach it, and theft from a locked car is excluded unless the phone was out of view in an enclosed compartment, boot or luggage space
verdict: For a phone bought outright and under three years old, this is a competitive standalone policy: £1.99 to £9.99 a month depending on the handset, unlimited claims, loss and theft included, worldwide cover and a two-working-day claims decision. The company's 94% acceptance figure for 2024 is its own, but it is a figure it is willing to put a definition against, which is more than most of this market offers. Work out the excess before you buy — it runs to £150 on the dearest handsets and is the difference between a policy worth having and one that costs more than a repair. And if you are buying Essential rather than Full, ask what the cheaper tier leaves out, because the site's own documents disagree with each other on the answer.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites an Insurance2go phone policy?
faqs.a: The current gadget documents name Collinson Insurance, a trading name of Astrenska Insurance Limited (FRN 202846). The phone-specific documents are older and name different insurers: Inter Partner Assistance S.A. UK Branch (FRN 202664) in the May 2021 product information document, and UK General Insurance on behalf of Watford Insurance Company Europe Limited in the September 2020 wording. Because no current phone wording is published, it is worth ringing 0333 999 7905 and asking who the insurer is before you buy.

faqs.q: How much is the excess?
faqs.a: It depends on the handset and is only confirmed on your certificate schedule. The iPhone pages show £50 on an iPhone 11, £100 on an iPhone 12, 13 or 14, £125 on the Pro models and £150 on an iPhone 13 Pro Max. The company's own guide puts the wider range at about £25 for older, cheaper phones up to around £150 for high-specification ones. An additional Early Excess also applies to any claim made within 31 days of the policy starting or of the insured device being changed.

faqs.q: Can I insure a phone that is more than three years old?
faqs.a: Not as a new policy. The device must be no more than 36 months old at the point the cover starts, must have been bought in the UK, and if it is refurbished or second-hand it must have come from a UK-registered supplier with a twelve-month warranty. A phone already on cover stays covered as it ages past three years.

faqs.q: Will I get a new phone if mine is stolen?
faqs.a: Usually not. The wording says the administrator will try to replace the phone with an identical, fully refurbished handset of the same age and condition, and will only supply a new one where no refurbished equivalent is available. Repairs and replacements are carried out in the UK. This is normal across gadget insurance, and it is also one of the complaint grounds the Financial Ombudsman Service lists for this product.

faqs.q: How many claims can I make in a year?
faqs.a: Insurance2go states there is no limit on the number of claims while cover is in place, which is unusual — most network and bank policies cap claims at one or two a year. The excess is payable on every claim, so the practical limit is financial rather than contractual.

faqs.q: How do I cancel?
faqs.a: You have 14 days from the policy starting, or from renewal, to cancel with a full refund provided no claim has been made. After that you can cancel at any time, but a monthly policy attracts no refund and an annual policy is refunded proportionately only if no claim has been made during the year.

title: Insure4Boats Review: Small Craft, Jet Skis and the Conditions Attached
meta_title: Insure4Boats Review: £3m Cover for Small Craft & Jet Skis
meta_description: Insure4Boats covers paddleboards to 27ft speedboats with £3m liability as standard. Underwriters, fees, exclusions and discounts, checked August 2026.
intro:
Insure4Boats sells cover for the end of the water most marine brokers treat as an afterthought. Paddleboards, kayaks, canoes, dinghies, RIBs, speedboats and jet skis sit alongside the narrowboats and yachts on its quote form, and all of them can be bought online in a single sitting. It is a trading name of Ripe Insurance Services Limited, a Stockport firm at One Stockport Exchange, incorporated on 9 August 2002 as company 04507332 and authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority under firm reference 313411. Hull cover carries £3,000,000 of third-party liability as standard, five claim-free years earn up to 25% off, and monthly payments over £50 are offered at 0% APR.

The parent business explains a good deal about how the buying feels. Ripe runs a family of single-hobby brands off one platform — Insure4Sport, Insure4Music, Cycleplan, Golf Care and a caravan arm among them — and now serves close to 350,000 policyholders with more than three million site visits a year. Aquiline Capital Partners, a private investment firm with $6.9 billion under management, took a majority stake when the group stood at 280,000 policyholders and was growing revenue 27% a year. The company was called JRW Insurance Services Limited for six weeks in 2002, then J R W Group Services Limited until 15 June 2017, when the Ripe name was adopted.

What that scale buys a small-boat owner is a quote journey that does not flinch at a £400 kayak. Most yacht brokers want a survey, a mooring address and a phone call before they will price anything. Insure4Boats will insure a stand-up paddleboard and a 25ft RIB through the same front door, with the same discounts and the same 14-day cooling-off period, and it publishes all five of its policy wordings and every product information document openly rather than sending them after the sale.

sections.heading: What £3 million of liability is actually holding up
sections.html:
The liability limit is the number that matters most on a small boat, because the boat itself is rarely the expensive part of an accident. A £2,000 dinghy can put someone in hospital or hole a moored cruiser worth fifty times its value, and the £3,000,000 that Insure4Boats includes as standard is what stands behind that.

It also clears the licensing bar comfortably. The Canal & River Trust will not issue a boat licence without third-party cover of at least £2,000,000, protecting the owner or the person in charge against claims for injury or damage. A standard Insure4Boats policy sits £1,000,000 above that floor before you spend anything extra, and the upgrade to £5,000,000 costs £40 plus insurance premium tax.

For a sense of how often small craft need help at all: RNLI crews launched more than 9,000 times in 2025 across 238 stations, an average of 25 lifeboats a day and the charity's sixth busiest year on record. Motorboats accounted for 951 of those launches and sailing vessels 713, with 272 lives saved. Salvage and towage charges are covered under the hull policy, which is the clause most owners of trailer-launched boats never think about until a gearbox fails two miles offshore.

sections.heading: You get one of two insurers, and which one depends on the product
sections.html:
This is the detail no competitor page carries, and it is worth reading the documents for. Buy hull and machinery cover with liability attached — the normal purchase — and the risk sits with Travelers Insurance Company Limited, registered at 30 Fenchurch Street in London as company 01034343, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority under firm reference 202549. That applies across the small craft, jet ski, sports craft and narrowboat wordings.

Buy third-party liability on its own, though, and the policy is written by Certain Underwriters at Lloyd's instead. It is a different contract with a different claims route: claims go to Charles Taylor Adjusting at 12–13 Essex Street, London, on 0800 997 8986, and complaints that Insure4Boats cannot settle escalate to Argo rather than to Travelers, with Lloyd's own complaints team on 020 7237 5693 behind that. The liability-only wording also carries its own £25 administration fee on cancellation after the first 14 days, separate from the broker's charge.

The practical consequence is that comparing the cheap liability-only quote against the full quote is not comparing two versions of one policy. Two insurers, two sets of conditions, two complaints routes.

sections.heading: Five wordings, and the 27ft line that decides yours
sections.html:
Insure4Boats splits its book into five documents rather than running one wording with endorsements. Small craft covers speedboats, RIBs and anything 27ft and under; large craft picks up motorboats and sailing yachts above that; jet ski, sports craft and narrowboat and inland craft each have their own. The 27ft line is worth checking before you quote, because it changes the conditions rather than only the price.

The sports craft wording is the one aimed squarely at kayaks, canoes and paddleboards, and it is drawn tighter than the name suggests. Windsurfers, sailboards, kiteboards, wakeboards, water skis and scuba or snorkelling equipment are all outside it. Theft cover on that wording is conditional in a way owners regularly fall foul of: at home the craft must be inside a locked building with evidence of forced entry, and away from home it must be locked to an immovable object or, on a vehicle, secured to a locked roof rack in a locked car. Personal accident cover on that wording pays nothing to anyone under 16 or over 65.

sections.heading: The conditions a small boat carries through the year
sections.html:
Three restrictions in the small craft wording catch people out, and none of them are obvious from the quote screen.

The first is winter. Between 1 November and 31 March the boat is expected to be ashore or in a professionally run marina, and using it in that window is not covered unless you have bought the optional winter cover. Anyone who takes a RIB out on a bright February morning is uninsured by default.

The second is unattended mooring. A vessel left afloat and unattended is covered only at a permitted mooring, and outside the hours of 10:00 to 18:00 the cover falls away in the circumstances the wording sets out. Swing, trot and pile moorings are accepted in England but with named exclusions around the Thames Estuary.

The third is age. A boat more than 30 years old needs an out-of-water survey carried out within the previous three years before the hull cover responds. On the liability-only Lloyd's wording the thresholds are different again: no vessel over 50 years old at inception, no wooden vessel over 10 years, and anything over 40 years needs a condition and valuation survey completed within five years. Single-handed sailing is permitted in daylight only and not at all above 26ft overall, and any vessel underway for 18 consecutive hours or more must carry at least two suitably experienced crew. European cruising is limited to Belgium, Holland and France, and not west of Brest.

sections.heading: Jet skis are policed harder than anything else on the site
sections.html:
The jet ski wording reads like a different company wrote it. The rider must be at least 18 and must have gained experience on a similar machine with the owner's permission — a claim involving anyone under 18 at the controls is excluded outright. The engine cut-out lanyard has to be operational and in use. Water ingestion is not covered if the drainage plugs were not fitted properly, which is the single most common way a personal watercraft engine dies.

The condition with the sharpest teeth is Datatag: theft is not covered unless the machine is Datatag registered. That is a marking and registration scheme you have to buy and apply yourself, and a policy bought without it leaves the most likely large claim uninsured. Towing water toys, ringos and inflatables is also excluded from the liability cover, which is what a great many jet skis are actually used for. The £5,000,000 liability upgrade is not sold on jet skis at all, so £3,000,000 is the ceiling.

sections.heading: Fees, discounts and what walking away costs
sections.html:
Ripe's terms of business are published openly, which is more than many brokers manage, and they set out the charges plainly. A mid-term adjustment costs up to £45 and a cancellation up to £45. New business and renewal fees are not fixed in the document — they are shown before you buy and in the confirmation afterwards, so read that screen rather than assuming the premium is the price. Cancel after the 14-day cooling-off period and a pro-rata refund may be due, but nothing under £10 is paid out, and no refund at all is due if a claim has been made during the term. Cooling off does not apply to policies shorter than one month.

On the other side of the ledger, the discounts are real: up to 25% for five claim-free years, a marina mooring discount, and monthly instalments at 0% APR on premiums above £50, which is unusual — most brokers charge 20% or more in credit interest on a spread payment.

The sale is non-advised. Ripe states that it provides information about a policy from one or more insurers without giving advice or a personal recommendation, and that it acts as agent of the insurer when arranging cover. It holds premium as the insurer's agent, so your policy counts as paid once you have paid Ripe. It is paid a percentage of the annual premium as commission, with a further bonus possible if profit targets are met, and you can ask what that commission is at any time.

sections.heading: The complaints record, and what the numbers around it show
sections.html:
Complaints go first to Ripe's own department on 0161 902 2666 or complaints@ripeinsurance.co.uk, then to the Financial Ombudsman Service on 0800 023 4567 if you are not satisfied. Unlike some specialist brokers, Insure4Boats does not publish its own complaints return, so there is no firm-level uphold rate to quote and that gap should be read as a gap rather than as a good record.

The market numbers around it are worth knowing. The Financial Ombudsman received 214,600 new complaints in 2025/26, down almost 30% from 305,700 the year before, and upheld 30% of everything it resolved. Marine insurance does appear as its own line, but only just: 50 new cases in the year at a 26% uphold rate. Set that against motor insurance on 13,420 cases and buildings insurance on 6,399, and the picture is of a product almost nobody escalates — partly because so few policies exist, and partly because the sums in dispute are smaller. It also means there is no meaningful pleasure-craft benchmark to hold this or any other boat insurer against.

Ripe is covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme, though the terms note that the protection depends on the type of insurance and the circumstances of the claim, and consumer credit arranged alongside is excluded.

pros: £3,000,000 third-party liability as standard, comfortably above the £2,000,000 the Canal & River Trust demands for a licence
Genuinely covers the small end — paddleboards, kayaks, canoes and dinghies as readily as yachts
All five policy wordings and every product information document published before you buy, not after
Up to 25% no-claims discount after five claim-free years, plus a marina mooring discount
Monthly instalments at 0% APR on premiums over £50
Salvage and towage charges included in the hull cover
Backed by Travelers Insurance Company Limited, a PRA-authorised insurer (FRN 202549)
cons: No excess figures appear anywhere in the published documents — every wording says only 'the excess shown in your schedule', so you cannot compare the real cost of a claim until you have quoted
The marina mooring discount is advertised as up to 15% on the home page and up to 10% on the cover and small-boat pages; both were live on 30 August 2026 and Ripe should say which is right
Winter use between 1 November and 31 March is excluded unless you buy the optional winter cover — an easy trap for anyone who boats all year
Jet ski theft is not covered at all unless the machine is Datatag registered, and the £5,000,000 liability upgrade is not offered on jet skis
The sale is non-advised, so nobody checks that the wording you have bought matches how you actually use the boat
Cancelling can cost up to £45, and refunds below £10 are not paid at all, so a cheap paddleboard policy refunds nothing
The firm publishes no complaints return of its own, and marine is too small a Financial Ombudsman line (50 cases in 2025/26) to benchmark it against
verdict: For a kayak, a paddleboard, a jet ski or a trailer-launched boat under 27ft, this is one of the few places that will quote online in minutes and still put £3,000,000 of liability behind you. The documents are open, the insurer is a substantial one, and the discounts are not window dressing. Read the winter dates, the unattended-mooring hours and the Datatag condition before you buy, and get the excess in writing from your schedule — those four details decide whether the policy works when you need it.

faqs.q: Who underwrites an Insure4Boats policy?
faqs.a: It depends what you buy. Hull and machinery cover with liability attached is underwritten by Travelers Insurance Company Limited, company 01034343, firm reference 202549. Third-party liability bought on its own is written by Certain Underwriters at Lloyd's, with claims handled by Charles Taylor Adjusting on 0800 997 8986. Insure4Boats itself is the broker: a trading name of Ripe Insurance Services Limited, FCA firm reference 313411.

faqs.q: Is £3 million of liability enough for a canal licence?
faqs.a: Yes. The Canal & River Trust requires third-party cover of at least £2,000,000 before it will issue a boat licence, so the standard £3,000,000 clears it with £1,000,000 to spare. The £5,000,000 upgrade costs £40 plus insurance premium tax and is aimed at larger craft; it is not sold on jet skis.

faqs.q: Can I use the boat in winter?
faqs.a: Not on the standard small craft wording. Between 1 November and 31 March the vessel is expected to be ashore or in a professionally run marina, and use in that period needs the optional winter cover added to the policy. Frost cover is a separate option again.

faqs.q: What does it cost to change or cancel a policy?
faqs.a: Ripe's terms of business set a mid-term adjustment fee of up to £45 and a cancellation fee of up to £45. You have 14 days from the start date, renewal or receipt of documents to cancel for a full refund provided no claim has been made. After that a pro-rata refund may apply, but amounts under £10 are not paid. The liability-only Lloyd's wording adds its own £25 administration fee.

faqs.q: Does the policy cover me abroad?
faqs.a: Only within the cruising limit printed on your schedule, and European cover is an option rather than a given. Where it applies, the small craft and jet ski wordings limit continental Europe to Belgium, Holland and France, and not west of Brest. Check the schedule rather than the brochure before travelling.

faqs.q: Does Insure4Boats give advice on which cover to pick?
faqs.a: No. The terms of business state that Ripe provides information about a policy from one or more insurers without giving advice or a personal recommendation, and that it acts as the insurer's agent when arranging the cover. Choosing the right wording, the right cruising limit and the right options is left to you.

title: InsureMore Travel Insurance Review
meta_title: InsureMore Travel Insurance: BIBA's Own Scheme, Sold Direct
meta_description: InsureMore sells the BIBA broker travel scheme straight to the public: £12m medical cover, Munich Re capacity, four policies and four age limits.
intro:
InsureMore is the public shopfront for a travel insurance scheme most people only ever meet across a broker's desk. It is run from a converted estate office at Berry Pomeroy, near Totnes, by Virtual Insurance Products Limited — a Devon underwriting agency incorporated on 13 June 2001 (company 04233964, Financial Services Register number 307038) that has held the British Insurance Brokers' Association's endorsed travel scheme since 19 May 2021 and also trades as Jackson Lee Underwriting. BIBA's 1,700-odd regulated member firms can sell the same policies; buying at insuremore.travel simply removes the middleman.

The money behind it belongs to Great Lakes Insurance UK Limited, the Munich Re subsidiary that took over the group's UK book on 1 January 2023 and wrote £1.73 billion of gross premium in 2024. ERGO Travel Insurance Services arranges cover on its behalf and DAS carries the legal expenses section. On the flagship Holiday Travel+ wording that buys £12,000,000 of emergency medical treatment and repatriation, £2,000,000 of personal liability and £5,000 of cancellation, with cruise cover and pet care built in rather than sold as extras.

Charges are unusually restrained for a broker-style operation: nothing to set up a policy, nothing to renew one, and £15 to change it part-way through. Premiums are held under risk transfer in an insurer trust account, so a payment that reaches InsureMore counts as reaching the insurer even if the agency were to fail.
