sections.heading: Four policies, and the one you pick sets your age limit
sections.html:
InsureMore does not sell a bronze-silver-gold ladder. It sells four separate policies sorted by what the trip is, and each one stops at a different birthday.

Holiday Traveller is the entry policy: up to 80 on a single trip, up to 75 on an annual multi-trip, and 30 days per trip. Personal possessions are capped at £2,000, gadgets at £500 for a single item, winter sports equipment at £750.

Holiday+ is the one the scheme is built around: up to 85 on a single trip, 75 annually, and 45 days per trip with an upgrade to 60 days for anyone aged 75 or under. Cancellation starts at £5,000 and can be bought up in steps to £10,000. Golf equipment runs to £1,500 with a £400 single-item cap, gadgets to £1,000, business equipment to £1,000 with £500 per item.

Sports+ stops at 65 and covers more than 350 activities across four graded categories, with sports equipment insured to £3,000 in total and £1,000 per item. Adventure Travel, the long-stay policy, also stops at 65 but runs for as long as 540 days and allows a voluntary break — a trip home for a wedding or a funeral without collapsing the policy. A separate business travel policy joined the range in 2026, capped at age 70 and 31 days a trip.

sections.heading: What £12 million of medical cover is actually for
sections.html:
Limits that large invite scepticism, and the claims record answers it. Association of British Insurers members paid £472 million on more than 500,000 travel claims in 2024. Emergency medical treatment accounted for £262 million of that — 34% of all claims, up from 29% the year before — at an average of £1,528 a claim. One insurer reported a single claim above £1 million for hospital treatment in the United States followed by repatriation to the UK.

That is the shape of the risk: thousands of small claims and a thin tail of enormous ones, almost all of them medical and most of them American. A £12,000,000 ceiling is not marketing; it is the number that makes the tail survivable. The £50 excess on the medical section is worth reading against the £1,528 average — it removes about 3% of a typical payout, which is mild by the standards of the market.

Cruise cover and pet care sit in the base policy rather than behind an upsell, which matters more than it sounds: cruise passengers are among the likeliest to need repatriation, and plenty of insurers charge separately for both.

sections.heading: Three companies stand behind one badge
sections.html:
Knowing who to ring saves hours when something goes wrong abroad, and here the answer depends entirely on what has happened.

A medical emergency goes to the assistance line on +44 (0)1403 788 719, or toll-free from the United States and Canada on +1-844-780-0494. Any other claim goes to +44 (0)1403 788 720, Monday to Friday between 09:00 and 17:00, or by email to claims@ergo-ias.co.uk. Those are ERGO's numbers in Horsham, not Devon.

Sales, amendments and cancellations go to 0330 111 3093 in Totnes. Pre-existing conditions are declared to a separate medical screening line on 0330 111 4078. A complaint starts with the complaints manager at the Totnes office on 0330 111 3998 or travel@insurevip.co.uk, is acknowledged within three working days, and must get a full answer within eight weeks; after that, or after a final response, the Financial Ombudsman Service at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR will take it for six months. The Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers 90% of an insurance claim with no upper cash limit.

sections.heading: The excesses move around more than the headline suggests
sections.html:
The £50 excess quoted everywhere is the general one. It is not the only one.

On Holiday Traveller, a gadget claim carries £100 and a winter sports equipment claim carries £100 — double the standard figure, against a £500 single-item gadget cap that a current phone will exceed on its own. Adventure Travel charges £75 on the same two sections. Personal money is limited to £500 and a replacement passport to £250, both subject to the excess, so a stolen wallet abroad is a claim worth making only if the loss is real.

Travel delay pays £50 for each full 12 hours and stops at £400, which is a benefit designed for airport meals rather than a rebooked flight. Personal accident death benefit is £25,000 between the ages of 18 and 65 — modest, and worth checking against life cover you may already hold. The excess applies per person and per section, so a family whose luggage and money both go missing pays it more than once.

sections.heading: Sports+ insures the activity but not always the liability
sections.html:
Sports+ is the most interesting policy in the range and the one most likely to be misread. Roughly 80 activities are covered as standard, from recreational cycling to scuba diving to 30 metres. Beyond that sit four graded categories — open-water swimming and competitive cycling at the lower end, heli-skiing and big-air competition at the top — each covered only if it is named on the schedule and the extra premium has been paid, and only then for training and competition.

The catch is in the wording rather than the price list. For the listed activities in categories one to four, personal liability is switched off. The policy will treat your broken collarbone; it will not defend you if you take somebody else down the slope with you. On a policy sold to people who race, that is the exclusion most likely to be discovered too late.

Winter sports is an optional extension on every policy in the range, not an inclusion, and equipment cover of £750 will not replace a modern ski set-up bought new.

sections.heading: Buying without advice, and what it costs to change your mind
sections.html:
The terms of business are blunt about it: "we will not provide you with advice or personal recommendations". The firm acts as your agent when arranging the policy and as the insurer's agent when it takes your money. Its income is commission out of the premium plus a possible share of profit, neither of which is quantified.

With four products, four age ceilings and four trip lengths, a non-advised sale puts the whole burden of choosing correctly on the buyer. A 66-year-old booking a diving holiday is outside Sports+ entirely and will not be told so by anyone. A 78-year-old is eligible for a Holiday+ single trip but capped at 31 days on it, where a 70-year-old gets 12 months.

The cooling-off period is 14 days from purchase or from receiving the documents, whichever comes later, with a full refund if the policy is unused and no claim is intended. The exception is worth knowing before you buy: single-trip policies lasting under a month may carry no refund entitlement at all. Changing anything after that costs £15.

sections.heading: Where the paperwork gets hard to follow
sections.html:
The brand moved house and left its documents behind. As at 31 August 2026 every address on insuremore.co.uk — including the JIM15A, JIM20A and JIM23A policy wordings that search engines still list — returns a 302 redirect to the new homepage at insuremore.travel. Anyone trying to read the wording they were actually sold under in 2023 or 2024 cannot get to it.

The current documents are reachable, but they sit behind long hashed addresses on abelonline.co.uk, the agency's own administration platform, rather than at readable paths on the brand's site. The product pages describe the cover as coming from "'A' rated UK insurers" without naming one; Great Lakes and DAS are named in the policy wording and in BIBA's own copy of it, not on the pages where a buyer decides.

No independent star rating for these policies could be verified from a primary source, and the firm publishes no complaints return of its own, so there is nothing to set against the market averages below. Great Lakes Insurance UK's own accounts show the strength behind the promise and the direction of travel: a £36.2 million profit after tax in 2024 against a £17.0 million loss in 2023, on solvency coverage that eased from 159% to 145%.

sections.heading: What the 2026 claims data says about buying any travel policy
sections.html:
Two free official datasets are worth more than any review, this one included.

The FCA's general insurance value measures for 2025, published on 21 July 2026, put travel insurance claims acceptance at 83–86%. That is better than home insurance at 62–71% and a long way below motor at 99% — roughly one travel claim in seven is turned down somewhere in the market. The same release shows claims costs jumping to 44–48% of premium from 31–37% a year earlier, with premiums up 12% while payouts rose 47%. Insurers under that kind of margin pressure get stricter, not looser.

The Financial Ombudsman Service's annual figures, published on 21 May 2026, recorded 4,451 new travel insurance complaints in 2025/26 with 36% upheld, against 214,649 complaints and a 30% average uphold rate across all financial products. Travel sits above the average and above motor's 35%. The ombudsman's own analysis of the trend attributes most of it to declined claims, and within that, to medical conditions the insurer says were not properly disclosed.

Which is the argument for spending twenty minutes on the screening line on 0330 111 4078 before you buy anything, from InsureMore or anyone else.

pros: £12,000,000 emergency medical and repatriation limit on Holiday Travel+, with a mild £50 excess
No fee to take out or renew a policy, and £15 to amend one — low for a broker-style seller
Cruise cover and pet care included as standard rather than sold as extensions
Munich Re capacity through Great Lakes Insurance UK, which wrote £1.73bn of premium in 2024
Single-trip cover available up to age 85 on Holiday+, and up to 540 days on Adventure Travel
Premiums held under risk transfer, so your payment reaches the insurer even if the agency fails
Cancellation cover can be bought up from £5,000 to £10,000 rather than fixed at one level
The same scheme BIBA's 1,700 member firms sell, available without going through a broker
cons: The sale is non-advised across four policies with four different age ceilings, so choosing the wrong one is entirely the buyer's problem and £15 to correct
Sports+ and Adventure Travel both stop at 65, and every annual multi-trip policy stops at 75, which rules out a large part of the travelling public
Personal liability is switched off for the graded category one to four activities on Sports+, the policy most likely to be sold to people who compete
Holiday Traveller charges a £100 excess on gadget and winter sports claims against a £500 single-item gadget cap, so a stolen phone may be barely worth claiming
Every document address on the old insuremore.co.uk domain now redirects to the homepage, putting historic policy wordings out of reach
The product pages promise "'A' rated UK insurers" without naming Great Lakes or DAS anywhere a buyer would look before paying
No independent star rating and no published complaints return could be verified from a primary source
Travel delay pays £50 per 12 hours to a £400 ceiling, and personal accident death benefit is £25,000 only between ages 18 and 65
verdict: InsureMore is a trade-body scheme sold retail, and it is priced and built like one: generous core limits, almost no fees, Munich Re behind the promise, and a cruise-and-pet inclusion that quietly beats a lot of high-street cover. The weakness is not the policy but the shopping. Four products with ceilings at 65, 75, 80 and 85 need an adviser, and the terms of business say plainly that you will not get one. Work out which policy you belong in before you look at the price, declare every medical condition on the screening line, and the cover behind it is stronger than the brand's profile suggests.

faqs.q: Who actually underwrites an InsureMore policy?
faqs.a: Great Lakes Insurance UK Limited, Financial Services Register number 955859, a Munich Re subsidiary registered at 1 Fen Court, London EC3M 5BN. ERGO Travel Insurance Services acts on its behalf, and the legal costs section is separately insured by DAS Legal Expenses Insurance Company Limited, FRN 202106. InsureMore itself is a trading name of Virtual Insurance Products Limited, FRN 307038, which arranges and administers the policy but does not carry the risk.

faqs.q: What is the oldest age InsureMore will insure?
faqs.a: 85, on a Holiday+ single trip. Holiday Traveller stops at 80 on a single trip. Every annual multi-trip policy in the range stops at 75, and Sports+ and Adventure Travel stop at 65 whichever way you buy them. Trip length tightens with age on the single-trip wording: up to 12 months at 70 and under, 60 days between 71 and 75, and 31 days from 76 to 85.

faqs.q: Does it cover pre-existing medical conditions?
faqs.a: Only where they have been declared, accepted in writing and any additional premium has been paid. Screening is done on a separate line, 0330 111 4078. This is the single most important step in buying travel cover: the Financial Ombudsman Service upheld 36% of the 4,451 travel complaints it received in 2025/26, and undeclared or disputed medical history is the most common cause behind declined claims.

faqs.q: What does it cost to change or cancel a policy?
faqs.a: Nothing to buy or renew, and £15 for a mid-term adjustment. There is a 14-day cooling-off period running from purchase or from receipt of the documents, whichever is later, with a full refund if the policy has not been used and no claim is intended. Single trips of under a month may carry no refund right at all, so check before you buy a short policy you might not need.

faqs.q: Do I have to be a BIBA member or go through a broker?
faqs.a: No. The Holiday Travel+ and Sports Travel+ scheme is endorsed by the British Insurance Brokers' Association and sold by its 1,700-plus member firms, but insuremore.travel sells the same policies directly to the public. Jackson Lee Underwriting has run the scheme since 19 May 2021 and offers brokers white-labelled portals, which is why the same cover appears under several different names online.

faqs.q: Is winter sports cover included?
faqs.a: No, it is an optional extension on every policy in the range. Equipment is covered to £750 on Holiday Traveller and Holiday+, with a £100 excess on Holiday Traveller and £75 on Adventure Travel. Cruise cover and pet care, by contrast, are included as standard.

headline.label: Emergency medical cover
headline.value: £12,000,000 on Holiday Travel+, £50 excess

title: John Lewis Home Insurance Review
meta_title: John Lewis Home Insurance 2026: Four Insurers, One Brand
meta_description: John Lewis Money now quotes from four insurers. What Bronze, Silver and Gold pay, the unlimited sums insured, and the limits worth reading first.
intro:
John Lewis has sold home insurance under the Partnership name for a long time, and in March 2026 it changed how. John Lewis Finance Limited became a regulated insurance broker rather than the front for a single insurer, and household quotes are now run across a panel: AXA, Covéa Insurance and Prestige Underwriting from April 2026, with Ageas added on 23 June 2026. The money business behind it reports 1.4 million active customers and £1.5 billion of customer spending across John Lewis and Waitrose in the past year.

At the top of the range the cover is unusually generous for a high-street name. Silver and Gold both carry unlimited buildings and contents sums insured — no rebuild figure to guess at, no contents valuation to get wrong — and both are rated 5 stars by Defaqto on John Lewis Money's own comparison pages. Accidental damage to drains, fixed glass and sanitaryware is standard and unlimited on both, and Gold makes alternative accommodation unlimited as well.

Nobody publishes a price until you ask, so the useful yardstick is the market: the Association of British Insurers put the average combined buildings and contents premium at £375 in its 6 May 2026 release, down £22 on the year across roughly 15.5 million policies. Against that backdrop the entry-level Bronze tier is a distinctly different animal from the two above it, and the panel arrangement has consequences worth knowing about. Both are set out below.

key_facts.value: AXA · Covéa Insurance · Prestige Underwriting · Ageas (added 23 June 2026)

key_facts.value: Bronze · Silver · Gold

key_facts.value: Bronze £400,000 · Silver unlimited · Gold unlimited

key_facts.value: Bronze £50,000 · Silver £100,000 · Gold unlimited

key_facts.value: Bronze £50,000 · Silver £100,000 · Gold unlimited

key_facts.value: Bronze £10,000 · Silver £15,000 · Gold unlimited

key_facts.value: Up to £15,000 in total, capped at £5,000 per bike

key_facts.value: Up to £5,000 per claim, £1,500 any one item

key_facts.value: Underwritten by Covéa Insurance plc — FCA reference 202277

sections.heading: The switch from single insurer to panel, and what it does to a quote
sections.html:
Until spring 2026 a John Lewis home policy meant one insurer standing behind it. Since March that year John Lewis Finance Limited has held FCA permission for insurance distribution and credit broking under firm reference 1018169, which is a broker's permission, not an insurer's. John Lewis plc sits alongside as an appointed representative under reference 416011. Both numbers are checkable on the FCA Register.

The panel went live in April 2026 with AXA, Covéa and Prestige Underwriting. Ageas was announced on 23 June 2026 and offers all three tiers. Prestige is the interesting one: it is a specialist in risks that fall outside standard acceptance criteria, which is how a broker widens the gate rather than declining people at the door. A flat above a shop, a long claims history, a home with an unusual construction — those are the cases a single-insurer arrangement tends to turn away and a four-insurer panel can often place.

Gary Davess, who runs insurance at John Lewis Money, framed the Ageas appointment as part of “a step change for our insurance business”. The same restructuring brought car insurance back in summer 2026, quoted across Ageas, AXA and Covéa on a two-tier premier and essentials split.

sections.heading: Bronze, Silver and Gold set against each other
sections.html:
The three tiers share one policy wording, which makes the differences easy to line up. On buildings, Bronze pays up to £400,000 to repair or rebuild; Silver and Gold are unlimited. On contents, Bronze caps at £50,000, Silver at £100,000 and Gold is unlimited. If your home has to be evacuated, Bronze funds £50,000 of alternative accommodation on the buildings side and £10,000 on the contents side; Silver lifts those to £100,000 and £15,000; Gold removes the ceiling on both.

Freezer contents scale the same way — £250, £500, £750 — which is a small figure that tells you a lot about where each tier sits.

The sharper split is accidental damage to drains, underground pipes, fixed glass and sanitaryware. On Silver and Gold it is standard and unlimited. On Bronze it is not there at all unless you buy the Extended accidental damage extension. A cracked soil pipe or a shattered shower screen is one of the more common household claims, so a Bronze quote that undercuts a Silver one is not comparing the same cover.

The £400,000 Bronze rebuild cap deserves a moment on its own. Rebuild cost is not market value, but on a larger family house in the South East, or anything with a period roof, it is a figure you can reach. Check yours before assuming the cheapest tier fits.

sections.heading: The bolt-ons, and what each one actually pays
sections.html:
Bicycle cover runs to £15,000 across all your bikes with a £5,000 ceiling on any single one, in the home and away from it. Student cover, for a family member living in halls or rented student accommodation in the UK or Ireland, pays up to £5,000 a claim with £1,500 on any one item; inside that sit sub-limits of £500 for bicycles, £500 for sports equipment, £500 for business equipment including a laptop used for work, £200 for cash and £1,000 for cards. Bikes have to be locked whenever they are not being ridden, and belongings must come home over the holidays.

Home emergency and legal expenses are both underwritten by ARAG Legal Expenses Insurance Company Limited, firm reference 202106, on policies starting from 1 April 2026. Legal expenses covers qualifying disputes to £100,000. ARAG runs its own claims lines — 0800 652 0259 for a home emergency, 0117 934 0416 for a legal claim — separate from the John Lewis Money support number on 0345 608 9031.

sections.heading: Listed buildings, seven bedrooms and £20,000 watches
sections.html:
Above the standard range sits Specialist Home Insurance, underwritten by Covéa Insurance plc under firm reference 202277. It is aimed at homes where contents exceed £40,000 or a single item exceeds £20,000, at listed buildings and properties built before 1800, at houses with 7 or more bedrooms, and at second and holiday homes.

The benefits are the part standard cover does not attempt. Alternative accommodation runs for up to 5 years. Rebuilding after a claim carries up to £10,000 towards solar or wind generation. Scheduled valuables can be replaced at up to 125% of the scheduled figure where an accredited valuer assessed them within the past 5 years, which is the clause that absorbs a rising gold price between valuations. Guests' belongings are covered to £10,000 in total and £500 an item, and the policy will accommodate up to 6 paying guests. After an approved claim over £20,000, Covéa contributes up to £2,500 towards leak-detection equipment. There is even £500 for a hole in one and £500 at £50 a day to hire clubs while yours are replaced.

The specialist line is reached on 0800 916 6880 rather than through the standard quote journey.

sections.heading: The market this policy launched into
sections.html:
Two free, dated sources put the cover in proportion, and neither belongs to an insurer.

The ABI's 6 May 2026 figures show home insurers paid £846 million to households in the first quarter of 2026 alone. The average household claim reached a record £6,340, up 20% year on year. Weather-related payouts averaged £6,040, a 38% jump from £4,390. Subsidence averaged £17,820. Theft claims rose 14% to £4,350. Premiums moved the other way: combined cover averaged £375, down 5%, with buildings-only at £306 and contents-only at £117.

Set the claim averages against Bronze's £50,000 contents ceiling and the case for Silver or Gold sharpens considerably.

The Financial Ombudsman Service published its 2025/26 annual data on 21 May 2026. It took 214,600 new complaints in the year. Buildings insurance produced 6,399 cases with a 38% uphold rate; contents insurance produced 1,685 with 30% upheld. Both sit at or above the 30% average across every financial product the service handles, which is a reminder that a home claim is one of the more contested things you can make.

sections.heading: Where the cover thins out
sections.html:
Bronze is the weak point of the range and it is worth naming plainly. The £400,000 rebuild cap and £50,000 contents cap are the tightest of the three, the drains, glass and sanitaryware cover has to be bought as an extra, and Bronze is not among the tiers John Lewis Money describes as 5-star Defaqto rated. Silver and Gold are.

The panel model has a flip side too. “John Lewis home insurance” is now a brand and a service wrapped around whichever of four insurers priced your risk that day. The wording is common across the panel, but the claims handling, the loss adjusters and the repair networks are not, and the quote journey does not tell you which insurer you have landed with until a price appears. Two neighbours on the same tier can have materially different claims experiences. It is also worth being clear that John Lewis carries the distribution and the brand, not the underwriting risk.

Paperwork is the third problem. The site currently hosts documents for policies starting on or after 3 September 2026, for those starting between 1 April and 3 September 2026, for pre-April-2026 policies with numbers beginning 1000, and for older Essential, Plus, Premier and Premier Select policies with numbers beginning H or J — four generations, with pre-April claims routed to 0345 608 9001 instead of the ARAG lines. Renewing customers can find the product changed under them without the branding changing at all.

Smaller catches: the older wording excludes theft and damage once a home has stood empty for more than 60 consecutive days, and the same 60-day rule applies to student accommodation; e-bikes and e-scooters are excluded from student cover outright; and single bicycles worth more than £500 need specifying rather than being assumed in.

One thing this review could not verify from John Lewis Money's own pages: cancellation charges, mid-term amendment fees and the length of the cooling-off period are not published on the site. Ask for the Terms of Business document before you buy rather than taking a figure from elsewhere.

pros: Silver and Gold both carry unlimited buildings and contents sums insured, removing the risk of under-insuring a rebuild
Silver and Gold are described by John Lewis Money as 5-star Defaqto rated
Accidental damage to drains, fixed glass and sanitaryware is standard and unlimited on Silver and Gold
A four-insurer panel including a non-standard specialist means awkward risks get quoted rather than declined
Gold makes alternative accommodation unlimited on both the buildings and contents sides
A genuine high-value arm for listed, pre-1800 and seven-bedroom homes, with 5 years of alternative accommodation and 125% extended replacement on scheduled valuables
cons: Bronze is a noticeably thinner product: a £400,000 rebuild cap, £50,000 contents, no accidental damage to drains, glass or sanitaryware without paying extra, and no 5-star Defaqto mark
Which of the four panel insurers you get is not visible until a price appears, and claims handling differs between them even though the wording does not
Four generations of policy documentation now sit on the site, with different claims numbers depending on whether your policy number starts 1000, H or J
Cancellation charges, amendment fees and the cooling-off period are not published on John Lewis Money's public pages
John Lewis is the distributor, not the insurer — the brand you are buying does not carry the risk
E-bikes and e-scooters are excluded from student cover, and bikes over £500 must be specified individually
verdict: Silver and Gold are strong policies: unlimited sums insured on buildings and contents, unlimited accidental damage to drains, glass and sanitaryware, and a 5-star Defaqto mark, sitting in a market where the average household claim has just hit a record £6,340. Bronze is a different proposition and should be priced against what it leaves out rather than against the tier above. The March 2026 move to a four-insurer panel is a real gain for anyone whose home does not fit a standard box — a listed cottage, a flat over a shop, a claims history — because Prestige Underwriting exists on the panel precisely to place those. The trade is that the John Lewis name now covers four different claims operations, and you will not know which one you have until you have a quote in front of you.

faqs.q: Who underwrites John Lewis home insurance?
faqs.a: Since April 2026 there is no single answer. John Lewis Finance Limited is a regulated broker (FCA firm reference 1018169) and quotes across a panel of AXA, Covéa Insurance, Prestige Underwriting and, from 23 June 2026, Ageas. Specialist high-value home cover is underwritten by Covéa Insurance plc, firm reference 202277, and the home emergency and legal expenses add-ons by ARAG Legal Expenses Insurance Company Limited, firm reference 202106.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Bronze, Silver and Gold?
faqs.a: Bronze pays up to £400,000 to rebuild and covers £50,000 of contents, with £50,000 and £10,000 of alternative accommodation and £250 of freezer food. Silver lifts contents to £100,000, makes the rebuild unlimited and pays £100,000 and £15,000 of alternative accommodation with £500 of freezer food. Gold is unlimited on buildings, contents and alternative accommodation, with £750 of freezer food. Silver and Gold also include unlimited accidental damage to drains, fixed glass and sanitaryware, which Bronze charges extra for.

faqs.q: Does John Lewis cover a listed building or a house with seven bedrooms?
faqs.a: Yes, through Specialist Home Insurance underwritten by Covéa. It is designed for listed properties, homes built before 1800, houses with 7 or more bedrooms, second and holiday homes, and households where contents pass £40,000 or a single item passes £20,000. The specialist line is 0800 916 6880.

faqs.q: Can I insure bikes and a student's belongings on the policy?
faqs.a: Both are optional extensions. Bicycle cover pays up to £15,000 across all bikes with a £5,000 cap on any one, at home and away, and single bikes over £500 must be specified. Student cover pays up to £5,000 a claim with £1,500 on any one item, and includes £500 for bicycles, £500 for sports equipment, £200 for money and £1,000 for cards. E-bikes and e-scooters are excluded, and cover stops if the accommodation is empty for 60 days or more.

faqs.q: What happens to my existing John Lewis policy?
faqs.a: It depends when it started. Policies beginning 1000 predate 1 April 2026 and use an earlier wording, with claims on 0345 608 9001. Older Essential, Plus, Premier and Premier Select policies beginning H or J have their own documents again. Policies starting from 1 April 2026 sit on the Bronze, Silver and Gold wording, and a further version applies to start dates from 3 September 2026. Check which set applies to you before relying on any limit quoted here.

title: John Lewis Televisions
meta_title: John Lewis TVs: 5-Year Guarantee, Prices From £139.99
meta_description: A free five-year guarantee on all 252 TVs John Lewis lists, from £139.99. What delivery, running costs and the small print add, checked 20 September 2026.

headline.label: Free guarantee included in the price
headline.value: 5 years on every television — all 252 sets listed, from £139.99, checked 20 September 2026

intro:
Every television John Lewis sells comes with a five-year guarantee at no extra cost. On 20 September 2026 that covered all 252 sets listed on johnlewis.com, from a £139.99 LG 32-inch to models priced past £6,000. Figures checked that day against John Lewis's own television pages.

The range runs across five brands — Samsung, LG, Sony, Hisense and TCL — in five price bands the site sets itself: £50–£430, £440–£670, £690–£1,100, £1,140–£1,690 and £1,690–£6,200. Forty-one of the 252 sets sit in that cheapest band. Which? put John Lewis second among technology shops on a customer score of 87% in its most recent survey and named it a Recommended Provider.

The price promise came back on 9 September 2024 after two years away. Never Knowingly Undersold now matches 25 named retailers rather than high-street rivals alone, and it runs for seven days after purchase, which matters on a product whose price moves weekly.

sections.heading: Five years included, and where the five years stop
sections.html:
The guarantee is advertised on the listing itself — "5 year guarantee included" appears against every one of the 252 televisions, at £139.99 and at £6,000 alike. John Lewis's own wording is that it offers "outstanding guarantees in addition to always honouring the manufacturers' guarantees" and that "all our guarantees are in addition to your statutory rights".

That second clause is worth holding on to. A guarantee is a contractual promise from the seller; your statutory rights run in parallel and are not shortened by it. The explanatory notes to the Consumer Rights Act 2015 set out the period you have to bring a claim for breach of contract: six years in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and five years in Scotland. A five-year guarantee therefore sits inside that window rather than extending it. What it buys is a shorter argument — no need to prove the fault was present at delivery, no need to commission a report — which on a television is worth having, but it is not five extra years of protection.

What the guarantee covers in years three, four and five is the gap. John Lewis does not publish the television guarantee terms at any page reachable from its customer services section; the guarantee hub points to a product-support portal instead. Whether labour and call-out are included throughout, and what condition the set has to be in, are worth asking on 0345 604 8835 before you buy something expensive on the strength of the badge.

sections.heading: How it scores when shoppers are asked
sections.html:
Which? surveys buyers rather than testing the shop, which makes it the one independent measure worth quoting here. In its latest technology and appliance retailer survey — 4,076 respondents for technology and 4,101 for appliances, fielded in July and August 2025 — John Lewis scored 87% for technology and 89% for appliances. Both placed it second, and it was named a Which? Recommended Provider in both categories.

The category average was 80% in each. Richer Sounds topped technology on 93% and Sainsbury's came last on 71%; in appliances Samsung led on 91% and Wickes trailed on 67%. On the individual measures John Lewis took five stars for product quality, customer service, delivery and after-sales service, and four for value for money — which is a fair summary of the whole proposition.

sections.heading: The price promise, and the 25 names behind it
sections.html:
Never Knowingly Undersold was retired in 2022 and brought back on 9 September 2024 in a different shape. The old version matched high-street competitors; the new one names 25 retailers and includes online-only sellers, which is the change that matters for televisions. The list runs AO.com, Amazon (technology only), Apple, Argos, Asos, Boots, Currys, Dunelm, Dreams, The Entertainer, Fenwick, Flannels, Furniture Village, Harrods, Harvey Nichols, Heal's, House of Fraser, Lakeland, M&S, Mama's and Papa's, Next, Richer Sounds, Selfridges, Smyths Toys and Space NK. For a television buyer the useful entries are AO.com, Amazon, Argos, Currys and Richer Sounds — which is most of the market.

It works after the sale rather than at the till. You have seven days from purchase to find the same product cheaper, in stock and ready for delivery, at one of the 25; you submit a form with screenshots and order details; John Lewis reviews it within 48 hours and pays a refund of the difference within five days. The same seven-day window applies if John Lewis itself drops the price after you have bought.

sections.heading: Who owns the shop and what the accounts show
sections.html:
John Lewis plc is company number 00233462, incorporated on 20 September 1928 — ninety-eight years to the day before these figures were checked — with its registered office at 1 Drummond Gate, Pimlico, London SW1V 2QQ and accounts last made up to 31 January 2026. It sits inside the John Lewis Partnership, the largest employee-owned business in the UK, with around 65,000 Partners who are also its owners.

The Partnership's full-year results, published on 12 March 2026 for the 53 weeks to 31 January 2026, give the scale behind the guarantee. Partnership sales were £13.4bn, up 5%; the John Lewis department store business took £4.9bn of that, up 3%, and Waitrose £8.5bn, up 7%. Profit before tax, bonus and exceptionals came in at £134m, up 6%, though the statutory position after exceptionals was a £21m loss. Operating cash flow was £595m and total liquidity £1.6bn. The Partner bonus was restored at 2%, alongside £108m put into base pay. Jason Tarry, the chairman, said: "Our multi-year plan to invest in customers and brands for the long term is working; we have grown customer numbers and achieved record satisfaction."

One small inconsistency is worth confirming rather than glossing: the results announcement counts 34 John Lewis shops plus johnlewis.com, while the Partnership's own corporate "about" page says 36. The audited announcement is the safer figure.

sections.heading: A £239 43-inch set, priced all the way through
sections.html:
Take the Samsung UE43U8000F (2025), a 43-inch 4K set at £239.00 on 20 September 2026 — mid-range, and the sort of television most of these listings are. Its listing carries the five-year guarantee, a 3,840 x 2,160 panel and an energy class of G.

Delivery is where the shop's headline stops helping. The listing showed a standard delivery charge of £19.95, arriving from three working days, with Click & Collect unavailable. Faster options are dearer and are priced as large-item deliveries: £29.95 for next day or a four-hour slot, £39.95 for a guaranteed two-hour slot. Small and medium items are a different tariff entirely — £7.95 next or named day, £10.95 before 11.30am, £9.95 for evening delivery inside the M25.

Then the running cost. The listing prints 52kWh per 1,000 hours in standard dynamic range, 102kWh in HDR, and an estimated annual consumption of 72kWh. At the Ofgem price cap direct debit rate of 26.32p per kWh for 1 October to 31 December 2026, that is about £18.95 a year, or roughly £94.75 across the five years the guarantee runs — comfortably more than the delivery charge and about 40% of the ticket price.

Finance is offered on the same page at £9.18 a month over 36 months at 24.9% APR. Multiply it out: £330.48 against £239.00 in cash, a difference of £91.48. The rate is printed on the listing, which is more than some retailers manage, but the arithmetic is worth doing before the box is ticked.

sections.heading: The energy label is the one number nobody can dress up
sections.html:
Televisions in Great Britain carry the rescaled energy label, running A to G rather than the old A+++ to G, and it has applied to electronic displays at the point of sale since 1 March 2021 under the Energy Information Regulations as amended by the Ecodesign for Energy-Related Products and Energy Information Regulations 2021.

The label has to show the model number and the supplier's name or trademark, the energy consumption data, the efficiency class from best to worst, the UK flag, English text and a QR code linking to the model information on a publicly accessible website. Selling at a distance does not remove the duty: an arrow carrying the energy class and the range of classes must sit alongside the product and link through to the full label.

John Lewis complies visibly, and goes further than most by letting you filter televisions by grade. The filters tell their own story: among the 41 televisions under £430, classes F and G dominate and nothing approaches the top of the scale. That is the trade in plain sight — a cheap large panel is a cheap large panel, and the label is the place the shop cannot spin it.

sections.heading: What happens to the television you are replacing
sections.html:
This is the part of a television purchase that most people discover late. John Lewis's published waste electrical and electronic equipment statement is blunt about it: the shop does not accept old electrical items in its branches, and instead contributes to funding a network of recycling points through the Distributor Take Back Scheme, pointing customers to recyclenow.com or their council. Its producer registration number is WEE/DC0065TW. Portable batteries are the exception and can be handed in at any John Lewis or Waitrose shop, provided they can be carried by hand.

Retailers selling electrical goods have to offer customers a way of disposing of the equivalent old item, and the government's guidance allows that duty to be met by in-store take-back, an alternative free service, or membership of the Distributor Take Back Scheme. John Lewis has taken the third route, which is lawful and also the least convenient of the three for somebody with a 43-inch set to shift.

The gap is partly filled by promotion rather than policy. On 20 September 2026 the television pages were running trade-in offers reading "Save £250 and get free recycling when you trade in your old TV", with £200 and £100 variants, each tied to a promotional code on the individual product page. Useful when one is running on the set you want; nothing to rely on if it is not.

sections.heading: Reading the small print before you check out
sections.html:
Returns. Change your mind and you have 30 days to send it back in original condition with proof of purchase. Small items are free to return by post or in a shop; large items are "free to return if they're damaged or faulty", but if you simply do not want it, "we charge a £29.95 collection fee". A manufacturing fault inside 30 days is exchanged or refunded; beyond that John Lewis says it will "repair or replace the product in accordance with the terms of the Consumer Rights Act 2015".

The free delivery line. The television pages carry the shop's standard "free standard delivery on orders above £50" message, and a television is not what it is talking about. The £239 Samsung above showed £19.95. John Lewis's own "free delivery TVs" filter returned one television — a £659 Samsung QE50QN90F — out of the 252 listed. That is not a hidden charge, because the figure is on the product page, but the banner and the basket do not agree and the difference is real money on a cheap set.

The price promise, narrowed. Never Knowingly Undersold does not apply to products reduced to clear, flash sales, multi-buy offers or refurbished items, and covers branded products only. Televisions are discounted through exactly those mechanisms, so the promise is at its weakest in the week you are most likely to be shopping. The seven-day window also runs from purchase, not from delivery.

Protect+. Sold alongside the guarantee, this is accidental damage insurance underwritten by Domestic & General Insurance PLC, firm reference 202111, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA and the PRA. It covers accidental damage including television screen burn, with unlimited repairs and no excess, and will replace a set it cannot repair. It expressly does not cover "mechanical or electrical breakdown of your product", loss, cosmetic damage, neglect or deliberate damage, or the cost of being without the television. Terms run 2, 3 or 5 years, there is a 45-day cooling-off period with a full refund, and the product must have been bought or received less than 60 days ago. Read that against the free guarantee: the paid cover handles accidents, the free guarantee handles faults, and neither is a substitute for the other.

If it goes wrong. A television bought outright is a retail purchase with no ombudsman behind it — the Financial Ombudsman Service covers the insurance and the credit agreement, not the set. Once John Lewis's own complaints route is exhausted, the free consumer helpline run by Citizens Advice is 0808 223 1133, and it is the route that passes reports on to Trading Standards, which a consumer cannot do directly.

pros: Five years of guarantee included in the ticket price on every television, against the one year most shops and manufacturers give
Which? scored John Lewis 87% for technology and 89% for appliances in July and August 2025, second in both, with five stars for product quality, customer service, delivery and after-sales service
Never Knowingly Undersold now reaches 25 named retailers including Amazon on technology, Currys, Argos, AO.com and Richer Sounds, and is claimed online rather than at a counter
A real spread of prices — 41 sets under £430 on 20 September 2026 and a top band running to £6,200 — so the guarantee is not restricted to the expensive end
The energy class and the kWh-per-1,000-hours figure are printed on every listing, and the site lets you filter televisions by energy grade
Employee-owned, with published full-year accounts: £13.4bn of sales, £134m of profit before bonus and exceptionals and a 2% Partner bonus for the 53 weeks to 31 January 2026
cons: The five-year guarantee sits inside the period the law already gives you, not beyond it — six years in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and five in Scotland — so it is a simpler route to a repair rather than extra time
John Lewis does not publish the full guarantee terms at any page we could reach, so what counts as fair wear, and whether call-outs and labour are included in years three to five, has to be asked for

The shop takes nothing back in store: its own WEEE statement says it does not accept old electrical items in its shops and funds the Distributor Take Back Scheme instead, so the old set is your problem unless a trade-in offer is running

The £50 free delivery threshold does not reach televisions — a £239 43-inch Samsung showed a £19.95 standard delivery charge, and the shop's own free-delivery television filter returned a single set out of 252 on 20 September 2026

Never Knowingly Undersold excludes products reduced to clear, flash sales, multi-buy offers and refurbished stock — which is how discounted televisions are most often sold — and covers branded products only

Protect+, the paid accidental damage cover sold alongside, must be bought within 60 days of receiving the product and expressly excludes mechanical or electrical breakdown, so it does not extend the guarantee at all
Changing your mind about a television costs £29.95 in collection charges if it is not faulty, and the window is 30 days
verdict: John Lewis is not trying to be the cheapest television retailer and the prices show it. What it sells instead is five years of guarantee, a price promise wide enough to include Amazon and Currys, and a customer-service record Which? has scored at 87%. On a £239 set the guarantee is worth more than the £19.95 delivery costs; on a £2,000 OLED it is worth a great deal more. Read the delivery line and the recycling arrangements before you check out, because neither works the way the £50 free-delivery banner suggests.

faqs.q: Is the five-year John Lewis television guarantee really free?
faqs.a: Yes. It is included in the ticket price on every television listed — all 252 of them on 20 September 2026, from £139.99 upwards — and John Lewis states that its guarantees are in addition to the manufacturer's and to your statutory rights. The paid product, Protect+, is separate and covers accidental damage rather than faults.

faqs.q: Does John Lewis take away my old television?
faqs.a: Not as a matter of course. Its WEEE statement says it does not accept old electrical items in its shops and that it funds recycling points through the Distributor Take Back Scheme instead. Trade-in promotions offering free recycling were running on the television pages on 20 September 2026, but they are tied to promotional codes on individual products rather than being a standing service.

faqs.q: How does the Never Knowingly Undersold price match work now?
faqs.a: Since 9 September 2024 it matches 25 named retailers, including Amazon on technology, Currys, Argos, AO.com and Richer Sounds. You have seven days from purchase to submit a form with screenshots; John Lewis reviews it within 48 hours and refunds the difference within five days. It excludes reduced-to-clear stock, flash sales, multi-buy offers and refurbished items.

faqs.q: Is delivery free on a television?
faqs.a: Usually not. A £239 43-inch Samsung showed a £19.95 standard delivery charge on 20 September 2026, and the shop's own free-delivery television filter returned a single set out of 252. Faster large-item slots are £29.95 for next day or a four-hour window and £39.95 for a guaranteed two-hour window.

faqs.q: What does a John Lewis television cost to run?
faqs.a: The listing prints the figure. The 43-inch Samsung above shows 52kWh per 1,000 hours in standard dynamic range and an estimated 72kWh a year, which at the Ofgem cap rate of 26.32p per kWh for 1 October to 31 December 2026 is roughly £18.95 a year, or about £94.75 over the five years the guarantee runs.

title: Kwik Fit Servicing Review: Prices, Guarantees and the Paperwork
meta_title: Kwik Fit Servicing: What the Fixed Prices Really Buy
meta_description: Kwik Fit servicing prices are published up front: interim from £186.95, full from £246.95, MOT bundles from £281.95. What each one covers, and what it misses.
intro:
Kwik Fit has been servicing cars in Britain since the first centre opened in Edinburgh in 1971, and the company behind the name is just as old: Kwik-Fit (GB) Limited was registered at Companies House on 27 April 1971, first as Euro Exhaust Centre Holdings Limited, then as Kwik-Fit-Euro Limited from 1981 until 1990. It now runs more than 600 centres across the UK including Northern Ireland, open seven days a week — 8.30am to 6pm Monday to Friday, 8.30am to 5pm on Saturday and 10am to 4pm on Sunday. Since June 2011 the group has been owned by the Japanese trading house ITOCHU.

What makes it worth a look for a service rather than just tyres is that the prices are published before you hand over the keys. A fixed grid on the site sets an interim service at £186.95 for an engine up to 1400cc rising to £251.95 above 3000cc, a full service from £246.95 to £311.95, an engine oil and filter change from £132.95, an electric vehicle service from £230.95, and a full service bundled with the MOT from £281.95. Most independent garages will not quote until they have seen the car. Service components and other mechanical parts fitted during the work carry a 12 month or 12,000 mile guarantee, and a service takes two to four hours depending on the vehicle.

One thing to settle by phone before you book. If you drive a hybrid, Kwik Fit's own pages disagree about whether it will take the car: the servicing FAQ says "We are not currently able to service hybrid vehicles of any type", while the service comparison page lists both the interim and the full service as suitable for hybrids, and the full service checklist includes a hybrid system check. Nobody has reconciled the two. The centre itself will know which answer is current.

sections.heading: The price grid, engine size by engine size
sections.html:
Kwik Fit publishes a full price table rather than a single headline. An engine oil and filter change runs £132.95 up to 1400cc, £152.95 to 2000cc, £172.95 to 3000cc and £192.95 above that. The interim service is £186.95, £211.95, £231.95 and £251.95 across the same four bands. The full service is £246.95, £271.95, £291.95 and £311.95. Add the MOT and the interim bundle starts at £221.95 and the full bundle at £281.95, rising to £286.95 and £346.95 for the largest engines. An electric vehicle service is £230.95, or £270.90 with the MOT.

Every one of those is a "from" price, and the site is straight about why: cost turns on engine size and on the oil the car needs, with synthetic and specialist grades costing more. The company says it will use "an oil equivalent to the manufacturer's specification" rather than naming a grade in advance, so the figure you see online is a floor rather than a quotation.

The intervals are conventional. Interim is every 6 months or 6,000 miles, full is every 12 months or 12,000 miles whichever comes first, and the EV service is every 24 months or 20,000 miles. The oil and filter change sits outside all of that: it includes safety checks but cannot reset the service light or stamp the book, which makes it a top-up between services rather than a cheap substitute for one.

sections.heading: What is on the checklist, and what is quietly left off it
sections.html:
The full service checklist runs to more than 60 inspection points, grouped into the cabin, the exterior, a pre-alignment check, under the bonnet, under the car, the replacement items and a road test. The cabin section covers instruments, warning lights, horn, wipers, the AdBlue or Eolys light, seat belts, clutch operation on a manual, climate control and an engine diagnostics read. The pre-alignment section takes in steering and suspension linkages, ball joints, shock absorbers, springs, a full tyre inspection covering tread, pressure and alignment, and the tyre pressure monitoring system. Under the bonnet it checks the battery, coolant, brake fluid, the brake, radiator and power steering hoses and the auxiliary drive belt. Under the car it covers a full brake inspection, fuel pipes, drive shaft joints and the exhaust.

The replacement items are shorter than the inspection list, and that is the part worth reading twice. A full service replaces the engine oil and filter and the air filter, and tops up the screen wash. An interim service replaces the oil and filter only. Kwik Fit states plainly that "Replacement spark plugs are not included in our service packages", and its interim service also excludes the fuel filter, the air filter, belts and power steering fluid, while the full service excludes spark plugs, the fuel filter and belts. Anything on those lists that your car is due comes as extra work on top of the published price.

The terms set out how that extra work is handled: "Once Services have started you will be informed immediately of any additional work identified. A new printed quotation will be produced on request and additional work will only be carried out with your agreement." Note the phrasing — the printed quotation appears if you ask for one.

sections.heading: MOT pricing, and the figure the government caps
sections.html:
The MOT is the one part of the bill nobody can inflate. The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency sets a maximum fee of £54.85 for a class 4 car with up to eight passenger seats, £64.00 for a class 4 test that includes a seat belt installation check, £58.60 for a class 7 goods vehicle between 3,001kg and 3,500kg and £29.65 for a motorcycle. Those are ceilings, not prices, and a test station is free to charge less. Kwik Fit does not advertise a standalone MOT price on its servicing pages; it prices the test inside the bundles, where the gap between the £246.95 full service and the £281.95 full-service-with-MOT works out at £35.00, comfortably under the cap.

The test is worth taking seriously on the numbers. DVSA's own quarterly data for class 3 and 4 vehicles in April to June 2025 puts the initial failure rate at 27.24%, so better than one car in four fails first time. Lamps, reflectors and electrical equipment accounted for 10.36% of tests, suspension 8.65%, tyres 6.23%, brakes 6.10% and visibility 4.65%. Most of those categories overlap with items a full service inspects but does not replace, which is the practical argument for booking the two together rather than a fortnight apart.

sections.heading: Servicing off the dealer forecourt without losing the warranty
sections.html:
This is the question that sends most people to a chain like this one, and the answer is better than the folklore. UK competition law contains a specific block exemption for motor vehicle agreements: The Competition Act 1998 (Motor Vehicle Agreements Block Exemption) Order 2023, SI 2023 No. 501, made on 28 April 2023, in force from 1 June 2023 and running until 31 May 2029. Article 6 stops a supplier restricting an independent operator's access to the "information, tools or training" needed to repair a vehicle in a way that puts that operator at a disadvantage against an authorised repairer, and Article 5 bars restrictions on selling aftermarket parts to independent garages.

Kwik Fit sells a Manufacturer Service built to the maker's own schedule for the car's age, model and mileage, quoted individually rather than from the grid, using what it calls "competitively-sourced parts of 'Original Equipment' standard" and oils that "match or exceed the quality of the manufacturer's original oil". Its own wording on the warranty point is unusually firm: "We guarantee you that a stamp in your car's logbook from Kwik Fit will uphold any warranty you have with your car dealer, supporting your full dealer service history."

Two caveats belong with that. The first is that a manufacturer's warranty and a dealer's own extended warranty are different contracts with different conditions, and it is the second one that tends to carry the awkward clauses. The second is the paperwork, which is the subject of the next section.

sections.heading: The digital service record it cannot sign
sections.html:
Kwik Fit says so itself, on the manufacturer servicing page: "If your vehicle has a Digital Service Record (DSR) we will not be able to update or reset this." For a car with a paper logbook that costs nothing. For a car whose service history exists only on the manufacturer's own system — which covers most mainstream brands sold new in the last decade — it means the work is done to schedule, the invoice proves it, and the manufacturer's record still shows a gap. You are relying on the invoice and the stamp, not on the file a franchised dealer or a future buyer will look at.

It sits awkwardly beside the guarantee quoted above, which is written entirely around the logbook. If your car has no logbook to stamp, the sentence does not describe your situation, and Kwik Fit has not written a version that does. Worth asking the centre, before booking, exactly what documentation you will leave with.

The same page repeats a description of the law that has been out of date in Britain for years, telling readers that "In 2002, the European Parliament took the view that the practice of manufacturers forcing car owners to go to dealerships to get a service to uphold their warranty was too restrictive". The practical outcome has not changed — the 2023 Order preserves the position — but the authority for it is now a British statutory instrument rather than a European decision, and a page written this year could say so.

sections.heading: Two Kwik Fit pages, two different prices for the same service
sections.html:
The service pricing table gives an interim service from £186.95 and a full service from £246.95. The company's own guide to choosing a service, on the same site, gives an interim service "From £84 (based on engine size and oil type required)" and a full service "From £167". That is a gap of £102.95 on the interim and £79.95 on the full, for the same two products described in the same terms, and neither page is dated.

Neither figure is dishonest on its face; one of them is simply stale, and a reader has no way of telling which. If you arrive quoting £84 you will be quoted £186.95, and the fixed-price grid — the best thing about buying a service here — loses some of its point when the site carries two versions of it. The same absence of dates affects the hybrid answer in the introduction: two pages, two positions, no way to tell which was written last.

sections.heading: How the guarantee is worded for brakes, and how it is worded for a service
sections.html:
The guarantees document is versioned and dated, which is more than most chains manage — Version 1.9, 30 January 2026 — and several of the promises in it are generous. Brake pads and shoes carry a lifetime guarantee, with replacement sets "for as long as you own the vehicle". Bosch and NAPA batteries carry five years and unlimited mileage. Exhausts and catalytic converters carry three years and unlimited mileage. Shock absorbers carry a two-year manufacturer defect guarantee plus a 14-day satisfaction promise: if the ride has not improved, you get a refund and the original units refitted free, provided you kept them.

Now compare two sentences. On brakes: "we will guarantee all other new brake parts fitted, including labour for the first 12 months after fitment or the first 12,000 miles". On servicing: "Service components and any other mechanical parts, including starters and alternators are guaranteed for 12 months or 12,000 miles, whichever comes first." The brake clause names labour. The service clause does not. Elsewhere the document promises to "dismantle and repair or replace at its discretion any defective parts and reassemble them on your vehicle free of charge, subject to these guarantee conditions", which reads as though labour is covered — but the explicit mention in one clause and its absence in the other is exactly the kind of drafting that gets argued about at a counter. Ask, and get the answer on the invoice.

All the guarantees exclude wear, tear and corrosion, criminal or malicious damage, fire, theft, third-party repairs, competitive motorsport, and "any monetary or compensatory claim, in particular consequential or additional losses". The battery and brake guarantees also exclude company vehicles, hire cars, taxis and commercial use, and all of them require the original receipt.

sections.heading: Who decides it if the job goes wrong
sections.html:
Kwik Fit's terms are Version 13, dated 8 July 2025, and they are clear about the routine things. Services and MOTs booked online carry a 14-day cancellation right, or until 4pm on the day before the MOT appointment if that comes sooner; cancel before work starts and there is no charge; cancel after it has started and the company "reserve[s] the right to charge you for any Products or Services supplied". The contract is with Kwik-Fit (GB) Limited, company 01009184, VAT number GB 380 0948 50, under English law.

The dispute clause is where it thins out. If Customer Care cannot settle a complaint, the terms tell you to "ask Our Customer Care department for details of the Alternative Dispute Resolution Scheme that We participate in". The scheme is not named there, on the contact page, or in the FAQs. Under regulation 19 of the Alternative Dispute Resolution for Consumer Disputes (Competent Authorities and Information) Regulations 2015, a trader obliged to use an ADR body must give "the name and website address of the ADR entity" both on its website and in its general terms; where use is voluntary, regulation 19(2) requires the name and website in writing once the internal procedure is exhausted. Either way, a customer deciding whether it is worth pursuing a complaint cannot find out who would hear it without making a phone call.

For context on what the sector's own scheme offers: The Motor Ombudsman runs a Service and Repair Code approved by the Chartered Trading Standards Institute, first approved in 2008 and granted full Office of Fair Trading approval in November 2011, with around 7,500 businesses accredited across its four codes as at its December 2023 audit. Accredited garages must put estimates and quotations in writing as a breakdown of costs, contact the customer "for authorisation prior to commencement" of extra work, make replaced parts available to view until the car is collected, itemise parts, labour, environmental disposal charges and VAT separately on the invoice, acknowledge a complaint within ten working days and issue a final response within eight weeks, after which the customer has one year to refer the matter onward. Whether Kwik Fit is accredited to that code could not be confirmed from the Ombudsman's own published material, and Kwik Fit does not claim it — so treat the list above as the benchmark to ask about rather than as a description of what you are buying.

sections.heading: The group behind the 600 centres
sections.html:
Ownership has changed hands repeatedly. Ford bought the Kwik Fit group in June 1999 for more than $1bn, sold it to CVC Capital Partners in 2002, and PAI Partners took it on in 2005 before ITOCHU completed its purchase in June 2011, adding the 110-location STS Tyre Pros network at the same time. Today the immediate parent recorded at Companies House is European Tyre Enterprise Limited, which was notified as the person with significant control on 25 June 2025, taking over from Kwik-Fit Holdings Limited. ETEL describes its group — Kwik Fit, Stapletons Tyre Services, STS Tyre Pros and Murfitts Industries — as having "total annual sales in excess of £1.2bn", though that figure carries no date on the page. Kwik Fit's most recent accounts cover the year to 31 March 2025, with the next set due by 31 December 2026. In 2024 the group bought Fettle, a London bicycle servicing business.

On training, the company's own about page credits it with "Ofsted Outstanding accreditation" for its training academy. Ofsted's published record tells a more recent story: the Outstanding grade was awarded at an inspection on 20 to 24 April 2015, and at the most recent inspection, from 16 to 19 July 2024, Kwik-Fit (GB) Limited was graded Good in all five areas — quality of education, behaviour and attitudes, personal development, leadership and management, and apprenticeships. The provider had around 550 apprentices at that inspection, three-quarters of them aged 19 or under, almost all on the level 2 autocare technician standard. Good is a solid grade and the report is complimentary about the training plans; the marketing copy is simply eleven years out of date.

One product is currently unavailable rather than merely undersold. Kwik Fit Club, the monthly subscription covering tyres, MOT, servicing, air conditioning, batteries, brakes, exhausts, alignment and wipers, has been closed to new members: "Our Kwik Fit Club service is currently being upgraded and new memberships have been temporarily paused." Existing members keep their benefits. Its terms are still Version 2, dated 2 March 2023, and they note that the subscription is non-transferable, that an early termination fee applies after the 14-day cooling-off period, and that unused allowances are not refunded.

pros: Prices published in a full grid by engine size before you book — £186.95 to £251.95 interim, £246.95 to £311.95 full — rather than quoted only after the car is on the ramp
Over 600 centres open seven days a week, including Sundays from 10am to 4pm
Service components and other mechanical parts guaranteed for 12 months or 12,000 miles, under a guarantees document that is versioned and dated (V1.9, 30 January 2026)
Bundling the MOT with a full service costs £35.00 on top, against the DVSA maximum test fee of £54.85
A Manufacturer Service to the maker's own schedule, with parts of Original Equipment standard, priced individually
Lifetime guarantee on brake pads and shoes, five years on Bosch and NAPA batteries, three years on exhausts and catalytic converters
Extra work only carried out with your agreement, with a printed quotation available on request
cons: Cannot update or reset a manufacturer Digital Service Record, so on most cars sold new in the last decade the maker's own service file will show a gap however good the work
Two pages on Kwik Fit's own site quote different starting prices for the same services — £84 and £167 on one, £186.95 and £246.95 on the other — and neither is dated
The servicing FAQ says hybrids cannot be serviced "of any type", while the service comparison page lists hybrids as suitable for both the interim and full service
The Alternative Dispute Resolution scheme is never named — the terms tell customers to telephone Customer Care to find out who would hear a complaint
The service guarantee covers parts for 12 months or 12,000 miles without mentioning labour, where the brake guarantee names labour explicitly
Spark plugs are excluded from every service package, and the interim service replaces nothing but the oil and filter
The about page still claims an Ofsted Outstanding rating awarded in April 2015; the July 2024 inspection graded the training provision Good in every category
Kwik Fit Club is closed to new members while the service is upgraded
verdict: For a straightforward annual service on a car that is out of its dealer warranty, Kwik Fit is an easy thing to buy: you can read the price before you book, there are more than 600 places to book it, and the parts carry a 12 month or 12,000 mile guarantee. The full service at £246.95 with the MOT at £281.95 is a fair price for a 60-point inspection and a road test, and bundling the test makes sense given that better than one class 4 car in four fails first time. The reservations are about paperwork rather than spanners: it cannot sign a digital service record, its own site carries two sets of prices, it will not say who arbitrates a dispute, and its hybrid answer depends on which page you read. Ring the centre with the registration, ask what documentation you will leave with, and get the quotation in writing before the car goes up.

faqs.q: How much does a service at Kwik Fit cost?
faqs.a: An interim service starts at £186.95 for engines up to 1400cc, rising through £211.95 and £231.95 to £251.95 above 3000cc. A full service starts at £246.95 and rises to £311.95. An engine oil and filter change starts at £132.95 and an electric vehicle service at £230.95. All are "from" prices: the final figure depends on engine size and on the oil your car requires, with synthetic and specialist grades costing more.

faqs.q: Will a Kwik Fit service invalidate my manufacturer warranty?
faqs.a: Not by itself. The Competition Act 1998 (Motor Vehicle Agreements Block Exemption) Order 2023, in force from 1 June 2023 to 31 May 2029, protects an independent garage's access to the information and tools needed to service a car properly. Kwik Fit's Manufacturer Service follows the maker's own schedule using parts of Original Equipment standard, and the company states that its logbook stamp "will uphold any warranty you have with your car dealer". Two things to check: a dealer's own extended warranty is a separate contract with its own conditions, and Kwik Fit cannot update a manufacturer Digital Service Record.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the interim and the full service?
faqs.a: The interim runs every 6 months or 6,000 miles and replaces the engine oil and filter, with a visual brake inspection and a range of checks. The full service runs every 12 months or 12,000 miles and adds the air filter, a full strip-down brake check and a wheel alignment, bearing and balancing inspection. Neither includes spark plugs; the interim also excludes the fuel filter, air filter, belts and power steering fluid.

faqs.q: Does Kwik Fit do MOTs, and what does it charge?
faqs.a: Yes — the company is licensed by the DVSA to carry out MOT testing. It prices the test inside its bundles rather than advertising it alone: a full service with MOT starts at £281.95 against £246.95 for the service on its own, a difference of £35.00. The legal maximum any test station may charge for a class 4 car is £54.85.

faqs.q: Can Kwik Fit service a hybrid or an electric car?
faqs.a: Electric vehicles, yes: there is a dedicated EV service at £230.95, recommended every 24 months or 20,000 miles. Hybrids are unclear. The servicing FAQ states that "We are not currently able to service hybrid vehicles of any type", while the service comparison page marks hybrids as suitable for both the interim and the full service and the full service checklist includes a hybrid system check. Telephone the centre with your registration before booking.

faqs.q: How do I complain about work done at a Kwik Fit centre?
faqs.a: Start with Customer Care on 0800 75 76 77 or customercare@kwik-fit.com, keeping the original receipt, which the guarantees require before any remedial work can start. If that does not settle it, the terms say to ask Customer Care for details of the Alternative Dispute Resolution scheme the company participates in — the scheme is not named anywhere on the website. Trade-body benchmarks are useful here: The Motor Ombudsman's Service and Repair Code requires accredited garages to acknowledge a complaint within ten working days and issue a final response within eight weeks.

title: Kwik Fit Tyres: Fitted Prices, the Label and What the Law Demands
meta_title: Kwik Fit Tyres: The Fitted Price, the Label and the Law
meta_description: Kwik Fit fits tyres at over 600 centres. What the fully fitted price covers, the £20.50 no discount touches, the guarantee, TyreCare and the tread rules.
intro:
Kwik Fit is the largest tyre-fitting chain in Britain, with over 600 centres across the UK and Northern Ireland and many of them open seven days a week. It stocks more than twenty makes, from Michelin, Continental, Pirelli, Goodyear, Bridgestone and Dunlop at the premium end through Hankook, Yokohama, Vredestein and Uniroyal in the middle to Giti, Leao, Maxxis, Triangle and Westlake at the budget end. Every price the website shows is a fully fitted price, and the company is unusually clear about what that means: the tyre, a replacement valve, wheel balancing, disposal of the tyre coming off and VAT are all inside the figure you see before you book.

You search by registration or by the size on the sidewall, pick a centre and pick a slot. The prices online are the cheapest Kwik Fit does, and the company says so plainly — its web prices are exclusive to the site and most of its promotions never appear in a centre. Mobile fitting is a genuine alternative rather than a token: over 200 mobile fitters work seven days a week, evening slots included, and fitting at your home or workplace is free when you buy four tyres online. The free tyre check is done properly, with the car raised so each wheel can be turned, rather than as a glance across a forecourt.

Every new tyre carries a guarantee against manufacturing defects for the legal life of the tyre. A puncture, where the damage allows, is repaired from £29.95 including a new valve and rebalancing, to the British Standard the trade works to. Tyre insurance against accidental and malicious damage is offered separately at the counter, underwritten by a company regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority, from £6.99 a tyre.
