sections.heading: What the price on the screen actually buys
sections.html:
The number beside each tyre is the fitted number. Kwik Fit builds it from the tyre itself plus a fixed charge of £20.50 per tyre covering fitting, wheel balancing, the new valve and disposal of the old casing, with VAT on top of all of it. That fixed element is worth holding on to, because it is the part of the bill that never goes on sale. Kwik Fit states in the small print of its own promotions that all tyre discounts "apply to the cost of the tyre only and exclude charges for fitting, balancing, valve and disposal". On a set of four, that leaves £82.00 of the bill outside any code you enter.

The codes themselves are generous enough on the rubber. At the time of checking the site was running 10% off two Pirelli tyres or 15% off four under SAVEPI, 10% off two or more Goodyears under KFGOOD, 10% off two Continentals under COTYKF, 15% off four Giti tyres under GITISAVE, 10% off two Hankooks under KFHAN and 15% off four Bridgestone Turanza All Season 6 under KFBRAS. Students and key workers are offered up to 15%. Codes cannot be stacked with any other offer unless the offer says so, and only the Continental promotion carried a visible countdown to its expiry.

One thing the site does not do is publish a price list you can check against a counter. Kwik Fit says the prices on kwik-fit.com "are exclusive to the website and may vary from the prices set in your local Kwik Fit centre", and explains the gap as web promotions plus the efficiency of ordering stock on demand rather than holding it in every branch. The web price is the low one. There is no published in-centre equivalent to compare it with, so booking online is the only way to know what you are being charged before you arrive.

sections.heading: Fitting at a centre, or on your own driveway
sections.html:
Two speeds are on offer. Express fitting covers same-day and next-day appointments where the tyre is already in the right place; otherwise the site typically offers appointments three or five days from the date of purchase, because the tyre is ordered in for you. If you want the work done where the car already is, mobile fitting reaches most urban postcodes seven days a week, with an anytime slot cheaper than a half-day slot and the charge running up to £30 depending on which you choose. Kwik Fit gives a two-hour arrival window, the customer has to be there, and the fitter needs a level surface and room to work — steep drives, lowered cars and some heavier electric vehicles are the awkward cases. Wheels are balanced off the car and refitted with a new valve, the same as in a centre.

Two limits are worth knowing before you book. Tyres bought from Kwik Fit have to be fitted by Kwik Fit: the company states flatly that it is "not our company policy to offer a cash and carry service", so you cannot buy at the online price and carry the tyre to a cheaper fitter or your own garage. And mobile appointments are fitment-only, so a tyre cannot be dropped off and left.

The free tyre check is booked the same way, by registration. The technician inspects the whole tread rather than the outer shoulder, checks both inner and outer sidewalls, looks at wear pattern, size, load index and speed rating, and raises the car so each wheel can be rotated. Kwik Fit makes the point itself that a look at a tyre on a forecourt, with a quarter of its circumference on the ground, is not a check at all.

sections.heading: The letters on the sidewall label, and what one class is worth
sections.html:
Every new car tyre sold in Great Britain carries a standardised label, and the rules behind it are assimilated Regulation (EU) 2020/740, the revised scheme that took effect in May 2021. A distributor has to make sure the label is visible at the point of sale or, where the tyres are not on display, that the information reaches you during the buying process, and the same figures must appear in brochures and on websites.

For a car tyre the fuel efficiency classes are set against rolling resistance measured in newtons per kilonewton: class A is 6.5 or below, B runs 6.6 to 7.7, C 7.8 to 9.0, D 9.1 to 10.5 and E is 10.6 or above. Wet grip uses an index instead, where A is 1.55 or better, B 1.40 to 1.54, C 1.25 to 1.39, D 1.10 to 1.24 and E 1.09 or below. The European Commission's own guidance puts a single class step at three to six metres of extra stopping distance in the wet, and about 80 litres of fuel across the life of a set on a petrol or diesel car. Noise is shown as a measured figure in decibels alongside a three-bar symbol, against type-approval ceilings that run between 70 and 77 dB(A) depending on the tyre class; three decibels is a doubling of sound energy, so the gap between quiet and loud is larger than it looks. Two pictograms sit outside the letter scales: the three-peak mountain snowflake for tyres that pass a snow braking test, and a separate icon for tyres that pass an ice test.

The one thing to watch is that the scale changed. The 2009 scheme it replaced ran from A to G, and some official guidance pages still describe tyre labels that way. On a current car tyre the bottom of both scales is E.

sections.heading: What the law asks of a tyre, and what ignoring it costs
sections.html:
The standard everyone quotes comes from regulation 27 of the Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) Regulations 1986. For cars, light goods vehicles up to 3,500kg, zero-emission goods vehicles up to 4,250kg and light trailers, the grooves of the tread pattern must be at least 1.6mm deep in a continuous band across the central three-quarters of the breadth of the tread and round the entire outer circumference. Vehicles with more than eight passenger seats, and anything first used before 3 January 1933, work to 1.0mm. The same regulation bans a cut longer than 25mm or 10% of the section width that reaches the ply or cord, any lump, bulge or tear from a structural failure, exposed ply or cord, and a tyre not inflated fit for the use it is being put to.

The MOT tester applies the same list. Tread below the limit, a bulge, exposed cords and a valve likely to deflate are dangerous defects. A cut to the cords, two different sizes on one axle, radial and cross-ply mixed on one axle and a tyre pressure monitoring system that is not working are major defects. That last one catches more drivers than it should: TPMS is inspected on every M1 vehicle first used on or after 1 January 2012, with motor caravans, ambulances and hearses over 2,500kg excluded, so a warning light left on after a tyre change is a fail on a car that is otherwise perfect.

Get it wrong on the road and the offence sits under section 41A of the Road Traffic Act 1988. For a car the maximum is a level 4 fine of £2,500 with three penalty points; over 3.5 tonnes it rises to level 5, which has been unlimited for offences committed since 13 March 2015. The detail people miss is that the fine is charged per defective tyre while the points are normally endorsed once, so four bald tyres is a four-figure sum rather than a ticket.

Whether 1.6mm is where you should actually stop is a different question, and Kwik Fit answers it the way most of the trade does: many manufacturers advise replacing at 3mm, because stopping distances lengthen sharply below that. The 20p test works because the outer rim of the coin is just under 3mm — if the rim disappears into the groove you are somewhere above the legal minimum, not necessarily above the sensible one. For scale, TyreSafe's reading of the Department for Transport casualty figures put tyre-related deaths and serious injuries at 172 in 2024 against a five-year average of 163, with a 24% jump among riders of powered two-wheelers, the highest in a decade. The Department's own 2025 report, published on 30 July 2026, recorded 1,538 road deaths and 29,918 people killed or seriously injured.

sections.heading: When a puncture can be repaired, and when the answer is a new tyre
sections.html:
Kwik Fit repairs to British Standard BS AU 159, which fixes where on a tyre a repair may be made, how big it may be and how many are allowed. In practice that means the central third of the tread, known as the minor repair area. A nail through the middle of the tread is usually repairable; the same nail in the shoulder, close to the sidewall, is not, because the flexing there will not tolerate a plug and patch.

A repair is also refused if the tread is already below 1.6mm, if the object has done secondary damage inside the casing, if the rubber has deteriorated with age, if the bead or sidewall is damaged, if cords are showing, if a previous repair has failed, or if the tyre is bulging. Run-flat tyres are not repaired at all, because their reinforced sidewalls hide the structural damage caused by driving on them deflated — which is precisely what they are designed to let you do. Owners of cars delivered on run-flats should price a puncture at the cost of a tyre, not at the £29.95 a repair starts from.

sections.heading: Tyre age: the ten-year rule that is not about your car
sections.html:
The ten-year figure attached to tyres is real law, and it does not apply to the car on your drive. The Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) (Amendment) Regulations 2020, in force from 1 February 2021, prohibit a tyre whose week of manufacture — the code moulded into the sidewall under ECE Regulation 30 or 54 — falls more than ten years before the day the vehicle is used, on the front axle of a bus, on any single-wheel axle of a minibus, and on the front axle of a goods vehicle over 3,500kg. Retreads are dated from the retreading. The MOT manual mirrors it, failing tyres over ten years old on any front steered axle and on a minibus rear axle with single wheels.

For an ordinary car there is no legal age limit at all. What there is instead is advice, and Kwik Fit gives the same figure the manufacturers do: around ten years is the outer limit for a tyre regardless of how much tread is left, because rubber hardens and cracks whether or not the car is driven. A caravan, a classic or a second car doing a thousand miles a year is the case where tread depth tells you almost nothing and the date code tells you everything.

sections.heading: Second-hand tyres are held to a higher number than the one on your car
sections.html:
Kwik Fit's range is new tyres, and it is worth understanding what the alternative is legally required to be. Under the Motor Vehicle Tyres (Safety) Regulations 1994, a part-worn tyre sold in England, Scotland or Wales must have at least 2mm of original tread across the full breadth of the tread and round the entire outer circumference, and must be marked "PART-WORN" in capitals at least 4mm high, permanently and legibly, next to every approval mark — and not by hot-branding or cutting. It must also be free of the same defects the road regulations ban: no cut over 25mm or 10% of the section width, no bulges or tears, no exposed cords, no unrepaired penetration damage.

Read those two numbers together and the oddity stands out. A part-worn tyre must have 2mm across its full width before it may legally be sold, while a tyre already on your car is legal at 1.6mm across the middle three-quarters. The second-hand tyre is held to the higher standard, which is a useful thing to know when a price two-thirds below a new fitted price is being explained to you.

sections.heading: TyreCare, the insurance sold at the tyre counter
sections.html:
TyreCare is a real insurance contract, not a warranty extension, and it is priced off what the tyre cost: £6.99 on a tyre under £50, then £11.99, £16.99, £21.99, £27.99 and £32.99 as the price climbs in fifty-pound steps, and £42.99 on anything over £300. Insurance premium tax is included. It is underwritten by London General Insurance Company Limited, company number 1865673 of Staines-upon-Thames, authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority and the PRA under firm reference 202689. Kwik-Fit (GB) Ltd arranges and administers it, and states in the paperwork that it gives information rather than a personal recommendation.

What it covers is accidental damage — sudden, unforeseen deflation or other damage to the tyre or the valve — and malicious damage by a third party, which needs a police crime reference number. Repairs and replacements come with fitting, valve and balancing at no extra cost. What it does not cover is a long list: any tyre below the UK legal tread depth, wear and tear, manufacturing defects, fire, theft, damage outside the UK, Isle of Man and Channel Islands, damage to anything other than the tyre, consequential loss, vehicles used for hire, driving instruction, chauffeuring, racing, track days or rallying, commercial and agricultural use, modified vehicles, tyres without DOT markings, and buyers under seventeen.

The shape of the cover matters more than the price. It runs twelve months from purchase, but it ends earlier on the first replacement of the tyre, on the third repair, or when you sell the car — so a single unrepairable puncture consumes the policy on that tyre rather than leaving cover in place for the new one. You have fourteen days to cancel for a full refund if you have not claimed, and afterwards a pro-rata refund with a £5 minimum retained. Complaints go to Kwik Fit customer services on 0800 757677 and then, if you are not satisfied within six months, to the Financial Ombudsman Service, and the Financial Services Compensation Scheme covers 90% of a general insurance claim without an upper limit.

Two things about the documents themselves. The policy wording carries the version reference V12_0420 and the insurance product information document is FV1.6, dated March 2021, while the premium ladder on the live page runs up to £42.99 — the paperwork is several years older than the prices it sits beside. And neither document states Kwik-Fit (GB) Ltd's own regulatory status or firm reference number, only the insurer's; it could not be confirmed from the material Kwik Fit publishes, and a buyer deciding whether to take a regulated product from a tyre counter would reasonably want it on the page.

sections.heading: One group fits the tyre, another arm delivers it and a third grinds it up
sections.html:
Kwik Fit sits inside European Tyre Enterprise Limited, formed in 2011 when ITOCHU Corporation brought several long-established tyre and automotive businesses together, with group sales above £1.2 billion. The retail chains are Kwik Fit and STS Tyre Pros. The wholesale arm is Stapletons Tyre Services, which distributes tyres to the trade through eleven hubs. And since 20 December 2021 the group has also owned Murfitts Industries, the tyre recycler at Lakenheath in Suffolk, which handles something like 20 million car tyres a year and turns them into granulate for sports surfaces, playgrounds, pathways, carpet underlay and modified asphalt.

That makes the disposal element of the £20.50 unusual: the charge for taking your old tyre away is paid to a group that also owns the business which processes it and sells the material on. None of this is hidden — ETEL says so on its own site — and it is a reasonable explanation of why Kwik Fit can quote one all-in figure while independents itemise disposal separately. It is simply worth knowing that the fitting price covers three stages of the same group's business.

sections.heading: If the tyre fails, or the bill turns out to be wrong
sections.html:
The guarantee document is versioned and dated, which is more than most chains manage — V1.9, 30 January 2026. On tyres it says all new tyres are covered against manufacturing defects throughout the legal life of the tyre, and that where a defect is confirmed by the manufacturer's inspection you receive a refund for the remaining tread. That is not the same as a free replacement: it is money back in proportion to the tread you had not used, and it depends on producing the original paperwork, which the document tells you twice to keep safe. Reasonable wear, tear and corrosion are excluded, as is damage from criminal or malicious acts, fire and theft, and anything another garage has worked on since.

Wheel alignment is treated separately and honestly: Kwik Fit says alignment is affected by road conditions and driving and therefore cannot be covered by its guarantees, but it will recheck and readjust free of charge within 30 days of the work.

The complaints route is Customer Care on 0800 75 76 77. There is a real asymmetry here worth understanding before you buy the add-on rather than after. A dispute about TyreCare is a dispute about a regulated insurance contract, so it can be taken to the Financial Ombudsman Service, free, with a binding outcome. A dispute about the tyre, the fitting or the bill is an ordinary consumer contract; Kwik Fit's terms refer to an alternative dispute resolution scheme without naming it, so the only certain route is the county court or a claim under the Consumer Rights Act. The insurance you might not need has a stronger complaints backstop than the fitting you definitely bought.

pros: Fully fitted prices published before you book, with the tyre, a new valve, balancing, disposal and VAT all inside the figure
Over 600 centres with many open seven days, plus more than 200 mobile fitters covering evenings and weekends
Free mobile fitting when four tyres are bought online, and free vehicle, battery, brake and exhaust checks alongside the tyre check
The free tyre check is done with the car raised, so the whole circumference and both sidewalls are inspected rather than the visible shoulder
Punctures repaired from £29.95 including a new valve and rebalancing, to British Standard BS AU 159
More than twenty brands stocked, from Michelin and Continental down to Giti, Leao and Westlake, so a budget option exists in most sizes
Manufacturing-defect cover on every new tyre for its legal life, set out in a guarantees document that is versioned and dated
TyreCare is a properly regulated insurance contract with Financial Ombudsman Service access and 90% FSCS protection
cons: Every advertised tyre discount excludes the £20.50 a tyre charged for fitting, balancing, valve and disposal, so a 15%-off-four code leaves £82.00 of a four-tyre bill untouched
Two of Kwik Fit's own pages give that charge differently — £20.50 on the online pricing page and £20.00 in the tyre FAQ — and neither page carries a date
Web prices are described as exclusive to the website and no in-centre price list is published anywhere, so a walk-in customer has nothing to check the counter price against
Tyres must be fitted by Kwik Fit and there is no cash and carry, so the online price cannot be taken to a cheaper fitter or used on a wheel you bring in
TyreCare ends on the first replacement of the tyre, so one unrepairable puncture uses up the whole twelve months of cover on that wheel
TyreCare excludes any tyre already below the legal tread depth, which is the condition in which damage is most likely to happen
The TyreCare paperwork is years older than the prices beside it — policy wording V12_0420 and an information document marked FV1.6, dated March 2021, against a premium ladder reaching £42.99
Neither TyreCare document gives Kwik-Fit (GB) Ltd's own regulatory status or firm reference number, only the insurer's, and it could not be confirmed from Kwik Fit's published material
Run-flat tyres are never repaired, so a puncture that would be a £29.95 repair on an ordinary tyre is a full replacement on a car delivered with them
The lifetime guarantee pays a refund for the remaining tread after a manufacturer's inspection rather than replacing the tyre, and it depends on producing the original receipt
The alternative dispute resolution scheme covering the tyre and the fitting is referred to in the terms but never named, while the optional insurance has a clearly signposted Ombudsman route
verdict: Kwik Fit is the most convenient way to buy tyres in Britain and it is honest about the number on the screen: the tyre, the valve, the balancing, the disposal and the VAT are all in it, at over 600 centres and through more than 200 mobile fitters seven days a week. Read the arithmetic before you enter a discount code, because £20.50 a tyre sits outside every promotion the site runs, and there is no published centre price to compare the web price with. The tyre guarantee is real but narrow — manufacturing defects only, settled as a refund for unused tread — and TyreCare is worth the £6.99 to £42.99 only if you understand that it stops at the first replacement. On price alone an online-only retailer with a local fitter will often beat it; on getting four tyres onto a car this weekend, at a published price, with a free check first and somebody to ring afterwards, very little else comes close.

faqs.q: Does the Kwik Fit price include fitting?
faqs.a: Yes. The price shown online is fully fitted and covers the tyre, a replacement valve, wheel balancing, disposal of the old tyre and VAT. The fitting element is £20.50 per tyre, and it is excluded from every discount code, so a promotional percentage applies only to the cost of the rubber.

faqs.q: What is the legal tread depth, and when should I actually replace a tyre?
faqs.a: The law requires at least 1.6mm across the central three-quarters of the tread and round the whole circumference of the tyre. Driving on less risks a level 4 fine of up to £2,500 and three penalty points, charged per tyre. Many manufacturers advise replacing at 3mm, because wet stopping distances lengthen quickly below that, and the outer rim of a 20p coin is just under 3mm if you want a rough check at home.

faqs.q: Can Kwik Fit repair my puncture rather than sell me a tyre?
faqs.a: Often, but not always. Repairs follow British Standard BS AU 159, which allows them only in the central third of the tread. A puncture near the shoulder or sidewall, a tyre already below 1.6mm, exposed cords, a bulge, ageing rubber or a previous failed repair all rule it out, and run-flat tyres are never repaired. A repair starts at £29.95 including a new valve and rebalancing.

faqs.q: Is TyreCare worth buying?
faqs.a: It insures the tyre against accidental and malicious damage for twelve months at £6.99 to £42.99 depending on what the tyre cost, and it is underwritten by an FCA-regulated insurer with Ombudsman and FSCS backing. The catch is that cover on a tyre ends at the first replacement or the third repair, and nothing is paid on a tyre already below the legal tread depth. On an expensive tyre in a city where kerbing and vandalism are likely it can pay for itself in one claim; on a cheap tyre it rarely will.

faqs.q: Can I buy tyres from Kwik Fit and fit them myself?
faqs.a: No. Kwik Fit states that all tyres must be fitted by its own staff and that it does not operate a cash and carry service. Mobile appointments are fitment-only as well, so a tyre cannot be delivered and left with you.

faqs.q: Will a tyre pressure warning light fail the MOT?
faqs.a: Yes, on most modern cars. A tyre pressure monitoring system that is not working is a major defect, and it is inspected on every M1 vehicle first used on or after 1 January 2012, with motor caravans, ambulances and hearses over 2,500kg excluded. Have the sensor or the service kit sorted at the same time as the tyre rather than after the test.

faqs.q: What are the rules on part-worn tyres?
faqs.a: They may be sold, but under the Motor Vehicle Tyres (Safety) Regulations 1994 they must carry at least 2mm of original tread across the full breadth and round the whole circumference, be marked PART-WORN in capitals at least 4mm high next to every approval mark, and be free of cuts over 25mm or 10% of the section width, bulges, exposed cords and unrepaired damage. That 2mm is a higher figure than the 1.6mm your own tyres are legal at.

title: LateRooms Hotel Deals
meta_title: LateRooms review: how cheap are its last-minute hotel deals?
meta_description: LateRooms lists UK rooms from £18 a night and London from £34, and free membership cuts up to 15% more. Prices and small print, checked 19 September 2026.

headline.label: Cheapest advertised London room
headline.value: £34 a night — LateRooms' own lead-in price for London, checked 19 September 2026

intro:
LateRooms advertises United Kingdom rooms from £18 a night, England from £26 and London from £34, with free membership knocking up to 15% off rates at more than 100,000 hotels. Those figures were taken from laterooms.com on 19 September 2026. The site has specialised in short-notice bookings since 1999, when it began as a place to shift rooms hotels had not sold that day.

The company behind it is not the one that built the name. The original LateRooms collapsed on 1 August 2019 when its parent, Malvern Group, ran out of cash and called in KPMG, after Cox & Kings India — which owned 49% of the group — defaulted on loan repayments. The brand was bought by Snaptrip Group and relaunched in 2024. Book today and your contract is with Snaptrip Group Limited, company number 08774859, of LG.03 Cargo Works, 1–2 Hatfields, London SE1 9PG.

What that buys is a search covering the same wholesale hotel stock the trade uses, with two ways to pay: prepay in full at the time of booking, or reserve now and settle with the hotel at check-in or check-out. Thousands of rooms carry free cancellation, and the app is priced separately from the website, so it is worth checking both before you commit.

key_facts.label: Who you are booking with
key_facts.value: Snaptrip Group Limited, company 08774859, trading as LateRooms; VAT 201864825; registered LG.03 Cargo Works, 1–2 Hatfields, London SE1 9PG

key_facts.label: Lead-in prices
key_facts.value: United Kingdom from £18 a night, England from £26, London from £34, City of London from £45, luxury London from £80 — checked 19 September 2026

key_facts.label: Membership
key_facts.value: Free to join; "save up to 15% on over 100,000 hotels"

key_facts.label: How you pay
key_facts.value: Prepaid in full at booking on some hotels, or "payment is taken directly by the hotel at check-in or check-out" on others

key_facts.label: Who supplies the rooms
key_facts.value: Hotelbeds and its hotel partners; LateRooms "act[s] as an intermediary" and the accommodation contract is with the supplier

key_facts.label: Liability cap
key_facts.value: "Our liability to you is limited to the amount you paid us for the booking"

key_facts.label: Price Promise
key_facts.value: Refunds the difference if the same room is found cheaper elsewhere, claimed within 24 hours of booking

key_facts.label: Rules that apply
key_facts.value: No financial regulator; hotel-only bookings sit outside ATOL, and the site names no ABTA membership or ADR scheme

sections.heading: £18 a night, and the cities where that number holds
sections.html:
The lead-in prices are published on LateRooms' own destination pages and they vary more than the headline suggests. United Kingdom shows from £18 per night; England from £26; London from £34; the City of London from £45; Greater London, which sweeps in the outer boroughs, from £92; and filtering London to luxury properties lifts the floor to £80. Abroad, the home page was showing Blackpool from £20, Amsterdam from £23 and Paris from £91 on 19 September 2026.

A lead-in price is the cheapest room the system can find on any date in the window, so it is a floor rather than a forecast. LateRooms is unusually candid about that in its own help text, which puts a three-star room at "between £70 and £120 per night", a four-star at "between £120 and £200 per night" and a five-star at "typically start at £200 per night". Those three bands are a better planning figure than the £18, and a shop that prints both is doing more than most.

Membership is the other lever. It is free, and the site claims savings of up to 15% at over 100,000 hotels — which on a £120 four-star room is £18, roughly the cost of the cheapest room in the country. The app also carries rates the website does not, so a serious price check means looking in both places.

sections.heading: The rooms are wholesale stock, and the wholesaler is listed in Madrid
sections.html:
LateRooms does not hold hotel contracts of its own for this inventory. Its accommodation booking terms say plainly: "We act as an intermediary: you make a booking through our platform, but the accommodation services are provided by Hotelbeds and its hotel partners." Hotelbeds is the business-to-business bed bank owned by HBX Group, and it is the largest of its kind.

That matters because it puts audited numbers behind the search box. HBX Group floated on the Spanish stock exchanges in February 2025, raising €725 million, and its results for the year to 30 September 2025, announced on 26 November 2025, show total transaction value of €8.2bn, up 8%; revenue of €720m; adjusted EBITDA of €431m at a 60% margin; operating free cash flow of €437m; and a net loss after tax of €70m, with net debt down 63% to €397m. The group's own site describes around 60,000 travel distributors across more than 170 countries, 3,500 staff and seven billion searches a day.

For a guest, the practical consequence is a three-party booking: you pay LateRooms, Hotelbeds supplies the room, and the hotel provides the stay. If something goes wrong at the desk, the hotel's answer is often that its contract is with the wholesaler, not with you.

sections.heading: Two ways to pay, and only one of them is well protected
sections.html:
The booking terms describe both models: "For some hotels, you must pay the full amount at the time of booking", while "[f]or other hotels, payment is taken directly by the hotel at check-in or check-out." Cancellation and amendment rules "vary by hotel and rate type, and are determined by the Supplier", and a no-show is treated as a cancellation with no refund.

Pay the hotel directly on arrival and LateRooms has taken no money, so there is nothing to claim back from it. Prepay by credit card and section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 makes the card issuer jointly liable with the seller on purchases costing more than £100 and up to £30,000 — and paying only the deposit on a card is enough to claim the full price. Debit and prepaid cards fall back on chargeback, which MoneyHelper describes as an agreement between Visa, Mastercard and American Express rather than legal protection, with a 120-day claim window.

A hotel room booked on its own is not a package holiday, so no ATOL certificate applies and none is offered. The site names no ABTA membership and no alternative dispute resolution scheme, and its terms are "governed by the laws of England and Wales" with disputes going to the English courts.

sections.heading: What the compared price leaves at the hotel desk
sections.html:
The terms list a set of charges that are settled on site rather than online: "local taxes, resort fees, deposits, incidental charges, or security deposits" are "payable directly at the hotel". None of those appears in the number a shopper is comparing across sites, and city tourist taxes in particular are now charged across much of Europe and are creeping into British cities.

The rules on how prices are shown have tightened since the LateRooms name last meant anything. The consumer provisions of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 took effect on 7 April 2025, banning drip pricing — quoting one figure and adding compulsory fees as the customer proceeds — and giving the Competition and Markets Authority power to fine up to 10% of global turnover without going to court first. The same Act carries an explicit prohibition on fake and incentivised reviews.

It is worth being accurate about what LateRooms is and is not bound by. It was not one of the 31 accommodation booking businesses that gave the CMA undertakings on 13 September 2019 over scarcity messaging, discount claims and the effect of commission on search order; six of those — Booking.com, Expedia, Agoda, Hotels.com, ebookers and trivago — had already given formal undertakings in February 2019. The current site is under the general law rather than any case-specific commitment.

sections.heading: Who actually awards the stars on a British hotel
sections.html:
Star ratings shown on LateRooms listings are supplied by the property or by third parties, not assessed by LateRooms. In Britain the assessment that does exist is run by the AA and VisitEngland, whose inspectors visit as mystery-shopper guests and grade hospitality, service, bedrooms, bathrooms, cleanliness and food. The AA awards black stars from three to five, adds silver stars for superior housekeeping and food, picks red stars annually as the best hotels at each level, and has a "Quality Assessed" grade for properties that pass a full inspection without earning a star rating.

The other number on a listing is a guest score — Claridge's showed 9.6 from 588 reviews on 19 September 2026, the Ned 9.2 from 1,005 and Park Grand Hyde Park 7.4 from 1,002. Those are crowd averages collected by booking platforms, not an inspection, and the two should not be read as though they measure the same thing. A five-star guest average on an unassessed property tells you people enjoyed their stay; it does not tell you the bathrooms were checked by anyone.

sections.heading: Snaptrip Group on paper
sections.html:
Snaptrip Group Limited was incorporated on 14 November 2013 as Rest Easy Rentals Limited, became Rest Easy Group Limited on 19 September 2019 and took its present name on 12 May 2021. Its SIC code is 47910, retail sale via mail order houses or via the internet, and it is registered for VAT under 201864825. Persons with significant control are Matthew Richard Fox and Forward Partners General Partner Limited, both notified on 6 April 2016; Luke Smith was appointed a director on 24 March 2022. Matt Fox, the group's chief executive, described LateRooms as "one of the country's biggest and most popular hotel booking sites in the early part of the 21st century" when the relaunch was announced.

The accounts are where the trail stops. The company files total exemption full accounts — the small-company regime — with the latest made up to 30 November 2025 and filed on 20 July 2026, and the next set not due until 31 August 2027. Small-company accounts carry a balance sheet but no profit and loss account, so there is no published turnover, no booking volume and no customer count for the business taking your money. The only audited revenue anywhere in this chain belongs to HBX Group, and that is the supplier rather than the seller.

sections.heading: The Price Promise has a hole where last-minute bookings go
sections.html:
LateRooms promises that "if you do spot the same hotel room cheaper elsewhere online, we'll do the decent thing and refund the difference". The claim form must be submitted within 24 hours of booking, and the comparison has to be the exact same room online — same room type, same hotel, same check-in and check-out dates, same conditions such as breakfast and parking — in the same currency.

The exclusions are where it thins out. Rates that have gone by the time the claim is investigated do not count, nor do cancelled bookings, membership or loyalty rates, reward programme prices, opaque rates where the hotel is not revealed until after booking, and — the awkward one — bookings made less than 24 hours before arrival. A site whose entire proposition is the last-minute room excludes the last-minute room from its price guarantee.

There is a second mismatch worth knowing about. The consumer site says "over 100,000 hotels"; the pitch on the LateRooms affiliate programme says "over 1 million properties worldwide". Both cannot be describing the same catalogue, and neither page explains the difference.

sections.heading: Where a last-minute room fits the British hotel year
sections.html:
Domestic demand is the backdrop. VisitBritain's figures published on 11 June 2026 show British residents took 87 million overnight trips in England during 2025, 3% down on 2024, while total domestic tourism spend rose 3% to £78bn and spend on overnight trips rose 6% to £29bn. Fewer trips, more money on each one.

The accommodation mix moved with it: the share of trips including a hotel stay rose to 40%, against 35–36% in previous years. Hotels are taking a larger slice of a slightly smaller market, which is the condition in which unsold rooms get discounted late — the thing this site was built to sell, and a reasonable argument for checking it within a day or two of travelling rather than weeks ahead.

pros: Lead-in prices are published openly by destination — £18 a night across the UK, £26 in England, £34 in London — rather than hidden behind a search
Free membership advertised at up to 15% off more than 100,000 hotels, with no subscription and no minimum spend
A choice between prepaying and paying the hotel at check-in or check-out, with free cancellation on a large part of the stock
The booking terms name the supplier outright, so it is possible to work out who holds the contract before paying
Realistic price guidance in its own help text — £70–£120 for three stars, £120–£200 for four, £200-plus for five — instead of leaving the lead-in price to do the talking
Inventory comes from Hotelbeds, whose parent HBX Group publishes audited results and put €8.2bn of transaction value through in the year to 30 September 2025
cons: The company behind the brand publishes no turnover. Snaptrip Group Limited files total exemption full accounts, so the latest filing, made up to 30 November 2025, carries a balance sheet and no profit and loss account
Liability is capped at what you paid: "Our liability to you is limited to the amount you paid us for the booking", which will not stretch to a missed event or a replacement room at a higher rate
There is no telephone number and no published complaints procedure — contact is by email to mybooking@laterooms.com — and the site names no ombudsman or alternative dispute resolution scheme
The Price Promise excludes bookings made less than 24 hours before arrival, opaque rates, membership and loyalty rates, which removes it from much of what a last-minute site sells
Local taxes, resort fees, deposits and incidental charges are payable at the hotel and sit outside the price being compared, so two sites' figures are not necessarily like for like
Star ratings on listings come from the property or third parties rather than an AA or VisitEngland inspection, and the guest scores beside them are crowd averages, not an assessment
The catalogue is described as "over 100,000 hotels" to shoppers and "over 1 million properties worldwide" to affiliates, with no explanation of the gap
Hotel-only bookings carry no ATOL protection and the site claims no ABTA membership, so a card payment is the practical safety net
verdict: LateRooms is a resurrected brand on wholesale plumbing, and it is more open about both than it needs to be. The booking terms name Hotelbeds as the supplier, the help text gives honest three-, four- and five-star price bands, and the lead-in prices — £18 across the UK, £34 in London — are published rather than buried. Free membership at up to 15% off more than 100,000 hotels is worth the two minutes it takes, and the pay-at-the-hotel option suits anyone who wants to keep the money until they arrive. The weaknesses are all about what happens when a booking goes wrong: liability is limited to what you paid, there is no phone number, no complaints procedure and no dispute scheme, and the operating company publishes no accounts beyond a small-company balance sheet. Prepay on a credit card if the room costs more than £100, note that taxes and resort fees are still to come at the desk, and treat the Price Promise as a discipline for bookings made more than a day ahead rather than a guarantee on the last-minute room.

faqs.q: Is LateRooms the same company it used to be?
faqs.a: No. The original business collapsed on 1 August 2019 when its parent Malvern Group ran out of cash and appointed KPMG as administrators, after Cox & Kings India, a 49% shareholder, defaulted on loan repayments. Snaptrip Group bought the brand and relaunched the site in 2024. Bookings today are made with Snaptrip Group Limited, company number 08774859.

faqs.q: How cheap do the rooms actually get?
faqs.a: On 19 September 2026 the site advertised United Kingdom rooms from £18 a night, England from £26, London from £34 and the City of London from £45. Those are floors rather than typical prices; LateRooms' own guidance puts a three-star room at £70 to £120 a night, a four-star at £120 to £200 and a five-star at £200 or more.

faqs.q: Do I pay LateRooms or the hotel?
faqs.a: Both models exist and the rate decides which. Some hotels require the full amount at the time of booking; on others, payment is taken by the hotel at check-in or check-out. Local taxes, resort fees, deposits and incidental charges are paid at the property either way.

faqs.q: What protection do I have if the room is not there?
faqs.a: LateRooms limits its liability to the amount you paid it for the booking, and no ATOL or ABTA protection applies to a hotel-only reservation. Where you prepaid more than £100 on a credit card, section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 makes the card issuer jointly liable with the seller on purchases up to £30,000. Debit card payments rely on chargeback, which is a card scheme agreement rather than a legal right and normally has to be raised within 120 days.

faqs.q: Is the Price Promise worth relying on?
faqs.a: Only within limits. The claim has to be made within 24 hours of booking, for the identical room, hotel, dates, conditions and currency, and the cheaper rate must still be available when it is checked. Bookings made less than 24 hours before arrival are excluded, as are membership, loyalty and reward rates and opaque deals that hide the hotel name until after purchase.

faqs.q: Who decides the star rating shown on a listing?
faqs.a: The property or a third-party feed, not an inspector. Britain's assessment scheme is run by the AA and VisitEngland, whose inspectors stay as mystery-shopper guests and award black stars from three to five, with silver stars for superior quality and red stars for the best at each level. A guest score of 9.2 or 7.4 beside a listing is an average of customer reviews and measures something different.

title: Legal & General Life Insurance Review: Underwriting, Cover and Claims
meta_title: Legal & General Life Insurance Review: Cover From £5 a Month
meta_description: Legal & General life cover from £5 a month, £527m of life claims paid in 2025, and what the health questions really decide. Limits, evidence rules and gaps.
intro:
Legal & General has been writing life assurance since 1836, and the company behind the policy carries the risk itself rather than placing it with somebody else. Legal and General Assurance Society Limited is registered in England and Wales as company 166055 at One Coleman Street, London EC2R 5AA, and holds firm reference 117659 — authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both the Financial Conduct Authority and the PRA. Cover starts at £5 a month. In 2025 the company paid nearly 14,000 life insurance claims worth £527 million, part of £992 million paid across 20,621 retail protection claims, or about 56 claims settled a day, and £4.6 billion over the past five years.

What you are buying is a fixed-term policy in one of two shapes. Level cover keeps the same sum assured from the first day to the last; decreasing cover falls roughly in step with a repayment mortgage and costs less for it. You can apply from 18 up to 77 (67 if you add Critical Illness Cover), the term runs from 5 to 50 years, and the policy has to end before your 90th birthday. Terminal illness cover is built in at no extra charge, accidental death benefit up to £300,000 covers you while the application is being assessed, and there is free cover between exchange and completion if you are buying a house. Premiums are guaranteed not to rise unless you change the policy.

The third thing shapes everything else: this is medically underwritten cover. L&G asks about your health, your build, your drinking and whether you have touched nicotine in the past twelve months, then prices you on the answers. More than 80% of applications are processed straight through, with 180 UK-based underwriters picking up the rest. Those questions are the reason the premiums are as low as they are — and they are the part worth taking slowly, because the answers are what a claim gets checked against years later.

sections.heading: £5 a month, £26.33 a month, and the gap between them
sections.html:
The £5 headline is real but it is a floor, not a typical price. L&G's own guide to what life cover costs puts the average premium at £26.33 a month on its 2025 figures, and the average valid life claim it paid that year at £37,788. Both numbers are the company's own, which makes them more useful than any comparison table: they describe what its actual customers pay and receive rather than what a quote engine advertises.

The published worked examples show how sharply age bites. Spend £25 a month over a 25-year term as a non-smoker in good health and L&G's own illustration gives roughly £563,838 of cover at 30, £214,688 at 40, £75,521 at 50 and £23,258 at 60. A 70-year-old paying the same gets about £8,645 over a maximum 19-year term. The same money buys about twenty-four times as much cover at 30 as it does at 60, which is the single strongest argument for buying early rather than shopping hard.

Premiums can be paid monthly or annually and are guaranteed for the life of the policy unless you alter it. There is no cash-in value at any point — this is pure protection, and if you stop paying, the cover stops. Cancel inside the first 30 days and every premium comes back. Cancel later on a monthly plan and nothing does; annual payers get a proportionate refund.

sections.heading: Decreasing cover, and the interest rate you cannot see until you have bought
sections.html:
Decreasing cover is built for a repayment mortgage. The sum assured steps down over the term, which is why it is cheaper than level cover for the same starting amount, and why it is the default choice for people whose only real liability is the house. L&G sets the rate of decline using an assumed mortgage interest rate, and that rate appears on your Policy Schedule when the policy starts.

The company is candid about the consequence in its own terms and conditions, document reference LG2022, dated 2026/07: "If the interest rate we apply is less than the interest rate that is actually applied to your repayment mortgage, or your mortgage changes, the amount we pay out may not be enough to repay your mortgage in full." That is the whole risk of decreasing cover in one sentence. If you remortgage onto a higher rate, extend the term, borrow more for an extension, or move to a bigger house, the two curves separate and nobody tells you.

What the pre-sale documents do not carry is the assumed rate itself. It is not on the product page, not in the FAQs and not in the policy summary — it is disclosed on the schedule after you have applied. A buyer choosing between level and decreasing cover cannot compare the two properly without it, and asking for the figure before the cooling-off period runs out is worth the phone call. The 30-day window exists precisely for that kind of check.

Level cover carries no equivalent uncertainty, and it is the sensible shape where the money is meant to replace an income or cover a fixed liability such as an inheritance tax bill rather than a shrinking debt.

sections.heading: Where the health questions stop and a doctor's report starts
sections.html:
L&G publishes the thresholds at which an application stops being a form and becomes a medical file. Its guide to underwriting limits, reference Q41806, dated 10/25, sets out which evidence is triggered automatically by a combination of age and sum assured. A GP's report first appears on life cover of £75,001 to £100,000 for applicants aged 71 to 74. A medical examination starts at £100,001 to £150,000 for ages 66 to 70. Nurse screening begins at £200,001 to £250,000 for ages 61 to 65, a full blood profile at £250,001 to £300,000 for ages 66 to 70, and an exercise ECG only at £2,000,001 to £3,000,000 for the same age band.

A 35-year-old asking for £250,000 of cover, in other words, is very unlikely to see a doctor at all. A 72-year-old asking for £80,000 almost certainly will. Financial evidence follows a separate ladder: nothing is required automatically up to £1,500,000 of cover, and a Personal Assurance Questionnaire is needed above £3,500,000.

Evidence has a shelf life. For life cover up to £500,000 it stays valid for 6 months; above £500,000 it is 3 months. Critical illness evidence runs to 6 months up to £350,000 and 3 months above it. Let an application drift and the tests may have to be repeated.

Two definitions do more work than any other. Smoker rates apply to anyone who has used cigarettes, e-cigarettes, cigars, pipes or nicotine replacement within the last 12 months — vaping counts, and so do patches. Ex-smoker rates can apply to someone who has smoked within the last 5 years but not the last 12 months. Stopping for a year and re-applying is one of the few levers a customer controls, and L&G says so on its own pages.

sections.heading: The medical report has your name on it, and the law gives you first look
sections.html:
Where an insurer does want a report from your GP, the Access to Medical Reports Act 1988 governs what happens next, and almost nobody buying life cover knows it exists. Section 3 says an insurer may not even ask your doctor for a report unless it has told you it intends to and you have said yes: "that person ... has notified the individual that he proposes to make the application; and the individual has notified the applicant that he consents to the making of the application."

Section 4 gives you the right to read the report before it goes anywhere. Your doctor must not send it until you have seen it, or until 21 days have passed from the date of the application without you arranging to. Section 5 lets you ask, before consenting to its release, for any part you think is "incorrect or misleading" to be amended — and if the doctor declines, you may attach your own written statement of disagreement, which travels with the report. Section 6 requires the practitioner to keep a copy for at least six months. Section 7 is the limit on all of this: a doctor may withhold anything likely to cause "serious harm to the physical or mental health" of you or somebody else.

The practical value is that GP records are frequently wrong in small ways — a coded condition that was ruled out, a drinking estimate written down in a hurry, a referral that came to nothing. Those errors are cheap to correct at application and expensive to argue about at claim. Twenty-one days is a short window, so if you want to exercise the right, say so when you give consent rather than afterwards.

sections.heading: Genetic tests: one condition, one threshold, and a code that binds the insurer
sections.html:
Anyone who has had genetic testing, or is thinking about it, has a specific and often misunderstood protection. Under the Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance, agreed between the Association of British Insurers and the government, an insurer "will never require or pressure any applicant to undertake a predictive or diagnostic genetic test", and may ask about a predictive test result in one situation only: Huntington's disease, and then only on life cover above £500,000. The equivalent ceilings are £300,000 for critical illness and £30,000 a year for income protection. Below those figures the result of a predictive test is simply none of the insurer's business.

The government's three-year review of the Code, published 5 March 2026, gives the compliance picture for 2024: 2,700 predictive test results and 5,013 diagnostic results reported by insurers, five complaints about how genetic information was used, all resolved directly with the customers, and 93% of life policies written below the £500,000 threshold. Diagnostic tests are a different matter — where a test confirms or rules out a condition you already have symptoms of, the result is ordinary medical history and is treated as such.

The Code is a commitment rather than a statute, which is worth knowing, but it is monitored, published and reviewed by government, and a family history of an inherited condition need not keep anybody out of a mainstream policy.

sections.heading: Getting an answer wrong does not always mean getting nothing
sections.html:
The received wisdom is that a mistake on the form voids the policy. The reality set out in the LG2022 terms is more graduated, and more useful. Where information was given carelessly rather than deliberately, L&G may reprice or reduce the cover using a formula based on the premium that would have been charged had the truth been known — so a policy bought at half the correct premium pays out roughly half the claim rather than nothing. Deliberate or reckless misrepresentation is the serious case, and that is where a policy is cancelled outright.

The company's own warning on its decreasing cover page is blunt: "If you fail to mention something like a medical condition, for example, we may not pay out in the event of a claim." The way to avoid the argument entirely is to over-declare. Nothing is lost by mentioning an investigation that came to nothing; a great deal can be lost by leaving it out.

Disputes are rare in this product line. The Financial Ombudsman Service's annual complaints data, published 21 May 2026, records 884 new term assurance complaints at a 17% uphold rate, against 214,600 complaints and a 30% average across all financial products. Critical illness cover ran at 647 complaints and 12% upheld, income protection at 942 and 21%. Older whole-of-life plans fare worse — 414 non-reviewable cases at 26% and 434 reviewable at 38% — which says something about the products, not about term cover. Term assurance is one of the least-disputed things a UK consumer can buy.

sections.heading: What L&G actually paid, and to whom
sections.html:
The most recent full breakdown L&G publishes for its retail protection book covers 2023, and it is worth reading alongside the 2025 totals. That year the company accepted 97% of life insurance claims — 13,007 payouts totalling £519 million, an average of £39,916, at an average age at claim of 70. Cancer accounted for 32.6% of causes, heart-related conditions 21.7% and neurological conditions 5.9%.

Terminal illness cover, the benefit that pays before death, was accepted on 92% of claims: 1,149 payouts worth £139 million, averaging £121,621 at an average age of 56, and 92.9% of them for cancer. Critical Illness Cover ran at 93% accepted across 3,597 claims worth £255 million, averaging £70,978 at an average age of 48, two-thirds of them cancer claims.

The 2025 figures fill in the rest: £1.388 billion paid across more than 26,000 retail and group claims, of which retail protection was £992 million; terminal illness alone accounted for £161 million at an average payout above £125,000, and critical illness for over £291 million. In 2024 the company paid 14,067 life claims worth £583 million, and its oldest claimant that year was 101.

Notice the pattern in the acceptance rates. The gap between 97% on life claims and 92% on terminal illness is not administrative meanness — it is the difference between a fact and a prognosis. Terminal illness requires a hospital consultant and L&G's own Medical Officer to agree the illness is "expected to lead to death within 12 months", and it cannot be claimed at all if the policy has less than two years left to run.

sections.heading: Trusts, probate and the tax threshold that has not moved since 2009
sections.html:
A life policy paid into your estate is part of your estate. The inheritance tax nil-rate band has stood at £325,000 since 6 April 2009 and is now legislated to stay there until 5 April 2031, with the residence nil-rate band at £175,000 and a taper starting on estates above £2 million. The freeze to 2029-30 was announced at Autumn Budget 2024, and the government's own costing expects it to pull an extra 1,400 estates into charge in 2028-29 and 2,900 in 2029-30. A £300,000 policy landing on top of a house is exactly the kind of sum that tips an estate over.

Writing the policy in trust changes both the tax position and the timing. L&G's own guidance is that money from a policy in trust "will usually not form part of your estate for Inheritance Tax purposes", and that beneficiaries "could receive the payout within a couple of weeks of the death certificate being issued" rather than waiting for probate. There are four options — discretionary, flexible, survivor's discretionary and absolute — and no added cost for using them, whether you set the trust up at outset or later.

The trade-off is real and L&G states it: with some trusts "you may not be able to change your mind", and trustees take on legal responsibilities for how the money is distributed. An absolute trust in particular fixes the beneficiaries permanently. For most people with a partner and children the discretionary or flexible route keeps enough room to manoeuvre, but it is a decision worth taking with advice rather than through a web form.

sections.heading: The gaps in the paperwork, and what the complaints figures show
sections.html:
Three things are missing from the pre-sale documents that a careful buyer would want. The assumed mortgage interest rate behind decreasing cover, as above, is not published anywhere before the schedule arrives. Neither is the minimum or maximum sum assured on the main life product — the FAQs, the policy summary QGI14768 (dated 2026/01) and the product page all leave it out, so the only way to discover what £5 a month buys a 45-year-old is to complete a quote. And the £5 figure itself carries no footnote saying how many customers achieve it. The Advertising Standards Authority's published position on "from" pricing is that a significant proportion of customers should be able to obtain the advertised price, and it has indicated that under 10% is unlikely to count as significant. L&G's own average of £26.33 a month is the more informative number, and it is buried in a guide rather than shown beside the headline.

The Defaqto 5 Star badge on both the life and critical illness pages carries no year. Defaqto reissues its ratings annually, so an undated star rating tells a reader nothing about whether the product still holds it. The Moneyfacts award is handled better: L&G names it as Life Insurance Provider of the Year (Direct) at the 2026 Consumer Moneyfacts awards, its seventh consecutive year, which is a dated, checkable claim.

On complaints, L&G publishes its own regulatory return. For the six months to 30 June 2026, its insurance and pure protection business opened 3,312 complaints and closed 3,172, a rate of 0.76 per 1,000 policies in force, with 46.40% closed inside three days, 49.65% within eight weeks and 34.96% upheld. The main cause was general administration and customer service. That is a low rate per policy, but the direction is worth noting: in the previous six months the same business opened 2,895 complaints at 0.66 per 1,000. Volumes went up, though the uphold rate came down from 39.25%.

One smaller thing. The £100 Amazon gift card offered to new customers is paid six months after the policy starts and only if premiums are up to date. It is a perfectly ordinary incentive, but it rewards starting a policy rather than choosing the right sum assured, and a hundred pounds is less than four months of the average premium. Buy the cover you need and treat the voucher as change.

pros: Underwritten and paid by the insurer itself — Legal and General Assurance Society Limited, firm reference 117659, with no broker or intermediary in the chain
£527 million of life claims paid in 2025 across nearly 14,000 payouts, and a 97% life acceptance rate in the last year L&G published a full breakdown
Premiums guaranteed for the term, from £5 a month, with terminal illness cover and accidental death benefit up to £300,000 included at no extra cost
Published underwriting limits (Q41806, 10/25) show exactly when a GP report or medical is triggered, so applicants can see what they are in for
Four trust options at no added cost, with payouts reaching beneficiaries in around two weeks instead of waiting for probate
Complaints running at 0.76 per 1,000 policies in force, with 46.40% resolved inside three days, on the company's own published return
cons: The assumed mortgage interest rate that decides how fast decreasing cover falls is not published anywhere before purchase — it appears only on the policy schedule, and L&G's own terms warn the payout "may not be enough to repay your mortgage in full"
No minimum or maximum sum assured is published in the FAQs, the policy summary or the product page, so a shopper cannot find out what a given premium buys without completing a quote
The "from £5 a month" headline carries no footnote naming the proportion of customers who get it, while L&G's own average premium of £26.33 a month sits in a separate guide
The Defaqto 5 Star rating shown on both the life and critical illness pages carries no year, and Defaqto reissues its ratings annually
Cancel after the 30-day cooling-off period on a monthly plan and nothing is refunded; miss a payment and the policy is deemed cancelled 60 days after the due date, with no value in it at any stage

Terminal illness cover cannot be claimed if the policy has less than two years left to run, and requires L&G's own Medical Officer to agree the 12-month prognosis — its acceptance rate was 92% against 97% on death claims
Complaints volumes in the insurance and pure protection book rose from 2,895 to 3,312 in consecutive half-years, and from 0.66 to 0.76 per 1,000 policies
verdict: For straightforward term cover from a company that carries its own risk, L&G is about as solid as the UK market gets: 1836, firm reference 117659, £527 million of life claims paid in 2025 and a 97% acceptance rate on the last full breakdown published. The product is plain — level or decreasing, 18 to 77, 5 to 50 years, premiums fixed — and the underwriting is unusually transparent for the sector, with the evidence thresholds published down to the pound. Where it disappoints is disclosure before the quote: the decreasing-cover interest rate, the cover limits and any proportion behind the £5 headline are all withheld until you have applied. Take the time over the health questions, ask for the assumed interest rate inside the 30-day window if you buy decreasing cover, and put the policy in trust while you are at it.

faqs.q: Does Legal & General pay out on life insurance claims?
faqs.a: On the most recent full breakdown, covering 2023, L&G accepted 97% of life insurance claims — 13,007 payouts worth £519 million at an average of £39,916. In 2025 it paid nearly 14,000 life claims totalling £527 million, with an average valid claim of £37,788, and £992 million across all 20,621 retail protection claims. Terminal illness claims were accepted at 92% and critical illness at 93%.

faqs.q: Will I need a medical to get cover?
faqs.a: Most applicants will not. L&G's underwriting limits guide (Q41806, 10/25) triggers a GP report on life cover of £75,001 to £100,000 only for applicants aged 71 to 74, a medical examination from £100,001 to £150,000 for ages 66 to 70, and nurse screening from £200,001 to £250,000 for ages 61 to 65. A healthy 35-year-old buying £250,000 of cover is unlikely to see anybody. Over 80% of applications are processed straight through.

faqs.q: Can I see the report my GP sends to the insurer?
faqs.a: Yes. The Access to Medical Reports Act 1988 requires your consent before the insurer may even apply for a report, and gives you the right to read it first. Your doctor must not send it until you have seen it or 21 days have passed since the application without you making arrangements. You can ask for anything incorrect or misleading to be amended, and if the doctor refuses you may attach your own written statement. Say you want to see it at the point you give consent.

faqs.q: What happens if I get a health question wrong?
faqs.a: It depends on how the mistake happened. Careless errors are dealt with proportionately under the LG2022 terms: the cover or payout is adjusted to reflect the premium that should have been charged, so a policy underpriced by half pays roughly half. Deliberate or reckless misrepresentation is the serious case and can cancel the policy. Declaring more than you think necessary costs nothing at application and removes the argument at claim.

faqs.q: Do I have to tell L&G about a genetic test?
faqs.a: Only in one narrow case. Under the ABI and government Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance, insurers will never require a test and may ask about a predictive result only for Huntington's disease, and only on life cover above £500,000 — £300,000 for critical illness and £30,000 a year for income protection. The government's three-year review of 5 March 2026 records 93% of life policies falling below that threshold. Diagnostic tests, which confirm a condition you already have symptoms of, are ordinary medical history and must be disclosed.

faqs.q: Is decreasing cover cheaper than level cover?
faqs.a: Generally yes, because the sum assured falls over the term. It is designed to track a repayment mortgage, using an assumed interest rate that appears on your policy schedule. If your actual mortgage rate is higher than the assumed one, or you extend or increase the loan, L&G's terms state the payout may not clear the balance. Level cover keeps the same amount throughout and suits anyone protecting an income or a fixed liability rather than a shrinking debt.

title: LG UK Televisions
meta_title: LG UK TVs: 12 Months Warranty, 36 on Its Projectors
meta_description: LG gives its televisions 12 months parts and labour, while its monitors get 24 and its projectors 36. The 5-year OLED panel cover excludes the C series.

headline.label: TV warranty
headline.value: 12 months parts and labour — against 24 on a monitor and 36 on a projector

disclosure: we earn a commission if you buy through the link on this page. It costs you nothing. The warranty table, the panel-cover exclusions and the delivery conditions below are taken from LG’s own support pages, including where they count against the sale.
intro:
Everyone can find an LG TV price in thirty seconds, so this page does the part that is harder: the terms you only discover after something goes wrong. Buying direct from LG Electronics U.K. Ltd, company number 02143888, registered at Velocity 2, Brooklands Drive, Weybridge and incorporated on 1 July 1987, gets you the maker’s own warranty and its own delivery service, and both are worth reading first.

Here is the figure that surprised us. LG’s own warranty page gives a television 12 months parts and 12 months labour. The same page gives a monitor 24 months, a WiFi soundbar 24 months, a washing machine 24 months and a projector 36 months.

So the most expensive thing in LG’s living-room range carries the shortest standard cover of almost anything it sells. That is not unusual across the television industry, but it is the single most useful thing to know before you spend four figures on a panel.

sections.heading: The warranty table, in LG's own numbers
sections.html:
Straight from LG UK’s consumer warranty page, labour and parts, for domestic use:

ProductLabourParts
Televisions12 months12 months
Projectors36 months36 months
Monitors24 months24 months
Soundbars and speakers, WiFi models24 months24 months
Soundbars, “WiFi Ready” models12 months12 months
Washers, dryers, fridge freezers24 months24 months
Dishwashers, Stylers, microwaves24 months24 months
Home cinema systems, Blu-ray players, laptops, earbuds12 months12 months

Read the soundbar rows together, because they are a trap worth avoiding: a soundbar with working WiFi gets 24 months, but one described as “WiFi Ready” gets 12. Same shelf, same brand, half the cover. If you are adding a soundbar to a TV order, check which description applies before you choose.

Projectors at 36 months is the standout. If you are weighing a big TV against a projector for a dark room, the projector comes with three times the standard cover.

sections.heading: The 5-year OLED panel warranty, and who does not get it
sections.html:
LG does offer longer cover on OLED panels, and it is a genuine benefit: a five-year premium OLED panel warranty, with no registration required. Two qualifications decide whether it applies to you.

First, which models. LG lists it on selected G, M, W and Z series OLED TVs. The C series is not in that list — and the C is the model most people actually buy, because it is the one that sits at the sensible end of the price range. If five-year panel cover is what you are buying, you have to buy up into the G series or above.

Second, it covers the panel and not the repair. LG’s wording is explicit: “The consumer will be charged for labour after the 12 month product warranty has expired”. So in year three, LG supplies the panel and you pay an engineer to fit it to a wall-mounted 65-inch television. That is not a trivial bill, and it is not covered.

Worth knowing alongside it: LG also publishes 10 years of parts cover on specific washer and dryer components and on the fridge freezer linear compressor, on the same labour-charged basis. The pattern across the whole range is long parts cover and short labour cover.

And one clause that voids everything, so protect against it on day one: if the serial number is “defaced, missing or illegible”, the LG UK warranty is void. Photograph the serial-number sticker on the back of the set before you mount it, along with the invoice — the warranty is valid only with the original invoice, receipt or LG’s own confirmation of the period.

sections.heading: What the warranty does not pay for
sections.html:
LG “guarantees free repair service to its products within the warranty period” through authorised service centres, and parts or units may be “new or remanufactured service exchanges” — so a replacement is not necessarily brand new.

Excluded, in LG’s own list:

  • Routine check-ups, maintenance and normal wear and tear.
  • Transport, removal and installation costs. On a large television that is the expensive part.
  • Misuse, “including incorrect installation” — which puts the risk of a DIY wall mount on you.
  • Damage from lightning, water, fire, acts of God, war, public disturbances, incorrect mains voltage or poor ventilation.

Two practical consequences. Poor ventilation being named means a set recessed into a tight cabinet or media wall is a risk to your cover, so leave the clearance the manual asks for. And because installation is excluded both ways — not covered by the warranty, and bad installation voids it — a professional wall mount with a receipt is worth more than the saving on doing it yourself.

Back up anything stored on the set before a repair: LG states it is not responsible for data loss during one.

There is a support life to factor in too. The 65-inch C-series page we read states that its “security update is supported until 31/12/2029”. That is a smart-TV software commitment, not a warranty, but on a television you expect to keep for a decade it tells you when the apps and the browser stop being maintained. Check that date on the model you are buying.

sections.heading: Delivery, and the word "members"
sections.html:
LG advertises free delivery on all LG.com orders, and then qualifies it in the footnotes. The three qualifications matter:

  • Free delivery is for members only — you have to be signed up.
  • It does not cover postcode-related fees. Delivery charges “vary by postcode and may include additional charges for Highland or remote areas”, with the final cost confirmed at the checkout.
  • Installation is not included unless stated when you order.

For the Scottish Islands and remote areas, LG says delivery is handled by a third-party carrier who contacts you to arrange a date. So if you are outside mainland Britain, do not treat “free delivery” as a price — get to the basket and read the real figure before you commit.

The ordering page does offer a delivery date and an optional time slot, plus a paid Installation Plus service, which for a 65-inch set delivered to a flat is worth pricing rather than dismissing.

On returns, one clause to watch if you buy a bundle: “In the event of a return, all products purchased in the bundle must be returned together”, and “A partial refund is not possible under any circumstances”. So a TV-and-soundbar deal is one object for returns purposes — you cannot keep the television and send back the soundbar.

sections.heading: Discounts and finance, with the numbers
sections.html:
The direct-from-LG discounts are structured around membership rather than sales:

  • Welcome voucher: 5% off your first purchase when you join, valid 90 days from sign-up, online only, and not combinable with other offers.
  • Membership discount: a further 2% off, for as long as you keep the membership.
  • Rotating promotions we saw included up to 15% off selected TVs, 10% off selected OLED TVs, up to 15% cashback on selected sets, and up to 50% off selected soundbars bought with an eligible TV.
  • A Trade-Up offer, one per order, which can be combined with the welcome voucher but not with other offers or an LG Flex subscription.

Note the combination rules, because they are where the stacking falls apart: the welcome voucher is not combinable with other offers, and the Trade-Up only pairs with the voucher. In practice you pick one route, not all of them.

On finance, the published terms are:

  • PayPal Credit: 0% interest for 4 months over £99, 12 months over £1,000, and up to 30 months over £2,500, subject to approval. The representative example is 23.9% APR variable.
  • Klarna Pay in 3 and Pay in 30, and PayPal Pay in 3.
  • Finance is limited to permanent UK residents aged 18 or over.

Thirty months at 0% on a £2,500 television is a real offer and the cheapest way to spread that cost — provided you clear it inside the term, because the rate behind it is 23.9% variable. Set the standing order to finish a month early.

sections.heading: One thing we could not do, and what we would do instead
sections.html:
We will be straight with you: we could not read LG’s prices. Its UK television pages render the price after the page loads, so on the 65-inch C-series page we read the model code OLED65C56LB, the EAN, the size options of 48, 55, 65 and 77 inches and the security-update date — but no figure we could quote honestly. We are not going to publish a price we did not see.

What that means for you in practice. Buying direct from LG is rarely the cheapest way to get an LG television, and the brand’s own site is not where you discover that. What buying direct does get you is the manufacturer’s warranty handled by the manufacturer, a chosen delivery date, an installation option, and the 0% finance above.

So the sensible sequence is: pick the exact model code from LG’s own pages, where the specification and the support date are reliable; check the warranty row above for that product type; then price that model code wherever you like, including here. If the gap to a retailer is small, buying direct is the easier life. If it is £150, it is not.

Five years' OLED panel cover on selected G, M, W and Z sets, with no registration required

cons: Televisions get only 12 months' parts and labour — the shortest cover on almost anything LG sells
