verdict: Buy the television from LG direct if you want the maker handling its own warranty, a delivery date you choose, an installation option and up to 30 months at 0% on a set over £2,500. Go in knowing two things. The standard television warranty is 12 months parts and labour, which is shorter than the 24 LG gives a monitor and the 36 it gives a projector — so the cover on the most expensive thing in the range is the thinnest. And the headline five-year OLED panel warranty does not cover the C series, and pays for the panel but not the engineer who fits it. Photograph the serial-number sticker and the invoice before the set goes on the wall, leave the ventilation gap the manual asks for, have it installed professionally with a receipt, and check the security-update date on the model page if you plan to keep it for a decade. Then price that exact model code elsewhere before you buy — direct from the brand is the easiest route, not usually the cheapest.

faqs.q: How long is the warranty on an LG television?
faqs.a: Twelve months parts and twelve months labour, according to LG UK’s own consumer warranty page. For comparison, the same page gives monitors 24 months, WiFi soundbars 24 months, washing machines 24 months and projectors 36 months. A television carries the shortest standard cover of almost anything LG sells.

faqs.q: Does my OLED get the five-year panel warranty?
faqs.a: Only if it is one of the selected G, M, W or Z series sets. The C series is not in that list, and it is the model most buyers choose. No registration is needed where it applies, but read the limit: it covers the panel, and LG states that “the consumer will be charged for labour after the 12 month product warranty has expired”. In year three LG supplies the panel and you pay to have it fitted.

faqs.q: What can void the warranty?
faqs.a: A serial number that is “defaced, missing or illegible” voids it outright, so photograph the sticker on the back before the set is mounted. Claims also need the original invoice, receipt or LG’s confirmation of the period. Misuse “including incorrect installation” is excluded, as is damage from poor ventilation — which matters if you are recessing the TV into a media wall or a tight cabinet.

faqs.q: Is delivery really free?
faqs.a: For members, on mainland orders, and not including postcode fees. LG says charges “vary by postcode and may include additional charges for Highland or remote areas”, confirmed at the checkout, and that Scottish Islands and remote deliveries are handled by a third-party carrier who contacts you to arrange a date. Installation is separate unless you add it when ordering.

faqs.q: Can I return just the soundbar from a TV bundle?
faqs.a: No. The bundle terms state that “in the event of a return, all products purchased in the bundle must be returned together” and that “a partial refund is not possible under any circumstances”. If you are unsure about the soundbar, buy it separately rather than as part of a bundle.

faqs.q: What finance is available?
faqs.a: PayPal Credit at 0% for four months on orders over £99, twelve months over £1,000 and up to thirty months over £2,500, all subject to approval, with a representative 23.9% APR variable behind them. Klarna Pay in 3 and Pay in 30 and PayPal Pay in 3 are also offered. Finance is limited to permanent UK residents aged 18 or over, and the 0% only stays free if you clear the balance inside the term.

title: LoungeKey Airport Lounge
meta_title: LoungeKey: What One Airport Lounge Visit Really Costs
meta_description: A LoungeKey visit costs £18.50 to £24 per person and your bank sets the price, against £38 to £48 at the desk. Who runs it and what the contract says.

headline.label: Cost of one lounge visit
headline.value: £18.50–£24 per person per visit — set by your card issuer, guests charged the same

intro:
One airport lounge visit through LoungeKey costs £24 per person if your card is a Monzo Premium or Monzo Max account, or £18.50 per person on a Barclaycard Avios Plus. Walk up to the same kind of desk without a card behind you and Which? found UK lounges charging £38 to £43 in advance and up to £48 on the door in its most recent round of visits. On a family of four, that gap is most of the price of the flight seats.

LoungeKey is run by Priority Pass Limited, a London company that has been trading under one name or another since 3 July 1992 and now sits inside the Collinson group at 3 More London Riverside. Collinson is family-owned, registered in England and Wales as company 11141096, employs more than 2,500 people across 19 locations and runs five businesses, of which airport experiences is the oldest. Its better-known sister brand, Priority Pass, reaches 1,900-plus lounges and airport experiences in over 600 cities and 143 countries. LoungeKey is the same machinery sold a different way.

You cannot buy LoungeKey. There is no membership page, no annual fee and no checkout — it only reaches you attached to a payment card, and the bank that issued that card, not LoungeKey, decides what a visit costs you, how many visits are free and whether guests are included. If you are shopping for a lounge pass you can buy outright for one trip, this is not that product, and the card comparison is where the decision actually gets made.

sections.heading: What a visit costs, and who sets the number
sections.html:
LoungeKey publishes no price. Its Conditions of Use say only that lounge and merchant visits are “subject to a per-person, per-visit, charge”, and Mastercard's own Airport Experiences FAQ, which runs on the same programme, says you will be charged “the prevailing lounge visit fee” without ever printing one. The figure lives in your card issuer's terms, so that is where to look.

Two UK issuers publish theirs plainly. Monzo says holders of Monzo Premium and Monzo Max, and their guests, get into around 1,100 lounges worldwide “for a flat fee of £24 per person, per visit”, with pre-booking adding at least £6 on top where a lounge offers it. Barclaycard puts the Avios Plus rate at £18.50 per lounge pass per person across more than 1,000 lounges, on a card costing £20 a month. For comparison, HSBC prices its Premier credit card's lounge benefit — the sister Priority Pass programme rather than LoungeKey — at £24 a visit for the cardholder and £24 per person for guests, while the Premier World Elite Mastercard gives the cardholder unlimited access and still charges £24 a head for anyone they bring.

Some cards include a number of free visits before the fee starts. Those are the issuer's, not LoungeKey's: the Mastercard FAQ confirms complimentary visits run from 1 January to 31 December, are set by the card issuer, and that “unused visits are not transferable and cannot be carried over to the following year”. Whatever you owe is debited later to the card on file rather than taken at the lounge desk, so no payment is made at the point of entry and nothing is signed except the record of how many people walked in.

sections.heading: One brand, two registered companies and a parent
sections.html:
The contract names its counterparty precisely: “LoungeKey means Priority Pass Limited of 3 More London Riverside, London, SE1 2AQ, Company No. 02728518.” That company is active at Companies House, was incorporated on 3 July 1992 under the name Assistsolve Limited and took its present name 24 days later, files as an activities-of-membership-organisations business and last made up accounts to 30 April 2025.

A second active company, Lounge Key Limited, number 08792537, was incorporated on 27 November 2013 at the same address with the same filing pattern, and it is the one the Conditions of Use send written data-protection requests to. The portal footer, meanwhile, reads “Copyright © 2025 LoungeKey Ltd”. The privacy notice on loungekey.com identifies the data controller as nothing more specific than “LoungeKey … a company registered in England and Wales, at 3 More London Riverside”, giving an email address but no company number, which leaves a reader who wants to know which legal entity holds their travel data with two candidates and no way to tell from the page itself.

Behind both sits Collinson, which also owns Priority Pass and Airport Dimensions, the business that builds and runs lounges rather than selling access to them. Which entity actually processes your payment depends on where you fly: the Conditions of Use name seven merchants of record by region, with Priority Pass Limited covering Europe, the Middle East and Africa, Priority Pass, Inc. covering the Americas outside Peru, and separate companies for Asia Pacific, mainland China, India, Peru and Taiwan.

sections.heading: Card, boarding pass, ID — and a seat that might not exist
sections.html:
Entry is conditional on three things together: a valid means of access, a valid boarding pass, and any further identification the lounge asks for, which can include a passport, national identity card or driving licence. A photograph of your card will not do, and neither will reading out the card number — the contract rules both out by name. You tell the desk you are entering on LoungeKey, staff read the card or digital code electronically, and they enter the number of guests, who have to register and walk in at the same time as you.

Two limits catch people out. Lounges inside a Schengen-designated pier are only reachable if you are travelling between Schengen countries, which quietly removes a slice of the European network from a UK departure. And your issuer may cap how often you can use the benefit in a period or at the same airport; where it does, the contract makes the issuer responsible for telling you, and expressly disclaims LoungeKey's liability if the issuer does not.

Nothing about the visit is guaranteed. The lounges belong to third parties, access is “subject to capacity restrictions”, and LoungeKey accepts that it has no control over whether you are admitted, how many people are let in, what is on offer, the opening hours or how long you are allowed to stay. It undertakes reasonable endeavours and no more. That is a normal arrangement for a distributor, and it is the reason a busy Friday evening at a single-lounge airport can end with a card that works and a door that does not open.

sections.heading: What Which? found inside 20 UK lounges
sections.html:
The trade has no ratings agency, but Which? runs the nearest thing to one. Its researchers visited 20 UK airport lounges anonymously between February and September 2024, scored each between one and five stars on facilities, quiet and family space, runway views and the food and drink, and published the results on 26 October 2024. Only five of the 20 managed three stars or better. Prices quoted alongside the scores were for an 8am Saturday entry booked through whichever of the airport's or the lounge's own site was cheaper.

Value was the recurring complaint. Lounges averaging £29 to pre-book in 2019 were reaching £40, a rise of 37 per cent, while made-to-order food and spa treatments were quietly withdrawn. The two one-star scores both went to Heathrow: Plaza Premium Terminal 5, at up to £47.50 on the door or £43 in advance, where the coffee machine was broken, and the No1 Lounge at Terminal 3. Plaza Premium Terminal 2 charged £48 at the door for two stars. At the other end, Gatwick My Lounge South and Edinburgh Plaza Premium both scored four, at £38 and with a children's area that keeps the noise away from the bar. Showers, where they exist, cost an extra £20 to £28 on top of entry.

Read against the card rates, that survey is the strongest argument for using a card benefit rather than paying at the desk: the £24 or £18.50 buys the identical room that somebody beside you paid £48 for. It is also a warning that the room may not be worth either figure, and the card fee buys no influence over which lounge you end up in.

sections.heading: The clauses that decide what happens when it goes wrong
sections.html:
Price changes reach you indirectly. LoungeKey may amend lounge or merchant charges “at any time on providing 30 days' notice”, but where the benefit came through a card, the notice goes to the card provider, who “is responsible for advising Customer”. Refusing a change means giving 30 days' written notice to the bank, not to LoungeKey. A separate clause reserves the right to increase fees of any kind on 30 days' notice.

Membership is held on a short lead. LoungeKey “reserves the right at any time in its sole discretion and without notice to revoke Programme membership or terminate Programme”, and may cancel without refund any membership it finds in breach. If your card is cancelled or moved to a product outside the programme and charges are left outstanding, the contract says it may pursue legal action to recover them — and any lounge entered on an invalid card, guests included, is charged to you.

Complaints have a clock on them. Anything arising from a lounge or merchant visit must be raised within six months, and it goes to LoungeKey rather than the venue that actually turned you away, on +44 (0) 208 865 0767 or by post to PO Box 815, Haywards Heath RH16 9LR. Cancellation, refunds and anything about the benefit itself go to the card provider instead. The Conditions of Use took effect on 28 June 2023, can be changed by being posted on the site, and are governed by English law with the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the English courts.

pros: A visit costs £18.50 to £24 per person against £38 to £48 paid at a UK lounge desk, for the same room
No membership fee of its own — the cost sits in the card, and the lounge rate is the only extra
Guests pay the same per-person rate as the cardholder rather than a penalty rate
Around 1,100 lounges worldwide, with the sister Priority Pass network reaching 1,900-plus in 143 countries
Nothing is paid at the desk: the charge goes to the card on file, and entry can be card-free with the digital membership card
The counterparty is named and traceable — Priority Pass Limited, company 02728518, trading since 1992 inside a 2,500-person group
cons: LoungeKey publishes no price anywhere: the contract says only “a per-person, per-visit, charge” and the FAQ only “the prevailing lounge visit fee”, so the cost has to be found in your bank's terms
You cannot buy it — access exists only as a card benefit, and the fee, the free-visit allowance and the guest rules are all the issuer's to change
Notice of a price rise is served on your bank, not on you, and it is then the bank's job to pass it on
Membership can be revoked “at any time in its sole discretion and without notice”, and a membership found in breach is cancelled without refund
Access is never guaranteed: lounges are third parties, entry is subject to capacity, and LoungeKey disclaims control over admission, hours and how long you stay
Complaints must be made within six months and go to LoungeKey, while cancellation goes to your card provider — three parties, none of them the lounge
One brand covers two registered companies at one address, and the privacy notice names neither company number
verdict: As a way of getting into an airport lounge, LoungeKey is genuinely cheap: £24 a head on a Monzo Premium or Max account and £18.50 on Barclaycard Avios Plus, against the £38 to £48 Which? recorded at UK desks in 2024. As a product to choose, it barely exists, because you cannot buy it and every number that matters is set by whichever bank put it on your card. Compare the cards, not the programme — and check the lounge itself, because only five of the 20 Which? visited scored three stars out of five.

faqs.q: How much does a LoungeKey visit cost?
faqs.a: It depends on the card. Monzo charges £24 per person per visit on Monzo Premium and Monzo Max, and Barclaycard charges £18.50 per person on Avios Plus. LoungeKey itself never publishes a figure — its Conditions of Use refer only to “a per-person, per-visit, charge” — so the number in your card's terms is the one that applies to you.

faqs.q: Can I buy LoungeKey membership directly?
faqs.a: No. LoungeKey is distributed only through card issuers and other organisations; there is no consumer checkout. If you want a pass you can buy outright, the sister brand Priority Pass sells annual membership at US$99, US$329 and US$469 depending on tier, covering 1,900-plus lounges and airport experiences in more than 600 cities.

faqs.q: Do guests pay the same as the cardholder?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Monzo applies the same £24 flat fee to guests, and HSBC charges £24 per guest even on its unlimited-access Premier World Elite card. Guests have to register and walk into the lounge at the same time as you, and the desk records how many people entered on your card.

faqs.q: What do I need to show at the lounge?
faqs.a: Three things: a valid means of access — an eligible payment card, digital membership card or code — a valid boarding pass, and any further identification the lounge asks for, which may be a passport, national identity card or driving licence. A photograph of the card or the card number read aloud will not be accepted.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if a lounge turns me away?
faqs.a: LoungeKey, not the lounge, and within six months of the visit — by phone on +44 (0) 208 865 0767 or by post to PO Box 815, Haywards Heath RH16 9LR. Anything about the benefit itself, including cancelling it, goes to your card provider instead. The Conditions of Use are governed by English law.

faqs.q: Is LoungeKey the same as Priority Pass?
faqs.a: They are separate brands run by the same company. The LoungeKey contract defines the programme as being provided by Priority Pass Limited, company 02728518, and both sit inside the Collinson group at 3 More London Riverside. Priority Pass is sold direct to consumers as an annual membership; LoungeKey is sold to banks as a benefit to attach to a card.

title: Loungepass.com Airport Lounge
meta_title: Lounge Pass Review: Every UK Price Is in US Dollars
meta_description: Lounge Pass sells single airport lounge visits from Priority Pass itself, with no membership. The catch for UK buyers: every price is quoted in US dollars.

headline.label: UK lounge prices
headline.value: US$20 to US$101 a visit — quoted in dollars, with no sterling option

disclosure: we earn a commission if you book a lounge through the link on this page. It costs you nothing and we have not been paid to say anything in particular. The criticisms below are ours and they stay in.
intro:
Lounge Pass does something useful that most lounge schemes do not: it sells you one visit, with no membership, no annual fee and no card to carry. Prices for UK lounges run from about US$20 at the smallest regional airports to US$101 for a six-hour stay at Heathrow Terminal 4.

It also has a pedigree worth knowing about. Every page on the site carries the line “A Division of Priority Pass Limited”, and the company behind it is Priority Pass Limited, registered number 02728518, part of the Collinson group. This is not a reseller sitting between you and the lounge operator — it is the pay-per-visit arm of the biggest lounge network there is.

Now the thing a UK buyer needs before clicking: the site quotes every price in US dollars. We searched the booking results for a pound sign and found none, and there is no currency selector. You will pay in dollars at whatever rate and non-sterling fee your card applies that day.

sections.heading: What UK lounges actually cost
sections.html:
These are the published adult and child prices we saw on 8 October 2026 for a country setting of United Kingdom, in the currency the site displayed them — US dollars.

LoungeAirportAdultChild
No1 LoungeHeathrow T3US$71US$35
Club AspireHeathrow T5US$71US$35
Plaza PremiumHeathrow T4US$66US$66
Plaza Premium, 3–6 hour stayHeathrow T4US$101US$101
ClubroomsGatwick NorthUS$73—
Club AspireGatwick SouthUS$56US$35
Escape LoungesManchester T2US$67US$48
No1 LoungeBirminghamUS$65US$35
Northern Lights ExecutiveAberdeen DyceUS$39US$22
Rockliffe LoungeTeessideUS$37US$17
Amelia Earhart LoungeCity of DerryUS$20—

Infants aged 0 to 1 go free, children are 2 to 11 inclusive, and a single booking takes a maximum of five people. Anything larger is a group booking and needs seven days’ notice by email.

Notice the shape of that table. The regional lounges are the bargains — Derry at US$20 and Teesside at US$37 are genuinely cheap for three hours indoors with a seat and a cup of tea. The London prices are not, and at Heathrow T4 the child pays the adult fare.

sections.heading: Three hours, and the clock is not generous
sections.html:
The standard entitlement is stated plainly in the terms: “A Means of Access provides for a maximum three hour stay in the Lounge unless otherwise indicated”. Several UK lounges spell it out on their own page as “Maximum 3 hour stay”.

There is a second clock most people miss. Entry “shall be at the discretion of the Lounge but in no event after three hours of the time shown” on your pass. So if your flight slips by four hours, the pass you bought for the earlier slot may simply not be honoured, and it is not refundable — the terms say Lounge Pass “will not refund Customers for any unused Means of Access for whatever reason however occurred”.

Heathrow T4 is the one UK lounge in the list that sells a longer stay: US$101 buys six hours instead of three. If you have a long connection, that is the option to look for.

One more line worth reading before you rely on it: a pass “entitles Customers to access the Lounge however seating in the Lounge is unreserved and cannot be guaranteed”, and Lounge Pass “has no control over the Lounge’s decision of whether to admit any Customer, the number of people allowed in at any time”. You are buying a ticket to try, not a reserved seat.

sections.heading: Book a day ahead: there is no walking up
sections.html:
This is the single most practical fact on the page. Lounge Pass requires that “all bookings must be made at least 24 hours in advance of your departure date”, and you need the confirmation to get in — “you will not be able to enter the lounge without it”.

So Lounge Pass is no use at all once you are at the airport staring at a four-hour delay. It is a planning tool, bought the day before. If you want to decide at the gate, you need the lounge’s own on-the-door price instead.

Cancellation runs on the same 24-hour hinge, and it must be in writing: “Cancellations must be advised in writing by letter, fax or by email to Lounge Pass within working hours at least 24 hours prior to the visit date and time at the lounge.” Inside that window, “no refund will be given”.

And here is a gap we could not close. Even when you cancel properly, the refund is the cost “less any cancellation charge advised at the time of booking”. That charge is never published. Not on the cancellation page, not in the terms. You find out what it is at the point of buying.

sections.heading: What you get once you are through the door
sections.html:
Food and drink vary by lounge, and Lounge Pass is careful not to promise: “generally lounges provide complimentary refreshments however this is not always the case. Where payment is required for refreshments or services you will be asked to pay directly at the lounge.”

Two concrete examples from the lounge pages themselves. No1 at Heathrow T3 offers a “Self-service buffet available” but notes “Champagne is subject to payment and payable directly to the lounge”. Aberdeen states “Premium alcoholic drinks are subject to additional payment by credit card only”. Read the individual lounge page before you assume the bar is open.

There is a dress code, and it is unusually specific. Lounges “do not allow certain items of clothing such as (but not limited to); sportswear, vest tops for men, football/rugby team shirts, sports tracksuits, clothing with offensive slogans or motifs, baseball caps, fancy dress, hair rollers or having hair rollers on show”. If you are travelling to a match in your shirt, change first.

Children’s rules are set by each lounge rather than centrally. At Gatwick South, “All children must be accompanied by an adult”; at Heathrow T3, “Children under 12 years may be restricted to use family areas and be supervised by an adult”. Alcohol is 18 and over everywhere.

sections.heading: The numbers on the site do not agree with each other
sections.html:
We check claims like these because they tell you how carefully a site is maintained, and this one has drifted.

The About page says Lounge Pass covers “over 500 airport VIP lounges worldwide – at over 300 airports across more than 100 countries”. The FAQ on the same site says “over 800 airport VIP lounges worldwide” at “over 400 airports”, and adds “48 UK airports”. Both cannot be right.

We tested the UK figure against the site’s own booking engine. A United Kingdom search returned 52 lounge listings across 24 UK airports — half the claimed number of airports. Twenty-four is still a good spread, and it includes places like Derry and Teesside that most schemes ignore. But 48 is not what the engine sells.

The “from £13.50” you may have seen on a search result is a third oddity. It appears only in the homepage’s meta description — the snippet Google shows — and nowhere on the site itself, where the equivalent claim is “from US$14.00”. The cheapest UK adult price we could actually find in the engine was US$20.

Even the company’s own PO Box postcode differs between pages: RH16 9LS on the contact page, RH16 9LR twice in the Conditions of Use. And the terms themselves are dated “Last updated 9 June 2022”, with an effective date of 1 May 2018.

sections.heading: Who you are buying from, and what protection you have
sections.html:
The trading entity is Priority Pass Limited, company number 02728518, VAT number GB 173 5401 21, registered at 3 More London Riverside, London SE1 2AQ. Companies House shows it incorporated on 3 July 1992 and active, with Priority Travel Group (Holdings) Limited holding 75% or more of the shares.

Lounge Pass itself “was founded in 2003” and describes itself as part of “Collinson Group which employs over 1,500 staff in 28 locations around the world”, alongside Priority Pass, Airport Lounge Development and the “The Club At” lounges. A thirty-four-year-old company filing accounts at Companies House is about as solid as this category gets.

On protection, be clear about what you are not getting. There is no ATOL and no ABTA, and neither is claimed — a lounge pass is not travel, so no bonding applies. If the company failed, your £50-odd lounge booking would be an unsecured claim. For a sum that size, paying by card is the protection that matters.

Complaints have a deadline: they must be “made within six months of the Lounge visit”, and the named alternative dispute resolution body is ADR Group of Rayleigh, Essex. Having a named ADR scheme at all is a point in its favour.

Contact details are published, which is more than some competitors manage: +44 (0)20 8865 3280, info@loungepass.com, and hours of 08:00–20:00 Monday to Friday and 09:00–17:00 Saturday.

pros: Pay for one visit with no membership, no annual fee and no card to carry
It is Priority Pass's own pay-per-visit arm, not a reseller standing between you and the lounge
Regional lounges are genuinely cheap — US$20 at City of Derry, US$37 at Teesside, US$39 at Aberdeen
Infants aged 0 to 1 go free and children pay roughly half at most UK lounges
Heathrow T4 sells a six-hour stay, which suits a long connection
Twenty-four UK airports are bookable, including small ones most schemes skip
A named ADR scheme and a six-month complaints window are published
A real phone number, email and published opening hours
Priority Pass Limited has filed at Companies House since 1992
Each lounge has its own page listing facilities, dress code and child rules before you buy
cons: Every price is in US dollars, so a UK buyer pays an exchange rate and probably a non-sterling card fee
No sterling option and no currency selector anywhere on the site
The “from £13.50” figure appears only in the Google snippet; the site's own lowest claim is US$14 and the cheapest UK lounge we found was US$20
Bookings must be made 24 hours ahead, so it is useless for a delay you discover at the airport
The cancellation charge is never published — you learn it at the checkout
Nothing is refunded for an unused pass, whatever the reason
Entry can be refused after three hours past the time on the pass, with no refund
A seat is explicitly not guaranteed, and admission is the lounge's decision, not Lounge Pass's
The FAQ claims 48 UK airports; the booking engine returned 24
The site contradicts itself on lounge numbers: 500 lounges at 300 airports on one page, 800 at 400 on another
The PO Box postcode differs between two pages on the same site
The terms have not been updated since June 2022
No ATOL or ABTA bonding, so your money is unprotected if the company fails
verdict: Lounge Pass is the right shape of product: one visit, one price, no membership, and it comes from Priority Pass itself rather than a middleman. At US$20 in Derry or US$37 at Teesside it is cheap enough to buy on a whim, and the six-hour option at Heathrow T4 for US$101 is the best thing here for a long connection. Two things should shape how you use it. First, it is priced in dollars with no sterling alternative, so compare the real cost including your card's non-sterling fee rather than the headline. Second, the 24-hour booking rule means this is something you buy the day before, not when a delay appears on the board — and once bought it is effectively non-refundable, with a cancellation charge the site never states. Read the individual lounge page for the dress code, the child rules and whether the drinks are actually included, then book a day ahead with a card that does not punish you for spending dollars.

faqs.q: Can I buy a Lounge Pass at the airport?
faqs.a: No. Its own rule is that “all bookings must be made at least 24 hours in advance of your departure date”, and you need the booking confirmation to get in. If you are already at the airport, you need the lounge’s own on-the-door price instead.

faqs.q: Why are the prices in dollars?
faqs.a: That is how the site displays them, even with the country set to the United Kingdom. We looked for a sterling price and a currency selector and found neither. So a UK buyer pays a US dollar amount converted by their card issuer, usually with a non-sterling transaction fee on top. Factor that in before comparing with a lounge’s own sterling price.

faqs.q: How long can I stay?
faqs.a: Three hours, unless the lounge page says otherwise. Plaza Premium at Heathrow T4 is the UK exception, selling a six-hour stay for US$101 against US$66 for three. There is also a cut-off on arrival: entry is at the lounge’s discretion and “in no event after three hours of the time shown” on the pass.

faqs.q: Can I get my money back if my flight is cancelled?
faqs.a: Almost certainly not. Cancellations must be made in writing at least 24 hours before the lounge visit, and inside that window “no refund will be given”. The terms also state that unused passes are not refunded “for whatever reason however occurred”. Even a valid cancellation is refunded less a charge that the site does not publish.

faqs.q: Is my seat guaranteed?
faqs.a: No. The terms say seating “is unreserved and cannot be guaranteed”, and that Lounge Pass has no control over the lounge’s decision on whether to admit anyone or how many people it lets in. In practice refusals are rare, but you are buying access rather than a reservation.

faqs.q: Who owns Lounge Pass?
faqs.a: Priority Pass Limited, company number 02728518, registered at 3 More London Riverside, London SE1 2AQ and incorporated in July 1992. Every page carries the line “A Division of Priority Pass Limited”, and the site describes itself as part of the Collinson group alongside Priority Pass and the The Club At lounges. The Lounge Pass brand itself dates from 2003.

title: Luxury Escapes – Exclusive Hotel Deals
meta_title: Luxury Escapes: Real Prices, but No ATOL Number Shown
meta_description: Luxury Escapes shows member and non-member prices openly, from £219 for two nights. It says it is ATOL protected but publishes no ATOL number we could find.

headline.label: Member saving, as published
headline.value: £30 to £70 a stay — for example £349 against £419 in Hong Kong

disclosure: we earn a commission if you book through the link on this page. It costs you nothing. The things we could not verify — the ATOL number, the contracting company, the refund terms — are reported as gaps rather than glossed over.
intro:
Luxury Escapes does the most useful thing a deal site can do: it shows you both prices. Every offer carries a member price and a non-member price side by side, so the value of joining is a number rather than a promise. On the day we looked, two nights at The Hoxton Edinburgh was £219 for members against £249, and three nights at the Harbour Grand Hong Kong was £349 against £419.

The stock is real luxury rather than rebadged mid-market: COMO Point Yamu in Phuket, L’Hôtel du Collectionneur in Paris, Mondrian Singapore Duxton. Five nights in a suite at The Little Shore Khao Lak was £849.

What we could not do is verify the paperwork, and on a site selling flight-inclusive holidays that matters. The pages say “ATOL protection provided for eligible flights and flight inclusive holidays” and show an ATOL badge — but we found no ATOL number and no named selling company anywhere we could read. Details below, including what to ask for before you pay.

sections.heading: The prices, exactly as published
sections.html:
These are live offers we read on 8 October 2026. Member price first, non-member in the second column:

HotelStayMemberNon-member
The Hoxton Edinburgh2 nights£219£249
Torel Avantgarde, Porto2 nights£219£249
Ellen Kensington, London2 nights£249£269
EQ Kuala Lumpur2 nights£249£289
Harbour Grand Hong Kong3 nights£349£419
Mondrian Singapore Duxton2 nights£359£419
L’Hôtel du Collectionneur, Paris2 nights£529£599
COMO Point Yamu, Phuket5 nights£849£889
The Little Shore Khao Lak, suite5 nights£849£889

The member gap runs from £20 to £70 across those nine. Notice how it is shaped: the two biggest gaps, £70 on Hong Kong and £70 on Paris, are on mid-priced city breaks, while the £849 long-haul stays save only £40. The membership is worth most on the cheaper bookings, which is the opposite of what you might assume.

One thing we could not establish: what the LuxPlus+ membership costs. The site invites you to “join our VIP Travel Club” and links to its terms, but no price appeared on any page we could read. Work out the sum yourself before joining — if the fee is more than the gap on the one trip you are booking, it only pays if you book again.

Prices are listed as “from” figures, and at least one offer carried an “ends in 3 days” countdown. Treat those as the usual deal-site urgency: the same hotel will have another offer.

sections.heading: The ATOL question, and what to ask before you pay
sections.html:
Here is the part we want you to read properly, because it is about your money rather than your room.

The site states: “ATOL protection provided for eligible flights and flight inclusive holidays”, and an “ATOL protected” badge appears near the top of the page. That is the right claim for a business selling flight-inclusive holidays to UK customers.

What we could not find, on the homepage, the booking policies page or the FAQ pages we read, is the ATOL number itself. An ATOL holder has a licence number, and the scheme works by you receiving an ATOL Certificate when you book, naming the licence holder and showing exactly what is protected. Without the number you cannot check the licence on the Civil Aviation Authority’s own register before you hand over money.

We are not suggesting the claim is untrue — we are telling you we could not verify it from the published pages, and that the verification is normally one click away. So:

  • Ask for the ATOL number before you pay for anything flight-inclusive. The 24-hour phone line is 0808 175 4987, and this is exactly what it is for.
  • Check that number on the CAA’s ATOL register yourself. It takes a minute and it is free.
  • Make sure the ATOL Certificate arrives with your confirmation, and read which parts of the trip it covers. A hotel-only booking is not ATOL protected, and never was — the protection attaches to the flight.
  • Pay by credit card. On a four-figure holiday that is the cheapest insurance you will ever buy.

We also found no ABTA membership claimed, and no named dispute resolution scheme or ombudsman on the pages we read.

sections.heading: Who you would be contracting with
sections.html:
This should be the simplest question on any travel site and here it is not. The pages we read publish no legal entity, no company number and no registered address in the footer. What we could establish from the public registers is that there are two British-registered companies in the picture, and they are very different things.

EntityWhat the register says
Luxury Escapes (Singapore) Pte. Ltd.
Overseas company FC038864		Registered as an overseas company with a UK establishment. Incorporated 1 March 2021, registered office OUE Downtown 2, 6 Shenton Way, Singapore. Accounts last made up to 30 June 2025. No Gazette notices.
Luxury Escapes Ltd
Company 15394496		Incorporated 7 January 2024, registered at 124–128 City Road, London EC1V 2NX. Status: active, with an active proposal to strike off. Its stated activities are hotels and accommodation, and letting and managing real estate — not travel agency.

We are reporting both because we could not determine which one sells to you, and we are not going to guess. The second one is the one to be aware of: an active proposal to strike off means a company is heading towards being removed from the register. Its stated activities suggest it is not the travel seller, and the overseas Singapore registration looks the likelier contracting party — but “looks likelier” is not good enough when you are paying a deposit.

So ask. The company you are contracting with should be named on your booking confirmation and on the ATOL Certificate. Read it when it arrives, and keep it.

The underlying business is large and real — an Australian-founded group that entered the UK market and trades across several countries — so this is a disclosure problem rather than a credibility one. But a travel site that takes four-figure payments should name its company on its own pages, and this one does not.

sections.heading: What we could not read, and why we are telling you
sections.html:
We tried to report the cancellation and refund terms for you and could not. The booking policies page we fetched returned navigation and metadata rather than policy text, and the same was true of the FAQ and shop terms pages. So, plainly: we do not know what this site’s cancellation terms say, and we are not going to summarise terms we have not read.

That matters more here than on most sites, because of how this kind of offer usually works. Deal-based luxury travel is often sold as a purchase now, choose your dates later arrangement, with a validity period, blackout dates and a surcharge on peak nights. Whether that is how these offers work, how long you have to redeem, and what happens if you never do, are the three questions we would want answered before buying.

Before you pay, get these in writing:

  • Is this a dated booking or a voucher I redeem later, and if it is a voucher, when does it expire?
  • What is the cancellation scale, and is any part non-refundable?
  • Is there an amendment fee for changing dates, and are there blackout periods or peak supplements?
  • What is the ATOL number, and will I receive a certificate?

One more thing we noticed in passing. The pages carry “4.7/5” and “4.8/5” rating badges with no source named and no number of reviews. A rating with no provenance is decoration, not evidence, and we would not weigh it either way.

On the positive side of service, the contact arrangement is better than most: a freephone number on 0808 175 4987, staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. For a long-haul booking in a different time zone, that is genuinely valuable, and it is the number to use for every question in the list above.

verdict: On price and presentation this is one of the better deal sites: real luxury hotels, short stays as well as long ones, and member against non-member prices printed side by side so you can see the saving rather than take it on faith. Two nights at The Hoxton Edinburgh for £219, or three at the Harbour Grand Hong Kong for £349 against £419, are offers worth looking at. Where we have to mark it down is the paperwork, and on a site taking four-figure payments for flight-inclusive holidays the paperwork is not a detail. It says it is ATOL protected and publishes no ATOL number; it names no selling company in its footer; the British company registered under the name is shown as active with a proposal to strike off and is classified as a hotel and property business rather than a travel seller; and we could not read its cancellation terms at all. None of that means anything is wrong — it means you should make one phone call before you pay. Ring 0808 175 4987, ask for the ATOL number and the name of the contracting company, check the number on the CAA register, confirm the cancellation scale and whether you are buying dates or a voucher, pay by credit card, and keep the ATOL Certificate.

faqs.q: Is Luxury Escapes ATOL protected?
faqs.a: It says so: “ATOL protection provided for eligible flights and flight inclusive holidays”, with an ATOL badge on the site. But we could not find the ATOL number published on the homepage, the booking policies page or the FAQ pages we read, and without it you cannot check the licence on the Civil Aviation Authority register. Ring 0808 175 4987 and ask for the number before you pay for anything flight-inclusive, then check it yourself and make sure the ATOL Certificate arrives with your confirmation.

faqs.q: Is my hotel-only booking protected too?
faqs.a: No. ATOL protection attaches to flights and flight-inclusive holidays, so a hotel-only stay is outside the scheme however prominent the badge is. For a hotel-only booking your protection is your card provider and your travel insurance, which is a good reason to pay by credit card.

faqs.q: How much does membership save?
faqs.a: Between £20 and £70 on the nine offers we read. The largest gaps were £70 on three nights at the Harbour Grand Hong Kong, £349 against £419, and £70 on two nights in Paris, £529 against £599. The £849 long-haul stays saved only £40. We could not find the membership price published anywhere, so compare the fee against the gap on the trip you are actually booking.

faqs.q: What is the cancellation policy?
faqs.a: We do not know, and we will not summarise terms we have not read. The booking policies and FAQ pages we fetched returned navigation rather than policy text. Before paying, get four things in writing: whether you are buying fixed dates or a voucher and when that voucher expires, the full cancellation scale, any amendment fee and peak-date supplements, and the ATOL number.

faqs.q: Which company am I buying from?
faqs.a: The site does not say, which is the problem. The public registers show two British-registered entities under the name: Luxury Escapes (Singapore) Pte. Ltd., an overseas company numbered FC038864, incorporated 1 March 2021 with accounts filed to 30 June 2025; and Luxury Escapes Ltd, number 15394496, incorporated 7 January 2024 in London and currently shown as active with a proposal to strike off, whose registered activities are hotels and real estate rather than travel. We could not establish which one contracts with you, so check the name on your confirmation and the ATOL Certificate.

faqs.q: Are the ratings on the site reliable?
faqs.a: We would not rely on them. The pages carry 4.7/5 and 4.8/5 badges with no source named and no number of reviews behind them, so there is nothing to check. Judge the offer on the hotel, the dates and the total price including any supplement, not on a score with no provenance.

title: LV= Home Insurance Review
meta_title: LV= Home Insurance 2026: Unlimited Rebuild, 5-Star Cover
meta_description: LV= holds a Defaqto 5 Star rating for Home and Home Plus. The rebuild limits, the £1,000 subsidence excess and the January 2027 change, explained.
intro:
LV= has held a Defaqto 5 Star rating on its Home and Home Plus policies for nineteen consecutive years, which is the longest run any home insurer on this site can point to. The top tier, Home Plus, carries an unlimited rebuild limit on the buildings section, so the single most common home insurance mistake — underinsuring the cost of putting the house back up — simply cannot happen on it. Contents on that tier run to £150,000 and alternative accommodation to £100,000.

Online quotes start at £119. LV= is specific about what that means: 10% of new customers paid £119 or less between November 2025 and April 2026. Buying online takes a further 5% off, and where buildings and contents are on one policy a single claim attracts one excess rather than two. Repairs arranged through LV='s approved network come with a 12-month guarantee, and the emergency helpline is UK-based and staffed around the clock.

Behind the brand sits real scale. Liverpool Victoria Insurance Company Limited is part of the Allianz UK group, which completed its purchase of LV= General Insurance on 2 January 2020 in a deal worth up to £1.078bn and became the second largest general insurer in the UK, with gross written premiums above £4bn and roughly 9% of the market. Three things are worth reading before you buy: your underwriter is changing on 1 January 2027, the subsidence excess is fixed at £1,000, and the gap between Essentials and the tiers above it is wider than the price suggests. All three are below.

sections.heading: Where the ladder actually steps
sections.html:
The three tiers are not simply cheap, medium and generous versions of one policy. The step from Essentials to Home changes what is insured, not just how much of it.

Buildings cover is capped at £500,000 on Essentials, rises to £1m on Home and becomes unlimited on Home Plus. Contents follow at up to £50,000, £100,000 and £150,000. If your home has to be rebuilt from the ground up, the relevant number is the reinstatement cost quoted by a surveyor, not the price you paid or the price it would fetch — and for most terraced and semi-detached houses £500,000 leaves room. Large detached properties, anything with a slate roof, and listed buildings are where a half-million cap starts to look thin.

The differences that catch people out are further down the schedule. Trace and access — the cost of digging up a floor to find a leaking pipe — is not covered at all on Essentials. It is £5,000 on Home and £10,000 on Home Plus. Escape of water is one of the most frequent household claims there is, and finding the leak routinely costs more than repairing it. Money cover runs £250, £500 and £1,000; garden plants £500, £1,500 and £10,000; business equipment £5,000 on Essentials against £15,000 on Home. Loss of keys is capped at £750 on the entry tier and included on the two above it.

Valuables are the other split. Any single item worth more than £2,000 has to be listed separately on Essentials and Home. Home Plus lifts that ceiling to £5,000, which quietly removes a lot of admin for anyone with an engagement ring, a decent watch or a camera. Bicycles sit at £1,000 per bike on every tier, and cover away from home only applies when the bike is locked to something immovable.

sections.heading: Your underwriter changes on 1 January 2027
sections.html:
This is the fact most reviews of LV= have not caught up with, and there is a date on it that has not passed yet.

Allianz is consolidating five UK insurance entities into Allianz Insurance plc. Liverpool Victoria Insurance Company Limited is one of them, alongside Highway Insurance Company Limited, Fairmead Insurance Limited and Trafalgar Insurance Limited. The mechanism is a Part VII transfer under the Financial Services and Markets Act, which needs a judge to approve it. The directions hearing was granted on 22 May 2026; the sanction hearing is listed for 2 October 2026 at the Rolls Building in London, with a parallel hearing in the Royal Court of Jersey on 6 October. If sanctioned, the transfer takes effect on 1 January 2027.

Allianz's position is that cover, terms, premiums, policy numbers, claims handling and contact routes all stay as they are; direct debit payers will see the reference on their bank statement change to ALLIANZ LV INS. The LV= name itself survives — Allianz abandoned its plan to retire the brand and announced a new multi-year licensing partnership on 24 April 2026, so policies will keep arriving with LV= on them.

The part worth acting on: any policyholder who believes they would be adversely affected can object, and the deadline for doing so is 25 September 2026. Objections go to Allianz on 0800 032 2799 or in writing, and a policyholder may also appear before the court in person. The scheme documents and the independent expert's report are published free on Allianz's transfer page. Nobody is likely to be worse off here, but a transfer that swaps the entity standing behind a claim is not a footnote, and the window to say anything about it closes before the hearing.

sections.heading: £1,000 before subsidence pays anything
sections.html:
LV= sets a compulsory excess of £1,000 for subsidence and £500 for escape of water. Those are fixed, they sit on top of any voluntary excess you choose to knock the premium down, and they are entirely normal for the UK market — which does not make them small.

Set that £1,000 against what subsidence now costs. The Association of British Insurers reported on 3 August 2026 that the average subsidence claim had reached a record £20,000 in the second quarter of the year, more than £2,000 up on the same quarter of 2025, with £72m paid out in three months. Prolonged dry weather shrinking clay soils is the driver. On a claim of that size a £1,000 excess is 5% — irritating rather than ruinous. On the small crack that turns out to cost £1,400 to underpin, it is most of the claim.

The policy is also specific about what subsidence cover excludes: damage arising from poor workmanship, poor design or faulty materials is not covered, which is where a good number of disputed claims live. Escape of water has a matching carve-out — the water damage is insured, but the tank, appliance or pipe that failed is not, and nothing caused by wear and tear is covered at all.

One more clause worth knowing before you need it. Where part of a matching set or suite is damaged — three of five kitchen units, one of two sofas — LV= contributes 50% toward the undamaged items, not the full cost of replacing the set. That is a common term and it is disclosed plainly, but it is the sort of thing people discover at the point of claim.

sections.heading: Sixty days empty, and the cover thins out
sections.html:
If the property is not lived in for more than 60 days in a row, the policy stops behaving like a normal home policy. LV='s definition of unoccupied covers both parts of the problem: nobody living there, or not enough furniture and services present for normal living. A long stay in hospital, an extended trip, a probate sale, a renovation that runs over — all of them count, and none of them feel like they should.

Two practical consequences. If you are going to be away past two months, tell LV= before the sixtieth day rather than after a claim, because a mid-term notification is a conversation and a declined theft claim is not. And if the house is genuinely standing empty for months, a home policy is the wrong product; unoccupied property cover exists for exactly this.

The claims conditions are equally firm. Theft and vandalism must be reported to the police immediately and a crime reference number obtained. You must not admit responsibility, negotiate, or arrange repairs without LV='s agreement — instructing your own builder before the insurer has seen the damage is a reliable way to have part of a claim refused.

The wider claims picture is worth having in mind whoever you insure with. The FCA's general insurance value measures data for calendar year 2025, published on 21 July 2026, put claims acceptance across combined buildings and contents policies at 62–71% — far below motor, which sits at 99%. Complaints about claims ran at 7–13% of claims registered, high against the 0–6% typical elsewhere in retail insurance, and claims costs took 48% of premium income. The Financial Ombudsman Service upholds around 41% of the buildings insurance complaints it decides, and claim decline is the single most common reason people go to it. Home insurance is simply a harder product to claim on than motor, and choosing a well-rated policy is the main lever an individual has.

sections.heading: What LV= is now, and how the money flows
sections.html:
The LV= you buy home insurance from is not the friendly society. Liverpool Victoria Insurance Company Limited is registered in England and Wales under number 3232514 and holds register number 202965 with the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority — a number you can check yourself on the FCA Register. Allianz took a 49% stake in the general insurance business in 2017 for £500m, raised it in 2019, and completed the purchase of the remainder on 2 January 2020. The life and pensions business that shares the name is a separate company under separate ownership; a complaint about one will not reach the other.

LV= sells direct rather than through a comparison panel, which cuts both ways: there is no intermediary commission in the price, and there is also no second quote in front of you. Cover is underwritten in-house rather than placed with a panel of insurers, so the entity setting the terms is the entity paying the claim.

If something goes wrong, the internal route is 0800 085 5664 or GIFeedback@LV.co.uk. If LV= does not resolve it to your satisfaction you have six months from its final response to take the case to the Financial Ombudsman Service on 0800 023 4567, free of charge. There is a 14-day cooling-off period from receiving your documents, and cancelling later attracts a charge for time on cover plus a cancellation fee.

For context on what all this is buying: the ABI recorded £846m paid out on home insurance claims in the first quarter of 2026 alone, at an average of £6,340 a claim — £6,040 for weather damage, £4,350 for theft. The average combined buildings and contents premium over that period was £375, with buildings-only at £306 and contents-only at £117. LV='s £119 entry price is a genuinely competitive number, provided the cover behind it matches the house.

pros: Defaqto 5 Star rating on Home and Home Plus for a nineteenth consecutive year
Unlimited buildings rebuild cover on Home Plus removes any risk of undervaluing the sum insured
Trace and access up to £10,000 on Home Plus, which covers the expensive half of a leak claim
One excess rather than two when buildings and contents are claimed on the same policy
Alternative accommodation up to £100,000 on the top tier, and £50,000 on Home
£5,000 single-item limit on Home Plus, against £2,000 on most competing policies
5% discount for buying online, and a 12-month guarantee on approved-network repairs
Underwritten in-house by an Allianz group company rather than placed with a broker panel
cons: Trace and access is not covered at all on Essentials — a £5,000 to £10,000 gap on one of the most common claim types
£1,000 compulsory subsidence excess and £500 for escape of water, neither reducible, against an ABI average subsidence claim of £20,000
The £119 headline price was paid by only 10% of new customers between November 2025 and April 2026
Cover is restricted once the home is empty for more than 60 days in a row, which catches hospital stays and probate sales
Accidental damage, personal belongings away from home and cycle cover are all paid extras except on Home Plus
Contents are capped at £150,000 even on the top tier, while buildings cover is unlimited
Matching sets and suites attract only a 50% contribution toward the undamaged items
Your underwriter becomes Allianz Insurance plc on 1 January 2027, and the deadline to object is 25 September 2026
No comparison quotes are shown alongside the price, so the market check is on you
verdict: Home Plus is the tier that justifies the LV= name: unlimited rebuild cover, £10,000 trace and access, a £5,000 single-item limit and £100,000 of alternative accommodation add up to a policy with very few holes in it, and nineteen straight years of a Defaqto 5 Star rating is not an accident. Essentials is a different proposition — the missing trace and access cover in particular means it should be priced against other entry-level policies rather than against the tier above it. Read the £1,000 subsidence excess and the 60-day unoccupancy rule before you buy, note that your underwriter changes on 1 January 2027, and get a quote online where the 5% discount applies.

faqs.q: Who underwrites LV= home insurance?
faqs.a: Liverpool Victoria Insurance Company Limited, registered in England and Wales under number 3232514 and holding register number 202965 with the FCA and PRA. It is part of the Allianz UK group, which completed its purchase of LV= General Insurance on 2 January 2020. From 1 January 2027, subject to court approval at the sanction hearing on 2 October 2026, policies transfer to Allianz Insurance plc.

faqs.q: What is the excess on an LV= home insurance claim?
faqs.a: There is a compulsory excess of £1,000 for subsidence and £500 for escape of water, plus any voluntary excess you choose when you set the policy up. Your exact figures are printed on your personal details schedule. Where buildings and contents are damaged in the same incident on a combined policy, only one excess applies.

faqs.q: How much contents cover do I get with LV=?
faqs.a: Up to £50,000 on Essentials, up to £100,000 on Home and up to £150,000 on Home Plus. Individual items worth more than £2,000 must be specified separately on Essentials and Home; the threshold rises to £5,000 on Home Plus. Bicycles are limited to £1,000 each on every tier.

faqs.q: Does LV= cover my home if I go away for a long time?
faqs.a: Cover is restricted once the property has been unoccupied for more than 60 days in a row. LV= treats a home as unoccupied if nobody is living there or if there is not enough furniture and services for normal living. Contact LV= before that point rather than after an incident, and consider dedicated unoccupied property cover for longer absences.

faqs.q: What happens if I want to complain about LV=?
faqs.a: Call 0800 085 5664 or email GIFeedback@LV.co.uk. If you are not satisfied with the final response, you have six months to refer the case free of charge to the Financial Ombudsman Service on 0800 023 4567. The Ombudsman upholds roughly 41% of the buildings insurance complaints it decides, with claim decline the most common reason for referral.

faqs.q: Can I object to my policy moving to Allianz Insurance plc?
faqs.a: Yes. Any policyholder who believes they would be adversely affected by the Part VII transfer can object in writing, by phone on 0800 032 2799, or by appearing at the High Court sanction hearing on 2 October 2026. The deadline for registering an objection is 25 September 2026, and the scheme documents and independent expert's report are published free on Allianz's transfer information page.

title: Monzo Current Account
meta_title: Monzo Current Account: 1st for Service, 3.65% Savings
meta_description: Monzo ranks 1st of 17 UK providers for service quality at 79%. Savings pots pay 2.75% to 3.65% AER depending on plan. Rates and fees checked 6 October 2026.

headline.label: Interest, first 12 months
headline.value: None on the account balance; 2.75% AER on Instant Access Savings on the free plan, up to 3.65% AER on Select Access with Perks at £9 a month

intro:
Monzo finished first of the 17 largest current account providers in the service quality survey every big UK bank is obliged to publish, with 79% of its customers in Great Britain saying they would recommend it and 85% on online and mobile banking. Ipsos surveyed 17,055 people for the August 2026 edition. Every figure on this page was checked on 6 October 2026 against Monzo's own pages, rate tables and legal documents.

The business behind that score has stopped being a startup. Monzo Bank Limited reported revenue of £1.7bn for the year to 31 March 2026, a 39% rise, with gross profit of £1.0bn, adjusted profit before tax of £172.6m and customer deposits of £25.7bn, up 55%. It counts 15.2 million customers, three million of them added during that year, and 10.4 million who open the app in a given month. Card spending through it came to £73.0bn. It sits on the Financial Services Register under firm reference number 730427, holds its own banking licence rather than riding on somebody else's, and eligible deposits are protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme up to £120,000 per person.

Two things are worth knowing before you open the app. The current account itself pays no interest on your balance on any plan: every rate Monzo advertises belongs to a separate savings pot, and which rate you get depends on which of four plans you pay for — free, Extra at £3 a month, Perks at £9, or Max from £19. And Monzo's own switching page carried no cash bonus on 6 October 2026 for moving an account across, which several rivals were offering. What it sells instead is the day-to-day product its own customers rank first in the country, and a savings rate that climbs with the subscription.
