sections.heading: What the four plans cost, and what the savings rate actually buys
sections.html:
Monzo puts all eight of its savings rates on one page, which is more than most banks manage, so the sum below is one anybody can check. Instant Access Savings pays 2.75% AER (variable) on the free plan, 3.00% on Extra, 3.25% on Perks and 3.50% on Max. Select Access pays 3.15% on the free plan and on Extra, and 3.65% on Perks and Max, provided you make two or fewer withdrawals a year and keep at least £500 in it. Interest is paid monthly.

Set those rates against what the plans cost over a year and the picture sharpens. Extra is £36 a year and lifts Instant Access by 0.25 of a percentage point, so the subscription only pays for itself once you hold £14,400 in the pot. Perks is £108 a year for half a point, which needs £21,600. Max is £228 a year for three quarters of a point, which needs £30,400. Below those balances the subscription costs more than the extra interest it unlocks, and the non-savings benefits have to carry it.

Select Access is where the arithmetic gets blunter. Free and Extra pay the identical 3.15%, so an Extra subscriber who keeps savings there pays £36 a year for a rate the free plan already has. Perks and Max both pay 3.65%, so the extra £120 a year that Max costs over Perks buys nothing at all on that pot. Only one of the three paid plans changes the Select Access rate.

There is a tax line worth drawing too. £30,400 at 3.50% produces about £1,064 of interest in a year, which is just past the £1,000 personal savings allowance a basic-rate taxpayer gets, and more than double the £500 a higher-rate taxpayer gets. The balance at which the Max subscription starts paying for itself is roughly the balance at which the interest starts being taxed.

For context, Bank Rate has been 3.75% since 18 December 2025, after 4.00% in August 2025 and 4.25% that May. Monzo's best advertised savings rate, 3.65% on Select Access with a paid plan, sits below Bank Rate, and the free plan's 2.75% sits a full percentage point below it.

sections.heading: From Focus FS Limited to 15.2 million customers
sections.html:
Companies House records Monzo Bank Limited, company number 09446231, as incorporated on 18 February 2015 under the name FOCUS FS LIMITED, renamed on 21 October 2016. Its registered office is Broadwalk House, 5 Appold Street, London EC2A 2AG, and it files under SIC code 64191, banks. Eleven and a half years from a shell company to £25.7bn of deposits is unusually fast for a British bank, and the growth has not stopped: deposits rose 55% in the year to 31 March 2026, revenue 39% and card spending 32%.

The single licence matters more than it sounds. Where a bank runs several brands on one authorisation, a customer holding accounts with two of those brands has one £120,000 of FSCS cover between them, not two. Monzo has no sibling brands to pool with, so the £120,000 is whole. Monzo's own FSCS page works the example: £80,000 in savings plus £50,000 in the current account is £130,000 of deposits, of which £120,000 is paid and £10,000 is not.

The same page is worth reading for what it excludes. A collective investment undertaking and a pension or retirement fund are both named as ineligible depositors, and Monzo now sells investments and pensions alongside the bank account. Money in those products is not covered by the deposit scheme in the way a savings pot is, and anybody moving a pension into the app should establish which protection does apply before they do it.

sections.heading: Moving an account across takes seven working days
sections.html:
Monzo is a full member of the Current Account Switch Service, which means a switch completes in seven working days on a date you pick, incoming and outgoing payments move with it, payments sent to the old account are redirected, and the guarantee refunds any interest or charges on either account caused by a failure of the switch.

Switching is busier than it has been. Pay.UK reported 608,528 switches between January and June 2026, up from 439,324 in the first half of 2025 — a 39% rise — with 12.9 million switches since the service launched and 1.2 million in the preceding twelve months. That release is dated 30 July 2026. Monzo was third among the named net gainers for the first quarter of 2026, with 21,894 more switchers arriving than leaving, behind Nationwide's 58,448.

Three things do not come across, and all three catch people out. Recurring payments taken on your card rather than by Direct Debit — the way most streaming and gym subscriptions are collected — have to be set up again with each merchant. Savings accounts and ISAs cannot be switched through the service at all. And a joint account can only switch to another joint account, so a couple moving to Monzo need the joint account open at both ends first. Permissions you have granted to third-party apps through open banking do not transfer either.

sections.heading: Three overdraft rates, and the one you get is decided for you
sections.html:
Monzo lends an arranged overdraft at 19%, 29% or 39% EAR (variable), and which of the three you are offered depends on your credit score. Its own representative example is a £1,200 overdraft used for 30 days at 39.0% EAR, costing £32.94. Limits run up to £2,000, subject to an affordability check. There are no arrangement fees, no usage fees and no charges for a declined payment — only interest, which accrues daily on the overdrawn balance and on interest already added.

Go past an arranged limit and Monzo charges the same rate it already charges you. With no arranged overdraft at all, an unarranged balance is charged at 39% EAR, capped at £15.50 a month. Stay overdrawn for more than 60 days without paying anything in and Monzo can ask for 5% of the balance, with a minimum of £10, giving at least 30 days' notice first.

Against Bank Rate at 3.75%, the top rung of 39% is more than ten times the cost of money, which is ordinary for an arranged overdraft since the fees were folded into the headline rate across the market. The structure is honest: one number, no fees behind it, and Monzo came first of 17 providers on overdraft services in the August 2026 survey, at 78%.

One oddity is worth flagging. The overdraft information document a customer is pointed to is version 1.2, dated 21 December 2021 — nearly five years old. The rates in it still match the live product pages, so nothing in it is wrong, but a document that old invites the question of what else has not been revisited.

sections.heading: The charges, and the test that decides which set applies to you
sections.html:
Monzo's fee information document is version 1.11, dated 18 August 2026, and it is the document to read rather than the marketing pages. Keeping the account, Direct Debits, standing orders, UK transfers, UK card payments, spending in foreign currency on the card and a replacement card for a stolen or expired one are all £0. Paying cash in costs £1 per deposit at a PayPoint or Post Office. A replacement card for any other reason is free twice a year and then £5, and £30 if you need one sent abroad.

Cash machine allowances depend on a test Monzo calls the Fee Criteria. Meet it and UK and European Economic Area withdrawals are free with no cap, while withdrawals outside the EEA are free up to £200 in a rolling 30 days and then cost 3%. Fail it and even UK and EEA withdrawals are only free up to £400 in a rolling 30 days, after which the same 3% applies. The criteria are published: you need at least one of four things, including £500 or more paid in with active Direct Debits running, eligible government payments, student loan payments, or a joint account shared with somebody who qualifies. Perks lifts the overseas allowance to £600 every 30 days and adds three fee-free cash deposits a month.

Receiving money in euros or another currency attracts a 1% conversion fee, capped at £1,000. Sending money abroad is about to change, and the same document gives both sides of it: until 31 October 2026 the fixed element is no more than £9 with a variable element between 0% and 1.80%, and from 1 November 2026 the fee is "less than £0.80" for most currencies but "may be up to £11 in some cases". For most people that is a sharp cut. Monzo does not say which currencies land on the £11, and anybody sending money to a thinly traded currency should check the quote in the app before 1 November rather than assume the lower figure.

sections.heading: A £21m penalty, and the detail inside it
sections.html:
On 7 July 2025 the Financial Conduct Authority fined Monzo Bank Limited £21,091,300 over financial crime controls. The figure is after a 30% settlement discount, from £30,130,475. The breaches were of Principle 3, which requires adequate risk management systems, and of a requirement imposed on Monzo under section 55L of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 that barred it from taking on new high-risk customers. The conduct covers 1 October 2018 to 4 August 2020, and then 5 August 2020 to 30 June 2022 once that requirement was in force.

The findings are specific. For most of the earlier period Monzo did not require address verification to open an account, so customers could register obviously implausible UK addresses. About 53,600 customers failed fraud screening at CIFAS, with more than half recommended for exit. After the restriction took effect, Monzo opened 33,039 accounts in breach of it, 26,325 of them for customers it had itself rated high-risk. And 45% of transaction monitoring alerts were closed as "undecided" rather than investigated to a conclusion.

Two points of fairness. The conduct ended in June 2022, three years before the notice landed, and the growth that caused it — the bank went from a few hundred thousand customers to millions in that window — is the same growth that produced the service scores at the top of this page. And the failures were of control rather than of customer money: nobody's balance was lost. It is still the hardest fact about Monzo on the public record, and it is one no comparison table will show you.

sections.heading: What Monzo's own complaints return admits
sections.html:
Banks publish their complaints twice a year, and Monzo's covers 1 October 2025 to 31 March 2026. In that half year it opened 67,488 banking and credit card complaints and closed 70,687, a rate of 2.39 per 1,000 accounts. It closed 35.91% within three days and a further 62.00% after three days but within eight weeks, which leaves about 2.1% running past the eight-week mark at which a customer can take the case to the Financial Ombudsman Service. It upheld 23.97%, and the main cause was recorded as "product performance / features".

The uphold rate is the flattering number. Roughly one complaint in four going the customer's way is low for a current account provider, and taken with the complaint rate per 1,000 accounts it suggests most of what comes in is a query rather than a grievance. The three-day figure is the unflattering one: close to two complaints in three take longer than three days to resolve, which for a bank that exists entirely inside an app is slower than the ranking at the top of this page would lead you to expect.

The rest of the return is where the uncomfortable numbers are. Credit-related complaints ran at 4.81 per 1,000 accounts, double the banking rate, on 951 cases and a 19.86% uphold rate. Investments produced 169 complaints with 31.65% upheld, and decumulation and pensions 101 complaints with 36.95% upheld — the two highest uphold rates in the table, on the two products that sit outside deposit protection.

sections.heading: Max at £19 a month: who provides the cover, and who cannot buy it
sections.html:
Max is the plan where the subscription buys something other than a savings rate, and Monzo names the firms behind each benefit, which is more than many packaged accounts do. Worldwide travel insurance comes from Zurich, arranged through Qover: cancellation up to £5,000, emergency medical up to £10 million, lost valuables up to £750, a car hire excess waiver up to £3,000, winter sports included, and a £50 excess per claim. Phone insurance comes from Assurant: up to £2,000 for the handset and £300 for accessories against loss, theft and accidental damage, with a £75 excess and no more than two claims in 12 months. Breakdown cover is the RAC, attached to the person rather than to one vehicle, with home start, onward travel and recovery. Family can be added to all three for £4 a month, covering up to five people.

Two conditions sit on it. Max carries a three-month minimum term, so the first commitment is £57 rather than £19. And it is sold to people aged 18 to 69, which is the one hard eligibility line on the whole range: the plan whose main attraction is travel and breakdown cover is closed to the age group most likely to want it, and it is not clear from the public pages what happens to an existing subscriber who turns 70. That needs confirming with Monzo before anybody in their late sixties signs a three-month term.

Perks, at £9, is the plan Monzo values at "over £300 a year" in partner benefits: an annual Railcard, a weekly Greggs item, Uber One membership, a monthly Vue cinema ticket with 10% off food, and YouTube Premium Lite. Against a £108 annual cost that would be good value, but Monzo does not itemise what it counts each benefit at, so the £300 cannot be checked the way the savings rates can. It is also worth noting that the benefits only pay if you were going to buy those things anyway.

pros: First of the 17 largest providers for overall service quality in Great Britain in the August 2026 Ipsos survey, at 79%, and first on online and mobile banking at 85%
Free plan with no monthly fee, no minimum pay-in to keep it open, and no interest charges unless you borrow
All eight savings rates published in a single table, so the cost of each plan can be measured against what it pays
£120,000 of FSCS cover on Monzo's own banking licence, with no sibling brand to share the limit with
Arranged overdrafts carry interest only, with no arrangement, usage or refused-payment fees, and a £15.50 monthly cap on unarranged charges
First of 17 providers on overdraft services in the same survey, at 78%
Switching completes in seven working days under the Current Account Switch Guarantee, which refunds interest and charges caused by a failed switch
Audited scale behind the app: £1.7bn of revenue, £172.6m of adjusted profit before tax and £25.7bn of deposits in the year to 31 March 2026
cons: The current account pays no interest on your balance on any plan, so every rate quoted sits in a separate savings pot you have to move money into
The £3-a-month Extra plan adds nothing to the Select Access rate — 3.15% on free and 3.15% on Extra — so an Extra subscriber saving that way pays £36 a year for a rate they already had
Max costs £120 a year more than Perks and pays the same 3.65% on Select Access, so the uplift has to come entirely from the insurance and the partner benefits
Max is sold only to people aged 18 to 69, so the plan built around travel, phone and breakdown cover is closed to anybody who has turned 70
Fined £21,091,300 by the FCA on 7 July 2025 for financial crime control failures, including 33,039 accounts opened in breach of a regulatory restriction
Only 35.91% of banking complaints were closed within three days in the six months to 31 March 2026, and about 2.1% ran past eight weeks
Fee-free overseas cash withdrawals are capped at £200 every 30 days on the free plan, a third of the £600 Perks allows, and cash deposits cost £1 each
No branches at all, so there is no counter service, no branch score in the service quality table, and paying in cash means a shop or a post office
The £300-a-year figure Monzo puts on the Perks benefits is not itemised anywhere, so unlike the savings rates it cannot be checked before you subscribe
verdict: Monzo is the best-rated current account provider in Britain by the only independent measure the product has, and the free plan is genuinely free: no fee, no minimum balance, no interest on your money and none charged unless you borrow. Judge it on that and it is hard to beat. The paid plans are a different question, and the arithmetic is the answer rather than the marketing: Extra needs £14,400 in a pot to pay for itself on interest alone, Perks £21,600 and Max £30,400, and on Select Access the £3 plan buys no uplift at all. Max earns its £19 through the Zurich travel cover, the Assurant phone policy and RAC breakdown rather than through the savings rate, and it is shut to anybody over 69. The £21,091,300 fine of July 2025 is real and worth reading, though the conduct ended in 2022 and concerned controls rather than customer money. Open the free account on the service record; buy a plan only after doing the sum on your own balance.

faqs.q: Does the Monzo current account pay interest on your balance?
faqs.a: No. On every plan, including Max at £19 a month, the current account balance earns nothing. The rates Monzo advertises — 2.75% to 3.50% AER on Instant Access Savings and 3.15% or 3.65% on Select Access — apply to money you move into a savings pot, not to money sitting in the account. Interest on the pots is paid monthly.

faqs.q: Is money in a Monzo account protected?
faqs.a: Yes. Monzo Bank Limited holds its own banking licence under firm reference number 730427, and eligible deposits are covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme up to £120,000 per person. Because Monzo does not run other deposit brands, that limit is not shared. Monzo's own worked example: £80,000 in savings plus £50,000 in the current account is £130,000, of which £120,000 is paid out. Investments and pensions bought through the app are not deposits and are not covered on the same basis.

faqs.q: Does Monzo pay a switching bonus?
faqs.a: Not on 6 October 2026. Monzo's switching page sets out the Current Account Switch Guarantee — seven working days, payments moved and redirected, interest and charges refunded if the switch goes wrong — but advertises no cash payment for switching. Offers of this kind come and go, so check the app or the switch page before assuming either way.

faqs.q: How much does a Monzo overdraft cost?
faqs.a: One of three rates, depending on your credit score: 19%, 29% or 39% EAR variable, with limits up to £2,000. Monzo's representative example is £1,200 borrowed for 30 days at 39.0% EAR, which costs £32.94. There are no fees of any kind on top. Without an arranged overdraft, an unarranged balance is charged at 39% EAR with a £15.50 monthly cap.

faqs.q: Is a paid Monzo plan worth it for the savings rate alone?
faqs.a: Only above a certain balance. Extra costs £36 a year for an extra 0.25 of a percentage point on Instant Access, which needs £14,400 in the pot to break even. Perks costs £108 for half a point, needing £21,600. Max costs £228 for three quarters of a point, needing £30,400. On Select Access, free and Extra both pay 3.15% and Perks and Max both pay 3.65%, so only Perks changes anything there.

faqs.q: Can you pay cash into a Monzo account?
faqs.a: Yes, at any PayPoint or Post Office, at a cost of £1 per deposit. Perks includes three fee-free cash deposits a month. Cash withdrawals in the UK and the EEA are free if you meet Monzo's Fee Criteria — which needs one of four things, such as £500 or more paid in with active Direct Debits — and otherwise free only up to £400 in a rolling 30 days, then 3%. Outside the EEA the free allowance is £200 every 30 days on the free plan and £600 on Perks.

title: MyMoneyComparison Breakdown Insurance Review
meta_title: MyMoneyComparison Breakdown Cover: One Form, Ten Quotes
meta_description: MyMoneyComparison sends one breakdown form to up to ten providers. Who runs the quote engine, what the £15.49 headline is based on, and what to check.
intro:
MyMoneyComparison.com Ltd has been quoting insurance from Jubilee House on Church Street in Morley, at the southern edge of Leeds, since it was incorporated on 27 March 2013. It is a small, owner-run business — Companies House holds micro-entity accounts for it, most recently made up to 31 March 2025 — and it does one job: it takes a single set of answers about your vehicle and puts them in front of a panel it describes as 50-plus specialist UK brokers. On breakdown cover the headline is “You could pay from £15.49”, and the form itself costs nothing.

The part that makes it worth a shot is not really the Leeds end. The quote journey runs on the platform built by Seopa Ltd of Belfast, the firm that has been on the FCA register since 2003 and has run Quotezone since 2005. Seopa now puts through more than nine million quotes a year for over four million UK customers, across 60-plus products and a panel of more than 300 providers. MyMoneyComparison names Seopa on its own compliance page as the separate data controller for insurance quote data, and the small print under its breakdown price credits Seopa for the figure. On this product the platform reaches up to ten breakdown providers.

What the questionnaire gathers is the five things any breakdown policy is assembled from — roadside assistance, recovery, home start, onward travel, and European or worldwide cover — with prices you can take monthly or annually. Nobody asks you for a card to see them. The providers pay for the introduction, which is how every comparison service of this shape earns its keep.

key_facts.value: A quote comparison and introduction service — not an insurer, and not an adviser

key_facts.label: Quote platform
key_facts.value: Seopa Ltd, Belfast · company NI46322 · FCA reference 313860

key_facts.label: Breakdown panel
key_facts.value: Up to 10 providers from one form

key_facts.value: From £15.49 — but read the section on where that number comes from

key_facts.value: None found — no Defaqto rating and no entry on Smart Money People

sections.heading: One questionnaire, ten breakdown panels
sections.html:
Breakdown cover is sold in layers, and the questionnaire behind this site is built around them. Roadside assistance brings a patrol to you, usually with a minimum distance from your own front door before it applies. Vehicle recovery pays to move the car when it cannot be fixed at the kerb. Home start removes that distance rule. Onward travel buys you a hire car, a hotel or train fares while the vehicle is in a garage. European or worldwide cover extends the lot beyond the Channel. The platform also quotes the common bolt-ons — tyre replacement, key replacement, misfuelling and battery replacement — and returns both monthly and annual prices.

The number that matters here is ten. That is the maximum number of breakdown providers the underlying platform will put in front of you, and it is a much narrower field than the 130-plus the same engine advertises for car insurance. Breakdown is a small market with a handful of very large names and a long tail of white-label schemes, so ten is a reasonable spread — but it is not the whole market, and no version of this form claims that it is.

The distance rule is the trap on cheap policies, and Greg Wilson, who founded the platform, says so on the Quotezone version of the same product: “The cheapest breakdown policies only cover you a set distance from your home, typically a quarter of a mile or more, which means a breakdown on your own driveway isn't covered.” If you are shopping on price alone, that quarter of a mile is the first thing to check on whichever quote comes back cheapest.

sections.heading: The Belfast platform behind a Leeds brand
sections.html:
Seopa Ltd is registered in Northern Ireland as company NI46322, at Floor 4, Blackstaff Studios, 8-10 Amelia Street, Belfast BT2 7GS, and carries FCA reference 313860 as a non-investment insurance intermediary with permission for credit brokerage. It was started by an engineer, Greg Wilson, in 2003; Quotezone followed in 2005 and CompareNI.com serves the Northern Irish market. Alongside Belfast there is an engineering office in Timișoara, Romania, and the firm was named in Deloitte's Best Managed Companies programme for three consecutive years, 2018 to 2021.

Selling that platform to other websites is a deliberate line of business rather than an accident. Seopa's own pitch to partners is blunt about the split: “Your brand leads the experience, carrying your logo, your colours and your wording, in a journey styled as your own. The Seopa platform runs behind it.” Partners choose from 60-plus products across seven categories — vehicle, business motoring, property, leisure, lifestyle, business and financial — and earn commission on what is bought through their site. Seopa's material says partners typically join as Introducer Appointed Representatives under its authorisation, though it also says the division of responsibility is settled in each contract. MyMoneyComparison holds its own FCA reference and publishes no detail of its arrangement, so the exact shape of the tie is something only the two firms can confirm.

Two things follow for anyone using the breakdown form. Your answers are handled by a business with two decades of quote traffic behind it, which is a good deal more reassuring than a form of unknown parentage. And the second data controller in the chain is named for you on the site's own compliance page — Seopa's ICO registration is Z8733752, sitting alongside MyMoneyComparison's own ZA460665. Very few small comparison brands bother to spell that out.

sections.heading: Who you end up contracting with
sections.html:
The footer on every page reads: “MyMoneyComparison.com Ltd, which does not provide financial advice and does not sell insurance policies. MyMoneyComparison.com Ltd is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) for insurance mediation and credit broking activity under FCA registration number 916241.” That number is the firm's own disclosure and can be checked against the FCA Register before you hand over anything.

The credit broking half is not decoration. Paying £15 a month for breakdown cover rather than a lump sum is a credit agreement, and a firm that introduces you to one needs permission to do it. It is the correct shape of authorisation for the job, and worth knowing about because monthly breakdown cover is usually more expensive over a year than paying once.

The terms of use, last updated in April 2026, say two useful things plainly. On money: “The use of our website is free. However, if you purchase a product or service from a third-party provider, MyMoneyComparison may receive a small commission.” On the contract: once you accept a quotation, “Their terms are not the same as ours, and they are the terms you agree to when you accept a quotation.” Whatever you buy is a contract with the provider. The Leeds company made an introduction and was paid for it; it is not a party to your cover, it does not handle your claim, and it cannot make the recovery truck arrive faster. The company's SIC code, 66220, describes it as an insurance agent and broker, and its micro-entity accounts mean no turnover figure is published — the site's own claim of 28,144 quotes requested in 2025 is the only measure of scale it offers.

sections.heading: An older car park is what keeps this market growing
sections.html:
The strongest argument for buying breakdown cover at all has nothing to do with any comparison site. The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders published its vehicles-in-use count on 24 April 2026: the British fleet reached a record 42,549,649 vehicles in 2025, up 1.4%, of which 36,676,185 are cars, 5,175,598 are vans and 626,566 are heavy goods vehicles.

The age figures inside that release are the ones worth carrying to a quote form. The average car on a British road is now 9.7 years old, up from 9.5 the year before, and a record 45.7% of all cars have been in service for more than a decade. Nearly half the national fleet is past the point where a manufacturer warranty or a dealer assistance package is still running. That, rather than any advertised saving, is what a breakdown policy is for.

Official counts of breakdowns themselves are thinner than you would expect. The most recent national figure that could be found is from a Highways England release of 24 June 2019, which recorded more than 48,500 breakdowns on its network over the summer holiday period of 2018, around 5,000 a week at the peak, with roughly a quarter caused by punctures or tyre problems. That is seven years old and covers only the strategic road network, so treat it as scale rather than as anything current — no newer equivalent appears to be published.

sections.heading: Where the £15.49 on the page came from
sections.html:
This is the part of the site that needs fixing, and it is easy to see because both halves are published. The MyMoneyComparison breakdown page reads: “You could pay from £15.49 per month*”, and its own footnote explains the source: “*Based on quote data provided by Seopa Ltd during September 2023. This quote was provided to the majority of customers.”

The same platform's own site carries the same number in different clothes: “You could pay from £15.49 per year*”, footnoted “*Based on quote data provided by Seopa Ltd during April 2026.” One figure, one source, two units, and two and a half years between the datestamps. Read as monthly, £15.49 is £185.88 a year, which is the price of a premium motoring club membership rather than the cheapest policy on a ten-provider panel. Read as annual, it is the entry-level roadside product the platform actually returns. Neither page is hiding anything — both cite their source and their date — but a shopper landing on the Leeds version will form the wrong idea of what breakdown cover costs, and the figure they are being shown was gathered in the autumn of 2023.

The same drift shows up on the other products the site advertises. Its car panel is given as “110+ providers” with a saving of “up to £518.14”, where the platform behind it currently publishes 130+ providers and “51% of consumers could save £535.17” on May 2026 data. The van figure of £685.51 matches exactly — but the platform's own footnote dates it to May 2025 and frames it as something half of customers could achieve rather than a maximum. That distinction matters: the Chartered Trading Standards Institute's pricing guidance, which the advertising regulator applies, expects a significant proportion of buyers to reach the advertised saving, and the regulator's published view is that less than 10% is unlikely to count as significant. No proportion is published alongside the “up to” figures here.

sections.heading: What you cannot find out before filling in the form
sections.html:
Not one breakdown provider is named. The page describes the cover types and the add-ons, and never says whose policies come back — not a single insurer, motoring club or scheme. For a product where the name on the van is most of what people are buying, that is a real gap, and it cannot be closed without handing over your registration and your details first.

There are also two breakdown landing pages rather than one. /breakdown-insurance/ and /breakdown-insurance-comparison carry the same five cover types, the same £15.49 headline and the same September 2023 footnote, with different headings above them. Duplicate pages of that kind tend to be a search-engine tactic rather than anything a reader benefits from, and they double the number of places a stale figure has to be corrected.

There is no independent rating to fall back on either. Defaqto rates insurance products, not comparison services, so its absence here is a fact about the ratings market rather than about this firm — but there is also no entry on Smart Money People, which does cover comparison brands. The site displays a 4.8 out of 5 Google Reviews score without publishing how many reviews sit behind it. A score with no sample size attached is not much use for deciding anything.

sections.heading: The number missing from the contact page
sections.html:
There is no telephone number anywhere on the site. Contact is by web form or by one of three departmental email addresses, the stated office hours are Monday to Friday, 9am to 5:30pm, and the firm aims to reply “to all enquiries within 24 hours”. For a service that only makes introductions that is defensible. For a motorist stuck on a hard shoulder it is worth knowing in advance, because the number you will need is the provider's, not this one's.

No complaints procedure and no reference to the Financial Ombudsman Service could be found anywhere on the site — not in the terms, not on the contact page, not in the compliance section. Any FCA-authorised firm has to have a complaints process and to tell eligible customers about their Ombudsman rights, so this is almost certainly a publishing omission rather than a missing process, but it is the sort of thing a shopper is entitled to read before they start. In practice complaints split in two: anything about the policy, the price or a callout goes to the provider whose name is on the certificate, and only a complaint about the introduction itself belongs with the comparison service. Either way the Ombudsman takes over eight weeks after a complaint is made, or sooner if a final response arrives.

The Ombudsman's 2025/26 annual data, published 21 May 2026, is a useful piece of background: roadside assistance produced 950 new complaints at a 44% uphold rate, well above the 30% average across every product it handles. The volume is far too small to say anything about any individual firm on a ten-provider panel, and breakdown cover does not appear in the FCA's general insurance value measures at all, so no published claims-acceptance rate exists for this product from anybody. What the uphold gap suggests is that assistance disputes are usually about whether the sales promise matched the callout — which is an argument for reading the policy summary on whichever quote you pick, rather than an argument against the panel.

pros: Free to use, with the provider paying for the introduction rather than it being added to your premium
One questionnaire reaches up to 10 breakdown providers, priced both monthly and annually
The quote platform is Seopa's, on the FCA register since 2003 and handling more than 9 million quotes a year
Panel described as 50+ specialist UK brokers, with routes into non-standard vehicles most mainstream sites skip
FCA reference 916241 and ICO registration ZA460665 published on every page, with Seopa's ICO number named alongside
Terms of use dated April 2026 state plainly that the contract you sign is the provider's, not the site's
A real registered company with a Leeds address, trading under the same name since 27 March 2013
cons: The breakdown headline of “from £15.49 per month” rests on Seopa quote data from September 2023, while the same platform's own site shows £15.49 per year on April 2026 data — a twelvefold difference in what a reader will expect to pay
The car figures are stale in the same way: 110+ providers and “up to £518.14” against the platform's current 130+ and £535.17, and no proportion of customers is published alongside any “up to” saving
Not one breakdown provider is named anywhere before you submit your details, so you cannot tell whose policies the panel will return
Two near-identical breakdown landing pages carry the same cover list and the same out-of-date price
No telephone number, no published complaints procedure and no mention of the Financial Ombudsman Service anywhere on the site
No verifiable independent rating: no Defaqto rating, no listing on Smart Money People, and the 4.8 out of 5 shown is a Google Reviews score with no review count attached
verdict: As a way of getting breakdown quotes in front of you quickly, this works, and the machinery underneath it is better than the brand's size suggests — a Belfast platform with twenty-odd years of quote traffic, up to ten providers on this product, and no cost to you. The weakness is the shop window rather than the engine. A £15.49 headline drawn from September 2023 data and printed as a monthly price, when the same source now publishes it as an annual one, is the sort of thing that makes a reader doubt everything else on the page. Use it for what it does well: run the form, then judge each quote on the distance rule, the recovery limit and the name on the certificate rather than on anything advertised beforehand.

faqs.q: Does MyMoneyComparison sell the breakdown policy itself?
faqs.a: No. Its own footer says the company “does not provide financial advice and does not sell insurance policies”. It introduces you to providers and is paid a commission if you buy. The policy, the certificate and the claim all sit with whoever quoted you, and the terms you agree to are theirs.

faqs.q: Is the £15.49 a month or a year?
faqs.a: The site says “from £15.49 per month” on data its footnote dates to September 2023. The platform that supplied the figure publishes the same £15.49 as an annual price on April 2026 data. Treat the annual figure as the live one and check the actual price on your own quote — monthly, £15.49 would be £185.88 a year.

faqs.q: How many breakdown providers will I actually see?
faqs.a: Up to ten. That is the ceiling on the platform behind the form, and it is far narrower than the 130-plus quoted for car insurance on the same engine. Nobody claims it covers the whole market, so treat the cheapest result as the best price on that panel rather than the best available anywhere.

faqs.q: Who is Seopa and why is its name on the small print?
faqs.a: Seopa Ltd of Belfast, company NI46322 and FCA reference 313860, builds and runs the comparison platform. It has been on the register since 2003, launched Quotezone in 2005, and sells the same technology to partner websites under their own branding. Its ICO registration, Z8733752, is named on MyMoneyComparison's compliance page as the controller of insurance quote data.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if the recovery never turns up?
faqs.a: The provider on your certificate, not the comparison site. Only a complaint about the introduction itself — the form, the data, the quote you were shown — belongs with the site, and no complaints procedure is published there, so ask for it by email. The Financial Ombudsman Service can take the case eight weeks after you complain, or sooner if you get a final response.

faqs.q: Is monthly payment worth taking?
faqs.a: Check the annual price first. Monthly breakdown cover is a credit agreement, which is why the firm holds a credit broking permission alongside its insurance one, and spreading the cost almost always costs more over twelve months than paying once. On a product this cheap the difference can be a large share of the premium.

title: MyMoneyComparison.com Life Insurance
meta_title: MyMoneyComparison: FCA Authorised, But No Advice
meta_description: MyMoneyComparison.com Ltd is FCA authorised under number 916241, says it does not sell insurance or give advice, and hands your quote to Seopa Ltd.

headline.label: Regulatory status
headline.value: FCA authorised for insurance mediation and credit broking, number 916241

disclosure: we earn a commission if you request a quote through the link on this page, and the programme pays on a cost-per-lead basis — which means we are paid when you submit your details, not only if you buy. We think you should know that before you fill anything in. Nothing below has been softened for it.
intro:
The first thing to check on any insurance comparison site is whether it is regulated, and this one is. Its own footer states that MyMoneyComparison.com Ltd is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority “for insurance mediation and credit broking activity under FCA registration number 916241”.

The company is real and settled: number 08464012, registered at Jubilee House, 55 Church Street, Morley, Leeds LS27 9JQ, incorporated on 27 March 2013 and classified at Companies House under SIC 66220, activities of insurance agents and brokers.

Equally to its credit, it tells you what it is not. In its own words: “We do not sell insurance directly” and “we do not give financial advice”. For life insurance in particular, that second sentence is the one that should shape how you use it, and we go into why below.

sections.heading: What the regulated permissions actually cover
sections.html:
Two activities are named in that footer, and they are worth separating.

Insurance mediation is the permission to arrange or introduce insurance — the regulated activity a comparison site or broker needs to put you in front of an insurer. Credit broking is the separate permission needed to introduce you to credit, which in insurance usually means monthly premium finance.

What is not in that list is any form of investment permission or advice permission. That is consistent with what the site says about itself, and it is the correct shape for a quote service. It also means nobody in the process is assessing whether a policy suits you.

One honest caveat about our own checking. We read the firm reference number 916241 on the company’s own pages. We did not reach the FCA’s public register to confirm the entry, so we are reporting it as the company’s published statement rather than as a register check we performed. Looking up an FRN is free and takes a minute on the FCA’s own register, and it is worth doing before you hand over medical details to any insurance site, this one included.

The company also publishes an ICO data-protection registration, ZA460665, which is what a business processing personal data at this scale should have.

sections.heading: Your quote is handled by a different company
sections.html:
This is the most useful thing we found, and most people filling in the form would never know it. The compliance page states plainly: “Seopa is the data controller for all insurance product quotes provided.”

Seopa Ltd is a separate regulated firm — FCA number 313860, ICO registration Z8733752 — and it runs the quote engine. So when you complete a quote journey you are, in data-protection terms, dealing with Seopa rather than with MyMoneyComparison, and the page describes the process as putting “your enquiry in front of brokers who write that kind of risk”.

Why that matters to you, practically:

  • Your data-protection rights — access, correction, deletion — run against Seopa for the quote itself, not against the website you started on.
  • Your details go to a network of brokers, so expect contact from firms you have not heard of. That is how the model works and it is disclosed, but it is not the same as a single insurer’s quote form.
  • The compliance page does not describe an opt-out for Seopa’s handling of quote data. If you want to limit who contacts you, read the consent wording on the quote form carefully before you submit, because that is where the choice is made.

On the advertising side it is more conventional: log data is “not linked to personally identifiable information”, the named advertising partner is Google, and third-party ad servers use “cookies, JavaScript and web beacons” which automatically share your IP address. Cookies can be refused through your browser.

sections.heading: Non-advised life cover: what you take on yourself
sections.html:
We are not advisers and this is information rather than a recommendation, but the practical difference between advised and non-advised life insurance is a matter of fact and it is worth understanding before you compare on price alone.

On a non-advised route — which is what a comparison form is — nobody is responsible for whether the policy fits your circumstances. You choose the type, the sum assured and the term, and the suitability of those choices is yours. That is fine if you know what you want. It is less fine if you are not sure of the answers to the following, which all change the outcome:

  • Level term or decreasing term. Decreasing cover is designed to track a repayment mortgage and is cheaper; level cover pays the same sum whenever you die within the term. They are not interchangeable.
  • Life cover or critical illness. Different products, different prices, often sold on the same page.
  • Whether the policy is written in trust. Putting a life policy in trust is a long-standing arrangement that affects who receives the money and when. A quote form does not do it for you.
  • Whether it is guaranteed or reviewable premiums. A reviewable premium can rise.

And the one that catches people out most: medical disclosure is your responsibility. Life cover is underwritten on what you tell the insurer, and an incomplete answer about a condition, a medication, your weight, your drinking or your family history can be the reason a claim is examined years later. If your history is at all complicated, that is the clearest case for talking to a regulated adviser rather than a form — and this site states it does not provide one.

Price-wise, there is one structural fact worth knowing: life insurance is priced by age at the start, and the premium you are quoted this year will be higher next year for the same cover. Comparing is sensible; postponing is expensive.

sections.heading: If the insurer fails, what is protected
sections.html:
This is the part of buying life cover nobody puts on a comparison page, and it is reassuring, so it is worth knowing. The Financial Services Compensation Scheme publishes the levels, and for life insurance they are the strongest in the scheme.

Term life assurance and critical illness cover are protected at 100% where the firm failed on or after 3 July 2015. Whole of life assurance is 100% protected. Income protection, annuities and insured personal pensions are also at 100% on that basis. For firms that failed before 3 July 2015, those categories are protected at 90%.

There is no published monetary cap on long-term insurance protection, only that cover is “subject to conditions, limits and requirements set out by the Prudential Regulation Authority”. Compare that with general insurance, where home, travel, pet and health cover are protected at 90%, and only compulsory classes such as third-party motor and employers’ liability reach 100%.

The practical point: on a life policy you are not exposed to the insurer going under in the way you might fear, and that is a reason to judge a quote on the policy terms and the underwriting rather than on how big a brand name is. What the scheme does not do is make a badly chosen policy pay out — protection against insurer failure and suitability of cover are different problems, and only the first one is solved for you.

If an intermediary rather than an insurer fails, the levels differ: 100% for compulsory general insurance and 90% for other general insurance, and the scheme does not publish a separate figure for a life policy arranged through a failed broker.

sections.heading: What this site is actually built for
sections.html:
Read the navigation and the shape of the business becomes clear. The strength here is not mainstream personal cover — it is specialist and commercial risk, and there is a lot of it:

  • Trade and commercial vehicles: taxi, private hire, HGV, courier, fleet, motor trade, minibus, coach, limousine, driving school, catering van, ice cream van.
  • Hard-to-place motor: convicted drivers, modified, kit car, import, classic, young drivers, over 50s, temporary and learner cover.
  • Specialist property: park home, holiday home, HMO, block of flats, unoccupied property, Airbnb, landlord and buy-to-let.
  • Trades and business: tradesman, plumber, roofer, auto electrician, public liability, employers’ liability, professional indemnity, shop, salon, restaurant, hotel, care home, surgery.
  • Leisure: horsebox, campervan, motorhome, caravan, boat, bicycle, horse.

That is a genuinely useful list. If you drive an ice cream van, run an HMO or have points on your licence, a panel of specialist brokers is exactly what you want, and the big-name comparison sites are often no help at all.

Life insurance, by contrast, is a sideline here. It appears in the navigation under “Lifestyle”, alongside health and pet, and it does not appear in the homepage’s own “What do you need to insure?” list or in its “Insurance by Category” block. For a product this large and this competitive, that placement tells you where the site’s attention is.

The claims it makes for itself are not quantified. It says it has helped “thousands of individuals and businesses across the UK”, refers to “hundreds of brokers” in the wider market without saying how many are on its own panel, and promises savings “by avoiding inflated premiums and unnecessary extras” with no figure attached. Its copyright notice runs from 2013 to 2026, which matches the Companies House incorporation date, and the founder’s biography cites “over a decade of experience”. There is also a “Rated 4.8/5” badge on the page that names no source and no number of reviews, which is not a rating anyone can check.

We should also report a maintenance problem we hit while checking that navigation: several menu items link only to “#” and go nowhere. Multi-Car, Buy-to-Let, HMO, Airbnb, Builders, Plumber and Roofer insurance are all advertised in the menu with no destination page behind them. That is a site that has grown faster than it has been tidied, and it is a reason to check that the specific product you came for actually has a working journey before you rely on it.

sections.heading: How it gets paid, and how to use it well
sections.html:
The business model is stated openly on the affiliate side: the programme pays on a cost-per-lead basis, with only valid leads paid. In other words, the site earns when a completed enquiry is generated, whether or not you ever take out a policy.

That is standard in this market and it is not a criticism on its own. It does explain two things you will notice: the form wants your details before it shows you much, and the number of product pages is very large relative to the depth of each one. We earn on the same basis, which is why we have put the disclosure at the top of this page rather than the bottom.

So, used sensibly:

  • Use it for the awkward risks — trade vehicles, convicted drivers, non-standard property. That is where a broker panel beats a mainstream comparison site, and where the lead model works in your favour because a human broker actually wants the business.
  • For life insurance, treat it as one quote among several, not as the market. It is a thin corner of this particular site.
  • Read the consent wording on the form before submitting, because your details go to a network of brokers and the compliance page describes no opt-out for the quote data itself.
  • Use an email address you can filter, and expect calls.
  • Check the FRN yourself — 916241 for MyMoneyComparison.com Ltd and 313860 for Seopa Ltd — on the FCA register before you submit medical information.
  • If your medical history is complicated, see a regulated adviser. This site says it does not give financial advice, and on underwritten life cover that gap is the thing most likely to cost you.

verdict: On the checks that matter, this one holds up: MyMoneyComparison.com Ltd is FCA authorised in its own right under number 916241 for insurance mediation and credit broking, it has been registered at Companies House since 2013, and it is upfront that it neither sells insurance nor gives advice. It also discloses something most comparison sites bury — that Seopa Ltd, a separate regulated firm, is the data controller for your quote and puts your enquiry in front of a broker network. Where we would steer you is on fit. This site is built for awkward risks: taxis, HGVs, motor trade, convicted drivers, HMOs, unoccupied property. For those it is better than the household-name comparison sites, and the per-lead model means a specialist broker genuinely wants the enquiry. Life insurance is a thin corner of it, tucked under “Lifestyle” and absent from the homepage categories, with no example premiums published. Use it as one quote among several, read the consent wording before you submit, check both firm reference numbers on the FCA register, and if your medical history is anything other than simple, pay for advice instead of filling in a form. We are not advisers either, and on underwritten life cover that is the gap worth closing.

faqs.q: Is MyMoneyComparison.com regulated?
faqs.a: Its own footer states that MyMoneyComparison.com Ltd is “authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority” for “insurance mediation and credit broking activity under FCA registration number 916241”. The company is number 08464012, registered in Leeds since March 2013. We read that number on the company’s pages rather than on the FCA register, so check it yourself on the register — it is free and takes a minute.

faqs.q: Will it advise me which life policy to take?
faqs.a: No. It says “we do not sell insurance directly” and “we do not give financial advice”. That means the choice of level or decreasing cover, the sum assured, the term, whether to add critical illness and whether to write the policy in trust are all yours, and nobody is responsible for whether the result suits you. If those questions are not obvious to you, that is the case for a regulated adviser rather than a quote form.

faqs.q: Who actually gets my details?
faqs.a: The compliance page states that “Seopa is the data controller for all insurance product quotes provided” and that the process puts “your enquiry in front of brokers who write that kind of risk”. Seopa Ltd is a separate firm with FCA number 313860 and ICO registration Z8733752. So your quote data sits with Seopa and goes out to a broker network — read the consent wording on the form, because the page describes no opt-out for that handling.

faqs.q: How does the site make money?
faqs.a: On a cost-per-lead basis: it is paid for a valid completed enquiry rather than for a policy you buy. That is normal in this market and it explains why the form asks for your details early. We are paid on the same basis if you use the link on this page, which is why our disclosure sits at the top of it.

faqs.q: Are there example premiums I can look at first?
faqs.a: None that we could find published anywhere on the site. There is no indicative price, no premium table and no named insurer on the life panel before you submit your details. If you want a sense of the market before giving anyone your medical history, get one quote directly from a well-known insurer first and use it as your yardstick.

faqs.q: Is it any good for anything other than life insurance?
faqs.a: That is where it is strongest. The site is built around specialist and commercial risk — taxi, private hire, HGV, courier, fleet, motor trade, minibus, horsebox, convicted drivers, modified and import cars, HMOs, park homes, unoccupied property, and a long list of trades liability covers. For risks the household-name comparison sites decline, a specialist broker panel is exactly the right tool. Do check your product has a working page first: several menu items link to “#” and go nowhere.

title: National Tyres and Autocare Servicing: Prices, the MOT Sum and the Halfords Stamp
meta_title: National Tyres Servicing: Prices and the MOT Discount
meta_description: National servicing prices run from £219.99 by engine size, parts are guaranteed two years or 24,000 miles, and the bundled MOT undercuts the legal cap.
intro:
National Tyres and Autocare has been fitting tyres in Britain since August 1970, when Marsham, Briggs and Gorrills were folded together into what the company called the country's first national network of tyre fitting centres. Servicing came later and now sits alongside the tyres, exhausts, brakes, batteries and MOT work at more than 200 National-branded garages. The prices are published before you book: an interim service starts at £219.99, a full service at £279.99 and a major service at £329.99, each stepping up with engine size, and every part fitted carries a guarantee of two years or 24,000 miles — twice the length the fast-fit trade usually offers.

National has been part of Halfords since December 2021, when the group paid £62m for it. That matters at the counter rather than in the boardroom. Halfords now runs around 600 consumer garages, of which National is roughly a third, and the branch finder on National's own site marks a long list of former National sites as "(Now a Halfords centre)" or "(Halfords Autocentres)". Book a service under the National name and the stamp that goes in your book reads "Halfords Autocentre Menu Service". Nothing about that is hidden, but it decides which brand your paperwork carries and which website you should be booking on, so it is worth knowing before you ring.

The most useful thing on the price list is the MOT. A test at National is £49.99 against a statutory maximum of £54.85, and buying it with a service brings it down again — to £29.85 alongside a major service, which is £25 below the most any garage in the country is allowed to charge.

sections.heading: What a service costs before anybody looks at the car
sections.html:
National publishes a full grid rather than a single headline price, and the only variable is engine size. An interim service is £219.99 up to 1499cc, £249.99 from 1500cc to 2499cc and £289.99 above that. A full service runs £279.99, £309.99 and £349.99 across the same three bands. A major service is £329.99, £359.99 and £399.99. The steps between the bands are £30 and £40 every time, which makes the grid easy to read and easy to check against a quotation.

The gaps between the service levels are worth doing in your head before you book. Moving from an interim to a full service costs £60 on a small engine; moving from a full to a major costs £50. The major is sold as a two-yearly job rather than an annual one, so on a car that does average mileage the real comparison is one major every other year against two fulls — £329.99 against £559.98 on the smallest band, with the major throwing in the brake fluid and cabin filter that the full service leaves alone.

Orders over £200 can go through Payment Assist and be spread across four months. Every service on the grid clears that threshold, the £219.99 interim included, so the option is there on any of them.

sections.heading: The MOT is priced off the government's cap, not off National's own MOT price
sections.html:
This is the part of the price list nobody seems to have taken apart, and it is the best value on the page. The Department for Transport sets a maximum fee of £54.85 for a class 4 MOT and a garage may charge anything below it. National charges £49.99 for a test on its own. Bundle it with a service and the grid shows the following: an interim service and MOT is £259.84 against £219.99 for the service alone, a full service and MOT is £314.84 against £279.99, and a major service and MOT is £359.84 against £329.99.

Subtract, and the MOT inside those bundles costs £39.85, £34.85 and £29.85. Those three numbers are exactly £15, £20 and £25 below the £54.85 statutory maximum, and they hold across all three engine bands — the arithmetic is identical on the £289.99 interim and the £399.99 major. The discount is built off the legal ceiling, not off National's own shelf price, and it rises with the size of the service you buy.

The marketing describes the same offer as "30% off your MOT (worth £49.99)" with a service, rising to 40% with a full service and 50% with a major. Those percentages applied to £49.99 would give £34.99, £29.99 and £24.99, and every actual bundle is £4.86 dearer than that — £4.86 being precisely the gap between National's £49.99 MOT and the £54.85 cap. Read against the cap the offer is honest and generous; read against the price on National's own MOT page it falls a fiver short of what it says. Either way, £29.85 for a test is a good deal, and it is the number to quote at the counter.

sections.heading: Fifty checks, sixty checks, seventy checks, and what the extra ten buy
sections.html:
The three service levels are sold on inspection counts: 50 or more points on the interim, 60 or more on the full, 70 or more on the major. The interim covers the oil and filter change, brake operation and pad condition, tyres, wipers, battery security, clutch, steering and suspension components and the exhaust. The full service adds an air filter that National values at up to £70, plus mirrors, seatbelts, door locks and an assessment of any chip or crack in the windscreen.

The major adds two items that genuinely cannot wait indefinitely: a cabin filter valued at up to £60 and a brake fluid change with the system bled, valued at up to £49.99, along with an alternator charging-rate test. Brake fluid absorbs water over time and most manufacturers ask for it every two years regardless of mileage, so the two-yearly major is priced around the interval that actually matters rather than an arbitrary one.

Add the quoted part values together and the major service includes up to £179.99 of consumables against a £329.99 price on the smallest engine. That is the company's own valuation rather than a shop price you could verify, so treat it as an indication of what is in the box, not as a saving.

sections.heading: Two years and 24,000 miles, which is longer than the trade norm
sections.html:
The servicing pages carry one line that does more for a buyer than any of the pricing: "All parts fitted at Halfords Autocentres and National Autocentres are guaranteed for a minimum of 2 years or 24,000 miles (whichever is sooner)." Fast-fit chains more commonly guarantee parts for twelve months or 12,000 miles, so National is offering double on both halves of the test, and the guarantee is honoured across the whole group estate rather than only at the branch that did the work.

What the sentence covers is parts. The labour position is set out separately under the fitting warranty on the rights page, alongside manufacturer guarantees on the goods themselves and an accidental damage guarantee that is sold as an extra rather than included. If the point of the visit is a repair rather than a service — a clutch, a set of discs, an exhaust — ask which of the three is doing the work before the car goes up, because they have different lengths and different claim routes.

sections.heading: Servicing away from the dealer, and the stamp that says Halfords
sections.html:
Having a car serviced outside the franchised network does not void a manufacturer warranty provided the schedule is followed and the parts meet the maker's specification, which is why a chain like National can sell against a main dealer at all. Halfords puts the saving at "on average, 20% less than a main dealer would charge", a group-wide claim without a worked example behind it, so it is a reason to get a dealer quotation for comparison rather than a figure to rely on.

Two details of the paperwork are worth knowing in advance. The stamp National puts in a paper service book records a "Halfords Autocentre Menu Service" — accurate, since that is the schedule being followed, but not the National name a buyer might expect to see later. And electronic service records cannot be stamped at all: the pages state plainly that "Electronic service books cannot be stamped with this service." Most manufacturers moved to digital records years ago, and a car whose history lives in the maker's system will come away from a National service with an invoice and nothing in the online record. Keep the invoice; on resale it is the only evidence you have.

sections.heading: £54 a year that includes an MOT, if you book on the right website
sections.html:
Halfords Motoring Club has around six million members, of whom about 420,000 pay for the Premium tier and generate roughly £22m of subscription revenue a year. Premium costs £54 and includes one MOT worth up to £49.99, a £10 welcome voucher, two ten-point car checks valued at £30, one free fitting, unlimited next-day delivery and 5% off member pricing. On the MOT alone the membership is close to paying for itself, and the 5% then runs against servicing.

The catch is procedural and easy to fall over. Halfords' own help page confirms that "You can use your benefits at any National Tyres garage", but to apply them to an online booking you have to book through Halfords.com and pick the National branch there, rather than booking on national.co.uk. A member who books the obvious way, on the National site, arrives without the discount attached. If you hold Premium, start on the Halfords side and choose the National garage from that end.

sections.heading: Where a complaint goes, and how far it can get
sections.html:
National's terms and conditions name an alternative dispute resolution body, which is more than many garages do: complaints can be taken to The National Conciliation Service at no charge. The NCS is accredited by the Chartered Trading Standards Institute under delegated powers from the Secretary of State for Business and Trade, under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, and it handles vehicle servicing, maintenance and repair disputes as well as vehicle sales. Conciliation is free to the consumer, you have twelve months from the business's final response to bring a case, the average process runs 72 days and an outcome is issued in writing within 90. Claims below £50 can be refused.

Two limits are worth understanding before you rely on it. The scheme's own rules state that "Any outcome of the ADR procedure is not legally binding" on either side, and if conciliation fails, arbitration carries a consumer fee running from £48 plus VAT on claims between £50 and £1,000 up to £345 plus VAT above £15,000, refundable if the claim succeeds. That is a materially weaker position than the Motor Ombudsman offers at Halfords-branded garages under the same ownership, where the final decision binds the accredited business once the consumer accepts it and the service is free throughout.

The gap between National's own two pages does not help. The rights page sets out a complaints procedure — email or write, or ring 0808 100 0015, examined within two working days and an aim to resolve within five — and then sends anyone still unhappy to "your local Trading Standards office or your local Citizens' Advice Bureau", without mentioning the conciliation scheme the terms and conditions point to. A customer who reads the rights page and not the terms will never learn the ADR route exists.

sections.heading: The estate is shrinking, so check the branch is still there
sections.html:
Halfords' preliminary results for the 53 weeks to 3 April 2026 report group revenue of £1,801.7m, with Autocentres at £739.7m and an underlying operating profit of £21.0m from that division. The estate finished the year at 588 locations — 496 consumer garages and 92 commercial fleet sites — down from 632, after 43 underperforming garages were closed during the year. The group also runs about 250 mobile vans trading as Halfords Mobile Expert and National.

Alongside the closures, 103 sites now trade under the Fusion format, which combines a retail store and a garage on one site, with roughly 35 more planned in the current financial year. Both programmes work through the same estate National sits in, and the company has flagged "ongoing weakness in the tyres market" with only some stabilisation late in the year. None of that is a reason to avoid a service, but it is a reason to ring the branch rather than trust a map pin, particularly if the one you use is the sort of small standalone site the closure programme has been aimed at.

sections.heading: Two price lists on one website
sections.html:
National's servicing pricing page and its MOT and service packages page do not agree, and the gap is wide enough to matter. The pricing grid puts an interim service and MOT at £259.84, a full service and MOT at £314.84 and a major service and MOT at £359.84 on the smallest engine band. The packages page advertises the same three bundles "from £189.99", "from £244.99" and "from £289.99" — £70, £70 and £70 apart respectively. A search listing for the pricing page itself shows a full service "price from £209.99", a third figure again.

A "from" price usually signals a promotional rate, a smaller vehicle class or a branch-specific offer, and none of those explanations is set out on either page. The practical answer is to put your registration and postcode into the quote tool, which is what both pages ask you to do, and to get the figure in writing before the car is booked in. Do not assume the higher grid is the one you will be charged, and do not assume the lower one is available at your branch either — this needs confirming with the garage, not with the website.

sections.heading: The company behind the name
sections.html:
The trading entity is National Tyre Service Limited, company number 00986754, incorporated on 12 August 1970 and VAT registered as 785 4130 19. Its registered office at Companies House is Icknield Street Drive, Washford West, Redditch — Halfords' own home town — while the consumer terms and conditions still give Regent House, Heaton Lane, Stockport, the address the business used under its previous owners. The last full accounts cover the period to 28 March 2025 and were filed on 19 November 2025. Henry Birch was appointed a director on 16 April 2025, the day after Graham Stapleton's termination, mirroring the change of chief executive at the parent.

The ownership history is unusually busy for a garage chain: BTR plc bought it in 1985, the German tyre maker Continental AG in May 1991, and a management buyout took it to Axle Group Holdings for £24m in December 2001. By 2018 it was running 235 locations with 1,192 employees. Halfords paid £62m in December 2021, creating a combined network of 604 garages and 235 mobile vans at the time. Roughly 7,500 people now work across the group's garages and its 400-plus retail stores.

pros: Prices published by engine size before you book, with no need to submit details first
Parts guaranteed for a minimum of two years or 24,000 miles, double the usual fast-fit term, and honoured across around 600 group garages
The bundled MOT costs £39.85, £34.85 or £29.85 — £15 to £25 below the £54.85 statutory maximum
A major service includes brake fluid and a cabin filter on a two-yearly cycle that matches most manufacturers' own interval
An ADR body is named in the terms and conditions, and it is CTSI-accredited
Payment Assist spreads anything over £200 across four months
Halfords Motoring Club Premium at £54 includes an MOT worth up to £49.99 and is usable at National garages
cons: Two of National's own pages price the same bundles £70 apart — £259.84 against "from £189.99" for an interim service and MOT — with no explanation of the difference on either page
The advertised "30% / 40% / 50% off your MOT (worth £49.99)" understates every bundle by £4.86, because the discount is calculated against the £54.85 cap rather than National's own £49.99 price

The rights page names no dispute scheme and sends unhappy customers to Trading Standards, while the terms and conditions point to The National Conciliation Service — a reader of the wrong page never learns the route exists

National Conciliation Service outcomes are "not legally binding", and arbitration costs the consumer £48 plus VAT and up, where Halfords-branded garages in the same group sit under an ombudsman whose decisions bind the business
Electronic service records cannot be stamped, so a car with a digital history leaves with an invoice and nothing in the manufacturer's system
The paper stamp reads "Halfords Autocentre Menu Service" rather than National, and many listed branches now trade as Halfords centres
Motoring Club benefits only attach to an online booking made through Halfords.com, not through national.co.uk
43 garages closed in the year to 3 April 2026, taking the estate from 632 sites to 588
The terms and conditions still give a Stockport registered office that Companies House no longer shows
verdict: National is a straightforward thing to buy a service from: the grid is published, the only variable is engine size, and the parts guarantee of two years or 24,000 miles is longer than most of the chains it competes with. The bundled MOT is the standout — £29.85 alongside a major service is £25 under the legal maximum, and it is worth asking for by that number. The reservations are about which page you happen to read. Two parts of the site price the same bundle £70 apart, the MOT discount is advertised as a percentage of a figure it is not actually calculated from, and the dispute route named in the terms is missing from the page about your rights — and is weaker than the ombudsman covering the Halfords-branded garages next door in the same group. Get the quotation in writing with your registration against it, ask whether the branch is National or now a Halfords centre, and if you hold a Motoring Club membership start the booking on the Halfords site.

faqs.q: How much is a service at National Tyres and Autocare?
faqs.a: As checked on 8 September 2026, an interim service is £219.99 up to 1499cc, £249.99 from 1500cc to 2499cc and £289.99 above 2499cc. A full service is £279.99, £309.99 and £349.99 across the same bands, and a major service is £329.99, £359.99 and £399.99. A separate packages page advertises lower "from" prices, so confirm the figure for your registration before booking.

faqs.q: Is the MOT cheaper if I book it with a service?
faqs.a: Yes, and by more than the headline suggests. On its own an MOT is £49.99. Added to an interim service it costs £39.85, to a full service £34.85 and to a major service £29.85 — £15, £20 and £25 below the £54.85 statutory maximum for a class 4 car. The discounts are the same in cash terms whatever your engine size.

faqs.q: How long are parts guaranteed for?
faqs.a: A minimum of two years or 24,000 miles, whichever comes first, on parts fitted at National and Halfords Autocentres. That is twice the twelve months or 12,000 miles common elsewhere in the fast-fit trade. Fitting is covered separately under the fitting warranty, so ask which applies if the visit is a repair rather than a scheduled service.

faqs.q: Will a National service affect my manufacturer warranty?
faqs.a: Not if the manufacturer's schedule is followed and the parts meet its specification. The practical risk is documentary rather than mechanical: National cannot stamp an electronic service record, so on a car with a digital history you should keep the invoice as your proof that the work was done on time.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if the work is wrong?
faqs.a: Start with National — email customersupport@national.co.uk or ring 0808 100 0015; the company says complaints are examined within two working days and it aims to resolve them within five. If that fails, the terms and conditions allow a free referral to The National Conciliation Service, which is CTSI-accredited and covers servicing and repair disputes. You have twelve months from the final response, the average case takes 72 days, and the outcome is not legally binding on either party.

faqs.q: Is National Tyres the same company as Halfords now?
faqs.a: It is a Halfords subsidiary. National Tyre Service Limited (company 00986754) has traded since August 1970 and was bought by Halfords for £62m in December 2021. Around 200 garages still carry the National name within a group estate of roughly 600, the branch finder marks a number of former National sites as Halfords centres, and the service book stamp records a Halfords Autocentre menu service.

title: Nationwide FlexDirect Review: 5% AER, £295 of Value, and the £1,500 a Month It Asks For
meta_title: Nationwide FlexDirect: 5% on £1,500 and £295 in Year One
meta_description: Nationwide's rebuilt FlexDirect pays 5% AER on £1,500, £175 for switching and up to £120 cashback. Here is what the £1,500 monthly pay-in really asks for.
intro:
Nationwide's FlexDirect pays 5% AER (4.89% gross a year), fixed, on balances up to £1,500 for the first twelve months, with £175 for switching in on top and no monthly fee. Every money figure on this page was re-read against Nationwide's own product page and its switch offer terms on 8 October 2026, and not one of them has moved since the account was rebuilt on 9 September 2026.

The society behind it is the largest of its kind in the world and it is owned by the people who bank with it — over 19 million members, no shareholders, and a board answerable to a membership rather than to a share price. Total assets stood at £382.3bn at 31 March 2026, retail deposits at £270.8bn, the CET1 capital ratio at 19.1% and underlying profit before tax at £2,026m. It runs 696 branches — 605 of its own and 91 Virgin Money — and has committed to keeping every one of them open until at least 2030, which on its own 21 May 2026 count makes it the biggest branch network in the country while other banks were on course to close more than 240 branches during the year. 6.7 million people used a Nationwide branch in 2025. In July 2026 the Institute of Customer Service put Nationwide top of the whole UK Customer Satisfaction Index on 87.3 out of 100, against an all-sector average of 78.3.

FlexDirect is the society's reward current account. Alongside the rate sit two separate £5 monthly cashback payments — one for putting at least £300 a month through Direct Debits, one for spending at least £500 a month on the debit card — each capped at £60 a year. Nationwide adds the switch payment and the cashback together and calls it £295 of value in year one; the same announcement prints a maximum of £370 once up to £75 of interest is counted in. Interest is paid monthly and there is no fee for maintaining the account at any point.

Three eligibility rules decide whether any of that is available to you, and they are worth knowing before you start an application. You have to pay in at least £1,500 every month for the interest and the cashback to run at all, and transfers from your other Nationwide accounts and refunds do not count towards it. You cannot have held a FlexDirect within the last three years. And the £175 goes only to your first eligible sole switch and your first eligible joint switch since 2021, and not at all if you are moving from an account already held with Nationwide — which since 2 April 2026 includes Virgin Money. Nationwide attaches the words exceptions apply to the last two rules without saying what the exceptions are.

key_facts.value: 1% AER / 0.99% gross a year, variable

key_facts.value: £1,500, excluding transfers from other Nationwide accounts and refunds
