sections.heading: What the £295 actually asks of you
sections.html:
The £295 headline is two things bolted together, and only one of them arrives without effort. The £175 is a one-off payment for completing a switch. The £120 is twelve months of two £5 cashback payments, each with its own monthly threshold. Interest sits outside the £295 altogether — Nationwide keeps it out of that figure and publishes a separate maximum of £370 that adds up to £75 of it, which is the honest way round, because the interest depends on your balance and the other two do not.

Put the requirements end to end and the year looks like this. To keep the rewards live you pay in £1,500 a month, which is £18,000 through the account over twelve months. To collect the full £60 of Direct Debit cashback you need £300 a month leaving by Direct Debit, twelve months running — £3,600. To collect the full £60 of card cashback you need £500 a month on the debit card, twelve months running — £6,000. Cashback for both is paid into the FlexDirect on the last day of each month, so a month where the card spend lands at £480 simply pays nothing rather than paying a reduced amount.

None of that is hidden. Nationwide prints every threshold on the product page and repeats them in the 9 September 2026 announcement of the account. What the arithmetic tells you is who it suits: somebody whose salary is comfortably above £1,500 a month and whose everyday spending already runs through a debit card rather than a credit card. If your card spending averages £300 a month, half the cashback is out of reach no matter what else you do, and the account is worth £175 plus £60 plus interest.

sections.heading: Five per cent, capped at £1,500, for twelve months
sections.html:
The rate is the reason most people look at this account, and the cap is the reason to be careful with it. 5% AER applies to balances up to £1,500. Hold exactly £1,500 in the account for a full year and the interest comes to roughly £75. Hold £5,000 and you still earn roughly £75, because the £3,500 above the cap earns the account's standard rate rather than the headline one.

That is worth setting against Bank Rate, which the Bank of England's own series puts at 3.75%, set on 18 December 2025 and unchanged since — the two steps before it were 4.00% on 7 August 2025 and 4.25% on 8 May 2025. A fixed 5% is 1.25 percentage points above that, on a small balance you can spend the same day, which is genuinely above the market for that shape of money — but it is above the market on £1,500, not on your savings. The sensible reading of FlexDirect is that it is a current account with a good rate on the float you keep in it, not a home for a rainy-day fund.

Tax rarely bites at this size. The personal savings allowance lets a basic-rate taxpayer earn £1,000 of interest a year tax-free and a higher-rate taxpayer £500, and £75 sits a long way inside either. Additional-rate taxpayers have no allowance at all, so for them the £75 is taxable — a small point, but the kind that comparison tables usually skip.

sections.heading: Two thresholds for one account, and a third page that still says £200
sections.html:
This is the part of FlexDirect most likely to catch somebody out, and it comes from the offer and the account having been written by different rulebooks. The switch offer terms — document SMD1863, dated May 2026 and still the live version on 8 October 2026 — require you to pay in at least £1,000 within 31 days of the account being opened, make at least one payment with the Nationwide debit card inside the same window, and carry across at least two active Direct Debits, with the switch itself completing within 28 days. The account's own interest and cashback require £1,500 every month.

So it is entirely possible to satisfy the £175 and earn nothing else, by paying in £1,000 in month one and stopping there. The two numbers are published in two different places and neither document mentions the other. If you are switching for the rewards rather than the bonus, the number to plan around is £1,500, not £1,000. The switching page also narrows what counts towards the £1,000: money already sitting in an existing account, a transfer from another Nationwide account — including one that is not in your name — and Visa credits are all excluded.

There is a third document, and it gives a different amount. Nationwide publishes a page of switch offer terms at /current-accounts/help/terms/current-account-online-switch-offer-terms-and-conditions whose clause 11 reads “We'll pay you £200”. Clause 1 dates that offer to 21 September 2023, the switch is allowed 60 days to complete rather than 28, there is no pay-in requirement at all, and the exclusion is anyone who has taken a Nationwide online switch offer since 18 August 2021 rather than since 2021. The page carries no withdrawal notice and no last-updated date. On the same day, the FlexDirect product page, the switch offer landing page and SMD1863 all said £175 on the conditions above. The figure to plan on is the £175, because that is the one on the product page and in the current terms document — but somebody searching for Nationwide's switch offer terms can land on a live Nationwide page promising £200, and that is the society's own page rather than a stale copy on somebody else's site.

One further condition is easy to miss: the FlexDirect must be your first in the last three years. A former FlexDirect customer who closed the account in 2025 is outside the 5% entirely, however long ago they last took it.

And one thing that is often written up as a five-year rule is not one. The £175 is payable once on an eligible sole switch and once on an eligible joint switch since 2021, and Nationwide publishes no date on which that resets. Anyone who has taken a Nationwide current account switch incentive at any point since 2021 is simply outside it, and the announcement's “exceptions apply” is the only qualification offered.

What Nationwide still does not publish, re-checked on 8 October 2026, is what happens in a month you fall short of the £1,500 — whether the interest stops for that month and resumes when the pay-in returns, or whether something more permanent happens to the twelve-month clock. The product page states the requirement and says nothing about the consequence. That needs confirming with Nationwide directly before you rely on it, and it is the one question worth asking on the phone before you switch.

sections.heading: Seven working days, and the people the £175 shuts out
sections.html:
The switch itself runs on the Current Account Switch Service, which the whole industry uses and which does the work for you: allow seven working days, and your Direct Debits, standing orders and incoming payments move across. In the second quarter of 2026, 99.3% of switches completed inside that window. Redirection sends an automatic message back to whoever made the payment so they can update their records. The Current Account Switch Guarantee makes your new provider responsible for anything that goes wrong — any charges or interest you incur on either the old or the new account because of a switching error are refunded, and it is the new bank's decision whether to pay anything beyond that.

The service is busy. Pay.UK recorded 288,999 switches in the second quarter of 2026 and 608,528 across the first half of the year, up 39% on the 439,324 in the first half of 2025, taking the total since the service started in 2013 to 12.9 million. Nationwide has been the main beneficiary by a wide margin: the participant table runs a quarter behind, and for the first quarter of 2026 it gives Nationwide 80,474 switches in and 22,026 out — a net gain of 58,448, the largest of any participant, against 21,894 at Monzo and 8,970 at TSB, and net losses of 20,780 at Barclays, 18,719 at NatWest, 14,368 at HSBC and 10,904 at Chase.

The £175 has a defined guest list. You need to move a full switch from a non-Nationwide and non-Virgin Money account carrying at least two active Direct Debits, complete it within 28 days of the account being opened, and pay in £1,000 and make one debit card payment within 31 days. SMD1863 rules out gambling and crypto transactions, cash withdrawals and money transfers as the qualifying card payment, and the switching page adds loan, lease and mortgage payments to that list. The offer is limited to your first eligible sole switch and your first eligible joint switch since 2021, and it is unavailable to anyone switching from an account already held with Nationwide under a different trading name, Virgin Money included. Payment lands within 10 days of the last condition being met, shows on the statement as Switching Offer, and only one payment is made on a joint switch. Nationwide reserves the right to end, change or replace the offer at any time.

sections.heading: Month thirteen, when the account becomes an ordinary one
sections.html:
Everything good about FlexDirect has a twelve-month fuse. The 5% drops to 1% AER (0.99% gross a year), variable. Both cashback streams stop. The £175 was a one-off. What remains is a fee-free current account paying 1% on up to £1,500, which is £15 a year, and still asking for £1,500 a month to be paid in.

Against a 3.75% Bank Rate, 1% is 2.75 percentage points adrift. That is not unusual for a standard current account — most pay nothing at all — but it does mean the account you hold in month thirteen is a different proposition from the one you switched to, and the switch payment is not available a second time on an eligible sole account to soften it. Anyone treating FlexDirect as a twelve-month product should diarise the anniversary; anyone treating it as a permanent home should judge it on the 1%, the branch network and the service scores rather than on the headline.

sections.heading: Membership, and the £100 that is not part of the £295
sections.html:
Being a building society customer is not purely sentimental here, though it is easy to overstate. Under the Building Societies Act 1986 at least 50% of a society's funding must come from shares held by individual members, and at least 75% of its business assets must be loans secured on residential property — the two rules that keep a society a society rather than a bank, and that the FCA and PRA can enforce under sections 36 and 37 by directing a restructuring plan or, at the far end, a winding-up petition.

The visible dividend of that structure is the Fairer Share Payment. In 2026 Nationwide paid £100 each to around 4.4 million members on 10 June, roughly £440m, taking the total paid since the scheme started in 2023 to about £1.5bn. Note where the bigger numbers in the press coverage come from: the Moneyfacts estimate quoted in Nationwide's own announcement, that FlexDirect could be worth up to £470 in the first year, gets there by adding roughly £75 of interest and an assumed £100 Fairer Share to the £295. Nationwide's wording in the same document is that the Fairer Share is not guaranteed and will depend on how the society performs financially.

The conditions are specific. For the 2026 payment you needed a qualifying current account open on 31 March 2026 and either at least £100 in Nationwide savings or cash ISAs at the end of any day in March 2026, or at least £100 owed on a Nationwide residential mortgage on 31 March 2026. For a FlexDirect, the activity test was, in two of the three months from January to March 2026, either receiving at least £500 and making at least two payments out, or making at least ten payments out. Buy-to-let and commercial mortgages do not count, and neither do Clydesdale or Virgin Money accounts. So a switcher planning on £470 is planning on a board decision that has not been taken.

sections.heading: 39.9% on the other side of zero
sections.html:
FlexDirect's arranged overdraft costs nothing on the first £50 and 39.9% a year, compounded and variable, on everything above it. The representative example is 38.2% APR on an assumed arranged limit of £1,200. That is at the expensive end of the high street, and it is not a hangover from the old days of daily fees — it is what the market settled at after the FCA's overdraft rules landed.

Those rules, from PS19/16, banned fixed daily and monthly fees, stopped firms charging more for unarranged borrowing than arranged, forced a single annual interest rate and required a representative APR. The FCA calculated in April 2023 that the reforms saved consumers close to £1bn — more than £500m from the pricing rules alone, an average of £17.40 per customer with overdraft access during 2021, and £153m in the most deprived areas. The side effect was headline rates in the high thirties and low forties where they had previously been buried in fees.

On a £1,000 arranged overdraft held for a full year, 39.9% is about £399 of interest, which dwarfs anything the account pays out on the credit side. The two published rates are worth reconciling, because the gap between them is the only thing the free slice buys you: apply 39.9% to the £1,150 that is actually charged on a £1,200 limit and you land on 38.2%, which is the representative APR to the decimal. The £50 buffer is useful for a mistimed Direct Debit and no use at all for genuine borrowing — on £1,000 it is worth about £20 a year.

sections.heading: The numbers Nationwide publishes about itself that are less comfortable
sections.html:
Two sets of figures sit awkwardly beside the customer-satisfaction awards, and both come from official sources rather than opinion.

The first is complaints. In its own regulatory return for 1 October 2025 to 31 March 2026 — still the most recent one published on 8 October 2026 — Nationwide Building Society opened 93,640 complaints across banking and credit cards, a rate of 2.24 per 1,000 banking accounts, and upheld 55.13% of the ones it closed. Just over half, 54.78%, were resolved inside three days. Home finance ran to 6,915 complaints, 3.57 per 1,000 accounts, with 56.36% upheld. General administration and customer service was the largest single driver in every category. An uphold rate above 50% is not in itself damning — it partly reflects a firm settling readily rather than arguing — but 93,640 complaints in six months is a large number by any reading.

The second is the fine. On 11 December 2025 the FCA published a final notice imposing a penalty of £44,078,500 on Nationwide for breaching Principle 3 and SYSC 6.1.1R and 6.3.1R between 1 October 2016 and 1 July 2021, after failures in its anti-money-laundering systems. The notice records a customer risk assessment that flagged only around 2,000 customers as high risk out of 18 million, no systematic process for refreshing customer due diligence, transaction monitoring run in monthly batches, and personal current accounts used for business activity in breach of Nationwide's own terms. In one case a customer fraudulently obtained £27.36m in Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme money, of which £820,687 was never recovered. The penalty already reflects a 30% settlement discount. The conduct is historic and the systems have been rebuilt since, but it is the largest single fact on this page that Nationwide's marketing does not mention.

A third point is structural rather than critical. Since the Virgin Money business legally transferred into Nationwide on 2 April 2026, money held with both brands sits under a single FSCS limit rather than two. That limit rose from £85,000 to £120,000 on 1 December 2025 (and from £1m to £1.4m for temporary high balances), so most people gained rather than lost — but anyone who deliberately spread savings across Nationwide and Virgin Money to double their protection no longer has it.

sections.heading: Who is on the hook, and where a complaint goes
sections.html:
Nationwide Building Society is authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by both the Financial Conduct Authority and the PRA under firm reference number 106078. It is on the FCA's Mutuals Public Register as well as the Financial Services Register. Deposits are covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme up to £120,000 per eligible person, or £240,000 on a joint account, across all Nationwide and Virgin Money holdings combined.

Complaints go to Nationwide first. If the society has not resolved matters within eight weeks, or issues a final response you disagree with, the Financial Ombudsman Service will consider the case free of charge, and its decisions bind the firm if you accept them. Nationwide's own data shows 44.70% of banking complaints taking between three days and eight weeks to close, so the eight-week clock is a live consideration rather than a formality.

On service, the independent benchmark is the survey the Competition and Markets Authority requires every large provider to publish. Ipsos surveyed 17,055 people between July 2025 and June 2026, around 1,000 customers of each of the 17 largest personal current account providers, and the results published in August 2026 put Nationwide joint third for overall service quality in Great Britain on 75%, level with first direct and behind Monzo on 79% and Starling on 76%. For a provider still running 605 branches, third out of seventeen against two app-only banks is a strong showing.

pros: 5% AER fixed for twelve months on up to £1,500, 1.25 percentage points above the 3.75% Bank Rate, on money you can spend the same day
£175 for switching, paid within 10 days of meeting the conditions, with no monthly account fee at any point
Up to £120 of cashback in year one for spending you were probably doing anyway, and Nationwide publishes every threshold
Joint third of 17 providers for overall service quality in the Ipsos survey published August 2026, on 75%
Top of the UK Customer Satisfaction Index in July 2026 on 87.3 out of 100, against a 78.3 all-sector average
696 branches — 605 Nationwide and 91 Virgin Money — committed to stay open until at least 2030, when other banks were closing more than 240 in 2026
A mutual with a 19.1% CET1 ratio that paid £100 each to about 4.4 million members in June 2026
cons: Everything worth having expires after twelve months: the rate falls to 1% AER, both cashback streams stop, and the £175 was a one-off
The £1,500 monthly pay-in is a high bar for an account that pays interest on a maximum of £1,500 — £18,000 through the account to earn about £75
Two different pay-in thresholds apply: £1,000 within 31 days for the £175, £1,500 every month for the rewards, published in separate documents that do not cross-reference

Nationwide still publishes a page of switch offer terms promising £200 on a 60-day switch with no pay-in, dated 21 September 2023, alongside the £175 terms in SMD1863 (May 2026) — with no withdrawal notice on the older page
Nationwide does not publish what happens if you miss the £1,500 in a given month, so the consequence needs confirming directly before you rely on the account
The arranged overdraft costs 39.9% a year compounded above the first £50 — about £399 on £1,000 held for a year

The £175 excludes anyone who has taken a Nationwide switch incentive since 2021, with no published date on which that resets, and anyone switching from Virgin Money, which has been part of Nationwide since 2 April 2026
You cannot have held a FlexDirect in the last three years, which shuts out every previous holder of the 5%
The FCA fined Nationwide £44,078,500 on 11 December 2025 over anti-money-laundering control failures between October 2016 and July 2021
Nationwide opened 93,640 banking and credit card complaints in the six months to 31 March 2026 and upheld 55.13% of those it closed
Nationwide and Virgin Money deposits now share one £120,000 FSCS limit rather than two
verdict: FlexDirect in its 9 September 2026 form is a well-built twelve-month account with an honest set of published thresholds and an unusually strong service record behind it, and every money figure on it was confirmed unchanged on 8 October 2026. If £1,500 a month lands in your account anyway, you spend £500 a month on a debit card and you have not taken a Nationwide switch incentive since 2021, £295 plus about £75 of interest is a straightforward return for filling in a switch form. If any of those three is untrue, the value falls quickly, and the account you are left with in month thirteen pays 1% on £1,500. Treat it as a year-long product with a diary reminder attached rather than a permanent home for savings, plan on the £175 rather than the £200 that one of Nationwide's own terms pages still advertises, ask what happens in a month you miss the £1,500 before you commit, and keep well clear of the 39.9% overdraft.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay in £1,500 a month, or is it £1,000?
faqs.a: Both numbers are real and they do different jobs. The £175 switch offer requires £1,000 paid in within 31 days of the account being opened, plus one qualifying debit card payment and two active Direct Debits carried across, with the switch completing inside 28 days. The account's own interest and cashback require at least £1,500 every month, and transfers from your other Nationwide accounts and refunds do not count towards it. Meeting the £1,000 gets you the bonus and nothing else.

faqs.q: Why does one Nationwide page say the switch offer is £200?
faqs.a: Because an older set of terms is still published. The live offer on the FlexDirect product page, on the switch offer page and in document SMD1863 (May 2026) is £175, on a 28-day switch with £1,000 paid in within 31 days. A separate terms page on nationwide.co.uk still sets out a £200 offer dated 21 September 2023, with 60 days to switch and no pay-in requirement, and carries no notice that it has been withdrawn. Plan on the £175 — that is the figure in the current terms document and on the product page.

faqs.q: How much interest will I actually earn?
faqs.a: About £75 over twelve months if you keep £1,500 in the account throughout. The 5% AER applies only to balances up to £1,500, so a larger balance does not earn more at the headline rate. Nationwide's own announcement puts the maximum first-year value at £370 on that basis — £175 plus £120 plus up to £75. For a basic-rate taxpayer the interest sits well inside the £1,000 personal savings allowance; additional-rate taxpayers have no allowance and would pay tax on it.

faqs.q: What happens after the first twelve months?
faqs.a: The rate falls to 1% AER (0.99% gross a year), variable, still capped at £1,500 — around £15 a year. Both £5 cashback payments stop. The £1,500 monthly pay-in requirement remains. Against a Bank Rate of 3.75%, set on 18 December 2025, the account becomes a fee-free everyday account rather than a rewarding one.

faqs.q: Can I get the £175 if I already bank with Nationwide or Virgin Money?
faqs.a: Not if you are switching from an account already held with Nationwide, and that now includes Virgin Money, whose business transferred into Nationwide on 2 April 2026. Existing Nationwide customers can qualify by switching in an account held elsewhere, provided it is their first eligible sole switch since 2021. The FlexDirect itself must also be your first in the last three years.

faqs.q: Is my money safe with a building society rather than a bank?
faqs.a: The protection is identical. Nationwide is authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA and PRA under firm reference number 106078, and deposits are covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme up to £120,000 per eligible person and £240,000 on a joint account — a limit that rose from £85,000 on 1 December 2025. The one thing to watch is that Nationwide and Virgin Money balances now count towards a single £120,000 limit rather than two separate ones.

faqs.q: Will I get the £100 Fairer Share payment as well?
faqs.a: Possibly, but it is not part of the £295 and it is not promised. The 2026 payment went to around 4.4 million members on 10 June and required a qualifying current account open on 31 March 2026 plus either £100 in Nationwide savings or £100 owed on a Nationwide residential mortgage. Nationwide's own wording is that the payment is not guaranteed and will depend on how the society performs financially.

title: Nationwide Mortgage Deals: 4.99% Fixed, a 4.09% Tracker and Six Times Income
meta_title: Nationwide Mortgages: 4.09% Tracker, 4.99% Fixed, 6x Income
meta_description: Nationwide's cheapest fix is 4.99% with a £1,499 fee and its two-year tracker 4.09%, with lending to six times income. Checked 10 October 2026.
intro:
Nationwide's cheapest fixed rate is 4.99%, on a two-year fix to 60% loan-to-value carrying a £1,499 product fee and a minimum loan of £300,000, and its cheapest two-year tracker is 4.09% — Bank Rate plus 0.34 points. Both figures are taken from Nationwide's own intermediary product guide, effective 30 September 2026 and read on 10 October 2026.

It is the biggest building society in the country and, on its own audited numbers for the year to 31 March 2026, the second-biggest mortgage lender: £286.3 billion of mortgage balances at a 16.3% share of the market, and £45.8 billion of new lending in twelve months at a 15.6% share. Arrears are low — 0.39% of residential accounts were more than three months behind — and it keeps 605 branches open under a Branch Promise now extended to 2030. It also publishes a dated product guide and an archive of every rate sheet it has issued since December 2023, which is more than most lenders will let a borrower see.

The thing that separates Nationwide from most of its rivals is not the rate. It is how much it will lend against a given income: six times for buyers, movers and remortgage customers, and six and a half on a like-for-like remortgage. The rate itself has been moving — Nationwide repriced on 18 and 24 August and on 10, 15 and 30 September 2026, and the direction since mid-August has been upward, so a 4.48% figure quoted anywhere else has been superseded.

sections.heading: Six times income, and the rule change that let Nationwide do it
sections.html:
Nationwide's own standard criteria stop at 4.49 times income. Its Helping Hand mortgage goes to six, which on a £30,000 salary is the difference between £134,700 and £180,000 — roughly £45,000 of extra borrowing from the same payslip. Nationwide's own worked examples put a single buyer on £30,000 at £180,000 against £225,000 for a couple on £50,000 without the product and £300,000 with it. It says Helping Hand helped over 17,000 customers onto the ladder during 2025.

The conditions are specific. You must be a first-time buyer, which Nationwide defines as not having had a mortgage in the last three years, and on a joint application both of you must qualify; you need at least a 5% deposit; and you have to take a five or ten-year fix. The five-year version runs to 95% LTV and the ten-year stops at 90%. Minimum income is £30,000 sole and £50,000 joint, cut from £35,000 and £55,000 on 15 July 2025. Self-employed income does not count towards it, and anyone buying through shared ownership or Right to Buy is excluded.

On 21 January 2026 Nationwide extended six times income beyond first-time buyers, to home movers and to remortgage customers borrowing more, at up to 95% LTV. That release set the entry price at £75,000 of income for a sole applicant and £100,000 for a joint one. The joint figure has since come down. Nationwide's current affordability criteria say the requirement is to "have an eligible income of £75,000 or more for both sole and joint applicants", a change its intermediary site dates to 16 July 2026, so a couple now needs £25,000 less between them than the January announcement demanded. Existing Nationwide members moving home face no minimum income at all — the criteria give the example of a £50,000 earner borrowing £300,000. And unlike Helping Hand, this route states plainly that "clients who are self employed are also eligible to borrow up to six times income".

The full ladder, as Nationwide publishes it, is worth reading as a whole: 6x on Helping Hand, 6x on a purchase or remortgage with extra borrowing where the income test is met, 6x for existing customers, 6.5x on a like-for-like remortgage (5.5x where the loan is interest-only), 4.75x on a further advance, 4.49x on standard lending and 4.49x on Equity Share. Six and a half times a £50,000 joint income is £325,000. Nationwide is careful to say these are ceilings rather than offers: they "represent the maximum possible amounts" and remain "subject to a Decision in Principle".

None of it was possible until the Financial Policy Committee moved in July 2025. The governing rule is the loan-to-income flow limit, which caps lending at 4.5 times income or above to 15% of a lender's new mortgages. The FPC recommended letting individual lenders exceed their own 15% while the market total held at 15%, on the reasoning that uneven use of the cap was keeping creditworthy households out. The Prudential Regulation Authority then consulted on removing the firm-level limit altogether in CP6/26, published on 1 April 2026 and closed on 1 July 2026, keeping the 15% aggregate and exempting firms with under £150 million of lending or fewer than 300 regulated mortgages.

Henry Jordan, Nationwide's Group Director of Mortgages, called the changes "a game changer for first-time buyers" and said the society had seen "a five-fold increase in the number of first-time buyers borrowing between 5.5 and six times income". A separate change on 15 May 2025 cut affordability stress rates by 0.75 to 1.25 percentage points, which Nationwide said let applicants borrow an average of £28,000 more.

sections.heading: Five repricings in six weeks, and where that leaves the rate
sections.html:
Nationwide changes its mortgage rates often, and it leaves a paper trail that makes the movement measurable rather than anecdotal. Its intermediary product guide carries an effective date on the front page and a document reference in the footer, and every superseded guide stays online with the dates it was valid between.

Follow one product through that archive and the picture is plain. The guide marked F6 (18.08.2026) priced the two-year fix for home movers at up to 60% LTV at 4.48% with a £1,499 fee on loans of £300,000 to £5 million, product code 205931. The current guide, F6 (30.09.2026), prices the same slot at 4.99% on the same fee and the same loan band, product code 207216. That is 0.51 percentage points in six weeks, or about £88 a month on a £300,000 loan over 25 years, and Bank Rate did not move in between: it has been 3.75% throughout, held again on 17 September 2026 with the next decision due on 5 November.

The archive dates the steps as well as the total. Nationwide's rate sheets ran from 4 August to 17 August, then 18 to 23 August, 24 August to 9 September, 10 to 14 September, 15 to 29 September, and from 30 September to now — five repricings in the period, announced to brokers on 17 August, 23 August, 9 September, 14 September and 29 September.

What the current guide gives a first-time buyer with a 5% deposit, at 90.01% to 95% LTV: a five-year fix at 5.64% with a £1,499 fee, 5.69% with a £999 fee or 5.74% with no fee, and a two-year fix at 5.79% with a £999 fee or 5.89% fee-free. At 60% LTV the same buyer pays 5.05% on a five-year fix with the larger fee and 5.54% on a two-year with none. A home mover at 85.01% to 90% pays 5.26% over five years with a £1,499 fee. The spread between the 60% and the 95% rate is roughly 0.6 to 0.7 percentage points, which is the price of a small deposit stated plainly.

Carlo Pileggi, Head of Mortgage Products, said in August that the cuts then brought "our lowest mortgage rate back below 4.5 per cent for new and existing borrowers moving home". That was accurate on the day and is no longer true of the range. The wider market has cooled with it: Nationwide's own house price index for September 2026, published on 2 October, put annual growth at 0.8%, halved from 1.6% in August, with prices down 0.2% on the month and the average house at £274,251. Robert Gardner, Nationwide's Chief Economist, called it "the weakest rate of growth since December 2025".

First-time buyers get £500 cashback paid within a month of completion — £500 per mortgage, not per applicant — with £250 to £500 more available through the Green Reward on an energy-efficient property. The stamp duty position in England and Northern Ireland is unchanged: nothing to £300,000, 5% from £300,001 to £500,000, and no first-time buyer relief at all above £500,000.

sections.heading: The fee tiers do not overlap, and one pound decides which one you get
sections.html:
Nationwide prices most fixed products three ways: a £1,499 fee, a £999 fee and no fee at all. The rate falls as the fee rises, which is ordinary. What is not ordinary is that the two fee-paying tiers are mutually exclusive by loan size. The £999 product at up to 60% LTV runs from £25,000 to £299,999. The £1,499 product at the same LTV runs from £300,000 to £5 million. There is no overlap, so the borrower never chooses between them — the size of the loan chooses.

Run the two-year numbers over a 25-year term and the boundary does something odd. At £299,999 a home mover takes 5.04% with a £999 fee: £1,760.76 a month, and £30,640 of true cost across the two years once the capital repaid is netted off. At £300,000 the same borrower is on 4.99% with a £1,499 fee: £1,752.02 a month, which looks better, and £30,842 of true cost, which is £202 worse. The extra pound of borrowing costs £201.78, because the 0.05-point rate cut does not pay for the extra £500 of fee.

The decision that does exist is fee against no fee, and it turns on size. The fee-free two-year at 60% LTV is 5.29% and is available from £25,000 to £5 million. On a £150,000 loan the £999 product costs £253 more over the two years than paying nothing and 5.29%. On £250,000 it saves £245. The crossover sits at roughly £200,800: below that the fee-free rate wins, above it the fee pays for itself. Spread across 24 payments, £1,499 is £62.46 a month and £999 is £41.63 — which is why the headline rate on its own tells a borrower under £200,000 almost nothing useful.

Maximum loan size also tightens as the deposit shrinks: £5 million to 75% LTV, £2 million from 75.01% to 85%, £1 million from 85.01% to 90% and £750,000 from 90.01% to 95%.

sections.heading: A tracker that undercuts every fix Nationwide sells
sections.html:
The cheapest way into a Nationwide mortgage in October 2026 is not a fixed rate. A home mover at up to 60% LTV can take a two-year tracker at Bank Rate plus 0.34%, which with Bank Rate at 3.75% is 4.09%, on a £999 fee and loans of £25,000 to £5 million. The fee-free version is Bank Rate plus 0.99%, or 4.74%. The cheapest fix in the same band is 4.99%.

On a £300,000 loan over 25 years that gap is £153.57 a month, or £1,843 a year, in the tracker's favour at today's Bank Rate. Two further features make it more attractive than the rate alone suggests. Nationwide states in the guide that "ERCs don't currently apply to tracker rate products", so there is no charge for leaving — a fixed-rate borrower in year one of a five-year deal pays 5%. And all tracker mortgages reserved on or after 2 May 2014 can be overpaid without limit, against the 10% a year allowed on a fix.

The catch is the obvious one and it deserves saying flatly: the rate moves with Bank Rate, there is no ceiling on it, and a borrower who takes 4.09% is betting that Bank Rate does not climb 0.90 points inside two years. The Monetary Policy Committee held at 3.75% on 17 September 2026 and reports again on 5 November. Nobody should read a tracker as a cheaper fix; it is a different product with the risk moved onto the borrower.

One more rate in the guide is worth knowing about because it is not a mortgage deal so much as a grant with repayments. Green Additional Borrowing is priced at 0% over two or five years, with no product fee, on amounts from £5,000 to £20,000 and up to 90% LTV. The condition is absolute: "you must use 100% of what you borrow for 'green purchases'", which Nationwide gives as solar panels, boiler upgrades or insulation. An existing borrower funding insulation out of a further advance at 4.75 times income should check this first.

sections.heading: Two reversion rates, and the 2009 line that decides which one you get
sections.html:
When a Nationwide fix ends the borrower moves to one of two variable rates, and the difference between them is real money. The Standard Mortgage Rate is 6.49% and the Base Mortgage Rate is 5.75%, both effective from 1 January 2026 and both unchanged since.

The BMR carries a promise: it "is guaranteed to be no more than 2% above the Bank of England base rate". With Bank Rate at 3.75% the BMR is sitting exactly on its ceiling. The SMR carries no such promise — Nationwide's own words are that it "has no upper limit or cap" — and at 6.49% it stands 2.74 points above Bank Rate.

Which rate you land on was settled years ago. Nationwide borrowers who reserved on or before 29 April 2009 are on the BMR, as are all former Portman customers, Cheshire members from before 15 June 2009 and Derbyshire members from before 31 May 2009. Anyone who reserved on or after 30 April 2009, every former Dunfermline customer, and anyone who switches to a new mortgage product goes to the SMR. That last clause is the one to read twice: taking a new deal from Nationwide moves a capped BMR borrower permanently onto the uncapped rate.

The size of the gap is the argument against drifting. A Helping Hand borrower on £180,000 over 30 years pays about £1,044 a month on the current 5.69% five-year fix at 95% LTV and £1,137 on the SMR — £93 a month, or £1,116 a year, for doing nothing at the end of a deal. On the older rates that gap was wider; rising fixes have narrowed it, which makes the end-of-deal letter easier to ignore and no less expensive.

sections.heading: Switching deal without advice, and the four-month window
sections.html:
Existing borrowers can take a new Nationwide deal through Mortgage Manager once they have fewer than four months left on a fixed rate; do it earlier and an early repayment charge applies. Borrowers already on a tracker, the SMR or the BMR can switch at any time. Retirement mortgage holders are restricted to the last three months of the deal and cannot do it online at all.

Two features of that route deserve stating together. Nationwide says there is "no affordability check when you switch deal", which is a genuine advantage for anyone whose income has fallen, whose circumstances have changed, or who has gone self-employed since they borrowed. It also says the online journey is execution-only: you must be "comfortable choosing a new rate without any advice". No affordability test and no advice is a fast, cheap route for someone who knows what they want, and nobody at all checking the choice for someone who does not. Free phone and video appointments with an adviser are available for that reason.

The pricing promise is that switcher rates are "as good as, or better than, those available to new customers remortgaging to us", and the 30 September figures bear it out by a wider margin than they did in the summer. A rate switch at up to 60% LTV with a £999 fee is 4.89% over two or three years and 4.97% over five. A new remortgage customer at the same LTV and fee pays 5.09% over two years and 5.11% over five. The existing member is 0.20 and 0.14 points ahead. At 90.01% to 95% LTV the switcher pays 5.69% over two years and 5.64% over five, against 5.74% and 5.69% for a new remortgage. That is the reverse of the loyalty penalty this market was criticised for, and Nationwide deserves the credit for publishing both sets in the same document.

One practical detail has gone missing. Nationwide's switching page used to publish the deadline for cancelling a switch; it now says only that the cancellation deadline sits inside Mortgage Manager, so a borrower cannot find out when it falls without logging in. The other warning in its own guide still stands: "If you want to switch and borrow more at the same time, you could end up paying more if you apply online. Please call us for advice."

sections.heading: Getting out early, and the 10% you are allowed first
sections.html:
Overpayments are generous by the standards of the market. Products reserved from 29 May 2013 allow 10% a year of the original loan amount with no charge; all tracker mortgages reserved from 2 May 2014 are unlimited, as are the SMR and BMR; older products from 1 February 2001 to 28 May 2013 run on a £500 a month allowance instead. Note the base: 10% of the original advance, not of the current balance, which on a loan you have been paying down for years is the more useful of the two definitions. On a £180,000 Helping Hand loan that is £18,000 a year.

Go beyond it and the early repayment charge lands. Nationwide's published ladder is 2% in year one and 1% in year two on a two-year fix; 3%, 2% then 1% across a three-year fix; 5% falling a point a year to 1% across a five-year fix; and 6% for each of the first five years of a ten-year fix, tapering a point a year to 1% by year ten. On a £180,000 loan that is £9,000 to leave a five-year fix in its first year and £10,800 to leave a ten-year one — which is the price of the six-times-income deal if life changes, because Helping Hand is only sold on those two terms. Borrowers who reserved before 13 September 2024 are a separate case: for them Nationwide says only that "ERC details can be found in their mortgage offer", so the published ladder cannot be relied on and the offer document has to be read.

The other charges are modest and published: £20 for a telegraphic transfer at completion, up to £100 plus VAT for a home visit if the account falls into arrears, and £65 for unpaid ground rent. Nationwide charges nothing for an unpaid cheque or an unpaid direct debit, which many lenders still do, and remortgage products include free standard legal work. The minimum it will lend at all is £10,000 except for home improvements.

sections.heading: The size of the lender behind the rate
sections.html:
For the year to 31 March 2026, Nationwide reported £45.8 billion of gross mortgage lending, a 15.6% share of all new lending, and £286.3 billion of balances at a 16.3% share. Total assets were £382.3 billion, underlying profit before tax £2,026 million, statutory profit before tax £1,490 million, and the CET1 capital ratio 19.1%. Arrears of more than three months stood at 0.39% of residential accounts, against a market figure of 1.1% of balances in the Bank of England's Q2 2026 statistics.

The mutual structure shows up in what it gave back: £1.8 billion of member value including a third Fairer Share payment of £0.4 billion, and £1.4 billion of member financial benefit through pricing, down from £1.8 billion the year before. It completed the Part VII transfer of most of Virgin Money's business on 2 April 2026, described in its own results as the largest non-ring-fencing banking business transfer ever made in the UK, and runs 605 Nationwide branches alongside 91 Virgin Money ones.

One number in those results runs against the direction of everything above. Nationwide helped 88,000 first-time buyers into a home in the year to March 2026, against 120,000 the year before — a fall of 26.7% in the same period it was loosening stress rates and extending six-times lending. The wider market moved the other way: Bank of England figures published on 8 September 2026 put gross advances at £77.4 billion in Q2 2026, up 31.7% on the year, with lending above 90% LTV at 8.4%, the highest share since 2008 Q2, and lending at 4.5 times income or more at 46.0% of advances. Nationwide has not explained the gap, and it is a fair question to put to it.

sections.heading: What the complaints return admits, and what it does not
sections.html:
Nationwide publishes its own complaints data every six months, broken down by product, and the latest return still covers 1 October 2025 to 31 March 2026. Home finance — the mortgage line — recorded 6,915 complaints opened at 3.57 per 1,000 accounts. 29.18% were closed within three days and a further 69.96% after three days but within eight weeks, which puts 99.14% inside the eight-week deadline. 56.36% were upheld, and the leading cause was general administration and customer service.

Two readings of that. More than half of mortgage complaints being upheld means most of the people who complained had a point, which is an argument for complaining rather than a reason not to borrow. And fewer than three in ten closing inside three days means a mortgage complaint here is usually not a quick phone call, even though almost all of them are resolved before the regulatory clock runs out.

The same return covers The Mortgage Works separately, and the comparison is useful: 1,477 complaints at 5.19 per 1,000 accounts, 26.64% closed in three days, 72.62% after three days but within eight weeks and 52.08% upheld. The buy-to-let arm generates complaints at almost half as much again per account as the residential book.

A complaint not resolved within eight weeks can go to the Financial Ombudsman Service. For completeness on the regulatory record, the FCA fined Nationwide £44,078,500 on 11 December 2025 over anti-money-laundering control failures between October 2016 and July 2021. That penalty concerns financial crime systems rather than mortgage lending, and reading it as a comment on the mortgage book would be wrong.

sections.heading: Buy-to-let is written by a different company
sections.html:
A landlord searching for a Nationwide buy-to-let mortgage will not find one under that name. Buy-to-let is written by The Mortgage Works, part of the Nationwide group, with its own criteria, its own products and, as the complaints table above shows, its own service record.

Those criteria moved on 3 September 2026. The maximum age at application for a first-time landlord rose from 70 to 75 for lending up to 70% LTV, and experienced landlords applying up to the same 70% now face no maximum age at all. Maximum total borrowing across the whole Nationwide group went from £7.5 million to £10 million, and TMW began accepting purchases of existing buy-to-let properties from family members. Dan Clinton, its Head of Buy-to-Let Mortgages, framed it as lending criteria evolving with landlords' circumstances.

The market context cuts the other way. Buy-to-let was 8.0% of gross advances in Q2 2026 on Bank of England figures, the lowest share since 2024 Q3 and down 1.2 points on the year. Loosening age and borrowing limits into a shrinking share of the market is a bid for the landlords who are still buying, not a sign that many are.

Residential lending into later life is tighter than the buy-to-let arm's. Nationwide's own borrower criteria put the maximum retirement age it will accept at 70, and require the mortgage term to end before the oldest applicant's 75th birthday.

pros: Six times income for first-time buyers, home movers and remortgage customers, and 6.5 times on a like-for-like remortgage — well beyond the 4.49 times its own standard criteria allow
The six-times route for movers and remortgage is open to self-employed applicants, which the first-time buyer version is not
A two-year tracker at 4.09% sits 0.90 points below the cheapest fix in the range, carries no early repayment charge at all, and can be overpaid without limit
Switcher rates are demonstrably better than new-customer remortgage rates: 4.89% against 5.09% on the two-year 60% LTV product with a £999 fee on 30 September 2026
No affordability check when an existing borrower moves to a new deal, which matters if income has dropped or work has become self-employed
Green Additional Borrowing at 0% on £5,000 to £20,000 over two or five years with no product fee, where every pound goes on energy-efficient work
10% of the original loan amount can be overpaid each year with no charge, and tracker, SMR and BMR borrowers can overpay without limit
£500 cashback for first-time buyers, up to £500 more on an energy-efficient property, and free standard legal work on remortgages
Every rate sheet since December 2023 is published and dated, so any figure on this page can be checked against the document that set it
cons: Fixed rates have risen while Bank Rate has not: the same two-year 60% LTV home mover product went from 4.48% on 18 August 2026 to 4.99% on 30 September, 0.51 points in six weeks, across five repricings

The September increases were published only to brokers. Nationwide's consumer newsroom carried rate releases on 3 and 17 August 2026, both headed as cuts, and has published nothing about mortgage rates since — while the intermediary site announced changes on 9, 14 and 29 September
The 4.99% headline needs 40% equity and a loan of at least £300,000, and the fee tiers do not overlap, so borrowing £300,000 rather than £299,999 costs £202 more over the two years

The only rate tables a reader can actually read are the intermediary ones, marked "For Intermediary use only. Under no circumstances should this communication be given, copied or distributed to customers"; the consumer rate finder will not load its figures at all

The Standard Mortgage Rate of 6.49% has no cap of any kind, sits 2.74 points above Bank Rate, and is where every new borrower ends up — taking any new Nationwide deal moves a capped BMR borrower onto it permanently
Early repayment charges on the long fixes Helping Hand requires are severe: 6% for each of the first five years of a ten-year fix, which is £10,800 on a £180,000 loan
Helping Hand ignores self-employed income and excludes shared ownership and Right to Buy, so the first-time buyer version of six-times lending is closed to two large groups
56.36% of the 6,915 home finance complaints opened in the six months to 31 March 2026 were upheld, and fewer than three in ten were closed within three days
Nationwide helped 88,000 first-time buyers in the year to March 2026 against 120,000 the year before, a 26.7% fall it has not explained, in a market where gross lending rose 31.7% year on year
The deadline for cancelling a product switch is no longer published anywhere on the switching page — it can only be seen inside Mortgage Manager
verdict: Nationwide is worth a quote for one reason above all others: it will lend more against the same income than almost anyone else, six times for buyers, movers and remortgage customers and six and a half on a like-for-like remortgage, at up to 95% loan-to-value, against the 4.49 times its own standard criteria allow. If the obstacle is affordability rather than deposit, that is the difference between buying and not. The rates are no longer the draw — the cheapest fix is 4.99% at 60% LTV with a £1,499 fee and a £300,000 floor, and a first-time buyer with a 5% deposit is paying 5.69% to 5.89% — but the two-year tracker at 4.09% with no early repayment charge is the most interesting number in the range, and existing members switching deal are priced 0.20 points better than new remortgage customers. The three things to hold in mind are the 6.49% uncapped Standard Mortgage Rate waiting at the end of every deal, the early repayment charges on the five and ten-year fixes the six-times product obliges you to take, and the direction of travel: this range has been repriced five times in six weeks and every move since mid-August has been upward, so check the figure on the day.

faqs.q: What is Nationwide's cheapest mortgage rate?
faqs.a: On the product guide effective 30 September 2026, the cheapest fixed rate is 4.99% — a two-year fix for home movers at up to 60% LTV, with a £1,499 product fee and a minimum loan of £300,000. Below £300,000 the equivalent two-year is 5.04% with a £999 fee, or 5.29% with no fee. The cheapest rate in the range overall is the two-year tracker at 4.09%, which is Bank Rate plus 0.34% with a £999 fee.

faqs.q: How much will Nationwide lend me?
faqs.a: Up to six times income for first-time buyers through Helping Hand, and since 21 January 2026 for home movers and remortgage customers borrowing more. A like-for-like remortgage can go to 6.5 times, or 5.5 times on interest-only. First-time buyers need £30,000 sole or £50,000 joint income; new borrowers using the mover and remortgage route need £75,000 whether applying alone or jointly, while existing members have no minimum. Standard lending is 4.49 times, so on a £30,000 salary the difference is £134,700 against £180,000.

faqs.q: Have Nationwide's mortgage rates gone up or down recently?
faqs.a: Up, since the middle of August 2026. The two-year fix for home movers at up to 60% LTV with a £1,499 fee was 4.48% on the guide effective 18 August and is 4.99% on the guide effective 30 September — 0.51 percentage points across five repricings, with Bank Rate unchanged at 3.75% throughout. Nationwide keeps every superseded rate sheet on its intermediary site, so the movement can be checked product by product.

faqs.q: What rate will I move to when my fixed deal ends?
faqs.a: Almost certainly the Standard Mortgage Rate, which is 6.49% and has been since 1 January 2026. It has no cap. The older Base Mortgage Rate of 5.75% is guaranteed never to exceed Bank Rate plus 2%, but it is closed to anyone who reserved on or after 30 April 2009 and is lost permanently if a BMR borrower takes a new Nationwide product.

faqs.q: Is a Nationwide tracker cheaper than a fix?
faqs.a: At today's Bank Rate, yes, and by a wide margin. The two-year tracker at up to 60% LTV is Bank Rate plus 0.34%, or 4.09%, against 4.99% on the cheapest two-year fix — about £154 a month on a £300,000 loan over 25 years. Trackers also carry no early repayment charge and, where reserved on or after 2 May 2014, can be overpaid without limit. The rate moves with Bank Rate and has no ceiling, so the saving is not guaranteed for the two years.

faqs.q: Can I overpay without being charged?
faqs.a: Yes, up to 10% a year of the original loan amount on any product reserved from 29 May 2013 — £18,000 a year on a £180,000 loan. Tracker mortgages reserved from 2 May 2014, and anything sitting on the SMR or BMR, can be overpaid without limit. Products from 1 February 2001 to 28 May 2013 are capped at £500 a month instead.

faqs.q: When can I switch to a new Nationwide deal?
faqs.a: Once there are fewer than four months left on a fixed rate, or at any time from a tracker, the SMR or the BMR. There is no affordability check, and the online route through Mortgage Manager is execution-only with no advice given. Switcher pricing is better than new-customer remortgage pricing — 4.89% against 5.09% on the two-year 60% LTV product with a £999 fee — but the cancellation deadline is only shown inside Mortgage Manager, and Nationwide advises phoning rather than applying online if you want to borrow more at the same time.

faqs.q: Does Nationwide do buy-to-let mortgages?
faqs.a: Not under the Nationwide name. Buy-to-let is written by The Mortgage Works, a Nationwide group company. From 3 September 2026 its maximum age at application for a first-time landlord rose from 70 to 75 at up to 70% LTV, experienced landlords lending to that level face no maximum age, and maximum total group borrowing rose from £7.5 million to £10 million.

title: NatWest Credit Cards: Eight Cards, from 12.9% to 40.7% APR
meta_title: NatWest Credit Cards: 0% for 36 Months and a 12.9% Card
meta_description: NatWest publishes eight credit cards, from a 12.9% APR card with no transfer fee to 36 months at 0%. The rates, the fees, and what the APR actually includes.

headline.label: Representative APR
headline.value: 12.9% to 40.7% variable across eight cards, all quoted on an assumed £1,200 credit limit

intro:
NatWest's cheapest credit card charges 12.9% representative APR with no annual fee and no balance transfer fee, and its longest 0% deal runs to 36 months for a 3.10% fee. Every rate on this page was re-read on 9 October 2026 against NatWest's own product pages and summary boxes, and none of the eight headline rates had moved since September. National Westminster Bank Plc appears on the Financial Services Register under firm reference number 121878, and its parent, NatWest Group, reported £8.7 billion of income, up 8.9%, and £4.3 billion of operating profit for the six months to 30 June 2026, serving more than 20 million customers. Six of the eight cards carry no annual fee at all, every one shows a representative example on its own product page against an assumed £1,200 credit limit, and the published representative APRs span 12.9% to 40.7% — a range wide enough that picking the wrong card in the same bank's own line-up costs more than picking the wrong bank.

The cheapest is the plainest. The NatWest Credit Card carries a 12.9% representative APR, no annual fee, no balance transfer fee, and it charges transferred balances the same 12.9% rather than parking them on a promotional clock — and it is open to people who do not already bank with NatWest. The longest 0% deal is elsewhere: the Longer Balance Transfer card gives up to 36 months interest free for a 3.10% transfer fee, the Purchase & Balance Transfer card gives up to 23 months on spending and 21 on transfers for 3.49%, and the plain Balance Transfer card gives up to 11 months for no fee whatsoever. Those three all quote 24.9% representative. Across the range the entry bar is the same: 18 or over, resident in the UK, earning at least £10,000 a year, and no bankruptcy in the last six years. The Reward Black asks for £15,000.

Two rules decide whether a transfer is possible at all, so they belong here rather than in the small print. The balance has to be moved within the first three months of the account being opened, and no NatWest card will accept a balance from another NatWest Group card. NatWest does not spell out which brands that second rule covers, so anyone hoping to shift a balance held elsewhere in the group onto a fresh 0% deal should establish it before applying rather than after — no version of the product gets round it.
