sections.heading: The ladder, priced in pounds
sections.html:
Percentages hide the size of the decision, so here are the rungs as monthly payments and total cost, worked from Santander's published APRs on a loan with no arrangement fee.

Borrow £3,000 over five years at 8.1% APR and the repayment is about £60.56 a month, £3,633.75 all told, of which £633.75 is interest. Take £10,000 over four years at 6.7% and it is roughly £237.16 a month and £11,383.76 in total; stretch the same £10,000 to five years and the monthly figure drops to about £195.67 while the total rises to £11,740.43. At £25,000 over five years the cost is in the region of £489.18 a month and £29,351.09 overall, and at the new top of the range £35,000 over five years runs to about £687.95 a month and £41,277, with £6,277 of interest.

Two things have moved since this page was last checked on 5 October 2026, and both are the lender's doing rather than the Bank of England's – Bank Rate has stood at 3.75% since 17 September 2026. The three lower rungs each went up by a tenth of a point, from 10.5%, 8.0% and 7.5% to 10.6%, 8.1% and 7.5%, and the representative rung went up by three tenths, from 6.4% to 6.7%. On £10,000 over five years that costs £79.39 more than the old rate; on £25,000 it costs £198.47 more. The smaller rises are trivial in cash – £8.08 on a £2,999 loan, £8 on a £3,000 one – but the direction is the point, because a lender announces a cut and says nothing about an increase.

The ceiling matters as much as the ladder. Each of the four pages states that “the maximum APR we could offer on any loan amount is 29.9%”, so the advertised rung is where pricing starts rather than where it lands. A rate between 6.7% and 29.9% is a spread of 23.2 points, and which end of it you see depends on the credit and affordability assessment behind the application.

sections.heading: The band edges now cut both ways
sections.html:
A price list arranged in bands has edges, and Santander's sit at £3,000, £5,000, £7,500 and now £25,000. Cross one of the first three and the rate on the entire balance falls, which produces an outcome worth checking before you type an amount into the calculator: borrowing slightly more can cost less.

Take a five-year term. £2,999 at 10.6% comes to roughly £3,833.60 in total. £3,000 at 8.1% comes to about £3,633.75. One extra pound of borrowing, £199.85 less to repay, and £3.33 a month cheaper for five years. The same thing happens at £5,000: £4,999 at 8.1% totals around £6,055.04 against £5,000 at 7.5% at £5,976.36, a £78.67 difference. And at the third edge, £7,499 at 7.5% runs to about £8,963.35 at £149.39 a month, while £7,500 at 6.7% runs to £8,805.33 at £146.76 – one pound more borrowed, £158.02 less repaid.

The fourth edge is new and it runs the other way. Santander extended the range from £25,000 to £35,000 and priced the extension at 6.9%, two tenths of a point above the representative rung, so crossing £25,000 raises the rate on the whole balance. £25,000 at 6.7% over five years totals £29,351.09 at £489.18 a month; £25,001 at 6.9% totals £29,484.75 at £491.41. One extra pound of borrowing costs £133.66 more to repay, and there is no amount inside the new band that undoes it – the 6.9% total is above the £25,000 figure from the first pound onwards.

None of that is a trick in the pricing; it is the arithmetic of banded rates, and the bands are published so anyone can do the sum. The practical move is to price the amount just below £25,000 and just above each of the three lower edges as well as the amount you had in mind. It is the single most useful thing this page can tell a reader who has already decided to borrow from Santander.

sections.heading: Where 6.7% sits against the rest of the market
sections.html:
An APR means very little on its own, and there is a free monthly figure that gives it a scale. The Bank of England's Money and Credit release of 29 September 2026 puts the effective interest rate on new personal loans to individuals at 9.96% in August, up from 9.86% in July. Santander's representative rung is 3.26 points below that average; its £1,000 to £2,999 rung, at 10.6%, is 0.64 points above it.

So the shape of this product is a cheap large loan and an expensive small one, measured against what lenders as a whole were actually charging in August. The same release puts interest-charging credit cards at 21.55% and interest-charging overdrafts at 20.27%, which is the comparison that matters if the money is going to clear a card: even the 10.6% rung is less than half the card rate. Net consumer credit borrowing rose to £2.5bn in August from £2.1bn in July, with the annual growth rate at 9.6%.

Industry volumes are flatter than that growth rate suggests. The Finance and Leasing Association's latest consumer finance figures are unchanged since this page was last checked and still cover July 2026, when its members advanced £10.3bn of new credit, 1% below July 2025, with credit card and personal loan new business together 2% lower and retail store and online credit 3% lower, while the first seven months of 2026 ran 4% ahead of 2025.

sections.heading: A second loan that pays your card companies instead of you
sections.html:
Alongside the main product Santander runs a separate agreement called the Personal Loan to pay off your credit card(s), and its Key Facts Document, effective 4 November 2024, describes something built differently. The money does not arrive in a current account: it is “paid directly to your existing credit card account(s) shown in your credit agreement”, and it “cannot be used for any other purpose”.

Two of its terms are more generous than the main loan's and one is tighter. It starts at £500 rather than £1,000, and it opens at 18 rather than 21. Its eligibility list asks only that an applicant has not been declared bankrupt or had an individual voluntary arrangement in six years, where the main loan's list adds a County Court judgment. But the term runs 1 to 4 years rather than 1 to 5, so the same balance has to be cleared a year sooner, and the upper limit is £25,000 against the £35,000 the main loan pages now advertise. The rate is fixed for the life of the agreement, with the document noting that the rate offered “may differ from the advertised Representative APR”.

Because Santander settles the card balances itself, the borrower never has the cash in hand to spend elsewhere, which is the whole point of the design. It is a narrower product than a general-purpose loan and it is easy to miss on the main loans page.

sections.heading: The list of things the money cannot be spent on
sections.html:
The car loan page says only that “we are unable to lend for certain purposes” and sends the reader to the Key Facts Document. The document has the list, and it is longer and more specific than a reader would guess: a house deposit, bridging negative equity, property in the UK or abroad, land “for example for parking space”, investment or business, household bills, living expenses, CSA payments, personal tax bills, time share, stocks and shares, gambling, borrowing on behalf of a third party “unless given as a genuine gift”, equity transfer, capital raising and any business purpose.

Two entries stand out. The first is that household bills and living expenses are excluded, which rules out the reason a good many people go looking for a loan at all, and which sits awkwardly beside the ombudsman decision further down this page. The second is that the document bars crypto currency and then names one company: a loan cannot be used “to pay for crypto currency or to make payments to Binance Markets Ltd”. That is the only company named anywhere in the list, and the exclusion has been sitting in a document effective 4 November 2024 for almost two years.

Santander's own framing of the same page is that “a personal loan from Santander can be used for a wide range of purposes”, and the rate “doesn't vary according to what you're taking the loan out for”. Both are true. The list is worth reading anyway, because the application asks what the money is for.

sections.heading: Five minutes, two working days, a search that leaves no mark
sections.html:
The mechanics are quick and documented. Santander's wording on the checker is that “using our checker will give you an idea of whether we'll accept you for a loan” and that “it won't leave a record on your credit file”, with the hard search attached to the full application: “once you submit your application, we'll do a credit check on you”. An application made between 6.30am and 11.30pm usually produces an accept, decline or refer decision by email within five minutes; one made overnight gets an answer by 7.30am, and a referred case takes up to two working days from the point the extra information arrives.

After approval, “once released, your loan funds will be in your chosen bank account within 2 working days”. Terms run from 12 to 60 months in six-month steps, and the Terms and Conditions set out how the money is priced day to day: “we'll work out interest each day on the outstanding loan amount” and “we will add interest to your loan on the last day of each month”. A maximum of two people can be named on one application.

The statutory escape hatch is spelled out too. Withdrawal is available “within 14 days, starting the day after your loan has been opened”, and the document is explicit that “you won't need to pay any interest if you change your mind during this time”.

sections.heading: A £3.2bn loan book inside a £235.3bn bank
sections.html:
The lender named on the agreement is Santander UK plc, and its own half-year report for the six months to 30 June 2026 gives a profit before tax of £517m against £746m a year earlier, on customer loans of £235.3bn and customer deposits of £220.7bn, with a CET1 capital ratio of 14.2% against 15.8% at the end of 2025. The holding company above it, Santander UK Group Holdings plc, reports the same half on a slightly wider basis – £528m of profit before tax, £238.9bn of loans, £227.2bn of deposits and a banking net interest margin of 2.25% against 2.26% – and it is worth saying which entity a figure belongs to, because the two sets are close enough to be mistaken for each other and only one of them is the lender.

Inside the plc, the unsecured personal loan book was £3.2bn, up from £2.0bn at the end of 2025. Mortgages were £202.6bn, up from £167.3bn, and credit cards £3.7bn against £3.1bn – so Santander still has more money out on plastic than on loans, and both are rounding errors beside the mortgage book. A reader deciding whether to borrow here is dealing with a mortgage bank that also writes loans, which explains why the loan proposition is priced to compete rather than designed to dominate.

Those jumps are an acquisition rather than a lending surge. Santander completed its purchase of TSB on 30 April 2026, and its own results commentary says the bank was “pleased to welcome 4 million customers and 4,500 colleagues to Santander UK”, that “Santander UK and TSB have 480 branches” between them, and that it does “not intend to close any additional Santander or TSB branches before 2028 at the earliest”. TSB continues to trade under its own brand, and existing loan terms are fixed, so nothing about an in-force agreement changes on acquisition.

sections.heading: 1,132 complaints, and a third fewer than six months earlier
sections.html:
Santander publishes its own complaints return and the latest covers 1 January to 30 June 2026. Across the bank it opened 62,497 complaints. The Credit Related line – where a personal loan grievance goes – accounted for 1,132 of them, at a rate of 2.9 per 1,000 loans, with 45% upheld and 1,143 closed.

The half before it is the useful comparison and it is on the same page. Between 1 July and 31 December 2025 the Credit Related line ran at 1,660 complaints, 3.9 per 1,000 loans and 53% upheld. So lending complaints fell 31.8% in volume, the rate per thousand loans fell by a full point, and the uphold rate fell eight points. That is a line moving in the right direction on all three measures at once, which is not something most of these returns show.

Set it against the bank's other products in the same return. Banking and credit cards drew 57,274 complaints at 2.4 per 1,000 accounts with 47% upheld; home finance 3,878 at 4.1 per 1,000 balances with 66% upheld; investments 86 at 0.4 per 1,000 client accounts with 47% upheld; insurance and pure protection 82 at 0.2 per 1,000 policies with 24% upheld. Read the speed columns carefully, because they are headed “Percentage closed within 3 days” and “Percentage closed after 3 days but within 8 weeks” and the two groups are separate: 54% and 46% on banking and credit cards means every complaint was closed inside eight weeks, not that 46% of them took longer. Both of those columns read N/A on the Credit Related line, so Santander publishes no speed figure for loan complaints at all.

One sum that cannot be done here is worth flagging, because it looks tempting. A rate of 2.9 per 1,000 loans against 1,132 complaints implies roughly 390,000 loan accounts, but the return's own heading covers “Santander & Cahoot” while the £3.2bn book is the consolidated figure that now includes the loans acquired with TSB, so dividing one by the other does not give an average balance. Independent ratings are thin too. Smart Money People shows the Santander loan at 3.20 out of 5 from 57 reviews, against 3.75 from 2,666 reviews for the brand, with only the business bank account and Options home insurance scoring lower among the 23 Santander products it rates. No Defaqto star rating or Fairer Finance score specific to the personal loan could be found, which needs confirming rather than reading as an absence of quality.

sections.heading: Fifty-eight days, and the twelve-month line that halves it
sections.html:
The sales pages lead with unlimited free overpayments. The Key Facts Document is where closing the agreement gets priced, and it carries a condition the headline number hides: to work out a settlement figure Santander will “assume that you'll repay your loan in full within 28 days”, and “if your original loan term was longer than 12 months, you'll also be charged an extra 30 days' interest”, which “means you'll be charged up to 58 days' interest in total”.

The twelve-month qualifier matters and it is easy to miss. A loan taken over 12 months settles on 28 days' interest, not 58, and the support page repeats the condition in the same terms. On £5,000 outstanding at 6.7% the whole 58 days is about £51.79, of which the extra 30 days is £26.86; at 10.6% the 58 days is about £80.69 with £41.90 of it the extra; and at the 29.9% ceiling on £10,000 it is about £424.45 with £221.74 of it the extra. Tens of pounds on a mid-range loan, a few hundred at the top of the rate range.

Credit where it is due: Santander does the addition for the reader and prints the total, which not every lender bothers to do, and the allowance itself comes from the Consumer Credit (Early Settlement) Regulations 2004 rather than from Santander. What the sales pages do not do is flag that free overpayments and up to 58 days' interest are answers to two different questions. Chipping away at the balance while the agreement runs is free; closing it is not. The exact figure comes from one phone call, on 0800 028 4055, and it stays “available for 28 days”.

The detail around a partial overpayment has a trap of its own. The default is that “your loan term will be reduced, but your monthly repayment will stay the same”. Keeping the original term and paying less each month is available, but it has to be asked for, and the reduction “may take up to 3 months to take full effect”. Any surplus is refunded within 30 days, and the Direct Debit should not be cancelled until the loan is repaid in full.

sections.heading: What the rulebook makes a lender do once the money has gone
sections.html:
Most of the attention on consumer credit rules goes on the decision to lend. The obligations that run for the next five years sit in CONC 6.7 of the FCA Handbook and are short enough to quote. CONC 6.7.2R, in force since 1 March 2018, requires that “a firm must monitor a customer's repayment record and take appropriate action where there are signs of actual or possible repayment difficulties”. That is a standing duty, not a response to a phone call.

The refinancing rules are the ones to read before consolidating anything. CONC 6.7.17R, from 25 November 2020, defines refinancing to cover replacing, varying or supplementing an agreement, exercising a contractual power, or “granting an indulgence or waiver to the customer”. CONC 6.7.18R, in force since 1 April 2014, is blunt: “a firm must not encourage a customer to refinance a regulated credit agreement if the result would be the customer's commitments are not sustainable”. CONC 6.7.19R, from the same date, bars refinancing other than by forbearance unless the firm acts “at the customer's request or with the customer's consent” and “reasonably believes that it is not against the customer's best interests to do so”.

Santander's debt consolidation page sits squarely in that territory and does not oversell itself. Its own caveat is that “we can't guarantee that this type of loan will reduce your overall cost of borrowing”. The same page sets out two routes to borrowing more and they are not equivalent: a top-up where “your new loan will pay off your existing loan”, which settles the original and therefore triggers the interest allowance described above, and a second loan alongside the first, which does not but leaves two repayments running.

The other end of the same chapter is less comfortable reading, and the published documents go further than this page previously recorded. If payments stop, Santander can demand the balance “straight away”, “use money you have in any other accounts held with us to pay off your outstanding balance” – a right of set off, named as such in section 12 of the Terms and Conditions – charge “our reasonable costs in trying to collect the loan amount from you, including legal costs”, “sell your loan to a different company who will continue to try and collect the loan from you”, take legal action, and report the account to credit reference agencies. Section 11 adds that Santander “can transfer all of our rights and duties under this agreement to someone else at any time”. The document promises only that “we'll usually let you know before we do any of these things”.

The support side has improved since this page was last checked, when the money worries page would not open at all. It now reads normally and lists three things a struggling borrower can ask for: “set up a repayment plan to get back on track”, “a temporary reduction in your monthly repayment” and “breathing space, 30 days to get free independent debt advice”, on a dedicated line, 0800 085 1152, which is not the complaints number. What it does not do is name a single free debt advice organisation, while the loan's own Key Facts Document names PayPlan and gives its number, 0800 280 2816.

sections.heading: One £1,000 loan, as an ombudsman read it
sections.html:
Published Financial Ombudsman Service decisions are the closest thing to watching a lender's affordability process tested from outside. Decision DRN-5688533, decided by ombudsman Robert Walker, concerns a £1,000 Santander personal loan taken in March 2019 at 24.89% APR, repayable in 60 monthly instalments of £27.87 – £672.20 of interest, fees and charges on top of the £1,000, and £1,672.20 to repay in all.

The bank statement Santander itself collected showed the customer already dependent on payday lending, and the ombudsman checked the credit file and found regular payday borrowing both before and after the loan, so the statement was not a one-off. The complaint was upheld. Santander was directed to “remove all interest, fees and charges applied” from the outset, treat payments already made as reducing the £1,000 balance, refund anything paid above it with interest “at 8% per year simple” from the date of each overpayment, and remove all adverse information about the loan from the credit file.

Three things in that for a reader today. The affordability assessment is a check Santander can get wrong, and the Ombudsman will unwind the cost of the credit when it does. A £1,000 loan written over five years at £27.87 a month looks affordable on the face of it, which is exactly what the decision says made it look affordable, and it is the shape the Key Facts Document's own ban on lending for “living expenses” is meant to prevent. And 24.89% on £1,000 is a reminder of how far the price can sit from the bottom rung: well inside the 29.9% ceiling, on an amount whose advertised rate today is 10.6%.

sections.heading: The figures Santander does not serve
sections.html:
For a product where the law is built around a worked example, the example is the hardest thing to read. On the main loans page and on the car, home improvement and debt consolidation pages, the representative example renders as labels without values – “Loan amount”, “Monthly repayment”, “Interest rate”, “Term”, “Total amount repayable” – because the calculator fills them in by script, with the note that “these figures will change every time you make changes to the calculator”. On two of the four pages the unrendered placeholders calc_rate and calc_rate_max are visible in the served text. A visitor using a browser normally almost certainly sees the numbers appear, so this is a rendering matter rather than a missing disclosure, and it is stated here as unestablished rather than absent. It still means the one passage designed for comparing lenders side by side cannot be read without running the page, and it has now been true on three separate checks over three weeks.

The same template carries a second oddity. All four pages state a maximum of 29.9% in their own text, twice, and all four also serve the sentence “maximum APR we could offer on a loan of £XX,XXX is 26.9%” with the amounts left as placeholders. A figure sitting beside £XX,XXX is template filler rather than a published rate, and it is read here as such; 29.9% is the number Santander states in prose.

The paperwork has not kept up with the product. The newest Key Facts Document that could be located is still effective 4 November 2024, and so are the Terms and Conditions, reference CONS 0055 NOV 24. Both describe loans “of between £1,000 and £25,000”, while every live loan page now advertises £1,000 to £35,000 and prices a 6.9% band above £25,000. The income requirement is published only in that document, which means there is no stated income floor at all for the £25,001 to £35,000 band, and the regulated pre-sale summary a borrower is pointed to describes a product narrower than the one on sale. Whether a 2025 or 2026 version exists behind the application journey could not be confirmed.

There is also no fee schedule anywhere in the open material. Beyond the 58-day settlement allowance, which is explained, and the undefined “reasonable costs” of collection, a prospective borrower cannot find out what anything else costs until the agreement is in front of them. The Terms and Conditions name the PRA and the FCA and make no mention of the Financial Services Compensation Scheme, which is correct rather than an omission – that scheme protects deposits and has nothing to pay out on a loan – and the complaints route they give is Santander on 0800 171 2171 and then the Financial Ombudsman Service, with no reference to the European online dispute resolution platform that several banks still signpost and that was discontinued in July 2025.

pros: Five rates published by loan size before you apply, rather than a single representative figure with nothing behind it
The representative 6.7% sits 3.26 points below the 9.96% market average for new personal loans in August 2026
No requirement to bank with Santander – the table is headed for new and existing customers alike
Soft-search eligibility checker that leaves no mark on a credit file, with an online decision usually inside five minutes
The written terms allow a change only to meet a legal or regulatory requirement and promise never to raise the rate or the monthly payment
Unlimited partial overpayments at no charge, with interest worked out daily on the outstanding balance
Settling early costs 28 days' interest rather than 58 where the original term was 12 months, and the settlement figure holds for 28 days
Lending complaints fell from 1,660 to 1,132 and the uphold rate from 53% to 45% between the two halves of the reporting year
No arrangement or set-up fee, and a separate credit-card payoff loan from £500 open from age 18
cons: Every rung went up on 6 October 2026 while Bank Rate stood still: 10.5% to 10.6%, 8.0% to 8.1% and 6.4% to 6.7%, which adds £198.47 to a £25,000 five-year loan
The 6.7% headline covers only £7,500 to £25,000 of a product sold to £35,000; the ceiling is 29.9%, a 23.2-point spread with no published table of who gets what
Crossing £25,000 raises the rate on the whole balance to 6.9%, so £25,001 costs £133.66 more to repay than £25,000 over five years
The Key Facts Document and Terms and Conditions are both still effective 4 November 2024 and both describe a product capped at £25,000, ten thousand pounds below what the pages advertise
No income requirement is published for the £25,001 to £35,000 band, because the only income figures appear in that superseded document
The representative example renders as empty labels on all four loan pages, and the served template quotes a 26.9% maximum where the pages state 29.9%
Missing a payment lets Santander take the money from any other account held with it, sell the loan on, and transfer the agreement to anyone at any time
The money worries page lists support options but names no free debt advice organisation, where the loan's own Key Facts Document names PayPlan
No published fee or charge schedule: collection costs are described only as reasonable, with no figures attached
An ombudsman found in DRN-5688533 that Santander lent £1,000 at 24.89% to a customer its own bank statement showed to be dependent on payday lending
No Defaqto or Fairer Finance rating specific to the loan could be found, and Smart Money People has only 57 reviews behind a 3.20 out of 5
verdict: Santander is one of the few large UK lenders that tells you the price before it tells you about itself: 10.6%, 8.1%, 7.5%, 6.7% and 6.9% APR, set by how much you borrow, published openly and open to people who bank elsewhere. The representative rung sits more than three points under the 9.96% the market charged on new personal loans in August, the written terms promise never to raise the rate or the payment, and the banded structure throws up a genuinely useful quirk at £3,000, £5,000 and £7,500, where borrowing a pound more drops the rate on the whole balance and cuts the total cost. The caveats have grown since the range was extended. Every rung rose on 6 October while Bank Rate stood still; the new £35,000 ceiling is priced above the representative rate, so crossing £25,000 costs more rather than less; and the Key Facts Document a borrower is pointed at still describes a £25,000 product and is the only place the income requirement appears. Worth a soft search if you are borrowing £3,000 or more, and worth pricing the amount just above each lower band edge – and just below £25,000 – before you commit.

faqs.q: What rate will Santander actually give me?
faqs.a: The advertised rate depends on the amount: 10.6% APR on £1,000 to £2,999, 8.1% on £3,000 to £4,999, 7.5% on £5,000 to £7,499, 6.7% APR representative on £7,500 to £25,000 and 6.9% on £25,001 to £35,000. Those are starting points. Santander states a maximum of 29.9%, and the rate offered follows its credit and affordability assessment. The eligibility checker uses a soft search, so it costs nothing on a credit file to find out.

faqs.q: Why did the rates change in October 2026?
faqs.a: Santander repriced the whole ladder with effect from 6 October 2026, the date stamped on each of its four loan pages. The three lower rungs each rose by a tenth of a point and the representative rung rose from 6.4% to 6.7%, while the range was extended from £25,000 to £35,000 with the new slice priced at 6.9%. Bank Rate has been 3.75% since 17 September 2026, so none of the increase follows a change there. On £10,000 over five years the new rate costs £79.39 more than the old one.

faqs.q: Do I need a Santander current account to get a loan?
faqs.a: No. The rate table is headed for new and existing Santander customers alike, and there is no requirement to hold a Santander account first. You do need to be able to repay by Direct Debit, be 21 or over, live permanently in the UK, be employed, self-employed or retired, and have had no bankruptcy, County Court judgment or individual voluntary arrangement in the last six years. The Key Facts Document adds a regular yearly income of at least £10,500 for loans up to £19,999 or £20,000 for loans of £20,000 to £25,000.

faqs.q: Is it really free to overpay?
faqs.a: Partial overpayments are, and interest is worked out daily, so the saving starts at once. The default is that the term shortens and the monthly payment stays the same; a lower payment over the original term has to be asked for and can take up to three months to take effect. Clearing the loan in full is different: the Key Facts Document assumes settlement within 28 days and adds an extra 30 days' interest where the original term was longer than 12 months, up to 58 days in total. On £5,000 outstanding at 6.7% that is about £51.79, of which £26.86 is the extra. Ask for a settlement figure on 0800 028 4055; it holds for 28 days.

faqs.q: What can a Santander loan not be used for?
faqs.a: The Key Facts Document rules out a house deposit, bridging negative equity, property in the UK or abroad, land, investment or business, household bills, living expenses, CSA payments, personal tax bills, time share, stocks and shares, gambling, borrowing for a third party unless it is a genuine gift, equity transfer, capital raising and any business purpose. It also bars crypto currency and payments to one named company, Binance Markets Ltd. The rate itself does not vary with the purpose.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss a payment?
faqs.a: Santander can ask for the whole balance back straight away, take money from any other account you hold with it under the right of set off in section 12 of the Terms and Conditions, charge its reasonable collection costs including legal costs, sell the loan to another company, take legal action and report the account to credit reference agencies, usually after telling you first. Before it gets that far the money worries line is 0800 085 1152, and the options listed there are a repayment plan, a temporary reduction in the monthly payment, or 30 days of breathing space to get free independent debt advice.

faqs.q: Who regulates Santander, and where does a complaint go?
faqs.a: Santander UK plc is on the Financial Services Register under firm reference number 106054, checkable at fca.org.uk/register. Complaints go to the bank first, on 0800 171 2171, and can then be referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service. Between 1 January and 30 June 2026 Santander opened 1,132 credit-related complaints, 2.9 per 1,000 loans, and upheld 45% of them, against 1,660 at 3.9 per 1,000 and 53% upheld in the previous six months.

title: Secret Flight Club Cheap Flights
meta_title: Secret Flight Club: £36 a Year, and It Auto-Renews
meta_description: Secret Flight Club emails flight deals for £36 a year after a 7-day trial. It books nothing itself, renews with no notice and refunds nothing.

headline.label: Price
headline.value: £36 a year after a 7-day trial — renewed automatically, with no notification

disclosure: we earn a commission if you subscribe through the link on this page. It costs you nothing. We have left in everything we found that counts against it, including the renewal terms, because that is the part people get caught by.
intro:
Secret Flight Club sends flight deals by email for £36 a year — about £3 a month — after a seven-day free trial. If one alert saves you £60 on a single fare, it has paid for itself twice, and that is a reasonable bet for someone with flexible dates.

It is also admirably clear about what it is not. Its own words: “Secret Flight Club finds and shares the deal, but we do not sell the flight.” You book with the airline. More bluntly, in the terms: “SecretFlightClub.com are strictly an advertising and marketing company.”

The company behind it is Secret Marketing Group Limited, number 12627422, registered at 167–169 Great Portland Street, London W1W 5PF, incorporated 27 May 2020 and active. It traded as Travel Circus Group Limited until 1 May 2024.

sections.heading: What you pay, and when the money actually leaves
sections.html:
There is one UK tier and no monthly option. The “£3 per month” you see on the homepage is the annual £36 divided by twelve, not a monthly plan you can stop in March.

ItemWhat is published
UK membership£36 per year, billed annually
US membershipUS$39 per year, on the same site
Trial7 days free, card required
RenewalAutomatic, on the trial’s anniversary, until cancelled
Payment handled byStripe, showing as “secretflightclub”
Free tierNone — the trial is the only free route in

The homepage calls the trial “no up front payment”. The terms describe something slightly different: “We will pre authorize payment of your membership fee… This may show as pending on your bank statement and will hold funds”, and anyone without the funds available “will be declined the trial period”. So nothing is taken, but £36 is reserved on your card from day one.

What the subscription buys, from its own list: international flight deals, European weekend deals, error fares, 8 to 12 deal newsletters a week, business fares, peak-travel fares, deals from UK airports, and a hotel-deal membership it values at £34. The FAQ describes the volume differently — “often daily, although the number varies” — so treat 8 to 12 as the ceiling rather than a promise.

sections.heading: The renewal terms, which are the most important thing here
sections.html:
If you read one section, read this one. Four clauses, all quoted from the site’s own terms, combine into something you need to diary.

One. “For first year subscriptions that go past the 7 day free trial, we cannot offer a refund if not cancelled before 00.01 am on the morning after the trial ends on day 8… Payments will be taken without notification.”

Two. “We do not issue notification of your membership renewing annually as we provide the service daily during working days.” No reminder email, by design.

Three. “We offer a no hassle free cancellation up to 7 days prior to your annual renewal… following renewal, if not cancelled we are unable to cancel any previous renewals or refund any previous years renewals.”

Four. “Please note that unsubscribing to the flight deal alerts does not cancel your membership. This must be done via our secure ‘My Account’ page.”

Put together: you must cancel through the account page, at least a week before an anniversary you will not be reminded of, or you are charged £36 again with no refund. The refund policy is explicit on all three points — automatic renewals are “non-refundable”, a post-trial charge gets no refund, and “we do not offer prorated refunds”.

That sits awkwardly beside the marketing. “FREE CANCELLATION” is listed as a membership benefit and the site says it is “free to cancel at any time”, while clause 17.3 restricts free cancellation to more than seven days before renewal. Both statements are on the same website.

There is also a clause we have not seen elsewhere: “Any customers/members joining and cancelling membership within the free cancellation period will and can be blacklisted and prevented from joining at Secret Flight Club management’s discretion without explanation or reason.” Cancelling in the trial is within your rights, and it may cost you the ability to rejoin later.

What to do about it: put a calendar reminder 14 days before the anniversary of the day your trial ended, and cancel through My Account rather than by unsubscribing from the emails.

sections.heading: It is not a travel company, and that changes your protection
sections.html:
Secret Flight Club does not hold ATOL and is not an ABTA member, and it does not claim to be either. It is registered at Companies House under SIC code 63110 — data processing and hosting — not travel.

It passes the check to you, in writing: “We check our advertisers hold all the relevant ATOL, ABTA and bonding where it is relevant to their model. However not all holidays and flights shown… feature bonding… Please check with the operator before booking that they hold the relevant bonding.” And on liability: “We accept no liability for any bookings made with any of our advertisers or the flights we promote.”

That is honest, and it is also the right way round for a deal-alert service — you are buying information, not a holiday. But it means the protection on your trip comes entirely from whoever you book with, so the practical advice is the old advice: book direct with the airline where you can, pay by credit card, and buy travel insurance at the same time as the flight rather than later.

One flat-footed line in the terms gives away how little of this is tailored to the UK: “even though the secret deals are often less than $32, please still ensure you take the usual precautions”. Dollars, on the page selling a sterling membership.

sections.heading: What an alert is actually worth
sections.html:
Error fares and mistake fares are real, and they are genuinely hard to find yourself. The service’s own caveats about them are fair:

“Rates are correct at the time we send emails… however flight prices change rapidly and we cannot guarantee rate remain available after publication for any amount of time.” And: “Some fares remain available for several days, while mistake fares and particularly low flight prices can disappear much sooner.”

There is a practical limitation in how the deals arrive, too: “The link may open a sample search showing one available combination of dates and airports. You can adjust the search to suit your plans, although changing the dates, route or number of passengers may change the price.” In other words, the advertised price exists for a specific combination, and your dates may not be it.

So the honest version of the value proposition is this: you are paying £36 for a stream of leads, most of which will not suit you, in the hope that two or three a year do. If your dates and your destination are both fixed, that hit rate will be poor and a fare alert from the airline itself may serve you better. If you can fly in February instead of April, or to Lisbon instead of Madrid, it is a much better buy.

On coverage, the claim is broad: deals “from airports across the UK, Ireland, Europe, the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand”, and the pricing box promises “DEALS FROM ALL UK AIRPORTS — Yes, all UK airports”. We could not verify that. No airport list is published, and the public feed we could see is labelled only “UK | IRELAND”. If you fly from a small regional airport, treat the trial as the test.

sections.heading: The savings claims do not hold still
sections.html:
The UK page is consistent, claiming an average saving of “£143+”. The US version of the same site, however, gives four different averages: US$196+, US$228, US$163 and US$169 per return flight.

Four numbers for one statistic means at most one of them is current. The methodology is described only as a comparison of “average fares for routes vs what our technology and flight deal experts find”, with no baseline, no sample size and no date range. We cannot check any version of it, so we would not lean on the £143 either.

Two more claims we could not stand behind. The “100,000+ members” figure is unaudited and unverifiable from outside. And the trademark cited in the terms as UK00004209765 may well be registered, but the Intellectual Property Office served a security check when we tried to look it up and we did not work around it, so we are reporting it as the company’s claim rather than a confirmed fact.

The terms themselves were “Last updated 5th March 2024” and contain no price at all. The £36 figure lives only in the marketing copy, which means the contract you agree to does not state what you are agreeing to pay.

sections.heading: Getting hold of them
sections.html:
There is no phone number. We looked across the homepage, the contact page, the about page and the team page and found none — no landline, no mobile, no click-to-call.

Support is one email address, members@secretflightclub.com, with the stated turnaround “During business days we usually respond within 24 hours”. No opening hours are published, and no UK trading address beyond the registered office in the terms.

Two limits are set out on the contact page itself. “We cannot issue cancellations or refunds via this email” — cancelling must go through My Account. And “we are unable due to the large amount of members, respond to individual flight deal requests”, so do not expect to ask for a route.

For a service costing £36 a year that is defensible. For a renewal dispute, an email address and no phone number is a thin channel, which is another reason to cancel early rather than argue later.

verdict: As a product this makes sense: £36 for a year of flight-deal emails is cheap next to one saved fare, and Secret Flight Club is honest that it sells information rather than flights — you book with the airline, and it tells you to check their bonding yourself. The trial is the right way to judge it, because the value depends entirely on whether the deals suit your airport and your flexibility. Where we would be careful is the renewal. The terms say the charge is taken without notification, free cancellation ends seven days before an anniversary you are not reminded of, nothing is refunded afterwards, and unsubscribing from the emails does not cancel anything. Treat it as a diary task: note the day the trial ends, set a reminder two weeks before that date next year, and cancel through My Account if the alerts have not earned their keep. Do that, and £36 is a fair gamble on a flexible traveller's luck. Forget it, and you will pay £36 a year for emails you stopped reading.

faqs.q: Does Secret Flight Club book my flight?
faqs.a: No. Its own wording: “Secret Flight Club finds and shares the deal, but we do not sell the flight. You will complete your booking with the airline or booking provider shown in the search results.” The terms go further and describe the business as “strictly an advertising and marketing company” that accepts “no liability for any bookings made with any of our advertisers”.

faqs.q: How much does it cost and is there a monthly option?
faqs.a: £36 a year in the UK, billed annually, after a seven-day free trial. There is no monthly plan — the “£3 per month” on the homepage is the annual price divided by twelve. The US version of the site charges US$39 a year.

faqs.q: How do I cancel, and when?
faqs.a: Through the My Account page on the website. Unsubscribing from the deal emails does not cancel the membership. Timing matters: free cancellation is offered only up to seven days before your annual renewal, the company says it does not notify you that renewal is coming, and after the charge there are no refunds and no prorated refunds. Set a reminder a fortnight before the anniversary of the day your trial ended.

faqs.q: Is my money protected if something goes wrong with the flight?
faqs.a: Not by Secret Flight Club. It holds no ATOL and is not an ABTA member, and its terms ask you to “check with the operator before booking that they hold the relevant bonding”. Whatever protection you have comes from the airline or agent you book with, so book direct where you can, pay by credit card and arrange insurance when you book rather than later.

faqs.q: Will the deal still be there when I click?
faqs.a: Sometimes not, and the site says so: prices “change rapidly and we cannot guarantee rate remain available after publication for any amount of time”, and “mistake fares and particularly low flight prices can disappear much sooner”. The link may also open a sample search for one specific combination of dates and airports, and changing those “may change the price”.

faqs.q: Can I speak to someone?
faqs.a: Only by email, at members@secretflightclub.com, usually answered within 24 hours on business days. There is no phone number published anywhere on the site, no opening hours and no UK trading address beyond the registered office. The contact page also says it cannot process cancellations or refunds by email, so those must go through My Account.

title: Simply Business Tradesman Insurance Review
meta_title: Simply Business Tradesman Insurance: What It Costs
meta_description: Simply Business quotes tradesman cover from £5.40 a month across a panel of 19 insurers. The prices, the limits, the excesses and the fees, checked.
intro:
Simply Business started in 2005 as a team of five people trying to sell business insurance online at a time when almost nobody did. It now covers more than one million small businesses and landlords across roughly 1,500 trades, employs over 900 people from offices in London and Northampton, and paid out £57 million in claims during 2025 — an average of about £156,000 a day. On the tradesman side alone it puts the figure at more than 253,000 tradespeople on cover. Quotes start at £5.40 a month and the site reckons on about seven minutes to complete one.

It does not carry the risk itself. Simply Business is the trading name of Xbridge Limited, an insurance broker, and the policy you end up with is written by one of the insurers on its panel — AXA, Aviva, Zurich, Allianz, QBE, Covéa, Hiscox, Markel, Churchill or AIG among them. That is a point in its favour rather than against it: a sole trader paying £7 a month is getting paper from companies that would not normally quote a one-person business directly. The whole operation has been owned by the American insurer Travelers since 2017, which bought it from Aquiline Capital Partners for around $490 million when it had 425,000 customers and had placed £93 million of premium in 2016.

What follows is what the cover actually contains, what the excesses look like on the two wordings the site publishes openly, what paying monthly adds, and where the paperwork runs out.

sections.heading: What £5.40 a month buys a tradesman
sections.html:
The advertised entry price is for public liability alone, and the site is unusually open about what real customers pay. Ten per cent of them paid £64.78 a year or less in the first half of 2026. Two worked examples are published with the date they were generated, 12 May 2026: a Manchester domestic cleaner with under a year's experience, no employees and £1,000,000 of public liability at £7.21 a month or £86.49 a year, underwritten by Covéa; and an Edinburgh barber renting a chair, with £1,000,000 of liability and £1,000 of tools cover, at £11.46 a month or £100.08 a year, underwritten by Chiswell. A separate builder's example on the trades page comes out at £7.32 a month, £87.89 for the year.

Four public liability limits are offered — £1m, £2m, £5m and £10m — and the split between them is published too: 85% of customers take £1,000,000 and 15% take £2,000,000. That figure is worth sitting with. The £1m limit is the cheapest box on the form and the one most people tick, but plenty of commercial clients, main contractors and accreditation schemes ask for more before they will let anyone on site, and the quote journey does not know what your customers demand. Employers' liability is the exception: it is set at £10,000,000 on both published wordings, which is double the £5,000,000 the law asks for.

Beyond liability, the trades journey will add tools and equipment, owned and hired plant, contract works, stock, business legal protection and personal accident. Cover can be bought the same day, with documents issued immediately.

sections.heading: Nineteen insurers on the panel, and three of them are the house
sections.html:
Simply Business publishes its panel, which is more than most brokers do. On the business side it lists AXA (with Select and Commercial Guard variants), QBE and QBE Essentials, Covéa with its Lexicon and Elements products, AIG and AIG Essentials, Allianz, Zurich, Hiscox, Markel, Churchill, and a Barclays-badged product — 19 named entries in all. Three of those entries are described on the same page as MGAs: Finsbury, Maltings and Chiswell.

Chiswell is the interesting one. It was established in 2016, it is available only through Simply Business, and its policies are underwritten by HDI Global Specialty SE and Great Lakes Insurance SE, the Munich Re subsidiary. Finsbury is presented in the same way, and Xbridge's own complaints page names Chiswell Insurance Services and Finsbury Insurance Group as associated brands. So when the barber in the published example was quoted at £11.46 a month, the quote came from the broker's own underwriting agency rather than from a third party on the panel. Nothing about that is improper — a managing general agent binds cover on a real insurer's behalf, and HDI Global Specialty and Great Lakes are substantial names — but a shopper who believes they are comparing 19 independent insurers is not quite getting that. The public liability page describes the exercise as comparing quotes from "up to 15 insurers", which is a fourth number again.

sections.heading: The wording you get is decided during the quote, not before it
sections.html:
Because the insurer is chosen by the quote engine, a tradesman cannot read the policy that will govern their claim until they have been matched to one. Two of the wordings are on open URLs, and they differ in ways that matter.

The AXA tradesmen summary (reference ACLD0784Z-A, dated 04/21) sets public liability at £1,000,000 as standard with an upgrade to a maximum of £5,000,000 — not the £10,000,000 AXA advertises on its own site. Employers' liability runs to £10,000,000 any one event. The public liability excess is £250, rising to £500 or £1,000 for certain trades. Portable tools are limited to £500 for any one item, with an excess of 10% of each claim, minimum £100 and maximum £500. Hired plant and contract works both carry a £250 excess that becomes £500 for theft. Contract works are capped at £500,000 for any one contract, stock in trade at £2,500 and constructional plant at £25,000. Personal accident pays £2,000 on death or permanent disability and up to £500 a week for 104 weeks of temporary disability. Exclusions include asbestos, defective workmanship, and work at aircraft installations, railways, docks, quarries and power stations.

The Covéa Small Business Plus wording (reference P187E, dossier 20110324E) carries the same £10,000,000 employers' liability figure, limits tools to £500 per tool or 20% of the sum insured whichever is greater, and imposes conditions precedent that a working tradesman would want to read before a claim rather than after — hot work and welding require named fire precautions, flammable solvents require further ones, and underground services must be located before digging starts. That document is dated May 2019, which is over seven years old at the time of writing. The site's own construction page puts the range of excesses across the panel at anything from nil to £750 on public liability and up to £4,000 on contents and stock, depending on which insurer you land with.

sections.heading: Taking on a first employee changes the paperwork permanently
sections.html:
Employers' liability cover is compulsory from the day a tradesman takes on staff, and Simply Business flags the fine of up to £2,500 for every day without it. The part nobody explains is what happens to the record afterwards. Since the rules in the regulator's policy statement PS11/4 of February 2011, which came into force on 6 March 2011, every insurer must maintain an employers' liability register of policies entered into, renewed or claimed on from 1 April 2011, and from 1 April 2012 must record the Employer Reference Number — the PAYE reference issued by HMRC — against each one. Directors have had to certify those registers annually, with an assurance report, since 1 July 2012. The regulator costed the set-up of the system at about £28.4 million.

The practical effect is that the ERN a tradesman gives at quote time is the thread that lets a former employee find the right insurer twenty years later, for a disease claim that may not surface until long after the business has closed. Give a wrong or missing reference and the policy is harder to trace. It takes ten seconds at the quote stage and no comparison journey makes any fuss about it.

sections.heading: Spreading the cost over twelve months
sections.html:
Monthly payments are run through a credit agreement with Premium Credit Limited rather than by Simply Business itself, and interest is charged. The rate is not published anywhere on the site: the help pages say only that "details of the interest will be shown before going ahead and included in your credit agreement, sent after purchase". The agreement has to be signed and returned electronically within ten days of receipt, and failing to do that attracts a one-off £25 penalty charge. Renewal payments are taken nine days before the current policy expires.

The two published example quotes tell slightly different stories about what the instalments cost. The cleaner's £7.21 a month multiplies out to £86.52 against an annual price of £86.49 — effectively no uplift. The barber's £11.46 a month multiplies out to £137.52 against an annual price of £100.08, which is £37.44 or roughly 37% more for paying in twelve pieces. Both are the provider's own figures, published side by side on the same page and generated on the same day.

For context, the regulator's premium finance market study MS24/2, published in February 2026, found weighted average APRs at the end of that period of 16.5% where the insurer lends, 23.5% at intermediary lenders and 29.4% at intermediary brokers — the last of those down from 35.1% in 2022. It also found that broker compensation accounted for 55% of the total cost of credit on agreements financed by specialist providers, and that commission averaged about £45 per policy and 8% of loan value in 2023. Falling rates have saved customers around £157 million a year across the market. That work looked at motor and home policies, so none of the numbers are Simply Business's, but they are the yardstick for what an insurance instalment plan usually costs, and they explain why the annual price is worth asking for.

sections.heading: The complaints numbers Simply Business publishes about itself
sections.html:
Xbridge puts its own regulatory complaints return on the website, which very few brokers do. For the six months to 31 December 2025 it opened 1,240 general insurance complaints and closed 1,319, a rate of 1.86 complaints for every 1,000 policies sold. Eleven per cent were closed within three days and 88% within eight weeks, and 40% were upheld. The preceding half year, to 30 June 2025, ran at 1,186 opened and 1,216 closed, 1.75 per 1,000 policies, 16% closed within three days, 84% within eight weeks and 46% upheld. Credit broking is reported separately and is small: 45 complaints opened in the second half of 2025 with 38% upheld, and 59 in the first half with 30% upheld.

Two things stand out. The uphold rate sits well above the 30% average the Financial Ombudsman Service records across all financial products, and only about one complaint in nine is settled inside three days. Against that, the volume is modest for a book of more than a million policies, and the firm is publishing figures it is under no obligation to make this easy to find. The rules are changing here too: the regulator's policy statement PS25/19, published in December 2025, merges five separate complaints returns into one, moves everybody to half-yearly calendar reporting and sets a publication threshold of 500 complaints or more, with the first return under the new regime covering January to June 2027.

Claims are a third party again. Simply Business states that "our specialist partner Sedgwick pays claims on behalf of the insurer", on 0333 207 0560 around the clock, with a call back within two days of an online form and payment usually within 24 hours of a settlement being agreed. So a tradesman who buys here deals with the broker at the quote, an insurer or MGA on the certificate, a loss adjuster at the claim and a separate lender if paying monthly.

sections.heading: Where the paperwork runs out
sections.html:
The one document a broker's customer most wants before buying is the terms of business agreement, because that is where set-up fees, mid-term adjustment charges and cancellation fees live. Simply Business does not publish it. Its help pages point to it repeatedly — cancelling after the 14-day cooling-off period gives "a proportionate refund of the premium you have paid, less any set up fees and the cancellation fee as set out in your Terms of Business Agreement" — and the website terms, dated June 2026, confirm the TOBA exists and governs the relationship without saying what is in it. Searching the site turns up no copy. The one piece of good news is explicit: "there is no admin fee to make a change to your policy."

Independent ratings are thin, and partly that is the market rather than the firm. Defaqto rates insurance products rather than the brokers who introduce them, and commercial cover is much less thoroughly rated than home or motor, so no star rating for this product could be found. Smart Money People carries a business insurance score of 4.61 out of 5 from 32 reviews, last reviewed on 20 August 2026, plus 4.27 from 8 reviews on liability and 4.14 from 44 on landlord cover — small samples, and worth treating as such. The 4.5 out of 5 from about 40,000 reviews shown across the site is collected by Feefo on the firm's own behalf and carries no date or product breakdown.

Xbridge files full accounts at Companies House, most recently made up to 31 December 2025 and filed on 15 July 2026, so its revenue and commission income are a matter of public record for anyone who wants to order the document; the filing itself could not be read for this review. The firm reference, 313348, is verifiable on the Financial Services Register.

The Covéa Small Business Plus wording on open display is dated May 2019, and the AXA tradesmen summary 04/21
Public liability through this route tops out at £5,000,000 on the AXA product, where AXA sells £10,000,000 direct
No Defaqto rating for the product, and the independent review samples that do exist are small (32 reviews on business insurance)
The service is non-advised, so nobody checks whether the £1,000,000 limit 85% of customers pick is enough for the contracts they work on
verdict: For a self-employed tradesman who wants liability cover quickly and cheaply, Simply Business does the job it advertises: real insurers, real prices, a quote in minutes and no charge for changing the policy later. The published claims and complaints figures are more than most brokers will show you, and the Travelers ownership means the business behind the website is not going anywhere. The reservations are about what happens after the quote. You cannot see the fee schedule before you buy, you cannot see the interest rate on instalments before you buy, and you cannot read the wording that will govern your claim until the engine has picked your insurer. None of that is unusual in this corner of the market, but it does mean the cheapest quote on the screen is not necessarily the cheapest policy over a year. Ask for the annual price, ask which insurer you have been placed with, and check the public liability limit against what your customers actually require before you tick the £1,000,000 box.

faqs.q: Does Simply Business insure me itself?
faqs.a: No. Simply Business is the trading name of Xbridge Limited, an insurance broker with FCA firm reference 313348. It arranges the policy and the risk is carried by one of the insurers or managing general agents on its panel, such as AXA, Covéa, Zurich, QBE or its own Chiswell agency, whose policies are underwritten by HDI Global Specialty SE and Great Lakes Insurance SE.

faqs.q: How much public liability cover do I actually need?
faqs.a: There is no legal minimum. Simply Business offers £1m, £2m, £5m and £10m, and 85% of its customers take £1,000,000. The limit that matters is whichever your clients, your accreditation scheme or your contract requires, which can be higher — so check before you pick the cheapest option, because the quote form will not ask.

faqs.q: What does it cost to cancel?
faqs.a: Within the first 14 days you are charged only for the time on cover. After that you get a proportionate refund less any set-up fees and a cancellation fee. Neither figure is published on the website; both are set out in the terms of business agreement issued with your policy, so ask for the amounts before you buy.

faqs.q: Is paying monthly more expensive?
faqs.a: Yes, interest is charged, through a credit agreement with Premium Credit Limited rather than with Simply Business. The rate is only shown at checkout. On the firm's own published examples, one quote works out at the same price either way while another costs £137.52 a year monthly against £100.08 paid up front. There is also a £25 charge if the credit agreement is not signed and returned within ten days.

faqs.q: Who handles a claim?
faqs.a: Sedgwick, which the site describes as paying claims on behalf of the insurer, on 0333 207 0560 at any hour. An online form gets a call back within two days, and once a settlement is agreed payment is usually made by bank transfer within 24 hours. Simply Business paid out £57 million in 2025, an average of about £156,000 a day.

faqs.q: Do I need to give my PAYE reference?
faqs.a: If you employ anyone, yes. Insurers must record the Employer Reference Number against every employers' liability policy renewed since 1 April 2012 and keep it on a register that a former employee can search years later. Getting it right at the quote stage is what allows an old claim to find the right insurer once the business has gone.

title: Smart Cover Plumbing and Drainage Insurance
meta_title: Smart Cover Plumbing & Drainage: £6.27 a Month Explained
meta_description: Smart Cover's plumbing and drainage plan starts at £6.27 a month. The claim limits, excesses, waiting periods and small print, checked at source.
intro:
Smart Cover has been selling household emergency policies since Smart-Cover Direct Limited was incorporated on 18 April 2013, and the plumbing and drainage plan is the cheapest thing it sells for the home: £6.27 a month, discounted from £6.96. That buys a 24-hour claims line, an approved engineer sent out within 24 hours of a claim being approved, and the callout, labour and parts included rather than billed separately. For a single blocked drain or a burst internal pipe, one claim can cost more than a year of premiums.

The range around it is broad for a firm this size. Plumbing and drainage on its own is £6.27; adding internal electrical emergencies takes it to £9.00 a month; the Smart Home Essential plan, which folds in the boiler, the central heating system and the external water supply pipe, is £10.90. Boiler-only cover starts at £7.90 and the top Smart Home Plus plan, which adds lock and key assistance and pest infestation, is £12.90. Every plan lets you pick an excess of £0, £49, £69 or £99, which is more choice than most home emergency products give you.

The claims line is 03333 449 559, staffed around the clock, and Smart Cover says calls are typically answered inside 60 seconds. There is a separate plumbing claims number, 03333 449 247. Complaints are acknowledged within five business days and answered inside the eight weeks the FCA allows, after which the Financial Ombudsman Service will take the case.
