sections.heading: Your client writes the limit; the scheme only writes it down
sections.html:
Nothing in law tells a builder how much public liability to buy. The number lands on the certificate because somebody further up the chain asked for it, and the pre-qualification schemes that gate most commercial work are more interesting for what they leave out than for what they demand.

Build UK's Common Assessment Standard question set, version 5, dated 1 July 2025 devotes five questions to cover: Q28 employers' liability, Q29 public liability, Q30 professional indemnity, Q31 product liability and Q32 contractors' all risks. Each asks for the same four things — “Policy number, Limit, Excess, Expiry date” — and insists the company name on the policy matches the legal name given at Q1. Q29 is the only one that is compulsory for everybody; Q28 falls away if you employ nobody, Q30 if you are neither Principal Designer nor Designer, Q31 if you supply no materials. Not one of the five sets a minimum figure.

Constructionline's Gold and Platinum supplier checklist guide of February 2026 goes further into the paperwork and no further into the money. It wants certificates, the insurer and the broker, the policy number — “we are unable to accept ‘TBC’ or anything else in place of a Policy Number” — the limit of indemnity, the limit for a single event, the excess, the expiry date, and the broker's business name and telephone number. Again there is no minimum. Design work categories trigger professional indemnity; directly employed staff trigger employers' liability; material supply triggers product liability. The schemes are auditing that you told the truth, not that you bought enough.

That is why the quoted ladder matters more than the ceiling. Cover is sold in £1m, £2m, £3m, £5m and £10m steps with higher limits “on request”, and the step you choose should be read off the contract you are bidding for, not off a brochure. A local authority framework and a domestic kitchen refit do not want the same number, and buying the £10m because it is there is as much of a mistake as buying the £1m because it is cheapest.

sections.heading: A trade policy asks more of you than your van policy does
sections.html:
This is the part most tradespeople have never been told, and it is worth more than any cover limit on the page. A sole trader's own car insurance is a consumer contract. The liability policy he buys the same afternoon is not, and the two sit under different statutes with different consequences for getting a question wrong.

A business policy falls under the Insurance Act 2015, which came into force eighteen months after Royal Assent, on 12 August 2016. Section 3 replaces the consumer's simple duty to answer carefully with a duty of fair presentation: before the contract is entered into, the insured must disclose “every material circumstance which the insured knows or ought to know”, or at minimum give “the insurer sufficient information to put a prudent insurer on notice” that it should ask more. It must be done “in a manner which would be reasonably clear and accessible to a prudent insurer”. In plain terms: the questions on the form are the floor, not the ceiling.

Schedule 1 sets out what happens when that duty is breached. Where the breach was deliberate or reckless the insurer may “avoid the contract and refuse all claims” and “need not return any of the premiums paid”. Where it was neither, the outcome depends on what the insurer would have done knowing the truth: if it would not have written the risk at all it may avoid and refuse claims but must hand the premium back; if it would have written it on different terms, the policy is read as though those terms had always applied. And if it would simply have charged more, paragraph 6 applies the arithmetic nobody expects — the insurer “need pay on the claim only X% of what it would otherwise have been under an obligation to pay”, X being the premium actually charged as a percentage of the premium that should have been. Pay 60% of the right premium and a £50,000 claim settles at £30,000, with the policy still perfectly valid.

Two practical consequences when you take the four-minute quote. Declare the turnover, the trades and the height and depth you actually work to, not the ones you mostly work to. And if there is something the questions never reach — a subcontractor arrangement, an unusual client, a past claim on a different policy — say it anyway, in writing, and keep the email.

sections.heading: Seven insurers, one certificate, and no wording until you ask
sections.html:
Everywhen is a broker, not an underwriter. The trade pages name the paper behind the schemes openly, which is more than many brokers do: AXA, Arch, Covéa, Markel, QBE, Zurich and Intact. That is seven, and every one is an established commercial insurer rather than a start-up MGA. On the contractors' all risks product the page names Markel Direct, a trading name of Markel International Insurance Company Limited, specifically.

What the pages do not tell you is which of the seven you will end up with, or on whose wording. There is no policy document, no insurance product information document and no specimen schedule published anywhere on the trade section; you find out what you have bought after you have given your details and taken a quote. That is normal for a scheme broker and it is still a gap, because the clauses that decide a claim — the tools conditions, the contract works exclusions, the height warranty — live in a document you cannot read in advance.

The product range itself is unusually wide. Twenty-seven separate trade products are sold, covering bathroom fitters, bricklayers, builders, builders' merchants, carpenters, carpet cleaners, construction, contractors, electrical contractors, electricians, engineering, gardeners, gas fitters, groundworkers, handymen, hired-in plant, landscapers, painters and decorators, plasterers, plumbers, professional indemnity, roofers, scaffolders, tools, tradesman, and tree surgeons. Contractors' all risks bundles contract works, hired-in plant, own plant and tools against “fire, flood, storm, malicious damage, and theft”, with legal defence costs from £100,000 and named options for scaffolding, hot roofing, underpinning and hazardous locations — the four things that get a small builder declined elsewhere.

sections.heading: What the van has to be doing at two in the morning
sections.html:
Tools cover is where trade policies are won and lost, and the condition attached to it is stated plainly enough to quote: “Overnight theft is excluded from vehicles unless locked in a secure building.” The van itself has to be “fully secured, all doors and windows closed with all locks fully engaged”, and “where alarms are fitted, they must be set”.

Read that against how most of the trade actually lives. A plumber who parks on the road outside his own house, or in an unlit bay at a travel inn between jobs, has no overnight tools cover at all under that clause — not reduced cover, none. A locked garage, a yard with a shut door, a secure compound: those work. The kerb does not.

The money is worth checking too. The range runs £1,000 to £5,000 per person with a single-article limit of £1,500, which is fine for a bag of hand tools and tight for one modern rotary laser or a decent SDS set. The excess is £100 on each claim. Wear and tear, electrical and mechanical breakdown, damage caused while a tool is in use, and anything “not listed or disclosed” are all outside cover — that last one making the schedule of items you supply at quote stage part of the contract rather than a formality.

sections.heading: The cover that has to outlive the job
sections.html:
Professional indemnity is quoted from £1,000,000 to £10,000,000 and it behaves differently from everything else on the page. Liability cover responds to when the accident happened; professional indemnity responds to when the claim is made. Let the policy lapse and the work you did while insured stops being covered, which is why run-off matters and why the pages raise the point that a claim in tort can arrive well after the six-year contractual limitation period has run out.

Any trade doing design as well as installation needs to take this seriously, because the pre-qualification schemes have already noticed. The Common Assessment Standard waives Q30 only if you are neither Principal Designer nor Designer; Constructionline requires professional indemnity from consultants and from “Contractors with Design work categories”. Specify the boiler as well as fit it, size the steel as well as install it, and you have crossed that line whether or not anyone called it design at the time.

One practical note on the contractors' all risks side: faulty workmanship, wear and tear, design errors, and damage occurring before the policy starts or after the project completes are all excluded. The first and third of those are the gap professional indemnity is meant to fill, so on a design-and-build job the two products are not alternatives — each is the other's hole.

sections.heading: The company that has been through three names
sections.html:
The entity you contract with is Advisory Insurance Brokers Limited, company 04043759, FCA firm reference 313250, registered at 2 Minster Court, Mincing Lane, London EC3R 7PD. Companies House records the history: incorporated on 31 July 2000 as Broomco (2274) Limited, renamed MIA General Insurance Service Managers Limited on 19 September 2000, then Towergate Underwriting Group Limited on 31 December 2003, and finally Advisory Insurance Brokers Limited on 22 March 2022. The Everywhen brand arrived on top of that in 2025; the legal person behind your certificate has not changed since the Towergate years.

Its parent is one of the largest brokers in the world. The Ardonagh Group's full-year 2025 results report pro forma income of $2.9 billion and pro forma adjusted EBITDA of $1.1 billion, income growth of 20.4%, EBITDA growth of 24.8%, a margin of 35.7% and organic income growth of 4%, across more than 12,000 staff in 250-plus locations in over 30 countries, after 95 acquisitions in the year of which 93 were outside the UK. Chief executive David Ross put it this way: “In the eight years since Ardonagh launched we've seen income grow ten-fold positioning us as a top 15 global insurance broker.”

If something goes wrong, the published timetable is specific. Staff aim to resolve a complaint within three business days; if more investigation is needed you should hear within five business days, again at four weeks with the reason for the delay, and a final response by eight weeks. After that, or if the answer does not satisfy you, the Financial Ombudsman Service at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR will take it — but you must go to them within six months of the final response letter. Policies written at Lloyd's route through Lloyd's own complaints team first.

Note the small-business gate on that last route. The Ombudsman only takes a business complaint where annual turnover is under £6.5 million and either the balance sheet total is under £5 million or there are fewer than 50 employees. Most readers of a tradesman page clear that comfortably; a growing contractor should check before assuming the backstop is there.

pros: Public, product and employers' liability all quoted to £10,000,000, with higher limits available on request
Seven named insurers on the panel — AXA, Arch, Covéa, Markel, QBE, Zurich and Intact — rather than an unnamed one
Twenty-seven separate trade products, including scaffolders, roofers, tree surgeons and groundworkers, which several online-only rivals decline
Work at height quoted to 15 metres and excavation to 2 metres, above the limits many schemes impose
Contractors' all risks bundles contract works, hired-in plant, own plant and tools, with legal defence costs from £100,000 and named options for hot roofing, underpinning and scaffolding
Premiums can be spread over ten monthly direct debits
A clear, published complaints timetable with three-day, five-day, four-week and eight-week stages, and the FCA reference and company number stated openly
cons: No price is published anywhere. Every one of the 27 trade pages gives limits and none gives a premium, so there is no way to benchmark before handing over your details — AXA, Hiscox and Simply Business all publish a starting monthly figure.
No policy wording, insurance product information document or specimen schedule is published for the trade products, so the clauses that decide a claim are unreadable until after you have quoted.
Overnight theft of tools is excluded from vehicles unless the van is locked inside a secure building, which removes cover entirely for any tradesperson who parks on a street or a drive.
The single-article limit of £1,500 inside a £5,000 maximum is low for one modern laser level, plant item or high-end SDS set.
Seven insurers are named but nothing tells you which of them will carry your risk or on whose wording, and the answer changes the claims conditions.

The only terms-of-business document findable on the site is a consumer version dated August 2023; no commercial fee schedule is published, and that document states fees and commission are non-refundable and that refunds under £10 are kept.

The Towergate name is gone from a market that still searches for it, so a tradesman renewing after several years has to satisfy himself the Everywhen site is the same firm before he types anything into it.
verdict: A broad, properly underwritten trade book with seven real insurers behind it and a product list that reaches the awkward trades — scaffolders, roofers, hot-work, underpinning — that the cheap online schemes turn away. The £10,000,000 ceiling on all three liability sections is as high as anyone offers and the 15-metre height and 2-metre depth allowances are genuinely useful. Against that, this is the least transparent of the five tradesman propositions on this site before you quote: no price, no wording, no commercial terms of business. If your work is straightforward and you want a number to compare, start with a provider that publishes one. If your work is the kind that gets declined online, or if you need £5m or £10m because a framework demands it, this is a broker worth the phone call.

faqs.q: Is Towergate tradesman insurance still available?
faqs.a: Yes, under a different name. The Ardonagh Group renamed its advisory arm Everywhen in May 2025 and completed the switch across offices and websites on 17 November 2025, bringing more than 35 broking brands under it. Old towergateinsurance.co.uk trade addresses 302-redirect to the matching everywhen.co.uk page. The regulated company, Advisory Insurance Brokers Limited (FCA reference 313250), is the same one that traded as Towergate Underwriting Group Limited until 22 March 2022.

faqs.q: How much public liability cover do I actually need?
faqs.a: Whatever your client's contract says, because no statute sets a figure. The limits sold here are £1m, £2m, £3m, £5m and £10m, with more on request. Neither of the two schemes that gate most commercial work sets a minimum: Build UK's Common Assessment Standard question set (version 5, 1 July 2025) asks at Q29 only for the policy number, limit, excess and expiry date, and Constructionline's February 2026 Gold and Platinum guide asks for the same plus the broker's name and phone number. Read the limit off the tender document, not off a brochure.

faqs.q: Are my tools covered if they are stolen from the van overnight?
faqs.a: Only if the van was locked inside a secure building. The published condition is that “overnight theft is excluded from vehicles unless locked in a secure building”, and the vehicle must in any case be fully secured with all locks engaged and any alarm set. A locked garage, yard or compound qualifies; a driveway or street does not. Cover runs from £1,000 to £5,000 per person with a £1,500 single-article limit and a £100 excess.

faqs.q: Does the same protection apply as on my own car insurance if I get a question wrong?
faqs.a: No, and this is the most important difference between a business policy and a personal one. A trade policy sits under the Insurance Act 2015, in force since 12 August 2016, which imposes a duty of fair presentation: you must disclose every material circumstance you know or ought to know, not merely answer the questions put to you. Schedule 1 allows an insurer to avoid the contract and keep the premium where a breach was deliberate or reckless, and where it was innocent but a higher premium would have been charged, to pay only the proportion of the claim that your premium bore to the correct one.

faqs.q: Can I take a complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service?
faqs.a: Usually yes. You get a final response within eight weeks, and you then have six months from that letter to refer the complaint to the Ombudsman at Exchange Tower, London E14 9SR. A business qualifies if annual turnover is under £6.5 million and either the balance sheet total is under £5 million or it has fewer than 50 employees. Policies placed at Lloyd's go through Lloyd's own complaints team first.

title: Trainline Review: The Booking Fee, the Refund Ladder and Who Pays When You Are Late
meta_title: Trainline Review: What the Booking Fee Really Costs
meta_description: Trainline's booking fee runs from 59p to £2.79, and nothing in the app on the day. The refund ladders, the 1 April 2026 rule change and who pays for delays.

headline.label: Booking fee per transaction
headline.value: 59p to £2.79 — nothing at all in the Trainline app on the day of travel

intro:
Trainline charges between 59p and £2.79 to book a British train ticket, and nothing at all if you book in its app on the day you travel. In the year to 28 February 2026 it put £6,319m of tickets through the platform and kept £453m of that as revenue. Both sets of figures are Trainline's own — the fee from its help centre, the money from its results — and were checked on 20 September 2026.

What the fee buys is reach. Trainline's about page describes bringing "the majority of rail and coach operators" in Europe onto one platform, across more than 40 countries, for 27 million active customers of whom 18 million are British. It holds 2.7 million digital railcards, 16% more than a year earlier, and 45% of the digital railcard market among 16 to 30 year olds. Its SplitSave tool, which quietly breaks one journey into several cheaper tickets, saved an average of £13 a trip on bookings between 1 July 2024 and 30 June 2025 by the company's own measurement.

One thing is worth knowing before you book, because it decides who you deal with when a train does not run. Trainline is a retailer, not a railway. The fares belong to the train companies, and so do the tickets, the seat reservations and the compensation. If your train is an hour late the claim goes to the operator that ran it — Trainline will spot the delay and send you a link, but somebody else signs the cheque.

key_facts.label: Who you are buying from
key_facts.value: Trainline.com Limited, company 03846791, incorporated 17 September 1999, at 1 Stonecutter Street, London EC4A 4AH

key_facts.label: Booking fee
key_facts.value: 59p to £2.79 per booking; none in the app on the day of travel; never refundable

key_facts.label: Delivery
key_facts.value: Digital tickets free; station collection £2.99; Royal Mail Special Delivery £12.99; no delivery fees at all through the app

key_facts.label: Refund fee (Trainline's own)
key_facts.value: Nothing under £2, then a ladder rising to £5 a ticket on anything costing £7 or more; £10 to refund a Season Ticket

key_facts.label: Exchange fee (Trainline's own)
key_facts.value: Nothing under £2, rising to £10 a ticket on fares of £15 and above

key_facts.label: Scale
key_facts.value: £6,319m of net ticket sales and £453m of revenue in the year to 28 February 2026; 27 million active customers

key_facts.label: Complaints
key_facts.value: Rail Ombudsman, named in Trainline's own terms; 40 working days with Trainline first, then a decision binding on Trainline

key_facts.label: Independent rating
key_facts.value: None found — no ratings agency scores rail ticket retailers

sections.heading: Two numbers for the same question
sections.html:
Trainline's own about page gives two counts of the same thing on the same screen. It says the company aggregates data from "over 70 carriers across Europe", and a few lines away it says it works with "270+ rail and coach companies". Both cannot be a count of the same set. The likeliest reading is that the smaller number counts carriers wired directly into the booking engine and the larger one counts every company whose tickets can appear in a search, but Trainline does not say so, and it is the sort of figure worth asking about rather than assuming.

What is not in doubt is the shape of the business. Net ticket sales split three ways in the year to 28 February 2026: £4,135m from UK consumers, up 6%; £1,104m from international consumers, up 5%; and £1,081m from Trainline Solutions, the business travel and white-label arm, up 15%. The fastest-growing third of the company is therefore the part most travellers never see.

sections.heading: The fee, to the penny
sections.html:
The booking fee "will vary between a minimum of 59p and a maximum of £2.79", and Trainline says it is calculated from the booking itself — the ticket price and the date of travel. It is shown in the basket before payment, which is a change the regulator pushed for rather than a courtesy. The app is treated differently: book in it on the day you are travelling and there is no booking fee, and the app charges no delivery fee on any ticket at any time.

On the website, delivery is free for digital tickets, £2.99 to collect from a station machine and £12.99 for a paper ticket by Royal Mail Special Delivery. That last figure is worth pausing on — it is more than many advance fares cost, and it exists because Special Delivery is a tracked, insured service rather than a stamp.

The comparison a reader will want is with buying the identical ticket somewhere else. Rail fares are set by the industry, not the retailer, so the ticket is the same ticket and the price of the travel is the same price. LNER's own site tells customers they can "[b]ook train tickets anywhere in England, Scotland and Wales through LNER and pay no bookings fees". On a £60 journey a fee of up to £2.79 is noise. On a £9 advance single it is nearer a third of the saving that made the advance worth booking.

sections.heading: How the money actually reaches Trainline
sections.html:
Put the two headline numbers side by side and the business model falls out of them. £6,319m of tickets sold produced £453m of revenue, which is a little over seven pence in every pound. Most of that is commission paid by the train and coach companies for selling their seats; the booking fee is the part the passenger sees. Trainline's terms put it plainly enough: "some of the fees come straight from the operators, so we have to charge them to you."

It is a profitable arrangement. Operating profit reached £122m in the year to 28 February 2026, up 43%, on adjusted EBITDA of £177m, up 11%, with basic earnings per share of 19.4p and £66m of adjusted free cash flow. The company has bought back £294m of its own shares since starting in September 2023, about 23% of its issued share capital, and had completed £94m of the current £150m programme by 30 April 2026. A retailer buying in a quarter of itself is a retailer with more cash than it has uses for.

sections.heading: Changing your mind costs money twice
sections.html:
Trainline runs two separate fee ladders, and they are its charges, levied on top of whatever the train company itself deducts. Refunding a UK ticket is free below £2, then £1 on a ticket costing £2 to £2.99, £1.50 from £3, £2 from £4, £3 from £5, £4 from £6 and £5 on anything from £7 upwards. Exchanging is dearer: free below £2, then £1 up to £4, £2.50 up to £6, £3 up to £8, £5 up to £11, £7.50 up to £13, £8.50 up to £15 and £10 above that. A Season Ticket refund costs a flat £10, though changing an eligible one is free.

Two details sit underneath the ladders. The booking fee itself is never returned — "booking fees cannot be refunded" — so a cancelled £8 ticket can lose its £5 refund fee and its booking fee together. And on European journeys the exchange fee is not Trainline's to set at all: it "vary[s] by carrier" and only appears during booking.

sections.heading: What changed on 1 April 2026
sections.html:
The biggest shift in years landed this April and it has nothing to do with Trainline's own charges. For Anytime tickets, Off-Peak tickets, Day Travelcards, Rovers and Rangers bought on or after 1 April 2026, a refund must be requested "before 23:59 on the day before your ticket becomes valid". Ask afterwards and it is "only considered in exceptional circumstances", with evidence that the ticket went unused. Tickets bought before that date keep the terms they were sold under, however far ahead the journey.

The industry administration fee sits on top: up to £5 a ticket and up to £10 a Season Ticket, and where the fee would swallow the refund, nothing is paid at all. Three things survive untouched, and they are the ones most often forgotten — a cancelled train still means a full refund, Delay Repay is a separate scheme that these rules do not reach, and the outward half of an Open Return cannot be refunded on its own once it becomes valid.

sections.heading: Delay Repay is the train company's job
sections.html:
Compensation thresholds are set by each operator and most follow the same shape: 25% of the fare for a delay of 15 to 29 minutes, 50% from 30 to 59 minutes, and the full fare at 60 minutes and beyond. Some operators pay nothing below 30 minutes. Trainline's part is to watch the journey and tell you: "We'll track your journey and let you know if you're eligible... we'll send you a push notification or email with a link to the train operator's website, where you can submit your claim."

That handover is not a design choice. In its own full-year statement Trainline told investors that operators are offering "1-click delay-repay, a feature third party retailers are expressly prohibited from providing to their customers". A company flagging its own competitive disadvantage in an investor document is as close to an unvarnished fact as this market produces, and it is the single clearest reason a frequent claimant might book on the operator's own app instead.

sections.heading: The regulator has already done the arithmetic on refund fees
sections.html:
The Office of Rail and Road studied refund administration across a full year to 31 March 2020: 341 million tickets issued and 5.8 million refunded. It found the average fee charged, where one was charged at all, was £6.96 a ticket, against an average cost of processing a refund — staff, systems, bank charges — of £3.77. Because 28% of fees were waived, the average across every refunded ticket came out at £4.64. The industry cap is £10, and the ORR has been working with the Department for Transport and the Rail Delivery Group on whether that cap should come down.

Read Trainline's £10 Season Ticket refund fee against those numbers and it sits precisely at the ceiling, at something under three times the regulator's estimate of what the work costs. That is legal, it is what the rules allow, and it is also the kind of figure a passenger only discovers at the moment they need the money back.

sections.heading: Who you are buying from, and who is watching
sections.html:
The contracting party for a British booking is Trainline.com Limited, company number 03846791, incorporated on 17 September 1999 and registered at 1 Stonecutter Street, London EC4A 4AH under SIC code 62090. Its last accounts were made up to 28 February 2025 and its next confirmation statement is due on 23 January 2027. A booking made in France is with Trainline SAS instead, trade register 512 277 450 in Paris, under French law and with a French tourism mediator rather than an ombudsman.

British customers get the Rail Ombudsman, named in Trainline's own terms. Give Trainline 40 working days to resolve a complaint — or less, if it sends a deadlock letter — and the Ombudsman can then take the case and issue a decision binding on Trainline, free to the passenger except for incidental costs. The ORR polices the selling itself. It reviewed 40 online rail ticket retailers in December 2023 and wrote to seven about how clearly they displayed booking, finder's, fulfilment and refund fees; Trainline was one of the seven. By March 2025 the regulator recorded that all of them had made changes, and the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 has since required fees to be folded into the total price at the earliest opportunity.

sections.heading: A state-owned rival is being built, and Trainline told its shareholders so
sections.html:
The government announced in January 2025 that Great British Railways would sell tickets, and the Railways Bill sets out how. Fourteen separate operator websites are to be folded into a single GBR app and site, alongside ticket offices, machines and onboard sales. Independent retailers are promised continued access — "[i]ndependent retailers, open access operators and devolved operators... will also be able to retail to passengers, just as they do today" — and a code of practice, owned and administered by the ORR, is meant to keep the state's retail arm at arm's length from the state's wholesale arm. Breaching that code will be a licence breach.

The detail that matters most to a retailer is quieter. The retail industry management functions the Rail Delivery Group performs today — setting commission rates, running technical standards, licensing retailers — move into a GBR back office. The body setting Trainline's commission will be part of the group competing with it. Trainline's own full-year statement records the company working on "development of the Code of Practice for GBR" and engaging with government on the Bill. None of this changes what a ticket costs this month, and all of it explains why the company is arguing publicly about fair retail market practices.

sections.heading: Where the savings are real
sections.html:
Two Trainline features genuinely move money, and both are worth naming precisely. SplitSave finds legal split tickets for a journey — you stay on the same train, it simply has to stop at each split point — and Trainline puts the average saving at £13 a trip for bookings between 1 July 2024 and 30 June 2025, measured against the next cheapest fare a Trainline customer could have bought. It is the company's own measurement against its own baseline, so treat it as a fair indication rather than an audited number, but split ticketing is real and most travellers never do it by hand.

The second is railcards. Trainline sells 2.7 million digital railcards, up 16% year on year, and holds 45% of the 16 to 30 market — a £30 card that takes a third off most fares pays for itself in two or three journeys, and the digital version cannot be left at home. Neither feature is exclusive to Trainline, but both are easier to find there than on most operator sites.

pros: No booking fee at all in the app on the day of travel, and no delivery fee on any app booking
One account covers more than 40 countries and, on Trainline's own account, the majority of Europe's rail and coach operators
Fees appear in the basket before payment, so the total is visible before you commit
SplitSave automates split ticketing — an average £13 a trip on Trainline's own 2024-25 measurement
2.7 million digital railcards sold, including 45% of the 16 to 30 market, and a digital card cannot be left in a drawer
The Rail Ombudsman is named in Trainline's own terms, and its decisions bind Trainline
Financially solid — £122m of operating profit and £66m of adjusted free cash flow in the year to 28 February 2026
cons: The booking fee of up to £2.79 buys nothing the train company would not sell you itself — LNER, for one, advertises no booking fees on tickets anywhere in England, Scotland and Wales
Booking fees are never refunded, so a cancelled cheap ticket can lose the fee and the £5 refund charge together
Trainline's refund and exchange ladders are its own charges and sit on top of whatever the train company deducts — up to £5 to refund and up to £10 to exchange
The £10 Season Ticket refund fee sits exactly at the industry cap, against the ORR's estimate of £3.77 as the average cost of processing a refund
No one-click Delay Repay: Trainline is, in its own words to shareholders, "expressly prohibited" from offering it, so every claim is handed to the operator's own form
£12.99 to post a paper ticket, which is more than many advance fares
Its own about page gives two irreconcilable counts of the operators it works with — "over 70 carriers" and "270+ rail and coach companies"
No independent rating exists for rail ticket retailers, so there is no Defaqto, Which? or Fairer Finance score to check this against
verdict: Trainline is the most complete rail shop in Europe and it charges between 59p and £2.79 for the privilege, which is a fair price for one account covering 40-odd countries and a poor one for a single advance single from Leeds. The honest way to use it is the way its own pricing points: search in the app, let SplitSave and the railcards do their work, and book on the day in the app where the fee disappears. For a regular commuter on one line, or anyone who claims Delay Repay more than occasionally, the operator's own app is the better tool — no booking fee, and a compensation claim that takes one tap rather than a link to somebody else's form. Nothing here is hidden; the fees are all published and the basket shows them before you pay. What the page above should change is when you use it, not whether.

faqs.q: Does Trainline charge a booking fee on UK train tickets?
faqs.a: Yes, on most bookings — "a minimum of 59p and a maximum of £2.79", worked out from the ticket price and the travel date, and shown in your basket before you pay. The exception is the app: book in it on the day you travel and there is no booking fee. The fee is never refunded, even when the ticket is.

faqs.q: Is a ticket cheaper if I buy it from the train company instead?
faqs.a: The fare is the same, because fares are set by the industry rather than by the retailer. What differs is the booking fee. LNER, for example, advertises that you can book tickets anywhere in England, Scotland and Wales through its own site and "pay no bookings fees". On a £60 fare the difference is trivial; on a £9 advance it is not.

faqs.q: What does it cost to refund or change a ticket bought on Trainline?
faqs.a: Trainline's own refund fee starts at nothing below £2 and rises in steps to £5 a ticket on anything costing £7 or more, with a flat £10 on Season Tickets. Its exchange fee runs from nothing below £2 up to £10 on fares of £15 and above. Those are Trainline's charges; the train company may deduct an administration fee of up to £5 a ticket as well, and since 1 April 2026 Anytime, Off-Peak, Day Travelcard, Rover and Ranger tickets must be refunded before 23:59 the day before they become valid.

faqs.q: Who pays me if my train is delayed?
faqs.a: The train operator, not Trainline. Most operators pay 25% of the fare for a delay of 15 to 29 minutes, 50% from 30 to 59 minutes and 100% at an hour or more, though the thresholds vary. Trainline tracks the journey and sends a link to the operator's claim form, but it cannot process the claim — it told its own shareholders that third-party retailers are "expressly prohibited" from offering one-click Delay Repay.

faqs.q: Who do I complain to if Trainline gets it wrong?
faqs.a: Trainline first. If it has not resolved matters after 40 working days, or it sends a deadlock letter sooner, the Rail Ombudsman can take the case — it is named in Trainline's own terms, it is free to passengers apart from incidental costs, and its decisions bind Trainline. The Office of Rail and Road handles the fee-transparency side; it wrote to Trainline and six other retailers about fee display in December 2023 and recorded the changes as complete by March 2025.

faqs.q: Will Great British Railways replace Trainline?
faqs.a: Not directly. GBR is folding fourteen train operator ticket websites into one app and site, and the Railways Bill says independent retailers "will also be able to retail to passengers, just as they do today". The part worth watching is that the body setting retailers' commission rates and licensing them moves inside GBR, and an ORR-administered code of practice is supposed to keep those decisions separate.

title: Trip.com – Global Hotel Deals
meta_title: Trip.com: ATOL 11572 for Flights, Singapore Law for Hotels
meta_description: Trip.com holds ATOL 11572 for flight-only sales through a UK company. Hotels run under Singapore law, and we found London, Kentucky in the results.

headline.label: Flight protection
headline.value: ATOL number 11572, held for flight-only sales — a licence you can check

disclosure: we earn a commission if you book through the link on this page. It costs you nothing. The jurisdiction clause and the search problem we found below are reported as they are, whether they help the sale or not.
intro:
Start with the thing that genuinely counts in Trip.com’s favour, because plenty of large booking sites cannot match it. Its UK terms state: “We provide full financial protection for our ATOL protected flight only sales”, citing Air Travel Organiser’s Licence number 11572.

That is a real, checkable licence number rather than a badge, and the UK party named alongside it is Trip Air Ticketing (UK) Limited, which holds an ICO data-protection registration, ZB360291, at Floor 10, 70 St Mary Axe, London EC3A 8BE, registered on 1 August 2022. You can verify the ATOL number yourself on the Civil Aviation Authority’s register before you pay, which is exactly how the scheme is meant to work.

Hotels are a different arrangement, and that is where this page spends its time. Your hotel contract runs to Trip.com Travel Singapore Pte. Ltd. at 30 Raffles Place, #29-01, Singapore 048622, under Singapore law. And when we searched its UK site for hotels in London, a good part of what came back was in London, Kentucky.

sections.heading: The search result that should worry you
sections.html:
We opened the page headed “Hotels in London” on the UK site on 8 October 2026 and read what it offered. These were the properties and prices:

Hotel as listedPrice shown
Fairfield Inn & Suites London£139 per night from
Hampton Inn London-North£118 per night from
Comfort Suites£81 in the listing, £66 in the page’s own FAQ
Baymont by Wyndham London KYfrom £56
Microtel Inn & Suites by Wyndham London£53 per night from
Motel 6 London, KYfrom £51
Quality Innfrom £50
Budget Host Westgate Innfrom £50

Fairfield Inn, Hampton Inn, Microtel, Baymont, Motel 6, Comfort Suites, Quality Inn, Budget Host. Those are American roadside chains, and two of them carry “KY” in the name. This is London, Kentucky — a town of a few thousand people off Interstate 75 — served up under a heading that says Hotels in London on a uk.trip.com address.

A £53-a-night Microtel looks like a bargain next to central London prices. It is not a bargain; it is a different continent. Nobody is being deliberately deceived here — it is a place-name collision in a database — but the consequence is the same if you book in a hurry.

What to do about it: before you book anything on this site, check the city, region and country on the property page, not the name in the list. Look at the map. If a price looks too good for the city you have in mind, that is usually because it is not that city. The same trap exists for Birmingham, Boston, Richmond, Hamilton and a dozen others.

The £81 against £66 inconsistency on the same hotel on the same page is a smaller problem of the same kind: the figure in the listing and the figure in the page’s own FAQ did not match. Treat any “from” price as an advertisement and the basket as the price.

sections.heading: Who you are contracting with, and under whose law
sections.html:
The terms name two companies and they do different jobs.

Trip.com Travel Singapore Pte. Ltd. is described as “a limited liability company with its address at 30 Raffles Place, #29-01 Singapore 048622”. Trip Air Ticketing (UK) Limited is the UK party, and the one that carries the ATOL licence — though the terms give no company number or registered address for it, which we had to find elsewhere.

The jurisdiction clause is the part to understand. The terms are “governed by and construed in accordance with the law of Singapore”, and “the courts of Singapore will have jurisdiction over any dispute or claim”.

Two saving clauses soften that, and they are worth knowing because they are genuinely in your favour:

  • Your mandatory consumer rights as a UK resident are preserved — a choice-of-law clause cannot strip them out.
  • You keep the right to sue in the courts of your own country of residence instead of Singapore.

So the position is better than a bare “Singapore law” clause sounds. But the default remains a Singapore contract interpreted under Singapore law, and that is a different footing from booking with a British company.

On its role, Trip.com calls itself “a global online travel agency” and says the travel products are “provided by third party suppliers”. The terms avoid the words agent and principal, but the practical effect is clear enough: on a hotel booking, the hotel’s own terms govern what you can change. The relevant line is “please check the relevant Supplier’s terms for information on your rights to change or cancel your booking”.

There is no ABTA membership and no named dispute resolution scheme in the terms.

sections.heading: Cancellations: the terms point you somewhere else
sections.html:
This is the honest shape of a marketplace booking, and it is worth being clear-eyed about rather than disappointed by later.

For hotels and other supplier-provided products, Trip.com does not set the cancellation rules — the supplier does, and the terms tell you to go and read them. On flights, the wording is: “if you are unsure whether your flight ticket permits changes and/or refunds for cancellation, please contact us”. On refunds generally: “any refunds will be paid back to the original payment method, unless we agree otherwise”, which is the right answer and worth having in writing.

What that means in practice:

  • The cancellation policy you are agreeing to is on the room, not on the website. Two rooms in the same hotel on the same page can have completely different terms, and the cheaper one is usually the non-refundable one.
  • Read the policy on the room you are about to pay for, on the payment page, not the one you read on the search results.
  • Screenshot it. If you later need to argue, the policy as displayed at the moment of payment is the thing you want evidence of.

One reassurance on price: for prepaid bookings the terms say “you will pay the exact amount shown on the payment page”. So the payment page figure is binding even if the search result was not. What the terms do not say anywhere we could find is whether displayed prices include taxes and fees — and the London hotel list we read made no statement about taxes or fees either. On a marketplace that often means the room rate is shown and local taxes or resort fees appear later, so check the total on the payment page against the per-night figure that attracted you.

sections.heading: Where the site is genuinely strong
sections.html:
We have spent most of this page on the cautions, so let us be fair about what this site is good at, because it is not nothing.

The ATOL licence is the headline, and it is real. Licence 11572 for flight-only sales puts Trip.com in a different category from the many international booking sites that sell UK customers flights with no UK financial protection at all. If you book a flight through it, that protection is a material benefit and you can check the number before you pay.

The refund route is the right one. Money goes back to the card you paid with, which is what you want.

The scale is the point of it. This is a genuinely global inventory, and it is strongest exactly where British agencies are weakest — domestic hotels across Asia, regional Chinese and Japanese cities, airlines that do not sell through European channels. For a trip across several Asian cities it will often show you rooms and routes that a UK-focused site does not have.

Member-only rates exist, unlocked by signing in, though we could not tie one to a specific hotel or quantify the discount, so treat it as worth a look rather than a reason to join.

Our overall read: use it for the inventory and the ATOL-covered flights, and apply the discipline above to the hotels. The problems we found are not dishonesty — they are the normal failure modes of a very large marketplace translated across dozens of countries. They are also entirely avoidable if you check the city, read the room’s own cancellation terms and compare the payment page against the headline.

verdict: Trip.com earns a real mark in its favour that most global booking sites cannot claim: ATOL licence 11572 for flight-only sales, held through a named UK company, with a number you can check on the CAA register before you pay. For flights, and for Asian hotels and airlines that British agencies simply do not carry, it is a sensible place to look. The hotel side needs discipline. Your contract runs to a Singapore company under Singapore law, the cancellation terms belong to the hotel rather than the website, the terms never say whether taxes and fees are in the price, and when we searched its UK site for hotels in London it offered us London, Kentucky at £51 a night with one property priced two different ways on the same page. None of that is dishonest, and all of it is avoidable. Check the city, the region and the map on the property page; read the cancellation policy on the exact room on the payment page and screenshot it; compare the payment total against the per-night figure that caught your eye; and pay by credit card.

faqs.q: Is Trip.com ATOL protected?
faqs.a: For flight-only sales, yes. Its UK terms state “we provide full financial protection for our ATOL protected flight only sales” under Air Travel Organiser’s Licence number 11572, with Trip Air Ticketing (UK) Limited as the UK party. You can check that number on the Civil Aviation Authority’s register before booking. A hotel-only booking is not ATOL protected — the licence attaches to flight sales.

faqs.q: Which company am I booking with, and under what law?
faqs.a: The terms name Trip.com Travel Singapore Pte. Ltd., at 30 Raffles Place, #29-01, Singapore 048622, and state that they are “governed by and construed in accordance with the law of Singapore” with the Singapore courts having jurisdiction. Two things soften that: your mandatory consumer rights as a UK resident are preserved, and you keep the right to bring a claim in the courts of your own country instead.

faqs.q: Why are the London hotel prices so cheap?
faqs.a: Because some of them are not in London, England. On 8 October 2026 the page headed “Hotels in London” on the UK site offered us Motel 6 London KY from £51, Baymont by Wyndham London KY from £56, a Microtel at £53 and several other American roadside chains — that is London, Kentucky. Always check the city, region and country on the property page and look at the map before booking.

faqs.q: Who sets the cancellation policy?
faqs.a: The hotel or supplier, not Trip.com. The terms say to “check the relevant Supplier’s terms for information on your rights to change or cancel your booking”. That means two rooms in the same hotel can carry completely different terms, and the cheapest rate is usually the non-refundable one. Read the policy on the exact room on the payment page, and take a screenshot of it.

faqs.q: Do the prices include taxes and fees?
faqs.a: The terms do not say, and the hotel list we read made no statement about taxes or fees either. What the terms do promise for prepaid bookings is that “you will pay the exact amount shown on the payment page”, so the payment page is the figure that binds. Compare that total against the per-night price that attracted you before you confirm.

faqs.q: What is it actually best for?
faqs.a: Flights, because of the ATOL cover, and Asia, because the inventory is deepest there — domestic hotels and airlines across China, Japan and south-east Asia that UK-focused sites often do not sell at all. For a trip around several Asian cities it will show you options others do not have. For a hotel in a European city, you are not gaining much over a British booking site and you are taking on a Singapore contract to get it.

title: Tyres.net Review: What 750 Prices for One Tyre Size Leave Out
meta_title: Tyres.net: 750 Prices for One Tyre Size, Compared
meta_description: Tyres.net lists 750 offers for a 205/55 R16, from £35.58. What the price covers, who you actually buy from, and the fitting charge nobody shows.

headline.label: Cheapest 205/55 R16 tyre listed
headline.value: £35.58 for a 91V Dovroad Zyphira — one of 750 offers in that size, delivered price, fitting not included

intro:
Search Tyres.net for a 205/55 R16, the size on more British family cars than any other, and it returns 750 separate offers running from £35.58 to £150.11 a corner. Figures checked on 20 September 2026 against the site's own search pages. It is a price comparison platform rather than a tyre shop: it gathers what other retailers are charging, sorts it, and hands you over to them.

The engine belongs to TyresNET GmbH, registered at Franz-Joseph-Straße 11 in Munich under HRB 221425 at the Amtsgericht München, VAT number DE301419717, with Andreas Prüfer and Nina Andree as managing directors. The same platform runs in 64 countries and 12 languages off a product feed of more than 10,000 items, and its UK callers get an 0330 number rather than a German one.

What it does well is show you the same tyre at several sellers on one line. Ask for a Continental ContiEcoContact 5 in 205/55 R16 91H and three shops come back at £70.48, £70.60 and £71.41 — a spread of 93p that would take three browser tabs to find anywhere else. Every listing also carries the tyre label grades: fuel efficiency, wet grip and the external noise figure in decibels, so a Bridgestone Turanza 6 in that size shows as B, A and 69 dB before you click anything.

sections.heading: 750 offers in one size, and who is actually behind them
sections.html:
The breadth is real. A 205/55 R16 search runs to 38 pages at roughly 20 products a page, and the budget end goes a long way below what a fitting chain will quote: Dovroad Zyphira at £35.58, Comforser PureSpeed at £36.19, Lanvigator Comfort 1 at £36.31, Tracmax F-109 at £36.75 and Saferich FRC16 at £37.65, all 91V or 94V and all from the same seller, tyresdirect. Move up to the names most drivers recognise and the ladder runs Continental ContiEcoContact 5 at £70.48, Continental UltraContact at £76.72, Continental PremiumContact 7 at £78.91, Bridgestone Turanza T005 at £83.24, Pirelli Cinturato P1 at £85.61, Bridgestone Turanza 6 at £88.96 and Michelin Primacy 5 Energy at £95.16. Continental alone accounts for 53 of the offers in that one size.

The seller names repeat: onlinecarparts.co.uk, tyres-outlet.co.uk, mytyres.co.uk and tyresdirect carry most of the listings on the front pages. Mytyres.co.uk is worth knowing about, because it is not an independent shop. It belongs to Delticom AG of Hedwig-Kohn-Straße 1, Sehnde, which by its own account runs over 300 online stores in more than 70 countries, carries 600-plus tyre brands and over 40,000 tyre models, and has served more than 17 million customers. A German platform comparing prices is therefore partly comparing the prices of another German group that sells the same tyres under a dozen different shopfronts. Nobody hides this — both companies publish it — but it is worth understanding that the number of shop names on a results page is larger than the number of businesses behind them.

sections.heading: The charge that never appears on the results page
sections.html:
A tyre bought this way arrives at your door. Getting it onto the car is a separate transaction with a separate business, and that is where a large part of the real cost sits. Kwik Fit publishes the number on its own site: all tyre discounts 'apply to the cost of the tyre only and exclude charges for fitting, balancing, valve and disposal', quoted at £20.00 per tyre in its tyre FAQ and at £20.50 in the footnote on the same page. Take the lower figure and a set of four is £80 before anyone touches a tyre; take the higher one and it is £82.

Run that against the headline. The £35.58 tyre becomes roughly £56 on the car if a fitter charges what Kwik Fit charges, and four of them come to about £222 rather than £142 — a 56% increase on the number that won the comparison. The £70.48 Continental goes to about £90. The gap narrows as the tyre gets dearer, which is why the saving on a premium tyre bought this way is usually genuine and the saving on the cheapest one on the page is usually a good deal smaller than it looks. Tyres.net does not raise fitting anywhere. Its FAQ covers searching, delivery, who the contract is with and how to contact a seller, and the word does not appear.

Delivery is the other absentee. Listings show a tyre price and nothing else; the site says only that 'each shop listed on Tyres.net has different delivery options' and that it 'does not carry the transport risk. The retailer is always responsible.' Since 6 April 2025, section 230 of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 has required a trader inviting a UK consumer to purchase to give the total price, meaning 'any fees, taxes, charges or other payments that the consumer will necessarily incur', and either to state any freight, delivery or postal charges not included in it or to say that such charges may apply. A comparison layer that passes you to a checkout where the carriage is finally revealed is exactly the shape that provision was written about, and a reader is entitled to treat the ranked price as incomplete until the basket confirms it.

sections.heading: Whose customer are you?
sections.html:
The general terms are blunt about it. Clause by clause they place Tyres.net outside the sale: 'the contracts about the products or services on the websites are concluded solely between the customers and the listed online shops', and 'TyresNET in this case is not representative of one contracting parties'. Liability is excluded 'regardless of the legal basis' apart from death or personal injury, product liability, intent or gross negligence, and breach of what the terms call cardinal duties. Warranty questions are pushed to the partner shop's own conditions, cancellation rights to 'the GTC of the online shops (including their cancellation policies)'. German law applies under clause 8.3.

Set that beside the site's return policy and the picture stops being consistent. That document is written in the first person by the platform itself: 'You are entitled to cancel this contract within fourteen days without having to state your reasons', addressed to 'TyresNET GmbH, Franz-Joseph-Str. 11, 80801 Munich Germany'; refunds 'without delay and no later than within fourteen days from the date of our receipt of your cancellation notice', by the same means of payment, with no extra charges; and, unusually generous, 'We collect the goods from you. We bear the cost of returning the goods.' Those are a seller's obligations, not an introducer's. The FAQ explains why both can be true — buyers either click through to a retailer or 'purchase directly via the marketplace' — but no page tells you which set of rules is governing the order you are about to place, and the difference decides who you chase when four tyres turn up in the wrong size.

sections.heading: What British law gives you here, whatever the terms say
sections.html:
A German choice-of-law clause does not strip a UK buyer of UK protection. Section 74 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 says that where the law of another country 'is chosen by the parties to be applicable to a consumer contract, but the consumer contract has a close connection with the United Kingdom, this Part applies despite that choice'. A platform trading at uk.tyres.net in sterling, with an 0330 phone number and a product feed of British sellers, is about as close a connection as a website gets. The 14 days in the return policy also match what the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 would give a UK buyer anyway.

The weak point is what happens when a complaint goes nowhere. Clause 10.1 of the terms directs unhappy customers to the European Commission's online dispute resolution portal at ec.europa.eu/consumers/odr. That portal stopped operating on 20 July 2025; the Commission has redirected the address and the underlying regulation has been repealed. It had not been open to UK consumers since Brexit in any case. No UK alternative dispute resolution scheme is named anywhere on the site, and there is no UK-registered company to complain to — the registered office, the commercial register entry, the VAT number and the bank account are all German. What is left is the seller's own complaints process, a card chargeback, or section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974, which makes a credit card provider jointly liable on a single purchase of more than £100 and up to £30,000. Four tyres at £70 clears that bar comfortably; one budget tyre at £35.58 does not.

sections.heading: The label data is there, and it is doing more work than it looks
sections.html:
Credit where it is due: the grades are on every row, and that is a legal duty rather than a courtesy. The government's guidance for tyre suppliers and distributors tells anyone selling where the customer cannot see the tyre before buying to 'give the information on the fuel efficiency, wet grip (where applicable) and external noise during the buying process'. Tyres.net does exactly that — the Bridgestone Turanza 6 in 205/55 R16 94V shows B for fuel, A for wet grip and 69 dB for noise before you leave the results page, which is more than several high-street sellers manage on a quotation. The guidance also expects the downloadable product information sheet to be available on a website selling tyres; whether the platform offers that, as opposed to the three grades, could not be confirmed and is worth checking on the product page before ordering.

One caution on the letters themselves. The government's own guidance page describes Great Britain as grading car tyres A to G while Northern Ireland uses A to E, which is not how the assimilated tyre labelling regulation reads, and the two have not been reconciled publicly. Treat the relative position as reliable — an A wet grip really does stop shorter than a C — and do not read anything into the letter at the bottom of whichever scale a given page is using.

sections.heading: How the site is paid, and why it does not say so
sections.html:
Nothing on Tyres.net explains its revenue. The FAQ covers searching, retailers, delivery and contact, and stops short of the commercial arrangement. The Awin affiliate network fills the gap: programme 12715, listed as Tyres UK, pays publishers 4% of a sale and 10p for a clickout, with a 30-day cookie and an average transaction value of about £115 net, across 64 countries and 12 languages. That is an ordinary arrangement and there is nothing improper in it — a comparison site has to be funded somehow, and this one is funded per click and per sale.

It does mean two things worth holding in mind as you read a results page. The platform earns whether or not you get the best tyre, provided you click; and a shop that is not part of the commercial arrangement has no obvious route onto the page at all, so 'the cheapest price' is the cheapest among participating sellers rather than the cheapest in Britain. Neither the ranking method nor the participation rules are published. Compare100 is itself an affiliate of this programme, which is the same disclosure being asked of them.

pros: Genuine breadth — 750 offers in a single common size, 53 of them from one premium brand, across 38 pages of results
Several sellers' prices for the identical tyre on one line, including margins as fine as 93p between three shops on a Continental ContiEcoContact 5
Budget tyres from £35.58 in 205/55 R16, well below anything a fitting chain advertises
Tyre label grades — fuel efficiency, wet grip and noise in decibels — shown on every listing, which satisfies the distance-selling duty in the government's guidance
A 14-day cancellation right with return carriage paid and collection arranged, which is better than the law requires
Covers wheels, oils and accessories as well as car, van, motorcycle, truck and bicycle tyres
cons: Fitting is never mentioned anywhere on the site, yet at Kwik Fit's published £20.00 to £20.50 a tyre it adds roughly £80 to £82 to a set of four — turning £142 of budget tyres into about £222 on the car

Delivery cost does not appear in the listings, so the ranked price is not the price you pay; section 230 of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 has required total pricing since 6 April 2025

The only dispute route named in the terms is the European ODR portal, which was switched off on 20 July 2025 and was closed to UK consumers before that; no UK alternative dispute resolution scheme is named

The general terms say the contract is 'concluded solely between the customers and the listed online shops', while the return policy is written in TyresNET GmbH's own name and promises to collect the goods and pay the carriage — nothing tells a buyer which applies to their order
No UK company, registered office or register entry; the registered office is in Munich, the commercial register is the Amtsgericht München and the bank account is with Commerzbank in euros
The site never discloses that it earns 4% of a sale and 10p a clickout, and publishes neither its ranking method nor the terms on which a shop gets listed
No independent rating exists for a tyre price comparison platform, so there is no external check on service quality
verdict: As a way of seeing what a tyre costs before you walk into a garage, Tyres.net earns its place: 750 offers in one common size, the label grades on every row, and several sellers priced against each other on a single line. Treat the number it gives you as the cost of the rubber and nothing else. Add £20 a tyre for fitting, balancing, a valve and disposal, add carriage, and then compare it with a fully fitted price — on a £35.58 budget tyre that arithmetic closes most of the gap, and on a £95 Michelin it does not. The paperwork is the part to go in with your eyes open: a Munich company, German law, a dispute portal that has been dark since July 2025, and a set of terms that cannot decide whether it is the seller or the introducer. Buy on a credit card, keep the order confirmation from the shop rather than the platform, and the risk is manageable.

faqs.q: Does Tyres.net sell the tyres itself?
faqs.a: Its general terms say no: contracts are 'concluded solely between the customers and the listed online shops'. Its own return policy says something closer to yes, promising a 14-day cancellation, collection of the goods and payment of the return carriage in TyresNET GmbH's own name, and the FAQ mentions buying 'directly via the marketplace' as well as clicking through to a retailer. Check the order confirmation to see whose name is on the sale.

faqs.q: Is the price shown the price I pay?
faqs.a: No. The listing price is for the tyre. Delivery is settled at the retailer's checkout and fitting is a separate job at a garage — Kwik Fit publishes £20.00 to £20.50 a tyre for fitting, balancing, a valve and disposing of the old one, so a set of four typically adds £80 to £82.

faqs.q: What can I do if something goes wrong with the order?
faqs.a: Start with the retailer, since the contract is most likely with them. Section 74 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 keeps UK protection in place despite the German choice of law where the contract has a close connection with the UK. The European ODR portal named in the terms has not operated since 20 July 2025, and no UK dispute scheme is offered in its place, so a card chargeback or a section 75 claim on a credit card purchase over £100 is the practical backstop.

faqs.q: Why does the same tyre appear at four different prices?
faqs.a: Because several retailers list the same product. A Continental ContiEcoContact 5 in 205/55 R16 91H came back at £70.48, £70.60 and £71.41 from three shops on the same row. Some of those shopfronts belong to the same group — mytyres.co.uk is one of the 300-plus stores run by Delticom AG — so the number of names is not the number of businesses.

faqs.q: Are the tyre label grades on the site reliable?
faqs.a: They come from the manufacturer's declared figures and showing them is a legal duty for distance sellers under the government's guidance, so the fuel efficiency letter, wet grip letter and decibel figure on each listing are the same data a shop would have to hand you. Use them comparatively: an A wet grip stops shorter than a C in the wet, which matters more on a British winter road than the fuel letter does.

title: Utility Warehouse Dual Fuel
meta_title: Utility Warehouse Dual Fuel: a £12.38 Discount, Per Fuel
meta_description: UW publishes a real dual-fuel discount: £12.38 a year per fuel off the standing charge. But only on its fixed tariffs, and the exit fee is £75 per fuel.

headline.label: Dual-fuel discount
headline.value: £12.38 a year per fuel ex VAT — £24.76 for both, off the standing charge

disclosure: the Utility Warehouse link on this page is our own UW Partner link. We are a registered UW Partner, which means UW pays us a one-off bonus and a percentage of the monthly bill if you join through it. It costs you nothing extra and it does not change what we say about UW — including the parts below that are critical. UW does not publish the Partner rules that govern where a Partner link may be used, so we have said so rather than claim an approval we cannot show you.
intro:
Utility Warehouse gives a dual-fuel discount of £12.38 a year per fuel, excluding VAT, taken off the standing charge on a daily basis. Take both gas and electricity and that is £24.76 a year. It is published in its own tariff information labels, in those words, with that figure.

That is worth stating plainly because the biggest name in this category does not have one. British Gas lists a dual-fuel discount as “Not applicable” on all 67 of its tariffs. UW’s £24.76 is not a fortune, but it is a real, quantified reward for consolidating, and it exists.

Two conditions matter. The discount appears on UW’s four fixed tariff labels only — the tracker and variable labels carry no dual-fuel clause at all. And a fixed tariff carries an exit fee of £75 including VAT per fuel, so leaving a dual-fuel fix early costs £150. The discount takes six years to pay off one early exit.

sections.heading: The real mechanism: your energy price depends on how many services you buy
sections.html:
UW’s dual-fuel discount is the small part. The large part is that which energy tariff you are allowed to buy depends on how many UW services you take, and the price difference between the rungs dwarfs £24.76.

Taking the Eastern region, gas, Direct Debit, excluding VAT, from UW’s own labels:

Services you takeTariff you qualify forGas unit rateStanding charge
Energy onlyUW Fixed Start 988.357p25.836p/day
Two servicesUW Fixed 987.725p24.789p/day
Three or fourUW Fixed Saver 987.725p19.620p/day

Read the first row carefully. The energy-only tariff has the highest gas unit rate UW sells. Buy nothing but energy from Utility Warehouse and you are on its worst gas price — 0.632p per kWh above the two-service rate, which on 9,500 kWh is £60 a year. Going from two services to three cuts the standing charge by 5.169p a day, another £18.87.

And there is a catch in how services are counted. UW’s Price Pledge terms state: “Multiple or different types of the same service (i.e. two types of mobile service, gas and electricity etc.) will be counted as one Eligible Service.” Gas and electricity together count as one service, not two. So “dual fuel” gets you onto the first rung of the ladder, not the second.

There is a clawback too. The Fixed Saver label says that if you cancel any service “they will automatically be transferred to the cheapest available fixed tariff of the same version number they are eligible to receive”. Drop your broadband and your energy price goes up.

sections.heading: The variable tariffs move the standing charge and nothing else
sections.html:
UW’s variable range runs Value, then Gold, then Double Gold, and this is the finding worth having: all three share an identical electricity unit rate in every one of UW’s 14 regions. We re-read the labels to be sure it was not a transcription error. It is not.

The entire variable multi-service discount comes off the standing charge. In the Eastern region, electricity: Value 51.779p a day, Gold 50.738p, Double Gold 49.094p. On gas the spread is larger and remarkably consistent — 10.230p a day from Value to Double Gold, and exactly 10.230p in all 14 regions.

So the variable discount is £37.34 a year on gas and about £9.80 on electricity, and it is worth the same to you whether you use 5,000 kWh or 25,000. That is the opposite of how most multi-service discounts work, and it means UW’s variable range rewards low users proportionally more than heavy ones.

One thing UW does not publish anywhere: how many services you need for Gold or Double Gold. It says only “not required — but getting it together unlocks the cheaper variable rate”. The fixed and tracker labels spell out their service requirements precisely; the variable ones do not, so you cannot work out in advance which rate you would land on.

sections.heading: What UW claims against the price cap, and what the numbers say
sections.html:
UW’s central promise is that you pay less than the Ofgem cap. On its variable tariffs it quantifies that as “a discount of up to £50 a year against the Government’s energy price cap”, and the tracker tariffs are described as tracking the cap “at a set discount”, with three tiers: Start for “a guaranteed discount”, Plus for “a bigger discount” and Saver for “our biggest discount”.

The size of the tracker discount is never published. Not in pence, not as a percentage, nowhere on UW’s site or in its tariff labels. “Guaranteed discount” with no number attached is a claim you cannot check before signing.

The fixed prices are published, and they need reading carefully against the right benchmark. The current Ofgem cap, which UW quotes itself, is £1,723 a year for a typical dual-fuel household on 9,500 kWh gas and 2,500 kWh electricity, for 1 October to 31 December 2026. UW’s own headline figures are UW Fixed at £1,735 and UW Fixed Saver at £1,710.

So on the current cap, UW Fixed is £12 above it and UW Fixed Saver is £13 below. UW’s “over £370 in savings” headline is measured against “January’s projected price cap” — a forecast of a future cap, not the one in force. That is a legitimate way to price a fix, and it is a bet on the cap rising. Just be clear which number you are being shown.

sections.heading: The rest of the bundle, with prices
sections.html:
Since the energy price depends on the bundle, here is what the bundle actually costs:

  • Full Fibre 150 (152Mbps) — £23.95 a month, rising to £27.95 in April 2027 and £31.95 in April 2028. Plus £5.99 postage.
  • Full Fibre 500 — £30, then £34, then £38.
  • Full Fibre 900 (944Mbps) — £35, then £39, then £43.
  • Mobile Go Unlimited — £13 a month, monthly rolling, with a 500GB fair use policy. On the EE network.
  • Mobile Go Essential — £6 a month for 10GB, monthly rolling.
  • Insurance — home, contents, boiler and home cover. No prices published at all.

Broadband connection is free, and UW guarantees it. Mobile is a monthly rolling contract with no early termination charge published, which is genuinely unusual and makes mobile the cheapest way to add a service and move up the energy ladder — £6 a month to unlock a better energy tariff may well pay for itself.

Broadband is the opposite. It runs 24 months, and leaving early costs £3.60 for each remaining month plus a cost recovery charge of £90 in months 1 to 12, £45 in months 13 to 17 and £22.50 in months 18 to 23, less a 1% discount. UW’s own worked example: ten months remaining in month 14 is £80.19.

sections.heading: The Cashback Card, and the cap nobody mentions
sections.html:
The Cashback Card is sold as “up to 10% cashback with our retail partners, and 1% everywhere else”. The 1% is where most people’s spending goes, and it is capped by how many services you take:

Services1% applies toMaximum a month
1First £500 of spend£5
2 or 3First £1,000£10
4 or moreFirst £1,500£15

So the very best case is £180 a year, and that needs four services and £1,500 of qualifying spend every month. Against it: a £5 application fee and a £3 monthly management fee — £36 a year — though UW runs it free for the first three months.

The exclusions matter. No 1% on anything “deemed to be cash or like cash”, on mortgage, rent, loan, insurance, pension, investment or savings payments, or on spending “with any other utility, telecoms, insurance company or a competitor of UW”. Non-sterling spending earns 3% uncapped, excluding ATM withdrawals, which is the best rate on the card and the least advertised. Cash machine withdrawals cost 50p, and there is a 3% foreign exchange fee on ATM transactions.

Cashback is credited to your next UW bill rather than paid out, and if it exceeds the bill the balance goes to your bank account.

sections.heading: The Price Pledge, and what it actually requires
sections.html:
UW’s strongest guarantee is the Price Pledge: if you do not save, “we’ll pay you double the difference and let you leave those services without incurring any exit fees”. That is a real commitment, and worth more than most of the discounts above.

The conditions are specific. You must have joined on or after 22 April 2024, take at least three different eligible services at sign-up or within 42 days, hold a Cashback Card and use it regularly, be on a credit meter, pay by valid direct debit, carry no debt on the account, and remain a customer for at least 12 months. Eligible services are energy, broadband, mobile SIM only and boiler and home cover.

Remember the counting rule: gas and electricity are one service. So three eligible services means energy plus two others. And where both fuels are at the address, you must switch both.

sections.heading: Where UW falls short
sections.html:
Its service record is poor, and about the same as British Gas’s. Citizens Advice scores Utility Warehouse 2.63 out of 5 for the April to June 2026 quarter, ranking it 13th. The complaints component scores 2.5 out of 5, on 40.6 complaints per 10,000 customers. British Gas, immediately above it in that table, scores 2.61.

Everything is priced excluding VAT. Every UW tariff label states “prices are excluding VAT”, so add 5% to the gas figures and compare carefully against suppliers who quote inclusive.

The exit fee is per fuel. £75 including VAT each, so £150 to leave a dual-fuel fix early — six years of the dual-fuel discount.

Your energy price is hostage to your other services. Cancel the broadband and you are moved to a worse tariff automatically.

The tracker discount is unquantified and the variable service thresholds are unpublished.

And UW does not generate its own energy. It states in its annual report: “we source our energy from E.ON”, holding supply licences through Electricity Plus Supply Limited and Gas Plus Supply Limited. Mobile runs on EE. You are buying a reseller’s bundle, which is fine, but it is not a vertically integrated supplier.

sections.heading: How it sells, and why that matters to you
sections.html:
Utility Warehouse does not advertise for customers in the usual way. It sells through 77,200 Partners, up from 71,710 a year earlier, who “refer Utility Warehouse to their friends, family and personal networks” in Telecom Plus’s own words.

Partners pay £10 to register and £3 a month, and are paid a one-off customer bonus plus a percentage of your bill for as long as you stay. UW publishes the full schedule in its own Opportunity Guide: the one-off bonus runs £50 for one service to £300 for four or more, and the residual is 2.5% of an energy bill for a homeowner, 4% on broadband and insurance.

It is also tiered across a downline, with group income paid at 100% on levels 2 to 8, 50% on 9 to 16 and 25% on 17 and above, and promotion bonuses from £200 to £20,000. Neither UW nor Telecom Plus calls this multi-level or network marketing — both consistently say “word-of-mouth” — but the published compensation plan is structured by level across a team.

Why this matters when you are buying: the person recommending UW to you is usually being paid for it, and the amount depends on how many services you take. That is not a reason to avoid UW. It is a reason to price the bundle yourself rather than accept the recommendation, and to notice that the advice to add a fourth service is advice that pays the adviser more.
